stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with acute chest pain and ST elevation in V1 to V4 after learning of her husband's sudden death. Urgent coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary artery disease. Echocardiogram shows apical ballooning with preserved basal function. Troponin is mildly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Left anterior descending artery spasm (Prinzmetal's variant)

why_correct: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress cardiomyopathy, broken heart syndrome) occurs predominantly in postmenopausal women following a significant emotional or physical stressor. It mimics STEMI with ST elevation and troponin rise but coronary angiography is normal. The characteristic finding is apical ballooning with preserved basal systolic function on echocardiogram (the apex dilates and is akinetic while the base contracts normally). The mechanism involves catecholamine surge and myocardial stunning. The vast majority recover with supportive treatment (ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker) over 4 to 8 weeks.
why_wrong: A. STEMI requires coronary occlusion — the angiogram is normal here. B. Myocarditis can mimic STEMI and cause troponin rise but does not produce the characteristic apical ballooning pattern. D. HCM causes asymmetric septal hypertrophy — not apical ballooning. E. Coronary spasm (Prinzmetal's) causes transient ST elevation but coronary anatomy appears normal at rest — however, spasm does not produce apical ballooning on echo and typically occurs at rest, not triggered by emotional stress.
pearl: Takotsubo diagnostic criteria (Mayo Clinic): transient akinesis or dyskinesis of LV apical and midventricular segments with regional wall motion abnormalities beyond a single epicardial coronary territory, no obstructive coronary disease, new ECG changes (ST elevation or T wave inversions) or mild troponin elevation, and no phaeochromocytoma or myocarditis. Recovery of LV function typically occurs within 4 to 8 weeks.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman + emotional stressor + chest pain ↓ ECG: ST elevation (anterior) ↓ Normal coronary angiogram ↓ Echo: apical ballooning + preserved basal function ↓ Takotsubo cardiomyopathy ↓ Management: supportive (ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker) ↓ Full recovery usually within 4–8 weeks
exam_trap: Takotsubo presents exactly like STEMI (chest pain, ST elevation, troponin rise) but coronary angiography is normal. The key distinguishing features are: emotional trigger, postmenopausal female, and apical ballooning on echo.
takeaway: Emotional trigger + normal coronaries + apical ballooning on echo = Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Recovery expected within 4 to 8 weeks.

stem: A 72-year-old man with stable heart failure (NYHA class II) has an Hb of 65 g/L following a lower GI bleed that has now stopped. He is haemodynamically stable, with mild breathlessness but no chest pain. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Transfuse several units, rechecking the Hb only at the end
options.B: Transfuse until the Hb is back within the normal range
options.C: Transfuse a single unit, then reassess and recheck the Hb
options.D: No transfusion now; observe and recheck the Hb tomorrow
options.E: Start oral iron and recheck the Hb in four weeks

correct_answer: C. Transfuse a single unit, then reassess and recheck the Hb
why_correct: His Hb of 65 g/L is below the level at which NICE NG24 recommends transfusion, whether the general restrictive threshold or the higher threshold suggested for acute coronary syndrome is applied, so transfusion is indicated. Because the bleeding has stopped, NICE NG24 advises single-unit red cell transfusion for adults who are not actively bleeding, followed by clinical reassessment and a repeat Hb after each unit, with further units given only if needed. This matters even more in heart failure, where every unit adds to the risk of transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO): transfuse slowly, monitor fluid balance and consider a diuretic. The source of the bleed still needs investigating, and iron deficiency should be treated once he is stable.
why_wrong: A. Giving several units without reassessing in between risks overtransfusion and TACO, particularly in heart failure; NICE advises clinical reassessment and a repeat Hb after each unit. B. Transfusing back to the normal range is a liberal strategy; NICE recommends restrictive transfusion, and overtransfusion increases the risk of TACO. D. His Hb is below the level at which NICE recommends transfusion and he is symptomatic, so withholding transfusion is unsafe. E. Oral iron takes weeks to raise the Hb and does not treat symptomatic anaemia now, although iron deficiency should be treated once he is stable.
pearl: NICE NG24: use restrictive thresholds — consider transfusing below 70 g/L with a post-transfusion target of 70 to 90 g/L, or below 80 g/L with a target of 80 to 100 g/L in acute coronary syndrome. In adults who are not actively bleeding, give single-unit transfusions and clinically reassess and check the Hb after each unit before giving more. In heart failure, transfuse slowly and consider a diuretic to reduce the risk of TACO.
thinking: Hb 65 g/L + bleeding stopped + haemodynamically stable ↓ Below the transfusion threshold whichever NICE figure applies ↓ Not actively bleeding → single-unit transfusion (NICE NG24) ↓ Reassess clinically and recheck Hb before any further unit ↓ Heart failure → transfuse slowly, watch for TACO
exam_trap: The trap is ordering several units at once or transfusing back to a 'normal' Hb. When the bleeding has stopped, give one unit at a time and reassess after each — especially in heart failure, where overtransfusion causes TACO.
takeaway: Hb clearly below the transfusion threshold and bleeding stopped = transfuse one unit, then reassess clinically and recheck the Hb before giving more.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents for her booking appointment at 10 weeks gestation. Her BMI is 34 kg/m² and her first child weighed 4.7 kg at birth. She has no other medical history. What is the most appropriate screening test for gestational diabetes?

options.D: Random plasma glucose at each antenatal visit
options.E: Urine dipstick for glucose at each visit

why_correct: NICE recommends a 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks for women with risk factors for GDM. This woman has two risk factors: BMI ≥30 and a previous macrosomic baby (≥4.5 kg). Screening is risk-based — not offered routinely to all pregnant women.
why_wrong: A. HbA1c is unreliable in pregnancy (haemodilution, increased red cell turnover). C. Fasting plasma glucose at booking is not a validated GDM screening tool. D. Random plasma glucose at antenatal visits is not a validated GDM screening tool. E. Urine dipstick glucose has poor sensitivity and specificity.
pearl: NICE GDM risk factors: BMI ≥30, previous macrosomic baby ≥4.5 kg, previous GDM, first-degree relative with diabetes, South Asian / Black Caribbean / Middle Eastern family origin. Any one risk factor = OGTT at 24–28 weeks, except previous GDM: early self-monitoring or an OGTT as soon as possible after booking, repeated at 24–28 weeks if normal.
thinking: BMI 34 + previous macrosomic baby ↓ Two GDM risk factors ↓ OGTT at 24–28 weeks indicated
exam_trap: GDM screening is risk-based, not universal. No risk factors = no OGTT. The stem must give you the risk factors for OGTT to be the correct answer.
takeaway: GDM screening = OGTT at 24–28 weeks if risk factors present.

stem: A 22-year-old woman at 8 weeks gestation presents with 5 days of persistent vomiting, weight loss of 3 kg, and inability to tolerate any oral fluids. Urine dipstick shows ketones 3+. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Oral cyclizine at home, with dietary advice and review
options.B: Oral metoclopramide and small frequent meals
options.C: Admit for IV fluids, IV antiemetics and IV thiamine
options.E: Reassurance — this is normal morning sickness

correct_answer: C. Admit for IV fluids, IV antiemetics and IV thiamine
why_correct: This presentation meets criteria for hyperemesis gravidarum: intractable vomiting with ketosis, dehydration, and weight loss. Hospital admission is required for IV fluid replacement (0.9% saline with potassium), IV antiemetics, and thiamine to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Oral antiemetics are appropriate for mild nausea and vomiting of pregnancy — this patient cannot tolerate oral intake. B. Oral metoclopramide likewise depends on oral intake, which she cannot manage. D. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory cases, not first-line treatment. E. Ketosis, dehydration and weight loss define hyperemesis — not normal morning sickness.
pearl: Thiamine must be given before IV glucose in any vomiting pregnant woman. Glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy (encephalopathy + oculomotor dysfunction + ataxia).
thinking: Vomiting 5 days + weight loss + ketones 3+ + oral fluids not tolerated ↓ Hyperemesis gravidarum ↓ Admit for IV fluids + IV antiemetics + thiamine before glucose
exam_trap: Never give IV glucose without thiamine first in a vomiting pregnant patient.
takeaway: Hyperemesis + ketosis + dehydration = admit, IV fluids, IV antiemetics, thiamine before glucose.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation presents with sudden, painless, bright red vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable and there is no fetal distress. The placental site was not documented at her anomaly scan. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.A: Digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
options.B: Speculum examination to visualise the cervix

correct_answer: C. Ultrasound to localise the placenta
why_correct: Painless APH in the third trimester is placenta praevia until proven otherwise. Digital vaginal examination is absolutely contraindicated — it can precipitate catastrophic haemorrhage if the placenta covers the os. Ultrasound is the immediate priority before any further clinical decisions.
why_wrong: A. Digital vaginal examination is absolutely contraindicated in suspected praevia — it risks catastrophic haemorrhage. B. Speculum examination is not contraindicated and can assess bleeding and the cervix, but it does not localise the placenta — ultrasound is the key diagnostic step. D. Caesarean section is the delivery mode for confirmed major praevia — not immediately in a stable patient. E. CTG is part of assessment but does not address the diagnosis.
pearl: Critical distinction: digital vaginal examination is absolutely contraindicated in suspected praevia. Speculum examination is not in the same category — but ultrasound always comes first regardless.
thinking: Painless bright red APH third trimester ↓ Praevia until proven otherwise ↓ Digital VE absolutely contraindicated ↓ Ultrasound first to localise placenta
exam_trap: The trap is confusing digital with speculum examination. Digital VE = absolutely contraindicated. Speculum examination = not automatically contraindicated, but ultrasound always comes first.
takeaway: Painless APH = placenta praevia until proven. Ultrasound first. Digital VE absolutely contraindicated.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, left iliac fossa pain, and dark brown vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable. Serum β-hCG is 1,500 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity and a left adnexal tubal ring. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The combination of β-hCG 1,500 IU/L (at or above the transvaginal discriminatory zone of ~1,000–1,500 IU/L), an empty uterine cavity, and a left adnexal tubal ring is diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy. At this β-hCG level a viable intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on TVUS.
why_wrong: A. Missed miscarriage would show products of conception within the uterine cavity. B. Complete miscarriage would show a thin endometrium with no adnexal mass. C. Mole presents with snowstorm appearance and very high β-hCG (>100,000 IU/L). E. A corpus luteum cyst is a normal incidental finding and does not explain the clinical picture.
pearl: Discriminatory zone: β-hCG level above which an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on TVUS (~1,000–1,500 IU/L). β-hCG above this level with empty uterus = ectopic until proven otherwise.
thinking: Amenorrhoea 6 weeks + LIF pain + spotting ↓ β-hCG 1,500 IU/L — at discriminatory zone ↓ Empty uterus on TVUS ↓ Left adnexal tubal ring ↓ Ectopic pregnancy
exam_trap: A negative ultrasound does not exclude ectopic. β-hCG above discriminatory zone + empty uterus = ectopic until proven otherwise.
takeaway: β-hCG above discriminatory zone + empty uterus + adnexal mass = ectopic pregnancy.

stem: A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks has a blood pressure of 152/96 mmHg on two readings four hours apart. Urine dipstick shows protein 2+. She has no headache, visual disturbance, or epigastric pain and is stable in a day assessment unit. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.A: Commence oral labetalol and review in 48 hours

why_correct: Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks with proteinuria or other maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction. NICE advises that a positive dipstick (1+ or more) is quantified with a PCR or ACR. Urine dipstick 2+ is a screening result only — it must be quantified with a PCR (≥30 mg/mmol confirms significant proteinuria) before the diagnosis can be formally made and management escalated.
why_wrong: A. Antihypertensive treatment is appropriate if BP stays above 140/90 mmHg, but it does not answer the question of confirming the diagnosis. B. Delivery is the definitive treatment but must follow confirmed diagnosis. D. IV labetalol is for acute severe hypertension (≥160/110) — not indicated at 152/96 in a stable patient. E. Discharge is unsafe with new hypertension and 2+ proteinuria in the third trimester.
pearl: Significant proteinuria (NICE): PCR ≥30 mg/mmol or ACR ≥8 mg/mmol. Do not routinely use 24-hour urine collection. Pre-eclampsia = new hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or other organ dysfunction.
thinking: New hypertension ≥140/90 twice ↓ Dipstick 2+ protein — screening only ↓ Must quantify with PCR ↓ PCR ≥30 mg/mmol = pre-eclampsia confirmed ↓ Then escalate management
exam_trap: Dipstick protein is not diagnostic. Do not start treatment or plan delivery based on dipstick alone in a stable patient — confirm with PCR first.
takeaway: Hypertension + dipstick protein → confirm with PCR ≥30 mg/mmol before diagnosing pre-eclampsia.

stem: A 25-year-old woman at 38 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds in the delivery suite. She is now post-ictal. Blood pressure is 168/108 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological management?

options.A: IV lorazepam 4 mg over 2 minutes, repeated once if needed
options.B: IV magnesium sulphate 4 g over 5–15 minutes
options.C: IV phenytoin 20 mg/kg at no more than 50 mg/minute

correct_answer: B. IV magnesium sulphate 4 g over 5–15 minutes
why_correct: Eclampsia is a seizure in a woman with pre-eclampsia. First-line is IV magnesium sulphate 4 g loading over 5–15 minutes, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours (continued for 24 hours after the last fit); recurrent fits get a further 2–4 g IV over 5–15 minutes. Magnesium is superior to diazepam and phenytoin for preventing recurrent seizures (Magpie Trial).
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines may terminate a prolonged fit but NICE advises against using diazepam or other anticonvulsants as an alternative to magnesium sulphate; recurrent fits are treated with further magnesium. C. Phenytoin is not recommended for eclampsia — magnesium is superior. D. Caesarean section is definitive but must follow maternal stabilisation — not during or immediately after the seizure. E. Nifedipine treats hypertension — it has no anticonvulsant effect.
pearl: MgSO4 toxicity: loss of patellar reflexes → respiratory depression → cardiac arrest. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output hourly. Antidote: IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10%.
thinking: Seizure in pre-eclamptic woman ↓ Eclampsia ↓ MgSO4 4 g IV loading immediately ↓ 1 g/hour maintenance ↓ Control BP ↓ Deliver after stabilisation
exam_trap: Do not give diazepam first. MgSO4 is always the first-line answer for eclampsia. Recurrent fits are treated with a further 2–4 g of MgSO4.
takeaway: Eclampsia = IV magnesium sulphate 4 g loading. Not diazepam. Not phenytoin.

stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman with BMI 35 kg/m² has a 75 g OGTT at 26 weeks. Fasting glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and 2-hour glucose is 8.2 mmol/L. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: NICE diagnostic criteria for GDM: fasting glucose ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour glucose ≥7.8 mmol/L. This patient meets both thresholds (fasting 5.8, 2-hour 8.2), confirming GDM.
why_wrong: A. Both values exceed diagnostic thresholds. C. Impaired fasting glucose is a non-pregnancy classification. D. Type 2 diabetes requires fasting ≥7.0 or 2-hour ≥11.1 mmol/L — not reached here. E. Diagnosis confirmed on single OGTT — no repeat needed.
pearl: NICE GDM diagnostic thresholds (75 g OGTT): fasting ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour ≥7.8 mmol/L. This follows NICE thresholds. Note: WHO 2013 uses fasting ≥5.1 mmol/L — do not confuse. Always apply NICE: fasting ≥5.6 OR 2-hour ≥7.8.
thinking: BMI 35 → risk factor → OGTT ↓ Fasting 5.8 (≥5.6) AND 2-hour 8.2 (≥7.8) ↓ Both thresholds met ↓ GDM confirmed
exam_trap: Do not use HbA1c to diagnose GDM — unreliable in pregnancy due to haemodilution. OGTT only.
takeaway: GDM diagnosis: OGTT fasting ≥5.6 mmol/L OR 2-hour ≥7.8 mmol/L.

stem: A 29-year-old woman is in spontaneous labour at 39 weeks. A vaginal swab at 36 weeks was positive for Group B Streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy. What is the most appropriate intrapartum management?

options.A: Oral clindamycin 300 mg four-hourly from admission until delivery
options.B: Vaginal chlorhexidine 0.2% wash every 4 hours until the baby is delivered
options.C: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g, then 1.5 g four-hourly until delivery
options.D: IV vancomycin 1 g twelve-hourly from onset of labour until delivery
options.E: No antibiotics — observe the baby for 12 hours and treat if symptomatic

correct_answer: C. IV benzylpenicillin 3 g, then 1.5 g four-hourly until delivery
why_correct: IAP with IV benzylpenicillin reduces early-onset neonatal GBS disease. Indications: GBS in current pregnancy (swab or bacteriuria), previous GBS-affected neonate, intrapartum fever with GBS risk factors. Regimen: benzylpenicillin 3 g IV loading, then 1.5 g four-hourly until delivery.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics do not achieve adequate levels for intrapartum prophylaxis, and clindamycin is no longer recommended for GBS prophylaxis because of increasing resistance. B. Chlorhexidine vaginal washes do not reduce early-onset neonatal GBS disease. D. Vancomycin is reserved for women with a significant penicillin allergy. E. Waiting for neonatal symptoms is inadequate — prophylaxis must be given intrapartum.
pearl: GBS IAP must be IV intrapartum — not oral antenatal. Antenatal oral antibiotics temporarily suppress colonisation but do not prevent neonatal GBS sepsis during delivery.
thinking: Positive GBS swab + now in labour ↓ IAP indicated ↓ No penicillin allergy ↓ IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading → 1.5 g four-hourly until delivery
exam_trap: IAP must be IV intrapartum. Antenatal oral antibiotics do not protect the baby during delivery.
takeaway: GBS positive in labour = IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.5 g four-hourly until delivery.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has a spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3.9 kg baby. Ten minutes later she has a sudden heavy vaginal bleed estimated at 1,500 mL. The uterus is soft and boggy. Blood pressure is 94/56 mmHg, heart rate 116 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: IM oxytocin 10 units, then reassess uterine tone and blood loss in 15 minutes
options.B: IV ergometrine 0.5 mg, then reassess uterine tone and bleeding in 15 minutes
options.C: IM carboprost 250 micrograms, repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses
options.D: Call for help, bimanual compression, IV oxytocin bolus then infusion
options.E: Transfer to theatre for subtotal hysterectomy

correct_answer: D. Call for help, bimanual compression, IV oxytocin bolus then infusion
why_correct: Uterine atony (soft boggy uterus) causes 80% of PPH. Immediate management: bimanual uterine compression (fastest method to reduce blood loss), IV oxytocin 5 units by slow injection (may be repeated), then 40 units in 500 mL infusion, and senior help. Physical compression and first-line uterotonic must happen simultaneously.
why_wrong: A. Oxytocin with a wait-and-see approach delays bimanual compression (the fastest way to reduce bleeding) and help in major PPH. B. Ergometrine alone omits uterine compression and senior help, and is contraindicated in hypertension. C. Carboprost is a later-line uterotonic after oxytocin and ergometrine, and is contraindicated in asthma. E. Hysterectomy is the last resort after balloon tamponade, compression sutures and arterial ligation.
pearl: PPH uterotonic sequence: oxytocin (first) → ergometrine (if no hypertension) → carboprost (if no asthma) → misoprostol. Surgical: balloon tamponade → B-Lynch suture → uterine artery ligation → hysterectomy.
thinking: Soft boggy uterus + 1,500 mL blood loss + haemodynamic compromise ↓ Uterine atony ↓ Bimanual compression immediately ↓ IV oxytocin bolus + infusion ↓ Senior help ↓ Escalate if no response
exam_trap: Bimanual compression reduces bleeding faster than waiting for drugs alone. Do not omit physical compression.
takeaway: PPH + boggy uterus = uterine atony. Bimanual compression + IV oxytocin immediately. Call for help.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with prolonged heavy vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal cramping 10 days after a spontaneous miscarriage at 12 weeks gestation. She is afebrile. Pelvic ultrasound shows heterogeneous echogenic material within the uterine cavity with Doppler flow. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral co-amoxiclav for 7 days with review in the EPAU
options.B: Expectant management with repeat ultrasound in 2 weeks
options.C: Surgical evacuation of retained products of conception

correct_answer: C. Surgical evacuation of retained products of conception
why_correct: Retained products of conception (RPOC) with heavy ongoing bleeding, Doppler flow (indicating viable trophoblastic tissue), and failure to resolve after 10 days is best managed by surgical management (evacuation of retained products, usually by vacuum aspiration). Surgical management is the most effective and definitive treatment, especially when bleeding is heavy.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics alone do not remove the retained tissue, and she has no signs of infection. B. Expectant management risks infection (endometritis) or severe haemorrhage when bleeding is heavy and ongoing. D. Misoprostol can be used for RPOC in mild cases but is less effective than surgical management when bleeding is heavy. E. MRI is not indicated — the ultrasound has already demonstrated retained products.
pearl: Septic miscarriage (RPOC + fever + uterine tenderness + purulent discharge) requires IV broad-spectrum antibiotics plus surgical evacuation of retained products. Intrauterine adhesions (Asherman's syndrome) are a recognised complication of uterine curettage.
thinking: Prolonged heavy bleeding 10 days post-miscarriage ↓ Ultrasound: RPOC with Doppler flow ↓ Surgical treatment most effective ↓ Answer: surgical evacuation of retained products of conception
exam_trap: Heavy ongoing bleeding with retained tissue 10 days after miscarriage favours surgical management over further expectant management.
takeaway: Prolonged bleeding post-miscarriage + RPOC on ultrasound with Doppler flow = surgical evacuation of retained products.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a confirmed unruptured ectopic pregnancy. Her β-hCG is 850 IU/L and has fallen by 20% in 48 hours. She is haemodynamically stable with no significant pain. She has a normal contralateral tube and wants to preserve fertility. What is the most appropriate management?
correct_answer: C. Expectant management with serial β-hCG
why_correct: Expectant management is appropriate when: β-hCG <1,000–1,500 IU/L, the trend is falling (≥15% fall in 48 hours), the patient is haemodynamically stable, there is no significant pain, and the patient can comply with follow-up. This patient meets all criteria. Success rate is >80% with a falling β-hCG below this threshold.
why_wrong: A. Salpingectomy removes the tube and is indicated for ruptured ectopic or failed medical management — not first-line here. B. Salpingostomy is fertility-preserving surgery but more invasive than needed when β-hCG is already falling. D. Methotrexate is indicated for plateauing or slowly rising β-hCG (first-line if hCG <1,500 IU/L, or as a choice with surgery at 1,500–5,000 IU/L, with no fetal heartbeat and mass <35 mm) — not for a falling β-hCG below 1,000. E. Mifepristone is not used for ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: Ectopic management by hCG (NICE NG126): ≤1,000 IU/L (consider up to 1,500), stable, pain free, mass <35 mm, no heartbeat → expectant (hCG days 2, 4 and 7). <1,500 IU/L → methotrexate first-line; 1,500–<5,000 IU/L → choice of methotrexate or surgery. ≥5,000 IU/L, fetal heartbeat, mass ≥35 mm or significant pain → surgery. Falling β-hCG = expectant management.
thinking: Stable ectopic + β-hCG 850 IU/L + falling 20% in 48 hours + no significant pain ↓ β-hCG below discriminatory zone and falling ↓ Expectant management with serial β-hCG
exam_trap: Falling β-hCG = expectant management. Methotrexate is not given to a patient whose ectopic is already resolving spontaneously.
takeaway: Stable ectopic + β-hCG <1,000 IU/L and falling = expectant management with serial β-hCG.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is in active labour at 39 weeks. She suddenly develops severe dyspnoea, cyanosis, and hypotension. She then has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure and becomes unconscious. Her coagulation results show prolonged PT, APTT, and low fibrinogen consistent with DIC. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare catastrophic condition occurring during labour or immediately postpartum. The classic triad is: sudden cardiovascular collapse (hypotension, hypoxia), seizure or altered consciousness, and DIC/coagulopathy. AFE is triggered by amniotic fluid entering the maternal circulation, activating complement and coagulation cascades.
why_wrong: A. PE causes hypoxia and hypotension but not typically DIC or seizures. B. Eclampsia causes seizures but not DIC or sudden profound cardiovascular collapse. D. Anaphylaxis causes hypotension and bronchospasm but not DIC. E. Acute MI is uncommon in young women in labour and does not cause DIC or seizures.
pearl: AFE management is supportive: basic life support, oxygenation/intubation, vasopressors, massive transfusion protocol for DIC, delivery of the fetus if undelivered. No specific pharmacological treatment exists. Mortality is 30–50%.
thinking: Active labour + sudden cardiovascular collapse + hypoxia + seizure + DIC ↓ Amniotic fluid embolism ↓ Supportive management ↓ Massive transfusion for DIC ↓ Deliver fetus
exam_trap: AFE is a diagnosis of exclusion — there is no definitive diagnostic test. The combination of cardiovascular collapse + seizure + DIC in active labour is the clinical triad.
takeaway: Sudden collapse + seizure + DIC in active labour = amniotic fluid embolism.

presentation: Cervical screening — HPV positive cytology negative
stem: A 35-year-old woman receives her cervical screening result: HPV positive, cytology negative (no abnormal cells). She has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: NHS cervical screening pathway: HPV positive + cytology negative → repeat HPV test in 12 months. If HPV is negative at 12 months, return to routine recall. If still HPV positive with negative cytology, rescreen again at a further 12 months. Refer for colposcopy if cytology becomes abnormal, or at the third consecutive HPV-positive result (24 months) regardless of cytology. This allows time for spontaneous HPV clearance while monitoring for persistent infection.
why_wrong: A. Five-year routine recall is for HPV-negative results, not HPV positive. C. Immediate colposcopy is for HPV positive + abnormal cytology, not HPV positive with normal cytology. D. HPV vaccination is for prevention, not treatment of existing infection. E. LLETZ is a treatment for CIN2+ confirmed at colposcopy, not for a screening test result.
pearl: HPV positive + abnormal cytology (borderline, low-grade, high-grade) → colposcopy referral. HPV positive + normal cytology → repeat in 12 months. HPV still positive at 24 months (third consecutive positive) → colposcopy.
thinking: HPV positive + cytology negative ↓ Low immediate risk ↓ Allow time for spontaneous clearance ↓ Repeat smear in 12 months
exam_trap: Do not refer directly to colposcopy for HPV positive with normal cytology. Rescreen at 12 months, and refer only if cytology becomes abnormal or HPV is still positive at the third consecutive test (24 months).
takeaway: HPV positive + normal cytology = repeat smear in 12 months.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with 4 weeks of persistent bloating, early satiety, and urinary frequency. She has no vaginal bleeding. CA-125 is 145 U/mL (normal <35). Pelvic ultrasound shows a complex, multiloculated right adnexal mass with solid components and ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Ovarian cancer classically presents with persistent non-specific symptoms: bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, and urinary symptoms. The combination of a raised CA-125 (well above the NICE NG12 threshold of 24 IU/ml for her age group), a complex multiloculated adnexal mass with solid components, and ascites gives a high Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) — highly suggestive of malignancy.
why_wrong: A. A benign serous cystadenoma is typically unilocular and thin-walled, without solid components or ascites. B. Endometriomas have a ground-glass appearance on ultrasound — not multiloculated with solid components. C. Dermoid cysts contain fat and calcifications on ultrasound — a different appearance. E. Ovarian torsion presents acutely with severe unilateral pain — not a 4-week history of vague symptoms.
pearl: Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) = ultrasound score × menopausal status × CA-125; RMI 250 or more = high risk → refer to specialist gynaecological oncology (NICE CG122). In primary care (NICE NG12, 2026), persistent symptoms in a woman aged 40 or over → measure CA-125 and arrange urgent ultrasound if it meets the age-specific threshold (24 IU/ml at 60–69); ascites or a pelvic/abdominal mass → suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Persistent bloating + early satiety + urinary frequency + age 65 ↓ Classic ovarian cancer symptoms ↓ CA-125 elevated + complex multiloculated mass + ascites ↓ High RMI ↓ Refer to gynaecological oncology
exam_trap: Do not diagnose IBS in a woman >50 with persistent bloating — ovarian cancer must be excluded first. Ovarian cancer kills because it is diagnosed late.
takeaway: Persistent bloating + complex adnexal mass + raised CA-125 = ovarian cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has not had a period for 14 months. She reports hot flushes, night sweats, and mood changes. She is otherwise healthy with no medical history. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_correct: In a woman over 45 with typical vasomotor symptoms and 12 months of amenorrhoea, menopause is a clinical diagnosis — no biochemical testing is required. NICE specifically recommends against routine FSH testing in this age group, as results are unreliable (FSH levels fluctuate during the perimenopause).
why_wrong: A. FSH testing is not required or recommended for diagnosing menopause in women >45 — it is unreliable due to fluctuating levels during perimenopause. B. Oestradiol is not a routine diagnostic test. D. DXA is indicated for fracture risk assessment, not to diagnose menopause. E. HRT is a treatment decision that follows diagnosis — not a diagnostic step.
pearl: FSH testing is only recommended for women aged 40–45 with menopausal symptoms and for women under 40 with suspected premature ovarian insufficiency (POI requires FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions 4–6 weeks apart).
thinking: Age 52 + 14 months amenorrhoea + vasomotor symptoms ↓ Classic menopausal presentation ↓ NICE: clinical diagnosis in women >45 ↓ No FSH testing required
exam_trap: Do not check FSH in a woman >45 with typical menopausal symptoms — it is not recommended and adds no clinical value. Diagnose clinically.
takeaway: Menopause in women >45: clinical diagnosis. No FSH testing needed.

presentation: Contraception — POP and migraine with aura
stem: A 25-year-old woman wishes to start hormonal contraception. She has a history of migraine with aura. She has no other medical problems. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP) is safe in migraine with aura
options.B: Progestogen-only pill (POP) is safe in migraine with aura
options.C: She requires neurology review before commencing any hormonal contraception
options.D: She must use barrier contraception only
options.E: POP may worsen her migraines and should be avoided

correct_answer: B. Progestogen-only pill (POP) is safe in migraine with aura
why_correct: COCP is contraindicated in women with migraine with aura (UKMEC 4 — absolute contraindication) due to increased risk of ischaemic stroke (oestrogen + migraine with aura synergistically increase stroke risk). Progestogen-only contraceptives (POP, implant, IUS, injection) contain no oestrogen and do not increase stroke risk — UKMEC 2 (safe to use) in migraine with aura.
why_wrong: A. COCP is absolutely contraindicated (UKMEC 4) in migraine with aura — it significantly increases stroke risk. C. No neurology review is needed — the POP is safe and can be prescribed directly. D. Barrier methods are not the only option — progestogen-only methods are safe and effective. E. POP has no established effect on stroke risk in migraine with aura.
pearl: UKMEC categories: 1 = use freely; 2 = benefits outweigh risks; 3 = risks outweigh benefits; 4 = absolute contraindication. COCP + migraine with aura = UKMEC 4. POP + migraine with aura = UKMEC 2.
thinking: Migraine with aura ↓ COCP = UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication — stroke risk) ↓ POP contains no oestrogen ↓ UKMEC 2 in migraine with aura ↓ POP safe
exam_trap: The trap is thinking all hormonal contraception is contraindicated with migraine. Only oestrogen-containing methods (COCP, combined patch, combined ring) are contraindicated. Progestogen-only methods are safe.
takeaway: Migraine with aura = COCP absolutely contraindicated (UKMEC 4). POP safe (UKMEC 2).

presentation: Combined oral contraceptive — one missed pill
stem: A 22-year-old woman takes a 21-day combined oral contraceptive. She missed one pill on day 15 of her pack and took it 14 hours late (less than 24 hours late). She has been sexually active. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop the pack, use condoms for 7 days, and start a new pack after 7 pill-free days
options.B: Take the missed pill now and use additional contraception (condoms) for 7 days
options.C: Take the late pill now and continue the pack; no extra precautions needed
options.E: The pack is invalid — start a new one immediately

correct_answer: C. Take the late pill now and continue the pack; no extra precautions needed
why_correct: FSRH guidance: a pill is 'late' if taken less than 24 hours after it was due and 'missed' if more than 24 hours late (more than 48 hours since the previous pill). This patient took her pill 14 hours late — which is less than 24 hours late. She should take the pill as soon as she remembers and continue the rest of the pack as normal. No additional contraception and no emergency contraception are needed.
why_wrong: A. Stopping the pack and taking a 7-day break lengthens the hormone-free interval and increases the risk of ovulation — a single late pill needs no change to pill taking. B. Additional precautions for 7 days are needed only when two or more consecutive pills are missed (more than 48 hours late) — not for a single pill taken late. D. Emergency contraception is not indicated — ovulation suppression has not been compromised by a pill less than 24 hours late. E. The pack remains valid.
pearl: FSRH missed pill rules: one pill late or missed (less than 48 hours since it should have been taken) = take it now, continue the pack, no additional contraception needed. Two or more pills missed (48 hours or more) = take the most recent missed pill, use condoms or abstain for 7 days, consider EC if pills were missed in week 1 and there was UPSI in the hormone-free interval or week 1, and omit the pill-free interval if pills were missed in week 3.
thinking: Pill taken 14 hours late = <24 hours late ↓ Not a true missed pill by FSRH definition ↓ Take pill now ↓ Continue pack normally ↓ No additional contraception or EC needed
exam_trap: A pill is only 'missed' if it is >24 hours late. 14 hours late = not missed. Many candidates incorrectly advise condoms for any late pill — the threshold is 24 hours.
takeaway: COC pill <24 hours late = take it and continue pack normally. No additional contraception needed.

presentation: Menorrhagia with fibroids — first-line medical management
stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with heavy regular menstrual bleeding with clots for 8 months. Pelvic ultrasound shows multiple intramural fibroids, the largest measuring 2.5 cm. The uterine cavity is not distorted on saline sonography. She wants medical management. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses

why_correct: NICE recommends LNG-IUS as first-line pharmacological management for heavy menstrual bleeding. It reduces menstrual blood loss by 90–95% at 12 months and is more effective than tranexamic acid, mefenamic acid, or the COCP. For fibroids <3 cm that do not distort the uterine cavity, LNG-IUS is appropriate and fits correctly.
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid is second-line if LNG-IUS is declined or unsuitable. B. Mefenamic acid is second-line and mainly addresses dysmenorrhoea. D. COCP is effective but less so than LNG-IUS — not first-line. E. GnRH agonists are used pre-operatively to shrink fibroids or treat anaemia — not for long-term first-line treatment.
pearl: Fibroid size matters for LNG-IUS suitability. Fibroids <3 cm without cavity distortion = LNG-IUS appropriate. Fibroids ≥3 cm or with cavity distortion = LNG-IUS may not sit correctly. Consider UAE, myomectomy, or hysterectomy for larger fibroids.
thinking: HMB + intramural fibroids <3 cm + undistorted cavity + wants medical treatment ↓ NICE first-line = LNG-IUS ↓ Reduces blood loss 90–95% ↓ Fibroids <3 cm = LNG-IUS fits correctly
exam_trap: Fibroid size matters. LNG-IUS is first-line for HMB with fibroids <3 cm without cavity distortion. Larger fibroids may prevent correct IUS placement.
takeaway: HMB + fibroids <3 cm + undistorted cavity = LNG-IUS (Mirena) first-line.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation presents with regular painful contractions (4 in 10 minutes) and a cervix that is 3 cm dilated. Membranes are intact. She is not in established labour. Fetal wellbeing is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
correct_answer: D. Oral nifedipine and antenatal steroids
why_correct: At 30 weeks with suspected preterm labour and intact membranes, NICE NG25 recommends tocolysis — nifedipine is preferred, with an oxytocin receptor antagonist such as atosiban if nifedipine is contraindicated — together with maternal corticosteroids, which are offered from 24+0 to 33+6 weeks to reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage and death. The main purpose of tocolysis is to delay birth long enough for the steroid course to take effect.
why_wrong: A. Nifedipine is the preferred tocolytic, but tocolysis alone omits antenatal corticosteroids — the main reason for delaying birth. B. Atosiban alone is the second-choice tocolytic (if nifedipine is contraindicated) and also omits corticosteroids. C. Magnesium sulphate is used for fetal neuroprotection (offered 24+0–29+6 weeks and considered 30+0–33+6 weeks in established labour or planned birth within 24 hours) — it is not the recommended tocolytic. E. Emergency delivery is not indicated when mother and fetus are stable — the goal is to delay birth for steroid administration.
pearl: Tocolysis is indicated between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks. Contraindications: chorioamnionitis, fetal distress, antepartum haemorrhage, severe pre-eclampsia. Magnesium sulphate for neuroprotection is given at <30 weeks in addition to tocolysis.
thinking: 30 weeks + contractions + 3 cm dilated + intact membranes + stable ↓ Suspected preterm labour ↓ Tocolysis (nifedipine first-line; atosiban if contraindicated) ↓ PLUS antenatal corticosteroids (24+0–33+6 weeks) ↓ Option that includes both = best answer
exam_trap: Tocolysis alone is not the answer — corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity must always accompany tocolysis. Also: magnesium sulphate is for neuroprotection, not tocolysis. Choose nifedipine as the tocolytic.
takeaway: Preterm labour 24–34 weeks = tocolysis (nifedipine first-line) + antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity.

presentation: Fetal growth restriction — absent end-diastolic flow
stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks has an ultrasound showing estimated fetal weight <3rd centile, absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, and oligohydramnios. CTG is normal today. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure and repeat growth scan and Doppler in 4 weeks
options.B: Twice-weekly outpatient CTG and umbilical Doppler monitoring
options.C: Admit, corticosteroids, daily CTG and plan delivery
options.D: Induction of labour with vaginal prostaglandin today

correct_answer: C. Admit, corticosteroids, daily CTG and plan delivery
why_correct: Absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) in the umbilical artery indicates significant placental insufficiency and the fetus is at risk of hypoxic injury and stillbirth. At 34 weeks, management is hospital admission for intensive monitoring, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and planning delivery — usually by caesarean section given the poor fetal reserve.
why_wrong: A. Review in 4 weeks is inappropriate for AEDF — the fetus is at significant risk of stillbirth. B. Outpatient surveillance is for milder FGR with normal or less severe Doppler findings — not for AEDF. D. A compromised fetus with AEDF is unlikely to tolerate induction and labour — caesarean section is usually safer. E. Maternal oxygen therapy has no evidence base for FGR.
pearl: Doppler severity in FGR: normal → elevated resistance (PI >95th centile) → absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) → reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF). REDF = near-immediate delivery. AEDF at 34 weeks = plan delivery after steroids.
thinking: FGR <3rd centile + AEDF + oligohydramnios ↓ Significant placental insufficiency ↓ Hospital admission + intensive monitoring ↓ Corticosteroids for lung maturity ↓ Plan delivery by CS
exam_trap: AEDF is not a reason to induce — it is a reason to deliver by caesarean after steroids. The fetal reserve is too poor to tolerate labour safely.
takeaway: FGR + AEDF = hospital admission + corticosteroids + plan for delivery (usually caesarean).

stem: A 28-year-old breastfeeding woman at 3 weeks postpartum presents with a tender, erythematous, warm left breast quadrant with fever of 38.4°C and myalgia. There is no fluctuant mass. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Stop breastfeeding and prescribe oral flucloxacillin
options.C: Urgent hospital admission for IV antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Continue breastfeeding + oral flucloxacillin + analgesia
why_correct: Lactational mastitis is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Management: continue breastfeeding from the affected breast (emptying the breast reduces pain and prevents abscess formation), oral flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS for 10–14 days (or erythromycin if penicillin allergic), and analgesia (ibuprofen is anti-inflammatory and analgesic). If no improvement in 48–72 hours, ultrasound to exclude abscess.
why_wrong: A. Stopping breastfeeding worsens engorgement and increases abscess risk — it is contraindicated. C. IV antibiotics are for sepsis or failed oral treatment — not first-line here. D. Needle aspiration is for a confirmed abscess (fluctuant mass on examination or collection on ultrasound) — not for uncomplicated mastitis. E. Paracetamol and compresses alone are insufficient with systemic symptoms and 38.4°C fever.
pearl: Breast abscess: fluctuant mass, failure to respond to 48–72 hours of antibiotics. Manage with ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (preferred over incision and drainage). Breastfeeding can continue on the unaffected breast.
thinking: Breastfeeding + tender erythematous breast + fever + no fluctuant mass ↓ Lactational mastitis (not abscess) ↓ Continue breastfeeding ↓ Oral flucloxacillin + analgesia ↓ Review if no improvement in 48–72 hours
exam_trap: Do not stop breastfeeding — emptying the breast is therapeutic. Stopping increases milk stasis and the risk of abscess formation.
takeaway: Lactational mastitis = continue breastfeeding + oral flucloxacillin. Stopping breastfeeding worsens outcome.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is 48 hours post-emergency caesarean section. She has a temperature of 39.2°C, heart rate of 104 bpm, lower abdominal pain, and offensive-smelling lochia. The uterus is tender on palpation. She has no urinary symptoms or breast symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Post-caesarean endometritis presents with fever, uterine tenderness, subinvolution of the uterus, and offensive-smelling lochia within 48–72 hours of delivery. It is the most common cause of puerperal pyrexia after caesarean section. Ascending infection (typically polymicrobial) causes inflammation of the endometrium.
why_wrong: A. Wound infection (cellulitis, dehiscence) presents with local signs at the incision site — erythema, swelling, or discharge — not offensive lochia or uterine tenderness. B. UTI presents with dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain — not offensive lochia. C. Mastitis presents with breast pain and erythema — onset is typically later (7–21 days postpartum). E. Pelvic haematoma presents with pain and a palpable mass — not primarily fever or offensive discharge.
pearl: Treatment: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (clindamycin + gentamicin is the standard regimen, or co-amoxiclav). Take blood cultures and high vaginal swab before starting antibiotics. If no improvement, consider pelvic haematoma or abscess on imaging.
thinking: Post-CS 48 hours + fever + tachycardia + uterine tenderness + offensive lochia + no breast/urinary symptoms ↓ Endometritis ↓ Blood cultures + HVS ↓ IV clindamycin + gentamicin
exam_trap: Offensive lochia + uterine tenderness is the specific combination for endometritis. Do not confuse with wound infection (local incision signs) or UTI (urinary symptoms).
takeaway: Post-caesarean fever + uterine tenderness + offensive lochia = endometritis. IV clindamycin + gentamicin.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida is 41+5 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy. She is not in labour. Fetal wellbeing is normal on CTG. What is the most appropriate management according to NICE?

options.A: Membrane sweep now and plan induction at exactly 42+0 weeks
options.B: Expectant management until 42+5 weeks with twice-weekly CTG
options.C: Offer a membrane sweep and induction of labour before 42+0
options.D: Immediate induction of labour today without further discussion
options.E: Elective caesarean section for the prolonged pregnancy today

correct_answer: C. Offer a membrane sweep and induction of labour before 42+0
why_correct: NICE NG207: discuss membrane sweeping at antenatal visits after 39+0 weeks, and discuss induction of labour from 41+0 weeks, explaining that the risks of stillbirth, neonatal death, neonatal unit admission and caesarean birth increase as pregnancy continues beyond 41+0 weeks. This patient is 41+5 — she should be offered a membrane sweep and induction now, so that birth can occur before 42+0 weeks.
why_wrong: A. Planning induction for exactly 42+0 needlessly delays it — NICE advises discussing induction from 41+0, so at 41+5 it should be offered now. B. Expectant management to 42+5 is not the recommended plan; if she declines induction, NICE advises discussing her options and additional fetal monitoring from 42 weeks, explaining that monitoring cannot reliably prevent stillbirth. D. Immediate induction today is not mandatory, and induction should be offered after an informed discussion with the woman, to proceed before 42+0 weeks. E. Caesarean section is not indicated for uncomplicated post-term pregnancy.
pearl: Risks of post-term pregnancy (>42 weeks): doubled stillbirth risk, meconium aspiration, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, need for instrumental or caesarean delivery. Membrane sweeping, discussed at antenatal visits after 39+0 weeks, makes spontaneous labour more likely and can reduce the need for formal induction.
thinking: 41+5 weeks + uncomplicated + normal CTG ↓ Approaching 42 weeks ↓ NICE: discuss induction from 41+0 weeks ↓ Offer sweep and induction now to aim for birth before 42+0
exam_trap: Do not let a pregnancy pass 42+0 weeks without a documented discussion of induction. If she declines, discuss her options and additional fetal monitoring from 42 weeks — monitoring cannot reliably prevent stillbirth.
takeaway: Uncomplicated post-term pregnancy = offer induction before 42+0 weeks (NICE).

stem: A 35-year-old woman wants long-acting reversible contraception (LARC) and has heavy menstrual bleeding. She has no contraindications to hormonal or copper devices. Which is the most appropriate intrauterine device?

options.C: Either device, as both are equally suitable
options.D: Neither — a systemic combined hormonal method is needed

why_correct: The LNG-IUS (Mirena) releases levonorgestrel locally into the uterine cavity, causing endometrial atrophy and reducing menstrual blood loss by 90–95%. It is first-line for both heavy menstrual bleeding and contraception. The copper IUD, by contrast, increases menstrual blood loss and dysmenorrhoea — it is unsuitable for women with menorrhagia.
why_wrong: A. The copper IUD tends to increase menstrual blood loss — it is unsuitable for women with heavy menstrual bleeding. C. They are not equally suitable — the copper IUD worsens heavy bleeding. D. Systemic hormones are not required — the LNG-IUS provides effective local treatment and contraception. E. The implant is not an intrauterine device and is less effective than the LNG-IUS at treating heavy menstrual bleeding.
pearl: Cu-IUD increases menstrual bleeding by 20–50%. LNG-IUS decreases menstrual bleeding by 90–95%. This distinction is tested directly and frequently.
thinking: Menorrhagia + wants LARC ↓ Cu-IUD worsens bleeding ↓ LNG-IUS reduces bleeding 90–95% ↓ LNG-IUS is the answer
exam_trap: Never offer a copper IUD to a woman whose primary complaint is heavy menstrual bleeding — it will make it significantly worse.
takeaway: Menorrhagia + LARC = LNG-IUS (Mirena). Never Cu-IUD — it worsens bleeding.

stem: A 30-year-old woman and her 32-year-old partner have been trying to conceive for 18 months without success. Neither has a known medical history. What is the most appropriate initial investigation for the male partner?
why_correct: Semen analysis is the first-line investigation for the male partner in a couple with subfertility. It assesses sperm count (>16 million/mL), motility (>42% motile), and morphology (>4% normal forms by WHO 2021 criteria). It is non-invasive, rapid, and identifies male factor subfertility in ~30% of couples.
why_wrong: A. Testicular ultrasound is indicated only if semen analysis is abnormal or if there is a clinical indication (varicocele, mass). B. Serum FSH/LH is indicated only if semen analysis shows azoospermia or severe oligospermia to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive causes. D. Karyotype is for severe oligospermia/azoospermia after initial investigations. E. Post-coital test is no longer recommended by NICE — it has poor predictive value.
pearl: Subfertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Refer earlier if: female >35 years, known risk factors (endometriosis, PMOS (formerly PCOS), previous PID, previous ectopic), or male factor suspected.
thinking: 18 months subfertility + male partner ↓ Initial investigation = semen analysis ↓ Non-invasive, rapid, identifies 30% of causes ↓ Then female investigations (hormones, ovulation, tubal assessment)
exam_trap: Post-coital test is no longer recommended by NICE — do not select it. Semen analysis is always the first investigation for the male partner.
takeaway: Initial male subfertility investigation = semen analysis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman had surgical evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole 4 weeks ago. Her β-hCG has fallen from 320,000 to 8,500 IU/L. She is registered with the regional trophoblastic disease screening centre. What is the recommended duration of β-hCG follow-up if her levels normalise?

options.A: No further follow-up needed once β-hCG normalises
options.B: Monthly β-hCG for 3 months after normalisation
options.C: β-hCG follow-up for 6 months from evacuation

correct_answer: C. β-hCG follow-up for 6 months from evacuation
why_correct: After complete mole evacuation, all patients are registered with a regional trophoblastic screening centre (Sheffield, Charing Cross, or Dundee). If β-hCG normalises within 8 weeks of evacuation, follow-up is 6 months from the date of evacuation. This detects gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), which occurs in ~15% of complete moles.
why_wrong: A. Stopping monitoring at normalisation is unsafe after a complete mole — GTN can still develop during the surveillance period. B. Three months is insufficient — follow-up continues to 6 months from evacuation. D. Two years of surveillance is not standard — when hCG normalises within 56 days, follow-up ends 6 months after evacuation. E. Indefinite annual monitoring is unnecessary once the surveillance period is complete.
pearl: After complete mole: if β-hCG normalises within 8 weeks of evacuation → monitor for 6 months from evacuation date. If normalisation takes >8 weeks → monitor for 6 months from normalisation. All patients registered with regional trophoblastic disease centre. Avoid pregnancy throughout follow-up.
thinking: Complete mole + falling β-hCG ↓ Registered at trophoblastic centre ↓ Monitor until normalised then 6 months from evacuation ↓ Avoid pregnancy during follow-up
exam_trap: Do not discharge a patient after molar evacuation without follow-up. GTN can develop even after β-hCG has normalised.
takeaway: Complete mole = β-hCG monitoring for 6 months from evacuation date. Avoid pregnancy throughout.

stem: A woman's membranes rupture spontaneously at 38 weeks during labour. The midwife notes a loop of umbilical cord in the vagina. The CTG shows a fetal heart rate of 55 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Replace the cord into the uterus and continue continuous CTG monitoring
options.B: Place her supine with a left lateral tilt and call for help
options.C: Manually elevate the presenting part and arrange category 1 caesarean
options.D: High-flow maternal oxygen and a rapid IV fluid bolus, then reassess the CTG
options.E: Attempt ventouse delivery in the room at the current cervical dilatation

correct_answer: C. Manually elevate the presenting part and arrange category 1 caesarean
why_correct: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency. The priority is to relieve pressure on the cord to restore fetal blood flow. The immediate action is to insert two fingers into the vagina and manually elevate the presenting part off the cord while simultaneously calling for emergency caesarean section. The mother should be placed in knee-chest or Trendelenburg position to reduce pressure.
why_wrong: A. Handling or replacing the cord risks vasospasm and cord damage — it is not recommended. B. The supine position does not relieve cord compression — knee-chest or exaggerated Sims' position with elevation of the presenting part is used. D. Maternal oxygen and fluids do not relieve cord compression — decompression and delivery are the immediate priorities. E. Instrumental vaginal delivery is appropriate only if the cervix is fully dilated and delivery is imminent — not at an unknown dilatation.
pearl: Alternatives to manual elevation: fill the bladder (instil 500 mL saline via Foley catheter to elevate the presenting part). Do not remove the cord from the vagina — keep it warm and moist. Emergency CS decision-to-delivery time target is <30 minutes.
thinking: Cord prolapse + FHR 55 bpm ↓ Obstetric emergency ↓ Manually elevate presenting part immediately ↓ Knee-chest position ↓ Emergency CS ↓ Do not push cord back
exam_trap: The first action is manual elevation of the presenting part — not oxygen, not changing position alone, not pushing the cord back. Cord decompression is the immediate priority.
takeaway: Cord prolapse = manually elevate presenting part + emergency caesarean section. Do not push cord back.

presentation: HIV in pregnancy — vertical transmission prevention
stem: A 30-year-old HIV-positive woman is 32 weeks pregnant. She has not yet started antiretroviral therapy (ART). Her viral load is 12,000 copies/mL. She wants to breastfeed. What is the most appropriate management to minimise vertical transmission?

options.A: Start ART, plan vaginal delivery, avoid breastfeeding
options.B: Start ART, plan caesarean section at 38 weeks, avoid breastfeeding
options.C: Start ART now, decide mode of birth on the 36-week viral load, recommend formula feeding
options.E: Delay ART until resistance results are back, then plan vaginal birth regardless of viral load

correct_answer: C. Start ART now, decide mode of birth on the 36-week viral load, recommend formula feeding
why_correct: Anyone presenting after 28 weeks not on ART should start a dolutegravir-based three-drug regimen immediately, before resistance results are available (BHIVA 2025). Viral load is checked 2 weeks after starting, then monthly until undetectable, and at 36 weeks; the 36-week result decides mode of birth (planned vaginal birth if <50 copies/mL, planned caesarean considered if 50–399, caesarean if ≥400). In the UK exclusive formula feeding is recommended because it removes the risk of postnatal transmission.
why_wrong: A. Committing to vaginal birth now is premature — it is supported only if viral load is <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks. B. Committing to caesarean section at 32 weeks is premature — with prompt ART many achieve <50 copies/mL by 36 weeks, and the 36-week viral load decides mode of birth. D. ART is essential — withholding it is unacceptable. E. ART must start immediately after 28 weeks without waiting for resistance results, and vaginal birth is planned only if viral load is <50 copies/mL at 36 weeks.
pearl: Vertical transmission: no interventions 25–30%; suppressed viral load on ART <0.3%. In the UK formula feeding is recommended; those who are virologically suppressed and choose to breastfeed are supported with enhanced monitoring. Infant PNP: 2 weeks zidovudine if low risk; combination PNP (zidovudine + lamivudine 4 weeks, nevirapine 2 weeks) if higher risk.
thinking: HIV + viral load 12,000 + 32 weeks, not on ART ↓ Late presenter (>28 weeks) → start dolutegravir-based triple ART immediately (do not wait for resistance tests) ↓ Viral load at 2 weeks, monthly, and at 36 weeks ↓ 36-week VL: <50 → vaginal birth; 50–399 → consider CS; ≥400 → CS ↓ Recommend formula feeding
exam_trap: Mode of birth is not fixed at diagnosis — it depends on the 36-week viral load. Do not delay ART for resistance results in a late presenter.
takeaway: HIV in pregnancy, late presentation = start dolutegravir-based ART now; 36-week viral load decides mode of birth; formula feeding recommended.

presentation: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy — first-line treatment
stem: A 10-week pregnant woman presents with nausea and vomiting. She has not yet tried any lifestyle or dietary measures. She is able to tolerate oral fluids, has no ketonuria, and has not lost weight. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
why_correct: NICE guidance for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy (NVP): first-line treatment is lifestyle and dietary measures — ginger (capsules or food), acupressure (P6 wristbands), small frequent meals, and avoiding spicy or fatty foods. Pharmacological antiemetics are second-line if these measures fail. This patient has not yet tried lifestyle measures, so these should be offered first.
why_wrong: A. Hospital admission is for hyperemesis with ketosis, dehydration, or significant weight loss — not mild NVP. B. Doxylamine/pyridoxine is a first-line antiemetic option (RCOG 2024), but drug treatment is offered when non-drug measures have not helped. C. Antiemetics (cyclizine, promethazine) are second-line — only after lifestyle measures have failed. E. Ondansetron is a second-line antiemetic; first-trimester use carries a very small increased risk of orofacial clefts, so it is not used before first-line options.
pearl: Ondansetron is second-line (very small increase in orofacial clefts with first-trimester use). Use cyclizine or promethazine first. Metoclopramide can cause extrapyramidal side effects but is safe in pregnancy.
thinking: NVP + tolerating oral fluids + no ketonuria ↓ Mild NVP ↓ Lifestyle measures first (ginger, dietary) ↓ If insufficient → antiemetics (cyclizine/promethazine) ↓ Ondansetron second-line
exam_trap: The trap is jumping straight to antiemetics. NICE first-line for NVP is lifestyle measures (ginger, acupressure). Antiemetics are second-line only if lifestyle has failed. If the stem does not say lifestyle has failed, ginger/acupressure is the answer.
takeaway: NVP first-line = ginger and acupressure. Antiemetics only if lifestyle measures have failed.

presentation: Down syndrome screening — first trimester combined test
stem: A 34-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation is offered first-trimester screening for Down syndrome. What does this involve?

options.A: Maternal age + nuchal translucency measurement only
options.B: Maternal age + nuchal translucency + free β-hCG + PAPP-A
options.C: Maternal age + serum AFP + β-hCG + uE3 (triple test)
options.D: Maternal age + AFP + β-hCG + uE3 + inhibin A (quadruple test)

correct_answer: B. Maternal age + nuchal translucency + free β-hCG + PAPP-A
why_correct: First-trimester combined screening (11+0 to 13+6 weeks) combines: nuchal translucency (NT) ultrasound measurement + serum free β-hCG + PAPP-A, together with maternal age. Detection rate is ~85–90% with a 3% false positive rate. This is the standard NHS first-trimester screen.
why_wrong: A. NT alone has a lower detection rate — serum markers are essential. C. Triple test is second-trimester (14–20 weeks), not first trimester. D. Quadruple test is second-trimester — used if first-trimester screening was missed. E. NIPT is offered after a high-risk combined test result — not as first-line.
pearl: Combined test detection rate: 85–90%, false positive 3%. Quadruple test (second trimester): 75–80% detection. NIPT: >99% detection for trisomy 21 but not offered universally.
thinking: First trimester Down screening ↓ 11+0 to 13+6 weeks ↓ NT + free β-hCG + PAPP-A + maternal age = combined test
exam_trap: Triple test is second trimester, not first trimester. The first-trimester test includes NT + free β-hCG + PAPP-A.
takeaway: First trimester Down syndrome screening = NT + free β-hCG + PAPP-A (combined test).

presentation: Gestational diabetes screening — timing in high-risk woman
stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman has a BMI of 33 kg/m². She has no previous history of gestational diabetes or family history of diabetes. At what gestation should she be offered an OGTT?

options.E: No screening needed — BMI 33 is not a sufficient risk factor

why_correct: NICE guidance: OGTT at 24–28 weeks for women with one or more GDM risk factors. BMI ≥30 is a recognised risk factor — BMI 33 qualifies. Women with a previous history of GDM are additionally offered an early OGTT at booking (to detect pre-existing diabetes) plus one at 24–28 weeks.
why_wrong: A. Early OGTT at booking is only for previous GDM — not for BMI alone. C. 16–20 weeks is too early and not recommended. D. 32–34 weeks is too late — GDM should be detected and managed earlier. E. BMI ≥30 is explicitly listed as a GDM risk factor by NICE.
pearl: Previous GDM = OGTT at booking AND at 24–28 weeks. BMI ≥30 alone = OGTT at 24–28 weeks only.
thinking: BMI 33 (≥30) ↓ GDM risk factor ↓ OGTT indicated ↓ Standard timing = 24–28 weeks
exam_trap: Do not give an OGTT at booking for BMI alone — that is reserved for previous GDM history. Standard timing is 24–28 weeks for all other risk factors.
takeaway: BMI ≥30 = OGTT at 24–28 weeks. Previous GDM = OGTT at booking AND 24–28 weeks.

stem: A woman at 32 weeks gestation develops severe pre-eclampsia: BP 172/112 mmHg, proteinuria 3+, epigastric pain, and a platelet count of 88 × 10⁹/L. She is 32 weeks pregnant. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Oral nifedipine and twice-weekly outpatient monitoring in the day assessment unit
options.B: IV labetalol or hydralazine, IV magnesium, steroids, then delivery once stable
options.C: Oral labetalol and expectant inpatient management aiming for delivery at 37 weeks
options.D: IV fluid bolus of 1 litre and a platelet transfusion, then reassess in one hour
options.E: Category 1 caesarean section immediately, before any antihypertensive treatment

correct_answer: B. IV labetalol or hydralazine, IV magnesium, steroids, then delivery once stable
why_correct: Severe pre-eclampsia at any gestation requires: acute antihypertensive treatment (IV labetalol or IV hydralazine to bring BP below 160/110 mmHg urgently, then aim for a target of 135/85 mmHg or less), magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, corticosteroids (betamethasone at 32 weeks for fetal lung maturity), and delivery after stabilisation — usually by caesarean section.
why_wrong: A. Outpatient oral management is unsafe with severe hypertension, thrombocytopenia and epigastric pain. C. Continued expectant management is inappropriate with these severe features (uncontrolled hypertension, epigastric pain, falling platelets) — delivery is planned once she is stabilised. D. Fluid loading risks pulmonary oedema in pre-eclampsia, and a platelet count of 88 × 10⁹/L does not need transfusion — it does not treat the disease. E. Operating before BP control and magnesium increases the risk of maternal stroke and eclampsia.
pearl: Threshold for acute antihypertensive treatment: systolic ≥160 mmHg or diastolic ≥110 mmHg. Do not use ACE inhibitors (teratogenic). Safe options: labetalol IV (first-line), hydralazine IV (second-line), nifedipine oral (alternative).
thinking: Severe pre-eclampsia: BP 172/112 + epigastric pain + thrombocytopenia ↓ IV antihypertensives ↓ MgSO4 prophylaxis ↓ Corticosteroids (32 weeks) ↓ Stabilise then deliver
exam_trap: Always stabilise before delivery — do not rush to CS without controlling BP and starting MgSO4. Uncontrolled severe hypertension during surgery greatly increases maternal risk.
takeaway: Severe pre-eclampsia = IV labetalol + MgSO4 + corticosteroids + deliver after stabilisation.

stem: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for primary postpartum haemorrhage?

options.A: Maternal age over 35 years at delivery

why_correct: Previous PPH is the strongest risk factor for recurrent PPH — it roughly triples the risk (OR about 3) and is the strongest of the listed factors. Other major risk factors include uterine overdistension (twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia), retained placenta, prolonged labour, and operative delivery.
why_wrong: A. Age over 35 is a modest risk factor. B. Obesity is a moderate risk factor. D. Induction increases PPH risk but is not the strongest predictor. E. Epidural is not a significant independent risk factor.
pearl: Active management of third stage reduces PPH risk by 60%: prophylactic oxytocin 10 units IM (or slow IV) + controlled cord traction after signs of placental separation.
thinking: Previous PPH → highest individual risk factor → risk roughly 3×
exam_trap: Do not choose induction or maternal age as the strongest risk factor. Previous PPH is the most powerful predictor.
takeaway: Strongest PPH risk factor = previous PPH.

stem: A woman delivers a baby with active management of the third stage. 35 minutes later the placenta has not delivered. There is no excessive bleeding. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Manual removal of placenta under anaesthesia
options.C: IV oxytocin + repeat controlled cord traction

correct_answer: B. Manual removal of placenta under anaesthesia
why_correct: The third stage is prolonged (placenta not delivered within 30 minutes of the birth with active management), so this is a retained placenta. NICE advises securing IV access, not using umbilical vein agents, and not using IV oxytocic agents routinely to deliver a retained placenta when the woman is not bleeding excessively. The next step is assessment and manual removal of the placenta in theatre under effective regional or general anaesthesia.
why_wrong: A. Further waiting after a diagnosed retained placenta delays definitive management and increases the risk of haemorrhage and infection. C. NICE advises against routine IV oxytocic agents to deliver a retained placenta; they are given only if she is bleeding excessively. D. Ergometrine is not used routinely for retained placenta and may cause cervical contraction, trapping the placenta. E. Hysterectomy is reserved for uncontrollable haemorrhage or placenta accreta spectrum.
pearl: Manual removal of placenta (MROP): performed in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia, with antibiotic prophylaxis. Risk of PPH and infection. If accreta is suspected, do not attempt manual removal without surgical backup.
thinking: Placenta undelivered at 35 min with active management ↓ Retained placenta ↓ No excessive bleeding → no routine IV oxytocics ↓ Secure IV access ↓ Manual removal under anaesthesia
exam_trap: IV oxytocin is given for retained placenta only if she is bleeding excessively; it is not routine.
takeaway: Retained placenta (>30 min with active management) without heavy bleeding = manual removal under anaesthesia; IV oxytocics only if bleeding excessively.

stem: A woman at 10 weeks gestation has been vomiting 6–8 times daily for 1 week. Weight loss is 3 kg. Ketones 3+ on dipstick. Unable to tolerate any oral intake. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral antiemetics + oral rehydration at home
options.B: IV fluids + IV antiemetics + IV thiamine
options.C: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg as first-line therapy
options.E: Total parenteral nutrition via a central line

correct_answer: B. IV fluids + IV antiemetics + IV thiamine
why_correct: Severe hyperemesis gravidarum: hospital admission required. IV 0.9% saline + potassium (correct electrolytes), IV antiemetics (cyclizine, promethazine, metoclopramide, or ondansetron for refractory), and IV thiamine before any glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. The oral route is not tolerated. C. Corticosteroids are third-line for refractory cases, not first-line. D. NG feeding is for cases failing IV antiemetics. E. TPN is very rarely needed.
pearl: IV glucose must never precede thiamine in a vomiting pregnant patient. Wernicke's encephalopathy is preventable — thiamine 100 mg IV/IM daily for 3 days minimum.
thinking: Severe HG + ketosis + cannot tolerate oral ↓ Admit ↓ IV fluids + IV antiemetics + thiamine before glucose
exam_trap: Thiamine before glucose — this rule is tested directly.
takeaway: Severe hyperemesis = IV fluids + IV antiemetics + thiamine before glucose.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with postcoital bleeding for 2 months. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill. She has had no intermenstrual bleeding. Speculum examination shows a red granular area around the external cervical os. What is the most common cause of her symptoms?
why_correct: Cervical ectropion (columnar epithelium extending onto the ectocervix) is the most common cause of postcoital bleeding in reproductive-aged women, especially those on the COCP (oestrogen stimulates ectropion) or pregnant. The red granular area around the external os is the classic clinical finding.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer is important to exclude but is not the most common cause. B is most common. C. Endometrial polyps cause intermenstrual bleeding, not primarily PCB. D. Chlamydia can cause PCB but is less common than ectropion in this age group. E. Vaginal atrophy occurs in postmenopausal women, not in a 32-year-old on COCP.
pearl: Always exclude cervical malignancy in postcoital bleeding: refer for colposcopy if age ≥40, if symptoms persist >4 weeks, or if there is a visible lesion. Normal smear does not exclude cancer.
thinking: 32-year-old + COCP + PCB + red granular area at os ↓ Classic cervical ectropion ↓ Most common cause in reproductive-aged women on COCP
exam_trap: Ectropion is the most common cause but always exclude cervical malignancy. A normal smear does not exclude cancer.
takeaway: Most common PCB cause in reproductive-aged women on COCP = cervical ectropion.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has a single episode of painless vaginal bleeding. She is 8 years postmenopausal. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_correct: PMB investigation pathway: first-line is TVUS to measure endometrial thickness. ET ≤4 mm = NPV >99% for endometrial cancer — no further investigation needed. ET >4 mm → endometrial biopsy (Pipelle) or hysteroscopy.
why_wrong: B. Endometrial biopsy is second-line (after ultrasound confirms ET >4 mm). C. Hysteroscopy is second-line if biopsy is inadequate or abnormal. D. CA-125 is for suspected ovarian cancer — not first-line for PMB. E. Colposcopy examines the cervix — not appropriate for suspected endometrial pathology.
pearl: Endometrial cancer risk factors: obesity, unopposed oestrogen, late menopause, nulliparity, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome. Unexplained PMB age ≥55 that cannot be attributed to HRT = suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12).
thinking: PMB ↓ Must exclude endometrial cancer ↓ TVUS first ↓ ET ≤4 mm = reassure ↓ ET >4 mm → biopsy
exam_trap: TVUS is first — biopsy is second. Do not go directly to biopsy without ultrasound.
takeaway: PMB = TVUS first. ET ≤4 mm reassure; ET >4 mm → biopsy.

stem: A woman has unprotected intercourse 72 hours ago. She is on day 14 of her cycle (expected ovulation in 1–2 days). She wants the most effective oral emergency contraceptive. What is the most appropriate choice?
why_correct: Near ovulation, ulipristal acetate is more effective than levonorgestrel. Ulipristal is a selective progesterone receptor modulator that delays or inhibits ovulation even when the LH surge has begun. Levonorgestrel becomes less effective once the LH surge is underway. The question specifies 'oral emergency contraceptive' — making ulipristal the best answer (copper IUD is more effective overall but the question specifies oral).
why_wrong: A. Levonorgestrel is less effective near or after the LH surge — ulipristal is superior in this scenario. B. Copper IUD is more effective than both but the question asks for oral EC. D. Yuzpe is the least effective hormonal method. E. POP at double dose is not recommended as EC.
pearl: Ulipristal effective up to 120 hours (5 days). Levonorgestrel effective up to 72 hours (with reduced efficacy after 48 hours). Copper IUD effective up to 5 days and most effective overall.
thinking: Day 14 + near ovulation + 72 hours after UPSI ↓ LH surge may have started ↓ Levonorgestrel less effective near ovulation ↓ Ulipristal more effective near ovulation ↓ Best oral option
exam_trap: Near ovulation = ulipristal, not levonorgestrel. Ulipristal retains efficacy when LH surge has begun. Levonorgestrel does not.
takeaway: Oral EC near ovulation = ulipristal acetate (more effective than levonorgestrel near ovulation).

stem: A 52-year-old woman has not had a period for 14 months and reports hot flushes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
why_correct: Menopause is confirmed after 12 consecutive months of amenorrhoea with no other cause. In a woman aged 52 with 14 months of amenorrhoea and vasomotor symptoms, menopause is a clinical diagnosis. No FSH testing is needed in women >45.
why_wrong: A. Late perimenopause = transition with irregular cycles — periods have not yet stopped for 12 months. C. POI = menopause before age 40. D. Secondary (central) hypogonadism implies pituitary or hypothalamic failure; this is physiological ovarian ageing, and 'postmenopause' is the clinical term. E. Pregnancy is possible but extremely unlikely at 52 with 14 months amenorrhoea.
pearl: Menopause: 12 months amenorrhoea in women >45 = clinical diagnosis. No FSH needed. POI (<40 years): FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions 4–6 weeks apart.
thinking: 52 years + 14 months amenorrhoea + vasomotor symptoms ↓ Clinical menopause ↓ No FSH needed
exam_trap: Do not check FSH in a woman >45 with classic menopausal symptoms — it is not recommended.
takeaway: Menopause in women >45 = clinical diagnosis after 12 months amenorrhoea. No FSH needed.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, and vaginal discharge for 3 days. Bimanual examination shows cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. She is afebrile with a temperature of 37.2°C. Pregnancy test is negative. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days while awaiting swab results
options.B: Admit for IV ceftriaxone, then oral doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
options.C: Swabs, then empirical IM ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline and metronidazole
options.E: Take endocervical swabs and start antibiotics once NAAT results are positive

correct_answer: C. Swabs, then empirical IM ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline and metronidazole
why_correct: PID is a clinical diagnosis based on minimal criteria: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. Treatment must be empirical (do not wait for swab results). BASHH/RCOG regimen: ceftriaxone 1 g IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days.
why_wrong: A. Metronidazole alone does not cover Chlamydia or gonorrhoea. B. Admission is for pregnancy, severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess or failed oral treatment — not mild PID. D. Laparoscopy is for diagnostic uncertainty or severe cases, and must not delay treatment. E. Treatment should not wait for swab results — a negative NAAT does not exclude PID, and delay risks tubal damage.
pearl: PID complications: tubo-ovarian abscess, Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis), infertility (10–20% after first episode, rising with recurrences). Contact tracing and treatment of partner is essential.
