thinking: Cervical motion tenderness + adnexal tenderness + vaginal discharge ↓ PID clinical diagnosis ↓ Do not wait for swabs ↓ Empirical antibiotics immediately
exam_trap: Do not wait for swab results before treating PID — delay increases risk of tubal damage and infertility.
takeaway: PID = clinical diagnosis. Treat empirically with ceftriaxone IM + doxycycline + metronidazole. Do not wait for swabs.

stem: A woman has a confirmed unruptured ectopic pregnancy. β-hCG is 2,100 IU/L (stable, not rising). There is no fetal heartbeat. She is haemodynamically stable with mild pain only. She wants to preserve her fertility. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Methotrexate criteria (NICE NG126): haemodynamically stable, no significant pain, unruptured ectopic with adnexal mass <35 mm, no visible heartbeat, no intrauterine pregnancy, and β-hCG <5,000 IU/L (methotrexate first-line below 1,500; between 1,500 and 5,000 NICE offers a choice of methotrexate or surgery). This patient meets these criteria and wishes to preserve fertility, so methotrexate (which avoids tubal surgery) is the best option. Success rate 65–95%.
why_wrong: A. Expectant management is for β-hCG <1,000 IU/L and clearly falling. β-hCG 2,100 IU/L (stable) is above the expectant threshold. B. Salpingectomy removes the tube — fertility-preserving alternatives should be tried first. C. Salpingostomy is also fertility-preserving but more invasive than methotrexate. E. Curettage is for intrauterine RPOC.
pearl: Methotrexate: folic acid antagonist, inhibits trophoblastic proliferation. Post-treatment: serial β-hCG weekly until negative. Avoid folic acid supplements, NSAIDs, alcohol, and pregnancy for 3 months. Side effects: oral mucositis, nausea, abdominal pain (from tubal abortion).
thinking: Stable ectopic + β-hCG 2,100 + no heartbeat + wants fertility ↓ Above expectant threshold ↓ Methotrexate criteria met ↓ Single-dose IM methotrexate
exam_trap: Methotrexate is NOT for tubal rupture or haemodynamic instability — surgery is required. For stable, low β-hCG, no heartbeat = methotrexate is first-line.
takeaway: Stable unruptured ectopic, hCG <5,000 IU/L, no heartbeat, mass <35 mm, no significant pain = methotrexate is an option (first-line if <1,500). Expectant management only if hCG ≤1,000–1,500 IU/L and pain free.

stem: A 6-week-old male infant is brought by his parents due to persistent jaundice since birth. He was born at term with no perinatal complications and is formula-fed. He is gaining weight appropriately and remains alert. On examination his liver is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, and the stools appear pale/acholic. Bilirubin fractionation shows conjugated bilirubin of 72 µmol/L (direct fraction >20% of total bilirubin). Total bilirubin is 135 µmol/L. What is the single most important next step in management?

options.A: Reassure as likely physiological jaundice and repeat split bilirubin at 8 weeks
options.B: Urgent abdominal ultrasound and same-day paediatric hepatology referral
options.C: Start phenobarbitone to stimulate bile flow and recheck bilirubin in a week
options.D: Switch to an extensively hydrolysed formula and review in 2 weeks
options.E: Arrange outpatient review in 4 weeks with stool colour chart

correct_answer: B. Urgent abdominal ultrasound and same-day paediatric hepatology referral
why_correct: Any conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia in an infant — defined as conjugated bilirubin >25 µmol/L or >20% of total bilirubin — is abnormal and must never be attributed to physiological jaundice or breast milk jaundice. The classic presentation with acholic stools and hepatomegaly at 6 weeks strongly suggests biliary atresia, which carries a window for curative surgery (Kasai portoenterostomy) that closes at approximately 60–70 days of age. Outcome is significantly better when the Kasai procedure is performed early, ideally before 60 days of age. Immediate ultrasound and same-day specialist referral are therefore a clinical emergency.
why_wrong: A. Waiting until 8 weeks risks missing the window for Kasai surgery — conjugated jaundice in an infant is not physiological and biliary atresia must be excluded urgently. C. Phenobarbitone has no role before the diagnosis is established and would delay urgent investigation. D. Dietary modification has no role — biliary atresia is a structural problem requiring surgery. E. An outpatient review in 4 weeks would cause irreversible harm. The stool colour chart is a community screening tool but has been superseded here by the clinical finding of acholic stools and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia.
pearl: NICE CG98: a conjugated bilirubin above 25 µmol/L in prolonged jaundice needs referral to a healthcare professional with expertise in neonatal hepatology. Biliary atresia (1:8,000–1:16,000 births) is the leading indication for paediatric liver transplantation. The stool colour chart is a validated community screening tool for early cholestasis detection.
thinking: Jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks in a formula-fed infant = ALWAYS investigate ↓ Conjugated bilirubin >20% of total = pathological cholestasis ↓ Acholic stools + hepatomegaly = biliary obstruction until proven otherwise ↓ Most likely: biliary atresia ↓ Surgery window closes ~60–70 days ↓ Same-day hepatology referral + hepatobiliary ultrasound
exam_trap: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is NEVER physiological at any age. Breast milk jaundice causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia only. A formula-fed infant with conjugated jaundice cannot have breast milk jaundice. Prolonged jaundice always requires bilirubin fractionation.
takeaway: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia + acholic stools in any infant = biliary atresia emergency. Same-day hepatology referral. Surgery before day 60 is critical.

stem: A 9-month-old infant is admitted with a 12-hour history of high fever (39.8°C), irritability, and progressive drowsiness. She is photophobic with marked neck stiffness. There is no rash. IV ceftriaxone is given immediately. CSF results: appearance = turbid; white cells = 1,200 × 10⁶/L (predominantly neutrophils); protein = 2.8 g/L; glucose = 1.1 mmol/L. Simultaneous blood glucose = 4.6 mmol/L. What do the CSF results confirm and what is the most likely causative organism in this age group?

options.B: Bacterial meningitis — Neisseria meningitidis most likely
options.C: Bacterial meningitis — Streptococcus pneumoniae most likely
options.E: Normal CSF — the LP was performed prematurely

correct_answer: C. Bacterial meningitis — Streptococcus pneumoniae most likely
why_correct: The CSF profile is classical for bacterial meningitis: turbid appearance, markedly elevated neutrophilic pleocytosis (>100 cells/µL), very high protein (>1 g/L), and critically low glucose. The CSF:blood glucose ratio is 1.1/4.6 = 0.24 — below 0.4 strongly suggests bacterial infection (normal >0.6). In a 9-month-old beyond the neonatal period, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of serious bacterial meningitis, followed by Neisseria meningitidis. The UK immunisation schedule (PCV and MenB/MenACWY) has reduced both, but S. pneumoniae remains most common in infants aged >3 months.
why_wrong: A. Viral meningitis (enterovirus): clear CSF, lymphocytic pleocytosis (<500 cells/µL), mildly elevated protein, NORMAL glucose — completely different. B. N. meningitidis is the second most common cause in this age group, not the most common. D. Tuberculous meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose but develops gradually over days to weeks — not 1,200 neutrophils acutely. E. This is unequivocally abnormal — turbid, 1,200 neutrophils/µL, CSF:blood glucose 0.24.
pearl: CSF patterns: BACTERIAL = turbid, neutrophils >100, protein very high (>1 g/L), glucose very low (ratio <0.4). VIRAL = clear, lymphocytes <500, protein mildly elevated, glucose normal. TUBERCULOUS = clear/xanthochromic, lymphocytes, protein very high, glucose low. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg QDS for 4 days (given with or before first antibiotic dose) reduces hearing loss and neurological sequelae.
thinking: Turbid CSF + neutrophils >100/µL = bacterial meningitis ↓ CSF:blood glucose = 1.1/4.6 = 0.24 (< 0.4 = bacterial) ↓ High protein >1 g/L ↓ Age 9 months: S. pneumoniae > N. meningitidis ↓ Continue IV ceftriaxone + add IV dexamethasone
exam_trap: Never delay IV antibiotics for LP if there are signs of raised ICP (papilloedema, focal neurology, GCS <13, seizures) — CT before LP in that case. However, antibiotics can be given before LP if LP follows within 4 hours without significantly affecting culture results.
takeaway: Turbid CSF + neutrophilic pleocytosis + protein >1 g/L + CSF:blood glucose <0.4 = bacterial meningitis. Age >3 months: S. pneumoniae most common. IV ceftriaxone + dexamethasone.

stem: A 38-week gestation male infant is 36 hours old and exclusively breastfed. He is clinically jaundiced. Serum total bilirubin is 245 µmol/L (unconjugated). He is feeding well, alert, with normal stools and wet nappies. There are no dysmorphic features, no pallor, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Blood group: mother O positive, baby A positive. Direct antiglobulin test (DAT): negative. According to NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: No action required — this is physiological jaundice and bilirubin will decline naturally
options.B: Start phototherapy now, as the level exceeds a fixed 200 µmol/L threshold at 36 hours of age
options.C: Plot the level on the NICE gestation-specific treatment threshold graph and act on it
options.D: Arrange double-volume exchange transfusion now, as the bilirubin level is rising rapidly
options.E: Discharge with safety netting and repeat the bilirubin at 48 hours as an outpatient review

correct_answer: C. Plot the level on the NICE gestation-specific treatment threshold graph and act on it
why_correct: NICE CG98 requires bilirubin to be plotted against age in hours on the gestation-specific treatment threshold graph, not judged against a single fixed number. For a baby of 38 weeks or more at 36 hours, the NICE threshold to start phototherapy is 225 µmol/L (exchange transfusion threshold 400 µmol/L). A level of 245 µmol/L is therefore above the phototherapy line, so the chart-based decision is to start phototherapy now and repeat the bilirubin 4–6 hours after starting.
why_wrong: A. 245 µmol/L at 36 hours in a 38-week infant is above the NICE phototherapy threshold (225 µmol/L) — dismissing it as physiological would withhold needed treatment. B. Phototherapy decisions use the age- and gestation-specific threshold graph, not a fixed figure such as 200 µmol/L; although phototherapy is indicated here, the stated basis is wrong. D. Exchange transfusion is for levels at or approaching the exchange threshold (400 µmol/L at 36 hours on the NICE table), and no serial rise has been shown. E. Discharging a 36-hour-old neonate above the phototherapy threshold is unsafe.
pearl: NICE CG98 uses HOUR-SPECIFIC, GESTATION-SPECIFIC bilirubin treatment threshold graphs; thresholds rise with postnatal age. NICE does not lower the plotted threshold for risk factors. Babies with haemolysis (e.g. Rh or ABO incompatibility with a positive DAT) need closer monitoring and may need IVIG if bilirubin keeps rising rapidly despite multiple phototherapy.
thinking: Unconjugated bilirubin 245 µmol/L + 36-hour-old 38-week infant ↓ Never use fixed thresholds ↓ ALWAYS plot on NICE age-in-hours + gestation chart ↓ At 36 h, ≥38 weeks: start-phototherapy line 225 µmol/L ↓ 245 is above the line ↓ Start phototherapy and repeat bilirubin 4–6 h after starting
exam_trap: Never cite a fixed bilirubin threshold as a universal cutoff. NICE guidance requires chart-based decisions using age in HOURS, not days. Quoting specific numbers from memory is unreliable.
takeaway: Neonatal jaundice management = plot bilirubin against NICE age-in-hours + gestation-specific chart. Never use fixed numerical cutoffs.

stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with 3 weeks of easy bruising and petechiae. He has also had reduced energy and intermittent limping without trauma. On examination he is pale with palpable cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy. Investigations: Hb 76 g/L, WBC 35 × 10⁹/L, platelets 18 × 10⁹/L, LDH 890 IU/L. Blood film shows blast cells with scant cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. No Auer rods. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?

options.A: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) — oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day
options.B: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia — same-day paediatric oncology referral
options.C: Aplastic anaemia — bone marrow trephine biopsy as the first investigation
options.D: Viral bone marrow suppression — reassure and repeat the FBC in 2 weeks
options.E: Acute myeloid leukaemia — start immediate induction chemotherapy on the ward

correct_answer: B. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia — same-day paediatric oncology referral
why_correct: This is the classic presentation of ALL — the most common childhood malignancy. Anaemia, thrombocytopenia, circulating blast cells, lymphadenopathy, markedly elevated LDH, and crucially BONE PAIN (limping) from leukaemic infiltration of bone marrow and periosteum in a 5-year-old is diagnostic until proven otherwise. ITP causes ISOLATED thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well child — this patient has anaemia, leucocytosis, blast cells, lymphadenopathy, and bone pain, making ITP impossible. Never give corticosteroids before specialist assessment as this may induce partial remission and complicate diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia with normal Hb and WBC in a systemically well child. This patient has anaemia, high WBC with blasts, lymphadenopathy and bone pain — ITP is excluded, and steroids before leukaemia is excluded are dangerous. C. Aplastic anaemia shows pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow and no blast cells. D. Viral bone marrow suppression is transient and mild without blast cells on the film. E. Auer rods are characteristic of AML; their absence, together with scant-cytoplasm blasts, lymphadenopathy and the child's age, favours ALL — and chemotherapy is not started before specialist diagnostic work-up.
pearl: ALL accounts for 25% of all childhood cancers, peak incidence ages 2–5. Survival exceeds 90% with current protocols. ALL blasts: high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, delicate chromatin, no Auer rods. AML blasts: larger, more cytoplasm, Auer rods pathognomonic. LDH elevation correlates with tumour burden.
thinking: Petechiae + bruising in a child ↓ Distinguish ITP from leukaemia ↓ ITP = isolated thrombocytopenia + well child + NO anaemia + NO lymphadenopathy ↓ Blast cells on film = haematological malignancy — NEVER reassure ↓ Bone pain + cytopenias with leucocytosis + blasts = ALL ↓ No Auer rods = lymphoblastic not myeloid ↓ NEVER give steroids before leukaemia excluded ↓ Same-day oncology referral
exam_trap: ITP vs ALL: ITP = isolated thrombocytopenia + normal Hb + normal WBC + well child. ALL = anaemia + thrombocytopenia + blast cells + lymphadenopathy + bone pain = EMERGENCY. Any abnormality beyond isolated thrombocytopenia demands a blood film and urgent specialist referral.
takeaway: Blast cells + anaemia + thrombocytopenia + lymphadenopathy + bone pain in a child = ALL. Same-day oncology referral. Never give steroids before diagnosis.

stem: A 7-year-old girl presented 3 weeks ago with palpable purpuric rash over lower limbs and buttocks, periarticular ankle swelling, and colicky abdominal pain. Platelet count was 312 × 10⁹/L (normal). She recovered over 10 days. She now returns with persistent headache, leg swelling, and reduced urine output. Urine dipstick: protein 3+, blood 2+. Blood pressure: 145/95 mmHg. Serum creatinine: 98 µmol/L (raised for age). Which statement most accurately describes the long-term risk and management priority?

options.A: This is self-limiting HSP nephritis; repeat urine dipstick at the 6-month review
options.B: Urgent paediatric nephrology referral and close BP and renal monitoring
options.C: Oral prednisolone given at the time of the rash would have prevented this nephritis
options.D: Start an ACE inhibitor in primary care and recheck urine and BP in 4 weeks
options.E: Arrange renal biopsy as the first step, before any antihypertensive is started

correct_answer: B. Urgent paediatric nephrology referral and close BP and renal monitoring
why_correct: HSP (IgA vasculitis) nephritis is the most important long-term complication of HSP. This patient has heavy proteinuria (3+), haematuria, hypertension, and oedema — significant nephritis requiring urgent specialist management. IgA vasculitis nephritis can cause chronic kidney disease in 2–5% of children. Pathologically, HSP nephritis is identical to IgA nephropathy on biopsy. UK practice (e.g. NICE CKS): urine dipstick and BP monitoring for at least 6 months after HSP, as nephritis can develop after resolution of other symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Significant nephritis with hypertension and 3+ proteinuria requires active specialist management — not observation. C. RCTs have NOT shown that early corticosteroids prevent HSP nephritis. D. ACE inhibitors may be part of specialist management, but starting one in primary care without specialist input is inappropriate for significant nephritis. E. Renal biopsy may be performed by the specialist, but it is not the first step and hypertension needs treating promptly.
pearl: HSP nephritis monitoring: urine dipstick and BP at presentation, then every 2 weeks for first month, then monthly for 6 months. GI bleeding in HSP is typically melaena or PR bleeding (lower GI), not haematemesis — vasculitis affects small bowel and colon.
thinking: Classic HSP: palpable purpura + arthritis + abdominal pain + NORMAL platelets ↓ Now: proteinuria 3+ + haematuria + hypertension + oedema ↓ Significant HSP nephritis ↓ Biopsy: IgA mesangial deposits ↓ Urgent paediatric nephrology referral
exam_trap: Normal platelet count is the crucial distinguishing feature of HSP from ITP. Purpura in ITP = non-palpable, thrombocytopenic. Purpura in HSP = PALPABLE (vasculitic) + NORMAL platelets. Palpable purpura + normal platelets = vasculitis, not ITP.
takeaway: HSP: palpable purpura + arthritis + abdominal pain + NORMAL platelets = IgA vasculitis. Monitor urine and BP for 6 months. Urgent nephrology if significant renal involvement.

stem: A 2.5-year-old boy had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes that self-terminated. Temperature is 39.2°C. No prior seizure history, no family history of epilepsy. After the seizure he is drowsy but arousable (post-ictal). There are no focal neurological signs and no neck stiffness. He has signs of a viral upper respiratory tract infection and returns to normal within 20 minutes. What is the classification of this seizure and the most appropriate management?

options.A: Complex febrile seizure — admit for urgent EEG and MRI brain within 48 hours
options.B: Simple febrile seizure — discharge with parental advice once recovered
options.C: Convulsive status epilepticus — give IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg now and admit
options.D: Absence epilepsy — routine paediatric neurology referral and sleep-deprived EEG
options.E: Possible meningitis — lumbar puncture and IV ceftriaxone before discharge

correct_answer: B. Simple febrile seizure — discharge with parental advice once recovered
why_correct: This is a SIMPLE febrile seizure — meeting all four defining criteria: (1) generalised, not focal, (2) brief (<15 minutes — lasted 3 minutes), (3) single episode within 24 hours, (4) in a febrile child aged 6 months to 5 years with no neurological deficit. Simple febrile seizures carry only a small increase in epilepsy risk (about 1–2%, versus 0.5–1% in the general population) and require no investigation — no LP, no EEG, no MRI — unless there are features suggesting meningitis or encephalitis.
why_wrong: A. EEG and MRI are not required for simple febrile seizures — they are for COMPLEX seizures (focal, >15 minutes, or multiple in 24 hours) or suspected epilepsy. C. Status epilepticus requires a seizure lasting >5 minutes — this lasted 3 minutes and self-terminated. D. Absence epilepsy presents with brief staring episodes without fever or a postictal phase — a different picture. E. LP and antibiotics are not required for a simple febrile seizure in a child who is fully alert after recovery with no signs of meningitis.
pearl: Simple vs complex febrile seizure: Simple = generalised + single + <15 min + age 6m–5y + normal neurology = discharge with education. Complex = ANY of: focal, >15 min, >1 episode in 24h = further investigation. Febrile seizures do NOT cause brain damage and do not significantly increase lifetime epilepsy risk.
thinking: Generalised + <15 min + single in 24h + age 6m–5y + no focal signs = SIMPLE febrile seizure ↓ 3 min, self-terminated = does NOT reach status threshold (>5 min) ↓ Post-ictal drowsiness 20 min = NORMAL ↓ No LP, no EEG, no MRI ↓ Educate parents + discharge once fully recovered
exam_trap: A 20-minute post-ictal drowsiness after simple febrile seizure is NORMAL and does NOT indicate meningitis or need for LP. The child must fully recover before discharge, but post-ictal drowsiness is expected.
takeaway: Simple febrile seizure: generalised + <15 min + single + age 6m–5y + no focal signs = discharge with parental education. No LP, EEG, or MRI required.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has been diagnosed with ADHD (combined presentation) following a multi-agency assessment. Despite an 8-week structured parent training programme and school-based behavioural interventions, his symptoms are significantly impairing his academic performance and social relationships. His weight is on the 45th centile and heart rate is 78 bpm. No significant past medical history. According to NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Continue behavioural intervention alone for a further 3 months
options.B: Refer for group CBT before considering medication
options.C: Offer methylphenidate with dose titration and regular review
options.D: Prescribe atomoxetine as first-line (non-stimulant, safer profile)
options.E: Refer for EEG to exclude epilepsy before starting any medication

correct_answer: C. Offer methylphenidate with dose titration and regular review
why_correct: NICE NG87 recommends offering methylphenidate as first-line medication for children aged 5 years and over whose ADHD symptoms are still causing persistent significant impairment in at least one domain after environmental modifications have been implemented and reviewed. This boy has had parent training and school-based support but remains significantly impaired, so medication is now appropriate. Methylphenidate is started at a low dose and titrated, with baseline and ongoing monitoring of weight, height, appetite, sleep, heart rate and blood pressure.
why_wrong: A. A further 3-month delay when symptoms remain significantly impairing despite environmental modifications is not in the child's best interests. B. Group CBT is not a required step before medication for school-aged children in the NICE ADHD pathway. D. Atomoxetine is not first-line. Under NICE NG87 it (or guanfacine) is reserved for children who cannot tolerate methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine, or whose symptoms have not responded to separate 6-week trials of each. E. EEG is not required before starting methylphenidate unless there are clinical features suggesting epilepsy.
pearl: NICE NG87 medication sequence for children aged 5 and over: methylphenidate first-line → lisdexamfetamine if a 6-week trial of methylphenidate has not helped enough → dexamfetamine if lisdexamfetamine helps but its longer effect is not tolerated → atomoxetine or guanfacine if methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine are not tolerated or have each failed after 6 weeks. Check pulse, BP, weight and height before and during treatment. Methylphenidate is a Schedule 2 controlled drug and is started by a specialist.
thinking: ADHD confirmed + environmental modifications and parent training done + persistent significant impairment ↓ NICE NG87: medication for children aged 5+ = methylphenidate first-line ↓ Start low, titrate, monitor growth and cardiovascular parameters ↓ Lisdexamfetamine = second-line; atomoxetine/guanfacine later
exam_trap: Atomoxetine is NOT first-line despite being perceived as safer (non-stimulant). NICE recommends methylphenidate first-line and lisdexamfetamine second-line. Atomoxetine takes several weeks to reach full effect (unlike stimulants, which work within hours) and carries an MHRA/SmPC warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviour.
takeaway: ADHD: environmental modifications and support first. If significant impairment persists in a child aged 5 or over, methylphenidate is first-line (NICE NG87) and lisdexamfetamine is second-line. Atomoxetine comes later.

stem: A 6-week-old infant is brought to the GP for a routine check. The mother asks about safe sleeping practices to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). The infant was born at 40 weeks, is thriving, and is breastfed. Both parents smoke outdoors only. The infant currently sleeps in a separate room. Which single intervention provides the greatest reduction in risk of SIDS according to UK guidance?

options.A: Using a firm, flat mattress with no soft bedding
options.C: Placing the baby on their back for every sleep

correct_answer: C. Placing the baby on their back for every sleep
why_correct: The supine sleeping position (back to sleep) is the single most important and evidence-based SIDS prevention strategy. Since the Back to Sleep campaign was implemented in the UK in 1992, SIDS rates fell by over 80%. NICE, the NHS, and Lullaby Trust guidance all identify supine sleeping as the number one recommendation. The prone sleeping position increases SIDS risk by 6–13-fold. All other measures are important but have smaller individual effect sizes.
why_wrong: A. A firm flat mattress is an important recommendation but has a smaller individual evidence base than supine sleeping position. B. Room temperature 16–20°C is correct guidance but has a smaller effect than sleep position. D. Breastfeeding is associated with reduced SIDS risk but its protective effect size is smaller than sleep position. E. Maternal alcohol consumption (particularly in co-sleeping contexts) is the SIDS risk factor, not alcohol in breast milk specifically.
pearl: Lullaby Trust/NHS Safe Sleep 2024: (1) Always back to sleep. (2) Same room for first 6 months. (3) Firm flat waterproof mattress — no pillows, duvets, bumpers. (4) Smoke-free environment. (5) Do not bed-share if smoking, alcohol, sedating medications, or baby premature/low birth weight. (6) Breastfeed if possible.
thinking: SIDS prevention ↓ Greatest single intervention = supine sleeping position ↓ Back to Sleep 1992 = >80% SIDS reduction ↓ Prone sleeping = 6–13× increased risk ↓ Room-sharing (not bed-sharing) for first 6 months
exam_trap: Room-sharing reduces SIDS risk. Bed-sharing is a RISK FACTOR — especially if either parent smokes, has consumed alcohol or drugs, or if the baby is premature. Infants should sleep on a separate surface in the same room, not in the parental bed.
takeaway: Greatest single SIDS prevention = supine sleeping position (back to sleep). UK Back to Sleep campaign reduced SIDS by >80% since 1992.

stem: A 6-week-old infant is brought to A&E after being 'floppy and unresponsive for 2 hours'. The father reports the baby 'rolled off the sofa' but cannot specify how. On examination the infant is drowsy (GCS 9/15) with a bulging tense fontanelle. Bilateral retinal haemorrhages are found on fundoscopy. There are no external injuries. CT head shows bilateral subdural haematomas with mixed density suggesting bleeds of different ages. What is the most appropriate immediate management pathway?

options.A: Accept the history of a sofa fall as consistent with the findings and admit for supportive care
options.B: Stabilise, make an urgent safeguarding referral and arrange a skeletal survey
options.C: Perform lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis before safeguarding referral
options.D: Await parental explanation before involving social services to preserve the family relationship
options.E: Discharge with safety netting if CT shows no acute bleed requiring surgery

correct_answer: B. Stabilise, make an urgent safeguarding referral and arrange a skeletal survey
why_correct: This presentation is highly suggestive of abusive head trauma. The triad of subdural haemorrhage, retinal haemorrhages, and encephalopathy in a young infant without a plausible mechanism of injury is highly specific for non-accidental head injury. A 6-week-old cannot roll off a sofa. Bilateral subdural haematomas of mixed density indicate bleeds of different ages — repeated injury. Simultaneous priorities: (1) clinical stabilisation; (2) immediate multi-agency safeguarding referral; (3) skeletal survey within 24 hours to identify occult fractures; (4) ophthalmology for formal retinal assessment.
why_wrong: A. A 6-week-old infant cannot roll. This history is implausible — accepting it is a serious safeguarding failure. C. LP must not be performed with raised ICP (bulging fontanelle) and must not delay safeguarding. D. Awaiting parental explanation before involving social services is dangerous — safeguarding must be initiated as soon as suspicion exists. E. Discharging the child returns them to a dangerous environment where repeated injury has occurred.
pearl: Abusive head trauma triad: subdural haemorrhage (typically bilateral, interhemispheric) + retinal haemorrhages (bilateral, multilayer, posterior pole) + encephalopathy. Skeletal survey findings: posterior rib fractures (highly specific for abuse — from squeezing), metaphyseal corner fractures, fractures of different ages.
thinking: 6-week-old cannot roll → stated history is IMPLAUSIBLE ↓ Classic abusive head trauma triad: SDH + retinal haemorrhages + encephalopathy ↓ Mixed-density bilateral SDH = bleeds of different ages = REPEATED injury ↓ Bulging fontanelle = raised ICP → stabilise + neurosurgery ↓ Do NOT do LP with raised ICP ↓ Immediate: stabilise + safeguarding referral + skeletal survey + ophthalmology
exam_trap: The implausible history is itself diagnostic. A 6-week-old cannot roll off a sofa. Short falls (<1 metre) in young infants do NOT cause bilateral subdural haematomas, retinal haemorrhages, or altered consciousness. Never accept such a history at face value.
takeaway: Abusive head trauma: bilateral SDH + retinal haemorrhages + encephalopathy + implausible history = immediate safeguarding referral + skeletal survey. Never delay for parental explanation.

presentation: Type 1 Diabetes — New Presentation Without DKA
stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with 3 weeks of polydipsia, polyuria, weight loss (3 kg), and fatigue. She is alert and clinically well hydrated with no vomiting, no abdominal pain, and no Kussmaul breathing. BMI is on the 30th centile. Random blood glucose: 21.8 mmol/L. Urine dipstick: glucose 3+, ketones 1+. Capillary blood gas: pH 7.38, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start basal insulin glargine in primary care and refer routinely
options.B: Admit for IV fluids and fixed-rate insulin infusion as for DKA
options.C: Same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team to start insulin
options.D: Start dietary modification and oral metformin pending specialist review
options.E: Reassure — this is likely type 2 diabetes in an obese child; recheck HbA1c in 4 weeks

correct_answer: C. Same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team to start insulin
why_correct: This child has new-onset type 1 diabetes without DKA — DKA is absent (pH 7.38, bicarbonate 21, clinically well, no Kussmaul breathing). NICE NG18 requires urgent same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes multidisciplinary team. Insulin must be initiated by specialist teams to ensure correct formulation selection, dosing, parental education in carbohydrate counting, hypoglycaemia management, sick-day rules, and glucose monitoring. Attempts to start insulin without specialist involvement risk serious dosing errors and hypoglycaemia in a newly diagnosed child.
why_wrong: A. Starting insulin in primary care with a routine referral risks dosing errors and delays specialist education — NICE requires same-day referral. B. The blood gas excludes DKA (pH >7.30, bicarbonate >15, clinically well hydrated) — DKA fluid and insulin protocols are inappropriate and risk cerebral oedema. D. Metformin has no role in type 1 diabetes. E. BMI on the 30th centile is normal — this child is not obese. Classic T1DM symptoms with glucose 21.8 mmol/L confirm diabetes needing insulin now.
pearl: NICE NG18: new-onset T1DM without DKA = same-day paediatric diabetes MDT referral. The team initiates insulin, provides structured education, sets up CGM, and establishes follow-up. DKA at presentation occurs in ~25–40% of new UK paediatric T1DM cases.
thinking: Classic T1DM: polydipsia + polyuria + weight loss + high random glucose ↓ pH 7.38 + bicarbonate 21 + clinically well = NO DKA ↓ Normal BMI, age 10, acute presentation = type 1 DM ↓ DO NOT start insulin without specialist ↓ NICE NG18: urgent same-day paediatric diabetes referral
exam_trap: Do NOT confuse hyperglycaemia without DKA (same-day specialist referral, no IV fluids) with DKA management (BSPED protocol: calculated fluid deficit, insulin infusion, potassium management). Wrong pathway causes cerebral oedema.
takeaway: New type 1 DM, no DKA = urgent same-day paediatric diabetes team referral. Never start insulin without specialist involvement.

stem: A 6-week-old infant presents with projectile vomiting. ABG shows: pH 7.52, PaCO₂ 6.3 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 37 mmol/L. What is the correct interpretation?
why_correct: pH 7.52 indicates alkalosis. HCO₃⁻ 37 mmol/L is elevated, making this a primary metabolic alkalosis. The body compensates by hypoventilating to retain CO₂. PaCO₂ of 6.3 kPa is raised, indicating some compensation — but pH remains elevated above 7.45, so compensation is incomplete. Pyloric stenosis causes hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis from repeated vomiting of hydrochloric acid.
why_wrong: A. Metabolic acidosis would show low pH and low HCO₃⁻. C. Respiratory alkalosis has low PaCO₂ as the primary disorder. D. Mixed alkalosis requires two independent causes simultaneously. E. Normal ABG has pH 7.35–7.45 and HCO₃⁻ 22–26.
pearl: Projectile vomiting in a 6-week-old = pyloric stenosis = hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. High pH + high HCO₃⁻ = metabolic alkalosis. Raised PaCO₂ with pH still high = partial respiratory compensation; a PaCO₂ within 4.7–6.0 kPa would mean no compensation.
thinking: pH 7.52 = alkalosis ↓ HCO₃⁻ 37 = primary metabolic alkalosis ↓ PaCO₂ 6.3 = raised (compensatory hypoventilation) ↓ pH still high = compensation incomplete ↓ Partially compensated metabolic alkalosis
exam_trap: Full compensation would return pH to normal. pH of 7.52 means compensation is partial. Pyloric stenosis causes metabolic alkalosis (vomiting acid), not acidosis.
takeaway: High pH + high HCO₃⁻ + projectile vomiting in an infant = partially compensated metabolic alkalosis (pyloric stenosis).

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with oliguria and peripheral oedema. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ and protein 3+. Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic red blood cells and red cell casts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Red cell casts in urine microscopy strongly suggest glomerulonephritis. Dysmorphic red blood cells indicate bleeding from the glomerular capillaries. Combined with haematuria, proteinuria, oedema, and oliguria, this is a classic nephritic presentation.
why_wrong: A. Pre-renal AKI produces a bland urine sediment (at most hyaline casts). B. Acute tubular necrosis produces muddy brown granular casts, not red cell casts. D. Acute interstitial nephritis produces white cell casts and eosinophiluria. E. Post-renal obstruction produces a bland sediment.
pearl: Red cell casts = glomerulonephritis. Muddy brown granular casts = ATN. White cell casts = interstitial nephritis.
thinking: Haematuria + proteinuria + oliguria + oedema + red cell casts on microscopy ↓ Red cell casts = glomerular bleeding ↓ Glomerulonephritis
exam_trap: Red cell casts are never seen in UTI or lower tract bleeding. Their presence always indicates a glomerular source.
takeaway: Red cell casts + haematuria + proteinuria = glomerulonephritis.

presentation: Hyperkalaemia — ECG changes and immediate management
stem: A 65-year-old man with chronic kidney disease presents with weakness. ECG shows tall peaked T waves in leads V2–V4, PR interval prolongation, and absent P waves. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Oral potassium binder and review in 24 hours

why_correct: This ECG shows progressive hyperkalaemia with cardiac toxicity: peaked T waves, PR prolongation, and absent P waves. IV calcium gluconate is the immediate treatment — it stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes, reducing the risk of ventricular fibrillation. It does not lower potassium but buys time for potassium-lowering measures (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, dialysis).
why_wrong: A. An oral potassium binder (e.g. sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) lowers potassium over hours — far too slow for a patient with ECG changes. C. IV sodium bicarbonate can shift potassium intracellularly but is not the immediate priority over membrane stabilisation. D. Dialysis is definitive but takes time to arrange — calcium gluconate must come first. E. Delaying with a repeat ECG when ECG changes are already present is dangerous.
pearl: Hyperkalaemia ECG progression: peaked T waves → PR prolongation + absent P waves → wide QRS → sine wave → VF → asystole. IV calcium gluconate = immediate membrane stabilisation when ECG changes present.
thinking: CKD + weakness + ECG: peaked T waves + absent P waves + PR prolongation ↓ Significant hyperkalaemia with cardiac toxicity ↓ IV calcium gluconate immediately ↓ Then insulin-dextrose ↓ Then consider dialysis
exam_trap: Calcium gluconate does not lower potassium — it protects the heart. Do not skip it while waiting for insulin-dextrose. Membrane stabilisation always comes first when ECG changes are present.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia + ECG changes = IV calcium gluconate immediately (membrane stabilisation).

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with palpitations. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm. Sawtooth flutter waves (F waves) are best seen in leads II, III, and aVF. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Atrial flutter has an atrial rate of approximately 300 bpm. With 2:1 AV conduction, the ventricular rate is approximately 150 bpm. The characteristic sawtooth flutter waves are best seen in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm with flutter waves is diagnostic.
why_wrong: B. Coarse AF is irregularly irregular with absent P waves — not regular with sawtooth waves. C. AVNRT has no sawtooth waves — P waves are hidden or retrograde. D. VT is wide-complex (>120 ms). E. Sinus tachycardia has normal upright P waves before each QRS, not sawtooth waves.
pearl: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm = think atrial flutter with 2:1 block. Sawtooth waves in inferior leads confirm it.
thinking: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia 150 bpm + sawtooth F waves in II, III, aVF ↓ Atrial rate ~300 + 2:1 AV block = ventricular rate 150 ↓ Atrial flutter
exam_trap: A regular tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm should always make you look for flutter waves. They are often subtle and best seen in II, III, aVF or V1.
takeaway: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm + sawtooth waves = atrial flutter (2:1 block).

presentation: DVT — Wells score and D-dimer pathway
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a swollen tender left calf. Her two-level Wells score for DVT is 1 (DVT unlikely). D-dimer is elevated at 800 ng/mL (normal <500). What is the next step?

options.E: No further action — D-dimer is a false positive

why_correct: In the two-level Wells DVT score, a score of 1 or less is DVT unlikely. A negative D-dimer in a low-probability patient excludes DVT. However, a positive D-dimer requires imaging — D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. Compression ultrasound of the proximal leg veins is the first-line imaging investigation.
why_wrong: A. Empirical treatment without imaging is not appropriate when imaging is available. B. Repeating D-dimer adds no diagnostic value — it will remain elevated. D. CT venography is not first-line — compression ultrasound is non-invasive and radiation-free. E. Assuming false positive without imaging risks missing a DVT.
pearl: D-dimer is a rule-out test (high sensitivity, low specificity). Negative D-dimer + low probability = DVT excluded. Positive D-dimer + low probability = ultrasound required.
thinking: DVT suspected + Wells 1 (unlikely) + D-dimer positive ↓ D-dimer cannot rule in DVT ↓ Positive D-dimer in low probability = compression ultrasound
exam_trap: A positive D-dimer does not diagnose DVT. It is a rule-out test only. Always move to imaging if D-dimer is positive regardless of clinical probability.
takeaway: Positive D-dimer + low DVT probability = compression ultrasound (not treat, not discharge).

stem: A 55-year-old woman with breast cancer presents with sudden breathlessness. Her Wells score for pulmonary embolism is 5. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: A Wells score of 5 places this patient in the PE-likely category (>4). In high-probability patients, D-dimer is not indicated — it will almost certainly be positive and only delays definitive imaging. CTPA is first-line for suspected PE in a haemodynamically stable patient.
why_wrong: A. D-dimer is only useful in low/intermediate probability patients to rule out PE. In high probability, it adds no value and delays diagnosis. C. V/Q scan is an alternative only when CTPA is contraindicated (pregnancy, contrast allergy, severe renal impairment). D. Chest X-ray cannot confirm or exclude PE. E. Echocardiogram is for haemodynamically unstable patients with suspected massive PE — not initial imaging in a stable patient.
pearl: Wells PE ≤4 = PE unlikely → D-dimer first. Wells >4 = PE likely → CTPA directly. Skip D-dimer in high-probability patients.
thinking: Breast cancer + sudden breathlessness + Wells 5 (PE likely) ↓ High probability = D-dimer not useful ↓ Proceed directly to CTPA
exam_trap: Do not order D-dimer when Wells >4. High probability = straight to CTPA.
takeaway: Wells PE score >4 = CTPA directly. No D-dimer.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain and hypotension. Serum lactate is 5.0 mmol/L (normal <2). What is the clinical significance of this lactate level?

options.A: Normal post-prandial rise after a carbohydrate-rich meal
options.B: Tissue hypoperfusion — sepsis or mesenteric ischaemia
options.C: Isolated dehydration — will correct with oral rehydration
options.D: Haemolysed sample — repeat with a free-flowing specimen
options.E: Expected effect of metformin, of no acute significance

correct_answer: B. Tissue hypoperfusion — sepsis or mesenteric ischaemia
why_correct: Lactate >4 mmol/L indicates severe tissue hypoperfusion. In a patient with abdominal pain and hypotension, mesenteric ischaemia or septic shock are the most likely causes. Elevated lactate reflects anaerobic metabolism due to inadequate oxygen delivery. This demands immediate resuscitation.
why_wrong: A. Post-prandial lactate stays below 2 mmol/L — 5.0 is pathologically elevated. C. Dehydration alone does not explain a lactate of 5.0 mmol/L with hypotension and severe pain, and oral fluids are inadequate. D. Haemolysis mainly affects potassium and LDH; it does not explain a lactate of 5.0 in a hypotensive patient, and repeating the sample delays resuscitation. E. Metformin can cause type B lactic acidosis, but with abdominal pain and hypotension this is type A (hypoperfusion) and is significant.
pearl: Lactate >4 mmol/L reflects severe tissue hypoperfusion and should prompt immediate senior review and resuscitation; NICE NG253 grades adult sepsis risk by NEWS2 (7 or more is high risk), with lactate part of the assessment rather than a stand-alone risk criterion. Abdominal pain with elevated lactate and hypoperfusion — think mesenteric ischaemia (pain out of proportion to examination is a classic warning sign).
thinking: Abdominal pain + hypotension + lactate 5.0 ↓ Lactate >4 = severe tissue hypoperfusion ↓ Sepsis or mesenteric ischaemia ↓ Immediate resuscitation
exam_trap: Lactate 5.0 in a patient with abdominal pain and hypotension is never normal. It demands immediate action — not observation.
takeaway: Lactate >4 mmol/L + abdominal pain + hypotension = severe tissue hypoperfusion. Treat urgently.

presentation: Peak flow diary — reversible airflow obstruction (asthma)
stem: A 45-year-old with suspected asthma records peak flow twice daily for two weeks. Results show >20% diurnal variability and >20% improvement after salbutamol. What does this indicate?
why_correct: Diurnal peak flow variability exceeding 20% combined with post-bronchodilator reversibility exceeding 20% are both highly characteristic of asthma. NICE includes peak flow variability ≥20% as a diagnostic criterion for asthma.
why_wrong: A. Fixed airflow obstruction (COPD) shows little or no reversibility and minimal variability. C. Normal peak flow variability is <10% — >20% is pathological. D. Poor effort causes consistently low or erratic readings without a consistent morning-evening pattern. E. COPD shows fixed or minimally reversible obstruction — not >20% reversibility.
pearl: NICE/BTS/SIGN NG245 (adults): diagnose asthma if FeNO ≥50 ppb (or raised eosinophils); otherwise BDR — FEV1 rise ≥12% and ≥200 mL; or PEF variability ≥20% on twice-daily monitoring for 2 weeks; then bronchial challenge if still unclear.
thinking: Peak flow diary: variability >20% + reversibility >20% ↓ Both classic asthma features ↓ Reversible airflow obstruction = asthma
exam_trap: Asthma = variable and reversible obstruction. COPD = fixed obstruction with minimal reversibility. Reversibility degree distinguishes them.
takeaway: Peak flow variability >20% + reversibility >20% = asthma.

stem: A 75-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (target INR 2.5) has a routine INR of 4.5. He has no bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Omit one dose, then restart warfarin at a reduced dose
options.B: Give vitamin K 5 mg IV and recheck INR tomorrow
options.D: Continue the current dose and recheck INR in 4 weeks
options.E: Admit for daily INR checks until within range

correct_answer: A. Omit one dose, then restart warfarin at a reduced dose
why_correct: For an INR above the target range but below 5.0 without bleeding, omit a dose and/or reduce the maintenance dose, then recheck the INR (the BNF 'withhold 1–2 doses and reduce the maintenance dose' band starts at INR 5.0–8.0). Vitamin K is not required at this level without bleeding.
why_wrong: B. IV vitamin K is not indicated for INR 4.5 without bleeding — it over-corrects and causes warfarin resistance for several days. C. Prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding or emergency reversal. D. Continuing unchanged would leave the INR above range and increase bleeding risk. E. Hospital admission is not required for INR 4.5 without bleeding.
pearl: INR above target but <5.0, no bleeding = omit a dose and/or reduce the maintenance dose. INR 5.0–8.0, no bleeding = withhold 1–2 doses and reduce the maintenance dose. INR >8.0, no bleeding = withhold + vitamin K 1–5 mg oral. Any INR with major bleeding = vitamin K IV + PCC + urgent haematology.
thinking: INR 4.5 (target 2.5) + no bleeding ↓ INR above target but <5, no bleeding = omit a dose and reduce the maintenance dose ↓ Restart at lower maintenance dose ↓ Recheck in 1–2 weeks
exam_trap: Vitamin K at INR 4.5 without bleeding is incorrect — causes prolonged warfarin resistance. Only use for INR >8 without bleeding, or any level with major bleeding.
takeaway: INR 4.5 without bleeding = withhold 1 dose, restart lower dose. No vitamin K.

presentation: Upper GI alarm features — urgent endoscopy
stem: A 68-year-old man presents with dull epigastric pain, early satiety, and unintentional weight loss of 8 kg over 4 months. Examination reveals a palpable epigastric mass. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Trial of proton pump inhibitor for 4 weeks

why_correct: This patient has multiple alarm features for upper GI malignancy: age >55, unexplained weight loss, early satiety, and a palpable epigastric mass. NICE recommends urgent upper GI endoscopy (suspected cancer pathway) for suspected upper GI cancer. Endoscopy allows direct visualisation and biopsy.
why_wrong: A. A PPI trial delays diagnosis when alarm features are present — never empirically treat when a palpable mass or weight loss is present. B. H. pylori testing is appropriate for dyspepsia without alarm features. D. Ultrasound may miss early gastric cancer and cannot provide tissue diagnosis. E. CT is for staging after diagnosis is confirmed endoscopically.
pearl: NICE suspected cancer pathway for upper GI cancer: age ≥55 with unexplained weight loss and upper abdominal pain; dysphagia; palpable epigastric mass at any age.
thinking: Age 68 + 8 kg weight loss + early satiety + palpable epigastric mass ↓ Multiple alarm features ↓ Urgent upper GI endoscopy (not PPI, not USS, not CT first)
exam_trap: Alarm features = investigate first. Never start a PPI trial when weight loss or a palpable mass is present. Endoscopy is the correct first step.
takeaway: Alarm features + palpable epigastric mass = urgent upper GI endoscopy (suspected cancer pathway).

stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related chronic pancreatitis presents with worsening epigastric pain radiating to the back and greasy, foul-smelling, floating stools. What is the most likely cause of his stool change?
why_correct: Chronic pancreatitis destroys pancreatic acinar cells, reducing lipase production. This causes steatorrhoea — greasy, foul-smelling, floating stools from fat malabsorption. The epigastric pain radiating to the back is consistent with pancreatic pathology.
why_wrong: A. Bile duct obstruction causes obstructive jaundice with pale stools and dark urine — not greasy floating stools in a known pancreatitis patient. B. SIBO can cause malabsorption but is not the primary explanation here. D. Coeliac disease is possible but does not explain the known chronic pancreatitis. E. Giardiasis can cause steatorrhoea, but it is usually acute with travel or water exposure, and established chronic pancreatitis better explains this picture.
pearl: Chronic pancreatitis → exocrine insufficiency → steatorrhoea. Investigation: faecal elastase-1. Treatment: pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT — e.g., Creon) with every meal.
thinking: Chronic pancreatitis + greasy floating foul-smelling stools ↓ Fat malabsorption = steatorrhoea ↓ Destroyed acinar cells = insufficient lipase ↓ Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency ↓ PERT
exam_trap: Steatorrhoea does not require jaundice. Greasy floating stools in chronic pancreatitis are from fat malabsorption, not biliary obstruction.
takeaway: Chronic pancreatitis + greasy floating stools = pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. Treat with PERT.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with acute severe epigastric pain radiating to her back. She leans forward to relieve the pain. She has a history of gallstones. Serum amylase is 1,200 U/L (normal <100). What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relief on leaning forward, gallstones, and amylase >3× the upper limit of normal (here 12× normal) confirm acute pancreatitis.
why_wrong: A. Acute cholecystitis causes RUQ pain with Murphy's sign — not radiation to the back and not this amylase level. C. Perforated peptic ulcer causes generalised peritonitis — amylase may be mildly elevated but not 12× normal. D. Biliary colic is episodic, resolves completely, and does not cause amylase elevation. E. Myocardial infarction may cause epigastric pain but does not cause amylase elevation.
pearl: Acute pancreatitis: amylase >3× upper limit is supportive. Gallstones and alcohol are the most common causes. Assess severity with a scoring system (e.g. Glasgow-Imrie) and organ failure; reserve CT for diagnostic uncertainty or suspected complications (ideally after 72 hours).
thinking: Epigastric pain radiating to back + leaning forward + gallstones + amylase 1,200 (12× normal) ↓ Acute pancreatitis ↓ Assess severity ↓ IV fluids + analgesia + NBM
exam_trap: Normal amylase does not exclude pancreatitis — it can be normal in late presentation or hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis.
takeaway: Epigastric pain radiating to back + leaning forward + elevated amylase + gallstones = acute pancreatitis.

presentation: Upper GI bleed — stable, endoscopy within 24 hours
stem: A 45-year-old man presents with haematemesis and a long history of NSAID use. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, heart rate is 100 bpm. There is epigastric tenderness but no peritonism. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Endoscopy within 2 hours of arrival, then start IV fluid resuscitation
options.B: Oral PPI, stop NSAIDs and arrange outpatient endoscopy in 2 weeks
options.C: Resuscitate, crossmatch and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours
options.D: IV ceftriaxone and terlipressin as for variceal bleeding
options.E: Surgical referral for emergency laparotomy and oversewing of the ulcer

correct_answer: C. Resuscitate, crossmatch and arrange endoscopy within 24 hours
why_correct: This patient has an upper GI bleed with compensated shock (tachycardia, maintained blood pressure). NICE guidance: IV access, fluid resuscitation, full blood count, crossmatch, coagulation, and urgent endoscopy within 24 hours. Endoscopy immediately after resuscitation is reserved for unstable patients with severe bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Resuscitation comes before endoscopy, and immediate endoscopy is for patients who remain unstable — this patient is compensated. B. Outpatient management is unsafe — haematemesis with tachycardia requires admission. D. Antibiotics and terlipressin are for suspected variceal bleeding — the history points to an NSAID-related peptic ulcer. E. Surgery is reserved for failed endoscopic and radiological haemostasis.
pearl: NICE: stable upper GI bleed = endoscopy within 24 hours. Unstable despite resuscitation = endoscopy as soon as possible (immediately after resuscitation). Resuscitate first.
thinking: Haematemesis + NSAID use + HR 100 + BP maintained ↓ Compensated upper GI bleed ↓ IV access + fluids + crossmatch ↓ Endoscopy within 24 hours
exam_trap: Stable = 24-hour endoscopy. Unstable = 2-hour endoscopy. Do not confuse the thresholds.
takeaway: Compensated upper GI bleed = IV access + resuscitation + endoscopy within 24 hours.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with known Crohn's disease presents with worsening abdominal pain, fever, and non-bloody diarrhoea. Examination reveals a tender palpable mass in the right iliac fossa. What is the most likely complication?
why_correct: Intra-abdominal abscess is a penetrating complication of Crohn's disease. The triad of fever, worsening abdominal pain, and a tender palpable mass points to abscess formation. CT abdomen with contrast is the investigation of choice. Management: percutaneous drainage plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Toxic megacolon is more common in UC and presents with distension and systemic toxicity — not a localised mass. C. Colorectal cancer is unlikely at 25 without longstanding extensive disease. D. Perianal fistula causes perianal symptoms — not an abdominal mass with fever. E. SBO causes vomiting, distension, absolute constipation — not a tender mass with fever.
pearl: Crohn's complications: inflammatory (flare), stricturing (obstruction), penetrating (abscess, fistula). Fever + tender abdominal mass = abscess until proven otherwise. CT confirms.
thinking: Crohn's + fever + tender RIF mass ↓ Penetrating disease → abscess ↓ CT abdomen ↓ Drainage + antibiotics
exam_trap: Not all acute deteriorations in Crohn's are flares. Exclude abscess and obstruction before treating as an inflammatory flare.
takeaway: Crohn's + fever + tender abdominal mass = intra-abdominal abscess. CT + drainage.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 10-year history of Crohn's disease presents with acute lower abdominal pain and vomiting. AXR shows multiple dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels. There is no peritonism and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.C: NG tube decompression and IV fluids

correct_answer: C. NG tube decompression and IV fluids
why_correct: SBO in Crohn's disease, without peritonism or signs of strangulation, should initially be managed conservatively: nil by mouth, nasogastric tube for decompression, IV fluids, and close monitoring. Most SBOs due to inflammatory strictures settle within 48–72 hours. Surgery is reserved for failure of conservative management or signs of strangulation.
why_wrong: A. Oral medication cannot be relied on in a vomiting, obstructed patient, and steroids do not decompress the bowel. B. Urgent surgery is not first-line without signs of strangulation (fever, peritonism, lactic acidosis, haemodynamic instability). D. Colonoscopy is contraindicated in acute obstruction — perforation risk. E. Antibiotics do not relieve obstruction, and oral fluids are inappropriate in a vomiting obstructed patient.
pearl: SBO in Crohn's: conservative first (NG tube + IV fluids + monitoring). Surgery if: no resolution at 48–72 hours, signs of strangulation, or complete obstruction. Surgery avoided where possible due to recurrence and short bowel risk.
thinking: Crohn's + SBO on AXR + no peritonism + stable ↓ No strangulation features ↓ Conservative management first ↓ NG tube + IV fluids ↓ Surgery only if fails or strangulation
exam_trap: Do not choose urgent surgery for SBO in Crohn's without strangulation. Conservative management is always first.
takeaway: Crohn's SBO without peritonism = conservative management (NG tube + IV fluids) first.

presentation: Lower GI alarm features — FIT to guide suspected cancer pathway referral
stem: A 60-year-old man presents with new-onset change in bowel habit to looser stools, rectal bleeding, and unintentional weight loss of 5 kg over 3 months. Abdominal and digital rectal examination are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Urgent colonoscopy via a suspected cancer pathway referral, without FIT

why_correct: NICE NG12 (recs 1.3.1–1.3.3, updated 2023): adults aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding or weight loss, or with a change in bowel habit, should be offered a quantitative faecal immunochemical test (FIT) to guide referral, and referred on a suspected cancer pathway if FIT is at least 10 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces. Only a rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration bypasses FIT, and none is present here. If FIT is below 10 but strong clinical concern persists (for example, ongoing unexplained symptoms), referral should not be delayed (NG12 1.3.3); colonoscopy follows the referral.
why_wrong: B. Referring straight for colonoscopy skips FIT, which NICE now uses to guide referral for these symptoms; direct referral without FIT is reserved for a rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or anal ulceration. C. CT colonography is an alternative investigation in secondary care if colonoscopy is unsuitable, not the first step. D. Flexible sigmoidoscopy only examines the left colon and would miss right-sided lesions. E. Ultrasound is not appropriate for suspected colorectal cancer.
pearl: NICE NG12 (2023): offer FIT to guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer in adults with an abdominal mass, a change in bowel habit or iron-deficiency anaemia; aged 40 and over with unexplained weight loss and abdominal pain; aged under 50 with rectal bleeding plus unexplained abdominal pain or weight loss; aged 50 and over with unexplained rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or weight loss; or aged 60 and over with anaemia. Refer on a suspected cancer pathway if FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g. A rectal mass, unexplained anal mass or anal ulceration → refer without FIT.
thinking: Age 60 + rectal bleeding + looser stools + weight loss 5 kg ↓ No rectal or anal mass ↓ NICE NG12: offer quantitative FIT ↓ FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g → Suspected cancer pathway referral (colonoscopy); FIT <10 with strong concern → do not delay referral
exam_trap: Referring straight for colonoscopy because the symptoms feel high-risk. Since 2023 NICE uses FIT to guide referral for these symptoms; only a rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or anal ulceration bypasses it.
takeaway: Rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit or weight loss at ≥50 with no rectal or anal mass = FIT first; refer on a suspected cancer pathway if FIT ≥10 µg Hb/g.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea, fatigue, and recurrent mouth ulcers. She has a reddish-purple tender nodular rash on her shins. Examination reveals mild lower abdominal tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The combination of chronic diarrhoea, aphthous stomatitis (mouth ulcers), and erythema nodosum (tender red-purple nodules on the shins) with abdominal tenderness points to Crohn's disease. Erythema nodosum and mouth ulcers are extra-intestinal manifestations that occur more commonly in Crohn's than UC.
why_wrong: A. UC typically causes bloody diarrhoea and is less commonly associated with mouth ulcers and erythema nodosum than Crohn's. C. Coeliac disease causes diarrhoea and fatigue but is not associated with erythema nodosum or mouth ulcers. D. IBS causes no extra-intestinal manifestations. E. Giardiasis is acute or subacute — not chronic with skin and mouth involvement.
pearl: Crohn's extra-intestinal manifestations: erythema nodosum, aphthous stomatitis, uveitis, and arthropathy. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is more common in UC.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea + mouth ulcers + erythema nodosum on shins ↓ Extra-intestinal clues ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: Erythema nodosum and mouth ulcers point away from IBS and coeliac — these are IBD manifestations, most commonly Crohn's.
takeaway: Chronic diarrhoea + mouth ulcers + erythema nodosum = Crohn's disease.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with painless obstructive jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. She has lost 6 kg over 2 months. Examination reveals a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Courvoisier's law: painless jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones and strongly suggests malignant biliary obstruction, most commonly from a pancreatic head tumour. Gallstones cause a contracted inflamed gallbladder that cannot distend.
why_wrong: A. Choledocholithiasis usually causes painful jaundice and the gallbladder is not palpable (contracted). B. Cholecystitis causes a tender inflamed gallbladder — not non-tender and palpable. D. Primary biliary cholangitis causes chronic cholestasis without a palpable gallbladder or acute weight loss. E. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis with raised transaminases — not obstructive jaundice.
pearl: Courvoisier's law: painless jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder = malignant obstruction until proven otherwise. In a jaundiced patient, gallstone obstruction rarely produces a palpable gallbladder because the chronically inflamed gallbladder is fibrosed.
thinking: Painless jaundice + weight loss + pale stools + palpable non-tender gallbladder ↓ Courvoisier's sign ↓ Malignant biliary obstruction ↓ Pancreatic head cancer ↓ Urgent CT + suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Non-tender gallbladder = malignancy. Tender gallbladder = inflammation. Tenderness is the key discriminator.
takeaway: Painless jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder = pancreatic cancer (Courvoisier's law).

stem: A 39-year-old man presents with 2 weeks of crampy lower abdominal pain, urgency, and bloody diarrhoea 6–8 times per day. He has no prior episodes and no recent antibiotics. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.A: Stool culture and C. difficile testing

correct_answer: A. Stool culture and C. difficile testing
why_correct: Acute bloody diarrhoea must have infective causes excluded before IBD is considered. Stool culture identifies bacterial pathogens (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli O157). C. difficile toxin should always be tested. NICE recommends excluding infection before colonoscopy for suspected IBD.
why_wrong: B. Colonoscopy is not the first investigation in the acute setting — infection must be excluded first, and it carries perforation risk in active colitis. C. CT can show colonic wall thickening but does not identify the causative organism. D. Faecal calprotectin is raised in both infection and IBD and does not distinguish between them. E. AXR has low diagnostic yield unless toxic megacolon is suspected.
pearl: Always exclude infection before diagnosing IBD. Stool culture + C. diff toxin are mandatory first steps in acute bloody diarrhoea. Infectious colitis can mimic IBD clinically and endoscopically.
thinking: Acute bloody diarrhoea 2 weeks + no prior episodes ↓ Must exclude infection first ↓ Stool culture + C. difficile toxin ↓ If negative → IBD workup
exam_trap: Never go straight to colonoscopy for acute bloody diarrhoea without first excluding infection.
takeaway: Acute bloody diarrhoea = stool culture + C. difficile toxin first.

presentation: Massive upper GI bleed — haemodynamically unstable
stem: A 32-year-old man with excess alcohol intake presents with multiple episodes of haematemesis. He appears pale and sweaty. Blood pressure is 88/60 mmHg and heart rate is 126 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: IV PPI infusion, IV fluids and endoscopy within 24 hours
options.B: Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood, then immediate endoscopy
options.C: Oral PPI and outpatient gastroscopy within 2 weeks
options.D: IV antibiotics as the first priority, then IV fluids
options.E: IV terlipressin and antibiotics, endoscopy within 24 hours

correct_answer: B. Resuscitate with IV fluids and blood, then immediate endoscopy
why_correct: This patient has a massive upper GI bleed with haemodynamic instability (hypotension 88/60, tachycardia 126). Immediate management: ABCDE resuscitation, IV fluid resuscitation, blood transfusion, and urgent endoscopy immediately after resuscitation. Resuscitation always precedes endoscopy. If variceal bleeding is suspected (alcohol excess), also give terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation (NICE CG141).
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy within 24 hours is for stable bleeds — this patient is unstable and needs endoscopy immediately after resuscitation. C. Oral PPI and outpatient investigation are wholly inappropriate with haemodynamic instability. D. Antibiotics may be appropriate if variceal bleeding is suspected, but resuscitation is the first priority. E. Terlipressin and antibiotics may be appropriate for suspected varices, but an unstable patient needs endoscopy immediately after resuscitation, not within 24 hours.
pearl: Stable upper GI bleed = endoscopy within 24 hours. Unstable upper GI bleed = resuscitate + endoscopy immediately after resuscitation. Always resuscitate first.
thinking: Haematemesis + BP 88/60 + HR 126 ↓ Haemodynamically unstable ↓ ABCDE + IV fluids + blood transfusion ↓ Urgent endoscopy immediately after resuscitation
exam_trap: Stable = 24-hour endoscopy. Unstable = endoscopy immediately after resuscitation. This is the exam trap — do not choose 24-hour endoscopy for an unstable patient.
takeaway: Massive upper GI bleed + haemodynamic instability = resuscitate + urgent endoscopy as soon as possible.

stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with intermittent severe colicky abdominal pain. Between episodes he is well. He passes a stool that looks like redcurrant jelly. A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The classic triad of intussusception: intermittent colicky abdominal pain, redcurrant jelly stool (blood and mucus from mucosal ischaemia), and a palpable sausage-shaped mass (usually right upper quadrant). Most common in children aged 3 months to 3 years, often post-viral. Ultrasound (target sign) confirms. Air enema is first-line reduction.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes constant RIF pain — not intermittent colicky pain with redcurrant stool. C. Meckel's causes painless rectal bleeding without a sausage mass. D. Constipation presents with hard stools and distension — no redcurrant jelly or sausage mass. E. Testicular torsion presents with scrotal pain — not an abdominal mass.
pearl: Intussusception: colicky pain + redcurrant jelly stool + sausage mass. Ultrasound (target sign). Air enema for reduction. Surgery if enema fails or perforation suspected.
thinking: 2-year-old + intermittent colicky pain + well between episodes + redcurrant stool + sausage mass ↓ Classic triad = intussusception ↓ Ultrasound → air enema
exam_trap: The child may be completely well between episodes — do not dismiss as gastroenteritis. The redcurrant stool and sausage mass are diagnostic.
takeaway: Colicky pain + redcurrant jelly stool + sausage mass = intussusception.

stem: A 6-week-old boy presents with projectile vomiting after feeds. The vomiting is non-bilious. He is hungry immediately after vomiting. Visible peristalsis moves left to right and an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: HPS presents at 3–8 weeks with projectile non-bilious vomiting immediately after feeds. The infant is hungry again after vomiting. Visible left-to-right peristalsis and a palpable olive-shaped mass are classic findings. More common in firstborn males. Ultrasound confirms (pyloric muscle thickness >3 mm, length >15 mm). Classic electrolyte disturbance: hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Treatment: correct alkalosis then Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
why_wrong: A. GOR causes non-projectile vomiting with no olive mass. C. Malrotation with volvulus causes bilious vomiting in a critically ill infant — non-bilious and otherwise well rules this out. D. Intussusception affects older infants with colicky pain and redcurrant stool. E. Milk protein allergy causes diarrhoea and rectal blood — not projectile vomiting.
pearl: HPS: projectile non-bilious vomiting at 6 weeks + hungry after + visible peristalsis + olive mass. Ultrasound confirms. Electrolyte: hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Fix alkalosis before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.
thinking: 6-week-old + projectile non-bilious vomiting + hungry after + visible peristalsis + olive mass ↓ HPS ↓ Ultrasound confirms ↓ Correct alkalosis → pyloromyotomy
exam_trap: Classic electrolyte = hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (loss of gastric acid). Do not confuse with hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
takeaway: Projectile vomiting + olive mass at 6 weeks = pyloric stenosis. Correct alkalosis before surgery.

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset drooling and dysphagia. He has no respiratory distress and can still swallow small amounts of saliva. His mother reports he was playing with small coins. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.C: Observation on the ward for 24 hours
options.D: Barium contrast swallow to locate the coin

correct_answer: A. Urgent chest X-ray (AP and lateral)
why_correct: In a child with suspected oesophageal foreign body (probable coin) with no respiratory distress and still able to swallow small amounts of saliva (partial obstruction), chest X-ray (AP and lateral) is the appropriate first-line investigation. It confirms the location and type of object. A coin in the oesophagus appears en face (round, flat) on AP view. X-ray also identifies a button battery (double-ring/halo sign) or magnets; an oesophageal button battery, or complete obstruction (cannot swallow saliva), needs immediate endoscopic removal without further delay.
why_wrong: B. Immediate endoscopy is for an oesophageal button battery, multiple magnets, sharp objects or complete obstruction once located; this child can swallow saliva, so X-ray comes first. C. Observation without imaging is unsafe — oesophageal foreign bodies can erode or perforate. D. A contrast swallow risks aspiration and is not needed to locate a radio-opaque coin. E. CT involves unnecessary radiation for a radio-opaque object.
pearl: Suspected oesophageal coin + partial obstruction (able to swallow saliva) = chest X-ray first. Button battery/magnet/sharp object/complete obstruction = immediate removal once located on urgent X-ray. Button batteries are surgical emergencies — endoscopy within 2 hours.
thinking: Child + coins + drooling + dysphagia + NO respiratory distress + still swallowing saliva ↓ Probable oesophageal coin (partial obstruction) ↓ Chest X-ray first ↓ If button battery or complete obstruction → immediate removal once located on X-ray
exam_trap: X-ray is not the end point — button batteries, magnets, sharp objects and complete obstruction require immediate removal once located on urgent X-ray, and imaging must not delay it. The ability to still swallow saliva makes X-ray the appropriate first step here.
takeaway: Suspected oesophageal coin + able to swallow saliva = chest X-ray first. Button battery/complete obstruction = immediate removal once located on urgent X-ray.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with effortless regurgitation of undigested food within 5–30 minutes of eating. She has no nausea or retching. Between episodes she is completely well. Endoscopy and oesophageal manometry are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rumination syndrome: effortless regurgitation of recently ingested food within 5–30 minutes of eating, with no preceding nausea or retching. The regurgitated food is recognisable and not acidic (unlike GORD). All investigations are normal. Treatment: diaphragmatic breathing biofeedback and behavioural therapy. No role for acid suppression.
why_wrong: A. Gastroparesis causes nausea, bloating and vomiting of partially digested food hours after eating — not immediate effortless regurgitation. B. Achalasia causes dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation hours later and abnormal manometry. D. Bulimia involves effortful self-induced vomiting after binge eating. E. GORD causes acidic regurgitation and heartburn, worse lying flat.
pearl: Rumination: effortless post-prandial regurgitation within 5–30 minutes + no nausea/retching + undigested food + normal investigations. Treatment: breathing biofeedback, not medications.
thinking: Young woman + effortless regurgitation 5–30 min post-meal + no nausea + normal endoscopy and manometry ↓ No obstructive or motor disorder ↓ Rumination syndrome ↓ Diaphragmatic breathing biofeedback
exam_trap: Key distinctions: no effort, no retching, food undigested and not acidic, within 5–30 minutes. Bulimia = deliberate vomiting. GORD = acidic. Achalasia = abnormal manometry.
takeaway: Effortless regurgitation within 5–30 min of eating, no nausea = rumination syndrome.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic alcoholism presents with chronic epigastric pain, steatorrhoea, and weight loss. AXR shows pancreatic calcifications. What is the most specific non-invasive test to confirm pancreatic exocrine insufficiency?
why_correct: Faecal elastase-1 (FE-1) is the most appropriate non-invasive marker of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. FE-1 <200 µg/g = mild-moderate insufficiency; <100 µg/g = severe. It is not affected by exogenous enzyme supplementation. Important limitation: FE-1 can be falsely low in watery diarrhoea (dilution effect) — a formed stool sample is required. CT pancreas (not AXR) is the gold standard for structural confirmation.
why_wrong: A. Serum amylase is often normal or low in chronic pancreatitis — not useful for exocrine function. C. Secretin-stimulated MRI is a research tool. D. Endoscopic ultrasound assesses structural changes — not exocrine function. E. Glucose tolerance test assesses endocrine function (diabetes) — not exocrine.
pearl: FE-1 confirms exocrine insufficiency. Requires formed stool — falsely low in watery diarrhoea. CT pancreas is gold standard for structural diagnosis. Treat with PERT (e.g., Creon).
thinking: Chronic pancreatitis + steatorrhoea + weight loss ↓ Confirm exocrine insufficiency = FE-1 ↓ Requires formed stool (falsely low in watery diarrhoea) ↓ If low → PERT
exam_trap: FE-1 can be falsely low in watery diarrhoea — requires formed stool. Serum amylase is often normal in chronic pancreatitis.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea in chronic pancreatitis = faecal elastase-1 (formed stool required).

stem: A 28-year-old man with Crohn's disease presents with perianal pain and purulent discharge. A draining fistula opening is visible externally. He has no abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate imaging to define the fistula anatomy?
why_correct: MRI pelvis is the gold standard for imaging perianal fistulas in Crohn's disease. It defines the primary tract, secondary extensions, internal opening, and associated abscesses. MRI is superior to endoanal ultrasound for complex or high fistulas. Endoanal ultrasound is acceptable for simple low fistulas. Treatment: drain any abscess before starting anti-TNF therapy (infliximab or adalimumab). Seton + biologic combination is standard for complex fistulas.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy cannot image fistula anatomy. B. CT has poor soft tissue contrast for fistula anatomy and involves radiation. D. Endoanal ultrasound is inferior to MRI for complex or high fistulas. E. Fistulography is obsolete and inaccurate.
pearl: Perianal Crohn's fistula: MRI pelvis (gold standard). Drain abscess before anti-TNF. Seton + anti-TNF (infliximab or adalimumab) combination for complex fistulas.
thinking: Crohn's + perianal fistula → define anatomy ↓ MRI pelvis (gold standard) ↓ Drain any abscess first ↓ Seton + anti-TNF
exam_trap: Drain any abscess before starting anti-TNF therapy. Endoanal ultrasound is acceptable for simple low fistulas but MRI is gold standard for complex disease.
takeaway: Perianal Crohn's fistula = MRI pelvis.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with known coeliac disease has persistent dyspepsia despite a gluten-free diet. Endoscopy shows varioliform gastritis (raised erosions with central depression) and normal mucosa between lesions. Biopsies show increased intraepithelial lymphocytes without H. pylori. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lymphocytic gastritis is characterised by varioliform gastritis on endoscopy (raised erosions with central depression) and histology showing increased intraepithelial lymphocytosis (>25 per 100 epithelial cells) without gland atrophy, without H. pylori. It is strongly associated with coeliac disease and often improves on a gluten-free diet. PPIs do not treat the underlying cause.
why_wrong: A. H. pylori gastritis shows organisms on biopsy — absent here. B. Autoimmune gastritis is body-predominant, atrophic, associated with pernicious anaemia. D. Eosinophilic gastritis shows eosinophilic infiltration with atopy. E. Ménétrier's causes giant folds and protein-losing enteropathy.
