why_correct: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction (systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve); the murmur increases with reduced preload (standing, Valsalva). Preload- or afterload-reducing agents (nitrates, and overdiuresis) worsen the obstruction and are avoided; beta-blockers are used.
why_wrong: A. Mitral regurgitation does not cause asymmetrical hypertrophy with SAM, and diuretics are used rather than avoided. B. The murmur of aortic stenosis does not increase with standing or Valsalva, and the echo shows HCM rather than valve stenosis. D. A murmur that increases with Valsalva in a symptomatic patient with LVH and SAM is pathological. E. A VSD causes a pansystolic murmur and is not associated with SAM; aspirin is not a relevant caution.
pearl: A systolic murmur that gets louder with Valsalva is HCM — avoid nitrates and overdiuresis, which deepen the obstruction.
thinking: Murmur louder on standing/Valsalva ↓ asymmetrical LVH + SAM ↓ HCM with dynamic obstruction ↓ avoid preload reduction such as nitrates (C)
exam_trap: B, aortic stenosis with beta-blockers to avoid — another systolic murmur, so a reasonable thought. But the murmur of aortic stenosis gets QUIETER (less flow) with Valsalva, whereas the HCM murmur gets LOUDER; HCM is the dynamic-obstruction diagnosis, treated with beta-blockers and avoiding preload reduction.
takeaway: A systolic murmur that gets louder with Valsalva is HCM — avoid nitrates and overdiuresis, which deepen the obstruction.

stem: A 58-year-old man with no cardiovascular disease has a calculated 10-year cardiovascular risk (QRISK) of 16%. His cholesterol is mildly raised. After lifestyle advice, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.B: Withhold a statin because his cholesterol is only mildly raised
options.C: Start a statin only once he develops symptoms
options.D: Treat to a specific cholesterol target with combination therapy first-line
options.E: No intervention, as he has no established disease

correct_answer: A. Offer atorvastatin for primary prevention
why_correct: Primary prevention is guided by overall 10-year cardiovascular risk: a QRISK at or above 10% warrants offering a statin (atorvastatin 20 mg) after lifestyle measures, regardless of whether the cholesterol itself is only modestly elevated.
why_wrong: B. The decision rests on the overall QRISK3 score, not the cholesterol level alone; a 10-year risk of 10% or more warrants offering a statin even with modestly raised cholesterol. C. Primary prevention aims to prevent a first event; waiting for symptoms defeats its purpose. D. NICE recommends atorvastatin 20 mg first-line for primary prevention, aiming for a greater than 40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol, not combination therapy to a fixed target. E. His 10-year risk of 16% exceeds the 10% threshold, so a statin should be offered despite no established disease.
pearl: Statins for primary prevention follow the QRISK score, not the cholesterol number — a QRISK ≥10% earns a statin.
thinking: No established CVD ↓ QRISK3 16% (≥10%) after lifestyle advice ↓ Decision is based on overall risk, not the cholesterol level ↓ Offer atorvastatin 20 mg
exam_trap: B, withhold the statin because cholesterol is only mildly raised — judging the decision on the cholesterol number feels intuitive. But the decision rests on the overall QRISK score, not the cholesterol level alone; a QRISK ≥10% warrants a statin even with near-normal cholesterol.
takeaway: Statins for primary prevention follow the QRISK score, not the cholesterol number — a QRISK ≥10% earns a statin.

stem: A child develops, a few weeks after a sore throat, a migratory polyarthritis of the large joints, a new heart murmur, and involuntary jerky movements (chorea). There is evidence of recent streptococcal infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A migratory polyarthritis, carditis (new murmur) and chorea occurring weeks after a streptococcal throat infection, with evidence of recent streptococcal infection, is acute rheumatic fever (diagnosed via the Jones criteria); it is treated with antibiotics and anti-inflammatories, with secondary prophylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes persistent (not migratory) arthritis for at least 6 weeks and is not associated with chorea or preceding streptococcal infection. B. Septic arthritis usually affects a single acutely infected joint, whereas the migratory polyarthritis with carditis and chorea here is rheumatic fever. C. Reactive arthritis follows gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection and causes asymmetric lower-limb arthritis, without carditis or chorea. E. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) causes palpable purpura, abdominal pain and nephritis, not carditis and chorea.
pearl: Migratory polyarthritis with carditis and chorea weeks after a strep throat is acute rheumatic fever (Jones criteria).
thinking: Weeks after strep throat ↓ Migratory polyarthritis + carditis + chorea (Jones major criteria) ↓ Acute rheumatic fever
exam_trap: B, septic arthritis — a hot joint after infection can suggest joint sepsis. But septic arthritis is a single acutely infected joint, whereas the MIGRATORY polyarthritis with carditis and chorea following a strep throat here is rheumatic fever.
takeaway: Migratory polyarthritis with carditis and chorea weeks after a strep throat is acute rheumatic fever (Jones criteria).

stem: An asymptomatic, thriving child is found on routine examination to have a soft, short systolic murmur that is louder when lying down and softer when standing. There is no thrill, no radiation, normal heart sounds and normal pulses. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Infective endocarditis — take three sets of blood cultures
options.B: A pathological murmur requiring urgent cardiology referral
options.C: Innocent murmur — reassure, no referral needed
options.D: Structural heart disease — refer for cardiac surgery
options.E: Early heart failure — start a diuretic

correct_answer: C. Innocent murmur — reassure, no referral needed
why_correct: A soft, short, systolic, asymptomatic murmur that varies with position, with normal heart sounds and pulses and no thrill or radiation, has the features of an innocent (functional) murmur; reassurance is appropriate, whereas certain features prompt referral.
why_wrong: A. A thriving, asymptomatic child has no features of endocarditis. B. A soft, short, positional murmur without a thrill, radiation or abnormal heart sounds has innocent features and does not need urgent referral. D. Nothing suggests structural disease, and surgery is not based on an innocent-sounding murmur. E. A thriving, asymptomatic child has no signs of heart failure.
pearl: A soft asymptomatic systolic murmur that varies with position is innocent; diastolic, loud/thrilling or symptomatic murmurs need referral.
thinking: Asymptomatic, thriving child ↓ Soft, short systolic murmur varying with posture; no thrill, radiation or abnormal sounds ↓ Innocent murmur — reassure
exam_trap: B, a pathological murmur needing urgent referral — any murmur can prompt worry. But the reassuring features here (soft, systolic, asymptomatic, varies with posture, no thrill) indicate an innocent murmur; diastolic, loud/thrilling, or symptomatic murmurs are the ones that need referral.
takeaway: A soft asymptomatic systolic murmur that varies with position is innocent; diastolic, loud/thrilling or symptomatic murmurs need referral.

stem: A patient with non-valvular atrial fibrillation is assessed for stroke prevention. Their stroke-risk score (CHA2DS2-VASc) indicates they would benefit from anticoagulation, and bleeding risk has been assessed. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy
options.B: Aspirin 75 mg daily for stroke prevention
options.C: Left atrial appendage occlusion as first-line
options.D: A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban

correct_answer: D. A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban
why_correct: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc score balanced against bleeding risk; when anticoagulation is indicated, a direct oral anticoagulant is generally preferred over warfarin, and antiplatelet drugs (aspirin) are not recommended for this purpose.
why_wrong: A. Dual antiplatelet therapy is less effective than anticoagulation for AF stroke prevention, with a similar bleeding risk. B. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF; it is ineffective and still causes bleeding. C. Left atrial appendage occlusion is reserved for those with contraindications to anticoagulation. E. Antiplatelet monotherapy does not adequately prevent AF-related stroke.
pearl: Stroke prevention in AF is anticoagulation (a DOAC, CHA2DS2-VASc-guided) — aspirin is not adequate.
thinking: Non-valvular AF ↓ CHA2DS2-VASc indicates benefit, bleeding risk assessed ↓ anticoagulation, not antiplatelets ↓ DOAC such as apixaban (D)
exam_trap: B, aspirin alone for stroke prevention — aspirin is an antithrombotic, so it seems plausible. But aspirin is ineffective for preventing AF-related strokes and is not recommended; proper stroke prevention requires anticoagulation, usually with a DOAC.
takeaway: Stroke prevention in AF is anticoagulation (a DOAC, CHA2DS2-VASc-guided) — aspirin is not adequate.

stem: A patient is recovering after a myocardial infarction. Alongside cardiac rehabilitation and lifestyle change, which combination of drugs is the cornerstone of secondary prevention?

options.A: DAPT, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker
options.B: Aspirin, a statin and a calcium-channel blocker
options.C: Aspirin, warfarin and a high-intensity statin
options.D: Clopidogrel, a nitrate, amlodipine and furosemide
options.E: DAPT and a statin, stopped after 3 months

correct_answer: A. DAPT, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker
why_correct: Secondary prevention after a myocardial infarction comprises dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a second agent), a high-intensity statin, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker, together with cardiac rehabilitation and lifestyle modification, to reduce further events and mortality.
why_wrong: B. This omits a second antiplatelet, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker, and a calcium-channel blocker is not routine secondary prevention. C. Warfarin is not routine after MI, adds bleeding risk and does not replace DAPT, an ACE inhibitor or a beta-blocker. D. Nitrates, amlodipine and diuretics treat symptoms rather than forming core prognostic secondary prevention. E. Secondary prevention is lifelong (DAPT usually for 12 months), and stopping at 3 months raises the risk of further events.
pearl: After an MI: dual antiplatelets, a statin, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker, plus cardiac rehab — not aspirin alone.
thinking: Post-myocardial infarction ↓ Prognostic secondary prevention drugs ↓ DAPT + high-intensity statin + ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker
exam_trap: B, aspirin, a statin and a calcium-channel blocker — this looks like a reasonable cardiovascular combination. But it omits a second antiplatelet, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker, and a calcium-channel blocker is not routine prognostic therapy after MI.
takeaway: After an MI: dual antiplatelets, a statin, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker, plus cardiac rehab — not aspirin alone.

presentation: Chronic Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction — Management
stem: A patient has chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Which treatment improves prognosis (survival), as opposed to only relieving symptoms?

options.B: A loop diuretic such as furosemide daily
options.C: Digoxin titrated to a target serum level
options.D: An ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker

correct_answer: D. An ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker
why_correct: In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, ACE inhibitors (or ARB/ARNI) and beta-blockers improve survival, and NICE also recommends a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) as prognostic therapy; loop diuretics relieve congestive symptoms but do not improve prognosis.
why_wrong: A. Nitrates alone do not improve survival in HFrEF (hydralazine with nitrate is used in specific groups). B. Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival. C. Digoxin improves symptoms and reduces admissions but not mortality. E. Amlodipine and thiazides do not improve survival in HFrEF.
pearl: In HFrEF, ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker (with an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor) improve survival; diuretics only relieve symptoms.
thinking: HFrEF ↓ question asks for prognostic benefit ↓ prognostic drugs vs symptomatic drugs ↓ ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker (D)
exam_trap: B, a loop diuretic improves survival — diuretics make patients feel much better, so they seem disease-modifying. But diuretics only relieve fluid symptoms; the prognosis-improving drugs are ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, MRAs and SGLT2 inhibitors.
takeaway: In HFrEF, ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker (with an MRA and an SGLT2 inhibitor) improve survival; diuretics only relieve symptoms.

stem: A patient with a cardiac valve abnormality is due to have a routine dental procedure and asks whether they need antibiotics beforehand to prevent infective endocarditis. According to current UK guidance, what is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Prophylactic antibiotics before every dental procedure for any valve lesion
options.B: No routine antibiotic prophylaxis; maintain good oral hygiene
options.C: Daily low-dose penicillin V as lifelong prophylaxis
options.D: Defer dental treatment until the valve is repaired

correct_answer: B. No routine antibiotic prophylaxis; maintain good oral hygiene
why_correct: Current UK (NICE) guidance does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis solely to prevent infective endocarditis in people undergoing dental or other procedures; emphasis is placed on maintaining good oral and dental health, with individualised specialist advice in selected high-risk cases.
why_wrong: A. NICE does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures solely to prevent endocarditis. C. Lifelong antibiotics are not indicated and promote resistance and adverse effects. D. Dental treatment should not be deferred; good dental health reduces endocarditis risk. E. Clindamycin prophylaxis is not recommended and carries a risk of C. difficile infection; routine prophylaxis is not advised whatever the allergy status.
pearl: UK guidance does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis before dental work — prioritise oral hygiene instead.
thinking: Valve abnormality + routine dental work ↓ NICE: no routine antibiotic prophylaxis ↓ good oral hygiene (B)
exam_trap: A, antibiotics before every dental procedure for all valve patients — historical practice routinely gave prophylaxis, so it feels expected. But current UK guidance does not recommend routine prophylaxis; the focus is on oral hygiene, not blanket antibiotics.
takeaway: UK guidance does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis before dental work — prioritise oral hygiene instead.

presentation: Atrial Fibrillation — Rate versus Rhythm Control
stem: A patient has established (non-acute) atrial fibrillation and is stable. Separate from anticoagulation, what is the most appropriate first-line strategy for controlling the arrhythmia in most patients?

options.A: Rhythm control with long-term oral amiodarone therapy
options.B: Elective DC cardioversion with flecainide afterwards
options.C: Rate control with a beta-blocker or diltiazem
options.D: Digoxin monotherapy in a physically active patient
options.E: Anticoagulation alone without any rate control

correct_answer: C. Rate control with a beta-blocker or diltiazem
why_correct: For most patients with established atrial fibrillation, rate control (a beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) is first-line; rhythm control is reserved for selected patients — new-onset AF, a reversible cause, heart failure thought to be caused by AF, or symptoms that persist despite rate control.
why_wrong: A. Amiodarone is not first-line because of its toxicity; rhythm control is reserved for selected patients. B. Cardioversion is a rhythm-control strategy for selected patients (e.g. new onset or a reversible cause), not first-line for most. D. Digoxin monotherapy is reserved for sedentary patients because it does not control the rate during exertion. E. Anticoagulation prevents stroke but does not control the ventricular rate or symptoms.
pearl: Rate control is first-line for most established AF; rhythm control is for new-onset, reversible causes, AF-related heart failure, or persistent symptoms.
thinking: Established, stable AF ↓ no indication for rhythm control first ↓ rate control with beta-blocker or diltiazem (C)
exam_trap: B, elective DC cardioversion with flecainide afterwards — restoring sinus rhythm seems the definitive fix. But rhythm control is reserved for specific situations; for most stable patients with established AF, rate control is the first-line strategy.
takeaway: Rate control is first-line for most established AF; rhythm control is for new-onset, reversible causes, AF-related heart failure, or persistent symptoms.

stem: A patient has an elevated blood pressure reading in clinic. Before diagnosing hypertension and starting treatment, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Confirm with ambulatory (ABPM) or home (HBPM) blood-pressure monitoring
options.B: Diagnose hypertension and start treatment on this single clinic reading
options.C: Ignore it unless the patient has symptoms
options.D: Repeat the clinic reading once more and diagnose if still high
options.E: Start treatment empirically and never confirm

correct_answer: A. Confirm with ambulatory (ABPM) or home (HBPM) blood-pressure monitoring
why_correct: An elevated clinic blood pressure should be confirmed with ambulatory (ABPM) or home (HBPM) monitoring before diagnosing hypertension, to exclude the white-coat effect and to stage severity, except where readings are very high or there is end-organ damage warranting immediate action.
why_wrong: B. A single clinic reading can reflect white-coat hypertension; confirmation with ABPM or HBPM is needed before diagnosis unless BP is very high or there is target-organ damage. C. Hypertension is usually asymptomatic, so waiting for symptoms misses it. D. Further clinic readings cannot exclude the white-coat effect; out-of-office monitoring is needed. E. Treating without confirmation risks lifelong treatment of white-coat hypertension.
pearl: Confirm a raised clinic BP with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing hypertension — don't diagnose on one clinic reading.
thinking: Elevated clinic blood pressure ↓ A single clinic reading may reflect white-coat effect ↓ Confirm with out-of-clinic monitoring ↓ ABPM (or HBPM if ABPM unsuitable or not tolerated)
exam_trap: B, diagnose and treat on the single clinic reading — a high reading seems enough to act on. But a single clinic reading can reflect white-coat hypertension; confirmation with ABPM/HBPM is needed before diagnosis (unless very severe).
takeaway: Confirm a raised clinic BP with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing hypertension — don't diagnose on one clinic reading.

stem: A patient has symptomatic complete (third-degree) heart block with syncope and a slow ventricular escape rhythm. After any acute stabilisation, what is the definitive management?

options.D: Reassurance and discharge with no device
options.E: A statin and an ACE inhibitor only

correct_answer: C. Insertion of a permanent pacemaker
why_correct: Symptomatic complete heart block (or symptomatic Mobitz II) is an indication for a permanent pacemaker; acutely, atropine and temporary (transcutaneous or transvenous) pacing may be used to stabilise, but the definitive treatment is permanent pacing.
why_wrong: A. Atropine is only a temporary IV measure; it is not a long-term oral treatment for heart block. B. Beta-blockers slow AV conduction and would worsen bradycardia. D. Symptomatic complete heart block with syncope is high-risk and needs pacing. E. A statin and ACE inhibitor do not treat a conduction block.
pearl: Symptomatic complete heart block (or Mobitz II) needs a permanent pacemaker — drugs only temporise.
thinking: Symptomatic complete heart block with syncope ↓ acute stabilisation (atropine/temporary pacing) ↓ definitive treatment = permanent pacemaker (C)
exam_trap: A, lifelong atropine tablets — atropine raises the heart rate acutely, so it seems a logical ongoing treatment. But atropine is only a temporary measure; symptomatic high-grade heart block requires a permanent pacemaker for definitive treatment.
takeaway: Symptomatic complete heart block (or Mobitz II) needs a permanent pacemaker — drugs only temporise.

stem: A young, asymptomatic patient is found to have a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur at the apex is the classic finding of mitral valve prolapse, usually benign; it can occasionally be associated with mitral regurgitation and, rarely, arrhythmia.
why_wrong: A. Aortic stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, with no mid-systolic click. C. Mitral stenosis causes a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap, not a systolic click and late systolic murmur. D. A VSD causes a harsh pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge. E. Tricuspid regurgitation causes a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration.
pearl: A mid-systolic click with a late systolic apical murmur is mitral valve prolapse — usually benign.
thinking: Young asymptomatic patient ↓ Mid-systolic click + late systolic apical murmur ↓ Mitral valve prolapse
exam_trap: A, aortic stenosis — both are systolic murmurs. But aortic stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, whereas the mid-systolic CLICK with a late apical murmur is mitral valve prolapse.
takeaway: A mid-systolic click with a late systolic apical murmur is mitral valve prolapse — usually benign.

stem: A patient presents with symptoms and signs of heart failure. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with globally reduced systolic function (low ejection fraction) and no significant valve or coronary disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle with a low ejection fraction, in the absence of significant valvular or coronary disease, is dilated cardiomyopathy; causes include idiopathic, alcohol, post-viral and genetic, and management follows heart-failure principles.
why_wrong: B. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows a thickened, non-dilated ventricle with preserved or increased contraction, the opposite of this picture. C. Constrictive pericarditis causes diastolic restriction with a thickened pericardium and usually preserved systolic function. D. Severe aortic stenosis is excluded by the absence of significant valve disease. E. Acute MI causes regional wall-motion abnormality from coronary disease, which is absent here.
pearl: A dilated, poorly-contracting left ventricle (low EF) without valve/coronary disease is dilated cardiomyopathy.
thinking: Heart failure ↓ Dilated LV with globally reduced EF, no valve or coronary disease ↓ Dilated cardiomyopathy
exam_trap: B, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — both are cardiomyopathies. But hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows a thickened, non-dilated ventricle with preserved/increased contraction, the opposite of the dilated, poorly-contracting ventricle here.
takeaway: A dilated, poorly-contracting left ventricle (low EF) without valve/coronary disease is dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A young patient with palpitations has an ECG showing a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS complex (a delta wave). What is the diagnosis, and what is an important management caution?

options.A: First-degree heart block — no further action is needed
options.B: Wolff-Parkinson-White — avoid AV-nodal blockers in AF
options.C: Complete heart block — arrange urgent permanent pacing
options.D: Normal variant — reassure and discharge with no follow-up
options.E: Long QT syndrome — avoid QT-prolonging drugs and stimulants

correct_answer: B. Wolff-Parkinson-White — avoid AV-nodal blockers in AF
why_correct: A short PR interval with a delta wave indicates Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (an accessory pathway); patients are prone to re-entrant tachycardias, and in pre-excited atrial fibrillation, AV-node-blocking drugs (e.g. adenosine, verapamil, digoxin) can dangerously accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway and are avoided.
why_wrong: A. First-degree block prolongs the PR interval; here it is short with a delta wave. C. Complete heart block shows AV dissociation, not a short PR with a delta wave. D. Pre-excitation with palpitations carries a risk of re-entrant and pre-excited arrhythmias and needs assessment. E. Long QT syndrome prolongs the QT interval and does not cause a short PR or delta wave.
pearl: A short PR with a delta wave is Wolff-Parkinson-White — avoid AV-node-blocking drugs in pre-excited AF.
thinking: Palpitations in a young patient ↓ Short PR + delta wave = pre-excitation ↓ Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome ↓ Avoid AV-nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited AF
exam_trap: A, first-degree heart block — PR-interval abnormalities can be conflated. But first-degree block is a LONG PR with no delta wave, whereas the SHORT PR with a delta wave here is Wolff-Parkinson-White.
takeaway: A short PR with a delta wave is Wolff-Parkinson-White — avoid AV-node-blocking drugs in pre-excited AF.

stem: A man with central chest pain has ST elevation in leads V1 to V4. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded, and which wall is affected?
correct_answer: E. Left anterior descending — anteroseptal wall
why_correct: ST elevation in V1–V4 localises an anteroseptal infarct, supplied by the left anterior descending artery — a large-territory, high-risk STEMI.
why_wrong: A. Right ventricular infarction is shown by ST elevation in right-sided leads (V4R), not V1–V4. B. The right coronary artery causes inferior ST elevation in II, III and aVF. C. The circumflex causes lateral changes in I, aVL, V5 and V6. D. Posterior infarction shows ST depression with tall R waves in V1–V3, not ST elevation.
pearl: V1–V4 elevation is an anterior (LAD) STEMI — read the lead group to name the artery.
thinking: ST elevation V1–V4 ↓ Anteroseptal territory ↓ Left anterior descending artery
exam_trap: B, the right coronary artery/inferior wall — the commonest single culprit overall, so a reflex answer. But inferior infarction shows in II, III and aVF, not the precordial V1–V4; the anterior leads point to the LAD.
takeaway: V1–V4 elevation is an anterior (LAD) STEMI — read the lead group to name the artery.

presentation: Inferior STEMI — Territory and a Critical Check
stem: A man has ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which artery is most often responsible, and what additional lead should you record before giving nitrates?
correct_answer: D. Right coronary artery — record V4R
why_correct: Inferior ST elevation (II, III, aVF) is usually a right coronary artery occlusion; a right-sided lead (V4R) is recorded because co-existing right ventricular infarction makes the patient preload-dependent and nitrate-sensitive.
why_wrong: A. Left main occlusion causes widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR, not inferior ST elevation. B. The LAD causes anterior ST elevation, and posterior leads do not check for RV involvement. C. The circumflex can cause inferior changes but less often than the RCA, and aVL is already part of the standard ECG. E. The RCA, not an isolated PDA lesion, is the usual culprit, and right ventricular involvement is best assessed with a right-sided lead (V4R) rather than V1.
pearl: Inferior STEMI is usually the RCA — record V4R, because right ventricular involvement makes nitrates dangerous.
thinking: ST elevation II, III, aVF ↓ Inferior STEMI, usually RCA ↓ Record V4R for RV infarction before nitrates
exam_trap: B, the LAD with V7–V9 — posterior leads are a real adjunct, but they pair with posterior, not inferior, infarction. Inferior STEMI is usually the RCA, and the key extra lead is V4R for the right ventricle.
takeaway: Inferior STEMI is usually the RCA — record V4R, because right ventricular involvement makes nitrates dangerous.

stem: A man with chest pain has tall R waves and horizontal ST depression in V1–V3, with upright T waves. The inferior leads show some ST elevation. What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.E: Pericarditis — give an NSAID and colchicine

correct_answer: A. Posterior STEMI — record leads V7–V9
why_correct: Tall R waves with ST depression in V1–V3 are the mirror image of posterior ST elevation; posterior leads (V7–V9) confirm a posterior STEMI, which is often missed and warrants the same urgent reperfusion.
why_wrong: B. ST depression with tall R waves and upright T waves in V1–V3, with inferior ST elevation, is a posterior STEMI needing reperfusion, not NSTEMI management. C. These changes are not a normal variant in a patient with chest pain. D. PE can cause a dominant R in V1 from RV strain but not this pattern with inferior ST elevation. E. Pericarditis causes widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression, not this regional pattern.
pearl: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves is a posterior STEMI in the mirror — record posterior leads and reperfuse.
thinking: Chest pain ↓ Tall R waves + horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with upright T waves, plus inferior ST elevation ↓ Reciprocal change of an (infero)posterior STEMI ↓ Record V7–V9 and proceed to urgent reperfusion
exam_trap: B, anterior ischaemia managed as NSTEMI — the anterior ST depression looks like anterior ischaemia. But it is reciprocal change from a posterior infarct; treating it as an NSTEMI would miss a STEMI needing reperfusion.
takeaway: Anterior ST depression with tall R waves is a posterior STEMI in the mirror — record posterior leads and reperfuse.

presentation: New Left Bundle Branch Block with Chest Pain
stem: A man with ongoing ischaemic chest pain has a broad QRS with a left bundle branch block pattern that was not present on a previous ECG. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Wait, as LBBB makes the ECG uninterpretable
options.B: Treat as a STEMI equivalent and activate primary PCI
options.E: Give a fibrinolytic only if ST elevation appears later

correct_answer: B. Treat as a STEMI equivalent and activate primary PCI
why_correct: New (or presumed-new) left bundle branch block in a patient with ischaemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent, because it can mask an acute occlusion; primary PCI is activated.
why_wrong: A. Waiting because LBBB obscures ST changes risks a completed infarct; new LBBB with ischaemic pain is itself an indication for reperfusion. C. NSTEMI management delays reperfusion of a possible acute coronary occlusion. D. New LBBB with ongoing ischaemic pain is not benign. E. Waiting for ST elevation delays reperfusion, and primary PCI is preferred to fibrinolysis where available.
pearl: New LBBB with ischaemic chest pain is a STEMI equivalent — reperfuse, do not wait for clearer ST changes.
thinking: Ongoing ischaemic chest pain ↓ LBBB not present on the previous ECG ↓ LBBB can mask an acute coronary occlusion ↓ Treat as a STEMI equivalent and activate primary PCI
exam_trap: A, wait because LBBB is uninterpretable — LBBB does obscure ST changes, so caution feels reasonable. But new LBBB with ischaemic pain is itself an indication for reperfusion; waiting risks a completed infarct.
takeaway: New LBBB with ischaemic chest pain is a STEMI equivalent — reperfuse, do not wait for clearer ST changes.

stem: An ECG shows a QRS duration of 140 ms with an 'RSR' (M-shaped) pattern in V1 and a broad slurred S wave in the lateral leads (I and V6). What does this represent?
why_correct: A broad QRS with an RSR' in V1 and a wide S wave laterally is right bundle branch block (the 'MaRRoW' pattern) — often benign but worth correlating with the clinical context.
why_wrong: B. LBBB gives a broad notched R in the lateral leads (WiLLiaM) without the RSR' in V1; the M in V1 here is RBBB. C. VT is a broad-complex tachycardia, whereas this trace describes a bundle-branch QRS morphology rather than a tachyarrhythmia. D. WPW causes a short PR with a delta wave, not an RSR' pattern. E. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves and diffuse QRS widening rather than a specific RSR' in V1 with lateral slurred S waves.
pearl: RSR' in V1 is RBBB (MaRRoW); a broad notched lateral R is LBBB (WiLLiaM) — read V1 to tell them apart.
thinking: QRS 140 ms + RSR' in V1 + broad slurred lateral S wave ↓ MaRRoW pattern ↓ Right bundle branch block
exam_trap: B, left bundle branch block — both widen the QRS, so they are easily confused. But LBBB gives a broad notched R in the lateral leads (William) without the V1 RSR'; the M in V1 here is RBBB.
takeaway: RSR' in V1 is RBBB (MaRRoW); a broad notched lateral R is LBBB (WiLLiaM) — read V1 to tell them apart.

stem: An asymptomatic patient's ECG shows the PR interval lengthening progressively over successive beats until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle repeats. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Insert a permanent pacemaker urgently today
options.C: IV atropine 500 micrograms now and repeat

correct_answer: E. Observe and review rate-slowing drugs
why_correct: Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block, usually benign and at low risk of progression; management is observation and review of rate-slowing drugs, with pacing only if symptomatic.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of acute infarction; thrombolysis is not indicated for an asymptomatic conduction finding. B. Mobitz I is usually benign with a low risk of progression; pacing is for symptomatic or high-risk blocks. C. Atropine is for symptomatic or unstable bradycardia, and this patient is asymptomatic. D. Beta-blockers slow AV conduction and could worsen the block.
pearl: Wenckebach (progressive PR then a dropped beat) is usually benign — observe; pacing is for Mobitz II and complete block.
thinking: Progressive PR lengthening then dropped QRS ↓ Mobitz I (Wenckebach), asymptomatic ↓ usually benign ↓ observe and review rate-slowing drugs (E)
exam_trap: B, urgent pacemaker — any dropped beat can prompt thoughts of pacing. But Mobitz I is generally benign; it is Mobitz II and complete block that need pacing, not asymptomatic Wenckebach.
takeaway: Wenckebach (progressive PR then a dropped beat) is usually benign — observe; pacing is for Mobitz II and complete block.

stem: An ECG shows intermittent dropped QRS complexes with a constant PR interval on the conducted beats. The patient has presyncope. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Mobitz type II block (dropped beats with a constant PR) carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block and asystole; a permanent pacemaker is indicated.
why_wrong: B. Mobitz II carries a high risk of progression to complete heart block and asystole, particularly with symptoms; observation is unsafe. C. Adenosine blocks the AV node and could precipitate asystole. D. Symptomatic Mobitz II is high-risk and needs pacing, not discharge. E. Beta-blockers slow AV conduction and would worsen the block.
pearl: Mobitz II (constant PR, dropped beats) needs a pacemaker — the fixed PR is the danger sign that separates it from Wenckebach.
thinking: Intermittent dropped QRS complexes ↓ Constant PR on conducted beats = Mobitz type II ↓ Symptomatic (presyncope) with high risk of complete heart block ↓ Permanent pacemaker
exam_trap: B, observation only — appropriate for benign Wenckebach, so the patterns are easily confused. But Mobitz II is dangerous and unpredictable; it needs pacing, not watchful waiting.
takeaway: Mobitz II (constant PR, dropped beats) needs a pacemaker — the fixed PR is the danger sign that separates it from Wenckebach.

stem: A patient on long-term diuretics has an ECG showing flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves. What is the most likely electrolyte abnormality?
why_correct: Flattened T waves, ST depression and U waves are the classic ECG features of hypokalaemia, which also predisposes to arrhythmia and potentiates digoxin toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT interval and does not cause U waves. B. Hyperkalaemia gives tall tented T waves and a broad QRS; the flat T waves and U waves here are hypokalaemia. D. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT through ST-segment lengthening, without prominent U waves. E. Hypermagnesaemia is rare with diuretics and causes conduction delay (prolonged PR, broad QRS) rather than U waves.
pearl: U waves with flat T waves is hypokalaemia; tented T waves with a wide QRS is hyperkalaemia.
thinking: Long-term diuretics ↓ Flat T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves ↓ Hypokalaemia
exam_trap: B, hyperkalaemia — the more feared potassium abnormality, so the reflex worry. But hyperkalaemia gives tall tented T waves and a broad QRS; the flat T waves and U waves here are hypokalaemia.
takeaway: U waves with flat T waves is hypokalaemia; tented T waves with a wide QRS is hyperkalaemia.

stem: A patient with vomiting (and likely electrolyte loss) is noted to have a markedly prolonged QTc. They are about to be prescribed an antiemetic. Which is the main danger, and what should guide prescribing?

options.A: Torsades de pointes — avoid QT-prolonging drugs
options.B: Bradycardia — give atropine before the antiemetic
options.C: Hyperkalaemia — give IV calcium gluconate first
options.D: Bronchospasm — give salbutamol with the antiemetic

correct_answer: A. Torsades de pointes — avoid QT-prolonging drugs
why_correct: A prolonged QTc predisposes to torsades de pointes; QT-prolonging drugs (many antiemetics, antipsychotics, macrolides) should be avoided and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium) corrected.
why_wrong: B. A prolonged QTc does not chiefly predispose to bradycardia, and atropine is not indicated. C. Vomiting causes hypokalaemia rather than hyperkalaemia, and calcium does not address QT prolongation. D. Bronchospasm is not a consequence of QT prolongation. E. Dystonia is a side effect of some antiemetics, but the major danger with a long QTc is torsades de pointes.
pearl: A long QT is a torsades waiting to happen — withhold QT-prolonging drugs and fix the electrolytes.
thinking: Vomiting with electrolyte loss + markedly prolonged QTc ↓ Substrate for torsades de pointes ↓ Avoid QT-prolonging antiemetics and correct electrolytes
exam_trap: B, bradycardia needing atropine — heart-rate concerns are common with rhythm problems. But the specific danger of a long QT is the polymorphic VT of torsades, driven by QT-prolonging drugs and low electrolytes, not bradycardia.
takeaway: A long QT is a torsades waiting to happen — withhold QT-prolonging drugs and fix the electrolytes.

stem: A patient with a long QT develops a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in which the QRS complexes appear to twist around the baseline. They have a pulse and no adverse features. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
why_correct: Torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT on a background of long QT) is treated with IV magnesium sulfate, alongside correcting electrolytes and stopping any QT-prolonging drug; unstable patients are cardioverted.
why_wrong: A. Adenosine has no role in polymorphic VT. B. Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and can worsen torsades de pointes. D. Digoxin is not used for torsades and is pro-arrhythmic. E. An oral beta-blocker is too slow to terminate active torsades; beta-blockers are used for prevention in some congenital long QT syndromes.
pearl: Torsades is treated with magnesium — never reach for a QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic like amiodarone.
thinking: Long QT ↓ polymorphic VT twisting around baseline = torsades de pointes ↓ avoid amiodarone ↓ IV magnesium sulfate (C)
exam_trap: B, amiodarone — a standard VT antiarrhythmic, so it feels right. But amiodarone prolongs the QT and can worsen torsades; the specific treatment is magnesium.
takeaway: Torsades is treated with magnesium — never reach for a QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic like amiodarone.

stem: A patient stable on therapeutic digoxin has an ECG showing down-sloping 'reverse-tick' ST depression. They are asymptomatic with a normal potassium and digoxin level. What does this represent?

options.B: Digoxin toxicity — give digoxin-specific antibody fragments
options.C: The expected digoxin effect — no action needed

correct_answer: C. The expected digoxin effect — no action needed
why_correct: The 'reverse tick' down-sloping ST segment is the expected ECG effect of digoxin at therapeutic levels and does not indicate toxicity; toxicity is diagnosed from arrhythmias and clinical features, not this ST change.
why_wrong: A. The reverse-tick ST depression of digoxin is a drug effect, not ischaemia, in an asymptomatic patient. B. The reverse tick is a benign therapeutic effect; with a normal level and no symptoms or arrhythmia, digoxin-specific antibody fragments are not indicated. D. The potassium is stated to be normal, so replacement is not needed. E. Hypothermia causes Osborn (J) waves and bradycardia, not reverse-tick ST depression.
pearl: The digoxin 'reverse tick' is an effect, not toxicity — toxicity is judged by arrhythmias and clinical features, not the ST change.
thinking: Therapeutic digoxin, asymptomatic, normal K+ and level ↓ Reverse-tick ST depression ↓ Expected digoxin effect — no action
exam_trap: B, treat as toxicity with antibody fragments — any digoxin-related ECG change can prompt fear of toxicity. But the reverse-tick is a benign therapeutic effect; with a normal level and no symptoms, no treatment is needed.
takeaway: The digoxin 'reverse tick' is an effect, not toxicity — toxicity is judged by arrhythmias and clinical features, not the ST change.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a previous myocardial infarction has a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 170/min. He is alert with a blood pressure of 105/70. What is the safest assumption and first-line treatment?

options.B: Assume SVT with aberrancy; give IV verapamil
options.C: Give IV adenosine as a diagnostic and therapeutic trial first
options.D: Assume VT; synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation

correct_answer: D. Assume VT; synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation
why_correct: A regular broad-complex tachycardia, especially with a history of ischaemic heart disease, is assumed to be ventricular tachycardia. In the RCUK 2025 adult tachyarrhythmia algorithm, a stable regular broad-complex tachycardia is treated as VT with synchronised shock(s) under sedation or anaesthesia; drug treatment (procainamide, or amiodarone if procainamide is unavailable or contraindicated) is considered only if the risk of sedation or anaesthesia is too high. Life-threatening features also call for synchronised shock.
why_wrong: A. A regular broad-complex tachycardia at 170/min after MI is not sinus tachycardia and needs treatment. B. Verapamil given to VT misdiagnosed as SVT can cause cardiovascular collapse. C. Adenosine is considered for a regular broad-complex tachycardia when SVT with aberrancy is known or likely; with prior MI, VT is assumed. E. The rhythm is regular, so AF is unlikely, and digoxin is not used for broad-complex tachycardia.
pearl: Treat a broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise — verapamil to a misdiagnosed VT can be fatal.
thinking: Regular broad-complex tachycardia + previous MI ↓ assume VT ↓ stable, no life-threatening features ↓ RCUK 2025: synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation; drugs only if sedation risk too high (D)
exam_trap: B, treat as SVT with verapamil — broad-complex tachycardias can occasionally be SVT with aberrancy. But verapamil given to true VT can cause haemodynamic collapse; the safe default is to treat a broad-complex tachycardia as VT.
takeaway: Treat a broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise — verapamil to a misdiagnosed VT can be fatal.

stem: A hypertensive patient's ECG shows very tall R waves in the lateral leads and deep S waves in V1–V2 that together exceed the voltage criteria, with lateral ST depression and T-wave inversion. What does this represent?
why_correct: Tall lateral R waves and deep right precordial S waves meeting voltage criteria, with a lateral 'strain' pattern, indicate left ventricular hypertrophy — common in long-standing hypertension or aortic stenosis.
why_wrong: A. Wellens syndrome shows deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 without voltage criteria for LVH. B. STEMI shows ST elevation in contiguous leads, not lateral ST depression with high voltages. C. LBBB causes a broad QRS (over 120 ms) with characteristic morphology, not isolated voltage criteria. D. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves, flattened P waves and QRS widening, not high voltages with strain.
pearl: High QRS voltages with a lateral strain pattern is LVH — the strain follows the hypertrophy, it is not an acute infarct.
thinking: Long-standing hypertension ↓ Voltage criteria met + lateral ST depression/T inversion ↓ LV hypertrophy with strain
exam_trap: B, anterolateral STEMI — the ST/T changes can resemble ischaemia. But they are the secondary 'strain' pattern of hypertrophy (down-sloping, in the leads with tall R waves), not the acute ST elevation of infarction.
takeaway: High QRS voltages with a lateral strain pattern is LVH — the strain follows the hypertrophy, it is not an acute infarct.

stem: A patient with recent chest pain, now pain-free, has deeply biphasic and then deeply inverted T waves in V2–V3, with no ST elevation and normal troponin. What does this signify and what is the appropriate action?

options.E: Wellens pattern — outpatient exercise tolerance test

correct_answer: B. Critical LAD stenosis — urgent angiography
why_correct: Biphasic or deep symmetric T-wave inversion in V2–V3 in a pain-free patient (Wellens syndrome) signals critical proximal LAD stenosis and an imminent large anterior infarct; the patient needs angiography, and stress testing is dangerous.
why_wrong: A. Early repolarisation causes J-point elevation with upright T waves, not evolving deep T-wave inversion after chest pain. C. Hyperventilation does not explain this specific evolving pattern in V2–V3 after chest pain. D. Pericarditis causes widespread ST elevation with PR depression, not localised deep T-wave inversion. E. Stress testing is contraindicated in Wellens syndrome because it can precipitate a large anterior infarction; urgent angiography is needed.
pearl: Wellens T waves in a pain-free patient mean a critical LAD — angiography, not a stress test or discharge.
thinking: Recent chest pain, now pain-free, normal troponin ↓ Biphasic/deep T inversion V2–V3 (Wellens) ↓ Critical LAD stenosis — urgent angiography
exam_trap: A, benign repolarisation and discharge — the patient is pain-free with a normal troponin, which feels reassuring. But Wellens T waves predict an impending anterior MI; discharging or stress-testing risks a catastrophic infarct.
takeaway: Wellens T waves in a pain-free patient mean a critical LAD — angiography, not a stress test or discharge.

stem: A patient with chest pain and signs of shock has ST elevation in lead aVR with widespread ST depression across the other leads. What does this pattern most suggest?

options.D: Left main stem or triple-vessel disease
options.E: Massive pulmonary embolism with RV strain

correct_answer: D. Left main stem or triple-vessel disease
why_correct: ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression elsewhere suggests global subendocardial ischaemia from left main stem or severe triple-vessel disease — a high-risk presentation needing urgent cardiology input.
why_wrong: A. Early repolarisation causes J-point elevation in healthy people, not aVR elevation with widespread ST depression and shock. B. Inferior STEMI shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF. C. Pericarditis causes widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and aVR shows reciprocal ST depression, the opposite of this pattern. E. PE may cause tachycardia, right heart strain or S1Q3T3, but this pattern indicates global subendocardial ischaemia.
pearl: aVR elevation with widespread depression is the left main pattern — a high-risk ECG that needs urgent cardiology, not an NSAID.
thinking: Chest pain with shock ↓ ST elevation in aVR + widespread ST depression ↓ Left main stem or triple-vessel disease
exam_trap: C, pericarditis — it also causes widespread ST changes, so a tempting alternative. But pericarditis causes widespread ST elevation with PR depression, not the aVR elevation with widespread depression of left main ischaemia.
takeaway: aVR elevation with widespread depression is the left main pattern — a high-risk ECG that needs urgent cardiology, not an NSAID.

stem: A patient brought in from the cold with a core temperature of 29°C has bradycardia and a distinctive positive deflection at the J point (the junction of the QRS and ST segment). What is this finding called?
why_correct: The Osborn (J) wave — a positive deflection at the J point — is characteristic of hypothermia, alongside bradycardia and prolonged intervals; it resolves with rewarming.
why_wrong: A. An epsilon wave is a small terminal notch after the QRS in V1–V3, seen in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. B. A delta wave is the slurred QRS upstroke of pre-excitation (WPW), not a J-point hump in a cold patient. D. A U wave follows the T wave and is typical of hypokalaemia. E. Pathological Q waves indicate previous myocardial infarction.
pearl: A J-point hump in the cold is the Osborn wave — it is hypothermia's signature, and it melts with rewarming.
thinking: Core temperature 29°C + bradycardia ↓ Positive deflection at the J point ↓ Osborn (J) wave
exam_trap: B, a delta wave — another named ECG waveform, so a plausible guess. But the delta wave is the slurred QRS upstroke of pre-excitation (WPW); the J-point hump in a cold patient is the Osborn wave.
takeaway: A J-point hump in the cold is the Osborn wave — it is hypothermia's signature, and it melts with rewarming.

stem: A breathless, hypotensive patient has an ECG showing low-voltage QRS complexes whose amplitude alternates from beat to beat. What does this most suggest?
why_correct: Beat-to-beat variation in QRS amplitude (electrical alternans), especially with low-voltage complexes, suggests a large pericardial effusion in which the heart swings within the fluid — a clue to possible tamponade.
why_wrong: A. AF causes an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves, not beat-to-beat alternation in QRS amplitude. C. Bundle branch block widens the QRS but does not cause low voltage with alternans. D. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves and QRS widening, not electrical alternans. E. Sinus arrhythmia varies the heart rate with breathing and does not cause low-voltage complexes with alternans in a hypotensive patient.
pearl: Low voltages with alternating QRS height is the swinging heart of a big pericardial effusion — look for tamponade.
thinking: Breathless and hypotensive ↓ Low-voltage QRS with beat-to-beat amplitude alternation ↓ Large pericardial effusion (possible tamponade)
exam_trap: A, atrial fibrillation — an irregular trace might suggest AF. But AF is irregular in rhythm with varying R-R intervals, whereas alternans is a regular rhythm with alternating QRS height; the latter points to a pericardial effusion.
takeaway: Low voltages with alternating QRS height is the swinging heart of a big pericardial effusion — look for tamponade.

stem: An ECG shows a broad, notched (bifid) P wave in lead II. In which condition is this 'P mitrale' classically seen?
why_correct: A broad, bifid P wave (P mitrale) reflects left atrial enlargement, classically from mitral stenosis; right atrial enlargement instead gives a tall, peaked P wave (P pulmonale).
why_wrong: A. Tricuspid stenosis causes right atrial enlargement with tall peaked P waves (P pulmonale pattern), not a broad bifid P. C. Chronic lung disease causes right atrial enlargement with a tall peaked P wave (P pulmonale); the broad bifid P here is left atrial. D. WPW causes a short PR interval with a delta wave, not an abnormal P wave. E. Acute pericarditis causes PR depression and widespread ST elevation, not a bifid P wave.
pearl: A broad bifid P (P mitrale) is left atrial enlargement; a tall peaked P (P pulmonale) is right — width versus height tells them apart.
thinking: Broad, bifid P wave in lead II ↓ Left atrial enlargement ↓ Mitral stenosis
exam_trap: C, chronic lung disease — it does cause atrial enlargement, so a fair thought. But lung disease causes RIGHT atrial enlargement with a tall peaked P (P pulmonale); the broad bifid P here is left atrial (P mitrale).
takeaway: A broad bifid P (P mitrale) is left atrial enlargement; a tall peaked P (P pulmonale) is right — width versus height tells them apart.

stem: An elderly patient with intermittent dizziness and palpitations has an ambulatory ECG showing episodes of marked sinus bradycardia and sinus pauses alternating with bursts of atrial tachyarrhythmia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Alternating bradyarrhythmia (sinus pauses, bradycardia) and tachyarrhythmia from sinus node dysfunction is sick sinus syndrome; symptomatic patients often need a pacemaker (and anticoagulation if AF features).
why_wrong: A. First-degree AV block is a constant prolonged PR interval without pauses or tachyarrhythmias. B. Complete heart block shows AV dissociation rather than sinus pauses alternating with atrial tachyarrhythmia. C. WPW shows pre-excitation (short PR, delta wave) and causes tachycardias, not sinus pauses and bradycardia. D. Atrial flutter does not explain the episodes of sinus bradycardia and pauses.
pearl: Alternating brady and tachy with sinus pauses is sick sinus syndrome — the failing sinus node, not the AV node.
thinking: Intermittent dizziness and palpitations ↓ Sinus pauses/bradycardia alternating with atrial tachyarrhythmia ↓ Sick sinus syndrome
exam_trap: B, complete heart block — another cause of bradycardia and dizziness. But complete heart block shows AV dissociation, whereas the brady-tachy alternation with sinus pauses here is sinus node disease.
takeaway: Alternating brady and tachy with sinus pauses is sick sinus syndrome — the failing sinus node, not the AV node.

stem: A patient with a prolonged QT interval, due specifically to a long ST segment (with a normal T-wave width), has tetany. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Hypocalcaemia prolongs the ST segment and therefore the QT interval, and can cause tetany; hypercalcaemia does the opposite, shortening the QT.
why_wrong: A. Hypomagnesaemia can cause tetany and QT prolongation, but the classic isolated ST-segment lengthening with a normal T wave is hypocalcaemia (low magnesium often coexists and should be checked). B. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves and QRS widening, not tetany with ST prolongation. C. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT; a long QT from ST-segment prolongation with tetany is hypocalcaemia. E. Hyponatraemia causes neurological symptoms (confusion, seizures) rather than tetany with a lengthened ST segment.
pearl: Low calcium lengthens the QT (and causes tetany); high calcium shortens it — the direction of the QT names the calcium.
thinking: Tetany ↓ QT prolonged by a long ST segment with normal T wave ↓ Hypocalcaemia
exam_trap: C, hypercalcaemia — calcium is clearly involved, so the opposite ion is a tempting trap. But hypercalcaemia SHORTENS the QT; a long QT from ST-segment prolongation with tetany is hypocalcaemia.
takeaway: Low calcium lengthens the QT (and causes tetany); high calcium shortens it — the direction of the QT names the calcium.

stem: A 24-year-old competitive endurance athlete has a routine ECG showing sinus bradycardia at 44/min. He is entirely asymptomatic with no syncope and a normal examination. What is the most appropriate action?

options.C: Oral theophylline to raise the heart rate
options.E: Stop training until a cardiology review

why_correct: Resting sinus bradycardia is a normal finding in trained endurance athletes due to high vagal tone; in an asymptomatic athlete with a normal examination, reassurance is appropriate.
why_wrong: B. Pacing is for symptomatic or high-grade bradyarrhythmia, not physiological athletic bradycardia. C. There is no indication to raise the heart rate in an asymptomatic athlete. D. Admission is unnecessary for an asymptomatic, physiological finding. E. Training need not stop; the bradycardia reflects fitness, not disease.
pearl: Sinus bradycardia in an asymptomatic athlete is normal vagal tone — reassure; pace only the symptomatic.
thinking: Sinus bradycardia 44/min ↓ Trained endurance athlete, asymptomatic, normal examination ↓ Physiological high vagal tone ↓ Reassure
exam_trap: B, urgent pacemaker — a heart rate of 44 can look alarming out of context. But an asymptomatic, fit athlete with a normal examination needs reassurance, not pacing; bradycardia here is physiological.
takeaway: Sinus bradycardia in an asymptomatic athlete is normal vagal tone — reassure; pace only the symptomatic.

stem: An ECG from a patient with a pacemaker shows a sharp narrow vertical spike immediately before each broad QRS complex. What does this represent?
why_correct: A pacing spike immediately preceding each broad QRS indicates a ventricular paced rhythm; ventricular pacing produces a broad, LBBB-like QRS because the impulse spreads from the pacing lead, not the conduction system.
why_wrong: A. Artefact — a consistent spike immediately before every broad QRS in a paced patient is a pacing stimulus, not random artefact. B. Ventricular tachycardia — VT is a fast broad-complex rhythm without pacing spikes before each complex. C. Left bundle branch block (intrinsic) — paced beats do look LBBB-like, so the confusion is understandable, but the preceding pacing spike marks this as paced, not an intrinsic conduction block. D. Hyperkalaemia — causes peaked T waves, flattened P waves and QRS widening, but no pacing spikes.
pearl: A spike before a broad QRS is a paced beat — pacing mimics LBBB, but the spike gives it away.
thinking: ECG from a paced patient: sharp vertical spike before each broad QRS ↓ The pacing SPIKE immediately before each QRS identifies a paced beat ↓ A ventricular paced rhythm
exam_trap: C, intrinsic left bundle branch block — paced beats do look LBBB-like, so the confusion is understandable. But the preceding pacing spike marks this as paced, not an intrinsic conduction block.
takeaway: A spike before a broad QRS is a paced beat — pacing mimics LBBB, but the spike gives it away.

stem: A patient with cardiac-sounding chest pain has an ECG showing ST depression and T-wave inversion (no ST elevation), and a raised troponin. What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.A: IV fibrinolysis followed by angiography within 24 hours
options.C: Aspirin and discharge with an outpatient exercise ECG
options.D: Activate primary PCI as for an ST-elevation MI
options.E: Treat as pericarditis with an NSAID and colchicine

correct_answer: B. Antiplatelets, antithrombin and risk-guided angiography
why_correct: ST depression/T-wave inversion with a troponin rise is an NSTEMI; management is antiplatelet and antithrombin therapy with risk stratification (e.g. GRACE) guiding the timing of angiography. Fibrinolysis is not used in NSTEMI.
why_wrong: A. Fibrinolysis gives no benefit and causes harm in NSTEMI, where the artery is usually not totally occluded. C. A troponin-positive NSTEMI needs admission and treatment, not discharge with outpatient testing. D. Primary PCI pathways are for STEMI; NSTEMI angiography timing is guided by risk stratification. E. ST depression with a raised troponin and cardiac-sounding pain is NSTEMI, not pericarditis, which causes widespread ST elevation.
pearl: NSTEMI (ST depression, raised troponin) is treated medically with risk-stratified angiography — fibrinolysis is for STEMI only.
thinking: Cardiac pain + ST depression/T inversion + raised troponin ↓ NSTEMI ↓ no fibrinolysis ↓ antiplatelets, antithrombin, risk-guided angiography (B)
exam_trap: A, immediate fibrinolysis — clot-busting is a reperfusion reflex for acute coronary syndromes. But fibrinolysis benefits STEMI, not NSTEMI, where it is ineffective or harmful; NSTEMI is managed medically with risk-stratified angiography.
takeaway: NSTEMI (ST depression, raised troponin) is treated medically with risk-stratified angiography — fibrinolysis is for STEMI only.

stem: An asymptomatic patient's routine ECG shows a constant PR interval of 240 ms, with every P wave followed by a QRS. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: First-degree AV block (a prolonged but constant PR with every beat conducted) is usually benign and asymptomatic, needing no specific treatment beyond reviewing rate-slowing drugs.
why_wrong: B. Asymptomatic first-degree AV block does not need pacing. C. Atropine is for symptomatic or unstable bradycardia, not an asymptomatic conduction finding. D. Admission is not needed for benign, asymptomatic first-degree block. E. Beta-blockers further slow AV conduction and could worsen the block.
pearl: First-degree block (long but constant PR, nothing dropped) is benign — reassure and check the drug chart, do not pace.
thinking: Constant PR 240 ms, every P conducted ↓ first-degree AV block, asymptomatic ↓ benign ↓ reassure and review medications (A)
exam_trap: B, permanent pacemaker — 'AV block' can trigger thoughts of pacing. But first-degree block conducts every beat and is benign; pacing is reserved for high-grade (Mobitz II, complete) block.
takeaway: First-degree block (long but constant PR, nothing dropped) is benign — reassure and check the drug chart, do not pace.

stem: A 48-year-old white man with stage 2 hypertension confirmed on ambulatory monitoring needs drug treatment. He has no diabetes. What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?
why_correct: For a patient under 55 who is not of Black African or African-Caribbean origin, first-line antihypertensive treatment is an ACE inhibitor (or ARB); calcium-channel blockers are first-line for those 55 or over or of Black African/Caribbean origin.
why_wrong: A. A calcium-channel blocker is first line for people aged 55 or over or of Black African/African-Caribbean origin, not for this 48-year-old white man. C. A thiazide-like diuretic is an add-on at later steps (or used first when a CCB is unsuitable in the CCB group), not first line here. D. Beta-blockers are not first line for uncomplicated hypertension. E. Alpha-blockers are reserved for resistant hypertension (step 4).
pearl: Under 55 and not of Black-African/Caribbean origin starts on an ACE inhibitor; 55-plus or Black-African/Caribbean starts on a calcium-channel blocker.
thinking: 48-year-old white man, stage 2 hypertension, no diabetes ↓ under 55 and not of Black African/African-Caribbean origin ↓ ACE inhibitor (or ARB) first line (B)
exam_trap: A, a calcium-channel blocker — also a first-line agent, so it feels interchangeable. But the choice is age- and ethnicity-dependent: under 55 and not of Black African/Caribbean origin selects an ACE inhibitor, not a CCB.
takeaway: Under 55 and not of Black-African/Caribbean origin starts on an ACE inhibitor; 55-plus or Black-African/Caribbean starts on a calcium-channel blocker.

stem: A 55-year-old man with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 58 mmol/mol) has established cardiovascular disease. Lifestyle measures alone have not reached target. He has normal renal function. What is the most appropriate first-line drug therapy?
correct_answer: C. Metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor
why_correct: Metformin is first-line in type 2 diabetes; in a patient with established cardiovascular disease, an SGLT2 inhibitor is added (or co-started) for its proven cardiovascular and renal benefit. NICE NG28 (2026) now offers modified-release metformin, an SGLT2 inhibitor and subcutaneous semaglutide (up to 1 mg weekly) for adults with atherosclerotic CVD; of the options listed, metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor is the correct choice.
why_wrong: A. Insulin is not needed at an HbA1c of 58 mmol/mol and offers no cardiovascular benefit at this stage. B. A sulfonylurea carries hypoglycaemia and weight-gain risk and no cardiovascular benefit; with established CVD, an SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred. D. Pioglitazone has no proven cardiovascular benefit in this setting and causes fluid retention and heart failure risk. E. DPP-4 inhibitors are cardiovascular-neutral; with established CVD an SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended for its proven benefit.
pearl: T2DM with ASCVD: metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor (+ semaglutide per NG28 2026).
thinking: New type 2 diabetes + established atherosclerotic CVD ↓ cardiovascular-protective therapy needed from the start ↓ metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor (C)
exam_trap: B, a sulfonylurea — an effective glucose-lowering drug, so a plausible choice. But it carries hypoglycaemia and weight-gain risk and no cardiovascular benefit; with established CVD, metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred.
takeaway: T2DM with ASCVD: metformin + SGLT2 inhibitor (+ semaglutide per NG28 2026).

stem: A 68-year-old woman has a fragility fracture of the wrist and a DXA T-score of -2.8. She has no contraindications. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: Oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D
options.B: Combined hormone replacement therapy with calcium and vitamin D
options.C: Calcium and vitamin D alone, with a falls assessment
options.D: Daily subcutaneous teriparatide with calcium and vitamin D
options.E: Six-monthly subcutaneous denosumab with calcium and vitamin D

correct_answer: A. Oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D
why_correct: A fragility fracture with osteoporotic bone density is treated first-line with an oral bisphosphonate (with adequate calcium and vitamin D), which reduces future fracture risk.
why_wrong: B. HRT is not first-line treatment for osteoporosis in a 68-year-old because of its risks. C. Calcium and vitamin D alone do not adequately reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis; a bisphosphonate is the first-line agent. D. Teriparatide is reserved for severe osteoporosis (e.g. multiple vertebral fractures or very low T-scores) or failure of other treatment. E. Denosumab is used when oral bisphosphonates are unsuitable or not tolerated, not first-line.
pearl: Osteoporosis after a fragility fracture is treated with a bisphosphonate plus calcium and vitamin D — supplements alone are not enough.
thinking: 68-year-old woman + wrist fragility fracture + T-score −2.8 ↓ established osteoporosis, high fracture risk ↓ oral alendronate with calcium and vitamin D (A)
exam_trap: C, calcium and vitamin D alone — they support bone and are co-prescribed, so they feel sufficient. But on their own they do not adequately reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis; a bisphosphonate is the first-line agent.
takeaway: Osteoporosis after a fragility fracture is treated with a bisphosphonate plus calcium and vitamin D — supplements alone are not enough.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with lupus develops breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis, alongside a rising creatinine and new confusion, over 48 hours. Imaging confirms pulmonary emboli, and she has widespread small-vessel thrombosis. She is known to be antiphospholipid-antibody positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rapid multi-organ thrombosis affecting three or more systems over days, in a patient with antiphospholipid antibodies, defines catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome — a rare, high-mortality emergency needing anticoagulation, steroids and often plasma exchange.
why_wrong: A. Lupus pneumonitis can cause breathlessness and haemoptysis, but it does not explain confirmed pulmonary emboli, renal failure and confusion from widespread small-vessel thrombosis. C. Pulmonary vasculitis is plausible with haemoptysis and renal involvement in lupus, but the dominant process here is thrombosis rather than vessel-wall inflammation, and her antiphospholipid status points to a clotting catastrophe. D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation needs a trigger such as sepsis or trauma and causes consumptive bleeding as well as clotting; the stem gives no trigger and the picture is pure thrombosis in an antibody-positive patient. E. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura causes microangiopathic haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia and confusion, but not large-vessel pulmonary emboli, and nothing here suggests haemolysis.
pearl: Simultaneous thrombosis in several organs plus antiphospholipid antibodies is catastrophic APS — recognise the clotting storm and treat it hard and fast.
thinking: Lupus patient known to be antiphospholipid-antibody positive ↓ Pulmonary emboli plus renal failure and confusion within 48 hours — three organ systems at once ↓ Widespread small-vessel thrombosis confirms a thrombotic storm rather than inflammation ↓ Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome
exam_trap: C, pulmonary vasculitis — plausible in a lupus patient with haemoptysis and renal involvement. But the dominant process here is widespread thrombosis, not inflammation of vessel walls, and the antiphospholipid status points to a clotting catastrophe.
takeaway: Simultaneous thrombosis in several organs plus antiphospholipid antibodies is catastrophic APS — recognise the clotting storm and treat it hard and fast.

stem: A 50-year-old woman had surgery 18 months ago for early oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer and takes adjuvant tamoxifen. Her recent oncology follow-up showed no evidence of recurrence. She now presents with a confirmed pulmonary embolism. She has had no recent surgery, immobility or long-distance travel. Which factor most likely provoked her thrombosis?
why_correct: Tamoxifen is a selective oestrogen receptor modulator with a recognised prothrombotic effect, and is the most likely provoking factor for venous thromboembolism in a patient otherwise free of surgery or immobility.
why_wrong: A. Age 50 adds only a modest background risk and is not a specific provoking factor for a new pulmonary embolism. B. Her recent follow-up showed no evidence of recurrence and she is not receiving antimitotic treatment, so occult progression of the cancer is unsupported, whereas tamoxifen carries a direct, well-described thrombotic risk. C. An undiagnosed inherited thrombophilia is speculative; it should not be assumed when a known prothrombotic drug is present, and testing is not routine. E. She is a 50-year-old with breast cancer, in whom combined oral contraception is contraindicated, and nothing in the stem says she takes it; the hormonal agent she is on is tamoxifen.
pearl: When VTE appears 'unprovoked', check the drug chart — tamoxifen and oestrogens provoke clots that are easy to label idiopathic.
thinking: New pulmonary embolism with no recent surgery or immobility ↓ She takes tamoxifen, a selective oestrogen receptor modulator ↓ Tamoxifen has a recognised prothrombotic effect and is a known drug provocation ↓ Tamoxifen
exam_trap: B, the cancer itself — malignancy is genuinely thrombogenic, so it is a reasonable thought. But she is in remission after surgery with no recurrence on recent follow-up, while tamoxifen carries a direct, well-described thrombotic risk and is the identifiable provocation here.
takeaway: When VTE appears 'unprovoked', check the drug chart — tamoxifen and oestrogens provoke clots that are easy to label idiopathic.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has jaundice, fatigue and dark urine. Hb 70, reticulocytes raised, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH high, haptoglobin low. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive for IgG. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Haemolysis (raised reticulocytes and LDH, low haptoglobin, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia) with a DAT positive for IgG is warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, treated first-line with corticosteroids.
why_wrong: A. Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia is DAT-negative and shows red-cell fragments (schistocytes), usually with low platelets; a positive DAT points to immune haemolysis. B. Cold agglutinin disease is IgM-mediated with a DAT positive for complement (C3), not IgG; the IgG-positive DAT marks the warm type. C. Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited membrane defect with a negative DAT, usually presenting earlier in life with a family history. D. G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidant-triggered haemolysis with a negative DAT and bite cells or Heinz bodies on the film.
pearl: A DAT positive for IgG is warm autoimmune haemolysis (treat with steroids); complement-positive points to the cold type instead.
thinking: Jaundice, dark urine and anaemia with raised reticulocytes ↓ High LDH and unconjugated bilirubin with low haptoglobin confirm haemolysis ↓ DAT positive for IgG means antibody-mediated, warm-reacting haemolysis ↓ Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
exam_trap: B, cold agglutinin disease — the other autoimmune haemolysis, so the natural pair. But cold agglutinin disease is IgM-mediated with the DAT positive for complement (C3), not IgG; the IgG-positive DAT here marks the warm type.
takeaway: A DAT positive for IgG is warm autoimmune haemolysis (treat with steroids); complement-positive points to the cold type instead.

stem: A 65-year-old man with low vitamin B12 has tingling feet, an unsteady gait, reduced vibration and proprioception, and brisk knee reflexes with up-going plantars. He is also anaemic. What is the most appropriate management sequence?

options.A: Replace B12 first, and replace folate only after or alongside
options.B: Replace folate first to correct the macrocytic anaemia quickly
options.C: Oral folic acid alone, then recheck B12 in three months
options.D: Oral ferrous sulfate, then repeat the full blood count in a month
options.E: Nerve conduction studies before starting any replacement

correct_answer: A. Replace B12 first, and replace folate only after or alongside
why_correct: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord from B12 deficiency is treated by replacing B12; giving folate before B12 in a deficient patient can precipitate or worsen the neurological damage, so B12 comes first.
why_wrong: B. Folate without B12 in a B12-deficient patient can worsen the cord degeneration; B12 must be replaced first. C. Folate alone in B12 deficiency risks precipitating or worsening neurological damage. D. There is no evidence of iron deficiency; the picture is B12-deficiency neurology. E. Treatment should not be delayed for investigations, as neurological damage may become permanent.
pearl: In B12 deficiency, replace B12 before folate — folate first can tip the cord into irreversible damage.
thinking: Low B12 + dorsal column loss + upper motor neurone signs ↓ subacute combined degeneration ↓ replace B12 before or with folate (A)
exam_trap: B, folate first — it would correct the macrocytic anaemia, so it looks helpful. But folate without B12 in a B12-deficient patient can worsen the cord degeneration; B12 must be replaced first.
takeaway: In B12 deficiency, replace B12 before folate — folate first can tip the cord into irreversible damage.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has lifelong easy bruising, heavy periods and prolonged bleeding after dental work. Her father has similar symptoms. Platelet count is normal, APTT is mildly prolonged, and von Willebrand factor and ristocetin cofactor activity are low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with an autosomal pattern, a mildly prolonged APTT and low von Willebrand factor activity is von Willebrand disease — the commonest inherited bleeding disorder.
why_wrong: A. Haemophilia A also prolongs the APTT, but it is X-linked and so rarely affects women severely, and causes deep joint and muscle bleeds; her mucocutaneous bleeding with low von Willebrand factor activity is von Willebrand disease. C. Immune thrombocytopenia causes mucocutaneous bleeding but with a low platelet count, whereas her count is normal and the bleeding is lifelong and familial. D. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a rare autosomal recessive platelet function disorder with a normal APTT and normal von Willebrand factor levels. E. Vitamin K deficiency is acquired and prolongs the PT more than the APTT; it does not explain lifelong bleeding inherited from her father or a low von Willebrand factor.
pearl: Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with low von Willebrand factor is vWD — haemophilia is X-linked and bleeds into joints, not gums.
thinking: Lifelong bruising, heavy periods and bleeding after dental work — mucocutaneous bleeding ↓ Father affected too, so inheritance is autosomal rather than X-linked ↓ Normal platelets, mildly prolonged APTT and low von Willebrand factor with low ristocetin cofactor activity ↓ Von Willebrand disease
exam_trap: A, haemophilia A — it also prolongs the APTT, making it a reasonable thought. But haemophilia is X-linked (affecting males) with deep joint and muscle bleeds, whereas this woman has mucocutaneous bleeding and a low von Willebrand factor.
takeaway: Lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding with low von Willebrand factor is vWD — haemophilia is X-linked and bleeds into joints, not gums.

stem: A 28-year-old woman, recently over a viral illness, develops widespread petechiae, bruising and gum bleeding. Her platelet count is 12 × 10⁹/L, but haemoglobin, white cells and the blood film are otherwise normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Isolated thrombocytopenia with an otherwise normal blood count and film, often after a viral illness, is immune thrombocytopenia — a diagnosis of exclusion caused by antibody-mediated platelet destruction.
why_wrong: A. Disseminated intravascular coagulation occurs in a seriously ill patient with a trigger such as sepsis, and causes prolonged clotting times and fragments on the film, not isolated thrombocytopenia in a well woman. B. Acute leukaemia usually disturbs the other cell lines and shows blasts on the film; isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film points to immune destruction. D. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura causes microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with fragments on the film, often with neurological or renal features, whereas her haemoglobin and film are normal. E. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia, not isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal haemoglobin and white count.
pearl: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film is ITP — when the other cell lines are affected, think marrow infiltration instead.
thinking: Recent viral illness, then petechiae, bruising and gum bleeding ↓ Platelet count 12 × 10⁹/L with normal haemoglobin, white cells and film — isolated thrombocytopenia ↓ No other line affected, so marrow failure, infiltration and microangiopathy are unlikely ↓ Immune thrombocytopenia
exam_trap: B, acute leukaemia — a feared cause of a low platelet count, so an understandable worry. But leukaemia usually disturbs the other cell lines and the film; here the isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film points to immune destruction.
takeaway: Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film is ITP — when the other cell lines are affected, think marrow infiltration instead.
