stem: A 35-year-old woman has had two unprovoked deep vein thromboses. Thrombophilia testing shows activated protein C resistance. What is the most likely underlying abnormality?
why_correct: Activated protein C resistance is caused, in the great majority of cases, by the Factor V Leiden mutation, which makes factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C — the commonest inherited thrombophilia.
why_wrong: A. The prothrombin gene mutation raises prothrombin levels and causes thrombosis, but it does not cause activated protein C resistance. B. Antithrombin deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia detected by a low antithrombin level, not by an activated protein C resistance assay. C. Protein C deficiency sounds like the obvious answer, but the abnormality here is resistance to protein C action, not a lack of protein C, and is due to the Factor V Leiden mutation. D. Antiphospholipid syndrome is an acquired thrombophilia diagnosed by persistent lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies, not by inherited activated protein C resistance.
pearl: Activated protein C resistance means Factor V Leiden — the clotting factor resists protein C, rather than protein C being lacking.
thinking: Two unprovoked DVTs in a young woman ↓ Thrombophilia screen shows activated protein C resistance ↓ Factor V is resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, which is almost always the inherited Factor V Leiden variant ↓ Factor V Leiden mutation
exam_trap: C, protein C deficiency — the name sounds like the obvious cause of 'protein C resistance'. But the abnormality is resistance to protein C action, not a deficiency of it, and is due to the Factor V Leiden mutation.
takeaway: Activated protein C resistance means Factor V Leiden — the clotting factor resists protein C, rather than protein C being lacking.

stem: A 65-year-old man has fatigue and a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low ferritin. He has no obvious source of blood loss and is not vegetarian. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Oral iron, repeating the full blood count in six months' time
options.B: Oral iron, with GI investigation if he fails to respond to it
options.C: Transfuse two units of red cells and arrange GP follow-up
options.D: Coeliac serology alone, with oral iron if the result is negative
options.E: Investigate the GI tract with upper and lower endoscopy

correct_answer: E. Investigate the GI tract with upper and lower endoscopy
why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man (or postmenopausal woman) mandates investigation of the gastrointestinal tract for occult bleeding, especially malignancy, in addition to iron replacement.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency is a sign, not a diagnosis; delaying investigation risks missing a GI cancer. B. Response to iron does not exclude malignancy; unexplained iron deficiency in this group needs GI investigation now. C. Transfusion is not indicated for a stable patient with fatigue, and it leaves the cause uninvestigated. D. Coeliac serology is part of the work-up, but a negative result does not remove the need for upper and lower GI endoscopy.
pearl: Iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man is a GI cancer until the scopes say otherwise — replace the iron and find the source.
thinking: Older man with unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ No obvious cause in this group means occult GI blood loss or malignancy ↓ Bidirectional endoscopy (E)
exam_trap: B, oral iron with GI investigation only if he fails to respond. Correcting the anaemia feels like completing the job, but a response to iron does not exclude a GI cancer. Unexplained iron deficiency in this group needs upper and lower GI investigation now, alongside iron replacement.
takeaway: Iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man is a GI cancer until the scopes say otherwise — replace the iron and find the source.

stem: A 70-year-old man has bone pain, fatigue, an acute kidney injury and hypercalcaemia. Blood film shows rouleaux, and there is a paraprotein band on serum electrophoresis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: The CRAB features (hyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions) with a serum paraprotein and rouleaux are multiple myeloma — a plasma-cell malignancy confirmed by electrophoresis, urinary light chains and marrow biopsy.
why_wrong: A. Metastatic prostate cancer can cause bone pain and hypercalcaemia in an older man, but it does not produce a serum paraprotein band or rouleaux, which point to a plasma-cell dyscrasia. C. Primary hyperparathyroidism explains hypercalcaemia and can cause bone pain, but it does not produce a paraprotein band or rouleaux. D. Chronic kidney disease alone would not explain the paraprotein band, rouleaux and hypercalcaemia; here the kidney injury is a consequence of myeloma. E. Iron-deficiency anaemia could cause fatigue but not hypercalcaemia, bone pain, renal injury or a paraprotein.
pearl: Bone pain with hyperCalcaemia, Renal failure and Anaemia plus a paraprotein is myeloma — CRAB plus the band makes the diagnosis.
thinking: Older man with bone pain, fatigue, AKI and hypercalcaemia ↓ These are the CRAB features of a plasma-cell disorder ↓ Rouleaux and a paraprotein band on electrophoresis confirm a monoclonal protein ↓ The diagnosis is multiple myeloma
exam_trap: A, metastatic prostate cancer — it also causes bone pain and hypercalcaemia in an older man. But the paraprotein band and rouleaux point specifically to a plasma-cell dyscrasia (myeloma), not a solid tumour.
takeaway: Bone pain with hyperCalcaemia, Renal failure and Anaemia plus a paraprotein is myeloma — CRAB plus the band makes the diagnosis.

stem: Minutes into a blood transfusion, a patient develops fever, loin pain, dark urine and hypotension, with a feeling of impending doom. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Stop the transfusion immediately and begin resuscitation
options.B: Slow the transfusion rate and recheck observations in 15 minutes
options.C: Give paracetamol and continue the same unit at a slower rate
options.D: Give IV chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion
options.E: Complete the unit, then send a direct antiglobulin test (DAT)

correct_answer: A. Stop the transfusion immediately and begin resuscitation
why_correct: Fever, loin pain, haemoglobinuria and shock soon after starting a transfusion suggests an acute haemolytic (ABO-incompatibility) reaction; the transfusion is stopped immediately and the patient resuscitated, with the unit and patient identity rechecked.
why_wrong: B. Slowing the rate suits a mild febrile reaction, but loin pain, haemoglobinuria and shock indicate a life-threatening haemolytic reaction; the transfusion must be stopped at once. C. Paracetamol treats a simple febrile reaction; continuing an incompatible unit worsens haemolysis. D. An antihistamine treats mild allergic reactions; this is acute haemolysis and the transfusion must stop. E. Completing the unit gives more incompatible blood; the transfusion is stopped immediately and investigations sent afterwards.
pearl: Stop the transfusion the moment haemolysis is suspected — loin pain and dark urine are not a 'slow it down' reaction.
thinking: Fever, loin pain, dark urine, hypotension minutes into transfusion ↓ acute haemolytic reaction ↓ stop and resuscitate (A)
exam_trap: B, slow and continue — milder febrile reactions can be managed by slowing the rate, so this feels proportionate. But the loin pain, haemoglobinuria and shock indicate a life-threatening haemolytic reaction; the transfusion must be stopped at once.
takeaway: Stop the transfusion the moment haemolysis is suspected — loin pain and dark urine are not a 'slow it down' reaction.

stem: A middle-aged person has fatigue, weight loss and massive splenomegaly. The blood film shows a markedly raised white cell count with the full spectrum of maturing granulocytes, and the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL) is present. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.B: Urgent allogeneic stem cell transplant for all
options.E: No treatment, as it is benign

correct_answer: C. A tyrosine kinase inhibitor (e.g. imatinib)
why_correct: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (raised granulocytes across the maturation spectrum, splenomegaly, Philadelphia chromosome/BCR-ABL) is treated first-line with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib, which targets the BCR-ABL fusion protein.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not treat CML; there is no infection described. B. CML is controlled effectively with tyrosine kinase inhibitors first-line; allogeneic transplant is reserved for resistant or advanced-phase disease. D. Splenectomy does not treat the underlying BCR-ABL-driven disease. E. CML is a malignancy that progresses to blast crisis without treatment.
pearl: CML with BCR-ABL is treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib) — the targeted drug is first-line, not upfront transplant.
thinking: Massive splenomegaly + granulocytes across maturation + BCR-ABL ↓ CML ↓ tyrosine kinase inhibitor (C)
exam_trap: B, allogeneic transplant for everyone — transplant is curative in some leukaemias, so it is tempting. But CML is controlled effectively with tyrosine kinase inhibitors first-line; transplant is reserved for resistant or advanced disease.
takeaway: CML with BCR-ABL is treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib) — the targeted drug is first-line, not upfront transplant.

stem: A young man of Mediterranean origin develops sudden jaundice and dark urine with anaemia after eating fava beans (or taking a new oxidant drug). The blood film shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Sickle cell disease with a haemolytic crisis

why_correct: Episodic haemolysis triggered by oxidant stress (fava beans, certain drugs, infection) with bite cells and Heinz bodies, in an X-linked pattern, is G6PD deficiency; management is to avoid triggers and treat the acute haemolysis supportively.
why_wrong: A. Autoimmune haemolysis is DAT-positive with spherocytes and is not triggered by fava beans or oxidant drugs. B. Spherocytosis causes chronic haemolysis with spherocytes, whereas OXIDANT-triggered haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies indicates G6PD deficiency. C. Sickle cell disease shows sickled cells on the film and is not precipitated by fava beans. E. Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic haemolysis that is not triggered by oxidant stress and does not produce Heinz bodies and bite cells.
pearl: Oxidant-triggered haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies is G6PD deficiency — avoid the triggers (fava beans, oxidant drugs).
thinking: Haemolysis after fava beans/oxidant drug + bite cells and Heinz bodies ↓ oxidant haemolysis ↓ G6PD deficiency (D)
exam_trap: B, hereditary spherocytosis — another inherited haemolytic anaemia, so a reasonable thought. But spherocytosis gives chronic haemolysis with spherocytes and a positive osmotic fragility, whereas the OXIDANT-triggered haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies here is G6PD deficiency.
takeaway: Oxidant-triggered haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies is G6PD deficiency — avoid the triggers (fava beans, oxidant drugs).

stem: A patient is admitted to hospital with reduced mobility. What is the most appropriate approach to venous thromboembolism prevention?

options.A: Encourage mobilisation and hydration, reserving LMWH for confirmed DVT
options.B: Prophylactic LMWH on admission, without a documented risk assessment
options.C: Assess VTE and bleeding risk, offering LMWH unless contraindicated
options.D: Graduated compression stockings as the sole method for medical patients
options.E: Treatment-dose LMWH until the patient is fully mobile

correct_answer: C. Assess VTE and bleeding risk, offering LMWH unless contraindicated
why_correct: All hospital admissions should have a documented assessment of VTE risk balanced against bleeding risk; those at risk are offered pharmacological prophylaxis (usually LMWH) unless contraindicated, with mechanical prophylaxis where drugs are unsuitable.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for a clot defeats the purpose of prophylaxis in an at-risk immobile patient. B. Anticoagulant prophylaxis must be balanced against bleeding risk through individual assessment; it is not given without one. D. Stockings alone are not adequate prophylaxis for an at-risk medical patient; NICE recommends pharmacological prophylaxis (LMWH first-line) when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, and advises against stockings altogether in acute stroke. E. Treatment-dose anticoagulation increases bleeding risk and is not used for prophylaxis.
pearl: Every admission gets a VTE and bleeding risk assessment — prophylaxis is offered when the balance favours it, not given blindly.
thinking: Admission with reduced mobility ↓ Assess VTE risk AND bleeding risk on admission ↓ Offer LMWH if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, unless contraindicated
exam_trap: B, give LMWH to everyone without assessment — universal prophylaxis seems safe. But anticoagulant prophylaxis must be balanced against bleeding risk through individual assessment; it is not given blindly to all.
takeaway: Every admission gets a VTE and bleeding risk assessment — prophylaxis is offered when the balance favours it, not given blindly.

stem: A patient of Mediterranean (or Southeast Asian) origin has a microcytic anaemia with a very low MCV that seems disproportionate to the mild drop in haemoglobin. Ferritin is normal, and the anaemia does not respond to a trial of iron. What is the most appropriate explanation and next test?

options.A: Occult GI blood loss — arrange bidirectional upper and lower GI endoscopy
options.B: Iron-deficiency anaemia — switch to IV iron and recheck the count in 4 weeks
options.C: Anaemia of chronic disease — check CRP and ESR and look for inflammation
options.D: Sideroblastic anaemia — bone marrow examination with iron stain
options.E: Thalassaemia trait — confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC

correct_answer: E. Thalassaemia trait — confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC
why_correct: A microcytic anaemia with a disproportionately low MCV, normal ferritin and no response to iron, in a relevant ethnic group, suggests thalassaemia trait; haemoglobin electrophoresis (a raised HbA2 in beta-thalassaemia trait) confirms it and avoids unnecessary iron.
why_wrong: A. A normal ferritin argues against iron loss from occult bleeding. B. The NORMAL ferritin and failure to respond to iron point away from iron deficiency and towards thalassaemia trait. C. Anaemia of chronic disease is usually normocytic or mildly microcytic, without a disproportionately low MCV, and no inflammatory illness is described. D. Sideroblastic anaemia is rare; the ethnic background and disproportionately low MCV with normal ferritin point to thalassaemia trait, so electrophoresis comes first.
pearl: Microcytic anaemia with normal ferritin that ignores iron is thalassaemia trait — check haemoglobin electrophoresis (raised HbA2).
thinking: Very low MCV out of proportion to Hb + normal ferritin + no iron response ↓ thalassaemia trait ↓ Hb electrophoresis/HPLC (E)
exam_trap: B, iron-deficiency anaemia — microcytosis usually means iron deficiency, so it is the default. But the NORMAL ferritin and failure to respond to iron point away from iron deficiency and towards thalassaemia trait, confirmed on electrophoresis.
takeaway: Microcytic anaemia with normal ferritin that ignores iron is thalassaemia trait — check haemoglobin electrophoresis (raised HbA2).

stem: A patient has persistent painless lymphadenopathy with night sweats, weight loss and fevers ('B symptoms'). Lymphoma is suspected. What is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis and type?

options.A: A trial of antibiotics and review
options.E: Reassurance and review in six months

why_correct: Suspected lymphoma (persistent painless lymphadenopathy with B symptoms) is investigated with an excisional lymph node biopsy, because the nodal architecture — not just cell morphology — is needed to diagnose and subtype the lymphoma; fine-needle aspiration is usually insufficient.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not treat lymphoma, and a trial of them delays a tissue diagnosis when B symptoms are present. B. FNA samples cells without preserving the nodal architecture, so it is usually inadequate to diagnose and subtype lymphoma. D. An FBC may be abnormal but cannot establish a diagnosis of lymphoma or its type. E. Persistent lymphadenopathy with B symptoms needs urgent tissue diagnosis, so waiting six months is unsafe.
pearl: Suspected lymphoma needs an excisional lymph node biopsy — FNA cannot show the architecture that defines the type.
thinking: Persistent painless lymphadenopathy with B symptoms ↓ Suspected lymphoma needs nodal architecture for diagnosis and subtyping ↓ Excisional lymph node biopsy (C)
exam_trap: B, fine-needle aspiration cytology alone — FNA is less invasive and useful for some lumps. But it samples cells without preserving the nodal architecture, so it is usually inadequate for lymphoma; an excisional biopsy is required.
takeaway: Suspected lymphoma needs an excisional lymph node biopsy — FNA cannot show the architecture that defines the type.

stem: A patient has anaemia with a raised mean cell volume (macrocytosis). What is the most appropriate set of initial investigations to find the cause?

options.A: Ferritin and a trial of oral iron for three months
options.B: Haemoglobin electrophoresis and a reticulocyte count
options.C: Faecal immunochemical test and urgent colonoscopy
options.D: B12, folate, TFTs and LFTs, with alcohol and drug history
options.E: Repeat the FBC in three months before any testing

correct_answer: D. B12, folate, TFTs and LFTs, with alcohol and drug history
why_correct: Macrocytic anaemia (raised MCV) is investigated for B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic causes) and for non-megaloblastic causes such as alcohol excess, liver disease, hypothyroidism, certain drugs and myelodysplasia; iron deficiency causes a MICROcytic, not macrocytic, anaemia.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency causes a MICROcytic anaemia; a high MCV points to B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism or drugs. B. Electrophoresis is for suspected haemoglobinopathy in microcytic anaemia, not the first-line work-up of macrocytosis. C. GI blood loss causes iron-deficiency (microcytic) anaemia, not macrocytosis. E. Delaying investigation risks missing B12 deficiency, which can cause irreversible neurological damage.
pearl: Macrocytic anaemia points to B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease or hypothyroidism — not iron deficiency, which is microcytic.
thinking: Anaemia with a high MCV ↓ Consider B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs and myelodysplasia ↓ B12, folate, TFTs, LFTs with alcohol and drug history (D)
exam_trap: A, ferritin and a trial of oral iron — iron is the reflex treatment for anaemia. But iron deficiency causes a low MCV (microcytic) anaemia; a HIGH MCV points instead to B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease or hypothyroidism, which should be investigated.
takeaway: Macrocytic anaemia points to B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, liver disease or hypothyroidism — not iron deficiency, which is microcytic.

stem: A boy has recurrent bleeding into joints (haemarthroses) and prolonged bleeding after minor injury. Coagulation studies show a prolonged APTT with a normal PT and normal platelets. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX and X)
options.C: Haemophilia A or B (factor VIII or IX deficiency)

correct_answer: C. Haemophilia A or B (factor VIII or IX deficiency)
why_correct: Recurrent haemarthroses and a prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets in a boy indicate haemophilia (X-linked deficiency of factor VIII — haemophilia A — or factor IX — haemophilia B); management involves factor replacement and avoiding intramuscular injections and NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT first (factor VII has the shortest half-life), not an isolated APTT. B. ITP causes a low platelet count with mucocutaneous bleeding and normal clotting times, whereas a prolonged APTT with normal platelets and haemarthroses indicates a clotting factor deficiency. D. DIC occurs in acute illness with low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT and low fibrinogen. E. Platelet function disorders cause mucocutaneous bleeding with a normal APTT, not haemarthroses.
pearl: Haemarthroses with an isolated prolonged APTT (normal PT/platelets) in a boy is haemophilia (factor VIII/IX deficiency, X-linked).
thinking: A boy has recurrent bleeding into joints (haemarthroses) and prolonged ↓ A prolonged APTT with NORMAL PT and NORMAL platelets, plus haemarthroses — that
exam_trap: B, immune thrombocytopenia — both cause bleeding. But ITP causes a low platelet count with mucocutaneous/petechial bleeding and normal clotting times, whereas the prolonged APTT with normal platelets and haemarthroses here indicates a clotting-factor deficiency (haemophilia).
takeaway: Haemarthroses with an isolated prolonged APTT (normal PT/platelets) in a boy is haemophilia (factor VIII/IX deficiency, X-linked).

stem: A patient who has had a splenectomy has a blood film showing Howell-Jolly bodies. What is the most important long-term management to reduce a serious risk?

options.B: Lifelong low-dose aspirin to prevent post-splenectomy thrombosis
options.C: Annual blood film and ultrasound to monitor for splenunculi
options.D: Avoidance of live vaccines, with no other specific measures
options.E: Regular haematology review with iron and folate supplementation

correct_answer: A. Encapsulated-organism vaccines and prophylactic antibiotics
why_correct: Howell-Jolly bodies on the film indicate hyposplenism/asplenia; these patients are at risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcus), so they need vaccination against these organisms and often prophylactic antibiotics, plus prompt treatment of febrile illness.
why_wrong: B. Thrombocytosis after splenectomy is usually transient; the major lifelong risk is overwhelming post-splenectomy infection. C. Monitoring the film or spleen does not reduce the risk of overwhelming infection. D. Asplenia does not contraindicate live vaccines, and vaccination against encapsulated organisms is essential. E. Haematinic supplements do not address the risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.
pearl: Howell-Jolly bodies indicate hyposplenism — vaccinate against encapsulated organisms and consider antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent overwhelming sepsis.
thinking: Splenectomy + Howell-Jolly bodies ↓ asplenia ↓ encapsulated-organism vaccines and antibiotic prophylaxis (A)
exam_trap: D, avoid live vaccines with no other measures — the patient may feel well. But asplenia does not contraindicate live vaccines, and lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection requires vaccination against encapsulated organisms and antibiotic prophylaxis.
takeaway: Howell-Jolly bodies indicate hyposplenism — vaccinate against encapsulated organisms and consider antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent overwhelming sepsis.

stem: An older patient is found incidentally to have a markedly raised lymphocyte count, with smear (smudge) cells on the blood film and painless lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: A reactive lymphocytosis from a simple viral infection

why_correct: An older patient with a persistent marked lymphocytosis, smudge cells on the film and lymphadenopathy most likely has chronic lymphocytic leukaemia; it is often indolent and may be monitored ('watch and wait') if asymptomatic and early-stage.
why_wrong: A. A viral illness can raise the lymphocyte count, but a marked lymphocytosis with smudge cells and lymphadenopathy in an older patient indicates chronic lymphocytic leukaemia rather than a transient reactive rise. B. Acute myeloid leukaemia presents with marrow failure and myeloblasts on the film, not an incidental mature lymphocytosis with smudge cells. C. Iron-deficiency anaemia causes a microcytic anaemia and does not raise the lymphocyte count or cause lymphadenopathy. E. Chronic myeloid leukaemia causes a neutrophilia with myelocytes and basophilia and marked splenomegaly, not a lymphocytosis with smudge cells.
pearl: Persistent lymphocytosis with smudge cells and lymphadenopathy in an older patient is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia — often watch-and-wait if early.
thinking: Older patient with an incidental marked lymphocytosis ↓ Smudge cells on the film reflect fragile neoplastic B lymphocytes ↓ Painless lymphadenopathy fits a chronic lymphoproliferative disorder ↓ The diagnosis is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
exam_trap: A, a reactive lymphocytosis from a simple viral infection — viral illness can raise lymphocytes. But a persistent, markedly raised lymphocyte count with smudge cells in an older patient indicates chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, not a transient reactive rise.
takeaway: Persistent lymphocytosis with smudge cells and lymphadenopathy in an older patient is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia — often watch-and-wait if early.

stem: An adult presents with fatigue, bruising and infections. The blood film shows myeloblasts, some containing rod-shaped inclusions (Auer rods). What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Marrow-failure symptoms (anaemia, bruising, infections) with myeloblasts and Auer rods on the film indicate acute myeloid leukaemia, which requires urgent haematology referral; it is commoner in adults.
why_wrong: A. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia shows mature lymphocytes and smudge cells, not myeloblasts with Auer rods. C. A reactive neutrophilia from infection raises mature neutrophils but does not produce myeloblasts containing Auer rods. D. Iron-deficiency anaemia causes fatigue but not bruising, infections or blasts on the film. E. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, not myeloblasts with Auer rods.
pearl: Myeloblasts with Auer rods and marrow failure is acute myeloid leukaemia — urgent haematology referral.
thinking: Adult with fatigue, bruising and infections ↓ This is a marrow-failure picture ↓ Myeloblasts with Auer rods are specific to a myeloid blast population ↓ The diagnosis is acute myeloid leukaemia
exam_trap: C, a reactive neutrophilia from infection — infection raises the white count. But a reactive picture does not produce myeloblasts with Auer rods; these indicate acute myeloid leukaemia.
takeaway: Myeloblasts with Auer rods and marrow failure is acute myeloid leukaemia — urgent haematology referral.

stem: A patient on warfarin has deranged clotting. Which pattern of the coagulation screen is most consistent with warfarin's effect?

options.A: An isolated prolonged thrombin time with a low fibrinogen
options.B: An isolated prolonged APTT with a normal prothrombin time
options.C: A low platelet count with normal PT/INR and APTT
options.E: Prolonged bleeding time with a normal PT/INR and APTT

correct_answer: D. A prolonged PT/INR (reduced vitamin-K-dependent factors)
why_correct: Warfarin inhibits vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), and because factor VII (extrinsic pathway) has a short half-life, the prothrombin time (PT/INR) is prolonged and is used for monitoring; heparin chiefly prolongs the APTT, while haemophilia gives an isolated prolonged APTT.
why_wrong: A. A prolonged thrombin time suggests heparin effect or low or abnormal fibrinogen (e.g. DIC or a fibrinogen disorder), not warfarin. B. An isolated prolonged APTT suggests heparin or a factor VIII/IX deficiency; warfarin prolongs the PT/INR, which is why the INR is used for monitoring. C. Warfarin does not lower the platelet count. E. A prolonged bleeding time reflects platelet dysfunction; warfarin acts on clotting factors and prolongs the PT/INR.
pearl: Warfarin prolongs the PT/INR (vitamin-K-dependent factors); heparin prolongs the APTT — match the test to the drug.
thinking: Patient on warfarin with deranged clotting ↓ Warfarin reduces the vitamin-K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X ↓ Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so the prothrombin time is prolonged first ↓ A prolonged PT/INR
exam_trap: B, an isolated prolonged APTT with a normal PT — clotting abnormalities are easily mixed up. But an isolated prolonged APTT suggests heparin or a factor VIII/IX deficiency; warfarin prolongs the PT/INR, which is why the INR is used to monitor it.
takeaway: Warfarin prolongs the PT/INR (vitamin-K-dependent factors); heparin prolongs the APTT — match the test to the drug.

stem: Partway through a red-cell transfusion a patient develops an isolated fever and chills, but remains haemodynamically stable with no pain, no hypotension and no signs of haemolysis or anaphylaxis. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Stop the transfusion and give IV furosemide for presumed fluid overload
options.B: Continue at the same rate and recheck observations at the end of the unit
options.C: Stop, return the unit and treat as an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction
options.D: Give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms and stop the transfusion
options.E: Pause or slow it, give paracetamol and continue if no other features

correct_answer: E. Pause or slow it, give paracetamol and continue if no other features
why_correct: An isolated fever with chills during transfusion, without hypotension, pain, haemolysis or anaphylaxis, is most likely a febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction; management is to temporarily stop or slow the transfusion, give an antipyretic (e.g. paracetamol), and — after excluding more serious reactions — restart cautiously if the patient remains otherwise well.
why_wrong: A. There are no signs of fluid overload, so a diuretic is not indicated. B. A new fever needs assessment and a temporary pause or slowing of the transfusion; continuing unchanged risks missing an evolving reaction. C. An acute haemolytic reaction causes pain, hypotension and haemolysis, none of which is present; an isolated fever with stability is a febrile non-haemolytic reaction. D. There are no features of anaphylaxis, so adrenaline is not indicated.
pearl: An isolated fever during transfusion in a stable patient is a febrile non-haemolytic reaction — antipyretic and cautious continuation after excluding serious reactions.
thinking: Isolated fever and chills, stable, no pain, hypotension or haemolysis ↓ febrile non-haemolytic reaction ↓ pause/slow, paracetamol, continue if well (E)
exam_trap: C, treat as an acute haemolytic reaction and never transfuse again — serious reactions must be excluded. But an acute haemolytic reaction causes pain, hypotension and haemolysis, none of which are present; an isolated fever with stability is a febrile non-haemolytic reaction.
takeaway: An isolated fever during transfusion in a stable patient is a febrile non-haemolytic reaction — antipyretic and cautious continuation after excluding serious reactions.

stem: Soon after a transfusion begins, a patient develops urticaria, angioedema, wheeze and hypotension. This is a known risk in patients with IgA deficiency. What is the immediate management?

options.A: Slow the transfusion, give IV paracetamol and recheck observations at 15 minutes
options.B: Stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline, treating as anaphylaxis
options.C: Stop the transfusion and give IV furosemide for fluid overload
options.D: Give IV chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion more slowly
options.E: Give IV hydrocortisone and restart the unit once wheeze settles

correct_answer: B. Stop the transfusion and give IM adrenaline, treating as anaphylaxis
why_correct: Urticaria, angioedema, wheeze and hypotension during transfusion indicate an anaphylactic transfusion reaction (a recognised risk in IgA-deficient recipients with anti-IgA antibodies); the transfusion must be stopped immediately and anaphylaxis treated with intramuscular adrenaline and supportive care, with future use of washed/IgA-deficient products.
why_wrong: A. That is the response to a mild febrile reaction; airway and circulatory compromise is anaphylaxis, demanding immediate cessation and intramuscular adrenaline. C. Urticaria, angioedema and hypotension indicate anaphylaxis, not fluid overload. D. An antihistamine alone is inadequate for anaphylaxis, and the transfusion must not continue. E. Steroids are not first-line for anaphylaxis, and the implicated unit must not be restarted.
pearl: Anaphylaxis during transfusion (urticaria, wheeze, hypotension; classic in IgA deficiency) — stop immediately and give IM adrenaline.
thinking: Urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension during transfusion ↓ anaphylactic reaction ↓ stop and give IM adrenaline (B)
exam_trap: A, slow the transfusion and give an antipyretic — that is the response to a mild febrile reaction. But the airway/circulatory compromise here is anaphylaxis, demanding immediate cessation and intramuscular adrenaline.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis during transfusion (urticaria, wheeze, hypotension; classic in IgA deficiency) — stop immediately and give IM adrenaline.

stem: A haemodynamically stable patient without acute coronary syndrome has anaemia. What is the most appropriate red-cell transfusion strategy?

options.A: Oral iron instead of transfusion until haemoglobin falls below 50 g/L
options.B: A liberal threshold of 100 g/L to optimise tissue oxygen delivery
options.C: A restrictive threshold of about 70 g/L, individualised
options.D: Transfuse to a target haemoglobin of 120 g/L in older adults
options.E: Two units per transfusion episode, then recheck haemoglobin

correct_answer: C. A restrictive threshold of about 70 g/L, individualised
why_correct: In stable patients without active bleeding or acute coronary syndrome, a restrictive transfusion threshold (about 70 g/L, with a target of 70–90 g/L after transfusion; NICE suggests 80 g/L only for acute coronary syndrome) is recommended, as restrictive strategies are at least as safe as liberal ones and reduce transfusion-related harm; the decision is individualised, not based on a number alone.
why_wrong: A. A threshold of 50 g/L is unsafely low; the recommended restrictive threshold is around 70 g/L. B. Liberal transfusion offers no benefit and adds risk in stable patients; a restrictive threshold around 70 g/L is recommended. D. A high target exposes patients to transfusion risks without benefit. E. NICE advises single-unit transfusion followed by reassessment in non-bleeding patients.
pearl: In stable patients use a restrictive transfusion threshold (about 70 g/L; 80 g/L is reserved for acute coronary syndrome) — liberal transfusion adds risk without benefit.
thinking: Stable, no ACS, no bleeding ↓ restrictive strategy ↓ threshold about 70 g/L, individualised (C)
exam_trap: B, transfuse everyone below 100 g/L — a higher target may feel safer. But liberal transfusion offers no benefit and adds risk in stable patients; a restrictive threshold around 70 g/L is recommended.
takeaway: In stable patients use a restrictive transfusion threshold (about 70 g/L; 80 g/L is reserved for acute coronary syndrome) — liberal transfusion adds risk without benefit.

stem: A patient has a microcytic anaemia. The serum ferritin is low and the transferrin saturation is reduced. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A low serum ferritin is the most specific indicator of iron deficiency; combined with a reduced transferrin saturation in a microcytic anaemia, it confirms depleted iron stores.
why_wrong: A. Haemochromatosis causes iron overload with a high ferritin and high transferrin saturation, the opposite of these results. B. Anaemia of chronic disease can be microcytic, but ferritin is normal or raised as an acute-phase reactant; a low ferritin points to true iron deficiency. C. Beta-thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis with normal iron studies and a raised HbA2, not a low ferritin. E. Sideroblastic anaemia shows ring sideroblasts with normal or raised ferritin and iron, not depleted stores.
pearl: A low ferritin is the most specific test for iron deficiency; in anaemia of chronic disease ferritin is normal or high (acute-phase reactant), so check transferrin saturation when inflammation may be masking deficiency.
thinking: Microcytic anaemia ↓ Low ferritin means iron stores are depleted ↓ Low transferrin saturation confirms too little iron is available for red cell production ↓ The cause is iron deficiency
exam_trap: B, anaemia of chronic disease — it also causes a microcytic or normocytic anaemia. But in anaemia of chronic disease ferritin is normal or HIGH (it is an acute-phase reactant) with a low total iron-binding capacity; a LOW ferritin points to true iron deficiency.
takeaway: A low ferritin is the most specific test for iron deficiency; in anaemia of chronic disease ferritin is normal or high (acute-phase reactant), so check transferrin saturation when inflammation may be masking deficiency.

stem: A 55-year-old man with bulky high-grade lymphoma and a raised baseline urate is about to start chemotherapy. He is at high risk of tumour lysis. Alongside IV hydration, which agent is most appropriate to prevent it?
why_correct: In a high-risk patient with a high baseline urate, rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) rapidly breaks down existing uric acid and is preferred over allopurinol, which only prevents new urate formation.
why_wrong: A. Allopurinol prevents new urate formation but cannot clear existing urate; in high-risk patients with a raised baseline urate rasburicase is preferred. C. Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended and can precipitate calcium phosphate deposition. D. Furosemide is not a prophylactic agent and can worsen volume depletion. E. Calcium gluconate is used only for cardiac protection in symptomatic hyperkalaemia or hypocalcaemia, not prophylaxis.
pearl: Allopurinol prevents new urate; rasburicase destroys existing urate — choose rasburicase when the risk is high and the urate is already up.
thinking: Bulky high-grade lymphoma + raised baseline urate ↓ high TLS risk ↓ rasburicase with IV hydration (B)
exam_trap: A, allopurinol — the standard agent for lower-risk patients, and the familiar choice. But allopurinol cannot clear the urate already present; in a high-risk patient with established hyperuricaemia, rasburicase is preferred.
takeaway: Allopurinol prevents new urate; rasburicase destroys existing urate — choose rasburicase when the risk is high and the urate is already up.

stem: Which tumour marker is most appropriately paired with its associated malignancy?
why_correct: Tumour markers must be matched correctly: CA 19-9 is associated with pancreatic cancer; AFP with hepatocellular carcinoma and germ-cell tumours; beta-hCG with germ-cell/trophoblastic disease; CA-125 with ovarian cancer; CEA with colorectal cancer (mainly for monitoring); and PSA with prostate cancer. Markers are generally used for monitoring, not population screening, given imperfect specificity.
why_wrong: A. CA-125 is associated with OVARIAN cancer, while prostate cancer is associated with PSA. B. PSA is associated with prostate cancer; colorectal cancer is associated with CEA. D. AFP is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and germ-cell tumours, not breast cancer. E. Germ-cell tumours are associated with AFP and beta-hCG; CEA is associated with colorectal cancer.
pearl: CA 19-9 → pancreatic, CA-125 → ovarian, PSA → prostate, CEA → colorectal, AFP/β-hCG → germ-cell — markers monitor, they don't screen.
thinking: The question asks for a correctly matched marker and cancer ↓ CA-125 is ovarian, PSA prostate, AFP hepatocellular and germ-cell, CEA colorectal ↓ CA 19-9 is the marker associated with pancreatic cancer ↓ CA 19-9 with pancreatic cancer
exam_trap: A, CA-125 with prostate cancer — markers and cancers are easily mismatched. But CA-125 is associated with OVARIAN cancer, while prostate cancer is associated with PSA; correct pairing is essential.
takeaway: CA 19-9 → pancreatic, CA-125 → ovarian, PSA → prostate, CEA → colorectal, AFP/β-hCG → germ-cell — markers monitor, they don't screen.

stem: A 60-year-old man on long-term prednisolone for polymyalgia is admitted with severe pneumonia. He looks unwell with a borderline blood pressure. Regarding his steroids, what is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Stop prednisolone while the infection is being treated
options.B: Increase his steroid dose to cover the acute illness
options.C: Continue the usual prednisolone dose unchanged
options.D: Switch to inhaled budesonide to limit immunosuppression
options.E: Halve the dose to reduce the risk of worsening infection

correct_answer: B. Increase his steroid dose to cover the acute illness
why_correct: Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal axis; during acute illness the body cannot mount its own cortisol response, so the dose must be increased (sick-day rules) and never abruptly stopped, to avoid an adrenal crisis.
why_wrong: A. Abruptly stopping steroids in an adrenally suppressed patient under stress precipitates an adrenal crisis; the dose must go up. C. The usual dose does not cover the increased cortisol requirement of severe illness. D. Inhaled steroids give no systemic glucocorticoid cover and would precipitate an adrenal crisis. E. Reducing the dose during acute illness risks an adrenal crisis; the dose should be increased.
pearl: Long-term steroids need increasing, never stopping, during acute illness — sick-day rules prevent adrenal crisis.
thinking: Long-term prednisolone + severe pneumonia + borderline BP ↓ Adrenal suppression with increased stress requirement ↓ Increase steroid dose (sick-day rules); never stop
exam_trap: A, stop the steroid — infection plus immunosuppression makes stopping feel protective. But abruptly stopping in an adrenally-suppressed patient under stress precipitates an addisonian crisis; the dose must go up, not away.
takeaway: Long-term steroids need increasing, never stopping, during acute illness — sick-day rules prevent adrenal crisis.

stem: A 70-year-old man stable on warfarin is prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection by an out-of-hours doctor. Three days later his INR is 9.0 with no bleeding. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Continue warfarin at the same dose and recheck the INR in a week
options.B: Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K, and review the interacting antibiotic
options.C: Give prothrombin complex concentrate urgently to reverse warfarin
options.D: Increase the warfarin dose to counteract the effect of the antibiotic
options.E: Reassure him, as a high INR is expected and needs no change in dose

correct_answer: B. Withhold warfarin and give oral vitamin K, and review the interacting antibiotic
why_correct: Clarithromycin inhibits warfarin metabolism and raises the INR. The BNF advises that for an INR above 8 without bleeding, warfarin is stopped and oral vitamin K (phytomenadione 1–5 mg) is given, with warfarin restarted once the INR is below 5. The interacting antibiotic should be reviewed and the INR monitored closely. (For an INR of 5–8 without bleeding, the BNF advises withholding one or two doses and reducing the maintenance dose, without vitamin K.)
why_wrong: A. Continue warfarin at the same dose and recheck the INR in a week — with an INR above 8 the bleeding risk is high; the BNF advises stopping warfarin and giving oral vitamin K now. C. Give prothrombin complex concentrate urgently to reverse warfarin — PCC is for major bleeding; in a non-bleeding patient with an INR above 8, withholding warfarin and giving oral vitamin K is correct. D. Increase the warfarin dose to counteract the effect of the antibiotic — clarithromycin increases the anticoagulant effect, so a higher dose would raise the INR further. E. Reassure him, as a high INR is expected and needs no change in dose — an INR of 9.0 is dangerous even without bleeding and needs action now.
pearl: An INR above 8 without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin and giving oral vitamin K — save PCC for active major bleeding, and check the drug chart for the culprit.
thinking: Warfarin + clarithromycin → INR 9.0, no bleeding ↓ INR >8 without bleeding ↓ Stop warfarin, oral vitamin K 1–5 mg, review the antibiotic, restart when INR <5
exam_trap: C, prothrombin complex concentrate — the reversal agent for major bleeding, so it feels thorough for a high INR. But PCC is reserved for serious bleeding; in a non-bleeding patient with an INR above 8, withholding warfarin and giving oral vitamin K is correct.
takeaway: An INR above 8 without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin and giving oral vitamin K — save PCC for active major bleeding, and check the drug chart for the culprit.

stem: A 55-year-old woman is started on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. What is the single most important safety instruction and co-prescription?

options.A: Take it once daily, stopping if nausea or mouth ulcers develop
options.B: Take it once daily, with folic acid on the same day
options.C: Take it once weekly, avoiding folic acid supplements
options.D: Take it once weekly, with folic acid on a different day
options.E: Take it twice weekly with food, plus daily folic acid tablets

correct_answer: D. Take it once weekly, with folic acid on a different day
why_correct: Methotrexate is dosed once weekly; daily dosing is a classic and potentially fatal medication error. Folic acid is co-prescribed (on a different day) to reduce side effects, with regular blood monitoring of FBC and LFTs.
why_wrong: A. Daily methotrexate is a classic and potentially fatal dosing error; it is taken once weekly. B. 'Once daily' is the default mental model for most drugs, which is why the weekly rule is missed; daily methotrexate causes severe, sometimes fatal, toxicity. C. Folic acid is co-prescribed to reduce side effects; it should not be avoided. E. Methotrexate is taken once weekly, not twice weekly.
pearl: Methotrexate is weekly, not daily, with folic acid cover — daily dosing is a lethal error to guard against.
thinking: Methotrexate started for RA ↓ once-WEEKLY dosing is the safety-critical fact; daily dosing can be fatal ↓ folic acid on a different day
exam_trap: B, daily dosing with folic acid — 'once daily' is the default mental model for most drugs, which is exactly why the weekly rule is so often missed. But methotrexate taken daily causes severe, sometimes fatal, toxicity.
takeaway: Methotrexate is weekly, not daily, with folic acid cover — daily dosing is a lethal error to guard against.

stem: A 75-year-old man with reduced renal function is treated with IV gentamicin for sepsis. Which monitoring and adverse effects are most important?

options.A: No routine monitoring for a course under 72 hours; watch for rash
options.B: Monitor liver function tests; watch for drug-induced hepatitis
options.C: Monitor levels and renal function; watch for nephro- and ototoxicity
options.D: Monitor INR and platelets; watch for bleeding and thrombocytopenia
options.E: Monitor glucose and QT; watch for dysglycaemia and arrhythmia

correct_answer: C. Monitor levels and renal function; watch for nephro- and ototoxicity
why_correct: Gentamicin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic, with a narrow therapeutic window; serum levels and renal function are monitored, and doses are adjusted for renal impairment to minimise harm.
why_wrong: A. Gentamicin has a narrow therapeutic window; levels and renal function are monitored from the first dose, especially with renal impairment. B. Gentamicin's key toxicities affect the kidney and the ear, not the liver. D. Bleeding and thrombocytopenia are not the principal toxicities of gentamicin. E. Dysglycaemia and QT prolongation are associated with fluoroquinolones, not aminoglycosides.
pearl: Gentamicin damages kidneys and ears — monitor levels and renal function, especially in the elderly.
thinking: Older patient + impaired renal function + IV gentamicin ↓ Narrow therapeutic index aminoglycoside, renally cleared ↓ Monitor levels and renal function; watch for nephro- and ototoxicity
exam_trap: B, monitor LFTs for hepatotoxicity — liver monitoring is a reflex for many drugs. But gentamicin's key toxicities are to the kidney and the ear, not the liver; level and renal monitoring are what matter.
takeaway: Gentamicin damages kidneys and ears — monitor levels and renal function, especially in the elderly.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy, planning pregnancy, currently takes sodium valproate with good seizure control. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Reduce valproate to the lowest effective dose and start folic acid 5 mg
options.B: Continue valproate unchanged, as her seizures are well controlled
options.C: Stop valproate now and avoid antiepileptics during pregnancy
options.D: Add lamotrigine and reduce valproate, keeping both through pregnancy
options.E: Urgent specialist switch to a safer antiepileptic, plus folic acid 5 mg

correct_answer: E. Urgent specialist switch to a safer antiepileptic, plus folic acid 5 mg
why_correct: Sodium valproate carries a high risk of neural tube and other malformations and neurodevelopmental harm; in a woman planning pregnancy it should be switched (under specialist care) to a safer agent, with high-dose folic acid.
why_wrong: A. Valproate remains teratogenic at lower doses; she should be switched to a safer drug under specialist care. B. Valproate's teratogenicity is too great to continue when planning pregnancy; specialist switching, not continuation, is correct. C. Stopping antiepileptics abruptly risks uncontrolled seizures, which are dangerous in pregnancy. D. Continuing valproate in combination still exposes the fetus to its risks; it should be replaced, not added to.
pearl: Valproate and pregnancy do not mix — switch under specialist care before conception, and load with folic acid.
thinking: Woman with epilepsy planning pregnancy on valproate ↓ High teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk ↓ Urgent specialist switch to a safer antiepileptic + folic acid 5 mg
exam_trap: B, continue valproate — its seizure control is good, so changing it feels risky for her epilepsy. But valproate's teratogenicity is too great to continue in pregnancy planning; specialist switching, not continuation, is correct.
takeaway: Valproate and pregnancy do not mix — switch under specialist care before conception, and load with folic acid.

stem: A 65-year-old man is started on ramipril for hypertension. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen 25% and potassium is 5.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation and action?

options.A: Stop ramipril now and switch to amlodipine, rechecking renal function in a week
options.B: Continue, recheck soon and assess for renal artery stenosis if it worsens
options.C: Continue unchanged, with renal function next checked at his annual review visit
options.D: Continue ramipril and add spironolactone 25 mg daily for blood pressure control
options.E: Double the ramipril dose today and recheck renal function in three months' time

correct_answer: B. Continue, recheck soon and assess for renal artery stenosis if it worsens
why_correct: ACE inhibitors can cause a modest, acceptable rise in creatinine (up to about 30%) and potassium; a larger or progressive rise raises concern for bilateral renal artery stenosis and warrants review.
why_wrong: A. A rise in creatinine of under 30% is expected and acceptable; stopping a prognostically valuable drug for this is an over-reaction. C. The rise is acceptable but needs a repeat check soon, not deferral to annual review. D. Adding spironolactone with a potassium already 5.2 mmol/L risks dangerous hyperkalaemia. E. Increasing the dose before confirming stability risks further renal and potassium deterioration.
pearl: A small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected — a big one suggests renal artery stenosis; check the magnitude before stopping.
thinking: Ramipril started; creatinine +25%, K+ 5.2 at 2 weeks ↓ Rise below 30% and K+ below 6.0 is acceptable ↓ Continue, recheck soon; assess for renal artery stenosis if it worsens
exam_trap: A, stop immediately for any rise — caution feels safe. But a small rise is expected and acceptable; reflexively stopping a prognostically valuable drug for a minor, anticipated change is an over-reaction. Recheck and contextualise.
takeaway: A small creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor is expected — a big one suggests renal artery stenosis; check the magnitude before stopping.

stem: A 50-year-old woman on long-term lithium develops a diarrhoeal illness and starts an NSAID for back pain. She becomes confused with a coarse tremor, ataxia and vomiting. What is the most likely problem?
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range; dehydration (diarrhoea) and NSAIDs both raise lithium levels, producing toxicity — coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion and GI upset — which is confirmed by a lithium level and managed by stopping it and rehydrating.
why_wrong: B. Serotonin syndrome is another drug-induced neuro-toxidrome, but she is on lithium with two clear precipitants (dehydration and an NSAID) raising its level; the coarse tremor and ataxia point to lithium toxicity. C. Hypoglycaemia can cause confusion, but not coarse tremor and ataxia following known lithium precipitants. D. Viral encephalitis would usually give fever, headache or seizures and does not explain the drug precipitants. E. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs antipsychotic exposure and causes rigidity and hyperthermia.
pearl: Dehydration and NSAIDs push lithium into toxicity — a coarse tremor and ataxia on lithium means check the level.
thinking: Lithium + diarrhoea + NSAID ↓ reduced renal lithium clearance ↓ coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion
exam_trap: B, serotonin syndrome — another drug-induced neuro-toxidrome, so a reasonable thought. But she is on lithium with two clear precipitants (dehydration and an NSAID) raising its level; the coarse tremor and ataxia point to lithium toxicity.
takeaway: Dehydration and NSAIDs push lithium into toxicity — a coarse tremor and ataxia on lithium means check the level.

stem: A finals candidate is asked which of the following drugs has a narrow therapeutic index and routinely requires plasma level monitoring. Which is the best example?
why_correct: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and requires regular plasma level monitoring (plus renal and thyroid checks), as toxicity occurs close to the therapeutic range. Other monitored drugs include digoxin, gentamicin, vancomycin, theophylline and phenytoin.
why_wrong: A. Amlodipine has a wide therapeutic index and is not monitored by drug level. C. Ramipril needs renal and electrolyte checks, but ACE inhibitors are monitored for their effects on the kidney, not by drug level; lithium is the classic narrow-therapeutic-index drug needing level monitoring. D. Atorvastatin is monitored with lipids and LFTs, not drug levels. E. Omeprazole does not need level monitoring.
pearl: Lithium, digoxin, gentamicin, vancomycin, theophylline and phenytoin have narrow windows and need level monitoring — most other drugs do not.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic index ↓ plasma level itself must be measured
exam_trap: C, ramipril — it needs renal/electrolyte checks, so 'monitoring' fits loosely. But ACE inhibitors are monitored for their effects on the kidney, not by drug level; lithium is the classic narrow-therapeutic-index drug needing level monitoring.
takeaway: Lithium, digoxin, gentamicin, vancomycin, theophylline and phenytoin have narrow windows and need level monitoring — most other drugs do not.

stem: In an overdose, which antidote is correctly matched to its poison?
why_correct: Flumazenil is the benzodiazepine antagonist (used cautiously because of seizure risk); the correct other pairings are naloxone for opioids, N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol, glucagon/high-dose insulin for beta-blockers, and vitamin K/PCC for warfarin.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; matching flumazenil to opioids is the classic mix-up. C. Paracetamol overdose is treated with N-acetylcysteine; naloxone is for opioids. D. Beta-blocker overdose is treated with glucagon or high-dose insulin; protamine reverses heparin. E. Warfarin is reversed with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate; N-acetylcysteine is for paracetamol.
pearl: Flumazenil is for benzodiazepines, naloxone for opioids, NAC for paracetamol — keep the antidote pairings straight.
thinking: Match each antidote to its poison ↓ flumazenil = benzodiazepines; naloxone = opioids
exam_trap: A, flumazenil for opioids — both are reversal agents for sedative overdoses, so they are easily swapped. But naloxone reverses opioids and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; matching flumazenil to opioids is the classic mix-up.
takeaway: Flumazenil is for benzodiazepines, naloxone for opioids, NAC for paracetamol — keep the antidote pairings straight.

stem: A patient on warfarin presents with major, life-threatening bleeding and a high INR. What is the most appropriate reversal treatment?

options.A: Intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
options.B: Oral vitamin K and withhold warfarin, rechecking INR at 24 hours
options.C: Fresh frozen plasma as the sole reversal agent
options.D: Withhold warfarin and transfuse red cells, rechecking the INR daily
options.E: IV protamine sulfate followed by IV vitamin K

correct_answer: A. Intravenous vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
why_correct: Major (life-threatening) bleeding on warfarin is reversed with intravenous vitamin K together with prothrombin complex concentrate, which rapidly replaces the vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors; PCC is preferred over fresh frozen plasma for speed and completeness.
why_wrong: B. Oral vitamin K works too slowly for life-threatening bleeding; immediate factor replacement with PCC plus IV vitamin K is required. C. FFP is slower and less complete than PCC and is not the agent of choice when PCC is available. D. Red cells replace blood loss but do not reverse anticoagulation; urgent reversal is needed. E. Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.
pearl: Major warfarin bleeding is reversed with PCC plus IV vitamin K — vitamin K alone is too slow when the bleeding is life-threatening.
thinking: Warfarin + major life-threatening bleeding + high INR ↓ Needs immediate factor replacement plus sustained reversal ↓ IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate
exam_trap: B, oral vitamin K alone — vitamin K does reverse warfarin, so it seems sufficient. But oral vitamin K works too slowly for life-threatening bleeding; immediate factor replacement with PCC (plus IV vitamin K) is required.
takeaway: Major warfarin bleeding is reversed with PCC plus IV vitamin K — vitamin K alone is too slow when the bleeding is life-threatening.

stem: An elderly patient with chronic kidney disease, already taking an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, requests an NSAID for joint pain. Why is an NSAID particularly hazardous here?

options.A: With an ACE inhibitor and diuretic it markedly raises the risk of AKI
options.B: It blunts the antihypertensive effect, but renal function is unaffected
options.C: It causes hepatotoxicity when combined with diuretics in older adults
options.D: Its main risk is sedation and falls in older people with CKD
options.E: It increases the diuretic effect, causing dehydration and gout

correct_answer: A. With an ACE inhibitor and diuretic it markedly raises the risk of AKI
why_correct: NSAIDs cause gastrointestinal ulceration/bleeding, fluid retention and renal impairment; combined with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic (the 'triple whammy'), they markedly increase the risk of acute kidney injury, and they should be used with great caution (or avoided) in the elderly and in CKD, heart failure or peptic ulcer disease.
why_wrong: B. NSAIDs do blunt antihypertensive effects, but the key danger is that the NSAID/ACE inhibitor/diuretic combination ('triple whammy') causes acute kidney injury. C. The combination is not hepatotoxic; the danger is renal. D. NSAIDs are not significantly sedating; the main hazard here is acute kidney injury. E. NSAIDs REDUCE the effect of diuretics through sodium and water retention.
pearl: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the 'triple whammy' for acute kidney injury — avoid NSAIDs in the elderly, CKD, heart failure or peptic ulcer disease.
thinking: Elderly CKD + ACE inhibitor + diuretic ↓ adding NSAID = triple whammy
exam_trap: B, blunted antihypertensive effect — NSAIDs do blunt antihypertensives, so this sounds plausible. But renal function is not unaffected: the NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic 'triple whammy' causes acute kidney injury, so an NSAID should be avoided in this patient.
takeaway: NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic is the 'triple whammy' for acute kidney injury — avoid NSAIDs in the elderly, CKD, heart failure or peptic ulcer disease.

stem: A patient with poorly controlled asthma is being considered for a beta-blocker. Why is caution required?

options.A: They reduce the anti-inflammatory effect of regular inhaled corticosteroids
options.B: They worsen the tachycardia caused by high-dose salbutamol
options.C: Cardioselective agents have no effect on airway smooth muscle
options.D: They can precipitate bronchospasm, so are generally avoided in asthma
options.E: They cause hypokalaemia that predisposes to severe asthma attacks

correct_answer: D. They can precipitate bronchospasm, so are generally avoided in asthma
why_correct: Beta-blockers can precipitate bronchospasm and are generally avoided in asthma (non-selective agents especially); they also require caution in significant bradycardia or high-degree heart block.
why_wrong: A. Beta-blockers do not reduce the effect of inhaled corticosteroids; the concern is bronchoconstriction. B. Beta-blockers slow the heart rate; the concern is that they block bronchodilation and provoke bronchospasm. C. Cardioselectivity reduces but does not abolish beta-2 blockade; even selective agents can cause bronchospasm in asthma. E. Beta-blockers do not cause hypokalaemia (beta-agonists do); the concern is bronchospasm.
pearl: Beta-blockers can trigger bronchospasm in asthma — avoid them (and use caution in significant bradycardia/heart block).
thinking: Poorly controlled asthma ↓ beta-blockade risks bronchospasm
exam_trap: C, cardioselective agents have no airway effect — a common assumption. But cardioselectivity reduces but does not abolish beta-2 blockade, so even selective agents can cause bronchospasm in asthma.
takeaway: Beta-blockers can trigger bronchospasm in asthma — avoid them (and use caution in significant bradycardia/heart block).

stem: A 35-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding with no structural cause found and no desire for pregnancy currently. She would like effective treatment that also provides contraception. What is the most appropriate first-line option?

options.A: Endometrial ablation as a first-line procedure
options.B: Tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily during menses
options.C: A combined oral contraceptive taken continuously

why_correct: For heavy menstrual bleeding without structural pathology, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first-line: it markedly reduces bleeding and provides contraception.
why_wrong: A. Endometrial ablation is a second-line surgical option and is not suitable for someone who may want future pregnancy. B. Tranexamic acid is an effective non-hormonal option, but she also wants contraception, and the levonorgestrel IUS is the first-line treatment that delivers both. C. The combined pill is a second-line option for heavy menstrual bleeding; the LNG-IUS is first-line. E. Hysterectomy is a last-resort option and is inappropriate as first-line treatment.
pearl: First-line for heavy periods without structural cause is the levonorgestrel IUS — it treats the bleeding and contracepts.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding, no structural cause, wants contraception ↓ Needs an option that treats bleeding and contracepts ↓ Levonorgestrel intrauterine system
exam_trap: B, tranexamic acid — an effective non-hormonal option taken only during periods, so it appeals. But she also wants contraception, and the levonorgestrel IUS is the first-line treatment that delivers both.
takeaway: First-line for heavy periods without structural cause is the levonorgestrel IUS — it treats the bleeding and contracepts.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 36 weeks has a blood pressure of 162/110, proteinuria, headache and visual disturbance with brisk reflexes. What is the most appropriate management of her blood pressure and seizure risk?

options.A: Ramipril to lower BP and diazepam for seizure prophylaxis
options.B: Oral methyldopa and bed rest, with BP review in one week
options.C: IV furosemide to lower BP, with phenytoin seizure prophylaxis
options.D: Immediate caesarean section before any antihypertensive
options.E: Labetalol plus magnesium sulfate, then planned delivery

correct_answer: E. Labetalol plus magnesium sulfate, then planned delivery
why_correct: Severe pre-eclampsia is managed with antihypertensives (labetalol first-line) and magnesium sulfate to prevent eclamptic seizures, with delivery the definitive treatment once the mother is stabilised.
why_wrong: A. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy, and magnesium sulfate, not diazepam, is used for seizure prophylaxis. B. Severe pre-eclampsia needs urgent inpatient treatment; a week's delay risks eclampsia and stroke. C. Diuretics are not used to treat pre-eclampsia, and magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin for seizure prophylaxis. D. The mother must be stabilised (blood pressure controlled, magnesium given) before delivery.
pearl: Pre-eclampsia is controlled with labetalol and magnesium, and cured by delivery — never an ACE inhibitor in pregnancy.
thinking: BP 162/110 + proteinuria + headache, visual disturbance, brisk reflexes ↓ Severe pre-eclampsia ↓ Labetalol + MgSO4, then planned birth
exam_trap: A, an ACE inhibitor — a standard antihypertensive, so it seems a reasonable choice. But ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and contraindicated in pregnancy; labetalol (or nifedipine) is used, with magnesium for seizure prophylaxis.
takeaway: Pre-eclampsia is controlled with labetalol and magnesium, and cured by delivery — never an ACE inhibitor in pregnancy.

stem: Shortly after a prolonged labour and delivery, a woman has heavy ongoing vaginal bleeding. The uterus feels soft and 'boggy' on palpation. What is the most likely cause and the first management step?

options.A: Uterine atony — fundal massage and oxytocin
options.B: Retained products — proceed to manual removal in theatre
options.C: Cervical laceration — examine and suture in theatre
options.D: Coagulopathy — give fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate
options.E: Uterine inversion — manual replacement of the uterus

correct_answer: A. Uterine atony — fundal massage and oxytocin
why_correct: Uterine atony (a soft, boggy uterus) is the commonest cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage; first-line management is uterine massage and uterotonics (oxytocin, then ergometrine, carboprost) alongside resuscitation.
why_wrong: B. A soft, boggy uterus indicates atony; the first steps are massage and uterotonics, with exploration for retained tissue only if bleeding continues. C. Genital tract trauma bleeds despite a well-contracted uterus; a soft, boggy uterus indicates atony. D. Coagulopathy is a less common cause; a boggy uterus points to atony, treated first with massage and uterotonics. E. Uterine inversion presents with shock and an absent or dimpled fundus, not a soft, palpable boggy uterus.
pearl: A boggy uterus after delivery is atony — rub it up and give uterotonics before anything more drastic.
thinking: Prolonged labour + heavy bleeding + boggy uterus ↓ Uterine atony ↓ Massage + oxytocin
exam_trap: B, retained products and manual removal — a recognised cause of PPH, so it seems plausible. But a soft, boggy uterus points to atony; massage and uterotonics come first.
takeaway: A boggy uterus after delivery is atony — rub it up and give uterotonics before anything more drastic.

stem: A pregnant woman with risk factors has an oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks showing a raised fasting glucose. After a trial of diet and exercise fails to control her glucose, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.E: Continue diet alone regardless of glucose

why_correct: Gestational diabetes is managed first with diet and exercise; if targets are not met, metformin and/or insulin are used (these are the agents considered safe in pregnancy).
why_wrong: A. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not recommended in pregnancy and are not part of gestational diabetes management. B. Sulfonylureas are not routine; glibenclamide is considered only if metformin is not tolerated or insulin is declined (NICE NG3). Metformin and/or insulin is the standard next step. C. SGLT2 inhibitors are not used in pregnancy. E. If diet and exercise do not meet glucose targets within 1–2 weeks, drug treatment is needed, because persistent hyperglycaemia raises the risk of macrosomia and other complications.
pearl: Gestational diabetes that fails diet is treated with metformin and/or insulin — the other glucose-lowering classes are not for pregnancy.
thinking: GDM not controlled by diet and exercise ↓ drug choice is limited by pregnancy safety ↓ metformin and/or insulin (glibenclamide only if metformin not tolerated or insulin declined)
exam_trap: B, a sulfonylurea — an oral glucose-lowering drug, so a plausible step. But the agents used in gestational diabetes are metformin and insulin; sulfonylureas, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists are not standard in pregnancy.
takeaway: Gestational diabetes that fails diet is treated with metformin and/or insulin — the other glucose-lowering classes are not for pregnancy.

stem: During labour, after the membranes rupture, the cord is felt below the presenting part in the vagina and the fetal heart rate drops. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Start an oxytocin infusion to expedite vaginal delivery
options.B: Replace the cord above the presenting part and keep monitoring
options.C: Continuous CTG monitoring and await spontaneous delivery
options.D: Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange immediate delivery
options.E: Apply fundal pressure and encourage pushing to speed vaginal delivery

correct_answer: D. Elevate the presenting part off the cord and arrange immediate delivery
why_correct: Cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency; pressure on the cord is relieved (manually elevating the presenting part, maternal positioning), the cord kept warm and moist, and the baby delivered immediately, usually by caesarean.
why_wrong: A. Oxytocin increases contractions and cord compression, worsening fetal hypoxia. B. Handling the cord causes vasospasm and worsens fetal hypoxia; pressure is relieved and the baby delivered urgently, not left to labour. C. With fetal bradycardia, waiting risks fetal death; immediate delivery is required. E. Fundal pressure increases cord compression; the presenting part is elevated and urgent delivery (usually caesarean) arranged.
pearl: Cord prolapse means relieve the pressure and deliver now — do not handle or replace the cord.
thinking: Cord palpable below the presenting part + fetal bradycardia ↓ cord prolapse, an obstetric emergency ↓ relieve compression and deliver immediately
exam_trap: B, push the cord back in — instinct says to replace it. But handling the cord causes vasospasm and worsens fetal hypoxia; the cord is not replaced — pressure is relieved and the baby delivered urgently.
takeaway: Cord prolapse means relieve the pressure and deliver now — do not handle or replace the cord.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has several weeks of persistent bloating, early satiety, abdominal distension and urinary urgency. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.A: Reassurance and review if symptoms persist beyond three months
options.B: Serum CA-125, with ultrasound if it meets the age threshold
options.C: Faecal calprotectin to exclude inflammatory bowel disease
options.D: Urgent colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer
options.E: A 6-week trial of a low-FODMAP diet for presumed IBS

correct_answer: B. Serum CA-125, with ultrasound if it meets the age threshold
why_correct: Persistent bloating, early satiety and abdominal/urinary symptoms in a woman over 50 are red flags for ovarian cancer; NICE NG12 (updated 2026) recommends serum CA-125 as the initial test, with an urgent ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis if it meets the age-specific threshold (24 IU/ml or more at age 60–69).
why_wrong: A. Persistent bloating and early satiety in a woman over 50 are red flags for ovarian cancer and need investigation now. C. Calprotectin tests for inflammatory bowel disease; ovarian cancer must be excluded first with CA-125. D. These symptoms point to ovarian cancer, for which CA-125 is the initial test, not colonoscopy. E. New persistent bloating in an older woman warrants exclusion of ovarian cancer with CA-125 first, not an assumption of IBS.
pearl: New persistent bloating in an older woman is ovarian cancer until CA-125 and ultrasound say otherwise — not new-onset IBS.
thinking: Woman over 50 + persistent bloating, early satiety, urinary urgency ↓ NICE NG12 ovarian cancer symptoms ↓ CA125 first, then urgent ultrasound if ≥24 IU/ml (age 60–69 threshold)
exam_trap: E, a low-FODMAP diet for presumed IBS — the symptoms can mimic IBS. But new persistent bloating in an older woman warrants exclusion of ovarian cancer with CA-125 first, not an assumption of IBS.
takeaway: New persistent bloating in an older woman is ovarian cancer until CA-125 and ultrasound say otherwise — not new-onset IBS.

stem: A woman attends for routine cervical screening. Under the current programme, what is tested first on her sample, and what determines whether cytology is examined?

options.A: Cytology first; HPV tested if cytology shows low-grade change
options.B: Cytology and HPV co-tested on every sample at each round
options.C: HPV genotyping first; colposcopy directly for any HPV-positive result
options.D: A CA-125 blood test first; cytology if CA-125 is raised
options.E: High-risk HPV first; cytology only on HPV-positive samples

correct_answer: E. High-risk HPV first; cytology only on HPV-positive samples
why_correct: The cervical screening programme uses primary high-risk HPV testing; cytology (reflex) is performed only on HPV-positive samples, as HPV-negative women are at very low risk.
why_wrong: A. Cytology-first with HPV triage of low-grade change was the previous model; the programme now uses primary HPV testing with reflex cytology. B. Co-testing every sample is not used in the UK programme; cytology is examined only on HPV-positive samples. C. HPV-positive samples undergo reflex cytology in the UK, with further management guided by the cytology result rather than direct colposcopy for every positive. D. CA-125 is not a cervical screening test; screening uses a cervical sample tested first for high-risk HPV.
pearl: Cervical screening is now HPV-first, cytology only if HPV-positive — the test order changed from the older cytology-first model.
thinking: Routine cervical screening sample ↓ Current programme tests high-risk HPV FIRST ↓ Cytology only as a reflex on HPV-positive samples
exam_trap: A, cytology first with HPV triage of low-grade change — this was the old model, so it feels familiar. But the programme now tests high-risk HPV first and reflexes to cytology only if HPV-positive.
takeaway: Cervical screening is now HPV-first, cytology only if HPV-positive — the test order changed from the older cytology-first model.

stem: A woman at 8 weeks has light bleeding; ultrasound confirms a missed miscarriage (no fetal heart, retained tissue). She is haemodynamically stable and not septic. What management options are appropriate?

options.A: Methotrexate injection and serial hCG monitoring
options.B: Surgical evacuation within 24 hours as the standard required route
options.C: Progesterone support and rescan in two weeks
options.D: Expectant, medical or surgical management, chosen with the patient
options.E: Admission for IV oxytocin infusion to induce passage of tissue

correct_answer: D. Expectant, medical or surgical management, chosen with the patient
why_correct: For a confirmed missed miscarriage in a stable woman, expectant, medical (oral mifepristone 200 mg followed 48 hours later by misoprostol 800 micrograms) and surgical management are all options, chosen through shared decision-making according to her preference and circumstances.
why_wrong: A. Methotrexate with serial hCG is a treatment for selected ectopic pregnancies, not for an intrauterine missed miscarriage. B. Surgery is one valid option, but in a stable woman it is not mandatory; expectant, medical and surgical options are discussed and she chooses. C. Progesterone is used for threatened miscarriage in selected women with previous miscarriage; it cannot help a confirmed non-viable pregnancy. E. Oxytocin infusion is not used to manage first-trimester miscarriage; medical management of missed miscarriage uses mifepristone followed by misoprostol.
pearl: Stable miscarriage offers expectant, medical or surgical management — it is a shared decision, not an automatic operation.
thinking: Missed miscarriage at 8 weeks ↓ stable, not septic ↓ expectant, medical or surgical management all appropriate ↓ shared decision
exam_trap: B, immediate surgery for all — surgery is one valid option, so it can seem the definitive route. But in a stable woman the choice between expectant, medical and surgical management is hers to make; surgery is not mandatory.
takeaway: Stable miscarriage offers expectant, medical or surgical management — it is a shared decision, not an automatic operation.

stem: A woman at 9 weeks has severe, persistent vomiting with weight loss, ketonuria and signs of dehydration. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassurance that morning sickness is normal, no treatment
options.B: IV fluids, antiemetics and thiamine, with admission if severe
options.E: Withhold all antiemetics as they harm the fetus

correct_answer: B. IV fluids, antiemetics and thiamine, with admission if severe
why_correct: Hyperemesis gravidarum (severe vomiting with weight loss, dehydration and ketosis) is treated with IV fluids, antiemetics (e.g. cyclizine, promethazine) and thiamine to prevent Wernicke's, with admission for severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Weight loss, ketonuria and dehydration mark hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs active treatment, not reassurance. C. She is dehydrated and cannot keep fluids down, so oral intake alone is inadequate. D. Termination is not a treatment for hyperemesis; it is considered only after all treatment options have been tried. E. Antiemetics such as cyclizine, prochlorperazine, promethazine, ondansetron and metoclopramide are recommended in pregnancy; withholding them is inappropriate.
pearl: Hyperemesis (weight loss, ketosis, dehydration) needs fluids, antiemetics and thiamine — it is not just morning sickness to reassure away.
thinking: Severe vomiting at 9 weeks + weight loss, ketonuria, dehydration ↓ hyperemesis gravidarum ↓ IV fluids, antiemetics, thiamine ± admission
