exam_trap: A, reassurance as normal morning sickness — nausea is common in pregnancy, so this is a tempting dismissal. But weight loss, ketonuria and dehydration mark hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs active treatment, not reassurance.
takeaway: Hyperemesis (weight loss, ketosis, dehydration) needs fluids, antiemetics and thiamine — it is not just morning sickness to reassure away.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with troublesome vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats) and a uterus wants treatment. She has no contraindications. What is the most appropriate hormone replacement regimen?

options.A: Oestrogen-only HRT via a transdermal patch
options.E: Vaginal oestrogen cream as sole treatment

correct_answer: B. Combined oestrogen and progestogen HRT
why_correct: A woman with a uterus who needs HRT for vasomotor symptoms is given combined oestrogen and progestogen; the progestogen protects the endometrium from the increased cancer risk of unopposed oestrogen.
why_wrong: A. Unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus increases endometrial hyperplasia and cancer risk; oestrogen-only HRT is for women without a uterus. C. Testosterone may be considered for low libido alongside HRT, not as monotherapy for vasomotor symptoms. D. Clonidine is a less effective non-hormonal alternative used when HRT is contraindicated or declined, which is not the case here. E. Vaginal oestrogen treats urogenital symptoms but does not control systemic vasomotor symptoms.
pearl: A woman with a uterus needs combined HRT — unopposed oestrogen risks endometrial cancer; oestrogen-only is for those without a uterus.
thinking: A 52-year-old woman with troublesome vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, ↓ The woman having an intact UTERUS — the presence of the uterus is what requires
exam_trap: A, oestrogen-only HRT — oestrogen treats the symptoms, so alone it seems sufficient. But unopposed oestrogen in a woman with a uterus increases endometrial cancer risk; a progestogen must be added (oestrogen-only is for women without a uterus).
takeaway: A woman with a uterus needs combined HRT — unopposed oestrogen risks endometrial cancer; oestrogen-only is for those without a uterus.

stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has an episode of vaginal bleeding. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Urgent referral for transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling
options.B: Treat as atrophic vaginitis with vaginal oestrogen and review if it recurs
options.C: Reassure and make a routine gynaecology referral if a second episode occurs
options.D: Cervical screening test now and refer if it is abnormal
options.E: Tranexamic acid and review in primary care in three months if bleeding persists

correct_answer: A. Urgent referral for transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial sampling
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise and warrants urgent referral; transvaginal ultrasound measures endometrial thickness, with hysteroscopy and biopsy if it is thickened.
why_wrong: B. Atrophy is a common cause, but postmenopausal bleeding must be investigated to exclude endometrial cancer before it is attributed to atrophy. C. Waiting for a second episode delays diagnosis; a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding warrants urgent referral. D. Cervical screening does not assess the endometrium and is not a diagnostic test for abnormal bleeding. E. Tranexamic acid treats heavy menstrual bleeding and would delay investigation of possible endometrial cancer.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until investigation says otherwise — refer urgently, never reassure.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman aged 62 + vaginal bleeding ↓ endometrial cancer until proven otherwise ↓ urgent suspected cancer referral (age ≥55) for TVUS ± sampling
exam_trap: B, treat as atrophic vaginitis — atrophy is a common cause of postmenopausal bleeding, so this is tempting. But endometrial cancer must be excluded by urgent investigation before the bleeding is attributed to atrophy.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until investigation says otherwise — refer urgently, never reassure.

stem: A rhesus-D-negative pregnant woman has a potentially sensitising event (e.g. antepartum bleeding). What is the most appropriate action to prevent haemolytic disease in this or future pregnancies?

options.B: Give the woman a blood transfusion
options.C: Give the fetus a transfusion now
options.D: No action, as the first pregnancy is unaffected

correct_answer: E. Give anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours
why_correct: In a rhesus-negative woman, a sensitising event risks the formation of anti-D antibodies; anti-D immunoglobulin given within 72 hours prevents sensitisation and protects future pregnancies from haemolytic disease of the newborn.
why_wrong: A. Iron treats iron deficiency and does not prevent RhD sensitisation. B. Maternal transfusion is not indicated and does not prevent anti-D formation. C. Fetal transfusion treats established fetal anaemia from haemolytic disease, not prevention of sensitisation. D. The current pregnancy is often unaffected, but sensitisation now endangers future pregnancies; anti-D must be given.
pearl: Rhesus-negative woman plus a sensitising event means anti-D within 72 hours — it protects the pregnancies to come.
thinking: RhD-negative woman ↓ potentially sensitising event ↓ anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours
exam_trap: D, no action as the first pregnancy is unaffected — the current pregnancy is often unharmed, so inaction is tempting. But preventing sensitisation now protects FUTURE pregnancies; anti-D must be given.
takeaway: Rhesus-negative woman plus a sensitising event means anti-D within 72 hours — it protects the pregnancies to come.

stem: A woman with placenta praevia and two previous caesarean sections has antenatal imaging suggesting the placenta is abnormally adherent and invading the uterine wall. Why does this matter, and what is the key management principle?

options.A: Vasa praevia — elective caesarean at 39 weeks in a standard unit
options.B: Placental abruption risk — routine vaginal birth with active third stage
options.C: Placenta accreta spectrum — planned MDT delivery for haemorrhage risk
options.D: Uncomplicated praevia — routine elective caesarean by any team
options.E: Placental insufficiency — serial growth scans and induction at 37 weeks

correct_answer: C. Placenta accreta spectrum — planned MDT delivery for haemorrhage risk
why_correct: Placenta praevia with previous caesarean sections is the major risk factor for placenta accreta spectrum (abnormal placental invasion); it carries a high risk of catastrophic haemorrhage at delivery and must be managed with planned delivery by an experienced multidisciplinary team.
why_wrong: A. Vasa praevia involves fetal vessels over the cervix; the imaging here shows abnormal placental invasion of the uterine wall, and delivery at 39 weeks would be wrong anyway. B. The placenta is praevia, so vaginal birth is not possible, and the problem is abnormal invasion rather than abruption. D. Praevia with prior caesareans and imaging signs of invasion is accreta spectrum, not uncomplicated praevia; delivery must be planned in a specialist centre with an experienced multidisciplinary team. E. The issue is abnormal adherence with major haemorrhage risk, not growth restriction; induction is inappropriate with a praevia.
pearl: Praevia plus a prior caesarean means assume accreta — plan a multidisciplinary delivery, because the bleeding risk is life-threatening.
thinking: Praevia + two previous caesareans ↓ imaging shows abnormal adherence/invasion ↓ placenta accreta spectrum ↓ planned MDT delivery in a specialist centre
exam_trap: D, uncomplicated praevia — the placenta might be assumed simply low-lying. But praevia plus prior caesareans with imaging signs of invasion is placenta accreta spectrum, which demands planned delivery by an experienced multidisciplinary team, not routine management.
takeaway: Praevia plus a prior caesarean means assume accreta — plan a multidisciplinary delivery, because the bleeding risk is life-threatening.

stem: A woman in the third trimester has nausea, vomiting, right-upper-quadrant pain and jaundice, with raised transaminases. Distinctively, she also has HYPOGLYCAEMIA and a coagulopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: A. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
why_correct: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a third-trimester emergency with nausea/vomiting, jaundice and liver dysfunction; hypoglycaemia (from impaired hepatic glucose production) and coagulopathy are characteristic, and the definitive treatment is prompt delivery with supportive care.
why_wrong: B. HELLP syndrome shares right-upper-quadrant pain and raised transaminases, but it is defined by haemolysis and low platelets and does not typically cause hypoglycaemia. C. Acute viral hepatitis can cause jaundice and raised transaminases, but marked hypoglycaemia with coagulopathy in the third trimester points to acute fatty liver of pregnancy. D. Gallstone disease causes biliary pain and possibly obstructive jaundice, but not hypoglycaemia or a coagulopathy from liver failure. E. Pre-eclampsia without liver involvement cannot explain jaundice, raised transaminases, hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy.
pearl: Third-trimester liver failure with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy is acute fatty liver of pregnancy — deliver promptly; the hypoglycaemia separates it from HELLP.
thinking: Third-trimester nausea, vomiting, RUQ pain and jaundice ↓ Raised transaminases show acute liver dysfunction ↓ Hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy mark failing hepatic synthetic function ↓ The diagnosis is acute fatty liver of pregnancy
exam_trap: B, HELLP syndrome — the overlapping picture of right-upper-quadrant pain and deranged liver tests makes it the key differential. But HELLP is defined by haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets and does not typically cause hypoglycaemia, whereas hypoglycaemia is a hallmark of acute fatty liver of pregnancy.
takeaway: Third-trimester liver failure with hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy is acute fatty liver of pregnancy — deliver promptly; the hypoglycaemia separates it from HELLP.

stem: A pregnant woman is found to carry group B Streptococcus on a swab in the current pregnancy. What is the most appropriate intrapartum management to reduce early-onset neonatal infection?

options.A: Elective caesarean section for all carriers
options.B: A course of oral antibiotics now, in the antenatal period

why_correct: Group B Streptococcus carriage in the current pregnancy is managed with intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis (benzylpenicillin) during labour to reduce early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis; antenatal treatment does not prevent recolonisation.
why_wrong: A. GBS carriage is not an indication for caesarean section. B. Antenatal oral antibiotics do not prevent recolonisation by the time of delivery; the effective measure is intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis. C. GBS colonisation can cause early-onset neonatal sepsis, so intrapartum prophylaxis is offered. E. Topical antiseptics do not reduce early-onset GBS disease.
pearl: GBS prophylaxis is given intravenously during labour, not as an antenatal course — the protection has to be present at delivery.
thinking: GBS carriage in current pregnancy ↓ risk is early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis ↓ intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin from onset of labour
exam_trap: B, treat antenatally with oral antibiotics — eradicating the organism in advance seems logical. But antenatal treatment does not prevent recolonisation by the time of delivery; the effective measure is intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis during labour.
takeaway: GBS prophylaxis is given intravenously during labour, not as an antenatal course — the protection has to be present at delivery.

stem: A woman requesting a trial of labour after a previous caesarean is reviewed. Which feature is an absolute contraindication to attempting vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC)?

options.B: A single previous lower-segment caesarean for breech presentation
options.C: A previous classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean section
options.D: An estimated fetal weight at the upper end of normal

correct_answer: C. A previous classical (vertical upper-segment) caesarean section
why_correct: A previous classical (vertical upper-segment) uterine incision carries a high risk of uterine rupture in labour and is an absolute contraindication to VBAC; a single previous lower-segment caesarean is not, and a prior vaginal birth actually increases VBAC success.
why_wrong: A. A previous vaginal birth is a favourable factor that increases the chance of successful VBAC. B. A single lower-segment scar carries a low rupture risk, and VBAC is offered regardless of the original indication. D. Suspected large fetal size may lower VBAC success but is not an absolute contraindication. E. A BMI of 30 is associated with lower success rates but does not contraindicate VBAC.
pearl: A classical (vertical) uterine scar contraindicates VBAC; a lower-segment scar does not — the incision type is what matters.
thinking: Woman considering VBAC ↓ The key risk in labour after caesarean is uterine rupture ↓ Rupture risk depends on the type of previous uterine incision ↓ A classical (vertical upper-segment) scar carries a high rupture risk ↓ Absolute contraindication: a previous classical caesarean section
exam_trap: B, a single previous lower-segment caesarean — having had a caesarean might seem to preclude labour. But a lower-segment scar has a low rupture risk and VBAC is offered; it is the classical (vertical) scar that is the absolute contraindication.
takeaway: A classical (vertical) uterine scar contraindicates VBAC; a lower-segment scar does not — the incision type is what matters.

stem: A woman in late pregnancy with hypertension and proteinuria has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. After securing the airway and ensuring safety, what is the most appropriate drug to control and prevent further seizures?
why_correct: Eclampsia (a seizure on a background of pre-eclampsia) is treated and prevented with intravenous magnesium sulphate, which is superior to conventional anticonvulsants in this setting; blood pressure is also controlled and delivery planned.
why_wrong: A. A benzodiazepine is first-line for most seizures, but in eclampsia magnesium sulphate is superior for controlling and preventing seizures. C. Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulphate in eclampsia. D. Nifedipine treats hypertension but does not control seizures. E. Levetiracetam is not used for eclamptic seizures.
pearl: Eclamptic seizures are treated with magnesium sulphate — not the benzodiazepine you would reach for in ordinary status epilepticus.
thinking: Seizure with hypertension and proteinuria in late pregnancy ↓ eclampsia ↓ IV magnesium sulphate
exam_trap: A, intravenous lorazepam — a benzodiazepine is the standard first-line for most seizures. But in eclampsia magnesium sulphate is the specific, evidence-based agent for controlling and preventing seizures, superior to benzodiazepines and phenytoin.
takeaway: Eclamptic seizures are treated with magnesium sulphate — not the benzodiazepine you would reach for in ordinary status epilepticus.

stem: A young woman has chronic cyclical pelvic pain, painful periods (dysmenorrhoea), deep pain during intercourse, and difficulty conceiving. Examination may show tender nodularity in the pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and subfertility, with pelvic nodularity, suggest endometriosis (ectopic endometrial tissue); laparoscopy is the definitive diagnostic test, and management includes analgesia, hormonal treatment and surgery.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome causes abdominal pain linked to bowel habit, not cyclical dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, subfertility and pelvic nodularity. B. Pelvic inflammatory disease is an infection that usually causes discharge, cervical motion tenderness and sometimes fever, whereas this pain is cyclical and tied to menstruation. D. Ovarian cancer typically presents in older women with bloating, early satiety and a pelvic mass, not cyclical pain in a young woman. E. A urinary tract infection causes dysuria and frequency, not cyclical pelvic pain, dyspareunia and subfertility.
pearl: Cyclical pelvic pain with dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and subfertility is endometriosis — the menstrual link is the clue.
thinking: Young woman with chronic pelvic pain ↓ The pain is cyclical with dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia ↓ Subfertility and tender pelvic nodularity add weight ↓ The diagnosis is endometriosis
exam_trap: B, pelvic inflammatory disease — another cause of pelvic pain and dyspareunia. But PID is an infective, often acute illness with discharge and fever, whereas the CYCLICAL pain tied to menstruation with subfertility here is endometriosis.
takeaway: Cyclical pelvic pain with dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia and subfertility is endometriosis — the menstrual link is the clue.

stem: During a vaginal delivery, after the head is delivered it retracts against the perineum ('turtle sign') and the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with routine traction. What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.A: Zavanelli manoeuvre and emergency caesarean section
options.B: Strong downward traction on the fetal head
options.D: Fundal pressure with continued maternal pushing
options.E: Internal rotation (Woods' screw) as the first manoeuvre

correct_answer: C. McRoberts' manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure
why_correct: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency; the first-line response is McRoberts' manoeuvre (sharply flexing the maternal hips onto the abdomen) with suprapubic pressure, escalating through further manoeuvres if needed, while avoiding excessive traction and fundal pressure.
why_wrong: A. Cephalic replacement (Zavanelli) with caesarean is a last resort after other manoeuvres have failed. B. Excessive downward traction risks brachial plexus injury and does not free the impacted shoulder. D. Fundal pressure worsens impaction and is associated with uterine rupture; it should not be used. E. Internal rotational manoeuvres such as Woods' screw are second-line, used if McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure fail.
pearl: Shoulder dystocia starts with McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure — never pull harder or push on the fundus.
thinking: Head delivered then retracts (turtle sign) and the anterior shoulder does not deliver ↓ Shoulder dystocia: call for help, avoid excessive traction or fundal pressure ↓ First-line manoeuvres increase the pelvic outlet and dislodge the shoulder ↓ McRoberts' manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure
exam_trap: B, strong downward traction on the head — pulling harder seems the instinctive response. But excessive traction risks brachial plexus injury; the correct first step is McRoberts' manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure.
takeaway: Shoulder dystocia starts with McRoberts' and suprapubic pressure — never pull harder or push on the fundus.

stem: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks is offered the combined test (nuchal translucency, PAPP-A and beta-hCG), which returns a 'higher-chance' result. How should this be interpreted and what comes next?

options.A: It confirms trisomy 21 — refer to fetal medicine for counselling
options.B: It is a screening result — reassure, as most such pregnancies are unaffected
options.C: A screening (risk) result — offer NIPT or CVS/amniocentesis
options.D: It suggests a structural anomaly — await the routine 20-week anomaly scan
options.E: Offer the quadruple test at 15 weeks to confirm the result

correct_answer: C. A screening (risk) result — offer NIPT or CVS/amniocentesis
why_correct: The combined test is a screening test that estimates the chance of trisomy; a higher-chance result is not diagnostic. The woman is offered further testing — a more accurate screening test (NIPT) or a diagnostic test (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis) — with informed choice.
why_wrong: A. The combined test gives a probability, not a diagnosis; confirmation requires a diagnostic test. B. Although many higher-chance results are unaffected, the woman should be offered further testing rather than reassurance alone. D. The combined test screens for trisomies 21, 18 and 13, not structural anomalies, and further testing should be offered now. E. Repeating serum screening adds little after a higher-chance combined result; the next step is NIPT or a diagnostic test.
pearl: The combined test gives a risk, not a diagnosis — a higher-chance result leads to NIPT or a diagnostic test, the woman's choice.
thinking: Combined test at 12 weeks ↓ higher-chance result = screening probability, not diagnosis ↓ offer NIPT or CVS/amniocentesis
exam_trap: A, the combined test is diagnostic — a higher-chance screen can feel definitive. But screening gives a probability, not a diagnosis; confirmation requires a diagnostic test (CVS/amniocentesis), or NIPT as a more accurate screen, chosen by the woman.
takeaway: The combined test gives a risk, not a diagnosis — a higher-chance result leads to NIPT or a diagnostic test, the woman's choice.

stem: A breastfeeding woman has a tender, red, wedge-shaped area on one breast with fever and flu-like symptoms. There is no fluctuant collection. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop feeding from the affected breast and express from the other side
options.B: Continue breastfeeding, with flucloxacillin if severe or not improving
options.C: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of the inflamed area as first-line
options.D: Cabergoline to suppress lactation, with oral analgesia
options.E: Admit for IV benzylpenicillin and pause breastfeeding

correct_answer: B. Continue breastfeeding, with flucloxacillin if severe or not improving
why_correct: Lactational mastitis is managed by continued effective milk removal (breastfeeding or expressing), analgesia and rest, with an antibiotic (flucloxacillin) if it is severe, associated with a nipple fissure, or not improving; ongoing drainage is key, and an abscess (fluctuant) needs drainage.
why_wrong: A. Stopping milk removal from the affected breast causes stasis and worsens mastitis; continued feeding or expressing is central. C. Aspiration is for a breast abscess (a fluctuant collection), which is absent here. D. Suppressing lactation is not a treatment for mastitis and removes the key therapeutic measure of milk drainage. E. Admission and IV antibiotics are for severe sepsis, pausing feeding worsens stasis, and benzylpenicillin lacks reliable staphylococcal cover.
pearl: Keep the milk moving in mastitis — continue breastfeeding/expressing, add flucloxacillin if severe, and drain a fluctuant abscess.
thinking: Breastfeeding woman with a tender, red, wedge-shaped area, fever and no fluctuant collection ↓ Lactational mastitis, not an abscess ↓ Milk stasis drives it, so effective drainage must continue ↓ Continue breastfeeding, with flucloxacillin if severe or not improving
exam_trap: A, stop breastfeeding immediately — pausing feeding from a painful infected breast feels protective. But stopping milk removal causes stasis and worsens mastitis (and risks abscess); continued effective drainage is central to treatment.
takeaway: Keep the milk moving in mastitis — continue breastfeeding/expressing, add flucloxacillin if severe, and drain a fluctuant abscess.

stem: A postmenopausal woman has vaginal dryness, soreness and pain during intercourse. Examination shows thin, pale, dry vaginal walls. There is no abnormal bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Chlamydia infection — doxycycline and partner notification
options.B: Vulvovaginal candidiasis — clotrimazole pessary and cream
options.C: Atrophic vaginitis — vaginal oestrogen and lubricants
options.D: Lichen sclerosus — potent topical corticosteroid ointment
options.E: Bacterial vaginosis — oral metronidazole for seven days

correct_answer: C. Atrophic vaginitis — vaginal oestrogen and lubricants
why_correct: Vaginal dryness, soreness and dyspareunia with thin, pale, atrophic vaginal walls after the menopause is atrophic vaginitis, due to oestrogen deficiency; topical vaginal oestrogen (with lubricants) is effective. Any postmenopausal bleeding must still be investigated separately to exclude cancer.
why_wrong: A. Chlamydia causes discharge, post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding and cervicitis, not thin, pale, dry vaginal walls. B. Candidiasis causes itch with a thick white discharge and erythema, not dry atrophic vaginal walls. D. Lichen sclerosus gives white, atrophic, intensely itchy vulval plaques; the findings here are in the vagina and reflect oestrogen deficiency. E. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin, fishy-smelling discharge, not dryness with atrophic walls.
pearl: Postmenopausal dryness and dyspareunia with thin pale walls is atrophic vaginitis — topical oestrogen helps; investigate any bleeding separately.
thinking: Postmenopausal dryness and dyspareunia ↓ thin, pale, dry vaginal walls ↓ oestrogen deficiency = atrophic vaginitis ↓ vaginal oestrogen plus lubricants
exam_trap: B, vulvovaginal candidiasis — another cause of vaginal soreness. But candidiasis causes itch with a thick white discharge, whereas the dryness and thin, pale atrophic walls in a postmenopausal woman here are atrophic vaginitis, treated with topical oestrogen.
takeaway: Postmenopausal dryness and dyspareunia with thin pale walls is atrophic vaginitis — topical oestrogen helps; investigate any bleeding separately.

stem: A woman aged 36 has stopped having periods and has hot flushes and night sweats. Pregnancy is excluded, and a raised FSH is confirmed on two occasions a few weeks apart. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Early physiological menopause — non-hormonal symptom control
options.B: Premature ovarian insufficiency — HRT until around 51
options.C: PMOS (formerly PCOS) — combined pill for cycle control
options.E: Hypothalamic amenorrhoea — weight gain and stress reduction

correct_answer: B. Premature ovarian insufficiency — HRT until around 51
why_correct: Menopausal symptoms with a raised FSH (on two occasions) before the age of 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency; hormone replacement therapy is offered (at least until the average age of natural menopause) to control symptoms and protect bone and cardiovascular health.
why_wrong: A. Menopause before 40 is by definition premature ovarian insufficiency, and HRT is recommended rather than symptom control alone. C. PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism and a normal FSH, not vasomotor symptoms with a raised FSH. D. Hyperprolactinaemia suppresses gonadotrophins, so FSH would be low or normal, not raised. E. Hypothalamic amenorrhoea is associated with low FSH, not a persistently raised FSH.
pearl: Menopausal symptoms with raised FSH before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency — offer HRT until the usual age of menopause.
thinking: Age 36 + amenorrhoea + vasomotor symptoms + raised FSH on two samples ↓ premature ovarian insufficiency ↓ HRT at least until the average age of natural menopause
exam_trap: A, normal physiological menopause needing no treatment — the symptoms and raised FSH resemble menopause. But occurring UNDER 40, this is premature ovarian insufficiency, for which HRT is recommended (unlike the default approach to menopause at the usual age).
takeaway: Menopausal symptoms with raised FSH before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency — offer HRT until the usual age of menopause.

stem: A young woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill has post-coital bleeding and a non-offensive vaginal discharge. On speculum examination the area around the cervical os looks reddened. What is the most likely diagnosis and the appropriate approach?

options.A: Cervical polyp — avulse in clinic today and send the polyp for histology
options.B: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia — LLETZ at the first colposcopy visit
options.C: Cervical ectropion — swabs and up-to-date screening before reassurance
options.D: A physiological change on the pill — stop the pill and review in three months
options.E: Pelvic inflammatory disease — IM ceftriaxone and oral doxycycline

correct_answer: C. Cervical ectropion — swabs and up-to-date screening before reassurance
why_correct: Post-coital bleeding and discharge with a reddened area around the os, in a young woman on oestrogen-containing contraception (or pregnant), suggests cervical ectropion (columnar epithelium on the ectocervix), which is benign; however, infection and cervical cancer must be excluded (swabs, up-to-date cervical screening) before reassurance, with cautery if symptomatic.
why_wrong: A. A cervical polyp is a discrete pedunculated lesion at the os, not a diffuse reddened area around it. B. Treatment of CIN is guided by screening and colposcopy; there is no screening abnormality to justify immediate excision. D. Ectropion is linked to oestrogen, but infection and cancer must be excluded before attributing post-coital bleeding to it; stopping contraception is not the first step. E. There is no pelvic pain or cervical motion tenderness to suggest PID; swabs are taken rather than treating empirically.
pearl: Post-coital bleeding from a cervical ectropion is usually benign — but exclude infection and cancer (swabs, up-to-date screening) first.
thinking: Young woman on the combined pill with post-coital bleeding and non-offensive discharge ↓ Reddened area around the os: oestrogen-driven ectropion is likely ↓ Still exclude infection and check screening is up to date ↓ Cervical ectropion: swabs and up-to-date screening before reassurance
exam_trap: B, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia treated with LLETZ at the first colposcopy — post-coital bleeding raises concern about cervical pathology. But a reddened area around the os in a young woman on the pill is typical of an ectropion; the approach is swabs and confirming screening is up to date, with colposcopy only if screening is abnormal or the cervix looks suspicious, not proceeding straight to excisional treatment.
takeaway: Post-coital bleeding from a cervical ectropion is usually benign — but exclude infection and cancer (swabs, up-to-date screening) first.

stem: A teenager has painful periods (crampy lower abdominal pain) that began around the time her periods started, with no other gynaecological symptoms and a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?

options.A: Pelvic inflammatory disease — oral ofloxacin and metronidazole
options.C: Primary dysmenorrhoea — an NSAID such as mefenamic acid
options.D: Uterine fibroids — pelvic ultrasound and tranexamic acid
options.E: Ovarian cyst — CA-125 and pelvic ultrasound

correct_answer: C. Primary dysmenorrhoea — an NSAID such as mefenamic acid
why_correct: Painful periods beginning around menarche, without pelvic pathology or other features, is primary dysmenorrhoea; first-line treatment is an NSAID (such as mefenamic acid), with the combined oral contraceptive pill as an alternative/addition. Later-onset or atypical pain (secondary dysmenorrhoea) prompts investigation for causes like endometriosis.
why_wrong: A. There is no fever, discharge or pelvic tenderness, and pain from menarche with a normal examination does not suggest PID. B. Endometriosis typically causes secondary dysmenorrhoea with later onset and other features; laparoscopy is not first-line for pain beginning at menarche. D. Fibroids are uncommon in teenagers, and tranexamic acid treats heavy bleeding rather than pain. E. Cyclical pain from menarche with a normal examination does not suggest an ovarian cyst, and CA-125 is not indicated.
pearl: Painful periods from menarche with no pathology is primary dysmenorrhoea — NSAID first-line (± combined pill); later-onset pain needs investigation.
thinking: Painful periods from around menarche ↓ normal examination, no other features ↓ primary dysmenorrhoea ↓ NSAID first-line
exam_trap: B, endometriosis requiring laparoscopy — painful periods can be due to endometriosis. But that is secondary dysmenorrhoea with later onset and additional features; pain beginning at menarche with a normal examination is primary dysmenorrhoea, treated first with an NSAID.
takeaway: Painful periods from menarche with no pathology is primary dysmenorrhoea — NSAID first-line (± combined pill); later-onset pain needs investigation.

stem: A woman who has migraine WITH aura requests contraception. Why should the combined oral contraceptive pill be avoided, and what are suitable alternatives?

options.A: No issue if migraines are infrequent — continue the combined pill
options.B: Oestrogen worsens migraine frequency — use a lower-dose combined pill
options.C: Progestogens provoke aura — avoid all hormonal methods, including the implant
options.D: Oestrogen raises VTE risk — use the combined vaginal ring instead
options.E: Oestrogen raises stroke risk — use progestogen-only methods or LARC

correct_answer: E. Oestrogen raises stroke risk — use progestogen-only methods or LARC
why_correct: Migraine with aura is a contraindication to oestrogen-containing (combined) contraception because the oestrogen increases ischaemic stroke risk; suitable alternatives are progestogen-only methods or long-acting reversible contraception (the implant or intrauterine methods), which are also the most effective.
why_wrong: A. Migraine with aura at any frequency is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk. B. The concern is ischaemic stroke, not migraine frequency; a lower oestrogen dose does not remove the contraindication. C. Progestogen-only methods, including the implant, are suitable in migraine with aura; there is no need to avoid hormonal contraception. D. The vaginal ring also contains oestrogen and carries the same contraindication; the key risk is ischaemic stroke.
pearl: Migraine with aura contraindicates the combined (oestrogen) pill — use a progestogen-only or LARC method; LARC is the most effective.
thinking: Migraine with aura ↓ Oestrogen adds to the already raised ischaemic stroke risk ↓ Combined hormonal methods are UKMEC 4 (contraindicated) ↓ Oestrogen raises stroke risk: use progestogen-only methods or LARC
exam_trap: B, a lower-dose combined pill — reducing the oestrogen dose seems a reasonable compromise. But the concern in migraine with aura is ischaemic stroke, not migraine frequency, and combined hormonal contraception at any dose is UKMEC 4; progestogen-only methods or LARC should be used.
takeaway: Migraine with aura contraindicates the combined (oestrogen) pill — use a progestogen-only or LARC method; LARC is the most effective.

stem: A woman has mood swings, irritability, bloating and breast tenderness that recur in the days before each period (the luteal phase) and resolve once menstruation begins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cyclical psychological and physical symptoms occurring in the luteal phase and resolving with the onset of menstruation are premenstrual syndrome; management ranges from lifestyle measures to the combined pill or an SSRI for severe symptoms (premenstrual dysphoric disorder).
why_wrong: B. A primary depressive disorder is persistent and does not reliably resolve each month when menstruation begins. C. Generalised anxiety disorder causes persistent worry most days, not symptoms confined to the luteal phase with bloating and breast tenderness. D. Hypothyroidism causes persistent fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance, not symptoms that come and go with the menstrual cycle. E. Bipolar affective disorder causes episodes of mania and depression lasting weeks, not short luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menstruation.
pearl: Cyclical luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menstruation is premenstrual syndrome — lifestyle, the combined pill, or an SSRI if severe.
thinking: Mood and physical symptoms recur each cycle ↓ They appear in the luteal phase before menstruation ↓ They resolve once the period starts, so they are tied to the cycle ↓ The diagnosis is premenstrual syndrome
exam_trap: B, a primary depressive disorder — the mood symptoms can resemble depression. But the strict CYCLICAL pattern, confined to the luteal phase and resolving with menstruation, distinguishes premenstrual syndrome from a persistent primary mood disorder.
takeaway: Cyclical luteal-phase symptoms that resolve with menstruation is premenstrual syndrome — lifestyle, the combined pill, or an SSRI if severe.

stem: A woman in the third trimester has intense itching, particularly of the palms and soles, WITHOUT a rash. Liver function tests and serum bile acids are raised. What is the most likely diagnosis and a key concern?

options.A: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy — urgent delivery after correcting coagulopathy
options.B: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy — reassure, emollients and topical steroid
options.C: HELLP syndrome — urgent delivery after stabilisation and IV magnesium sulfate
options.D: Pemphigoid gestationis — potent topical or oral steroids and dermatology review
options.E: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — stillbirth risk; monitor, plan birth

correct_answer: E. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — stillbirth risk; monitor, plan birth
why_correct: Itching of the palms and soles without a rash, with raised bile acids and transaminases in later pregnancy, is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (obstetric cholestasis). The risk of stillbirth rises with peak bile acid concentration (particularly at 100 micromol/L or above), so management centres on monitoring bile acids and planning the timing of birth; ursodeoxycholic acid may slightly reduce itch but does not reduce stillbirth risk.
why_wrong: A. Acute fatty liver presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy rather than isolated pruritus. B. Polymorphic eruption causes an itchy urticarial rash starting in the abdominal striae; there is no rash here, and bile acids are raised. C. HELLP causes haemolysis, low platelets and raised liver enzymes, usually with hypertension and epigastric pain, not palmar itch. D. Pemphigoid gestationis is a blistering rash around the umbilicus; this woman has itch without any rash.
pearl: Itchy palms/soles without a rash plus raised bile acids in late pregnancy is obstetric cholestasis — increased stillbirth risk; monitor and plan delivery.
thinking: Third-trimester itching of palms and soles without a rash ↓ Raised bile acids and liver function tests ↓ Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, with stillbirth risk rising with bile acid level ↓ Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy: monitor and plan birth
exam_trap: B, a simple pregnancy rash needing only emollients — itching in pregnancy is common. But the palmar/plantar itch WITHOUT a rash plus raised bile acids indicates obstetric cholestasis, which carries fetal risk and needs monitoring, not just emollients.
takeaway: Itchy palms/soles without a rash plus raised bile acids in late pregnancy is obstetric cholestasis — increased stillbirth risk; monitor and plan delivery.

stem: A pregnant woman has vaginal bleeding, severe hyperemesis and a uterus larger than expected for dates. The beta-hCG is very high, and ultrasound shows a 'snowstorm'/cluster-of-grapes appearance with no fetus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: A threatened miscarriage of a normal fetus

why_correct: Markedly raised beta-hCG, a 'snowstorm'/cluster-of-grapes ultrasound appearance with no fetus, a large-for-dates uterus and exaggerated pregnancy symptoms indicate a molar pregnancy (gestational trophoblastic disease); management is uterine evacuation with follow-up of beta-hCG, as a minority progress to persistent trophoblastic disease/choriocarcinoma.
why_wrong: A. An ectopic pregnancy shows an empty uterus, often with an adnexal mass, and a lower hCG, not a snowstorm intrauterine appearance. B. A normal early pregnancy shows a gestational sac and fetus, not a snowstorm appearance with no fetus. D. A threatened miscarriage has a viable fetus seen on ultrasound with a closed cervix, not a snowstorm uterus with a very high hCG. E. Placenta praevia is a later-pregnancy cause of painless bleeding with a low-lying placenta, not a snowstorm appearance without a fetus.
pearl: Very high hCG with a 'snowstorm' uterus and no fetus is a molar pregnancy — evacuate and follow up hCG for persistent disease.
thinking: Bleeding with severe hyperemesis and a large-for-dates uterus ↓ The hCG is very high ↓ Ultrasound shows a snowstorm appearance with no fetus ↓ The diagnosis is a molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole)
exam_trap: A, an ectopic pregnancy — both present with bleeding and abnormal hCG. But ectopic pregnancy shows an empty uterus with an adnexal mass and lower hCG, whereas the very high hCG with a snowstorm intrauterine appearance here indicates a molar pregnancy.
takeaway: Very high hCG with a 'snowstorm' uterus and no fetus is a molar pregnancy — evacuate and follow up hCG for persistent disease.

stem: A woman has post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding, and on speculum examination there is an irregular, friable mass on the cervix. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Take a cervical screening sample now and refer if HPV-positive
options.B: Treat as ectropion with cryocautery at a routine gynaecology clinic
options.C: Take swabs and give empirical doxycycline for presumed cervicitis
options.D: Urgent suspected cancer referral for colposcopy and biopsy
options.E: Routine gynaecology referral for outpatient cervical polypectomy

correct_answer: D. Urgent suspected cancer referral for colposcopy and biopsy
why_correct: An irregular, friable cervical mass with abnormal bleeding (post-coital, intermenstrual) is suspicious for cervical cancer and requires urgent referral for colposcopy and biopsy — a visible suspicious lesion should be referred regardless of recent smear results.
why_wrong: A. Screening is for asymptomatic women; a visible suspicious lesion needs urgent referral whatever the screening result. B. An irregular friable mass is not an ectropion; cautery would delay diagnosis of possible cancer. C. Infection can cause bleeding, but a friable mass must be referred urgently rather than treated empirically. E. An irregular friable mass is not a simple polyp, and routine referral is too slow for suspected cancer.
pearl: An irregular friable cervical mass with abnormal bleeding needs urgent referral for colposcopy/biopsy — refer a visible suspicious lesion whatever the smear shows.
thinking: Post-coital and intermenstrual bleeding + irregular friable cervical mass ↓ appearance consistent with cervical cancer ↓ suspected cancer pathway referral for colposcopy and biopsy
exam_trap: B, treat as an ectropion with cryocautery — an ectropion can also bleed post-coitally. But a visibly irregular, friable mass is suspicious for malignancy and needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for colposcopy and biopsy, not ablative treatment of a presumed benign lesion.
takeaway: An irregular friable cervical mass with abnormal bleeding needs urgent referral for colposcopy/biopsy — refer a visible suspicious lesion whatever the smear shows.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is haemodynamically stable with a confirmed tubal ectopic pregnancy. The serum beta-hCG is 1500 IU/L, the mass is 2.5 cm with no fetal cardiac activity, and she has minimal pain and no free fluid. She wishes to avoid surgery if safe. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: A stable, unruptured tubal ectopic with no significant pain, an adnexal mass under 35 mm with no visible heartbeat, no intrauterine pregnancy and serum hCG of at least 1500 but below 5000 IU/L can be offered a choice of methotrexate or surgery (NICE NG126); as she wishes to avoid surgery and can attend follow-up, single-dose intramuscular methotrexate is appropriate. Expectant management requires hCG of 1000 IU/L or below.
why_wrong: A. Mifepristone is used in medical management of miscarriage, not ectopic pregnancy. B. Expectant management requires hCG of 1000 IU/L or below; at 1500 it is not offered. C. Salpingectomy is right if she is unstable or the criteria are not met, but she meets the criteria for medical management and wants to avoid surgery, so methotrexate is appropriate. D. Salpingostomy is a surgical option mainly for women with contralateral tubal damage; it is surgery she wishes to avoid and needs hCG follow-up.
pearl: A stable ectopic that meets the low-hCG, small-mass, no-heartbeat criteria can be treated medically — methotrexate spares the tube and the theatre.
thinking: Stable, unruptured ectopic ↓ hCG 1500 (1500–<5000 band), mass <35 mm, no heartbeat, no significant pain ↓ methotrexate or surgery offered as a choice ↓ she wants to avoid surgery
exam_trap: C, salpingectomy — the definitive answer for an ectopic, and the right one when she is unstable or the criteria are not met. But this patient meets every criterion for medical management and has asked to avoid surgery, so methotrexate is appropriate.
takeaway: A stable ectopic that meets the low-hCG, small-mass, no-heartbeat criteria can be treated medically — methotrexate spares the tube and the theatre.

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation presents with severe right-upper-quadrant and epigastric pain, nausea and malaise. Her blood pressure is 158/104. Bloods show a haemolytic picture, platelets of 78, and ALT of 210. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes and Low Platelets in a hypertensive woman in the third trimester is HELLP syndrome — a severe variant of pre-eclampsia and an obstetric emergency.
why_wrong: A. Acute cholecystitis causes right-upper-quadrant pain, but not hypertension, haemolysis and thrombocytopenia in the third trimester. B. Acute pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised amylase, and does not explain haemolysis, low platelets and hypertension. C. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy causes liver dysfunction, but it is characterised by hypoglycaemia and coagulopathy rather than this hypertensive haemolytic picture. E. Peptic ulcer disease causes epigastric pain but not hypertension, haemolysis, low platelets or a raised ALT.
pearl: Epigastric pain with hypertension and low platelets in late pregnancy is HELLP until proven otherwise — it is pre-eclampsia attacking the liver, and the treatment is delivery.
thinking: Third-trimester woman with RUQ and epigastric pain ↓ Blood pressure is raised, so pre-eclampsia is in play ↓ Haemolysis, raised ALT and low platelets complete the triad ↓ The diagnosis is HELLP syndrome
exam_trap: A, cholecystitis — right-upper-quadrant pain in a young woman points there first. But the hypertension, the haemolysis, the thrombocytopenia and the gestation together make a pregnancy-specific liver disorder far more likely than gallstones.
takeaway: Epigastric pain with hypertension and low platelets in late pregnancy is HELLP until proven otherwise — it is pre-eclampsia attacking the liver, and the treatment is delivery.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden severe left iliac fossa pain and vomiting. She has a known ovarian cyst. She is tender in the left adnexa, and a pregnancy test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden severe unilateral pelvic pain with vomiting in a woman with an ovarian cyst is ovarian torsion — a surgical emergency, because a twisted ovary loses its blood supply and infarcts.
why_wrong: A. A ruptured appendix causes right-sided pain with fever and peritonism, not sudden left iliac fossa pain in a woman with a known ovarian cyst. C. Pelvic inflammatory disease usually causes bilateral pain with fever and discharge that builds over days, not sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting. D. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is the must-not-miss diagnosis, but the negative pregnancy test excludes it. E. Mittelschmerz is mild mid-cycle ovulation pain lasting hours, not sudden severe pain with vomiting.
pearl: Acute pelvic pain with a cyst and a negative pregnancy test is torsion until the ovary is seen — it is a time-critical, ovary-threatening emergency.
thinking: Sudden severe left iliac fossa pain with vomiting ↓ She has a known ovarian cyst ↓ The negative pregnancy test excludes ectopic pregnancy ↓ The diagnosis is ovarian torsion
exam_trap: D, ruptured ectopic — the must-not-miss diagnosis in a woman with acute pelvic pain, so it is the anxious first thought. But the negative pregnancy test removes an ectopic from the running and leaves torsion of the known cyst.
takeaway: Acute pelvic pain with a cyst and a negative pregnancy test is torsion until the ovary is seen — it is a time-critical, ovary-threatening emergency.

stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) develops a sudden, painful, pale, cold and pulseless left leg over a few hours, with reduced sensation but intact power. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Primary amputation, as the limb is non-viable
options.B: Elevate the leg and arrange arterial duplex as an outpatient
options.C: Aspirin and clopidogrel with vascular clinic in two weeks
options.D: Start a DOAC and arrange outpatient vascular follow-up
options.E: IV heparin and urgent referral for revascularisation

correct_answer: E. IV heparin and urgent referral for revascularisation
why_correct: Acute limb ischaemia, usually embolic in atrial fibrillation, is a limb-threatening emergency: immediate IV heparin limits clot propagation while urgent vascular assessment arranges embolectomy or other revascularisation.
why_wrong: A. With intact power and only reduced sensation the limb is threatened but salvageable; amputation is for an irreversibly ischaemic limb. B. Elevation further reduces perfusion, and outpatient imaging wastes the window for revascularisation. C. Antiplatelets do not treat an acute embolus, and delayed review risks limb loss. D. Oral anticoagulation is appropriate long term, but this limb-threatening emergency needs immediate heparin and urgent revascularisation, not outpatient care.
pearl: A sudden pulseless leg in AF is an arterial embolus — heparinise immediately and get the vascular team; the clock decides whether the limb survives.
thinking: Sudden painful, pale, cold, pulseless leg in untreated atrial fibrillation ↓ Embolic acute limb ischaemia ↓ Reduced sensation but intact power: threatened but salvageable limb ↓ IV heparin and urgent referral for revascularisation
exam_trap: D, a DOAC with outpatient follow-up — anticoagulation is part of the answer, so it feels right. But oral anticoagulation with outpatient management wastes the narrow window in which the limb can be saved; the patient needs heparin now and urgent revascularisation.
takeaway: A sudden pulseless leg in AF is an arterial embolus — heparinise immediately and get the vascular team; the clock decides whether the limb survives.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant has 18 hours of right iliac fossa pain with guarding and rebound tenderness, a white cell count of 14, and a low-grade fever. What is the most appropriate first imaging investigation?

options.A: Ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis
options.E: No imaging — proceed straight to appendicectomy

correct_answer: A. Ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis
why_correct: In pregnancy, ultrasound is the first-line imaging for suspected appendicitis because it avoids ionising radiation; if it is inconclusive, MRI is the next step, with CT avoided where possible.
why_wrong: B. CT is the default test in non-pregnant adults, but its ionising radiation makes it the wrong first choice in pregnancy, where ultrasound then MRI is preferred. C. MRI is the second-line test if ultrasound is inconclusive, not the first investigation. D. A plain abdominal X-ray uses radiation and does not reliably show appendicitis. E. Appendicitis is harder to diagnose clinically in pregnancy, and ultrasound is quick and safe, so imaging should come before going to surgery.
pearl: Image the pregnant abdomen with ultrasound first and MRI second — keep CT and its radiation as the last resort.
thinking: Right iliac fossa pain with peritonism, raised white cells and fever ↓ Appendicitis is suspected ↓ She is 10 weeks pregnant, so ionising radiation should be avoided ↓ The first imaging is ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis
exam_trap: B, CT abdomen — the most sensitive test for appendicitis, and the default in a non-pregnant adult. But its ionising radiation makes it the wrong first choice in pregnancy, where ultrasound (then MRI) is preferred.
takeaway: Image the pregnant abdomen with ultrasound first and MRI second — keep CT and its radiation as the last resort.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with painless visible haematuria, a dull loin ache and a new left-sided varicocele that does not empty on lying down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Painless haematuria with a loin ache, and a new non-emptying left varicocele from renal vein involvement, strongly suggests renal cell carcinoma. The classic (but uncommon) triad is haematuria, loin pain and a palpable loin mass; a varicocele is an associated sign, not part of the triad.
why_wrong: A. A simple renal cyst is usually asymptomatic and does not cause haematuria or obstruct the renal vein. C. A bladder calculus can cause haematuria, but it does not explain a loin ache or a varicocele that does not empty on lying down. D. Benign prostatic hyperplasia causes lower urinary tract symptoms and occasionally haematuria, but not loin ache or a non-emptying varicocele. E. Pyelonephritis causes fever, loin pain and dysuria, not painless haematuria with a varicocele.
pearl: Painless haematuria with a new non-emptying varicocele is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise — the varicocele betrays the renal vein.
thinking: Older man with painless visible haematuria and loin ache ↓ A new left varicocele does not empty on lying down ↓ The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, so a tumour may be obstructing it ↓ The diagnosis is renal cell carcinoma
exam_trap: C, a bladder calculus — a cause of haematuria, so a reasonable thought. But it does not explain the varicocele, and the loin ache plus the non-emptying varicocele point to a renal tumour invading the renal vein.
takeaway: Painless haematuria with a new non-emptying varicocele is renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise — the varicocele betrays the renal vein.

stem: A 22-year-old man has central abdominal pain that has migrated to the right iliac fossa over a day, with anorexia, low-grade fever, and guarding and rebound tenderness at McBurney's point. What is the most appropriate management?

options.C: A trial of oral antibiotics at home

why_correct: Migratory right-iliac-fossa pain with anorexia and peritonism is acute appendicitis, a clinical diagnosis warranting urgent surgical assessment and appendicectomy to prevent perforation.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy has no role in acute appendicitis and risks perforation. B. A week's delay risks perforation; imaging, if needed, is done urgently. C. Antibiotic-only treatment is for selected uncomplicated cases under surgical care, not peritonism at home. D. Analgesia alone does not treat appendicitis.
pearl: Migratory right-iliac-fossa pain with peritonism is appendicitis — refer for surgery, do not manage peritonitis at home.
thinking: Central pain migrating to the RIF with anorexia and fever ↓ guarding and rebound at McBurney's point ↓ appendicitis with peritonism
exam_trap: C, oral antibiotics at home — antibiotic-only management exists for selected uncomplicated cases, so it has some basis. But with peritonism (guarding and rebound) the patient needs urgent surgical assessment, not home treatment.
takeaway: Migratory right-iliac-fossa pain with peritonism is appendicitis — refer for surgery, do not manage peritonitis at home.

stem: A fit patient has acute cholecystitis (right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, a positive Murphy's sign and ultrasound showing a thick-walled gallbladder with stones). They are systemically stable. What is the preferred timing of cholecystectomy?

options.A: Antibiotics alone, with surgery reserved for any recurrent attacks
options.B: Interval surgery 6–8 weeks after cooling off with antibiotics
options.C: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis
options.D: Emergency open cholecystectomy within 24 hours of admission

correct_answer: C. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis
why_correct: Current evidence favours early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (during the index admission, within 1 week of diagnosis, as recommended by NICE CG188) for acute cholecystitis in fit patients, as it shortens overall illness and reduces complications compared with delayed interval surgery.
why_wrong: A. Fit patients should have early cholecystectomy; antibiotics alone risk recurrent attacks and complications. B. Delayed interval surgery is the older approach; early surgery in fit patients shortens illness and reduces recurrent admissions. D. Laparoscopic surgery is preferred, and emergency open surgery is not needed in a stable patient. E. Cholecystostomy is reserved for patients too unwell or unfit for surgery, not a fit, stable patient.
pearl: Acute cholecystitis in a fit patient is taken to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy — the 'cool off and come back' delay is the worse option.
thinking: Acute cholecystitis confirmed clinically and on ultrasound ↓ Fit and systemically stable patient ↓ NICE offers early surgery within 1 week of diagnosis ↓ Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within a week of diagnosis
exam_trap: B, delayed interval surgery after antibiotics — the older 'let it settle, operate later' approach feels safer. But early cholecystectomy in fit patients gives better outcomes than interval surgery; delaying risks recurrent attacks and a longer total course.
takeaway: Acute cholecystitis in a fit patient is taken to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy — the 'cool off and come back' delay is the worse option.

stem: A patient with a long-standing inguinal hernia presents with a tender, irreducible, tense lump and now has colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. The overlying skin is becoming erythematous. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassurance and an outpatient hernia clinic referral
options.C: Manual reduction under sedation and discharge
options.D: A truss and review in six weeks
options.E: Oral analgesia and observation at home

correct_answer: B. Urgent surgery (the hernia is strangulated/obstructed)
why_correct: A previously reducible hernia that becomes tender, irreducible and tense with signs of obstruction (vomiting, colic) and skin changes is strangulated — the blood supply is compromised — and requires urgent surgery to prevent bowel ischaemia and perforation.
why_wrong: A. An outpatient referral is for a reducible hernia; a strangulated hernia risks dead bowel. C. Reducing a possibly ischaemic hernia can return non-viable bowel to the abdomen. D. A truss is never used for an irreducible or strangulated hernia. E. Home observation delays emergency surgery.
pearl: A tender, irreducible, obstructing hernia is strangulated — to theatre urgently; the elective clinic is for the reducible ones.
thinking: Long-standing inguinal hernia now tender, tense and irreducible ↓ colic, vomiting and skin erythema ↓ strangulation
exam_trap: A, an outpatient clinic referral — elective repair is routine for a simple reducible hernia. But a tender, irreducible hernia with obstruction is a surgical emergency; delaying for an outpatient appointment risks dead bowel.
takeaway: A tender, irreducible, obstructing hernia is strangulated — to theatre urgently; the elective clinic is for the reducible ones.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has a new, painless, hard, irregular, fixed breast lump with overlying skin dimpling. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
options.B: Mammogram via the screening programme, referring if abnormal
options.C: A course of flucloxacillin and review in two weeks
options.D: Re-examine in 4–6 weeks to see if it persists
options.E: Fine-needle aspiration in primary care, referring if blood-stained

correct_answer: A. Suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
why_correct: A new hard, irregular, fixed breast lump with skin dimpling in an older woman is suspicious for cancer and warrants urgent referral for triple assessment (clinical examination, imaging and biopsy).
why_wrong: B. Screening mammography is not a diagnostic pathway for a symptomatic lump; a suspicious lump needs urgent referral. C. There are no features of infection, and antibiotics would delay assessment of a suspicious lump. D. Watchful waiting is inappropriate for a hard, fixed lump with skin dimpling in a woman over 30. E. Aspiration in primary care is not appropriate for a suspicious solid lump; it needs triple assessment in a breast clinic.
pearl: A hard, fixed, irregular breast lump with skin dimpling is cancer until triple assessment says otherwise — refer urgently.
thinking: 55-year-old woman with a new, hard, irregular, fixed breast lump and skin dimpling ↓ Suspected breast cancer ↓ A: suspected cancer referral to a breast clinic for triple assessment
exam_trap: B, a screening mammogram — imaging seems a reasonable first step. But screening is for asymptomatic women; a suspicious symptomatic lump needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for triple assessment.
takeaway: A hard, fixed, irregular breast lump with skin dimpling is cancer until triple assessment says otherwise — refer urgently.

stem: A patient has severe, sharp pain on defecation lasting some time afterwards, with a small amount of bright red blood on the toilet paper. Examination (when tolerable) suggests a tear in the posterior midline of the anal margin. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: A topical corticosteroid cream with a stimulant laxative
options.B: Early referral for lateral internal sphincterotomy
options.C: A course of oral metronidazole and review in two weeks
options.D: Rubber band ligation of presumed internal haemorrhoids
options.E: Fibre, fluids and topical GTN or diltiazem

correct_answer: E. Fibre, fluids and topical GTN or diltiazem
why_correct: Severe pain on defecation with bright red bleeding and a posterior midline tear is an anal fissure; first-line management is conservative — stool softening (fibre and fluids), analgesia and a topical agent such as GTN or diltiazem to relax the sphincter and aid healing.
why_wrong: A. Steroid creams do not heal fissures, and stimulant laxatives can worsen pain; stool softening with fibre and fluids is preferred. B. Sphincterotomy is reserved for chronic fissures that fail topical treatment. C. A fissure is not an infection; oral antibiotics have no role in first-line management. D. Banding treats internal haemorrhoids, not an anal fissure.
pearl: Painful defecation with bright-red blood and a posterior midline tear is an anal fissure — fibre, fluids and topical GTN first.
thinking: Severe pain on defecation with bright red blood on the paper ↓ Tear in the posterior midline of the anal margin: acute anal fissure ↓ First line is to soften stools and relax the sphincter ↓ Fibre, fluids and topical GTN or diltiazem
exam_trap: B, urgent surgery for all fissures — the pain may seem to demand intervention. But most fissures heal with conservative measures and topical treatment; surgery (e.g. sphincterotomy) is reserved for chronic, refractory cases.
takeaway: Painful defecation with bright-red blood and a posterior midline tear is an anal fissure — fibre, fluids and topical GTN first.

stem: A woman in her early twenties has a smooth, firm, painless, highly mobile breast lump (it slips under the examining fingers). What is the most likely diagnosis and the appropriate approach?

options.A: Breast cyst — aspirate in primary care and discharge
options.C: Phyllodes tumour — wide local excision with clear margins
options.D: Breast abscess — ultrasound-guided aspiration and antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Fibroadenoma — triple assessment, then observation
why_correct: A smooth, firm, painless, very mobile breast lump in a young woman is most likely a fibroadenoma (a benign 'breast mouse'); it is still confirmed with triple assessment (examination, imaging and biopsy/cytology as appropriate), after which it can be observed or removed by choice.
why_wrong: A. Cysts are commoner in women aged 35–50 and are smooth and fluctuant rather than firm and highly mobile; aspiration in primary care is not appropriate. C. Phyllodes tumours are rarer, larger and faster growing, typically in older women; a small mobile lump in a woman in her twenties is most likely a fibroadenoma. D. An abscess is painful, red and tender, often during lactation, unlike this painless lump. E. Discrete breast lumps should be referred for triple assessment to confirm the benign diagnosis; clinical reassurance alone risks missing cancer.
pearl: A smooth, very mobile breast lump in a young woman is likely a fibroadenoma — still confirm it with triple assessment.
thinking: Young woman with a smooth, firm, painless lump ↓ Highly mobile ('breast mouse'): fibroadenoma is most likely ↓ Every discrete breast lump still needs triple assessment ↓ Fibroadenoma: triple assessment, then observation
exam_trap: E, simple reassurance with no assessment — fibroadenomas are benign, so reassurance feels sufficient. But all discrete breast lumps undergo triple assessment to confirm the benign diagnosis; reassurance without assessment risks missing cancer.
takeaway: A smooth, very mobile breast lump in a young woman is likely a fibroadenoma — still confirm it with triple assessment.

stem: An elderly, constipation-prone nursing-home resident has marked abdominal distension, pain and absolute constipation. An abdominal X-ray shows a large, distended, inverted-U ('coffee bean') loop of bowel arising from the pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial management?

options.A: Faecal impaction — phosphate enema and oral macrogol daily
options.C: Caecal volvulus — urgent laparotomy and right hemicolectomy
options.D: Colonic pseudo-obstruction — IV neostigmine and supportive care
options.E: Diverticular stricture — CT colonography and elective resection

correct_answer: B. Sigmoid volvulus — flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression
why_correct: Massive abdominal distension with a 'coffee bean'/inverted-U loop on X-ray in an elderly, constipated patient is sigmoid volvulus; initial management is endoscopic decompression with a flatus tube (or sigmoidoscopy), with surgery if decompression fails or there is bowel ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. Impaction does not produce a coffee-bean loop; this is a closed-loop obstruction needing decompression. C. A caecal volvulus arises in the right iliac fossa, whereas a loop arising from the pelvis is a sigmoid volvulus. D. Pseudo-obstruction causes diffuse colonic dilatation without a twisted inverted-U loop. E. A stricture causes gradual obstruction without the coffee-bean sign, and decompression of the volvulus is the immediate priority.
pearl: A hugely distended abdomen with a 'coffee bean' loop in an elderly patient is sigmoid volvulus — decompress with a flatus tube/sigmoidoscopy.
thinking: Elderly constipated nursing-home resident with gross distension ↓ 'coffee bean' loop arising from the pelvis ↓ sigmoid volvulus
exam_trap: A, simple constipation managed with a laxative — constipation is common in this group. But the gross distension with a coffee-bean loop indicates a sigmoid volvulus (a closed-loop obstruction), which needs decompression, not just a laxative.
takeaway: A hugely distended abdomen with a 'coffee bean' loop in an elderly patient is sigmoid volvulus — decompress with a flatus tube/sigmoidoscopy.

stem: A woman has a groin lump located BELOW and LATERAL to the pubic tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?

options.A: Femoral hernia — high strangulation risk; repair even if painless
options.B: Direct inguinal hernia — low strangulation risk; watchful waiting
options.C: Indirect inguinal hernia — elective repair if symptomatic
options.D: Saphena varix — venous duplex scan and compression stockings
options.E: Inguinal lymphadenopathy — examine drainage area and observe

correct_answer: A. Femoral hernia — high strangulation risk; repair even if painless
why_correct: A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is a femoral hernia (an inguinal hernia lies above and medial); femoral hernias are commoner in women and carry a high risk of strangulation, so surgical repair is recommended even when asymptomatic.
why_wrong: B. Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is the femoral canal; direct inguinal hernias lie above and medial. C. Indirect inguinal hernias also emerge above and medial to the tubercle; the femoral position mandates repair because of strangulation risk. D. A saphena varix is a soft, compressible swelling with a cough thrill that disappears on lying down; a groin hernia in this position is femoral. E. A groin lump in this position should be assessed as a femoral hernia rather than assumed to be a lymph node.
pearl: A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is a femoral hernia — high strangulation risk, so repair even if asymptomatic; inguinal is above and medial.
thinking: Groin lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle ↓ Inguinal hernias lie above and medial; this is the femoral canal ↓ Narrow femoral neck gives a high strangulation risk ↓ Femoral hernia: repair even if painless
exam_trap: B, a direct inguinal hernia managed by watchful waiting — groin hernias are often grouped together. But the position below and lateral to the pubic tubercle marks a FEMORAL hernia, whose high strangulation risk mandates repair, unlike a small, minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia.
takeaway: A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is a femoral hernia — high strangulation risk, so repair even if asymptomatic; inguinal is above and medial.

stem: A 30-year-old man has sudden severe colicky left flank pain radiating to the groin, with microscopic haematuria. He is afebrile and writhing in pain. What is the most appropriate first-line analgesia and key investigation?

options.A: Rectal or IV NSAID, with non-contrast CT KUB
options.B: IV morphine, with renal ultrasound as first-line imaging
options.C: Oral paracetamol and codeine with a plain KUB X-ray
options.D: IV paracetamol and contrast-enhanced CT abdomen

correct_answer: A. Rectal or IV NSAID, with non-contrast CT KUB
why_correct: Ureteric colic is best relieved by an NSAID (more effective than opioids for this pain), and non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder is the gold-standard investigation to confirm and locate the stone.
why_wrong: B. NSAIDs are more effective first-line analgesia than opioids for renal colic, and non-contrast CT is more accurate than ultrasound in adults. C. Paracetamol and codeine are weaker options, and a plain X-ray misses many stones. D. Contrast is not needed and may obscure stones; non-contrast CT KUB is the investigation of choice. E. Nephrostomy is reserved for an obstructed, infected kidney; he is afebrile.
pearl: Renal colic responds better to NSAIDs than opioids, and CT KUB is the test — reach for the anti-inflammatory and the CT.
thinking: A 30-year-old man has sudden severe colicky left flank pain radiating ↓ Colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria in an afebrile patient — the classic
exam_trap: B, morphine and ultrasound — opioids and imaging both feature in stone care, so it seems reasonable. But NSAIDs are the more effective first-line analgesia for renal colic, and CT KUB outperforms ultrasound for detecting stones.
takeaway: Renal colic responds better to NSAIDs than opioids, and CT KUB is the test — reach for the anti-inflammatory and the CT.

presentation: Acute Urinary Retention in Benign Prostatic Enlargement
stem: A 70-year-old man cannot pass urine for 12 hours and has a painful, palpable bladder. He has a history of poor urinary flow and nocturia. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Suprapubic catheter insertion as first-line drainage
options.B: Oral tamsulosin and review in the urology clinic in a week
options.C: Urethral catheterisation to relieve the retention
options.D: Urgent TURP on the next available list
options.E: Bladder scan, then a trial of voiding in a warm bath

correct_answer: C. Urethral catheterisation to relieve the retention
why_correct: Acute urinary retention is relieved immediately by urethral catheterisation, which decompresses the bladder and relieves pain; an alpha-blocker is then started to improve the chance of a successful trial without catheter.
why_wrong: A. Suprapubic catheterisation is used if urethral catheterisation fails or is contraindicated, not first-line. B. Tamsulosin is started alongside catheterisation to aid a later trial without catheter; it does not relieve retention now. D. Surgery is not an emergency treatment for retention; the bladder is drained first and the prostate managed later. E. A painful palpable bladder after 12 hours of retention needs immediate drainage, not attempts at spontaneous voiding.
pearl: Acute retention is decompressed first by catheter — the alpha-blocker comes after, for the trial without catheter.
thinking: Unable to void for 12 hours with a painful palpable bladder ↓ acute urinary retention ↓ drain the bladder now
exam_trap: B, tamsulosin and review — an alpha-blocker has a role, so it feels like reasonable management. But it does not relieve the painful, obstructed bladder now; the immediate need is catheter drainage, with the alpha-blocker added afterwards.
takeaway: Acute retention is decompressed first by catheter — the alpha-blocker comes after, for the trial without catheter.

stem: A 68-year-old man has lower urinary tract symptoms and a hard, irregular, nodular prostate on digital rectal examination. His PSA is raised. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent suspected cancer referral for MRI and biopsy
options.B: Repeat the PSA in six weeks before deciding on referral
options.C: Start tamsulosin and review symptoms in three months
options.D: Treat as prostatitis with a four-week quinolone course
options.E: Start finasteride and recheck the PSA in six months

correct_answer: A. Urgent suspected cancer referral for MRI and biopsy
why_correct: A hard, irregular prostate with a raised PSA raises suspicion of prostate cancer and warrants urgent referral, with multiparametric MRI and prostate biopsy to confirm and stage.
why_wrong: B. A hard, nodular prostate warrants urgent referral regardless of PSA; repeating the test delays diagnosis. C. An alpha-blocker treats symptoms of benign enlargement but does not address suspected cancer. D. There are no features of infection, and antibiotics would delay assessment of a suspicious gland. E. Finasteride lowers PSA and can mask cancer; the abnormal examination needs urgent referral.
pearl: A hard nodular prostate with a raised PSA is cancer until biopsy says otherwise — refer urgently, do not reassure.
thinking: LUTS with a hard, irregular, nodular prostate ↓ raised PSA ↓ suspected prostate cancer
exam_trap: B, repeat the PSA in six weeks — PSA can fluctuate, so rechecking feels prudent. But a hard, nodular prostate on DRE warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral regardless of PSA; repeating the test only delays diagnosis.
takeaway: A hard nodular prostate with a raised PSA is cancer until biopsy says otherwise — refer urgently, do not reassure.

stem: A 70-year-old man who smokes has a single episode of painless visible haematuria. He has no pain, no infection on dipstick, and no other symptoms. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Send an MSU and treat empirically for a UTI
options.B: Routine urology referral if a second episode occurs
options.C: Urgent suspected cancer referral for cystoscopy and imaging
options.D: Check renal function and repeat dipstick in six weeks
options.E: Renal ultrasound in primary care and review the result

correct_answer: C. Urgent suspected cancer referral for cystoscopy and imaging
why_correct: Painless visible haematuria in an older patient (especially a smoker) is bladder cancer until proven otherwise and warrants urgent referral for cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of infection, and painless visible haematuria in an older smoker needs urgent referral. B. A single episode of visible haematuria at this age is a red flag; waiting for recurrence delays diagnosis. D. Repeating tests delays assessment; visible haematuria warrants urgent referral now. E. Ultrasound alone cannot exclude bladder cancer; cystoscopy is required via urgent referral.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria is bladder cancer until cystoscopy says otherwise — refer urgently, do not treat as a UTI.
thinking: 70-year-old smoker with painless visible haematuria ↓ no infection ↓ suspected bladder cancer
exam_trap: A, treat as a UTI — haematuria can accompany infection, so antibiotics seem reasonable. But there is no evidence of infection, and painless visible haematuria in this group is a red flag for malignancy requiring urgent referral.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria is bladder cancer until cystoscopy says otherwise — refer urgently, do not treat as a UTI.

stem: A man in his late twenties notices a painless, hard lump within the body of one testis that does not transilluminate. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Reassurance, as testicular lumps are always benign
options.C: A trial of antibiotics for epididymitis
options.D: Aspiration of the lump in clinic

correct_answer: B. Urgent scrotal ultrasound (with tumour markers)
why_correct: A painless, hard intratesticular lump in a young man is testicular cancer until proven otherwise; urgent scrotal ultrasound (with serum tumour markers AFP, beta-hCG and LDH) is the next step, and it is highly curable when treated.
why_wrong: A. Testicular lumps are not always benign; an intratesticular mass is cancer until proven otherwise. C. A hard painless lump within the testis is not epididymitis; antibiotics delay diagnosis. D. Aspiration or biopsy through the scrotum is avoided in suspected testicular cancer. E. Waiting six months delays diagnosis of a highly curable cancer.
pearl: A painless hard intratesticular lump in a young man is testicular cancer until ultrasound says otherwise — not epididymitis.
thinking: Painless hard lump within the testis in a man in his late twenties ↓ does not transilluminate ↓ suspected testicular cancer
exam_trap: C, a trial of antibiotics for epididymitis — an inflammatory scrotal cause might be assumed. But a hard, painless lump WITHIN the testis is not epididymitis; it needs urgent ultrasound to exclude testicular cancer, not empirical antibiotics.
takeaway: A painless hard intratesticular lump in a young man is testicular cancer until ultrasound says otherwise — not epididymitis.

stem: A woman has fever with rigors, loin pain and tenderness in the renal angle, with dysuria and nausea. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Mechanical back pain — NSAIDs and physiotherapy referral
