options.B: Uncomplicated lower UTI — 3-day course of nitrofurantoin
options.C: Ureteric colic — NSAID analgesia and CT KUB
options.D: Pelvic inflammatory disease — ceftriaxone, doxycycline and metronidazole
options.E: Acute pyelonephritis — antibiotic course; admit if systemically unwell

correct_answer: E. Acute pyelonephritis — antibiotic course; admit if systemically unwell
why_correct: Fever with rigors, loin pain and renal-angle tenderness plus urinary symptoms is acute pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection); it is treated with an appropriate antibiotic course, with admission and intravenous therapy if the patient is systemically unwell or pregnant.
why_wrong: A. Fever, rigors, urinary symptoms and positive nitrites indicate infection, not mechanical pain. B. Fever, rigors and loin pain indicate upper-tract infection; nitrofurantoin does not achieve adequate renal levels and a short course is insufficient. C. Ureteric colic causes colicky pain radiating to the groin; fever with rigors and nitrites indicates pyelonephritis. D. PID causes lower abdominal pain with cervical motion tenderness and discharge, not loin pain with nitrite-positive urine.
pearl: Loin pain and fever with rigors is pyelonephritis (upper tract) — it needs a proper antibiotic course, not short-course cystitis treatment (nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate renal levels).
thinking: Fever with rigors, loin pain and renal-angle tenderness plus dysuria and nitrite-positive urine ↓ Acute pyelonephritis (upper urinary tract infection) ↓ E: antibiotic course; admit if systemically unwell
exam_trap: B, a simple lower UTI with a 3-day nitrofurantoin course — the urinary symptoms suggest a basic cystitis. But fever, rigors and LOIN pain indicate upper-tract infection (pyelonephritis), which needs a fuller antibiotic course, not short-course cystitis treatment (nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate renal levels).
takeaway: Loin pain and fever with rigors is pyelonephritis (upper tract) — it needs a proper antibiotic course, not short-course cystitis treatment (nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate renal levels).

stem: A man in his fifties has gradual-onset erectile dysfunction. Beyond addressing the symptom, what is an important consideration, and what is the first-line drug treatment (and its key contraindication)?

options.A: Prescribe a PDE5 inhibitor, which is safe to combine with GTN spray
options.B: Treat as psychogenic; psychosexual therapy as first-line
options.C: Testosterone replacement as first-line; avoid in prostate cancer
options.D: Assess cardiovascular risk; a PDE5 inhibitor, avoided with nitrates
options.E: Refer for a penile prosthesis as first-line treatment

correct_answer: D. Assess cardiovascular risk; a PDE5 inhibitor, avoided with nitrates
why_correct: Erectile dysfunction (especially gradual, organic) warrants assessment of cardiovascular risk and metabolic/endocrine factors, as it can be an early marker of vascular disease; first-line treatment is a PDE5 inhibitor (e.g. sildenafil), which is contraindicated with nitrates (risk of profound hypotension).
why_wrong: A. PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates such as GTN cause profound hypotension and are contraindicated together. B. Gradual onset in a man in his fifties suggests an organic (often vascular) cause, so cardiovascular assessment is needed. C. Testosterone is given for confirmed hypogonadism, not as first-line treatment of erectile dysfunction. E. Surgical options such as a prosthesis are reserved for failure of medical treatment.
pearl: Erectile dysfunction can herald vascular disease — assess CV risk; PDE5 inhibitors are first-line but never with nitrates.
thinking: Gradual-onset ED in a man in his fifties ↓ marker of vascular disease ↓ PDE5 inhibitor, never with nitrates
exam_trap: A, a PDE5 inhibitor regarded as safe with GTN spray — treating the ED pharmacologically seems straightforward. But PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates cause dangerous hypotension and are contraindicated together; nitrate use must be checked first.
takeaway: Erectile dysfunction can herald vascular disease — assess CV risk; PDE5 inhibitors are first-line but never with nitrates.

stem: A sexually active man has a gradual onset (over a day or two) of unilateral scrotal pain and swelling, with relief of pain on elevating the testis (a positive Prehn's sign) and an intact cremasteric reflex. What is the most likely diagnosis and a crucial differential?

options.A: Indirect inguinal hernia extending into the scrotum
options.C: Torsion of a testicular appendage (hydatid of Morgagni)
options.D: Epididymo-orchitis — torsion must still be excluded
options.E: Testicular tumour — urgent ultrasound and tumour markers

correct_answer: D. Epididymo-orchitis — torsion must still be excluded
why_correct: Gradual-onset unilateral scrotal pain and swelling with a positive Prehn's sign and a preserved cremasteric reflex, in a sexually active man, suggests epididymo-orchitis (often chlamydia/gonorrhoea in younger men, or urinary organisms in older men); the crucial differential is testicular torsion (sudden severe pain, absent cremasteric reflex), which is a surgical emergency and must be excluded.
why_wrong: A. A hernia arises from the groin with a cough impulse and does not cause gradual testicular pain relieved by elevation. B. Torsion is typically sudden and severe with an absent cremasteric reflex; the gradual onset and positive Prehn's sign favour epididymo-orchitis, although torsion must still be excluded. C. Appendage torsion mainly affects prepubertal boys and causes a tender nodule at the upper pole ('blue dot' sign). E. Testicular tumours usually present as a painless lump rather than gradual painful swelling relieved by elevation.
pearl: Gradual scrotal pain with positive Prehn's sign and intact cremasteric reflex suggests epididymo-orchitis — but always exclude testicular torsion.
thinking: Gradual unilateral scrotal pain and swelling in a sexually active man ↓ Positive Prehn's sign and intact cremasteric reflex favour infection ↓ Torsion must still be actively excluded ↓ Epididymo-orchitis, with torsion still to be excluded
exam_trap: B, definitely testicular torsion requiring no further thought — torsion must never be missed. But torsion is typically sudden and severe with an absent cremasteric reflex; the gradual onset with a positive Prehn's sign here suggests epididymo-orchitis, while still keeping torsion in mind.
takeaway: Gradual scrotal pain with positive Prehn's sign and intact cremasteric reflex suggests epididymo-orchitis — but always exclude testicular torsion.

stem: A retracted foreskin has become trapped behind the glans (often after catheterisation) and cannot be returned, leading to a swollen, painful glans. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent manual reduction of the foreskin with analgesia
options.B: Elective circumcision on the next available routine list
options.C: Topical steroid cream to the foreskin and review in 48 hours
options.D: Oral flucloxacillin for balanitis and review
options.E: Remove the catheter and observe for spontaneous reduction

correct_answer: A. Urgent manual reduction of the foreskin with analgesia
why_correct: Paraphimosis — a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans causing a constricting band and swelling — is a urological emergency, because progressive oedema can compromise blood flow to the glans; management is prompt manual reduction (with analgesia and measures to reduce swelling), and dorsal slit/circumcision if reduction fails.
why_wrong: B. Circumcision may be offered later, but the trapped foreskin needs urgent reduction now to protect the glans. C. Topical steroids treat phimosis; they do not relieve a constricting band around the glans. D. This is not balanitis; antibiotics do not relieve the constriction. E. Paraphimosis does not reliably resolve on its own, and delay risks ischaemia of the glans.
pearl: Paraphimosis (foreskin trapped behind the glans) is a urological emergency — reduce it promptly to protect the glans.
thinking: Retracted foreskin trapped behind a swollen, painful glans ↓ Paraphimosis, a urological emergency threatening the glans ↓ A: urgent manual reduction of the foreskin with analgesia
exam_trap: B, elective circumcision — circumcision may be offered later, so it can seem definitive. But paraphimosis threatens the viability of the glans through constriction and requires urgent reduction, not delayed review.
takeaway: Paraphimosis (foreskin trapped behind the glans) is a urological emergency — reduce it promptly to protect the glans.

stem: A 16-month-old boy had a 3-minute generalised seizure during a fever of 39.5°C. He has fully recovered and is now alert and playing. This is his first such event and examination is normal. What is the most appropriate advice to the parents?

options.A: Simple febrile convulsion; safety-net, with 999 if over 5 minutes
options.B: Arrange an urgent EEG and an outpatient paediatric neurology review
options.C: Give paracetamol regularly during fevers to prevent further seizures
options.D: Admit him for a full septic screen, including a lumbar puncture today
options.E: Arrange an MRI brain scan to exclude an underlying structural cause

correct_answer: A. Simple febrile convulsion; safety-net, with 999 if over 5 minutes
why_correct: A brief, generalised seizure with fever in a well, fully recovered young child is a simple febrile convulsion — common, benign, not requiring investigation, with reassurance and safety-netting the appropriate management.
why_wrong: B. A simple febrile convulsion does not require EEG or neurology referral. C. Antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions; they are given for comfort only. D. A full septic screen and lumbar puncture are not needed in a well, fully recovered child with a simple febrile convulsion and normal examination. E. Neuroimaging is not indicated after a simple febrile convulsion with a normal examination.
pearl: Simple febrile convulsions are benign and need reassurance, not investigation — and antipyretics do not prevent them.
thinking: 16-month-old, single brief (3-minute) generalised seizure with fever, full recovery and normal examination ↓ Simple febrile convulsion — benign, no investigation needed, antipyretics do not prevent recurrence ↓ A: reassure and safety-net (999 if a seizure lasts over 5 minutes)
exam_trap: C, regular paracetamol to prevent recurrence — intuitively the antipyretic should stop fever-triggered fits. But antipyretics do not prevent febrile convulsions; the correct management is reassurance and safety-netting.
takeaway: Simple febrile convulsions are benign and need reassurance, not investigation — and antipyretics do not prevent them.

stem: A 9-month-old has 3 days of high fever and is otherwise well; as the fever resolves, a pink maculopapular rash appears on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: High fever for several days followed by a rash that appears as the fever breaks, in a well infant, is roseola infantum (human herpesvirus 6) — a benign, self-limiting illness.
why_wrong: A. In measles the rash appears while the fever is high, with coryza, cough, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots. C. Rubella causes a mild fever at the same time as the rash, with suboccipital lymphadenopathy, rather than a rash after the fever settles. D. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue, appearing with the fever. E. Meningococcal disease causes a non-blanching rash in an unwell child, not a pink maculopapular rash as fever settles in a well infant.
pearl: Fever first, rash as the fever breaks, child well throughout, is roseola — measles rashes appear while the child is still hot and ill.
thinking: 9-month-old with 3 days of high fever, otherwise well ↓ Rash appears as the fever resolves ↓ Pink maculopapular rash on the trunk in this age group ↓ Roseola infantum (HHV-6)
exam_trap: A, measles — a febrile rash illness, so a reasonable thought. But in measles the rash appears while the fever is still high and is accompanied by coryza, cough and Koplik spots; here the rash comes as the fever resolves.
takeaway: Fever first, rash as the fever breaks, child well throughout, is roseola — measles rashes appear while the child is still hot and ill.

stem: A newborn fails to pass meconium in the first 48 hours and develops abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops with a 'soap-bubble' (granular) appearance. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
why_correct: Meconium ileus — thick, inspissated meconium obstructing the distal ileum with a granular 'soap-bubble' appearance — is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis and warrants a sweat test or genetic confirmation.
why_wrong: B. Hirschsprung's disease also delays passage of meconium, but it is aganglionosis without the inspissated soap-bubble meconium of meconium ileus. C. Necrotising enterocolitis mainly affects premature infants after feeding, with bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis on X-ray. D. Duodenal atresia causes bilious vomiting from birth with a double-bubble sign, not distal ileal obstruction with soap-bubble meconium. E. Malrotation with volvulus causes sudden bilious vomiting and is a surgical emergency, but it does not cause the granular soap-bubble appearance.
pearl: Meconium ileus means cystic fibrosis until the sweat test says otherwise — the inspissated soap-bubble meconium is the clue.
thinking: Newborn fails to pass meconium with distension and bilious vomiting ↓ The X-ray shows a soap-bubble appearance of inspissated meconium ↓ This is meconium ileus ↓ The underlying diagnosis is cystic fibrosis
exam_trap: B, Hirschsprung's disease — it also presents with delayed meconium passage, making it the close differential. But Hirschsprung's is aganglionosis without the inspissated, soap-bubble meconium of meconium ileus, which points specifically to cystic fibrosis.
takeaway: Meconium ileus means cystic fibrosis until the sweat test says otherwise — the inspissated soap-bubble meconium is the clue.

stem: A 12-month-old child with a history of egg anaphylaxis is due the MMRV vaccine. The parents are worried. What is the correct advice?

options.B: MMRV is contraindicated in egg allergy
options.C: MMRV must be given in hospital under specialist supervision
options.D: MMRV can be given as normal, including in egg anaphylaxis
options.E: MMRV should be deferred until the child is older

correct_answer: D. MMRV can be given as normal, including in egg anaphylaxis
why_correct: All children with egg allergy, including previous anaphylaxis, should receive MMRV as a routine procedure in primary care. The measles and mumps components are grown in chick-embryo cell culture, but egg-derived products are not in the vaccine itself, and the varicella component is not made using egg; anaphylaxis to MMR-containing vaccines relates to other components such as gelatine, not egg.
why_wrong: A. Skin testing is not needed, because MMRV contains no meaningful egg protein. B. MMRV is not contraindicated in egg allergy; the egg caution applies to vaccines such as yellow fever. C. Hospital administration is not needed; the Green Book advises giving MMRV in primary care even after egg anaphylaxis. E. Deferring MMRV is unnecessary and leaves the child unprotected against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox.
pearl: MMRV is safe in egg allergy, even anaphylaxis — give it in primary care; the egg caution belongs to yellow fever and some flu vaccines.
thinking: Child with egg anaphylaxis is due MMRV ↓ Measles/mumps components grown in chick-embryo cell culture; no egg protein of significance in the vaccine; varicella component egg-free ↓ Give routinely in primary care
exam_trap: B, MMRV contraindicated in egg allergy — a common misconception, since some vaccines do carry egg-allergy cautions. But that caution applies to vaccines such as yellow fever and some influenza vaccines, not MMRV, which is safe.
takeaway: MMRV is safe in egg allergy, even anaphylaxis — give it in primary care; the egg caution belongs to yellow fever and some flu vaccines.

stem: A 2-year-old, after a sudden fright, cries briefly, then goes silent, turns pale, stiffens and loses consciousness for a few seconds before recovering fully and quickly. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: 24-hour ECG to exclude long QT, then antiarrhythmics
options.B: Start an antiepileptic such as levetiracetam
options.C: Urgent EEG and paediatric neurology referral

correct_answer: D. Reassure: benign breath-holding/reflex anoxic spells
why_correct: A typical breath-holding or reflex anoxic spell — triggered by upset or pain, with brief pallor or cyanosis, stiffening and rapid full recovery — is benign and managed with parental reassurance.
why_wrong: A. A typical provoked spell with rapid full recovery does not need antiarrhythmics; long QT is suspected with exercise- or startle-triggered collapse without the typical crying prodrome. B. These provoked, rapidly resolving spells are not epileptic, and antiepileptics are not effective. C. The history is typical of a benign spell; EEG is not indicated. E. Admission is unnecessary for a typical spell with full recovery and normal examination.
pearl: Provoked spells with rapid full recovery are benign breath-holding/reflex anoxic episodes — reassure, do not medicate.
thinking: Brief fright → cry → pallor, stiffening and brief LOC with rapid full recovery; normal examination ↓ provoked, self-limiting reflex anoxic/breath-holding spell ↓ reassure
exam_trap: B, start an antiepileptic — the brief stiffening can look like a seizure. But these provoked, rapidly self-resolving spells are not epilepsy, and antiepileptics are neither needed nor effective.
takeaway: Provoked spells with rapid full recovery are benign breath-holding/reflex anoxic episodes — reassure, do not medicate.

stem: A 3-year-old has a low fever, painful mouth ulcers, and a vesicular rash on the palms and soles. He is otherwise well and eating a little. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Supportive care with fluids and analgesia
options.B: Oral aciclovir and exclusion from nursery for a week
options.C: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for a ten-day course
options.D: Admission for IV fluids and observation overnight
options.E: Topical hydrocortisone to the palms and soles

correct_answer: A. Supportive care with fluids and analgesia
why_correct: Hand, foot and mouth disease (usually coxsackievirus A16) is a self-limiting viral illness managed supportively with fluids and analgesia; it resolves within about a week.
why_wrong: B. This is hand, foot and mouth disease (coxsackievirus), not herpes; aciclovir is not indicated and exclusion is not required. C. This is a viral illness; antibiotics have no role. D. He is eating a little and not dehydrated, so admission is not needed. E. The rash is self-limiting, and topical steroids are not indicated.
pearl: Hand, foot and mouth disease is supportive care only — the palm-sole-mouth distribution is coxsackie, not herpes.
thinking: Low fever, painful mouth ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles in a well toddler ↓ Hand, foot and mouth disease (coxsackievirus), self-limiting ↓ A: supportive care with fluids and analgesia
exam_trap: B, oral aciclovir — the oral ulcers might suggest herpes, so an antiviral is tempting. But this is a coxsackievirus illness, not herpes, and aciclovir is neither indicated nor effective; care is supportive.
takeaway: Hand, foot and mouth disease is supportive care only — the palm-sole-mouth distribution is coxsackie, not herpes.

stem: A 4-month-old has 2 days of coryza followed by cough, wheeze, fine crackles and mild respiratory distress. He is feeding at about three-quarters of normal and saturations are 94%. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Supportive care, monitoring feeding and saturations
options.B: Oral amoxicillin for a presumed bacterial chest infection
options.C: A trial of nebulised salbutamol and review in an hour
options.D: A three-day course of oral prednisolone
options.E: Nebulised 3% hypertonic saline given as routine treatment

correct_answer: A. Supportive care, monitoring feeding and saturations
why_correct: Bronchiolitis (usually RSV) in infants is managed supportively — monitoring feeding, hydration and oxygenation — as bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not effective; admission is for feeding or oxygenation concerns.
why_wrong: B. Bronchiolitis is viral; antibiotics do not help unless there is a secondary bacterial infection. C. Bronchodilators are not effective in bronchiolitis and are not recommended. D. Corticosteroids do not improve outcomes in bronchiolitis. E. Hypertonic saline is not recommended as routine treatment for bronchiolitis.
pearl: Bronchiolitis is supportive care — bronchodilators and steroids do not work in the wheezy infant under one.
thinking: Infant with coryza, then cough, wheeze and fine crackles ↓ Bronchiolitis ↓ Saturations 94% (above the 92% referral threshold) and feeding only modestly reduced, so supportive care with close review of intake ↓ Supportive care, monitoring feeding and saturations
exam_trap: C, nebulised salbutamol — the wheeze invites a bronchodilator. But bronchodilators do not help bronchiolitis (the airways are plugged with debris, not bronchospasm); care is supportive.
takeaway: Bronchiolitis is supportive care — bronchodilators and steroids do not work in the wheezy infant under one.

stem: A 2-year-old has a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor that is worse when upset, following a coryzal illness. He is not drooling and looks otherwise well. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: A single dose of oral dexamethasone
options.D: Throat examination to inspect the airway

correct_answer: B. A single dose of oral dexamethasone
why_correct: Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis) with a barking cough and stridor is treated with a single dose of oral dexamethasone, which reduces airway oedema; nebulised adrenaline is added for severe distress.
why_wrong: A. Intubation and IV antibiotics are for epiglottitis (toxic, drooling child); this well child with a barking cough has croup. C. Salbutamol does not relieve upper-airway oedema; nebulised adrenaline is the rescue treatment for severe croup. D. Examining the throat can precipitate airway obstruction in a child with stridor and is not needed to diagnose croup. E. Croup is viral; antibiotics have no role.
pearl: Croup is the barking cough treated with oral dexamethasone — drooling and toxaemia instead would point to epiglottitis.
thinking: Barking cough, hoarse voice and stridor after coryza; not drooling or toxic ↓ Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis), not epiglottitis ↓ B: single dose of oral dexamethasone
exam_trap: A, intubation and antibiotics — appropriate for the look-alike emergency, epiglottitis. But this child is not toxic or drooling, and has a barking cough; this is croup, treated with oral steroids, not airway instrumentation.
takeaway: Croup is the barking cough treated with oral dexamethasone — drooling and toxaemia instead would point to epiglottitis.

stem: An unimmunised 4-year-old is acutely unwell with a high fever, drooling, a muffled voice and a soft stridor, sitting forward and refusing to lie down. What is the most important immediate action?

options.A: Lie the child flat and give high-flow oxygen by mask
options.B: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor to confirm the diagnosis
options.C: Call senior anaesthetic and ENT help; do not examine the throat
options.D: Lateral neck X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
options.E: Nebulised adrenaline and oral dexamethasone, managing as for croup

correct_answer: C. Call senior anaesthetic and ENT help; do not examine the throat
why_correct: Epiglottitis (now rare, in unimmunised children) is a true airway emergency; the child is kept calm and upright while senior anaesthetic and ENT help secure the airway, because any throat examination can precipitate complete obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Lying the child flat can precipitate complete airway obstruction; the child is kept upright and calm. B. Examining the throat can trigger fatal airway obstruction; the airway is secured first. D. Sending the child for X-ray delays securing the airway and moves them away from expert help. E. Treating as croup misses a true airway emergency; the priority is senior airway management.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis, do not touch the throat — keep the child calm and get the airway secured by experts.
thinking: Unimmunised child + high fever, drooling, muffled voice, soft stridor, sitting forward ↓ epiglottitis, a true airway emergency ↓ call senior anaesthetic and ENT help; do not examine the throat
exam_trap: B, examine the throat — confirming the diagnosis feels like good practice. But examining or distressing the throat in epiglottitis can trigger fatal airway obstruction; the airway is secured first, and the throat is left alone.
takeaway: In suspected epiglottitis, do not touch the throat — keep the child calm and get the airway secured by experts.

stem: A 9-month-old has episodes of screaming with drawing-up of the legs, vomiting, and a 'redcurrant jelly' stool. A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right abdomen. What is the most appropriate management if the child is stable?

options.E: Abdominal X-ray then home with safety-net

why_correct: Intussusception (telescoping of bowel) with colicky pain, a sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant-jelly stool is reduced, in a stable child, by air or contrast enema; surgery is reserved for failure, perforation or peritonitis.
why_wrong: B. Immediate laparotomy is reserved for peritonitis, perforation, haemodynamic instability or failed enema reduction; a stable child should have air (or contrast) enema reduction first. C. Discharging a child with suspected intussusception risks bowel ischaemia and perforation; it needs urgent reduction. D. Antibiotics and observation do not reduce the intussusception and delay definitive treatment. E. An abdominal X-ray is neither sensitive nor reassuring, and sending the child home misses a surgical emergency; ultrasound confirmation and enema reduction are needed.
pearl: Stable intussusception is reduced by air enema, not the knife — reserve surgery for peritonitis or failed reduction.
thinking: 9-month-old + colicky screaming, vomiting, redcurrant-jelly stool, sausage-shaped mass, stable ↓ intussusception without peritonism ↓ air (or contrast) enema reduction
exam_trap: B, immediate laparotomy for all — surgery is definitive, so it feels safe. But in a stable child without peritonitis, air-enema reduction is both diagnostic and therapeutic and avoids an operation; surgery is for the unstable or failed reduction.
takeaway: Stable intussusception is reduced by air enema, not the knife — reserve surgery for peritonitis or failed reduction.

stem: A 3-year-old has had a high fever for 6 days with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a strawberry tongue and cracked lips, a polymorphous rash, swollen red hands and feet, and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the most important treatment and why?

options.A: Supportive care and paracetamol for a viral exanthem
options.B: IV ceftriaxone for presumed toxic shock syndrome
options.C: IV immunoglobulin and aspirin, to prevent coronary aneurysms
options.D: Oral penicillin for presumed scarlet fever

correct_answer: C. IV immunoglobulin and aspirin, to prevent coronary aneurysms
why_correct: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis whose feared complication is coronary artery aneurysm; IV immunoglobulin and aspirin, given promptly, markedly reduce that risk.
why_wrong: A. Five or more days of fever with these features is Kawasaki disease, which needs active treatment to protect the coronary arteries. B. There is no hypotension or multi-organ failure to suggest toxic shock; the features meet criteria for Kawasaki disease. D. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue but not non-purulent conjunctivitis or swollen hands and feet. E. The conjunctivitis is non-purulent and part of the vasculitis; antibiotic drops do not address the coronary risk.
pearl: Kawasaki disease is treated with immunoglobulin and aspirin to save the coronary arteries — do not dismiss the prolonged fever as viral.
thinking: Fever for 5 or more days with conjunctivitis, mucositis, rash, extremity changes and cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ Kawasaki disease, risk of coronary artery aneurysm ↓ C: IV immunoglobulin and aspirin
exam_trap: A, reassurance as viral — many febrile rash illnesses in toddlers are viral, so this is the easy miss. But Kawasaki disease threatens the coronary arteries and must be actively treated with immunoglobulin to prevent aneurysms.
takeaway: Kawasaki disease is treated with immunoglobulin and aspirin to save the coronary arteries — do not dismiss the prolonged fever as viral.

presentation: Neonatal Jaundice in the First 24 Hours
stem: A baby develops visible jaundice at 18 hours of age. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Reassure and recheck at the routine day-5 midwife visit
options.B: Physiological jaundice — observe and encourage frequent breastfeeds
options.C: Breast-milk jaundice — continue breastfeeding and observe
options.D: Pathological — needs urgent bilirubin measurement and investigation
options.E: Start phototherapy and defer investigation unless it worsens

correct_answer: D. Pathological — needs urgent bilirubin measurement and investigation
why_correct: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is always pathological (often haemolytic, e.g. rhesus or ABO incompatibility, or sepsis) and requires urgent bilirubin measurement and investigation.
why_wrong: A. Jaundice under 24 hours cannot wait for routine review; bilirubin should be measured urgently. B. Physiological jaundice does not appear before 24 hours; jaundice this early is pathological until proven otherwise. C. Breast-milk jaundice appears later and persists beyond two weeks; it does not explain jaundice at 18 hours. E. Phototherapy may be needed, but the cause (e.g. haemolysis or sepsis) must be investigated urgently, not deferred.
pearl: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise — investigate urgently; physiological jaundice never comes that early.
thinking: Visible jaundice at 18 hours of age ↓ Onset within the first 24 hours is never physiological ↓ Consider haemolysis (rhesus, ABO) or sepsis ↓ Pathological: urgent bilirubin measurement and investigation
exam_trap: B, physiological — most neonatal jaundice is benign and physiological, so it is the comfortable assumption. But physiological jaundice never appears before 24 hours; jaundice this early is pathological until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise — investigate urgently; physiological jaundice never comes that early.

stem: A 6-month-old, not yet mobile, is brought in with a spiral fracture of the femur. The history is vague and inconsistent and changes between carers, and presentation was delayed. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Confront the parents about abuse before deciding on discharge
options.B: Treat the fracture and discharge with GP and health visitor letters
options.C: Arrange a skeletal survey as an outpatient after discharge
options.D: Test for osteogenesis imperfecta before considering safeguarding
options.E: Treat the injury and escalate to senior and safeguarding teams

correct_answer: E. Treat the injury and escalate to senior and safeguarding teams
why_correct: A spiral femoral fracture in a non-mobile infant, with an inconsistent, changing and delayed history, raises strong safeguarding concerns; the injury is treated and child-protection processes (senior review, referral) are activated.
why_wrong: A. Confronting carers can compromise the child's safety and the investigation; concerns are escalated through child protection procedures. B. Letters to the GP and health visitor do not protect the child; a child protection referral is needed before discharge. C. Investigations such as a skeletal survey are done within the safeguarding process with the child kept safe, not after discharge. D. Bone disorders are considered as part of the assessment, but they must not delay safeguarding escalation.
pearl: Injuries that do not fit the child's development or the story are safeguarding red flags — treat and escalate, do not just discharge.
thinking: Non-mobile 6-month-old + spiral femoral fracture + inconsistent, changing, delayed history ↓ suspected non-accidental injury ↓ treat the injury and escalate to senior and safeguarding teams
exam_trap: B, treat and discharge — focusing only on the medical injury feels like completing the task. But the inconsistent history and an unusual fracture in a non-mobile baby are red flags for non-accidental injury that must be escalated, not sent home.
takeaway: Injuries that do not fit the child's development or the story are safeguarding red flags — treat and escalate, do not just discharge.

stem: The parents of an 18-month-old child are concerned about his development. Which single feature would most clearly indicate an abnormal finding needing referral rather than normal variation?

options.A: Saying six to ten single words at 18 months
options.B: Not yet running or kicking a ball at 18 months
options.C: Not sitting by 12 months or not walking by 18 months
options.D: Not yet building a tower of six cubes at 18 months
options.E: Mild stranger anxiety and clinging to parents at 18 months

correct_answer: C. Not sitting by 12 months or not walking by 18 months
why_correct: Developmental delay is judged against limit ages: not sitting unsupported by 9 months (certainly by 12 months), or not walking by 18 months, are red flags warranting assessment, whereas later skills (running, drawing) are not yet expected at this age.
why_wrong: A. Six to ten single words at 18 months is within the normal range; the speech limit is no words at 18 months. B. Running and kicking a ball are later skills, so their absence at 18 months is not a red flag. D. A tower of six cubes is expected around two years, so its absence at 18 months is not abnormal. E. Stranger anxiety and clinginess are normal at this age.
pearl: Judge development against limit ages — not walking by 18 months is a red flag; not yet running is not.
thinking: Parents concerned about an 18-month-old's development ↓ Compare against limit ages (sit unsupported by 9 months, walk by 18 months) ↓ Later skills such as running and a six-cube tower are not yet expected ↓ Not sitting by 12 months or not walking by 18 months is the red flag
exam_trap: B, not running at 18 months — comparing against an advanced skill seems strict. But running is not expected at 18 months; the genuine red flag is failure to reach the limit ages for sitting or walking.
takeaway: Judge development against limit ages — not walking by 18 months is a red flag; not yet running is not.

stem: A 13-month-old child due the MMRV vaccine has a mild coryzal illness with a low-grade temperature but is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate action?

options.B: Defer the vaccine until completely well

correct_answer: D. Give the vaccine as scheduled
why_correct: Minor illnesses without fever (or with only a low-grade temperature) are not contraindications to vaccination; the vaccine should be given to avoid missed opportunities. Vaccination is deferred only for an acute severe febrile illness.
why_wrong: A. Fractional doses are not used; a partial dose may not give adequate protection. B. A minor coryzal illness without significant fever or systemic upset is not a reason to postpone; deferral risks a missed opportunity to immunise. C. A minor illness is not a contraindication, so there is no reason to cancel MMRV. E. Antibiotics are not indicated for a viral coryzal illness and are not needed before vaccination.
pearl: Minor illness is not a reason to defer vaccination — only acute severe febrile illness is; do not miss the opportunity.
thinking: 13-month-old due MMRV + mild coryza, low-grade temperature, otherwise well ↓ minor illness is not a contraindication ↓ give the vaccine as scheduled
exam_trap: B, defer until completely well — caution feels safe. But minor coryzal illness is not a contraindication, and deferring causes missed immunisations; only an acute severe febrile illness warrants postponement.
takeaway: Minor illness is not a reason to defer vaccination — only acute severe febrile illness is; do not miss the opportunity.

stem: At the newborn check, a baby has a positive Ortolani/Barlow test (a clunk on hip examination). She was breech and has a family history of hip problems. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: No imaging; re-examine at 6 weeks only

why_correct: A positive Barlow/Ortolani test or risk factors (breech, family history) for developmental dysplasia of the hip is investigated with hip ultrasound, as the cartilaginous infant hip is not well seen on X-ray.
why_wrong: A. A positive Ortolani/Barlow test is a screen-positive result that needs hip ultrasound (at 4 to 6 weeks of age under NIPE, with an outcome decision by 6 weeks), not simply re-examination. B. The young infant's femoral head is cartilaginous and poorly seen on X-ray; X-ray is used after about 4–6 months once ossification begins. C. MRI is not a first-line screening test and usually needs sedation. E. CT involves radiation and is not used to diagnose DDH in infants.
pearl: Image the young infant's hip with ultrasound — the cartilage is invisible to X-ray until ossification.
thinking: Positive Ortolani/Barlow test plus breech and family history ↓ Suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip; the infant femoral head is cartilaginous ↓ D: hip ultrasound
exam_trap: B, a plain X-ray — imaging the hip seems logical. But in young infants the femoral head is cartilaginous and not visible on X-ray; ultrasound is the appropriate investigation.
takeaway: Image the young infant's hip with ultrasound — the cartilage is invisible to X-ray until ossification.

presentation: Urinary Tract Infection in a Child
stem: An 18-month-old has a fever with no obvious focus, vomiting and is generally unwell. A clean-catch urine sample is positive on dipstick and culture. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Long-term antibiotic prophylaxis after this first UTI
options.B: Oral antibiotics, with a DMSA scan after every first UTI
options.C: Admit for IV antibiotics because of age under two years
options.D: Cranberry products and fluids without antibiotics
options.E: Prompt antibiotics; imaging if atypical or recurrent

correct_answer: E. Prompt antibiotics; imaging if atypical or recurrent
why_correct: A urinary tract infection in a young child is treated promptly with antibiotics, and atypical or recurrent infections (and infections in young infants) prompt imaging to detect structural abnormalities or reflux that predispose to renal scarring.
why_wrong: A. Prophylaxis is not routinely recommended after a first UTI. B. Routine DMSA is not recommended after a first typical UTI that responds to treatment; imaging is targeted at atypical or recurrent infection. C. Children over 3 months can usually be treated with oral antibiotics unless very unwell or unable to take them. D. A confirmed UTI in a young child needs antibiotics; cranberry products are not a treatment.
pearl: A young child's UTI is treated promptly and may need imaging — it can be the first sign of a structural problem, not just a simple infection.
thinking: 18-month-old, fever without focus, vomiting, unwell; urine positive on dipstick and culture ↓ UTI in a young child: treat promptly with antibiotics ↓ Imaging targeted at atypical or recurrent UTI, not every first UTI
exam_trap: B, a DMSA scan after every first UTI — imaging feels thorough in a young child. But routine DMSA is not recommended after a first typical UTI that responds to treatment; imaging is targeted at atypical or recurrent UTI.
takeaway: A young child's UTI is treated promptly and may need imaging — it can be the first sign of a structural problem, not just a simple infection.

stem: A 4-year-old has hard, infrequent, painful stools with some overflow soiling, and no red-flag features. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: Behavioural measures and a reward chart before any laxative
options.B: A stimulant laxative (senna) as the first-line single agent
options.C: Increased dietary fibre and fluids for four weeks first
options.D: A phosphate enema for disimpaction, then lactulose

correct_answer: E. Macrogol, with disimpaction then maintenance
why_correct: Idiopathic childhood constipation is treated first-line with an osmotic laxative (macrogol), using a disimpaction regimen if impacted, followed by maintenance, alongside diet, fluids and behavioural advice.
why_wrong: A. Behavioural measures support treatment, but established constipation with overflow needs a macrogol now. B. Stimulant laxatives are added if macrogol alone is insufficient; they are not first-line. C. Diet and fluids should not be used alone as first-line treatment for faecal impaction. D. Enemas are not used for disimpaction in children unless oral macrogol fails, and lactulose is not first-line.
pearl: Childhood constipation with soiling is treated with macrogol (disimpact then maintain) — diet alone will not clear an impacted bowel.
thinking: 4-year-old + hard, infrequent, painful stools with overflow soiling, no red flags ↓ idiopathic constipation with faecal impaction ↓ macrogol, disimpaction then maintenance
exam_trap: C, dietary advice alone — diet matters, so it feels sufficient. But established constipation with overflow soiling needs a macrogol (disimpaction and maintenance); diet alone will not clear an impacted rectum.
takeaway: Childhood constipation with soiling is treated with macrogol (disimpact then maintain) — diet alone will not clear an impacted bowel.

stem: A 9-year-old has a few weeks of marked thirst, frequent urination (including new bedwetting), weight loss and tiredness. A finger-prick glucose is markedly raised. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team
options.B: Urgent outpatient referral to the paediatric diabetes clinic within 2 weeks
options.C: Arrange a fasting glucose and HbA1c, then review the results
options.D: Start oral metformin and dietary advice in primary care
options.E: Treat for a urinary tract infection and recheck glucose in a week

correct_answer: A. Same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team
why_correct: New type 1 diabetes in a child (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, hyperglycaemia) requires same-day referral to specialist paediatric services because of the risk of rapidly developing diabetic ketoacidosis.
why_wrong: B. Suspected type 1 diabetes in a child needs same-day referral, as ketoacidosis can develop within hours. C. Further tests in primary care delay treatment; suspected type 1 diabetes needs same-day referral. D. This presentation is type 1 diabetes, which needs insulin; metformin is not appropriate. E. The polyuria and weight loss are explained by hyperglycaemia; treating a presumed UTI delays urgent referral.
pearl: A child with thirst, polyuria and weight loss is new type 1 diabetes — same-day referral; DKA can be hours away.
thinking: Child with weeks of polydipsia, polyuria/new enuresis, weight loss and raised capillary glucose ↓ New type 1 diabetes with risk of DKA within hours ↓ A: same-day referral to the paediatric diabetes team
exam_trap: B, a routine outpatient appointment — the symptoms have been present for weeks, so it feels non-urgent. But a child with new hyperglycaemia can deteriorate into DKA within hours; same-day specialist referral is required.
takeaway: A child with thirst, polyuria and weight loss is new type 1 diabetes — same-day referral; DKA can be hours away.

stem: A 5-year-old seen at the GP surgery is febrile, drowsy and mottled, with a rapidly spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: IM/IV benzylpenicillin now and emergency transfer
options.B: Wait for blood culture and lumbar puncture results before antibiotics
options.C: Oral amoxicillin and review in the morning
options.D: Do a glass test and observe for 4 hours
options.E: Emergency transfer, withholding antibiotics until hospital

correct_answer: A. IM/IV benzylpenicillin now and emergency transfer
why_correct: A non-blanching purpuric rash with fever and systemic illness suggests meningococcal septicaemia; immediate parenteral antibiotics (IV/IM benzylpenicillin or ceftriaxone in the community unless it delays transfer; IV ceftriaxone in hospital) are given without delay, as the condition can be fatal within hours.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics must not be delayed for investigations in suspected meningococcal sepsis. C. Oral antibiotics and delayed review are inadequate for life-threatening sepsis. D. A drowsy, mottled child with a non-blanching rash needs immediate treatment, not observation. E. Parenteral antibiotics should be given before transfer, as delay increases mortality.
pearl: A non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise — antibiotics now, before any investigation.
thinking: Febrile, drowsy, mottled child with a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash in primary care ↓ Meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise ↓ A: parenteral antibiotic now (unless it delays transfer) and emergency transfer
exam_trap: B, wait for cultures and LP — confirming the diagnosis first feels thorough. But meningococcal sepsis kills within hours; antibiotics are given immediately, and investigations must not delay treatment.
takeaway: A non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise — antibiotics now, before any investigation.

stem: A 6-year-old, after a recent upper respiratory infection, develops a palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and extensor surfaces of the legs, with abdominal pain and joint pain. Urine shows some blood and protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and legs with abdominal pain, arthralgia and renal involvement, following an infection in a child, is Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) — usually self-limiting with monitoring of renal function.
why_wrong: A. ITP causes flat petechiae and bruising with a low platelet count, without arthralgia, abdominal pain or renal involvement. C. Meningococcal disease causes a rapidly spreading rash in a toxic child, not palpable purpura over the buttocks with joint and renal features. D. The symmetrical distribution with joint, abdominal and renal features is typical of HSP rather than inflicted injury. E. Leukaemia causes pallor, bruising and bone pain with abnormal blood counts, not palpable purpura with haematuria after an infection.
pearl: Palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks with joints, gut and kidney in a well child is HSP — but always exclude meningococcal sepsis first.
thinking: Child after an upper respiratory infection, systemically well ↓ Palpable purpura over buttocks and extensor legs ↓ Abdominal pain, arthralgia and haematuria with proteinuria ↓ Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis)
exam_trap: C, meningococcal septicaemia — a purpuric rash always raises this fear, and it must be excluded. But the child is systemically well with a typical distribution and the joint/abdominal/renal features of HSP, not the toxic, rapidly deteriorating picture of meningococcal sepsis.
takeaway: Palpable purpura on the legs and buttocks with joints, gut and kidney in a well child is HSP — but always exclude meningococcal sepsis first.

stem: An unimmunised infant has paroxysms of severe coughing followed by an inspiratory 'whoop', with vomiting after coughing and apnoeic episodes. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Supportive care at home, as the cough is likely viral
options.B: Macrolide, notification and prophylaxis for contacts
options.C: An inhaled bronchodilator with a course of oral prednisolone
options.D: Oral amoxicillin and review in 48 hours at home
options.E: Oral co-amoxiclav and notification of the case

correct_answer: B. Macrolide, notification and prophylaxis for contacts
why_correct: Whooping cough (Bordetella pertussis) causes paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting; a macrolide is given (most useful early), the case is notified, and close contacts are offered chemoprophylaxis where UKHSA criteria are met (onset within 21 days and a vulnerable/priority-group contact); an apnoeic infant is admitted.
why_wrong: A. Paroxysmal cough with a whoop and apnoea in an unimmunised infant is pertussis; an apnoeic infant also needs admission. C. Bronchodilators and steroids do not help pertussis. D. Pertussis is treated with a macrolide, and an apnoeic infant needs admission rather than home review. E. Co-amoxiclav is not the recommended treatment; a macrolide is used, with prophylaxis for close contacts.
pearl: A whooping, paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting is pertussis — treat, notify, and protect the contacts.
thinking: Unimmunised infant with paroxysmal cough, inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting and apnoea ↓ Pertussis, notifiable; apnoeic infant needs admission ↓ B: macrolide, notification and contact prophylaxis per UKHSA criteria
exam_trap: A, reassurance as viral — cough is usually viral, so this is a tempting default. But the paroxysmal whooping cough with apnoea in an unimmunised infant is pertussis, a notifiable bacterial infection needing antibiotics and contact prophylaxis.
takeaway: A whooping, paroxysmal cough with post-tussive vomiting is pertussis — treat, notify, and protect the contacts.

stem: A young child with gastroenteritis is lethargic with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, a prolonged capillary refill time and reduced urine output. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: IV or IO 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, then reassess
options.B: Oral rehydration solution via nasogastric tube on the ward
options.C: A bolus of 5% glucose intravenously, then reassess
options.D: Check electrolytes and start fluids once results return
options.E: Loperamide and oral rehydration solution at home

correct_answer: A. IV or IO 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, then reassess
why_correct: A child with clinical shock/severe dehydration (lethargy, prolonged capillary refill, reduced urine output) needs prompt intravenous (or intraosseous) isotonic fluid resuscitation with a saline bolus, then reassessment; oral rehydration is for mild-to-moderate dehydration.
why_wrong: B. Nasogastric oral rehydration suits moderate dehydration; a shocked child needs IV or IO fluid resuscitation. C. Hypotonic glucose is not used for resuscitation and risks hyponatraemia; isotonic saline is required. D. Fluid resuscitation in shock must not wait for blood results. E. Antidiarrhoeal drugs are not used in young children with gastroenteritis, and home care is inappropriate for shock.
pearl: A shocked, severely dehydrated child gets an IV isotonic fluid bolus and reassessment — oral rehydration is for the milder end.
thinking: Gastroenteritis with lethargy, prolonged capillary refill and reduced urine output ↓ Severe dehydration with shock ↓ A: IV or IO 0.9% sodium chloride bolus, then reassess
exam_trap: B, oral rehydration at home — oral fluids are correct for mild dehydration, so this is a tempting de-escalation. But a lethargic, shocked child with prolonged capillary refill needs intravenous resuscitation, not home oral rehydration.
takeaway: A shocked, severely dehydrated child gets an IV isotonic fluid bolus and reassessment — oral rehydration is for the milder end.

stem: A neonate in the first days of life is lethargic and feeding poorly, with temperature instability, grunting and a high respiratory rate. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin and review in the community tomorrow
options.B: Observe with 4-hourly observations and review in the morning
options.C: Septic screen and immediate empirical IV antibiotics
options.D: Check a blood glucose and encourage feeding, then reassess
options.E: Take blood cultures and start antibiotics once they are positive

correct_answer: C. Septic screen and immediate empirical IV antibiotics
why_correct: Neonatal sepsis presents with non-specific signs (poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability, respiratory distress); because it can deteriorate rapidly, the approach is a septic screen and immediate broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics without waiting for results.
why_wrong: A. A sick neonate needs IV antibiotics in hospital; oral treatment and discharge are unsafe. B. Neonatal sepsis can deteriorate rapidly; observation alone delays treatment. D. Glucose should be checked, but these signs need a septic screen and immediate antibiotics, not feeding support alone. E. Antibiotics must start immediately after cultures are taken, not once they turn positive.
pearl: A non-specifically unwell neonate is sepsis until proven otherwise — screen and start IV antibiotics immediately, do not wait.
thinking: Neonate with poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability, grunting and tachypnoea ↓ Neonatal sepsis until proven otherwise ↓ C: septic screen and immediate empirical IV antibiotics
exam_trap: B, observe overnight — the non-specific signs can seem mild. But neonatal sepsis is rapidly progressive and easily missed; a septic screen with immediate empirical antibiotics is required, not watchful waiting.
takeaway: A non-specifically unwell neonate is sepsis until proven otherwise — screen and start IV antibiotics immediately, do not wait.

stem: A child has a sore throat and fever followed by a widespread fine, rough 'sandpaper' rash, flushed cheeks with circumoral pallor, and a 'strawberry' tongue. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: Supportive care, as it is a viral exanthem
options.D: Oral penicillin V for 10 days and notification
options.E: Oral aciclovir and exclusion from school

correct_answer: D. Oral penicillin V for 10 days and notification
why_correct: Scarlet fever (group A streptococcal infection) causes a sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue and circumoral pallor following a sore throat; it is treated with oral penicillin (or a macrolide if penicillin-allergic) and is a notifiable disease.
why_wrong: A. There is no oral thrush; the features are of streptococcal infection. B. Scarlet fever is bacterial and should be treated with penicillin and notified. C. The rash is caused by streptococcal toxin; topical steroids do not treat the infection. E. Aciclovir treats herpesviruses, not streptococcal infection.
pearl: A sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue is scarlet fever — give penicillin and notify; it is bacterial, not just another viral rash.
thinking: Sore throat and fever then sandpaper rash, circumoral pallor and strawberry tongue ↓ Scarlet fever (group A streptococcus), notifiable ↓ D: phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days and notify
exam_trap: B, no treatment as viral — many childhood rashes are viral and self-limiting. But scarlet fever is a streptococcal (bacterial) infection that should be treated with penicillin and notified, to reduce complications and spread.
takeaway: A sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue is scarlet fever — give penicillin and notify; it is bacterial, not just another viral rash.

stem: An unimmunised child has a few days of high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, with small white spots on the buccal mucosa. A blotchy maculopapular rash then appears, starting behind the ears and spreading down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots (white buccal spots), followed by a descending maculopapular rash, is measles; it is a notifiable disease, managed supportively, with important complications (otitis media, pneumonia, encephalitis).
why_wrong: A. Kawasaki disease causes at least five days of fever with non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips or strawberry tongue, extremity changes and cervical lymphadenopathy, but not Koplik spots or a cough-and-coryza prodrome. B. Rubella is milder, with tender suboccipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy, little prodrome and no Koplik spots, whereas this child has a marked cough, coryza and conjunctivitis prodrome with Koplik spots. C. Roseola affects infants and causes several days of high fever with the rash appearing as the fever settles, without Koplik spots or a descending blotchy rash. D. Scarlet fever follows a streptococcal sore throat with a fine sandpaper-like rash, strawberry tongue and circumoral pallor, not a coryzal prodrome with Koplik spots.
pearl: Koplik spots with a prodrome and a descending rash is measles — notify it and watch for pneumonia and encephalitis.
thinking: Unimmunised child with high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis ↓ White buccal spots are Koplik spots, pathognomonic of measles ↓ Blotchy maculopapular rash starting behind the ears and spreading downwards fits the measles pattern ↓ Diagnosis: measles, a notifiable disease
exam_trap: B, rubella — another viral exanthem with a similar rash. But rubella is milder with tender suboccipital lymphadenopathy and no Koplik spots or marked prodrome, whereas the Koplik spots and the cough/coryza/conjunctivitis prodrome here are measles.
takeaway: Koplik spots with a prodrome and a descending rash is measles — notify it and watch for pneumonia and encephalitis.

stem: A child has perianal itching that is worse at night, and tiny white thread-like worms have been seen around the anus. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Mebendazole for the affected child, with hygiene advice at home
options.B: Mebendazole for the whole household, plus hygiene measures
options.C: Topical hydrocortisone to the perianal skin and an emollient
options.D: Oral metronidazole for the child and any symptomatic siblings
options.E: Stool microscopy for ova before any treatment

correct_answer: B. Mebendazole for the whole household, plus hygiene measures
why_correct: Perianal itch worse at night with visible thread-like worms is threadworm (Enterobius); treatment is an anthelmintic such as mebendazole for the whole household simultaneously, with hygiene measures (handwashing, laundering, nail care) to prevent reinfection.
why_wrong: A. Threadworm spreads readily within households, so all members are treated at the same time to prevent reinfection. C. Steroids do not treat the infestation. D. Threadworm is not treated with antibiotics; an anthelmintic is needed. E. Diagnosis is clinical when worms are seen; stool microscopy is unreliable and delays treatment.
pearl: Threadworm means treat the whole household with mebendazole plus hygiene — treating the child alone invites reinfection.
thinking: Nocturnal perianal itch with visible thread-like worms ↓ Threadworm, which spreads readily within households ↓ B: mebendazole for the whole household plus hygiene measures
exam_trap: A, treat only the child — focusing on the symptomatic child seems sufficient. But threadworm spreads readily within households (including asymptomatic members), so the whole household is treated together to prevent reinfection.
takeaway: Threadworm means treat the whole household with mebendazole plus hygiene — treating the child alone invites reinfection.

stem: A 2-year-old is brought to the GP with a fever that started yesterday. To decide on the urgency of action, what is the most appropriate basis for risk assessment?

options.A: Assess red-flag features using a traffic-light system
options.B: Base the decision mainly on the height of the temperature
options.C: Give empirical oral antibiotics to febrile children under five
options.D: Assess response to antipyretics to judge severity
options.E: Use CRP and white cell count as the primary basis

correct_answer: A. Assess red-flag features using a traffic-light system
why_correct: A febrile child is risk-assessed using a traffic-light system that looks at colour, activity, respiratory and circulatory signs and other red-flag features; children with red features need urgent assessment, as the height of the temperature alone is a poor guide to serious illness.
why_wrong: B. The height of the temperature correlates poorly with serious illness (except in young infants); clinical features guide risk. C. Antibiotics should not be given to febrile children without an apparent source unless serious infection is suspected. D. Response to antipyretics does not distinguish serious from minor illness. E. Blood tests may support assessment, but initial risk is judged clinically using red-flag features.
pearl: A febrile child is assessed by clinical red-flag features (traffic lights), not by how high the temperature is.
thinking: Febrile young child ↓ Temperature height alone predicts serious illness poorly ↓ Assess colour, activity, respiratory, circulation and other red-flag features ↓ Assess red-flag features using a traffic-light system
exam_trap: B, use the height of the temperature alone — a very high fever feels like the key danger signal. But the temperature value correlates poorly with serious illness; the clinical red-flag features (appearance, activity, perfusion) are what determine urgency.
takeaway: A febrile child is assessed by clinical red-flag features (traffic lights), not by how high the temperature is.

stem: An unimmunised teenage boy has fever, malaise and painful bilateral swelling of the parotid glands (in front of and below the ears). What is the most likely diagnosis and an important complication to counsel about?

options.A: Acute bacterial parotitis — IV flucloxacillin and drainage
options.B: Mumps — warn about orchitis; notifiable, supportive care
options.C: Cervical lymphadenitis — oral co-amoxiclav for a week
options.E: Infectious mononucleosis — counsel to avoid contact sports

correct_answer: B. Mumps — warn about orchitis; notifiable, supportive care
why_correct: Bilateral painful parotid swelling with fever in an unimmunised person is mumps (a paramyxovirus); it is managed supportively and is notifiable, and complications include orchitis, viral meningitis and pancreatitis.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial parotitis is usually unilateral in dehydrated or older patients with pus from the duct; bilateral swelling in an unimmunised teenager is mumps. C. The swelling is of the parotid glands themselves, in front of and below the ears, not cervical lymph nodes. D. Salivary stones cause unilateral swelling related to meals, without fever or bilateral involvement. E. Glandular fever causes cervical lymphadenopathy and tonsillitis rather than bilateral parotid swelling.
pearl: Bilateral parotid swelling in an unimmunised young person is mumps — supportive care; counsel about orchitis and meningitis; notify it.
thinking: Unimmunised teenage boy with fever and malaise ↓ Painful bilateral parotid swelling ↓ Mumps, which is notifiable and managed supportively ↓ Mumps: warn about orchitis
exam_trap: A, a bacterial parotid abscess needing drainage — parotid swelling can suggest a localised collection. But bilateral parotid swelling in an unimmunised young person is characteristic of mumps (viral), managed supportively and notified, not surgically drained.
takeaway: Bilateral parotid swelling in an unimmunised young person is mumps — supportive care; counsel about orchitis and meningitis; notify it.

stem: A young child develops a limp and hip pain a week after a viral upper respiratory infection. He is systemically well, afebrile, and can (reluctantly) bear weight; inflammatory markers are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis, and the key thing to exclude?

options.A: Transient synovitis — but septic arthritis must be excluded
options.B: Definite septic arthritis requiring immediate joint washout

correct_answer: A. Transient synovitis — but septic arthritis must be excluded
why_correct: A well, afebrile child who can weight-bear, with normal inflammatory markers after a viral illness, most likely has transient synovitis (irritable hip), which is self-limiting; however, septic arthritis must always be excluded, as missing it is limb- and life-threatening.
why_wrong: B. Definite septic arthritis requiring immediate washout over-calls the diagnosis: this child is afebrile, can bear weight and has normal inflammatory markers, which make transient synovitis likely, although septic arthritis must still be actively excluded. C. Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head) usually presents with an insidious limp over weeks in a child of about 4–8, rather than an acute limp a week after a viral illness. D. A soft-tissue (muscular) strain needs a history of injury and, more importantly, attributing hip pain in a child to a strain risks missing septic arthritis, which must always be considered. E. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis requires arthritis persisting for at least six weeks, whereas this is an acute, post-viral presentation.
pearl: A well, afebrile, weight-bearing child after a viral illness is transient synovitis — but fever, non-weight-bearing and raised CRP mean septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
thinking: Young child with acute limp and hip pain a week after a viral illness ↓ Afebrile, weight-bearing, with normal inflammatory markers: reassuring features ↓ This favours transient synovitis (irritable hip), which is self-limiting ↓ But septic arthritis must still be excluded, so the answer is transient synovitis with septic arthritis excluded
exam_trap: B, definite septic arthritis needing washout — septic arthritis is the dangerous diagnosis, so over-calling it feels safe. But the reassuring features here (afebrile, weight-bearing, normal markers) favour transient synovitis; septic arthritis is suggested by fever, inability to weight-bear and raised inflammatory markers (Kocher criteria).
takeaway: A well, afebrile, weight-bearing child after a viral illness is transient synovitis — but fever, non-weight-bearing and raised CRP mean septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

stem: A boy aged about 6 has an insidious onset of hip pain and a limp over weeks, with no systemic upset and no recent trauma. X-ray shows changes in the femoral head (flattening/sclerosis). What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: E. Perthes disease (femoral head avascular necrosis)
why_correct: Insidious hip pain and limp in a young boy (typically 4–8 years), without systemic upset, with femoral-head changes on X-ray, is Perthes disease — idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head; management ranges from observation to surgery depending on age and severity.
why_wrong: A. DDH causes a limp from walking age without femoral-head flattening and sclerosis appearing over weeks. B. Septic arthritis is acute with fever, systemic upset and refusal to weight-bear. C. Transient synovitis is acute and self-limiting after a viral illness, with a normal X-ray. D. SUFE affects adolescents (often overweight), with slippage of the epiphysis rather than flattening and sclerosis.
pearl: Insidious hip pain and limp in a young boy with femoral-head changes is Perthes (avascular necrosis).
thinking: A boy aged about 6 has an insidious onset of hip pain and a limp over ↓ An INSIDIOUS course over weeks with femoral-head changes on X-ray in a young boy
exam_trap: C, transient synovitis — both cause a limp in a young child. But transient synovitis is acute and self-limiting after a viral illness with a normal X-ray, whereas the insidious course over weeks with femoral-head changes here is Perthes disease.
takeaway: Insidious hip pain and limp in a young boy with femoral-head changes is Perthes (avascular necrosis).

stem: An overweight adolescent boy has hip and knee pain with a limp. The affected leg is held externally rotated, and hip internal rotation is restricted and painful. What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the key learning point?

options.A: Transient synovitis — rest and analgesia, expecting resolution
options.B: Knee ligament injury — arrange MRI of the knee, where the pain is
options.C: Growing pains — reassure and give simple analgesia
options.D: Slipped upper femoral epiphysis — image the hip despite knee pain
options.E: Osgood-Schlatter disease — rest from sport and ice

correct_answer: D. Slipped upper femoral epiphysis — image the hip despite knee pain
why_correct: An overweight adolescent with hip/knee pain, an externally rotated leg and restricted internal rotation has slipped upper femoral epiphysis; knee pain is often referred from the hip, so the hip must be imaged (frog-leg lateral), and the child should not bear weight pending orthopaedic referral.
why_wrong: A. Transient synovitis affects younger children after a viral illness; restricted internal rotation in an overweight adolescent suggests SUFE. B. Knee pain can be referred from the hip; imaging only the knee risks missing SUFE. C. Growing pains are bilateral and nocturnal, without a limp or restricted hip movement. E. Osgood-Schlatter causes tibial tuberosity pain and swelling, not restricted hip rotation.
pearl: An overweight teenager with hip/knee pain and an externally rotated leg is SUFE — always image the hip, even when the knee is what hurts.
thinking: An overweight adolescent boy has hip and knee pain with a limp ↓ Hip pain referred to the KNEE in an overweight adolescent with an externally rot
exam_trap: B, a knee injury investigated at the knee — the child reports knee pain, so examining the knee seems logical. But hip pathology refers pain to the knee; in an adolescent (especially if overweight) with an externally rotated hip, SUFE must be excluded by imaging the hip.
takeaway: An overweight teenager with hip/knee pain and an externally rotated leg is SUFE — always image the hip, even when the knee is what hurts.

stem: On examination of a baby boy, one side of the scrotum is empty and the testis cannot be brought down into the scrotum. It remains undescended at review beyond a few months of age. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Reassure that it will always descend eventually, with no follow-up
options.E: Refer for orchidopexy (ideally by 12 months of age)

correct_answer: E. Refer for orchidopexy (ideally by 12 months of age)
why_correct: If a testis is still undescended at 4–5 months of age (corrected for gestational age), NICE CKS advises referral to paediatric surgery or urology, to be seen by 6 months of age, because spontaneous descent is unlikely after 6 months. Orchidopexy is then ideally performed between 6 and 12 months of age (European Association of Urology; the British Association of Paediatric Surgeons advises around 12 months). Early surgery reduces the later risks of impaired fertility and testicular malignancy and makes the testis easier to examine.
why_wrong: A. Review again only in adolescence — far too late; a testis still undescended after 6 months is unlikely to descend, and delay increases the risks of impaired fertility and testicular malignancy. B. Reassure that it will always descend eventually, with no follow-up — many testes descend in the first few months, but spontaneous descent is unlikely after 6 months (NICE CKS); one still undescended at 4–5 months needs referral, to be seen by 6 months. C. Start testosterone therapy — hormonal treatment is not routinely recommended for an undescended testis; the treatment is orchidopexy. D. Remove the testis routinely — orchidectomy is not routine in infancy; the aim is to bring a viable testis into the scrotum by orchidopexy.
pearl: An undescended testis still present at 4–5 months (corrected age) needs referral, to be seen by 6 months, and orchidopexy ideally by 12 months — it lowers later infertility and testicular-cancer risk.
thinking: Testis undescended and not manipulable into the scrotum beyond a few months ↓ spontaneous descent unlikely after 6 months ↓ refer for orchidopexy (ideally by 12 months)
exam_trap: B, reassure that it will always descend — many testes do descend in the first months, making 'watchful waiting' tempting. But one persisting beyond a few months needs referral for orchidopexy; leaving it indefinitely raises fertility and malignancy risks.
takeaway: An undescended testis still present at 4–5 months (corrected age) needs referral, to be seen by 6 months, and orchidopexy ideally by 12 months — it lowers later infertility and testicular-cancer risk.

stem: A toddler has bow legs, swelling at the wrists and costochondral junctions, delayed walking and bone discomfort. Bloods show low vitamin D and calcium with a raised alkaline phosphatase, and X-rays show widened, cupped metaphyses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bowing of the legs with metaphyseal swelling (wrists, costochondral 'rosary'), a raised alkaline phosphatase and low vitamin D/calcium, with characteristic X-ray changes, is rickets due to vitamin D deficiency; treatment is vitamin D (and calcium) replacement.
why_wrong: A. Achondroplasia causes disproportionate short stature with short proximal limbs and a large head from birth, with normal vitamin D, calcium and alkaline phosphatase. B. Physiological bow legs are a normal variant in toddlers with normal bloods and X-rays, whereas this child has low vitamin D and calcium, a raised alkaline phosphatase and cupped metaphyses. C. Osteogenesis imperfecta presents with recurrent low-trauma fractures and often blue sclerae, without metaphyseal swelling or the biochemistry of vitamin D deficiency. D. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes persistent joint inflammation and does not produce low vitamin D, a raised alkaline phosphatase or widened, cupped metaphyses on X-ray.
pearl: Bow legs with bony swelling, low vitamin D and raised alkaline phosphatase is rickets — treat with vitamin D.
thinking: Toddler with bow legs, wrist swelling and a costochondral 'rosary' ↓ Bloods show low vitamin D and calcium with a raised alkaline phosphatase ↓ X-rays show widened, cupped metaphyses: defective mineralisation of growing bone ↓ Diagnosis: rickets due to vitamin D deficiency
exam_trap: B, physiological bow legs — mild bowing is a normal variant in toddlers, so it is a reasonable thought. But physiological bowing has normal bloods and X-rays, whereas the low vitamin D, raised alkaline phosphatase and metaphyseal changes here indicate rickets.
takeaway: Bow legs with bony swelling, low vitamin D and raised alkaline phosphatase is rickets — treat with vitamin D.

stem: A toddler, previously well, suddenly has a coughing and choking episode while playing, followed by a persistent cough and a unilateral wheeze with reduced air entry on one side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A sudden choking episode followed by a persistent cough and UNILATERAL wheeze/reduced air entry in a well toddler is an inhaled foreign body (often lodging in a main bronchus); a chest X-ray may show hyperinflation or collapse, and bronchoscopy is used to remove it.
why_wrong: A. Croup causes a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor after a coryzal illness, not a sudden choking episode followed by unilateral wheeze. B. Acute asthma causes bilateral, widespread wheeze without a witnessed choking event, whereas this toddler has sudden onset after choking and one-sided signs. D. Bronchiolitis occurs mainly in infants under one year after a coryzal prodrome and gives bilateral crackles and wheeze, not a sudden choking episode with unilateral signs. E. Community-acquired pneumonia would usually bring fever and systemic illness with focal crackles, whereas this child was well until a sudden choking episode while playing.
pearl: Sudden choking then a unilateral wheeze in a toddler is an inhaled foreign body — think bronchoscopy, not an asthma label.
thinking: Previously well toddler with a sudden coughing and choking episode while playing ↓ Persistent cough afterwards ↓ Unilateral wheeze and reduced air entry suggest a localised airway obstruction ↓ Diagnosis: inhaled foreign body, needing bronchoscopy
exam_trap: B, acute asthma — wheeze in a child often suggests asthma. But asthma causes bilateral, widespread wheeze without a sudden choking event, whereas the SUDDEN onset with a witnessed choking episode and UNILATERAL signs here indicates an inhaled foreign body.
takeaway: Sudden choking then a unilateral wheeze in a toddler is an inhaled foreign body — think bronchoscopy, not an asthma label.

stem: A young child is noticed to have a persistent inward turning of one eye. The corneal light reflex is asymmetrical and the cover test confirms a manifest squint. What is the most appropriate action and why?

options.A: Review at the school-entry vision screen
options.B: Reassure and recheck in a year, as many squints resolve
options.C: Start patching of the good eye in primary care
options.D: Refer to the optometrist for a routine eye test
options.E: Refer to ophthalmology — risk of amblyopia

correct_answer: E. Refer to ophthalmology — risk of amblyopia
why_correct: A persistent (manifest) squint with an asymmetrical corneal light reflex and abnormal cover test should be referred to ophthalmology; if untreated, the brain suppresses the image from the deviating eye, causing amblyopia (permanent reduced vision), which is treatable when addressed early.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for school screening delays treatment while amblyopia develops; a manifest squint needs referral now. B. A persistent manifest squint does not resolve spontaneously and risks amblyopia. C. Patching is part of specialist amblyopia treatment after assessment (including refraction), not started in primary care. D. A manifest squint in a young child needs referral to the hospital eye service (orthoptics and ophthalmology), not a routine sight test.
pearl: A true persistent squint needs referral — untreated it causes amblyopia (suppression of the deviating eye).
thinking: Persistent inward eye turn + asymmetrical corneal reflex + abnormal cover test ↓ manifest squint with risk of amblyopia ↓ refer to ophthalmology
exam_trap: B, reassure it will be outgrown — some intermittent squints in early infancy do resolve, making reassurance tempting. But a persistent manifest squint risks amblyopia and needs referral and treatment, not simple reassurance.
takeaway: A true persistent squint needs referral — untreated it causes amblyopia (suppression of the deviating eye).

stem: An infant has episodes of becoming acutely cyanosed and distressed ('spells'), which improve when the child squats or is held in a knee-to-chest position. There is an ejection systolic murmur, and the chest X-ray shows a 'boot-shaped' heart. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: An isolated small ventricular septal defect (acyanotic)

why_correct: Cyanotic 'spells' relieved by squatting (or the knee-to-chest position), with an ejection systolic murmur and a boot-shaped heart, are characteristic of Tetralogy of Fallot — the commonest cyanotic congenital heart disease; squatting raises systemic resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting.
why_wrong: B. An innocent flow murmur occurs in a well child with no cyanosis and a normal chest X-ray, not cyanotic spells and a boot-shaped heart. C.
