An isolated small ventricular septal defect is acyanotic and usually gives a pansystolic murmur, whereas this infant has cyanotic spells relieved by squatting and a boot-shaped heart. D. Patent ductus arteriosus is acyanotic (left-to-right shunt) with a continuous 'machinery' murmur, not cyanotic spells. E. Coarctation of the aorta is acyanotic and presents with weak or delayed femoral pulses, upper-limb hypertension or heart failure, not hypercyanotic spells relieved by squatting.
pearl: Cyanotic spells relieved by squatting with a boot-shaped heart is Tetralogy of Fallot.
thinking: Infant with episodic cyanosis and distress ('spells') ↓ Relieved by squatting or knee-to-chest, which raises systemic resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting ↓ Ejection systolic murmur (pulmonary stenosis) and a boot-shaped heart on chest X-ray ↓ Diagnosis: Tetralogy of Fallot
exam_trap: C, an isolated small acyanotic VSD — a VSD is part of the lesion, so it is a plausible distractor. But an isolated small VSD is acyanotic, whereas the cyanotic spells relieved by squatting and the boot-shaped heart here indicate Tetralogy of Fallot.
takeaway: Cyanotic spells relieved by squatting with a boot-shaped heart is Tetralogy of Fallot.

stem: A young child has persistent difficulties with social communication and interaction, alongside restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests, present from early development and impairing function. What is the most likely diagnosis and approach?

options.A: Autism spectrum disorder — start risperidone and review in primary care
options.B: Hearing impairment — audiology and speech therapy referral
options.C: Normal variation — review at the next developmental check
options.D: Autism spectrum disorder — specialist multidisciplinary assessment
options.E: ADHD — refer for specialist assessment and parent training

correct_answer: D. Autism spectrum disorder — specialist multidisciplinary assessment
why_correct: Persistent difficulties in social communication/interaction combined with restricted, repetitive behaviours, present from early development with functional impairment, characterise autism spectrum disorder; diagnosis is via specialist multidisciplinary assessment, with educational and supportive interventions (there is no curative drug).
why_wrong: A. There is no drug treatment for the core features of autism; antipsychotics are specialist-initiated only for specific behaviours. B. Hearing should be checked, but hearing loss does not explain restricted, repetitive behaviours. C. Persistent, impairing difficulties in two domains are not normal variation and need referral. E. ADHD involves inattention and hyperactivity; social-communication difficulties with restricted, repetitive behaviours indicate autism.
pearl: Autism is persistent social-communication difficulty plus restricted/repetitive behaviours from early development — refer for multidisciplinary assessment.
thinking: Young child with persistent social-communication difficulties ↓ Plus restricted, repetitive behaviours from early development, impairing function ↓ Pattern fits autism; hearing should still be checked ↓ Autism spectrum disorder: specialist multidisciplinary assessment
exam_trap: B, a hearing impairment alone — hearing must indeed be checked, so it is a sensible consideration. But the combination of social-communication difficulty AND restricted, repetitive behaviours points to autism spectrum disorder, requiring specialist assessment beyond a hearing test.
takeaway: Autism is persistent social-communication difficulty plus restricted/repetitive behaviours from early development — refer for multidisciplinary assessment.

stem: A well child has a mild fever followed by a bright red rash on both cheeks ('slapped cheek' appearance), and then a lacy, reticular rash on the trunk and limbs. What is the most likely diagnosis and an important caution?

options.A: Measles — isolation and immunoglobulin for contacts
options.B: Parvovirus B19 — risk in pregnancy and haemolytic anaemia
options.C: Scarlet fever — oral penicillin and notification
options.D: Rubella — caution with non-immune pregnant contacts
options.E: Kawasaki disease — IV immunoglobulin and echocardiography

correct_answer: B. Parvovirus B19 — risk in pregnancy and haemolytic anaemia
why_correct: A 'slapped cheek' facial rash followed by a lacy reticular body rash in a well child is erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), caused by parvovirus B19; it is self-limiting, but parvovirus B19 can cause hydrops fetalis in pregnancy and aplastic crisis in those with haemolytic anaemias (e.g. sickle cell).
why_wrong: A. Measles causes a marked prodrome with Koplik spots and a descending rash in an unwell child, not slapped cheeks followed by a lacy rash. C. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue. D. Rubella causes a fine rash spreading from the face with suboccipital lymphadenopathy, not slapped cheeks. E. Kawasaki disease causes prolonged fever with conjunctivitis, mucosal and extremity changes in an unwell child.
pearl: A slapped-cheek then lacy rash in a well child is fifth disease (parvovirus B19) — beware in pregnancy and sickle cell.
thinking: Well child with mild fever ↓ Slapped-cheek rash followed by a lacy reticular rash on trunk and limbs ↓ Erythema infectiosum ↓ Parvovirus B19: risk in pregnancy and haemolytic anaemia
exam_trap: A, measles requiring isolation and immunoglobulin — another childhood exanthem. But measles has a marked prodrome with Koplik spots and a descending maculopapular rash in an unwell child, whereas the slapped-cheek then lacy rash in a well child here is parvovirus B19.
takeaway: A slapped-cheek then lacy rash in a well child is fifth disease (parvovirus B19) — beware in pregnancy and sickle cell.

stem: An unimmunised child has a mild illness with a low-grade fever and a fine pink-red maculopapular rash that started on the face and spread, with notably tender lymph nodes behind the ears and at the back of the head (suboccipital). What is the most likely diagnosis and the key public-health concern?

options.A: Rubella — risk of congenital rubella syndrome in pregnancy
options.B: Measles — immunoglobulin for exposed infants and pregnant women
options.C: Scarlet fever — penicillin and exclusion from school for 24 hours
options.D: Parvovirus B19 — risk of fetal hydrops in non-immune pregnant women
options.E: Roseola infantum — risk of febrile convulsions in young infants

correct_answer: A. Rubella — risk of congenital rubella syndrome in pregnancy
why_correct: A mild illness with a fine maculopapular rash and tender suboccipital/postauricular lymphadenopathy is rubella; it is usually mild in children but causes congenital rubella syndrome (cataracts, deafness, cardiac defects) if a non-immune woman is infected in early pregnancy, and it is notifiable.
why_wrong: B. Measles causes a severe prodrome with Koplik spots in an unwell child; this mild illness with suboccipital nodes is rubella. C. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue, not suboccipital lymphadenopathy. D. Parvovirus causes slapped cheeks followed by a lacy rash, not a face-to-body rash with suboccipital nodes. E. Roseola affects infants with high fever followed by a rash as the fever settles.
pearl: A mild rash with tender suboccipital lymphadenopathy is rubella — the key danger is congenital rubella in early pregnancy; notify it.
thinking: Mild illness, face-to-body maculopapular rash and tender suboccipital/postauricular nodes ↓ Rubella ↓ A: key public-health risk is congenital rubella syndrome in non-immune pregnant women
exam_trap: B, measles requiring immunoglobulin for contacts — both are childhood exanthems. But measles is more severe with a marked prodrome and Koplik spots, whereas the mild illness with suboccipital lymphadenopathy here is rubella, whose key danger is to the fetus in pregnancy.
takeaway: A mild rash with tender suboccipital lymphadenopathy is rubella — the key danger is congenital rubella in early pregnancy; notify it.

stem: A teenage girl has short stature and has not started her periods (primary amenorrhoea). Examination shows a webbed neck and widely spaced nipples, and she has a history of coarctation of the aorta. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Short stature and primary amenorrhoea with a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples and a history of coarctation of the aorta in a girl indicate Turner syndrome (45,X); it is confirmed by karyotype and managed with growth hormone, oestrogen replacement and screening for associated cardiac, renal and thyroid problems.
why_wrong: B. Down syndrome causes characteristic facial features, learning disability and hypotonia with atrioventricular septal defects, not a webbed neck, primary amenorrhoea and coarctation. C. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) affects phenotypic males, who are typically tall with small testes, so it cannot explain this girl's presentation. D. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature with long limbs, lens dislocation and aortic root dilatation, the opposite of this girl's short stature. E. PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism in a normally grown woman, whereas the short stature, webbed neck and coarctation here indicate Turner syndrome.
pearl: Short stature and primary amenorrhoea with a webbed neck and coarctation is Turner syndrome (45,X) — confirm by karyotype.
thinking: Teenage girl with short stature and primary amenorrhoea ↓ Webbed neck and widely spaced nipples are dysmorphic features ↓ Coarctation of the aorta is the classic cardiac association ↓ Diagnosis: Turner syndrome (45,X), confirmed by karyotype
exam_trap: E, PMOS (formerly PCOS) — both can present with menstrual disturbance. But PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism in a normally-grown woman, whereas the short stature, webbed neck and coarctation here indicate Turner syndrome.
takeaway: Short stature and primary amenorrhoea with a webbed neck and coarctation is Turner syndrome (45,X) — confirm by karyotype.

stem: A 30-year-old woman, 6 weeks postpartum, has 3 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep despite the baby sleeping, and feelings of worthlessness. Her PHQ-9 is 18. She has fleeting thoughts that her family would be better off without her but no plan and no thoughts of harming the baby. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Reassure her this is normal 'baby blues' and review in two weeks
options.B: Start sertraline and refer to the perinatal mental health team
options.C: Admit her to a mother-and-baby unit today
options.D: Advise her to stop breastfeeding before any treatment
options.E: Refer to a parenting class only

correct_answer: B. Start sertraline and refer to the perinatal mental health team
why_correct: A PHQ-9 of 18 with persistent symptoms beyond two weeks is moderate-to-severe postnatal depression, not baby blues; an SSRI (sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding) plus perinatal mental health referral is appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Baby blues resolve within two weeks; persistent symptoms at six weeks with a PHQ-9 of 18 are depression needing treatment. C. Mother-and-baby unit admission is for severe illness, psychosis or high risk; she has no plan and no thoughts of harming the baby. D. Sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding, so stopping is unnecessary. E. A parenting class does not treat depression.
pearl: Low mood persisting past two weeks postpartum is depression, not baby blues — treat it, and sertraline is breastfeeding-compatible.
thinking: 6 weeks postpartum, 3 weeks of low mood, anhedonia, worthlessness, PHQ-9 18, passive thoughts without plan ↓ Postnatal depression (beyond baby blues) ↓ SSRI compatible with breastfeeding (sertraline) plus perinatal mental health referral
exam_trap: A, reassure as baby blues — the common, self-limiting early-postpartum low mood, so a tempting benign label. But baby blues resolve within two weeks; persistent symptoms at six weeks with a high PHQ-9 are depression needing treatment.
takeaway: Low mood persisting past two weeks postpartum is depression, not baby blues — treat it, and sertraline is breastfeeding-compatible.

stem: A 50-year-old man with alcohol dependence stops drinking. About 72 hours later he becomes acutely confused, agitated and tremulous with vivid visual hallucinations, sweating, tachycardia and a low-grade fever. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: A benzodiazepine regimen plus parenteral thiamine
options.B: Haloperidol as first-line sedation, plus oral thiamine
options.D: Oral thiamine with zopiclone at night for agitation
options.E: Acamprosate started now to prevent relapse

correct_answer: A. A benzodiazepine regimen plus parenteral thiamine
why_correct: Delirium tremens, peaking around 48–72 hours after cessation, is treated with benzodiazepines (which reduce mortality, seizures and autonomic instability) plus parenteral thiamine to prevent Wernicke's.
why_wrong: B. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat the withdrawal; benzodiazepines are first-line, and thiamine should be parenteral. C. Glucose without thiamine risks precipitating Wernicke's, and fluids alone do not treat withdrawal. D. Zopiclone does not treat delirium tremens, and oral thiamine is inadequate here. E. Acamprosate is for maintaining abstinence after withdrawal, not for treating delirium tremens.
pearl: Delirium tremens is a GABA-withdrawal emergency — benzodiazepines and thiamine, not antipsychotics.
thinking: Alcohol cessation ~72 h ago ↓ Confusion, visual hallucinations, tremor, autonomic instability, fever = delirium tremens ↓ Benzodiazepines plus parenteral thiamine
exam_trap: B, an antipsychotic first-line — the reflex for hallucinations and agitation. But antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat the underlying GABA withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the mainstay.
takeaway: Delirium tremens is a GABA-withdrawal emergency — benzodiazepines and thiamine, not antipsychotics.

stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol dependence, 12 hours after his last drink, has tremor, sweating, agitation, a heart rate of 112 and mild anxiety, but no confusion or hallucinations. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral fluids and observation, with no medication
options.D: A reducing dose of zopiclone plus thiamine
options.E: A reducing benzodiazepine regimen plus thiamine

correct_answer: E. A reducing benzodiazepine regimen plus thiamine
why_correct: Early alcohol withdrawal is treated with a reducing benzodiazepine regimen (such as chlordiazepoxide) to prevent progression to seizures and delirium tremens, with thiamine to prevent Wernicke's.
why_wrong: A. He has significant withdrawal (tremor, tachycardia); without treatment he risks seizures and delirium tremens. B. Antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal. C. Naltrexone helps prevent relapse after withdrawal; it does not treat acute withdrawal. D. Zopiclone does not prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are first-line.
pearl: Alcohol withdrawal is managed with a benzodiazepine taper and thiamine — not antipsychotics, which lower the seizure threshold.
thinking: Alcohol dependence, 12 h since last drink ↓ Tremor, sweating, tachycardia, agitation without confusion or hallucinations = early alcohol withdrawal ↓ Prevent seizures and delirium tremens ↓ Reducing benzodiazepine regimen (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) plus thiamine
exam_trap: B, an antipsychotic — the agitation might prompt it. But antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and do not treat the GABA withdrawal; benzodiazepines are the mainstay.
takeaway: Alcohol withdrawal is managed with a benzodiazepine taper and thiamine — not antipsychotics, which lower the seizure threshold.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has marked, persistent fear of social situations with avoidance, blushing and sweating, impairing her work. After discussion she opts for medication alongside psychological therapy. What is the most appropriate first-line drug?
why_correct: First-line psychological treatment for social anxiety disorder is CBT; when medication is used, an SSRI such as sertraline is first-line, whereas benzodiazepines are avoided because of dependence.
why_wrong: A. Propranolol is not recommended for social anxiety disorder; it may blunt performance-related tremor but does not treat the disorder. B. Regular benzodiazepine use causes tolerance and dependence and is not recommended for social anxiety disorder. C. Antipsychotics have no role in social anxiety disorder. E. Pregabalin is not a first-line drug for social anxiety disorder; an SSRI (escitalopram or sertraline) is.
pearl: Anxiety disorders are treated with an SSRI (and CBT), not a daily benzodiazepine — avoid creating dependence.
thinking: Persistent fear and avoidance of social situations impairing work ↓ Social anxiety disorder ↓ Patient chooses medication alongside therapy ↓ SSRI (sertraline or escitalopram) first-line; avoid daily benzodiazepines
exam_trap: B, a daily benzodiazepine — it would quickly relieve anxiety, so it seems effective. But regular benzodiazepine use causes tolerance and dependence and is not recommended for an anxiety disorder; an SSRI is first-line.
takeaway: Anxiety disorders are treated with an SSRI (and CBT), not a daily benzodiazepine — avoid creating dependence.

stem: A 20-year-old man has 4 months of auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions and social withdrawal, with no drug use and a normal organic screen. After assessment by mental health services, what is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?
why_correct: First-line drug treatment for a first episode of psychosis is an oral antipsychotic, chosen jointly with the patient after discussing side effects (NICE does not prefer one class), and combined with psychological intervention (CBTp and family intervention). An oral atypical is a usual first choice and is the only appropriate option listed.
why_wrong: B. Depot (long-acting injectable) antipsychotics are considered later — for people who prefer them after an acute episode or where avoiding covert non-adherence is a priority — not as first-line for a new first episode. C. Benzodiazepines may help short-term agitation but do not treat psychosis. D. SSRIs do not treat psychotic symptoms. E. Mood stabilisers alone are not treatment for first-episode psychosis without a mood disorder.
pearl: First-episode psychosis: oral antipsychotic chosen jointly with the patient, plus psychological therapy — depots are not first-line.
thinking: 4 months of hallucinations, paranoid delusions and withdrawal; organic causes and drugs excluded ↓ First-episode psychosis ↓ Oral antipsychotic chosen with the patient, plus CBTp and family intervention ↓ Oral atypical antipsychotic (A)
exam_trap: B, a depot antipsychotic — it guarantees adherence, so it can look attractive. But NICE starts first-episode psychosis with an oral antipsychotic chosen with the patient; depots are considered later if the person prefers them or covert non-adherence is a concern.
takeaway: First-episode psychosis: oral antipsychotic chosen jointly with the patient, plus psychological therapy — depots are not first-line.

stem: A severely malnourished patient is admitted and feeding is restarted. Within days he becomes weak and develops cardiac and neurological signs. Which electrolyte abnormality is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome and must be monitored and replaced?
why_correct: When feeding restarts after starvation, the insulin surge drives phosphate (and potassium and magnesium) into cells, causing hypophosphataemia — the hallmark of refeeding syndrome — which can precipitate cardiac and neurological failure; feeding is started cautiously with electrolyte monitoring and replacement.
why_wrong: A. Calcium is not the hallmark and is not typically raised in refeeding syndrome. C. Sodium and fluid retention occur, but hypernatraemia is not the hallmark. D. The insulin surge drives potassium into cells, causing hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia. E. Magnesium falls, not rises, as it shifts into cells with the insulin surge.
pearl: Refeeding syndrome is marked by falling phosphate — reintroduce feeding cautiously and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
thinking: A severely malnourished patient is admitted and feeding is restarted ↓ The fall in phosphate as feeding restarts — the insulin-driven intracellular shi
exam_trap: D, hyperkalaemia — electrolyte shifts are central, so a potassium abnormality is a reasonable guess. But the cellular shift in refeeding LOWERS potassium and especially phosphate; the hallmark is hypophosphataemia, not a high potassium.
takeaway: Refeeding syndrome is marked by falling phosphate — reintroduce feeding cautiously and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

stem: A 30-year-old man with bipolar disorder, currently on an SSRI for a past depressive episode, presents elated, grandiose, overactive and barely sleeping, with pressured speech. What is the most appropriate medication change?

options.A: Stop the SSRI and start an antimanic agent
options.B: Continue the SSRI and add a benzodiazepine
options.C: Continue the SSRI and add lamotrigine
options.D: Switch the SSRI to mirtazapine at night
options.E: Reduce the SSRI dose and add zopiclone

correct_answer: A. Stop the SSRI and start an antimanic agent
why_correct: Acute mania is treated by stopping any antidepressant (which can drive or worsen mania) and starting an antimanic agent — an antipsychotic and/or a mood stabiliser such as lithium or valproate.
why_wrong: B. Continuing the antidepressant can drive the mania; a benzodiazepine may help agitation but is not antimanic treatment. C. Lamotrigine helps prevent bipolar depression but is not effective for acute mania, and the SSRI should be stopped. D. Any antidepressant can worsen mania; switching does not treat it. E. The antidepressant should be stopped, not reduced, and a hypnotic does not treat mania.
pearl: In acute mania, stop the antidepressant and start an antimanic — antidepressants pour fuel on the mania.
thinking: Known bipolar disorder on an SSRI ↓ Elation, grandiosity, overactivity, reduced sleep, pressured speech = acute mania ↓ Antidepressant may be driving the mania ↓ Stop the SSRI and start an antimanic agent
exam_trap: B, continue the SSRI and add a benzodiazepine — calming the agitation feels supportive. But antidepressants precipitate and worsen mania; the SSRI should be stopped and an antimanic agent started.
takeaway: In acute mania, stop the antidepressant and start an antimanic — antidepressants pour fuel on the mania.

stem: A patient has intrusive, unwanted thoughts about contamination causing marked anxiety, which they relieve by repeated, time-consuming handwashing rituals, recognising these as excessive. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: CBT (exposure and response prevention) and/or an SSRI
options.B: Long-term diazepam to control the anxiety and the urge to wash
options.C: Risperidone monotherapy as first-line treatment for the obsessions
options.D: Psychodynamic psychotherapy as first-line to explore underlying conflict
options.E: Supportive counselling and a mood stabiliser such as lithium

correct_answer: A. CBT (exposure and response prevention) and/or an SSRI
why_correct: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (intrusive obsessions relieved by compulsions, with insight) is treated first-line with CBT incorporating exposure and response prevention, and/or an SSRI (often at higher doses than for depression).
why_wrong: B. Benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and risk dependence. C. Antipsychotics are used as augmentation in resistant OCD, not as first-line monotherapy. D. Psychodynamic therapy is not an evidence-based first-line treatment for OCD. E. Mood stabilisers and non-specific counselling are not treatments for OCD.
pearl: OCD is treated with exposure-and-response-prevention CBT and an SSRI — not benzodiazepines.
thinking: Intrusive contamination thoughts relieved by washing rituals, with insight ↓ Obsessive-compulsive disorder ↓ First-line: CBT with exposure and response prevention and/or an SSRI
exam_trap: B, a long-term benzodiazepine — the anxiety might invite an anxiolytic. But benzodiazepines do not treat OCD and risk dependence; the evidence-based treatments are ERP-based CBT and SSRIs.
takeaway: OCD is treated with exposure-and-response-prevention CBT and an SSRI — not benzodiazepines.

stem: A month after a serious assault, a patient has recurrent intrusive flashbacks and nightmares, hyperarousal, and avoidance of reminders of the event, with significant distress and impairment. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.D: Debriefing alone immediately after the event
options.E: No treatment, as it will always self-resolve

why_correct: Post-traumatic stress disorder (re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal beyond a month) is treated first-line with trauma-focused psychological therapy — trauma-focused CBT or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR).
why_wrong: B. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD (dependence, no benefit on core symptoms). C. Antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD. D. Single-session psychological debriefing is not recommended and may be harmful. E. Symptoms persisting at a month with impairment warrant treatment; they do not reliably self-resolve.
pearl: PTSD is treated first-line with trauma-focused CBT or EMDR — not benzodiazepines, and not routine immediate debriefing.
thinking: One month after assault: flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance, hyperarousal with impairment ↓ PTSD ↓ First-line: trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT or EMDR) — not benzodiazepines
exam_trap: B, a benzodiazepine first-line — sedation might seem to calm the hyperarousal. But benzodiazepines are not recommended for PTSD (dependence, poor evidence); trauma-focused psychological therapy is first-line.
takeaway: PTSD is treated first-line with trauma-focused CBT or EMDR — not benzodiazepines, and not routine immediate debriefing.

stem: A patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia is started on clozapine. Which is the most important adverse effect to monitor for with regular blood tests?
why_correct: Clozapine can cause life-threatening agranulocytosis, so it is dispensed only with mandatory regular full blood count monitoring; treatment is stopped if the neutrophil count falls. (Myocarditis and constipation/ileus are other serious effects.)
why_wrong: B. Thyroid monitoring is for lithium, not clozapine. C. Hyponatraemia is linked with SSRIs and carbamazepine; it is not the reason for clozapine's mandatory blood monitoring. D. Clozapine can raise liver enzymes, but mandatory monitoring is for neutropenia. E. Clozapine does not typically cause haemolytic anaemia; the risk is agranulocytosis.
pearl: Clozapine demands regular full-blood-count monitoring for agranulocytosis — the blood count, not the thyroid, is the one to watch.
thinking: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia started on clozapine ↓ Clozapine carries a risk of life-threatening neutropenia ↓ Mandatory regular full blood count monitoring ↓ Agranulocytosis (neutropenia)
exam_trap: B, hypothyroidism — thyroid monitoring belongs to lithium, so this is a cross-over trap. But clozapine's mandatory monitoring is of the full blood count for agranulocytosis, not thyroid function.
takeaway: Clozapine demands regular full-blood-count monitoring for agranulocytosis — the blood count, not the thyroid, is the one to watch.

stem: Within two weeks of giving birth, a woman develops rapidly fluctuating mood, confusion, delusions and hallucinations, with thoughts that may put her or the baby at risk. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Referral to the perinatal mental health team within two weeks
options.B: Reassurance that this is the baby blues, with health visitor review
options.C: Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit
options.D: Start an SSRI for postnatal depression and review in a week
options.E: A short course of zopiclone and review by her GP

correct_answer: C. Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit
why_correct: Postpartum (puerperal) psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with rapid onset of psychotic symptoms and risk to mother and baby; it requires urgent assessment and admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit.
why_wrong: A. Postpartum psychosis is an emergency; a two-week referral is far too slow given the risk to mother and baby. B. The baby blues are mild, transient tearfulness without psychosis or confusion. D. This is psychosis, not depression; an SSRI with routine review is inadequate. E. Hypnotics and primary care review do not address an emergency with psychosis and risk.
pearl: Puerperal psychosis is an emergency with risk to mother and baby — urgent admission, not reassurance as baby blues.
thinking: Onset within 2 weeks of birth: fluctuating mood, confusion, delusions, hallucinations, risk to mother/baby ↓ Postpartum psychosis = psychiatric emergency ↓ Urgent admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit
exam_trap: B, reassurance as baby blues — early postpartum mood change is common, so the label is tempting. But psychosis with delusions and risk is an emergency, far beyond the transient baby blues, and needs urgent admission.
takeaway: Puerperal psychosis is an emergency with risk to mother and baby — urgent admission, not reassurance as baby blues.

stem: An infant has repeated hospital admissions for unexplained episodes (e.g. apnoea or seizures) that are only ever witnessed by one parent, never occur during monitored periods, and have no organic explanation despite extensive investigation. What is the most appropriate concern and action?

options.A: Discharge home with an apnoea monitor and arrange outpatient review
options.B: Reassure the parent and arrange further invasive tests for the child
options.C: Suspect an inborn error of metabolism and start empirical treatment
options.D: Suspect fabricated or induced illness; escalate via safeguarding
options.E: Confront the parent with your suspicions before involving any others

correct_answer: D. Suspect fabricated or induced illness; escalate via safeguarding
why_correct: Recurrent unexplained events occurring only in one carer's presence, never witnessed on monitoring, with no organic cause despite thorough investigation, should raise the possibility of fabricated or induced illness — a safeguarding concern requiring escalation through child-protection procedures rather than ever-more invasive tests.
why_wrong: A. Home monitoring does not address the safeguarding concern raised by this pattern. B. Repeated invasive tests can themselves harm the child; the pattern should prompt safeguarding. C. Extensive investigation has found no organic cause; empirical treatment exposes the child to harm. E. Confronting the carer alone can increase risk to the child; concerns are escalated through safeguarding procedures first.
pearl: Unexplained events seen only when one carer is present and never on monitoring is a safeguarding concern (fabricated or induced illness) — escalate, do not just keep testing.
thinking: An infant has repeated hospital admissions for unexplained episodes (e ↓ Events occurring ONLY in one carer's presence and never on monitoring, with no o
exam_trap: B, reassure and keep investigating — clinicians naturally keep searching for a medical cause. But repeating invasive tests can itself harm the child, and the pattern (events only with one carer, never on monitoring) should trigger safeguarding action, not further investigation alone.
takeaway: Unexplained events seen only when one carer is present and never on monitoring is a safeguarding concern (fabricated or induced illness) — escalate, do not just keep testing.

stem: A patient has moderate depression with persistent low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and appetite, and impaired functioning, with no immediate risk to safety. What is an appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: Active monitoring with review in two to four weeks
options.D: St John's wort prescribed alongside an SSRI
options.E: An SSRI such as sertraline and/or individual CBT

correct_answer: E. An SSRI such as sertraline and/or individual CBT
why_correct: Moderate depression is treated first-line with an antidepressant (an SSRI such as sertraline) and/or a high-intensity psychological therapy (e.g. CBT), chosen with the patient; benzodiazepines and antipsychotics are not first-line.
why_wrong: A. Active monitoring suits mild symptoms; moderate depression with impaired functioning warrants an SSRI and/or high-intensity psychological therapy. B. Benzodiazepines do not treat depression and risk dependence. C. Antipsychotics are not first-line for depression without psychotic features. D. St John's wort interacts with SSRIs (serotonin syndrome risk) and is not recommended.
pearl: Moderate depression is treated with an SSRI and/or CBT first-line — not benzodiazepines.
thinking: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, sleep/appetite change, impaired function, no immediate risk ↓ Moderate depression ↓ Antidepressant (SSRI) and/or individual CBT, chosen with the patient
exam_trap: B, a long-term benzodiazepine — the sleep and anxiety symptoms might invite a sedative. But benzodiazepines do not treat depression and risk dependence; the first-line options are an SSRI and/or psychological therapy.
takeaway: Moderate depression is treated with an SSRI and/or CBT first-line — not benzodiazepines.

stem: A young adult has a longstanding, pervasive pattern of unstable intense relationships, marked impulsivity, chronic feelings of emptiness, fear of abandonment, and recurrent self-harm. What is the most appropriate first-line management approach?

options.A: Long-term diazepam to manage emotional crises
options.B: Lamotrigine as the primary long-term mood treatment
options.C: An antipsychotic as the primary long-term treatment
options.D: Structured psychological therapy such as DBT
options.E: Brief supportive counselling with contact during crises

correct_answer: D. Structured psychological therapy such as DBT
why_correct: Emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder is managed primarily with a structured psychological therapy such as dialectical behaviour therapy; medication is not the mainstay and is used only for specific comorbidities or short-term crises.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines risk dependence and disinhibition and are not a treatment for the disorder. B. Medication is not the core treatment; it is used for comorbidities or short-term crises. C. Antipsychotics are not recommended as the primary treatment; structured psychological therapy is the mainstay. E. Brief non-specific counselling is not effective; structured, longer-term psychological therapy is recommended.
pearl: Emotionally unstable personality disorder is treated primarily with structured psychotherapy (e.g. DBT) — medication is adjunctive, not the mainstay.
thinking: Longstanding pervasive instability of relationships, impulsivity, emptiness, abandonment fear, self-harm ↓ Emotionally unstable personality disorder, not an episodic mood disorder ↓ Structured psychological therapy (e.g. DBT); medication only adjunctive
exam_trap: B, a mood stabiliser as primary treatment — the mood instability invites a pharmacological fix. But no drug is licensed as the core treatment for the disorder; the evidence-based mainstay is structured psychological therapy, with medication playing only a limited adjunctive role.
takeaway: Emotionally unstable personality disorder is treated primarily with structured psychotherapy (e.g. DBT) — medication is adjunctive, not the mainstay.

stem: Some weeks after a bereavement, a person has waves of sadness and tearfulness with preoccupation about the deceased, but retains their self-worth, can still experience moments of pleasure, and is gradually functioning again. Which is the most appropriate assessment?

options.A: An anxiety disorder requiring a short benzodiazepine course
options.B: A major depressive episode — start an SSRI such as sertraline
options.C: A normal grief reaction — support and monitoring
options.D: Prolonged grief disorder — refer for specialist therapy
options.E: Psychotic depression requiring informal psychiatric admission

correct_answer: C. A normal grief reaction — support and monitoring
why_correct: Normal grief comes in waves, fluctuates, preserves self-worth and the capacity for some pleasure, and gradually eases; it is supported rather than medicated. Features such as pervasive worthlessness, persistent global impairment, or active suicidality would suggest a depressive illness needing treatment.
why_wrong: A. Waves of sadness and preoccupation with the deceased are features of grief, not an anxiety disorder; benzodiazepines can impair grieving. B. Preserved self-worth, moments of pleasure and gradual recovery indicate normal grief rather than depression. D. Prolonged grief disorder requires persistent impairing grief well beyond six months; this is weeks after the loss and improving. E. There are no psychotic features, and functioning is improving.
pearl: Grief comes in waves with preserved self-worth; pervasive worthlessness and persistent impairment signal depression needing treatment.
thinking: Waves of sadness and preoccupation weeks after a bereavement ↓ Self-worth and capacity for pleasure preserved ↓ Gradual return of functioning, no psychotic features ↓ A normal grief reaction — support and monitoring
exam_trap: B, a major depressive episode needing antidepressants — low mood after loss can look like depression. But the preserved self-worth, retained capacity for pleasure and gradual recovery here are consistent with normal grief, which is supported, not medicated.
takeaway: Grief comes in waves with preserved self-worth; pervasive worthlessness and persistent impairment signal depression needing treatment.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that are present both at home and at nursery, began before age 3, and impair his functioning and social development. What is the most appropriate diagnosis and initial approach?

options.A: An anxiety disorder requiring a benzodiazepine prescription
options.B: Normal variation — behavioural advice and review in six months
options.C: ADHD — start methylphenidate in primary care straight away
options.D: Conduct disorder — refer for a group-based parenting programme
options.E: ADHD — specialist assessment, with parent training first

correct_answer: E. ADHD — specialist assessment, with parent training first
why_correct: ADHD requires persistent, developmentally inappropriate inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity present in MORE than one setting (e.g. home and nursery) with functional impairment; diagnosis is made by a specialist (child psychiatrist or paediatrician with ADHD expertise). For a child under 5, NICE NG87 makes an ADHD-focused group parent-training programme the first-line treatment, and medication is not offered without a second specialist opinion.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety can cause restlessness, but pervasive inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity from early childhood across settings indicate ADHD, and benzodiazepines are inappropriate. B. Symptoms across settings with functional impairment are not normal variation and need specialist assessment. C. ADHD medication is started only after specialist diagnosis, not in primary care, and in a child under 5 only after a second specialist opinion. D. Conduct disorder involves persistent antisocial, defiant behaviour, not primarily inattention and hyperactivity.
pearl: ADHD needs pervasive symptoms across settings with impairment — specialist diagnosis; under 5, parent training first; 5 and over, medication if impairment persists after environmental changes.
thinking: 4-year-old with inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity since early childhood ↓ Pervasive across settings (home AND nursery) with functional impairment ↓ ADHD: specialist assessment; under 5, group parent training first
exam_trap: B, normal childhood behaviour — children are often active, so symptoms can be dismissed. But pervasive symptoms across settings WITH functional impairment distinguish ADHD from normal behaviour and warrant specialist assessment.
takeaway: ADHD needs pervasive symptoms across settings with impairment — specialist diagnosis; under 5, parent training first; 5 and over, medication if impairment persists after environmental changes.

stem: A 34-year-old man who uses heroin daily has opioid dependence and asks his GP for help. What is the most appropriate evidence-based management approach?

options.A: Methadone or buprenorphine with psychosocial support
options.B: Abrupt cessation with symptomatic relief and no follow-up
options.C: Long-term oral diazepam prescribed to manage cravings
options.D: Naltrexone started while he is still using heroin daily
options.E: Defer treatment until he is abstinent for a month

correct_answer: A. Methadone or buprenorphine with psychosocial support
why_correct: Opioid dependence is managed with opioid substitution therapy (methadone or buprenorphine) alongside psychosocial support and harm-reduction measures (such as needle exchange and take-home naloxone); abrupt unsupported cessation has high relapse and risk.
why_wrong: B. Unsupported abrupt cessation has high relapse and overdose risk; substitution therapy with support is evidence-based. C. Benzodiazepines do not treat opioid dependence and increase overdose risk. D. Naltrexone precipitates withdrawal in current users and is used only after detoxification. E. Withholding treatment until abstinence increases harm; treatment should be offered now.
pearl: Opioid dependence is managed with substitution therapy (methadone/buprenorphine) plus psychosocial support and harm reduction — not abrupt cessation.
thinking: Opioid (heroin) dependence, wants help ↓ Evidence-based treatment = opioid substitution ↓ Methadone or buprenorphine with psychosocial support and harm reduction
exam_trap: B, immediate abrupt cessation with no support — stopping the drug seems the obvious goal. But unsupported abrupt cessation has poor outcomes and high relapse; structured substitution therapy with psychosocial support is the evidence-based approach.
takeaway: Opioid dependence is managed with substitution therapy (methadone/buprenorphine) plus psychosocial support and harm reduction — not abrupt cessation.

stem: A patient has recurrent, unexpected episodes of intense fear with palpitations, sweating, chest tightness, shortness of breath and a feeling of impending doom, lasting minutes. Between episodes they worry about having another. Cardiac and other organic workup is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.C: Panic disorder — CBT and/or an SSRI

correct_answer: C. Panic disorder — CBT and/or an SSRI
why_correct: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory anxiety between episodes, and a normal organic workup, is panic disorder; first-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy and/or an SSRI.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism causes persistent rather than episodic symptoms, and the organic workup is normal. B. Recurrent brief attacks with a normal cardiac workup and anticipatory anxiety indicate panic disorder. D. Phaeochromocytoma has been excluded by a normal organic workup; the anticipatory anxiety points to panic disorder. E. GAD involves persistent worry rather than discrete attacks, and long-term benzodiazepines are not recommended.
pearl: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory anxiety and a normal workup is panic disorder — CBT and/or an SSRI.
thinking: Recurrent unexpected attacks of intense fear with autonomic symptoms, anticipatory worry, normal organic workup ↓ Panic disorder ↓ CBT and/or an SSRI
exam_trap: B, an acute coronary syndrome requiring admission — the somatic symptoms (chest tightness, palpitations) mimic cardiac disease and must be excluded. But with recurrent attacks and a normal workup plus anticipatory anxiety, the diagnosis is panic disorder, treated with CBT and/or an SSRI.
takeaway: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory anxiety and a normal workup is panic disorder — CBT and/or an SSRI.

stem: A patient has persistent physical symptoms accompanied by excessive and disproportionate thoughts, anxiety and time devoted to them, despite repeated normal investigations and reassurance. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Explain the symptoms are psychological and discharge
options.B: Further investigations at each visit to reassure the patient
options.C: One coordinating clinician, limited investigations and CBT
options.D: Long-term opioid analgesia for symptom control
options.E: Refer to several specialists in parallel for second opinions

correct_answer: C. One coordinating clinician, limited investigations and CBT
why_correct: Persistent physical symptoms with disproportionate health-related thoughts and anxiety, despite negative investigations, characterise somatic symptom disorder; management is a consistent, supportive relationship (ideally one coordinating clinician), avoiding unnecessary repeated investigations, validating distress, and considering psychological therapy (CBT).
why_wrong: A. Dismissing symptoms damages trust and does not help; the distress is real and needs a supportive approach. B. Repeated investigations reinforce health anxiety and risk iatrogenic harm. D. Long-term opioids carry dependence risk and are not effective for these symptoms. E. Multiple parallel referrals fragment care and drive further unnecessary tests.
pearl: Persistent symptoms with disproportionate health anxiety and negative tests is somatic symptom disorder — a consistent supportive approach, not endless investigation.
thinking: Persistent physical symptoms despite normal investigations ↓ Disproportionate health anxiety and time devoted to symptoms ↓ Somatic symptom disorder ↓ One coordinating clinician, limited investigations and CBT
exam_trap: B, continue ordering more investigations — the patient's distress can pull clinicians into endless testing. But repeated investigations reinforce illness behaviour and risk harm; a consistent supportive approach with limited testing is appropriate.
takeaway: Persistent symptoms with disproportionate health anxiety and negative tests is somatic symptom disorder — a consistent supportive approach, not endless investigation.

stem: During a routine consultation, a patient is found to be drinking at hazardous levels but is not dependent. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Refer for assisted alcohol withdrawal in the community
options.B: Record the intake and review if dependence develops
options.C: Start acamprosate to help reduce drinking
options.D: Refer to specialist alcohol services for therapy
options.E: AUDIT screening and a brief intervention on low-risk limits

correct_answer: E. AUDIT screening and a brief intervention on low-risk limits
why_correct: Hazardous (but non-dependent) drinking is identified with a validated tool such as AUDIT and addressed with a brief intervention — structured feedback, advice and goal-setting — together with advice on lower-risk limits; this tackles alcohol harm early, before dependence develops.
why_wrong: A. The patient is not dependent, so assisted withdrawal is not needed. B. Waiting for dependence misses the opportunity for an effective brief intervention now. C. Acamprosate is for maintaining abstinence in dependent drinkers after withdrawal. D. Specialist referral is for harmful or dependent drinking or failure of brief interventions; hazardous drinking is managed first with a brief intervention.
pearl: Hazardous drinking is identified with a tool like AUDIT and addressed with a brief intervention — tackle alcohol harm early, not only at dependence.
thinking: Hazardous drinking, not dependent ↓ intervene early with validated screening (AUDIT) and a brief intervention
exam_trap: B, take no action unless dependence develops — it can seem that only dependence needs intervention. But early identification and brief intervention at the hazardous stage are effective and recommended; waiting for dependence misses the opportunity to prevent harm.
takeaway: Hazardous drinking is identified with a tool like AUDIT and addressed with a brief intervention — tackle alcohol harm early, not only at dependence.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash over his right forehead and the tip of his nose, with eye pain and redness. What does the involvement of the nose tip signify, and what is needed?

options.B: Recurrent herpes simplex — topical aciclovir cream
options.C: Facial cellulitis — oral flucloxacillin and review
options.E: Hutchinson's sign — antivirals and urgent eye review

correct_answer: E. Hutchinson's sign — antivirals and urgent eye review
why_correct: Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and a high risk of sight-threatening ocular disease; oral antivirals and urgent ophthalmology review are required.
why_wrong: A. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief paroxysms of pain without a rash. B. A dermatomal vesicular rash in an older adult is shingles, and topical treatment does not protect the eye. C. The dermatomal vesicular rash is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, which needs antivirals and an eye review, not antibiotics. D. Contact dermatitis is itchy rather than painful and does not follow a dermatome or involve the eye.
pearl: Nose-tip vesicles in shingles is Hutchinson's sign — the eye is at risk; give antivirals and refer to ophthalmology urgently.
thinking: A 70-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash over his right forehead ↓ Vesicles on the tip of the nose — Hutchinson's sign flags nasociliary (and there
exam_trap: C, bacterial cellulitis — a red, painful facial rash can look infected, so antibiotics are tempting. But the dermatomal vesicular rash with nose-tip involvement is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, needing antivirals and an eye review, not antibiotics.
takeaway: Nose-tip vesicles in shingles is Hutchinson's sign — the eye is at risk; give antivirals and refer to ophthalmology urgently.

presentation: Microbial Keratitis in a Contact Lens Wearer
stem: A 25-year-old contact lens wearer has a painful red eye, photophobia, watering and blurred vision, with a white corneal infiltrate seen on fluorescein staining. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Topical chloramphenicol and GP review in one week
options.B: Stop lens wear and refer same day to ophthalmology
options.C: Lubricating drops and a two-week break from lenses
options.E: Patch the eye and review in clinic in 48 hours

correct_answer: B. Stop lens wear and refer same day to ophthalmology
why_correct: A painful red eye with a corneal infiltrate in a contact lens wearer is microbial keratitis, a sight-threatening emergency; lens wear is stopped and the patient referred urgently for corneal scraping and intensive topical antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Microbial keratitis in a lens wearer needs same-day specialist assessment and intensive treatment; chloramphenicol with delayed review is inadequate. C. A corneal infiltrate is not dry eye; it needs urgent referral. D. Steroids can worsen corneal infection and should not be started outside specialist care. E. Patching a lens-related infection encourages bacterial growth and delays treatment.
pearl: A contact lens wearer with a corneal infiltrate has microbial keratitis — refer urgently and never reach for a steroid.
thinking: A 25-year-old contact lens wearer has a painful red eye, photophobia, ↓ A corneal infiltrate in a contact lens wearer — the infiltrate signals infection
exam_trap: D, a topical steroid — it would calm the inflammation and redness, so it feels soothing. But steroids on an infected cornea accelerate the infection and can perforate the eye; the need is urgent antimicrobial treatment.
takeaway: A contact lens wearer with a corneal infiltrate has microbial keratitis — refer urgently and never reach for a steroid.

stem: An 80-year-old man has rapid-onset distortion of central vision, with straight lines appearing wavy, in one eye. Fundoscopy and OCT suggest a neovascular (wet) process. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: Reassurance, as it is age-related and untreatable
options.C: Urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF injection

correct_answer: C. Urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF injection
why_correct: Wet (neovascular) age-related macular degeneration causes rapid central visual distortion; urgent intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy can preserve vision, so prompt referral is essential.
why_wrong: A. Reading glasses do not correct distortion from macular neovascularisation. B. Wet AMD is treatable with anti-VEGF if caught early; reassurance as 'untreatable' applies only to dry AMD. D. Oral steroids have no role in neovascular AMD. E. Cataract does not cause sudden metamorphopsia and surgery would not treat the macular lesion.
pearl: Sudden wavy central vision is wet AMD — refer urgently for anti-VEGF; it is treatable if caught fast.
thinking: Rapid-onset central distortion (wavy lines) in an 80-year-old ↓ neovascular (wet) AMD on OCT ↓ treatable if caught early
exam_trap: B, reassurance as untreatable — dry AMD has no specific treatment, making 'untreatable' a tempting generalisation. But wet AMD is treatable with anti-VEGF if caught early; rapid distortion demands urgent referral, not reassurance.
takeaway: Sudden wavy central vision is wet AMD — refer urgently for anti-VEGF; it is treatable if caught fast.

stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes is found on screening to have new vessels growing on the retina (neovascularisation). What does this indicate and what is the treatment?

options.A: Background retinopathy — annual screening and glucose control

correct_answer: B. Proliferative retinopathy — panretinal laser photocoagulation
why_correct: Neovascularisation defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which threatens sight through vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment; pan-retinal laser photocoagulation (with anti-VEGF in some cases) is the treatment.
why_wrong: A. New vessels mark the proliferative stage, which needs laser treatment, not routine screening. C. Pre-proliferative disease has ischaemic features but no new vessels; neovascularisation indicates proliferative retinopathy needing treatment. D. Maculopathy involves exudates or oedema at the macula; retinal neovascularisation is proliferative retinopathy. E. Neovascular glaucoma involves new vessels on the iris with raised pressure; the finding here is retinal neovascularisation.
pearl: New vessels mean proliferative retinopathy — treat with pan-retinal laser; background changes only need monitoring.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes with retinal neovascularisation on screening ↓ New vessels define proliferative diabetic retinopathy ↓ Risk of vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment ↓ Proliferative retinopathy — panretinal laser photocoagulation
exam_trap: A, background retinopathy needing no treatment — earlier stages indeed need only monitoring and glucose control. But NEW VESSELS mark the proliferative, sight-threatening stage that requires laser treatment.
takeaway: New vessels mean proliferative retinopathy — treat with pan-retinal laser; background changes only need monitoring.

stem: A patient has a sudden increase in floaters and flashing lights, followed by a 'curtain' or shadow descending across the vision in one eye, which is progressing. What is the most appropriate action?

options.D: Routine optician appointment in two weeks

correct_answer: C. Urgent referral to ophthalmology (same day)
why_correct: Flashes and floaters with a progressing visual field 'curtain' suggest retinal detachment, a sight-threatening emergency requiring same-day ophthalmology assessment for surgical repair.
why_wrong: A. Lubricating drops treat dry eye, not a retinal tear or detachment. B. Isolated floaters may be benign, but flashes with a progressing curtain indicate detachment. D. A two-week delay risks macular involvement and permanent visual loss. E. There is no infection; antibiotics are irrelevant.
pearl: Flashes, floaters and a curtain over the vision is retinal detachment — refer the same day; isolated floaters alone are benign.
thinking: Flashes and floaters followed by a progressing 'curtain' ↓ retinal detachment ↓ sight-threatening emergency
exam_trap: B, reassurance as benign floaters — isolated floaters are often harmless, so reassurance can be a trap. But floaters and flashes with a descending curtain indicate detachment, which is an emergency, not a benign floater.
takeaway: Flashes, floaters and a curtain over the vision is retinal detachment — refer the same day; isolated floaters alone are benign.

stem: A 65-year-old man is found at a routine optician visit to have raised intraocular pressure, an enlarged optic disc cup and peripheral visual field loss, but no pain or redness. An ophthalmologist confirms chronic open-angle glaucoma. He declines laser treatment. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Urgent laser iridotomy for presumed angle closure
options.C: Observation with repeat visual field testing in a year
options.E: Topical pilocarpine drops as first-line treatment

correct_answer: B. Topical prostaglandin analogue, e.g. latanoprost
why_correct: Primary (chronic) open-angle glaucoma presents with painless, gradual peripheral field loss, raised pressure and disc cupping. NICE NG81 recommends 360-degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) first-line for newly diagnosed COAG. When SLT is declined, unsuitable or awaited, a generic topical prostaglandin analogue (e.g. latanoprost) is the first-line drop to lower intraocular pressure and preserve vision.
why_wrong: A. This is painless chronic open-angle glaucoma, not acute angle closure; iridotomy is not the treatment. C. Established field loss with raised pressure needs treatment now to prevent progression. D. Systemic acetazolamide has significant side effects and is not used long term as first-line. E. Pilocarpine is not a first-line treatment for open-angle glaucoma; a prostaglandin analogue is.
pearl: Open-angle glaucoma is painless and chronic. NICE first-line is 360° SLT; if declined or unsuitable, lower the pressure with a generic prostaglandin analogue. The painful, sudden one is angle closure.
thinking: Painless, gradual peripheral field loss + raised IOP + disc cupping ↓ Chronic open-angle glaucoma ↓ NICE NG81: 360° SLT first-line, but he declines laser ↓ Generic prostaglandin analogue drop (e.g. latanoprost)
exam_trap: A, urgent surgery for acute glaucoma — glaucoma can prompt thoughts of an emergency. But this is the chronic, painless open-angle form managed with pressure-lowering drops, not the acute painful angle-closure emergency.
takeaway: Open-angle glaucoma is painless and chronic. 360° SLT is first-line; if declined, a prostaglandin analogue drop. The painful, sudden one is angle closure.

stem: A patient has a red eye with severe, boring pain that wakes them at night and a bluish hue to the deep vessels, which do not blanch with topical phenylephrine. They have rheumatoid arthritis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Scleritis causes a deeply red, painful eye (severe boring pain), often with systemic disease such as rheumatoid arthritis; the deep vessels do not blanch with phenylephrine, and it is sight-threatening, needing urgent ophthalmology and systemic treatment.
why_wrong: A. Anterior uveitis causes photophobia, blurred vision and a small irregular pupil with anterior-chamber cells, and is not characterised by bluish, non-blanching deep scleral vessels. B. Episcleritis is the milder mimic: it is relatively painless and its superficial vessels blanch with phenylephrine, whereas the severe pain and non-blanching deep vessels here indicate scleritis. C. Conjunctivitis causes a gritty or itchy eye with discharge and superficial injection, not severe boring pain that wakes the patient at night. E. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is a painless, well-demarcated patch of blood under the conjunctiva, not a painful inflamed eye.
pearl: Severe pain with non-blanching deep vessels is scleritis (serious); mild and blanching is episcleritis (benign).
thinking: Red eye with severe boring pain waking the patient at night ↓ Bluish deep vessels that do not blanch with phenylephrine ↓ Background of rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Scleritis, the sight-threatening condition, not episcleritis
exam_trap: B, episcleritis — the milder mimic. But episcleritis is relatively painless and its vessels blanch with phenylephrine, whereas the severe pain and non-blanching deep vessels here indicate the more serious scleritis.
takeaway: Severe pain with non-blanching deep vessels is scleritis (serious); mild and blanching is episcleritis (benign).

stem: A patient has a painful red eye with blurred vision, marked photophobia, and a small, irregular pupil. They have a history of ankylosing spondylitis. Slit-lamp examination shows cells in the anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful, photophobic red eye with blurred vision, an irregular/small pupil and anterior-chamber cells is anterior uveitis (iritis), associated with HLA-B27 conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis; treatment is topical steroids and cycloplegics under ophthalmology.
why_wrong: B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is another painful red eye, but it causes a fixed, mid-dilated pupil with a hazy cornea and very high pressure, whereas this patient has a small irregular pupil with anterior-chamber cells. C. Bacterial conjunctivitis causes a gritty eye with purulent discharge, normal vision and a normal pupil, not photophobia with anterior-chamber cells. D. Episcleritis is a mild, often painless sectoral redness without photophobia, visual loss or pupil change. E. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is a painless patch of blood with normal vision and pupil, not a photophobic eye with anterior-chamber cells.
pearl: A painful, photophobic red eye with a small irregular pupil and anterior-chamber cells (especially with ankylosing spondylitis) is anterior uveitis.
thinking: Painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision ↓ Small irregular pupil with anterior-chamber cells on slit lamp ↓ HLA-B27 link with ankylosing spondylitis ↓ Anterior uveitis (iritis)
exam_trap: B, acute angle-closure glaucoma — another painful red eye, so an important differential. But angle-closure causes a FIXED, mid-dilated pupil with a hazy cornea and very high pressure, whereas anterior uveitis has a small/irregular pupil with anterior-chamber cells and a relevant rheumatological history.
takeaway: A painful, photophobic red eye with a small irregular pupil and anterior-chamber cells (especially with ankylosing spondylitis) is anterior uveitis.

stem: A child has a red, swollen, painful eyelid with fever, and now has pain on eye movement, restricted eye movements and proptosis. What is the diagnosis and the most appropriate management?

options.A: Allergic angio-oedema — oral antihistamine and review
options.B: Preseptal cellulitis — oral co-amoxiclav and review
options.C: Orbital cellulitis — admit for IV antibiotics and CT imaging
options.D: Infected chalazion — warm compresses and chloramphenicol

correct_answer: C. Orbital cellulitis — admit for IV antibiotics and CT imaging
why_correct: Pain on eye movement, restricted eye movements and proptosis with eyelid swelling and fever indicate orbital (post-septal) cellulitis — a sight- and life-threatening emergency requiring admission, urgent IV antibiotics and imaging (CT) to assess for abscess.
why_wrong: A. Allergic swelling is itchy and painless, without fever, restricted movements or proptosis. B. Pain on eye movement, restricted movement and proptosis indicate post-septal infection, which needs admission and IV antibiotics. D. A chalazion is a localised lid lump without fever, proptosis or restricted eye movements. E. Conjunctivitis does not cause proptosis or painful, restricted eye movements.
pearl: Painful, restricted eye movements and proptosis with eyelid swelling is orbital cellulitis — admit for IV antibiotics and imaging; preseptal cellulitis spares the movements.
thinking: Eyelid swelling with fever plus pain on eye movement, restricted movement and proptosis ↓ post-septal (orbital) cellulitis ↓ admit, IV antibiotics, CT
exam_trap: B, preseptal cellulitis with oral antibiotics — superficial eyelid cellulitis is treated this way. But the presence of painful, RESTRICTED eye movements and proptosis means the infection is behind the septum (orbital cellulitis), which is an emergency needing IV antibiotics and imaging.
takeaway: Painful, restricted eye movements and proptosis with eyelid swelling is orbital cellulitis — admit for IV antibiotics and imaging; preseptal cellulitis spares the movements.

stem: A baby's parents notice that one pupil looks white in photographs, and on examination the red reflex is absent on that side. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Repeat the red reflex at the 6–8 week check
options.B: Reassure that it is a camera-flash artefact and recheck in a month
options.D: Urgent ophthalmology referral for possible retinoblastoma
options.E: Refer to an optometrist for a refraction test

correct_answer: D. Urgent ophthalmology referral for possible retinoblastoma
why_correct: An absent or white red reflex (leukocoria) in a child must be referred urgently, as it can indicate retinoblastoma (a potentially life-threatening but treatable eye cancer) or other serious pathology such as congenital cataract.
why_wrong: A. An absent red reflex needs urgent referral now; waiting delays diagnosis of a possible cancer. B. A white reflex in photographs confirmed by an absent red reflex on examination is not an artefact. C. Leukocoria warrants urgent, not routine, referral because retinoblastoma is time-critical. E. A refraction test does not assess for retinoblastoma or cataract; urgent specialist referral is needed.
pearl: A white pupil or absent red reflex in a child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise — refer urgently.
thinking: A baby's parents notice that one pupil looks white in photographs, and ↓ An ABSENT red reflex (leukocoria) on examination — that finding, not a photograp
exam_trap: B, reassure as a flash artefact — a white reflex in a photo can be dismissed as a camera effect. But a genuinely absent red reflex on examination is a red flag for retinoblastoma and demands urgent referral, not reassurance.
takeaway: A white pupil or absent red reflex in a child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise — refer urgently.

stem: A patient has a red, gritty eye with discharge. Crucially, there is NO pain, NO photophobia and NO reduction in visual acuity, and the pupil is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Conjunctivitis — hygiene advice, antibiotic drops only if needed
options.B: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — urgent pressure-lowering treatment
options.C: Anterior uveitis — same-day eye referral for topical steroid drops
options.D: Microbial keratitis — corneal scrape and urgent ophthalmology referral
options.E: Scleritis — high-dose oral NSAIDs and urgent ophthalmology referral

correct_answer: A. Conjunctivitis — hygiene advice, antibiotic drops only if needed
why_correct: A red eye with discharge but NO pain, photophobia or visual loss and a normal pupil is conjunctivitis, which is usually self-limiting; advice on hygiene is given, with topical antibiotics reserved for bacterial cases that are troublesome.
why_wrong: B. Angle closure causes severe pain, haloes, reduced vision and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, none of which are present. C. Uveitis causes pain, photophobia and a small irregular pupil. D. Keratitis causes pain, photophobia and reduced vision, usually with a corneal infiltrate. E. Scleritis causes severe, boring pain and tenderness, often with systemic disease, rather than a painless red eye with discharge.
pearl: A red eye with no pain, no photophobia and normal vision is conjunctivitis — any of those red flags means a sight-threatening cause instead.
thinking: Red gritty eye with discharge ↓ no pain, photophobia or visual loss and a normal pupil ↓ conjunctivitis
exam_trap: D, microbial keratitis needing urgent referral — sight-threatening causes must always be excluded in a red eye. But keratitis, uveitis and angle-closure all cause pain, photophobia or visual loss; their ABSENCE here, with a normal pupil, points to benign conjunctivitis.
takeaway: A red eye with no pain, no photophobia and normal vision is conjunctivitis — any of those red flags means a sight-threatening cause instead.

stem: A patient with very high blood pressure undergoes fundoscopy, which shows arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nipping, flame-shaped haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, with swelling of the optic disc (papilloedema). What does the papilloedema signify?

options.E: Central retinal vein occlusion — routine eye referral

correct_answer: B. Malignant hypertension — a hypertensive emergency
why_correct: Fundal changes of arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nipping, flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are hypertensive retinopathy; the addition of papilloedema indicates accelerated (malignant) hypertension — a hypertensive emergency requiring prompt, controlled blood-pressure reduction.
why_wrong: A. These changes with papilloedema in very high blood pressure are hypertensive, not diabetic, retinopathy. C. Papilloedema indicates grade 4 (accelerated) hypertensive retinopathy, which is an emergency, not a grade 2 finding for routine care. D. The disc swelling here occurs with severe hypertensive retinal changes, indicating malignant hypertension rather than idiopathic intracranial hypertension. E. Vein occlusion is usually unilateral with widespread haemorrhages, and papilloedema with very high blood pressure needs urgent treatment.
pearl: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are hypertensive retinopathy — added papilloedema means accelerated (malignant) hypertension, an emergency.
thinking: Very high blood pressure with AV nipping, flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots ↓ Hypertensive retinopathy ↓ Papilloedema marks grade 4 (accelerated) change ↓ Malignant hypertension — a hypertensive emergency
exam_trap: A, diabetic retinopathy — both cause retinal haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots. But the arteriovenous nipping/arteriolar changes with papilloedema in the context of very high blood pressure indicate hypertensive (accelerated) retinopathy, an emergency, rather than diabetic retinopathy.
takeaway: AV nipping, flame haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots are hypertensive retinopathy — added papilloedema means accelerated (malignant) hypertension, an emergency.

stem: An older patient has a gradual, progressive loss of central vision over months. Fundoscopy shows drusen at the macula, without sudden distortion of straight lines. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Dry AMD — no specific cure; monitor for sudden distortion
options.B: Wet (neovascular) AMD — urgent referral for intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy
options.C: Primary open-angle glaucoma — start prostaglandin analogue eye drops
options.D: Cataract — routine phacoemulsification with an intraocular lens implant

correct_answer: A. Dry AMD — no specific cure; monitor for sudden distortion
why_correct: Gradual progressive central visual loss with drusen and no acute distortion is dry (atrophic) age-related macular degeneration, for which there is no specific cure (supplements may slow progression); the wet (neovascular) form causes sudden distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) and requires urgent anti-VEGF treatment.
why_wrong: B. Wet AMD causes sudden distortion (metamorphopsia) and rapid loss; gradual loss with drusen is the dry form. C. Open-angle glaucoma causes peripheral, not central, field loss with disc cupping. D. Cataract causes generalised blurring and glare, and drusen are a retinal finding. E. Central serous chorioretinopathy affects younger adults with sudden blurring from subretinal fluid, not drusen.
pearl: Gradual central vision loss with drusen is dry AMD; sudden distortion (metamorphopsia) is wet AMD needing urgent anti-VEGF.
thinking: Older patient, gradual progressive central visual loss over months ↓ Drusen at the macula, no sudden distortion of straight lines ↓ Dry (atrophic) AMD; wet AMD would be sudden with metamorphopsia and need anti-VEGF
exam_trap: B, wet AMD requiring urgent anti-VEGF — both are macular degeneration. But wet AMD presents with SUDDEN distortion (metamorphopsia) and needs urgent intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy, whereas the GRADUAL loss with drusen here is the dry form.
takeaway: Gradual central vision loss with drusen is dry AMD; sudden distortion (metamorphopsia) is wet AMD needing urgent anti-VEGF.

stem: A patient describes a transient loss of vision in one eye, like 'a curtain coming down', that fully resolved within minutes. What does this most likely represent, and what does it require?

options.A: Posterior vitreous detachment — routine optometry review
options.B: Retinal migraine — reassurance and migraine prophylaxis
options.D: Amaurosis fugax — urgent TIA assessment and carotid imaging
options.E: Transient visual obscuration from papilloedema — urgent CT head

correct_answer: D. Amaurosis fugax — urgent TIA assessment and carotid imaging
why_correct: Transient monocular visual loss described as a descending curtain that resolves is amaurosis fugax — a transient ischaemic event, often from carotid embolism; it carries a high risk of stroke and warrants urgent assessment (including carotid imaging) and secondary prevention (antiplatelet, risk-factor and possibly carotid intervention).
why_wrong: A. A vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes, not a transient curtain that fully resolves. B. Retinal migraine is a diagnosis of exclusion; a monocular curtain must be treated as ischaemic until proven otherwise. C. A detachment causes a persistent curtain-like field loss that does not resolve within minutes. E. Obscurations from papilloedema last seconds, are often bilateral and are triggered by posture, unlike this descending curtain.
pearl: Transient monocular 'curtain' visual loss is amaurosis fugax (a TIA) — urgent stroke-risk assessment and secondary prevention.
thinking: Transient monocular 'curtain' visual loss resolving within minutes ↓ Retinal ischaemia, often carotid embolism ↓ A TIA with high early stroke risk ↓ Amaurosis fugax — urgent TIA assessment and carotid imaging
exam_trap: B, a benign migraine aura needing no action — transient visual symptoms can be migrainous. But a sudden monocular 'curtain' that resolves is an ischaemic event (amaurosis fugax) signalling stroke risk, requiring urgent assessment, not reassurance.
takeaway: Transient monocular 'curtain' visual loss is amaurosis fugax (a TIA) — urgent stroke-risk assessment and secondary prevention.

stem: A patient with proliferative diabetic retinopathy has sudden loss of vision with numerous new floaters, and the fundal (red) reflex is reduced or absent with an obscured retinal view. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: A simple posterior vitreous detachment with no bleeding

why_correct: Sudden visual loss with new floaters and a reduced/absent red reflex and obscured retinal view, especially in proliferative diabetic retinopathy (or after retinal tear), indicates vitreous haemorrhage; management is treating the underlying cause and ophthalmology review, as many clear spontaneously.
why_wrong: A. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with haloes, a hazy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, not painless floaters with loss of the red reflex. B. Central retinal artery occlusion also causes sudden visual loss, but the fundus can be seen and shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot, whereas the obscured view and lost red reflex here indicate blood in the vitreous. D. Optic neuritis causes painful eye movements and reduced colour vision with a normal red reflex, not new floaters with an obscured fundal view. E. A posterior vitreous detachment without bleeding causes floaters and flashes, but the red reflex and retinal view are preserved and vision is not suddenly lost.
pearl: Sudden floaters with an obscured view and reduced red reflex (often in proliferative diabetic retinopathy) is vitreous haemorrhage.
thinking: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy with fragile new vessels ↓ Sudden visual loss with many new floaters ↓ Reduced red reflex and obscured retinal view ↓ Vitreous haemorrhage
exam_trap: B, central retinal artery occlusion — both cause sudden visual loss. But artery occlusion allows a view of a pale retina with a cherry-red spot, whereas the obscured view with loss of the red reflex here indicates blood in the vitreous (vitreous haemorrhage).
takeaway: Sudden floaters with an obscured view and reduced red reflex (often in proliferative diabetic retinopathy) is vitreous haemorrhage.

stem: A patient has a painful, watering, red eye with a foreign-body sensation after something flew into it. What is the most appropriate initial assessment?

options.A: Double-pad the eye and review in clinic in 48 hours
options.B: Topical anaesthetic drops to use at home for the pain
options.C: Fluorescein staining and eversion of the upper eyelid
options.D: Topical steroid drops to settle the inflammation
options.E: Visual acuity and slit-lamp check without fluorescein

correct_answer: C. Fluorescein staining and eversion of the upper eyelid
why_correct: A painful, watering eye with a foreign-body sensation after trauma is assessed with fluorescein staining under a blue light to reveal a corneal abrasion (a green-staining epithelial defect) or to find a retained foreign body, and the upper lid should be everted to look for a subtarsal foreign body; treatment includes removing any foreign body, topical antibiotic and analgesia.
why_wrong: A. Patching does not aid healing and delays proper examination for an abrasion or retained foreign body. B. Topical anaesthetics impair epithelial healing and mask injury, so they are not given for home use. D. Steroids risk infection and delayed healing in a corneal abrasion. E. Without fluorescein a corneal abrasion is easily missed, and the upper lid must be everted to find a subtarsal foreign body.
pearl: A painful watering eye after trauma needs fluorescein examination and lid eversion to find a corneal abrasion or foreign body — never give topical anaesthetic for home use.
thinking: Painful, watering red eye with foreign-body sensation after trauma ↓ Suspect corneal abrasion or retained foreign body ↓ Fluorescein shows abrasion; lid eversion finds subtarsal foreign body ↓ Fluorescein staining and eversion of the upper eyelid
exam_trap: B, prescribe a topical anaesthetic for ongoing home use — anaesthetic drops relieve the pain. But topical anaesthetics impair healing and mask injury, so they are not given for home use; the eye should be examined with fluorescein and treated appropriately.
takeaway: A painful watering eye after trauma needs fluorescein examination and lid eversion to find a corneal abrasion or foreign body — never give topical anaesthetic for home use.
