stem: A patient notices a flat, bright-red patch on the white of one eye. There is no pain, no visual disturbance and no discharge, and the rest of the examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Chloramphenicol drops and review in a week
options.B: Same-day ophthalmology referral to exclude acute scleritis
options.C: An urgent clotting screen and same-day haematology referral
options.D: Topical steroid drops to speed resolution
options.E: Reassure it is benign; check BP and any anticoagulant use

correct_answer: E. Reassure it is benign; check BP and any anticoagulant use
why_correct: A painless, flat, bright-red patch on the sclera with normal vision and no discharge is a subconjunctival haemorrhage, which is benign and resolves spontaneously over a couple of weeks; it is worth checking blood pressure and considering anticoagulant/antiplatelet use or recurrent bleeding, but no specific treatment is needed.
why_wrong: A. A subconjunctival haemorrhage is not infective; antibiotics are not needed. B. Scleritis is painful with reduced vision; a painless flat red patch with normal vision does not need urgent referral. C. An isolated subconjunctival haemorrhage does not need urgent haematology input; INR is checked if the patient takes warfarin. D. Steroids do not speed resolution and carry risks; no treatment is needed.
pearl: A painless subconjunctival haemorrhage with normal vision is benign and self-limiting — reassure, check BP, review anticoagulation.
thinking: Flat bright-red patch on the sclera ↓ painless, normal vision, no discharge ↓ subconjunctival haemorrhage
exam_trap: B, same-day referral to exclude scleritis — a bright-red eye can look alarming. But scleritis is painful with reduced vision; a painless, flat subconjunctival haemorrhage with normal vision is benign and self-limiting, so reassurance with a BP check is appropriate.
takeaway: A painless subconjunctival haemorrhage with normal vision is benign and self-limiting — reassure, check BP, review anticoagulation.

stem: An older patient presents with a sudden, severely painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes around lights, and nausea and vomiting. The eye is hard, the cornea is hazy, and the pupil is fixed and mid-dilated. What is the diagnosis and immediate priority?

options.B: Acute anterior uveitis — same-day topical steroids and cycloplegia
options.C: Bacterial keratitis — intensive topical antibiotics and same-day review
options.D: Acute angle-closure glaucoma — urgent IOP reduction and referral
options.E: Primary open-angle glaucoma — routine ophthalmology outpatient referral

correct_answer: D. Acute angle-closure glaucoma — urgent IOP reduction and referral
why_correct: A sudden painful red eye with haloes, a hazy cornea, a hard globe and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, with systemic upset, is acute angle-closure glaucoma — a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent intraocular-pressure reduction and immediate ophthalmology referral.
why_wrong: A. Episcleritis is mildly uncomfortable with normal vision, not a hard eye with haloes. B. Uveitis causes a small, irregular pupil with photophobia, not a fixed mid-dilated pupil with a hard eye. C. Keratitis causes a corneal infiltrate rather than a hard eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and haloes. E. Open-angle glaucoma is painless and chronic; this acute presentation needs immediate treatment.
pearl: A sudden painful red eye with haloes, a hazy cornea, a hard globe and a fixed mid-dilated pupil is acute angle-closure glaucoma — an emergency needing urgent IOP reduction and ophthalmology referral.
thinking: Sudden painful red eye with haloes and vomiting ↓ hard eye, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil ↓ acute angle closure
exam_trap: B, acute anterior uveitis — it is also an acutely painful red eye. But uveitis causes a small, irregular pupil with photophobia, not a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and the eye is not hard with haloes; the fixed mid-dilated pupil and raised pressure mark angle closure.
takeaway: A sudden painful red eye with haloes, a hazy cornea, a hard globe and a fixed mid-dilated pupil is acute angle-closure glaucoma — an emergency needing urgent IOP reduction and ophthalmology referral.

stem: A 22-year-old man with a worsening sore throat now has severe unilateral throat pain, difficulty swallowing his saliva (drooling), a muffled 'hot potato' voice and trismus. One tonsil is displaced medially with uvular deviation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Unilateral severe throat pain with trismus, a muffled voice, drooling and a displaced tonsil with uvular deviation is a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy), needing drainage and antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Retropharyngeal abscess mainly affects young children, causing neck stiffness and a posterior pharyngeal bulge, without tonsillar displacement. B. Tonsillitis is bilateral without trismus or uvular deviation. C. Epiglottitis causes stridor and drooling without a displaced tonsil or trismus. D. Glandular fever causes bilateral tonsillar enlargement with lymphadenopathy, not unilateral displacement with trismus.
pearl: A unilateral, uvula-deviating, trismus-causing sore throat is quinsy — it needs drainage, not just antibiotics.
thinking: Worsening sore throat, now severe and unilateral ↓ Trismus, drooling and muffled hot-potato voice ↓ Tonsil displaced medially with uvular deviation ↓ Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
exam_trap: B, simple tonsillitis — the obvious antecedent, so a tempting label. But tonsillitis is bilateral without trismus or uvular deviation; the unilateral swelling pushing the uvula across marks an abscess.
takeaway: A unilateral, uvula-deviating, trismus-causing sore throat is quinsy — it needs drainage, not just antibiotics.

stem: A patient has sudden, unilateral hearing loss over hours to a day, with no obvious cause. Weber's test lateralises to the opposite (better) ear and Rinne's test is normal in the affected ear. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Routine audiology referral for a hearing aid assessment
options.B: Reassure and review in four weeks if it has not improved
options.C: Ear irrigation for presumed wax impaction
options.D: Nasal decongestant for presumed Eustachian tube dysfunction
options.E: Urgent ENT referral for prompt corticosteroid treatment

correct_answer: E. Urgent ENT referral for prompt corticosteroid treatment
why_correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (a sensorineural pattern on tuning-fork tests) is an emergency; prompt ENT referral and corticosteroids within days give the best chance of recovery.
why_wrong: A. Routine referral misses the window for steroid treatment of sudden sensorineural loss. B. Delay reduces the chance of recovery; this is time-critical. C. Wax causes conductive loss (Weber to the affected ear, Rinne negative), not this sensorineural pattern. D. Eustachian tube dysfunction causes conductive loss, whereas the tuning-fork tests here indicate sensorineural loss.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency — urgent ENT and steroids; do not wait or assume it is wax.
thinking: Sudden unilateral hearing loss ↓ Weber to the better ear, Rinne normal = sensorineural ↓ time-critical
exam_trap: B, reassure and review in a month — hearing loss can seem non-urgent. But sudden sensorineural loss is time-critical; delay reduces the chance of recovery, so urgent referral and steroids are needed.
takeaway: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an emergency — urgent ENT and steroids; do not wait or assume it is wax.

stem: A 45-year-old has recurrent episodes of spontaneous rotational vertigo lasting hours, with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and a sensation of aural fullness in one ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness is Meniere's disease (endolymphatic hydrops); management includes lifestyle measures, betahistine and acute vestibular sedatives.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular neuronitis causes a single prolonged attack of vertigo lasting days after a viral illness, without hearing loss, tinnitus or aural fullness. B. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo gives brief vertigo lasting seconds, triggered by head movement, with normal hearing, not hours-long spontaneous attacks with hearing loss. D. Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) causes progressive unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus with imbalance rather than discrete recurrent attacks of rotational vertigo lasting hours. E. Labyrinthitis causes a single acute episode of vertigo with hearing loss, usually after a viral infection, not recurrent episodes with fluctuating hearing.
pearl: Hours of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness is Meniere's — BPPV is brief, positional and spares the hearing.
thinking: Recurrent spontaneous rotational vertigo lasting hours ↓ Fluctuating unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus ↓ Aural fullness in the same ear suggests endolymphatic hydrops ↓ Meniere's disease
exam_trap: B, BPPV — another episodic vertigo, so a reasonable thought. But BPPV gives brief, positionally-triggered vertigo of seconds without hearing loss, whereas the hours-long attacks with hearing loss and fullness here are Meniere's.
takeaway: Hours of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness is Meniere's — BPPV is brief, positional and spares the hearing.

stem: A 3-year-old has ear pain, fever and a red, bulging tympanic membrane. He is otherwise well, eating and drinking, and the eardrum is intact. What is the most appropriate management for most such children?

options.B: Analgesia with no or delayed antibiotics
options.D: Ciprofloxacin ear drops for seven days

correct_answer: B. Analgesia with no or delayed antibiotics
why_correct: Most acute otitis media in otherwise well children is self-limiting; analgesia with a no-antibiotic or delayed-antibiotic strategy is appropriate, reserving immediate antibiotics for those systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications, and considering them for under-2s with bilateral AOM or any child with otorrhoea.
why_wrong: A. Most acute otitis media resolves without antibiotics; immediate antibiotics are for those who are systemically unwell, have otorrhoea, or are under 2 with bilateral disease. C. Grommets are for persistent otitis media with effusion or recurrent infections, not a single acute episode. D. Topical drops do not reach the middle ear through an intact eardrum. E. Decongestants and antihistamines do not help acute otitis media.
pearl: Most acute otitis media is treated with analgesia and watchful waiting — reserve immediate antibiotics for under-2s with bilateral disease, the discharging or the unwell.
thinking: 3-year-old with ear pain, fever and a red, bulging drum, otherwise well ↓ Uncomplicated acute otitis media, no high-risk features ↓ Analgesia with a no-antibiotic or delayed-antibiotic strategy
exam_trap: A, immediate antibiotics for all — an obvious-looking ear infection invites antibiotics. But most cases resolve without them; a no-/delayed-antibiotic approach with analgesia is appropriate for the otherwise-well child.
takeaway: Most acute otitis media is treated with analgesia and watchful waiting — reserve immediate antibiotics for under-2s with bilateral disease, the discharging or the unwell.

stem: A patient has an active nosebleed from the front of the nose. They are haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate first-aid measure?

options.A: Insert an anterior nasal pack before trying compression
options.B: Tilt the head back and pinch the bony bridge
options.C: Lie flat and press firmly on the bony bridge for 5 minutes
options.D: Sit forward and pinch the soft nose for 10–15 minutes
options.E: Silver nitrate cautery before any compression

correct_answer: D. Sit forward and pinch the soft nose for 10–15 minutes
why_correct: Most nosebleeds are anterior; first aid is to sit upright and lean FORWARD, pinch the soft (cartilaginous) part of the nose firmly for 10–15 minutes and breathe through the mouth; if bleeding continues, cautery or packing is used.
why_wrong: A. Packing is used if bleeding persists after first aid and cautery, not before compression. B. Tilting back lets blood run into the throat, and pressure on the bony bridge does not compress Little's area. C. Lying flat risks swallowing or aspirating blood, and pressing the bony bridge does not compress the bleeding point. E. Cautery is used once first aid has failed and the bleeding point is visible, not before compression.
pearl: Stop a nosebleed by leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose — leaning back just sends blood down the throat.
thinking: A patient has an active nosebleed from the front of the nose ↓ Pinching the SOFT (cartilaginous) part while leaning FORWARD — that technique co
exam_trap: B, tilt the head back and pinch the bony bridge — leaning back feels natural to stop blood dripping out. But tilting back lets blood run down the throat (risking aspiration and obscuring blood loss), and pinching the bony bridge does not compress the bleeding point; lean forward and pinch the soft part.
takeaway: Stop a nosebleed by leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose — leaning back just sends blood down the throat.

stem: A patient has an acute sore throat. To decide whether antibiotics are appropriate, what is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Throat swab for culture before deciding, treating if positive
options.B: Prescribe penicillin V whenever the tonsils are visibly enlarged
options.C: Base the decision on whether symptoms have lasted over a week
options.D: Point-of-care CRP test, prescribing antibiotics if it is raised
options.E: Use FeverPAIN or Centor to estimate streptococcal likelihood

correct_answer: E. Use FeverPAIN or Centor to estimate streptococcal likelihood
why_correct: Most sore throats are viral and self-limiting; a scoring tool (Centor or FeverPAIN — features such as tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, fever and absence of cough) estimates the likelihood of streptococcal infection and guides whether antibiotics are warranted.
why_wrong: A. Routine throat swabs are not recommended; results are slow and do not distinguish carriage from infection. B. Tonsillar enlargement alone does not indicate bacterial infection; a scoring tool targets antibiotics. C. Duration alone does not predict streptococcal infection; validated scoring tools are used. D. CRP testing is not part of the recommended assessment of acute sore throat in UK primary care.
pearl: Antibiotics for a sore throat follow a Centor/FeverPAIN score — most sore throats are viral and need none.
thinking: A patient has an acute sore throat ↓ The use of a scoring tool (Centor/FeverPAIN) to risk-stratify — antibiotic decis
exam_trap: B, antibiotics for everyone — treating all sore throats seems to cover infection. But most are viral, and indiscriminate antibiotics drive resistance and side effects; a scoring tool targets antibiotics to those most likely to have streptococcal infection.
takeaway: Antibiotics for a sore throat follow a Centor/FeverPAIN score — most sore throats are viral and need none.

stem: A patient develops acute, severe, persistent vertigo lasting days, with nausea and vomiting, following a viral illness. There is NO hearing loss or tinnitus, and no other neurological signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute, sustained vertigo lasting days after a viral illness, with no hearing loss or tinnitus and no central signs, is vestibular neuronitis (inflammation of the vestibular nerve); it is managed supportively, with a short course of a vestibular sedative and vestibular rehabilitation.
why_wrong: B. Ménière's disease gives recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting hours with hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, whereas this is a single sustained attack lasting days without hearing symptoms. C. Posterior circulation stroke must be considered in acute sustained vertigo, but there are no other neurological signs here; a central cause would be suggested by focal signs, severe ataxia or a normal head impulse test (no corrective saccade). D. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief episodes lasting seconds triggered by head movement, not continuous vertigo lasting days. E. Labyrinthitis involves the inner ear and so causes hearing loss or tinnitus alongside the vertigo; their absence here points to the vestibular nerve alone.
pearl: Days of vertigo with no hearing loss after a viral illness is vestibular neuronitis — hearing loss points to labyrinthitis/Ménière's; focal signs point to a stroke.
thinking: Acute, severe vertigo lasting days with nausea and vomiting after a viral illness ↓ No hearing loss or tinnitus, so the cochlea is spared ↓ No other neurological signs, so a central cause is less likely ↓ Vestibular neuronitis
exam_trap: B, Ménière's disease — another peripheral cause of vertigo. But Ménière's gives episodic vertigo WITH hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, whereas the sustained vertigo WITHOUT hearing loss after a viral illness here is vestibular neuronitis.
takeaway: Days of vertigo with no hearing loss after a viral illness is vestibular neuronitis — hearing loss points to labyrinthitis/Ménière's; focal signs point to a stroke.

presentation: Head and Neck Cancer — Red-Flag Referral
stem: A 60-year-old smoker has had a hoarse voice for more than three weeks with no improvement, and now reports a persistent lump in the neck. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Oral antibiotics and review in two weeks
options.B: A further trial of voice rest and review in three months
options.C: Arrange a chest X-ray and refer if it is abnormal
options.D: Urgent suspected cancer referral to ENT

correct_answer: D. Urgent suspected cancer referral to ENT
why_correct: Persistent unexplained hoarseness lasting over three weeks, or an unexplained persistent neck lump, in an at-risk person (older smoker) warrants urgent suspected cancer pathway referral to exclude head and neck cancer.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of infection, and further delay is inappropriate for red-flag symptoms. B. Persistent hoarseness beyond three weeks with a neck lump in a smoker needs urgent referral, not further watchful waiting. C. A normal chest X-ray does not exclude laryngeal or other head and neck cancer; urgent ENT referral is needed. E. These red-flag symptoms need an urgent suspected cancer referral, not a routine one.
pearl: Persistent unexplained hoarseness or a neck lump warrants urgent suspected cancer pathway ENT referral — do not keep watching and waiting.
thinking: 60-year-old smoker with persistent hoarseness ↓ plus a persistent neck lump ↓ head and neck cancer red flags
exam_trap: B, a further trial of voice rest and review in three months — hoarseness often has benign causes, so watchful waiting is tempting. But persistent unexplained hoarseness beyond three weeks in a smoker is a red flag requiring urgent referral, not further delay.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained hoarseness or a neck lump warrants urgent suspected cancer pathway ENT referral — do not keep watching and waiting.

stem: A child with a recent middle-ear infection develops a fever and a tender, red, fluctuant swelling behind the ear, pushing the pinna forward and down. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.B: Acute mastoiditis — admit for IV antibiotics and ENT review
options.C: Persistent otitis media — oral co-amoxiclav with GP review in 48 hours
options.D: Infected sebaceous cyst — incision and drainage

correct_answer: B. Acute mastoiditis — admit for IV antibiotics and ENT review
why_correct: A red, tender, swelling behind the ear that displaces the pinna forward and down, following otitis media, is acute mastoiditis — a serious complication; it requires admission, intravenous antibiotics and urgent ENT assessment (with imaging/surgery if needed).
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa affects the ear canal and does not push the pinna forward with a fluctuant postauricular swelling. C. A fluctuant postauricular swelling displacing the pinna indicates mastoiditis, which needs admission and IV antibiotics. D. A sebaceous cyst would not follow otitis media with fever and displace the pinna. E. Lymphadenitis does not displace the pinna forward and down; this is mastoid involvement.
pearl: A red, tender swelling behind the ear pushing the pinna forward is mastoiditis — admit for IV antibiotics and ENT, not oral treatment at home.
thinking: Recent otitis media with fever ↓ Tender, red, fluctuant postauricular swelling ↓ Pinna pushed forward and down ↓ Acute mastoiditis — admit for IV antibiotics and ENT review
exam_trap: C, simple otitis media managed at home — mastoiditis follows otitis media, so it can be mistaken for ongoing ear infection. But the postauricular swelling with a protruding pinna marks spread to the mastoid; this needs admission and IV antibiotics, not home oral treatment.
takeaway: A red, tender swelling behind the ear pushing the pinna forward is mastoiditis — admit for IV antibiotics and ENT, not oral treatment at home.

stem: A patient has seasonal sneezing, an itchy and runny nose, nasal congestion and itchy, watery eyes. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Xylometazoline nasal spray used throughout the season
options.B: A course of oral amoxicillin for sinusitis
options.C: Ipratropium nasal spray as first-line treatment
options.E: Avoid allergens; nasal steroid and/or antihistamine

correct_answer: E. Avoid allergens; nasal steroid and/or antihistamine
why_correct: Seasonal sneezing, nasal itch/rhinorrhoea, congestion and itchy watery eyes is allergic rhinitis; management is allergen avoidance plus an intranasal corticosteroid (for persistent/moderate-severe symptoms) and/or a non-sedating antihistamine.
why_wrong: A. Topical decongestants cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) if used for more than about a week. B. Allergic rhinitis is not infective; antibiotics are inappropriate. C. Ipratropium only reduces rhinorrhoea and is not first-line for allergic rhinitis. D. Depot steroid injections carry systemic risks and are not recommended.
pearl: Allergic rhinitis is treated with allergen avoidance, intranasal steroids and/or non-sedating antihistamines — not antibiotics.
thinking: Seasonal sneezing, itchy runny nose and congestion ↓ Itchy, watery eyes ↓ Allergic rhinitis ↓ Avoid allergens; nasal steroid and/or antihistamine
exam_trap: B, a course of oral antibiotics — nasal symptoms can be mistaken for infection. But allergic rhinitis is not infective; antibiotics are inappropriate, and treatment is allergen avoidance with intranasal steroids and/or antihistamines.
takeaway: Allergic rhinitis is treated with allergen avoidance, intranasal steroids and/or non-sedating antihistamines — not antibiotics.

stem: A patient has facial pain/pressure, nasal congestion and discharge for five days following a cold. They are systemically well. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Supportive care without antibiotics, as it is usually viral
options.B: Oral amoxicillin for five days, as symptoms persist
options.C: CT sinuses to confirm before deciding on treatment
options.D: A five-day course of oral prednisolone for the pain
options.E: Routine ENT referral for nasal endoscopy and review

correct_answer: A. Supportive care without antibiotics, as it is usually viral
why_correct: Acute sinusitis is usually viral and self-limiting; for symptoms of 10 days or less, give no antibiotic and advise self-care (analgesia, antipyretics, fluids). If symptoms persist beyond 10 days without improvement, consider a high-dose nasal corticosteroid and a no-antibiotic or back-up antibiotic strategy; immediate antibiotics are for those systemically very unwell or at high risk of complications.
why_wrong: B. Symptoms of 10 days or less are usually viral; antibiotics are not recommended. C. Imaging is not needed for uncomplicated acute sinusitis. D. Oral steroids are not recommended for acute sinusitis. E. ENT referral is for recurrent, chronic or complicated sinusitis, not a five-day post-viral illness.
pearl: Acute sinusitis is usually viral and self-limiting — antibiotics only for severe or prolonged (>10 days) or worsening symptoms.
thinking: Facial pain, congestion and discharge for 5 days after a cold, systemically well ↓ Acute sinusitis of 10 days or less, usually viral ↓ Self-care without antibiotics
exam_trap: B, immediate antibiotics for everyone — sinus symptoms feel bacterial. But most acute sinusitis is viral and resolves without antibiotics; these are reserved for severe or prolonged (beyond ~10 days) or worsening illness.
takeaway: Acute sinusitis is usually viral and self-limiting — antibiotics only for severe or prolonged (>10 days) or worsening symptoms.

stem: An adult has gradual bilateral nasal obstruction with reduced sense of smell (anosmia) and a runny nose. Examination shows bilateral, pale, grey, painless swellings in the nasal cavity. They also have asthma. What is the diagnosis, and what would be a red flag?

options.A: Allergic rhinitis — recurrent nosebleeds would be the key red flag
options.B: Nasal polyps — a unilateral polyp is a red flag needing referral
options.C: Inverted papilloma — the bilateral swellings themselves are the red flag
options.D: Adenoidal hypertrophy — snoring would be a red flag
options.E: Nasal polyps — the coexisting asthma is a red flag for malignancy

correct_answer: B. Nasal polyps — a unilateral polyp is a red flag needing referral
why_correct: Bilateral, pale, painless nasal polyps causing obstruction and anosmia (often with asthma and sometimes aspirin sensitivity) are managed with intranasal corticosteroids; a UNILATERAL polyp in an adult, or any nasal polyp in a child, is a red flag warranting referral to exclude malignancy or (in children) cystic fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. Pale grey swellings in the nasal cavity are polyps, not the swollen turbinates of allergic rhinitis, and the key red flag is unilaterality. C. Bilateral pale smooth swellings are typical of benign polyps; it is unilateral disease that raises concern for inverted papilloma or malignancy. D. Adenoids lie in the postnasal space, not visible as pale swellings in the nasal cavity, and are uncommon in adults. E. Asthma (and aspirin sensitivity) is commonly associated with benign nasal polyps and is not a red flag; unilateral polyps are.
pearl: Bilateral nasal polyps cause obstruction and anosmia (linked to asthma/aspirin sensitivity) — a unilateral polyp needs referral to exclude malignancy.
thinking: Adult with gradual bilateral nasal obstruction, anosmia and rhinorrhoea, plus asthma ↓ Pale, grey, painless bilateral swellings in the nasal cavity = nasal polyps ↓ Bilateral polyps with asthma are benign; unilateral disease raises concern for malignancy ↓ Answer: nasal polyps, with a unilateral polyp as the red flag needing referral
exam_trap: E, nasal polyps with asthma as the red flag for malignancy — asthma is so often linked with polyps that it can seem significant. But asthma (and aspirin sensitivity) is associated with benign bilateral polyps; it is a UNILATERAL polyp that is the red flag needing referral to exclude malignancy.
takeaway: Bilateral nasal polyps cause obstruction and anosmia (linked to asthma/aspirin sensitivity) — a unilateral polyp needs referral to exclude malignancy.

stem: A 40-year-old swimmer has an itchy, painful, discharging ear. The canal is red and swollen with debris, but the tympanic membrane appears intact. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.D: Antibiotic–steroid ear drops and aural toilet
options.E: Oral decongestant and keep the ear dry

correct_answer: D. Antibiotic–steroid ear drops and aural toilet
why_correct: Acute otitis externa is treated with topical antibiotic/steroid ear drops and cleaning of the canal (aural toilet); systemic antibiotics are reserved for spreading infection or immunocompromise.
why_wrong: A. Systemic steroids are not used for otitis externa. B. Oral antibiotics are reserved for spreading cellulitis or immunocompromise; first-line treatment is topical. C. Antifungal drops are for fungal otitis externa; this presentation is treated first with antibiotic–steroid drops. E. Keeping the ear dry helps, but decongestants do not treat canal inflammation.
pearl: Otitis externa is treated with topical drops and aural toilet — save oral antibiotics for spread beyond the canal.
thinking: Swimmer + itchy, painful, discharging ear + red swollen canal + intact drum ↓ Acute otitis externa confined to the canal ↓ Topical antibiotic–steroid drops + aural toilet
exam_trap: B, oral flucloxacillin — the reflex 'antibiotic for an ear infection'. But otitis externa is a canal problem treated topically; oral antibiotics are unnecessary unless the infection spreads beyond the canal.
takeaway: Otitis externa is treated with topical drops and aural toilet — save oral antibiotics for spread beyond the canal.

presentation: Palliative Pain — Opioid Conversion and Breakthrough
stem: A patient with cancer pain is well controlled on a regular oral morphine total of 60 mg per 24 hours. What is the appropriate dose for a breakthrough (as-required) pain dose?

options.A: The same as the total 24-hour dose (60 mg)
options.B: Between one-tenth and one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (6–10 mg)
options.C: Half of the total 24-hour dose (30 mg) each time
options.D: A fixed 5 mg dose regardless of the background dose
options.E: No breakthrough dose while the pain is well controlled

correct_answer: B. Between one-tenth and one-sixth of the 24-hour dose (6–10 mg)
why_correct: The BNF states that the standard rescue dose of morphine for breakthrough pain is usually one-tenth to one-sixth of the regular 24-hour dose, repeated every 2–4 hours as required. For 60 mg per 24 hours that is 6–10 mg of immediate-release oral morphine, reviewed regularly.
why_wrong: A. The same as the total 24-hour dose (60 mg) — a single rescue dose this size would be a dangerous overdose. C. Half of the total 24-hour dose (30 mg) each time — far above the BNF range of one-tenth to one-sixth, risking opioid toxicity. D. A fixed 5 mg dose regardless of the background dose — the rescue dose should be proportional to the regular 24-hour dose; 5 mg is below the 6–10 mg range here. E. No breakthrough dose while the pain is well controlled — anyone on regular opioids for cancer pain should have an as-required rescue dose prescribed for breakthrough pain.
pearl: The breakthrough opioid dose is one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour total — 60 mg/day gives a 6–10 mg rescue dose.
thinking: Regular oral morphine 60 mg per 24 hours ↓ breakthrough dose = one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour total ↓ 6–10 mg immediate-release oral morphine
exam_trap: C, half the 24-hour dose — a larger rescue dose might seem to ensure relief. But the standard breakthrough dose is one-tenth to one-sixth of the daily total; half would risk toxicity.
takeaway: The breakthrough opioid dose is one-tenth to one-sixth of the 24-hour total — 60 mg/day gives a 6–10 mg rescue dose.

presentation: Choosing an Antiemetic in Palliative Care
stem: A palliative patient has nausea. What is the most appropriate principle for selecting an antiemetic?

options.A: Avoid antiemetics and use relaxation techniques and reassurance instead
options.B: Use cyclizine as the default first-line drug, adding a second agent if it fails
options.C: Match the antiemetic to the cause (e.g. metoclopramide for gastric stasis)
options.D: Start levomepromazine in a syringe driver as the first-line choice
options.E: Use a benzodiazepine for sedation as the first-line antiemetic approach

correct_answer: C. Match the antiemetic to the cause (e.g. metoclopramide for gastric stasis)
why_correct: Antiemetic choice in palliative care is guided by the likely mechanism: prokinetics (metoclopramide) for gastric stasis, a centrally acting agent (haloperidol) for chemical/metabolic/opioid-related nausea, and cyclizine for raised intracranial pressure or vestibular causes.
why_wrong: A. Nausea in palliative care is distressing and should be treated pharmacologically as well as supportively. B. A single default drug ignores the mechanism and fails for nausea driven by a different pathway. D. Levomepromazine is a broad-spectrum second-line agent, not first-line for every cause. E. Sedation is not an antiemetic strategy and is not first-line.
pearl: In palliative care, pick the antiemetic by the mechanism of the nausea — there is no universal antiemetic.
thinking: A palliative patient has nausea ↓ Identify the likely cause/mechanism of the nausea ↓ Choose the antiemetic that targets that mechanism
exam_trap: B, use the same single antiemetic for all causes — one default drug seems simpler. But effectiveness depends on matching the drug to the underlying mechanism; a single agent will fail for nausea driven by a different pathway.
takeaway: In palliative care, pick the antiemetic by the mechanism of the nausea — there is no universal antiemetic.

stem: A 55-year-old man has a 3-day history of a painful, swollen, warm left calf after a long period of immobility. The two-level DVT Wells score is 3 (DVT likely). What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Class 2 compression stockings and repeat clinical review in 48 hours
options.B: D-dimer test, with leg ultrasound arranged only if the D-dimer is raised
options.C: Start warfarin with a target INR of 2.5 and treat for six months without imaging
options.D: Proximal leg vein ultrasound (with interim anticoagulation if delayed)
options.E: Advise mobilisation and analgesia, with review in one week if no better

correct_answer: D. Proximal leg vein ultrasound (with interim anticoagulation if delayed)
why_correct: When DVT is 'likely' on the two-level Wells score (2 points or more), NICE recommends a proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours if possible, followed by a D-dimer if the scan is negative. If the scan result cannot be obtained within 4 hours, take a D-dimer, give interim therapeutic anticoagulation and arrange the scan within 24 hours. A D-dimer-first pathway is used only when DVT is 'unlikely'.
why_wrong: A. Compression does not diagnose or treat a likely DVT. B. A D-dimer-first pathway is used when DVT is 'unlikely'; with a Wells score of 3, ultrasound is needed. C. Treatment without imaging confirmation is inappropriate; the diagnosis must be confirmed. E. Delaying assessment of a likely DVT risks propagation and pulmonary embolism.
pearl: When DVT is 'likely' on Wells, scan the vein rather than D-dimer — the score decides whether the blood test can exclude.
thinking: Painful, swollen, warm calf after a long period of immobility ↓ Two-level Wells score of 3 = DVT likely ↓ In the 'likely' group a D-dimer cannot safely exclude DVT, so imaging comes first ↓ Answer: proximal leg vein ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if the scan is delayed
exam_trap: B, D-dimer — the standard first test when DVT is 'unlikely', so it feels routine. But with a 'DVT likely' Wells score, a D-dimer cannot safely exclude it; ultrasound is required.
takeaway: When DVT is 'likely' on Wells, scan the vein rather than D-dimer — the score decides whether the blood test can exclude.

stem: A patient has visible, tortuous, dilated superficial leg veins with aching and mild ankle swelling after standing. There are no skin changes, bleeding or ulceration. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Referral to a vascular service for assessment and treatment
options.B: Urgent open surgery to strip all visible varicose veins
options.C: Immediate therapeutic anticoagulation for venous thrombosis
options.D: Compression hosiery as treatment, without vascular referral
options.E: Reassurance only, as varicose veins are purely cosmetic

correct_answer: A. Referral to a vascular service for assessment and treatment
why_correct: Varicose veins with troublesome symptoms (aching, swelling, heaviness, discomfort, itching) are symptomatic. NICE CG168 recommends referral to a vascular service for duplex ultrasound and, if truncal reflux is confirmed, endothermal ablation (then ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy, then surgery). Compression hosiery is not offered as treatment unless interventional treatment is unsuitable.
why_wrong: B. Surgery is not urgent, and open surgery is third-line after endothermal ablation and foam sclerotherapy. C. There is no thrombosis to anticoagulate. D. NICE advises against compression hosiery as treatment unless interventional treatment is unsuitable; symptomatic varicose veins should be referred. E. Symptomatic varicose veins merit information, advice and referral, not dismissal as cosmetic.
pearl: Symptomatic varicose veins (aching, swelling, heaviness) are referred to a vascular service; compression hosiery is only for those unsuitable for intervention.
thinking: Visible varicose veins + aching and ankle swelling after standing ↓ Troublesome symptoms = symptomatic varicose veins (NICE CG168) ↓ Refer to vascular service for duplex ultrasound and treatment ↓ Compression hosiery only if intervention unsuitable
exam_trap: D, compression hosiery — stockings feel like the safe first step. But NICE CG168 advises against offering compression hosiery to treat varicose veins unless interventional treatment is unsuitable; symptomatic varicose veins are referred to a vascular service.
takeaway: Symptomatic varicose veins (aching, swelling, heaviness) are referred to a vascular service; compression hosiery is only for those unsuitable for intervention.

presentation: Best Interests in a Patient Lacking Capacity
stem: An 85-year-old man with advanced dementia has painful urinary retention and is at risk of acute kidney injury. He says 'no' to a catheter. On assessment he cannot understand or retain information about the procedure or weigh it up. He has no advance decision and no lasting power of attorney. He is calm. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Sedate him to allow the procedure
options.B: Do not catheterise, because he has refused
options.C: Apply to the Court of Protection
options.D: Catheterise him as a best-interests decision
options.E: Wait until a family member can consent on his behalf

correct_answer: D. Catheterise him as a best-interests decision
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a patient who cannot understand, retain or weigh the relevant information lacks capacity for that decision. With no advance decision or LPA, the treating clinician decides in his best interests, consulting those close to him, and may give necessary treatment by the least restrictive means.
why_wrong: A. He is calm and not resisting; sedation is not necessary and is not the least restrictive option (any restraint must be necessary and proportionate under MCA s6). B. A refusal only binds if the person has capacity; he fails the understand/retain/weigh test for this decision, so his 'no' is not a valid refusal, though his wishes are considered in best interests. C. Court of Protection applications are for genuine disputes or particular serious decisions, not routine best-interests treatment like catheterisation. E. Family cannot consent for an adult without an LPA (health and welfare) or deputyship; they should be consulted to inform best interests, but delay risks pain and AKI.
pearl: A refusal only counts if the patient has capacity to make it — assess capacity first, then act in best interests by the least restrictive route.
thinking: Advanced dementia, painful retention, says 'no' ↓ fails the understand/retain/weigh test for this specific decision ↓ no ADRT or LPA ↓ D: catheterise in best interests, least restrictive option
exam_trap: B, respecting the refusal — autonomy is rightly the default, so 'he said no' feels like the safe, respectful answer. But a valid refusal requires capacity, and a refusal made without the ability to weigh the information does not bind.
takeaway: A refusal only counts if the patient has capacity to make it — assess capacity first, then act in best interests by the least restrictive route.

stem: A 15-year-old girl requests contraception and does not want her parents informed. She understands the advice and its implications and is judged to have sufficient maturity. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Refer to children's social care before prescribing, given her age
options.B: Defer prescribing until a parent or guardian gives consent
options.C: Prescribe, but inform her parents as she is under 16
options.D: Advise her to return with a parent and give condom advice meanwhile
options.E: Provide contraception, encouraging her to involve a parent

correct_answer: E. Provide contraception, encouraging her to involve a parent
why_correct: A young person under 16 who is Gillick competent (understands the advice and its implications) can consent to contraception confidentially; the doctor still encourages parental involvement but does not require it. (Note: Gillick competence is UK-wide common law; specific guidance on prescribing contraception to under-16s varies slightly across the four nations.)
why_wrong: A. Age alone is not a safeguarding concern; referral is needed only if there are specific concerns. B. A Gillick-competent young person can consent without parental involvement. C. Informing her parents against her wishes breaches confidentiality without justification. D. Insisting on parental attendance denies a competent young person care she can consent to.
pearl: A Gillick-competent minor can consent confidentially to contraception — encourage parental involvement, but it is not required.
thinking: 15-year-old requests contraception, wants confidentiality ↓ assessed as Gillick/Fraser competent ↓ E: provide contraception, encourage parental involvement
exam_trap: B, refuse without parental consent — under-16 status makes parental consent feel necessary. But Gillick competence allows a mature minor to consent confidentially to contraception; refusing would breach her rights.
takeaway: A Gillick-competent minor can consent confidentially to contraception — encourage parental involvement, but it is not required.

stem: A man with epilepsy that is poorly controlled continues to drive against medical advice and refuses to notify the DVLA. You have advised him repeatedly. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Inform his employer that he should not drive for work
options.B: Maintain confidentiality and document the advice given in his notes
options.C: Report him to the police so his driving licence can be revoked
options.D: Inform the DVLA, having told the patient you intend to do so
options.E: Ask his wife to persuade him to stop driving

correct_answer: D. Inform the DVLA, having told the patient you intend to do so
why_correct: When a patient who poses a risk to others continues to drive against advice and will not notify the DVLA, the doctor may break confidentiality and inform the DVLA, after telling the patient of that intention — the public-safety duty outweighs confidentiality here.
why_wrong: A. Disclosure to the employer is not the appropriate route; the DVLA is the licensing authority. B. Confidentiality is not absolute; ongoing risk to the public justifies disclosure to the DVLA. C. The police do not revoke licences for medical reasons; the DVLA does. E. Disclosing to a relative breaches confidentiality and does not address the risk.
pearl: Confidentiality yields to public safety — when a dangerous driver will not self-report, inform the DVLA, having told him you will.
thinking: Poorly controlled epilepsy, still driving, refuses to tell DVLA despite repeated advice ↓ ongoing risk to others ↓ D: tell him you will inform the DVLA, then do so
exam_trap: B, maintain confidentiality — it is a core duty, so it feels like the safe ethical default. But confidentiality is not absolute; when a patient endangers others and will not act, the doctor must inform the DVLA.
takeaway: Confidentiality yields to public safety — when a dangerous driver will not self-report, inform the DVLA, having told him you will.

stem: A patient requests a chaperone of a particular sex for an intimate examination, but the only person immediately available does not meet that preference. The examination is not urgent. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Proceed with the available chaperone, explaining they are fully trained
options.B: Offer to find a suitable chaperone or rearrange the examination
options.C: Proceed without a chaperone, as the patient is competent to consent
options.D: Explain a chaperone is not a legal requirement and continue the examination
options.E: Decline to examine and refer the patient to another clinician

correct_answer: B. Offer to find a suitable chaperone or rearrange the examination
why_correct: A chaperone should be offered for intimate examinations and the patient's preferences respected; if a suitable chaperone is not available and the examination is not urgent, it should be rescheduled rather than proceeding against the patient's wishes.
why_wrong: A. Training does not override the patient's reasonable preference for a non-urgent intimate examination. C. Proceeding without the chaperone the patient requested ignores their wishes. D. Whether or not it is a legal requirement, overriding the patient's preference is inappropriate. E. Refusing care and referring on is unnecessary when a suitable chaperone or a new appointment can be arranged.
pearl: Offer a chaperone and respect the patient's reasonable preference — for a non-urgent intimate examination, reschedule rather than override it.
thinking: Patient requests a chaperone of a particular sex ↓ examination is non-urgent and the preference is reasonable ↓ B: find a suitable chaperone or rebook
exam_trap: A, proceed with whoever is available — a chaperone is present, so it seems adequate. But the patient's reasonable preference (including the chaperone's sex) should be respected; for a non-urgent examination, rescheduling is appropriate rather than overriding that preference.
takeaway: Offer a chaperone and respect the patient's reasonable preference — for a non-urgent intimate examination, reschedule rather than override it.

stem: A patient refuses a recommended treatment. To decide whether they can make this decision for themselves, what must they be able to do for capacity to be present (for this specific decision)?

options.A: Achieve a score of 24 or more out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination
options.B: Agree with the treatment option that has been recommended by the clinical team
options.C: Understand, retain and weigh the information, and communicate a decision
options.D: Have no diagnosis of a mental disorder or any form of cognitive impairment
options.E: Understand the information and repeat it back accurately to the clinician

correct_answer: C. Understand, retain and weigh the information, and communicate a decision
why_correct: Capacity is decision-specific and present if the person can understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it in making the decision, and communicate that decision; a capacitous patient may refuse treatment even if others disagree with the choice.
why_wrong: A. Capacity is decision-specific and not determined by a cognitive test threshold. B. A capacitous person may make an unwise decision and refuse treatment. D. A diagnosis does not in itself remove capacity. E. Understanding and repeating information is insufficient; the person must also retain, weigh it and communicate a decision.
pearl: Capacity means understand, retain, weigh and communicate — a person with capacity can refuse treatment, even unwisely.
thinking: A patient refuses a recommended treatment ↓ The four functional abilities (understand, retain, weigh, communicate) for THIS
exam_trap: B, simply agree with the doctor — equating capacity with compliance is a common error. But a person with capacity is entitled to make an 'unwise' decision and refuse treatment; capacity depends on the process of decision-making, not on agreeing with the clinician.
takeaway: Capacity means understand, retain, weigh and communicate — a person with capacity can refuse treatment, even unwisely.

stem: A patient who previously had capacity made a valid, applicable written advance decision refusing a specific treatment. They now lack capacity, and that treatment is being considered. Their family wants the treatment given. What is the correct course of action?

options.A: Respect the valid advance decision and withhold the refused treatment
options.B: Give the treatment because the family requests it
options.C: Give the treatment in the patient's 'best interests' regardless of the advance decision
options.D: Ask a court for permission to override the document
options.E: Ignore the document because the patient now lacks capacity

correct_answer: A. Respect the valid advance decision and withhold the refused treatment
why_correct: A valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment, made when the person had capacity, is legally binding once they lose capacity; it must be respected, and family members cannot override it.
why_wrong: B. The family's wishes do not override a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment; under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 it is legally binding, and relatives have no power to consent on the patient's behalf unless they hold an LPA made later that covers this treatment. C. Best-interests decisions apply only where there is no valid applicable advance decision; one that is valid and applicable takes precedence for the treatment it covers. D. Applying to the Court of Protection is appropriate only where there is genuine doubt about whether the advance decision is valid or applicable; here it is stated to be both, so there is nothing to override. E. Loss of capacity is exactly when an advance decision takes effect, so ignoring it because the patient now lacks capacity defeats its purpose.
pearl: A valid advance decision to refuse treatment, made with capacity, is binding once capacity is lost — family cannot override it.
thinking: Patient made a written advance decision refusing a specific treatment while they had capacity ↓ The decision is valid and applicable, and the patient now lacks capacity ↓ Under the Mental Capacity Act it is binding and neither family wishes nor a best-interests judgement can override it ↓ Respect the advance decision and withhold the refused treatment
exam_trap: C, give it in 'best interests' regardless — the best-interests framework applies when someone lacks capacity, so it seems to apply here. But a valid applicable advance decision takes precedence over a best-interests judgement for the treatment it covers; it cannot be overridden on best-interests grounds.
takeaway: A valid advance decision to refuse treatment, made with capacity, is binding once capacity is lost — family cannot override it.

stem: A patient suffers harm because of a mistake in their care. What does the professional and statutory duty of candour require?

options.A: Inform the patient once the incident investigation has been completed
options.B: Disclose the error if the patient or family asks what happened
options.C: Explain what happened but avoid apologising, as it may imply liability
options.D: Report it via the incident system and inform the patient's GP
options.E: Tell the patient what happened, apologise and explain the next steps

correct_answer: E. Tell the patient what happened, apologise and explain the next steps
why_correct: The duty of candour requires healthcare professionals (and organisations) to be open and honest when something goes wrong and a patient is harmed: informing them promptly, offering an apology, and explaining what happened and what will be done.
why_wrong: A. Candour requires prompt disclosure, not waiting for the investigation to finish. B. The duty is proactive; disclosure should not depend on the patient asking. C. An apology is required and is not an admission of legal liability. D. Incident reporting is necessary but does not replace telling the patient.
pearl: When care harms a patient, the duty of candour means tell them promptly, apologise and explain — concealment is not an option.
thinking: A patient suffers harm because of a mistake in their care ↓ The occurrence of HARM from care — that trigger creates a duty to be open, apolo
exam_trap: C, avoid apologising for fear of liability — clinicians may worry an apology admits fault. But an apology is an expression of regret, not an admission of legal liability, and openness is required; withholding it breaches the duty of candour.
takeaway: When care harms a patient, the duty of candour means tell them promptly, apologise and explain — concealment is not an option.

stem: In a trial, a drug reduces the rate of an event from 20% to 10% over a year. What is the number needed to treat (NNT) for one year?
why_correct: The absolute risk reduction is 20% − 10% = 10% (0.1); the NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction, so 1/0.1 = 10 patients treated for one year to prevent one event.
why_wrong: B. 2 comes from dividing the control event rate by the treated event rate (20/10), which is the inverse of the relative risk (0.5), not the NNT; the NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (1/0.1 = 10). C. 5 is the reciprocal of the control event rate (1/0.2), not of the absolute risk reduction. D. 20 is simply the control event rate expressed as a percentage, not a number of patients needed to treat. E. 100 would correspond to an absolute risk reduction of only 1%, ten times smaller than the 10% reduction in this trial.
pearl: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction — here 1/0.1 = 10; do not confuse it with the ratio of the event rates.
thinking: Event rate falls from 20% to 10% over one year ↓ Absolute risk reduction = 20% − 10% = 10%, or 0.1 ↓ NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction = 1 ÷ 0.1 ↓ The NNT is 10
exam_trap: B, 2 — dividing the two percentages (20/10) gives 2, a tempting but wrong shortcut. But the NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction (1/0.1 = 10), not the ratio of the two event rates.
takeaway: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction — here 1/0.1 = 10; do not confuse it with the ratio of the event rates.

stem: In a case-control study of diet and a disease, people WITH the disease are more likely to remember and report past dietary exposures than the controls, because their illness has made them reflect on possible causes. What type of error does this introduce?
why_correct: When cases systematically recall or report exposures differently from controls, the resulting systematic error is recall bias — a particular risk in retrospective case-control studies.
why_wrong: A. Confounding is distortion by a third variable associated with both the exposure and the outcome; here the error comes from cases remembering exposures differently from controls, which is recall bias. C. Random error is non-systematic variation due to chance, which would not consistently push cases towards reporting more exposure than controls. D. Lead-time bias is an apparent survival gain from earlier diagnosis in screening studies and has nothing to do with remembering past exposures. E. Selection at randomisation relates to how participants are allocated in a trial; a case-control study does not randomise, and the error here arises in recall, not recruitment.
pearl: Differential memory of exposure between cases and controls is recall bias — a hazard of retrospective studies.
thinking: Case-control study asking about past dietary exposures ↓ Cases remember and report exposures more fully than controls because of their illness ↓ A systematic difference in recall between groups distorts the association ↓ Recall bias
exam_trap: A, confounding — another systematic distortion, so a tempting choice. But confounding is distortion by a third variable linked to both exposure and outcome, whereas the DIFFERENTIAL accuracy of memory between cases and controls here is recall bias.
takeaway: Differential memory of exposure between cases and controls is recall bias — a hazard of retrospective studies.

stem: A study finds that coffee drinkers have more lung cancer. However, coffee drinkers in the study also smoke far more than non-coffee-drinkers, and smoking causes lung cancer. What does smoking represent in this association?
why_correct: Smoking here is a confounder: a factor associated with both the exposure (coffee) and the outcome (lung cancer) that distorts the apparent association; confounding is addressed by design (randomisation, matching, restriction) or analysis (stratification, adjustment).
why_wrong: B. Recall bias concerns differential accuracy of reported information between groups, whereas smoking is a third factor linked to both coffee drinking and lung cancer. C. A placebo effect is a response to receiving an inactive treatment and has no role in an observational association between coffee and lung cancer. D. Smoking is not the exposure being studied (coffee is); it is an extraneous factor that distorts the apparent effect of coffee. E. Incidence is the rate of new cases in a population over time, a measure of frequency rather than an explanation for a distorted association.
pearl: A variable associated with both exposure and outcome is a confounder — control it by randomisation or statistical adjustment.
thinking: Coffee drinkers appear to have more lung cancer ↓ Coffee drinkers also smoke more, so smoking is associated with the exposure ↓ Smoking independently causes lung cancer, so it is associated with the outcome ↓ Smoking is a confounder
exam_trap: B, recall bias — another threat to validity. But recall bias concerns differential reporting of information, whereas a third factor (smoking) linked to BOTH the exposure and the outcome is, by definition, a confounder.
takeaway: A variable associated with both exposure and outcome is a confounder — control it by randomisation or statistical adjustment.

stem: A public health team reports the number of NEW cases of a condition diagnosed in a population over the course of one year. Which measure does this describe?
why_correct: Incidence is the number of NEW cases arising in a defined population over a specified period; prevalence is the total number of existing cases (new and pre-existing) at a point or over a period.
why_wrong: A. Mortality rate counts deaths in a population over a period, not new diagnoses. B. Prevalence counts all existing cases (new and pre-existing) at a point or over a period, whereas only new cases over a year are being counted here. D. Relative risk compares the risk of an outcome in an exposed group with that in an unexposed group, so it needs two groups rather than a single count of new cases. E. Positive predictive value is the proportion of people with a positive test who truly have the disease, a test-performance measure rather than a measure of disease frequency.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases over time; prevalence counts all existing cases — new arising vs total present.
thinking: The team counts cases newly diagnosed in a defined population ↓ The count covers a specified time period of one year ↓ Only new cases are included, not pre-existing ones ↓ This is incidence
exam_trap: B, prevalence — both describe how common a condition is, so they are easily confused. But prevalence counts ALL existing cases, whereas the count of NEW cases over a time period here is incidence.
takeaway: Incidence counts new cases over time; prevalence counts all existing cases — new arising vs total present.

stem: A drug reduces the risk of an outcome from 2% to 1%. A headline states it 'halves the risk' (a 50% relative risk reduction). How is this benefit best understood for an individual patient?

options.A: The 50% relative risk reduction best guides individual benefit
options.B: Absolute risk reduction is 1% (NNT 100), which is more informative
options.C: The drug prevents the outcome in half of the patients who take it
options.D: The number needed to treat is 2, as the risk is halved
options.E: The absolute risk reduction is 50%, as the risk falls by half

correct_answer: B. Absolute risk reduction is 1% (NNT 100), which is more informative
why_correct: A large relative risk reduction can correspond to a small absolute benefit when baseline risk is low: here the absolute risk reduction is 1% and the number needed to treat is 100 (NNT = 1/ARR), which conveys the real-world benefit better than the relative figure.
why_wrong: A. The relative figure overstates benefit when baseline risk is low. C. Only 1 in 100 treated patients avoids the outcome, not half. D. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.01 = 100, not 2. E. The absolute reduction is 2% − 1% = 1%; 50% is the relative reduction.
pearl: Judge benefit by the absolute risk reduction and NNT (1/ARR), not the headline relative reduction — a big relative cut can be a tiny absolute one.
thinking: A drug reduces the risk of an outcome from 2% to 1% ↓ The reliance on ABSOLUTE risk reduction (and NNT) rather than the relative figur
exam_trap: A, the 50% relative figure reflects the true individual benefit — relative reductions sound impressive and are often quoted. But relative risk reduction ignores baseline risk; the absolute risk reduction (and NNT) is what reflects the benefit an individual can expect.
takeaway: Judge benefit by the absolute risk reduction and NNT (1/ARR), not the headline relative reduction — a big relative cut can be a tiny absolute one.

stem: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.85 for an outcome with a treatment, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.70 to 1.05. How should this result be interpreted?

options.A: Statistically significant, as the point estimate of 0.85 lies below 1
options.B: Not statistically significant, as the confidence interval crosses 1
options.C: Statistically significant harm, as the upper limit of 1.05 exceeds 1
options.D: Significant benefit, as most of the confidence interval lies below 1
options.E: Significant at the 5% level, as the interval excludes 0

correct_answer: B. Not statistically significant, as the confidence interval crosses 1
why_correct: For a ratio measure (relative risk, odds ratio, hazard ratio), a 95% confidence interval that crosses 1 includes the possibility of no effect, so the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level; a narrower interval indicates greater precision.
why_wrong: A. Significance depends on the confidence interval, not the point estimate alone. C. An interval spanning 1 shows neither significant benefit nor harm. D. Where most of the interval lies does not matter; it crosses 1, so the result is not significant. E. For ratio measures the null value is 1, not 0.
pearl: A 95% CI for a ratio that crosses 1 (or a difference that crosses 0) is not statistically significant — the point estimate alone is not enough.
thinking: RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.70–1.05 ↓ For a ratio, the no-effect value is 1 ↓ The interval crosses 1, so the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level
exam_trap: A, the point estimate of 0.85 proves benefit — the central value suggests a reduction, so it looks beneficial. But because the confidence interval crosses 1, the true effect could be null or even harmful; the result is not statistically significant.
takeaway: A 95% CI for a ratio that crosses 1 (or a difference that crosses 0) is not statistically significant — the point estimate alone is not enough.

stem: When appraising evidence to answer a question about treatment effectiveness, which source generally provides the strongest evidence?

options.A: Expert opinion from a national specialist panel
options.C: A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
options.D: A single well-conducted randomised controlled trial
options.E: A systematic review of observational cohort studies

correct_answer: C. A systematic review of randomised controlled trials
why_correct: In the hierarchy of evidence for treatment effectiveness, a systematic review or meta-analysis of well-conducted randomised controlled trials sits at the top, followed by individual RCTs, then observational studies, with case reports and expert opinion at the bottom.
why_wrong: A. Expert opinion is the lowest level of evidence. B. Cohort studies are observational and prone to confounding. D. A single RCT ranks below a systematic review of several RCTs. E. Pooling observational studies does not remove their confounding; it ranks below a review of RCTs.
pearl: A systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs is the strongest evidence for treatment effect; expert opinion is the weakest.
thinking: The question is about treatment effectiveness ↓ RCTs minimise confounding through randomisation ↓ Pooling several RCTs in a systematic review gives a more precise, less biased estimate than any single study ↓ Answer: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials
exam_trap: A, expert opinion — an authority's view can feel persuasive. But expert opinion is near the bottom of the evidence hierarchy; a systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs provides the strongest evidence for effectiveness.
takeaway: A systematic review/meta-analysis of RCTs is the strongest evidence for treatment effect; expert opinion is the weakest.

stem: In a randomised controlled trial, some participants in the treatment group did not take the drug and some crossed over. To analyse the results without undermining randomisation, which approach should be used?

options.A: As-treated analysis, by the treatment actually received
options.B: Per-protocol analysis of those who completed the assigned treatment
options.C: Exclude non-adherent participants and analyse the remaining patients
options.D: Intention-to-treat analysis, by group of original randomisation
options.E: Complete-case analysis of those with full follow-up data

correct_answer: D. Intention-to-treat analysis, by group of original randomisation
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their originally randomised groups regardless of adherence or crossover; this preserves the benefits of randomisation (balanced confounders) and avoids overestimating treatment effect, as a per-protocol analysis can.
why_wrong: A. Analysing by treatment received breaks randomisation and reintroduces confounding. B. Per-protocol analysis excludes non-adherent participants, undermining randomisation and tending to overestimate benefit. C. Excluding non-adherent participants biases the comparison. E. Restricting to complete cases introduces attrition bias and breaks randomisation.
pearl: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone as randomised — it preserves randomisation and avoids overestimating benefit.
thinking: Some participants did not take the drug and some crossed over ↓ Analysing by treatment received, or excluding non-adherers, breaks the balance created by randomisation ↓ Keeping everyone in the group to which they were randomised preserves it ↓ Answer: intention-to-treat analysis
exam_trap: B, per-protocol analysis only — analysing just the adherent completers seems to test the drug 'fairly'. But excluding non-adherers breaks randomisation and can bias the result (usually overestimating benefit); intention-to-treat preserves randomisation.
takeaway: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone as randomised — it preserves randomisation and avoids overestimating benefit.

stem: A study reports a difference between two treatments with a p-value of 0.01. What does this p-value mean?

options.A: There is a 99% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
options.B: There is a 1% probability that the null hypothesis is true
options.C: The difference is large enough to be clinically important
options.D: There is a 1% probability of a result this extreme if the null were true
options.E: There is a 1% probability the result would not be replicated in a new study

correct_answer: D. There is a 1% probability of a result this extreme if the null were true
why_correct: A p-value is the probability of obtaining the observed result (or one more extreme) if the null hypothesis were true; p<0.05 is conventionally called statistically significant. It does not measure effect size, clinical importance, or the probability that a hypothesis is true.
why_wrong: A. A p-value does not give the probability that any hypothesis is true. B. The p-value is calculated assuming the null is true; it is not the probability that the null is true. C. A p-value says nothing about effect size or clinical importance. E. A p-value does not measure the probability of replication.
pearl: A p-value indicates statistical significance (probability of the data if the null were true) — not the size or importance of an effect.
thinking: A study reports a difference between two treatments with a p-value of ↓ The p-value as the probability of the data UNDER the null hypothesis — not a mea
exam_trap: C, the effect is large and clinically important — a small p-value feels impressive. But the p-value reflects statistical significance, not the magnitude or clinical importance of the effect; a tiny, unimportant effect can be highly significant in a large study.
takeaway: A p-value indicates statistical significance (probability of the data if the null were true) — not the size or importance of an effect.

stem: In a study, the way participants were recruited means the sample systematically differs from the population it is meant to represent (for example, only the healthiest volunteers were enrolled). What type of error is this?
why_correct: A systematic error arising from how participants are selected into a study (or into its groups), making the sample unrepresentative, is selection bias; it threatens the validity and generalisability of results.
why_wrong: A. Recall bias arises from differential accuracy of remembered information between groups, not from how participants are recruited. C. Confounding is distortion by a third variable associated with both exposure and outcome, not an unrepresentative sample created by the recruitment process. D. Random error is non-systematic variation due to chance, whereas enrolling only the healthiest volunteers is a systematic error. E. Publication bias arises when positive studies are more likely to be published, which affects the literature and meta-analyses rather than recruitment into a single study.
pearl: Systematic error from how participants are selected into a study is selection bias.
thinking: Recruitment produces a sample that differs systematically from the target population ↓ Only the healthiest volunteers were enrolled ↓ The error arises from who gets into the study, not from measurement or chance ↓ Selection bias
exam_trap: A, recall bias — both are systematic errors. But recall bias concerns differential accuracy of remembered information, whereas an error arising from HOW participants are selected is selection bias.
takeaway: Systematic error from how participants are selected into a study is selection bias.

stem: Researchers conduct a case-control study. Which measure of association is appropriate, and what is its relationship to relative risk?

options.A: The relative risk, calculated directly from the exposure proportions
options.B: The odds ratio, which approximates relative risk if the outcome is rare
options.C: The incidence rate ratio, calculated from person-time at risk
options.D: The hazard ratio, which equals the odds ratio with full follow-up
options.E: The attributable risk, which equals relative risk for common outcomes

correct_answer: B. The odds ratio, which approximates relative risk if the outcome is rare
why_correct: Case-control studies report the odds ratio (relative risk cannot be calculated directly because the underlying population at risk is not sampled); the odds ratio approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare, but overstates it when the outcome is common.
why_wrong: A. Relative risk cannot be calculated directly because the population at risk is not sampled. C. Person-time is not available in a case-control design. D. Hazard ratios come from time-to-event (cohort/trial) data and do not equal the odds ratio. E. Attributable risk needs incidence data and does not equal relative risk.
pearl: Case-control studies give odds ratios, not relative risk — the OR approximates RR only when the outcome is rare.
thinking: Researchers conduct a case-control study ↓ The study being CASE-CONTROL — that design yields the odds ratio (not a directly
exam_trap: A, the relative risk calculated directly — relative risk is intuitive, so it is the natural choice. But case-control studies start from outcome status and cannot yield relative risk directly; the appropriate measure is the odds ratio.
takeaway: Case-control studies give odds ratios, not relative risk — the OR approximates RR only when the outcome is rare.

stem: An observational study finds a strong statistical association between an exposure and a disease. Before concluding that the exposure causes the disease, what must be considered?

options.A: Whether the p-value is below 0.05, which establishes a causal link
options.B: The strength of association, as a strong association establishes cause
options.C: The sample size, as large studies exclude confounding and bias
options.D: The size of the association, regardless of which came first: exposure or disease
options.E: Confounding, bias and chance, and criteria such as temporality and dose-response

correct_answer: E. Confounding, bias and chance, and criteria such as temporality and dose-response
why_correct: A statistical association does not establish causation; one must exclude confounding, bias and chance, and weigh considerations such as temporality (cause precedes effect), dose-response, consistency, strength and biological plausibility (Bradford Hill considerations) before inferring cause.
why_wrong: A. Statistical significance addresses chance only and does not establish causation. B. Strength supports but does not prove causation; confounding and bias can produce strong associations. C. Large samples reduce chance error but not confounding or bias. D. Temporality is essential: the exposure must precede the disease.
pearl: Association is not causation — exclude confounding, bias and chance and weigh criteria like temporality and dose-response first.
thinking: An observational study finds a strong statistical association between ↓ The principle that association ≠ causation — requiring exclusion of confounding/
exam_trap: B, a strong association alone proves causation — a strong, significant link feels conclusive. But strength and significance do not establish cause; confounding and bias must be excluded and causal criteria (especially temporality) considered.
takeaway: Association is not causation — exclude confounding, bias and chance and weigh criteria like temporality and dose-response first.

stem: A meta-analysis may overstate a treatment's benefit because studies with positive, statistically significant results are more likely to be published than those with negative results. What is this phenomenon called, and how can it be assessed?

options.A: Publication bias — assessed using a funnel plot
options.D: Lead-time bias — assessed by screening intervals

correct_answer: A. Publication bias — assessed using a funnel plot
why_correct: Publication bias is the tendency for studies with positive or significant findings to be published preferentially, which can distort meta-analyses by overstating effects; asymmetry on a funnel plot is used to detect it.
why_wrong: B. Recall bias concerns differential memory of exposures in individual studies and is not assessed by interview; it does not explain preferential publication of positive results. C. Confounding is distortion by a third variable within a study, and randomisation prevents it rather than assessing it; it does not explain selective publication. D. Lead-time bias is an apparent survival gain from earlier diagnosis in screening, unrelated to which studies reach publication. E. Random error is chance variation that averages out as studies accumulate, whereas selective publication is a systematic distortion that pooling cannot correct.
pearl: Preferential publishing of positive studies is publication bias — look for funnel-plot asymmetry.
thinking: A meta-analysis may overstate benefit ↓ Positive, significant studies are more likely to be published than negative ones ↓ Systematic loss of small negative studies makes a funnel plot asymmetrical ↓ Publication bias, assessed using a funnel plot
exam_trap: B, recall bias — both are systematic distortions. But recall bias concerns differential memory of exposures, whereas the preferential publication of positive studies is publication bias, detected with a funnel plot.
takeaway: Preferential publishing of positive studies is publication bias — look for funnel-plot asymmetry.

stem: A diagnostic test is described as having high sensitivity. What does this mean, and what is it most useful for?

options.A: A high proportion of those without the disease test negative, so it is best for ruling in
options.B: Most true cases test positive, so a negative result helps rule disease out
options.C: A high probability that a positive result is a true positive, so it rules disease in
options.D: Few false positives, so a positive result reliably confirms the disease
options.E: A high proportion of true cases test positive, so a positive result rules disease in

correct_answer: B. Most true cases test positive, so a negative result helps rule disease out
why_correct: Sensitivity is the proportion of people WITH the disease who test positive; a highly sensitive test has few false negatives, so a negative result helps rule the disease OUT (SnNout). Specificity is the proportion WITHOUT the disease who test negative; a highly specific test helps rule disease IN when positive (SpPin).
why_wrong: A. This describes specificity, not sensitivity. C. This describes positive predictive value. D. Few false positives reflects high specificity. E. A highly sensitive test is useful when negative (SnNout); a positive result may be a false positive.
pearl: High sensitivity means few false negatives — a negative result helps rule OUT (SnNout); high specificity helps rule IN (SpPin).
thinking: A diagnostic test is described as having high sensitivity ↓ Sensitivity = the proportion of TRUE cases detected, so a negative result RULES
exam_trap: C, the probability that a positive test is a true positive — that describes the positive predictive value, which depends on prevalence. Sensitivity instead is the proportion of diseased people correctly identified.
takeaway: High sensitivity means few false negatives — a negative result helps rule OUT (SnNout); high specificity helps rule IN (SpPin).

stem: In a randomised controlled trial, what is the main purpose of randomisation, and of blinding?

options.A: Randomisation increases statistical power; blinding improves participant adherence
options.B: Randomisation ensures a representative sample; blinding removes confounding
options.C: Randomisation balances confounders; blinding reduces bias in care and assessment
options.D: Randomisation conceals allocation; blinding balances baseline characteristics
options.E: Randomisation reduces loss to follow-up; blinding increases generalisability

correct_answer: C. Randomisation balances confounders; blinding reduces bias in care and assessment
