why_correct: Randomisation allocates participants to groups by chance, balancing known AND unknown confounders so the groups are comparable; blinding (of participants, clinicians and/or assessors) reduces performance and detection bias. Allocation concealment additionally prevents foreknowledge of the next assignment from influencing enrolment.
why_wrong: A. Power depends on sample size and effect size, and blinding is not primarily for adherence. B. Representativeness depends on sampling, not randomisation, and blinding does not remove confounding. D. Allocation concealment is a separate step, and baseline balance comes from randomisation, not blinding. E. Neither process primarily addresses attrition or generalisability.
pearl: Randomisation balances confounders between groups; blinding reduces bias in outcome influence/assessment.
thinking: Two separate processes are asked about ↓ Randomisation allocates by chance, balancing known and unknown confounders ↓ Blinding stops knowledge of allocation influencing care or outcome assessment (performance and detection bias) ↓ Answer: randomisation balances confounders; blinding reduces bias in care and assessment
exam_trap: D, randomisation conceals allocation and blinding balances baseline characteristics — both terms sound familiar, so the pairing is tempting. But allocation concealment is a separate step, and baseline balance comes from randomisation; blinding reduces performance and detection bias.
takeaway: Randomisation balances confounders between groups; blinding reduces bias in outcome influence/assessment.

stem: A health technology assessment expresses the value of a treatment in terms of cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. What does a QALY capture?

options.A: Length of life gained, weighted by its quality, in a single measure
options.B: Number of years of life gained, without adjustment for their quality
options.C: Quality-of-life scores on the EQ-5D, without any adjustment for survival
options.D: The cost of the treatment per year of life gained
options.E: Disability-adjusted life years lost to the disease in the population

correct_answer: A. Length of life gained, weighted by its quality, in a single measure
why_correct: A quality-adjusted life year combines the QUANTITY of life (years gained) with the QUALITY of those years (weighted by a utility from 0 to 1), giving a single measure used in cost-effectiveness analysis (cost per QALY) to compare interventions and inform funding decisions against a willingness-to-pay threshold.
why_wrong: B. A QALY adjusts years gained for quality of life. C. A QALY also incorporates survival. D. Cost is the numerator of cost per QALY, not what a QALY measures. E. That describes a DALY, a measure of disease burden, not a QALY.
pearl: A QALY combines length and quality of life into one measure — cost per QALY informs funding against a willingness-to-pay threshold.
thinking: A QALY is the outcome unit of cost-utility analysis ↓ It multiplies years of life by a utility weight from 0 (death) to 1 (full health) ↓ So it combines quantity and quality of life in one number ↓ Answer: length of life gained, weighted by its quality, in a single measure
exam_trap: B, only the number of years of life gained ignoring quality — survival is part of it. But the QALY deliberately also incorporates the QUALITY of those years, not just their number.
takeaway: A QALY combines length and quality of life into one measure — cost per QALY informs funding against a willingness-to-pay threshold.

stem: A new screening test for a disease is being evaluated. The developers want it to miss as few true cases as possible, accepting some false positives. Which property should be prioritised?
why_correct: A screening test should have high sensitivity so that it detects (does not miss) as many true cases as possible; the inevitable false positives are then resolved by a more specific confirmatory test.
why_wrong: A. Prevalence is a property of the population, not of the test, and cannot be chosen when designing a screening test. B. High specificity minimises false positives and is the priority for a confirmatory test, but the aim here is to miss as few true cases as possible, which is sensitivity. C. Positive predictive value depends on disease prevalence and reflects how likely a positive result is to be correct, which is not the stated aim of missing few cases. D. A low negative predictive value would mean many negative results are false, which is the opposite of what a screening test should achieve.
pearl: Screening tests are built for sensitivity (rule out, miss few); confirmatory tests are built for specificity (rule in).
thinking: The aim is to miss as few true cases as possible ↓ Missing few cases means minimising false negatives ↓ Some false positives are accepted and can be resolved by a confirmatory test ↓ Prioritise high sensitivity
exam_trap: B, high specificity — minimising false positives sounds desirable. But specificity is the priority for a confirmatory (not a screening) test; a screen prioritises sensitivity to avoid missing cases.
takeaway: Screening tests are built for sensitivity (rule out, miss few); confirmatory tests are built for specificity (rule in).

stem: A team measures how their current practice compares with an agreed best-practice standard, identifies gaps, introduces changes, and then re-measures practice against the same standard to see if it has improved. What process does this describe?
why_correct: Comparing current practice against an established standard, implementing change, and re-measuring to 'close the loop' is clinical audit — a quality-improvement process distinct from research, which seeks to generate new knowledge.
why_wrong: B. A randomised controlled trial randomly allocates participants to interventions to answer a research question, rather than comparing current practice with an agreed standard. C. A cohort study follows groups defined by exposure over time to see who develops an outcome; it does not measure practice against a standard and re-audit. D. Original research asks what best practice should be and generates new knowledge, whereas this team measures existing practice against an already-agreed standard and re-measures after change. E. A systematic review synthesises existing published studies on a question; it does not measure local practice or implement change.
pearl: Audit checks practice against a standard and re-measures after change; research creates new knowledge — different purposes.
thinking: Current practice is measured against an agreed best-practice standard ↓ Gaps are identified and changes introduced ↓ Practice is re-measured against the same standard to close the loop ↓ Clinical audit
exam_trap: D, original research generating new knowledge — both involve data and rigour, so they are easily confused. But research asks what the best practice should be (creating new knowledge), whereas audit measures existing practice against an already-agreed standard and re-checks after change.
takeaway: Audit checks practice against a standard and re-measures after change; research creates new knowledge — different purposes.

stem: A clinician strongly suspects a case of a notifiable infectious disease (for example measles or meningococcal disease) but laboratory confirmation is not yet available. What is the correct action regarding notification?

options.A: Notify once the patient has given written consent to share their details with public health
options.B: Notify once the diagnosis is confirmed by the reference laboratory
options.C: Notify public health on clinical suspicion, without awaiting lab confirmation
options.D: Ask the laboratory to notify, as clinicians do not hold this duty
options.E: Notify the patient's GP, who will then decide on public health reporting

correct_answer: C. Notify public health on clinical suspicion, without awaiting lab confirmation
why_correct: Notifiable diseases must be reported to the relevant public health authority on clinical suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation, so that public health action (contact tracing, prophylaxis, outbreak control) can begin promptly; this statutory duty overrides routine confidentiality.
why_wrong: A. Notification is a statutory duty and does not require consent. B. Waiting for confirmation delays contact tracing and prophylaxis. D. The registered medical practitioner has a statutory duty to notify on suspicion. E. The attending clinician must notify public health directly.
pearl: Notifiable diseases are reported on clinical suspicion, not after lab confirmation — speed protects the public.
thinking: A notifiable disease is strongly suspected but not yet confirmed ↓ The registered medical practitioner has a statutory duty to notify on clinical suspicion ↓ Waiting for laboratory confirmation delays contact tracing and prophylaxis ↓ Answer: notify public health on clinical suspicion without awaiting laboratory confirmation
exam_trap: B, wait for laboratory confirmation — reporting only a confirmed diagnosis feels more accurate. But delaying notification until confirmation could allow spread; notifiable diseases are reported on clinical suspicion to enable timely public health action.
takeaway: Notifiable diseases are reported on clinical suspicion, not after lab confirmation — speed protects the public.

stem: A patient who smokes wants to stop. What is the most effective approach to support cessation?

options.A: Prescribe a short benzodiazepine course for withdrawal anxiety
options.B: Very brief advice alone, followed by review at the next annual check
options.C: Advise stopping abruptly on a set quit date, without medication
options.D: Behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy (NRT, varenicline or bupropion)
options.E: Advise cutting down gradually over a year, without setting a quit date

correct_answer: D. Behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy (NRT, varenicline or bupropion)
why_correct: The most effective smoking cessation combines behavioural support with pharmacotherapy — nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, or bupropion — which together substantially increase quit rates compared with advice alone.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines are not a smoking cessation treatment. B. Brief advice alone is far less effective than combined support. C. Unsupported quitting has the lowest success rates. E. Indefinite cutting down without a quit date is less effective than a supported quit attempt.
pearl: Smoking cessation works best as behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy (NRT/varenicline) — not advice on its own.
thinking: A patient who smokes wants to stop ↓ COMBINING behavioural support with pharmacotherapy — that combination, rather th
exam_trap: B, brief advice alone — advice is a useful start and is recommended at every opportunity. But advice alone has modest effect; combining behavioural support with pharmacotherapy is considerably more effective.
takeaway: Smoking cessation works best as behavioural support plus pharmacotherapy (NRT/varenicline) — not advice on its own.

stem: A national cervical screening programme detects pre-cancerous changes before symptoms develop. Which level of prevention does screening represent?

options.A: It is not a form of prevention
options.B: Primary prevention (preventing disease before it occurs)
options.C: Tertiary prevention (reducing the impact of established disease)
options.E: Secondary prevention (early detection of existing/early disease)

correct_answer: E. Secondary prevention (early detection of existing/early disease)
why_correct: Screening is secondary prevention: it detects disease at an early or pre-symptomatic stage to allow earlier intervention. Primary prevention stops disease arising (e.g. vaccination, smoking cessation); tertiary prevention reduces the impact and complications of established disease (e.g. rehabilitation).
why_wrong: A. Screening is a recognised form of prevention: by detecting pre-cancerous changes early, treatment can stop progression to invasive cancer. B. Primary prevention stops disease arising at all, such as HPV vaccination, whereas cervical screening detects changes that are already present. C. Tertiary prevention reduces the impact and complications of established, symptomatic disease, such as rehabilitation, not the detection of pre-symptomatic changes. D. Quaternary prevention protects patients from overmedicalisation and unnecessary intervention; it does not describe early detection of disease.
pearl: Primary prevention stops disease arising (vaccination); secondary detects it early (screening); tertiary limits its impact (rehab).
thinking: Cervical screening detects pre-cancerous changes before symptoms develop ↓ The abnormality already exists, so this is not primary prevention ↓ Early detection allows treatment before invasive disease, not management of established disease ↓ Secondary prevention
exam_trap: B, primary prevention — screening 'prevents' bad outcomes, so it can seem primary. But primary prevention stops disease occurring at all, whereas screening detects disease that is already present early — that is secondary prevention.
takeaway: Primary prevention stops disease arising (vaccination); secondary detects it early (screening); tertiary limits its impact (rehab).

stem: In a population with a high vaccination uptake, an unvaccinated infant is nonetheless less likely to catch a vaccine-preventable infection. What concept explains this indirect protection?

options.A: Passive immunity from a recent vaccine

why_correct: Herd (population) immunity occurs when a sufficiently high proportion of a population is immune, reducing transmission and thereby indirectly protecting non-immune individuals (such as the unvaccinated or immunocompromised); the threshold needed depends on how transmissible the infection is.
why_wrong: A. Passive immunity means receiving preformed antibodies (via the placenta or immunoglobulin), and vaccines produce active rather than passive immunity; this infant is unvaccinated in any case. B. Active immunity requires the infant's own immune response to vaccination or infection; this infant has no vaccine-induced immunity, and the protection described is indirect, coming from the immune people around them. D. Antigenic drift is gradual mutation of viral surface antigens (as in influenza) that reduces protection, so it cannot explain an unvaccinated infant being protected. E. Notification bias is a reporting artefact in surveillance data and does not reduce an individual's actual risk of infection.
pearl: Herd immunity protects the non-immune indirectly by cutting transmission when enough of the population is immune.
thinking: High vaccination uptake in the population ↓ The unvaccinated infant has no vaccine-induced immunity of its own ↓ Few susceptible people means transmission is reduced, so the infant is less likely to be exposed ↓ Herd immunity
exam_trap: A, passive immunity from a recent vaccine — immunity terms are easily conflated. But the infant here is unvaccinated; the protection comes from reduced spread in the surrounding immune population, which is herd immunity, not passive immunity in the infant.
takeaway: Herd immunity protects the non-immune indirectly by cutting transmission when enough of the population is immune.

presentation: Health Inequalities and the Social Determinants of Health
stem: Populations living in more deprived areas have systematically worse health outcomes and shorter life expectancy than those in affluent areas. What does this best illustrate?

options.A: Genetic differences in disease susceptibility between populations
options.B: Health inequalities due to the social determinants of health
options.C: Individual lifestyle choices such as smoking and diet
options.D: Selection bias, as healthier people move to more affluent areas
options.E: Random variation between areas, expected by chance alone

correct_answer: B. Health inequalities due to the social determinants of health
why_correct: Systematic, avoidable differences in health outcomes linked to social and economic circumstances are health inequalities, arising from the social determinants of health (income, education, housing, employment, environment); they are addressed through upstream policy and proportionate universalism, not by attributing them solely to individuals.
why_wrong: A. Systematic area-level gradients are not explained by genetics. C. Lifestyle factors are themselves shaped by social determinants and do not explain the gradient alone. D. Health-related migration contributes little and does not explain the consistent gradient. E. A consistent, systematic gradient is not random variation.
pearl: Health inequalities are systematic, avoidable differences driven by social determinants (income, education, housing) — not just individual choices.
thinking: Worse outcomes follow a systematic gradient by area deprivation ↓ A consistent gradient is not explained by chance, genetics or migration ↓ Income, education and housing shape both lifestyle and health ↓ Answer: health inequalities due to the social determinants of health
exam_trap: C, differences explained solely by individual lifestyle choices — lifestyle does contribute, so this is tempting. But the systematic gradient by deprivation reflects the social determinants of health, not merely individual choices; effective action targets these wider determinants.
takeaway: Health inequalities are systematic, avoidable differences driven by social determinants (income, education, housing) — not just individual choices.

stem: A 74-year-old woman with known hypertension and ischaemic heart disease presents with sudden-onset palpitations, shortness of breath, and dizziness. She is sweaty and pale. Her ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 162 bpm. Her blood pressure is 84/52 mmHg. She is alert but confused. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.E: Oral apixaban and rate control with diltiazem

why_correct: In unstable AF with a rapid ventricular response, the priority is immediate restoration of sinus rhythm because the heart is not adequately filling or perfusing the brain and coronaries. Pharmacological rate control (beta-blockers, digoxin, amiodarone) takes 30–60 minutes to work. This patient does not have 30 minutes. Synchronised DC cardioversion is the definitive and time-critical intervention.
why_wrong: A. IV digoxin acts too slowly to restore perfusion in an unstable patient. B. Amiodarone is given only if synchronised shocks (up to 3) fail; it acts slowly and can worsen hypotension. C. IV beta-blockade would worsen hypotension and does not restore sinus rhythm quickly. E. Oral anticoagulation and diltiazem do not treat life-threatening instability, and diltiazem would worsen hypotension.
pearl: In AF, if the BP is low and the patient is slow (confused), shock them fast. Rate control is for the stable; volts are for the unstable.
thinking: Fast AF (162/min) ↓ BP 84/52 with confusion = life-threatening features ↓ unstable tachyarrhythmia ↓ synchronised DC cardioversion (D)
exam_trap: Trap — B, IV amiodarone infusion Amiodarone is the go-to pharmacological agent for acute rate and rhythm control in AF on many medical wards. Candidates see "AF with fast rate" and instinctively reach for the infusion. However, amiodarone is not the first-line treatment for unstable AF (RCUK: synchronised shock up to 3 attempts, then amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min) because: - It takes too long to take effect. - It can transiently worsen hypotension (due to its vasodilator properties). - In unstable patients, you do not "try" medical therapy—you shock first and ask questions later.
takeaway: In AF, if the BP is low and the patient is slow (confused), shock them fast. Rate control is for the stable; volts are for the unstable.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents to a rural Emergency Department with a 90-minute history of central crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm. ECG shows 4mm ST-elevation in leads V1–V4 (Anterior STEMI). He is haemodynamically stable. He has a history of a massive haemoptysis 2 weeks ago (awaiting bronchoscopy). The nearest PCI centre is 90 minutes away by ambulance. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Immediate transfer to PCI centre for primary PCI (door-to-balloon >120 mins)
options.C: Administer aspirin, clopidogrel, and fondaparinux, and wait for spontaneous reperfusion
options.D: Administer IV metoprolol and GTN infusion and defer reperfusion
options.E: Administer high-dose statin and heparin only

correct_answer: A. Immediate transfer to PCI centre for primary PCI (door-to-balloon >120 mins)
why_correct: The UK guidelines (NICE/ESC) state: - If PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given, PCI is preferred. - If the delay to PCI is >120 minutes *and* there is no contraindication, give fibrinolysis. - However, if fibrinolysis is contraindicated (as here), you must transfer for PCI even if the transfer time exceeds 120 minutes. You cannot give a contraindicated drug.
why_wrong: B. Fibrinolysis is contraindicated after a recent massive haemoptysis from an uninvestigated source. C. Waiting for spontaneous reperfusion abandons reperfusion therapy in an anterior STEMI. D. Deferring reperfusion increases infarct size and mortality; beta-blockers and GTN do not reperfuse. E. A statin and heparin alone do not reperfuse the occluded artery.
pearl: A contraindication to lysis is an absolute mandate for PCI. Time does not make a contraindication disappear.
thinking: Anterior STEMI ↓ PCI centre 90 min away ↓ fibrinolysis contraindicated by recent massive haemoptysis ↓ transfer for primary PCI (A)
exam_trap: Trap — B, Administer fibrinolytic therapy immediately Candidates see "rural hospital" and "90 minutes to PCI" and think, "Door-to-balloon >120 mins, so I must use fibrinolysis." They overlook the recent major internal bleed (massive haemoptysis from an uninvestigated source 2 weeks ago), which contraindicates fibrinolysis. Giving a fibrinolytic here could cause catastrophic, fatal intracranial or pulmonary haemorrhage. The presence of a contraindication overrides the time-based algorithm.
takeaway: A contraindication to lysis is an absolute mandate for PCI. Time does not make a contraindication disappear.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to ED with palpitations and dizziness. His ECG shows an irregularly irregular broad-complex tachycardia with a rate of 220 bpm. There are delta waves present in sinus rhythm on a previous ECG (known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome). He is haemodynamically stable (BP 110/70, alert). What is the single most appropriate *antiarrhythmic* management?
why_correct: In WPW, the accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) can conduct rapidly. If you give an AV nodal blocker (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, or beta-blockers), you block the normal AV node, forcing *all* the atrial impulses to go down the accessory pathway. This can precipitate ventricular fibrillation (VF). The Resuscitation Council UK adult tachyarrhythmia algorithm (V3, March 2026) gives: “Atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation: procainamide or cardioversion”. Amiodarone is not listed for pre-excited AF (its fallback role in the algorithm is for broad-complex VT). In this stable patient the antiarrhythmic of choice is IV procainamide; if he becomes unstable, synchronised DC cardioversion. IV procainamide is unlicensed in the UK and may not be stocked, so seek expert (cardiology) help early; synchronised DC cardioversion is the alternative the algorithm gives.
why_wrong: A. Adenosine blocks the AV node and can precipitate VF in pre-excited AF. B. Amiodarone is not recommended for pre-excited AF and has AV-nodal blocking effects. C. Verapamil blocks the AV node and can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway, causing VF. E. Digoxin is an AV nodal blocker and can precipitate VF in pre-excited AF.
pearl: In WPW with AF, never block the node. You will send all the traffic down the fast lane and crash the heart.
thinking: Irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 220/min + known WPW ↓ pre-excited AF ↓ avoid AV-nodal blockers ↓ procainamide (D)
exam_trap: Trap — A, IV adenosine (or C, Verapamil) Candidates see "narrow-complex tachycardia" (or broad-complex in this case due to pre-excitation) and reflexively give adenosine to break the re-entry circuit. In WPW with AF, adenosine is contraindicated. It blocks the AV node, leaving the accessory pathway unprotected, and can cause the ventricular rate to accelerate to 300+ BPM, degenerating into VF. This is a classic, high-stakes trap.
takeaway: In WPW with AF, never block the node. You will send all the traffic down the fast lane and crash the heart.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a known 5.5 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm is awaiting elective repair; a CT angiogram 2 weeks ago showed anatomy suitable for endovascular repair. He presents with sudden-onset severe back pain and collapse. He is pale, sweaty and increasingly drowsy. His BP is 70/35 mmHg and HR 135 bpm, and his BP is falling despite initial resuscitation. He has a tender, pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Immediate CT angiogram of the aorta to plan repair
options.B: Bedside FAST ultrasound to confirm free intraperitoneal fluid
options.C: Immediate transfer to theatre for open or endovascular repair
options.D: IV crystalloid to restore a systolic BP above 120 mmHg
options.E: Cross-match 6 units and request an urgent echocardiogram

correct_answer: C. Immediate transfer to theatre for open or endovascular repair
why_correct: This is a suspected ruptured AAA in a patient who is not responding to resuscitation. NICE NG156 advises considering CT angiography for people with a suspected rupture who are being evaluated for repair, but this man is deteriorating despite resuscitation and already has a recent CT angiogram showing anatomy suitable for EVAR. A further scan would only delay haemorrhage control. The vascular surgeon, anaesthetist and theatre team should be called and he should go immediately to theatre for repair; NICE notes that EVAR gives more benefit than open repair for most people, especially men over 70. Permissive hypotension is used while awaiting repair.
why_wrong: A. He is deteriorating despite resuscitation and his anatomy is already known from a CT angiogram 2 weeks ago; a further scan only delays haemorrhage control. B. A rupture is often retroperitoneal, FAST is unreliable and it delays definitive care. D. Aggressive fluid resuscitation worsens bleeding; permissive hypotension is used. E. Echocardiography is irrelevant and delays surgery.
pearl: Suspected ruptured AAA: a stable patient can have CT angiography to plan repair; a patient deteriorating despite resuscitation goes straight to theatre. Use permissive hypotension.
thinking: Known AAA with suitable EVAR anatomy on a recent CT angiogram ↓ Sudden back pain, collapse and a tender pulsatile mass ↓ BP 70/35 and falling despite resuscitation, drowsy = unstable rupture ↓ Further CT only delays haemorrhage control ↓ Straight to theatre for endovascular or open repair
exam_trap: Trap — A, immediate CT angiogram. CT angiography is appropriate for a suspected rupture when the patient is stable enough, and EVAR planning needs it. But this patient is deteriorating despite resuscitation and his anatomy was imaged 2 weeks ago, so another scan only delays haemorrhage control.
takeaway: Suspected ruptured AAA: CT angiography if stable enough; deteriorating despite resuscitation = straight to theatre, with permissive hypotension.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with 36 hours of severe right upper quadrant pain, fever (38.5°C), and vomiting. She has a positive Murphy's sign. Blood tests show WBC 16 x 10⁹/L and CRP 140 mg/L. An ultrasound confirms a thickened, oedematous gallbladder wall with pericholecystic fluid; no ductal dilatation. She is stable and has no significant comorbidities. What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.A: IV antibiotics and fluids, then interval cholecystectomy at 6–8 weeks
options.B: IV antibiotics and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission
options.C: Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction
options.D: Percutaneous cholecystostomy followed by interval cholecystectomy
options.E: Analgesia and discharge on oral co-amoxiclav with surgical clinic follow-up

correct_answer: B. IV antibiotics and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission
why_correct: NICE CG188 recommends laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acute cholecystitis, carried out within 1 week of diagnosis, in patients fit for surgery. Early surgery reduces the risk of recurrent symptoms, complications (perforation, empyema), and total hospital stay compared to delayed surgery (6-8 weeks). It is safe and has similar complication rates to delayed surgery.
why_wrong: A. Delayed surgery carries a higher risk of recurrent attacks and complications in a fit patient. C. There is no ductal dilatation or cholangitis, so ERCP is not indicated. D. Cholecystostomy is reserved for patients too unwell or frail for surgery. E. Acute cholecystitis with fever and raised inflammatory markers needs admission and definitive treatment.
pearl: For a fit patient with acute cholecystitis, do it early. The old 'wait 6 weeks' rule is dead—do it in the same admission.
thinking: RUQ pain, fever, Murphy's sign, raised WBC and CRP, thickened gallbladder wall with pericholecystic fluid ↓ Acute cholecystitis, no ductal dilatation ↓ Fit and stable ↓ IV antibiotics and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission
exam_trap: Trap — A, IV antibiotics and delayed cholecystectomy (6-8 weeks) Older surgical practice (and older exam candidates) default to "cool down" the inflammation with antibiotics and do the surgery later to avoid operating in an inflamed field. This is outdated. Randomised evidence and meta-analyses show that early cholecystectomy in the acute phase is safe and reduces the risk of readmission for recurrent cholecystitis or gallstone pancreatitis while waiting for the delayed operation. Unless the patient is critically unwell or has severe cardiorespiratory comorbidities, they get the surgery *now*.
takeaway: For a fit patient with acute cholecystitis, do it early. The old 'wait 6 weeks' rule is dead—do it in the same admission.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a 6-hour history of sudden-onset severe pain in his right groin and nausea. He has a known right inguinal hernia that has been present for years. On examination, the hernia is tense, tender, and irreducible. The overlying skin is erythematous. He has a tachycardia of 110 bpm and a fever of 38.2°C. Bowel sounds are absent. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Attempt manual reduction (taxis) after IV analgesia
options.B: Emergency surgical exploration and hernia repair
options.C: Abdominal X-ray to confirm small bowel obstruction
options.D: IV fluids and antibiotics, with review in 12 hours
options.E: CT abdomen and pelvis to confirm strangulation

correct_answer: B. Emergency surgical exploration and hernia repair
why_correct: Manual reduction (taxis) is contraindicated in a strangulated hernia because: - You cannot reliably tell if the bowel is viable or dead. - Reducing dead bowel into the abdomen converts a *contained* strangulation into an *intra-abdominal* perforation/peritonitis, which is catastrophic. - The definitive treatment is emergency surgery (exploration, resection of non-viable bowel, and hernia repair).
why_wrong: A. Reduction of a strangulated hernia risks returning non-viable bowel to the abdomen, causing perforation and peritonitis. C. Imaging adds nothing to a clinically strangulated hernia and delays surgery. D. Conservative management allows bowel necrosis to progress. E. CT delays definitive surgery when strangulation is clinically evident.
pearl: Red skin and fever means dead bowel inside. You do not push dead bowel back in—you cut it out.
thinking: Long-standing inguinal hernia now tense, tender and irreducible ↓ Erythematous skin, fever, tachycardia and absent bowel sounds = strangulation ↓ Reduction risks returning non-viable bowel; imaging only delays theatre ↓ Answer: emergency surgical exploration and hernia repair
exam_trap: Trap — A, Attempt manual reduction (taxis) under sedation Candidates think, "If the hernia is strangulated, just push it back to relieve the obstruction." This is a dangerous fallacy. "Taxis" is reserved for incarcerated (irreducible but viable) hernias without signs of strangulation (no erythema, no systemic upset, no tenderness). Once the skin is red, the patient has fever, and bowel sounds are absent – you must assume the bowel is dead. You do NOT push dead bowel back inside.
takeaway: Red skin and fever means dead bowel inside. You do not push dead bowel back in—you cut it out.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of headache, fatigue, and jaundice. Blood tests show: Hb 72 g/L (normocytic), Platelets 18 x 10⁹/L, Creatinine 180 µmol/L, and an elevated LDH. Blood film shows schistocytes. She is slightly confused. What is the single most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: The definitive, life-saving treatment is urgent plasma exchange (to remove the pathogenic antibodies and replace the missing enzyme). This is a haematological emergency with high mortality if untreated.
why_wrong: A. Platelet transfusion is avoided in TTP (unless life-threatening bleeding) because it can fuel microthrombi. B. Steroids are an adjunct to plasma exchange, not a substitute for it. D. Folic acid supports haemolysis-driven erythropoiesis but does not treat the ADAMTS13 deficiency. E. Bone marrow biopsy is not needed; the diagnosis is MAHA with thrombocytopenia and plasma exchange must not be delayed.
pearl: In TTP, you do not give platelets—you take plasma. Platelet transfusions are fuel for the fire.
thinking: Schistocytes (MAHA) + platelets 18 + confusion + renal impairment ↓ TTP ↓ urgent plasma exchange (C)
exam_trap: Trap — A, Platelet transfusion Candidates see a platelet count of 18 and reflexively order a platelet transfusion to prevent bleeding. In TTP, platelet transfusions are absolutely contraindicated (unless there is life-threatening haemorrhage). They fuel the thrombotic microangiopathy by providing more platelets to form the microthrombi that clog the capillaries, leading to worsening end-organ damage (brain, kidneys, heart). Platelet transfusions in TTP can precipitate a stroke or acute myocardial infarction.
takeaway: In TTP, you do not give platelets—you take plasma. Platelet transfusions are fuel for the fire.

stem: A 62-year-old man with septic shock (source: perforated diverticulum) is intubated in ITU. He is bleeding from his IV sites, his surgical drain, and his gums. Blood tests show: Platelets 40 x 10⁹/L, PT 22 secs (normal 12), APTT 58 secs (normal 30), Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L (normal 2-4), and D-dimers > 20 mg/L. What is the most appropriate management of his coagulopathy?

options.A: One adult dose of platelets, then recheck the count
options.B: FFP and cryoprecipitate, guided by coagulation results
options.C: IV tranexamic acid 1 g, repeated if bleeding continues
options.D: IV vitamin K 10 mg and recheck the PT in 6 hours

correct_answer: B. FFP and cryoprecipitate, guided by coagulation results
why_correct: The key biochemical features are: - Low platelets (consumption) - Prolonged PT/APTT (consumption of clotting factors) - Low fibrinogen (consumption > production) - Elevated D-dimers (breakdown of clots) In DIC with active bleeding, the management is replacement of what is being consumed: - FFP replaces clotting factors (PT/APTT correction) - Cryoprecipitate (or fibrinogen concentrate) replaces fibrinogen (target >1.5 g/L) - Platelets if <50 and actively bleeding The *most important* step is treating the underlying cause (sepsis), but the immediate supportive measure is factor/fibrinogen replacement.
why_wrong: A. Platelets alone do not replace the consumed clotting factors and fibrinogen. C. Antifibrinolytics are generally avoided in DIC as they may worsen thrombosis. D. Vitamin K does not correct a consumptive coagulopathy. E. PCC is for warfarin reversal and lacks fibrinogen; it is not first-line in DIC.
pearl: In bleeding DIC, you replace the factors and fibrinogen. TXA blocks the brake, not the leak.
thinking: Septic shock + bleeding + low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, high D-dimer ↓ DIC with active bleeding ↓ FFP and cryoprecipitate guided by coagulation (B)
exam_trap: Trap — C, IV tranexamic acid 1g (antifibrinolytic) Candidates see "bleeding + raised D-dimers" and think of hyperfibrinolysis, reaching for tranexamic acid. In DIC, the problem is widespread microvascular thrombosis and consumption. Giving an antifibrinolytic (tranexamic acid) in DIC is dangerous because it can precipitate massive thrombosis (strokes, MI, pulmonary embolism) by preventing the breakdown of the pathological microthrombi. Antifibrinolytics are reserved for *primary* hyperfibrinolysis (e.g., trauma, or specific haematological conditions), not for consumptive DIC.
takeaway: In bleeding DIC, you replace the factors and fibrinogen. TXA blocks the brake, not the leak.

stem: A 12-year-old girl in Year 8 attends her school's routine vaccination session. According to the UK vaccination schedule, which HPV vaccine is currently used?

options.B: Cervarix (2-valent: HPV 16 and 18), given as a three-dose course
options.C: Gardasil (4-valent: HPV 6, 11, 16 and 18), given as two doses
options.D: No HPV vaccine; cervical screening from age 25 is used instead
options.E: A 9-valent vaccine offered to girls in Year 8 but not offered to boys

why_correct: Gardasil 9 covers HPV types 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. Since September 2023 the routine UK programme gives a single dose to eligible adolescents and young people, with additional doses for some groups (e.g. immunosuppressed or HIV-positive individuals). The previous vaccines were Cervarix (bivalent) and Gardasil (quadrivalent), but Gardasil 9 is now standard.
why_wrong: B. Cervarix was used in the UK until 2012 and has been replaced. C. Quadrivalent Gardasil has been replaced by Gardasil 9 in the UK programme. D. HPV vaccination is part of the routine UK schedule alongside screening. E. The UK programme is gender-neutral; boys have been vaccinated since 2019.
pearl: UK HPV vaccine: Gardasil 9 protects against 9 types. It's given to boys and girls.
thinking: Routine UK school-age HPV vaccination ↓ Cervarix was replaced in 2012 by quadrivalent Gardasil ↓ Quadrivalent Gardasil has since been replaced by the 9-valent vaccine, offered to boys and girls ↓ Answer: Gardasil 9
exam_trap: Trap — B, Cervarix (2-valent: HPV 16 and 18). Candidates remember an older vaccine. Cervarix was replaced by quadrivalent Gardasil in 2012, and Gardasil 9 (9-valent) has since replaced quadrivalent Gardasil in the UK programme. The exam tests this update.
takeaway: UK HPV vaccine: Gardasil 9 protects against 9 types. It's given to boys and girls.

stem: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD is admitted with a type 2 respiratory exacerbation (pCO₂ 9.2 kPa). He is confused, agitated, and pulling off his BiPAP mask. The medical team wants to intubate and ventilate him. His wife produces a valid, signed, and witnessed Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT) which explicitly states: "I refuse endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation under any circumstances, even if my life is at risk." He is currently delirious and lacks capacity. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Intubate and ventilate immediately under the doctrine of necessity (emergency treatment)
options.B: Override the ADRT because he is delirious and lacks capacity
options.C: Respect the ADRT and do not intubate; commence palliative symptom control
options.D: Seek a Court of Protection ruling before making any decision
options.E: Ask the consultant psychiatrist to assess capacity and overturn the ADRT

correct_answer: C. Respect the ADRT and do not intubate; commence palliative symptom control
why_correct: A valid and applicable Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment does not require the patient to have capacity at the time of the emergency; it is designed for when they lose capacity. A valid ADRT (made with capacity, in writing, signed, witnessed, and stating it applies even if life is at risk) has the same legal force as a contemporaneous refusal, so intubation and mechanical ventilation must not be given. Withholding refused treatment is not euthanasia. Other treatment not covered by the ADRT continues in his best interests, with symptom control/palliation if he deteriorates.
why_wrong: A. Emergency necessity does not override a valid and applicable advance decision; refusing life-sustaining treatment is binding even in an emergency (MCA 2005 s26). B. Loss of capacity is precisely when an ADRT takes effect; delirium is not a reason to override it. D. A Court of Protection ruling is only needed if there is genuine doubt about validity or applicability; here the ADRT is valid and applicable. E. Capacity is already lacking; a psychiatrist cannot 'overturn' a valid ADRT.
pearl: An ADRT is legally binding in an emergency. You do not need capacity to enact it—you needed capacity to make it.
thinking: Life-threatening type 2 respiratory failure + lacks capacity ↓ valid, applicable ADRT refusing intubation/ventilation ↓ ADRT is binding ↓ do not intubate; continue other treatment and symptom control
exam_trap: Option A (intubate under the doctrine of necessity) is the trap. Candidates see "respiratory failure + confused + lacks capacity" and feel compelled to intervene to save the patient's life. They mistakenly think that *emergency necessity* overrides an ADRT. It does not. The Mental Capacity Act explicitly states that a valid ADRT cannot be overridden by a clinician, even in an emergency. The only exceptions are if the ADRT is invalid (e.g., not signed, ambiguous, or if the patient has since acted inconsistently with it).
takeaway: An ADRT is legally binding in an emergency. You do not need capacity to enact it—you needed capacity to make it.

stem: A 17-month-old previously well boy is brought to the Emergency Department by his parents. 15 minutes ago, he had a 4-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. He has now returned to his normal, playful self. He has a temperature of 39.2°C. He is fully immunised (including Hib and MenB). On examination, he is smiling, interacting, and has no neck stiffness, no rash, and a normal fundoscopy. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Lumbar puncture, as this is his first febrile seizure
options.B: IV ceftriaxone and aciclovir pending blood cultures
options.C: Observe for 1–2 hours and discharge with safety netting
options.D: CT head followed by a lumbar puncture if the CT is normal
options.E: Admit for an EEG and start regular prophylactic antipyretics

correct_answer: C. Observe for 1–2 hours and discharge with safety netting
why_correct: In a fully immunised, well-appearing child who has returned to baseline with no meningeal signs and no features of serious infection, this is a simple febrile seizure and no investigations are required. He can be observed until fully recovered and then discharged with safety-netting advice for the parents. Antibiotics and LP are not indicated.
why_wrong: A. LP is not indicated in a well, fully immunised child with no meningeal signs who has returned to baseline. B. Empirical antimicrobials are not indicated in a well child with no features of meningitis or encephalitis. D. Neuroimaging is not indicated for a simple febrile seizure. E. EEG is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure, and antipyretics do not prevent recurrence.
pearl: In a febrile seizure, if the child is back to normal, you don't need to tap. Treat the fever, not the seizure.
thinking: Fully recovered febrile child + generalised seizure <15 min + no meningism, fully immunised ↓ Simple febrile seizure ↓ Observe, treat fever source, safety-net and discharge
exam_trap: Trap — A, Lumbar puncture immediately Candidates see "fever + seizure" and immediately think of bacterial meningitis, reflexively reaching for an LP. However, in a child who has fully recovered and has no signs of meningitis (no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no rash, alert and interactive), the risk of meningitis is extremely low. Performing an LP here is unnecessary, traumatic for the child, and can cause a false positive due to a traumatic tap. Examiners want you to differentiate between a *simple febrile seizure* and a *seizure with CNS infection*—the discriminator is the post-ictal neurological status.
takeaway: In a febrile seizure, if the child is back to normal, you don't need to tap. Treat the fever, not the seizure.

stem: A 6-week-old male infant is brought to the ED with a 3-day history of coryza, cough, and poor feeding. He is tachypnoeic (RR 70/min), has intercostal and subcostal recessions, and nasal flaring. On auscultation, you hear bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and high-pitched expiratory wheeze. His SpO₂ is 89% in air. He is alert but irritable. What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.B: Oxygen and nasogastric or orogastric fluids

correct_answer: B. Oxygen and nasogastric or orogastric fluids
why_correct: This is bronchiolitis, and management is supportive. His oxygen saturation is 89% in air, so NICE NG9 recommends supplemental oxygen (for babies aged 6 weeks and over, give oxygen if saturation is persistently below 90%; below 92% if under 6 weeks or with underlying conditions). He is feeding poorly, so give fluids by nasogastric or orogastric tube; NG9 reserves intravenous isotonic fluids for children who do not tolerate nasogastric or orogastric fluids or who have impending respiratory failure, and he is alert with no sign of that. NG9 advises against salbutamol, corticosteroids and antibiotics in bronchiolitis and against a routine chest X-ray.
why_wrong: A. Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg — NICE NG9 advises not to use salbutamol in bronchiolitis; the wheeze comes from small-airway inflammation and mucus, not bronchospasm. C. Oral corticosteroids (prednisolone) 1 mg/kg — NG9 advises not to use systemic or inhaled corticosteroids in bronchiolitis. D. Chest X-ray to exclude pneumonia — NG9 advises against a routine chest X-ray; crackles are typical of bronchiolitis and an X-ray would not change management. E. Antibiotics (IV amoxicillin) — bronchiolitis is viral, and NG9 advises not to use antibiotics to treat it.
pearl: In bronchiolitis, you support the breathing, you do not bronchodilate. Salbutamol is for asthma, not for a 6-week-old with RSV.
thinking: 6-week-old + coryza + crackles/wheeze + recession ↓ Bronchiolitis ↓ SpO2 89% (<90%) → oxygen; poor feeding → NG/OG fluids ↓ No salbutamol, steroids, antibiotics or routine CXR
exam_trap: Trap — A, Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg Candidates see "wheeze" and immediately think of an asthma attack, reaching for the nebulised salbutamol. In a 6-week-old, this is bronchiolitis, not asthma (asthma is rarely diagnosed under 12 months). Salbutamol may cause tachycardia, hypoxia, and distress without any clinical benefit. NICE explicitly advises against using salbutamol in bronchiolitis.
takeaway: In bronchiolitis, you support the breathing, you do not bronchodilate. Salbutamol is for asthma, not for a 6-week-old with RSV.

stem: A 10-year-old boy with known type 1 diabetes presents with a 2-day history of vomiting, polyuria, and polydipsia. He is drowsy but rousable. His capillary glucose is 28 mmol/L. Blood gas shows: pH 7.10, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, and ketones 4.5 mmol/L. He is clinically dehydrated. What is the single most important principle regarding intravenous fluid resuscitation in paediatric DKA?

options.A: Give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 30 minutes, subtracted from the deficit
options.B: Give a 20 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 15 minutes routinely to every child with DKA
options.C: Restrict total fluid to 1.5 x maintenance over 48 hours, regardless of dehydration
options.D: Replace the fluid deficit over 24 hours using 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose
options.E: Add sodium bicarbonate to the IV fluids to correct the acidosis rapidly

correct_answer: A. Give a 10 mL/kg 0.9% saline bolus over 30 minutes, subtracted from the deficit
why_correct: BSPED 2021: a child with DKA who is not shocked but needs IV fluids receives a 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes, which is subtracted from the deficit. This boy is clinically dehydrated and drowsy but not described as shocked, so this applies. A child in shock (weak thready pulses, hypotension) instead receives 10 mL/kg boluses over 15 minutes, repeated after reassessment (up to 40 mL/kg before inotropes), which are not subtracted from the deficit. The deficit (5% if pH ≥7.1, 10% if pH <7.1) is then replaced with 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium over 48 hours plus maintenance. Large rapid boluses in the absence of shock are avoided.
why_wrong: B. Large (20 mL/kg) rapid boluses are reserved for shock, not given routinely. C. Fluid volume is calculated from deficit plus maintenance, not a fixed multiple of maintenance. D. BSPED replaces the deficit over 48 hours with 0.9% sodium chloride, not over 24 hours with 0.45% saline. E. Bicarbonate is not used routinely and may increase the risk of cerebral oedema.
pearl: Paediatric DKA (BSPED 2021): shocked → 10 mL/kg boluses over 15 minutes, reassess and repeat; not shocked but needs IV fluids → one 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes, subtracted from the deficit; never a routine large rapid bolus.
thinking: 10-year-old with DKA, pH 7.10 (moderate, 5% deficit) ↓ Is he shocked? Not described as shocked ↓ BSPED 2021: shock = 10 mL/kg over 15 min, repeated; non-shocked = 10 mL/kg over 30 min ↓ Deficit + maintenance over 48 h with 0.9% NaCl + KCl
exam_trap: Trap — B, a routine 20 mL/kg rapid bolus. Candidates trained in adult medicine resuscitate anyone who looks dry with large fast boluses. BSPED 2021 reserves rapid 10 mL/kg boluses for shock (reassessing between each); a non-shocked child who needs IV fluids gets a single 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes, which is subtracted from the deficit. Genuine shock must still be treated fully.
takeaway: Paediatric DKA (BSPED 2021): shocked → 10 mL/kg boluses over 15 minutes, reassess and repeat; not shocked but needs IV fluids → one 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 minutes, subtracted from the deficit; never a routine large rapid bolus.

stem: A 2-year-old girl is treated for an atypical urinary tract infection (poor urine flow, non-E. coli organism). Renal ultrasound during the acute illness shows bilateral hydronephrosis with ureteric dilatation. According to UK NICE guidelines, what is the most appropriate next imaging investigation?

options.B: DMSA scan (to look for renal scarring)

why_correct: For a child aged 6 months to under 3 years with atypical UTI, NICE NG224 recommends ultrasound during the acute infection and a DMSA scan 4–6 months later. MCUG is not routine in this age group but should be considered when there is dilatation on ultrasound, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or a family history of vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) — the first three are present here. MCUG is therefore the next imaging test, to look for VUR; give 3 days of oral prophylactic antibiotics with the MCUG on the second day. DMSA follows 4–6 months after the infection to detect scarring.
why_wrong: B. DMSA is recommended for atypical UTI in this age group, but it is done 4–6 months after the acute infection, so it is not the next test. C. A repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks is not part of the NICE schedule for atypical UTI and would not show reflux. D. CT urogram involves high radiation and is not used to investigate UTI in children. E. IVU is obsolete for this purpose and does not demonstrate reflux.
pearl: NICE NG224 (6 months–3 years): MCUG is not routine but is considered with dilatation on ultrasound, poor urine flow, non-E. coli infection or family history of VUR. Give 3 days of prophylactic antibiotics, with the MCUG on day 2.
thinking: 2-year-old with atypical UTI ↓ Ultrasound during acute infection shows hydronephrosis and ureteric dilatation ↓ NICE: consider MCUG if dilatation, poor flow or non-E. coli ↓ DMSA later at 4–6 months
exam_trap: Trap — B, DMSA scan. DMSA is indicated for atypical UTI, but it is timed 4–6 months after the infection to detect scarring. When ultrasound shows dilatation in a child under 3 with atypical UTI, the next test is MCUG to look for reflux.
takeaway: Child under 3 + atypical UTI + dilatation on ultrasound → MCUG next; DMSA at 4–6 months.

stem: A 4-year-old girl has had three episodes of cystitis (lower urinary tract infection) in the past 9 months, each confirmed on urine culture and each responding to antibiotics within 48 hours. A renal and bladder ultrasound performed within 6 weeks of the latest episode is normal. According to UK NICE guidelines, what is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.D: CT urogram – for upper tract pathology
options.E: No further investigations – ultrasound is normal

why_correct: Three or more lower UTIs meets the NICE definition of recurrent UTI. For children aged 3 years or older with recurrent UTI, NICE NG224 recommends an ultrasound within 6 weeks and a DMSA scan 4–6 months after the acute infection to detect renal parenchymal defects (scarring). MCUG is not recommended in children aged 3 years or older. Children with recurrent UTI should also be referred for paediatric specialist assessment.
why_wrong: A. MCUG is not recommended in children aged 3 years or older (and is not routine from 6 months to 3 years); it is invasive and requires catheterisation. C. The ultrasound within 6 weeks has already been done and is normal; repeating it adds nothing. D. CT urogram exposes the child to high radiation and is not part of the NICE imaging schedule. E. A normal ultrasound does not exclude renal scarring; NICE still recommends DMSA for recurrent UTI.
pearl: NICE NG224 recurrent UTI imaging: under 6 months — ultrasound during the acute infection, DMSA and MCUG; 6 months–3 years — ultrasound within 6 weeks and DMSA, MCUG only if specific features; 3 years or older — ultrasound within 6 weeks and DMSA only.
thinking: 4-year-old with three lower UTIs = recurrent UTI ↓ Ultrasound within 6 weeks is normal ↓ NICE (3 years or older): DMSA at 4–6 months; MCUG not recommended
exam_trap: Trap — A, MCUG. Candidates link recurrent UTI with reflux and reach for MCUG, but NICE does not recommend MCUG in children aged 3 years or older. The recommended test is a DMSA scan 4–6 months after the infection to look for scarring.
takeaway: Recurrent UTI in a child aged 3 or over: ultrasound within 6 weeks, then DMSA 4–6 months after the infection; no MCUG.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation (G3 P2) presents with sudden-onset, severe constant abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. She is pale, tachycardic (HR 120 bpm), and hypotensive (BP 88/54 mmHg). Her uterus is tense and woody-hard on palpation. The cardiotocograph (CTG) shows a flat trace with no accelerations and late decelerations. What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Administer IV atosiban to stop uterine contractions
options.B: Perform a bedside ultrasound to confirm fetal viability
options.D: IV fluid resuscitation and wait for the CTG to improve
options.E: Administer IV dexamethasone for fetal lung maturation

why_correct: The uterus is tense and woody (concealed or revealed haemorrhage). In a viable pregnancy (>24 weeks) with maternal instability and fetal compromise, the definitive management is immediate delivery (category 1 caesarean section) – within 30 minutes. The abruption is causing a consumptive coagulopathy and depriving the fetus of oxygen. You cannot "wait and see".
why_wrong: A. Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption with fetal compromise. B. Fetal viability is already shown by the CTG; scanning delays delivery. D. Resuscitation is given alongside, not instead of, immediate delivery when the CTG is pathological. E. Steroids at 34 weeks must not delay delivery of a compromised fetus.
pearl: A woody uterus and a flat CTG = deliver immediately. Fluids are for the mother; the knife is for the baby.
thinking: Pain + bleeding + woody uterus + shock ↓ Placental abruption ↓ Pathological CTG at 34 weeks ↓ Resuscitate and deliver by category 1 CS
exam_trap: Trap — D, IV fluid resuscitation and wait for the CTG to improve Candidates see "hypotension" and reflexively start fluids to stabilise the mother. While fluid resuscitation is critical for the mother, in a severe abruption the fetus is already compromised and the bleeding is ongoing inside the uterus. The only way to save the baby is to get them out. Delaying delivery while "optimising" the mother with fluids alone wastes the critical window and increases the risk of stillbirth and maternal DIC.
takeaway: A woody uterus and a flat CTG = deliver immediately. Fluids are for the mother; the knife is for the baby.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has just delivered a 3.8 kg baby vaginally. The third stage of labour was managed actively with 10 units of oxytocin IM. Fifteen minutes after delivery, the placenta is delivered intact. However, the midwife notices a large gush of bright red blood, and the uterus is soft, boggy, and palpable above the umbilicus. Her BP drops from 120/80 to 85/50 mmHg. Her HR is 130 bpm. What is the single most appropriate immediate pharmacological step to address the *cause* of the haemorrhage?

options.A: Give IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes and repeat if needed
options.B: Further uterotonic: IV oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost
options.C: Give 2 litres of warmed crystalloid rapidly via two large-bore cannulae
options.D: Insert an intrauterine balloon for tamponade of the uterine cavity
options.E: Cross-match 4 units and give O-negative blood

correct_answer: B. Further uterotonic: IV oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost
why_correct: The immediate pharmacological management is to give additional uterotonics to contract the uterus: - First-line (already given): Oxytocin 5-10 units IV/IM. - Second-line: Ergometrine 500 mcg IV (contraindicated in hypertension), or Carboprost (PGF2α) 250 mcg IM (contraindicated in asthma). - Third-line: Misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or rectally (prostaglandin E1). While fluid resuscitation and blood products are critical, the cause is the atony. You must treat the atony with more uterotonics.
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid is an adjunct but does not treat uterine atony. C. Fluid resuscitation is supportive and does not address the cause. D. Balloon tamponade is a mechanical, not pharmacological, step used if uterotonics fail. E. Blood replacement is supportive and does not treat the atony.
pearl: A boggy uterus is a bleeding uterus. Fluids fill the tank, but uterotonics stop the leak.
thinking: Atonic uterus after delivery + shock ↓ Cause = atony ↓ Further uterotonic (oxytocin, ergometrine or carboprost)
exam_trap: Trap — C, 2 litres of warmed crystalloid Candidates see the hypotension and tachycardia and reflexively start massive fluid resuscitation. Fluids are absolutely indicated to maintain perfusion, but fluids do not contract the uterus. If you give fluids without giving more oxytocin/ergometrine, the uterus will continue to bleed, and the patient will suffer a dilutional coagulopathy from massive crystalloid infusion. The sequence is: Uterotonics first (to stop the bleeding), fluids second (to support the circulation).
takeaway: A boggy uterus is a bleeding uterus. Fluids fill the tank, but uterotonics stop the leak.

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation has pre-eclampsia. Her blood film shows fragmented red cells, LDH is raised, ALT is 310 U/L and platelets are 62 × 10⁹/L. She has no previous uterine surgery and is not in labour. She suddenly develops severe right upper quadrant pain. Her BP is 80/40 mmHg, HR 130 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% on air. Her uterus is soft and non-tender. What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate management?

options.A: Uterine rupture — resuscitation and immediate laparotomy with caesarean section
options.B: Hepatic capsule rupture — resuscitation, laparotomy and delivery
options.C: Placental abruption — resuscitation and emergency caesarean delivery
options.D: Pulmonary embolism — CTPA and systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
options.E: Perforated peptic ulcer — erect chest X-ray and emergency laparotomy

correct_answer: B. Hepatic capsule rupture — resuscitation, laparotomy and delivery
why_correct: Haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets in pre-eclampsia indicate HELLP syndrome. Sudden severe right upper quadrant pain with shock indicates a subcapsular hepatic haematoma with capsular rupture, a life-threatening complication. Management is resuscitation with activation of the major haemorrhage protocol, urgent delivery, and laparotomy with liver packing (or interventional radiology embolisation where appropriate) with hepatobiliary surgical support. This is a catastrophic obstetric emergency.
why_wrong: A. Uterine rupture causes abdominal pain with fetal compromise, usually in labour with a scarred uterus, not right upper quadrant pain in HELLP. C. Abruption causes uterine pain and a tender, hard uterus rather than right upper quadrant pain. D. PE presents with dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain, not right upper quadrant pain. E. Perforated ulcer is not the expected complication in HELLP with right upper quadrant pain and shock.
pearl: HELLP + epigastric pain + shock = liver rupture. Don't just deliver; pack the liver.
thinking: 35 weeks, pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets = HELLP ↓ Sudden severe right upper quadrant pain and shock ↓ Soft non-tender uterus and no uterine scar argue against abruption and uterine rupture ↓ Hepatic capsule rupture ↓ Resuscitate, deliver, laparotomy with liver packing
exam_trap: Trap — C, placental abruption with emergency delivery. Candidates see shock in pregnancy and think of abruption. Here the uterus is soft and non-tender, and HELLP (haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, low platelets) with right upper quadrant pain points to the liver. Hepatic rupture is the classic catastrophic complication of HELLP; management is haemorrhage control at laparotomy plus delivery.
takeaway: HELLP + epigastric pain + shock = liver rupture. Don't just deliver; pack the liver.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department 18 hours after taking a single ingestion of 20g of paracetamol. She reports mild nausea but is otherwise well. Her paracetamol level is 15 mg/L (plotted on the treatment nomogram). Liver function tests are normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: No treatment, as the level is below the treatment line
options.C: Oral methionine 2.5 g and repeat LFTs in 4 hours
options.D: Activated charcoal 50 g orally, then repeat the level
options.E: Medically fit; refer for psychiatric assessment

correct_answer: B. Start IV acetylcysteine without delay
why_correct: She presented 18 hours after a large single ingestion (20 g, well over 150 mg/kg). TOXBASE/MHRA guidance for patients presenting 8–24 hours after taking 150 mg/kg or more is to start IV acetylcysteine immediately, without waiting for the level. The UK treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours) becomes less reliable after 15 hours, and here 15 mg/L at 18 hours lies above the line in any case. Acetylcysteine is most effective within 8 hours but still beneficial when started later, so treatment should not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. The level is not reassuring. At 18 hours, 15 mg/L lies above the UK treatment line, and after a 150 mg/kg-plus ingestion presenting late, acetylcysteine is started immediately. C. Methionine is not a standard UK treatment and is less effective, especially late. D. Charcoal is only useful within about 1 hour of ingestion. E. She needs acetylcysteine before being considered medically fit.
pearl: At 18 hours, you treat the patient, not the level. If they took 20g, give the NAC.
thinking: Single 20 g paracetamol ingestion, presenting at 18 hours ↓ Treatment line is less reliable after 15 hours, and 15 mg/L at 18 hours is above it anyway ↓ Large ingestion presenting 8–24 hours later = start acetylcysteine immediately
exam_trap: Trap — A, No treatment required (level is below line). Candidates see a low-looking number (15 mg/L) and discharge the patient. This is a dangerous error. On the UK treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours, halving about every 4 hours) the threshold at 18 hours is roughly 9 mg/L, so 15 mg/L is above the line, and the nomogram is less reliable after 15 hours anyway. After an ingestion of 150 mg/kg or more presenting 8–24 hours later, acetylcysteine is started immediately.
takeaway: At 18 hours, you treat the patient, not the level. If they took 20g, give the NAC.

stem: A 24-year-old man sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture playing rugby 6 hours ago. He was placed in a backslab and sent home with analgesia. He returns to the Emergency Department because his pain is unbearable, despite taking oral morphine. On examination, his foot is pale and cool, with prolonged capillary refill (>3 seconds). He has severe pain on passive dorsiflexion of his toes. The posterior tibial pulse is palpable but weak. What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.A: Elevate the leg above heart level on pillows and reassess in 30 minutes
options.B: IV morphine titrated to pain and senior review of the limb in 1 hour
options.C: Split the backslab and padding down to skin, then reassess
options.D: Urgent CT angiogram of the leg to exclude a popliteal artery injury
options.E: IV mannitol infusion to reduce the intracompartmental pressure

correct_answer: C. Split the backslab and padding down to skin, then reassess
why_correct: The classic features are: severe pain out of proportion to the injury, pain on passive stretch, and paraesthesia. The immediate first step is to remove any circumferential dressings or casts that are restricting the limb. Splitting the backslab (and cutting the underlying padding) can reduce the intracompartmental pressure by up to 30-40%. You do this *before* calling for surgical fasciotomies, and you reassess the limb afterwards.
why_wrong: A. Elevation above the heart reduces arterial perfusion pressure and worsens compartment syndrome; the limb is kept at heart level. B. Escalating analgesia masks progression and delays decompression. D. A palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome; imaging delays decompression. E. Mannitol has no established role and delays definitive treatment.
pearl: In compartment syndrome, split the cast to skin and keep the leg at heart level. Never elevate—you starve the muscle.
thinking: Tibial fracture in a backslab + pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch ↓ A palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome ↓ Acute compartment syndrome ↓ First remove constriction: split the backslab and padding to skin, keep the leg at heart level
exam_trap: Trap — A, Elevate the leg on pillows Candidates instinctively think "swelling = elevate." In compartment syndrome, elevating the leg above the heart is dangerous. It reduces the arterial perfusion pressure gradient (mean arterial pressure minus compartment pressure), thereby *worsening* ischaemia. The leg should be kept at heart level (not elevated) while awaiting definitive management.
takeaway: In compartment syndrome, split the cast to skin and keep the leg at heart level. Never elevate—you starve the muscle.

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with a 4-hour history of sudden-onset severe pain in his right testicle. He feels nauseous and vomited once. On examination, the right testis is swollen, tender, and lies horizontally (high-riding). The left testis is normal. There is no urinary frequency or dysuria. What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler to assess blood flow
options.D: Analgesia and observe for 4 hours (likely torsion of a hydatid of Morgagni)

correct_answer: B. Urgent surgical exploration (scrototomy) and detorsion/fixation
why_correct: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency. The testicle has a viability window of 4–6 hours. If surgery is performed within 4 hours, salvage rates are >90%. Salvage falls to roughly 20–50% at 12–24 hours and is poor beyond 24 hours. Do not delay for an ultrasound (which takes time and may be unavailable at night). The definitive management is immediate surgical exploration (bilateral orchidopexy). If torsion is confirmed, the testis is untwisted and fixed. If the testis is non-viable, it is removed.
why_wrong: A. Doppler delays theatre and can be falsely reassuring; a classic clinical picture needs exploration. C. Sudden onset with a horizontal high-riding testis and no urinary symptoms points to torsion, not epididymo-orchitis. D. Observation wastes the salvage window; torted appendages are diagnosed at exploration. E. Urinalysis does not change management and must not delay surgery.
pearl: In a teenager with acute scrotal pain and a horizontal testis, the clock is ticking. Do not scan—go straight to the theatre.
thinking: Teenager + sudden severe testicular pain + vomiting + horizontal high-riding testis ↓ Testicular torsion until proven otherwise ↓ Within the salvage window; imaging would only delay theatre ↓ Urgent scrotal exploration
exam_trap: Trap — A, Urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler Candidates know that Doppler ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice to diagnose torsion (showing absent flow). However, in a classic presentation in a teenager, ultrasound delays definitive management. If the clinical picture is clear (sudden pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex), you go straight to theatre. Ultrasound is only indicated if the diagnosis is *uncertain* (e.g., intermittent pain, or early presentation with mild signs). Imaging should not delay exploration when the clinical diagnosis is clear.
takeaway: In a teenager with acute scrotal pain and a horizontal testis, the clock is ticking. Do not scan—go straight to the theatre.

stem: A 22-year-old man is undergoing a general anaesthetic for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. He is induced with propofol and suxamethonium (for rapid sequence induction). Five minutes after intubation, the anaesthetist notices a significant and rapid rise in end-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂) despite adequate ventilation. The patient's heart rate is 140 bpm, and his temperature is rising (38.5°C). There is muscle rigidity. What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.A: Increase the minute ventilation (to blow off CO₂)
options.C: Administer IV sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis
options.D: Change the soda lime in the anaesthetic circuit
options.E: Administer IV atracurium (non-depolarising muscle relaxant) to break the rigidity

why_correct: This is Malignant Hyperthermia (MH) – a life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction triggered by suxamethonium or volatile anaesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane). The cardinal signs are: - Unexplained rise in ETCO₂ (first and most sensitive sign) - Tachycardia - Muscle rigidity (masseter spasm) - Rapid temperature rise The definitive and specific treatment is IV dantrolene (a ryanodine receptor blocker). It must be given immediately, alongside stopping trigger agents, 100% oxygen with increased minute ventilation, and active cooling. Give dantrolene 2–3 mg/kg (e.g. 2.5 mg/kg) IV, then 1 mg/kg every 5 minutes until ETCO₂ is below 6 kPa with normal minute ventilation and core temperature is below 38.5°C; reappraise the diagnosis if 10 mg/kg has been given. Without dantrolene, the patient will develop severe acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and cardiac arrest.
why_wrong: A. Increasing minute ventilation with 100% oxygen is part of the immediate supportive response, but it only removes CO₂ and does not stop the hypermetabolic process. C. Bicarbonate treats the consequence (acidosis), not the cause. D. Exhausted soda lime does not explain rigidity, tachycardia and hyperthermia. E. Non-depolarising relaxants do not relieve MH rigidity, which arises within the muscle cell.
pearl: In MH, CO₂ rises because the muscles are burning. You don't ventilate the fire out—you put the fire out with dantrolene.
thinking: Suxamethonium given ↓ Rapid rise in ETCO₂ despite adequate ventilation + tachycardia + rising temperature + rigidity ↓ Malignant hyperthermia ↓ Stop triggers and give IV dantrolene immediately
exam_trap: Trap — A, Increase the minute ventilation. Candidates see a rise in ETCO₂ and treat the number. In MH, the CO₂ rise is due to increased production (hypermetabolism), not decreased excretion. Hyperventilation with 100% oxygen is done as part of the initial response, but on its own it does nothing to stop the muscle hypermetabolism or the temperature rise. Dantrolene is the only treatment that addresses the cause.
takeaway: In MH, CO₂ rises because the muscles are burning. You don't ventilate the fire out—you put the fire out with dantrolene.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 12-hour history of severe sore throat, drooling of saliva, muffled voice ("hot potato" voice), and significant stridor. He is sitting upright, leaning forward, and appears anxious. He is febrile (39°C) and tachycardic (HR 110). What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.A: Flexible nasendoscopy in the ED to visualise the epiglottis before calling anaesthetics
options.B: Lay the patient flat for direct laryngoscopy in the ED to inspect the epiglottis
options.C: Urgent anaesthetic review for airway assessment and possible intubation
options.D: IV dexamethasone and IV ceftriaxone, then reassess the airway in one hour
options.E: Nebulised adrenaline and close observation in the ED resuscitation area

correct_answer: C. Urgent anaesthetic review for airway assessment and possible intubation
why_correct: The classic signs are stridor, drooling, muffled voice, and tripod positioning. The cardinal rule: Do NOT attempt to examine the throat or perform a nasendoscopy in the ED unless you are prepared for immediate airway intervention. Reflex laryngospasm or complete airway obstruction can be precipitated by instrumentation. The immediate step is to call the anaesthetist (or ENT) to assess the airway in a controlled environment (theatre or ITU) where they can secure it.
why_wrong: A. Instrumenting the airway before senior anaesthetic support is available risks complete obstruction. B. Lying flat and laryngoscopy can precipitate complete airway obstruction. D. Steroids and antibiotics are part of treatment but do not secure a threatened airway. E. Nebulised adrenaline may buy time but does not replace definitive airway assessment and control.
pearl: If the patient is drooling, sitting up, and stridulous, you do not look—you call for the tube. Examination is for the theatre, not the ED.
thinking: Severe sore throat, drooling, muffled voice and stridor in a febrile adult sitting forward ↓ Acute epiglottitis/supraglottitis with a threatened airway ↓ Examining the throat or lying the patient flat in ED can precipitate complete obstruction ↓ Answer: urgent anaesthetic review for airway assessment and possible intubation
exam_trap: Trap — A, Perform a flexible nasendoscopy Candidates (and inexperienced clinicians) want to "look" to confirm the diagnosis. In a patient with stridor and drooling, passing a scope can trigger total laryngeal obstruction. If you do perform a nasendoscopy, it must be done *only* by an ENT surgeon in a theatre with a fully prepared anaesthetic team and surgical airway kit (cricothyroidotomy) ready. The *immediate* action is the referral to the specialist team, not the diagnostic test.
takeaway: If the patient is drooling, sitting up, and stridulous, you do not look—you call for the tube. Examination is for the theatre, not the ED.

stem: A 68-year-old male smoker with peripheral arterial disease presents with sudden-onset severe rest pain in his left foot, which has become pale and cold over the last 4 hours. On examination, the left foot is mottled and pulseless (no Doppler signal), with reduced sensation and a dropped foot (foot drop). The right leg has normal pulses. What is the single most appropriate immediate management step?

options.A: Oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose and aspirin, then reassess
options.B: Urgent CT angiogram of the lower limb before any vascular referral
options.C: Immediate vascular referral for emergency revascularisation
options.D: IV heparin infusion and reassessment of the limb in 24 hours
options.E: Elevate the foot and apply warm packs to aid perfusion, then review

correct_answer: C. Immediate vascular referral for emergency revascularisation
why_correct: The presence of sensory loss and motor deficit (foot drop) indicates *severe* ischaemia (Rutherford class IIb – threatened limb). The limb has a window of viability of 4–6 hours. Medical therapy (heparin/antiplatelets) is an *adjunct*; the definitive treatment is immediate vascular surgery (embolectomy or bypass; thrombolysis is generally too slow when motor deficit is present). You must refer the patient to the vascular surgeon *before* you do anything else.
why_wrong: A. Antiplatelets do not restore flow to an acutely threatened limb. B. Imaging before referral delays revascularisation in a limb with sensory and motor loss. D. Heparin is an adjunct; delaying revascularisation for 24 hours risks limb loss. E. Elevation reduces perfusion and warming increases metabolic demand.
pearl: When the foot is pulseless and numb, the clock is ticking. Call the surgeon before you touch the heparin.
thinking: Sudden pale, cold, mottled, pulseless foot with sensory loss and foot drop ↓ Acute limb ischaemia with motor deficit (Rutherford IIb, immediately threatened) ↓ Viability window of hours; heparin is only an adjunct ↓ Immediate vascular referral for emergency revascularisation
exam_trap: Trap — D, IV heparin 5000 units bolus Candidates think "acute thrombosis/embolism = anticoagulate." While IV heparin is indicated to prevent further clot propagation, it does not dissolve the existing clot that is occluding the artery. In an acutely threatened limb, heparin is a bridge—but it is not the answer. Delaying surgical referral to "start heparin" wastes the 4-6 hour window. The correct order is: Call vascular surgeon NOW, and *while waiting*, start heparin.
takeaway: When the foot is pulseless and numb, the clock is ticking. Call the surgeon before you touch the heparin.

stem: A 20-year-old university student is admitted with confirmed meningococcal meningitis. He lives in a shared house with five other students, and his girlfriend, who does not live there, stayed overnight with him several times in the week before he became unwell. He also attended lectures with the rest of his year group. Who should be offered chemoprophylaxis to prevent secondary cases?

options.C: Only the housemates who share a bedroom with the case
options.D: The girlfriend and the housemates who share a bathroom
options.E: All students in the same university year

correct_answer: A. All 5 housemates and the girlfriend
