why_correct: UKHSA guidance (Dec 2025) offers chemoprophylaxis to close contacts, defined as people who had prolonged close contact with the case in a household-type setting during the 7 days before onset of illness: those living or sleeping in the same household, and boyfriends or girlfriends. All 5 housemates qualify because they live in the same house, and the girlfriend qualifies through intimate contact and staying overnight in that week. Thus all 6 contacts (5 + 1) should be offered prophylaxis; ciprofloxacin is the UK chemoprophylaxis of choice, with rifampicin as an alternative.
why_wrong: B. Limiting prophylaxis to the girlfriend ignores the housemates, who had prolonged household-type contact and are also close contacts under UK guidance. C. Limiting prophylaxis to bedroom-sharers is wrong because everyone living in the same household in the preceding seven days counts as a close contact, not just those sharing a bedroom. D. Sharing a bathroom is not the criterion; all housemates qualify through prolonged household-type contact, so excluding some of them would be wrong. E. Students in the same university year have only casual contact and are not close contacts, so blanket prophylaxis is not recommended outside a managed outbreak.
pearl: Meningococcal prophylaxis is for everyone who lived or slept under the same roof as the case, or had intimate kissing contact, in the 7 days before onset.
thinking: Index case with meningococcal disease living in a shared student house ↓ Close contacts are those with prolonged household-type contact in the seven days before onset ↓ That includes all housemates and the girlfriend, but not the wider university year ↓ All five housemates and the girlfriend receive prophylaxis
exam_trap: Trap — B, Only the girlfriend (close intimate contact) Candidates think only of sexual/intimate contacts. In meningococcal disease, household contacts (living under the same roof) are also at high risk (even without kissing) due to prolonged exposure. You must include all household members.
takeaway: Meningococcal prophylaxis is for everyone who lived or slept under the same roof as the case, or had intimate kissing contact, in the 7 days before onset.

stem: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman attends her GP 6 weeks after a Colles' fracture sustained in a fall from standing height. Her mother had a hip fracture. She takes no regular medication. According to UK (NICE) guidelines, what is the most appropriate next step to assess her fracture risk?

options.A: DXA scan of the hip and lumbar spine
options.B: FRAX risk calculation using clinical risk factors
options.E: Referral to a community falls prevention clinic first

correct_answer: A. DXA scan of the hip and lumbar spine
why_correct: A Colles' (distal radius) fracture from a fall from standing height is a fragility fracture, and the wrist is a major osteoporotic fracture site. NICE NG259 (2026), which replaced CG146, recommends offering a DXA scan to measure bone mineral density, with or without completing a risk prediction tool, to anyone aged 30 or over who has had a single major osteoporotic fragility fracture in the last 2 years (rec 1.4.1). She is 6 weeks from the fracture, so she goes straight to DXA; FRAX or QFracture can be completed alongside but is not a prerequisite. Source: NICE NG259, Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng259/chapter/Fragility-fracture-risk-assessment
why_wrong: B. NICE NG259 (1.4.1) offers a DXA scan directly after a major osteoporotic fragility fracture in the last 2 years, with or without a risk prediction tool, so a FRAX calculation is optional here and is not the most appropriate next step (FRAX first, then DXA only at intermediate risk, was the older CG146/NOGG pathway). C. Urine calcium/creatinine does not assess fracture risk. D. Vitamin D helps assess bone health and secondary causes but does not estimate fracture risk. E. Falls assessment matters but is separate from assessing bone fracture risk.
pearl: Wrist, hip, spine or shoulder fragility fracture in the last 2 years: offer a DXA scan directly (NICE NG259 1.4.1).
thinking: Fall from standing height ↓ Colles' fracture = major osteoporotic fragility fracture, 6 weeks ago ↓ NICE NG259 1.4.1: offer DXA (with or without a risk tool)
exam_trap: Trap — B, FRAX first. Under the old CG146/NOGG pathway a risk tool came first and DXA followed at intermediate risk. NICE NG259 (July 2026) offers DXA directly after a major osteoporotic fragility fracture in the last 2 years; the risk tool is optional.
takeaway: Major osteoporotic fragility fracture (wrist, hip, spine, shoulder) in the last 2 years: offer DXA — FRAX first is not needed (NICE NG259).

stem: According to the UK NHS Breast Screening Programme, what is the age range for routine screening?
why_correct: The NHS Breast Screening Programme invites women from age 50 up to their 71st birthday for mammography every 3 years; women aged 71 and over can self-refer every 3 years. The AgeX trial, which randomised women aged 47–49 and 71–73 to test an age extension, stopped randomising in 2020 and is now in follow-up; the routine range is unchanged. For comparison, cervical screening is 25 to 64 years and bowel screening in England is 50 to 74 years.
why_wrong: A. Routine NHS breast screening does not start at 40. C. Routine invitations stop at 70; 74 is not the upper limit. D. Routine screening does not start at 45. E. Routine screening continues to 70, not 65.
pearl: Breasts are 50 to 70 (three-yearly). Bowels are 50 to 74 (England). Cervix is 25 to 64.
thinking: UK breast screening age range ↓ Invited from 50 up to the 71st birthday, every 3 years ↓ 50 to 74 is the bowel screening range in England, not breast
exam_trap: Trap — C, 50 to 74 years. Candidates confuse breast screening with bowel screening, which in England now covers 50 to 74, or with US guidance. The UK breast screening range is 50 to 70 (up to the 71st birthday), with self-referral after that.
takeaway: Breasts are 50 to 70. Bowels are 50 to 74 (England). Cervix is 25 to 64.

stem: A mother asks when her 9-month-old son will have his first MMR vaccine. According to the UK childhood immunisation schedule, at what age is the first dose given?
why_correct: On the current schedule the first dose of measles-containing vaccine (now MMRV) is given at 12 months, on or after the first birthday. Children born on or after 1 January 2025 then have the second MMRV dose at 18 months, and the 3 years 4 months visit is the pre-school dTaP/IPV booster only; older cohorts follow transitional arrangements in the UKHSA complete routine immunisation schedule. MMR/MMRV is a live attenuated vaccine.
why_wrong: B. At 3 months the infant is due primary-course vaccines such as the second dose of the 6-in-1; a live measles-containing vaccine is not given this early because maternal antibody would blunt the response. C. There is no routine vaccine appointment at 6 months; MMR given before the first birthday (for example in an outbreak or before travel) does not count towards the routine two-dose course. D. 18 months is the second-dose visit for MMRV on the current schedule, not the first dose. E. Around 3 years 4 months is the pre-school booster visit; waiting until then for a first dose would leave the toddler unprotected against measles for years.
pearl: MMR(V): first dose at 12 months, second at 18 months on the current schedule. The 6-in-1 is the early one.
thinking: Routine schedule question: first dose of the measles-containing vaccine ↓ Live attenuated vaccine, so it is given once maternal antibody has waned ↓ Early infant visits (8, 12, 16 weeks) are for the 6-in-1 and other primary vaccines; nothing routine at 6 months ↓ First dose is given at 12 months, the second at 18 months on the current schedule ↓ Answer: 12 months
exam_trap: Trap — B, 3 months. Candidates might think of the 6-in-1 vaccine (DTaP/IPV/Hib/HepB), which is given at 8, 12 and 16 weeks. The measles-containing vaccine is given later: at 12 months and, on the current schedule, 18 months. The exam tests this distinction.
takeaway: MMR(V): first dose at 12 months, second at 18 months on the current schedule. The 6-in-1 is the early one.

stem: A 19-year-old student who lives in a shared house with four other students is admitted with meningococcal septicaemia. She has no partner, and she attended lectures with her year group in the week before becoming unwell. Who should be offered chemoprophylaxis to prevent secondary cases?

options.B: Only the housemates who share a bedroom
options.D: All students in the same university year
options.E: No one – prophylaxis is not needed

why_correct: All 4 housemates qualify as close contacts because they had prolonged close contact with the case in the same household during the 7 days before onset. Casual contacts such as classmates do not qualify. Ciprofloxacin is the UK chemoprophylaxis of choice, with rifampicin as an alternative.
why_wrong: B. Restricting prophylaxis to bedroom-sharers is too narrow: everyone living in the same household in the 7 days before onset counts as a close contact. C. An intimate kissing partner would qualify, but offering prophylaxis only to a sexual partner misses the other household contacts who share the same exposure. D. Students in the same year are casual contacts; UK guidance does not offer them prophylaxis after a single case. E. Close household contacts of a case of meningococcal disease are at increased risk of secondary cases and should be offered chemoprophylaxis promptly.
pearl: Meningitis prophylaxis: household contacts and intimate contacts.
thinking: Index case of meningococcal disease in a shared student house ↓ Close contact means prolonged household-type contact in the 7 days before onset ↓ All housemates meet this; classmates and colleagues do not ↓ Answer: offer chemoprophylaxis to all four housemates
exam_trap: Trap — D, All students in the same university year. Candidates think of all contacts, but casual contacts (classmates, work colleagues) are not offered chemoprophylaxis after a single case. The exam tests this distinction.
takeaway: Meningitis prophylaxis: household contacts and intimate contacts.

stem: A 30-year-old man who holds a Group 1 (car) driving licence has a first unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Brain MRI shows no relevant structural abnormality, EEG shows no epileptiform activity, and no underlying cause is found. He has notified the DVLA and stopped driving. Provided he has no further seizures, when can he be considered to regain his car licence?

options.A: 6 months from the date of the seizure
options.B: 12 months from the date of the seizure
options.C: 3 months from the date of the seizure
options.D: 2 years from the date of the seizure

correct_answer: A. 6 months from the date of the seizure
why_correct: After a first unprovoked seizure, a Group 1 driver must stop driving and notify the DVLA; driving must cease for 6 months from the date of the seizure, or 12 months if there is an underlying causative factor that may increase risk. His normal MRI and EEG and the absence of any cause mean the 6-month standard applies. If he has a further unprovoked seizure, the epilepsy standard (12 months seizure-free) applies instead. Group 2 (bus/lorry): 5 years off driving after a first unprovoked seizure, with no epilepsy medication throughout and a neurologist assessing the annual recurrence risk as 2% or lower (10 years seizure-free without medication for epilepsy).
why_wrong: B. 12 months applies to epilepsy (two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart) or to a first unprovoked seizure with an underlying causative factor that may increase the risk; neither is described here. C. 3 months is too short; the DVLA standard for a first unprovoked seizure is 6 months seizure-free for a car licence. D. 2 years is not the Group 1 standard for a first unprovoked seizure and would keep him off the road far longer than required. E. A single unprovoked seizure does not mean permanent loss of a car licence; he can reapply once he has been seizure-free for the required period.
pearl: First unprovoked seizure with normal imaging and EEG: 6 months off driving (car). Epilepsy, or a first seizure with a risk-raising cause: 12 months.
thinking: First unprovoked seizure in a car (Group 1) driver ↓ He must stop driving and notify the DVLA ↓ Normal MRI and EEG, no underlying cause, so no factor increasing recurrence risk ↓ DVLA standard is 6 months (12 months if a causative factor may increase risk; 12 months for epilepsy) ↓ Answer: 6 months from the date of the seizure
exam_trap: Trap — B, 12 months. The 12-month rule applies to epilepsy (two or more unprovoked seizures) or to a first unprovoked seizure with an underlying causative factor that may increase risk, such as a relevant lesion on imaging or epileptiform EEG. With normal MRI and EEG, a single unprovoked seizure requires 6 months off driving (Group 1).
takeaway: First unprovoked seizure with normal MRI and EEG: 6 months off driving (car); epilepsy: 12 months.

stem: A 6-week-old infant is brought to the GP by his mother. She is concerned that he is increasingly jaundiced, and his urine is dark yellow. He has been feeding poorly and is not gaining weight well. On examination, he has hepatomegaly. The mother asks if it is normal for his stools to be pale yellow/white (clay-coloured). What is the single most appropriate immediate next step?

options.A: Reassure that breastfed babies can have pale yellow stools
options.B: Request a conjugated bilirubin and review the result next week
options.C: Same-day paediatric referral for urgent investigation
options.D: Start home phototherapy and recheck bilirubin in 48 hours
options.E: Start ursodeoxycholic acid and review in 2 weeks

correct_answer: C. Same-day paediatric referral for urgent investigation
why_correct: Biliary atresia is a surgical emergency in neonates. The Kasai procedure (hepatoportoenterostomy) must be performed within 60 days of life to preserve liver function and avoid liver transplantation. NICE CG98 identifies pale chalky stools and/or dark urine in prolonged jaundice as features of possible biliary obstruction needing urgent paediatric assessment. Do not wait for outpatient investigations. Admit them.
why_wrong: A. Pale stools with dark urine suggest biliary obstruction and are not normal. B. Conjugated bilirubin is needed but waiting a week delays possible Kasai surgery. D. Phototherapy treats unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not address cholestasis. E. Medical treatment without diagnosis delays investigation of biliary atresia.
pearl: Pale stools and dark urine in a jaundiced baby is a red flag. They are not just 'yellow' – they are obstructed. Admit immediately.
thinking: 6-week-old + prolonged jaundice + dark urine + pale (clay-coloured) stools + hepatomegaly ↓ Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia — suspect biliary atresia ↓ Same-day paediatric referral
exam_trap: Trap — B, Check a conjugated bilirubin level Candidates think, "Let's do the blood test to confirm." While a conjugated (direct) bilirubin >20% of total is the key biochemical discriminator for biliary atresia, this test is done in the hospital, not in the GP surgery. If a GP suspects biliary atresia (pale stool + dark urine + hepatomegaly), they do NOT wait for blood tests in primary care. They make an urgent same-day referral to the paediatric unit, where the tests and ultrasound will be performed. The *immediate* action is the referral, not the blood draw.
takeaway: Pale stools and dark urine in a jaundiced baby is a red flag. They are not just 'yellow' – they are obstructed. Admit immediately.

stem: A 76-year-old woman with hypertension is taking ramipril and bendroflumethiazide. She starts taking ibuprofen regularly for knee osteoarthritis. Two weeks later her blood tests show a rise in creatinine and urea consistent with acute kidney injury. Which of her medications most likely precipitated the acute kidney injury?

options.A: Ramipril, by reducing efferent arteriolar tone
options.C: Ibuprofen (with the ACE inhibitor and diuretic)

correct_answer: C. Ibuprofen (with the ACE inhibitor and diuretic)
why_correct: The combination of an ACE inhibitor (ramipril) + a diuretic (bendroflumethiazide) + an NSAID (ibuprofen) is the classic 'triple whammy': the NSAID reduces renal perfusion while the other two impair autoregulation, precipitating acute kidney injury. Adding the NSAID was the trigger.
why_wrong: A. Ramipril was tolerated until the NSAID was added. B. The thiazide was tolerated until the NSAID was added. D. Paracetamol is not among her medications and is not nephrotoxic at usual doses. E. Amlodipine is not among her medications and does not cause AKI.
pearl: ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID = 'triple whammy' acute kidney injury.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID = 'triple whammy' acute kidney injury. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: The NSAID looks like harmless OTC pain relief; in a patient already on an ACE inhibitor and diuretic it is the nephrotoxic trigger.
takeaway: Avoid adding NSAIDs to patients on an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic.

presentation: Patient on anti-coagulant therapy / prescribing safety
stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes weekly oral methotrexate. She attends a different GP with dysuria and frequency, and a urine dip suggests a lower urinary tract infection. Which antibiotic should be avoided because of a potentially dangerous interaction with her methotrexate?
why_correct: Trimethoprim and methotrexate are both antifolates. Given together they act synergistically to suppress folate metabolism, markedly increasing the risk of bone-marrow suppression and pancytopenia. Trimethoprim should be avoided in patients taking methotrexate.
why_wrong: A. Nitrofurantoin is a recommended first-line choice for lower UTI and has no antifolate interaction with methotrexate; it is avoided mainly in significant renal impairment or near term in pregnancy. C. Cefalexin is a reasonable alternative for lower UTI and does not add to the antifolate effect of methotrexate. D. Fosfomycin is an alternative option for lower UTI and has no clinically important interaction with methotrexate. E. Pivmecillinam does not share trimethoprim's antifolate action; penicillins can reduce renal clearance of methotrexate, so a short course is used with caution and monitoring for toxicity rather than avoided.
pearl: Methotrexate + trimethoprim = double antifolate hit → risk of pancytopenia. Avoid the combination.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate + new UTI ↓ trimethoprim is also a folate antagonist ↓ additive antifolate effect → bone-marrow suppression/pancytopenia ↓ avoid trimethoprim (and co-trimoxazole)
exam_trap: A routine-looking UTI prescription hides a dangerous interaction; always check existing methotrexate before prescribing trimethoprim or co-trimoxazole.
takeaway: Never co-prescribe trimethoprim with methotrexate.

stem: A health visitor is concerned that an infant's weight has fallen across two major centile lines over several months. What is the most common underlying cause of faltering growth in this setting?
why_correct: The most common cause of faltering growth is inadequate nutritional intake (feeding difficulties, insufficient calories), which should be assessed first, including feeding history and observation of a feed.
why_wrong: A. Malabsorption from cystic fibrosis is an important but much less common cause. B. Congenital heart disease is a less common cause. D. Coeliac disease is a less common cause. E. Chronic kidney disease is a rare cause.
pearl: Faltering growth: inadequate intake is the commonest cause — assess feeding first.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Faltering growth: inadequate intake is the commonest cause — assess feeding first. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: Reaching for rare organic causes before assessing intake is the trap.
takeaway: Faltering growth: think feeding/intake first.

stem: A toddler with faltering growth develops diarrhoea, abdominal distension and irritability after weaning onto cereals. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Faltering growth with GI symptoms appearing after the introduction of gluten-containing cereals on weaning is characteristic of coeliac disease; screening (e.g. anti-tTG with total IgA) is appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric stenosis presents at a few weeks of age with projectile non-bilious vomiting, not diarrhoea and distension after weaning. B. Hirschsprung's disease typically presents with delayed passage of meconium and constipation, not diarrhoea starting with cereals. C. Lactose overload causes loose stools in infants on large milk volumes; it is not linked to starting cereals and does not explain faltering growth. D. Appendicitis is an acute illness with pain and fever, not chronic diarrhoea and faltering growth after weaning.
pearl: Faltering growth with symptoms after introducing gluten = consider coeliac disease.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Faltering growth with symptoms after introducing gluten = consider coeliac disease. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: E.
exam_trap: The timing relative to weaning onto cereals is the clue pointing to coeliac.
takeaway: Symptoms after gluten introduction: think coeliac.

stem: When assessing an infant with faltering growth, which initial step is most appropriate?

options.B: Take a detailed feeding history and observe a feed
options.D: Refer immediately for inpatient tube feeding
options.E: Perform a sweat test as the first investigation

correct_answer: B. Take a detailed feeding history and observe a feed
why_correct: Initial assessment of faltering growth centres on a detailed feeding history and observing a feed, alongside plotting growth and a focused history/examination, before investigations or interventions.
why_wrong: A. Abdominal CT involves significant radiation and is not part of the initial assessment of faltering growth without specific findings. C. Starting high-calorie supplements without assessment skips identifying the cause, such as feeding technique or an underlying illness. D. Inpatient tube feeding is reserved for severe or refractory cases after assessment, not the first step. E. A sweat test is indicated when features suggest cystic fibrosis; it is not a routine first investigation for every infant with faltering growth.
pearl: Faltering growth assessment starts with feeding history and observing a feed.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Faltering growth assessment starts with feeding history and observing a feed. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: B.
exam_trap: Jumping to investigations or interventions before the feeding assessment is the error.
takeaway: Faltering growth: assess feeding before investigating.

stem: A 7-year-old shows persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity for over six months, present both at home and at school, impairing his functioning. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start methylphenidate in primary care and review in 4 weeks
options.B: Reassure that this is normal behaviour for his age
options.C: Advise the school to arrange a fixed-term exclusion
options.D: Refer to paediatrics or CAMHS for specialist assessment
options.E: Give a parenting leaflet and review in 6 months

correct_answer: D. Refer to paediatrics or CAMHS for specialist assessment
why_correct: Where symptoms of inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity persist over time, occur in more than one setting and cause impairment, referral for specialist assessment is appropriate — diagnosis of ADHD is made by specialists, not in primary care.
why_wrong: A. ADHD medication is started by specialists after diagnosis. B. Persistent impairing symptoms in two settings are not normal. C. Exclusion does not address the likely underlying condition. E. Symptoms have persisted for six months with impairment, so further delay is inappropriate.
pearl: ADHD requires specialist diagnosis: symptoms in 2+ settings, persistent, and impairing — then refer.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ ADHD requires specialist diagnosis: symptoms in 2+ settings, persistent, and impairing — then refer. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: D.
exam_trap: Starting stimulant medication in primary care before specialist diagnosis is the trap.
takeaway: Suspected ADHD: refer for specialist assessment.

stem: For a child newly diagnosed with ADHD whose symptoms cause moderate impairment, which initial management is generally recommended before medication in many cases?

options.B: Long-term risperidone to reduce hyperactivity and impulsivity
options.C: Methylphenidate for all children at the point of diagnosis
options.D: Restricting screen time at home as the main intervention
options.E: Watchful waiting until adolescence before any treatment

correct_answer: A. Parent training and behavioural/environmental support
why_correct: Non-pharmacological measures — parent training/education programmes, behavioural strategies and school support — are recommended early, with medication considered when impairment persists or is severe (per specialist guidance).
why_wrong: B. Antipsychotics are not a treatment for ADHD. C. Medication is not routinely started at diagnosis for moderate impairment. D. Screen restriction alone is not an evidence-based ADHD intervention. E. Delaying intervention allows impairment to continue.
pearl: ADHD management often begins with parent training and behavioural/school support before medication.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ ADHD management often begins with parent training and behavioural/school support before medication. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: A.
exam_trap: 'Medicate everyone immediately' ignores first-line non-pharmacological support.
takeaway: ADHD: behavioural/parent support first in many cases.

stem: A child being assessed for possible ADHD shows symptoms only at school but not at home or elsewhere. How does this affect the likelihood of an ADHD diagnosis?

options.A: It confirms ADHD, as school is the key setting for diagnosis
options.B: It does not matter; severity and duration determine the diagnosis
options.C: It indicates a trial of medication to clarify the diagnosis
options.D: It suggests parents are under-reporting, so ADHD remains likely
options.E: It makes ADHD less likely; symptoms must occur in two or more settings

correct_answer: E. It makes ADHD less likely; symptoms must occur in two or more settings
why_correct: ADHD requires symptoms to be present in more than one setting (e.g. home and school). Symptoms confined to a single setting make ADHD less likely and prompt consideration of setting-specific factors.
why_wrong: A. A single setting does not meet the diagnostic criteria. B. Pervasiveness across settings is a diagnostic requirement. C. Medication is not used as a diagnostic test. D. Single-setting symptoms prompt consideration of setting-specific factors rather than presumed under-reporting.
pearl: ADHD symptoms must span more than one setting; single-setting symptoms point elsewhere.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ ADHD symptoms must span more than one setting; single-setting symptoms point elsewhere. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: E.
exam_trap: Assuming school symptoms alone confirm ADHD ignores the cross-setting criterion.
takeaway: ADHD needs symptoms in 2+ settings.

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of fever, lethargy and vomiting. His parents report that he has become increasingly drowsy. Examination reveals a temperature of 39.5°C, tachycardia and a widespread non-blanching purpuric rash over his trunk and legs. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Take blood cultures and await the Gram stain result before treatment
options.B: Give IV ceftriaxone immediately; investigations must not delay it
options.C: Request an urgent CT head to exclude raised ICP before any antibiotics
options.D: Lumbar puncture to confirm meningococcal infection before antibiotics
options.E: Give IV fluids and await senior paediatric review before antibiotics

correct_answer: B. Give IV ceftriaxone immediately; investigations must not delay it
why_correct: A febrile child with a non-blanching purpuric rash should be assumed to have meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. In hospital, NICE NG240 recommends intravenous ceftriaxone (1.7.1), given without delay (NG240 1.5.1 sets a 1-hour target from arrival for suspected meningococcal disease). Blood tests are taken first if they cause no delay, but investigations must not hold up antibiotics, and lumbar puncture is not performed first in suspected meningococcal septicaemia. Outside hospital, NG240 (1.2.5) advises IV or IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin as soon as possible, unless this would delay transfer.
why_wrong: A. Cultures may be taken but must not delay antibiotics. C. Imaging must not delay antibiotics. D. LP is contraindicated in suspected meningococcal septicaemia and delays treatment. E. Antibiotics must not wait for senior review.
pearl: Fever + non-blanching rash = meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Fever + non-blanching rash = meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: B.
exam_trap: Candidates often choose investigations first. In meningococcal sepsis, treatment comes before confirmation.
takeaway: Suspected meningococcal disease in hospital → intravenous ceftriaxone without delay (pre-hospital: IV/IM ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin unless it delays transfer).

stem: A parent brings a well-looking 2-year-old with a mild self-limiting viral illness, anxious that something serious is being missed. Examination is reassuring with no red flags. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Admit the child for 24 hours of observation to reassure the parent
options.B: Prescribe amoxicillin as a precaution against bacterial infection
options.C: Arrange blood tests and a chest X-ray to exclude serious illness
options.D: Reassure the parent and give clear safety-netting advice
options.E: Reassure the parent and discharge without further advice

correct_answer: D. Reassure the parent and give clear safety-netting advice
why_correct: A well child with no red flags needs reassurance plus explicit safety-netting: telling the parent which specific features should prompt re-presentation and where to seek help. This respects the parent's concern while avoiding over-medicalisation.
why_wrong: A. Admission of a well child without red flags is unnecessary. B. Antibiotics are not indicated for a viral illness. C. Investigations are not indicated in a well child without red flags. E. Reassurance without safety-netting leaves the parent unsure when to return.
pearl: Well child, anxious parent: reassurance plus explicit safety-netting.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Well child, anxious parent: reassurance plus explicit safety-netting. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: D.
exam_trap: Both over-investigation and curt dismissal are wrong; safety-netting is the balance.
takeaway: Worried parent, well child: reassure and safety-net.

stem: Which tool helps assess the risk of serious illness in a feverish young child and guides the response to a worried parent?
correct_answer: B. The NICE traffic light system
why_correct: The NICE traffic light system stratifies the risk of serious illness in feverish under-5s using colour-coded features, guiding management and what to tell parents.
why_wrong: A. The Glasgow Coma Scale measures conscious level only and is not designed to stratify the risk of serious illness in a feverish child. C. CHA2DS2-VASc estimates stroke risk in adults with atrial fibrillation and has no role in childhood fever. D. The Wells score estimates the probability of venous thromboembolism in adults, not serious illness in feverish children. E. CURB-65 grades the severity of community-acquired pneumonia in adults and is not validated in children.
pearl: Feverish young child risk stratification: NICE traffic light system.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Feverish young child risk stratification: NICE traffic light system. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: B.
exam_trap: Adult risk scores (Wells, CURB-65, CHA2DS2-VASc) are distractors for a paediatric fever question.
takeaway: Feverish child: use the NICE traffic light system.

stem: A parent is hesitant about routine childhood immunisations and asks for your advice. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Explain that routine vaccines are a legal requirement in the UK
options.B: Explain the practice will deregister the child unless vaccinated
options.C: Agree to delay all vaccines until the immune system is stronger
options.D: Explore concerns, give evidence-based information and respect their decision
options.E: Refer to children's social care on the grounds of medical neglect

correct_answer: D. Explore concerns, give evidence-based information and respect their decision
why_correct: Vaccine hesitancy is best addressed by exploring the parent's specific concerns, providing clear evidence-based information, and supporting informed consent — which in the UK is the parent's decision for routine immunisation.
why_wrong: A. Vaccination is not compulsory in the UK. B. Threatening deregistration is coercive and damages trust. C. Delaying vaccines increases the period of vulnerability and is not evidence-based. E. Vaccine hesitancy alone is not a safeguarding concern.
pearl: Vaccine hesitancy: explore concerns, inform, respect parental consent.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Vaccine hesitancy: explore concerns, inform, respect parental consent. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: D.
exam_trap: Coercive or dismissive options are wrong; informed consent and dialogue are key.
takeaway: Vaccine hesitancy: explore, inform, respect consent.

presentation: Mental health problems in pregnancy or postpartum / seizures
stem: A 29-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation presents with severe headache, visual disturbance and epigastric pain. Her blood pressure is 170/115 mmHg and urinalysis shows 3+ protein. While being assessed she develops a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
why_correct: This patient has eclampsia. Magnesium sulfate is the first-line treatment for prevention and control of eclamptic seizures. Blood pressure management and delivery planning are important but follow immediate seizure management.
why_wrong: A. Diazepam is not first-line for eclamptic seizures; magnesium sulfate is more effective at stopping and preventing recurrent fits. B. Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulfate in eclampsia and is not recommended as first-line. D. Labetalol is needed to control her severe hypertension, but stopping the seizure with magnesium sulfate comes first. E. Delivery is the definitive treatment, but the mother must be stabilised (seizure controlled, blood pressure treated) before delivery is undertaken.
pearl: Eclamptic seizure = magnesium sulfate.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Eclamptic seizure = magnesium sulfate. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: Do not treat eclampsia like standard epilepsy.
takeaway: Seizure in pre-eclampsia → IV magnesium sulfate first.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with 6 weeks of amenorrhoea, left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. A urine pregnancy test is positive and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.D: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast

why_correct: In a haemodynamically stable woman with a positive pregnancy test and pain or bleeding, transvaginal ultrasound is the initial investigation to locate the pregnancy and assess for an ectopic pregnancy, often alongside serial serum beta-hCG.
why_wrong: A. X-ray has no role in suspected ectopic pregnancy. C. Laparoscopy is not the first investigation in a stable patient. D. CT involves radiation and is not the investigation for early pregnancy. E. Serum progesterone is not recommended to diagnose ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: Positive pregnancy test + pain/bleeding + stable = transvaginal ultrasound (with serial beta-hCG).
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Positive pregnancy test + pain/bleeding + stable = transvaginal ultrasound (with serial beta-hCG). ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: B.
exam_trap: If the woman were haemodynamically unstable, the answer shifts to resuscitation and urgent surgery — read the stability detail.
takeaway: Suspected ectopic, stable patient: transvaginal ultrasound first.

stem: A 72-year-old reports transient loss of vision in one eye, a tender scalp, jaw pain when chewing, and a raised ESR. What is the most appropriate immediate action to prevent permanent blindness?

options.D: Reassure and review in two weeks
options.E: Start aspirin alone and wait for biopsy

why_correct: This is giant cell (temporal) arteritis; high-dose corticosteroids must be started urgently on clinical suspicion to prevent irreversible visual loss, without waiting for temporal artery biopsy.
why_wrong: A. A routine ophthalmology appointment risks irreversible blindness in suspected giant cell arteritis; treatment must start the same day. B. Topical antibiotics treat surface eye infection and are irrelevant to an arteritic cause of visual loss. D. Reassuring and reviewing in two weeks risks permanent visual loss, especially after transient visual symptoms. E. Waiting for biopsy delays steroids and risks blindness; biopsy remains positive for some time after steroids are started, so treatment should not be withheld.
pearl: Suspected giant cell arteritis: start high-dose steroids immediately — do not wait for biopsy.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Suspected giant cell arteritis: start high-dose steroids immediately — do not wait for biopsy. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: 'Confirm with biopsy first' is the dangerous trap; treat on suspicion to save sight.
takeaway: GCA: urgent high-dose steroids to save vision.

stem: A patient describes sudden floaters and flashing lights followed by a 'curtain' descending across the vision of one eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Flashes and floaters followed by a progressing 'curtain' or shadow over the visual field is the classic description of retinal detachment, which requires urgent ophthalmology referral.
why_wrong: A. Migraine aura usually causes positive visual phenomena such as zigzags that resolve within an hour, not a persisting curtain over one eye. B. Cataract causes gradual painless blurring or glare, not sudden flashes, floaters and a curtain. C. Dry age-related macular degeneration causes gradual central visual loss, not an acute peripheral shadow. D. Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins and does not cause flashes, floaters or field loss.
pearl: Flashes, floaters, then a 'curtain' = retinal detachment — urgent referral.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Flashes, floaters, then a 'curtain' = retinal detachment — urgent referral. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: E.
exam_trap: Gradual conditions (cataract, AMD) don't cause the acute curtain of detachment.
takeaway: Curtain over vision with flashes/floaters = retinal detachment.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with sudden severe pain in her right eye. She reports blurred vision, seeing haloes around lights and feeling nauseated. Examination reveals a red eye, cloudy cornea and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Routine ophthalmology referral and lubricating eye drops meanwhile
options.B: Chloramphenicol eye drops four times daily and review in 48 hours
options.C: Urgent ophthalmology referral and pressure-lowering drugs
options.D: High-dose oral prednisolone today and an urgent ESR and CRP check
options.E: Dilating drops (tropicamide 1%) to examine the fundus fully

correct_answer: C. Urgent ophthalmology referral and pressure-lowering drugs
why_correct: This is acute angle-closure glaucoma, a sight-threatening emergency caused by a sudden rise in intraocular pressure. Immediate pressure reduction and urgent ophthalmology involvement are required to prevent permanent visual loss.
why_wrong: A. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency, not for routine referral. B. This is not infective conjunctivitis. D. Steroids with ESR and CRP are for giant cell arteritis, which does not cause a fixed mid-dilated pupil with corneal clouding. E. Dilating the pupil worsens angle closure.
pearl: Painful red eye + haloes + fixed mid-dilated pupil = acute angle-closure glaucoma.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Painful red eye + haloes + fixed mid-dilated pupil = acute angle-closure glaucoma. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: Do not mistake acute angle-closure glaucoma for conjunctivitis.
takeaway: Acute angle-closure glaucoma → urgent ophthalmology referral and immediate pressure-lowering treatment.

stem: A patient has multiple persistent physical symptoms for which thorough, appropriate investigation has found no organic cause. They remain distressed and request further tests. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Order a broad further panel of blood tests and whole-body imaging to reassure the patient
options.B: Explain that the symptoms are psychological in origin and discharge them to their GP
options.C: Acknowledge distress, avoid needless tests, offer regular review with one clinician
options.D: Refer to several different specialists at once to exclude rare organic causes of symptoms
options.E: Discharge from follow-up, advising them to return if new or changing symptoms develop

correct_answer: C. Acknowledge distress, avoid needless tests, offer regular review with one clinician
why_correct: For medically unexplained (functional) symptoms after adequate assessment, best practice is to validate the patient's distress, avoid repeated unnecessary investigations (which reinforce illness behaviour and risk iatrogenic harm), and provide continuity through regular review with one clinician.
why_wrong: A. Repeated tests reinforce illness concern and risk harm. B. Dismissive explanations damage trust and do not help. D. Multiple referrals fragment care and increase harm. E. Discharge removes the continuity of care that helps these patients.
pearl: Medically unexplained symptoms: validate, avoid over-investigation, provide continuity of care.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Medically unexplained symptoms: validate, avoid over-investigation, provide continuity of care. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: C.
exam_trap: Both extremes — endless tests and dismissive discharge — are wrong; the answer is validation plus continuity.
takeaway: MUS: acknowledge, don't over-investigate, ensure continuity.

stem: Which principle best reduces iatrogenic harm when managing a patient with medically unexplained symptoms?

options.A: Repeat normal tests at each visit to provide ongoing reassurance to the patient
options.B: Prescribe opioid analgesia early to control the patient's physical symptoms
options.C: Avoid offering any explanation of symptoms, to prevent increasing patient worry
options.D: Rotate the responsible clinician regularly to gain fresh diagnostic perspectives
options.E: Limit repeat tests and referrals while keeping a supportive relationship

correct_answer: E. Limit repeat tests and referrals while keeping a supportive relationship
why_correct: Limiting unnecessary repeated tests and referrals, while keeping a consistent supportive therapeutic relationship, reduces the iatrogenic harm and reinforcement of illness behaviour that can result from over-medicalisation.
why_wrong: A. Repeating tests reinforces illness concern and risks harm. B. Early opioids carry risk of dependence and harm. C. A clear explanation is part of management. D. Changing clinicians fragments care and leads to more investigation.
pearl: Continuity plus restraint in investigation limits iatrogenic harm in functional disorders.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Continuity plus restraint in investigation limits iatrogenic harm in functional disorders. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: E.
exam_trap: 'Reassuring' repeat tests actually perpetuate the problem.
takeaway: MUS: fewer tests, steady relationship, clear explanation.

stem: A patient with a functional symptom disorder might benefit from which evidence-based treatment alongside a supportive doctor–patient relationship?
why_correct: Cognitive behavioural therapy has evidence for functional/medically unexplained symptom disorders, helping patients understand and manage symptoms alongside a supportive clinical relationship.
why_wrong: A. Long-term opioids carry dependence risk and do not help functional symptoms. C. Courses of antibiotics have no role without infection. D. Repeated endoscopy reinforces illness concern and risks harm. E. Prolonged rest leads to deconditioning and worsens symptoms.
pearl: CBT is an evidence-based option in functional symptom disorders.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ CBT is an evidence-based option in functional symptom disorders. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: B.
exam_trap: Pharmacological/procedural distractors offer harm, not help, here.
takeaway: MUS: consider CBT, not opioids or more procedures.

stem: A 75-year-old woman reports a sensation of 'something coming down' from her back passage on defecation, with mucus discharge and occasional bleeding. On examination during straining, a protruding mass with concentric (circular) mucosal folds is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Full-thickness rectal prolapse classically produces a protruding mass with concentric (circular) mucosal folds, often with mucus discharge and bleeding, typically in older women. The concentric folds distinguish it from haemorrhoids.
why_wrong: A. An anal skin tag is a small, fixed external fold of skin present at rest; it does not protrude on straining or show concentric mucosal folds. B. Prolapsing internal haemorrhoids appear as discrete vascular cushions separated by radial folds, not as a circumferential mass with concentric rings. C. An anal fissure causes sharp pain on defecation with bright red blood and sometimes a sentinel tag; it does not produce a prolapsing mass. D. Rectal carcinoma must be excluded (by endoscopy) because it can cause bleeding and mucus, but it presents as an irregular mass or change in bowel habit, not a reducible prolapse with concentric folds on straining.
pearl: Concentric (circular) mucosal folds = rectal prolapse; radial folds = haemorrhoids.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Concentric (circular) mucosal folds = rectal prolapse; radial folds = haemorrhoids. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: E.
exam_trap: Distinguishing rectal prolapse from prolapsing haemorrhoids hinges on the pattern of the folds — concentric versus radial.
takeaway: Protruding mass with concentric folds in an older woman = rectal prolapse.

stem: An otherwise fit 70-year-old man has a symptomatic full-thickness rectal prolapse that recurs after each bowel motion. Conservative measures for his constipation have not resolved it. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
correct_answer: B. Surgical repair, such as rectopexy
why_correct: Definitive treatment of full-thickness rectal prolapse is surgical. In a fit patient, an abdominal rectopexy is commonly chosen; frailer patients may have a perineal procedure (e.g. Delorme's or Altemeier's). Addressing constipation is supportive but not definitive.
why_wrong: A: Laxatives help underlying constipation but do not correct an established full-thickness prolapse. C: Banding treats haemorrhoids, not rectal prolapse. D: Steroid cream has no role in correcting prolapse. E: A symptomatic, recurrent prolapse warrants definitive treatment.
pearl: Definitive treatment of full-thickness rectal prolapse is surgical — rectopexy (abdominal) in the fit, perineal procedures in the frail.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Definitive treatment of full-thickness rectal prolapse is surgical — rectopexy (abdominal) in the fit, perineal procedures in the frail. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: B.
exam_trap: Banding and laxatives are distractors borrowed from haemorrhoid/constipation management — they do not fix a true prolapse.
takeaway: Symptomatic full-thickness rectal prolapse = surgical repair.

stem: A 2-year-old child is brought in after a recurrent rectal prolapse. The parents have noticed the child has bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools and poor weight gain. Which underlying condition is most important to exclude?
why_correct: Rectal prolapse in a young child is a recognised presentation of cystic fibrosis, especially with steatorrhoea (bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools) and faltering growth from pancreatic insufficiency. CF should be actively excluded (e.g. sweat test).
why_wrong: A. Cow's milk protein allergy can cause loose stools and faltering growth in infancy, but it presents with atopic or GI symptoms such as vomiting, eczema or bloody stools, not steatorrhoea with recurrent rectal prolapse. B. Coeliac disease can cause faltering growth and loose stools, but recurrent rectal prolapse with greasy, foul-smelling stools is the classic pancreatic-insufficiency picture of cystic fibrosis, which must be excluded first. C. Hirschsprung's disease presents with delayed passage of meconium, constipation and abdominal distension, not steatorrhoea and rectal prolapse. E. Intussusception presents acutely with colicky pain, vomiting and redcurrant-jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass, not recurrent prolapse with chronic malabsorption.
pearl: Rectal prolapse in a child — exclude cystic fibrosis, particularly with steatorrhoea and faltering growth.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ Rectal prolapse in a child — exclude cystic fibrosis, particularly with steatorrhoea and faltering growth. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: D.
exam_trap: This is the classic paediatric link: child + rectal prolapse should immediately prompt thoughts of cystic fibrosis.
takeaway: Child with rectal prolapse = exclude cystic fibrosis.

stem: A patient who has been off work for 5 days with a self-limiting viral illness asks you to provide a fit note for their employer. They have now recovered and are returning to work. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Refer them to occupational health, who certify short absences
options.B: Issue a fit note backdated to the first day of illness, covering all 5 days
options.C: Issue a fit note covering the 5 days off, as they are now well
options.D: Explain that they can self-certify for up to 7 days; no fit note is needed
options.E: Decline and refer them to the employer's occupational health for a certificate

correct_answer: D. Explain that they can self-certify for up to 7 days; no fit note is needed
why_correct: For absences of 7 calendar days or fewer, employees self-certify (e.g. form SC2); a fit note from a healthcare professional is not required. The patient simply informs their employer.
why_wrong: A. Occupational health is not needed; the employee self-certifies short absences. B. A fit note is not required for 7 days or fewer. C. A fit note is not required for an absence of 5 days. E. Self-certification covers this absence; no certificate from occupational health is needed.
pearl: 7 calendar days or fewer: self-certification (SC2). A fit note is only needed beyond 7 days.
thinking: Absence of 5 days, now recovered ↓ 7 calendar days or fewer = self-certification (SC2 if the employer needs a form) ↓ fit note only needed after 7 days
exam_trap: Issuing an unnecessary fit note for a short illness is the wrong move — recognise the self-certification window.
takeaway: First 7 days off = self-certify; no fit note required.

stem: A patient recovering from a back injury has been off work for three weeks. They feel able to return if they avoid heavy lifting and start with shorter hours. Which option on the fit note best reflects this?

options.A: 'May be fit for work', suggesting amended duties and a phased return
options.B: 'Not fit for work' for four more weeks to allow full recovery
options.C: Leave both boxes blank and let the employer decide on duties
options.D: 'Fit for work', with a note suggesting he avoid heavy lifting
options.E: A private letter to the employer recommending light duties

correct_answer: A. 'May be fit for work', suggesting amended duties and a phased return
why_correct: The fit note offers two options: 'not fit for work' or 'may be fit for work'. The latter lets the clinician suggest adjustments — phased return, amended duties, altered hours, or workplace adaptations — which fits this patient exactly.
why_wrong: B. He feels able to return with adjustments, so 'not fit' prolongs absence unnecessarily. C. The fit note must state the clinician's assessment. D. The fit note has no 'fit for work' option; 'may be fit' is used with adjustments. E. The fit note is the appropriate statutory document for this advice.
pearl: 'May be fit for work' lets you recommend phased return, amended duties, altered hours or workplace adaptations.
thinking: Identify what the question is really asking. ↓ 'May be fit for work' lets you recommend phased return, amended duties, altered hours or workplace adaptations. ↓ Eliminate the inferior options. ↓ Select the single best answer: A.
exam_trap: There is no 'fit for work' tick box that mandates full duties — the choice is 'not fit' or 'may be fit', the latter carrying adjustment advice.
takeaway: Able to return with adjustments = 'may be fit for work' with suggested amendments.

stem: A patient tells you their employer 'has to' put in place the amended duties suggested on their fit note. Which statement reflects the correct understanding of the fit note?

options.A: It is a binding medical instruction that the employer must follow
options.B: The employer is legally obliged to implement every adjustment suggested
options.C: It is advice; the employer decides whether adjustments can be accommodated
options.D: Adjustments can be suggested by occupational health, not the treating clinician
options.E: Adjustments are mandatory for 12 weeks and then become optional

correct_answer: C. It is advice; the employer decides whether adjustments can be accommodated
why_correct: The fit note provides professional advice about fitness for work and possible adjustments. It is not binding: the employer considers the advice and decides what is feasible. If the employer cannot accommodate the suggested adjustments, the fit note effectively functions as not fit for work for the duration stated.
why_wrong: A. The fit note is advice, not a binding instruction. B. The employer is not legally obliged to follow the fit note's suggested adjustments. D. The treating clinician can suggest adjustments on the fit note. E. There is no period in which adjustments become mandatory.
pearl: A fit note advises; the employer decides. If adjustments cannot be accommodated, the note effectively functions as not fit for work for the duration stated.
thinking: 'May be fit for work' with adjustments ↓ fit note is advice, not a binding instruction ↓ employer decides whether adjustments are feasible ↓ if not, it is treated as not fit for work for the stated period
exam_trap: Candidates assume the fit note compels the employer — it does not. It is advice, not instruction.
takeaway: Fit note = advice to the employer, not a binding order.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with sudden onset severe abdominal and back pain. He is pale, clammy, hypotensive (BP 78/50 mmHg) and confused. You feel a pulsatile abdominal mass. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent CT angiography to confirm rupture before intervention
options.B: IV antibiotics for presumed sepsis and observe
options.C: IV morphine and reassess after fluid resuscitation
options.D: Emergency vascular surgery referral and transfer to theatre
options.E: Admit to the surgical ward for observation and serial examination

correct_answer: D. Emergency vascular surgery referral and transfer to theatre
why_correct: This is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm with haemodynamic instability — a time-critical surgical emergency. The correct action is immediate vascular surgical activation and transfer to theatre; imaging must not delay definitive treatment in an unstable patient.
why_wrong: A. Formal CT must not delay vascular referral in a shocked patient; any CT angiography is decided by the vascular team once the patient is under their care. B. The picture is a ruptured AAA, not sepsis. C. Analgesia and reassessment delays definitive treatment, and aggressive fluid resuscitation is avoided (permissive hypotension). E. Ward observation delays definitive vascular treatment of a ruptured AAA.
pearl: Ruptured AAA (pulsatile mass + back pain + shock): bedside ultrasound in ED can confirm the aneurysm, but discuss immediately with the regional vascular service, use permissive hypotension, and do not let imaging delay transfer.
thinking: Pulsatile mass + abdominal/back pain + shock in an older man ↓ Ruptured AAA until proven otherwise ↓ Immediate vascular surgical referral; imaging must not delay it ↓ Permissive hypotension during transfer
exam_trap: Do not let formal imaging delay vascular referral in a shocked patient with a pulsatile mass.
takeaway: Suspected ruptured AAA with instability → straight to emergency vascular surgery.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 2 hours of crushing central chest pain radiating to his left arm. His ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.E: IV morphine and await cardiology review

why_correct: Inferior STEMI (ST elevation in II, III, aVF). Primary PCI is the gold-standard reperfusion strategy when deliverable within 120 minutes of first medical contact — superior vessel patency and mortality benefit over thrombolysis.
why_wrong: B: thrombolysis is reserved for when PCI is unavailable within 120 minutes. C: aspirin is adjunctive, not definitive reperfusion. D: CABG is not first-line acute reperfusion. E: symptom relief without reperfusion is inadequate.
pearl: Inferior STEMI — check V3R/V4R for right ventricular involvement; avoid nitrates if RV infarction present.
thinking: Identify territory from leads: inferior = II,III,aVF; anterior = V1-V4; lateral = I,aVL,V5-V6.
exam_trap: Choosing thrombolysis when PCI is available — the clinical context implies a PCI centre.
takeaway: Primary PCI is first-line for STEMI when deliverable within 120 minutes.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 30%) is on bisoprolol, ramipril, and furosemide. eGFR 52, potassium 4.2 mmol/L. What additional drug should be started?
why_correct: A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone) is Class I indicated in HFrEF on top of ACEi and beta-blocker. It reduces mortality and hospitalisation. eGFR >45 and K+ <5.0 make it safe here. The four pillars of HFrEF now include an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin) as a standard agent regardless of diabetes status (NICE NG106; ESC 2021).
why_wrong: B. Digoxin is an add-on for persistent symptoms or AF and does not reduce mortality. C. Amlodipine has no prognostic benefit in HFrEF. D. Ivabradine is considered in sinus rhythm with HR ≥75 despite optimised therapy. E. Nitrates (with hydralazine) are an alternative when ACE inhibitors/ARBs are not tolerated, not an add-on here.
pearl: The four pillars of HFrEF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2 inhibitor.
thinking: Optimise guideline-directed medical therapy before considering device therapy.
exam_trap: Adding ivabradine without first checking that heart rate criteria are met.
takeaway: MRA is the standard third agent in HFrEF on ACEi and beta-blocker, provided renal function and K+ allow.

stem: An 80-year-old woman presents with exertional dyspnoea and near-syncope. There is a slow-rising pulse, ejection systolic murmur loudest at the right second intercostal space radiating to the carotids, and soft S2. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
why_correct: Clinical features are classic for severe aortic stenosis. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirms diagnosis, quantifies gradient and valve area, and assesses LV function — essential before any further management.
why_wrong: A: exercise testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe AS due to haemodynamic compromise risk. B: angiogram may follow for surgical planning but is not the first investigation. C: MRI is not first-line for valve assessment. E: carotid Doppler does not assess cardiac valves.
pearl: The triad of AS: angina, syncope, dyspnoea (heart failure). Once symptoms appear, average survival without valve replacement is approximately 5, 3 and 2 years respectively.
thinking: Slow-rising pulse + ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids = AS until proven otherwise.
exam_trap: Ordering exercise testing in a symptomatic patient — it is contraindicated in severe symptomatic AS.
takeaway: Echo is the investigation of choice for suspected aortic stenosis.

stem: A 55-year-old Black African man is diagnosed with stage 1 hypertension (clinic BP 148/92). He has no other comorbidities. What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?
why_correct: NICE recommends a calcium channel blocker as first-line for people of Black African or Caribbean origin at any age, or for those over 55. Black African patients have low renin states, making CCBs more effective than ACE inhibitors.
why_wrong: A: ACE inhibitors are less effective as first-line in Black African patients and carry higher angioedema risk. C: beta-blockers are not first-line antihypertensives. D: alpha-blockers are fourth-line agents. E: thiazide-like diuretics are an alternative but CCB is preferred.
pearl: ABCD rule: A = ACEi/ARB (younger, non-Black), B = beta-blocker (4th line), C = CCB (older or Black), D = diuretic (thiazide-like).
thinking: Ethnicity and age guide first-line antihypertensive choice per NICE guidance.
exam_trap: Prescribing ramipril first-line in a Black patient — less effective and higher angioedema risk.
takeaway: CCB is first-line antihypertensive for Black African patients and those over 55.

stem: A 45-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer presents with progressive dyspnoea, hypotension (BP 88/60), and elevated JVP. Heart sounds are muffled. ECG shows electrical alternans. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_correct: Beck's triad (hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled heart sounds) plus electrical alternans confirms cardiac tamponade — a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate pericardiocentesis to relieve pericardial pressure.
why_wrong: B. Fluid may temporise but does not relieve tamponade. C. Diuretics reduce preload and worsen haemodynamics in tamponade. D. Thoracotomy is not indicated when pericardiocentesis can relieve tamponade. E. Steroids do not relieve acute tamponade.
pearl: Electrical alternans (beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation) on ECG is highly specific for large pericardial effusion with tamponade.
thinking: Tamponade = obstructive shock. The only definitive treatment is drainage.
exam_trap: Giving furosemide — this worsens tamponade by reducing preload in an already preload-dependent state.
takeaway: Cardiac tamponade requires immediate pericardiocentesis — diuretics are harmful.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with 90 minutes of chest pain. Troponin T is elevated at 65 ng/L (normal <14). ECG shows ST depression in V4-V6. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial antiplatelet regimen?
correct_answer: E. Aspirin 300 mg plus ticagrelor 180 mg
why_correct: NSTEMI requires dual antiplatelet therapy. Current NICE and ESC guidance favours aspirin plus ticagrelor over aspirin plus clopidogrel, given superiority demonstrated in the PLATO trial. Ticagrelor is preferred unless contraindicated or there is a high bleeding risk.
why_wrong: A: single antiplatelet therapy is inferior. B: monotherapy is insufficient. C: aspirin plus clopidogrel is acceptable but ticagrelor is preferred. D: ticagrelor without aspirin is not standard practice.
pearl: Ticagrelor does not require hepatic activation unlike clopidogrel — faster and more consistent platelet inhibition.
thinking: NSTEMI = non-ST elevation with troponin rise; manage with DAPT and risk-stratify with GRACE score.
exam_trap: Using clopidogrel instead of ticagrelor — ticagrelor is now the preferred P2Y12 inhibitor in ACS.
takeaway: Aspirin plus ticagrelor is the preferred dual antiplatelet therapy in NSTEMI.

stem: A 70-year-old man collapses. ECG shows P waves at 80 bpm with no fixed relationship to broad QRS complexes occurring at 38 bpm. He is haemodynamically compromised. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.A: IV atropine 500 micrograms (up to 3 mg total in incremental doses)

why_correct: Complete (third-degree) heart block with haemodynamic compromise requires immediate transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous or permanent pacing — the most rapidly available intervention.
why_wrong: A: RCUK 2025 advises not giving atropine in high-degree AV block with a wide QRS — it is ineffective and may worsen the block. B: a 1 mg IV bolus is the cardiac arrest dose; in bradycardia adrenaline is used only as a 2–10 mcg/min infusion interim measure. D: permanent pacemaker requires assessment and planning. E: observation is inappropriate in haemodynamic compromise.
pearl: In complete heart block, atropine may accelerate atrial rate but rarely improves ventricular rate — transcutaneous pacing is preferred.
thinking: P waves and QRS complexes marching independently = complete heart block.
exam_trap: Giving maximum-dose atropine expecting it to work reliably in complete heart block.
takeaway: Haemodynamically unstable complete heart block: immediate transcutaneous pacing.

stem: A 35-year-old IV drug user presents with 2 weeks of fever, night sweats, and fatigue. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge and splinter haemorrhages. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which valve is most likely affected?
why_correct: IV drug users are predisposed to right-sided endocarditis, most commonly the tricuspid valve. Pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge = tricuspid regurgitation. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common organism.
why_wrong: A: mitral valve is more commonly affected in community-acquired endocarditis in non-drug users. B: aortic valve endocarditis produces an early diastolic murmur. D: pulmonary valve endocarditis is rare. E: tricuspid predominates specifically in IV drug use.
pearl: Right-sided endocarditis causes septic pulmonary emboli — multiple nodular opacities on CXR.
thinking: IV drug use = tricuspid endocarditis. Native valve disease / prosthetic = left-sided.
exam_trap: Assuming mitral or aortic valve — always consider right-sided endocarditis in IV drug users.
takeaway: IV drug use classically causes tricuspid valve endocarditis with Staphylococcus aureus.

stem: A 78-year-old woman presents with acute severe breathlessness, SpO2 88%, bilateral crackles to mid-zones. CXR shows bilateral alveolar shadowing and upper lobe diversion. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_correct: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema requires IV furosemide, which provides rapid venodilation within minutes before its diuretic effect, reducing preload and relieving pulmonary congestion. IV route gives faster and more reliable effect than oral. Initial management also includes oxygen and, if the patient is hypertensive, nitrates (e.g. GTN); furosemide is not the only first-line element.
why_wrong: A: salbutamol treats bronchospasm, not fluid overload. C: oral furosemide absorption is reduced in acute congestion. D: oxygen corrects hypoxaemia but does not treat the underlying cause. E: dexamethasone treats inflammatory pulmonary oedema, not cardiogenic.
pearl: IV furosemide's first action is venodilation (within 15 minutes); diuresis follows within 30-60 minutes.
thinking: Acute pulmonary oedema = cardiogenic emergency. Priorities: oxygenation, venodilation, diuresis.
exam_trap: Giving oral furosemide — splanchnic hypoperfusion in acute heart failure impairs oral absorption.
takeaway: IV furosemide is first-line for acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents with sharp central chest pain worse on lying flat, relieved by sitting forward. He had a viral URTI 2 weeks ago. ECG shows saddle-shaped ST elevation in multiple leads with PR depression. What is the first-line treatment?
why_correct: Viral pericarditis is treated with NSAIDs plus colchicine. The COPE and ICAP trials demonstrated that adding colchicine to NSAIDs significantly reduces recurrence. Ibuprofen is preferred; avoid in post-MI pericarditis.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin without colchicine carries a higher recurrence risk. B. Corticosteroids increase recurrence risk and are reserved for specific causes or when NSAIDs/colchicine are contraindicated. D. Viral pericarditis does not require antibiotics. E. Pericardiocentesis is for tamponade or suspected purulent effusion, not uncomplicated pericarditis.
pearl: PR depression on ECG in multiple leads is highly specific for pericarditis.
thinking: Saddle-shaped ST elevation + PR depression + pleuritic positional chest pain = pericarditis.
exam_trap: Prescribing steroids first-line — they increase recurrence rates in viral pericarditis.
takeaway: Acute pericarditis: NSAID plus colchicine — steroids are not first-line.

stem: A 40-year-old male athlete attends for a health check. His resting ECG shows PR interval of 220 ms. He is entirely asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: First-degree heart block (PR >200 ms) in an asymptomatic athlete is a common benign finding related to high vagal tone. No treatment or referral is required and it often resolves with exercise.
why_wrong: B. Holter and exercise testing are not needed for asymptomatic first-degree block in an athlete. C. Referral is unnecessary for an isolated benign finding. D. Pacing is for symptomatic or advanced (second/third-degree) block. E. Bisoprolol would further slow AV conduction.
pearl: Athletes commonly have first-degree block, Wenckebach, and sinus bradycardia due to high vagal tone — all benign.
thinking: First-degree block = prolonged PR, all P waves conduct, no dropped beats.
exam_trap: Over-investigating asymptomatic first-degree block in an athlete.
takeaway: First-degree heart block in an asymptomatic athlete requires only reassurance.

stem: A 65-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy presents with palpitations. ECG shows broad complex tachycardia at 160 bpm. He is conscious with BP 95/60. What is the most appropriate management?
why_correct: Broad complex tachycardia in ischaemic cardiomyopathy is VT until proven otherwise; RCUK 2025 recommends synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation/anaesthesia for monomorphic VT with structural heart disease, and borderline BP makes this more urgent.
why_wrong: A: amiodarone (or procainamide) is reserved for when cardioversion fails or sedation risk is high. B: adenosine is for narrow complex SVT and is dangerous in VT. D: unsynchronised is for VF or pulseless VT. E: verapamil is contraindicated in broad complex tachycardia/VT.
pearl: Never give verapamil for broad complex tachycardia — it causes haemodynamic collapse in VT.
thinking: Broad complex tachycardia in a patient with cardiac disease = VT until proven otherwise.
exam_trap: Using adenosine or verapamil in broad complex tachycardia — both are dangerous if it is VT.
takeaway: Haemodynamically unstable VT requires synchronised DC cardioversion.

stem: A 22-year-old woman attends A&E with an acute asthma attack. She is too breathless to complete sentences. Peak flow is 40% predicted, SpO2 92%, pulse 115 bpm. She has had one salbutamol nebuliser. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: IV aminophylline loading dose followed by a continuous infusion now
options.B: Discharge on a higher-dose ICS/LABA inhaler with GP review in 48 hours
options.C: Oral prednisolone 40-50 mg and back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers
options.D: IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 20 minutes and repeat the assessment
options.E: Rapid sequence induction, intubation and ICU admission

correct_answer: C. Oral prednisolone 40-50 mg and back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers
why_correct: PEFR 33-50% with inability to complete sentences = acute severe asthma. BTS/SIGN acute asthma management: back-to-back (oxygen-driven) salbutamol nebulisers, adding ipratropium, and oral prednisolone 40-50 mg promptly.
why_wrong: A. IV aminophylline is a later, senior-led option after nebulised bronchodilators, steroids and magnesium. B. Discharge is unsafe in acute severe asthma with SpO2 92%. D. IV magnesium is considered if response to initial bronchodilators is poor, but it does not replace systemic steroids and repeated nebulisers. E. Intubation is for life-threatening or near-fatal asthma with exhaustion or rising CO2.
pearl: Life-threatening asthma: SpO2 <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor respiratory effort, PEFR <33%, confusion, exhaustion.
thinking: Classify severity, then escalate management stepwise — steroids within 1 hour.
exam_trap: Giving IV magnesium before steroids and adequate bronchodilators.
takeaway: Acute severe asthma: back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers plus oral prednisolone within 1 hour.

stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD is admitted with increased dyspnoea and purulent sputum. ABG on air: pH 7.29, PaO2 7.1 kPa, PaCO2 7.8 kPa, HCO3 31 mmol/L. What does this pattern represent?

options.B: Acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure, partially compensated
options.D: Chronic type 2 respiratory failure, fully metabolically compensated

correct_answer: B. Acute-on-chronic type 2 respiratory failure, partially compensated
why_correct: pH 7.29 = acidosis. PaCO2 7.8 kPa = raised (hypercapnia). PaO2 7.1 kPa = hypoxaemia. Elevated bicarbonate (31) = chronic metabolic compensation. This is type 2 respiratory failure with partial metabolic compensation.
why_wrong: A. Type 1 failure has a normal or low PaCO2; here PaCO2 is raised. C. Metabolic acidosis would have a low bicarbonate; HCO3 here is 31. D. Full compensation would give a normal pH; pH 7.29 shows acute decompensation. E. The bicarbonate of 31 is in keeping with the expected renal compensation for chronic hypercapnia, so there is no evidence of an additional metabolic acidosis.
pearl: Type 1 RF = low PaO2, normal/low PaCO2. Type 2 RF = low PaO2 + raised PaCO2.
thinking: Step through ABG: pH → primary disorder → compensation → identify cause.
exam_trap: Calling it type 1 failure when CO2 is clearly elevated.
takeaway: Elevated CO2 + hypoxia + acidosis = type 2 respiratory failure.

stem: A 25-year-old tall, slim man presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild breathlessness. CXR shows a primary spontaneous pneumothorax with a 2.5 cm rim. He is haemodynamically stable, SpO2 96%, and not significantly breathless. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Needle aspiration and discharge if the lung re-expands
options.B: Conservative management with planned outpatient review
options.C: Small-bore chest drain insertion and admission
options.D: Admission for high-flow oxygen and serial chest X-rays
options.E: Referral for VATS pleurectomy on this admission

correct_answer: B. Conservative management with planned outpatient review
why_correct: The BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline moved away from the rim-size-driven algorithm. For a primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a patient who is haemodynamically stable and not significantly breathless, conservative management with observation and planned outpatient review is an appropriate first-line option, even with a rim of 2 cm or more, provided there are no high-risk features. The decision to intervene is guided by symptoms, high-risk features and patient priorities through shared decision-making, rather than size alone.
why_wrong: A. Needle aspiration is for patients who are significantly breathless, have high-risk features or choose intervention; it is not the default for a stable PSP. C. A chest drain is for patients needing intervention, not a stable, minimally breathless patient. D. Admission for oxygen is not required for a stable patient suitable for conservative management. E. Surgery is reserved for recurrence, persistent air leak or failure of other measures.
pearl: BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline: management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax is driven by symptoms, high-risk features and patient choice, not rim size alone. Conservative care is first-line for the stable, minimally symptomatic patient.
thinking: The BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline reframed pneumothorax management around symptoms, high-risk features and shared decision-making rather than the old rim-size cut-off.
exam_trap: Applying the old rule of "rim 2 cm or more -> aspirate". The BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline superseded this; conservative management is now first-line for a stable, minimally breathless patient.
takeaway: Stable, minimally breathless primary spontaneous pneumothorax: conservative management with outpatient review is now first-line (BTS 2023 pleural disease guideline).

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea 5 days after a long-haul flight. CTPA confirms bilateral pulmonary emboli. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_correct: Haemodynamically stable PE is treated with a DOAC. Apixaban (or rivaroxaban) is NICE-recommended first-line for acute PE — no need for initial parenteral anticoagulation. Simple, effective, and safe.
why_wrong: A: unfractionated heparin is reserved for massive PE or when rapid reversal is needed. C: warfarin requires bridging and is no longer first-line. D: thrombolysis is for massive PE with haemodynamic compromise. E: aspirin is not anticoagulation.
pearl: Massive PE = systolic BP <90 or drop ≥40 mmHg for >15 min → thrombolysis. Stable PE → DOAC.
thinking: Risk-stratify PE: massive/high-risk vs submassive vs low-risk.
