why_correct: An unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy (empty uterus with an adnexal mass) in a stable woman with hCG 1,500-4,999 IU/L, a mass under 35 mm, no visible heartbeat, no significant pain and able to attend follow-up can be offered a choice of systemic methotrexate or surgery (NICE NG126 1.15.3). Expectant management is only for pain-free women with hCG 1,500 IU/L or less; methotrexate alone is first-line only when hCG is under 1,500 IU/L. Surgery is first-line if there is significant pain, a mass 35 mm or larger, a visible heartbeat or hCG 5,000 IU/L or more.
why_wrong: A: laparotomy is for a ruptured ectopic with haemodynamic compromise; when surgery is chosen in a stable woman, a laparoscopic approach is preferred. B: the ectopic is already visible on scan, so serial hCG and discharge delays treatment of a pregnancy that needs active management at this hCG level. C: progesterone supplementation has no role in ectopic pregnancy. D: oxytocin is used in labour and the third stage, not ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: Discriminatory zone: hCG level above which TVS should see an IUP. No IUP above this level = ectopic or failed pregnancy.
thinking: Tubal ectopic seen on scan + stable → management depends on pain, hCG, mass size and heartbeat: hCG 1,500-4,999, no significant pain, mass <35 mm, no heartbeat → choice of methotrexate or surgery.
exam_trap: Choosing expectant management or methotrexate alone at hCG above 1,500 IU/L, or laparotomy in a stable patient — NICE offers a choice of methotrexate or laparoscopic surgery for hCG 1,500-4,999.
takeaway: Stable tubal ectopic with hCG 1,500-4,999 and no significant pain: choice of methotrexate or surgery; expectant only if pain-free and hCG ≤1,500.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 34 weeks gestation has BP 158/105, 2+ proteinuria, and headache. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate and planned delivery
options.B: Bed rest, IV fluids and repeat BP in 4 hours on the antenatal ward
options.C: Oral labetalol and twice-weekly day-unit review as an outpatient
options.D: Immediate caesarean section before controlling the BP or giving magnesium

correct_answer: A. Antihypertensives, magnesium sulphate and planned delivery
why_correct: Severe pre-eclampsia: admit, antihypertensives (labetalol IV or oral nifedipine), magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis (eclampsia prevention), and plan for delivery (a senior obstetric decision: at 34-36+6 weeks birth is planned when there are severe features such as ongoing severe headache or visual disturbance, uncontrolled BP or worsening bloods).
why_wrong: B. Bed rest and fluids do not control BP and risk fluid overload. C. Severe hypertension with proteinuria and headache requires admission, not outpatient care. D. BP must be controlled and magnesium sulphate given before delivery. E. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion in pre-eclampsia.
pearl: MgSO4 reduces eclampsia risk by 50% in severe pre-eclampsia. Diazepam is not recommended for eclamptic seizures.
thinking: Severe pre-eclampsia = BP control + MgSO4 + delivery planning.
exam_trap: Giving diuretics — pre-eclampsia causes vasoconstriction and relative hypovolaemia; diuretics worsen organ perfusion.
takeaway: Severe pre-eclampsia: antihypertensives + MgSO4 seizure prophylaxis + plan for delivery.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has cyclical severe pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, and bloating. CA-125 mildly elevated. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: Combined oral contraceptive pill or progestogen
options.B: Diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of endometriosis
options.C: Referral to a fertility clinic for IVF assessment
options.D: Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral oophorectomy
options.E: Monthly GnRH agonist depot injections for 6 months

correct_answer: A. Combined oral contraceptive pill or progestogen
why_correct: Endometriosis first-line: hormonal suppression with combined OCP or progestogen (norethisterone, desogestrel). These reduce symptoms in 70-80% of women. Laparoscopy is diagnostic/surgical — medical treatment first unless pregnancy is desired or medical therapy fails.
why_wrong: B. Laparoscopy is diagnostic/surgical; hormonal treatment is tried first unless fertility is a priority or medical therapy fails. C. IVF is for infertility, not primary pain management. D. Radical surgery is a last resort. E. GnRH agonists are second-line because of menopausal side effects and bone loss.
pearl: GnRH analogues with add-back HRT are second-line; laparoscopic excision is gold standard for refractory disease.
thinking: Endometriosis: hormonal suppression first, surgery if medical treatment fails or fertility is a concern.
exam_trap: Offering laparoscopy as the first intervention — medical therapy should be tried first.
takeaway: Endometriosis first-line: OCP or progestogen to suppress cyclical hormonal drive.

stem: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman has abdominal bloating, early satiety, and urinary frequency over 4 months. CA-125 420 U/ml. USS shows a complex right ovarian mass. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
correct_answer: C. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis
why_correct: Suspected ovarian cancer: NICE recommends CT of the abdomen and pelvis (with chest imaging as clinically indicated, commonly done as CT CAP in practice) to establish the extent of disease before surgical planning. CT guides operability and extent of disease. CA-125 + USS + CT is the standard diagnostic pathway.
why_wrong: A: MRI pelvis is complementary and may follow CT. B: diagnostic laparoscopy should not be first. D: 6-week delay is inappropriate with elevated CA-125 and concerning mass. E: core biopsy risks peritoneal seeding.
pearl: Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) = USS score x menopausal status x CA-125. RMI I of 250 or more = refer to a specialist MDT (NICE CG122).
thinking: Suspected ovarian cancer: CA-125 + USS → CT for staging → specialist MDT.
exam_trap: Biopsy before surgical staging — risks peritoneal seeding of malignancy.
takeaway: Suspected ovarian cancer: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging — not biopsy.

stem: A 51-year-old woman with hot flushes, night sweats, mood changes, and vaginal dryness. Last period 14 months ago. FSH 72 IU/L. No contraindications to HRT. What is the most appropriate treatment?
why_correct: Symptomatic menopause with intact uterus: combined HRT (oestrogen + progestogen) is first-line per NICE NG23. Progestogen is required to protect the endometrium from unopposed oestrogen. HRT is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms.
why_wrong: A: oestrogen-only HRT is for women post-hysterectomy — without uterus, no progestogen needed. B: SSRIs are second-line for women who cannot take HRT. D: clonidine has modest benefit for flushes — not first-line. E: symptoms can be severe and persistent.
pearl: HRT: low risk in healthy women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause. Discuss cardiovascular, breast, and VTE risk.
thinking: Intact uterus = combined HRT. No uterus = oestrogen only.
exam_trap: Prescribing oestrogen-only HRT in a woman with an intact uterus — causes endometrial hyperplasia and cancer risk.
takeaway: Symptomatic menopause with intact uterus: combined HRT (oestrogen plus progestogen).

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. Examination reveals a pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex radiating to the axilla with a soft S1. What is the most appropriate investigation?
why_correct: Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla is classic mitral regurgitation. Transthoracic echocardiography confirms diagnosis, quantifies severity, assesses LV function, and guides management including timing of surgical repair.
why_wrong: A. ECG and Holter monitoring may show AF or LV hypertrophy but cannot diagnose or quantify MR. C. Stress testing is not the first investigation. D. Catheterisation follows echocardiography. E. CXR may show cardiomegaly but does not quantify MR.
pearl: Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture post-MI) causes flash pulmonary oedema with a soft pansystolic or early systolic murmur that may be inaudible in severe cases due to rapid equalisation of LA and LV pressures.
thinking: Pansystolic murmur at apex = MR. Echo quantifies it and assesses LV function.
exam_trap: Missing MR because the murmur is soft in acute severe MR — severity is not proportional to murmur loudness.
takeaway: Suspected mitral regurgitation: transthoracic echocardiography is the first investigation.

stem: A 20-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of syncope, particularly during exercise. Her ECG shows a QTc of 510 ms. Her younger brother died suddenly aged 18. What is the most important initial management?

options.A: Avoid QT-prolonging drugs and sport, beta-blocker, cardiology referral
options.B: Urgent ICD implantation as the first step, before starting any medication
options.C: Amiodarone loading and referral to cardiology for an electrophysiology study
options.D: No specific treatment required as she is asymptomatic between syncopal episodes
options.E: Reassure as vasovagal syncope and discharge with hydration and lifestyle advice

correct_answer: A. Avoid QT-prolonging drugs and sport, beta-blocker, cardiology referral
why_correct: Congenital long QT syndrome with symptoms and family history of sudden death: initial management includes avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs, restriction from competitive sport, and beta-blockers (reduce ventricular arrhythmia risk). ICD is considered for high-risk cases after cardiology assessment.
why_wrong: B. An ICD may be needed but follows cardiology risk stratification; beta-blockers are first-line. C. Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and is contraindicated. D. Exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death are high-risk features needing treatment. E. Exertional syncope with a long QT is not vasovagal; discharge is unsafe.
pearl: Common QT-prolonging drugs: amiodarone, sotalol, erythromycin, haloperidol, methadone, ondansetron. Check before prescribing.
thinking: QTc >500 ms in a symptomatic patient with family history = high-risk LQTS.
exam_trap: Prescribing amiodarone for arrhythmia in LQTS — it prolongs QT and can precipitate torsades de pointes.
takeaway: Symptomatic LQTS: avoid QT-prolonging drugs, restrict sport, refer to cardiology, consider beta-blocker.

stem: A 25-year-old footballer collapses during training. He recovers spontaneously. His father died suddenly aged 40. ECG shows LV hypertrophy and deep T-wave inversions. Echo shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Return to sport after 6 weeks of rest and a repeat echocardiogram
options.B: Start amiodarone and continue training with a pitch-side AED
options.C: Stop competitive sport; refer to inherited cardiac conditions team
options.D: Coronary angiogram and return to competitive sport if it is normal
options.E: Reassure that this is athlete's heart and allow play to continue

correct_answer: C. Stop competitive sport; refer to inherited cardiac conditions team
why_correct: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes. Features confirmed: exertional syncope, family history, ECG changes, and echo diagnosis. Patients must be disqualified from competitive sport and referred to a specialist inherited cardiac conditions (ICC) service.
why_wrong: A. Rest does not alter the risk; HCM with exertional syncope carries a high risk of sudden death. B. Amiodarone does not make continued competitive sport safe. D. Coronary angiography does not assess HCM risk. E. Athlete's heart does not cause asymmetric septal hypertrophy, SAM and deep T-wave inversion.
pearl: HOCM: differentiate from athlete's heart — HOCM has asymmetric hypertrophy, SAM, abnormal ECG, diastolic dysfunction, and family history.
thinking: Young athlete + exertional syncope + LVH on ECG + family history of SCD = HOCM until proven otherwise.
exam_trap: Returning to sport after normal coronary angiogram — HOCM risk is not related to coronary disease.
takeaway: HOCM: disqualify from competitive sport immediately and refer to specialist inherited cardiac conditions service.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker presents with calf pain on walking 200 metres that relieves within 5 minutes of rest. ABI is 0.65. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Supervised exercise, smoking cessation and antiplatelet therapy
options.B: Angioplasty and stenting of the femoral artery
options.D: Rest, leg elevation and compression stockings
options.E: Naftidrofuryl oxalate first, with review in 3 months

correct_answer: A. Supervised exercise, smoking cessation and antiplatelet therapy
why_correct: Intermittent claudication (stable PAD, ABI 0.4-0.9): first-line management is supervised exercise programme (improves collateral circulation and walking distance), risk factor modification (smoking cessation, statins, antihypertensives), and antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel 75 mg preferred in PAD per NICE CG147 / TA210).
why_wrong: B. Revascularisation is for failed supervised exercise or critical limb ischaemia. C. Anticoagulation is not standard for stable claudication. D. Elevation and compression worsen arterial insufficiency. E. Naftidrofuryl is considered only when supervised exercise has not helped and revascularisation is unsuitable.
pearl: ABI <0.9 = PAD. ABI <0.4 = critical limb ischaemia (rest pain, ulceration, gangrene). ABI >1.4 = non-compressible vessels (diabetes).
thinking: Claudication + ABI 0.65 = stable PAD. Conservative management first.
exam_trap: Anticoagulating claudication — warfarin has no benefit in stable PAD and increases bleeding risk.
takeaway: Intermittent claudication: supervised exercise + smoking cessation + antiplatelet therapy first-line.

stem: A 55-year-old farmer presents with recurrent episodes of breathlessness, fever, and malaise 4-6 hours after entering his hay barn. Between episodes he feels well. Serum precipitins to Faeni rectivirgula are positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Occupational asthma from grain mite exposure

why_correct: Farmer's lung is a type III/IV hypersensitivity pneumonitis to thermophilic actinomycetes (Faeni rectivirgula) in mouldy hay. Characterised by delayed onset (4-8 hours after exposure), systemic symptoms, and serum precipitins. Avoidance is the cornerstone of management.
why_wrong: A. Occupational asthma is IgE-mediated with immediate wheeze, not delayed fever and malaise. B. Sarcoidosis is not exposure-related and causes hilar lymphadenopathy. C. Miliary TB causes progressive illness, not recurrent episodes tied to exposure. E. ABPA requires underlying asthma or CF.
pearl: HP causes: farmer's lung (hay), bird fancier's lung (birds/droppings), humidifier fever (water systems), mushroom worker's lung.
thinking: Delayed breathlessness after specific exposure + precipitins = hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
exam_trap: Diagnosing asthma — HP has a delayed (not immediate) onset after exposure and systemic features.
takeaway: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: delayed onset breathlessness after antigen exposure + positive precipitins.

stem: A 50-year-old man has the following spirometry: FEV1 2.1 L (68% predicted), FVC 3.5 L (90% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.60. What is the pattern?
why_correct: Obstructive pattern: FEV1/FVC <0.70 (0.60 here). FVC is relatively preserved (90% predicted). Reduced FEV1 with low FEV1/FVC ratio = obstruction to airflow. Causes: COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis.
why_wrong: A: restrictive pattern = low FVC + normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio (>0.70). B: mixed = both FVC and FEV1/FVC are reduced. C: FEV1/FVC <0.70 is not normal. D: a clear obstructive pattern is present.
pearl: FEV1/FVC <0.70 = obstruction. Low FVC + normal ratio = restriction. Both reduced = mixed.
thinking: Always calculate FEV1/FVC first: <0.70 = obstruction; then assess FVC for restriction component.
exam_trap: Calling it restrictive because FEV1 is below normal — the FEV1/FVC ratio is the key discriminator.
takeaway: FEV1/FVC <0.70 = obstructive spirometry pattern.

stem: A 60-year-old man with confirmed exudative pleural effusion has a pH of 7.18, glucose 2.1 mmol/L, LDH 4200 U/L, and frank pus is aspirated. What is the most appropriate management?
correct_answer: A. Chest drain and IV antibiotics
why_correct: Empyema (frank pus or pH <7.2 with positive culture or loculations): requires chest drain insertion (intercostal drain) plus IV antibiotics. Drain allows drainage of infected fluid and instillation of fibrinolytics if needed.
why_wrong: B. Repeat aspiration does not adequately drain empyema. C. Antibiotics without drainage are inadequate. D. Observation is inappropriate for empyema. E. Surgery is considered after failed drainage.
pearl: BTS 2023: frank pus, positive Gram stain/culture, or pleural fluid pH ≤7.2 = chest drain; if pH is unavailable, glucose <3.3 mmol/L indicates high probability of complicated parapneumonic effusion; pH 7.2–7.4 with LDH >900 IU/L = consider drainage.
thinking: Empyema = chest drain + antibiotics. Simple parapneumonic effusion = antibiotics alone.
exam_trap: Giving antibiotics alone for empyema — drain is essential for infected collections.
takeaway: Empyema: chest drain plus IV antibiotics — antibiotics alone are insufficient.

stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe periumbilical pain disproportionate to his relatively soft abdomen. WBC is 22 x 10(9)/L, lactate is 5.8 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate priority?

options.A: Acute pancreatitis — IV fluids, analgesia, nil by mouth and serum lipase
options.B: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — emergency open repair in theatre
options.C: Renal colic — IM diclofenac and CT KUB
options.D: Perforated diverticulitis — IV antibiotics and CT abdomen with contrast
options.E: Mesenteric ischaemia — urgent CT angiography and surgical referral

correct_answer: E. Mesenteric ischaemia — urgent CT angiography and surgical referral
why_correct: Acute mesenteric ischaemia: sudden severe pain disproportionate to peritonism, AF (embolic source), markedly elevated lactate and WBC. This is a surgical emergency. CT mesenteric angiography confirms the diagnosis; revascularisation must be undertaken urgently.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised amylase/lipase. B. A ruptured AAA usually causes back pain, shock and a pulsatile mass. C. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain with haematuria. D. Perforated diverticulitis causes left-sided peritonism, not pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen in a patient with AF.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to peritonism + AF + elevated lactate = mesenteric ischaemia until proven otherwise.
thinking: High index of suspicion in elderly AF patients with sudden severe abdominal pain — mortality is >50% if diagnosis is delayed.
exam_trap: Reassuring on the basis of a relatively soft abdomen — peritonism is a late sign in mesenteric ischaemia.
takeaway: Acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain disproportionate to signs + AF + high lactate = CT angiography urgently.

stem: A 55-year-old obese man with 10 years of GORD undergoes OGD which shows salmon-pink mucosa extending 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy confirms intestinal metaplasia. What is the most appropriate management?

options.B: PPI and discharge without further endoscopy
options.D: PPI and endoscopic surveillance every 2-3 years

correct_answer: D. PPI and endoscopic surveillance every 2-3 years
why_correct: Barrett's oesophagus (intestinal metaplasia replacing normal squamous epithelium) is a pre-malignant condition for oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Management: PPI for symptom control and to reduce progression risk, plus endoscopic surveillance to detect dysplasia early.
why_wrong: A. Oesophagectomy is reserved for cancer or some high-grade dysplasia. B. Surveillance is required to detect dysplasia. C. Anti-reflux surgery does not reliably reverse Barrett's or remove the need for surveillance. E. Ablation is not offered for non-dysplastic Barrett's.
pearl: Barrett's surveillance interval depends on segment length: <1 cm = no surveillance; 1-3 cm = 3-5 yearly; >3 cm = 2-3 yearly.
thinking: Barrett's = metaplasia → dysplasia → adenocarcinoma. Surveillance detects progression.
exam_trap: Stopping follow-up after diagnosing Barrett's — surveillance is essential.
takeaway: Barrett's oesophagus: high-dose PPI plus endoscopic surveillance to detect dysplasia.

stem: A 48-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes has persistently elevated ALT (2x upper limit of normal). USS shows a bright echogenic liver. He drinks minimal alcohol. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Weight loss, exercise and metabolic risk control
options.B: Percutaneous liver biopsy to stage fibrosis first
options.D: Increase metformin to treat the fatty liver
options.E: Referral for bariatric surgery as first-line treatment

correct_answer: A. Weight loss, exercise and metabolic risk control
why_correct: MASLD (formerly NAFLD): first-line management is lifestyle modification — weight loss of 5-10% improves steatosis; 10% weight loss can improve fibrosis. Optimising diabetes, dyslipidaemia, and hypertension is essential. This is the most effective treatment for MASLD (formerly NAFLD).
why_wrong: B. Biopsy is not first-line; non-invasive fibrosis assessment (e.g. ELF) is used first. C. Ursodeoxycholic acid has no proven benefit in MASLD (formerly NAFLD). D. Metformin has no specific hepatic benefit in MASLD (formerly NAFLD). E. Bariatric surgery is considered after lifestyle measures within obesity criteria, not first-line.
pearl: FIB-4 score or liver stiffness measurement (transient elastography) grades fibrosis non-invasively. NAFLD was renamed MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) by international consensus in 2023; both terms may appear in practice.
thinking: MASLD (formerly NAFLD): lifestyle first. Severity assessment guides surveillance interval.
exam_trap: Biopsy as first step — non-invasive fibrosis assessment (FIB-4, elastography) comes before biopsy.
takeaway: MASLD (formerly NAFLD): weight loss and metabolic risk factor optimisation is the cornerstone of management.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with ptosis and diplopia that worsen throughout the day, improving after rest. She also has fatigable proximal limb weakness. Anti-AChR antibodies are positive. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
why_correct: Myasthenia gravis first-line symptom control: pyridostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) improves neuromuscular transmission by increasing synaptic acetylcholine. It provides good symptomatic control. Immunosuppression (prednisolone, azathioprine) is added for long-term disease modification.
why_wrong: B: prednisolone alone without pyridostigmine is not the initial step — and high-dose steroids can initially worsen MG. C: thymectomy is considered in AChR-positive patients with thymoma or generalised MG, not as immediate first-line. D: IVIg is for myasthenic crisis. E: beta-blockers are contraindicated in MG.
pearl: Myasthenic crisis: respiratory failure requiring ICU, ventilation, IVIg or plasmapheresis. Cholinergic crisis: excess pyridostigmine causing muscle fasciculations and secretions.
thinking: Fatigable weakness worse later in day = MG. Pyridostigmine first for symptom control.
exam_trap: Immediately prescribing high-dose steroids without first trying pyridostigmine — steroids can precipitate initial worsening.
takeaway: Myasthenia gravis: pyridostigmine for symptom control first-line — add immunosuppression for disease modification.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with brief (seconds) severe electric shock-like facial pain in the distribution of V2 and V3, triggered by eating, talking, or touching the face. Neurological examination is normal. What is the first-line treatment?
why_correct: Trigeminal neuralgia first-line: carbamazepine is the recommended first-line treatment. It reduces the frequency and severity of attacks in 70-80% of patients. It acts on voltage-gated sodium channels in the trigeminal nucleus.
why_wrong: A: amitriptyline is for neuropathic pain and post-herpetic neuralgia, not trigeminal neuralgia. B: gabapentin is second-line for trigeminal neuralgia. C: morphine is ineffective for trigeminal neuralgia. D: microvascular decompression is for drug-refractory cases.
pearl: Secondary trigeminal neuralgia causes: MS (demyelinating plaque), cerebellopontine angle tumour, vascular compression. Always image to exclude.
thinking: Electric shock facial pain in trigeminal distribution, triggered by touch/eating = trigeminal neuralgia.
exam_trap: Prescribing morphine for trigeminal neuralgia — opioids are ineffective for this neuropathic pain.
takeaway: Trigeminal neuralgia: carbamazepine is the first-line treatment.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive weakness, wasting, and fasciculations in his arms and legs. He has no sensory symptoms. Examination shows mixed UMN and LMN signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: ALS/MND: combination of UMN signs (hyperreflexia, spasticity, extensor plantars) AND LMN signs (wasting, fasciculations, weakness) in the same limbs, with NO sensory involvement. Progressive and incurable. Riluzole slows progression modestly.
why_wrong: B. MS usually causes sensory symptoms and does not cause fasciculations or wasting. C. MG causes fatigable weakness without fasciculations or UMN signs. D. GBS is acute and ascending, with areflexia and sensory symptoms. E. Myelopathy typically causes sensory symptoms and does not cause LMN signs in the legs.
pearl: MND does not affect: sensation, sphincters, eye movements, cognition (usually). 'Motor only' is the key feature.
thinking: Mixed UMN + LMN signs + progressive + no sensory involvement = ALS/MND.
exam_trap: Missing MND because of the combination of UMN and LMN signs — this mixed picture is characteristic.
takeaway: ALS/MND: progressive mixed UMN and LMN signs, no sensory deficit — riluzole for disease modification.

stem: A 45-year-old man has resistant hypertension on three antihypertensives, with plasma potassium 3.1 mmol/L and metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone/renin ratio is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome): hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis + suppressed renin + elevated aldosterone/renin ratio. Caused by aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma (most common) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Adrenal CT and adrenal vein sampling confirm.
why_wrong: A: Cushing's can cause hypertension and hypokalaemia but with hypercortisolaemia. B: phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension, not typically hypokalaemia. C: renal artery stenosis raises renin (secondary hyperaldosteronism). D: diuretics cause hypokalaemia but with normal or elevated renin.
pearl: Conn's: unilateral adenoma = surgery (adrenalectomy). Bilateral hyperplasia = medical treatment (spironolactone).
thinking: Resistant HTN + hypokalaemia + elevated aldosterone/renin ratio = primary hyperaldosteronism.
exam_trap: Attributing hypokalaemia to diuretics without checking aldosterone/renin ratio — primary hyperaldosteronism is under-diagnosed.
takeaway: Primary hyperaldosteronism: resistant hypertension + hypokalaemia + elevated aldosterone/renin ratio.

stem: A 75-year-old woman on an SSRI has sodium 118 mmol/L. She has mild confusion but no seizures or coma. She is euvolaemic. Rate of correction is being planned. What is the maximum safe rate of sodium correction to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome?

options.A: Normalise sodium to 135 mmol/L within the first 24 hours
options.B: 20 mmol/L per 24 hours (15 mmol/L if high risk)
options.C: 2 mmol/L per hour, sustained for the first 24 hours
options.D: 10 mmol/L per 24 hours (8 mmol/L if high risk)
options.E: No correction needed as she is not seizing

correct_answer: D. 10 mmol/L per 24 hours (8 mmol/L if high risk)
why_correct: Chronic hyponatraemia correction: maximum 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis). In high-risk patients (malnourished, alcoholic, liver disease) limit to 8 mmol/L per 24 hours.
why_wrong: A. Rapid normalisation causes osmotic demyelination. B. 20 mmol/L per 24 hours carries a high risk of ODS. C. 2 mmol/L per hour sustained over 24 hours far exceeds safe limits. E. Symptomatic severe hyponatraemia needs controlled correction.
pearl: Severe symptoms (seizures, reduced consciousness): give 150 mL of 3% sodium chloride IV over 20 minutes, check sodium and repeat (usually up to twice) aiming for a 5 mmol/L rise, with specialist/critical-care input; the 24-hour limit on total correction still applies.
thinking: Chronic hyponatraemia correction is a process, not a single action — monitor closely and limit rate.
exam_trap: Correcting sodium too rapidly — osmotic demyelination syndrome is irreversible.
takeaway: Chronic hyponatraemia: maximum 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with AKI, fever, rash, and eosinophilia 2 weeks after starting naproxen. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria and white cell casts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN): classic triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia + AKI following drug exposure (NSAIDs, beta-lactams, PPIs, sulfonamides). Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria and white cell casts. Treatment: stop offending drug; steroids if no improvement.
why_wrong: A. ATN follows ischaemia or nephrotoxins and lacks rash, fever and eosinophilia. B. RPGN causes haematuria with red cell casts, not drug-related rash and eosinophilia. D. Pyelonephritis would give positive cultures and loin pain, not sterile pyuria with rash. E. Prerenal AKI has bland urine without white cell casts or systemic features.
pearl: Most common drug causes of AIN: NSAIDs, beta-lactams, PPIs. Stop the drug — most cases resolve, but steroids may accelerate recovery.
thinking: Drug exposure + fever + rash + eosinophilia + AKI = AIN until proven otherwise.
exam_trap: Attributing AKI to the NSAID via haemodynamic mechanism without recognising the immune-mediated AIN.
takeaway: Acute interstitial nephritis: drug + fever + rash + eosinophilia + AKI — stop the offending drug.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with haematuria, left flank pain, and a palpable left renal mass. CT confirms a 7 cm solid left renal mass with no distant metastases. What is the most appropriate management?

options.E: Observation with repeat CT in 6 months

why_correct: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) presenting with the classic triad (haematuria, flank pain, palpable mass) is potentially curable with surgical resection. Radical nephrectomy (partial nephrectomy preferred for T1 tumours ≤7 cm where feasible, and for a solitary kidney) is the treatment of choice for localised RCC.
why_wrong: A: biopsy is not routinely required pre-operatively for solid masses — resection is both diagnostic and therapeutic. C: radiofrequency ablation is for patients unfit for surgery or small tumours. D: sunitinib is for metastatic RCC. E: observation is inappropriate for a 7 cm solid mass.
pearl: Classic triad of RCC (haematuria + loin pain + mass) occurs in only 10-15% but indicates advanced disease.
thinking: Solid renal mass + localised = surgical resection. Metastatic = targeted therapy.
exam_trap: Biopsy before surgery — for solid renal masses, surgical resection is both diagnostic and curative.
takeaway: Localised renal cell carcinoma: surgical nephrectomy is the treatment of choice.

stem: A 20-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa has a BMI of 12.5, HR 38 bpm, BP 80/50, and blood glucose 2.8 mmol/L. She is confused and cold. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Direct admission to a specialist eating disorder unit
options.B: Oral refeeding at home with weekly outpatient psychiatry
options.C: Emergency medical admission for stabilisation under MEED
options.D: Nasogastric feeding at home with community dietitian support
options.E: Mental Health Act detention to a psychiatric ward for feeding

correct_answer: C. Emergency medical admission for stabilisation under MEED
why_correct: MEED (Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders, RCPsych 2022; replaced MARSIPAN): BMI <13 with medical instability (bradycardia, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, confusion) = high physical risk requiring emergency medical admission for stabilisation, cardiac monitoring, and careful refeeding under medical supervision.
why_wrong: A. A specialist eating disorder unit is for medically stable patients; she needs medical stabilisation first. B. Outpatient management is unsafe with this degree of instability. D. Home NG feeding is inappropriate for a medically unstable patient. E. The MHA may be needed, but medical admission and stabilisation come first.
pearl: MEED BMI triggers: BMI <13 or rapid weight loss = very high risk. Monitor for refeeding syndrome during reintroduction.
thinking: Medical instability in severe AN = medical ward first. ED unit or psychiatric admission follows stabilisation.
exam_trap: Sending directly to an eating disorder unit without addressing life-threatening medical instability.
takeaway: Medically unstable severe anorexia: emergency medical admission for physical stabilisation before psychiatric treatment.

stem: A 30-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been started on clozapine. Three weeks later his neutrophil count falls to 1.2 x 10(9)/L. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Continue clozapine and recheck the FBC twice weekly
options.B: Halve the clozapine dose and recheck FBC in 1 week
options.C: Add lithium to raise the neutrophil count
options.D: Continue clozapine and add G-CSF support for neutrophils
options.E: Stop clozapine and inform the monitoring service

correct_answer: E. Stop clozapine and inform the monitoring service
why_correct: Clozapine and neutropenia: a neutrophil count below 1.5 x 10(9)/L (here 1.2) is a red result — stop clozapine immediately and inform the clozapine monitoring service; daily FBC until recovery and do not rechallenge without specialist advice. Amber (neutrophils 1.5-2.0) allows continuation with twice-weekly FBC. Agranulocytosis (neutrophils <0.5) is life-threatening. Mandatory FBC monitoring: weekly for 18 weeks, then fortnightly to 1 year, then monthly.
why_wrong: A. Twice-weekly monitoring while continuing is the amber-range action; a neutrophil count below 1.5 x 10(9)/L is a red result requiring clozapine to be stopped. B. Dose reduction does not protect against agranulocytosis. C. Lithium does not reliably prevent clozapine-induced agranulocytosis. D. G-CSF does not make it safe to continue clozapine after a red result.
pearl: Clozapine is only dispensed on mandatory FBC monitoring. Agranulocytosis rate: 0.5-2% with weekly monitoring protocols.
thinking: Clozapine + neutrophil count: <1.5 = stop immediately. This is a mandatory requirement.
exam_trap: Continuing clozapine with a neutrophil count below safe thresholds — agranulocytosis is life-threatening.
takeaway: Clozapine: neutrophils <1.5 x 10(9)/L = withhold immediately and notify clozapine monitoring service.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset left arm weakness with inconsistent examination findings (give-way weakness, Hoover's sign positive), normal MRI brain, and normal EMG. She had a stressful life event recently. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Functional neurological disorder (FND/conversion disorder): neurological symptoms inconsistent with organic disease (positive Hoover's sign = involuntary hip extension when contralateral hip flexes), normal investigations, positive FND signs. It is a genuine disorder, not feigned illness. Treated with physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
why_wrong: A. Malingering is deliberate feigning for external gain, which is not suggested here. B. MS would show demyelinating lesions on MRI. C. Stroke causes consistent signs and usually imaging changes; Hoover's sign is a positive functional sign. D. Factitious disorder involves deliberate symptom production to adopt the sick role, which is not suggested here.
pearl: Hoover's sign: patient cannot voluntarily extend the paretic hip but does so involuntarily when extending the contralateral hip against resistance — positive in functional weakness.
thinking: Positive FND signs + inconsistent examination + normal investigations = FND.
exam_trap: Labelling FND as malingering — it is a genuine neurological condition with real disability.
takeaway: Functional neurological disorder: genuine, not feigned — positive FND signs + normal investigations.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to A&E after being found by his wife with an empty bottle of paracetamol. He took 32 tablets 3 hours ago. He states he was 'trying to end it all'. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Urgent psychiatric assessment, then discharge if he denies ongoing intent
options.B: Activated charcoal now and repeat the paracetamol level at 4 hours
options.C: Reassure and discharge as blood paracetamol will be low
options.D: Gastric lavage followed by oral methionine
options.E: IV acetylcysteine per the nomogram and urgent psychiatric assessment

correct_answer: E. IV acetylcysteine per the nomogram and urgent psychiatric assessment
why_correct: Paracetamol overdose: >150 mg/kg or >12 g is significant. 32 tablets (16 g) is a major overdose. IV NAC treatment should be started according to the nomogram (4-hour paracetamol level determines treatment). Urgent psychiatric assessment for deliberate self-harm is mandatory before any decision about discharge.
why_wrong: A. Medical treatment of a major overdose must not be bypassed, and denial of intent does not make discharge safe. B. Activated charcoal is useful only within 1 hour and does not replace NAC. C. A 16 g overdose with suicidal intent is potentially fatal; reassurance and discharge are unsafe whatever the expected level. D. Gastric lavage is not recommended in paracetamol overdose.
pearl: Staggered or uncertain-time overdose: the nomogram cannot be interpreted, so start IV acetylcysteine without waiting for a level. There is one UK treatment line (100 mg/L at 4 hours) for all patients; the separate high-risk line was withdrawn in 2012. Take levels at least 4 hours after ingestion.
thinking: Paracetamol OD: NAC + psychiatric assessment. Never discharge without both.
exam_trap: Discharging without psychiatric assessment — suicide intent expressed = psychiatric assessment is mandatory.
takeaway: Paracetamol overdose: IV NAC per nomogram plus mandatory psychiatric assessment before any discharge decision.

stem: A 78-year-old man with moderate dementia (MMSE 14/30) and heart failure is admitted. His family ask that 'everything be done' if his condition deteriorates. He previously told his GP he would not want CPR. A DNACPR form was completed 6 months ago. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Rescind the DNACPR and attempt CPR as the family request
options.B: Apply to the Court of Protection before any CPR decision
options.C: Treat the family as decision-makers since they are next of kin
options.D: Uphold the DNACPR and discuss care goals with the family
options.E: Suspend the DNACPR until the patient himself repeats his refusal

correct_answer: D. Uphold the DNACPR and discuss care goals with the family
why_correct: A DNACPR completed when the patient had capacity reflects his previously expressed capacitous wishes, which carry significant weight under the MCA 2005 best-interests framework. A DNACPR is a clinical recommendation, not a legally binding document, but family members cannot demand CPR that is clinically inappropriate, nor override the patient's prior wishes. The team should acknowledge the family's distress, explain the decision and its rationale, and focus on comfort and quality-of-care goals.
why_wrong: A. CPR against the patient's documented capacitous wishes is inappropriate; family cannot demand it. B. Court involvement is not needed for this clinical decision. C. Next of kin are not legal decision-makers unless they hold a health and welfare LPA. E. A DNACPR made with his earlier capacitous input does not lapse because he cannot restate it now; he should be involved as far as his capacity allows, but his prior wishes and best interests guide the decision.
pearl: Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment (ADRT): legally binding if it meets MCA criteria (written, signed, witnessed, specific). DNACPR is a clinical decision, not a legal document, but reflects patient wishes.
thinking: DNACPR reflecting the patient's previously expressed wishes + family disagreement = uphold the DNACPR, explain the rationale and support the family.
exam_trap: Deferring to family wishes over the patient's documented prior wishes — family cannot demand CPR or override his previously expressed capacitous wishes unless they hold a relevant health and welfare LPA.
takeaway: A DNACPR reflecting prior capacitous wishes carries strong ethical and professional weight under the MCA — family cannot override it — though the DNACPR itself is a clinical recommendation, not a legally binding document.

stem: A 90-year-old woman with end-stage heart failure and dementia is clearly in the last days of life. She is agitated and appears to be in pain. She cannot swallow. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: IV fluids, IV diuretics and escalation of heart failure therapy
options.B: Subcutaneous syringe driver with morphine and midazolam
options.C: Transfer to the ICU for non-invasive ventilation and inotropes
options.D: Withhold all medications to allow a natural death to occur
options.E: NG tube for enteral feeding and her usual oral medications

correct_answer: B. Subcutaneous syringe driver with morphine and midazolam
why_correct: End-of-life symptom management: when a patient cannot swallow in the last days of life, subcutaneous continuous infusion via syringe driver (morphine for pain/dyspnoea, midazolam for agitation, haloperidol for nausea) provides continuous symptom control. This is standard palliative care.
why_wrong: A. Escalation is inconsistent with comfort-focused care in the last days of life. C. ICU is inappropriate without a realistic prospect of recovery. D. Withholding symptom control causes unnecessary suffering. E. NG feeding at the end of life does not improve comfort and may prolong dying.
pearl: Anticipatory prescriptions for the dying patient: morphine (pain/dyspnoea), midazolam (agitation/seizures), haloperidol (nausea/vomiting), hyoscine butylbromide (secretions).
thinking: End of life + cannot swallow + symptomatic = syringe driver for continuous subcutaneous symptom control.
exam_trap: Starting enteral feeding or IV fluids in the actively dying patient — this prolongs distress.
takeaway: Last days of life with inability to swallow: subcutaneous syringe driver for continuous symptom control.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness, worse in the mornings lasting over 1 hour. She has difficulty raising her arms above her head and getting out of a chair. ESR is 85 mm/hr, CRP 62 mg/L. Muscle strength is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid
options.D: Prednisolone 60 mg daily with gradual tapering
options.E: Prednisolone 15 mg daily with gradual tapering

correct_answer: E. Prednisolone 15 mg daily with gradual tapering
why_correct: Polymyalgia rheumatica: proximal muscle stiffness (shoulders and hips), elevated inflammatory markers, age >50, no muscle weakness. First-line: prednisolone 15 mg daily (not 60 mg used for GCA). Dramatic response within days is diagnostic. Taper over 12-24 months.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs give partial relief but do not control PMR. B. Methotrexate is a steroid-sparing agent, not first-line. C. Physiotherapy and analgesia are inadequate. D. 60 mg is the GCA dose; PMR responds to 15 mg.
pearl: PMR and GCA often co-exist. All PMR patients should be asked about headache and jaw claudication — if present, treat as GCA with 60 mg prednisolone.
thinking: Proximal stiffness + elevated ESR/CRP + age >50 = PMR. Prednisolone 15 mg — dramatic response confirms diagnosis.
exam_trap: Using 60 mg prednisolone for PMR — 60 mg is for GCA. PMR requires only 15 mg.
takeaway: Polymyalgia rheumatica: prednisolone 15 mg daily — dramatic response within days is both therapeutic and diagnostic.

stem: A 72-year-old man is diagnosed with epilepsy after two seizures. He drives professionally as a lorry driver. What are the DVLA notification requirements?

options.A: Notify DVLA; no driving for 6 months (5 years for Group 2)
options.B: Notify DVLA; may drive lorries once seizure-free on medication
options.C: GP notifies DVLA; he may drive cars while awaiting the decision
options.D: Notify DVLA; no driving for 1 year (10 years for Group 2)
options.E: No DVLA notification needed if he restricts himself to car driving

correct_answer: D. Notify DVLA; no driving for 1 year (10 years for Group 2)
why_correct: Epilepsy and DVLA: Group 1 (car): must not drive for 1 year from last seizure. Group 2 (lorry/bus/HGV): must be seizure-free for 10 years off all anticonvulsants. Patient has a legal duty to notify DVLA. Professional driving licence will be revoked.
why_wrong: A. Group 1 requires 1 year seizure-free after an epilepsy diagnosis, and Group 2 requires 10 years seizure-free off medication. B. Group 2 driving requires 10 years seizure-free without anti-seizure medication. C. The patient has a legal duty to notify DVLA and must stop driving. E. Epilepsy must be notified for all licence groups.
pearl: Patient's legal duty: notify DVLA. GP duty: advise patient to notify; can notify DVLA if patient refuses and there is a risk to public safety.
thinking: Always think Group 1 vs Group 2 licence — the requirements differ significantly.
exam_trap: Applying Group 1 (car) rules to a Group 2 (HGV/bus) licence holder — requirements are much stricter.
takeaway: Epilepsy in a Group 2 licence holder: 10 years seizure-free required — professional driving licence revoked.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions and flaccid blisters on her trunk that rupture easily leaving raw areas. Nikolsky sign is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pemphigus vulgaris: positive Nikolsky sign (pressure causes skin to slip), flaccid intraepidermal bullae that rupture easily, painful oral mucosa involvement, middle-aged. Caused by anti-desmoglein IgG antibodies. Treated with high-dose prednisolone +/- azathioprine.
why_wrong: A: bullous pemphigoid has tense bullae (subepidermal), no oral involvement (usually), negative Nikolsky sign, affects elderly. B: dermatitis herpetiformis causes intensely itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces, associated with coeliac. C: SJS causes mucocutaneous target lesions, drug-induced. D: impetigo causes honey-coloured crusted lesions, not bullae.
pearl: Pemphigus = flaccid blisters + oral involvement + Nikolsky positive. Pemphigoid = tense blisters + elderly + Nikolsky negative.
thinking: Nikolsky sign positive = intraepidermal blistering = pemphigus. Negative = subepidermal = pemphigoid.
exam_trap: Confusing pemphigus with pemphigoid — tense vs flaccid and Nikolsky sign are the key differentiators.
takeaway: Pemphigus vulgaris: flaccid bullae + oral erosions + positive Nikolsky sign — treat with high-dose prednisolone.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with persistent central facial erythema, flushing, papules, and pustules on her nose and cheeks. There are no comedones. She notices flares with alcohol and spicy food. What is the first-line treatment for papulopustular rosacea?

options.B: Topical adapalene 0.1% gel once at night

correct_answer: C. Topical metronidazole or azelaic acid
why_correct: Mild-moderate papulopustular rosacea: first-line topical treatment is metronidazole gel or azelaic acid cream. These reduce inflammatory lesions. Oral antibiotics (doxycycline) are used for more extensive or resistant disease. Topical ivermectin 1% once daily is first-line in UK guidance; topical metronidazole or azelaic acid are the alternatives (the best option listed here).
why_wrong: A. Oral doxycycline is for more extensive or resistant papulopustular rosacea. B. Topical retinoids are for acne and can irritate rosacea. D. Isotretinoin is for severe, refractory rosacea under specialist care. E. Topical steroids worsen rosacea.
pearl: Rosacea triggers: alcohol, hot beverages, spicy food, UV exposure, temperature extremes. No comedones (unlike acne).
thinking: Central facial erythema + papules/pustules + no comedones = rosacea. Topical metronidazole first-line.
exam_trap: Prescribing topical corticosteroid for facial redness — it causes steroid rosacea with rebound worsening.
takeaway: Papulopustular rosacea: topical metronidazole or azelaic acid first-line — avoid topical corticosteroids.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with a scaly patch of hair loss on his scalp with broken hair stumps. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.B: Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 6-8 weeks
options.D: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly for 4 weeks
options.E: Observation, as most cases resolve at puberty

correct_answer: B. Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 6-8 weeks
why_correct: Tinea capitis (scalp ringworm): dermatophyte infection requiring systemic antifungal because topical agents do not penetrate the hair follicle. Fluorescence suggests Microsporum, for which oral griseofulvin (6–8 weeks) is preferred; terbinafine (about 4 weeks) is preferred for Trichophyton species.
why_wrong: A. Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the hair follicle. C. Flucloxacillin treats bacterial, not fungal, infection. D. Antifungal shampoo reduces spore shedding but is an adjunct, not treatment. E. Untreated tinea capitis can cause kerion and scarring alopecia and spreads to others.
pearl: Trichophyton tonsurans (common in Afro-Caribbean children): does not fluoresce under Wood's lamp. Microsporum (fluorescent). Both need oral treatment.
thinking: Scalp ringworm = systemic antifungal required — topical insufficient.
exam_trap: Prescribing topical antifungal for tinea capitis — it is ineffective.
takeaway: Tinea capitis: oral griseofulvin or terbinafine for 6-8 weeks — topical antifungals are insufficient.

stem: A 70-year-old outdoor worker presents with a rapidly growing, ulcerated, keratinous lesion on his lower lip that has grown over 6 weeks. He has significant sun exposure history. On examination there is a firm 1.5 cm ulcerated lesion with raised indurated edges. What is the most appropriate management?

options.C: Suspected cancer pathway referral for excision
options.D: Routine dermatology referral and review in 3 months

correct_answer: C. Suspected cancer pathway referral for excision
why_correct: Rapidly growing ulcerated keratinous lesion with indurated edges on the lip in an elderly patient with sun exposure = squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. SCC has metastatic potential, particularly on the lip. Urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for excision biopsy and histological diagnosis is required.
why_wrong: A. Imiquimod is for superficial BCC, Bowen's disease and actinic keratoses, not suspected SCC. B. Cryotherapy is inappropriate for suspected SCC. D. Routine referral and delay risk progression and metastasis. E. Actinic keratosis does not grow rapidly or ulcerate with indurated edges.
pearl: SCC risk factors: sun exposure, immunosuppression, chronic wounds, radiation. Higher metastatic risk: lip, ear, non-sun-exposed sites.
thinking: Rapidly growing ulcerated lesion with indurated edges = SCC until proven otherwise. Do not delay.
exam_trap: Treating with topical therapy or delaying for SCC — rapid growth and ulceration require urgent excision.
takeaway: Suspected SCC: urgent suspected cancer pathway referral for excision and histological confirmation.

stem: A 65-year-old man has an incidental finding of WBC 42 x 10(9)/L on a routine FBC. Blood film shows predominantly small mature-looking lymphocytes with smear cells. He is asymptomatic with no lymphadenopathy. CD5+/CD23+ on flow cytometry. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Start ibrutinib now to delay progression
options.D: Watch and wait — monitor without treatment

correct_answer: D. Watch and wait — monitor without treatment
why_correct: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia: Binet stage A (no lymphadenopathy in ≥3 regions, no anaemia, no thrombocytopenia) — watchful waiting is the standard approach. Treatment for CLL is initiated when symptomatic or at Binet stage B/C. CLL in stage A does not benefit from early treatment.
why_wrong: A. Early treatment of asymptomatic early-stage CLL gives no survival benefit and adds toxicity. B. Transplant is reserved for high-risk refractory disease. C. Steroids have no role in early CLL (they are used for autoimmune complications). E. Splenectomy is not CLL management.
pearl: CLL smear cells (Gumprecht shadows) on blood film are characteristic. CD5/CD23 co-expression is diagnostic.
thinking: Asymptomatic CLL stage A = watch and wait. Treatment triggers: symptomatic, progressive, cytopenia.
exam_trap: Starting treatment for incidental asymptomatic CLL — early treatment does not improve prognosis.
takeaway: Asymptomatic Binet stage A CLL: watchful waiting — treatment does not benefit asymptomatic early disease.

stem: A 72-year-old man on warfarin (INR 8.2) presents with haematuria and visible right flank bruising. He is haemodynamically stable and alert. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Give fresh frozen plasma to correct the INR
options.B: Reduce the warfarin dose and recheck INR tomorrow
options.D: Withhold warfarin and give IV vitamin K

correct_answer: D. Withhold warfarin and give IV vitamin K
why_correct: INR >8 with minor bleeding: withhold warfarin and give phytomenadione 1–3 mg by slow IV injection, repeating after 24 hours if the INR remains too high; restart warfarin when INR <5. Major bleeding: vitamin K 5 mg IV plus 4-factor PCC. This patient is stable with minor bleeding.
why_wrong: A: FFP provides clotting factors but is volume-dependent and slower than PCC — used if PCC unavailable for major bleeding. B: warfarin should be withheld, not reduced. C: tranexamic acid does not reverse warfarin. E: protamine sulphate reverses heparin, not warfarin.
pearl: 4-factor PCC (Octaplex/Beriplex) rapidly reverses warfarin for life-threatening bleeding. Vitamin K takes 6-12 hours to work.
thinking: INR >8 with bleeding: withhold warfarin + vitamin K. Life-threatening bleeding: add PCC.
exam_trap: Giving FFP when PCC is available for major bleeding — PCC is faster and more effective.
takeaway: INR >8 with minor bleeding: withhold warfarin + IV vitamin K 1–3 mg; major bleeding: IV vitamin K 5 mg + PCC.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has widespread musculoskeletal pain for 6 months, fatigue, non-restorative sleep, and diffuse tenderness. All bloods including CRP, ESR, RF, and ANA are normal. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily with a slow taper over weeks
options.B: Disease-modifying therapy with weekly methotrexate and folic acid
options.D: Exercise, CBT and an antidepressant (e.g. amitriptyline)
options.E: Pregabalin titrated to 300 mg daily with regular GP review

correct_answer: D. Exercise, CBT and an antidepressant (e.g. amitriptyline)
why_correct: Fibromyalgia: widespread pain + fatigue + sleep disturbance + normal investigations. Management: aerobic exercise (most evidence), CBT for pain management, and low-dose amitriptyline (sleep) or duloxetine (pain). NSAIDs and opioids are generally ineffective and should be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Fibromyalgia is not inflammatory; steroids are not indicated. B. DMARDs have no role in fibromyalgia. C. Opioids should not be started for chronic primary pain and cause dependence. E. NICE advises against starting gabapentinoids for chronic primary pain.
pearl: Fibromyalgia = central sensitisation. Exercise and CBT target the pain processing mechanism. Opioids worsen outcomes.
thinking: Normal bloods + widespread pain + fatigue = fibromyalgia. Exercise and psychological therapy first.
exam_trap: Prescribing long-term opioids for fibromyalgia — they worsen central sensitisation and cause dependence.
takeaway: Fibromyalgia: graded exercise + CBT + amitriptyline or duloxetine — opioids should be avoided.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with painful swollen right knee and left ankle, urethritis, and conjunctivitis 3 weeks after an episode of diarrhoea caused by Campylobacter. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Reactive arthritis: asymmetric oligoarthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis following GI or urogenital infection (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Chlamydia). The classic triad: 'can't see, can't pee, can't bend the knee'. HLA-B27 associated. Most cases self-limiting.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis is usually monoarticular with fever and does not explain urethritis and conjunctivitis. B. RA is a symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis without this triad. C. Gonococcal arthritis causes migratory arthritis, tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions after sexual exposure. D. AS causes chronic inflammatory back pain, not acute oligoarthritis with this triad.
pearl: Reactive arthritis: self-limiting in most (3-6 months). NSAIDs for symptoms. 15-20% develop chronic joint disease.
thinking: Post-infection arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis = reactive arthritis.
exam_trap: Treating reactive arthritis as septic arthritis without joint aspiration evidence.
takeaway: Reactive arthritis: post-infectious asymmetric oligoarthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis — manage with NSAIDs.

stem: A 35-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve is about to undergo dental extraction. What is the current NICE guidance on antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.A: Amoxicillin 3 g orally 1 hour before the procedure
options.C: IV gentamicin and amoxicillin immediately before
options.D: Prophylaxis required for all dental procedures in all patients with cardiac history
options.E: No routine antibiotic prophylaxis — NICE does not recommend it for dental procedures

correct_answer: E. No routine antibiotic prophylaxis — NICE does not recommend it for dental procedures
why_correct: NICE CG64 (2008, updated 2016): routine antibiotic prophylaxis is NOT recommended for dental or other procedures in patients at risk of endocarditis, including those with prosthetic valves. Evidence of benefit is unclear, and risks of widespread antibiotic use (resistance, adverse reactions) outweigh benefit.
why_wrong: A. Amoxicillin prophylaxis before dental procedures is no longer recommended routinely by NICE. B. Clindamycin is no longer recommended (and carries C. difficile risk). C. IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin is an obsolete regimen. D. NICE does not recommend routine prophylaxis for any group having dental procedures.
pearl: NICE guidance is controversial — ESC/AHA still recommend prophylaxis for high-risk cardiac conditions. Good oral hygiene is emphasised as more important than procedure prophylaxis.
thinking: NICE 2008: no antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures regardless of cardiac history.
exam_trap: Prescribing prophylaxis because it 'feels right' for a high-risk patient — current NICE guidance does not recommend it.
takeaway: NICE: no routine antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures even in high-risk cardiac patients.

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman (32 weeks) presents with a widespread vesicular rash that appeared 12 hours ago. She has no prior history of chickenpox. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Give varicella vaccine now, with a second dose 4–8 weeks later
options.B: Varicella-zoster immunoglobulin and observation at home for 7 days
options.C: Calamine lotion and paracetamol with routine GP review in a week
options.D: Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily and obstetric referral
options.E: Check VZV IgG and start aciclovir if the result comes back negative

correct_answer: D. Oral aciclovir 800 mg five times daily and obstetric referral
why_correct: Chickenpox in pregnancy (especially >20 weeks) carries risk of varicella pneumonia in the mother (5-20% mortality) and neonatal varicella if near term. Oral aciclovir within 24 hours of rash onset reduces severity. Obstetric referral is urgent. For susceptible pregnant women exposed to chickenpox without a rash, UKHSA recommends oral antiviral post-exposure prophylaxis first, with VZIG only if antivirals are unsuitable.
why_wrong: A. Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. B. VZIG (or, preferably, oral antiviral) is post-exposure prophylaxis for women without a rash; it has no role once chickenpox has developed. C. Symptomatic treatment alone ignores the risk of maternal varicella pneumonia. E. Treatment should not wait for serology; the diagnosis is clinical.
pearl: Varicella pneumonia complicates up to about 10% of chickenpox in pregnancy — smokers at highest risk. Severe neonatal chickenpox is most likely if delivery occurs within 7 days of maternal rash onset or the mother develops the rash up to 7 days after delivery — the neonate then needs post-exposure prophylaxis per UKHSA.
thinking: Chickenpox in pregnancy = high-risk. Treat with aciclovir and refer to obstetrics urgently.
exam_trap: Treating as self-limiting — maternal varicella pneumonia is a life-threatening complication.
takeaway: Chickenpox in pregnancy: oral aciclovir + urgent obstetric referral — risk of maternal varicella pneumonia.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with painful right eye visual loss developing over 3 days. Visual acuity is 6/60 in the right eye. There is a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). Fundoscopy is normal (retrobulbar neuritis). What is the most likely underlying condition and most appropriate management?

options.A: Acute angle closure glaucoma — IV acetazolamide and pilocarpine
options.C: Central retinal artery occlusion — IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours
options.D: Demyelination — IV methylprednisolone and neurology referral
options.E: Ischaemic optic neuropathy — urgent ESR and prednisolone

correct_answer: D. Demyelination — IV methylprednisolone and neurology referral
why_correct: Optic neuritis in a young woman: painful visual loss + RAPD + normal fundus (retrobulbar) = demyelinating optic neuritis, most commonly associated with MS. High-dose IV methylprednisolone hastens recovery but does not improve final visual acuity. Urgent MRI and neurology referral are essential.
why_wrong: A. Angle closure causes a red eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil and raised IOP. B. Retinal detachment is painless with a field defect and abnormal fundus. C. CRAO is sudden and painless with a pale retina. E. Ischaemic optic neuropathy occurs in older patients, is usually painless and typically shows disc swelling.
pearl: Optic neuritis is the first presentation of MS in 25% of patients. MRI brain shows demyelinating lesions.
thinking: Painful visual loss + RAPD + young woman = optic neuritis = possible MS. MRI and neurology urgently.
exam_trap: Reassuring without MRI — optic neuritis is a sentinel event for MS requiring investigation.
takeaway: Optic neuritis: IV methylprednisolone + urgent MRI and neurology referral to investigate for MS.

stem: A 30-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis presents with painful right eye, photophobia, and blurred vision. Examination reveals circumcorneal injection (ciliary flush) and a small, irregular pupil. Slit-lamp examination shows cells and flare in the anterior chamber. What is the diagnosis and most appropriate management?

options.A: Bacterial conjunctivitis — chloramphenicol drops and review in 1 week
options.B: Anterior uveitis — steroid and cycloplegic drops, urgent eye referral
options.C: Acute angle closure glaucoma — IV acetazolamide and pilocarpine
options.D: Bacterial keratitis — topical antibiotic drops hourly
options.E: Scleritis — oral NSAIDs and rheumatology review

correct_answer: B. Anterior uveitis — steroid and cycloplegic drops, urgent eye referral
why_correct: Anterior uveitis (iritis): ciliary flush + irregular small pupil (posterior synechiae) + anterior chamber cells and flare. Associated with HLA-B27 conditions (AS, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis). Treatment: topical corticosteroids (prednisolone acetate) + cycloplegic drops (atropine/cyclopentolate) to prevent synechiae.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis causes diffuse injection without anterior chamber cells or pupil changes. C. Angle closure causes a fixed mid-dilated pupil and raised IOP. D. Bacterial keratitis shows a corneal infiltrate or ulcer on fluorescein, usually with contact lens use. E. Scleritis causes deep boring pain and scleral injection, without the anterior chamber activity described.
pearl: HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies: remember PAIR — Psoriatic arthritis, Ankylosing spondylitis, Inflammatory bowel disease arthropathy, Reactive arthritis.
thinking: Ciliary flush + irregular small pupil + cells in anterior chamber = uveitis. Urgent ophthalmology.
exam_trap: Treating uveitis as conjunctivitis with chloramphenicol — this delays treatment and risks sight.
takeaway: Anterior uveitis: ciliary flush + anterior chamber cells + irregular pupil — urgent ophthalmology, topical steroids.

stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought by parents with fever, poor feeding, and bulging fontanelle. He appears unwell and is irritable when handled. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin and GP review in 24 hours
options.B: IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin now; LP when safe
options.C: Lumbar puncture first, then IV cefotaxime
options.D: Paracetamol and observe for 4 hours before deciding
options.E: Urine culture and await result before antibiotics

correct_answer: B. IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin now; LP when safe
why_correct: Meningitis in a 3-month-old infant: bulging fontanelle + fever + irritability = bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. In an unwell infant, IV antibiotics must not be delayed: a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone, or cefotaxime if ceftriaxone is contraindicated) PLUS IV amoxicillin to cover Listeria in young infants (cephalosporins do not cover Listeria). NICE NG240 advises LP before antibiotics only if it is safe and will not cause a clinically significant delay; otherwise perform LP as soon as it is safe after antibiotics have started.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for suspected bacterial meningitis. C. LP must not delay antibiotics in an unwell infant. D. A febrile 3-month-old with a bulging fontanelle needs immediate IV antibiotics, not observation. E. Awaiting urine culture delays critical treatment.
pearl: Infants under 3 months are at risk of Group B Streptococcus and Listeria — add amoxicillin (also called ampicillin) to cover Listeria (not covered by cephalosporins).
thinking: Infant with fever + meningism signs = presumed bacterial meningitis. Treat immediately.
exam_trap: Delaying antibiotics to obtain an LP in a sick infant — LP comes first only if it is safe and will not cause a clinically significant delay.
takeaway: Suspected meningitis in an infant ≤3 months: IV cefotaxime PLUS amoxicillin (Listeria cover) immediately — LP after if safe, not before.

stem: A 4-week-old male infant presents with a 2-week history of projectile vomiting after every feed. He is hungry immediately after vomiting. On examination there is visible gastric peristalsis and an olive-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant. What is the diagnosis and management?

options.A: GORD — thickened feeds and a trial of oral omeprazole
options.B: Intussusception — air enema reduction under fluoroscopy
options.C: Meconium ileus — Gastrografin enema and IV fluid support
options.D: Hirschsprung's disease — rectal biopsy, then pull-through surgery
options.E: Pyloric stenosis — IV fluids to correct alkalosis, then pyloromyotomy

correct_answer: E. Pyloric stenosis — IV fluids to correct alkalosis, then pyloromyotomy
why_correct: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis: projectile (non-bilious) vomiting + hungry infant + olive mass in RUQ = classic presentation. Metabolic consequence: hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Management: IV fluid resuscitation to correct electrolytes BEFORE surgery (Ramstedt pyloromyotomy).
why_wrong: A. GORD does not cause projectile vomiting with visible peristalsis and a palpable olive mass. B. Intussusception presents later (around 5–10 months) with colicky pain and redcurrant jelly stools. C. Meconium ileus presents in the first days of life with bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium. D. Hirschsprung's disease presents with delayed passage of meconium and constipation, not projectile vomiting with an olive mass.
pearl: Electrolytes in pyloric stenosis: low Na, low K, low Cl, high bicarbonate (hypochloraemic alkalosis). Never operate until corrected.
thinking: Projectile non-bilious vomiting + olive mass + male infant = pyloric stenosis. Correct electrolytes first.
exam_trap: Operating without correcting metabolic alkalosis — anaesthetic risk is dangerously high.
takeaway: Pyloric stenosis: IV fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction before Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

stem: A 3-year-old boy who was born at 27 weeks gestation and required ventilation is referred by his health visitor. He has delayed motor milestones, tip-toe walking, increased tone in his legs with brisk reflexes, and scissor gait. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Global developmental delay from chromosomal abnormality

why_correct: Spastic diplegia: the most common form of CP in premature infants — periventricular leukomalacia damages the corticospinal fibres controlling the legs more than arms. Features: increased tone, brisk reflexes, scissor gait, tip-toe walking, predominantly affecting lower limbs.
why_wrong: A: DMD presents in boys aged 3-5 with proximal weakness, pseudohypertrophy, Gowers' sign, elevated CK. B: developmental delay does not explain UMN signs. D: ASD does not explain the motor findings. E: chromosomal causes have specific features.
pearl: IVH (intraventricular haemorrhage) and PVL are the main causes of CP in premature infants. MRI cranial confirms PVL.
thinking: Premature + increased tone + UMN signs + predominantly lower limb = spastic diplegia CP.
exam_trap: Attributing the findings to prematurity alone — CP is a specific diagnosis requiring assessment and intervention.
takeaway: Spastic diplegic CP: common in premature infants due to PVL — multidisciplinary management including physiotherapy.

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with a painless episode of bright red vaginal bleeding. She has no contractions. USS confirms complete placenta praevia. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Category 1 caesarean section within 30 minutes of arrival
options.B: Speculum and digital examination to assess the cervix
options.C: Amniotomy and oxytocin augmentation of labour
options.D: Discharge home with pelvic rest and review in 1 week
options.E: Admit, IV access, crossmatch and antenatal corticosteroids

correct_answer: E. Admit, IV access, crossmatch and antenatal corticosteroids
why_correct: Placenta praevia with antepartum haemorrhage: admit, IV access, blood crossmatch, maternal and fetal monitoring. Betamethasone for fetal lung maturation if <34 weeks. Delivery timing depends on haemodynamic stability and gestation. Vaginal delivery is contraindicated in placenta praevia.
why_wrong: A. Category 1 caesarean section is for haemodynamic instability or fetal compromise, which are not described here. B. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated in placenta praevia because it can provoke major haemorrhage. C. Amniotomy and vaginal delivery are contraindicated with a complete placenta praevia. D. Discharge is unsafe after an antepartum haemorrhage with a placenta praevia.
pearl: Placenta praevia: digital vaginal examination is CONTRAINDICATED — it can precipitate massive haemorrhage (a gentle speculum examination is acceptable).
thinking: Painless APH = placenta praevia until proven otherwise. Admit, stabilise, no digital vaginal examination.
exam_trap: Performing a digital vaginal examination in placenta praevia — catastrophic haemorrhage can result.
takeaway: Placenta praevia with bleeding: admit, IV access, crossmatch, steroids if <34 weeks — no digital vaginal examination.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, and acne. USS shows bilateral polycystic ovaries with 20+ follicles per ovary. She has no pregnancy wish currently. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.B: Clomifene citrate from day 2 of the cycle
options.D: GnRH analogue with add-back HRT for 6 months
options.E: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling as a day case

why_correct: PMOS (formerly PCOS) without fertility wish: combined OCP is first-line for menstrual regulation, hirsutism, and acne. It suppresses LH, reduces androgen production, and prevents endometrial hyperplasia. Co-cyprindiol (cyproterone + ethinylestradiol) has additional antiandrogen effect.
why_wrong: A. Metformin is not first-line for menstrual or skin symptoms — it is a useful adjunct if BMI >25 or metabolic features are present, or for ovulation induction, but the priority here (menstrual regulation and antiandrogen effects without a fertility wish) is the combined OCP. B. Clomifene is for ovulation induction when fertility is desired. D. GnRH analogues, even with add-back HRT, are not first-line for PMOS (formerly PCOS) symptoms. E. Ovarian drilling is for clomifene-resistant anovulatory infertility.
pearl: PMOS (formerly PCOS) long-term risks: endometrial hyperplasia/cancer (anovulation), metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes. Assess glycaemic status at diagnosis and every 1-3 years depending on risk.
thinking: PMOS (formerly PCOS) without fertility wish + menstrual and androgen symptoms = combined OCP first-line.
exam_trap: Starting clomifene in a patient who does not want fertility treatment — it is specifically for ovulation induction.
takeaway: PMOS (formerly PCOS) without fertility wish: combined OCP for menstrual regulation and antiandrogen effects.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with exertional dyspnoea and a collapsing pulse. Examination reveals a high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge, visible carotid pulsations, and wide pulse pressure (160/40). What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.E: MR angiography of the thoracic aorta

why_correct: Collapsing (waterhammer) pulse + early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge + wide pulse pressure = aortic regurgitation. Transthoracic echo confirms diagnosis, quantifies severity, assesses LV function and dimensions — essential for timing of surgical intervention.
why_wrong: A. A chest radiograph may show cardiomegaly but does not diagnose or quantify aortic regurgitation. B. Coronary angiography assesses the coronary arteries, typically before valve surgery, not as the initial investigation. C. An ECG may show LV hypertrophy but does not diagnose aortic regurgitation. E. MR angiography of the aorta may be needed if aortic root dilatation is suspected, but echocardiography comes first.
pearl: Signs of severe AR: Corrigan's pulse, de Musset's sign (head bobbing), Quincke's sign (nail bed pulsation), Traube's sign (pistol shot femoral sounds).
thinking: Early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge = AR. Echo is the first investigation.
exam_trap: Ordering coronary angiogram before echo in suspected valve disease.
takeaway: Suspected aortic regurgitation: transthoracic echocardiogram is the investigation of choice.

stem: A 72-year-old man with severe COPD is admitted with an exacerbation. ABG on 28% oxygen: pH 7.28, PaCO2 9.2 kPa, PaO2 7.8 kPa. He is drowsy. What is the most appropriate respiratory support?

options.A: High-flow oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreathe mask

why_correct: Type 2 respiratory failure with acidosis (pH 7.28) in COPD exacerbation: NIV (BiPAP) is the treatment of choice — it reduces respiratory muscle work, improves ventilation, reduces CO2, and avoids intubation. NICE and BTS recommend NIV for pH 7.25-7.35 with appropriate clinical assessment.
why_wrong: A: high-flow oxygen will worsen hypercapnia in COPD by abolishing hypoxic drive. B: intubation is reserved for NIV failure or contraindications (pH <7.25 with deterioration). D: controlled oxygen is not sufficient treatment for acidotic type 2 failure. E: bronchodilators alone are insufficient.
pearl: NIV targets: pH >7.35, RR reduction, improved consciousness within 1-4 hours. If no improvement, escalate to ITU.
thinking: COPD + acidosis (pH 7.25-7.35) + hypercapnia = NIV. Not high-flow O2.
exam_trap: High-flow oxygen in type 2 respiratory failure with COPD — worsens CO2 retention.
takeaway: COPD exacerbation with type 2 failure and acidosis: NIV is first-line respiratory support.

stem: A 55-year-old man with established hepatitis B cirrhosis attends for review. He is clinically well with no new symptoms. What surveillance is recommended to detect hepatocellular carcinoma early?

options.A: Annual contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
options.B: Six-monthly ultrasound with or without AFP
options.C: Clinical review only, imaging if symptoms develop
options.E: Annual liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast

correct_answer: B. Six-monthly ultrasound with or without AFP
why_correct: EASL/NICE: patients with cirrhosis (any cause) and chronic hepatitis B (without cirrhosis) should undergo 6-monthly liver ultrasound surveillance for HCC. AFP is used alongside USS but has limited sensitivity alone. This allows detection at a resectable/transplantable stage.
why_wrong: A. Annual CT involves radiation and contrast and is not the standard surveillance modality or interval. C. HCC is silent until advanced, so waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of surveillance. D. Biopsy is for tissue diagnosis of a detected lesion, not surveillance. E. MRI is used to characterise detected lesions; annual MRI is not standard surveillance.
pearl: HCC diagnosis: LIRADS criteria on CT/MRI in cirrhotic patients can diagnose without biopsy if typical features are present.
thinking: Cirrhosis = HCC risk. Six-monthly USS is the established surveillance standard.
exam_trap: Stopping surveillance because the patient is clinically well — HCC is asymptomatic until advanced.
takeaway: Cirrhosis: 6-monthly liver ultrasound (+/- AFP) for HCC surveillance.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive hand clumsiness, difficulty walking, and urinary urgency over 6 months. Examination shows reduced power in the hands, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, and extensor plantars. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cervical myelopathy: UMN signs in the legs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantars) + LMN signs in the hands (due to cord compression at C5/6/7) + bladder symptoms = classic presentation. MRI cervical spine confirms cord compression.
