why_wrong: A: MND has mixed UMN and LMN signs without sensory symptoms but does affect both arms and legs — cervical myelopathy has clear dermatomal distribution and bladder involvement. C: Parkinson's does not cause UMN signs or extensor plantars. D: peripheral neuropathy causes absent reflexes. E: syringomyelia has dissociated sensory loss (pain/temperature affected, proprioception spared).
pearl: Cervical myelopathy: hands weak (LMN — cord level) + legs spastic (UMN — below level). Urgency = spinothalamic tract compression.
thinking: UMN legs + LMN hands + bladder = cervical myelopathy. MRI confirms.
exam_trap: Missing the level-specific pattern — UMN in legs and LMN in hands together indicate cord compression, not brain or peripheral disease.
takeaway: Cervical myelopathy: hand weakness + spastic legs + bladder symptoms — MRI cervical spine urgently.

stem: A 70-year-old man with CKD (eGFR 28) requires urgent CT with contrast for suspected aortic dissection. What is the most important pre-procedure measure to reduce risk of contrast-induced nephropathy?

options.A: IV 0.9% saline before and after contrast
options.B: Withhold metformin for 48 hours after contrast
options.C: Oral N-acetylcysteine before and after contrast
options.D: Haemodialysis immediately after the contrast scan
options.E: Proceed with no precautions as the scan is urgent

correct_answer: A. IV 0.9% saline before and after contrast
why_correct: Contrast-induced nephropathy prevention: IV hydration with normal saline before and after contrast is the most effective intervention. It maintains renal perfusion and dilutes nephrotoxic contrast. Use minimum contrast volume and low-osmolarity agents.
why_wrong: B. Metformin may need to be withheld (lactic acidosis risk if AKI develops), but this is not a renal protective measure. C. N-acetylcysteine has mixed evidence and is not recommended in place of IV hydration. D. Prophylactic haemodialysis does not prevent contrast-induced nephropathy. E. Urgency does not negate the importance of IV hydration if time allows.
pearl: For urgent procedures with insufficient time to pre-hydrate: use minimum contrast volume and monitor renal function post-procedure.
thinking: CKD + contrast = pre-hydrate with IV saline. This is the single most evidence-based intervention.
exam_trap: Relying on NAC alone — hydration is the primary evidence-based intervention.
takeaway: Contrast nephropathy prevention: IV saline pre- and post-procedure is the most effective measure.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents 6 weeks after delivery with persistent low mood, tearfulness, inability to bond with her baby, poor sleep, and feelings of worthlessness. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 16. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Reassure that this is postnatal blues; review in 2 weeks
options.B: Immediate admission to a mother and baby unit
options.C: Oral haloperidol with community mental health team follow-up
options.D: Watchful waiting with self-help advice and repeat EPDS in 4 weeks
options.E: SSRI plus referral for CBT or IPT, with close follow-up

correct_answer: E. SSRI plus referral for CBT or IPT, with close follow-up
why_correct: Postnatal depression (EPDS ≥13 = probable PND): for moderate-severe depression NICE CG192 advises high-intensity psychological therapy (e.g. CBT), with an SSRI if she prefers medication, declines psychological therapy or does not respond, and combination treatment if the response is inadequate. Sertraline is usually preferred when breastfeeding. Close follow-up and safeguarding awareness are essential.
why_wrong: A. Postnatal blues occur in the first days and resolve within about 10 days; persistent symptoms at 6 weeks with a high EPDS indicate postnatal depression needing treatment. B. Mother and baby unit admission is for severe depression with psychotic features or significant risk, not described here. C. Haloperidol is for postpartum psychosis, not depression. D. Self-help alone with further delay risks harm to mother and child.
pearl: Sertraline: lowest breast milk transfer of SSRIs — preferred for breastfeeding mothers with PND.
thinking: EPDS ≥13 at 6 weeks postpartum = PND requiring active treatment. Safeguard the baby.
exam_trap: Dismissing as postnatal blues — blues resolves within 10 days; PND persists beyond 2 weeks.
takeaway: Postnatal depression: SSRI (sertraline) plus psychological therapy — distinguish from self-limiting postnatal blues.

stem: A 78-year-old man is found at home by neighbours. He is confused and unresponsive to voice. Core temperature is 30.2 degrees C. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Rapid rewarming by immersion in a hot bath
options.B: External rewarming, warmed IV fluids and cardiac monitoring
options.C: Cold 0.9% saline IV fluids to prevent rewarming shock
options.D: Discharge home with blankets and community nurse rewarming
options.E: Heated humidified oxygen as the only rewarming measure

correct_answer: B. External rewarming, warmed IV fluids and cardiac monitoring
why_correct: Moderate hypothermia (28-32 degrees C): passive rewarming (blankets, warm environment) plus active external rewarming (warm blankets, heat pads to trunk). Cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias (especially VF risk). Warmed IV fluids. Avoid rapid rewarming — causes afterdrop and rewarming shock.
why_wrong: A. Rapid peripheral rewarming (hot bath) causes afterdrop and rewarming shock as cold peripheral blood returns to the core. C. Cold IV fluids worsen hypothermia. D. Moderate hypothermia with reduced consciousness requires hospital care with monitoring. E. Heated humidified oxygen helps but is not sufficient as the only rewarming measure.
pearl: Hypothermia ECG: Osborn (J) waves — positive deflection at J-point. Risk of VF below 30 degrees C.
thinking: Moderate hypothermia: passive + active external rewarming, avoid peripheral rewarming before core.
exam_trap: Rapid rewarming in a hot bath — causes dangerous afterdrop and peripheral vasodilation.
takeaway: Hypothermia: passive and active external rewarming — never rapid peripheral rewarming.

stem: A 30-year-old woman started allopurinol 3 weeks ago. She presents with fever, widespread blistering skin lesions, and painful oral and genital erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. Skin detachment involves 35% body surface area. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Stop allopurinol; specialist unit for fluids, wound and eye care
options.B: Continue allopurinol and prescribe oral antihistamines
options.C: Start high-dose oral prednisolone and arrange community follow-up
options.D: Reassure as a viral exanthem and review again in 48 hours
options.E: Start oral trimethoprim for a secondary skin infection

correct_answer: A. Stop allopurinol; specialist unit for fluids, wound and eye care
why_correct: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN): skin detachment >30% BSA caused by drug reaction (allopurinol, anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, NSAIDs). Mortality 20-30%. Immediate management: stop causative drug, admit to specialist burns/dermatology unit, IV fluids, meticulous wound care, ophthalmology (corneal erosions), nutritional support.
why_wrong: B. Continuing the causative drug is catastrophic. C. Evidence for systemic steroids in TEN is mixed, and this life-threatening condition with 35% detachment cannot be managed in the community. D. TEN is a life-threatening emergency, not a viral exanthem. E. Trimethoprim is itself a recognised cause of SJS/TEN, and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated without proven infection.
pearl: SCORTEN score predicts TEN mortality. Ciclosporin or IV immunoglobulin are used in specialist centres.
thinking: >30% BSA detachment = TEN. <10% = SJS. 10-30% = overlap. Stop the drug immediately.
exam_trap: Continuing the causative drug — drug cessation is the single most important intervention.
takeaway: TEN: immediately stop the causative drug and transfer to burns/dermatology specialist unit.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with cold-induced triphasic colour change in her fingers (white to blue to red) that is symmetric and has occurred for 5 years with no other symptoms. ANA is negative. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent vascular surgery referral for sympathectomy
options.B: Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for 2 weeks then taper
options.C: Warfarin anticoagulation with a target INR of 2–3
options.D: Keep warm and avoid cold; nifedipine if severe
options.E: Rheumatology referral for an IV iloprost infusion

correct_answer: D. Keep warm and avoid cold; nifedipine if severe
why_correct: Primary Raynaud's phenomenon (no underlying cause): affects young women, symmetric, no tissue damage, ANA negative. Management: lifestyle measures (gloves, avoid cold triggers, smoking cessation). Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) are first-line pharmacotherapy for frequent/severe episodes.
why_wrong: A. Vascular surgery or sympathectomy is reserved for severe secondary Raynaud's with digital ischaemia or ulceration. B. Steroids have no role in primary Raynaud's. C. Anticoagulation is not indicated in primary Raynaud's. E. IV iloprost is reserved for severe secondary Raynaud's with digital ischaemia; there is no tissue damage here.
pearl: Secondary Raynaud's: associated with scleroderma, SLE, RA — investigate with ANA, anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70. Asymmetric onset, tissue damage, male gender, older age = investigate.
thinking: Young woman + symmetric + triphasic + ANA negative = primary Raynaud's. Lifestyle + nifedipine.
exam_trap: Investigating aggressively without distinguishing primary from secondary Raynaud's.
takeaway: Primary Raynaud's: lifestyle modifications first — nifedipine for frequent/severe episodes.

stem: A 60-year-old patient is found to be MRSA positive on pre-operative screening before elective hip replacement. He is currently asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Postpone surgery until three consecutive negative MRSA screens
options.B: Proceed with surgery as he has no symptoms
options.C: Nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine washes for 5 days
options.D: Oral flucloxacillin for 7 days before surgery
options.E: IV vancomycin for 2 weeks, then proceed with surgery

correct_answer: C. Nasal mupirocin and chlorhexidine washes for 5 days
why_correct: Pre-operative MRSA decolonisation: nasal mupirocin (3 times daily for 5 days) + chlorhexidine body wash + hair wash for 5 days before surgery significantly reduces surgical site infection rates. This is standard UK practice per PHE guidance.
why_wrong: A. Surgery can proceed after a decolonisation course; postponing for repeated negative screens is unnecessary. B. MRSA carriage increases peri-operative infection risk, so proceeding without decolonisation is inappropriate. D. Flucloxacillin does not treat MRSA (it is resistant to beta-lactams). E. IV vancomycin is for treating MRSA infection, not colonisation.
pearl: MRSA decolonisation failure: consider mupirocin resistance — use alternative topical agent. Prophylactic teicoplanin IV is given at induction for MRSA carriers.
thinking: MRSA carriage + planned surgery = decolonise first to reduce surgical site infection.
exam_trap: Using flucloxacillin for MRSA — MRSA is resistant to all beta-lactam antibiotics.
takeaway: Pre-operative MRSA carriage: nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine body wash for 5 days before surgery.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with ruddy complexion, headache, pruritus after bathing, and splenomegaly. FBC shows Hb 198 g/L, HCT 0.62, WBC 14, platelets 580. JAK2 V617F mutation is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?

options.A: Secondary polycythaemia — treat the underlying hypoxia
options.D: Reactive thrombocytosis — treat the underlying cause
options.E: Polycythaemia vera — aspirin and venesection to HCT <0.45

correct_answer: E. Polycythaemia vera — aspirin and venesection to HCT <0.45
why_correct: Polycythaemia vera: JAK2 V617F positive (>95% of PV), raised RBC mass, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus. First-line: low-dose aspirin (reduces thrombosis risk) plus venesection to HCT <0.45 (reduces hyperviscosity and thrombotic events). Hydroxycarbamide is added for high-risk patients.
why_wrong: A. Secondary polycythaemia has a raised or appropriate EPO and no JAK2 mutation, and does not explain splenomegaly with raised WBC and platelets. B. ET has markedly elevated platelets with normal Hb/HCT. C. Myelofibrosis presents with cytopenias, a leucoerythroblastic film and massive splenomegaly rather than a raised haematocrit. D. Reactive thrombocytosis does not explain the raised haematocrit or JAK2 positivity.
pearl: PV complications: thrombosis (arterial and venous), haemorrhage, transformation to myelofibrosis or AML.
thinking: JAK2 positive + raised RBC + splenomegaly + aquagenic pruritus = PV.
exam_trap: Missing PV because the presenting feature is itch — aquagenic pruritus is a classic PV symptom.
takeaway: Polycythaemia vera: aspirin + venesection to HCT <0.45 — add hydroxycarbamide for high-risk patients.

stem: A 19-year-old is seen in a community mental health clinic, having been referred by their GP. Since early adolescence they have felt a persistent and distressing sense that their body does not match who they are, describing a specific discomfort with their chest and voice. They avoid mirrors, stopped swimming at 14, and change clothes only in private. They describe feeling calmer and more themselves when addressed by a chosen name and different pronouns, which they have used with friends for two years. They are not preoccupied with a perceived flaw in their appearance, are comfortable socialising and presenting publicly in their chosen role, and there has been no recent identifiable life stressor. Mood is reactive and there is no weight or eating concern. What is the most likely explanation for this young person's distress?

options.E: Anorexia nervosa with body image disturbance

why_correct: The distress is anchored to a marked and persistent incongruence between experienced gender and sex assigned at birth, present since early adolescence, focused on sexed characteristics such as chest and voice, and relieved by being recognised in the experienced gender. Avoidance of mirrors, swimming and communal changing follows from that incongruence rather than from social evaluation or a perceived appearance defect. Recognition and referral for specialist assessment is the appropriate step; foundation doctors are not expected to initiate or manage gender-affirming treatment.
why_wrong: A: body dysmorphic disorder centres on preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, not on sexed characteristics being incongruent with experienced gender, and is not relieved by being recognised in another gender role. B: social anxiety disorder is driven by fear of scrutiny and negative evaluation across social situations; this patient is comfortable socialising and presenting publicly in the chosen role. D: adjustment disorder requires an identifiable recent stressor with symptoms that are time-limited, whereas this distress has been persistent since early adolescence. E: anorexia nervosa involves weight and shape preoccupation with dietary restriction, absent here.
pearl: Gender dysphoria is distinguished from its lookalikes by what relieves it: distress that eases when the person is recognised and addressed in their experienced gender points to incongruence rather than to appearance preoccupation or social fear.
thinking: Persistent distress since early adolescence ↓ Focused on sexed characteristics, not a perceived appearance flaw ↓ Eased by recognition in experienced gender ↓ No recent stressor, no social evaluation fear, no eating pathology ↓ Gender dysphoria (gender incongruence) — recognise and refer
exam_trap: Mirror and changing room avoidance reads as body dysmorphic disorder or social anxiety if taken at face value. The discriminator is the object and the relief: in gender dysphoria the distress attaches to sexed characteristics and eases with recognition in the experienced gender, whereas BDD centres on a perceived defect and social anxiety on being judged.
takeaway: Persistent distress at incongruence between experienced gender and sex assigned at birth, eased by recognition in the experienced gender = gender dysphoria; recognise and refer, do not manage.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found confused in a garage with a petrol-powered generator running. He has a headache, dizziness and nausea. His pulse is 105/min and oxygen saturation is 99% on air. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Carbon monoxide from an idling combustion engine in an enclosed space displaces oxygen from haemoglobin, producing headache, dizziness, nausea and confusion; pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin so saturation reads falsely normal.
why_wrong: B. Methanol poisoning typically causes visual disturbance and a severe metabolic acidosis rather than this exposure pattern. C. Salicylate toxicity causes tinnitus and hyperventilation, not a normal-saturation confusional state from engine exhaust. D. Opioid toxicity causes reduced consciousness with respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils, not a normal saturation and tachycardia. E. Cyanide poisoning is linked to combustion of synthetic materials in fires and causes a more dramatic, rapidly progressive toxic picture.
pearl: A normal pulse oximetry reading never excludes carbon monoxide poisoning — the probe cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin apart from oxyhaemoglobin, so a co-oximeter or blood gas is needed to measure carboxyhaemoglobin directly.
thinking: Enclosed garage + running petrol generator + headache, dizziness, confusion ↓ classic combustion-source exposure ↓ normal SpO2 despite hypoxic symptoms (oximeter can't detect COHb) ↓ Carbon monoxide poisoning
exam_trap: Candidates are often reassured by the normal oxygen saturation and look past CO poisoning, or are drawn to cyanide because of the combustion setting — but cyanide is linked far more with burning plastics/synthetics in structure fires than with idling engine exhaust.
takeaway: Enclosed space + engine exhaust + normal SpO2 with confusion is carbon monoxide until proven otherwise.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with profuse sweating, salivation, abdominal cramps, vomiting and pinpoint pupils after working with agricultural pesticides. Which type of poisoning is most likely?
why_correct: Organophosphate pesticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing excess cholinergic activity at muscarinic receptors: salivation, sweating, abdominal cramps, vomiting and miosis.
why_wrong: A. Tricyclic overdose typically causes arrhythmias, seizures and a broad QRS rather than a secretory cholinergic picture. B. Paracetamol poisoning is initially asymptomatic and later causes hepatotoxicity, not acute secretions. C. Opioids cause miosis and respiratory depression but not the marked salivation, sweating, cramps and vomiting seen here. E. Anticholinergic poisoning causes the opposite picture — dry skin, dilated pupils and urinary retention.
pearl: The cholinergic toxidrome is remembered with the mnemonic SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis) plus miosis — the mirror image of an anticholinergic overdose.
thinking: Agricultural pesticide exposure + salivation, sweating, cramps, vomiting ↓ excess muscarinic cholinergic drive ↓ pinpoint pupils confirm the cholinergic toxidrome ↓ Organophosphate poisoning
exam_trap: A well-meaning candidate may pick opioid poisoning because both cause miosis, but opioids cause respiratory depression and drowsiness rather than the drenching secretions and cramping of cholinergic excess.
takeaway: Occupational pesticide exposure with SLUDGE symptoms and miosis points straight to organophosphate poisoning.

stem: A 34-year-old man has taken an overdose of a tricyclic antidepressant. He is confused and hypotensive. ECG shows a broad QRS complex. Which treatment is indicated?
why_correct: Sodium bicarbonate increases extracellular sodium and alkalinises the blood, overcoming tricyclic-induced sodium-channel blockade and narrowing the QRS in significant toxicity with cardiovascular instability.
why_wrong: A. Activated charcoal may have a role very early after ingestion but does not reverse established cardiotoxicity. B. Vitamin K treats bleeding from vitamin K antagonists, not tricyclic overdose. C. Magnesium is used mainly for torsades de pointes, not broad-complex tricyclic toxicity. D. Calcium is used in selected calcium-channel blocker toxicity and other specific indications, not tricyclic overdose.
pearl: A widening QRS on the ECG is the key marker of severe tricyclic toxicity and the trigger for giving sodium bicarbonate, regardless of the measured drug level.
thinking: Tricyclic overdose + confusion and hypotension ↓ sodium-channel blockade shown by a broad QRS ↓ alkalinisation and sodium loading reverse the block ↓ Intravenous sodium bicarbonate
exam_trap: Candidates may reach for magnesium because it is the reflex answer for any broad-complex rhythm, but magnesium is reserved for torsades, not the sodium-channel-mediated QRS widening of tricyclic toxicity.
takeaway: A widening QRS in tricyclic overdose is treated with sodium bicarbonate, not magnesium.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has progressive difficulty swallowing. She initially struggled with solids, but now also has difficulty swallowing liquids. She has lost 7 kg unintentionally. What is the most appropriate investigation?
why_correct: Dysphagia progressing from solids to liquids together with unintentional weight loss is an alarm presentation for oesophageal malignancy and warrants urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to visualise and biopsy the oesophagus.
why_wrong: A. Hydrogen breath testing investigates carbohydrate malabsorption, not progressive mechanical dysphagia. B. Abdominal ultrasound does not adequately assess the oesophageal lumen. C. Flexible sigmoidoscopy examines the distal colon, unrelated to this presentation. D. Faecal calprotectin assesses intestinal inflammation, not swallowing difficulty.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia that moves from solids to liquids suggests a worsening mechanical narrowing, whereas dysphagia to solids and liquids together from the outset is more typical of a motility disorder such as achalasia.
thinking: Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) + unintentional 7 kg weight loss ↓ alarm features suggesting a structural, possibly malignant, oesophageal lesion ↓ direct visualisation and biopsy are needed urgently ↓ Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
exam_trap: A candidate might reach for a hydrogen breath test because malabsorption also causes weight loss, but breath testing has no role once alarm features point to a structural oesophageal problem needing endoscopy.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm symptom that goes straight to urgent endoscopy.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and bloating. Blood tests show iron deficiency and low vitamin levels. She reports symptoms after eating bread and pasta. Which condition should be suspected?
why_correct: Chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and bloating with iron and vitamin deficiencies, triggered by gluten-containing foods such as bread and pasta, are characteristic of malabsorption from coeliac disease.
why_wrong: B. GORD causes upper gastrointestinal symptoms rather than malabsorption. C. Lactose intolerance causes symptoms after lactose ingestion but does not typically cause significant nutritional deficiency. D. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause objective malabsorption or nutritional deficiencies. E. Acute appendicitis is an acute surgical condition, unrelated to chronic malabsorptive symptoms.
pearl: Nutritional deficiencies such as iron deficiency in the context of gluten-triggered gastrointestinal symptoms should prompt serological testing for coeliac disease before the patient reduces gluten intake.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea + weight loss + iron/vitamin deficiency + symptoms after bread/pasta ↓ gluten-triggered malabsorption ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: Candidates might consider lactose intolerance given the food-related trigger, but lactose intolerance does not explain the objective iron and vitamin deficiencies seen with true malabsorption from coeliac disease.
takeaway: Gluten-triggered diarrhoea with objective nutritional deficiencies points to coeliac disease rather than a food intolerance.

stem: A 58-year-old man has severe central chest pain radiating to his back. His blood pressure is different in each arm and there is a new early diastolic murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, together with unequal blood pressure between the arms and a new early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, strongly suggests dissection extending along the aorta and involving the aortic valve.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis typically causes pleuritic, positional chest pain and may produce a pericardial rub rather than an interarm blood pressure difference. B. Reflux disease does not cause these cardiovascular examination findings. C. Stable angina causes predictable, exertional discomfort rather than sudden severe tearing pain. E. Pulmonary embolism can cause pleuritic pain, dyspnoea and tachycardia but does not explain the blood pressure discrepancy or new regurgitant murmur.
pearl: A difference in blood pressure between the two arms in a patient with severe chest or back pain should always raise suspicion of aortic dissection, since it reflects compromised flow through a dissected arch vessel.
thinking: Sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back + unequal arm blood pressures ↓ suggests a dissecting intimal tear propagating along the aorta ↓ new early diastolic murmur shows aortic valve involvement ↓ Acute aortic dissection
exam_trap: A candidate focused on the chest pain alone might pick pulmonary embolism, but neither the interarm blood pressure gap nor the new aortic regurgitation murmur fits PE — both point specifically to dissection.
takeaway: Tearing chest/back pain with unequal arm pressures and a new diastolic murmur is aortic dissection.

stem: A 76-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of her right arm and leg with difficulty speaking. Which vascular territory is most likely affected?
why_correct: Right-sided arm and leg weakness combined with speech difficulty localises to the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, and this combined motor and language deficit is most typical of a left middle cerebral artery territory stroke.
why_wrong: A. A right posterior cerebral artery lesion would not typically impair dominant-hemisphere language function. B. Basilar artery disease causes brainstem signs, which does not fit this purely hemispheric pattern. C. Posterior cerebral artery lesions primarily cause visual field deficits, not this motor-language combination. D. A right MCA lesion would more typically cause left-sided, not right-sided, weakness.
pearl: Language is lateralised to the dominant hemisphere (left in almost all right-handed and most left-handed people), so any stroke causing both contralateral weakness and speech disturbance localises to that side.
thinking: Sudden right arm and leg weakness + difficulty speaking ↓ combined motor and language deficit ↓ language localises to the dominant hemisphere ↓ Left middle cerebral artery territory
exam_trap: A candidate might default to 'right MCA' by pattern-matching weakness to the wrong side of the brain, forgetting that motor tracts cross and the deficit is contralateral to the affected hemisphere.
takeaway: Right-sided weakness with speech disturbance localises to the left (dominant) MCA territory.

stem: A 70-year-old woman develops acute confusion over several hours while being treated for a urinary infection. She is disorientated and has fluctuating attention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute onset confusion with fluctuating attention in the setting of an acute infection is the classic picture of delirium, a reversible disturbance of consciousness driven by an underlying physical illness.
why_wrong: A. Dementia with Lewy bodies is a chronic progressive neurodegenerative disorder, not an acute illness-triggered state. B. Depression can affect concentration but does not typically cause this acute fluctuating disorientation. C. Alzheimer disease causes gradual, progressive cognitive decline rather than acute fluctuation. E. Schizophrenia is not characterised by acute fluctuating inattention tied to a physical illness.
pearl: Fluctuating attention over hours, rather than a fixed level of impairment, is the feature that most reliably distinguishes delirium from dementia at the bedside.
thinking: Acute confusion over hours + being treated for a urinary infection ↓ acute physical illness as the trigger ↓ fluctuating attention rather than a fixed chronic deficit ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: A candidate might assume an underlying dementia given the patient's age, but the acute onset and clear infective trigger point to delirium, which is reversible with treatment of the underlying cause.
takeaway: New acute confusion with fluctuating attention during an infection is delirium until proven otherwise.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has recurrent intrusive thoughts that she may have contaminated her family with germs. She repeatedly washes her hands to reduce her anxiety. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent, unwanted intrusive thoughts (obsessions) about contamination, followed by repetitive hand washing performed to reduce the resulting anxiety (compulsions), are the defining features of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
why_wrong: B. Mania causes elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and activity, not contamination fears. C. Panic disorder causes discrete attacks of autonomic fear rather than persistent intrusive thoughts and rituals. D. Generalised anxiety disorder causes broad excessive worry without the specific obsession-compulsion pattern. E. In a psychotic disorder the person would hold the belief as fixed and true rather than recognising the thoughts as intrusive and unwanted.
pearl: Insight is the key differentiator here — a person with OCD usually recognises their obsessions as excessive or irrational, unlike the fixed, unshakeable beliefs of a psychotic disorder.
thinking: Recurrent intrusive contamination thoughts (obsessions) + repetitive washing to relieve the anxiety (compulsions) ↓ classic obsession-compulsion cycle ↓ thoughts recognised as intrusive, not delusional ↓ Obsessive-compulsive disorder
exam_trap: A candidate might consider a psychotic disorder because the contamination fear sounds extreme, but the patient's insight that the thoughts are intrusive rather than a fixed belief rules psychosis out.
takeaway: Intrusive thoughts plus ritual behaviours performed to relieve the anxiety they cause define OCD.

stem: A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia stops taking his medication. His family reports increasing social withdrawal and that he is hearing voices again. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Refer directly for cognitive behavioural therapy without assessing risk
options.B: Reassure him and review in six months
options.E: Advise him to stop all medication

why_correct: Medication non-adherence with re-emergence of auditory hallucinations and social withdrawal indicates a psychotic relapse, which needs prompt clinical and risk assessment to guide safe management.
why_wrong: A. Psychological therapy may support longer-term management but cannot replace urgent clinical and risk assessment during an acute relapse. B. Delaying review for months risks further deterioration and harm. D. Antidepressants do not treat an acute psychotic relapse. E. Advising him to stop all medication would worsen an already deteriorating psychotic state.
pearl: Relapse risk rises sharply after stopping antipsychotic medication, which is why adherence support and early recognition of returning symptoms are central to relapse prevention.
thinking: Stopped antipsychotic medication + return of auditory hallucinations and withdrawal ↓ features of psychotic relapse ↓ needs prompt clinical review and risk assessment ↓ Arrange urgent psychiatric assessment
exam_trap: A candidate might reach for talking therapy as a gentler first step, but an active psychotic relapse needs urgent risk assessment before any purely psychological intervention is considered.
takeaway: Returning psychotic symptoms after stopping antipsychotic treatment need urgent assessment, not a delayed review.

stem: A 68-year-old man taking warfarin presents with melaena. He is hypotensive and his INR is markedly elevated. Which treatment is appropriate?

options.A: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus over 10 minutes
options.B: Oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg twice daily with food
options.D: Protamine sulfate by slow intravenous injection
options.E: Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate

correct_answer: E. Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
why_correct: Major bleeding with a markedly elevated INR on warfarin requires urgent reversal of anticoagulation, achieved with intravenous vitamin K together with prothrombin complex concentrate for rapid factor replacement.
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid does not reverse the underlying warfarin-induced coagulopathy. B. Oral iron does not treat active major haemorrhage. C. Aspirin would add to bleeding risk rather than treat it. D. Protamine sulfate reverses heparin, not warfarin.
pearl: Prothrombin complex concentrate reverses warfarin far faster than vitamin K alone, because it directly replaces the clotting factors whose synthesis warfarin has suppressed.
thinking: Melaena and hypotension on warfarin + markedly raised INR ↓ major bleeding driven by excess anticoagulation ↓ rapid factor replacement is needed alongside reversing further vitamin K antagonism ↓ Vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
exam_trap: A candidate might choose tranexamic acid as it 'stops bleeding', but it does nothing to correct the underlying coagulopathy, which is the priority in major warfarin-related haemorrhage.
takeaway: Major bleeding on warfarin with a high INR needs vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate, not tranexamic acid alone.

stem: A 30-year-old woman taking lithium develops vomiting and diarrhoea during an episode of gastroenteritis. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop drinking fluids until the vomiting has fully settled
options.B: Continue lithium unchanged without further assessment
options.C: Double the lithium dose until the symptoms have settled
options.D: Take ibuprofen regularly for the abdominal cramping pain
options.E: Seek urgent medical advice as toxicity is possible

correct_answer: E. Seek urgent medical advice as toxicity is possible
why_correct: Vomiting and diarrhoea cause dehydration and sodium loss, both of which reduce renal lithium clearance and can precipitate lithium toxicity, so urgent advice should be sought rather than continuing as normal.
why_wrong: A. Stopping fluid intake would worsen dehydration and increase toxicity risk. B. Continuing lithium unchanged ignores a real risk of rising lithium levels during fluid loss. C. Doubling the dose would further increase toxicity risk. D. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce renal lithium clearance and can themselves precipitate toxicity.
pearl: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index, and anything that causes dehydration or alters sodium handling — vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors — can push levels into the toxic range.
thinking: Lithium therapy + vomiting and diarrhoea from gastroenteritis ↓ dehydration reduces renal lithium clearance ↓ rising lithium levels risk toxicity ↓ Seek urgent medical advice because lithium toxicity is possible
exam_trap: A candidate might assume lithium should simply be 'carried on as normal' since it treats a chronic condition, overlooking how acute fluid loss sharply narrows its safety margin.
takeaway: Dehydrating illness in a patient on lithium is a red flag for toxicity and needs urgent review, not routine continuation.

stem: A 58-year-old man taking an ACE inhibitor develops a persistent dry cough. He has no respiratory infection and is otherwise well. Which medication is an appropriate alternative?

options.C: A loop diuretic such as furosemide
options.D: A beta blocker to suppress the cough

why_correct: ACE inhibitors commonly cause a persistent dry cough through accumulation of bradykinin; when this is not tolerated, switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker gives similar cardiovascular benefit without the bradykinin-mediated cough.
why_wrong: A. Switching to another ACE inhibitor is unlikely to resolve a class effect. B. Nitrates do not substitute for ACE inhibition in the usual indications. C. Loop diuretics are not a direct substitute for an ACE inhibitor. D. Beta blockers have no specific role in treating ACE inhibitor-induced cough.
pearl: The bradykinin-mediated cough of ACE inhibitors is a class effect, so switching within the class rarely helps — an angiotensin receptor blocker avoids the bradykinin pathway entirely.
thinking: Persistent dry cough on an ACE inhibitor + no infective cause ↓ bradykinin accumulation as the likely mechanism ↓ an alternative that spares bradykinin is needed ↓ An angiotensin receptor blocker
exam_trap: A candidate might try switching to a different ACE inhibitor, not recognising that the cough is a class effect that will persist on any drug in that group.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor cough is a class effect best managed by switching to an angiotensin receptor blocker, not another ACE inhibitor.

stem: A 60-year-old man develops severe pain in his calf and swelling after a long-haul flight. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Unilateral calf pain and swelling after a period of prolonged immobility, such as a long-haul flight, are typical features of deep vein thrombosis and should prompt assessment for it.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not typically cause acute unilateral calf swelling. B. Achilles tendinopathy causes localised tendon pain rather than the diffuse calf swelling described. C. Cellulitis can mimic this picture with erythema and warmth, but the clear immobility-related risk factor here points more strongly to a thrombotic cause. D. Gout typically affects a joint rather than causing diffuse calf swelling.
pearl: Prolonged immobility, such as on a long-haul flight, promotes venous stasis in the calf veins, a core part of Virchow's triad driving deep vein thrombosis.
thinking: Long-haul flight (prolonged immobility) + unilateral calf pain and swelling ↓ venous stasis is a recognised thrombotic risk factor ↓ pattern fits a provoked deep vein thrombosis ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: A candidate might default to cellulitis because of the swelling, but the clear immobility trigger makes DVT the diagnosis that must be actively considered and excluded first.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling after prolonged travel immobility should always raise suspicion of DVT.

stem: A 76-year-old woman presents with unilateral painful swelling and redness of the lower leg. She has fever and feels unwell. The skin is hot and tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute unilateral swelling with hot, tender, erythematous skin and systemic upset such as fever is the typical presentation of cellulitis, a bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral arterial disease causes chronic ischaemic symptoms rather than an acute infective skin process. B. Gout causes acute joint inflammation, not diffuse skin infection. C. DVT can cause swelling and pain but does not typically produce hot, clearly infected skin with systemic fever. D. Osteoarthritis affects joints, not the skin.
pearl: Cellulitis is usually a clinical diagnosis based on spreading erythema, warmth and tenderness with systemic upset — marking the visible margin can help track whether it is responding to antibiotics.
thinking: Unilateral leg swelling + hot, tender, erythematous skin + fever and feeling unwell ↓ acute infective process of the skin and soft tissue ↓ systemic symptoms support infection over a non-infective cause ↓ Cellulitis
exam_trap: A candidate might consider DVT because both cause a swollen, painful leg, but the clearly infected-looking hot skin with systemic fever favours cellulitis over a purely thrombotic process.
takeaway: Hot, tender, erythematous leg swelling with fever points to cellulitis rather than DVT.

stem: A 26-year-old man has recurrent episodes of severe pain in his big toe. The joint is red, hot and swollen. He has no fever. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent, severe monoarthritis affecting the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is the classic presentation of gout, caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis remains an important differential in any acutely hot joint and should be considered, but recurrent episodic podagra without fever favours gout. C. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, not a hot toe joint. D. Osteoarthritis is a chronic, less inflammatory process. E. Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes a symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis rather than episodic monoarthritis of the big toe.
pearl: Recurrent monoarthritis of the first MTP joint is podagra and remains the most common presentation of gout, even without a known history of hyperuricaemia.
thinking: Recurrent severe big-toe pain + red, hot, swollen joint + afebrile ↓ classic podagra ↓ Gout
exam_trap: Because any hot swollen joint raises concern for septic arthritis, candidates may over-select it here — but the recurrent nature and absence of fever both point away from an acute bacterial infection.
takeaway: Recurrent podagra without fever is gout until aspiration proves otherwise.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss and increased sweating. She has a fine tremor and a resting tachycardia. Her TSH is suppressed and free T4 is elevated. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A suppressed TSH with an elevated free T4, together with weight loss, sweating, tremor and tachycardia, confirms primary hyperthyroidism, in which excess thyroid hormone suppresses pituitary TSH release.
why_wrong: B. Hypoparathyroidism causes hypocalcaemia rather than thyrotoxicosis. C. Secondary hypothyroidism causes a low free T4 with an inappropriately low or normal TSH, the opposite biochemical pattern. D. Euthyroid sick syndrome occurs during severe systemic illness and does not produce this classic clinical and biochemical picture. E. Primary hypothyroidism causes a raised TSH with a low free T4.
pearl: In primary thyroid disease, TSH and free T4 move in opposite directions — a suppressed TSH with a raised T4 confirms hyperthyroidism, while a raised TSH with a low T4 confirms hypothyroidism.
thinking: Weight loss, sweating, tremor, tachycardia ↓ hyperadrenergic, hypermetabolic features ↓ suppressed TSH with raised free T4 confirms a primary thyroid cause ↓ Primary hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: A candidate might be distracted by the word 'primary' and mismatch it with hypothyroidism purely by habit — the biochemistry (low TSH, high T4) is what actually confirms hyperthyroidism here.
takeaway: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 confirms primary hyperthyroidism.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe headache, sweating, palpitations and marked hypertension. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Recurrent episodes of headache, sweating, palpitations and marked hypertension reflect intermittent catecholamine surges, which is the classic presentation of a phaeochromocytoma.
why_wrong: A. Addison disease causes hypotension and features of adrenal insufficiency, not episodic hypertension. C. Primary hyperaldosteronism usually causes sustained hypertension with hypokalaemia rather than episodic catecholamine symptoms. D. Primary hypothyroidism causes fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance, not episodic hypertensive surges. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia, unrelated to this presentation.
pearl: The classic triad of phaeochromocytoma — episodic headache, sweating and palpitations — occurring alongside hypertension should always prompt screening for catecholamine excess before symptoms are dismissed as anxiety.
thinking: Recurrent episodic headache, sweating, palpitations + marked hypertension ↓ pattern of intermittent catecholamine surges ↓ classic triad for an adrenal medullary tumour ↓ Phaeochromocytoma
exam_trap: A candidate might mistake this for panic disorder because of the episodic fear-like symptoms, but the combination with marked hypertension points specifically to a catecholamine-secreting tumour rather than a primary psychiatric cause.
takeaway: Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension together suggest phaeochromocytoma.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation and dizziness. Her blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg. Blood tests show hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia together reflect primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), in which loss of cortisol and aldosterone production drives this electrolyte and pigmentary picture.
why_wrong: B. Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss and adrenergic symptoms but does not explain this electrolyte pattern or hyperpigmentation. C. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic catecholamine excess and hypertension, not hypotension. D. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension with hypokalaemia, the opposite electrolyte picture. E. Cushing syndrome causes cortisol excess, typically with weight gain and hypertension rather than hypotension and weight loss.
pearl: Hyperpigmentation in Addison disease arises because low cortisol drives increased ACTH and its precursor melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which is why it is absent in secondary adrenal insufficiency caused by pituitary disease.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation + hypotension ↓ features of adrenal insufficiency ↓ hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency ↓ Addison disease
exam_trap: A candidate might confuse this with Cushing syndrome purely because both involve the adrenal glands, but the hypotension, weight loss and hyperkalaemia here are the opposite of cortisol excess.
takeaway: Hypotension with hyperpigmentation, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia points to Addison disease.

stem: A 38-year-old woman has marked thirst and passes very large volumes of dilute urine both day and night. Her blood glucose is normal. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Marked thirst with large volumes of dilute urine, occurring both day and night, in the absence of hyperglycaemia is characteristic of diabetes insipidus, caused by insufficient ADH action on the kidney.
why_wrong: A. SIADH causes water retention and hyponatraemia rather than large-volume dilute urine output. B. Hyperthyroidism does not typically cause this degree of polyuria with dilute urine. D. Cystitis causes frequency and dysuria with small, often painful voids, not large-volume dilute urine. E. Diabetes mellitus can cause polyuria through glycosuria but would be expected to show hyperglycaemia, which is absent here.
pearl: Distinguishing diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia often relies on a water deprivation test, since both cause large-volume dilute urine but respond differently to fluid restriction and desmopressin.
thinking: Marked thirst + very large volumes of dilute urine day and night + normal glucose ↓ excludes osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia ↓ pattern fits impaired urinary concentration ↓ Diabetes insipidus
exam_trap: A candidate might jump to type 1 diabetes because of the polyuria and polydipsia, but the normal blood glucose specifically rules out an osmotic, glucose-driven cause.
takeaway: Polyuria and polydipsia with a normal glucose points to diabetes insipidus, not diabetes mellitus.

stem: A 64-year-old man with small-cell lung cancer develops confusion. Blood tests show a sodium concentration of 119 mmol/L. He appears euvolaemic. Which diagnosis best explains this finding?
why_correct: Small-cell lung cancer can ectopically secrete ADH, causing water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia while the patient remains clinically euvolaemic, which is the hallmark of SIADH.
why_wrong: A. Addison disease can cause hyponatraemia but typically with hypotension and hyperkalaemia from mineralocorticoid deficiency, not this euvolaemic picture. C. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state is associated with severe hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolarity, not isolated hyponatraemia. D. Diabetes insipidus causes excessive water loss and tends towards hypernatraemia, the opposite pattern. E. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia, not hyponatraemia.
pearl: Small-cell lung cancer is the classic paraneoplastic cause of SIADH, reflecting ectopic ADH production by the tumour independent of normal osmotic regulation.
thinking: Small-cell lung cancer + confusion + sodium 119 mmol/L + clinically euvolaemic ↓ dilutional hyponatraemia without volume depletion or overload ↓ pattern fits inappropriate ADH secretion ↓ SIADH
exam_trap: A candidate might choose Addison disease because it also causes hyponatraemia, but the euvolaemic state and lack of hyperkalaemia here point instead to inappropriate water retention from SIADH.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia in a patient with small-cell lung cancer suggests paraneoplastic SIADH.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain, vomiting and confusion. He has had several similar episodes. Blood tests show hyponatraemia and mild tachycardia. His urine is dark and he has recently started a very restrictive diet. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent severe abdominal pain with neuropsychiatric features, hyponatraemia and dark urine, precipitated by a restrictive diet, is characteristic of acute intermittent porphyria, in which fasting can trigger an attack through haem pathway dysregulation.
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorptive gastrointestinal symptoms rather than acute recurrent neurovisceral attacks. C. Acute pancreatitis usually causes severe persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back with supportive enzyme abnormalities, not recurrent episodic attacks like this. D. Crohn disease causes chronic or relapsing inflammatory gastrointestinal symptoms rather than this acute neurovisceral pattern. E. Familial Mediterranean fever causes recurrent febrile serositis attacks, not confusion, hyponatraemia and dark urine triggered by dieting.
pearl: Fasting, alcohol and certain drugs can all trigger acute intermittent porphyria attacks by inducing haem synthesis enzymes, which is why a very restrictive diet is a recognised precipitant worth asking about directly.
thinking: Recurrent severe abdominal pain + confusion + hyponatraemia, dark urine + recent restrictive diet ↓ recurring neurovisceral attacks with a precipitating trigger ↓ pattern fits disordered haem synthesis rather than a structural abdominal cause ↓ Acute intermittent porphyria
exam_trap: A candidate may choose acute pancreatitis because of severe abdominal pain with vomiting, but the recurrent attacks, neuropsychiatric features, hyponatraemia, dark urine and dietary trigger point to acute intermittent porphyria.
takeaway: Recurrent abdominal pain with confusion, hyponatraemia and dark urine after fasting suggests acute intermittent porphyria.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty hearing. She has no tinnitus, vertigo or neurological symptoms. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry demonstrates conductive hearing loss. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive conductive hearing loss with a normal-appearing tympanic membrane and no vestibular or neurological symptoms is typical of otosclerosis, caused by abnormal bone remodelling around the stapes footplate.
why_wrong: A. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus, features absent here. C. Vestibular neuritis causes acute vertigo without a persistent conductive hearing loss. D. Vestibular schwannoma causes sensorineural, not conductive, hearing loss. E. Presbycusis causes bilateral sensorineural hearing loss related to ageing, not a conductive pattern.
pearl: A normal-looking eardrum with progressive conductive hearing loss, particularly in a younger adult, should prompt consideration of otosclerosis rather than a middle-ear problem visible on otoscopy.
thinking: Progressive hearing loss + no tinnitus, vertigo or neurological symptoms + normal otoscopy + conductive pattern on audiometry ↓ middle-ear conduction problem without a visible structural cause ↓ fits abnormal stapes bone remodelling ↓ Otosclerosis
exam_trap: A candidate might assume any progressive hearing loss in an older-leaning population is presbycusis, but presbycusis is sensorineural, not conductive, which the audiometry here clearly excludes.
takeaway: Progressive conductive hearing loss with a normal eardrum points to otosclerosis.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of wheeze, cough and chest tightness, particularly at night and after exercise. Between episodes she feels completely well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent, variable episodes of wheeze, cough and chest tightness, worse at night and after exercise, with complete symptom-free periods in between, are the hallmark of asthma.
why_wrong: B. COPD usually causes persistent airflow limitation and is uncommon at this age without a significant relevant exposure history. C. Pleural effusion causes more persistent respiratory symptoms rather than episodic wheeze. D. Pulmonary fibrosis causes progressive, not variable, breathlessness. E. Bronchiectasis typically causes chronic productive cough with recurrent infections rather than episodic wheeze.
pearl: Symptom variability — attacks interspersed with completely well periods, and worsening at night or with exercise — is the clinical fingerprint that separates asthma from the fixed airflow limitation of COPD.
thinking: Episodic wheeze, cough, chest tightness + worse at night and after exercise + well between episodes ↓ variable airflow obstruction ↓ pattern distinct from the fixed limitation of COPD ↓ Asthma
exam_trap: A candidate might consider COPD given the respiratory symptoms, but the patient's age and complete recovery between episodes are inconsistent with the persistent airflow limitation that defines COPD.
takeaway: Episodic, variable wheeze with symptom-free periods in between is the clinical signature of asthma.

stem: A 3-month-old infant has persistent cough, recurrent chest infections and poor weight gain. The parents report that the child's sweat tastes unusually salty. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent chest infections, poor weight gain and unusually salty-tasting sweat in an infant are characteristic features of cystic fibrosis, caused by abnormal chloride channel function affecting sweat and airway secretions.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease causes gastrointestinal malabsorption rather than recurrent chest infections and salty sweat. B. Asthma causes variable wheeze but does not cause salty sweat or this pattern of failure to thrive. D. Epiglottitis is an acute upper-airway emergency, not a chronic failure-to-thrive picture. E. Croup causes an acute barking cough and stridor, not chronic infections and poor growth.
pearl: A sweat chloride test remains the key confirmatory investigation when cystic fibrosis is suspected clinically, even though most cases in the UK are now first picked up on newborn screening.
thinking: Recurrent chest infections + poor weight gain + salty-tasting sweat reported by parents ↓ classic triad pointing to abnormal chloride channel function ↓ pattern fits an exocrine, multisystem disorder rather than isolated respiratory disease ↓ Cystic fibrosis
exam_trap: A candidate might consider asthma because of the recurrent chest symptoms, but asthma does not cause salty sweat or failure to thrive, both of which are specific pointers to cystic fibrosis.
takeaway: Recurrent chest infections with poor growth and salty sweat in an infant points to cystic fibrosis.

stem: A 4-year-old child has a barking cough and hoarse voice. There is no drooling or stridor at rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A barking cough and hoarse voice without drooling or stridor at rest, in a preschool-age child, is typical of mild croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), usually caused by a viral infection.
why_wrong: A. Meningitis causes neurological and systemic features rather than an isolated barking cough. B. Epiglottitis is associated with severe systemic illness, drooling and significant airway danger, not this mild picture. C. Bronchiolitis mainly affects infants and causes wheeze, crackles and respiratory distress rather than a barking cough. E. Foreign-body aspiration often has a sudden onset and may produce focal respiratory findings rather than a barking cough with hoarseness.
pearl: The absence of stridor at rest and drooling helps distinguish mild croup, which can usually be managed with oral steroids, from the airway emergency of epiglottitis or severe croup.
thinking: Barking cough + hoarse voice + no drooling or stridor at rest ↓ upper airway inflammation without significant obstruction ↓ mild severity distinguishes this from an airway emergency ↓ Mild croup
exam_trap: A candidate might jump to epiglottitis because both cause a hoarse voice and cough, but the absence of drooling and stridor at rest are reassuring features that point to mild croup instead.
takeaway: Barking cough and hoarse voice without drooling or resting stridor indicates mild, not severe, croup.

stem: A 2-year-old child develops sudden coughing and choking while eating peanuts. He remains wheezy and has reduced air entry on the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden coughing and choking while eating, followed by persistent unilateral wheeze and reduced air entry, strongly suggests an aspirated foreign body lodged in one main bronchus.
why_wrong: A. An asthma exacerbation causes bilateral wheeze and does not typically start abruptly during eating with choking. C. Bronchiolitis follows a viral prodrome and causes bilateral, not unilateral, respiratory signs. D. Croup causes upper-airway stridor and a barking cough rather than unilateral wheeze. E. Pneumonia usually develops over a longer period in the context of infection, not immediately after choking.
pearl: A unilateral wheeze with reduced air entry on one side, especially with a clear choking episode, should always prompt consideration of an inhaled foreign body and urgent airway assessment.
thinking: Sudden choking while eating peanuts + persistent wheeze + reduced air entry on one side ↓ acute onset tied directly to eating ↓ unilateral signs suggest a lodged object rather than diffuse airway disease ↓ Foreign body aspiration
exam_trap: A candidate might default to asthma because of the wheeze, but the sudden onset during eating and the unilateral (not bilateral) findings are the clues that point specifically to aspiration.
takeaway: Sudden choking during eating with unilateral wheeze points to foreign body aspiration, not asthma.

stem: A 6-year-old child has fever, sore throat and a widespread fine, rough-textured erythematous rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever and sore throat with a widespread fine, rough 'sandpaper' rash is the classic presentation of scarlet fever, caused by an exotoxin-producing group A streptococcal infection.
why_wrong: A. Kawasaki disease causes prolonged fever with mucocutaneous and extremity changes rather than this specific sandpaper rash following pharyngitis. C. Impetigo causes localised superficial bacterial skin lesions, often with honey-coloured crusting, not a widespread febrile rash. D. Tinea corporis causes annular scaly lesions rather than a widespread febrile rash. E. Chickenpox produces itchy vesicular lesions, not a fine rough erythematous rash.
pearl: Scarlet fever's rash typically spares the area around the mouth (circumoral pallor) and has a texture often described as feeling like sandpaper — a distinctive bedside clue.
thinking: Fever + sore throat + widespread fine, rough-textured erythematous rash ↓ pattern fits a toxin-mediated streptococcal illness ↓ texture and timing distinguish it from viral exanthems ↓ Scarlet fever
exam_trap: A candidate might consider chickenpox purely because of 'rash and fever' in a child, but chickenpox is vesicular and itchy, not the fine sandpaper texture described here.
takeaway: Fever, sore throat and a fine sandpaper rash together point to scarlet fever.

stem: A 15-year-old boy with suspected infectious mononucleosis is mistakenly prescribed amoxicillin. Two days later he develops a widespread maculopapular rash. What is the most likely explanation?
correct_answer: B. Amoxicillin-induced rash in EBV infection
why_correct: Aminopenicillins such as amoxicillin commonly provoke a widespread maculopapular rash when given to a patient with infectious mononucleosis, a well-recognised drug-disease interaction rather than a true penicillin allergy.
why_wrong: A. A maculopapular rash alone does not establish Stevens–Johnson syndrome, which involves mucosal involvement and skin necrosis. C. Scarlet fever has a distinct fine sandpaper-like rash with streptococcal infection, not this drug-triggered reaction in suspected glandular fever. D. Meningococcal septicaemia causes a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash with systemic illness, not this amoxicillin-associated rash. E. The rash in infectious mononucleosis is a non-allergic drug–disease interaction; there are no urticarial or anaphylactic features to suggest IgE-mediated allergy.
pearl: This amoxicillin-associated rash in infectious mononucleosis does not necessarily predict true penicillin allergy, and many patients go on to tolerate penicillins again once the acute EBV illness has resolved.
thinking: Suspected infectious mononucleosis + amoxicillin given + widespread maculopapular rash two days later ↓ recognised drug-disease interaction rather than anaphylaxis ↓ timing and rash type fit the amoxicillin-EBV phenomenon ↓ Antibiotic-associated rash in infectious mononucleosis
exam_trap: A candidate might label this event as an immediate penicillin allergy and record it as such for life, when it actually reflects a specific, well-described reaction linked to concurrent EBV infection.
takeaway: A maculopapular rash after amoxicillin in suspected glandular fever reflects an EBV drug interaction, not necessarily true penicillin allergy.

stem: A 19-year-old woman develops unilateral calf pain and swelling five days after starting a combined oral contraceptive pill. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: The combined oral contraceptive pill increases the risk of venous thromboembolism, and new unilateral calf pain and swelling shortly after starting it should raise concern for deep vein thrombosis.
why_wrong: A. Gout usually causes acute inflammation confined to a joint rather than diffuse calf swelling. B. Chronic venous insufficiency develops gradually with longstanding oedema and skin changes, not an acute five-day history. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute calf swelling. E. Cellulitis can cause redness and warmth but does not explain the clear thrombotic risk factor of a new combined contraceptive.
pearl: The combined oral contraceptive pill roughly doubles to triples the background risk of venous thromboembolism, which is why a personal or family history of clots is specifically screened for before prescribing it.
thinking: Started combined oral contraceptive + five days later unilateral calf pain and swelling ↓ recognised drug-related thrombotic risk factor ↓ acute unilateral pattern fits venous thrombosis ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: A candidate might consider cellulitis because of the swelling, but the clear temporal link to starting a prothrombotic medication makes DVT the diagnosis that needs active exclusion first.
takeaway: New unilateral calf swelling soon after starting the combined pill should prompt assessment for DVT.

stem: A 34-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill develops sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain in a woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill, a recognised risk factor for venous thromboembolism, must be urgently assessed for pulmonary embolism.
why_wrong: A. Tension headache does not explain the respiratory symptoms described. C. Stable angina causes predictable exertional chest discomfort rather than sudden dyspnoea. D. Panic attacks can mimic some features of PE but a dangerous cause must be excluded first rather than assumed. E. Reflux disease does not cause sudden unexplained dyspnoea and pleuritic pain.
pearl: A validated clinical prediction score (such as the Wells score) alongside D-dimer testing helps stratify the probability of PE and guide whether imaging such as CTPA is needed.
thinking: Combined oral contraceptive use + sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain ↓ recognised prothrombotic risk factor present ↓ acute respiratory presentation fits thromboembolism rather than a benign cause ↓ Pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: A candidate might default to panic disorder because anxiety can mimic breathlessness and chest pain, but a potentially life-threatening cause like PE must always be excluded first in this risk-factor context.
takeaway: Sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic pain on the combined pill must be assessed for pulmonary embolism before any other cause is assumed.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness and ankle swelling. He has bilateral basal crackles and raised jugular venous pressure. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Increasing breathlessness with ankle swelling, bilateral basal crackles and a raised jugular venous pressure together indicate fluid overload from congestive heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Acute bronchitis usually causes cough without raised JVP or peripheral oedema. B. GORD causes reflux symptoms rather than signs of fluid overload. C. Pneumothorax typically causes sudden unilateral respiratory symptoms, not this gradual bilateral picture. D. Pulmonary fibrosis causes progressive breathlessness and crackles but does not typically cause marked systemic venous congestion.
pearl: A raised jugular venous pressure is a key bedside sign of right heart congestion and helps distinguish heart failure from primary respiratory causes of breathlessness and crackles.
thinking: Increasing breathlessness + ankle swelling + bilateral basal crackles + raised JVP ↓ combination of pulmonary and systemic venous congestion ↓ fits a failing heart rather than a purely respiratory cause ↓ Heart failure
exam_trap: A candidate might attribute the crackles to a chest infection, but the combination with raised JVP and peripheral oedema points to cardiac, not purely respiratory, congestion.
takeaway: Breathlessness, ankle swelling, crackles and a raised JVP together point to heart failure.

stem: A 65-year-old man with heart failure develops increasing ankle swelling after stopping his prescribed diuretic. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Stopping a prescribed diuretic in a patient with known heart failure removes the mechanism controlling fluid retention, leading to re-accumulation of fluid and worsening peripheral oedema.
why_wrong: A. DVT usually causes unilateral, not bilateral, swelling. B. Appendicitis does not cause bilateral ankle oedema. D. Cellulitis causes localised inflammatory skin changes, is rarely bilateral, and does not explain fluid retention after stopping a diuretic. E. Nephrotic syndrome can cause oedema, but the clear temporal relationship to stopping heart-failure treatment here makes worsening heart failure the more likely explanation.
pearl: Diuretic adherence is a common and reversible cause of heart failure decompensation, which is why checking medication continuity is one of the first steps when oedema worsens.
thinking: Known heart failure + stopped prescribed diuretic + increasing ankle swelling ↓ clear temporal link to loss of diuretic control ↓ fluid retention re-accumulates without treatment ↓ Fluid retention due to worsening heart failure
exam_trap: A candidate might consider nephrotic syndrome given the oedema, but the obvious temporal link to stopping the diuretic makes decompensated heart failure by far the more likely explanation here.
takeaway: New oedema after a patient with heart failure stops their diuretic usually reflects simple fluid re-accumulation.

stem: A 71-year-old woman develops a painful ulcer on the tip of her toe. Her foot is cool and pedal pulses are absent. Which type of ulcer is most likely?
why_correct: A painful distal ulcer on a cool foot with absent pedal pulses reflects poor arterial perfusion, the hallmark of an arterial ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Venous ulcers typically occur around the medial malleolus and are associated with oedema, not distal pain and absent pulses. C. Neuropathic ulcers are typically painless and occur at pressure points, unlike this painful presentation. D. Malignant ulcers have different chronic features and are not defined by arterial insufficiency. E. Pressure ulcers occur over bony prominences in vulnerable, often immobile patients, a different mechanism to arterial disease.
pearl: Arterial ulcers are classically painful and occur at the most distal, poorly perfused sites such as the toes, in contrast to venous ulcers which are typically painless (or only mildly uncomfortable) and gaiter-area.
thinking: Painful ulcer at the toe tip + cool foot + absent pedal pulses ↓ signs of inadequate arterial perfusion at the most distal point ↓ pattern contrasts with the gaiter-area, oedema-associated venous ulcer ↓ Arterial ulcer
exam_trap: A candidate might default to venous ulcer purely because 'leg ulcer' is a common exam theme, but the painful, distal location with absent pulses is the specific signature of arterial, not venous, disease.
takeaway: A painful distal toe ulcer with absent pulses is an arterial ulcer, not a venous one.

stem: A 48-year-old man has recurrent episodes of severe pain in his big toe. The joint becomes red, hot and swollen. He has recently started treatment that lowers his serum urate. What is an important counselling point when starting long-term urate-lowering therapy?

options.A: It can initially precipitate an acute gout flare
options.C: It should only be taken during acute attacks
options.D: It is contraindicated in all patients with gout
options.E: It immediately cures the current flare

correct_answer: A. It can initially precipitate an acute gout flare
why_correct: Starting urate-lowering therapy can mobilise and destabilise existing urate crystal deposits, which can trigger an acute gout flare in the initial weeks of treatment, so patients should be counselled about this before starting.
why_wrong: B. Its purpose is to reduce, not increase, serum urate over the long term. C. It is intended as continuous long-term treatment, not something taken only during attacks. D. Urate-lowering therapy is an important long-term treatment for appropriate patients with recurrent gout, not contraindicated in all cases. E. It is for long-term prevention and does not provide immediate relief of a current acute flare.
pearl: Because urate-lowering therapy can trigger flares when started, prophylaxis with a low-dose NSAID or colchicine is often given for the first few months alongside it.
thinking: Recurrent gout attacks + starting long-term urate-lowering treatment ↓ mobilisation of existing urate deposits during the transition ↓ risk of an early flare that patients should be warned about ↓ It can initially precipitate an acute gout flare
exam_trap: A candidate might assume urate-lowering therapy immediately relieves the current flare, but it is a preventive long-term treatment and can even worsen symptoms in the short term when first started.
takeaway: Starting urate-lowering therapy can trigger an early flare — patients need counselling about this, not reassurance that it will relieve current pain.

stem: A 45-year-old woman reports pain and stiffness in both hands that is worse in the morning and lasts for more than an hour. Several MCP and PIP joints are swollen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Symmetrical pain and swelling of the small joints of the hands, with morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, is the classic pattern of inflammatory arthritis seen in rheumatoid arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms (numbness/tingling in specific fingers) rather than multiple swollen joints. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without objective joint swelling. C. Gout usually causes acute attacks affecting individual joints rather than this symmetrical small-joint pattern. D. Osteoarthritis typically causes shorter morning stiffness and favours the DIP and first CMC joints rather than MCP/PIP joints.
pearl: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour is a key discriminator for inflammatory arthritis, whereas osteoarthritis stiffness classically eases within about thirty minutes.
thinking: Symmetrical hand pain and stiffness + worse in the morning, lasting over an hour + swollen MCP and PIP joints ↓ inflammatory, not mechanical, pattern ↓ prolonged morning stiffness supports synovitis ↓ Rheumatoid arthritis
exam_trap: A candidate might default to osteoarthritis because hand pain is common at any age, but the prolonged morning stiffness and MCP/PIP joint involvement are specific markers of an inflammatory, not degenerative, process.
takeaway: Symmetrical MCP/PIP swelling with morning stiffness over an hour points to rheumatoid arthritis.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness that is particularly severe in the morning. He has no true muscle weakness. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: New bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, particularly severe in the morning and without true muscle weakness, in an older adult is characteristic of polymyalgia rheumatica.
why_wrong: B. Osteoarthritis usually affects specific joints with mechanical, activity-related symptoms rather than this girdle-pattern stiffness. C. Motor neurone disease causes progressive true muscle weakness, which is specifically absent here. D. Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor rather than girdle stiffness. E. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable true weakness rather than painful morning stiffness.
pearl: The absence of true muscle weakness on examination, despite the patient's report of stiffness and difficulty moving, is a key feature that helps separate polymyalgia rheumatica from primary muscle or neurological disease.
thinking: Older adult + bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness + worse in the morning + no true weakness ↓ inflammatory girdle pattern without primary muscle disease ↓ excludes neuromuscular causes of weakness ↓ Polymyalgia rheumatica
exam_trap: A candidate might consider myasthenia gravis because of the girdle distribution, but myasthenia causes genuine fatigable weakness, whereas this vignette specifically states there is no true weakness.
takeaway: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness without true weakness in an older adult points to polymyalgia rheumatica.

stem: A 67-year-old man develops sudden facial drooping, arm weakness and difficulty speaking. His symptoms began 45 minutes ago. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.C: Give oral antibiotics and review tomorrow
options.D: Wait for symptoms to resolve completely

correct_answer: B. Activate the acute stroke pathway
why_correct: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness and speech difficulty beginning only 45 minutes ago fall within the window for potential reperfusion treatment, so the acute stroke pathway must be activated immediately.
why_wrong: A. Routine outpatient review would cause unacceptable delay in a time-critical presentation. C. Antibiotics have no role in treating an acute stroke. D. Waiting for spontaneous resolution risks losing the opportunity for time-dependent treatment. E. Sedation would obscure neurological assessment and does not address the underlying emergency.
pearl: For thrombolysis and thrombectomy, 'time is brain' — every minute of delay in reperfusion is associated with loss of viable brain tissue, which is why recognising and acting on stroke symptoms within minutes matters so much.
thinking: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty + onset 45 minutes ago ↓ classic FAST-positive stroke symptoms within a treatable time window ↓ immediate action needed to preserve reperfusion options ↓ Activate the acute stroke pathway
exam_trap: A candidate might consider a 'watch and wait' approach given some strokes self-resolve (TIA), but with active FAST-positive symptoms in a treatable window the correct action is always urgent activation of the stroke pathway, not observation.
takeaway: FAST-positive symptoms within the treatable window mean immediate activation of the stroke pathway, not observation.

stem: A 69-year-old man develops a unilateral facial droop. He cannot close the affected eye and has difficulty raising the eyebrow on that side. There are no limb neurological deficits. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A unilateral facial palsy affecting the whole side of the face, including the forehead (unable to close the eye or raise the eyebrow), with no limb involvement, indicates a lower motor neurone facial nerve lesion — Bell palsy.
why_wrong: A. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness that typically varies through the day, not an acute complete unilateral palsy. B. Temporal arteritis can cause visual symptoms and headache but does not typically cause an isolated complete facial palsy. D. A stroke affecting the internal capsule typically causes an upper motor neurone pattern that spares the forehead, with weakness mainly of the lower face. E. Trigeminal neuralgia causes episodic facial pain, not facial weakness.
pearl: Forehead involvement is the key examination finding that distinguishes a lower motor neurone facial palsy (Bell palsy) from an upper motor neurone (central/stroke) facial weakness, which typically spares the forehead.
thinking: Unilateral facial droop + cannot close the eye + cannot raise the eyebrow + no limb signs ↓ whole side of the face affected, including forehead ↓ lower motor neurone pattern ↓ Bell palsy
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with the forehead-sparing rule may consider stroke, but the involvement of the forehead and eye closure specifically indicates a lower motor neurone lesion, pointing to Bell palsy rather than a central cause.
takeaway: Forehead involvement in a facial palsy means it's a lower motor neurone lesion — Bell palsy, not stroke.
