pearl: The defining feature separating dementia from delirium is the time course: dementia is gradual and progressive over months to years, while delirium is acute and fluctuates over hours to days.
thinking: Gradual progressive memory loss over years + impaired instrumental function (finances) ↓ chronic neurodegenerative course ↓ Alzheimer disease
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with the time-course distinction may consider delirium, but the multi-year progressive course rules out an acute confusional state.
takeaway: Gradual decline over years = dementia; sudden fluctuating confusion = delirium.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has episodes of painful electric-shock sensations over one side of her face, triggered by brushing her teeth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Brief, severe, electric-shock-like unilateral facial pain triggered by light stimuli such as brushing teeth is the characteristic presentation of trigeminal neuralgia.
why_wrong: A. Cluster headache causes severe unilateral orbital pain with autonomic features such as lacrimation, not brief trigger-evoked shocks. C. Giant cell (temporal) arteritis occurs mainly in older adults and causes headache with systemic or visual symptoms, not brief triggered facial shocks. D. Bell palsy causes facial weakness rather than paroxysmal facial pain. E. Migraine produces a longer-lasting headache syndrome rather than brief trigger-evoked shocks.
pearl: Trigger factors such as touching the face, chewing or brushing teeth are highly characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia and help distinguish it from other facial pain syndromes.
thinking: Brief electric-shock facial pain + specifically triggered by touch (brushing teeth) ↓ hallmark trigger-evoked paroxysmal pain pattern ↓ Trigeminal neuralgia
exam_trap: Candidates may think of cluster headache because both cause severe facial/head pain, but the brief, trigger-evoked, electric-shock quality is specific to trigeminal neuralgia.
takeaway: Brief trigger-evoked electric-shock facial pain = trigeminal neuralgia.

stem: A 70-year-old man develops a new unilateral headache associated with scalp tenderness. He has pain when chewing and transient visual disturbance. What is the most important diagnosis to consider?
why_correct: New unilateral headache with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and transient visual disturbance in an older adult is highly suggestive of giant cell arteritis, which requires urgent recognition to prevent irreversible visual loss.
why_wrong: B. Migraine is less likely with this new presentation in an older adult with these systemic features. C. Sinusitis does not explain this characteristic vascular presentation with jaw claudication. D. Cluster headache has a different pattern, with severe orbital pain and autonomic symptoms rather than scalp tenderness and jaw claudication. E. Tension headache does not explain jaw claudication or visual disturbance.
pearl: Jaw claudication and any visual disturbance in suspected giant cell arteritis are urgent red flags, since visual loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy can be sudden and permanent without prompt treatment.
thinking: New headache in an older adult + scalp tenderness + jaw claudication + transient visual disturbance ↓ classic features of cranial vasculitis ↓ risk of permanent visual loss if untreated ↓ Giant cell arteritis
exam_trap: Candidates may consider migraine because of headache and visual symptoms, but a genuinely new headache pattern in an older adult with jaw claudication and scalp tenderness should always raise giant cell arteritis as the priority diagnosis.
takeaway: New headache with jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual disturbance in an older adult is giant cell arteritis until excluded.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with severe unilateral headache associated with nausea and vomiting. She reports that similar attacks have occurred several times before. She prefers to lie in a dark, quiet room during attacks. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent unilateral headache with nausea, vomiting and a preference for a dark, quiet room (photophobia/phonophobia) during similar previous attacks is characteristic of migraine.
why_wrong: A. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically causes a sudden thunderclap headache, unlike this recurrent pattern. B. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief facial pain rather than prolonged headache with nausea. C. Cluster headache is associated with prominent ipsilateral autonomic symptoms and occurs in shorter, repeated attacks. D. Giant cell arteritis occurs mainly in older adults, not a 29-year-old.
pearl: A history of previous, similar recurrent attacks is one of the most reassuring features supporting migraine over a more sinister acute headache cause, alongside the classic photophobia/phonophobia pattern.
thinking: Recurrent similar headaches + nausea/vomiting + preference for a dark, quiet room ↓ classic migrainous triggers and relieving behaviours ↓ pattern consistent with previous attacks ↓ Migraine
exam_trap: Candidates might over-worry about subarachnoid haemorrhage given the severity described, but the recurrent nature matching previous typical attacks, rather than a sudden new thunderclap onset, favours migraine.
takeaway: Recurrent unilateral headache with nausea and a preference for dark, quiet surroundings is classic migraine.

stem: A pregnant woman at routine antenatal screening has bacteria detected in her urine but has no urinary symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Repeat urine culture at the next antenatal visit
options.B: Treat with a course of antibiotics
options.C: Renal tract ultrasound before any treatment
options.D: Urgent CT KUB to exclude obstruction

correct_answer: B. Treat with a course of antibiotics
why_correct: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated with an appropriate antibiotic because, unlike in non-pregnant adults, it carries a meaningful risk of progressing to pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes if left untreated.
why_wrong: A. Repeating the culture later without treating delays therapy and risks progression to pyelonephritis. C. Renal tract imaging is not required before treating uncomplicated asymptomatic bacteriuria. D. Urgent CT is not appropriate and involves radiation in pregnancy. E. Withholding treatment is inappropriate because pregnancy is a specific exception to the usual 'no treatment needed' approach to asymptomatic bacteriuria.
pearl: Pregnancy is the key exception to the general rule that asymptomatic bacteriuria does not need treatment — in pregnancy it is actively screened for and treated to reduce the risk of pyelonephritis and preterm birth.
thinking: Pregnant + asymptomatic bacteriuria on screening ↓ pregnancy changes the usual approach to bacteriuria ↓ untreated bacteriuria risks ascending infection ↓ Treat the bacteriuria with an appropriate antibiotic
exam_trap: Candidates familiar with the non-pregnant rule ('don't treat asymptomatic bacteriuria') may wrongly apply it here, missing that pregnancy is specifically the exception where treatment is indicated.
takeaway: Unlike in non-pregnant adults, asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should always be treated.

stem: A 42-year-old man has fever, a new murmur and splinter haemorrhages. Infective endocarditis is suspected, but he is haemodynamically stable. What should be done before starting antibiotics?
why_correct: When infective endocarditis is suspected in a haemodynamically stable patient, blood cultures should be taken before starting antibiotics, since prior antibiotic exposure can suppress growth and prevent identification of the causative organism.
why_wrong: A. Starting antibiotics before cultures reduces the chance of identifying the causative organism. B. Lumbar puncture is not the routine initial investigation for suspected endocarditis. D. CT head is not routinely required as the initial step here. E. Anticoagulation is not treatment for infective endocarditis.
pearl: Obtaining blood cultures before starting antibiotics is essential for suspected infective endocarditis, since identifying the organism guides targeted, often prolonged, antimicrobial therapy.
thinking: Fever + new murmur + splinter haemorrhages + stable patient ↓ suspected infective endocarditis ↓ organism identification is essential before treatment starts ↓ Take appropriate blood cultures
exam_trap: Candidates might prioritise starting antibiotics immediately given the concerning features, but in a stable patient cultures should be taken first, since early antibiotics can compromise microbiological diagnosis.
takeaway: In stable suspected endocarditis, take blood cultures before starting antibiotics.

stem: A 12-year-old develops migratory pain and swelling affecting several large joints several weeks after a sore throat. What condition should be suspected?
why_correct: Migratory large-joint arthritis occurring weeks after a streptococcal sore throat in a child is a classic feature of acute rheumatic fever, an autoimmune reaction to preceding group A streptococcal infection.
why_wrong: B. Gout is extremely unusual in a child and does not fit a preceding sore throat. C. Osteoarthritis is uncommon at this age. D. JIA is a chronic inflammatory arthritis rather than a typical post-streptococcal migratory arthritis. E. Septic arthritis usually affects a single joint and is an acute bacterial infection, not a migratory post-infectious process.
pearl: A migratory (rather than fixed) pattern of large-joint arthritis following a sore throat by several weeks should specifically prompt consideration of acute rheumatic fever, given its risk of cardiac involvement.
thinking: Child + migratory large-joint pain/swelling + weeks after a sore throat ↓ post-streptococcal autoimmune arthritis pattern ↓ classic migratory joint involvement ↓ Acute rheumatic fever
exam_trap: Candidates may consider septic arthritis because of joint swelling, but septic arthritis typically affects a single joint acutely, whereas the migratory, multi-joint pattern after a preceding sore throat is specific to rheumatic fever.
takeaway: Migratory large-joint arthritis weeks after a sore throat in a child suggests acute rheumatic fever.

stem: A 38-year-old man has had a persistent cough, night sweats, weight loss and intermittent fever for several weeks. What infection should be considered particularly strongly?
why_correct: A persistent cough with night sweats, weight loss and intermittent fever over several weeks is a classic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis and should prompt specific investigation for this diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms, not chronic cough and constitutional symptoms. B. Viral gastroenteritis is usually acute and predominantly gastrointestinal. C. Otitis media causes ear symptoms. D. Cellulitis causes a localised skin and soft-tissue infection, not systemic respiratory symptoms.
pearl: The combination of chronic cough, night sweats and weight loss over weeks should always prompt active consideration of tuberculosis, particularly in patients with relevant risk factors or exposure history.
thinking: Persistent cough + night sweats + weight loss + intermittent fever, over weeks ↓ classic constitutional and respiratory pattern ↓ chronic infective process ↓ Pulmonary tuberculosis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a simple chest infection, but the chronicity (weeks) combined with night sweats and weight loss is specifically suggestive of tuberculosis rather than an acute bacterial pneumonia.
takeaway: Chronic cough with night sweats and weight loss over weeks should prompt active consideration of tuberculosis.

stem: A 4-month-old infant has repeated bouts of coughing followed by a high-pitched inspiratory "whoop". The episodes sometimes cause vomiting. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Paroxysmal coughing fits followed by a characteristic high-pitched inspiratory whoop, sometimes with post-tussive vomiting, in an infant are classic for pertussis.
why_wrong: B. Croup typically causes a barking cough and inspiratory stridor, a different pattern. C. Epiglottitis causes severe sore throat, drooling and airway compromise, not this coughing pattern. D. Asthma causes variable wheeze and breathlessness rather than paroxysmal coughing with a whoop. E. Bronchiolitis causes wheeze, crackles and increased work of breathing, without the characteristic whoop.
pearl: Young infants with pertussis are at particular risk of apnoea and may not always produce the classic whoop, making vigilance for paroxysmal coughing with cyanotic or apnoeic episodes especially important in this age group.
thinking: Repeated coughing fits + inspiratory whoop + post-tussive vomiting ↓ classic Bordetella pertussis symptom pattern ↓ Pertussis
exam_trap: Candidates may consider croup because both involve a distinctive cough sound, but croup's barking cough with stridor is a different sound and pattern from pertussis's paroxysmal whoop.
takeaway: Paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory whoop and vomiting is pertussis.

stem: A 30-year-old man has well-demarcated plaques with silvery-white scales over his elbows and knees. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery-white scale over the extensor surfaces (elbows, knees) is the classic clinical appearance of plaque psoriasis.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is an acute bacterial skin infection with warmth, tenderness and spreading erythema, not well-demarcated scaly plaques. B. Tinea corporis usually produces annular lesions with an active scaly edge, not extensor plaques. C. Pityriasis rosea usually follows a herald patch with a characteristic distribution, not well-demarcated silvery plaques. D. Atopic eczema is typically intensely itchy and often affects flexures rather than extensor surfaces.
pearl: Involvement of the extensor surfaces (elbows and knees) with silvery scale on well-demarcated plaques is the classic distribution and appearance that distinguishes psoriasis from eczema, which favours the flexures.
thinking: Well-demarcated plaques + silvery-white scale + extensor surfaces (elbows, knees) ↓ classic distribution and morphology ↓ pattern specific to a chronic scaling dermatosis ↓ Psoriasis
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse this with eczema because both are chronic itchy skin conditions, but the extensor distribution and silvery scale (rather than flexural, ill-defined eczema) are specific to psoriasis.
takeaway: Well-demarcated, silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces are classic psoriasis.

stem: A 6-year-old child has recurrent intensely itchy, dry skin lesions predominantly affecting the flexures of the elbows and knees. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intensely itchy, dry skin lesions predominantly affecting the flexures (elbows, knees) in a child are the classic distribution and character of atopic eczema.
why_wrong: B. Cellulitis is usually painful, warm and acutely inflamed, not chronically itchy and dry. C. Tinea corporis causes annular fungal lesions with an active scaly edge, a different morphology. D. Herpes zoster produces painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution, not chronic flexural itch. E. Psoriasis typically produces well-demarcated scaly plaques, often on extensor surfaces, not flexures.
pearl: Flexural distribution (antecubital and popliteal fossae) with intense itch is the classic pattern of atopic eczema in children, in contrast to the extensor distribution typical of psoriasis.
thinking: Recurrent intensely itchy dry lesions + flexural distribution (elbows, knees) + child ↓ classic atopic dermatitis pattern ↓ flexural, not extensor, involvement ↓ Atopic eczema
exam_trap: Candidates might consider psoriasis given the chronic itchy skin lesions, but the flexural (not extensor) distribution and intense itch specifically point to eczema rather than psoriasis.
takeaway: Intensely itchy, dry, flexural skin lesions in a child are classic atopic eczema.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has an itchy circular lesion on her forearm with central clearing and a scaly advancing edge. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An itchy, circular lesion with central clearing and a scaly, advancing edge is the classic appearance of a dermatophyte (fungal) skin infection — tinea corporis.
why_wrong: A. Pityriasis rosea usually presents with multiple oval lesions following a herald patch, not a single advancing ring. B. Eczema is not usually characterised by this classic ring-shaped border with central clearing. C. Psoriasis usually causes thicker plaques rather than an annular advancing edge. D. Cellulitis produces diffuse warmth, erythema and tenderness rather than a well-defined annular lesion.
pearl: The active, scaly advancing edge with relative central clearing is the feature that identifies a fungal (dermatophyte) infection and distinguishes it from other annular skin lesions.
thinking: Itchy circular lesion + central clearing + scaly advancing edge ↓ classic 'ring' morphology of a dermatophyte infection ↓ active border with clearing centre ↓ Tinea corporis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider eczema given the itch, but the specific annular shape with central clearing and an active scaly border is characteristic of a fungal infection rather than eczema.
takeaway: An itchy ring-shaped lesion with central clearing and a scaly advancing edge is tinea corporis.

stem: A woman at 34 weeks' gestation develops severe itching, particularly affecting her palms and soles, but has no rash. Which investigation is particularly important?
why_correct: Severe pruritus, especially affecting the palms and soles, without a rash, in later pregnancy is characteristic of intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, for which serum bile acids are the key diagnostic investigation.
why_wrong: A. Serum calcium does not diagnose cholestasis. B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury, unrelated to this presentation. D. D-dimer is not the diagnostic test for pregnancy-associated cholestasis. E. Thyroid function tests are not the key investigation; palmar and plantar itch without rash in late pregnancy points to intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
pearl: Pruritus without a visible rash, particularly affecting the palms and soles and worsening later in pregnancy, should always prompt testing for intrahepatic cholestasis because of its associated fetal risks.
thinking: Late pregnancy + severe pruritus of palms/soles + no rash ↓ pattern suggests a cholestatic, not dermatological, cause ↓ raised bile acids are the diagnostic marker ↓ Serum bile acids
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with cholestasis may look for a dermatological cause given the itch, but the absence of a rash together with the palm/sole distribution specifically points to a hepatic, bile-acid-mediated process.
takeaway: Pruritus without a rash, especially of the palms and soles, in pregnancy warrants checking serum bile acids for cholestasis.

stem: A woman with a previous caesarean section develops sudden severe abdominal pain during labour. The fetal heart rate becomes persistently abnormal. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain during labour in a woman with a previous caesarean section, together with acute fetal compromise, should immediately raise concern for uterine rupture along the previous scar.
why_wrong: A. Hyperemesis occurs mainly in early pregnancy, not during labour. B. Gestational diabetes does not cause this acute intrapartum presentation. D. Placenta praevia typically causes painless vaginal bleeding rather than sudden pain with fetal compromise during labour. E. Intrahepatic cholestasis causes maternal pruritus, not acute abdominal pain and fetal compromise.
pearl: Previous caesarean section is the leading risk factor for uterine rupture in a subsequent labour, and sudden pain with fetal heart rate abnormality is the classic warning sign requiring immediate action.
thinking: Previous caesarean section + sudden severe abdominal pain in labour + persistent abnormal fetal heart rate ↓ scar dehiscence under labour stress ↓ acute fetal compromise follows ↓ Uterine rupture
exam_trap: Candidates might attribute the pain simply to normal labour, but the sudden severity combined with fetal heart rate abnormality in a scarred uterus is specific to rupture and demands emergency action.
takeaway: Sudden severe pain with fetal compromise in a woman with a previous caesarean scar means think uterine rupture.

stem: Immediately after spontaneous rupture of the membranes, a woman develops vaginal bleeding and the fetal heart rate suddenly becomes severely abnormal. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Vaginal bleeding occurring immediately after spontaneous rupture of the membranes, with sudden severe fetal heart rate abnormality, suggests rupture of unprotected fetal vessels running through the membranes — vasa praevia.
why_wrong: B. Intrahepatic cholestasis causes pruritus rather than acute bleeding. C. Placenta praevia causes maternal bleeding from the placenta itself rather than rupture of exposed fetal vessels immediately after membrane rupture. D. Hyperemesis is an early-pregnancy vomiting disorder, unrelated to this presentation. E. Maternal sepsis does not characteristically cause sudden bleeding with immediate fetal compromise directly after membrane rupture.
pearl: Because the bleeding in vasa praevia is fetal, not maternal, even a small amount of blood loss can rapidly cause severe fetal compromise — timing relative to membrane rupture is the critical diagnostic clue.
thinking: Bleeding begins immediately after membrane rupture + sudden severe fetal heart rate abnormality ↓ timing suggests exposed fetal vessels have torn ↓ fetal, not maternal, blood loss ↓ Vasa praevia
exam_trap: Candidates may default to placenta praevia whenever antepartum bleeding is described, but the precise timing — bleeding starting right at membrane rupture with severe fetal compromise — is the specific clue pointing to vasa praevia.
takeaway: Bleeding immediately at membrane rupture with severe fetal distress points to vasa praevia, a fetal vessel emergency.

stem: A woman shortly after delivery develops fever, lower abdominal pain and uterine tenderness. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, lower abdominal pain and uterine tenderness developing after delivery are the classic features of postpartum endometritis, an infection of the uterine lining.
why_wrong: A. Mastitis causes a painful, inflamed breast, not uterine tenderness. C. Calf DVT causes limb symptoms and does not explain uterine tenderness. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms rather than uterine tenderness. E. Postpartum psychosis causes psychiatric symptoms rather than fever and uterine tenderness.
pearl: Postpartum endometritis typically presents with fever, uterine tenderness and sometimes offensive lochia, and requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent progression to more serious sepsis.
thinking: Recent delivery + fever + lower abdominal pain + uterine tenderness ↓ localises to the uterus after delivery ↓ infection of the uterine lining ↓ Postpartum endometritis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a urinary or breast source given the postpartum setting, but the specific finding of uterine tenderness points directly to an endometrial, not urinary or breast, source of infection.
takeaway: Fever with uterine tenderness after delivery is postpartum endometritis.

stem: A newborn becomes unwell shortly after birth. The mother had suspected chorioamnionitis during labour. What should be considered?
why_correct: Maternal chorioamnionitis is an important risk factor for early-onset neonatal infection, so a newborn who becomes unwell shortly after birth in this context should be assessed and managed for possible sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric stenosis presents later with projectile vomiting, not immediate neonatal illness. C. Hirschsprung disease usually presents with delayed meconium passage or bowel obstruction, not sepsis-type illness. D. Eczema does not cause acute neonatal systemic illness. E. Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a musculoskeletal condition, unrelated to acute illness.
pearl: Maternal risk factors such as chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes or maternal fever should prompt close monitoring and a low threshold for treating a newborn for possible early-onset sepsis.
thinking: Maternal suspected chorioamnionitis + newborn unwell shortly after birth ↓ recognised risk factor for vertical transmission of infection ↓ prompts assessment for neonatal sepsis ↓ Early-onset neonatal infection
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a structural neonatal condition, but the specific maternal risk factor of chorioamnionitis should redirect thinking towards infection as the most important and time-critical diagnosis to consider.
takeaway: Maternal chorioamnionitis plus an unwell newborn means think early-onset neonatal infection.

stem: A newborn of a mother with diabetes becomes jittery and lethargic. What investigation should be performed promptly?
why_correct: Infants of mothers with diabetes are at increased risk of neonatal hypoglycaemia due to fetal hyperinsulinaemia, which can present with jitteriness and lethargy; blood glucose should be checked promptly.
why_wrong: A. D-dimer is not the appropriate investigation for this presentation. C. Troponin assesses myocardial injury, unrelated to jitteriness in this context. D. Amylase is relevant to pancreatic disease, not the immediate presentation. E. Serum urate has no role in assessing neonatal jitteriness.
pearl: In infants of diabetic mothers, fetal hyperinsulinaemia in response to maternal hyperglycaemia persists after birth once the maternal glucose supply stops, creating a window of risk for hypoglycaemia that needs active monitoring.
thinking: Infant of a mother with diabetes + jitteriness and lethargy ↓ fetal hyperinsulinaemia predisposes to postnatal hypoglycaemia ↓ symptoms are consistent with low blood glucose ↓ Blood glucose
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a cardiac or infective cause of lethargy, but in an infant of a diabetic mother, hypoglycaemia is the specific and immediately checkable explanation that must be excluded first.
takeaway: Jitteriness and lethargy in an infant of a diabetic mother means check blood glucose promptly.

stem: A premature newborn develops abdominal distension, feeding intolerance and blood-stained stools. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Abdominal distension, feeding intolerance and blood-stained stools in a premature newborn are highly suggestive of necrotising enterocolitis, a serious bowel condition of prematurity.
why_wrong: B. Hirschsprung disease causes distal bowel obstruction and delayed meconium passage, a different pattern. C. Infantile colic does not cause systemic illness or bloody stools. D. Pyloric stenosis causes progressive projectile vomiting, usually presenting later in infancy, not in the neonatal period with bloody stools. E. Reflux does not typically cause abdominal distension with bloody stools in a premature infant.
pearl: Prematurity is the single most important risk factor for necrotising enterocolitis, and the combination of distension, feeding intolerance and bloody stools should prompt urgent assessment and imaging.
thinking: Premature newborn + abdominal distension + feeding intolerance + blood-stained stools ↓ classic triad in a high-risk (premature) infant ↓ bowel wall injury with possible necrosis ↓ Necrotising enterocolitis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a feeding-related or reflux explanation, but the combination of distension, intolerance and bloody stools in a premature infant is specifically concerning for NEC and needs urgent management, not reassurance.
takeaway: Distension, feeding intolerance and bloody stools in a premature newborn means think necrotising enterocolitis.

stem: A patient is admitted to hospital taking several regular medicines prescribed by different clinicians. What is the most important initial step to reduce medication-related errors?

options.A: Replace all medicines with intravenous treatment
options.B: Prescribe all medicines at their previous doses without checking
options.E: Ask the patient to remember every dose

why_correct: Medicines reconciliation on admission establishes an accurate picture of what the patient was actually taking, helping identify omissions, duplications or dosing errors before further prescribing decisions are made.
why_wrong: A. Intravenous treatment is unnecessary for most regular medicines and does not itself reduce error. B. Prescribing previous doses without checking risks perpetuating errors or inappropriate medicines. D. Stopping all medicines may cause harm from untreated conditions or withdrawal. E. Patient recall alone may be incomplete or inaccurate.
pearl: Medicines reconciliation should ideally cross-check at least two independent sources (such as the patient, GP records and community pharmacy) to build the most accurate picture of actual medication use.
thinking: Admission + multiple regular medicines from different prescribers ↓ risk of errors, omissions or duplications across sources ↓ need a structured way to establish the true regimen ↓ Perform medicines reconciliation
exam_trap: Candidates might think simply asking the patient is sufficient, but reconciliation specifically means cross-checking multiple sources, not relying on recall alone.
takeaway: Medicines reconciliation on admission is the key step to catch errors, omissions and duplications.

stem: A doctor identifies a suspected serious adverse reaction to a newly started medicine. What UK reporting system is used to report suspected adverse drug reactions?
why_correct: The Yellow Card Scheme is the UK's established system for reporting suspected adverse drug reactions and other safety concerns relating to medicines and certain healthcare products.
why_wrong: A. The Confidential Inquiry into Maternal Deaths investigates maternal mortality, not drug reactions. B. The NHS Cervical Screening Programme concerns cervical screening. C. The Cancer Registry records cancer diagnoses. E. The National Joint Registry concerns joint replacement procedures.
pearl: Reporting is particularly encouraged for reactions to newer medicines (marked with a black triangle) and for any serious or unexpected suspected adverse drug reaction, even if causation is uncertain.
thinking: Suspected serious adverse reaction to a new medicine ↓ UK has a dedicated national reporting system for this ↓ identify the correct named scheme ↓ Yellow Card Scheme
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with UK-specific systems might guess at a generic 'cancer' or 'death inquiry' registry; recognising the Yellow Card Scheme as the specific named system for drug safety reporting is the key knowledge point.
takeaway: Suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK are reported through the Yellow Card Scheme.

presentation: Police Request For Records Without Consent
stem: The police ask a doctor to provide a patient's medical records. The patient has not consented. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Disclose once the police put the request in writing
options.B: Assess the lawful basis and disclose only what is relevant
options.C: Decline as a matter of policy without assessment
options.D: Provide the full record as the police have requested it
options.E: Disclose the records once the patient's GP agrees

correct_answer: B. Assess the lawful basis and disclose only what is relevant
why_correct: Confidentiality remains the default position; disclosure without consent may only be justified where there is a genuine lawful basis, and even then only the minimum relevant information should be disclosed.
why_wrong: A. A written police request is not in itself a lawful basis for disclosure without consent. C. Blanket refusal is wrong because there are circumstances where disclosure without consent may be lawful or required. D. Providing the entire record breaches the principle of disclosing only what is relevant. E. Another doctor's agreement does not create a lawful basis for disclosure.
pearl: When disclosure without consent is being considered, the guiding principles are: is there a lawful basis, is disclosure proportionate, and is only the minimum necessary information being shared.
thinking: Police request records without patient consent ↓ confidentiality remains the default position ↓ disclosure requires an identified lawful basis and proportionate scope ↓ Consider lawful basis and disclose only relevant information if justified
exam_trap: Candidates often swing to an extreme — either refusing every police request outright or handing over the full record — missing that the correct approach is a case-by-case assessment of lawful basis and proportionality.
takeaway: Police requests for records without consent require an assessed lawful basis and disclosure of only the minimum relevant information.

stem: A patient has a valid decision indicating that cardiopulmonary resuscitation should not be attempted if cardiac arrest occurs. The patient later develops pneumonia. What does the decision mean?

options.A: The patient can no longer refuse any other treatments offered
options.B: The patient should be discharged to a hospice for palliation
options.C: It applies to CPR only; other treatment may still be given
options.D: Active treatment should be withdrawn, including antibiotics
options.E: Antibiotics should be given orally rather than intravenously

correct_answer: C. It applies to CPR only; other treatment may still be given
why_correct: A DNACPR decision applies specifically to cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest; it does not mean that other clinically appropriate treatments, such as antibiotics for pneumonia, should automatically be withheld.
why_wrong: A. Treatment decisions remain subject to consent, capacity and best-interests principles regardless of a DNACPR decision. B. A DNACPR decision does not determine the patient's place of care or discharge. D. DNACPR does not mean withdrawing active treatment such as antibiotics. E. A DNACPR decision does not dictate the route of antibiotic administration.
pearl: A DNACPR decision should always be interpreted narrowly — it addresses resuscitation alone, and all other appropriate treatment decisions continue to be made on their own clinical merits.
thinking: Valid DNACPR decision + patient develops pneumonia ↓ DNACPR only concerns response to cardiac arrest ↓ other treatment decisions are made independently on clinical merit ↓ The decision specifically concerns CPR and does not automatically prevent other treatment
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes assume DNACPR implies a broader 'do not treat' approach, but it is a narrow decision limited to CPR and must never be extrapolated to withholding other appropriate care.
takeaway: DNACPR covers resuscitation only — all other appropriate treatment decisions are made independently.

stem: A study reports a relative risk of 0.50 for an intervention compared with control. What does this mean?

options.A: The absolute risk is reduced by 50 percentage points
options.B: The intervention causes the outcome in 50% of patients
options.C: The intervention prevents the outcome in 50% of patients
options.D: The outcome risk is halved compared with control
options.E: The outcome is twice as common with the intervention

correct_answer: D. The outcome risk is halved compared with control
why_correct: A relative risk of 0.50 means the risk of the outcome in the intervention group is half the risk in the control group — the intervention halves the relative risk compared with control.
why_wrong: A. Relative risk alone does not give the absolute risk reduction, which depends on the baseline risk. B. An RR of 0.50 does not mean the intervention causes the outcome in 50% of patients. C. An RR of 0.50 does not mean the outcome is prevented in 50% of patients; the proportion prevented depends on the baseline risk. E. An RR of 2.0, not 0.50, would mean the outcome is twice as common with the intervention.
pearl: Relative risk describes a proportional change compared with the baseline risk, so the same relative risk reduction can translate into very different absolute risk reductions depending on how common the outcome is.
thinking: RR reported as 0.50 ↓ this is a ratio of risk with intervention versus risk with control ↓ 0.50 means half the risk of the comparator ↓ The intervention halves the relative risk compared with control
exam_trap: Candidates commonly confuse relative and absolute risk reduction, wrongly assuming an RR of 0.50 tells you the absolute drop in risk, when it only describes the proportional change relative to the baseline.
takeaway: RR 0.50 means the outcome risk is halved relative to control — it says nothing about the absolute risk reduction on its own.

stem: A case-control study reports an odds ratio of 3.0 for an exposure and a disease. What does this indicate?

options.A: The disease occurs in 3% of exposed patients
options.B: Three times as many exposed as unexposed patients died
options.C: Cases had three times the odds of exposure of controls
options.D: This is equivalent to a relative risk of 3.0
options.E: The exposure reduces the odds of disease by a third

correct_answer: C. Cases had three times the odds of exposure of controls
why_correct: In a case-control study, an odds ratio of 3.0 means the odds of having been exposed are three times higher among cases (with the disease) than among controls (without the disease).
why_wrong: A. An odds ratio does not provide disease incidence or prevalence figures. B. An OR does not directly indicate the number of deaths or any absolute outcome count. D. The OR approximates the RR only when the outcome is rare; it is not equivalent to it, particularly when the outcome is common. E. An OR above 1 indicates increased odds of exposure among cases, not a protective effect.
pearl: In a case-control study, incidence cannot be directly calculated, so the odds ratio — comparing exposure odds between cases and controls — is used instead of relative risk.
thinking: Case-control study + OR of 3.0 reported for exposure and disease ↓ case-control design compares exposure odds, not incidence, between groups ↓ OR expresses how much higher exposure odds are in cases versus controls ↓ The odds of exposure among cases are three times those among controls
exam_trap: Candidates often conflate OR with RR and assume OR 3.0 directly means 'three times the risk', missing that OR specifically compares the odds of exposure between cases and controls in a case-control design.
takeaway: In a case-control study, the odds ratio compares exposure odds between cases and controls — it is not the same as relative risk.

presentation: Interpreting A Confidence Interval Crossing The Null
stem: A clinical trial reports a treatment effect with a 95% confidence interval that crosses the value representing no difference between treatment groups. What does this generally imply?

options.A: The treatment effect is statistically significant
options.B: The study proves the treatments are equally effective
options.D: The treatment is shown to cause harm
options.E: The result is compatible with no treatment difference

correct_answer: E. The result is compatible with no treatment difference
why_correct: When a 95% confidence interval for a treatment effect crosses the value representing no difference (the null), the result is generally interpreted as statistically compatible with there being no true difference between groups at that significance level.
why_wrong: A. A 95% CI that crosses the null value indicates a result that is not statistically significant at the 5% level. B. A non-significant result does not prove equivalence; it means the study could not rule out no effect. C. A 95% CI crossing the null corresponds to a p-value of 0.05 or more, not less. D. A CI spanning the null does not show that the treatment causes harm.
pearl: A wide confidence interval crossing the null often reflects an underpowered study rather than definitive proof of 'no effect' — the correct interpretation is uncertainty, not a confirmed null result.
thinking: 95% CI for treatment effect crosses the 'no difference' value ↓ this range includes zero (or 1, depending on the measure) effect ↓ result cannot confidently rule out no true difference ↓ The result is statistically compatible with no treatment difference
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes over-interpret a confidence interval crossing the null as definitive proof the treatment does not work, rather than recognising it only reflects statistical compatibility with no difference, not certainty.
takeaway: A confidence interval crossing the null means the result is compatible with no difference — it is not proof of no effect.

stem: A 68-year-old man has fatigue and numbness in both feet. Blood tests show macrocytic anaemia and a low vitamin B12 level. Which additional neurological feature is particularly associated with vitamin B12 deficiency?
why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological dysfunction, including peripheral neuropathy and posterior column involvement, alongside the macrocytic anaemia and fatigue described.
why_wrong: B. Monocular blindness suggests an ocular or optic vascular/neurological disorder, not a typical feature of B12 deficiency. C. Resting tremor is characteristic of parkinsonism rather than B12 deficiency. D. Hemiplegia suggests a focal central neurological lesion such as stroke, not B12 deficiency. E. A lower motor neurone facial palsy (e.g. Bell palsy) has different causes and is not typically linked to B12 deficiency.
pearl: B12 deficiency can cause a spectrum of neurological findings including peripheral neuropathy and, in more advanced cases, posterior column signs (impaired vibration/proprioception) — neurological features can precede the anaemia becoming apparent.
thinking: Fatigue + bilateral foot numbness + macrocytic anaemia + low B12 ↓ B12 is essential for myelin maintenance ↓ deficiency produces peripheral nerve and posterior column dysfunction ↓ Peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: Candidates may pick an unrelated neurological sign because 'neurological feature' sounds broad, but only peripheral neuropathy among the options reflects the recognised mechanism of B12-related nerve dysfunction.
takeaway: B12 deficiency classically causes peripheral neuropathy, alongside macrocytic anaemia.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with fatigue and jaundice. Blood tests show a raised bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, with a low haptoglobin. Which process is most likely occurring?
why_correct: Raised bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase with a low haptoglobin are the classic laboratory triad indicating increased red-cell breakdown — haemolysis — explaining the fatigue and jaundice.
why_wrong: A. B12 deficiency may cause ineffective erythropoiesis but does not produce this classic combination of raised LDH with low haptoglobin from red-cell destruction. B. Iron deficiency causes reduced haemoglobin and iron stores rather than this haemolytic biochemical pattern. D. Acute blood loss has a different clinical and laboratory pattern, without this specific haemolysis signature. E. Bone marrow failure causes reduced production of blood cells rather than increased breakdown.
pearl: Low haptoglobin is a particularly useful marker of haemolysis because haptoglobin is consumed as it binds free haemoglobin released from destroyed red cells.
thinking: Fatigue + jaundice + raised bilirubin and LDH + low haptoglobin ↓ classic biochemical signature of red-cell breakdown ↓ haptoglobin consumed mopping up free haemoglobin ↓ Haemolysis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a hepatic cause of jaundice given the bilirubin rise, but the combination with raised LDH and low haptoglobin specifically indicates a haemolytic, not primarily hepatic, process.
takeaway: Raised bilirubin and LDH with low haptoglobin is the classic laboratory pattern of haemolysis.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of jaundice during periods of illness and fasting. She is otherwise well and has normal liver function tests apart from a mild increase in unconjugated bilirubin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intermittent mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia triggered by fasting or illness, with otherwise normal liver function and no evidence of significant liver disease, is characteristic of Gilbert syndrome, a benign inherited condition of bilirubin conjugation.
why_wrong: B. Biliary obstruction typically causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, not isolated mild unconjugated elevation. C. Haemochromatosis causes iron overload rather than isolated intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. D. Primary biliary cholangitis causes chronic cholestatic liver disease with abnormal liver enzymes, unlike this otherwise normal picture. E. Acute hepatitis usually causes significant liver enzyme abnormalities and systemic symptoms, not just mild intermittent jaundice.
pearl: Gilbert syndrome is a benign, common condition requiring only reassurance once other causes of jaundice have been excluded — recognising the classic fasting/illness trigger avoids unnecessary further investigation.
thinking: Recurrent mild jaundice triggered by fasting/illness + otherwise normal liver function + mildly raised unconjugated bilirubin ↓ pattern fits a benign conjugation defect rather than structural liver disease ↓ classic trigger and biochemical pattern ↓ Gilbert syndrome
exam_trap: Candidates might worry about an evolving liver disease given recurrent jaundice, but the otherwise normal liver function tests and classic fasting/illness trigger are reassuring features specific to benign Gilbert syndrome.
takeaway: Recurrent mild jaundice triggered by fasting or illness, with normal liver function otherwise, is Gilbert syndrome.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss. Coeliac disease is suspected. Which antibody test is usually used initially?
why_correct: IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody is the recommended first-line serological test for suspected coeliac disease, usually combined with a total IgA level to exclude IgA deficiency as a cause of a false-negative result.
why_wrong: B. Antimitochondrial antibody is associated with primary biliary cholangitis, not coeliac disease. C. Anti-CCP antibody supports a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. D. Anti-GBM antibody is associated with certain forms of glomerulonephritis. E. Anti-dsDNA antibody is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
pearl: A diagnosis of coeliac disease should not be confirmed on serology alone and normally requires histological confirmation on duodenal biopsy while the patient remains on a gluten-containing diet.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea + bloating + weight loss ↓ suspected malabsorptive small bowel disease ↓ first-line serology ↓ IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody
exam_trap: Candidates may be drawn to antimitochondrial antibody because it sounds like a generic autoimmune gut test, but it is specific to primary biliary cholangitis, not coeliac disease.
takeaway: IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody (with total IgA) is the initial test of choice when coeliac disease is suspected.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with coeliac disease continues to have diarrhoea despite treatment. What should be checked first?

options.B: Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis

correct_answer: C. Adherence to a gluten-free diet
why_correct: Ongoing inadvertent gluten exposure is the most common cause of persistent symptoms in a patient already diagnosed with and treated for coeliac disease, so dietary adherence should be checked before further investigation.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatic insufficiency is a recognised cause of non-response, but it is considered only after gluten exposure has been excluded. B. CT imaging is not the first check in non-responsive coeliac disease; ongoing gluten exposure must be excluded first. D. D-dimer assesses thrombotic risk and does not explain ongoing diarrhoea. E. Repeat biopsy is part of the work-up of non-responsive disease, not the first check before dietary adherence.
pearl: Persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet should prompt a structured review of dietary adherence before considering refractory coeliac disease or an alternative diagnosis.
thinking: Known coeliac disease + ongoing diarrhoea on treatment ↓ most common explanation is continued gluten exposure ↓ check dietary adherence first
exam_trap: Candidates may jump to invasive or rare investigations, but the pragmatic and evidence-based first step is confirming whether gluten is truly being avoided.
takeaway: In treated coeliac disease with persistent symptoms, check dietary adherence before pursuing further work-up.

stem: A 45-year-old man develops severe diarrhoea after returning from a holiday abroad. He is passing frequent watery stools but has no blood and is haemodynamically stable. What is the most important initial management?
why_correct: In a haemodynamically stable patient with acute watery diarrhoea and no blood, the priority is replacing fluid and electrolyte losses, which is the cornerstone of managing most acute diarrhoeal illnesses.
why_wrong: A. Insulin infusion has no role in managing acute infective diarrhoea. B. There is no evidence of significant blood loss to warrant transfusion. C. Long-term corticosteroids are not indicated for acute infectious diarrhoea. D. There is no indication of an acute surgical abdomen requiring laparotomy.
pearl: Most acute infectious diarrhoeal illnesses are self-limiting and managed supportively with rehydration; antibiotics are reserved for specific indications.
thinking: Watery diarrhoea after travel + haemodynamically stable + no blood ↓ acute infective gastroenteritis ↓ supportive fluid replacement ↓ Oral rehydration
exam_trap: Candidates may over-medicalise a stable presentation by reaching for antibiotics or invasive options, when simple rehydration is the appropriate first step.
takeaway: Oral rehydration is the mainstay of initial management for acute watery diarrhoea in a stable patient.

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhoea after completing a course of antibiotics. She has abdominal cramping but no recent travel. What infection should be suspected?
why_correct: Diarrhoea developing after a course of antibiotics is the classic risk pattern for Clostridioides difficile infection, which disrupts normal gut flora and allows toxin-producing overgrowth.
why_wrong: A. Enterotoxigenic E. coli is the classic cause of travellers' diarrhoea, and there is no recent travel; it is not linked to antibiotic exposure. C. Influenza causes respiratory and systemic symptoms rather than diarrhoea after antibiotics. D. Malaria causes a febrile systemic illness rather than this characteristic post-antibiotic diarrhoeal pattern. E. Measles causes a febrile illness with respiratory symptoms and a rash.
pearl: Recent or recurrent antibiotic use is the single most important risk factor to elicit when C. difficile infection is suspected.
thinking: Recent antibiotics + new profuse watery diarrhoea + abdominal cramping ↓ disrupted gut flora ↓ Clostridioides difficile infection
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a travel-related pathogen, but the absence of travel and the clear antibiotic trigger point specifically to C. difficile.
takeaway: Diarrhoea shortly after antibiotic exposure should always raise suspicion of Clostridioides difficile.

stem: A 32-year-old woman develops bloody diarrhoea and abdominal cramps after eating undercooked chicken. Which organism is most likely?
why_correct: Campylobacter jejuni is strongly associated with undercooked poultry and typically causes fever, cramping abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea.
why_wrong: A. Vibrio cholerae causes profuse watery ('rice water') diarrhoea rather than this bloody, cramping picture. B. Giardia lamblia typically causes prolonged greasy, offensive diarrhoea and bloating rather than an acute bloody illness. C. Norovirus usually causes acute vomiting with watery diarrhoea rather than blood. D. Clostridioides difficile is particularly linked to recent antibiotic exposure, not undercooked poultry.
pearl: A clear dietary exposure history, such as undercooked poultry, is a key clue that helps narrow the likely causative organism in infective diarrhoea.
thinking: Undercooked chicken + bloody diarrhoea + cramps ↓ poultry-associated bacterial enteritis ↓ Campylobacter jejuni
exam_trap: Candidates may pick Clostridioides difficile because it is a familiar cause of diarrhoea, but there is no antibiotic history here, making a food-source organism far more likely.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea after undercooked poultry is the classic vignette for Campylobacter jejuni.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has recurrent diarrhoea, abdominal discomfort and weight loss. She also has a chronic itchy rash consisting of grouped vesicles over her elbows. What condition is associated with this skin finding?
why_correct: Dermatitis herpetiformis, an intensely itchy, grouped vesicular rash typically on extensor surfaces such as the elbows, is strongly and specifically associated with coeliac disease.
why_wrong: B. Ulcerative colitis is linked to different extraintestinal features such as erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum. C. Crohn disease has its own characteristic extraintestinal manifestations, not a grouped vesicular rash. D. Lactose intolerance does not cause an associated skin eruption. E. Irritable bowel syndrome does not produce an inflammatory vesicular rash.
pearl: The gut and skin manifestations of coeliac disease often coexist, and the rash can be the presenting feature even when gastrointestinal symptoms are mild.
thinking: Diarrhoea + weight loss + itchy grouped vesicles on elbows ↓ recognised gut-skin association ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: Candidates familiar with inflammatory bowel disease might reach for Crohn or ulcerative colitis, but neither is linked with a grouped vesicular extensor rash the way coeliac disease is.
takeaway: Grouped, itchy vesicles on extensor surfaces alongside gut symptoms should prompt testing for coeliac disease.

stem: A 58-year-old man reports flashes of light followed by a sudden increase in floaters and a dark curtain moving across his visual field. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: New flashes of light, a sudden shower of floaters and a curtain-like visual field defect are the classic warning symptoms of retinal detachment.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual, progressive visual deterioration rather than sudden flashes and a curtain effect. C. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden profound painless visual loss rather than the typical flashes-and-curtain presentation. D. Anterior uveitis causes pain, photophobia and reduced vision rather than flashes and a field defect. E. Conjunctivitis causes redness and discharge rather than a visual field disturbance.
pearl: Any patient describing flashes, new floaters or a curtain over their vision needs urgent same-day ophthalmic assessment, as delay risks permanent visual loss.
thinking: Flashes + sudden floaters + curtain-like visual field loss ↓ posterior vitreous separation pulling on retina ↓ Retinal detachment
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse this with central retinal artery occlusion because both cause sudden visual disturbance, but CRAO causes painless loss of vision rather than the flashes-and-curtain pattern described here.
takeaway: Flashes, floaters and a curtain across the vision are the classic triad of retinal detachment.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has gradually worsening difficulty reading small print and needs to hold books further away. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Gradual, age-related loss of the lens's ability to accommodate causes progressive difficulty focusing on near objects, which is presbyopia.
why_wrong: A. Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden, profound monocular visual loss, not gradual near-vision difficulty. C. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with visual disturbance, not a chronic reading difficulty. D. Optic neuritis causes acute or subacute visual loss, often with pain. E. Retinal detachment causes acute visual field symptoms rather than gradual near-vision loss.
pearl: Presbyopia is a near-universal, age-related change that typically becomes noticeable from the mid-40s onwards and is managed with reading glasses.
thinking: Older adult + gradual difficulty with near vision + holding print further away ↓ age-related loss of lens accommodation ↓ Presbyopia
exam_trap: Candidates might overthink this as a pathological process, but the gradual onset and classic pattern of holding reading material at arm's length is simply age-related presbyopia.
takeaway: Gradual difficulty with near vision in an older adult is typically presbyopia, not an acute eye disease.

stem: A 33-year-old man develops painful urination and a urethral discharge. What infection should be considered particularly strongly?
why_correct: A purulent urethral discharge with dysuria in a man is the classic presentation of gonococcal urethritis.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial vaginosis causes vaginal discharge and is not a cause of male urethritis. B. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is a vaginal fungal infection and does not affect the male urethra in this way. C. Syphilis classically causes a painless genital chancre in its primary stage, not urethral discharge. D. Genital herpes typically causes painful grouped genital vesicles or ulcers, not a purulent discharge.
pearl: Symptomatic urethral discharge should prompt testing for both gonorrhoea and chlamydia, as co-infection is common.
thinking: Male patient + dysuria + purulent urethral discharge ↓ classic bacterial urethritis pattern ↓ Gonorrhoea
exam_trap: Candidates may consider chlamydia as an alternative, but a markedly purulent discharge is the feature that points more specifically towards gonorrhoea, which tends to cause a more overt discharge than chlamydia.
takeaway: Purulent urethral discharge with dysuria in a man should prompt testing specifically for gonorrhoea.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with painless jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. He has lost weight over several months. What is the most likely underlying cause?
why_correct: Progressive painless obstructive jaundice with dark urine, pale stools and unintentional weight loss is the classic presentation of a malignancy obstructing the distal bile duct, most often a pancreatic head tumour.
why_wrong: B. Peptic ulcer disease does not typically cause painless obstructive jaundice. C. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause obstructive jaundice or this pattern of weight loss. D. Acute appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain and systemic inflammation, not jaundice. E. Haemorrhoids cause rectal bleeding or local anal symptoms, not jaundice.
pearl: Painless jaundice should always be treated as a red flag for malignant biliary obstruction until proven otherwise.
thinking: Painless jaundice + dark urine + pale stools + weight loss ↓ obstructive biliary picture without pain ↓ Pancreatic head malignancy
exam_trap: Candidates may expect gallstone disease when they see jaundice, but gallstones typically cause pain, whereas this painless, progressive pattern with weight loss is a classic malignancy red flag.
takeaway: Painless progressive jaundice with weight loss should be treated as pancreatic head cancer until excluded.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive difficulty swallowing. Initially she struggled with solid foods, but she now has difficulty swallowing liquids as well. Which diagnosis is most concerning?
why_correct: Dysphagia progressing from solids to liquids is the alarm pattern most concerning for a structural, obstructing oesophageal lesion such as malignancy, requiring urgent investigation.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause dysphagia. B. Haemorrhoids are unrelated to swallowing difficulty. C. Lactose intolerance causes gastrointestinal symptoms but not progressive dysphagia. E. Reflux can cause oesophageal symptoms but progressive dysphagia requires investigation rather than assuming uncomplicated reflux.
pearl: Any progressive dysphagia, particularly solids-then-liquids, should prompt urgent endoscopic assessment rather than being attributed to reflux without investigation.
thinking: Progressive dysphagia solids then liquids ↓ pattern suggesting mechanical obstruction ↓ Oesophageal malignancy
exam_trap: Candidates might attribute this to uncomplicated reflux given how common GORD is, but progressive dysphagia is an alarm feature that always warrants exclusion of malignancy rather than presumptive reflux management.
takeaway: Progressive solids-then-liquids dysphagia is the most concerning pattern for oesophageal malignancy and needs urgent investigation.

stem: A 76-year-old woman develops sudden pain, pallor and coldness of her left foot. The foot has no palpable distal pulses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness and absent distal pulses represent acute arterial occlusion of the limb, a vascular emergency.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes warmth, redness and tenderness, the opposite of a cold, pulseless limb. C. Chronic venous insufficiency causes chronic swelling and skin changes, not sudden pulselessness. D. Osteoarthritis causes chronic joint pain, not acute vascular compromise. E. DVT generally causes swelling and pain but does not cause an acutely pulseless, pale limb.
pearl: Acute limb ischaemia is time-critical; prolonged ischaemia risks irreversible tissue damage and limb loss, so urgent vascular assessment is required.
thinking: Sudden pain + pallor + coldness + absent pulses ↓ acute arterial occlusion ↓ Acute limb ischaemia
exam_trap: Candidates might consider DVT because it also causes an acutely symptomatic limb, but DVT causes a swollen, warm limb with preserved pulses rather than a pale, pulseless, cold one.
takeaway: Sudden pain, pallor, coldness and absent pulses define acute limb ischaemia, a vascular emergency.

stem: A 76-year-old woman has a chronic ulcer near the medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is oedematous and has brown pigmentation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A chronic ulcer near the medial malleolus with surrounding oedema and brown (haemosiderin) pigmentation reflects chronic venous hypertension, characteristic of a venous leg ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Malignant melanoma presents as a pigmented tumour rather than this typical venous ulcer pattern. B. Arterial ulcers are commonly painful, occur over pressure points, and are associated with features of arterial insufficiency rather than pigmentation and oedema. C. Neuropathic ulcers are commonly associated with loss of protective sensation rather than venous skin changes. E. Pressure ulcers occur over bony, pressure-bearing areas rather than the gaiter region.
pearl: Venous leg ulcers are the most common type of leg ulcer and are managed primarily with compression therapy once arterial disease has been excluded.
thinking: Medial malleolar ulcer + oedema + brown pigmentation ↓ chronic venous hypertension ↓ Venous leg ulcer
exam_trap: Candidates may assume any leg ulcer in an older patient is arterial, but arterial ulcers are typically painful and occur over pressure points rather than the gaiter region with pigmentation and oedema seen here.
takeaway: A gaiter-region ulcer with oedema and brown pigmentation is the classic picture of a venous leg ulcer.

stem: A patient with diabetes has reduced sensation in both feet and develops a painless ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.A: Acute gouty arthritis of the first MTP joint
options.B: Acute arterial embolism to the foot
options.C: Loss of protective sensation from neuropathy
options.D: Primary bacterial infection of the skin

correct_answer: C. Loss of protective sensation from neuropathy
why_correct: Loss of protective sensation from diabetic peripheral neuropathy allows repetitive unnoticed pressure over bony prominences, such as the first metatarsal head, to produce a painless plantar ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes an acutely painful inflammatory arthritis rather than a painless ulcer. B. Acute arterial embolism causes acute painful ischaemia rather than a chronic painless plantar ulcer. D. Infection may complicate an ulcer but is not the underlying mechanism of a painless pressure ulcer. E. Venous hypertension typically causes ulceration in the gaiter region rather than under the metatarsal head.
pearl: Regular foot inspection and protective footwear are key preventive measures in diabetic patients, since loss of protective sensation means injury can go unnoticed until ulceration develops.
thinking: Diabetes + reduced foot sensation + painless plantar ulcer under metatarsal head ↓ unnoticed repetitive pressure injury ↓ Peripheral neuropathy causing loss of protective sensation
exam_trap: Candidates might assume infection is the primary driver, but cellulitis would be a secondary complication rather than the underlying mechanism explaining why the ulcer formed painlessly in the first place.
takeaway: Painless plantar ulceration in diabetes reflects loss of protective sensation from peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness shortly after a long flight. Her heart rate is 115/min. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness with tachycardia after a period of immobility, such as a long flight, is a classic presentation of pulmonary embolism.
why_wrong: A. GORD can cause chest discomfort but does not explain the thromboembolic risk pattern here. B. Stable angina typically causes exertional chest discomfort rather than sudden pleuritic pain after immobility. C. Otitis media does not cause chest pain or breathlessness. E. Acute bronchitis usually causes cough and respiratory infection symptoms rather than this sudden presentation.
pearl: Prolonged immobility, such as long-haul travel, is a recognised provoking factor for venous thromboembolism and should raise suspicion of pulmonary embolism in a breathless, tachycardic patient.
thinking: Long flight (immobility) + sudden pleuritic pain + breathlessness + tachycardia ↓ provoked venous thromboembolism ↓ Pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: Candidates may consider a cardiac cause given the chest pain, but the pleuritic quality, recent immobility and tachycardia point specifically towards thromboembolic disease rather than ischaemic heart disease.
takeaway: Pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after a long journey should prompt consideration of pulmonary embolism.

stem: A 29-year-old woman develops sudden unilateral weakness and difficulty speaking. She is found to have atrial fibrillation. Which mechanism most likely explains the neurological event?

options.A: Migraine without aura triggered by stress
options.B: Hypoglycaemia presenting as a stroke mimic
options.E: Lacunar infarct from small vessel disease

why_correct: Atrial fibrillation predisposes to stasis and thrombus formation within the atria, and dislodged thrombus can embolise to the cerebral circulation, causing sudden focal neurological deficit.
why_wrong: A. Migraine without aura can cause headache but the presentation here still requires urgent stroke assessment rather than being attributed to migraine. B. Hypoglycaemia can mimic neurological symptoms but does not explain the embolic risk from atrial fibrillation. D. Bell palsy causes isolated lower motor neurone facial weakness rather than the weakness and speech difficulty described. E. Lacunar infarcts occur in older patients with vascular risk factors and do not usually cause dysphasia; in a young patient with AF an embolic mechanism is far more likely.
pearl: Atrial fibrillation is a major, modifiable risk factor for ischaemic stroke, and anticoagulation is central to secondary (and often primary) prevention.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation + sudden unilateral weakness + speech difficulty ↓ atrial thrombus embolising to brain ↓ Cardioembolic cerebral infarction
exam_trap: Candidates might consider migraine given the neurological symptoms, but the known atrial fibrillation and sudden onset make an embolic stroke far more likely and require urgent stroke pathway assessment regardless.
takeaway: Atrial fibrillation with sudden focal neurological deficit should be treated as a cardioembolic stroke until proven otherwise.

stem: A 70-year-old man develops sudden painless loss of vision in one eye. The eye itself is not painful or red. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Reassure him and arrange routine optometry review
options.C: Wait several weeks to see whether vision returns
options.D: Treat it as an ophthalmic emergency

correct_answer: D. Treat it as an ophthalmic emergency
why_correct: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye can represent a sight-threatening vascular or retinal emergency and must be assessed and investigated urgently.
why_wrong: A. Routine optometry review is inappropriate for sudden visual loss. B. Lubricating drops do not address a potential vascular or retinal emergency. C. Delaying assessment risks permanent, irreversible visual loss. E. Empirical treatment for conjunctivitis is inappropriate, as conjunctivitis does not cause sudden profound visual loss.
pearl: Sudden painless monocular visual loss covers several sight- and sometimes life-threatening causes, including retinal artery occlusion and giant cell arteritis, so urgent same-day ophthalmic review is essential.
thinking: Sudden painless monocular visual loss + no red eye ↓ possible vascular/retinal catastrophe ↓ treat as an ophthalmic emergency
exam_trap: Candidates might be reassured by the absence of pain or redness and consider a benign cause, but painlessness does not reduce urgency here — several sight-threatening causes of sudden visual loss are painless.
takeaway: Sudden painless visual loss in one eye is an ophthalmic emergency regardless of the absence of pain or redness.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has gradually worsening difficulty hearing conversations, particularly in noisy environments. Both ears are similarly affected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradual, bilateral, symmetrical difficulty hearing, especially in background noise, in an older adult is the typical pattern of age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).
why_wrong: A. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss develops acutely rather than gradually. B. Acute otitis media causes acute ear pain and conductive hearing loss, not a gradual bilateral pattern. C. Otitis externa causes ear canal pain and inflammation rather than progressive bilateral hearing loss. D. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus rather than a steady bilateral decline.
pearl: Presbycusis particularly affects high-frequency hearing, which is why patients often struggle most with speech discrimination in noisy environments.
thinking: Older adult + gradual bilateral hearing difficulty + worse in noise ↓ age-related sensorineural change ↓ Presbycusis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider Ménière disease, but that causes episodic vertigo and fluctuating hearing loss, not this steady, symmetrical, gradual decline.
takeaway: Gradual, symmetrical hearing loss worse in noisy settings in an older adult is typical presbycusis.

stem: A 76-year-old woman falls and is unable to weight-bear because of severe hip pain. Her leg appears shortened and externally rotated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A fall with inability to weight-bear and a leg that is shortened and externally rotated is the classic presentation of a hip fracture.
why_wrong: A. Lumbar disc prolapse causes radicular leg symptoms rather than this acute deformity. C. An ankle fracture does not cause shortening and external rotation of the whole leg. D. Anterior cruciate ligament injury affects the knee. E. Achilles tendon rupture causes difficulty plantar-flexing the ankle, not hip deformity.
pearl: Hip fracture is common after falls in older adults, particularly those with osteoporosis, and requires prompt orthopaedic assessment and analgesia.
thinking: Fall in older adult + severe hip pain + cannot weight-bear + shortened externally rotated leg ↓ classic fracture deformity ↓ Hip fracture
exam_trap: Candidates could consider a lumbar disc problem given the leg pain, but the specific shortened, externally rotated deformity after a fall is characteristic of a fractured neck of femur rather than a radicular back problem.
takeaway: A shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall in an older person is the classic sign of hip fracture.

stem: A 63-year-old smoker presents with persistent hoarseness for six weeks. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent referral to exclude laryngeal cancer
options.B: Oral antibiotics and review in two weeks
options.D: Routine ENT referral with an 18-week wait
options.E: Trial of a PPI for laryngopharyngeal reflux

correct_answer: A. Urgent referral to exclude laryngeal cancer
why_correct: Persistent hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks in a smoker is a red-flag symptom and warrants urgent assessment to exclude laryngeal malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of bacterial infection and delay assessment of a red-flag symptom. C. Voice rest is inappropriate as sole management given persistent hoarseness in a smoker. D. A routine referral would delay diagnosis; persistent unexplained hoarseness in a smoker over 45 meets suspected cancer pathway criteria. E. An empirical PPI trial delays urgent assessment of a red-flag symptom.
pearl: Persistent, unexplained hoarseness beyond a few weeks, particularly in smokers, should always prompt urgent ENT referral to exclude laryngeal cancer.
thinking: Smoker + persistent hoarseness for six weeks ↓ red-flag symptom for upper airway malignancy ↓ urgent assessment for possible laryngeal malignancy
exam_trap: Candidates may be tempted by an infective or inflammatory explanation and consider antibiotics, but persistent hoarseness in a smoker is a recognised cancer red flag requiring urgent referral rather than empirical treatment.
takeaway: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker for several weeks is a red flag requiring urgent assessment for laryngeal cancer.

stem: A 22-year-old woman develops sudden central abdominal pain that later localises to the right lower quadrant. She has nausea, anorexia and a low-grade fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pain that begins centrally and migrates to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia, nausea and low-grade fever, is the classic presentation of acute appendicitis.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant or epigastric pain rather than migrating right iliac fossa pain. B. Cystitis causes lower urinary tract symptoms rather than migratory abdominal pain. C. Renal colic typically causes severe flank-to-groin pain. E. Acute pancreatitis usually causes severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back.
pearl: The migration of pain from central abdomen to the right iliac fossa reflects the transition from visceral to somatic (parietal peritoneal) pain as inflammation progresses.
thinking: Central pain migrating to right iliac fossa + anorexia + nausea + low-grade fever ↓ classic appendiceal inflammation pattern ↓ Acute appendicitis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider a urinary cause given the lower abdominal location, but the classic migratory pain pattern with anorexia strongly favours appendicitis over a urinary tract source.
takeaway: Pain migrating from the centre of the abdomen to the right iliac fossa with anorexia is the classic pattern of acute appendicitis.

stem: A 74-year-old man has a painless scrotal swelling. On examination, the testis cannot be palpated separately from the swelling, which is translucent when a light is shone through it. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: A painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates, with the testis not separately palpable, indicates a fluid collection around the testis, i.e. a hydrocele.
why_wrong: A. Epididymitis causes painful inflammatory swelling, not a painless transilluminating mass. B. Testicular cancer usually presents as a solid intratesticular mass, which would not transilluminate. D. Testicular torsion causes acute severe pain, not a painless chronic swelling. E. Varicocele typically feels like a 'bag of worms' rather than a transilluminating fluid collection.
pearl: Transillumination is the key bedside test that distinguishes a fluid-filled hydrocele from a solid testicular mass, which does not transilluminate.
thinking: Painless scrotal swelling + testis not separately palpable + transilluminates ↓ fluid collection around the testis ↓ Hydrocele
exam_trap: Candidates might worry about testicular cancer given a scrotal mass, but a solid tumour would not transilluminate, and this swelling's transillumination points clearly to a fluid-filled hydrocele.
takeaway: A painless, transilluminating scrotal swelling is characteristic of a hydrocele.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus. Imaging shows a diffusely thickened heterogeneous myometrium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Heavy, painful menstrual bleeding with a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus and a diffusely thickened heterogeneous myometrium on imaging is characteristic of adenomyosis.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian torsion causes acute unilateral pelvic pain rather than chronic heavy bleeding with a diffusely enlarged uterus. C. Ectopic pregnancy requires a pregnancy and typically causes acute pain and bleeding rather than this chronic pattern. D. Fibroadenoma is a benign breast lesion, unrelated to the uterus. E. PMOS (formerly PCOS) is associated with ovulatory dysfunction rather than a diffusely enlarged, tender uterus.
pearl: Adenomyosis results from endometrial tissue within the myometrium and characteristically produces a globally (rather than focally) enlarged, tender uterus, unlike the discrete masses of fibroids.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding + uniformly enlarged tender uterus + diffuse myometrial thickening ↓ endometrial tissue within the myometrium ↓ Adenomyosis
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse this with fibroids given the heavy bleeding and enlarged uterus, but fibroids typically produce discrete focal masses rather than the diffuse, uniform, heterogeneous myometrial thickening described here.
takeaway: A uniformly enlarged, tender uterus with diffuse myometrial thickening on imaging points to adenomyosis rather than fibroids.

stem: A 24-year-old woman notices a smooth, firm, mobile breast lump. It is not painful and she has no skin or nipple changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A smooth, firm, highly mobile, painless breast lump in a young woman without skin or nipple changes is the classic description of a fibroadenoma.
why_wrong: A. Breast cancer can occur at this age but is less characteristic of this classic smooth, mobile, benign presentation. C. Paget disease usually causes nipple or areolar skin changes, which are absent here. D. A breast abscess is usually painful and associated with inflammatory changes. E. Mastitis causes breast pain, erythema and inflammation, not a painless mobile lump.
