stem: A 22-year-old man develops wheeze and facial swelling after eating peanuts. His blood pressure is currently normal. Which treatment should be given first?
why_correct: Wheeze and facial swelling after a known allergen exposure indicate anaphylaxis with airway or breathing compromise; IM adrenaline is required even though blood pressure is currently normal.
why_wrong: A. Iron has no role in managing anaphylaxis. B. Saline nebulisers do not treat the underlying allergic reaction. D. Antihistamines alone do not address airway compromise. E. Corticosteroids are adjunctive, not first-line, treatment.
pearl: Anaphylaxis is defined by airway, breathing or circulatory compromise after allergen exposure — hypotension is not required for the diagnosis or for giving adrenaline.
thinking: Peanut exposure + wheeze and facial swelling + normal blood pressure ↓ airway/breathing compromise still meets anaphylaxis criteria ↓ Intramuscular adrenaline
exam_trap: Candidates may withhold adrenaline because the blood pressure is normal, but breathing compromise alone is sufficient to diagnose anaphylaxis and mandate adrenaline.
takeaway: Normal blood pressure does not rule out anaphylaxis if there is airway or breathing compromise.

stem: A 40-year-old man develops widespread urticaria after eating strawberries. He has no breathing difficulty, throat swelling, dizziness or vomiting. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_correct: Widespread urticaria after a food trigger, without any airway, breathing, circulatory or gastrointestinal red flags, is uncomplicated urticaria and can usually be managed with an oral non-sedating antihistamine.
why_wrong: A. This is an allergic reaction, not a bacterial infection requiring antibiotics. B. There is no airway compromise requiring intubation. C. IM adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis, not isolated uncomplicated urticaria without airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. E. Thrombolysis is unrelated to an allergic skin reaction.
pearl: The absence of breathing difficulty, throat swelling, dizziness or vomiting is what distinguishes simple urticaria from anaphylaxis and guides the choice of a non-sedating antihistamine over adrenaline.
thinking: Widespread urticaria after strawberries + no airway/breathing/circulatory symptoms ↓ isolated cutaneous allergic reaction ↓ Oral non-sedating antihistamine
exam_trap: Candidates may over-treat with adrenaline out of caution, but adrenaline is reserved for true anaphylaxis with systemic compromise, not isolated skin involvement.
takeaway: Isolated urticaria without systemic features is treated with an antihistamine, not adrenaline.

stem: A 62-year-old man notices that objects appear distorted and straight lines look wavy. His central vision is deteriorating. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Distortion of straight lines (metamorphopsia) with deteriorating central vision is characteristic of macular disease, most commonly age-related macular degeneration in this age group.
why_wrong: B. Cataract typically causes generalised blur rather than the specific distortion of straight lines described. C. Bacterial conjunctivitis causes discharge and conjunctival redness, not central visual distortion. D. Retinal vein occlusion can cause visual loss but does not typically present with this classic metamorphopsia pattern. E. Otitis externa affects the ear, not vision.
pearl: Metamorphopsia (wavy lines) on an Amsler grid is a hallmark symptom of macular pathology and should prompt urgent ophthalmology referral, particularly to exclude the wet form of AMD.
thinking: Central vision worsening + straight lines appear wavy ↓ distortion localises the problem to the macula ↓ Age-related macular degeneration
exam_trap: Candidates may default to cataract for any gradual visual change in an older patient, but distortion of straight lines specifically localises the pathology to the macula, not the lens.
takeaway: Distorted, wavy straight lines with central vision loss point to macular, not lens, pathology.

stem: A 24-year-old woman develops painful swelling and redness of the outer ear after having a cartilage piercing. The earlobe is relatively spared. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Painful swelling and redness of the pinna after cartilage piercing, with relative sparing of the earlobe (which lacks cartilage), is characteristic of perichondritis, an infection of the auricular cartilage.
why_wrong: A. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo with hearing symptoms, not pinna inflammation. C. Otitis externa primarily affects the ear canal rather than the external cartilage. D. Otitis media affects the middle ear, behind an intact eardrum. E. Mastoiditis causes tenderness and swelling behind the ear, over the mastoid bone.
pearl: Cartilage (helix) piercings carry a higher risk of perichondritis than lobe piercings because cartilage has a poorer blood supply, making infection harder to clear and potentially disfiguring.
thinking: Cartilage piercing + painful red pinna + lobe relatively spared ↓ infection tracking through avascular cartilage ↓ Perichondritis
exam_trap: Candidates may default to otitis externa given the ear symptoms, but sparing of the earlobe and the cartilage-piercing history point specifically to perichondritis.
takeaway: Sparing of the earlobe with painful pinna swelling after a cartilage piercing signals perichondritis.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with fatigue, night sweats and weight loss. Blood tests show a very high lymphocyte count. Which condition should be considered?

options.E: Iron-deficiency anaemia from occult GI loss

why_correct: Fatigue, night sweats, weight loss and a markedly raised lymphocyte count in an older adult are typical of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
why_wrong: A. CML causes a raised neutrophil and granulocyte count with splenomegaly, not a lymphocytosis. C. ITP primarily causes thrombocytopenia, not a raised lymphocyte count. D. Sickle cell disease usually presents much earlier in life with a different pattern. E. Iron deficiency from occult GI loss causes anaemia, not marked lymphocytosis.
pearl: CLL is often diagnosed incidentally on a routine blood count showing lymphocytosis in an otherwise asymptomatic older adult, but it can also present with constitutional symptoms as described here.
thinking: Older adult + fatigue, night sweats, weight loss + very high lymphocyte count ↓ clonal lymphocyte proliferation ↓ Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
exam_trap: Candidates may consider an acute leukaemia given the systemic symptoms, but the age and the specific lymphocytosis pattern point to the chronic, indolent CLL.
takeaway: Marked lymphocytosis with constitutional symptoms in an older adult suggests CLL.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of painful swelling of her hands and feet. She has no urticaria or itching. Her father has similar episodes. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent, non-itchy swelling of the hands and feet without urticaria, particularly with a positive family history, is characteristic of hereditary angioedema, caused by C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Chronic spontaneous urticaria causes itchy wheals, which are absent here. C. Cellulitis usually causes localised painful erythema and warmth, not recurrent symmetrical swelling. D. Contact dermatitis causes an inflammatory eruption at the site of an exposure, not recurrent limb swelling. E. Anaphylaxis is an acute systemic allergic reaction, usually with urticaria or airway/circulatory compromise; the family history points to a hereditary cause.
pearl: Hereditary angioedema does not respond to antihistamines or adrenaline in the way allergic angioedema does, because it is driven by bradykinin, not histamine.
thinking: Recurrent non-itchy hand/foot swelling + no urticaria + family history ↓ bradykinin-mediated, inherited swelling ↓ Hereditary angioedema
exam_trap: Candidates may treat this as an allergic reaction, but the absence of itch or urticaria and the strong family history point to a hereditary, bradykinin-driven cause rather than histamine-mediated allergy.
takeaway: Recurrent non-itchy swelling without urticaria, especially with a family history, suggests hereditary angioedema.

stem: A 60-year-old man develops severe pain and swelling in his calf after starting a new medication. Blood tests show a markedly elevated creatine kinase. Which complication is most important to recognise?
why_correct: Severe muscle pain and swelling with a markedly elevated creatine kinase after starting a new medication (classically a statin) indicates rhabdomyolysis, which carries a risk of acute kidney injury.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency does not cause markedly elevated CK. C. Hypothyroidism can contribute to muscle symptoms but does not explain this acute presentation with markedly raised CK. D. Hyperbilirubinaemia does not explain severe muscle injury with raised CK. E. Neutropenia affects white-cell counts, not muscle enzymes.
pearl: Statins are a recognised cause of drug-induced rhabdomyolysis; the drug should be stopped and the patient assessed and hydrated to protect renal function.
thinking: New medication started + severe calf pain and swelling + markedly raised creatine kinase ↓ muscle breakdown releasing CK and myoglobin ↓ Rhabdomyolysis
exam_trap: Candidates may consider a DVT given the calf swelling, but the markedly raised creatine kinase is the key discriminator pointing to muscle breakdown rather than a clot.
takeaway: Severe muscle pain with a markedly raised CK after a new drug points to rhabdomyolysis, not DVT.

stem: A 42-year-old man develops episodes of wheeze, nasal congestion and worsening asthma after taking ibuprofen. Which drug class should he avoid?
why_correct: Wheeze, nasal congestion and worsening asthma after taking an NSAID indicate NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease, and NSAIDs should be avoided in this patient.
why_wrong: A. Antacids do not typically precipitate bronchospasm. B. Proton-pump inhibitors are not typical triggers. C. Penicillins can cause allergic reactions but do not characteristically produce this NSAID-related pattern. D. Statins are not typical triggers for this reaction.
pearl: NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease often occurs alongside nasal polyps and asthma (Samter's triad) and reflects abnormal arachidonic acid metabolism rather than a classic IgE allergy.
thinking: Wheeze and nasal congestion after ibuprofen + worsening asthma ↓ cross-reactive reaction to cyclo-oxygenase inhibition ↓ Avoid NSAIDs
exam_trap: Candidates may treat this as a coincidental asthma flare, but the clear temporal link to ibuprofen is the key clue to an NSAID-triggered respiratory reaction.
takeaway: Asthma that worsens after NSAIDs signals NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease — avoid the drug class.

stem: A 45-year-old man has persistent nasal congestion, reduced sense of smell and recurrent episodes of sinusitis. Examination shows pale, smooth masses within both nasal cavities. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent nasal congestion, reduced smell and recurrent sinusitis with pale, smooth masses on examination are characteristic of nasal polyps.
why_wrong: B. A foreign body is usually unilateral and more common in children, not this bilateral chronic pattern. C. Epistaxis describes nasal bleeding, not a mass. D. A septal haematoma usually follows nasal trauma. E. A peritonsillar abscess affects the oropharynx, not the nasal cavity.
pearl: Bilateral nasal polyps in an adult can be associated with conditions such as asthma and NSAID sensitivity, so this history should be explored.
thinking: Chronic nasal blockage, reduced smell, recurrent sinusitis + pale smooth bilateral masses ↓ oedematous inflammatory nasal tissue ↓ Nasal polyps
exam_trap: Candidates may consider a foreign body given the nasal obstruction, but bilateral, pale, smooth masses in an adult with chronic symptoms are characteristic of polyps, not an object.
takeaway: Bilateral pale, smooth nasal masses with chronic congestion are nasal polyps.

stem: A 70-year-old man suddenly develops double vision. Examination shows that his right eye is unable to move laterally. Which cranial nerve is affected?
why_correct: Inability to abduct the eye reflects lateral rectus weakness, and the lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens (sixth cranial) nerve.
why_wrong: A. The trochlear nerve supplies superior oblique, which causes depression and intorsion, not abduction. B. The oculomotor nerve supplies most other extraocular muscles, not lateral rectus. C. The optic nerve carries visual information and does not control eye movement. D. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression, not eye movement.
pearl: Because the abducens nerve has the longest intracranial course of the ocular motor nerves, it is particularly vulnerable to compression from raised intracranial pressure, producing a false localising sign.
thinking: Sudden double vision + right eye cannot abduct ↓ lateral rectus weakness localises the lesion ↓ Abducens nerve
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse this with a trochlear or oculomotor palsy, but the specific inability to move the eye laterally (abduction) localises the lesion to the abducens nerve.
takeaway: Failure of lateral eye movement (abduction) localises to the abducens (VI) nerve.

stem: A 69-year-old man develops gradually worsening personality changes, disinhibition and inappropriate social behaviour. Memory is initially relatively preserved. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Early personality change, disinhibition and inappropriate social behaviour with relatively preserved memory are characteristic of behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia.
why_wrong: A. Delirium has an acute, not gradually progressive, onset. C. Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically causes gait, cognitive and urinary problems rather than early personality change. D. Dementia with Lewy bodies is associated with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism, not primarily personality change. E. Alzheimer disease commonly presents initially with memory impairment, the opposite pattern to this case.
pearl: Frontotemporal dementia tends to present at a younger age than Alzheimer disease and is often initially misattributed to a psychiatric or personality disorder because memory is relatively spared early on.
thinking: Progressive personality change + disinhibition + memory relatively preserved ↓ early frontal lobe, not memory-circuit, involvement ↓ Frontotemporal dementia
exam_trap: Candidates may assume any dementia in an older adult is Alzheimer disease, but preserved early memory with prominent personality and behavioural change points instead to frontotemporal dementia.
takeaway: Early personality and behaviour change with preserved memory suggests frontotemporal, not Alzheimer, dementia.

stem: A 31-year-old woman develops diarrhoea, abdominal pain and bloating after consuming wheat products. She is being investigated for coeliac disease. What should she do before coeliac serological testing?

options.D: Start a strict gluten-free diet immediately

why_correct: Coeliac serology relies on an ongoing immune response to gluten, so patients should continue eating gluten-containing foods before testing; stopping gluten early can suppress antibody levels and cause a false-negative result.
why_wrong: A. There is no requirement to stop all carbohydrates. B. Prolonged fasting is unnecessary before serological testing. D. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing can make the diagnosis harder to establish by lowering antibody levels. E. Antibiotics do not improve the diagnostic accuracy of coeliac serology.
pearl: Patients should continue eating gluten in more than one meal a day for at least six weeks before coeliac testing to avoid a false-negative result.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease + testing planned ↓ antibody levels depend on ongoing gluten exposure ↓ Continue eating gluten-containing foods before testing
exam_trap: Candidates may assume starting a gluten-free diet early is sensible "precaution", but doing so before testing can suppress antibodies and produce a false-negative, delaying diagnosis.
takeaway: Never start a gluten-free diet before coeliac testing — it can cause a false-negative result.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. She also has painful red nodules on her shins. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent bloody diarrhoea with abdominal pain, together with erythema nodosum, is compatible with inflammatory bowel disease, and the pattern of bloody diarrhoea is particularly characteristic of ulcerative colitis.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause rectal bleeding or extraintestinal inflammatory manifestations. B. Lactose intolerance causes symptoms after dairy intake but not bloody diarrhoea or skin manifestations. D. Functional dyspepsia affects upper gastrointestinal symptoms, not bloody lower GI symptoms. E. Constipation does not explain recurrent bloody diarrhoea and erythema nodosum.
pearl: Bloody diarrhoea is a more prominent and earlier feature of ulcerative colitis than of Crohn disease, which more often causes non-bloody diarrhoea with abdominal pain and weight loss.
thinking: Recurrent bloody diarrhoea + abdominal pain + erythema nodosum ↓ inflammatory bowel disease with a bloody-diarrhoea-predominant pattern ↓ Ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: Candidates may select Crohn disease reflexively whenever IBD is suspected, but the prominent bloody diarrhoea here specifically favours ulcerative colitis.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea with erythema nodosum points towards ulcerative colitis.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has sudden severe abdominal pain followed by abdominal rigidity and guarding. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Sudden severe abdominal pain followed by rigidity and guarding indicates peritonitis, most likely from perforation of a hollow abdominal viscus, and requires urgent surgical assessment.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms, not generalised peritonism. B. IBS does not cause peritonitis. C. Biliary colic causes episodic upper abdominal pain without generalised guarding and rigidity. E. Uncomplicated constipation does not cause an acute rigid abdomen.
pearl: Generalised guarding and rigidity are signs of peritonitis and warrant urgent imaging and surgical review, since a perforated viscus is a time-critical surgical emergency.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain + rigidity and guarding ↓ signs of peritonitis from a ruptured hollow organ ↓ Perforated viscus
exam_trap: Candidates may consider biliary colic given the abdominal pain, but the generalised rigidity and guarding indicate peritonitis, well beyond the pain pattern of simple biliary colic.
takeaway: Sudden pain followed by rigidity and guarding signals peritonitis from a perforated viscus.

stem: A 22-year-old woman develops a painful blistering rash in the distribution of the right fifth cranial nerve. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.C: Acute guttate psoriasis of the face

why_correct: A painful blistering rash confined to the distribution of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (fifth cranial) nerve is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis usually causes an itchy inflammatory eruption at the site of an exposure, not a dermatomal blistering rash. C. Psoriasis causes scaly papules or plaques, not acute painful dermatomal vesicles. D. Impetigo causes superficial bacterial lesions, commonly with honey-coloured crusts, not a dermatomal blistering pattern. E. Tinea faciei causes annular fungal lesions, not dermatomal vesicles.
pearl: A vesicular rash on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicates nasociliary nerve involvement and predicts a higher risk of ocular complications, warranting urgent ophthalmology review.
thinking: Painful vesicular rash + confined to the ophthalmic (fifth cranial nerve) distribution ↓ reactivated varicella-zoster virus in that dermatome ↓ Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
exam_trap: Candidates may think of simple contact dermatitis given the rash, but the strict dermatomal distribution and pain are the specific clues pointing to zoster reactivation.
takeaway: A painful vesicular rash strictly confined to one dermatome, especially around the eye, is herpes zoster ophthalmicus.

stem: A 19-year-old man develops a rapidly spreading painful skin infection with fever and systemic illness. The affected area is extremely tender and there is pain extending beyond the visible erythema. Which diagnosis is most concerning?
why_correct: Rapidly spreading skin infection with systemic illness and pain out of proportion to visible skin changes are red-flag features of necrotising fasciitis, a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement.
why_wrong: A. Infected eczema occurs on a background of chronic eczema and does not cause pain beyond the visible erythema with rapid systemic deterioration. B. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis, not an acute infective emergency. D. Urticaria with angioedema causes transient itchy wheals and swelling, not severe systemic illness. E. Even extensive tinea corporis is a superficial fungal infection, not a deep, rapidly progressive one.
pearl: Pain disproportionate to the visible skin findings is one of the most important early clues to necrotising fasciitis, since skin changes can initially appear deceptively mild.
thinking: Rapidly spreading infection + fever, systemic illness + pain beyond visible erythema ↓ deep soft-tissue necrosis outrunning surface signs ↓ Necrotising fasciitis
exam_trap: Candidates may underestimate severity because the visible skin changes can look mild early on; the key red flag is pain extending well beyond what is visibly inflamed.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion to visible skin findings is the critical early warning sign of necrotising fasciitis.

stem: A 58-year-old man develops a new, rapidly enlarging pigmented skin lesion with irregular borders and multiple colours. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: A new, rapidly enlarging pigmented lesion with irregular borders and multiple colours shows features of the ABCDE criteria (asymmetry, border irregularity, colour variation, diameter, evolution) that are concerning for melanoma.
why_wrong: B. Seborrhoeic keratoses are usually benign, stable, 'stuck-on' lesions. C. Dermatofibromas are usually firm, stable, benign nodules. D. Viral warts are rough, keratotic lesions rather than pigmented and changing. E. Molluscum contagiosum causes small umbilicated papules, not a changing pigmented lesion.
pearl: Any lesion that is changing in size, shape or colour, or that has irregular borders and multiple colours, should be urgently referred for dermoscopic assessment and, if indicated, excision biopsy to exclude melanoma.
thinking: New pigmented lesion ↓ rapidly enlarging with irregular borders ↓ multiple colours present ↓ Melanoma
exam_trap: A candidate might consider a benign pigmented lesion such as a seborrhoeic keratosis, but the rapid change, irregular borders and colour variation are the red-flag features specifically concerning for melanoma.
takeaway: A changing pigmented lesion with irregular borders and multiple colours is concerning for melanoma.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has epigastric pain related to meals. She regularly takes ibuprofen for chronic joint pain. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Epigastric pain related to meals in a regular NSAID user reflects the well-established risk of NSAIDs causing gastric or duodenal ulceration through inhibition of protective prostaglandins.
why_wrong: A. IBS causes abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habit, not meal-related epigastric pain linked to NSAID use. B. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. D. Appendicitis is an acute inflammatory condition, not chronic meal-related pain. E. Gastroenteritis is usually an acute infectious illness with diarrhoea and/or vomiting.
pearl: Regular NSAID use is one of the most common and modifiable risk factors for peptic ulcer disease, and gastroprotection should be considered when NSAIDs are needed long-term.
thinking: Regular NSAID use + epigastric pain related to meals ↓ prostaglandin-mediated loss of mucosal protection ↓ Peptic ulcer disease
exam_trap: Candidates may consider gastroenteritis given the abdominal pain, but the chronic, meal-related nature and the clear NSAID exposure point to peptic ulcer disease instead.
takeaway: Regular NSAID use with meal-related epigastric pain points to peptic ulcer disease.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea and weight loss. She also has a history of autoimmune thyroid disease. Which gastrointestinal condition is particularly associated with autoimmune disease?
why_correct: Coeliac disease is strongly associated with other autoimmune conditions, including autoimmune thyroid disease, and should be considered in a patient with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss who has such a history.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids are vascular structures in the anorectal region, unrelated to autoimmune associations. B. GORD relates primarily to reflux of gastric contents, not an autoimmune-associated GI condition. D. Appendicitis is an acute inflammatory condition. E. Biliary colic is caused by gallstones, not autoimmune disease.
pearl: Screening for coeliac disease should be considered in patients with other autoimmune conditions, such as type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease, even with atypical or minimal gastrointestinal symptoms.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea and weight loss + known autoimmune thyroid disease ↓ recognised clustering of autoimmune conditions ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: Candidates may treat the thyroid disease and GI symptoms as unrelated, but coeliac disease's strong autoimmune clustering is exactly the link the question is testing.
takeaway: Coeliac disease clusters with other autoimmune conditions, including autoimmune thyroid disease.

stem: A 58-year-old man has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and a low haemoglobin concentration. Which finding would most strongly support malabsorption?
why_correct: A low ferritin indicates true iron deficiency, which can result from impaired intestinal absorption in malabsorptive conditions such as coeliac disease, making it the finding that best supports malabsorption here.
why_wrong: A. Troponin indicates myocardial injury, unrelated to malabsorption. B. A raised platelet count alone is nonspecific and does not indicate malabsorption. D. Hyponatraemia is not a specific marker of malabsorption. E. Isolated bilirubin elevation does not demonstrate malabsorption.
pearl: Iron-deficiency anaemia with a low ferritin in a patient with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss should prompt investigation for malabsorptive conditions such as coeliac disease.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, low haemoglobin ↓ which finding best confirms malabsorption? ↓ Low ferritin (true iron deficiency)
exam_trap: Candidates may be drawn to more dramatic-sounding options like a raised troponin, but only a low ferritin directly demonstrates the iron deficiency expected with malabsorption.
takeaway: A low ferritin, confirming true iron deficiency, is the finding that best supports malabsorption.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has dry eyes and a persistent dry mouth. She finds it difficult to swallow dry food and needs to drink water frequently. Which autoimmune condition is most likely?
why_correct: Dry eyes and dry mouth with difficulty swallowing dry food reflect autoimmune destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands, characteristic of Sjögren syndrome.
why_wrong: B. Osteoarthritis causes degenerative joint symptoms, not glandular dryness. C. Ankylosing spondylitis causes inflammatory spinal and sacroiliac disease. D. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis from urate crystal deposition. E. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal muscle-region pain and stiffness in older adults, not glandular dryness.
pearl: Sjögren syndrome can occur alone (primary) or alongside other autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus (secondary), and dryness of multiple mucosal surfaces is the clue to look for.
thinking: Dry eyes + dry mouth + difficulty swallowing dry food ↓ autoimmune exocrine gland destruction ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: Candidates may attribute dryness symptoms to simple ageing or medication effect, missing that the combination of ocular and oral dryness together points to an autoimmune exocrinopathy.
takeaway: Dry eyes plus dry mouth with swallowing difficulty = Sjögren syndrome.

stem: A 37-year-old woman has progressive tightening of the skin of her fingers and difficulty opening her mouth. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive skin tightening, particularly of the fingers and face (leading to reduced mouth opening, or microstomia), is characteristic of systemic sclerosis.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory joint disease, not skin tightening. B. Psoriasis causes characteristic scaly plaques, not diffuse skin thickening. C. Osteoarthritis causes degenerative joint symptoms, unrelated to skin changes. D. Dermatomyositis causes proximal muscle weakness and characteristic skin changes (such as heliotrope rash), a different pattern from diffuse skin tightening.
pearl: Skin thickening in systemic sclerosis typically begins in the fingers (sclerodactyly) and can progress centrally, so assessing hand and facial skin is central to diagnosis and monitoring.
thinking: Progressive finger skin tightening + reduced mouth opening ↓ diffuse cutaneous sclerosis pattern ↓ Systemic sclerosis
exam_trap: Candidates might consider rheumatoid arthritis given joint-area symptoms, but the defining feature here - progressive skin tightening, not joint inflammation - points to systemic sclerosis.
takeaway: Progressive skin tightening of the fingers and face is the hallmark of systemic sclerosis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman taking long-term corticosteroids asks why she has been advised to take measures to protect her bones. Which complication is particularly associated with prolonged corticosteroid use?
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroid treatment accelerates bone loss and increases the risk of fragility fractures, which is why bone-protection measures are advised.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids do not characteristically cause appendicitis. B. Corticosteroids do not cause Parkinson disease. D. Corticosteroids do not cause primary hyperthyroidism. E. Corticosteroids can contribute to cataracts, but this does not explain the specific bone-protection advice being asked about here.
pearl: Bone protection (such as calcium, vitamin D and consideration of bisphosphonates) should be considered early in patients expected to need long-term corticosteroids, rather than waiting for a fracture to occur.
thinking: Long-term corticosteroids + advised to protect bones ↓ steroid-accelerated bone loss ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: Candidates may think of cataracts as the classic long-term steroid complication being tested, but the specific advice about protecting bones points to osteoporosis, not the eyes.
takeaway: Long-term corticosteroids accelerate bone loss, which is why bone-protection advice is given.

stem: A 63-year-old man has persistent unilateral breast enlargement and a firm mass beneath the nipple. Which diagnosis requires exclusion?
why_correct: A persistent, firm, unilateral subareolar breast mass in a man requires urgent assessment to exclude male breast cancer.
why_wrong: A. IBS causes abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habit, unrelated to a breast mass. B. Gout causes crystal arthritis, unrelated to a breast mass. C. Biliary colic causes episodic upper abdominal pain, unrelated to a breast mass. D. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain, unrelated to a breast mass.
pearl: Unlike gynaecomastia, which is typically bilateral, soft and centred on the nipple, a firm, unilateral, eccentric breast mass in a man is a red flag requiring a suspected cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Man + persistent unilateral breast enlargement + firm subareolar mass ↓ atypical for benign gynaecomastia ↓ Male breast cancer must be excluded
exam_trap: Candidates may assume any male breast enlargement is benign gynaecomastia, but a firm, unilateral, persistent mass is atypical for gynaecomastia and needs malignancy excluded.
takeaway: A firm, unilateral breast mass in a man is treated as suspicious for malignancy until proven otherwise.

stem: A 32-year-old man develops an expanding, painless, red skin lesion several days after returning from a camping trip. He recalls removing a tick. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: An expanding, painless, red skin lesion appearing several days after a tick bite is erythema migrans, the characteristic early skin manifestation of Lyme disease.
why_wrong: A. Tinea corporis typically has a scaly, active advancing edge, unlike the smooth expanding rash described here. B. Cellulitis is usually painful, warm and tender, unlike this painless lesion. D. Herpes zoster causes a painful vesicular rash confined to a dermatome, not a slowly expanding painless patch. E. Psoriasis causes chronic scaly plaques, not an acutely expanding rash after a tick bite.
pearl: Erythema migrans often shows a "target" or "bullseye" appearance with central clearing and typically appears one to four weeks after a tick bite, though it can occur earlier.
thinking: Tick bite while camping + expanding painless red lesion days later ↓ classic erythema migrans ↓ Lyme disease
exam_trap: Candidates may consider cellulitis given the expanding redness, but cellulitis is typically painful and tender, unlike the painless erythema migrans of Lyme disease.
takeaway: A painless, expanding red rash after a tick bite is erythema migrans, the hallmark of early Lyme disease.

stem: A 45-year-old farmer develops fever, severe headache and muscle pains after working in water contaminated with animal urine. Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, severe headache and marked muscle pains after exposure to water contaminated with animal urine are characteristic of leptospirosis, transmitted through contact with infected urine.
why_wrong: A. Lyme disease follows exposure to infected ticks, not contaminated water. B. Malaria is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, not contaminated water. C. Toxoplasmosis is not characteristically associated with contaminated water exposure in this way. E. Hepatitis B is transmitted through infected blood and body fluids, not contaminated water.
pearl: Occupational exposure (farmers, sewage workers, those in contact with rodents or livestock) to water contaminated with animal urine is the key epidemiological clue for leptospirosis.
thinking: Farmer + water contaminated with animal urine + fever, headache, myalgia ↓ zoonotic spirochaete transmitted via contaminated water ↓ Leptospirosis
exam_trap: Candidates may consider a mosquito-borne illness given the fever, but the specific exposure to contaminated water rather than travel is the clue pointing to leptospirosis.
takeaway: Fever and severe myalgia after exposure to water contaminated with animal urine points to leptospirosis.

stem: A 36-year-old man has fever, night sweats and weight loss. He has recently returned from an area where tuberculosis is common. Which investigation is appropriate when pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected?
why_correct: Chest X-ray is a key initial investigation when pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected, alongside sputum microscopy and culture for confirmation.
why_wrong: A. ECG does not investigate suspected pulmonary TB. B. Abdominal ultrasound does not assess the lungs. D. DXA assesses bone mineral density, unrelated to TB. E. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury, unrelated to TB.
pearl: Chest X-ray findings in pulmonary TB classically include upper-lobe shadowing, cavitation or consolidation, but sputum testing is needed to confirm the diagnosis microbiologically.
thinking: Fever, night sweats, weight loss + TB-endemic exposure ↓ initial investigation for suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Chest X-ray
exam_trap: Candidates may jump straight to sputum culture as the only relevant test, but chest imaging is an equally important and immediate first step in the initial assessment.
takeaway: Chest X-ray is a standard initial investigation for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis.

stem: A 20-year-old woman develops a widespread non-blanching rash with fever and rapidly becomes unwell. Which diagnosis must be treated as an emergency?
why_correct: A widespread non-blanching rash with fever and rapid clinical deterioration is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment for possible invasive meningococcal disease.
why_wrong: A. Pityriasis rosea causes a herald patch and scaly oval plaques in a well patient, not an emergency. B. Guttate psoriasis causes small scaly plaques, often after a sore throat, not an acute emergency with a non-blanching rash. C. Erythema multiforme minor causes target lesions without rapid systemic deterioration or a non-blanching rash. D. Urticaria produces blanching, itchy wheals rather than a typical non-blanching purpuric rash.
pearl: A non-blanching rash (confirmed with the glass test) combined with fever and systemic illness should prompt immediate empirical antibiotic treatment without waiting for confirmatory tests.
thinking: Non-blanching rash + fever + rapid deterioration ↓ signature of invasive meningococcal sepsis ↓ Meningococcal disease (treat as an emergency)
exam_trap: Candidates may consider urticaria given the widespread rash, but urticaria blanches on pressure, unlike the non-blanching purpuric rash of meningococcal disease, which is the critical distinguishing test.
takeaway: A non-blanching rash with fever is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise, and is treated as an emergency.

stem: A 22-year-old man has a painless genital ulcer. Which infection is classically associated with a painless chancre?
why_correct: Primary syphilis classically causes a painless genital ulcer (chancre), making it the infection most associated with this presentation.
why_wrong: B. Genital herpes typically causes painful grouped vesicles or ulcers, not a painless chancre. C. Trichomoniasis more commonly causes genital discharge and irritation, not an ulcer. D. Candidiasis usually causes itching and inflammation rather than a chancre. E. Gonorrhoea commonly causes urethral discharge and dysuria, not a painless ulcer.
pearl: Because the chancre of primary syphilis is painless and may go unnoticed, patients can progress to secondary syphilis without ever seeking treatment for the initial lesion.
thinking: Genital ulcer + no pain ↓ classic painless chancre ↓ Syphilis
exam_trap: Candidates may default to genital herpes as the classic cause of genital ulcers, but herpes ulcers are painful, whereas the defining feature here — painlessness — points specifically to syphilis.
takeaway: A painless genital ulcer is the classic chancre of primary syphilis.

stem: A 40-year-old man is found to have HIV infection. Which condition is an important cause of opportunistic infection in advanced untreated HIV?

options.C: Migraine with aura and visual disturbance

why_correct: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a classic opportunistic infection occurring in advanced, untreated HIV infection once significant immunosuppression has developed.
why_wrong: B. Mycoplasma pneumonia occurs in immunocompetent people and is not an opportunistic infection of advanced HIV. C. Migraine is unrelated to immune suppression. D. H. pylori gastritis is common in the general population and is not an HIV opportunistic infection. E. Appendicitis is not characteristically associated with advanced HIV.
pearl: PCP typically occurs once CD4 counts fall to low levels, so its occurrence is a marker of significant immunosuppression and an indication for starting antiretroviral therapy and prophylaxis.
thinking: New HIV diagnosis + concern about opportunistic infection risk ↓ classic AIDS-defining infection in advanced disease ↓ Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
exam_trap: Candidates may think of more common respiratory infections, but in the context of advanced untreated HIV, PCP is the classic opportunistic pathogen being tested here.
takeaway: PCP is a classic opportunistic infection marking advanced, untreated HIV disease.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has recurrent painful mouth ulcers, genital ulcers and episodes of painful red eyes. She also has tender red nodules on her lower legs. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with painful red eyes and tender skin nodules together form the classic multisystem picture of Behçet disease, a vasculitis affecting mucous membranes, eyes and skin.
why_wrong: B. Systemic sclerosis causes skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon and internal-organ involvement, not this combination of ulcers and eye disease. C. Osteoarthritis causes mechanical joint pain and stiffness, unrelated to mucocutaneous and ocular findings. D. Coeliac disease primarily causes gastrointestinal and nutritional manifestations, not this triad. E. Rheumatoid arthritis primarily causes inflammatory polyarthritis, not recurrent ulcers and eye disease.
pearl: Recurrent oral ulceration is almost universal in Behçet disease and is often the presenting feature, with genital ulcers, uveitis and erythema-nodosum-like skin lesions supporting the diagnosis.
thinking: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers + painful red eyes + tender leg nodules ↓ multisystem mucocutaneous and ocular vasculitis ↓ Behçet disease
exam_trap: Candidates may consider Crohn disease because of the oral ulcers, but the combination with genital ulcers and painful red eyes points specifically to Behçet disease rather than an isolated bowel condition.
takeaway: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers with eye inflammation together point to Behçet disease.

stem: A woman with a known autosomal dominant genetic condition asks about the chance that each of her children will inherit the condition. Assuming she is heterozygous and her partner is unaffected, what is the risk for each pregnancy?
why_correct: A heterozygous parent passes one of two alleles to each child at random, so each pregnancy carries a 50% chance of inheriting the pathogenic dominant allele, independent of previous pregnancies.
why_wrong: A. The affected parent can and does pass on the condition. B. This is too low for straightforward Mendelian dominant transmission. C. 25% is the recurrence risk for an autosomal recessive condition when both parents are carriers. E. Not every pregnancy inherits the allele; transmission is probabilistic, not certain.
pearl: Each pregnancy is an independent event — the risk applies afresh each time and does not decrease because a previous child was unaffected.
thinking: Heterozygous parent with autosomal dominant condition ↓ one of two alleles passed at random each pregnancy ↓ 50% risk per pregnancy
exam_trap: Candidates confuse this with autosomal recessive carrier-by-carrier risk (25%) because both are common genetics questions with similar wording.
takeaway: Autosomal dominant, heterozygous parent = 50% risk to each child, every time.

stem: A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive condition and her partner is unaffected. Which child has the highest risk of being affected?

options.B: Both sons and daughters have equal risk of being affected

why_correct: A carrier mother has one normal and one pathogenic X allele. Sons, who have only one X (inherited from the mother), have a 50% chance of inheriting the pathogenic allele and being affected, since they have no second X to compensate.
why_wrong: A. Sons are at meaningful risk in X-linked recessive inheritance. B. The risks are not equal — sons are affected far more often than daughters. D. Daughters inherit a normal paternal X, so they are typically unaffected carriers rather than affected. E. Males, not females, are predominantly affected in X-linked recessive conditions.
pearl: In X-linked recessive inheritance, sons of a carrier mother carry the highest risk of being clinically affected, while daughters are typically unaffected carriers.
thinking: Mother is carrier, father unaffected ↓ sons have only one X, inherited from mother ↓ no compensating paternal X ↓ sons at highest risk of being affected
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes assume 'carrier' automatically means equal risk to all children, missing the sex-linked mechanism that concentrates risk in sons.
takeaway: X-linked recessive: carrier mother, unaffected father — sons carry the affected risk, daughters are usually carriers.

stem: A doctor realises that a prescribing error has resulted in a patient receiving the wrong dose of medication, but no harm has occurred. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Report it as an incident but not inform the patient
options.B: Alter the medical record to remove evidence of the error
options.C: Be open with the patient and report it as an incident
options.D: Apologise to the patient but not record the incident
options.E: Ask the pharmacist to inform the patient on their behalf

correct_answer: C. Be open with the patient and report it as an incident
why_correct: Professional duty of candour requires openness with patients about errors, even when no harm resulted, alongside appropriate incident reporting so that systems can learn and prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Reporting alone without informing the patient is a failure of candour. B. Altering records to conceal an error is dishonest and a serious professional breach. D. Openness must be accompanied by incident reporting so that the system can learn. E. The duty of candour rests with the responsible doctor and should not be delegated to another professional.
pearl: The professional duty of candour applies when something goes wrong that causes, or has the potential to cause, harm or distress — a wrong dose given qualifies even if no harm results; all such incidents, including near misses, should also be reported for learning.
thinking: Prescribing error identified, no harm occurred ↓ duty of candour and safety-learning obligations still apply ↓ Be open with the patient and follow incident reporting
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes assume no harm means no obligation to disclose or report, which misunderstands the professional duty of candour.
takeaway: No harm done does not remove the duty to be open and to report the error.

stem: A 9-year-old child tells a doctor that an adult at home regularly hits them. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Document the disclosure and review at the next appointment
options.B: Discuss the disclosure with the adult before any referral
options.C: Promise to keep it secret as the child requests
options.D: Ask the child's teacher to monitor for further injuries
options.E: Follow safeguarding procedures and escalate the concern

correct_answer: E. Follow safeguarding procedures and escalate the concern
why_correct: A disclosure of physical abuse by a child requires the clinician to follow local safeguarding procedures, document the disclosure accurately and escalate promptly to protect the child from further harm.
why_wrong: A. Delaying action until a later appointment risks further harm to the child. B. Discussing the disclosure with the alleged abuser before referral may put the child at further risk. C. Secrecy cannot be promised when a child is at risk of significant harm. D. Delegating monitoring to a teacher does not fulfil the duty to refer and escalate the concern.
pearl: Confidentiality is not absolute in safeguarding — a child's safety takes priority, and disclosures must be documented and escalated through local procedures.
thinking: Child discloses regular hitting at home ↓ safeguarding concern overrides routine confidentiality ↓ Follow local safeguarding procedures and escalate appropriately
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes over-value confidentiality in paediatric safeguarding scenarios, forgetting that protecting the child from harm takes precedence.
takeaway: A child's disclosure of abuse triggers safeguarding escalation, not a promise of silence.

stem: A 31-year-old woman develops severe vomiting and diarrhoea. Blood tests show potassium of 2.7 mmol/L. Which ECG abnormality may occur with significant hypokalaemia?

options.A: Complete heart block in every case

why_correct: Hypokalaemia slows ventricular repolarisation, producing flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves on the ECG.
why_wrong: A. Hypokalaemia does not invariably cause complete heart block. C. Delta waves reflect ventricular pre-excitation, as in Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, not hypokalaemia. D. Hypokalaemia tends to prolong rather than shorten repolarisation, so the QT interval is typically lengthened. E. ST elevation in contiguous leads suggests acute myocardial injury rather than an electrolyte disturbance.
pearl: U waves following the T wave are a classic but easily missed ECG sign of significant hypokalaemia.
thinking: Severe vomiting and diarrhoea + potassium 2.7 mmol/L ↓ hypokalaemia slows repolarisation ↓ U waves on ECG
exam_trap: Delta waves are a tempting distractor because they sound like an unusual ECG finding, but they belong to pre-excitation syndromes, not electrolyte disturbance.
takeaway: Hypokalaemia on ECG: flat T waves, ST depression, and prominent U waves.

stem: A 64-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has a potassium concentration of 7.2 mmol/L. ECG shows broad QRS complexes. What is the immediate concern?

options.A: Iron-deficiency anaemia of chronic kidney disease

why_correct: A potassium of 7.2 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes indicates severe hyperkalaemia with impending cardiac conduction failure, which can progress rapidly to a fatal arrhythmia without emergency treatment.
why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia does not cause this electrolyte or ECG picture. C. Hyperthyroidism does not explain severe hyperkalaemia. D. Mild dehydration would not produce a potassium this high with broad QRS changes. E. Hypocalcaemia may coexist in CKD but prolongs the QT interval and does not explain broad QRS complexes with a potassium of 7.2 mmol/L.
pearl: Broad QRS complexes in a patient with renal impairment and a very high potassium is a cardiac emergency requiring immediate stabilisation and potassium-lowering treatment.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease + potassium 7.2 mmol/L + broad QRS ↓ conduction system toxicity from severe hyperkalaemia ↓ Life-threatening hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: Candidates may underestimate urgency by focusing on the underlying CKD rather than recognising the ECG changes as signalling an imminent arrhythmic emergency.
takeaway: Very high potassium plus broad QRS complexes is a cardiac emergency — treat immediately.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has fatigue, diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness. Her vitamin D level is severely reduced and alkaline phosphatase is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe vitamin D deficiency impairs bone mineralisation, causing diffuse bone pain, proximal myopathy and a compensatory rise in alkaline phosphatase, the classic biochemical picture of osteomalacia.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes acute monoarticular inflammatory arthritis rather than diffuse bone pain and myopathy. B. Osteoarthritis causes localised degenerative joint pain, not vitamin D deficiency with raised alkaline phosphatase. C. Septic arthritis presents as an acutely infected, hot joint. D. Rheumatoid arthritis causes symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis rather than this metabolic bone picture.
pearl: Proximal muscle weakness combined with diffuse bone pain and a low vitamin D level should raise suspicion of osteomalacia rather than a primary joint disease.
thinking: Fatigue + diffuse bone pain + proximal weakness ↓ severely low vitamin D with raised alkaline phosphatase ↓ Osteomalacia
exam_trap: Candidates may anchor on 'bone pain' and think of a primary arthritic or malignant process, missing that the biochemical picture points to defective mineralisation.
takeaway: Bone pain, proximal weakness, low vitamin D, raised ALP = osteomalacia.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is found to have a low bone mineral density on a DXA scan. Which lifestyle measure is particularly important in reducing future fracture risk?

options.B: Increasing caffeine to five cups daily
options.C: Avoiding sunlight to prevent skin cancer
options.D: Bed rest after any minor fall or strain
options.E: Restricting dairy foods and calcium intake

correct_answer: A. Weight-bearing exercise and falls prevention
why_correct: Weight-bearing exercise helps maintain bone density, and falls-prevention strategies directly reduce the likelihood of a fragility fracture, making this combination particularly effective in someone with low bone mineral density.
why_wrong: B. High caffeine intake does not protect bone and may increase calcium loss. C. Avoiding sunlight can worsen vitamin D status and bone health. D. Bed rest accelerates bone loss and deconditioning. E. Restricting calcium intake worsens bone health.
pearl: Osteoporosis management is about more than medication — weight-bearing activity and falls-prevention measures meaningfully reduce fracture risk.
thinking: Low bone mineral density on DXA ↓ fracture risk is driven by both bone fragility and fall likelihood ↓ Weight-bearing exercise and falls prevention
exam_trap: Candidates focused purely on pharmacological bone treatment may underweight the practical importance of exercise and falls prevention in reducing fracture risk.
takeaway: Reducing fracture risk means building bone strength and preventing falls, not just treating density alone.

stem: A 48-year-old man has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and steatorrhoea. He is found to have iron-deficiency anaemia. Which mechanism best explains the anaemia?
why_correct: Chronic malabsorptive conditions such as coeliac disease damage the proximal small bowel mucosa where iron is predominantly absorbed, leading to iron-deficiency anaemia alongside steatorrhoea and weight loss.
why_wrong: A. Increased iron absorption would protect against, not cause, deficiency. B. Erythropoietin drives red-cell production but does not itself cause iron deficiency. D. Menstrual blood loss is not relevant in this male patient. E. Increased red-cell production would consume rather than explain a deficiency state without another driving cause.
pearl: Unexplained iron deficiency with chronic diarrhoea and steatorrhoea should prompt coeliac screening, since small bowel malabsorption is a common and treatable cause.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea + weight loss + steatorrhoea + iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ small bowel disease impairs iron absorption ↓ Intestinal malabsorption
exam_trap: Candidates may default to chronic blood loss as the explanation for iron deficiency, overlooking the clearly malabsorptive clinical context described.
takeaway: Chronic diarrhoea with steatorrhoea and iron deficiency points to small bowel malabsorption, not just blood loss.

stem: A 45-year-old man has chronic diarrhoea and weight loss. He reports greasy, difficult-to-flush stools. What does this stool description suggest?
why_correct: Bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that are difficult to flush describe steatorrhoea, reflecting excess undigested fat from malabsorption or pancreatic insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Haematochezia describes passage of fresh or partly digested blood per rectum. C. Constipation describes infrequent or difficult stool passage, not greasy stool character. D. Melaena describes black, tarry stool from upper gastrointestinal bleeding. E. Tenesmus describes a sensation of incomplete rectal emptying, unrelated to stool fat content.
pearl: Greasy, difficult-to-flush stools are a specific clue to fat malabsorption and should prompt evaluation for pancreatic or small bowel disease.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea + weight loss + greasy, hard-to-flush stool ↓ description specifically reflects excess faecal fat ↓ Steatorrhoea
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with stool terminology may confuse this with melaena or haematochezia, which describe blood rather than fat content.
takeaway: Greasy, floating, hard-to-flush stool = steatorrhoea, a marker of fat malabsorption.

stem: A 62-year-old man with chronic alcohol dependence presents with confusion, unsteady gait and abnormal eye movements. Which vitamin deficiency should be suspected?
why_correct: The triad of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with chronic alcohol dependence is classic for Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin A deficiency mainly causes visual (night blindness) and epithelial problems, not this triad. C. Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired clotting. D. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone and muscle problems rather than this acute neurological picture. E. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, with bleeding gums and poor wound healing.
pearl: Wernicke encephalopathy is often under-recognised because the full triad is not always present — any alcohol-dependent patient with acute confusion should be treated as at risk.
thinking: Chronic alcohol dependence + confusion + ataxia + abnormal eye movements ↓ classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy ↓ Thiamine deficiency
exam_trap: Candidates may attribute confusion in an alcohol-dependent patient purely to intoxication or withdrawal, missing the specific triad that signals thiamine deficiency.
takeaway: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in an alcohol-dependent patient = suspect thiamine deficiency.

stem: A patient with suspected Wernicke encephalopathy requires treatment. What should be given promptly?
why_correct: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy is a medical emergency, and prompt parenteral (rather than oral) thiamine is required because oral absorption is unreliable and delay risks irreversible brain injury.
why_wrong: A. Calcium does not address the underlying thiamine deficiency. C. Vitamin K corrects clotting factor deficiency, not encephalopathy. D. Oral iron does not treat thiamine deficiency. E. Antibiotics have no role unless a separate infection is identified.
pearl: Thiamine should be given before or alongside glucose in at-risk patients, since glucose administration alone can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
thinking: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy ↓ oral thiamine absorption is unreliable and delay risks permanent damage ↓ Parenteral thiamine
exam_trap: Candidates may select oral thiamine or assume any vitamin replacement will do, missing that parenteral administration is specifically required in this emergency.
takeaway: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy needs urgent parenteral thiamine, not oral replacement.

stem: A 34-year-old man reports excessive daytime sleepiness and repeatedly falls asleep unintentionally. He also describes brief episodes of sudden loss of muscle tone when laughing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Excessive daytime sleepiness with irresistible sleep episodes, combined with cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion such as laughter), is diagnostic of narcolepsy.
why_wrong: A. Restless legs syndrome causes uncomfortable leg sensations with an urge to move, not cataplexy. B. Shift-work sleep disorder relates to circadian misalignment rather than cataplexy. C. Insomnia causes difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, not sudden sleep attacks with cataplexy. D. OSA causes sleepiness from repeated airway obstruction during sleep, without the specific feature of emotion-triggered muscle tone loss.
pearl: Cataplexy — sudden, emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness — is the single most specific clinical clue to narcolepsy.
thinking: Excessive daytime sleepiness + sudden loss of muscle tone when laughing ↓ cataplexy is a specific marker of hypocretin/orexin deficiency ↓ Narcolepsy
exam_trap: Candidates may pick obstructive sleep apnoea because of the daytime sleepiness, missing that cataplexy is a highly specific feature pointing to narcolepsy instead.
takeaway: Daytime sleepiness plus emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone (cataplexy) = narcolepsy.

stem: A 55-year-old man is told by his partner that he snores loudly and repeatedly stops breathing during sleep. He is excessively sleepy during the day. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeic episodes and excessive daytime sleepiness form the classic clinical triad of obstructive sleep apnoea, caused by repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep.
why_wrong: A. Insomnia involves difficulty sleeping rather than witnessed breathing pauses. B. Panic disorder does not cause repeated nocturnal airway obstruction. C. Narcolepsy causes sleepiness and may include cataplexy, but not witnessed apnoeas. D. Nocturnal seizures can disturb sleep but do not typically produce this classic snoring–apnoea pattern.
pearl: A partner's report of witnessed apnoeic episodes during sleep is one of the most reliable clinical clues to obstructive sleep apnoea.
thinking: Loud snoring + witnessed breathing pauses + daytime sleepiness ↓ repeated upper-airway obstruction during sleep ↓ Obstructive sleep apnoea
exam_trap: Candidates may consider narcolepsy purely because of daytime sleepiness, overlooking that the witnessed apnoeas and snoring specifically point to OSA.
takeaway: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness = obstructive sleep apnoea.

stem: A 73-year-old woman has gradually progressive memory impairment over several years. She remains alert and her symptoms do not fluctuate significantly. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Gradual, progressive memory impairment over years, with preserved alertness and no significant fluctuation, is characteristic of dementia rather than an acute confusional state.
why_wrong: B. Acute psychosis primarily involves disturbed perception, thought or behaviour rather than gradual memory decline. C. Panic disorder causes recurrent discrete panic attacks, not progressive cognitive decline. D. Delirium has an acute onset with fluctuating attention and consciousness, the opposite of this picture. E. Alcohol withdrawal occurs shortly after reducing or stopping alcohol use, not as a chronic progressive process.
pearl: The key distinguishing features between dementia and delirium are onset (gradual vs acute) and course (progressive vs fluctuating), with alertness generally preserved in dementia.
thinking: Gradually progressive memory loss over years + alert + no fluctuation ↓ chronic, stable trajectory rather than acute confusion ↓ Dementia
exam_trap: Candidates may confuse dementia with delirium simply because both affect cognition; the stem's emphasis on gradual onset and lack of fluctuation is the key discriminator.
takeaway: Gradual, progressive memory decline without fluctuation in an alert patient = dementia, not delirium.

stem: A 70-year-old man with advanced illness has severe pain despite regular paracetamol. His treatment plan is being changed to include an opioid. What is an important adverse effect that should usually be anticipated and managed?
why_correct: Constipation is a very common and predictable opioid adverse effect that does not resolve with tolerance, so a laxative should routinely be co-prescribed when starting regular opioid treatment.
why_wrong: A. Opioids do not cause appendicitis. B. Polycythaemia is unrelated to opioid use. C. Opioids do not cause cataracts, and certainly not within hours. E. Opioids do not cause hyperthyroidism.
pearl: Unlike most opioid adverse effects, constipation does not improve with continued use, so a laxative should be prescribed prophylactically alongside regular opioids, not just reactively.
thinking: Starting a regular opioid for pain in advanced illness ↓ opioids reliably slow gut motility ↓ Constipation should be anticipated and managed
exam_trap: Candidates may pick a rarer, more dramatic-sounding adverse effect, forgetting that the most clinically important and predictable opioid effect to plan for is constipation.
takeaway: Starting regular opioids means anticipating and co-prescribing for constipation.

stem: A 70-year-old man receiving morphine for advanced cancer becomes very drowsy with slow, shallow breathing. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Profound drowsiness with slow, shallow breathing in a patient receiving morphine is the classic presentation of opioid toxicity, reflecting central respiratory depression.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute respiratory depression. B. Iron deficiency causes anaemia-related symptoms, not respiratory depression. C. Hyperthyroidism increases sympathetic drive rather than suppressing respiration. E. Panic attacks typically cause rapid, not depressed, breathing.
pearl: Respiratory rate and level of consciousness are the key bedside indicators of opioid toxicity and should be monitored closely whenever opioid doses are titrated.
thinking: Patient on morphine + very drowsy + slow, shallow breathing ↓ central respiratory depression from excess opioid effect ↓ Opioid toxicity
exam_trap: Candidates may attribute drowsiness to disease progression alone, missing that the combination with respiratory depression specifically signals opioid toxicity requiring dose review.
takeaway: Drowsy with slow, shallow breathing on morphine = opioid toxicity until proven otherwise.

stem: A new treatment reduces the risk of stroke from 10% to 6%. What is the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction is the simple arithmetic difference between the control and treatment event rates: 10% minus 6% equals a 4 percentage-point reduction.
why_wrong: A. 2% does not match the arithmetic difference between the two given risks. C. 6% is the treated-group event risk itself, not the reduction achieved. D. 40% is the relative risk reduction, calculated as a proportion of the baseline risk. E. 60% represents the relative risk of the treated group compared with the untreated group, not the absolute reduction.
pearl: Absolute risk reduction is a simple subtraction of event rates, while relative risk reduction expresses that same difference as a proportion of the baseline risk — the two numbers can look very different for the same data.
thinking: Baseline risk 10%, treated risk 6% ↓ subtract to find the absolute difference ↓ Absolute risk reduction = 4%
exam_trap: Candidates often calculate the relative risk reduction (40%) instead, confusing it with the simpler absolute risk reduction that the question specifically asks for.
takeaway: Absolute risk reduction = baseline risk minus treated risk, a straightforward subtraction.

stem: A trial reports that a new treatment has a relative risk of 0.6 for an outcome compared with standard treatment. What does this mean?

options.C: There is no difference in risk

why_correct: Relative risk reduction is calculated as 1 minus the relative risk: 1 − 0.6 = 0.4, meaning the treatment reduces the outcome risk by 40% relative to standard treatment.
why_wrong: A. The figure does not represent a 6% reduction. B. An RR of 0.6 does not equal a 60% reduction; that would require an RR of 0.4. C. An RR of 1.0, not 0.6, would indicate no difference in risk. D. The relative risk itself is 0.6, not 0.6%, and this is not the reduction being asked for.
pearl: To convert a relative risk into a relative risk reduction, subtract it from 1 and express as a percentage — an easy calculation that is frequently tested.
thinking: Relative risk given as 0.6 ↓ subtract from 1 to find the proportional reduction ↓ Relative risk reduction = 40%
exam_trap: Candidates often mistakenly read the relative risk value itself (0.6, i.e. 60%) as the percentage reduction, rather than subtracting it from 1 first.
takeaway: Relative risk reduction = 1 minus the relative risk, expressed as a percentage.

stem: A study reports an association between coffee consumption and heart disease. The association disappears after adjustment for smoking. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Smoking is associated with both coffee consumption and heart disease, so it distorted the apparent coffee–heart disease association until it was adjusted for — the classic definition of confounding.
why_wrong: A. Blinding concerns whether participants or assessors know treatment allocation, unrelated to this scenario. B. Publication bias concerns selective publication of favourable results. C. Randomisation is a method used to reduce confounding, not the phenomenon being described here. E. Recall bias concerns inaccurate recollection of past exposures, not a third variable linked to both exposure and outcome.
pearl: A confounder is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, and adjusting for it can reveal that an apparent association was spurious.
thinking: Coffee–heart disease association disappears after adjusting for smoking ↓ smoking is linked to both coffee drinking and heart disease ↓ Confounding
exam_trap: Candidates may label this as bias in general without identifying the specific mechanism, but the disappearance of an association after adjustment for a third factor is the textbook definition of confounding.
takeaway: An association that vanishes after adjusting for a third factor linked to both variables is confounding.

stem: A pharmaceutical company submits safety reports about a newly marketed medicine to the UK's medicines regulator. Which system is primarily used by the public and healthcare professionals to report suspected adverse drug reactions?

options.B: National Cancer Registration and Analysis Service

why_correct: The Yellow Card Scheme is the UK system through which healthcare professionals and the public report suspected adverse drug reactions and other safety concerns about medicines and healthcare products.
why_wrong: B. This concerns cancer registration and data analysis, not general adverse drug reaction reporting. C. This relates to immunisation records rather than a general adverse-reaction reporting system. D. This is a newborn hearing screening programme, unrelated to drug safety. E. This is a bowel cancer screening programme, unrelated to drug safety reporting.
pearl: Suspected adverse drug reactions, including those to newer medicines under additional monitoring, should be reported through the Yellow Card Scheme even when causation is uncertain.
thinking: New medicine + safety reporting question ↓ system for reporting suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK ↓ Yellow Card Scheme
exam_trap: Candidates may be distracted by other national screening or registry programmes listed as options, which sound plausible but serve entirely different purposes.
takeaway: Suspected adverse drug reactions in the UK are reported via the Yellow Card Scheme.

stem: A patient taking a medicine with a narrow therapeutic index starts another medicine that affects its metabolism. Why is this potentially important?

options.A: The new medicine will always improve efficacy
options.B: Small changes in concentration may cause toxicity or treatment failure
options.C: Drug interactions cannot occur with narrow therapeutic index medicines
options.E: The original medicine should automatically be doubled

correct_answer: B. Small changes in concentration may cause toxicity or treatment failure
why_correct: Because the effective and toxic concentrations are close together for a narrow therapeutic index medicine, even small interaction-driven changes in concentration can tip the balance towards toxicity or loss of efficacy.
why_wrong: A. An interacting medicine can either increase or decrease drug exposure, not reliably improve efficacy. C. Interactions can be particularly clinically significant for narrow therapeutic index medicines. D. Monitoring may well be necessary depending on the specific medicine and interaction. E. Dose changes should never be made automatically without properly assessing the interaction.
pearl: When starting any new medicine in a patient on a narrow therapeutic index drug, checking for pharmacokinetic interactions is essential, since the safety margin is small.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic index drug + new interacting medicine started ↓ small concentration shift risks crossing into toxicity or subtherapeutic range ↓ Small changes may cause toxicity or treatment failure
exam_trap: Candidates may assume a small interaction is clinically trivial, forgetting that for narrow therapeutic index drugs even modest concentration shifts can be clinically significant.
takeaway: For narrow therapeutic index drugs, even small interaction effects can cause toxicity or treatment failure.

stem: A patient is prescribed a medicine and asks what the most important information on the label is for safe use. Which information should always be clear?

options.B: Number of employees at the pharmaceutical company

why_correct: Clear instructions on dose and frequency are essential for safe medicine use, since errors in how much and how often a medicine is taken are a major preventable cause of harm.
why_wrong: A. Manufacturer profit has no bearing on safe administration. B. Staffing numbers at the manufacturer are irrelevant to patient safety. C. Logo colour has no clinical relevance. E. Advertising expenditure does not affect how safely a medicine is used.
pearl: Clear, unambiguous dose and frequency instructions are one of the simplest and most effective safeguards against medication error.
thinking: Patient asks what matters most for safe use of a labelled medicine ↓ safe administration depends on correct dosing information ↓ Dose and frequency
exam_trap: The distractor options are obviously irrelevant, but the question tests whether candidates correctly identify dose/frequency as the clinically essential labelling element amid plausible-sounding noise.
takeaway: Clear dose and frequency information is the core of safe medicine labelling.

stem: A patient receives a medicine in error but suffers no harm. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Report it via the local safety system and learn from it
options.B: Identify the staff member at fault and issue a formal warning
options.C: Note it in the patient record without any further reporting
options.D: Avoid informing the patient to prevent unnecessary worry
options.E: Alter the drug chart and medical record to hide the error

correct_answer: A. Report it via the local safety system and learn from it
why_correct: Even when no harm results, medication errors should be reported through the appropriate local safety system so that contributing factors can be identified and future incidents prevented.
why_wrong: B. Focusing on individual blame undermines a systems-based approach to patient-safety learning. C. Recording without reporting prevents the system from learning, even when no harm occurred. D. Patients should be told about errors that affect them; concealment is not appropriate. E. Altering records to hide an error is dishonest and unacceptable.
pearl: A 'no harm' outcome does not remove the value of reporting — near misses are some of the richest sources of learning for preventing future, more serious errors.
thinking: Medication error occurs, no harm results ↓ patient-safety learning still depends on reporting ↓ Report through the appropriate local safety system and learn from it
exam_trap: Candidates may think 'no harm, no foul', but PLAB 1 professionalism questions consistently test the principle that reporting matters regardless of outcome.
takeaway: No harm still means the error should be reported and learned from.

stem: A patient is prescribed penicillin despite a clearly documented previous anaphylactic reaction to penicillin. The error is identified before administration. What is this event best described as?
why_correct: A documented anaphylaxis risk was not acted upon at prescribing, but the error was identified and the medicine was not administered, making this a prescribing near miss rather than an actual adverse event.
why_wrong: A. Tolerance describes a reduced drug response over time, not an error-detection event. B. The prescription was inappropriate given the documented allergy, so this was not a successful treatment. D. Therapeutic drug monitoring involves measuring drug concentrations, unrelated to this scenario. E. Anaphylaxis, if it had occurred, would be an adverse reaction, not an expected drug effect.
pearl: A near miss — an error caught before it reaches the patient — is just as important to report as an actual adverse event, since it reveals the same underlying system weakness.
thinking: Documented penicillin anaphylaxis + penicillin prescribed in error + caught before administration ↓ potentially fatal error intercepted before harm occurred ↓ A prescribing near miss
exam_trap: Candidates may assume that because no harm occurred, this is a minor or irrelevant event, rather than recognising it as a reportable near miss.
takeaway: An error caught before it reaches the patient is a near miss, and still warrants reporting.

stem: A 63-year-old man with a long smoking history has progressive hoarseness lasting six weeks. There is no obvious upper respiratory infection. What diagnosis should be excluded?
why_correct: Persistent hoarseness lasting more than a few weeks in a smoker, without an obvious infective cause, is a red flag that must prompt urgent assessment to exclude laryngeal cancer.
why_wrong: B. Otitis externa causes external ear canal symptoms, not voice change. C. Allergic rhinitis produces nasal symptoms rather than persistent isolated hoarseness. D. Viral pharyngitis is typically short-lived and resolves within days to two weeks. E. Tonsillitis causes sore throat and inflamed tonsils rather than isolated prolonged hoarseness.
pearl: Hoarseness persisting beyond several weeks, especially in a smoker, should always trigger urgent referral to exclude laryngeal malignancy.
thinking: Long smoking history + hoarseness for six weeks + no infective cause ↓ persistent unexplained voice change is a cancer red flag ↓ Laryngeal cancer must be excluded
exam_trap: Candidates may default to a benign infective cause because sore throat/hoarseness is usually self-limiting, missing the red-flag duration and smoking history that demand urgent exclusion of malignancy.
takeaway: Persistent hoarseness beyond a few weeks in a smoker must be urgently assessed to exclude laryngeal cancer.

stem: A 63-year-old man has progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and occasional imbalance. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus and imbalance is the classic presentation of vestibular schwannoma, a benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
why_wrong: B. Noise-induced hearing loss is usually bilateral and does not cause imbalance. C. Otitis externa causes external ear canal inflammation and pain rather than progressive sensorineural loss. D. Sinusitis does not cause this characteristic progressive auditory and balance syndrome. E. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo without progressive unilateral hearing loss.
pearl: Any unilateral, progressive sensorineural hearing loss should prompt consideration of vestibular schwannoma, as asymmetry is the key red flag distinguishing it from age-related hearing loss.
