why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment is unrelated to the usual sports restriction advice. B. Hearing loss is not the principal concern. D. Pancreatitis is not the main reason for restricting contact sports. E. Renal failure is not the characteristic complication prompting this advice.
pearl: Patients with infectious mononucleosis are typically advised to avoid contact sports for a few weeks while splenomegaly resolves, to reduce the risk of rupture.
thinking: Infectious mononucleosis diagnosed + question about returning to contact sport ↓ splenomegaly increases vulnerability to trauma ↓ Splenic rupture
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with this specific advice may guess an unrelated complication; the key association to remember is splenomegaly with mononucleosis and its rupture risk from trauma.
takeaway: Avoid contact sports in early glandular fever because of the risk of splenic rupture.

stem: A 72-year-old woman develops a painful vesicular rash affecting the right side of her forehead and the tip of her nose. Which complication requires particular concern?
why_correct: A vesicular rash affecting the forehead and tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) indicates involvement of the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve, which predicts corneal involvement requiring urgent ophthalmic assessment.
why_wrong: A. Renal failure is not a characteristic complication of this presentation. C. Pancreatitis is unrelated. D. Otitis externa is not the key concern with ophthalmic-distribution shingles. E. Achilles tendon rupture is unrelated.
pearl: Involvement of the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) is a useful clinical marker predicting a higher likelihood of ocular involvement in herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
thinking: Vesicular rash on forehead and nose tip + ophthalmic trigeminal distribution ↓ Hutchinson sign predicting ocular spread ↓ Corneal involvement
exam_trap: Candidates may overlook the significance of nasal-tip involvement, but this specific sign is the clue that predicts a heightened risk of sight-threatening corneal disease.
takeaway: A vesicular rash on the tip of the nose in shingles predicts corneal involvement and needs urgent ophthalmic review.

stem: A 27-year-old man develops fever, sore throat and bilateral conjunctivitis. He also has tender cervical lymphadenopathy. Which viral infection is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, pharyngitis and bilateral conjunctivitis with tender cervical lymphadenopathy is the classic triad of pharyngoconjunctival fever, typically caused by adenovirus.
why_wrong: A. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis, particularly in young children. B. Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox or shingles. C. Hepatitis B primarily causes hepatic infection. E. Norovirus primarily causes acute gastroenteritis.
pearl: The combination of pharyngitis plus conjunctivitis is a distinctive clue that points specifically to adenoviral infection rather than typical bacterial tonsillitis.
thinking: Fever + sore throat + bilateral conjunctivitis + tender cervical nodes ↓ classic pharyngoconjunctival triad ↓ Adenovirus
exam_trap: A bacterial cause of sore throat might be assumed, but the addition of conjunctivitis is the specific clue that shifts the diagnosis to a viral, adenoviral cause.
takeaway: Sore throat plus conjunctivitis together points to adenovirus.

stem: A 15-year-old girl has primary amenorrhoea. She has normal breast development but very little pubic and axillary hair. Examination shows a short blind-ending vagina. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Normal breast development with absent or sparse pubic/axillary hair and a short blind-ending vagina reflects a 46,XY individual whose tissues cannot respond to androgens, producing female external genitalia with testicular oestrogen driving breast development.
why_wrong: A. PMOS (formerly PCOS) usually causes hyperandrogenism and irregular menstruation rather than primary amenorrhoea with absent pubic hair. B. Hypothyroidism can disturb menstruation but does not produce this characteristic phenotype. D. Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser syndrome (Müllerian agenesis) causes an absent uterus but with normal pubic and axillary hair, since androgen function is intact. E. Turner syndrome usually causes short stature and poor breast development from ovarian failure.
pearl: The combination of normal breast development with absent pubic/axillary hair is the key discriminator between androgen insensitivity syndrome and Müllerian agenesis, both of which cause primary amenorrhoea with a short vagina.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea + normal breasts + sparse pubic/axillary hair + blind-ending vagina ↓ androgen resistance despite testicular oestrogen production ↓ Androgen insensitivity syndrome
exam_trap: Müllerian agenesis is the classic distractor because it also causes a blind-ending vagina with normal breasts, but it does not cause the sparse pubic and axillary hair seen here, since androgen action is normal.
takeaway: Normal breasts but absent pubic/axillary hair with primary amenorrhoea points to androgen insensitivity, not Müllerian agenesis.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has primary amenorrhoea and normal breast development. She has normal pubic hair. Examination suggests absence of the uterus. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development and normal pubic hair, but an absent uterus, reflects congenital failure of Müllerian duct development with preserved ovarian (and therefore androgen) function.
why_wrong: A. Primary ovarian insufficiency causes reduced oestrogen and impaired secondary sexual development. B. Hyperprolactinaemia causes menstrual disturbance but not congenital absence of the uterus. D. Turner syndrome usually causes ovarian failure and impaired secondary sexual development. E. Androgen insensitivity typically causes sparse or absent pubic and axillary hair.
pearl: Normal pubic hair distinguishes Müllerian agenesis (normal androgen action) from androgen insensitivity syndrome (absent androgen action), even though both can present with a blind-ending vagina.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea + normal breasts + normal pubic hair + absent uterus ↓ functioning ovaries but failed Müllerian duct development ↓ Müllerian agenesis
exam_trap: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is the classic distractor for this presentation, but normal pubic hair here indicates intact androgen action, which rules it out.
takeaway: Absent uterus with normal pubic hair and breast development points to Müllerian agenesis, not androgen insensitivity.

stem: A 71-year-old man has urinary urgency, frequency and nocturia. He has no dysuria or haematuria. Which condition is most likely to cause these lower urinary tract symptoms?
why_correct: Urgency, frequency and nocturia without dysuria or haematuria in an older man are typical lower urinary tract symptoms of benign prostatic enlargement.
why_wrong: A. Epididymo-orchitis causes painful scrotal swelling. B. Acute pyelonephritis usually causes fever and flank pain. C. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain. D. An obstructing ureteric calculus causes severe loin-to-groin pain.
pearl: Absence of dysuria or haematuria helps distinguish uncomplicated benign prostatic enlargement from infective or malignant causes of lower urinary tract symptoms, which still warrant exclusion.
thinking: Older man + urgency, frequency, nocturia + no dysuria/haematuria ↓ typical bladder outlet obstruction pattern ↓ Benign prostatic enlargement
exam_trap: Pyelonephritis might be considered because of urinary symptoms, but the absence of fever, flank pain or dysuria argues against an infective process.
takeaway: Frequency, urgency and nocturia without dysuria or haematuria in an older man suggests benign prostatic enlargement.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with severe loin pain and fever. Urinalysis shows blood and leukocytes. CT confirms a ureteric stone. What complication is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Fever and infection above an obstructing ureteric stone indicate an infected, obstructed urinary system, which can progress rapidly to sepsis and requires urgent urological decompression.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause urinary obstruction or fever. B. Dehydration does not explain fever in the context of an obstructed, infected system. D. Migraine does not explain these findings. E. Chronic venous insufficiency is unrelated.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression alongside antibiotics, since antibiotics alone cannot clear infection behind an obstruction.
thinking: Loin pain + fever + confirmed ureteric stone ↓ infection trapped behind an obstruction ↓ Infected obstructed urinary system
exam_trap: Simple dehydration might be considered given the acute illness, but it does not explain the fever in combination with a confirmed obstructing stone.
takeaway: Fever with an obstructing ureteric stone signals an infected obstructed system — a urological emergency.

stem: A child with suspected Kawasaki disease is treated promptly because of the risk of a cardiovascular complication. Which complication is particularly associated with Kawasaki disease?
why_correct: Kawasaki disease causes vasculitis that can involve the coronary arteries, leading to aneurysm formation, which is why prompt treatment is important.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary hypertension is not a typical complication. B. DVT is not the characteristic vascular complication. D. Aortic dissection is not the characteristic cardiovascular complication. E. Mitral stenosis is not associated with Kawasaki disease.
pearl: Early treatment of Kawasaki disease substantially reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysm formation, making timely recognition and treatment important.
thinking: Suspected Kawasaki disease + concern about prompt treatment ↓ vasculitic process targets coronary arteries ↓ Coronary artery aneurysm
exam_trap: Candidates may reach for a more generic cardiovascular complication, but coronary artery aneurysm is the specific, well-recognised complication that defines the urgency of treatment.
takeaway: The key complication that drives urgent treatment of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysm.

stem: A 30-year-old woman develops recurrent episodes of palpitations, sweating and tremor several hours after meals. During an episode, her capillary glucose is 2.4 mmol/L. What is the immediate treatment for symptomatic hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient who can swallow?

options.C: Give a beta-blocker for the tremor

why_correct: A conscious patient with symptomatic hypoglycaemia who is able to swallow safely should be given fast-acting oral carbohydrate as immediate treatment.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics have no role in treating hypoglycaemia. B. A slow-release snack alone acts too slowly; it follows, rather than replaces, fast-acting carbohydrate. C. A beta-blocker masks symptoms and does not correct hypoglycaemia. E. IM glucagon is for patients who cannot safely take oral treatment, not for a conscious patient able to swallow.
pearl: Fast-acting oral carbohydrate is the first-line treatment for conscious patients with hypoglycaemia, followed by a longer-acting carbohydrate to prevent rebound.
thinking: Symptomatic episode + capillary glucose 2.4 mmol/L + conscious and able to swallow ↓ needs immediate glucose replacement by the safest route ↓ Fast-acting oral carbohydrate
exam_trap: Candidates may overthink the underlying cause (reactive hypoglycaemia) rather than focus on what the question actually asks — the immediate emergency treatment.
takeaway: A conscious, swallowing patient with hypoglycaemia gets fast-acting oral carbohydrate first.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with fatigue and proximal muscle weakness. He has recently been prescribed high-dose corticosteroids for an inflammatory condition. He has developed easy bruising and facial rounding. Which diagnosis best explains these features?
why_correct: Proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising and facial rounding following high-dose corticosteroid treatment reflect glucocorticoid excess, producing iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
why_wrong: B. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness without these characteristic steroid-related systemic features. C. Parkinson disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor. D. Addison disease results from cortisol deficiency, the opposite process. E. Hyperthyroidism causes weight loss, tremor and heat intolerance rather than this pattern.
pearl: Long-term high-dose corticosteroid therapy is the commonest cause of Cushing syndrome seen in clinical practice, more so than endogenous causes.
thinking: High-dose corticosteroid therapy + proximal weakness + bruising + facial rounding ↓ classic features of glucocorticoid excess ↓ Cushing syndrome
exam_trap: Addison disease might be confused with Cushing syndrome as 'the opposite adrenal condition', but the features described (weakness, bruising, facial rounding) reflect excess, not deficiency, of cortisol.
takeaway: High-dose steroids causing weakness, bruising and facial rounding = iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.

stem: A 70-year-old woman taking warfarin presents with severe headache and confusion after falling and hitting her head. Her INR is markedly elevated. What complication must be urgently excluded?
why_correct: Head trauma in a patient taking warfarin with a markedly elevated INR carries a significant risk of intracranial bleeding, which must be urgently excluded with imaging.
why_wrong: A. Tension-type headache is not the priority diagnosis after significant head trauma in an anticoagulated patient. B. Post-concussion syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion and must not be assumed before haemorrhage is excluded. D. Otitis media does not explain this acute neurological presentation. E. Acute sinusitis is not the immediate concern.
pearl: Any anticoagulated patient with head injury and new neurological symptoms should be treated as a medical emergency, with low-threshold imaging even for apparently minor trauma.
thinking: Warfarin + elevated INR + head trauma + headache/confusion ↓ anticoagulation markedly raises bleeding risk after trauma ↓ Urgently exclude intracranial haemorrhage
exam_trap: Candidates might be reassured by an ordinary-sounding headache, but the combination of anticoagulation, trauma and confusion makes intracranial haemorrhage the diagnosis that must be actively excluded.
takeaway: Head trauma on warfarin with a high INR must urgently exclude intracranial haemorrhage.

stem: A 64-year-old man taking warfarin has an INR of 8.5 but has no active bleeding and is otherwise well. What is the key principle of management?

options.B: Switch to aspirin until the INR is normal
options.C: Withhold warfarin and manage the excess anticoagulation
options.D: Continue warfarin and recheck INR in a week
options.E: Reduce the warfarin dose slightly and recheck next week

correct_answer: C. Withhold warfarin and manage the excess anticoagulation
why_correct: A markedly elevated INR (above 8.0) in a well patient without bleeding: stop warfarin and give oral phytomenadione (vitamin K) 1–5 mg (BNF), repeating the dose if the INR is still too high after 24 hours; restart warfarin when the INR is below 5.0.
why_wrong: A. Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding, not a raised INR without bleeding. B. Aspirin would add antithrombotic effect rather than correct the excessive INR. D. Continuing warfarin at an INR of 8.5 would increase bleeding risk. E. A small dose reduction is insufficient at an INR of 8.5; warfarin should be withheld.
pearl: Management of an excessively high INR depends on both the degree of elevation and whether bleeding is present, ranging from simply withholding doses to giving vitamin K or clotting factor concentrates.
thinking: Warfarin + INR 8.5 + no active bleeding + otherwise well ↓ excess anticoagulation needs correction before it causes harm ↓ Withhold warfarin and manage appropriately
exam_trap: Continuing the same dose might tempt candidates who focus only on 'otherwise well', but an INR this high carries significant bleeding risk even without current symptoms.
takeaway: A very high INR without bleeding still needs warfarin withheld and anticoagulation actively managed.

stem: A 63-year-old woman develops sudden facial flushing, wheeze and hypotension shortly after receiving an antibiotic intravenously. Which mechanism best explains anaphylaxis?
why_correct: Classical immediate anaphylaxis is mediated by IgE-triggered activation of mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators that cause flushing, wheeze and hypotension.
why_wrong: A. Delayed T-cell-mediated reactions occur over a much longer timescale than this immediate event. C. Immune-complex deposition is characteristic of type III hypersensitivity. D. Autoimmune haemolysis causes red-cell destruction, not anaphylaxis. E. Anaphylaxis is not caused by direct bacterial tissue invasion.
pearl: Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction, with mast-cell mediator release producing its rapid onset within minutes of exposure.
thinking: IV antibiotic exposure + sudden flushing, wheeze, hypotension ↓ classic immediate hypersensitivity time course ↓ IgE-mediated mast-cell activation
exam_trap: Immune-complex deposition might be confused with an immune mechanism, but it describes a type III reaction with a much slower, different clinical picture than acute anaphylaxis.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis is a type I, IgE-mediated mast-cell reaction.

stem: A 44-year-old woman develops a widespread itchy rash 48 hours after starting a new antibiotic. She is haemodynamically stable and has no airway or breathing problems. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is most consistent with this presentation?
why_correct: A widespread itchy rash developing 48 hours after a new medication, without airway or haemodynamic compromise, is consistent with a delayed (non-IgE) drug hypersensitivity reaction.
why_wrong: B. Autoimmune haemolysis affects red blood cells, not the skin. C. Immune-complex disease has a different clinical pattern and timescale. D. Complement deficiency is not the mechanism of a typical delayed antibiotic rash. E. IgE-mediated reactions typically occur rapidly and may cause urticaria, angioedema or anaphylaxis, not a rash appearing after two days.
pearl: The timing of a drug reaction is a key clue to its mechanism: minutes-to-hours suggests IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity, while days suggests a delayed T-cell-mediated reaction.
thinking: New antibiotic + itchy rash 48 hours later + haemodynamically stable, no airway compromise ↓ timescale excludes immediate IgE reaction ↓ Delayed drug hypersensitivity
exam_trap: Immediate IgE-mediated reaction might be chosen simply because a drug rash is described, but the 48-hour delay and absence of anaphylactic features point to a delayed hypersensitivity mechanism instead.
takeaway: A drug rash appearing after days, without airway or circulatory compromise, suggests delayed rather than immediate hypersensitivity.

stem: A 31-year-old woman taking combined hormonal contraception develops sudden unilateral calf swelling and pain. She is haemodynamically stable. Which risk factor is particularly relevant?

options.D: Daily topical emollient use for eczema
options.E: Seasonal allergic rhinitis with antihistamine use

why_correct: Oestrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception is a well-recognised risk factor for venous thromboembolism, presenting here as sudden unilateral calf swelling and pain suggestive of a DVT.
why_wrong: A. A vegetarian diet is not a recognised VTE risk factor. C. Vitamin D supplementation is not a recognised VTE risk factor. D. Topical emollients do not increase VTE risk. E. Allergic rhinitis and antihistamine use are not major VTE risk factors.
pearl: Oestrogen increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors, which is why combined hormonal contraception (and HRT) raises venous thromboembolism risk, particularly in women with additional risk factors.
thinking: COCP use + sudden unilateral calf swelling and pain ↓ classic DVT presentation with an identifiable hormonal risk factor ↓ Oestrogen-containing contraception
exam_trap: Candidates may look past the contraception history for an unrelated cause, but oestrogen exposure is the specific, well-recognised risk factor the question is testing.
takeaway: Oestrogen-containing contraception is a recognised risk factor for venous thromboembolism.

stem: A 79-year-old woman taking several antihypertensive medications has recurrent dizziness when standing. Her seated blood pressure is 145/80 mmHg and her standing blood pressure is 112/65 mmHg. What is an important initial management approach?
correct_answer: D. Review medications and contributing factors
why_correct: Reviewing medications and other contributing factors is a key initial step in managing orthostatic hypotension, since antihypertensives and other drugs are common reversible contributors.
why_wrong: A. Adding another antihypertensive may worsen the problem. B. Unnecessary fluid restriction may worsen hypotension. C. Fludrocortisone is not an initial step while potentially causative antihypertensives remain unchanged. E. Anticoagulation does not treat orthostatic hypotension.
pearl: In older adults on multiple antihypertensives, medication review and simplification is often the single most effective first step in managing symptomatic orthostatic hypotension.
thinking: Multiple antihypertensives + confirmed postural BP drop + recurrent dizziness ↓ likely drug-related contributor ↓ Review medications and contributing factors
exam_trap: Starting another antihypertensive is sometimes wrongly chosen as a reflex response to the underlying hypertension history, but this would worsen the postural drop rather than help it.
takeaway: Medication review is a key first step in managing orthostatic hypotension in older patients on multiple drugs.

stem: A 55-year-old man suddenly develops slurred speech and weakness of the left side of his body. He remains conscious. Which vascular territory is most likely to be affected if the dominant hemisphere is involved?
why_correct: The middle cerebral artery supplies large areas of the lateral cerebral hemisphere and commonly produces contralateral weakness with language disturbance when the dominant hemisphere is involved.
why_wrong: A. The renal artery supplies the kidney, not the brain. B. Posterior cerebral artery infarction more typically causes visual deficits. C. The external carotid artery does not supply the cerebral hemisphere. E. Basilar artery disease can cause brainstem syndromes but is not the typical territory for this hemispheric presentation.
pearl: The middle cerebral artery is the most commonly affected vessel in ischaemic stroke and, when the dominant hemisphere is involved, typically produces aphasia alongside contralateral weakness.
thinking: Sudden focal weakness and speech disturbance + dominant hemisphere involvement ↓ typical distribution of large-vessel hemispheric stroke ↓ Middle cerebral artery
exam_trap: Posterior cerebral artery is sometimes chosen for any stroke question, but it classically produces visual field deficits rather than the motor and language pattern described here.
takeaway: Contralateral weakness with language disturbance in dominant hemisphere stroke points to middle cerebral artery territory.

stem: A 64-year-old man suddenly develops weakness and numbness affecting his right face, arm and leg equally. He has no visual symptoms or speech disturbance. Which lesion is most likely?
why_correct: Weakness and numbness affecting the face, arm and leg equally, without cortical signs such as visual or speech disturbance, is characteristic of a lacunar infarct from small-vessel disease.
why_wrong: B. A single nerve-root lesion cannot explain this face, arm and leg distribution. C. A peripheral nerve lesion would not affect face, arm and leg together. D. An inner-ear disorder causes vestibular symptoms rather than hemibody sensorimotor loss. E. A cerebellar lesion usually produces coordination and gait abnormalities rather than this pattern.
pearl: Lacunar strokes classically spare 'cortical' functions such as language, neglect and visual fields, because they involve small perforating vessels supplying deep structures rather than the cortex.
thinking: Equal face/arm/leg weakness and numbness + no visual or speech disturbance ↓ absence of cortical signs points to a subcortical small-vessel lesion ↓ Lacunar infarction
exam_trap: Candidates might expect a cortical stroke syndrome given the hemibody symptoms, but the equal involvement of face, arm and leg with no cortical signs is the specific clue for a lacunar, not cortical, stroke.
takeaway: Equal face/arm/leg deficit without cortical signs (speech, vision) suggests a lacunar stroke.

stem: A 22-year-old student develops bilateral red, watery eyes after several friends at university have had similar symptoms. There is mild gritty discomfort but no significant pain or visual loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Bilateral red, watery, gritty eyes with a contagious contact history and no significant pain or visual loss are typical of viral conjunctivitis.
why_wrong: B. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and/or a visual field defect. C. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe pain, visual disturbance and often headache or nausea. D. Anterior uveitis typically causes pain and photophobia. E. Bacterial keratitis causes significant pain, photophobia and potentially reduced vision.
pearl: Viral conjunctivitis is highly contagious and self-limiting, so management focuses on hygiene advice and symptomatic relief rather than antibiotics.
thinking: Bilateral red watery eyes + contact cluster + no pain/vision loss ↓ benign contagious surface inflammation ↓ Viral conjunctivitis
exam_trap: A candidate might reach for antibiotic eye drops assuming a bacterial cause, but the bilateral watery presentation with a contagious contact history points to a viral aetiology instead.
takeaway: Bilateral watery red eyes spreading among contacts, without pain or vision loss, is viral conjunctivitis.

stem: A 59-year-old man notices a new dark irregularly pigmented lesion on his back that has increased in size and changed colour over the past six months. Which feature is most concerning?

options.B: Recent change in size and colour
options.C: Small size with no change over time
options.D: A symmetrical outline and regular border

correct_answer: B. Recent change in size and colour
why_correct: Recent change in size and colour of a pigmented lesion is one of the most important warning features ('evolution') suggesting possible melanoma.
why_wrong: A. Long-standing stability is generally reassuring rather than concerning. C. A small stable lesion without change is less suspicious. D. Symmetry and a regular border are generally reassuring. E. Uniform pigmentation is less concerning than irregular colour variation.
pearl: The ABCDE features (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter, Evolution) are a useful framework for assessing a pigmented lesion, with evolution over time being one of the most significant warning signs.
thinking: Pigmented lesion + recent growth and colour change over months ↓ evolution is a key melanoma warning feature ↓ Recent change in size and colour
exam_trap: Uniform colour might be misread as reassuring in a way that distracts from the correct answer, but the key finding here is specifically the recent evolution of the lesion, which is the concerning feature.
takeaway: A pigmented lesion that is changing in size or colour is the most concerning feature for melanoma.

stem: A 66-year-old woman falls and sustains a fracture through a vertebra after minimal trauma. She has no history of major trauma. What does this fracture represent?

options.B: Pathological fracture due to major trauma

why_correct: A vertebral fracture occurring after minimal trauma, with no history of major injury, represents a fragility fracture and should prompt assessment for underlying bone weakness such as osteoporosis.
why_wrong: A. Tendon rupture is a soft-tissue injury, not a bone fracture. B. Major trauma is specifically absent from this scenario. C. A dislocation is displacement of a joint, not a fracture. E. Stress fractures result from repetitive loading, a different mechanism to this low-energy fall.
pearl: Fragility fractures, particularly of the hip, spine and wrist, are sentinel events that should trigger assessment and treatment for osteoporosis to prevent further fractures.
thinking: Vertebral fracture + minimal trauma + no major injury history ↓ bone breaking under low-energy load ↓ Fragility fracture
exam_trap: Option B mixes two concepts: a pathological fracture occurs through abnormal bone with little force, whereas major trauma is specifically absent here. A low-energy vertebral fracture with no evidence of tumour is best classified as a fragility fracture.
takeaway: A fracture from minimal trauma is a fragility fracture and should prompt osteoporosis assessment.

stem: A 74-year-old woman has gradually worsening back pain and loses height over several years. Imaging shows a vertebral compression fracture without significant trauma. What is the most likely underlying condition?
why_correct: Gradual height loss and back pain from vertebral compression fractures occurring with little or no trauma are characteristic of osteoporosis.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis primarily affects joints rather than causing vertebral compression fractures. C. Gout causes crystal-induced arthritis, not fracture. D. Septic arthritis causes an acutely inflamed joint, not a chronic compression fracture. E. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without structural vertebral collapse.
pearl: Vertebral compression fractures are often asymptomatic or attributed to 'normal ageing' back pain, so height loss over time is a useful clue to underlying osteoporosis.
thinking: Gradual height loss + back pain + minimal-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ fragility fracture pattern ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: Candidates may attribute chronic back pain in an older patient simply to degenerative disease, but the minimal-trauma vertebral fracture and height loss specifically indicate osteoporosis.
takeaway: Height loss with a minimal-trauma vertebral fracture points to osteoporosis.

stem: A 56-year-old woman has taken minocycline for acne for 18 months. She develops painful swelling of the wrists, widespread arthralgia and a photosensitive rash. Which adverse drug reaction should be suspected?
why_correct: Arthralgia, joint swelling and a photosensitive rash developing after prolonged exposure to minocycline are consistent with drug-induced lupus. Minocycline is a recognised cause, typically after months to years of treatment for acne.
why_wrong: A. Viral conjunctivitis does not explain this systemic presentation. B. Iron deficiency causes anaemia rather than this inflammatory syndrome. D. Hypothyroidism does not typically cause a drug-related photosensitive inflammatory presentation. E. Osteoarthritis causes mechanical joint symptoms without a rash.
pearl: Drug-induced lupus typically improves after stopping the causative medication, distinguishing it from idiopathic systemic lupus erythematosus.
thinking: Long-term minocycline + painful wrist swelling + photosensitive rash + arthralgia ↓ prolonged exposure to a recognised causative drug with lupus-like features ↓ Drug-induced lupus
exam_trap: Idiopathic causes of joint pain and rash may be considered, but prolonged exposure to a recognised causative drug points specifically towards a drug-induced cause. Drug-induced lupus develops over months to years, so do not attribute a reaction that appears within days of starting a drug to it.
takeaway: New joint pain, arthralgia and a photosensitive rash after months to years on a recognised causative drug (e.g. minocycline, hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid) suggest drug-induced lupus.

stem: A 35-year-old man has been taking metronidazole for an infection. He drinks alcohol while taking the medication and subsequently develops flushing, nausea and palpitations. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Increase alcohol intake to overcome tolerance
options.E: Take an additional dose of metronidazole

correct_answer: C. Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole
why_correct: Alcohol should be avoided while taking metronidazole because of the risk of an unpleasant disulfiram-like reaction, causing flushing, nausea and palpitations.
why_wrong: A. Increasing alcohol intake would worsen symptoms, not overcome them. B. Aspirin does not prevent this reaction. D. Water restriction is inappropriate and unrelated. E. An additional antibiotic dose does not treat the reaction.
pearl: The metronidazole–alcohol interaction is a classic prescribing counselling point and should always be mentioned when this antibiotic is dispensed.
thinking: Metronidazole use + alcohol intake + flushing, nausea, palpitations ↓ classic disulfiram-like drug interaction ↓ Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole
exam_trap: Candidates might look for a pharmacological treatment for the reaction, but the correct answer is simple counselling advice to avoid the interacting substance.
takeaway: Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole to prevent a disulfiram-like reaction.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is prescribed doxycycline. She asks whether she should take it immediately before going to bed. What advice is appropriate?

options.A: Take it with an antacid to protect the gullet lining
options.B: Take it immediately before lying flat to sleep at night
options.C: Take it dry, without any fluid, to aid its absorption
options.D: Take it with plenty of water and stay upright
options.E: Stop drinking water for several hours afterwards

correct_answer: D. Take it with plenty of water and stay upright
why_correct: Doxycycline can cause oesophageal irritation and ulceration, so it should be taken with plenty of water while remaining upright afterwards to reduce this risk.
why_wrong: A. Antacids reduce doxycycline absorption and do not prevent oesophageal injury. B. Lying down immediately after taking it increases oesophageal exposure and risk of irritation. C. Taking it without fluid increases the risk of oesophageal irritation and ulceration. E. Adequate fluid intake, not restriction, is appropriate.
pearl: Tetracyclines such as doxycycline are classically associated with oesophageal irritation, which is why patients are advised to take them with water and stay upright for a period afterwards.
thinking: Doxycycline prescribed + question about bedtime dosing ↓ tablet contact time with the oesophagus must be minimised ↓ Take with plenty of water and remain upright
exam_trap: Taking the medication immediately before lying flat might seem like routine bedtime dosing advice, but this specifically increases the risk of oesophageal irritation with doxycycline.
takeaway: Take doxycycline with plenty of water and stay upright afterwards to avoid oesophageal irritation.

stem: A 30-year-old woman taking combined hormonal contraception is prescribed a course of an antibiotic. She asks whether she must stop her contraception because antibiotics always make it ineffective. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce efficacy by altering gut flora
options.B: Condoms are needed for 7 days after any antibiotic course
options.C: Amoxicillin induces liver enzymes that lower circulating hormone levels
options.D: Most non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do not reduce its efficacy
options.E: Contraception should be paused until the antibiotic course has ended

correct_answer: D. Most non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do not reduce its efficacy
why_correct: Most non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do not reduce the effectiveness of combined hormonal contraception; important exceptions are enzyme-inducing drugs, and vomiting or severe diarrhoea can independently affect oral contraceptive reliability.
why_wrong: A. The gut-flora theory is not supported; non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics do not reduce CHC efficacy. B. Additional precautions are not routinely needed with non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics. C. Amoxicillin is not an enzyme inducer. E. Pausing contraception is unnecessary and would leave her unprotected.
pearl: The common belief that 'all antibiotics stop the pill working' is outdated; only enzyme-inducing drugs (such as rifampicin) are a genuine concern for reduced contraceptive efficacy.
thinking: Patient starting antibiotics + worried about contraceptive failure ↓ most antibiotics are not enzyme-inducing ↓ Additional precautions are not routinely needed
exam_trap: Candidates influenced by outdated teaching may pick an option suggesting antibiotics always reduce contraceptive efficacy, but current guidance limits this concern to enzyme-inducing drugs.
takeaway: Routine antibiotics generally do not reduce combined hormonal contraceptive efficacy — only enzyme-inducing drugs do.

stem: A 24-year-old man has periods of abnormally elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, increased energy, rapid speech and excessive spending. During one episode he becomes unable to function normally at work. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Episodes of abnormally elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, increased energy, rapid speech and impaired functioning describe mania, characteristic of bipolar disorder.
why_wrong: A. Generalised anxiety disorder causes persistent excessive worry rather than episodic elevated mood. B. OCD causes intrusive thoughts and compulsive behaviours. C. Panic disorder causes recurrent unexpected panic attacks. E. Major depression does not explain episodes of pathological elevated mood.
pearl: Functional impairment distinguishes a manic episode from hypomania, which is milder and does not significantly disrupt daily functioning.
thinking: Elevated mood + reduced sleep need + rapid speech + overspending + functional impairment ↓ pattern of an episodic manic syndrome ↓ Bipolar disorder
exam_trap: Major depressive disorder is sometimes wrongly chosen because bipolar disorder also involves depressive episodes, but the symptoms described here are specifically manic, not depressive.
takeaway: Episodic elevated mood with impaired functioning is a manic episode, pointing to bipolar disorder.

stem: A 42-year-old man reports hearing voices speaking to him when nobody is present. He is convinced that his neighbours are transmitting thoughts into his head. Which combination of symptoms is present?
why_correct: Hearing voices with no external stimulus is an auditory hallucination, and a fixed false belief such as thought insertion by neighbours is a delusion — together these are core features of psychosis.
why_wrong: B. Obsessions are intrusive thoughts and compulsions are repetitive behaviours or mental acts, distinct from hallucinations and delusions. C. Phobias involve specific fears and panic attacks are acute episodes of intense anxiety. D. An illusion is a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus, and dysphasia is impaired language. E. Confabulation involves filling memory gaps with fabricated information.
pearl: Distinguishing a hallucination (a perception without a stimulus) from an illusion (a misperception of a real stimulus) is a commonly tested psychiatric definition.
thinking: Hears voices with no one present + fixed belief of thoughts being transmitted ↓ perception without stimulus plus a fixed false belief ↓ Hallucination and delusion
exam_trap: Illusion and dysphasia might be confused with hallucination and delusion, but an illusion requires a real external stimulus to be misperceived, which is absent here.
takeaway: Voices with no stimulus is a hallucination; a fixed false belief is a delusion — together, features of psychosis.

stem: A 25-year-old man develops painful neck and jaw muscle spasms several hours after receiving an antipsychotic medication. Which adverse effect is most likely?
why_correct: Painful muscle spasms affecting the neck and jaw within hours of starting an antipsychotic are typical of acute dystonia, an early dopamine-blockade-related movement disorder.
why_wrong: A. Metabolic syndrome develops over a much longer period. B. Hyperprolactinaemia causes endocrine effects such as galactorrhoea, not muscle spasms. C. Tardive dyskinesia develops after prolonged exposure, not within hours. E. Agranulocytosis is a blood disorder rather than an acute movement disorder.
pearl: Acute dystonia typically occurs within hours to days of starting or increasing an antipsychotic dose and responds rapidly to an anticholinergic agent.
thinking: Antipsychotic started + painful neck/jaw spasms within hours ↓ early-onset dopamine-blockade movement reaction ↓ Acute dystonia
exam_trap: Tardive dyskinesia might be chosen simply because it is a well-known antipsychotic movement disorder, but its onset is after prolonged treatment, not hours after a single dose.
takeaway: Painful muscle spasms soon after starting an antipsychotic = acute dystonia.

stem: A 67-year-old man with long-standing diabetes develops burning pain and numbness affecting both feet symmetrically. Examination shows reduced vibration sensation. Which type of neuropathy is most likely?
why_correct: Symmetrical burning pain, numbness and reduced vibration sense in the feet of a patient with long-standing diabetes reflect a distal symmetrical (length-dependent) peripheral neuropathy.
why_wrong: A. Radiculopathy follows a nerve-root distribution with back or leg pain rather than a symmetrical distal glove-and-stocking pattern. C. Motor neurone disease primarily causes progressive motor weakness without sensory symptoms. D. Vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex affects individual peripheral nerves in an asymmetric pattern. E. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than distal sensory loss.
pearl: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy follows a length-dependent 'glove and stocking' pattern, starting distally in the feet before progressing proximally.
thinking: Long-standing diabetes + symmetrical burning feet + reduced vibration sense ↓ length-dependent nerve damage ↓ Distal symmetrical peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: Mononeuritis multiplex might be considered given the diabetes history, but its pattern is asymmetric, affecting individual nerves, unlike the symmetrical distribution described here.
takeaway: Symmetrical distal sensory loss in diabetes is classic distal symmetrical peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with weakness of both legs, urinary retention and a sensory level on the trunk. Symptoms have developed over several hours. Which diagnosis requires urgent consideration?
why_correct: Bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention developing over hours are red-flag features of spinal cord compression requiring urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause a sensory level with urinary retention. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand, not the legs or bladder. D. Tension headache does not cause spinal cord signs. E. Otitis media does not cause this neurological syndrome.
pearl: A sensory level combined with bilateral leg weakness and bladder dysfunction is a classic triad for spinal cord compression and demands emergency imaging.
thinking: Bilateral leg weakness + urinary retention + sensory level on the trunk ↓ classic cord-level red flags ↓ Spinal cord compression
exam_trap: Candidates might underestimate acute bilateral leg symptoms as a peripheral problem, but the sensory level and bladder involvement specifically localise the lesion to the spinal cord.
takeaway: Bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level and bladder dysfunction requires urgent exclusion of spinal cord compression.

stem: A 61-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer develops severe back pain followed by bilateral leg weakness and urinary difficulty. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Increase analgesia and review in two weeks
options.B: Urgent assessment for metastatic cord compression
options.C: Arrange a routine outpatient spinal MRI
options.D: Treat as uncomplicated mechanical back pain
options.E: Refer to physiotherapy for core strengthening

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment for metastatic cord compression
why_correct: New back pain with bilateral leg weakness and urinary difficulty in a patient with known metastatic cancer are classic red flags for metastatic spinal cord compression, an oncological emergency requiring urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Delaying review risks permanent neurological damage. C. MRI of the whole spine is needed urgently (within 24 hours), not routinely. D. The cancer history and neurological signs make simple mechanical back pain an inappropriate working diagnosis. E. Physiotherapy would dangerously delay emergency investigation.
pearl: Any patient with known cancer presenting with new back pain and neurological symptoms should be treated as metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise, given the narrow window to prevent permanent paralysis.
thinking: Known metastatic cancer + severe back pain + bilateral leg weakness + urinary difficulty ↓ classic oncological emergency red flags ↓ Urgent assessment for metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: Treating this as uncomplicated mechanical back pain is a dangerous trap; the cancer history combined with new neurological deficits demands urgent emergency evaluation, not routine management.
takeaway: Back pain with new neurological signs in a cancer patient is metastatic spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.

stem: A 64-year-old man with peripheral arterial disease asks about a treatment that reduces his cardiovascular risk. He continues to smoke. Which lifestyle intervention is particularly important?
why_correct: Smoking cessation is the single most important modifiable lifestyle intervention for reducing cardiovascular and limb-related risk in patients with peripheral arterial disease.
why_wrong: A. Increasing smoking would worsen vascular risk. B. Appropriate exercise is generally an important, not harmful, part of vascular risk management. C. Fruit and vegetables should not be restricted. D. Increasing saturated fat intake is not beneficial.
pearl: Smoking cessation has one of the largest evidence-based impacts on reducing both cardiovascular events and disease progression in peripheral arterial disease.
thinking: Peripheral arterial disease + ongoing smoking + question about risk-reducing lifestyle change ↓ smoking is the dominant modifiable risk factor ↓ Smoking cessation
exam_trap: Candidates sometimes overlook smoking cessation in favour of dietary advice, but it remains the single most impactful lifestyle intervention in this condition.
takeaway: Smoking cessation is the most important lifestyle intervention in peripheral arterial disease.

stem: A 47-year-old man has a painless ulcer on the sole of his foot. He has longstanding diabetes and reduced sensation in both feet. What is the most likely type of ulcer?

options.D: Pressure ulcer from prolonged bed rest

why_correct: A painless plantar ulcer in a patient with longstanding diabetes and reduced sensation reflects loss of protective sensation, causing a neuropathic ulcer at a pressure-bearing site.
why_wrong: A. Malignant ulceration is far less likely than a neuropathic cause given this clinical context. C. Arterial ulcers are usually painful and associated with reduced perfusion, not painless. D. The patient is not described as immobile or bedbound. E. Venous ulcers usually occur around the gaiter area, not the sole.
pearl: Loss of protective sensation in diabetic neuropathy allows repeated unnoticed trauma at pressure points, which is why regular foot checks are essential in diabetic care.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes + reduced foot sensation + painless plantar ulcer ↓ loss of protective sensation at a weight-bearing point ↓ Neuropathic ulcer
exam_trap: Candidates may assume any diabetic foot ulcer is arterial, but the painless nature and sole location here specifically indicate a neuropathic rather than ischaemic mechanism.
takeaway: A painless plantar ulcer with diabetic sensory loss is a neuropathic ulcer.

stem: A 58-year-old woman develops a swollen, painful lower leg with a shallow ulcer around the medial ankle. The leg is oedematous and the skin is hyperpigmented. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: Oedema, hyperpigmentation and a shallow ulcer around the medial ankle reflect chronic venous hypertension causing chronic venous insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes acute joint inflammation, not chronic skin and ulcer changes. C. Neuropathy causes sensory loss and pressure-related ulcers rather than this venous pattern. D. Lymphoma does not characteristically produce this combination. E. Arterial disease causes cold, poorly perfused limbs with typically distal painful ulcers.
pearl: Chronic venous insufficiency produces a spectrum of skin changes — oedema, haemosiderin pigmentation and, eventually, ulceration — reflecting long-standing venous hypertension.
thinking: Swollen, painful leg + medial ankle ulcer + oedema and pigmentation ↓ chronic venous hypertension skin changes ↓ Chronic venous insufficiency
exam_trap: Peripheral arterial disease could be considered for any leg ulcer, but the oedema and hyperpigmentation here, rather than coldness and poor perfusion, point to a venous rather than arterial process.
takeaway: Medial ankle ulceration with oedema and pigmentation reflects chronic venous insufficiency.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with worsening breathlessness, ankle swelling and difficulty lying flat. He wakes at night gasping for breath. Which symptom is particularly characteristic of left-sided heart failure?
why_correct: Breathlessness when lying flat (orthopnoea) reflects redistribution of fluid into the lungs and is a characteristic symptom of left-sided heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Haematemesis indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding. C. Dysuria indicates urinary tract symptoms. D. Tinnitus is an auditory symptom. E. Photophobia is associated with conditions such as migraine or meningitis.
pearl: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea both reflect pulmonary congestion from left-sided heart failure, worsening when fluid redistributes on lying flat.
thinking: Breathlessness + ankle swelling + waking gasping at night + worse lying flat ↓ pulmonary congestion from left heart failure ↓ Orthopnoea
exam_trap: Candidates might be drawn to unrelated symptoms simply because they are unfamiliar terms, but orthopnoea is the specific, classic symptom of left-sided heart failure being tested here.
takeaway: Breathlessness on lying flat (orthopnoea) is a classic symptom of left-sided heart failure.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure has worsening peripheral oedema despite treatment. Her weight has increased by 3 kg over one week. What does the rapid weight gain most likely represent?
why_correct: A rapid weight gain of several kilograms over one week in a patient with worsening heart failure symptoms most likely reflects fluid retention rather than a change in body tissue.
why_wrong: B. Dehydration would reduce, not increase, weight. C. Bone density changes occur slowly over years. D. Fat loss would reduce body weight. E. Muscle mass cannot increase by several kilograms within a single week.
pearl: Daily weighing is a simple and effective way for heart failure patients to detect early fluid retention before overt symptoms worsen, allowing timely diuretic adjustment.
thinking: Heart failure + worsening oedema + rapid weight gain over one week ↓ timescale too fast for tissue change ↓ Fluid retention
exam_trap: Candidates might try to find a more complex physiological explanation, but a rapid weight change over days in heart failure is almost always due to fluid shifts.
takeaway: Rapid weight gain over days in heart failure reflects fluid retention, not tissue change.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with fever, a new heart murmur and several small painless lesions on his palms. He has recently had a dental procedure. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever, a new heart murmur and painless palmar lesions (Janeway lesions) following a dental procedure are suggestive of infective endocarditis, arising from transient bacteraemia seeding a heart valve.
why_wrong: B. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis, not this febrile cardiac syndrome. C. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory polyarthritis. D. Psoriasis causes characteristic skin plaques, not the syndrome described. E. Cellulitis causes a localised, painful erythematous infection rather than this systemic picture.
pearl: A new murmur with fever after a dental or invasive procedure should always raise suspicion of infective endocarditis, particularly in patients with predisposing valve disease.
thinking: Recent dental procedure + fever + new murmur + palmar lesions ↓ bacteraemia seeding a heart valve with peripheral stigmata ↓ Infective endocarditis
exam_trap: Cellulitis might be considered given the skin lesions, but the combination of fever, a new murmur and a preceding dental procedure specifically points to endocarditis rather than a localised skin infection.
takeaway: Fever, a new murmur and peripheral skin lesions after a dental procedure suggest infective endocarditis.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with Graves disease develops painful red eyes, photophobia and difficulty moving her eyes. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Painful red eyes, photophobia and restricted eye movements in a patient with Graves disease indicate orbital inflammation from thyroid eye disease.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes progressive visual impairment rather than painful restricted eye movements. B. Retinal detachment usually causes flashes, floaters and visual-field loss. C. Conjunctivitis typically causes conjunctival inflammation and discharge without restricted movement. D. A hordeolum is a localised painful eyelid infection, not orbital inflammation.
pearl: Thyroid eye disease results from autoimmune inflammation of the orbital tissues and can occur independently of current thyroid hormone levels.
thinking: Graves disease + painful red eyes + photophobia + restricted eye movement ↓ orbital autoimmune inflammation ↓ Thyroid eye disease
exam_trap: Conjunctivitis might be considered for red, uncomfortable eyes, but restricted eye movement is not a feature of simple conjunctivitis and points instead to orbital involvement.
takeaway: Painful, restricted eye movements with Graves disease indicate thyroid eye disease.

stem: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat and tender anterior cervical lymph nodes. There is no cough. Which organism is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Fever, sore throat and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy without cough in a school-age child are typical of streptococcal (group A Streptococcus) pharyngitis.
why_wrong: A. Rhinovirus typically causes a common-cold picture with cough and coryza. B. EBV commonly causes prominent fatigue and posterior, rather than anterior, cervical lymphadenopathy. C. RSV primarily causes lower respiratory disease in young children. E. Influenza usually causes prominent systemic symptoms such as myalgia and high fever with cough.
pearl: The absence of cough, along with fever and tender anterior lymphadenopathy, helps clinically favour a bacterial (streptococcal) over a viral cause of pharyngitis.
thinking: School-age child + fever + sore throat + tender anterior cervical nodes + no cough ↓ features favouring a bacterial cause ↓ Streptococcus pyogenes
exam_trap: EBV might be considered for any sore throat with lymphadenopathy, but it typically causes posterior cervical nodes and prominent fatigue, differing from this presentation.
takeaway: Sore throat with tender anterior nodes and no cough favours streptococcal pharyngitis.

stem: A 71-year-old man suddenly develops severe breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. He is hypotensive and has raised jugular venous pressure. Which diagnosis should be considered particularly urgently?
why_correct: Sudden severe breathlessness with pleuritic chest pain, hypotension and a raised jugular venous pressure indicate right heart strain from a life-threatening, massive pulmonary embolism.
why_wrong: A. Simple bronchitis does not cause sudden severe hypotension. B. Stable angina does not cause sudden haemodynamic collapse. D. Reflux does not cause shock. E. Musculoskeletal pain does not explain acute cardiovascular instability.
pearl: Hypotension with a raised JVP in the context of sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain suggests acute right ventricular strain, a hallmark of massive pulmonary embolism requiring emergency management.
thinking: Sudden severe breathlessness + pleuritic chest pain + hypotension + raised JVP ↓ acute right heart strain from vascular obstruction ↓ Massive pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: Stable angina might be superficially considered given the chest pain, but the combination of hypotension and a raised JVP indicates acute haemodynamic compromise, which angina alone does not cause.
takeaway: Sudden breathlessness with hypotension and a raised JVP points to massive pulmonary embolism.

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with fever, dysuria, perineal pain and a tender prostate on examination. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever plus urinary symptoms plus a tender, boggy prostate on examination is the classic triad of acute bacterial prostatitis.
why_wrong: B. Benign prostatic enlargement causes chronic obstructive urinary symptoms without fever or a tender prostate. C. Epididymitis causes scrotal, not prostatic, pain and swelling. D. Prostate cancer is usually asymptomatic early and does not cause an acutely tender, febrile prostate. E. Renal colic causes severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, not perineal pain with a tender prostate.
pearl: Avoid vigorous prostate massage in suspected acute bacterial prostatitis, as it can seed bacteraemia; a gentle digital rectal examination is sufficient to find tenderness.
thinking: Fever + dysuria + perineal pain ↓ tender prostate on exam ↓ acute infective process, not obstructive or malignant ↓ Acute bacterial prostatitis
exam_trap: Candidates may jump to benign prostatic enlargement because of the age and urinary symptoms, missing that fever and tenderness point to infection rather than chronic obstruction.
takeaway: Fever + tender prostate + urinary symptoms = acute bacterial prostatitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 46-year-old man has persistent epigastric discomfort and bloating. Testing confirms *Helicobacter pylori* infection. Which condition is strongly associated with *H. pylori*?
why_correct: *H. pylori* colonises the gastric antrum and disrupts the mucosal barrier, and it is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease, particularly duodenal ulcers.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids are vascular anal cushions unrelated to gastric bacterial infection. B. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic oesophageal disorder not caused by *H. pylori*. C. Diverticulosis reflects colonic wall weakness, with no causal link to *H. pylori*. E. Ulcerative colitis is an autoimmune colitis, not caused by *H. pylori*.
pearl: Testing for and eradicating *H. pylori* is a key step in the management of peptic ulcer disease, alongside acid suppression.
thinking: Epigastric discomfort and bloating ↓ confirmed *H. pylori* infection ↓ organism strongly linked to mucosal ulceration ↓ Peptic ulcer disease
exam_trap: A candidate might be tempted by ulcerative colitis as 'another GI inflammatory disease', but UC has no established causal link to *H. pylori*.
takeaway: *H. pylori* is the classic driver of peptic ulcer disease, especially duodenal ulcers.

stem: A 73-year-old man develops progressive change in bowel habit with weight loss and intermittent rectal bleeding. Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: A change in bowel habit, unintentional weight loss and rectal bleeding in an older adult are red-flag features that mandate urgent investigation for colorectal cancer.
why_wrong: A. Anal fissure causes sharp pain on defecation with minor bleeding, not systemic weight loss. C. IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not explain weight loss or bleeding. D. Gastroenteritis is acute and self-limiting. E. Haemorrhoids alone would not explain the change in bowel habit and weight loss.
pearl: Any combination of new bowel habit change, weight loss and rectal bleeding in a patient over 60 warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal assessment.
thinking: Older age + progressive bowel habit change ↓ weight loss ↓ intermittent rectal bleeding ↓ Colorectal cancer
exam_trap: A candidate might default to haemorrhoids because bleeding is present, but haemorrhoids do not explain systemic weight loss or a genuine change in bowel habit.
takeaway: Weight loss plus bowel habit change plus bleeding in an older adult is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 52-year-old woman develops severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Her abdomen is distended and bowel sounds are initially high-pitched. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and early high-pitched (tinkling) bowel sounds reflect mechanical bowel obstruction.
why_wrong: A. GORD causes reflux symptoms, not obstruction. B. Haemorrhoids are unrelated to intra-abdominal obstruction. C. Chronic pancreatitis causes recurrent epigastric pain and malabsorption rather than this acute obstructive picture. E. IBS does not cause marked distension or high-pitched bowel sounds.
pearl: Early in bowel obstruction, bowel sounds are typically high-pitched and hyperactive as the bowel tries to overcome the blockage; they become quiet later as the bowel fatigues.
thinking: Abdominal pain + vomiting + distension ↓ high-pitched bowel sounds ↓ mechanical obstruction pattern ↓ Small bowel obstruction
exam_trap: Candidates may be thrown by 'high-pitched' bowel sounds and think of a benign cause; in fact hyperactive, tinkling sounds are an early feature of mechanical obstruction, not evidence against it.
takeaway: Pain + vomiting + distension + altered bowel sounds = think bowel obstruction.

stem: A 48-year-old woman develops widespread muscle pain, poor sleep and fatigue. Examination is normal and there is no objective joint swelling. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Widespread pain with fatigue and poor sleep, in the absence of any objective joint swelling or inflammatory signs, is characteristic of fibromyalgia.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis causes an acutely hot, swollen single joint with systemic illness. B. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects older adults with proximal girdle stiffness, not generalised diffuse pain. C. Osteomyelitis causes localised bone pain with infective signs. E. Rheumatoid arthritis produces objective synovitis and joint swelling, which is absent here.
pearl: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis based on widespread pain and associated symptoms (fatigue, poor sleep, cognitive difficulty); investigations are usually normal and mainly used to exclude other causes.
thinking: Widespread pain + fatigue + poor sleep ↓ normal examination, no joint swelling ↓ no inflammatory findings ↓ Fibromyalgia
exam_trap: Candidates may reach for rheumatoid arthritis because of 'muscle pain', but RA requires objective joint swelling, which this patient does not have.
takeaway: Widespread pain with fatigue and a normal joint exam suggests fibromyalgia, a diagnosis of exclusion.

stem: A 70-year-old man with long-standing inflammatory arthritis develops a new, firm swelling over the back of his elbow. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules over extensor pressure points such as the elbow are a recognised extra-articular feature of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes an acute, painful, warm, erythematous area rather than a firm chronic nodule. B. A lipoma is typically soft and mobile rather than firm. C. A ganglion cyst characteristically occurs around the wrist or hand. E. Melanoma is a malignant skin lesion, usually pigmented, not a firm subcutaneous nodule at a pressure point.
pearl: Rheumatoid nodules are a marker of more severe, seropositive (rheumatoid-factor-positive) disease and can also occur at other pressure points such as the fingers.
thinking: Long-standing inflammatory arthritis ↓ firm swelling at a pressure point (elbow) ↓ extra-articular rheumatoid feature ↓ Rheumatoid nodule
exam_trap: A candidate might worry about melanoma given a 'new' lesion, but the firm, non-pigmented nature at a classic pressure point in a patient with known inflammatory arthritis points to a rheumatoid nodule instead.
takeaway: Firm nodules over extensor surfaces in rheumatoid arthritis are rheumatoid nodules.

stem: A 32-year-old man develops jaundice and dark urine after taking a new antibiotic. Blood tests show haemolytic anaemia. Which condition can predispose to this reaction?
why_correct: G6PD deficiency leaves red cells vulnerable to oxidative stress; certain drugs (including some antibiotics) can trigger acute haemolysis, jaundice and dark urine in affected individuals.
why_wrong: B. Sickle-cell trait is usually asymptomatic and does not typically cause this acute drug-triggered haemolytic pattern. C. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia from ineffective erythropoiesis, not acute drug-triggered haemolysis. D. Haemochromatosis causes iron overload, not haemolysis. E. Iron-deficiency anaemia reflects reduced red-cell production, not increased destruction.
pearl: G6PD deficiency is X-linked and more common in patients of Mediterranean, African, Middle Eastern and Asian ancestry; a known trigger list (certain antibiotics, antimalarials, fava beans) is worth recognising.
thinking: New antibiotic + jaundice and dark urine ↓ haemolytic anaemia confirmed ↓ oxidative drug trigger in a susceptible enzyme deficiency ↓ Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
exam_trap: A candidate might pick sickle-cell trait as 'another inherited red-cell condition', but trait status rarely causes overt drug-triggered haemolysis, unlike G6PD deficiency.
takeaway: Drug-triggered haemolysis after a new medication points to underlying G6PD deficiency.

stem: A 28-year-old man with sickle-cell disease develops severe pain in his back and limbs. There is no evidence of infection or trauma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: In sickle-cell disease, severe bone and limb pain without evidence of infection or trauma is most often caused by microvascular occlusion from sickled red cells — a vaso-occlusive crisis.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis causes chronic mechanical pain, not acute severe crises. B. Osteomyelitis is an infection, and there is no evidence of infection here. D. Renal colic causes severe flank pain radiating to the groin, a different pattern. E. Appendicitis causes abdominal pain localising to the right lower quadrant.
pearl: Vaso-occlusive crises are the most common acute complication of sickle-cell disease and are managed with analgesia, hydration and treatment of any precipitating factor.
thinking: Sickle-cell disease + severe back/limb pain ↓ no infective or traumatic cause found ↓ microvascular sickling process ↓ Vaso-occlusive crisis
exam_trap: Candidates may over-investigate for infection given severe pain, but the stem explicitly excludes infection and trauma, pointing instead to the classic sickle-cell vaso-occlusive process.
takeaway: Severe pain without infection or trauma in sickle-cell disease is a vaso-occlusive crisis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with sickle-cell disease develops sudden severe chest pain, fever, cough and increasing breathlessness. Oxygen saturation is reduced. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: New respiratory symptoms, fever and hypoxia in a patient with sickle-cell disease represent acute chest syndrome, a life-threatening complication requiring urgent treatment.
why_wrong: A. Viral rhinitis does not cause hypoxia or severe chest pain. C. Reflux does not cause fever or hypoxia. D. Stable angina causes predictable exertional discomfort without fever or hypoxia. E. Panic disorder does not explain objective hypoxia and fever.
pearl: Acute chest syndrome is a leading cause of death in sickle-cell disease and needs prompt recognition, oxygen, analgesia and consideration of transfusion or exchange transfusion.
thinking: Sickle-cell disease + chest pain, fever, cough ↓ falling oxygen saturation ↓ acute pulmonary sickle complication ↓ Acute chest syndrome
exam_trap: A candidate might assume a simple chest infection, but in sickle-cell disease new respiratory symptoms with hypoxia specifically raise acute chest syndrome, which needs a different urgency of response.
takeaway: New respiratory symptoms with hypoxia in sickle-cell disease = acute chest syndrome until excluded.

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with recurrent headaches and fatigue. Blood tests show haemoglobin of 176 g/L and a raised haematocrit. She is a heavy smoker. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic hypoxia from smoking drives increased erythropoietin production, raising red-cell mass and producing secondary erythrocytosis with a high haemoglobin and haematocrit.
why_wrong: A. Neutropenia is a low neutrophil count, unrelated to the findings. B. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia, not a raised haemoglobin. C. Thrombocytopenia is a low platelet count. E. Iron-deficiency anaemia causes a low, not raised, haemoglobin.
pearl: Secondary erythrocytosis from smoking is distinguished from polycythaemia vera by a normal (not suppressed) erythropoietin level and absence of the JAK2 mutation.
thinking: Heavy smoker + raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ chronic hypoxic drive ↓ compensatory red-cell overproduction ↓ Secondary erythrocytosis
exam_trap: Candidates may jump to a primary marrow disorder, but a clear smoking history with chronic hypoxia points to a secondary, reactive cause rather than a primary myeloproliferative process.
takeaway: Smoking-related chronic hypoxia is a classic cause of secondary erythrocytosis.

stem: A 58-year-old man develops recurrent infections. His blood tests show a very low neutrophil count. Which term describes this finding?
why_correct: Neutropenia denotes an abnormally low neutrophil count, which reduces the ability to fight bacterial infection and explains the recurrent infections described.
why_wrong: A. Lymphocytosis describes a raised lymphocyte count. B. Neutrophilia describes a raised neutrophil count, the opposite of what is described. C. Thrombocytopenia refers to a low platelet count, not white cells. D. Polycythaemia describes an increased red-cell mass.
pearl: Severe neutropenia with fever is a medical emergency (neutropenic sepsis) and requires urgent empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics, regardless of the apparent severity of illness.
thinking: Recurrent infections ↓ blood tests show very low neutrophil count ↓ matching terminology for reduced neutrophils ↓ Neutropenia
exam_trap: Candidates unfamiliar with haematology terminology may confuse 'neutropenia' with 'neutrophilia'; the prefix and the clinical context (infection-prone, low count) should clarify the direction.
takeaway: A low neutrophil count is neutropenia and predisposes to infection.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of unexplained bruising. His platelet count is normal, but his activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. Which inherited disorder is a common cause?
why_correct: An isolated prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time with a normal platelet count reflects a defect in the intrinsic coagulation pathway, classically an inherited factor VIII or IX deficiency (haemophilia).
why_wrong: A. Sickle-cell disease causes vaso-occlusive and haemolytic problems, not a coagulation factor deficiency. B. G6PD deficiency predisposes to haemolysis, not abnormal clotting times. C. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolytic anaemia. D. Iron-deficiency anaemia affects red-cell production, not coagulation factors.
pearl: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) are X-linked recessive, so they classically present in males, with an isolated prolonged APTT and normal PT.
thinking: Unexplained bruising + normal platelets ↓ prolonged APTT ↓ intrinsic pathway coagulation factor defect ↓ Haemophilia
exam_trap: A candidate might be drawn to sickle-cell disease because of 'bruising', but sickle-cell disease does not prolong the APTT; the clotting-screen abnormality is the key discriminator here.
takeaway: Normal platelets with an isolated prolonged APTT points to an inherited coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia.

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 39 weeks has regular painful contractions occurring every 5 minutes. Her cervix is progressively dilating. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Regular, painful contractions with progressive cervical dilatation at term define established (active) labour.
why_wrong: A. Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular and do not cause progressive cervical change. C. Hyperemesis causes severe vomiting, not contractions. D. Placenta praevia classically presents with painless vaginal bleeding, not labour pain alone. E. Ectopic pregnancy occurs early in pregnancy, outside the uterus.
pearl: Established labour is defined by regular painful contractions accompanied by progressive cervical dilatation, distinguishing it from the latent phase or false labour (Braxton Hicks).
thinking: Term pregnancy + regular painful contractions every 5 minutes ↓ progressive cervical dilatation ↓ meets definition of active labour ↓ Established labour
exam_trap: Candidates may consider Braxton Hicks contractions because they are common near term, but Braxton Hicks are irregular and do not cause progressive dilatation, unlike the pattern here.
takeaway: Regular contractions plus progressive cervical dilatation define established labour.

stem: A 29-year-old woman develops heavy bleeding immediately after giving birth. The uterus feels soft and enlarged. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A soft, poorly contracted ('boggy') uterus immediately after delivery with heavy bleeding is the hallmark of uterine atony, the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer does not present as an acute postpartum hemorrhage with a boggy uterus. B. Ectopic pregnancy is incompatible with an ongoing term delivery. D. Endometriosis does not cause acute postpartum bleeding. E. Placenta praevia relates to abnormal placental location and typically causes antepartum, not primary postpartum, bleeding of this type.
pearl: Uterine atony is managed with uterine massage, uterotonic drugs (such as oxytocin) and, if needed, escalation to surgical measures to control bleeding.
thinking: Immediate postpartum heavy bleeding ↓ uterus soft and enlarged on palpation ↓ failure of the uterus to contract down ↓ Uterine atony
exam_trap: A candidate might consider retained placenta as an alternative, but the stem's emphasis on a soft, poorly contracted uterus specifically signals atony as the primary mechanism.
takeaway: A soft, boggy uterus with heavy postpartum bleeding is uterine atony.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is 10 weeks pregnant and asks which vitamin should be taken to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. Which supplement is recommended?
why_correct: Folic acid taken before conception and through early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin K supports coagulation but has no established neural-tube protective role. C. Vitamin C has no established role in preventing neural tube defects. D. B12 is important generally but is not the standard supplement for this specific indication. E. Vitamin D supports bone health but does not replace folic acid for neural-tube protection.
pearl: Folic acid is recommended from before conception until at least the end of the first trimester, with a higher dose advised for women at increased risk of neural tube defects.
thinking: Pregnant patient asks about neural tube defect prevention ↓ recognised protective micronutrient ↓ standard recommended supplement ↓ Folic acid
exam_trap: A candidate might think of vitamin D as 'the standard pregnancy supplement', but vitamin D supports bone health, not neural tube closure, which is specifically linked to folic acid.
takeaway: Folic acid supplementation reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to clinic because his parents are concerned that he has become increasingly thirsty and urinates frequently, including overnight. He has also lost weight. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Polyuria (including nocturnal), polydipsia and unexplained weight loss in a child are the classic presenting triad of new-onset type 1 diabetes.
why_wrong: A. Cystic fibrosis can impair growth through malabsorption but does not characteristically cause polyuria and polydipsia. C. Hypothyroidism causes lethargy and weight gain, not this pattern. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and heavy proteinuria rather than polyuria with weight loss. E. Cranial diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia but not weight loss from hyperglycaemic catabolism.
pearl: Any child with new polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss needs an urgent capillary or laboratory glucose check, as delayed diagnosis risks progression to diabetic ketoacidosis.
thinking: Child + increasing thirst and urination, including at night ↓ associated unexplained weight loss ↓ classic hyperglycaemic triad ↓ Type 1 diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: Candidates may be tempted by diabetes insipidus because of polyuria and polydipsia, but DI does not explain the weight loss, which points instead to a catabolic, hyperglycaemic process.
takeaway: Polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss in a child are new type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise.

stem: A 9-year-old child has difficulty sustaining attention at school, frequently interrupts others and is constantly moving around. Symptoms occur both at school and at home. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.D: Specific phobia relating to school settings

why_correct: Pervasive inattention, impulsivity (interrupting) and hyperactivity occurring across more than one setting (school and home) meet the diagnostic pattern for ADHD.
why_wrong: B. Bipolar disorder causes discrete episodes of mood disturbance, not persistent inattention and hyperactivity across settings. C. Autism spectrum disorder is characterised by social-communication difficulties and restricted/repetitive behaviours, not primarily inattention and hyperactivity. D. A specific phobia causes marked fear of a specific trigger. E. Oppositional defiant disorder involves angry, defiant and argumentative behaviour rather than inattention and hyperactivity per se.
pearl: A defining diagnostic requirement for ADHD is that symptoms are present and impairing in more than one setting, which helps distinguish it from situational behavioural problems.
thinking: Inattention + interrupting + constant movement ↓ symptoms present at both school and home ↓ meets cross-setting ADHD criteria ↓ Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
