correct_answer: E. Explain honestly what happened, apologise and outline next steps
why_correct: Professional duty includes openness and honesty when things go wrong.
why_wrong: A. An investigation does not justify withholding basic information unnecessarily. B. Responsibility should not be misrepresented. C. Significant discussions should be documented appropriately. D. Describing an error as a recognised complication is misleading and breaches the duty of candour.
pearl: The professional duty of candour requires openness, honesty, explanation and apology when a patient has been harmed by an error.
thinking: Select the option embodying transparency and apology, rejecting any approach that delays disclosure, shifts blame, or avoids documentation.
exam_trap: Waiting for investigation completion before discussing the incident is a common wrong answer; duty of candour requires timely open disclosure, not silence pending formal review.
takeaway: Error causing harm = be open, honest, apologise, and explain next steps promptly.

stem: An 84-year-old woman is admitted after a fall. She takes multiple medications and has difficulty walking. She lives alone. Which intervention is most likely to reduce her future risk of falls?

options.A: Prescribing night sedation to reduce nocturnal wandering
options.B: Advising her to stay indoors to avoid outdoor trip hazards
options.C: A period of bed rest to allow full recovery from the fall
options.D: Multifactorial falls assessment with medication review
options.E: Providing a walking stick and hip protectors for home use

correct_answer: D. Multifactorial falls assessment with medication review
why_correct: Falls are multifactorial, so assessment should include medications, gait and balance, vision, environment and other relevant factors.
why_wrong: A. Sedatives increase falls risk. B. Restricting her activity reduces mobility and is not an effective preventive strategy. C. Bed rest causes deconditioning and increases falls risk. E. Hip protectors may reduce fracture risk but do not reduce falls, and a walking aid without assessment does not address multifactorial causes.
pearl: Falls in older adults are multifactorial, so a comprehensive assessment (medications, mobility, vision, environment) is the most effective preventive intervention.
thinking: Reject single, restrictive interventions (sedation, immobility, isolation) in favour of a holistic multifactorial falls assessment, which is the evidence-based approach.
exam_trap: Prescribing a sedative or recommending bed rest are dangerous distractors that would actually increase falls risk.
takeaway: Falls prevention = comprehensive multifactorial assessment, not restriction or sedation.

stem: A 65-year-old man has progressive difficulty swallowing and is found to have oesophageal cancer. He asks whether he should continue smoking. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: Cutting down gradually is sufficient during treatment
options.B: Defer stopping until cancer treatment is complete
options.C: Stopping now offers no benefit once cancer is diagnosed
options.D: Smoking cessation is contraindicated during cancer treatment
options.E: Encourage and support him to stop smoking now

correct_answer: E. Encourage and support him to stop smoking now
why_correct: Smoking cessation remains beneficial after a cancer diagnosis and should be supported.
why_wrong: A. Reducing intake is less beneficial than stopping; cessation should be supported. B. There is no reason to delay cessation. C. Stopping smoking still benefits treatment outcomes and general health. D. Cancer treatment is not a contraindication to smoking cessation.
pearl: Smoking cessation remains beneficial even after a cancer diagnosis and should always be encouraged.
thinking: Recognise that ongoing smoking continues to harm outcomes and increase risk even once malignancy is diagnosed, so cessation advice is never 'irrelevant'.
exam_trap: Options suggesting cessation is contraindicated or irrelevant after diagnosis are distractors testing whether candidates know cessation advice always applies.
takeaway: Cancer diagnosed: still encourage smoking cessation, it still helps.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has obesity, hypertension and a strong family history of type 2 diabetes. She has normal glucose testing. What is the most appropriate general preventive advice?

options.A: Repeat HbA1c every month to detect diabetes early
options.B: Start low-dose gliclazide to prevent onset of diabetes
options.C: Strict carbohydrate exclusion from her diet long term
options.D: Healthy diet, increased activity and weight loss
options.E: Start a course of antibiotics to alter the gut flora

correct_answer: D. Healthy diet, increased activity and weight loss
why_correct: Lifestyle modification can reduce the risk of developing type 2 diabetes in people at increased risk.
why_wrong: A. Monthly testing is not indicated; periodic review is appropriate for people at high risk. B. Sulfonylureas are not used to prevent diabetes and risk hypoglycaemia. C. Complete carbohydrate exclusion is unnecessary. E. Antibiotics do not prevent type 2 diabetes.
pearl: For people at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, lifestyle measures (diet, activity, weight management) are the cornerstone of prevention.
thinking: Favour the balanced lifestyle-modification answer over extreme or premature pharmacological options when glucose testing is currently normal.
exam_trap: Starting insulin immediately is a clear overcorrection distractor, since glucose testing is normal and no diabetes diagnosis has been made.
takeaway: High-risk, normal glucose = lifestyle advice, not drug treatment.

presentation: Family History and Breast Cancer Screening
stem: A 43-year-old woman asks about breast cancer screening because her mother was diagnosed with breast cancer at age 82. What is the most appropriate response?

options.B: She should have a prophylactic mastectomy
options.C: Her family history means she needs annual MRI surveillance
options.D: Screening is contraindicated because she has a family history
options.E: Assess familial risk, including her mother’s age at diagnosis

correct_answer: E. Assess familial risk, including her mother’s age at diagnosis
why_correct: Familial risk assessment considers the number and relationship of affected relatives, ages at diagnosis and cancer patterns.
why_wrong: A. There is no indication for chemotherapy in an unaffected person. B. Prophylactic surgery is not indicated. C. A single relative diagnosed at 82 does not place her in a high-risk group for MRI surveillance. D. Family history does not contraindicate screening.
pearl: Familial breast cancer risk assessment depends on the number of affected relatives, their relationship and especially their age at diagnosis.
thinking: Recognise that a mother's late-onset breast cancer (age 82) carries much lower familial risk implications than an early-onset case, so age at diagnosis must be factored into risk assessment rather than reacting to family history alone.
exam_trap: Jumping to prophylactic mastectomy or annual MRI overstates risk from a single late-onset relative; age at diagnosis is the discriminating factor being tested.
takeaway: Assess familial cancer risk using relatives' age at diagnosis, not family history alone.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has a cervical screening sample showing high-risk HPV but no significant cell changes. What does the HPV result indicate?

options.A: She needs urgent colposcopy and LLETZ treatment of the cervix
options.B: She should receive chemotherapy for early-stage cervical cancer
options.C: She has a risk factor for cervical changes needing follow-up
options.D: She has cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 needing treatment
options.E: She can return to routine recall without any further follow-up

correct_answer: C. She has a risk factor for cervical changes needing follow-up
why_correct: High-risk HPV is associated with cervical precancer and cancer but does not itself mean that cancer is present.
why_wrong: A. Colposcopy and LLETZ are not indicated for HPV positivity with normal cytology; early repeat testing is arranged. B. HPV positivity with normal cytology is not cancer, and chemotherapy is not treatment for isolated HPV positivity. D. CIN is diagnosed histologically, and normal cytology does not indicate CIN3. E. HPV positivity requires earlier repeat testing rather than routine recall.
pearl: A high-risk HPV-positive result with normal cytology indicates increased risk of cervical cell changes and requires appropriate follow-up, not immediate treatment.
thinking: Understand HPV as a risk factor rather than a diagnosis of cancer, guiding the response toward surveillance/follow-up rather than invasive treatment.
exam_trap: Assuming HPV positivity means cancer or requires hysterectomy is a dangerous overreaction distractor.
takeaway: HPV positive, normal cytology = risk factor needing follow-up, not a cancer diagnosis.

stem: A 14-year-old asks a doctor for advice about contraception and says she is sexually active. She appears frightened when asked whether anyone is forcing her to have sex. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Inform her parents straight away without discussing it with her
options.B: Provide contraception and focus on the reason she attended
options.C: Accept her account as consensual and prescribe contraception
options.D: Explore possible coercion sensitively and assess safeguarding risk
options.E: Refuse contraception until a parent attends with her

correct_answer: D. Explore possible coercion sensitively and assess safeguarding risk
why_correct: A disclosure or indication of possible coercion requires sensitive safeguarding assessment.
why_wrong: A. Disclosure to parents without discussion is not the first step and may deter her from seeking help; information sharing should follow safeguarding assessment. B. Signs of possible coercion cannot be set aside. C. Consent must not be assumed where there are safeguarding concerns. E. Refusing care may deter her from seeking help and fails to address the risk.
pearl: Signs of fear or possible coercion in a sexually active young person must trigger sensitive safeguarding exploration, regardless of the original reason for attendance.
thinking: Recognise behavioural red flags (fear when asked about coercion) as overriding the stated reason for the consultation, requiring a shift to safeguarding assessment.
exam_trap: Focusing only on the contraception request and ignoring the fear response is the key error the question is testing against.
takeaway: Fear or possible coercion disclosed = explore safeguarding concerns, don't just address the presenting request.

stem: A 7-year-old repeatedly arrives at school hungry, poorly dressed and with untreated skin infections. The teacher reports that the parents rarely respond to concerns. What should the clinician consider?

options.A: Immediate diagnosis of a psychiatric disorder in the child
options.E: Ignoring the issue unless the child requests help

correct_answer: C. Safeguarding concern requiring appropriate assessment
why_correct: Persistent neglect of basic needs and healthcare may indicate neglect and warrants safeguarding consideration.
why_wrong: A. The presentation does not establish a psychiatric diagnosis. B. Clinicians should follow safeguarding procedures rather than punish families. D. Persistent unmet basic needs are not simply normal variation. E. Children may not recognise or disclose neglect themselves.
pearl: Persistent signs of unmet basic needs (hunger, poor hygiene, untreated infections) despite parental awareness should raise a safeguarding concern for neglect.
thinking: Recognise the pattern of repeated, unaddressed basic needs as a safeguarding trigger requiring formal assessment, rather than normalising it as parenting variation.
exam_trap: Dismissing this as 'normal variation in parenting' is the dangerous distractor the question is testing against.
takeaway: Repeated unmet basic needs + unresponsive parents = safeguarding concern.

stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to hospital with a spiral fracture of the femur. The explanation given by the parent does not fit the developmental abilities of the child. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Treat the fracture and arrange GP follow-up in one week
options.B: Accept the explanation if the child appears well cared for and thriving
options.C: Request bone biochemistry to exclude metabolic bone disease before acting
options.D: Consider non-accidental injury and follow safeguarding procedures
options.E: Discharge with the parent once the fracture is immobilised in plaster

correct_answer: D. Consider non-accidental injury and follow safeguarding procedures
why_correct: An injury inconsistent with the history or developmental ability should raise safeguarding concerns.
why_wrong: A. Routine follow-up fails to address an injury inconsistent with the history. B. A well-cared-for, thriving appearance does not exclude abuse. C. Investigation for alternative causes may form part of assessment but must not delay safeguarding action. E. Discharge could place the child at risk.
pearl: An injury inconsistent with the child's developmental stage or the history given should raise suspicion of non-accidental injury and trigger safeguarding procedures.
thinking: Match the mismatch between injury type/mechanism and the child's developmental ability as the trigger for safeguarding action, rather than accepting the explanation at face value.
exam_trap: Accepting the parental explanation without question is the dangerous distractor; inconsistency with development is a key red flag for NAI.
takeaway: History doesn't fit developmental stage = consider non-accidental injury, follow safeguarding procedures.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has been prescribed a new medicine. She asks the pharmacist how she should take it because she cannot read the written instructions easily. What is the most appropriate response?

options.B: Assume she cannot consent to treatment
options.C: Explain in an accessible format and check understanding
options.D: Tell her to ask a relative to administer all medication

correct_answer: C. Explain in an accessible format and check understanding
why_correct: Patients should receive information in a form they can understand, with reasonable adjustments where necessary.
why_wrong: A. Online information may not be appropriate or accessible. B. Literacy difficulties do not imply lack of capacity. D. The patient should not unnecessarily lose independence. E. Difficulty reading does not justify withholding medication.
pearl: Information should be provided in a form the patient can understand (e.g. for low literacy), with understanding checked, as a reasonable adjustment.
thinking: Favour the inclusive, adjusted-communication option over options that either assume incapacity or exclude the patient from managing their own medication.
exam_trap: Assuming the patient cannot consent because of a literacy difficulty is a discriminatory distractor the question is testing against.
takeaway: Literacy difficulty = adapt information format and check understanding, don't assume incapacity.

stem: A doctor is asked to prescribe an antibiotic for a patient with a viral upper respiratory tract infection. There are no features suggesting bacterial infection. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Prescribe a 5-day course of amoxicillin to prevent secondary bacterial complications
options.B: Give a single dose of azithromycin to cover atypical organisms
options.C: Prescribe amoxicillin with clarithromycin to cover all the likely causative organisms
options.D: Prescribe phenoxymethylpenicillin because the patient has responded to it before
options.E: Explain antibiotics are unlikely to help; give symptom and safety-net advice

correct_answer: E. Explain antibiotics are unlikely to help; give symptom and safety-net advice
why_correct: Antibiotics should be used when clinically indicated; unnecessary prescribing contributes to antimicrobial resistance and exposes patients to adverse effects.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated to prevent complications of a viral URTI and cause adverse effects and resistance. B. A single dose is not indicated and still contributes to resistance. C. Dual antibiotic therapy increases unnecessary exposure without benefit. D. Previous response is not an indication; there are no features of bacterial infection.
pearl: Antibiotics should not be prescribed for viral upper respiratory infections; explain the rationale and give safety-netting advice instead.
thinking: Resist prescribing to meet patient expectation and instead choose the stewardship-aligned answer of explanation plus safety-netting.
exam_trap: Prescribing 'to meet patient expectations' is the classic antimicrobial stewardship trap tested here.
takeaway: Viral URTI, no bacterial features = explain and safety-net, don't prescribe antibiotics.

stem: A patient asks why a generic medicine looks different from the branded medicine they previously received. Which explanation is correct?

options.A: They contain a lower dose of the active ingredient to reduce their cost
options.B: They contain a similar but chemically different active ingredient
options.C: They are licensed for milder disease than the branded product
options.D: They contain the same active ingredient and must meet quality standards
options.E: They are newer formulations still undergoing phase III clinical trials

correct_answer: D. They contain the same active ingredient and must meet quality standards
why_correct: A generic medicine contains the same active pharmaceutical ingredient as the corresponding branded medicine, although appearance and some inactive ingredients may differ.
why_wrong: A. Generics contain the same dose of the active ingredient. B. The active ingredient is the same, not a chemically different analogue. C. Generics are not restricted to milder disease. E. They are established medicines, not experimental treatments.
pearl: Generic medicines contain the same active ingredient as the branded version and must meet the same quality and regulatory standards, though appearance may differ.
thinking: Dismiss options implying generics are inferior or inactive, and select the factually accurate explanation of bioequivalence and quality standards.
exam_trap: Options A and B are tempting myths that generics contain a lower dose or a different active ingredient; generics contain the same active ingredient at the same dose and must meet the same regulatory quality standards.
takeaway: Generic = same active ingredient, same quality standard, different appearance.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painful, swollen knee. She has psoriasis and has previously had episodes of swelling in several fingers. Which finding is particularly characteristic of psoriatic arthritis?
why_correct: Dactylitis (“sausage digit”) is a characteristic feature of psoriatic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid nodules occur in rheumatoid arthritis. C. Clubbing is associated with several systemic and pulmonary conditions, not specifically psoriatic arthritis. D. Heberden's nodes occur in osteoarthritis. E. Tophi are associated with chronic gout.
pearl: Dactylitis ('sausage digit') is a hallmark feature of psoriatic arthritis.
thinking: Link the history of psoriasis with prior finger swelling episodes to dactylitis as the classic associated sign, distinguishing it from rheumatoid or gouty features.
exam_trap: Rheumatoid nodules and tophi are distractors associated with other arthritides (RA and gout respectively), not psoriatic arthritis.
takeaway: Psoriasis + sausage digit = dactylitis, think psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a new diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. He asks why early treatment is important. What is the main reason?

options.A: To reverse joint erosions that are already established on X-ray
options.B: To eradicate the disease so that treatment can later be stopped
options.C: To control inflammation and limit irreversible joint damage
options.D: To relieve pain while the disease runs a self-limiting course
options.E: To avoid the need for regular blood test monitoring in future

correct_answer: C. To control inflammation and limit irreversible joint damage
why_correct: Early effective treatment of inflammatory arthritis reduces inflammation and helps prevent irreversible structural joint damage.
why_wrong: A. Established erosions are largely irreversible; early treatment aims to prevent them. B. Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic; DMARDs control rather than cure it. D. Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic and progressive rather than self-limiting. E. Disease-modifying treatment requires regular monitoring.
pearl: Early, effective treatment of rheumatoid arthritis reduces inflammation and limits irreversible joint damage.
thinking: Select the answer centred on preventing structural damage through inflammation control, rejecting absolute claims (curing genetic predisposition, preventing all infections).
exam_trap: Absolute options like 'cure the underlying genetic predisposition' are distractors that overstate what treatment can achieve.
takeaway: Early RA treatment = control inflammation to prevent permanent joint damage.

stem: A 59-year-old woman has severe hip pain and cannot weight-bear after a fall. Her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows an intracapsular fracture of the neck of femur. What is the major immediate concern?

options.A: Sciatic nerve injury from the fracture
options.E: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

correct_answer: E. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
why_correct: Intracapsular femoral neck fractures can disrupt the blood supply to the femoral head, causing avascular necrosis.
why_wrong: A. Sciatic nerve injury is associated mainly with posterior hip dislocation or acetabular fracture rather than intracapsular femoral neck fracture. B. Thigh compartment syndrome is rare and not the characteristic concern with this fracture. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve at the wrist. D. Chronic sinusitis is unrelated to the fracture.
pearl: Intracapsular femoral neck fractures risk disrupting the retinacular blood supply to the femoral head, causing avascular necrosis.
thinking: Recognise that the fracture's location (intracapsular) specifically threatens the vascular supply, distinguishing the major concern from unrelated musculoskeletal conditions listed as distractors.
exam_trap: Unrelated conditions (tennis elbow, carpal tunnel) are obvious distractors; the key teaching point is the vascular risk unique to intracapsular (vs extracapsular) fractures.
takeaway: Intracapsular NOF fracture = risk of avascular necrosis from disrupted blood supply.

stem: A 36-year-old woman develops sudden severe pain in her lower back after lifting a heavy box. The pain radiates down the posterior aspect of her leg to the foot. Which nerve root is most commonly affected in a typical L5/S1 disc prolapse causing this pattern?
why_correct: A typical L5/S1 disc prolapse can compress the S1 nerve root, causing pain radiating down the posterior leg.
why_wrong: A. S4 is not the usual root affected in a typical L5/S1 disc prolapse. B. C7 is a cervical nerve root. C. C5 is a cervical nerve root. D. T10 is a thoracic nerve root.
pearl: A classic L5/S1 disc prolapse compresses the S1 nerve root, causing pain radiating down the posterior leg.
thinking: Match the described radiation pattern (posterior leg to foot) with the dermatomal distribution of S1, the nerve root typically affected at this disc level.
exam_trap: Other root levels listed are distant distractors; the key is knowing L5/S1 prolapse classically affects S1, not L5, despite the naming of the disc level.
takeaway: L5/S1 disc prolapse classically compresses the S1 nerve root.

stem: A 44-year-old man has low back pain radiating down the lateral leg to the dorsum of the foot. Examination suggests weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
why_correct: L5 radiculopathy can cause pain over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot and weakness of ankle dorsiflexion.
why_wrong: B. S2 is not the typical root for this pattern. C. L3 contributes to knee extension and anterior thigh sensation. D. L4 is associated particularly with knee extension and the medial leg. E. L2 mainly contributes to hip flexion and upper anterior thigh sensation.
pearl: L5 radiculopathy causes pain over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot with weakness of ankle dorsiflexion.
thinking: Match the lateral leg/dorsum of foot distribution and dorsiflexion weakness to the L5 dermatome and myotome specifically.
exam_trap: S1 (associated with plantarflexion weakness and posterior leg pain) is the classic confusable root level distractor.
takeaway: Lateral leg/dorsum of foot pain + weak dorsiflexion = L5 nerve root.

stem: A newborn develops respiratory distress shortly after birth. The mother received no antenatal corticosteroids and the baby was born prematurely. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Prematurity increases the risk of surfactant deficiency, causing neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Meconium aspiration typically affects term or post-term infants. C. Transient tachypnoea is more typical after term caesarean delivery and is usually mild and self-limiting. D. Epiglottitis is an acute upper-airway infection in children. E. Croup occurs in older infants and young children.
pearl: Prematurity with lack of antenatal corticosteroids increases the risk of surfactant deficiency causing neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
thinking: Link prematurity and absent antenatal steroids (which promote surfactant production) directly to the diagnosis of neonatal RDS.
exam_trap: Other paediatric respiratory conditions (croup, bronchiolitis) are distractors that occur later in infancy, not immediately after premature birth.
takeaway: Preterm birth, no antenatal steroids, early respiratory distress = neonatal RDS.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a new sexual partner and asks whether she should have an STI screen despite having no symptoms. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Advise testing if symptoms develop after the new relationship
options.B: STI testing is unnecessary in asymptomatic people
options.C: Offer testing guided by her sexual history and risk
options.D: Give empirical doxycycline for chlamydia without testing first
options.E: Offer HIV testing alone because it is the main risk to her

correct_answer: C. Offer testing guided by her sexual history and risk
why_correct: STI screening can be appropriate in asymptomatic people depending on sexual history and individual risk.
why_wrong: A. Many STIs are asymptomatic, so waiting for symptoms may miss infection and allow transmission. B. Many STIs can be asymptomatic. D. Empirical antibiotics without testing are not appropriate in an asymptomatic person. E. Testing should cover relevant infections such as chlamydia and gonorrhoea, not HIV alone.
pearl: STI testing in asymptomatic patients should be guided by individual sexual history and risk factors, not withheld simply because they are symptom-free.
thinking: Reject blanket 'no testing needed' or 'test only if symptomatic' answers in favour of individualised risk-based discussion.
exam_trap: 'STI testing is unnecessary in asymptomatic people' is a dangerous absolute-statement distractor.
takeaway: New partner, asymptomatic = discuss risk-based STI screening, don't dismiss it.

stem: A patient taking spironolactone develops breast tenderness and enlargement. Which adverse effect is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Spironolactone can cause gynaecomastia because of its anti-androgenic effects.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment is not an adverse effect of spironolactone. B. Pulmonary fibrosis is associated with drugs such as amiodarone, methotrexate and nitrofurantoin, not spironolactone. C. Peptic ulceration is associated with NSAIDs and corticosteroids rather than spironolactone. E. Osteoporosis is associated with long-term corticosteroids, not spironolactone.
pearl: Spironolactone's anti-androgenic activity commonly causes gynaecomastia and breast tenderness.
thinking: Link the anti-androgenic pharmacology of spironolactone directly to its known adverse effect of gynaecomastia, a frequently tested drug-effect pairing.
exam_trap: Unrelated adverse effects (pulmonary fibrosis, osteoporosis) are distractors that belong to other drug classes entirely.
takeaway: Spironolactone = anti-androgenic effects including gynaecomastia.

stem: A patient taking a thiazide diuretic develops acute pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Which adverse metabolic effect may have contributed?
why_correct: Thiazide diuretics can increase serum urate and may precipitate gout in susceptible patients.
why_wrong: A. They do not characteristically cause vitamin B12 deficiency. B. Hyperbilirubinaemia does not explain the presentation. C. Hypocalcaemia is not the characteristic effect relevant here. E. Thiazides do not cause hyperthyroidism.
pearl: Thiazide diuretics can raise serum urate and precipitate gout attacks in susceptible patients.
thinking: Connect the known metabolic effect of thiazides (reduced urate excretion, hyperuricaemia) to the acute gout presentation described.
exam_trap: Unrelated metabolic effects (B12 deficiency, hypocalcaemia) are distractors; thiazides actually cause hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia, reinforcing the correct mechanism here.
takeaway: Thiazide diuretics can precipitate gout via hyperuricaemia.

stem: A patient taking metformin is scheduled for an investigation involving iodinated contrast. The clinician reviews whether metformin should be temporarily withheld based on renal function and the specific clinical circumstances. Why is renal function relevant?

options.A: Metformin directly increases the nephrotoxicity of contrast
options.B: Metformin can accumulate in significant renal impairment
options.C: Metformin is directly nephrotoxic, in the same way as gentamicin
options.D: Metformin is mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism, not the kidney
options.E: Metformin commonly causes acute kidney injury after contrast

correct_answer: B. Metformin can accumulate in significant renal impairment
why_correct: Metformin is renally cleared, so significant renal impairment increases the risk of accumulation and lactic acidosis.
why_wrong: A. Metformin does not increase contrast nephrotoxicity; the concern is accumulation if renal function deteriorates. C. Metformin is not directly nephrotoxic; the concern is accumulation if renal function deteriorates. D. Metformin is excreted unchanged by the kidneys rather than hepatically metabolised. E. Metformin does not commonly cause acute kidney injury, after contrast or otherwise.
pearl: Metformin is renally cleared, so significant renal impairment increases the risk of accumulation and lactic acidosis, relevant when iodinated contrast is used.
thinking: Apply the pharmacokinetic principle that renal clearance governs metformin safety, explaining why renal function is reviewed before and after contrast exposure.
exam_trap: Claiming metformin is nephrotoxic itself, or mainly cleared by hepatic metabolism (it is excreted unchanged by the kidneys), are factually incorrect distractors confusing mechanism.
takeaway: Metformin + contrast: renal function matters because of accumulation/lactic acidosis risk in renal impairment.

stem: A patient taking levothyroxine asks why they should take it consistently at the same time and in relation to food. What is the main reason?

options.A: It has a short half-life, so levels fall quickly
options.B: Food and some medicines can reduce its absorption

correct_answer: B. Food and some medicines can reduce its absorption
why_correct: Consistent administration helps maintain predictable levothyroxine absorption and thyroid hormone replacement.
why_wrong: A. Levothyroxine has a long half-life of about a week, so levels do not fall within hours. C. It is orally absorbed. D. It does not convert into insulin. E. Levothyroxine is thyroid hormone replacement.
pearl: Levothyroxine absorption can be affected by food and other medicines, so consistent timing helps maintain stable thyroid hormone levels.
thinking: Link the rationale for consistent dosing timing to variable absorption with food/interacting drugs, rather than unrelated or incorrect mechanisms.
exam_trap: Options describing levothyroxine as an antibiotic or converting to insulin are clearly incorrect distractors testing basic pharmacology knowledge.
takeaway: Levothyroxine: take consistently because food/other drugs affect its absorption.

stem: A 58-year-old man has newly diagnosed hypertension. His clinician asks about alcohol intake. Why is this relevant?

options.A: Alcohol mainly affects cholesterol rather than blood pressure
options.B: Alcohol lowers blood pressure in moderate drinkers
options.D: Excess alcohol intake can raise blood pressure
options.E: Alcohol is required for effective antihypertensive treatment

correct_answer: D. Excess alcohol intake can raise blood pressure
why_correct: Excessive alcohol intake is a modifiable risk factor for hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
why_wrong: A. Alcohol raises blood pressure directly, independent of its effects on lipids. B. Alcohol does not reliably lower blood pressure, and regular intake tends to raise it. C. Alcohol does not prevent stroke. E. Alcohol is not required for antihypertensive treatment.
pearl: Excessive alcohol consumption is a modifiable contributor to raised blood pressure and should be assessed in all hypertensive patients.
thinking: Recognise alcohol intake as a reversible, lifestyle-related risk factor for hypertension that should routinely be assessed and addressed.
exam_trap: Claims that alcohol 'prevents stroke' or 'is required for effective treatment' are clearly incorrect distractors testing basic risk-factor knowledge.
takeaway: Excess alcohol is a modifiable risk factor for hypertension — always ask about intake.

stem:
A woman taking an ACE inhibitor discovers that she is pregnant.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Continue it until the end of the first trimester, then stop
options.B: Halve the dose and continue it under close obstetric review
options.C: Review the medicine promptly and switch to an alternative
options.D: Continue it, as ACE inhibitors are considered safe in pregnancy
options.E: Continue it but stop at 36 weeks in preparation for delivery

correct_answer: C. Review the medicine promptly and switch to an alternative
why_correct: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity (risk of renal damage and oligohydramnios). The medicine should be reviewed promptly and switched to an alternative such as labetalol, ideally within 2 days of the pregnancy being found (NICE NG133).
why_wrong: A. ACE inhibitors should be stopped promptly once pregnancy is known. B. Any dose of an ACE inhibitor carries fetal risk. D. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity. E. Continuing until 36 weeks risks fetal harm.
pearl: ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic, particularly in the second and third trimesters, where they can cause oligohydramnios, renal impairment and skull ossification defects.
thinking: Any pregnancy-plus-ACE-inhibitor stem is testing a known fetotoxicity principle: stop the drug and switch to a pregnancy-safe alternative rather than continuing or escalating it.
exam_trap: Candidates who are unsure sometimes default to 'continue but monitor', missing that ACE inhibitors are an absolute reason to switch antihypertensive class in pregnancy.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor plus pregnancy equals stop and switch, not continue and monitor.

stem: Which route is an important mode of transmission of hepatitis B virus?
why_correct: Hepatitis B is transmitted through infected blood and body fluids, including sexual transmission and perinatal transmission.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis B is not spread through respiratory droplets. B. Swimming pools are not a recognised transmission route. C. Casual contact does not transmit hepatitis B. E. Foodborne transmission is not the usual route of hepatitis B infection.
pearl: Hepatitis B is transmitted through blood, body fluids, sexual contact and perinatally, not via the faecal-oral or airborne routes.
thinking: Recall the bloodborne virus transmission pattern shared with HIV and hepatitis C, and eliminate options describing faecal-oral or airborne spread, which fit other pathogens.
exam_trap: Eating contaminated food is tempting because of the general 'hepatitis' association, but faecal-oral spread belongs to hepatitis A (and E), not hepatitis B.
takeaway: Hepatitis B travels in blood and body fluids, not food or air.

stem: Why does atrial fibrillation increase the risk of ischaemic stroke?

options.A: It accelerates carotid atherosclerotic plaque growth
options.B: It causes paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
options.C: It raises blood viscosity through secondary polycythaemia
options.D: It causes inflammation of the small cerebral arteries
options.E: Atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation

correct_answer: E. Atrial blood stasis promotes thrombus formation
why_correct: Ineffective atrial contraction can cause blood stasis and thrombus formation, with subsequent systemic embolisation.
why_wrong: A. AF does not cause carotid atherosclerosis; carotid disease is a separate stroke mechanism. B. Paradoxical embolism requires a venous thrombus crossing a right-to-left shunt and is not the AF mechanism. C. AF does not cause polycythaemia or raised blood viscosity. D. AF does not cause cerebral vasculitis.
pearl: Loss of coordinated atrial contraction in AF causes blood stasis (especially in the left atrial appendage), promoting thrombus formation and embolic stroke.
thinking: Trace the mechanism from ineffective atrial contraction to stasis, clot formation and systemic embolisation to the brain.
exam_trap: Carotid atherosclerosis and paradoxical embolism through a PFO are real stroke mechanisms, which makes them tempting, but neither is how AF causes stroke. AF stroke is cardioembolic, from thrombus forming in the stagnant left atrium (especially the appendage).
takeaway: AF causes stasis, stasis causes clots, clots cause stroke.

stem:
A patient taking an oral bisphosphonate asks how it should generally be taken.

Which instruction is appropriate?

options.A: Swallow with a full glass of water and stay upright afterwards
options.B: Crush it and mix with yoghurt if swallowing tablets is difficult
options.C: Take it at bedtime so it acts overnight while lying down
options.D: Take it with an antacid or calcium supplement to reduce irritation
options.E: Take it with a large meal to maximise absorption

correct_answer: A. Swallow with a full glass of water and stay upright afterwards
why_correct: Oral bisphosphonates can irritate the oesophagus and have specific administration requirements to improve absorption and reduce oesophageal injury.
why_wrong: B. Crushing and mixing with food is inappropriate; food and dairy reduce absorption and oesophageal irritation risk increases. C. Lying down soon after taking it increases oesophageal irritation risk. D. Antacids and calcium reduce absorption and should be separated in time. E. Food can reduce absorption of oral bisphosphonates.
pearl: Oral bisphosphonates should be swallowed whole with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, remaining upright for at least 30 minutes (60 minutes for oral ibandronic acid) to reduce oesophageal irritation and aid absorption.
thinking: Recall the specific administration instructions designed to maximise absorption and prevent oesophagitis, rejecting any option involving food, antacids or calcium, lying down, or crushing the tablet.
exam_trap: Taking it with a meal or lying down afterward are classic wrong answers that would reduce absorption or risk oesophageal injury.
takeaway: Oral bisphosphonates: empty stomach, plain water, stay upright at least 30 minutes (60 for ibandronic acid).

stem: A patient with severe vomiting develops weakness. Blood tests show hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis. What is the main mechanism causing the potassium loss?

options.B: Renal loss driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism
options.C: Reduced aldosterone secretion due to volume overload
options.D: Direct potassium loss in the vomited gastric fluid
options.E: Intracellular potassium shift from insulin excess

correct_answer: B. Renal loss driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism
why_correct: Vomiting loses H⁺ and Cl⁻, causing metabolic alkalosis and volume depletion; the resulting secondary hyperaldosteronism and increased distal bicarbonate delivery drive renal potassium wasting, which is the main cause of hypokalaemia.
why_wrong: A. Phosphate absorption does not affect potassium balance in this way. C. Aldosterone secretion is increased, not reduced, by volume depletion in vomiting. D. Gastric fluid contains relatively little potassium, so direct losses contribute only a small amount. E. Insulin excess is not a feature of vomiting; the main potassium loss is renal.
pearl: Vomiting causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis mainly through renal potassium wasting driven by volume depletion and secondary hyperaldosteronism, not by direct potassium loss in the vomitus.
thinking: This requires two-step reasoning: vomiting loses hydrochloric acid causing alkalosis and volume depletion, which triggers aldosterone-mediated renal potassium wasting, the indirect renal mechanism rather than direct GI loss that explains the hypokalaemia.
exam_trap: The most common error is picking direct potassium loss in the vomitus, since it seems intuitive, but gastric fluid is actually low in potassium, and the real mechanism is renal.
takeaway: Vomiting causes hypokalaemia mainly via the kidney through aldosterone, not from the vomit itself.

stem:
A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency department with a unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge. Examination reveals a small object in the right nostril.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Prescribe a topical nasal steroid spray for a week
options.B: Refer for immediate septoplasty by the ENT team
options.C: Start oral antibiotics and review again in one week
options.D: Attempt removal with a nasal suction catheter
options.E: Arrange urgent CT of the sinuses before removal

correct_answer: D. Attempt removal with a nasal suction catheter
why_correct: A visible nasal foreign body should generally be removed. Suction is one appropriate method when the object can be safely accessed.
why_wrong: A. Steroids do not treat the underlying problem. B. Septoplasty is not indicated. C. Antibiotics do not remove the foreign body. E. Imaging is usually unnecessary when the object is visible and delays removal.
pearl: Unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge in a young child is a classic sign of a retained nasal foreign body; button batteries and magnets need emergency removal due to tissue damage risk.
thinking: Unilateral, not bilateral, foul discharge in a toddler is the pattern-recognition clue for a foreign body, and management follows a stepwise approach of attempting removal and escalating to ENT if unsuccessful.
exam_trap: Candidates might reach for antibiotics to treat the 'infection' implied by the discharge, missing that the underlying foreign body must be removed first.
takeaway: Unilateral foul nasal discharge in a toddler means foreign body until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient is prescribed a medicine with a narrow therapeutic index. What does this mean?

options.A: The medicine is only available intravenously
options.B: Small changes in dose can cause toxicity
options.C: The medicine is ineffective at therapeutic doses
options.D: The medicine can never cause adverse effects
options.E: The medicine has no measurable plasma concentration

correct_answer: B. Small changes in dose can cause toxicity
why_correct: A narrow therapeutic index means the toxic and therapeutic concentrations are relatively close.
why_wrong: A. Route of administration is unrelated to therapeutic index. C. Narrow therapeutic index does not mean ineffective. D. These medicines may cause significant adverse effects. E. Plasma concentrations may be measurable and often require monitoring.
pearl: Medicines with a narrow therapeutic index, such as warfarin, lithium and digoxin, typically require closer monitoring because small concentration changes can tip into toxicity.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic index means the therapeutic and toxic concentrations lie close together, so a small change in dose or plasma level (e.g. from an interacting drug or reduced renal function) can push the patient into toxicity: option B.
exam_trap: Candidates may pick an absolute distractor (never causes adverse effects, no measurable concentration). A narrow therapeutic index simply means a small margin between the effective and toxic concentration, so monitoring is often needed.
takeaway: Narrow therapeutic index = small gap between an effective dose and a toxic one.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a routine health check. She is asymptomatic. Thyroid function tests: TSH 6.5 mIU/L (normal 0.4–4.0), free T4 14 pmol/L (normal 10–22). What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as an elevated TSH with a normal free T4. The thyroid is beginning to fail but free T4 remains within the normal range. TSH of 6.5 is clearly elevated — this is not normal thyroid function.
why_wrong: A. Primary hypothyroidism requires a low free T4 — free T4 here is 14 pmol/L, which is normal. C. Euthyroid sick syndrome occurs in acute illness with low T3 — not in a well outpatient. D. Secondary hypothyroidism shows low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4. E. Normal TSH is 0.4–4.0 — 6.5 is elevated.
pearl: High TSH + normal free T4 = subclinical hypothyroidism. NICE NG145: confirm with repeat TFTs in 3 months; consider levothyroxine if TSH ≥10 mIU/L on 2 occasions 3 months apart, or a 6-month trial if under 65 with TSH above range but <10 and symptoms of hypothyroidism.
thinking: Asymptomatic woman at a routine check ↓ TSH raised above the reference range ↓ Free T4 still within the normal range ↓ Raised TSH with normal free T4 defines the diagnosis ↓ B, subclinical hypothyroidism
exam_trap: Do not call TSH 6.5 normal. Subclinical hypothyroidism does not require immediate treatment in all patients but does need follow-up and monitoring.
takeaway: High TSH + normal free T4 = subclinical hypothyroidism.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with 6 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and fatigue. HbA1c is 52 mmol/mol (6.9%). What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.D: Requires a second confirmatory test before diagnosis

why_correct: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) diagnoses diabetes mellitus. This patient has an HbA1c of 52 mmol/mol with classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue). In a symptomatic patient, a single elevated HbA1c is sufficient for diagnosis — a second test is only needed in asymptomatic patients.
why_wrong: A. Normal HbA1c is <42 mmol/mol. B. Prediabetes is 42–47 mmol/mol — 52 exceeds this. D. A second test is required only in asymptomatic patients — this patient has classic symptoms, so one result is sufficient. E. No information suggests anaemia; assuming artefact without evidence is inappropriate.
pearl: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol = diabetes. 42–47 = prediabetes. <42 = normal. Symptomatic patient = one result sufficient. Asymptomatic = two results required.
thinking: Classic osmotic symptoms: polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue ↓ HbA1c 52 is above the 48 mmol/mol diagnostic cut-off ↓ Symptomatic, so one diagnostic result is enough ↓ C, type 2 diabetes mellitus
exam_trap: Symptomatic patients need only one abnormal HbA1c for diagnosis. The presence of classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) removes the need for confirmation.
takeaway: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol + symptoms = type 2 diabetes. One test sufficient when symptomatic.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has a DXA scan showing a T-score of -3.0 at the left hip. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: WHO DXA classification for postmenopausal women and men over 50: T-score -1.0 to -2.5 = osteopenia; T-score ≤-2.5 = osteoporosis. A T-score of -3.0 meets the threshold for osteoporosis. No fragility fracture is mentioned, so this is osteoporosis (not severe osteoporosis).
why_wrong: A. Osteopenia is T-score -1.0 to -2.5 — -3.0 is below this range. C. Normal is T-score ≥-1.0. D. Severe osteoporosis requires T-score ≤-2.5 AND a fragility fracture — none described. E. Osteomalacia cannot be diagnosed on DXA — it requires biochemistry and X-ray.
pearl: T-score: ≥-1.0 = normal. -1.0 to -2.5 = osteopenia. ≤-2.5 = osteoporosis. ≤-2.5 + fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis.
thinking: DXA T-score of −3.0 at the hip ↓ T-score at or below −2.5 means osteoporosis ↓ No fragility fracture described, so not 'severe' ↓ B, osteoporosis
exam_trap: Do not call it severe osteoporosis without a fragility fracture. T-score -3.0 without fracture = osteoporosis.
takeaway: T-score ≤-2.5 = osteoporosis. Severe = T-score ≤-2.5 + fragility fracture.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with epigastric burning pain that worsens after meals and at night when lying down. The pain is partially relieved by antacids. She has no weight loss or dysphagia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Burning epigastric pain worsened after meals and when lying flat, with relief from antacids, is classic for GORD. The absence of alarm features (weight loss, dysphagia, bleeding) makes malignancy unlikely.
why_wrong: A. Gastric cancer presents with alarm features — weight loss, early satiety, dysphagia. B. Peptic ulcer disease is not characteristically worsened by lying flat. D. Gallstones cause RUQ pain after fatty meals, not a burning quality worsened by lying flat. E. Chronic pancreatitis causes persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back with steatorrhoea.
pearl: GORD: burning epigastric or retrosternal pain, worse after meals and lying flat, relieved by antacids. No alarm features = 4-week trial of PPI. Alarm features = urgent referral, not a PPI trial.
thinking: Burning epigastric pain ↓ Worse after meals and when lying flat ↓ Relieved by antacids, no weight loss or dysphagia ↓ Reflux pattern without alarm features ↓ C, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
exam_trap: Do not trial a PPI in a patient with alarm features. Alarm features (dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 with weight loss plus dyspepsia, reflux or upper abdominal pain) = suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12, 2025); haematemesis = immediate assessment.
takeaway: Burning epigastric pain, worse after meals and lying flat, relieved by antacids = GORD.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with epigastric pain that awakens him at night. Eating food relieves the pain. He has no weight loss or vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Epigastric pain that awakens at night and is relieved by food is classic for duodenal ulcer. Food temporarily buffers gastric acid, relieving the pain. Nocturnal pain is characteristic because acid secretion peaks at night without the buffering effect of food.
why_wrong: A. Gastric ulcer pain is typically worsened by food — patients may avoid eating, leading to weight loss. C. GORD causes burning pain worsened after meals and lying flat — not relieved by eating. D. Gastric cancer presents with alarm features such as weight loss. E. Pancreatitis causes severe persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.
pearl: Duodenal ulcer: pain relieved by food, nocturnal pain. Gastric ulcer: pain worsened by food. Both associated with H. pylori — test and treat.
thinking: Epigastric pain that wakes him at night ↓ Eating relieves the pain ↓ No weight loss or vomiting to suggest malignancy ↓ Nocturnal, food-relieved pain is the duodenal pattern ↓ B, duodenal ulcer
exam_trap: The key discriminator: duodenal ulcer pain is RELIEVED by food; gastric ulcer pain is WORSENED by food.
takeaway: Epigastric pain relieved by food + nocturnal pain = duodenal ulcer.

presentation: Irritable bowel syndrome — diagnosis and coeliac exclusion
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with 2 years of recurrent central abdominal pain, bloating, and alternating diarrhoea and constipation. She has no weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, or rectal bleeding. Examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis and what investigation must be excluded first?

options.A: Crohn's disease — colonoscopy with ileal biopsies first
options.B: IBS — exclude coeliac disease with anti-tTG first
options.C: Colorectal cancer — urgent CT colonography first
options.D: Lactose intolerance — lactose hydrogen breath test first
options.E: Diverticular disease — CT abdomen and pelvis first

correct_answer: B. IBS — exclude coeliac disease with anti-tTG first
why_correct: The clinical picture is consistent with IBS: chronic abdominal pain related to bowel habit change, bloating, alternating bowel habit, no alarm features, and young age. However, NICE mandates that coeliac disease is excluded with anti-tTG antibodies in all suspected IBS before confirming the diagnosis, as coeliac disease can present identically.
why_wrong: A. IBD typically causes diarrhoea with weight loss, nocturnal symptoms or bleeding — none present here. C. Colorectal cancer is very unlikely at 35 without alarm features. D. Lactose intolerance causes symptoms related to dairy intake — not a 2-year history of alternating bowel habit. E. Diverticular disease is uncommon at 35 and does not explain this pattern.
pearl: NICE: exclude coeliac disease (anti-tTG + IgA) in ALL suspected IBS before confirming the diagnosis. If negative, diagnose IBS and manage with dietary advice, antispasmodics, and low-FODMAP diet.
thinking: Two years of pain, bloating and alternating bowel habit ↓ Young, with no weight loss, nocturnal symptoms or bleeding ↓ Fits IBS, but coeliac disease can mimic it exactly ↓ B, IBS, after excluding coeliac disease with anti-tTG
exam_trap: IBS is a diagnosis of exclusion — coeliac must be excluded first. The exam tests whether you know to check anti-tTG before labelling a patient with IBS.
takeaway: Chronic abdominal pain + altered bowel habit + no red flags = IBS. Exclude coeliac first with anti-tTG.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with severe right iliac fossa pain, nausea, and anorexia. Temperature is 38.2°C. Examination reveals tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: RIF pain, anorexia (highly specific for appendicitis), fever, and peritonism (guarding, rebound tenderness) in a young adult is classic for acute appendicitis. Urgent surgical referral is required.
why_wrong: B. Diverticulitis causes left iliac fossa pain in older patients. C. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain without peritonism. D. Mesenteric adenitis typically affects younger children with less localised tenderness and no peritonism. E. Psoas abscess causes pain on hip extension and is much less common.
pearl: Anorexia is one of the most discriminating features of appendicitis. In women of childbearing age, always exclude ectopic pregnancy with a urine pregnancy test.
thinking: Young adult with RIF pain, nausea and anorexia ↓ Fever of 38.2°C ↓ Localised guarding and rebound mean peritonism ↓ Classic inflamed appendix picture ↓ A, acute appendicitis
exam_trap: Always exclude ectopic pregnancy in women of childbearing age before diagnosing appendicitis — ectopic can mimic it exactly. The stem specifies a man here.
takeaway: RIF pain + anorexia + fever + peritonism = acute appendicitis. Urgent surgical referral.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with severe left iliac fossa pain, fever, and constipation. Examination reveals LIF tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute diverticulitis classically presents in older patients with left iliac fossa pain (sigmoid colon), fever, and change in bowel habit. This triad in a 72-year-old is the classic presentation.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis, including retrocaecal, causes right-sided pain — not left. C. Sigmoid volvulus causes massive abdominal distension and absolute constipation, not localised LIF tenderness with fever. D. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain without fever or localised tenderness. E. Ovarian torsion is less common at 72 and presents differently — not fever with constipation.
pearl: Diverticulitis: LIF pain + fever + change in bowel habit in older patient. Uncomplicated: consider no antibiotics if systemically well; oral antibiotics if systemically unwell, immunosuppressed or significant comorbidity. Complicated (abscess, perforation, obstruction) = CT + admission.
thinking: Older woman with left iliac fossa pain ↓ Fever with change in bowel habit ↓ Localised LIF tenderness, no gross distension ↓ Sigmoid diverticular inflammation ↓ B, acute diverticulitis
exam_trap: Appendicitis = right-sided. Diverticulitis = left-sided. Side of pain is the key differentiator.
takeaway: LIF pain + fever + older patient = diverticulitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with acute onset nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhoea. He returned from Egypt 2 days ago. He has no blood in his stool. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute onset nausea, vomiting, and watery diarrhoea in a returning traveller is most likely infectious gastroenteritis. Common pathogens include enterotoxigenic E. coli, Campylobacter, Salmonella, and viruses. Management is oral rehydration; antibiotics for severe or prolonged cases.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes RIF pain with peritonism — not acute watery diarrhoea in a traveller. C. IBD typically causes chronic or relapsing symptoms, not acute onset after travel. D. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorption — not acute diarrhoea after travel. E. Giardiasis causes subacute or chronic diarrhoea (1–3 weeks post-exposure) — too slow for symptoms 2 days after return.
pearl: Most travellers' diarrhoea is self-limiting (3–5 days). Rehydration is the mainstay. Consider Giardia if symptoms persist >2 weeks.
thinking: Acute vomiting and watery diarrhoea ↓ Onset within two days of returning from Egypt ↓ No blood; too soon for giardiasis ↓ Infective, traveller's pattern ↓ B, acute gastroenteritis
exam_trap: Giardia takes 1–3 weeks to cause symptoms after exposure — too slow for symptoms appearing 2 days after return. Acute onset = bacterial or viral gastroenteritis.
takeaway: Acute diarrhoea and vomiting in a returning traveller = gastroenteritis. Rehydration first.

presentation: Drug side effects — metformin and GI symptoms
stem: A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes presents with recurrent central abdominal bloating and nausea. She takes metformin, ramipril, and atorvastatin. Examination is normal. Which medication is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Metformin commonly causes gastrointestinal side effects: nausea, abdominal bloating, diarrhoea, and abdominal pain. These are dose-related and occur in up to 30% of patients. They can be reduced by taking metformin with food, starting at a low dose, or switching to modified-release metformin.
why_wrong: A. Ramipril causes dry cough and angioedema — not abdominal bloating. B. Atorvastatin occasionally causes myalgia and rarely elevated LFTs — not bloating. D. Omeprazole is not listed in this patient's medications — do not introduce drugs not in the stem. E. Bisoprolol causes fatigue, bradycardia — not GI symptoms.
pearl: Metformin GI side effects are dose-related and often improve with modified-release formulation or taking with meals. The most common reason for dose reduction in T2DM management.
thinking: Recurrent GI symptoms: bloating and nausea ↓ Drug list: metformin, ramipril, atorvastatin ↓ Only metformin commonly causes GI upset ↓ Normal examination supports a drug effect ↓ C, metformin
exam_trap: Always consider medication side effects when a patient on metformin presents with GI symptoms. This is one of the most common drug-related GI complaints in primary care.
takeaway: Abdominal bloating and nausea in a patient on metformin = metformin side effect until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with asthma presents with severe breathlessness and wheeze. She is unable to complete sentences comfortably and has marked respiratory distress.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Treat as an acute severe asthma attack and escalate urgently
options.B: Give a sedative and allow her to rest
options.C: Discharge her if she has no fever
options.D: Give antibiotics routinely before bronchodilator treatment

correct_answer: A. Treat as an acute severe asthma attack and escalate urgently
why_correct: Severe breathlessness and difficulty speaking in a patient with asthma are warning features requiring urgent treatment and reassessment. Source: NICE/BTS/SIGN guidance on asthma.
why_wrong: B. Sedatives can worsen respiratory compromise. C. Absence of fever does not exclude severe asthma. D. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for asthma attacks. E. Routine spirometry is inappropriate during an acute severe attack.
pearl: Do not let the presence or absence of wheeze alone determine severity; a very unwell patient may have a quiet chest.
thinking: Asthma + severe symptoms  ↓  recognise severity  ↓  immediate treatment and reassessment.
exam_trap: C, discharging her if she has no fever — fever has nothing to do with asthma severity; inability to complete sentences marks a severe attack needing urgent treatment.
takeaway: Inability to complete sentences in asthma signals an acute severe attack: treat and escalate urgently.

stem:
A 70-year-old man with severe COPD presents with an acute exacerbation and hypoxaemia. He is at risk of carbon dioxide retention.

What is the most appropriate oxygen strategy?

options.A: Give 15 L/min oxygen via a non-rebreather mask
options.B: Withhold oxygen until arterial blood gas results are available
options.C: Give controlled oxygen to an appropriate target saturation
options.D: Titrate oxygen to keep saturations between 94% and 98%
options.E: Give oxygen via nasal cannula at 6 L/min regardless of saturations

correct_answer: C. Give controlled oxygen to an appropriate target saturation
why_correct: Patients with COPD who are at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure require controlled oxygen therapy with an appropriate target saturation rather than indiscriminate high-concentration oxygen. Source: NICE NG115, COPD.
why_wrong: A. High-concentration oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients. B. Hypoxaemia should be treated while awaiting blood gas results. D. 94–98% is the target for patients not at risk of hypercapnia. E. Fixed oxygen without titration to a target risks hyperoxia and hypercapnia.
pearl: The key PLAB 1 concept is controlled oxygen, not simply "oxygen is dangerous in COPD."
thinking: COPD + acute hypoxaemia + risk of hypercapnia  ↓  controlled oxygen.
exam_trap: D, a 94–98% target — correct for most patients, but those at risk of carbon dioxide retention need a lower, controlled target of 88–92%.
takeaway: COPD at risk of hypercapnia: controlled oxygen to 88–92%, and never withhold oxygen while awaiting gases.

stem:
A 55-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Her pulse is 112/min. She has unilateral calf swelling.

What should guide the initial diagnostic approach?

options.A: Request a D-dimer before any clinical probability assessment
options.B: Use a normal chest X-ray to exclude pulmonary embolism
options.C: Assess PE probability with a validated prediction rule
options.D: Assume pneumonia because she has chest pain
options.E: Give antibiotics and review in one week

correct_answer: C. Assess PE probability with a validated prediction rule
why_correct: Suspected PE should be assessed using an appropriate validated clinical probability assessment, which then guides further investigation and treatment. Source: NICE NG158, Venous thromboembolic diseases.
why_wrong: A. D-dimer should be interpreted after clinical probability assessment; a likely Wells score warrants imaging. B. A normal chest X-ray cannot exclude PE. D. The presentation contains significant PE features. E. Delayed assessment could be dangerous.
pearl: PLAB 1 questions often test the sequence of investigation rather than memorisation of a single test.
thinking: Suspected PE  ↓  assess clinical probability  ↓  follow the appropriate diagnostic pathway.
exam_trap: A, a D-dimer before any probability assessment — it seems a quick first test, but D-dimer is only interpreted after a Wells score; if PE is likely, go straight to imaging.
takeaway: Suspected PE: score the clinical probability first, as that decides between D-dimer and imaging.

stem:
A 19-year-old student presents with fever, headache, vomiting and a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash. He is becoming drowsy.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Treat suspected meningococcal disease as a medical emergency
options.C: Wait for lumbar puncture before giving treatment
options.E: Wait for the rash to become widespread before treatment

correct_answer: A. Treat suspected meningococcal disease as a medical emergency
why_correct: Suspected meningococcal disease can deteriorate rapidly and requires urgent treatment and escalation. Source: NICE NG240, Meningitis and meningococcal disease.
why_wrong: B. Antihistamines do not treat meningococcal disease. C. Investigations must not cause clinically significant treatment delay. D. This is a medical emergency. E. Treatment should not be delayed.
pearl: A non-blanching rash in an unwell patient is a red flag, not simply a dermatological finding.
thinking: Fever + non-blanching rash + systemic illness  ↓  emergency meningococcal pathway.
exam_trap: C, waiting for a lumbar puncture — confirming the diagnosis seems sensible, but delaying antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease can be fatal within hours.
takeaway: Fever with a spreading non-blanching rash and drowsiness: treat as meningococcal disease immediately.

stem:
A 74-year-old man develops vomiting and diarrhoea. He takes an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and regular ibuprofen for osteoarthritis. His creatinine has risen significantly from baseline.

Which medication-related principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Review nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active medicines
options.B: Arrange contrast CT to exclude renal obstruction
options.C: Attribute it to dehydration and continue medicines
options.D: Switch ibuprofen to naproxen for better analgesia
options.E: Continue his medicines and recheck creatinine in a week

correct_answer: A. Review nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active medicines
why_correct: AKI requires identification and correction of reversible causes, including volume depletion and potentially harmful medicines. Source: NICE NG148, Acute kidney injury.
why_wrong: B. Iodinated contrast should be avoided where possible in AKI; ultrasound is used to look for obstruction. C. Dehydration does not make medicine review unnecessary; the ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID can worsen AKI. D. Another NSAID would also worsen renal perfusion. E. Medication review is needed now rather than delayed.
pearl: A common PLAB 1 pattern is acute illness + medication + organ injury.
thinking: AKI  ↓  identify cause  ↓  review medicines  ↓  correct reversible factors  ↓  monitor renal function.
exam_trap: C, blaming dehydration and continuing his medicines — dehydration is a cause, but the ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID all worsen AKI and need review now.
takeaway: In AKI, always review nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active drugs such as ACE inhibitors, diuretics and NSAIDs.

stem:
A 46-year-old man is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. He has no relevant cardiovascular, renal or other major comorbidity.

According to current NICE recommendations, which initial medication approach should be offered?

options.A: Modified-release metformin plus an SGLT-2 inhibitor
options.B: Basal insulin at diagnosis to achieve rapid glycaemic control
options.C: Diet and exercise advice, adding metformin after 3 months
options.D: Standard-release metformin monotherapy, titrated over weeks

correct_answer: A. Modified-release metformin plus an SGLT-2 inhibitor
why_correct: NICE updated NG28 in February 2026. For adults with type 2 diabetes without relevant comorbidity, current guidance recommends modified-release metformin and an SGLT-2 inhibitor. Source: NICE NG28, Type 2 diabetes in adults: management, updated 18 February 2026.
why_wrong: B. Insulin is not routinely required at diagnosis in uncomplicated type 2 diabetes. C. Delaying drug treatment is not the current recommendation; lifestyle measures accompany medication. D. Metformin monotherapy reflects older treatment recommendations. E. Sulfonylurea monotherapy is not the current general initial regimen.
pearl: This is a particularly important 2026 update for a current PLAB 1 bank.
thinking: New type 2 diabetes  ↓  assess comorbidity  ↓  use current NICE medication pathway.
exam_trap: D, standard-release metformin monotherapy — the long-standing first-line choice, but current NICE guidance now recommends modified-release metformin plus an SGLT-2 inhibitor.
takeaway: Current NICE initial therapy for uncomplicated type 2 diabetes: modified-release metformin plus an SGLT-2 inhibitor.

stem:
A patient with insulin-treated diabetes is conscious, confused and sweaty. His capillary glucose is 2.4 mmol/L. He is able to swallow safely.

What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.E: Wait for a laboratory glucose result

why_correct: A conscious patient with hypoglycaemia who can swallow safely should receive rapid-acting carbohydrate, followed by reassessment and further treatment as appropriate. Source: NICE guidance on diabetes and hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: A. Oral carbohydrate is appropriate when safe. B. Water does not correct hypoglycaemia. C. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia. E. Treatment should not be delayed for laboratory confirmation.
pearl: First establish whether the patient can safely swallow before choosing oral treatment.
thinking: Hypoglycaemia + conscious + safe swallow  ↓  fast-acting carbohydrate.
exam_trap: E, waiting for a laboratory glucose — confirmation feels safe, but a symptomatic patient with a low capillary glucose needs treatment now, not after a delay.
takeaway: Conscious hypoglycaemic patient who can swallow safely: fast-acting oral carbohydrate first, then recheck.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with acute kidney injury has a potassium concentration of 7.0 mmol/L. ECG shows broad QRS complexes.

What is the most urgent treatment priority?

options.A: Repeat the potassium on a non-haemolysed sample before starting any treatment
options.B: Give an oral potassium binder now and recheck the potassium level again tomorrow
options.C: Start oral sodium bicarbonate and restrict the patient's dietary potassium intake
options.D: Give IV furosemide first to increase renal potassium excretion in the AKI
options.E: Emergency hyperkalaemia treatment, starting with membrane stabilisation

correct_answer: E. Emergency hyperkalaemia treatment, starting with membrane stabilisation
why_correct: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG abnormalities is a life-threatening emergency. Immediate treatment is required to reduce the risk of fatal arrhythmia. Source: UK Kidney Association guidance on acute hyperkalaemia.
why_wrong: A. With ECG changes, treatment must not be delayed for a repeat sample. B. Potassium binders act slowly and do not protect the myocardium. C. Bicarbonate and dietary restriction are inadequate for severe acute hyperkalaemia. D. Loop diuretics are not first-line emergency treatment and do not stabilise the myocardium.
pearl: When hyperkalaemia produces ECG changes, think cardiac emergency, not simply "abnormal blood test."
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia + ECG changes  ↓  emergency  ↓  protect the heart and lower potassium.
exam_trap: A, repeating the potassium first — haemolysis can falsely raise potassium, but ECG changes show real myocardial danger, so treatment must start immediately.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: give IV calcium to stabilise the myocardium first, then shift potassium.

stem:
A 45-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Serum lipase is markedly elevated.

Which combination best supports a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?

options.A: Epigastric pain with an amylase just above the normal range
options.B: A raised CRP with epigastric tenderness on examination
options.C: Jaundice with a raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin
options.D: Typical pain with a markedly raised lipase or amylase
options.E: Fever with a raised white cell count and persistent vomiting

correct_answer: D. Typical pain with a markedly raised lipase or amylase
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed using the clinical presentation together with appropriate laboratory and/or imaging findings. Typical pain with a significant pancreatic enzyme elevation strongly supports the diagnosis. Source: NICE guidance on acute pancreatitis.
why_wrong: A. Diagnosis requires enzyme elevation of at least three times the upper limit of normal, not a marginal rise. B. Raised CRP is non-specific. C. Cholestatic liver tests suggest biliary disease and do not establish pancreatitis. E. Fever, leucocytosis and vomiting are non-specific.
pearl: PLAB 1 questions commonly test whether a diagnosis can be made clinically without unnecessarily ordering every available investigation.
thinking: Typical epigastric pain  ↓  pancreatic enzymes  ↓  consider cause and severity.
exam_trap: A, epigastric pain with an amylase just above normal — the enzyme is 'raised', but the diagnosis needs a marked rise, typically around three times the upper limit.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis: typical pain plus a markedly raised lipase or amylase, not a marginal rise.

stem:
A 63-year-old man presents with unexplained change in bowel habit and iron-deficiency anaemia.

What investigation is recommended in primary care to help guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer?

options.A: Abdominal ultrasound as the sole investigation

why_correct: Current NICE guidance recommends quantitative FIT to guide referral for suspected colorectal cancer in several symptom groups, including adults with iron-deficiency anaemia and changes in bowel habit. Source: NICE NG12, Suspected cancer: recognition and referral.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound is not the standard primary investigation for this presentation. C. Amylase is unrelated to colorectal cancer assessment. D. This examines the wrong anatomical area. E. Stool microscopy does not perform the same role.
pearl: A negative FIT does not mean that cancer is impossible when there are concerning clinical features.
thinking: Possible colorectal cancer in primary care  ↓  FIT where indicated  ↓  appropriate referral pathway.
exam_trap: A, abdominal ultrasound — it feels like a sensible first scan, but it does not assess the colon; NICE uses quantitative FIT to guide colorectal referral.
takeaway: Suspected colorectal cancer in primary care: use quantitative FIT to guide referral.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain and jaundice. She is hypotensive and confused.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Give oral antibiotics and discharge with GP review in 48 hours
options.B: Treat as uncomplicated biliary colic with analgesia
options.C: Treat as severe acute cholangitis needing urgent hospital care
options.D: Arrange liver biopsy to establish the cause of jaundice
options.E: Arrange a routine outpatient MRCP to look for stones

correct_answer: C. Treat as severe acute cholangitis needing urgent hospital care
why_correct: The combination of systemic infection, biliary symptoms and physiological deterioration is concerning for severe acute cholangitis. Source: NICE guidance on gallstone disease and management of acute biliary infection.
why_wrong: A. Discharge is unsafe in a hypotensive, confused patient. B. Fever, jaundice and shock are not consistent with uncomplicated biliary colic. D. Liver biopsy is not the appropriate initial investigation. E. Urgent treatment and biliary drainage take priority over routine imaging.
pearl: The key is recognising the septic biliary obstruction pattern.
thinking: Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain + deterioration  ↓  ascending biliary infection  ↓  urgent management.
exam_trap: E, routine outpatient MRCP — imaging for stones seems logical, but fever, jaundice and RUQ pain with shock need resuscitation, antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage.
takeaway: Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice with shock is severe cholangitis: resuscitate, give antibiotics, drain urgently.

stem:
A 73-year-old woman develops sudden right-sided weakness and expressive dysphasia 90 minutes ago. Symptoms persist on arrival at hospital.

What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Give oral aspirin before assessing whether thrombolysis may be appropriate
options.B: Activate the acute stroke pathway urgently
options.D: Assume it is a transient ischaemic attack because symptoms may improve
options.E: Wait 24 hours to see whether symptoms resolve

correct_answer: B. Activate the acute stroke pathway urgently
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficit is a medical emergency. Rapid specialist assessment and brain imaging are required to determine appropriate acute treatment. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s.
why_wrong: A. Antiplatelet treatment must be considered in the context of acute stroke imaging and reperfusion eligibility. C. Outpatient imaging is inappropriate. D. Persistent deficits indicate an acute stroke syndrome. E. Time-sensitive treatment may be lost.
pearl: In stroke, time from symptom onset matters.
thinking: Sudden focal deficit  ↓  stroke pathway  ↓  urgent imaging  ↓  assess reperfusion eligibility.
exam_trap: A, oral aspirin first — antiplatelets are part of stroke care, but they must wait until imaging excludes haemorrhage and thrombolysis eligibility is assessed.
takeaway: Persistent focal deficit within hours of onset: activate the stroke pathway for urgent brain imaging.

stem:
A 28-year-old man has been continuously convulsing for more than 5 minutes.

What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological approach?

options.A: Give a benzodiazepine per the emergency protocol
options.C: Give an oral dose of levetiracetam
options.E: Give IM haloperidol to control agitation

correct_answer: A. Give a benzodiazepine per the emergency protocol
why_correct: Convulsive status epilepticus requires immediate emergency treatment. A benzodiazepine is used as first-line pharmacological treatment according to the clinical setting and available route. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults.
why_wrong: B. Prolonged seizures can cause significant harm; treatment is needed at 5 minutes. C. Oral medication is inappropriate during an active prolonged seizure. D. Levetiracetam is second-line after benzodiazepine treatment. E. Antipsychotics do not terminate status epilepticus.
pearl: The first question is often "Has this seizure become status epilepticus?"
thinking: Prolonged convulsion  ↓  status epilepticus  ↓  emergency benzodiazepine treatment  ↓  reassess.
