thinking: AF  ↓  stroke risk + bleeding risk  ↓  don't use falls alone as an automatic reason to withhold treatment.
exam_trap: A, withholding anticoagulation because of falls — bleeding after falls worries clinicians, but NICE advises that falls risk alone is not a reason to withhold it.
takeaway: Do not withhold anticoagulation in AF solely because of age or risk of falls.

stem:
A patient taking a direct-acting oral anticoagulant realises that he has missed a dose.

What is the most appropriate general principle?

options.A: Take a double dose at the next scheduled time to catch up
options.B: Stop the anticoagulant and see the GP before restarting it
options.C: Take the missed dose whenever remembered, even at the next dose time
options.D: Follow that medicine's specific missed-dose instructions
options.E: Omit the next two doses to avoid drug accumulation and bleeding

correct_answer: D. Follow that medicine's specific missed-dose instructions
why_correct: Missed-dose advice varies between medicines and dosing schedules. The specific product instructions should be followed. Source: BNF/MHRA and individual DOAC product information.
why_wrong: A. Doubling is not appropriate and increases bleeding risk. B. One missed dose does not justify stopping treatment. C. Taking it at the next dose time effectively doubles the dose. E. Omitting further doses increases thromboembolic risk.
pearl: For prescribing questions, avoid assuming that all drugs in a class have identical administration instructions.
thinking: Medication error  ↓  identify exact medicine  ↓  follow product-specific missed-dose guidance.
exam_trap: C, taking the missed dose whenever remembered — catching up seems logical, but taking it at the next dose time effectively doubles the dose.
takeaway: Missed DOAC dose: follow that drug's specific missed-dose instructions; never double up.

stem:
A 75-year-old woman taking anticoagulation asks for regular ibuprofen for osteoarthritis pain.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Consider the bleeding risk and offer an alternative analgesic strategy
options.B: Prescribe ibuprofen with a PPI, as this removes the added bleeding risk
options.C: Stop her anticoagulant so that ibuprofen can be used safely
options.D: Prescribe ibuprofen and reduce her anticoagulant dose to compensate for it
options.E: Prescribe ibuprofen and recheck her blood count and renal function in a year

correct_answer: A. Consider the bleeding risk and offer an alternative analgesic strategy
why_correct: NSAIDs can increase gastrointestinal and other bleeding risks, particularly when combined with anticoagulants. Source: BNF/MHRA and NICE medication-safety guidance.
why_wrong: B. A PPI reduces but does not remove gastrointestinal bleeding risk, and other bleeding risks remain. C. Anticoagulation should not be stopped for analgesia without appropriate clinical assessment. D. Reducing the anticoagulant dose increases thromboembolic risk. E. Annual monitoring does not address the increased bleeding risk.
pearl: Drug–drug interaction questions often test risk recognition rather than a specific replacement drug.
thinking: Anticoagulant + NSAID  ↓  think bleeding risk  ↓  consider safer alternatives.
exam_trap: B, ibuprofen with a PPI — gastroprotection reduces GI bleeding risk, but it does not remove the added bleeding risk of combining an NSAID with an anticoagulant.
takeaway: Avoid regular NSAIDs in patients on anticoagulants; choose an alternative analgesic strategy.

stem:
A patient with uncomplicated viral upper respiratory symptoms asks for antibiotics.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Prescribe amoxicillin for 5 days to prevent a secondary bacterial infection
options.B: Prescribe clarithromycin because the patient expects to receive antibiotics
options.C: Prescribe a broad-spectrum antibiotic to cover possible atypical organisms
options.D: Take a throat swab and prescribe antibiotics while awaiting the result
options.E: Explain that antibiotics will not help and give safety-netting advice

correct_answer: E. Explain that antibiotics will not help and give safety-netting advice
why_correct: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections and unnecessary prescribing contributes to antimicrobial resistance and adverse effects. Source: NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidance.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not usefully prevent complications of uncomplicated viral infection. B. Patient expectation alone is not an indication. C. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are not justified. D. Swabbing and empirical antibiotics are not indicated for uncomplicated viral symptoms.
pearl: Good antimicrobial stewardship combines not prescribing with good communication.
thinking: Likely viral illness  ↓  no routine antibiotics  ↓  explain + safety-net.
exam_trap: B, clarithromycin to meet the patient's expectation — pleasing the patient is tempting, but antibiotics do not help viral illness and drive resistance and side effects.
takeaway: Uncomplicated viral URTI: no antibiotics; explain why and give clear safety-netting advice.

stem:
A patient says, "I'm allergic to penicillin." When questioned, he recalls that as a child he developed mild nausea after taking amoxicillin, with no rash, breathing difficulty or swelling.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Record a severe penicillin allergy and avoid beta-lactams in future
options.B: Remove the allergy label without discussing it with the patient
options.C: Record it as anaphylaxis to amoxicillin to be on the safe side in future
options.D: Clarify and document the actual reaction rather than assume true allergy
options.E: Give a full treatment course of amoxicillin without any further enquiry

correct_answer: D. Clarify and document the actual reaction rather than assume true allergy
why_correct: The term "penicillin allergy" covers a range of reactions. Accurate history is important because inappropriate allergy labels can affect antibiotic choice. Source: NICE antimicrobial prescribing/allergy guidance.
why_wrong: A. Nausea alone does not establish severe allergy, and an inaccurate label restricts antibiotic choice. B. The history remains relevant and should be discussed and documented. C. Documentation must reflect the actual history. E. The reaction should be clarified and documented before decisions are made.
pearl: "Allergy" and intolerance are not synonymous.
thinking: Reported allergy  ↓  clarify reaction + timing + features  ↓  document accurately.
exam_trap: A, recording a severe allergy and avoiding beta-lactams — it feels safe, but nausea is an intolerance, and a false label needlessly narrows antibiotic choice.
takeaway: Clarify and document the actual reaction; side effects such as nausea are not a true allergy.

stem:
An 81-year-old patient is admitted to hospital taking eight regular medicines. The admission team is unsure whether he still takes one of them.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Perform medicines reconciliation using reliable sources
options.B: Guess based on the medication list
options.E: Ask the patient to remember every dose without checking

correct_answer: A. Perform medicines reconciliation using reliable sources
why_correct: Accurate medicines reconciliation reduces prescribing errors, omissions and duplication during transitions of care. Source: NICE NG5, Medicines optimisation.
why_wrong: B. Guessing risks medication errors. C. Errors can occur throughout admission. D. Stopping all medication may be harmful. E. Patient history is useful but should be verified where appropriate.
pearl: Transitions of care are high-risk points for medication errors.
thinking: Admission + multiple medicines  ↓  reconcile medicines accurately.
exam_trap: E, relying on the patient's memory — the patient's account is useful, but it should be verified against reliable sources such as GP records.
takeaway: On admission, reconcile medicines using reliable sources such as GP records, the patient and their supply.

stem:
A capacitous adult with a serious infection refuses intravenous antibiotics after the risks and benefits have been explained.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Ask the next of kin to give consent to treatment on the patient's behalf instead
options.B: Discharge the patient from the ward as soon as the refusal form has been signed
options.C: Give the antibiotics under the doctrine of necessity, as the infection is serious
options.D: Respect the refusal, check understanding of consequences and explore reasons
options.E: Assess for detention under the Mental Health Act so that treatment can be given

correct_answer: D. Respect the refusal, check understanding of consequences and explore reasons
why_correct: A capacitous adult has the right to refuse treatment, even if the decision may result in serious harm. Source: GMC Good medical practice; Mental Capacity Act 2005.
why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot override a capacitous patient's decision. B. The discussion should be documented and the patient's reasons and ongoing care explored. C. Necessity does not apply to a capacitous adult who refuses treatment. E. The Mental Health Act cannot be used to treat a physical illness in a capacitous adult.
pearl: Capacity is not the same as agreeing with the doctor.
thinking: Refusal  ↓  establish capacity  ↓  ensure informed decision  ↓  respect capacitous refusal.
exam_trap: C, the doctrine of necessity — the infection is serious, but necessity applies only when a patient lacks capacity, never to a capacitous refusal.
takeaway: A capacitous adult may refuse treatment even if harmful: respect it, explore reasons and document.

stem:
A junior doctor notices repeated unsafe prescribing by a colleague that could place patients at risk.

What is the most appropriate professional response?

options.A: Raise the concern through appropriate professional and organisational channels
options.B: Discuss it informally with fellow junior doctors and wait for their consensus view
options.C: Leave it for the consultant to notice during routine supervision of the colleague
options.D: Amend the colleague's prescriptions quietly without documentation or discussion
options.E: Wait until a clear patient-safety incident occurs and then report it formally to the trust

correct_answer: A. Raise the concern through appropriate professional and organisational channels
why_correct: Doctors have a professional responsibility to act when they have concerns about patient safety. Source: GMC Good medical practice (2024).
why_wrong: B. Informal discussion delays action on a patient-safety concern. C. Patient safety is everyone's responsibility. D. Unauthorised alteration of prescribing creates further risk. E. Waiting for harm is inappropriate.
pearl: Professionalism questions often ask what protects patients, not colleagues' reputations.
thinking: Repeated safety concern  ↓  document appropriately  ↓  escalate through proper channels.
exam_trap: C, leaving it for the consultant to notice — supervision exists, but every doctor has a duty to raise patient-safety concerns promptly themselves.
takeaway: Concern about a colleague's unsafe practice: raise it promptly through appropriate channels.

stem:
The daughter of a competent 60-year-old patient phones the GP and asks for details of her mother's new cancer diagnosis. The patient has not consented to sharing information.

What should the GP do?

options.A: Confirm the diagnosis but withhold details of the treatment plan
options.B: Share the information because the daughter is her next of kin
options.C: Maintain confidentiality unless there is a lawful basis to disclose
options.D: Ask the daughter to collect a copy of the medical record from reception
options.E: Share the diagnosis if the daughter can confirm her mother's date of birth

correct_answer: C. Maintain confidentiality unless there is a lawful basis to disclose
why_correct: Confidential medical information should not be disclosed to relatives simply because they are family members. Source: GMC confidentiality guidance.
why_wrong: A. Partial disclosure is still disclosure. B. Being next of kin does not establish consent. D. Medical records are not accessible to relatives without consent. E. Verifying identity does not provide a basis for disclosure without consent.
pearl: Being a spouse, parent or child does not automatically confer access to adult medical information.
thinking: Relative asks for information  ↓  check consent/legal basis  ↓  maintain confidentiality.
exam_trap: A, confirming the diagnosis only — it seems a compromise, but any disclosure without consent or a lawful basis breaches confidentiality.
takeaway: Next of kin has no automatic right to information about a competent adult patient.

stem:
A healthy 55-year-old man is invited for a screening programme. He asks whether screening can ever lead to unnecessary investigations or treatment.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Reassure him that screening has no meaningful disadvantages and encourage uptake
options.B: Advise him that participation is expected of all eligible men in his age group
options.C: Explain that a positive screening test confirms cancer and that treatment follows
options.D: Explain the benefits, limitations and harms so he can make an informed choice
options.E: Explain that a negative result means he cannot go on to develop that cancer later

correct_answer: D. Explain the benefits, limitations and harms so he can make an informed choice
why_correct: Screening involves potential benefits as well as harms such as false positives, overdiagnosis and unnecessary investigation. People should receive balanced information. Source: UK National Screening Committee / NHS screening guidance.
why_wrong: A. Screening is not risk-free; false positives and overdiagnosis occur. B. Screening participation is a choice. C. A positive screening result does not diagnose cancer and needs further investigation. E. Screening does not eliminate cancer risk; interval cancers occur.
pearl: Screening is offered to people without symptoms; anyone with symptoms should be investigated rather than screened, and screening has harms as well as benefits.
thinking: Screening  ↓  benefits + limitations + possible harms  ↓  informed choice.
exam_trap: A, saying screening has no disadvantages — encouraging uptake seems helpful, but false positives and overdiagnosis are real harms that must be explained.
takeaway: Screening is a choice: explain benefits, limitations and harms so the person can decide.

stem:
A CT scan performed for renal colic incidentally identifies a small pulmonary nodule. The patient is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Reassure the patient that the nodule is benign and needs no further follow-up
options.B: Refer for urgent surgical resection of the nodule
options.C: Tell the patient that it is likely to be lung cancer and refer to oncology
options.D: Leave the finding for the GP to consider at the patient's next routine visit
options.E: Assess it against nodule guidelines and arrange follow-up if indicated

correct_answer: E. Assess it against nodule guidelines and arrange follow-up if indicated
why_correct: Incidental findings require risk-based assessment rather than automatic reassurance or immediate invasive treatment. Source: British Thoracic Society pulmonary nodule guidance.
why_wrong: A. Benignity cannot be assumed without risk assessment. B. Surgery is not indicated for a small incidental nodule. C. A small pulmonary nodule does not mean cancer. D. Responsibility for acting on the finding should not be deferred without a plan.
pearl: Avoid both over-investigation and false reassurance.
thinking: Incidental finding  ↓  characterise  ↓  assess risk  ↓  follow appropriate pathway.
exam_trap: D, leaving it for the GP at a routine visit — the patient is well, but the team that finds an incidental result is responsible for a clear plan.
takeaway: Incidental pulmonary nodule: assess it against nodule guidance and arrange follow-up where indicated.

stem:
A 36-year-old woman presents with a mild, non-specific abdominal pain. Examination is reassuring and no immediate serious diagnosis is identified. She is discharged.

What is an important part of safe management?

options.A: Arrange routine GP review in six weeks without further advice
options.B: Avoid discussing diagnostic uncertainty so as not to cause her anxiety
options.C: Arrange an outpatient CT abdomen before discharge to be safe
options.D: Give clear safety-netting advice about symptoms that need reassessment
options.E: Tell her that serious causes have been excluded by examination

correct_answer: D. Give clear safety-netting advice about symptoms that need reassessment
why_correct: When a serious diagnosis has not been established but cannot be completely excluded, patients should receive clear advice about what deterioration or new symptoms should trigger further assessment. Source: GMC Good medical practice (2024); NICE guidance across acute presentations.
why_wrong: A. Without safety-netting advice she will not know which symptoms need earlier reassessment. B. Patients need to understand what to look out for. C. Investigation should be proportionate to clinical risk. E. Examination cannot exclude all serious causes; uncertainty should be acknowledged.
pearl: Safety-netting is a clinical intervention, not merely a communication courtesy.
thinking: No clear diagnosis + reassuring assessment  ↓  safety-net clearly.
exam_trap: E, saying examination has excluded serious causes — reassurance feels kind, but examination cannot exclude everything; acknowledge uncertainty and safety-net.
takeaway: When discharging with diagnostic uncertainty, give specific safety-netting advice on when to return.

stem:
A vegan patient has macrocytic anaemia, paraesthesia and impaired proprioception.

Which deficiency should be strongly considered?
why_correct: A strict vegan diet lacks dietary vitamin B12, and deficiency causes macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia plus neurological damage such as peripheral neuropathy and dorsal column loss (impaired proprioception). The combination of macrocytosis and neurological signs points to B12 rather than folate.
why_wrong: A. Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia but not dorsal column loss, and vegan diets are usually folate-rich. B. Iron deficiency causes microcytic, not macrocytic, anaemia. C. Thiamine deficiency causes neuropathy and Wernicke encephalopathy but not macrocytic anaemia. D. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia and proximal myopathy, not macrocytic anaemia or loss of proprioception.
pearl: Neurological manifestations make timely recognition particularly important.
thinking: Strict vegan diet lacks dietary B12 ↓ Macrocytic anaemia ↓ Paraesthesia and lost proprioception mean dorsal column involvement ↓ Macrocytosis plus neurology points to B12, not folate ↓ E, vitamin B12
exam_trap: A, folate — it also causes macrocytic anaemia, but it does not cause dorsal column loss, and vegan diets are usually rich in folate.
takeaway: Macrocytosis with neurological signs in a vegan: think vitamin B12 deficiency, not folate.

stem:
A patient has a platelet count of 12 × 10⁹/L and develops spontaneous mucosal bleeding.

What is the key clinical concern?

options.A: Expected bleeding that needs a repeat count next week
options.B: Significant bleeding risk requiring urgent assessment
options.C: Pseudothrombocytopenia from clumping needing no action
options.D: Mild thrombocytopenia suitable for routine outpatient review
options.E: Bleeding from vitamin K deficiency needing oral vitamin K

correct_answer: B. Significant bleeding risk requiring urgent assessment
why_correct: A platelet count of 12 × 10⁹/L with spontaneous mucosal bleeding indicates severe thrombocytopenia with a high risk of serious (including intracranial) haemorrhage, so urgent assessment of the cause and same-day haematology input are needed.
why_wrong: A. A platelet count of 12 × 10⁹/L with spontaneous bleeding needs urgent assessment, not a repeat next week. C. Pseudothrombocytopenia does not cause spontaneous bleeding. D. 12 × 10⁹/L is severe, not mild, thrombocytopenia. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes a coagulopathy, not severe thrombocytopenia.
pearl: Spontaneous mucosal bleeding with a severely low platelet count is a warning sign of possible serious or intracranial haemorrhage: it needs same-day haematology input, not routine follow-up.
thinking: Platelets 12 × 10⁹/L = severe thrombocytopenia ↓ spontaneous mucosal bleeding = active bleeding tendency ↓ high risk of serious haemorrhage ↓ urgent assessment of the cause with same-day haematology input
exam_trap: D, mild thrombocytopenia for routine review — tempting if the count is read as merely low, but a count this low with spontaneous bleeding is severe and needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Very low platelets plus spontaneous bleeding is an emergency, not a result to repeat next week.

stem:
A 68-year-old man collapses without warning while walking. He has no prodrome and has a history of structural heart disease.

What feature makes a cardiac cause particularly concerning?
why_correct: Syncope during exertion suggests that cardiac output cannot rise to meet demand, as in aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or ventricular arrhythmia. In a patient with structural heart disease, exertional syncope without prodrome is a red flag requiring urgent cardiac assessment (NICE CG109).
why_wrong: A. Seasonal allergies do not increase the likelihood of cardiac syncope. B. Feeling hungry beforehand may suggest hypoglycaemia but does not point to a cardiac cause. C. Previous motion sickness is unrelated to cardiac syncope. E. Mild chronic back pain has no bearing on the likelihood of a cardiac cause.
pearl: Syncope during exertion can indicate a cardiac cause and warrants appropriate assessment.
thinking: Collapse without prodrome ↓ known structural heart disease ↓ exertion is when cardiac output must rise ↓ an obstructed or arrhythmic heart fails on effort ↓ collapse during exertion
exam_trap: B, feeling hungry beforehand — tempting as a recognised pre-syncope clue, but it points towards hypoglycaemia rather than a cardiac cause, and this patient had no prodrome.
takeaway: Exertional syncope, especially with structural heart disease, needs urgent cardiac assessment.

stem:
A 73-year-old woman develops a new temporal headache and jaw pain when chewing. She reports transient visual disturbance.

What is the key concern?

options.A: Tension-type headache related to jaw clenching
options.D: Giant cell arteritis with risk of visual loss
options.E: Trigeminal neuralgia affecting the mandibular branch

correct_answer: D. Giant cell arteritis with risk of visual loss
why_correct: New headache with jaw claudication and transient visual disturbance in a patient over 50 is giant cell arteritis until proven otherwise. Visual symptoms signal a risk of permanent visual loss, so high-dose glucocorticoids should be started immediately and urgent specialist assessment arranged.
why_wrong: A. Tension headache does not cause jaw claudication or visual disturbance and rarely begins de novo at 73. B. TMJ dysfunction does not cause new temporal headache with visual disturbance. C. Migraine rarely starts in older age and does not cause jaw claudication; assuming migraine risks missing GCA. E. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock pains, not jaw claudication or visual symptoms.
pearl: In suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms, start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and refer urgently; never wait for biopsy or imaging, as visual loss can become permanent.
thinking: > Older patient + new headache + jaw claudication/visual symptoms  ↓  GCA emergency.
exam_trap: C, migraine with visual aura — tempting because of headache with visual disturbance, but migraine rarely starts at 73 and does not cause jaw claudication; missing GCA risks blindness.
takeaway: New headache with jaw claudication over 50 is GCA until proven otherwise: treat immediately.

stem:
A 74-year-old man suddenly develops facial droop, arm weakness and speech difficulty.

What is the appropriate response?

options.E: Wait for symptoms to resolve completely

why_correct: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness and speech disturbance (positive FAST) indicate an acute stroke until proven otherwise. NICE NG128 requires immediate emergency transfer and urgent brain imaging because thrombolysis and thrombectomy are time-critical.
why_wrong: A. A routine GP appointment would delay time-critical reperfusion treatment. B. There is no indication for antibiotics in an acute focal neurological deficit. C. Rehabilitation follows diagnosis and acute treatment; it does not replace urgent assessment. E. Waiting for resolution wastes the treatment window, and resolved symptoms would still need urgent TIA assessment.
pearl: A positive FAST (face, arm, speech) means emergency transfer for urgent brain imaging, because thrombolysis and thrombectomy are only possible within a limited time window.
thinking: > Sudden focal neurological deficit  ↓  stroke pathway.
exam_trap: E, wait for symptoms to resolve — tempting because this might be a TIA, but waiting wastes the reperfusion window, and resolved symptoms would still need urgent TIA assessment.
takeaway: Sudden face, arm or speech deficit: treat as stroke and act immediately, as time is brain.

stem:
A 69-year-old woman develops sudden unilateral arm weakness that completely resolves after 20 minutes.

What should this be regarded as?

options.A: Possible transient ischaemic attack requiring urgent assessment
options.B: Migraine aura without headache, needing routine review
options.C: Focal seizure with Todd's paresis, needing an outpatient EEG
options.D: Hypoglycaemic episode needing dietary advice and monitoring
options.E: Peripheral nerve compression needing routine nerve studies

correct_answer: A. Possible transient ischaemic attack requiring urgent assessment
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms that resolve completely within 24 hours should be treated as a suspected TIA. NICE NG128 recommends immediate aspirin 300 mg (unless contraindicated) and specialist assessment within 24 hours because of the high early stroke risk.
why_wrong: B. Migraine aura is usually positive and spreading; sudden negative motor symptoms should not be attributed to migraine. C. There was no seizure; sudden focal weakness that resolves should be treated as a TIA. D. Hypoglycaemia should be excluded, but it does not explain the episode without evidence and the TIA must be assessed. E. Nerve compression causes gradual symptoms, not sudden transient unilateral weakness.
pearl: Resolution of symptoms does not make a transient focal neurological event safe to ignore.
thinking: Sudden-onset focal deficit ↓ unilateral arm weakness is a negative symptom ↓ complete resolution within 24 hours ↓ high early stroke risk ↓ possible TIA needing urgent assessment
exam_trap: B, migraine aura without headache — tempting as a transient neurological event, but aura is usually positive and spreading; sudden negative motor loss should be managed as TIA.
takeaway: A sudden focal deficit that fully resolves is a TIA until proven otherwise: assess urgently.

stem:
A patient is told that a biopsy has confirmed cancer. He becomes silent and visibly distressed.

What is the most appropriate immediate response?

options.A: Move on to the treatment plan to give him some hope
options.B: Continue with the remaining information so it is all covered
options.C: Leave him alone to absorb it and return another day
options.D: Reassure him that his treatment is very likely to succeed
options.E: Pause, acknowledge his reaction and let him respond

correct_answer: E. Pause, acknowledge his reaction and let him respond
why_correct: When a patient becomes silent and distressed after bad news, the clinician should pause, acknowledge the emotion and give the patient space to respond before continuing at their pace, consistent with the SPIKES approach and GMC guidance on good communication.
why_wrong: A. Moving on dismisses his distress before he is ready. B. Continuing ignores his emotional reaction, and information given now is unlikely to be retained. C. Leaving abandons the patient at a vulnerable moment. D. Premature reassurance may be false and undermines trust.
pearl: After breaking bad news, silence is part of the conversation: pause, acknowledge the emotion you see and let the patient lead before giving more information.
thinking: Bad news ↓ pause ↓ acknowledge emotion ↓ allow response ↓ then continue at the patient's pace.
exam_trap: D, reassuring him that treatment is very likely to succeed — tempting as a kind response, but premature reassurance may be false, dismisses his distress and undermines trust.
takeaway: Respond to emotion before information: pause, acknowledge and let the patient respond.

stem:
A patient notices that a pigmented lesion has recently changed in size, shape and colour.

Which feature should raise concern for melanoma?

options.B: Recent change in a pigmented lesion
options.C: A stable lesion unchanged for 20 years
options.D: A lesion that has never changed

correct_answer: B. Recent change in a pigmented lesion
why_correct: Recent change in size, shape or colour of a pigmented lesion is a major feature on the weighted 7-point checklist recommended by NICE NG12 and should prompt suspected cancer pathway referral for melanoma.
why_wrong: A. Symmetrical, uniform pigmentation is a reassuring feature; asymmetry and irregular colour raise concern. C. A lesion that has been stable for 20 years is reassuring rather than suspicious. D. A lesion that has never changed is less concerning than one with recent change. E. Amelanotic melanoma exists, but absence of pigmentation is not itself the warning feature described here.
pearl: Change in a pigmented lesion is an important warning feature.
thinking: Pigmented lesion ↓ recent change in size, shape and colour ↓ major features on the weighted 7-point checklist ↓ suspicion of melanoma ↓ recent change in a pigmented lesion
exam_trap: E, complete absence of pigmentation — tempting because amelanotic melanoma exists, but lack of pigment is not the warning feature here; recent change in a lesion is.
takeaway: Change in a mole is the key melanoma warning feature; stable, uniform lesions are reassuring.

stem:
A 24-year-old student has intense itching, particularly at night. His partner has developed similar symptoms. There are itchy lesions around the finger webs and wrists.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Intense itch that is worse at night, affected close contacts, and lesions in the finger webs and wrists are characteristic of scabies. Management is permethrin 5% cream for the patient and all close contacts at the same time.
why_wrong: B. Psoriasis causes well-demarcated scaly plaques on extensor surfaces and does not spread to contacts. C. Cellulitis causes a painful, hot, spreading erythema, usually of one limb, not itchy finger-web lesions. D. Herpes simplex causes painful grouped vesicles, typically around the lips or genitals, not nocturnal finger-web itch. E. Melanoma is a pigmented skin cancer and does not cause intense generalised nocturnal itch in contacts.
pearl: In scabies, treat the patient and all close contacts at the same time, even if contacts have no symptoms, to prevent reinfection; itch can persist for weeks after successful treatment.
thinking: > Nocturnal itch + close contacts affected + finger webs  ↓  scabies.
exam_trap: B, psoriasis — tempting as a common itchy rash, but it causes well-demarcated scaly extensor plaques and does not spread to a partner or favour the finger webs.
takeaway: Nocturnal itch, finger-web lesions and an itchy contact mean scabies until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman develops sudden severe unilateral eye pain, headache, nausea and blurred vision. The affected eye is red and the pupil appears abnormal.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Bacterial conjunctivitis requiring topical chloramphenicol drops
options.C: Mature cataract needing a routine ophthalmology surgical referral
options.D: Acute angle-closure glaucoma requiring urgent ophthalmology
options.E: Migraine with visual aura needing an oral triptan and antiemetic

correct_answer: D. Acute angle-closure glaucoma requiring urgent ophthalmology
why_correct: Sudden painful red eye with headache, nausea, blurred vision and an abnormal (typically mid-dilated, fixed) pupil in an older woman indicates acute angle-closure glaucoma. It is an ophthalmic emergency needing same-day ophthalmology to lower intraocular pressure and prevent permanent visual loss.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis causes a gritty red eye with discharge but not severe pain, reduced vision, abnormal pupil or vomiting. B. Episcleritis causes mild discomfort without reduced vision, pupil abnormality or systemic upset. C. Cataract causes gradual painless visual loss, not an acute painful red eye. E. Migraine does not cause a red eye with an abnormal pupil; attributing these signs to migraine risks blindness.
pearl: Acute angle-closure glaucoma can mimic a neurological or abdominal illness because of headache and vomiting: always look at the eye, as a red eye with an abnormal pupil needs same-day ophthalmology.
thinking: > Painful red eye + visual disturbance + systemic symptoms  ↓  emergency eye condition.
exam_trap: E, migraine with visual aura — tempting because of headache, nausea and blurred vision, but migraine does not cause a red eye with an abnormal pupil; missing angle closure risks blindness.
takeaway: Painful red eye, blurred vision, vomiting and abnormal pupil: acute angle closure, urgent ophthalmology.

stem:
An elderly care-home resident develops fever, cough, myalgia and malaise during an influenza outbreak.

What is an important preventive measure for eligible people?

options.E: Annual chest X-ray screening for residents

why_correct: Annual influenza vaccination is the key preventive measure for eligible groups, including older people, care-home residents, and health and social care workers, under the UKHSA national immunisation programme (Green Book chapter 19). It reduces infection, outbreaks and complications.
why_wrong: A. Pneumococcal vaccine does not prevent influenza and is not given annually. C. Vitamin C supplements do not prevent influenza. D. Antibiotics do not prevent viral influenza and promote antimicrobial resistance. E. Chest X-ray screening has no role in preventing influenza.
pearl: Annual influenza vaccination of older people, care-home residents and health and social care workers is the main measure that reduces outbreaks and their complications.
thinking: Fever, cough and myalgia during an outbreak ↓ influenza in a vulnerable care-home resident ↓ question asks about prevention ↓ circulating strains change each season ↓ annual influenza vaccination
exam_trap: A, pneumococcal vaccination every year — tempting as another vaccine for older people, but it does not prevent influenza and is not given annually.
takeaway: Influenza prevention in vulnerable groups means vaccination every year, before each season.

stem:
A parent asks why vaccines can protect not only the vaccinated child but also vulnerable people in the community.

What concept is being described?
why_correct: Herd (population) immunity occurs when enough people are immune to interrupt transmission, so people who cannot be vaccinated or respond poorly, such as infants and the immunocompromised, are indirectly protected.
why_wrong: A. Tachyphylaxis is a rapidly diminishing response to repeated doses of a drug. B. Genetic drift is a random change in allele frequency within a population, not community protection from vaccination. C. Negative feedback is a physiological control mechanism, not an epidemiological concept. E. Antibiotic resistance is the ability of bacteria to survive antibiotics and is unrelated to vaccine community protection.
pearl: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated or respond poorly, such as infants and immunocompromised people, so high vaccine uptake protects the whole community.
thinking: Vaccination makes individuals immune ↓ enough immune people interrupt transmission ↓ the pathogen struggles to reach susceptible people ↓ unvaccinated vulnerable people are indirectly protected ↓ herd immunity
exam_trap: E, antibiotic resistance — tempting as a familiar population-level public health concept, but it concerns bacteria surviving antibiotics and has nothing to do with vaccine protection.
takeaway: When enough people are immune, transmission breaks and the vulnerable are protected: herd immunity.

stem:
A patient has an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Use antibiotics to prevent all future viral infections
options.C: Avoid antibiotics when there is no indication for them

correct_answer: C. Avoid antibiotics when there is no indication for them
why_correct: Uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infections are self-limiting and do not benefit from antibiotics. NICE NG15 antimicrobial stewardship advice is to avoid unnecessary prescribing, give self-care advice and safety-net, because antibiotics cause adverse effects and drive resistance.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics have no activity against viruses and cannot prevent future viral infections. B. Dual antibiotic therapy is not indicated for a viral infection. D. Indefinite antibiotics are never appropriate for a self-limiting viral illness. E. Routine broad-spectrum antibiotics give no benefit in viral infection and increase resistance and C. difficile risk.
pearl: Unnecessary antibiotic use contributes to antimicrobial resistance and exposes patients to adverse effects.
thinking: Uncomplicated viral URTI ↓ self-limiting illness ↓ antibiotics do not act on viruses but cause side effects and resistance ↓ self-care advice and safety-netting ↓ avoid antibiotics without an indication
exam_trap: E, routine broad-spectrum antibiotics — tempting as a cover-all-bases approach, but they give no benefit in viral infection and increase resistance and C. difficile risk.
takeaway: No bacterial indication, no antibiotic: give self-care advice and safety-net instead.

stem:
A patient reports that they developed widespread urticaria and facial swelling shortly after taking penicillin in the past.

How should this history be regarded?

options.A: As an indication to give penicillin again routinely
options.E: As proof that all antibiotics are contraindicated

correct_answer: B. As potentially significant immediate hypersensitivity
why_correct: Urticaria and facial swelling shortly after penicillin suggest an immediate (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. NICE CG183 advises documenting it as an allergy, avoiding penicillins, and considering specialist allergy referral where penicillin would be needed.
why_wrong: A. Re-challenge with penicillin after a probable immediate hypersensitivity reaction risks anaphylaxis. C. Drug allergy history is central to safe prescribing and must be recorded. D. Hypersensitivity is a patient immune reaction, not bacterial antibiotic resistance. E. A penicillin allergy does not contraindicate all antibiotics; many non-beta-lactam alternatives are suitable.
pearl: Record the type of reaction, not just the word allergy: urticaria and facial swelling suggest immediate hypersensitivity, so avoid penicillins and consider allergy referral if penicillin is needed.
thinking: Urticaria and facial swelling ↓ onset shortly after penicillin ↓ pattern of an immediate IgE-mediated reaction ↓ risk of anaphylaxis on re-exposure ↓ potentially significant immediate hypersensitivity
exam_trap: E, proof that all antibiotics are contraindicated — tempting as the safest reading, but a penicillin allergy does not rule out all antibiotics, and many non-beta-lactam alternatives remain suitable.
takeaway: Rash and facial swelling soon after penicillin suggest true allergy: document it and avoid penicillins.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin is prescribed another medication that can significantly alter anticoagulant effect.

What is an appropriate principle?

options.A: Double the warfarin dose pre-emptively when it is started
options.B: Halve the warfarin dose and check the INR in three months
options.C: Continue usual INR checks, as most interactions are minor
options.D: Check for interactions and monitor the INR more closely
options.E: Stop warfarin while the new medicine is taken

correct_answer: D. Check for interactions and monitor the INR more closely
why_correct: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index and many interactions (for example macrolides, azoles, some antibiotics and enzyme inducers). The BNF advises checking for interactions and monitoring the INR more closely when another drug is started or stopped.
why_wrong: A. Empirical dose changes without INR monitoring risk major bleeding or thrombosis. B. Empirical dose changes with delayed monitoring are unsafe. C. Many interactions with warfarin are clinically important and need closer monitoring. E. Stopping warfarin unnecessarily increases thromboembolic risk.
pearl: Whenever a medicine is started or stopped in a patient on warfarin, check for interactions and monitor the INR more closely; common culprits include macrolides, azoles and enzyme inducers.
thinking: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index ↓ a new drug can raise or lower its effect ↓ the size of the effect cannot be reliably predicted ↓ measure rather than guess ↓ check interactions and monitor the INR more closely
exam_trap: E, stop warfarin while the new medicine is taken — tempting as a way to avoid bleeding, but interrupting anticoagulation unnecessarily exposes the patient to thromboembolism.
takeaway: Warfarin plus a new drug: check interactions and monitor the INR closely, rather than guessing the dose.

stem:
A 78-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease asks for regular ibuprofen for osteoarthritis.

Which consideration is most important?

options.A: Prescribe ibuprofen, as NSAIDs are safe in stable chronic kidney disease
options.B: Prescribe the maximum ibuprofen dose for long-term regular use in her case
options.C: Prescribe ibuprofen with a PPI, which also removes the renal risk
options.D: Assess GI, renal and cardiovascular risk before any oral NSAID
options.E: Prescribe regular ibuprofen and check her renal function annually

correct_answer: D. Assess GI, renal and cardiovascular risk before any oral NSAID
why_correct: Oral NSAIDs can worsen renal function, cause GI bleeding and raise cardiovascular risk, and these risks are higher in older people with CKD. NICE NG226 advises considering individual risk factors before using an oral NSAID, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, with a PPI, and topical NSAIDs are preferred for knee osteoarthritis.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion and can cause acute kidney injury, particularly in CKD. B. NSAIDs should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time. C. A PPI reduces gastrointestinal risk but has no effect on renal risk. E. Annual monitoring is inadequate given the renal risk in CKD.
pearl: Older age and CKD raise the renal, GI and cardiovascular risks of oral NSAIDs; consider topical treatment and non-drug measures first, and use any oral NSAID only after weighing her individual risks, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
thinking: Older patient with CKD ↓ oral NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion, cause GI bleeding and raise cardiovascular risk ↓ these risks are higher in her ↓ individual risk must be weighed first ↓ assess GI, renal and cardiovascular risk
exam_trap: C, ibuprofen with a PPI — tempting because a PPI is advised alongside oral NSAIDs, but it only reduces GI risk and does nothing to protect the kidneys.
takeaway: Before an oral NSAID, weigh renal, GI and cardiovascular risk, especially in older people with CKD.

stem:
An 83-year-old man has had three falls over six months. He takes several medications and reports occasional dizziness when standing.

What is an appropriate approach?

options.A: No further action is needed at present, as he has not sustained a fracture
options.B: Advise bed rest and a bedside commode to prevent further falls at home
options.C: Stop all his regular medicines at once and review him again in a month
options.D: Multifactorial falls assessment, including medication and postural BP
options.E: Arrange a CT head and routine outpatient EEG as the first investigations

correct_answer: D. Multifactorial falls assessment, including medication and postural BP
why_correct: Recurrent falls warrant a multifactorial falls risk assessment, including medication review and lying and standing blood pressure for orthostatic hypotension, as recommended by NICE NG249 and the 2022 World Falls Guidelines.
why_wrong: A. Recurrent falls predict future injury and require assessment even without a fracture. B. Bed rest causes deconditioning and increases falls risk. C. Abruptly stopping all medicines may cause harm; a structured review should target the culprits. E. Neuroimaging and EEG are not first-line and do not address postural dizziness or medicines.
pearl: Recurrent falls are a warning, not bad luck: review medicines, check lying and standing blood pressure, and assess gait, balance, vision and home hazards as part of a multifactorial assessment.
thinking: Recurrent falls  ↓  look for modifiable contributors rather than attributing them simply to age.
exam_trap: A, no action as there is no fracture — tempting because he is uninjured, but recurrent falls predict future injury and need a multifactorial assessment now.
takeaway: Recurrent falls warrant multifactorial assessment, including medicines review and postural BP.

stem:
An elderly inpatient is at increased risk of delirium.

Which measure can help reduce risk?

options.A: Limit conversation and visitors to reduce overstimulation at night
options.B: Prescribe a regular low-dose benzodiazepine at night to aid sleep
options.C: Perform hourly observations overnight, waking the patient each time
options.D: Promote orientation, hydration, sensory aids and normal sleep
options.E: Store glasses and hearing aids safely away from the bed at night

correct_answer: D. Promote orientation, hydration, sensory aids and normal sleep
why_correct: NICE CG103 recommends multicomponent interventions to prevent delirium, including reorientation, adequate hydration and nutrition, glasses and hearing aids, good sleep hygiene, early mobilisation and avoidance of unnecessary medicines.
why_wrong: A. Clear, regular communication and familiar visitors support orientation and reduce delirium risk. B. Sedatives, especially benzodiazepines, can precipitate or worsen delirium. C. Sleep disruption is a recognised risk factor for delirium. E. Sensory impairment increases delirium risk, so glasses and hearing aids should be available.
pearl: Delirium is often preventable: keep patients oriented, hydrated and mobile, with glasses and hearing aids to hand, protect their sleep and avoid unnecessary sedatives.
thinking: Elderly inpatient at risk of delirium ↓ triggers include dehydration, sensory loss, sleep disruption and sedatives ↓ reduce these triggers ↓ multicomponent prevention ↓ promote orientation, hydration, sensory aids and sleep
exam_trap: B, a regular low-dose benzodiazepine at night — tempting as a way to improve sleep, but benzodiazepines can precipitate or worsen delirium in older people.
takeaway: Prevent delirium with orientation, hydration, sensory aids and good sleep, not sedation.

stem:
A child repeatedly attends healthcare services with unexplained injuries. The explanations given by carers are inconsistent.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Treat the injuries and discharge without further documentation
options.B: Promise the child that anything they say will stay confidential
options.C: Wait for the child to disclose directly before acting
options.D: Consider safeguarding concerns and follow safeguarding procedures
options.E: Confront the carers about the injuries before taking any action

correct_answer: D. Consider safeguarding concerns and follow safeguarding procedures
why_correct: Repeated unexplained injuries with inconsistent explanations should raise suspicion of maltreatment, and NICE CG89 and GMC guidance require the clinician to act on concerns through local safeguarding procedures, without waiting for a disclosure.
why_wrong: A. Failing to document and refer may leave the child at continued risk. B. Clinicians cannot promise secrecy when a child may be at risk of harm. C. Children often do not disclose abuse, so a pattern of concerning injuries must be acted on. E. Confronting carers may increase risk to the child and is not appropriate.
pearl: A child does not need to make a direct disclosure before safeguarding concerns are taken seriously.
thinking: Repeated unexplained injuries ↓ inconsistent explanations from carers ↓ pattern raises suspicion of maltreatment ↓ a disclosure is not needed to act ↓ consider safeguarding and follow local procedures
exam_trap: E, confronting the carers first — tempting as an honest, direct approach, but it may increase the risk to the child and is not part of safeguarding procedures.
takeaway: Suspected maltreatment: document and follow safeguarding procedures without waiting for disclosure.

stem:
A woman attends repeatedly with injuries. Her partner insists on answering all questions for her.

What is an appropriate approach?

options.A: See her alone and sensitively assess her safety
options.B: Take the history from the partner, as he knows the details
options.C: Treat the injuries and document them as accidental
options.D: Challenge the partner about the injuries in front of her
options.E: Advise her that she must leave the relationship today

correct_answer: A. See her alone and sensitively assess her safety
why_correct: Repeated injuries and a controlling partner who answers for the patient raise concern about domestic abuse. NICE PH50 advises creating an opportunity to see the patient alone, asking sensitively about safety and offering support and referral.
why_wrong: B. Relying on the partner prevents disclosure and may increase risk. C. Repeated injuries with controlling behaviour should not be dismissed as accidental. D. Confronting the partner in front of the patient could escalate risk. E. The patient's autonomy should be respected; leaving immediately can be the most dangerous time and needs safe planning.
pearl: When a partner insists on answering for a patient with repeated injuries, create a chance to see the patient alone, ask sensitively about safety and abuse, and offer support and referral.
thinking: > Possible domestic abuse  ↓  private, safe, non-judgemental conversation.
exam_trap: E, advising her to leave today — tempting as a protective response, but it overrides her autonomy, and leaving can be the most dangerous time without safety planning.
takeaway: Possible domestic abuse: see the patient alone, ask sensitively and respect her choices.

stem:
A patient with advanced cancer has severe breathlessness despite treatment of the underlying disease.

What is an important principle of palliative care?

options.A: Manage symptoms alongside the underlying disease and the patient's goals
options.B: Defer palliative care referral until the last days of life
options.C: Escalate disease-directed treatment before addressing symptoms
options.D: Stop all active treatment once palliative care is involved
options.E: Avoid discussing prognosis to protect the patient from distress

correct_answer: A. Manage symptoms alongside the underlying disease and the patient's goals
why_correct: Palliative care focuses on relieving distressing symptoms, such as breathlessness, alongside disease-directed treatment where appropriate, guided by the patient's priorities and goals of care.
why_wrong: B. Palliative care can be provided early in a serious illness, not only at the end of life. C. Symptoms should be managed alongside treatment, with treatments reviewed for benefit and burden. D. Palliative care can be delivered alongside appropriate active treatment. E. Honest, sensitive communication about prognosis is central to palliative care.
pearl: Palliative care is not only for the last days of life: it can run alongside disease-directed treatment, focusing on symptoms such as breathlessness and on what matters most to the patient.
thinking: Advanced cancer with severe breathlessness ↓ underlying disease already treated ↓ symptom still distressing ↓ palliative care addresses symptoms at any stage ↓ manage symptoms alongside disease and the patient's goals
exam_trap: D, stop all active treatment once palliative care is involved — tempting because palliative care is linked with end of life, but it can be delivered alongside appropriate active treatment.
takeaway: Palliative care runs alongside treatment, guided by symptoms and the patient's goals.

stem:
A competent patient asks whether a DNACPR decision means that all medical treatment will be stopped.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Explain that it means a move to comfort-focused care
options.B: Explain that antibiotics and intravenous fluids will no longer be offered
options.C: Discuss the question with the family rather than the patient
options.D: Explain that it stops admission to hospital in future
options.E: Explain that it applies only to CPR, and other appropriate treatment continues

correct_answer: E. Explain that it applies only to CPR, and other appropriate treatment continues
why_correct: A DNACPR decision applies only to cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest. All other appropriate treatment, such as antibiotics, fluids and symptom control, continues as clinically indicated (BMA/RCUK/RCN guidance).
why_wrong: A. DNACPR does not mean stopping active treatment. B. DNACPR does not prohibit antibiotics or other appropriate treatments. C. A patient with capacity should be involved in discussions about DNACPR. D. DNACPR does not determine place of care or hospital admission.
pearl: DNACPR means only that CPR will not be attempted if the heart or breathing stops; all other appropriate treatment, such as antibiotics, fluids and hospital admission, continues.
thinking: Competent patient asks about DNACPR ↓ DNACPR covers only CPR in cardiac or respiratory arrest ↓ it is not a decision about other treatment ↓ give an honest, clear explanation ↓ CPR only; other treatment continues
exam_trap: A, a move to comfort-focused care — tempting because DNACPR is often discussed near the end of life, but it does not stop active treatment, which continues as clinically indicated.
takeaway: DNACPR means no CPR, not no treatment: all other appropriate care continues.

stem:
A doctor is asked by police for confidential medical information about a patient.

What is the most appropriate general principle?

options.A: Provide a copy of the full medical record on request from any investigating officer
options.B: Refuse the request, as police cannot access medical information
options.C: Disclose whatever is requested once the officer has shown valid police identification
options.D: Disclose the information once a senior nurse on the ward has agreed to the disclosure
options.E: Consider whether there is a lawful basis and disclose only what is justified

correct_answer: E. Consider whether there is a lawful basis and disclose only what is justified
why_correct: Confidentiality is the default, and disclosure to the police requires a lawful basis, such as patient consent, a statutory requirement, a court order or a public interest justification. GMC confidentiality guidance requires disclosure of only the minimum necessary information.
why_wrong: A. Disclosing the whole record is disproportionate and breaches confidentiality. B. Disclosure may be required or justified in some circumstances, so blanket refusal is inappropriate. C. Identification does not establish a lawful basis for disclosure. D. Another professional's agreement does not establish a lawful basis for disclosure.
pearl: A police request alone does not justify disclosure: identify a lawful basis such as consent, a legal requirement, a court order or a public interest justification, then share only the minimum necessary.
thinking: > Confidentiality is the default; disclosure requires an appropriate legal/ethical basis and should be proportionate.
exam_trap: C, disclosing once police identification is shown — tempting because the request seems official, but identification is not a lawful basis for breaching confidentiality.
takeaway: Disclose to the police only with a lawful basis, and only what is necessary.

stem:
A 61-year-old man presents with prolonged central chest pain. ECG demonstrates ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF.

Which anatomical territory is most likely affected?
why_correct: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior surface of the heart, usually supplied by the right coronary artery, so ST elevation in these leads indicates an inferior STEMI.
why_wrong: A. Right bundle branch block is a conduction abnormality, not a myocardial territory indicated by inferior ST elevation. B. Anterior STEMI shows ST elevation in V1–V4, mainly V3–V4. D. Septal changes appear in V1–V2. E. Lateral changes appear in I, aVL and V5–V6.
pearl: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery; inferior infarction can be complicated by bradycardia and heart block.
thinking: II, III, aVF  ↓  inferior.
exam_trap: B, anterior territory — tempting as the most familiar STEMI, but anterior changes appear in V1–V4; ST elevation in II, III and aVF localises to the inferior wall.
takeaway: II, III and aVF are the inferior leads; ST elevation there means the inferior territory.

stem:
A patient with severe renal impairment has potassium of 7.0 mmol/L. ECG shows tall peaked T waves.

What electrolyte disturbance best explains this finding?
why_correct: A potassium of 7.0 mmol/L is severe hyperkalaemia, and tall peaked T waves are its earliest ECG sign. Renal impairment is a common cause because potassium excretion is reduced.
why_wrong: A. Hypomagnesaemia is associated with QT prolongation and arrhythmias, not peaked T waves. C. Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves, ST depression and U waves. D. Hyponatraemia does not cause peaked T waves. E. Hypercalcaemia mainly shortens the QT interval.
pearl: Peaked T waves are the earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia; with severe hyperkalaemia and ECG changes, give IV calcium first to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin–glucose to shift potassium.
thinking: Severe renal impairment reduces potassium excretion ↓ potassium 7.0 mmol/L is markedly raised ↓ tall peaked T waves are the first ECG change ↓ cardiac excitability is affected ↓ hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: C, hypokalaemia — tempting because potassium disorders are easily confused, but hypokalaemia flattens T waves and causes U waves; peaked T waves point to a high potassium.
takeaway: Peaked T waves in renal impairment mean hyperkalaemia until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with acute heart failure has bilateral perihilar fluffy air-space shadowing and vascular congestion on chest X-ray.

Which diagnosis is most consistent?
why_correct: Bilateral perihilar (bat's wing) alveolar shadowing with vascular congestion in acute heart failure indicates pulmonary oedema. Other typical features are upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines and pleural effusions.
why_wrong: A. Lobar collapse causes volume loss and a localised opacity, not bilateral perihilar shadowing. B. Lung cancer usually appears as a mass or hilar enlargement, not bilateral perihilar shadowing with vascular congestion. C. An isolated pleural effusion causes costophrenic angle blunting, not bilateral air-space shadowing. E. Pneumothorax shows a visible pleural edge with absent lung markings peripherally.
pearl: Know the chest X-ray signs of heart failure: alveolar bat's wing shadowing, Kerley B lines, cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion and pleural effusions.
thinking: Known acute heart failure ↓ raised pulmonary venous pressure ↓ fluid moves into the interstitium and alveoli ↓ bilateral perihilar shadowing with vascular congestion ↓ pulmonary oedema
exam_trap: C, isolated pleural effusion — tempting because effusions occur in heart failure, but an effusion blunts the costophrenic angle rather than causing bilateral perihilar air-space shadowing.
takeaway: Bilateral perihilar shadowing with congestion in heart failure means pulmonary oedema.

stem:
A chest X-ray demonstrates blunting of one costophrenic angle with a meniscus-shaped opacity.

What is the most likely finding?
why_correct: Blunting of the costophrenic angle with a meniscus-shaped opacity is the classic chest X-ray appearance of a pleural effusion.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary oedema causes bilateral perihilar shadowing and congestion, not a unilateral meniscus. B. Hyperinflation causes flattened diaphragms and increased lung volume, not costophrenic blunting. C. Pneumothorax shows a visible pleural line with absent lung markings, not a meniscus opacity. E. A rib fracture shows a cortical break in the rib, not a meniscus-shaped opacity.
pearl: A pleural effusion blunts the costophrenic angle with a meniscus; a large one can push the mediastinum away, and an unexplained unilateral effusion needs investigation.
thinking: Unilateral chest X-ray change ↓ fluid gravitates to the lung base ↓ the costophrenic angle is blunted ↓ fluid tracks up the pleura, forming a meniscus ↓ pleural effusion
exam_trap: A, pulmonary oedema — tempting because fluid is involved, but oedema causes bilateral perihilar shadowing, not a unilateral meniscus at the costophrenic angle.
takeaway: A blunted costophrenic angle with a meniscus means pleural effusion.

stem:
A patient has jaundice, itching and markedly raised ALP and GGT.

Which pattern is most likely?
why_correct: Jaundice with pruritus and a predominant rise in ALP and GGT indicates cholestasis, which may be intrahepatic or due to biliary obstruction (for example gallstones or pancreatic cancer).
why_wrong: A. A hepatocellular pattern is dominated by raised transaminases rather than ALP and GGT. B. Thyrotoxicosis does not typically cause cholestatic jaundice with marked ALP and GGT elevation. C. Haemolysis causes an unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without raised ALP or GGT. E. Renal failure does not cause this liver test pattern.
pearl: Match the liver test pattern to the cause: transaminases dominate in hepatocellular injury, while ALP and GGT dominate in cholestasis, which should prompt ultrasound of the biliary tree.
thinking: Jaundice with itching ↓ itching suggests retained bile salts ↓ markedly raised ALP with raised GGT confirms a biliary origin ↓ intrahepatic or obstructive cause ↓ cholestatic liver-test pattern
exam_trap: A, isolated hepatocellular pattern — tempting because jaundice suggests liver injury, but hepatocellular disease is led by raised transaminases, not ALP and GGT.
takeaway: Raised ALP and GGT with jaundice and itch means cholestasis: look for obstruction.

stem:
A 62-year-old man has visible painless haematuria without evidence of urinary infection.

What is the important principle?

options.A: Treat as renal colic with analgesia and review in clinic if it recurs
options.B: Investigate for an underlying cause, including urinary tract cancer
options.C: Advise increased fluid intake and repeat urine dipstick in three months
options.D: Attribute it to recent strenuous exercise and recheck after a week's rest
options.E: Check renal function and reassure if it is normal

correct_answer: B. Investigate for an underlying cause, including urinary tract cancer
why_correct: Visible haematuria in an adult aged 45 or over without infection should be referred via a suspected cancer pathway (NICE NG12) to exclude bladder or renal malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Painless haematuria does not suggest stones, which typically cause pain. C. Haematuria should not be attributed to dehydration, and delay risks missing malignancy. D. Exercise-related haematuria is a diagnosis of exclusion. E. Normal renal function does not exclude urological malignancy.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult, once infection is excluded, is urological cancer until proven otherwise; refer on a suspected cancer pathway for cystoscopy and imaging.
thinking: Visible haematuria ↓ painless, so stones less likely ↓ no urinary infection ↓ older man at risk of bladder or renal cancer ↓ investigate for an underlying cause, including cancer
exam_trap: E, check renal function and reassure if normal — tempting as a sensible screen, but normal renal function does not exclude bladder or renal cancer.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult needs urgent investigation for urological cancer.

stem:
A patient has persistent significant proteinuria on testing.

Which organ system is most directly implicated?
why_correct: Persistent proteinuria indicates glomerular or tubular kidney damage and is used with eGFR to stage chronic kidney disease (NICE NG203).
why_wrong: A. Skin disease does not directly cause proteinuria. C. Thyroid disease does not directly cause persistent proteinuria. D. Pancreatic disease does not directly cause persistent proteinuria. E. Lung disease does not directly cause proteinuria.
pearl: Persistent proteinuria is a marker of kidney damage and increased cardiovascular risk; quantify it with a urine albumin:creatinine ratio and interpret it alongside eGFR.
thinking: Proteinuria on repeated testing ↓ healthy glomeruli prevent significant protein loss ↓ persistent leakage implies glomerular or tubular damage ↓ used with eGFR to stage CKD ↓ kidney
exam_trap: D, pancreas — tempting because diabetes is a common cause of proteinuric kidney disease, but the protein leak itself comes from damaged kidneys, not the pancreas.
takeaway: Persistent proteinuria points to the kidney: quantify it and assess renal function.

stem:
A patient with malignancy develops constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion. Calcium is markedly elevated.

Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
why_correct: Constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion ("bones, stones, groans and moans") with a markedly raised calcium indicate hypercalcaemia, commonly due to malignancy through PTHrP or bone metastases. It is treated with IV fluids and a bisphosphonate.
why_wrong: A. Hypocalcaemia causes paraesthesia, tetany and seizures. B. Hypokalaemia causes weakness and arrhythmias and does not explain the raised calcium. C. Hypoglycaemia causes acute neuroglycopenic and autonomic symptoms, not polyuria and constipation. D. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion but does not explain a markedly raised calcium.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy causes bones, stones, groans and moans; treat with IV fluid rehydration first, followed by an IV bisphosphonate.
thinking: Known malignancy ↓ constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion ↓ classic symptoms of a raised calcium ↓ markedly elevated calcium confirms it ↓ hypercalcaemia
exam_trap: D, hyponatraemia — tempting because confusion in cancer is often due to low sodium, but it does not explain the polyuria, constipation or markedly raised calcium.
takeaway: Thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion in cancer: check calcium and rehydrate.

stem:
A doctor is about to prescribe a new medicine.

Which information is particularly important to check before prescribing?

options.A: The patient's preferred community pharmacy and full next-of-kin details
options.B: Allergies, current medicines, relevant conditions and correct dose
options.C: The patient's blood group and the result of their most recent chest X-ray
options.D: The patient's registered GP practice and prescription charge exemption
options.E: The patient's current occupation, smoking status and immunisation history

correct_answer: B. Allergies, current medicines, relevant conditions and correct dose
why_correct: Safe prescribing requires checking allergies, current medicines (for interactions), relevant conditions such as renal or hepatic impairment and pregnancy, and the correct dose, route and frequency.
why_wrong: A. Pharmacy preference and next of kin are not key prescribing safety checks. C. Blood group and chest imaging are not routine prescribing safety checks. D. Administrative details do not determine prescribing safety. E. Occupation, smoking status and immunisation history are not the key safety checks before prescribing.
pearl: Before every new prescription, check allergies, current medicines for interactions, relevant conditions such as renal or hepatic impairment and pregnancy, and the correct dose, route and frequency.
thinking: > Safe prescribing = right patient + right drug + right dose + relevant contraindications/interactions + monitoring.
exam_trap: E, occupation, smoking status and immunisation history — tempting as broad clinical background, but these are not the key safety checks that prevent prescribing errors.
takeaway: Safe prescribing starts with allergies, current medicines, relevant conditions and the right dose.

stem:
A patient with type 1 diabetes is admitted to hospital.

Which principle is important?

options.A: Insulin should not be omitted without an appropriate clinical reason
options.B: Insulin should be withheld whenever the patient is nil by mouth
options.C: Capillary glucose can be checked once a day on the ward
options.D: Basal insulin should be stopped and replaced by a sliding scale
options.E: Insulin doses should be halved for the duration of admission

correct_answer: A. Insulin should not be omitted without an appropriate clinical reason
why_correct: People with type 1 diabetes are insulin-deficient and need basal insulin at all times, even when not eating, to prevent DKA. JBDS inpatient guidance states that insulin should not be omitted without a clear clinical reason.
why_wrong: B. Basal insulin is required even when the patient is not eating, to prevent DKA. C. Regular capillary glucose monitoring is essential in hospital. D. Basal insulin should usually be continued, even when a variable-rate infusion is used. E. Arbitrary dose reduction risks hyperglycaemia and DKA; doses should be individualised.
pearl: People with type 1 diabetes require insulin to prevent ketosis and DKA.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes ↓ absolute insulin deficiency ↓ basal insulin is needed even when not eating ↓ omission risks ketosis and DKA ↓ do not omit insulin without a clear clinical reason
exam_trap: B, withhold insulin when nil by mouth — tempting because of fear of hypoglycaemia, but people with type 1 diabetes still need basal insulin to prevent DKA.
takeaway: Never omit insulin in type 1 diabetes without a clear reason; basal insulin continues.

stem:
A patient has been taking systemic corticosteroids for several months.

Which prescribing principle is important?

options.A: Stop them abruptly, as adrenal suppression resolves quickly
options.B: Stop them abruptly if the original condition is controlled
options.C: Switch to an equivalent dose of inhaled corticosteroid and stop
options.D: Double the dose for a week and then stop
options.E: Taper the dose gradually rather than stopping abruptly

correct_answer: E. Taper the dose gradually rather than stopping abruptly
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroids suppress the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, so abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis. The BNF and NICE CKS advise gradual tapering after more than 3 weeks of treatment (or other specified risk situations).
why_wrong: A. HPA suppression after months of treatment can persist, and abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis. B. Disease control does not remove the risk of adrenal insufficiency on abrupt withdrawal. C. Inhaled corticosteroids do not provide adequate systemic replacement. D. Escalating then stopping abruptly still risks adrenal insufficiency.
pearl: Long-term systemic steroids suppress the adrenal axis: taper gradually, and make sure the patient has a steroid emergency card and sick day advice to prevent adrenal crisis.
thinking: Several months of systemic corticosteroids ↓ HPA axis suppressed ↓ the adrenals cannot respond immediately ↓ abrupt stopping risks adrenal crisis ↓ taper the dose gradually
exam_trap: B, stop abruptly once the condition is controlled — tempting because the drug is no longer needed for the disease, but adrenal suppression persists and abrupt withdrawal risks crisis.
takeaway: After prolonged systemic steroids, taper gradually; never stop abruptly.

stem:
A patient is admitted to hospital with a long list of medicines from several sources.

What is the purpose of medication reconciliation?

options.A: To stop medicines that are not needed during the hospital admission
options.B: To establish an accurate medicines list and identify discrepancies
options.C: To transfer responsibility for all prescribing to the ward pharmacist
options.D: To identify which medicines can be switched to generics
options.E: To record the cost of the patient's medicines for the hospital trust

correct_answer: B. To establish an accurate medicines list and identify discrepancies
why_correct: Medicines reconciliation, recommended by NICE NG5, compares sources to establish an accurate current medicines list on admission and identifies discrepancies, omissions and potential errors.
why_wrong: A. Reconciliation establishes what the patient takes; it is not primarily about stopping medicines. C. Reconciliation supports, but does not transfer, prescribing responsibility. D. Generic switching is not the purpose of reconciliation. E. Cost recording is not the purpose of reconciliation.
pearl: Medicines reconciliation compares several sources, such as the patient, the GP record and their own medicines, to produce one accurate list and catch omissions, duplications and errors on admission.
thinking: Admission with medicines from several sources ↓ lists may conflict ↓ compare all sources with the patient's account ↓ identify omissions, duplications and discrepancies ↓ accurate medicines list
exam_trap: A, stopping medicines not needed during admission — tempting as part of reviewing medicines, but reconciliation first establishes what is taken; stopping drugs is a separate decision.
takeaway: Reconciliation establishes an accurate medicines list and identifies discrepancies.

stem:
In a clinical trial, an event occurs in 15% of patients receiving standard treatment and 10% receiving the new treatment.

What is the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction is the control event rate minus the experimental event rate: 15% − 10% = 5%.
why_wrong: A. 2% does not correspond to the difference between the event rates. C. 10% is the event rate in the new treatment group, not the risk reduction. D. 15% is the event rate in the standard treatment group. E. 25% is the sum of the two rates, not their difference.
thinking: Standard treatment event rate 15% (control) ↓ new treatment event rate 10% (experimental) ↓ ARR = control rate minus experimental rate ↓ 15% − 10% = 5%
exam_trap: C, 10% — tempting because it appears in the stem, but it is the event rate on the new treatment, not the difference between the two groups.
takeaway: ARR is a simple subtraction: control event rate minus experimental event rate.

stem:
A study reports an absolute risk increase of 5% for an adverse effect associated with a treatment.

What is the number needed to harm?
why_correct: The number needed to harm is 1 divided by the absolute risk increase: 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20.
why_wrong: A. An NNH of 2 would correspond to an absolute risk increase of 50%. B. 5 is the absolute risk increase expressed as a percentage, not the NNH. C. An NNH of 10 would correspond to an absolute risk increase of 10%. E. An NNH of 100 would correspond to an absolute risk increase of 1%.
thinking: > NNH uses absolute risk increase, just as NNT uses absolute risk reduction.
exam_trap: B, 5 — tempting because the stem quotes 5%, but that is the absolute risk increase itself; the NNH is its reciprocal, 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20.
takeaway: NNH = 1 ÷ absolute risk increase (as a decimal), just as NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding three years after her menopause.

What is the appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Treat as atrophic vaginitis with topical oestrogen first
options.B: Arrange CA125 testing for ovarian cancer as the main step
options.C: Reassure that bleeding is common in the years after menopause
options.D: Investigate the cause, including endometrial pathology
options.E: Repeat assessment if bleeding recurs within six months

correct_answer: D. Investigate the cause, including endometrial pathology
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding (bleeding 12 months or more after the last period) must be investigated, and NICE NG12 (amended 2026) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 and over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to HRT. This woman aged 63 needs referral for transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial assessment to exclude endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: A. Atrophic vaginitis is a common cause, but malignancy must be excluded first. B. Endometrial pathology, not ovarian cancer, is the main concern. C. Bleeding after menopause is not normal and needs investigation. E. A single episode of postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding needs investigation for endometrial cancer; first-line assessment is transvaginal ultrasound of endometrial thickness, with endometrial sampling when indicated.
thinking: > Any postmenopausal bleeding  ↓  investigate.
exam_trap: A, atrophic vaginitis treated with topical oestrogen — tempting because atrophy is a common cause, but it can be accepted only after endometrial cancer has been excluded.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding is never normal: investigate to exclude endometrial cancer.

stem:
A 51-year-old woman has hot flushes, night sweats and irregular periods. Her symptoms are affecting her quality of life.

Which is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Arrange FSH testing to confirm menopause before any treatment
options.B: Discuss options, including menopausal hormone therapy
options.C: Advise that symptoms should be tolerated until periods stop
options.E: Refer for hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy

correct_answer: B. Discuss options, including menopausal hormone therapy
why_correct: NICE NG23 recommends discussing management options for menopausal symptoms affecting quality of life, with HRT the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms after individual benefits and risks are considered.
why_wrong: A. FSH testing is not needed to diagnose perimenopause in women over 45 with typical symptoms. C. Effective treatments are available and symptoms affecting quality of life should be managed. D. Non-hormonal options are not first line; HRT is most effective for vasomotor symptoms. E. Surgery is not indicated for menopausal symptoms.
pearl: Over 45 with typical vasomotor symptoms, perimenopause is a clinical diagnosis without FSH testing; HRT is the most effective treatment, discussed with individual benefits and risks.
