thinking: Woman aged 51 ↓ hot flushes, night sweats and irregular periods ↓ clinical diagnosis of perimenopause ↓ symptoms affect quality of life ↓ discuss options, including menopausal hormone therapy
exam_trap: A, FSH testing before any treatment — tempting as objective confirmation, but it is unnecessary over 45 with typical symptoms, and levels fluctuate in perimenopause.
takeaway: Perimenopause over 45 is a clinical diagnosis; HRT is the most effective symptom treatment.

stem:
A woman with six weeks of amenorrhoea develops severe abdominal pain and collapses. She has a positive pregnancy test and is hypotensive.

What is the priority?

options.A: Transvaginal ultrasound in the early pregnancy unit the next morning
options.B: Serial serum hCG measurements 48 hours apart
options.C: Analgesia and discharge with safety-netting advice and GP review
options.D: Intramuscular methotrexate for a presumed unruptured ectopic pregnancy
options.E: Emergency resuscitation for possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy

correct_answer: E. Emergency resuscitation for possible ruptured ectopic pregnancy
why_correct: Abdominal pain and collapse with hypotension and a positive pregnancy test at six weeks indicate a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise. ABCDE resuscitation, cross-matched blood and immediate gynaecology referral for surgery are required (NICE NG126).
why_wrong: A. Delaying assessment would be dangerous in a shocked patient. B. Serial hCG monitoring is for stable patients and would delay life-saving treatment. C. Discharge in shock would be dangerous. D. Methotrexate is for stable unruptured ectopic pregnancy, not haemodynamic collapse.
pearl: Any woman of reproductive age who collapses with abdominal pain needs a pregnancy test; if positive and shocked, resuscitate and involve the gynaecology team for surgery immediately.
thinking: > Early pregnancy + pain + collapse  ↓  ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.
exam_trap: D, methotrexate for a presumed unruptured ectopic — tempting because ectopic pregnancy is suspected, but methotrexate is only for stable patients; hypotension signals rupture needing surgery.
takeaway: Positive pregnancy test, pain and shock: ruptured ectopic, so resuscitate and go to theatre.

stem:
A woman at term is found to have a persistent breech presentation.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Discuss management options, taking account of her preferences
options.B: Book a planned caesarean section without discussing other options
options.C: Offer external cephalic version once labour has started
options.D: Arrange an immediate caesarean section on the day of diagnosis
options.E: Await spontaneous labour and plan a vaginal birth as usual

correct_answer: A. Discuss management options, taking account of her preferences
why_correct: Persistent breech presentation at term requires discussion of options, including external cephalic version, planned caesarean section or planned vaginal breech birth, considering gestation, maternal and fetal factors and patient preference (RCOG Green-top Guideline 20b and NICE NG192).
why_wrong: B. Options such as external cephalic version should be discussed. C. External cephalic version is offered before labour, not during it. D. Breech at diagnosis does not mandate immediate caesarean section. E. Breech presentation significantly influences delivery planning.
pearl: For breech at term, offer external cephalic version to suitable women; if declined or unsuccessful, discuss planned caesarean birth and vaginal breech birth so she can make an informed choice.
thinking: Persistent breech at term ↓ several reasonable options exist ↓ ECV, planned caesarean or vaginal breech birth ↓ choice depends on clinical factors and her preference ↓ discuss options with her
exam_trap: B, book a caesarean without discussing other options — tempting as a common outcome for breech, but it ignores ECV and her right to an informed choice.
takeaway: Breech at term: discuss ECV and birth options and let the woman make an informed choice.

stem:
A breastfeeding mother needs a medicine for a significant medical condition.

What is the most appropriate general principle?

options.A: Check whether the medicine is compatible with breastfeeding
options.B: Advise her to stop breastfeeding while taking any medicine
options.C: Advise her to express and discard milk for the whole course
options.D: Prescribe it, as most drugs do not pass into breast milk
options.E: Defer treatment until she has finished breastfeeding

correct_answer: A. Check whether the medicine is compatible with breastfeeding
why_correct: Many medicines are compatible with breastfeeding. Resources such as the BNF and UKDILAS should be used to check safety, often allowing treatment and continued breastfeeding.
why_wrong: B. Breastfeeding often does not need to stop when medication is required. C. Discarding milk is unnecessary for many medicines; compatibility should be checked. D. Many medicines pass into breast milk, so compatibility should be checked. E. A significant condition may need treatment, so deferring it could harm the mother.
pearl: Many medicines are compatible with breastfeeding: check a specialist source such as UKDILAS or the BNF before advising a mother to stop feeding or delay treatment.
thinking: Breastfeeding mother ↓ significant condition needs treatment ↓ some drugs pass into milk, but many are safe ↓ check compatibility using a reliable source ↓ check whether the medicine is compatible with breastfeeding
exam_trap: B, stop breastfeeding while taking any medicine — tempting as the cautious option, but many medicines are compatible, and stopping unnecessarily loses the benefits of breastfeeding.
takeaway: Check compatibility before prescribing in breastfeeding; stopping feeding is often unnecessary.

stem:
A patient with severe loin-to-groin pain also has fever, rigors and systemic illness.

What is the important concern?

options.A: Uncomplicated renal colic manageable with oral NSAIDs and fluids at home
options.B: Acute pyelonephritis without obstruction, needing oral antibiotics at home
options.C: Biliary colic requiring an outpatient ultrasound of the gallbladder
options.D: An infected obstructed urinary system requiring urgent assessment
options.E: Mechanical musculoskeletal back pain needing physiotherapy referral

correct_answer: D. An infected obstructed urinary system requiring urgent assessment
why_correct: Fever and rigors with renal colic suggest infection behind an obstructing stone (obstructive pyelonephritis), which is a urological emergency needing urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent plus antibiotics (NICE NG118).
why_wrong: A. Fever and systemic illness make this more than simple renal colic. B. Loin-to-groin colic suggests obstruction; oral antibiotics alone are inadequate. C. Biliary colic does not cause loin-to-groin pain with rigors. E. Musculoskeletal pain does not cause fever and rigors.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: antibiotics alone are not enough, and urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent is needed.
thinking: > Renal colic + infection  ↓  don't treat as uncomplicated stones.
exam_trap: B, pyelonephritis treated with oral antibiotics at home — tempting because fever suggests kidney infection, but loin-to-groin colic implies obstruction, which needs urgent decompression.
takeaway: Renal colic with fever or rigors: suspect an infected obstructed kidney needing urgent decompression.

stem:
A 67-year-old woman has chronic knee pain that is worse with activity. Morning stiffness lasts less than 30 minutes. Examination shows bony swelling and crepitus, and there are no systemic features.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Activity-related knee pain with brief morning stiffness (under 30 minutes), bony swelling and crepitus in a person aged 45 or over, without systemic features, allows a clinical diagnosis of osteoarthritis without investigations (NICE NG226).
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis causes an acutely hot, swollen joint, often with fever. B. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes proximal shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness with raised inflammatory markers. D. Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes symmetrical small-joint synovitis with prolonged morning stiffness. E. Acute gout causes sudden severe pain with redness and swelling, usually not chronic activity-related pain.
pearl: Osteoarthritis can be diagnosed clinically in people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and no or only brief morning stiffness; imaging is not needed to confirm it.
thinking: Older patient with chronic knee pain ↓ worse with activity, brief morning stiffness ↓ bony swelling and crepitus ↓ no systemic features ↓ osteoarthritis
exam_trap: D, rheumatoid arthritis — tempting because morning stiffness is mentioned, but RA causes prolonged stiffness and symmetrical small-joint synovitis, not brief stiffness with bony swelling.
takeaway: Activity-related pain, brief stiffness and bony swelling: a clinical diagnosis of osteoarthritis.

stem:
A 69-year-old man with a history of metastatic cancer develops new severe persistent back pain.

Which feature is a red flag?

options.D: Symptoms lasting one day after exercise

why_correct: A history of malignancy is a key red flag for back pain because it raises the probability of spinal metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression, requiring urgent assessment and MRI (NICE NG234).
why_wrong: B. Pain that improves with movement suggests mechanical back pain. C. Age under 20 is a red flag, but it does not apply to this 69-year-old patient. D. Short-lived pain after exercise suggests a benign mechanical cause. E. A normal neurological examination is reassuring but does not exclude metastases.
pearl: New back pain in someone with a history of cancer is spinal metastasis until proven otherwise; urgent assessment and MRI aim to catch cord compression before neurological deficit develops.
thinking: History of metastatic cancer ↓ new severe persistent back pain ↓ risk of spinal metastases ↓ possible spinal cord compression ↓ previous malignancy is the red flag
exam_trap: C, age under 20 — tempting because it is a recognised back pain red flag, but it does not apply to this 69-year-old; his history of malignancy is the relevant red flag.
takeaway: Back pain plus a history of cancer is a red flag for spinal metastases: assess urgently.

stem:
A patient develops sudden facial weakness. Examination shows weakness of the lower face but preservation of forehead movement. He also has new arm weakness.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Treat as Bell's palsy with oral prednisolone
options.B: Treat as Ramsay Hunt syndrome with aciclovir
options.C: Arrange a routine outpatient MRI of the brain
options.D: Refer for nerve conduction studies of the arm
options.E: Treat as a possible stroke and arrange urgent assessment

correct_answer: E. Treat as a possible stroke and arrange urgent assessment
why_correct: Lower facial weakness with forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion, and the accompanying arm weakness strongly suggests stroke, so urgent stroke assessment is needed (NICE NG128).
why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion involving the forehead and does not cause limb weakness. B. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a lower motor neuron palsy and does not cause arm weakness. C. Routine imaging delays urgent stroke assessment. D. The combination of findings indicates a central cause, not a peripheral nerve problem.
pearl: Forehead sparing marks an upper motor neuron facial palsy because the forehead has bilateral cortical supply; with limb weakness, it is stroke until proven otherwise.
thinking: Facial weakness with forehead sparing + limb deficit ↓ upper motor neuron lesion ↓ stroke pathway.
exam_trap: A, Bell's palsy with prednisolone — tempting because of sudden facial weakness, but Bell's palsy involves the forehead and does not cause arm weakness.
takeaway: Facial weakness sparing the forehead plus limb weakness: think stroke, not Bell's palsy.

stem:
A 35-year-old man has persistent low mood, loss of interest, poor concentration and sleep disturbance for several weeks.

Which additional assessment is particularly important?

options.C: Assume there is no risk because he attended voluntarily
options.D: Arrange a CT head for every patient
options.E: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm

correct_answer: E. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm
why_correct: This presentation is consistent with depression, and NICE NG222 and NG225 advise asking directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and self-harm. Asking directly does not increase risk and allows appropriate safety planning.
why_wrong: A. Childhood history may be relevant but is not the priority risk assessment. B. Avoiding the question may miss significant risk. C. Attending voluntarily does not exclude suicide risk. D. Routine CT head is not indicated for depression.
pearl: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea or increase risk; it allows proper risk assessment and safety planning in anyone with depressive symptoms.
thinking: Low mood and loss of interest for weeks ↓ poor concentration and disturbed sleep ↓ likely depression ↓ depression carries a risk of suicide and self-harm ↓ ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm
exam_trap: C, assuming no risk because he attended voluntarily — tempting as help-seeking seems protective, but attending does not exclude suicidal thoughts, so risk must be asked about.
takeaway: In low mood, always ask directly about suicidal thoughts and self-harm.

stem:
A 23-year-old man develops auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions and marked social withdrawal.

Which broad syndrome is present?
why_correct: Hallucinations and delusions are positive psychotic symptoms. With social withdrawal (a negative symptom), this indicates a psychotic syndrome, for which NICE CG178 advises urgent referral to an early intervention in psychosis service.
why_wrong: A. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions with preserved insight, not delusions. B. Simple phobia is fear of a specific object or situation. C. Panic disorder causes episodes of acute anxiety, not hallucinations or delusions. E. Adjustment disorder involves emotional distress after a stressor, without psychotic features.
pearl: Hallucinations and delusions are positive symptoms and social withdrawal a negative one; a first presentation of psychosis needs urgent referral to an early intervention in psychosis service.
thinking: Auditory hallucinations ↓ persecutory delusions ↓ positive psychotic symptoms with impaired reality testing ↓ social withdrawal as a negative symptom ↓ psychosis
exam_trap: A, OCD — tempting because intrusive thoughts can seem bizarre, but obsessions are recognised as the person's own with insight preserved, unlike fixed persecutory delusions.
takeaway: Hallucinations and delusions define psychosis; refer urgently to early intervention.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of sudden intense fear associated with palpitations, trembling, breathlessness and a feeling that she is going to die. Episodes peak rapidly and resolve.

Which diagnosis is most consistent?
why_correct: Sudden intense fear with autonomic symptoms such as palpitations, trembling and breathlessness, a fear of dying and a rapid peak (usually within 10 minutes) then resolution is characteristic of a panic attack. Recurrent attacks suggest panic disorder (NICE CG113).
why_wrong: B. Mania causes elevated mood, overactivity and grandiosity. C. Delirium causes fluctuating confusion and inattention, not discrete episodes of fear. D. Dementia causes progressive cognitive decline. E. Schizophrenia involves hallucinations, delusions and thought disorder.
pearl: Panic attacks peak within minutes and then settle; consider physical mimics such as arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism or asthma before attributing recurrent episodes to panic.
thinking: Sudden intense fear ↓ palpitations, trembling and breathlessness ↓ fear of dying ↓ rapid peak then resolution, recurring ↓ panic attack
exam_trap: C, delirium — tempting because of the sudden onset and distress, but delirium causes fluctuating confusion and inattention, not discrete self-limiting episodes of fear.
takeaway: Abrupt intense fear with autonomic symptoms that peaks fast and resolves is a panic attack.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with no cognitive impairment refuses a recommended operation because he does not consider the benefits worth the risks.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Ask his next of kin to consent to the operation for him
options.B: Proceed, as the operation is clearly in his best interests
options.C: Apply to the Court of Protection to authorise the operation
options.D: Treat him as lacking capacity because he declined treatment
options.E: Respect his informed decision, as he has capacity

correct_answer: E. Respect his informed decision, as he has capacity
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, an adult is presumed to have capacity, and an unwise decision does not imply incapacity. A capacitous, informed refusal must be respected (GMC Decision making and consent).
why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot consent on behalf of an adult with capacity. B. Doctors cannot override a capacitous refusal because they disagree. C. There is no basis for a court order when the patient has capacity. D. Refusal alone does not indicate a lack of capacity.
pearl: Capacity is presumed in adults, and an unwise decision does not prove incapacity; a capacitous, informed refusal must be respected even if it may lead to harm.
thinking: An unwise decision is not, by itself, evidence of lack of capacity.
exam_trap: B, proceed in his best interests — tempting when the operation is clearly beneficial, but best-interests decisions apply only when capacity is lacking; operating would be unlawful.
takeaway: An adult with capacity may refuse treatment; respect the decision even if it seems unwise.

stem:
A 68-year-old man presents with an acutely painful, hot swollen knee and fever. Septic arthritis is suspected.

Which investigation is particularly important to establish the diagnosis?

options.A: Joint aspiration for fluid analysis and culture
options.B: Plain X-ray of the knee to confirm joint infection
options.C: Serum urate level to confirm or exclude the diagnosis
options.D: C-reactive protein and white cell count as the main test
options.E: MRI of the knee as the first-line imaging investigation

correct_answer: A. Joint aspiration for fluid analysis and culture
why_correct: Urgent joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy, ideally before antibiotics, is the key investigation for suspected septic arthritis, and blood cultures should also be taken.
why_wrong: B. Plain X-ray cannot confirm early joint infection. C. Serum urate does not diagnose or exclude septic arthritis. D. Inflammatory markers are supportive but cannot establish the diagnosis. E. MRI is not the first investigation and does not identify the organism.
pearl: Aspirate a suspected septic joint urgently, ideally before antibiotics; send fluid for Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy, and take blood cultures as well.
thinking: Acute hot swollen joint + systemic features ↓ urgently investigate for septic arthritis.
exam_trap: D, CRP and white cell count — tempting as quick markers of infection, but they are only supportive and cannot confirm septic arthritis or identify the organism.
takeaway: Suspected septic arthritis: aspirate the joint for Gram stain, culture and crystals.

stem:
A 46-year-old patient has persistent swelling and morning stiffness affecting several small joints.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Advise rest and regular paracetamol for osteoarthritis
options.B: Refer for assessment for inflammatory arthritis
options.C: Request a hand X-ray and review in six months
options.D: Check rheumatoid factor and reassure if it is negative
options.E: Start prednisolone 30 mg daily and review in a month

correct_answer: B. Refer for assessment for inflammatory arthritis
why_correct: Persistent synovitis of several small joints with morning stiffness suggests inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis, and NICE NG100 recommends urgent referral to rheumatology.
why_wrong: A. Small-joint swelling with morning stiffness suggests inflammatory, not degenerative, disease. C. Persistent synovitis needs prompt referral, not delayed review. D. A negative rheumatoid factor does not exclude inflammatory arthritis; referral should not be delayed. E. Steroids before diagnosis may mask the disease and cause harm.
pearl: Persistent synovitis of small joints needs urgent rheumatology referral even if rheumatoid factor is negative, because early disease-modifying treatment reduces joint damage.
thinking: Several small joints affected ↓ persistent swelling suggests synovitis ↓ morning stiffness suggests inflammation ↓ likely inflammatory arthritis such as RA ↓ refer for assessment
exam_trap: D, check rheumatoid factor and reassure if negative — tempting as a quick test, but a negative result does not exclude inflammatory arthritis and must not delay referral.
takeaway: Persistent small-joint synovitis needs prompt rheumatology referral, whatever the RF result.

stem:
A 55-year-old man has shoulder pain that is particularly troublesome when lifting his arm overhead. There is no history of trauma or systemic illness.

Which broad group of conditions should be considered?

options.C: Acute myocardial infarction in every case

why_correct: Pain on overhead activity without trauma or systemic illness is typical of a rotator cuff or subacromial disorder, such as tendinopathy or impingement.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain. B. Cauda equina syndrome affects lumbosacral nerve roots. C. Myocardial infarction is not suggested by mechanical overhead shoulder pain. E. Septic arthritis causes an acutely hot joint with systemic features.
pearl: Pain on overhead activity without trauma suggests rotator cuff or subacromial pathology; a painful arc on abduction is a typical examination finding.
thinking: Shoulder pain ↓ worse lifting the arm overhead ↓ no trauma or systemic illness ↓ mechanical cuff or subacromial irritation ↓ rotator cuff/subacromial disorders
exam_trap: E, septic arthritis in every case — tempting as a do-not-miss diagnosis, but septic arthritis causes an acutely hot joint with systemic features, which are absent here.
takeaway: Overhead-activity shoulder pain without trauma points to rotator cuff or subacromial disorders.

stem:
A young man develops severe increasing pain and tense swelling of the lower leg following a tibial fracture. The pain is particularly severe on passive stretching.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Elevate the leg well above heart level and review in 4 hours
options.B: Urgent assessment for acute compartment syndrome
options.C: Give opioid analgesia and reassess on the morning ward round
options.D: Measure the circumference of the leg and repeat tomorrow
options.E: Apply a firmer circumferential bandage to control the swelling

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment for acute compartment syndrome
why_correct: Severe pain out of proportion to the injury, a tense compartment and pain on passive stretch after a tibial fracture indicate acute compartment syndrome. This is an orthopaedic emergency: release all circumferential dressings, keep the limb at heart level and arrange urgent fasciotomy (BOAST guidance).
why_wrong: A. Elevation above heart level reduces perfusion, and delay risks muscle necrosis. C. Analgesia and delay can mask progression of a limb-threatening emergency. D. Delay can lead to muscle necrosis and limb loss. E. A tighter bandage would increase compartment pressure.
pearl: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome; distal pulses are often still present, so a palpable pulse never excludes it.
thinking: > Severe disproportionate pain + tense compartment + pain on passive stretch  ↓  emergency.
exam_trap: A, elevate the leg above heart level — tempting as standard care for swelling, but elevation reduces perfusion in compartment syndrome, and delay risks muscle necrosis.
takeaway: Disproportionate pain after a fracture: suspect compartment syndrome and act immediately.

stem:
A patient is suspected of having bacterial sepsis and antibiotics are being considered.

When should blood cultures generally be obtained?

options.A: After the first dose of antibiotics has been given
options.B: If the temperature is above 38.5 °C at the time
options.C: After 48 hours if there is no response to antibiotics
options.D: Before antibiotics, provided this does not delay treatment
options.E: Before antibiotics, even if this delays them for hours

correct_answer: D. Before antibiotics, provided this does not delay treatment
why_correct: Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics where this does not delay treatment, to identify the organism, but antibiotics must not be delayed in high-risk sepsis (NICE NG253).
why_wrong: A. Cultures taken after antibiotics have a reduced yield. B. Blood cultures are indicated in suspected sepsis regardless of temperature. C. Delayed cultures are less useful for the initial diagnosis. E. Antibiotics must not be delayed in sepsis to obtain cultures.
pearl: Take blood cultures before antibiotics when this causes no delay, but in high-risk sepsis antibiotics come first if cultures cannot be taken promptly.
thinking: Suspected bacterial sepsis ↓ cultures identify the organism and guide therapy ↓ antibiotics reduce culture yield ↓ but delayed antibiotics increase harm ↓ take cultures before antibiotics, without delaying them
exam_trap: E, cultures first even if antibiotics are delayed for hours — tempting because it maximises yield, but delaying antibiotics in sepsis worsens outcomes.
takeaway: Blood cultures before antibiotics, but never let cultures delay antibiotics in sepsis.

stem:
A doctor is about to take blood from a patient.

Which action is essential immediately before the procedure?

options.A: Check identity using the bed number and name above the bed
options.B: Confirm identity with the nurse looking after the patient
options.C: Pre-label the sample tubes at the nurses' station
options.D: Check the request form, as the patient is known to you
options.E: Confirm the patient's identity and explain the procedure

correct_answer: E. Confirm the patient's identity and explain the procedure
why_correct: Positive patient identification and explanation of the procedure, with verbal consent, are essential before venepuncture to prevent wrong-patient errors.
why_wrong: A. Bed numbers and signs are unreliable identifiers. B. Identity should be confirmed directly with the patient and wristband. C. Pre-labelling risks wrong blood in tube errors. D. Familiarity does not replace positive patient identification.
pearl: Positive identification means asking the patient to state their name and date of birth and checking these against the wristband and request form, never relying on bed position or familiarity.
thinking: Venepuncture planned ↓ wrong-patient and wrong blood in tube errors are key risks ↓ identity must be confirmed with the patient directly ↓ consent requires an explanation ↓ confirm identity and explain the procedure
exam_trap: D, relying on the request form because the patient is known to you — tempting through familiarity, but recognition does not replace positive identification at the bedside.
takeaway: Before any procedure, positively identify the patient and explain what you will do.

stem:
A doctor has taken blood from a patient.

When should the sample be labelled?

options.A: Back at the doctors' office before sending
options.C: At the end of the ward round, in one batch
options.D: At the nurses' station using the request form
options.E: At the bedside, immediately after collection

correct_answer: E. At the bedside, immediately after collection
why_correct: Samples should be labelled at the bedside immediately after collection, using positive patient identification, to prevent wrong blood in tube errors.
why_wrong: A. Labelling away from the patient risks identification errors. B. Pre-labelling before collection risks wrong blood in tube errors. C. Batch labelling greatly increases the risk of mislabelling. D. Labelling away from the patient risks identification errors.
pearl: Label blood tubes at the bedside, immediately after collection, from the patient's positive identification; never pre-label or batch-label, as both cause wrong blood in tube errors.
thinking: > Correct patient identification and specimen labelling are fundamental patient-safety steps.
exam_trap: B, pre-printed labels before collection — tempting because it saves time, but pre-labelled tubes can be used for the wrong patient, causing wrong blood in tube errors.
takeaway: Label samples at the bedside, immediately after collection, one patient at a time.

stem:
A patient develops fever, chills, back pain and hypotension shortly after a blood transfusion starts.

What is the immediate action?

options.A: Slow the transfusion rate and give paracetamol
options.B: Give chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion
options.C: Complete the unit, then send a sample to the lab
options.D: Continue and recheck observations in an hour
options.E: Stop the transfusion and begin emergency assessment

correct_answer: E. Stop the transfusion and begin emergency assessment
why_correct: Fever, rigors, loin pain and hypotension soon after starting a transfusion suggest an acute haemolytic or other serious transfusion reaction. Stop the transfusion immediately, keep the line open with saline, check patient and unit identity and begin emergency management (BSH and SHOT guidance).
why_wrong: A. Slowing the rate continues exposure in a potentially fatal reaction. B. Continuing the transfusion is unsafe with hypotension and back pain. C. Completing the unit would worsen the reaction. D. Continuing the transfusion would worsen the reaction.
pearl: In any suspected serious transfusion reaction, stop the transfusion first, keep the line open, recheck patient and unit identity, and report; ABO incompatibility usually follows an identification error.
thinking: > Suspected serious transfusion reaction  ↓  stop transfusion first.
exam_trap: A, slow the rate and give paracetamol — tempting because mild febrile reactions can be managed this way, but hypotension and back pain suggest a serious reaction needing the transfusion stopped.
takeaway: Fever with hypotension or back pain during transfusion: stop it immediately and assess.

stem:
A patient is receiving supplemental oxygen in hospital.

What is an important principle?

options.A: Titrate oxygen upwards to maintain oxygen saturations at 100% on monitoring
options.B: Give 15 L/min via a reservoir mask until the patient is ready for discharge
options.C: Use 88–92% as the default target saturation range for most hospital patients
options.D: Give oxygen without a prescription, as it is not classed as a medicine
options.E: Prescribe oxygen to a target saturation range suited to the patient

correct_answer: E. Prescribe oxygen to a target saturation range suited to the patient
why_correct: Oxygen is a drug and should be prescribed to a target saturation range, usually 94–98% or 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, in line with BTS guidance.
why_wrong: A. Hyperoxaemia can cause harm; target ranges are below 100%. B. Excessive oxygen can cause harm, including hypercapnia in at-risk patients. C. 88–92% is for patients at risk of hypercapnia; most patients target 94–98%. D. Oxygen is a drug and requires prescription.
pearl: Oxygen is a medicine: prescribe a target saturation range, usually 94–98%, or 88–92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, and titrate to it.
thinking: Hospital patient on oxygen ↓ oxygen is a drug that harms in excess ↓ hyperoxaemia, and hypercapnia in some patients ↓ the right target depends on the patient ↓ prescribe to a suitable target range
exam_trap: C, 88–92% as the default target — tempting as a familiar figure, but it applies to patients at risk of hypercapnia; most hospital patients target 94–98%.
takeaway: Prescribe oxygen to a target saturation range that fits the individual patient.

stem:
A standard 12-lead ECG is being recorded.

Which lead is a limb lead?
why_correct: Lead I is a limb lead, recording the potential between the right and left arm electrodes. The limb leads are I, II, III, aVR, aVL and aVF.
why_wrong: A. V6 is a chest (precordial) lead. C. V2 is a chest (precordial) lead. D. V5 is a chest (precordial) lead. E. V1 is a chest (precordial) lead.
pearl: The 12-lead ECG has six limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) viewing the frontal plane and six chest leads (V1–V6) viewing the horizontal plane.
thinking: Twelve leads in a standard ECG ↓ V1–V6 are chest (precordial) leads ↓ I, II, III, aVR, aVL and aVF are limb leads ↓ lead I records between the two arm electrodes ↓ lead I
exam_trap: E, lead V1 — tempting because it is often listed first, but V1 is a chest lead placed at the right sternal edge; of these options, only lead I is a limb lead.
takeaway: Limb leads are I, II, III, aVR, aVL and aVF; V1–V6 are chest leads.

stem:
A patient with acute kidney injury has potassium of 7.1 mmol/L. The ECG shows broad QRS complexes.

What is the immediate concern?

options.B: Moderate hyperkalaemia treated with oral calcium resonium alone
options.C: Pseudohyperkalaemia needing a repeat venous sample first
options.D: Incidental bundle branch block unrelated to the potassium

correct_answer: A. Life-threatening hyperkalaemia needing urgent treatment
why_correct: A potassium of 7.1 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes indicates life-threatening hyperkalaemia with imminent risk of arrhythmia. Give IV calcium immediately to stabilise the myocardium, followed by insulin–glucose (UK Kidney Association and RCUK guidance).
why_wrong: B. A potassium over 6.5 mmol/L with ECG changes is an emergency needing IV calcium and insulin–glucose. C. ECG changes confirm true hyperkalaemia; treatment must not wait for a repeat sample. D. Broad QRS complexes with potassium of 7.1 mmol/L should be attributed to hyperkalaemia. E. Hypercalcaemia does not explain the raised potassium and QRS widening.
pearl: With hyperkalaemia and ECG changes, give IV calcium first to protect the heart, then insulin–glucose to shift potassium; calcium does not lower the potassium level itself.
thinking: AKI ↓ potassium 7.1 mmol/L, severely raised ↓ broad QRS complexes show cardiac toxicity ↓ imminent risk of fatal arrhythmia ↓ life-threatening hyperkalaemia needing urgent treatment
exam_trap: C, pseudohyperkalaemia needing a repeat sample — tempting as haemolysed samples are common, but ECG changes confirm true hyperkalaemia, so treatment must not wait.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is an emergency: IV calcium now, then insulin–glucose.

stem:
A doctor sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle.

What should they do first?

options.A: Give immediate first aid and report it via the local procedure
options.B: Scrub the wound with alcohol and report it at the end of the shift
options.C: Wash the wound and report it if the patient is high risk
options.D: Finish the procedure, then report it at the next appraisal
options.E: Squeeze the wound firmly and apply a plaster, without reporting

correct_answer: A. Give immediate first aid and report it via the local procedure
why_correct: After a needlestick injury, encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water (without scrubbing) and report immediately to occupational health or the emergency department for risk assessment and post-exposure prophylaxis (UKHSA guidance).
why_wrong: B. Scrubbing is not recommended, and delayed reporting may delay post-exposure prophylaxis. C. All exposures need reporting and risk assessment, whatever the presumed source risk. D. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective when started as soon as possible. E. Aggressive squeezing is not recommended, and failing to report prevents risk assessment.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage the wound to bleed, wash it with soap and running water without scrubbing, and report immediately so post-exposure prophylaxis can start promptly if needed.
thinking: Needlestick from a used needle ↓ risk of blood-borne virus transmission ↓ first aid reduces exposure ↓ HIV PEP works best when started as soon as possible ↓ first aid and immediate reporting
exam_trap: C, wash and report only if the patient is high risk — tempting to save time, but source risk is often unknown; every exposure needs reporting and risk assessment.
takeaway: Needlestick injury: first aid, then report immediately, every time.

stem:
A healthcare worker is about to examine a patient with a suspected transmissible infection.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Use precautions suited to the likely infection and procedure
options.B: Rely on gloves alone, without hand hygiene before or after
options.C: Use the same droplet precautions regardless of the organism
options.D: Defer precautions until the lab confirms the infection
options.E: Wear an apron, which removes the need for hand hygiene

correct_answer: A. Use precautions suited to the likely infection and procedure
why_correct: Infection prevention measures should be standard precautions plus transmission-based precautions tailored to the likely route of spread and the procedure (National Infection Prevention and Control Manual).
why_wrong: B. Hand hygiene is still required before and after glove use. C. Contact, droplet and airborne infections require different precautions. D. Precautions should be based on the suspected infection, not delayed until confirmation. E. PPE does not replace hand hygiene.
pearl: Apply standard precautions to every patient, adding contact, droplet or airborne precautions according to the likely organism and procedure; PPE never replaces hand hygiene.
thinking: Suspected transmissible infection ↓ standard precautions apply to everyone ↓ routes differ: contact, droplet or airborne ↓ the procedure may add risk ↓ precautions suited to the infection and procedure
exam_trap: D, defer precautions until the lab confirms infection — tempting to avoid unnecessary PPE, but transmission can occur before results return, so precautions follow suspicion.
takeaway: Base infection precautions on the suspected organism and the procedure, plus hand hygiene.

stem:
A patient has a persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats. Chest imaging suggests pulmonary tuberculosis.

What is the important immediate consideration?

options.A: Nurse in an open bay with standard precautions
options.B: Start empirical TB therapy and discharge without isolation
options.C: Repeat the chest X-ray in six weeks before acting
options.D: Treat as community-acquired pneumonia with amoxicillin

correct_answer: E. Infection-control precautions and specialist assessment
why_correct: Suspected pulmonary TB requires airborne isolation (respiratory precautions) and specialist assessment with sputum testing (NICE NG33).
why_wrong: A. An open bay risks transmission to other patients. B. Treatment should follow specialist assessment and sputum testing, with appropriate infection control. C. Abnormal imaging with these symptoms requires prompt investigation. D. Antibiotics for pneumonia do not address suspected TB.
pearl: Suspected pulmonary TB needs a side room with respiratory precautions, sputum samples for microscopy and culture, and specialist assessment before treatment starts.
thinking: Persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats ↓ imaging suggests pulmonary TB ↓ possibly infectious by airborne spread ↓ protect others and confirm the diagnosis ↓ infection control and specialist assessment
exam_trap: D, treat as pneumonia with amoxicillin — tempting because cough with an abnormal X-ray is common, but weight loss and night sweats point to TB, which amoxicillin will not treat.
takeaway: Suspected pulmonary TB: isolate with respiratory precautions and arrange specialist assessment.

stem:
A patient presents with a clinical picture in which HIV infection is a possible diagnosis.

Which approach is appropriate?

options.A: Offer HIV testing with consent and confidentiality
options.B: Avoid testing unless the patient belongs to a high-risk group
options.C: Test without informing the patient to avoid causing distress
options.D: Arrange formal specialist pre-test counselling before offering a test
options.E: Test and inform the GP and employer of the result

correct_answer: A. Offer HIV testing with consent and confidentiality
why_correct: HIV testing should be offered whenever HIV is in the differential diagnosis (BHIVA testing guidelines and NICE NG60), with informed verbal consent and confidentiality maintained.
why_wrong: B. Testing should be offered whenever HIV is clinically possible, regardless of risk group. C. Testing without informing the patient breaches consent. D. Lengthy specialist pre-test counselling is not required; any clinician can offer the test. E. Disclosure to an employer breaches confidentiality.
pearl: Offer an HIV test whenever HIV is in the differential diagnosis, regardless of perceived risk group; informed verbal consent is enough, and lengthy pre-test counselling is not required.
thinking: Clinical picture compatible with HIV ↓ late diagnosis worsens outcomes ↓ testing is offered whatever the risk group ↓ consent and confidentiality apply ↓ offer HIV testing with consent
exam_trap: D, formal specialist pre-test counselling first — tempting as a careful approach, but it is not required and delays diagnosis; any clinician can offer the test.
takeaway: If HIV is possible, offer a test with consent, whatever the patient's risk group.

stem:
A healthcare worker has an occupational exposure to blood from a patient known to have hepatitis B.

What is important?

options.A: Start a 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis
options.B: Check the worker's hepatitis B serology in three months and act if positive
options.C: Give a course of oral antibiotics as prophylaxis
options.D: Report it at the next annual occupational-health review
options.E: Urgent occupational-health assessment for post-exposure management

correct_answer: E. Urgent occupational-health assessment for post-exposure management
why_correct: Exposure to hepatitis B–positive blood requires urgent occupational health assessment of the worker's immunity, with consideration of a hepatitis B vaccine booster or immunoglobulin as soon as possible (UKHSA Green Book).
why_wrong: A. HIV prophylaxis does not address hepatitis B exposure. B. Hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive and should not wait months. C. Antibiotics have no role in hepatitis B exposure. D. Delayed reporting misses the window for prophylaxis.
pearl: After exposure to hepatitis B–positive blood, the worker's vaccination and antibody status decide management: a vaccine booster or course, with immunoglobulin when indicated, as soon as possible.
thinking: Occupational exposure to blood ↓ source is hepatitis B positive ↓ protection depends on the worker's immunity ↓ prophylaxis is time-sensitive ↓ urgent occupational-health assessment
exam_trap: A, a 28-day course of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis — tempting as the familiar needlestick response, but it does not address the known hepatitis B exposure.
takeaway: Hepatitis B exposure needs urgent occupational-health review for time-critical prophylaxis.

stem: Why is unnecessary antibiotic prescribing undesirable?

options.A: It delays recovery from viral infections by suppressing immunity
options.B: It drives antimicrobial resistance and causes avoidable adverse effects
options.C: It is mainly undesirable because of the cost to the NHS
options.D: It increases the risk of acquiring viral infections from others
options.E: It masks fever, so infections are diagnosed at a later stage

correct_answer: B. It drives antimicrobial resistance and causes avoidable adverse effects
why_correct: Unnecessary antibiotics drive antimicrobial resistance and expose patients to adverse effects such as allergy, C. difficile infection and drug interactions, without benefit (NICE NG15).
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not suppress immunity; their main harms are resistance and adverse effects. C. Cost is not the main concern; resistance and adverse effects are. D. Antibiotics do not increase the risk of acquiring viral infections. E. Antibiotics do not mask fever; this is not the reason to avoid unnecessary use.
pearl: Every unnecessary antibiotic carries harm without benefit: it selects for resistant bacteria and exposes the patient to allergy, C. difficile infection and drug interactions.
thinking: Antibiotic given without a bacterial indication ↓ no benefit to the patient ↓ selects resistant organisms ↓ exposes the patient to side effects ↓ drives resistance and causes avoidable adverse effects
exam_trap: C, mainly the cost to the NHS — tempting as a familiar argument, but cost is not the main concern; the key harms are antimicrobial resistance and avoidable adverse effects.
takeaway: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics because they drive resistance and cause avoidable harm.

stem:
A diagnostic test is negative in 95 of 100 patients who do not have the disease.

What is the specificity?
why_correct: Specificity is true negatives divided by all people without the disease: 95 ÷ 100 = 95%.
why_wrong: A. 5% is the false-positive rate (1 − specificity). B. 50% does not correspond to the given data. C. 75% does not correspond to the given data. E. 100% would require no false positives.
pearl: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative; a highly specific test rarely gives false positives, so a positive result helps rule the disease in.
thinking: > Specificity = true negatives ÷ all patients who do not have the disease.
exam_trap: A, 5% — tempting because 5 of the 100 people without disease tested positive, but that is the false-positive rate (1 − specificity), not the specificity.
takeaway: Specificity = true negatives ÷ all people without the disease.

stem:
A study tests 1,000 people:

- 100 have the disease.
- The test is positive in 90 of those 100.
- Of the 900 without disease, 90 also test positive.

What is the positive predictive value?
why_correct: PPV is true positives divided by all positive tests: 90 ÷ (90 + 90) = 50%.
why_wrong: A. 10% is the disease prevalence (100/1,000). B. 25% does not correspond to the given data. D. 75% does not correspond to the given data. E. 90% is the sensitivity (90/100), not the PPV.
pearl:
PPV = true positives ÷ all positive tests

= 90 ÷ (90 + 90)

= 50%
thinking: PPV asks how many positive tests are true positives ↓ true positives = 90 ↓ false positives = 90 ↓ all positives = 180 ↓ 90 ÷ 180 = 50%
exam_trap: E, 90% — tempting because the test detects 90 of 100 people with the disease, but that is the sensitivity; PPV uses all positive results, including the 90 false positives.
takeaway: PPV = true positives ÷ all positive tests; it falls when disease prevalence is low.

stem:
A study finds that people who drink more coffee have a higher incidence of cardiovascular disease. However, heavy coffee drinkers in the study are also substantially more likely to smoke.

What is the major methodological issue?
why_correct: Smoking is associated with both coffee drinking (the exposure) and cardiovascular disease (the outcome), so it confounds the observed association.
why_wrong: A. Blinding addresses observer and performance bias, not this problem. B. Randomisation is a method that reduces confounding, not a methodological flaw. C. Recall bias concerns inaccurate exposure recall, which is not the issue described. D. Publication bias concerns selective publication of studies.
pearl: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome without lying on the causal pathway; randomisation, matching, restriction or statistical adjustment reduce its effect.
thinking: > A third variable is associated with both the exposure and outcome and may distort the observed association.
exam_trap: B, randomisation — tempting because it is closely linked to this problem, but randomisation is the remedy that controls confounding, not the methodological flaw itself.
takeaway: A third factor linked to both exposure and outcome is a confounder.

stem:
A systematic review presents a forest plot comparing a treatment with placebo. The pooled confidence interval for the treatment effect crosses the line of no effect.

What does this indicate?

options.A: None of the individual studies showed a significant effect
options.B: The treatment has been shown to be harmful compared with placebo
options.C: There is significant heterogeneity between the included studies
options.D: The treatment has been shown to have no clinical effect
options.E: The pooled result is not statistically significant at that level

correct_answer: E. The pooled result is not statistically significant at that level
why_correct: A pooled confidence interval crossing the line of no effect includes the null value, so the result is not statistically significant at that confidence level. This does not prove that there is no effect.
why_wrong: A. Individual studies may still show significant results. B. An interval spanning no effect does not demonstrate harm. C. Heterogeneity is assessed separately (for example with I²), not from the pooled interval. D. A non-significant result does not exclude a clinically important effect.
pearl: Statistical non-significance does not prove that there is no clinically important effect.
thinking: > Crossing the line of no effect  ↓  the confidence interval includes the null value.
exam_trap: D, the treatment has no clinical effect — tempting because the result is not significant, but absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; an important effect may still exist.
takeaway: A pooled CI crossing the line of no effect means not statistically significant, not no effect.

stem:
A 5-year-old child develops high fever, severe sore throat, drooling and difficulty breathing. He is sitting forward and appears very unwell.

What is the most important principle?

options.A: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor to confirm the cause
options.B: Lie the child flat and obtain an urgent lateral neck X-ray
options.C: Insert a cannula and take bloods before calling for help
options.D: Give oral antibiotics and fluids and review in 24 hours
options.E: Treat as an airway emergency and seek urgent senior airway help

correct_answer: E. Treat as an airway emergency and seek urgent senior airway help
why_correct: High fever, drooling, stridor or respiratory difficulty and a tripod posture suggest epiglottitis or another upper airway obstruction. Keep the child calm and upright, avoid examining the throat, and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help urgently.
why_wrong: A. Throat examination may precipitate complete airway obstruction. B. Lying flat may worsen airway obstruction, and imaging delays airway management. C. Distressing procedures may precipitate obstruction and delay senior help. D. Delay risks airway loss.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis, keep the child calm and upright, avoid examining the throat or other distressing procedures, and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway.
thinking: > Toxic child + drooling + airway symptoms  ↓  protect the airway; avoid actions that may precipitate deterioration.
exam_trap: A, examining the throat with a tongue depressor — tempting to confirm the diagnosis, but it can precipitate complete airway obstruction in epiglottitis.
takeaway: Drooling, toxic child sitting forward: airway emergency, so do not examine the throat.

stem:
A 4-year-old child has fever, lethargy, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Perform a glass test and review again in four hours if the rash fades
options.B: Give paracetamol and reassess the rash once the fever has settled
options.C: Treat as a medical emergency for possible meningococcal disease
options.D: Arrange an urgent lumbar puncture before giving any antibiotic treatment
options.E: Refer routinely to dermatology for further assessment of the rash

correct_answer: C. Treat as a medical emergency for possible meningococcal disease
why_correct: Fever with a non-blanching rash and neck stiffness suggests meningococcal disease. NICE NG240 requires emergency treatment with immediate parenteral antibiotics (benzylpenicillin in the community, ceftriaxone in hospital) and urgent transfer.
why_wrong: A. Waiting delays life-saving treatment. B. Paracetamol does not treat meningococcal disease, and waiting delays antibiotics. D. Antibiotics must not be delayed for lumbar puncture in suspected meningococcal disease. E. A routine dermatology review would cause fatal delay.
pearl: A non-blanching rash with fever in an unwell child is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; give parenteral antibiotics immediately and never delay them for a lumbar puncture.
thinking: Fever and lethargy in a child ↓ neck stiffness suggests meningitis ↓ non-blanching rash suggests meningococcal septicaemia ↓ can be rapidly fatal without antibiotics ↓ treat as a medical emergency
exam_trap: D, lumbar puncture before antibiotics — tempting as the diagnostic test for meningitis, but antibiotics must not be delayed for LP in suspected meningococcal disease.
takeaway: Fever with a non-blanching rash: give antibiotics immediately and treat as an emergency.

stem:
A 9-year-old with asthma develops increasing wheeze and difficulty speaking in full sentences.

What is the appropriate broad response?

options.A: Assess severity and start acute asthma treatment
options.B: Give oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
options.C: Double the inhaled steroid dose and review next week
options.D: Advise use of a peak flow diary and routine GP review
options.E: Give oral montelukast and observe for an hour

correct_answer: A. Assess severity and start acute asthma treatment
why_correct: Inability to complete sentences indicates at least acute severe asthma, so severity should be assessed promptly and treatment started with oxygen if needed, bronchodilators and oral steroids (BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024).
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated and do not treat bronchospasm. C. Inability to complete sentences needs acute treatment, not a delayed review. D. Routine review is unsafe in acute severe asthma. E. Montelukast is not an acute treatment for a severe exacerbation.
pearl: Inability to complete sentences marks at least acute severe asthma in a child; give inhaled bronchodilators and oral steroids promptly, with oxygen if hypoxic, and escalate if there is no response.
thinking: Child with known asthma ↓ increasing wheeze ↓ cannot speak in full sentences ↓ at least an acute severe exacerbation ↓ assess severity and start acute asthma treatment
exam_trap: C, double the inhaled steroid and review next week — tempting as an asthma step-up, but an acute severe attack needs immediate bronchodilators and oral steroids now.
takeaway: Unable to complete sentences in asthma means acute severe: assess and treat now.

stem:
A patient with diabetes is unconscious and has severe hypoglycaemia.

Which principle applies?

options.A: Give the usual insulin dose to prevent ketoacidosis
options.B: Give oral glucose tablets once propped up
options.C: Recheck glucose in 15 minutes before acting
options.D: Treat by a non-oral route and protect the airway
options.E: Give fruit juice by mouth and recheck in 15 minutes

correct_answer: D. Treat by a non-oral route and protect the airway
why_correct: An unconscious patient with severe hypoglycaemia needs emergency treatment with IV glucose (for example 10% glucose) or IM glucagon, and the airway must be protected (JBDS guidance).
why_wrong: A. Giving insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia. B. Oral glucose is unsafe in an unconscious patient because of aspiration risk. C. Waiting risks brain injury and death. E. Oral treatment is unsafe in an unconscious patient.
pearl: Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious hypoglycaemic patient: use IV glucose or IM glucagon, protect the airway, and give oral carbohydrate once awake and able to swallow.
thinking: Diabetes with severe hypoglycaemia ↓ unconscious, so cannot swallow safely ↓ oral treatment risks aspiration ↓ glucose must be given by another route ↓ treat by a non-oral route and protect the airway
exam_trap: E, fruit juice by mouth — tempting because it is standard for a conscious patient, but in an unconscious patient oral fluids risk aspiration.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia: IV glucose or IM glucagon, never oral treatment.

stem:
A patient has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that continues for several minutes without stopping.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Wait until the seizure has lasted 30 minutes before giving any drug
options.B: Insert a bite block to protect the tongue
options.C: Restrain the limbs to prevent injury
options.D: Give an oral benzodiazepine tablet once it stops
options.E: Treat as status epilepticus and start the emergency pathway

correct_answer: E. Treat as status epilepticus and start the emergency pathway
why_correct: A generalised convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more should be treated as convulsive status epilepticus, a medical emergency (NICE NG217). Follow the status epilepticus pathway: ABC, oxygen, check glucose and give a first-line benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, IV lorazepam if access is available).
why_wrong: A. Treatment starts at 5 minutes; waiting risks hypoxic brain injury and makes the seizure harder to terminate. B. Putting an object in the mouth can damage teeth or the airway and obstruct breathing. C. Restraining the limbs can cause injury and does not stop the seizure. D. An ongoing prolonged seizure needs prompt buccal, rectal or IV benzodiazepine, not oral treatment afterwards.
pearl: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus: give a benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam, rectal diazepam or IV lorazepam) without waiting longer.
thinking: Prolonged ongoing seizure  ↓  emergency treatment; don't put anything in the mouth.
exam_trap: A, wait 30 minutes before giving any drug — tempting from older definitions of status epilepticus, but treatment starts at 5 minutes, as prolonged seizures cause harm and become harder to stop.
takeaway: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus: treat now.

stem:
A 28-year-old has a first witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure and has recovered fully.

What is the appropriate next step?

options.B: Tell the patient no further assessment is necessary
options.D: Start lifelong antiseizure treatment without assessment
options.E: Arrange appropriate assessment for a first seizure

correct_answer: E. Arrange appropriate assessment for a first seizure
why_correct: After a first suspected seizure, NICE NG217 recommends urgent referral to a specialist first seizure service (ideally seen within 2 weeks) to confirm the diagnosis and identify any cause. The patient should also be given safety advice, including DVLA driving guidance.
why_wrong: A. Epilepsy is not diagnosed automatically after a single seizure; it requires specialist assessment of recurrence risk and exclusion of other causes. B. A first seizure always needs specialist assessment because there may be a structural, metabolic or cardiac cause and there are safety and driving implications. C. There is no basis for assuming the event was deliberate; this would be inappropriate and unsafe. D. Antiseizure medicines should be started only after specialist assessment, not routinely after a single unassessed seizure.
pearl: After a first seizure, refer urgently to a first seizure specialist service and give safety advice, including that the patient should stop driving and inform the DVLA.
thinking: First generalised tonic-clonic seizure ↓ full recovery does not exclude a cause ↓ one seizure is not automatically epilepsy ↓ needs specialist review plus safety advice ↓ arrange appropriate first-seizure assessment
exam_trap: A, automatically diagnose epilepsy — tempting after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure, but epilepsy needs specialist assessment of recurrence risk and exclusion of other causes.
takeaway: First seizure: urgent specialist assessment and safety advice, not an automatic diagnosis.

stem:
A patient notices that a pigmented skin lesion has recently changed in size, shape and colour.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Review in three months with photographs to monitor change
options.B: Reassure as the lesion is painless and not bleeding
options.C: Arrange appropriate assessment for possible melanoma
options.D: Treat as seborrhoeic keratosis with cryotherapy
options.E: Shave biopsy in primary care to confirm the diagnosis

correct_answer: C. Arrange appropriate assessment for possible melanoma
why_correct: A pigmented lesion that has changed in size, shape or colour scores 2 points on each of these major features of the weighted 7-point checklist, so it needs a suspected cancer pathway referral for possible melanoma (NICE NG12). Dermoscopic assessment by a specialist is required.
why_wrong: A. Change in size, shape and colour scores highly on the 7-point checklist and needs suspected-cancer referral, not monitoring. B. Melanoma is often painless, so absence of pain gives no reassurance. D. Change in size, shape and colour suggests melanoma; destructive treatment would prevent histology. E. Suspicious pigmented lesions should be referred, not partially sampled in primary care.
pearl: Never destroy or partially sample a suspicious pigmented lesion in primary care: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for dermoscopic assessment and, if needed, excision for full histology.
thinking: Pigmented lesion ↓ recent change in size ↓ change in shape and colour ↓ high score on the weighted 7-point checklist ↓ arrange assessment for possible melanoma
exam_trap: A, review in three months with photographs — tempting as monitoring for change, but change has already occurred and needs suspected cancer referral now, not observation.
takeaway: A changing pigmented lesion needs suspected cancer referral for possible melanoma.

stem:
A patient with severe limb pain develops rapidly progressive swelling, systemic toxicity and skin changes. The pain appears disproportionate to the visible findings.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Treat as possible necrotising infection; urgent surgical review
options.B: Treat as cellulitis with oral flucloxacillin
options.C: Mark the erythema and reassess the spread after 24 hours
options.D: Arrange a routine MRI before any surgical referral
options.E: Treat as a deep vein thrombosis and start anticoagulation

correct_answer: A. Treat as possible necrotising infection; urgent surgical review
why_correct: Pain out of proportion to the visible findings, rapid progression and systemic toxicity are the hallmarks of necrotising fasciitis. This is a surgical emergency: give urgent broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and arrange immediate surgical review for debridement.
why_wrong: B. Disproportionate pain and systemic toxicity are red flags that simple cellulitis does not explain. C. Necrotising infection spreads within hours, so waiting greatly increases mortality. D. Imaging must not delay surgical assessment of a suspected necrotising infection. E. DVT does not explain systemic toxicity, skin changes and rapid progression.
pearl: Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical suspicion: pain out of proportion to skin findings with rapid systemic deterioration means IV antibiotics and immediate surgical debridement, not imaging first.
thinking: > Severe disproportionate pain + rapid progression + systemic toxicity  ↓  surgical emergency.
exam_trap: B, cellulitis with oral flucloxacillin — tempting as limb erythema and swelling look like cellulitis, but disproportionate pain and systemic toxicity point to necrotising infection.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion with rapid spread and toxicity: necrotising infection, call the surgeons.

stem:
A hospitalised patient develops a rise in creatinine after several days of vomiting and poor oral intake.

Which potentially reversible factor should be assessed?
why_correct: Vomiting and poor oral intake cause hypovolaemia and reduced renal perfusion, which is a common and reversible prerenal cause of acute kidney injury. Assess fluid status and correct it (NICE NG148).
why_wrong: B. Skin pigmentation does not contribute to AKI. C. Visual acuity is unrelated to the cause of a rising creatinine. D. Hair colour has no bearing on renal function. E. Hearing threshold is not a factor in acute kidney injury.
pearl: Much hospital AKI has a reversible prerenal component: assess fluid status, correct hypovolaemia and review nephrotoxic or contributing medicines early.
thinking: > AKI  ↓  look actively for reversible causes, including hypovolaemia and medicines.
exam_trap: B, skin pigmentation — may tempt as a visible skin sign, as if assessing skin turgor, but pigmentation says nothing about volume; vomiting and poor intake point to volume depletion.
takeaway: Rising creatinine after vomiting and poor intake: assess and correct volume depletion.

stem:
A patient is found to have persistent proteinuria on repeated testing.

What is the appropriate general approach?

options.A: Assess and investigate it rather than dismissing it as incidental
options.B: Repeat the urine dipstick annually provided the patient feels well
options.C: Stop any ACE inhibitor treatment to reduce urinary protein leakage
options.D: Send a urine culture and treat it as a lower urinary tract infection
options.E: Give a course of oral antibiotics and recheck the urine in a month

correct_answer: A. Assess and investigate it rather than dismissing it as incidental
why_correct: Persistent proteinuria is a marker of chronic kidney disease and of increased cardiovascular risk. It should be quantified (urine ACR) and assessed with eGFR, blood pressure and the clinical context (NICE NG203).
why_wrong: B. Proteinuria is often asymptomatic, so feeling well does not make it safe to defer assessment. C. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are often indicated in proteinuric CKD, so stopping them would be harmful. D. Persistent proteinuria has many causes and is not usually caused by UTI. E. Antibiotics are not indicated for proteinuria without evidence of infection.
pearl:
Persistent proteinuria can be an important marker of kidney disease and cardiovascular risk.


Bank total: 468 questions.

A useful change from the earlier batches is that these questions now more deliberately test the GMC's “apply knowledge to patient care” principle rather than simply asking for a disease name. The GMC explicitly states that PLAB 1 is not intended to test memorisation/recitation and that questions use short clinical scenarios with five answer options.
thinking: Proteinuria on repeated testing ↓ persistent, not transient ↓ marker of CKD and cardiovascular risk ↓ quantify with urine ACR and check eGFR and blood pressure ↓ assess and investigate it
exam_trap: C, stop the ACE inhibitor — tempting if ACE inhibitors are seen as harmful to kidneys, but they are often indicated in proteinuric CKD to reduce proteinuria and slow progression.
takeaway: Persistent proteinuria is never just incidental: quantify it and assess for CKD.

stem:
A 78-year-old patient has newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation.

What important issue should be assessed as part of management?

options.A: Whether 24-hour Holter monitoring is needed first to confirm the AF
options.B: Whether aspirin should be started as the main stroke-prevention therapy
options.C: Whether a cardiac MRI is needed to assess structure before any treatment
options.D: Risk of thromboembolism and whether anticoagulation is indicated
options.E: Whether lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis against endocarditis is required

correct_answer: D. Risk of thromboembolism and whether anticoagulation is indicated
why_correct: Atrial fibrillation greatly increases the risk of stroke. Every patient should have their stroke risk assessed (CHA2DS2-VASc) and bleeding risk considered (e.g. ORBIT), and a DOAC should be offered where indicated (NICE NG196). At 78 years, he already scores at least 2.
why_wrong: A. AF is already diagnosed; Holter monitoring does not address stroke risk. B. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF. C. Cardiac MRI is not routinely needed and does not replace stroke-risk assessment. E. Antibiotic prophylaxis has no role in AF.
pearl: In every new AF diagnosis, assess stroke risk with CHA2DS2-VASc and bleeding risk, then offer a DOAC where indicated; aspirin alone is not used for stroke prevention in AF.
thinking: New atrial fibrillation ↓ stasis in the left atrium promotes thrombus ↓ high risk of embolic stroke ↓ age 78 alone raises the stroke-risk score ↓ assess thromboembolic risk and need for anticoagulation
exam_trap: B, aspirin as the main stroke prevention — tempting as a familiar antiplatelet, but aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF; anticoagulation is.
takeaway: New AF: always assess stroke and bleeding risk and offer anticoagulation where indicated.

stem:
A patient with atrial fibrillation develops hypotension, chest pain and acute pulmonary oedema.

What is the key principle?

options.A: Give oral bisoprolol and recheck the rate in an hour
options.B: Treat as unstable AF needing emergency management
options.C: Start a DOAC and arrange outpatient cardioversion
options.D: Give oral digoxin and arrange admission for monitoring
options.E: Give IV furosemide alone and review the rhythm later

correct_answer: B. Treat as unstable AF needing emergency management
why_correct: Hypotension, chest pain (myocardial ischaemia) and pulmonary oedema (heart failure) are adverse features. Under the Resuscitation Council UK tachycardia algorithm, they mean the patient needs emergency synchronised DC cardioversion.
why_wrong: A. Oral rate control is too slow and may worsen hypotension in an unstable patient. C. Adverse features require emergency treatment, not outpatient cardioversion. D. Oral digoxin does not address haemodynamic compromise quickly. E. Treating pulmonary oedema alone does not address the unstable arrhythmia.
pearl: A tachyarrhythmia with adverse features (shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia or heart failure) needs synchronised DC cardioversion, not oral rate control.
thinking: Arrhythmia + haemodynamic compromise  ↓  emergency management.
exam_trap: A, oral bisoprolol and recheck in an hour — tempting as standard AF rate control, but it is too slow and may worsen hypotension in a patient with adverse features.
takeaway: AF with shock, ischaemia or heart failure is unstable: emergency synchronised DC cardioversion.

stem:
A 29-year-old has a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 beats/min. He is haemodynamically stable.

Which approach is appropriate initially?
why_correct: In a stable patient with regular narrow-complex tachycardia (probable SVT), first-line treatment is vagal manoeuvres such as the modified Valsalva manoeuvre. IV adenosine is given if these fail (Resuscitation Council UK tachycardia algorithm).
why_wrong: A. Thrombolysis treats thrombotic occlusion, not SVT. B. A chest drain has no role in arrhythmia management. C. Lumbar puncture is irrelevant to a tachyarrhythmia. D. Electrical treatment is reserved for patients with adverse features; this patient is stable, and defibrillation (unsynchronised) is for cardiac arrest rhythms.
pearl: For a stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia, try vagal manoeuvres such as the modified Valsalva first, then IV adenosine as a rapid bolus with ECG recording if they fail.
thinking: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia ↓ probable SVT ↓ haemodynamically stable with no adverse features ↓ first-line non-drug treatment ↓ appropriate vagal manoeuvres
exam_trap: D, immediate defibrillation — tempting because the rate is very fast, but electrical treatment is reserved for adverse features, and unsynchronised defibrillation is for cardiac arrest.
takeaway: Stable SVT: vagal manoeuvres first, then adenosine.

stem:
A trauma patient develops severe respiratory distress, hypotension and markedly reduced breath sounds on one side.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Arrange an urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before intervening
options.B: Treat as possible tension pneumothorax needing emergency treatment
options.C: Give high-flow oxygen and observe for 30 minutes
options.D: Give a 1-litre crystalloid bolus for presumed haemorrhagic shock alone
options.E: Request an urgent CT chest to confirm the diagnosis before intervening

correct_answer: B. Treat as possible tension pneumothorax needing emergency treatment
why_correct: Respiratory distress, hypotension and unilateral reduced breath sounds after trauma suggest tension pneumothorax. This is a clinical diagnosis that needs immediate decompression (needle or finger thoracostomy) followed by a chest drain, without waiting for imaging.
why_wrong: A. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for imaging delays decompression. C. Observation delays life-saving decompression. D. Fluids do not treat an obstructive shock state. E. Waiting for CT delays life-saving decompression.
pearl: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: decompress immediately by needle or finger thoracostomy and follow with a chest drain, without waiting for an X-ray.
thinking: > Trauma + respiratory compromise + hypotension + unilateral absent breath sounds  ↓  tension pneumothorax.
exam_trap: A, urgent chest X-ray before intervening — tempting to confirm the diagnosis, but tension pneumothorax is clinical and imaging delays life-saving decompression.
takeaway: Trauma with respiratory distress, hypotension and unilateral reduced breath sounds: decompress now.

stem:
A patient with COPD develops increasing breathlessness and a change in sputum volume and purulence.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Treat as acute heart failure with intravenous furosemide alone
options.B: Assess severity and manage as a possible COPD exacerbation
options.C: Start long-term oxygen therapy at home without further assessment
options.D: Stop the regular inhalers and start oral theophylline instead
options.E: Arrange routine spirometry in six weeks

correct_answer: B. Assess severity and manage as a possible COPD exacerbation
why_correct: More breathlessness with a change in sputum volume and purulence is the classic presentation of an acute exacerbation of COPD. Assess severity to decide where to treat, then manage with increased bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics if the sputum is purulent (NICE NG114/NG115).
why_wrong: A. Heart failure is a differential diagnosis, but sputum purulence points to an infective COPD exacerbation. C. Long-term oxygen therapy needs formal assessment when stable and is not a treatment for an exacerbation. D. Bronchodilator inhalers should be increased, not stopped, during an exacerbation. E. An acute exacerbation needs assessment and treatment now, not routine spirometry.
pearl: A COPD exacerbation is managed with increased bronchodilators and a short course of oral prednisolone, adding antibiotics when sputum is purulent or other features suggest infection.
thinking: Known COPD ↓ worsening breathlessness ↓ change in sputum volume and purulence ↓ acute exacerbation, likely infective ↓ assess severity and manage as a COPD exacerbation
exam_trap: A, acute heart failure with IV furosemide alone — tempting because heart failure also causes breathlessness, but the change in sputum points to a COPD exacerbation.
takeaway: COPD with more breathlessness and purulent sputum: assess severity and treat the exacerbation.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy presents with fever and neutropenia.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Give oral antibiotics and review in clinic within one week
options.B: Delay antibiotics until blood cultures confirm infection
options.C: Give G-CSF and wait for the neutrophil count to recover first
options.D: Treat as possible neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency
options.E: Give paracetamol and review if the fever persists 24 hours

correct_answer: D. Treat as possible neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency
why_correct: Fever in a patient receiving chemotherapy should be treated as neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency. Give empirical IV antibiotics (piperacillin with tazobactam) within 1 hour of presentation (NICE CG151).
why_wrong: A. Suspected neutropenic sepsis needs IV antibiotics within 1 hour, not outpatient review. B. Antibiotics must not be delayed for culture results. C. Waiting for neutrophil recovery risks rapid, fatal sepsis. E. Delay risks rapid, fatal sepsis.
pearl: Fever during chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise: give empirical IV antibiotics within an hour, without waiting for the neutrophil count or culture results.
thinking: Recent chemotherapy ↓ fever with neutropenia ↓ impaired defence against bacteria ↓ sepsis can progress rapidly ↓ treat as possible neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency
exam_trap: B, delay antibiotics until cultures confirm infection — tempting to target therapy, but neutropenic sepsis can be rapidly fatal, so empirical IV antibiotics come first.
takeaway: Fever on chemotherapy: empirical IV antibiotics within an hour, before results.

stem:
A 78-year-old man develops painful inability to pass urine with a palpable distended bladder.

What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Encourage oral fluids and reassess bladder volume in a few hours
options.B: Urgent catheterisation and assessment of the underlying cause
options.C: Start tamsulosin and review in the urology clinic in two weeks
options.D: Give laxatives and review once bowels have opened
options.E: Arrange a routine prostate assessment in clinic

correct_answer: B. Urgent catheterisation and assessment of the underlying cause
why_correct: A painful, palpable bladder with inability to void is acute urinary retention. It needs urgent catheterisation to decompress the bladder, followed by assessment of the cause (e.g. BPH, constipation or medicines) and monitoring of renal function.
why_wrong: A. Drinking more fluid increases bladder distension and pain when the patient cannot void. C. An alpha-blocker alone does not relieve acute retention; decompression is needed now. D. Constipation may contribute, but laxatives alone will not relieve an acutely distended bladder. E. Acute retention needs treatment immediately, not routine review.
pearl: Acute urinary retention needs urgent catheterisation; then look for the cause, such as prostatic enlargement, constipation or anticholinergic medicines, and check renal function.
thinking: Older man unable to pass urine ↓ painful, palpable distended bladder ↓ acute urinary retention ↓ the bladder needs decompression now ↓ urgent catheterisation and assessment of the cause
