thinking: Receiving chemotherapy ↓ Fever ↓ Severe neutropenia ↓ Cannot fight infection and may deteriorate rapidly ↓ Neutropenic sepsis requiring urgent assessment and treatment
exam_trap: E, simple viral infection managed at home — tempting if the patient looks well. Neutropenic patients can deteriorate rapidly and need immediate IV antibiotics in hospital.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy: immediate IV antibiotics; do not wait for the blood count.

stem:
A patient with known malignancy develops new confusion, constipation and thirst. Calcium is markedly elevated.

What important cause should be considered?

options.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency with cognitive decline
options.C: Hypokalaemia secondary to poor oral intake

why_correct: Confusion, constipation and thirst with high calcium in a patient with cancer suggest malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (from PTHrP or bone metastases), which needs IV fluids and bisphosphonate.
why_wrong: A. B12 deficiency does not cause raised calcium. C. Hypokalaemia may cause weakness and constipation but does not explain raised calcium. D. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion but does not explain thirst or raised calcium. E. Hypoglycaemia does not cause thirst, constipation or raised calcium.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia means bones, stones, groans and psychic moans. In known cancer, confusion, constipation and thirst should prompt a calcium check; treat with IV fluids, then an IV bisphosphonate.
thinking: Known malignancy ↓ Confusion, constipation and thirst ↓ Markedly raised calcium ↓ Caused by PTHrP or bone metastases ↓ Malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia
exam_trap: D, SIADH-related hyponatraemia — tempting because tumours cause SIADH and confusion. It does not explain thirst or a markedly raised calcium.
takeaway: Cancer plus confusion, constipation and thirst: check calcium; rehydrate, then bisphosphonate.

stem:
A patient's investigations raise concern for possible cancer, but the diagnosis has not yet been confirmed.

How should this uncertainty be communicated?

options.A: Reassure the patient that the result is probably benign to reduce anxiety
options.B: Explain what is known, what is uncertain and the planned next steps
options.C: Give a printed leaflet on cancer and arrange discussion after the scan
options.D: Tell the patient they have cancer so they can prepare for treatment
options.E: Avoid discussing the result until all investigations are complete

correct_answer: B. Explain what is known, what is uncertain and the planned next steps
why_correct: Good communication of uncertainty means being honest about what is known and unknown and explaining the plan, so the patient can take part in decisions (GMC Good medical practice).
why_wrong: A. False reassurance is dishonest and damages trust. C. A leaflet without discussion fails the duty to communicate clearly and may cause distress. D. The diagnosis is not confirmed, so stating it as certain would be inaccurate. E. Avoiding discussion leaves the patient uninformed and anxious.
pearl: Communicating uncertainty means being honest about what is known and unknown, explaining the plan and when results are expected, and checking understanding and support, without false reassurance.
thinking: Good communication does not mean eliminating uncertainty. It means being honest about what is known and unknown while explaining the plan.
exam_trap: A, reassure that the result is probably benign — tempting to ease anxiety. It is false reassurance that is dishonest and damages trust if cancer is later confirmed.
takeaway: Possible cancer, not yet confirmed: be honest about uncertainty and explain the next steps.

stem:
A 34-year-old presents with symptoms of depression and says, "Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me."

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Avoid discussing suicide because it may worsen the situation
options.B: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent and plans
options.C: Arrange routine review in one year
options.D: Reassure the patient without further assessment
options.E: Prescribe an antidepressant without assessing risk

correct_answer: B. Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent and plans
why_correct: NICE advises asking directly about suicidal thoughts, intent and plans when someone with depression expresses hopelessness; asking does not increase risk.
why_wrong: A. Asking about suicide does not increase risk and is necessary to assess it. C. A one-year review is unsafe when the patient has expressed possible suicidal ideation. D. Reassurance without assessment may miss significant risk. E. An antidepressant should not be started without first assessing risk.
pearl: NICE recommends asking people with depression directly about suicidal ideation and intent.
thinking: Symptoms of depression ↓ Says everyone would be better off without them ↓ Possible suicidal ideation ↓ Risk must be assessed directly ↓ Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent and plans
exam_trap: A, avoid discussing suicide in case it makes things worse — a common fear. Asking directly does not increase risk and is essential to assessing it.
takeaway: Hints of hopelessness: ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent and plans.

stem:
A patient with severe depression has a clear plan to end their life and says they intend to act today.

What is the appropriate response?

options.C: Tell the patient to return if things become worse
options.D: Reassure the patient and send them home alone
options.E: Arrange routine GP follow-up in one month

correct_answer: A. Arrange urgent specialist mental-health assessment
why_correct: A clear plan with stated intent to act today is high and immediate suicide risk, so the patient needs urgent same-day mental-health crisis assessment and should not be left alone.
why_wrong: B. The disclosure and actions taken must be clearly documented. C. The patient is already at immediate risk and needs urgent assessment now. D. Sending a high-risk patient home alone exposes them to serious harm. E. Routine follow-up is unsafe given the immediate risk.
pearl: A clear plan with intent to act today means immediate high risk: arrange same-day crisis or specialist mental-health assessment, do not leave the patient alone, and document clearly.
thinking: Severe depression ↓ Clear plan to end their life ↓ Intends to act today ↓ Immediate high risk ↓ Arrange urgent specialist mental-health assessment
exam_trap: C, tell the patient to return if things get worse — tempting as safety-netting. The patient is already at immediate risk; urgent assessment is needed now.
takeaway: Plan plus intent to act now: urgent same-day mental-health assessment, never left alone.

stem:
A patient with depression denies suicidal thoughts but reports previous self-harm.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Discharge with a leaflet, as current suicidal thoughts are denied
options.B: Explore past and current self-harm and suicide risk in a broad assessment
options.C: Refer for personality disorder assessment because of the past self-harm
options.D: Use a risk-scoring tool to classify the patient as low risk and discharge
options.E: Avoid asking about past self-harm, as this may cause distress

correct_answer: B. Explore past and current self-harm and suicide risk in a broad assessment
why_correct: Previous self-harm is an important risk factor even when current suicidal thoughts are denied, so NICE NG225 advises a broad psychosocial assessment of past and present self-harm and risk.
why_wrong: A. Denial of current thoughts does not remove the risk associated with previous self-harm, so assessment is needed before discharge. C. Previous self-harm does not establish a diagnosis of personality disorder. D. NICE advises against using risk tools or scales to predict suicide or to decide on care. E. Asking about self-harm does not increase risk and is essential to assessment.
pearl: Previous self-harm is an important risk factor even when current suicidal thoughts are denied. NICE advises a broad psychosocial assessment rather than risk scores to predict suicide or decide care.
thinking: Depression ↓ Denies current suicidal thoughts ↓ Past self-harm remains a major risk factor ↓ Risk needs fuller exploration ↓ Explore past and current self-harm and suicide risk in a broad assessment
exam_trap: D, use a risk-scoring tool to classify as low risk — tempting because it looks objective. NICE advises against risk tools to predict suicide or decide on discharge.
takeaway: Past self-harm: do a broad psychosocial assessment, not a risk score.

stem:
A patient presents with persistent low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and loss of appetite.

What is important when assessing possible depression?

options.A: Request a CT head to exclude an organic cause before making a diagnosis
options.B: Focus on mood symptoms alone and defer any physical health assessment
options.C: Treat as generalised anxiety disorder, as the poor sleep is prominent
options.D: Assess symptoms, function, physical health and psychosocial factors
options.E: Use a PHQ-9 score alone to confirm both the diagnosis and its severity

correct_answer: D. Assess symptoms, function, physical health and psychosocial factors
why_correct: NICE NG222 advises a holistic assessment of depression, covering symptoms, severity, function, physical health and psychosocial factors.
why_wrong: A. Routine CT head is not needed in depression without specific neurological features. B. Physical illness can cause or worsen depression and should be assessed. C. Low mood and anhedonia suggest depression, and anxiety should not be assumed without assessment. E. Questionnaire scores support but do not replace clinical assessment of symptoms, severity and function.
pearl: Assess depression holistically: core symptoms, severity, duration, function, physical health, medicines, substance use and social context. Questionnaires support but never replace clinical judgement.
thinking: Low mood and anhedonia ↓ Poor sleep and appetite ↓ Possible depression ↓ Severity, function and causes all shape management ↓ Assess symptoms, function, physical health and psychosocial factors
exam_trap: E, PHQ-9 score alone to confirm diagnosis and severity — tempting as a validated tool. Scores support but do not replace a full clinical assessment.
takeaway: Depression assessment is holistic: symptoms, function, physical health and social factors.

stem:
A patient starts an antidepressant and reports increased agitation and new suicidal thoughts during the early stages of treatment.

What should happen?

options.A: Reassure them that this is always harmless
options.C: Ignore the symptoms until the next annual review
options.E: Tell them to stop all medication without assessment

correct_answer: B. Promptly reassess risk and treatment
why_correct: Increased agitation and new suicidal thoughts can occur early in antidepressant treatment, particularly in younger people, so risk and treatment should be reassessed promptly.
why_wrong: A. These symptoms can indicate increased risk and should not be dismissed. C. New suicidal thoughts need prompt review, not waiting until annual review. D. Increasing the dose without review may worsen agitation. E. Stopping abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms and should be done only after assessment.
pearl: Early in antidepressant treatment, agitation and suicidal thoughts can increase, particularly in younger people. Warn about this when starting, review early and reassess promptly if it happens.
thinking: New antidepressant ↓ Increased agitation ↓ New suicidal thoughts ↓ Recognised early-treatment risk ↓ Promptly reassess risk and treatment
exam_trap: D, increase the dose automatically — tempting if symptoms are seen as under-treatment. A higher dose may worsen agitation; risk and treatment need prompt review.
takeaway: New suicidal thoughts or agitation on starting an antidepressant: review urgently.

stem:
A patient presents with recurrent depressive episodes. On further questioning, they describe a previous period lasting several weeks during which they slept very little, were unusually energetic, spent large amounts of money and behaved in a markedly disinhibited way.

What should be considered?
why_correct: A previous episode of reduced need for sleep, increased energy, overspending and disinhibition lasting several weeks suggests mania or hypomania, so bipolar disorder should be considered.
why_wrong: A. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions, not manic episodes. B. Specific phobia involves fear of a particular object or situation, not manic episodes. C. The history of a manic-type episode means this is not uncomplicated recurrent depression. E. Panic disorder causes episodes of intense fear, not prolonged elevated mood and disinhibition.
pearl: Always ask about past elevated mood in anyone with depression: a history of mania or hypomania changes the diagnosis to bipolar disorder and makes antidepressant monotherapy risky.
thinking: Recurrent depressive episodes ↓ Past weeks of little sleep, high energy, overspending and disinhibition ↓ Manic or hypomanic episode ↓ Bipolar disorder
exam_trap: C, uncomplicated recurrent depression — tempting because depression is the presenting complaint, but a past manic-type episode excludes a purely unipolar diagnosis.
takeaway: Depression plus any past manic or hypomanic episode means bipolar disorder until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient presenting in primary care has clear symptoms suggesting a current manic episode.

What is the appropriate action?

options.C: Reassure and arrange routine annual review
options.D: Start an antidepressant without further assessment

correct_answer: B. Arrange urgent specialist mental-health assessment
why_correct: NICE CG185 advises urgent referral to specialist mental-health services for people with suspected mania or severe depression who may pose a risk to themselves or others.
why_wrong: A. The presentation is manic, so treating it as depression is incorrect. C. Mania needs urgent assessment, not reassurance and routine review. D. Antidepressants without a mood stabiliser can worsen mania. E. Diagnosing ADHD without assessment would miss the manic episode.
pearl: Suspected mania in primary care needs urgent specialist mental-health assessment; do not start an antidepressant, which can worsen or prolong mania.
thinking: Clear features of current mania ↓ Impaired judgement and possible risk to self or others ↓ Needs specialist diagnosis and treatment ↓ Urgent specialist mental-health assessment
exam_trap: D, starting an antidepressant — tempting if low mood is also reported, but antidepressants without mood stabilisation can worsen mania, and the patient has not been assessed.
takeaway: Suspected mania in primary care: refer urgently to specialist mental-health services.

stem:
A patient reports hearing voices when nobody is present and has fixed beliefs that others are deliberately trying to harm them.

What does this presentation suggest?
why_correct: Hallucinations and fixed persecutory delusions are positive psychotic symptoms, which indicate psychosis.
why_wrong: A. Specific phobia involves fear of a particular object or situation, not psychotic symptoms. B. OCD involves intrusive thoughts recognised as one's own, not hallucinations or delusions. C. Panic disorder causes episodes of anxiety without hallucinations or delusions. E. Insomnia does not cause hallucinations and fixed delusions.
pearl: Hallucinations (perceptions without a stimulus) and delusions (fixed false beliefs) are the positive symptoms that define psychosis.
thinking: Hears voices when nobody is present: hallucinations ↓ Fixed belief that others want to harm them: persecutory delusions ↓ Positive psychotic symptoms ↓ Psychosis
exam_trap: B, OCD — tempting because of distressing intrusive thoughts, but OCD thoughts are recognised as the patient's own and are neither voices nor fixed false beliefs.
takeaway: Hallucinations plus fixed delusions mean psychosis, whatever the underlying cause.

stem:
A previously well young adult develops hallucinations, delusions and marked social withdrawal.

What is the appropriate response?

options.B: Assume recreational drug use without asking
options.D: Arrange assessment by an appropriate mental-health service

correct_answer: D. Arrange assessment by an appropriate mental-health service
why_correct: A first episode of psychosis needs referral to early intervention in psychosis services for prompt assessment, as NICE CG178 recommends.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of infection, so antibiotics are not indicated. B. Drug use should be asked about, not assumed. C. Schizophrenia should be diagnosed only after full specialist assessment. E. Delaying assessment worsens outcomes in first-episode psychosis.
pearl: A first episode of psychosis should be referred promptly to an early intervention in psychosis service; a shorter duration of untreated psychosis is linked to better outcomes.
thinking: Previously well young adult ↓ New hallucinations, delusions and social withdrawal ↓ Possible first-episode psychosis ↓ Prompt assessment by an appropriate mental-health service
exam_trap: C, diagnosing schizophrenia immediately — tempting as the picture fits, but diagnosis needs full specialist assessment, including exclusion of organic and drug-related causes.
takeaway: First-episode psychosis: refer promptly for specialist assessment; do not label or wait.

stem:
A patient with psychosis is taking an antipsychotic and has gained substantial weight.

What should be considered?

options.A: Advise a very-low-calorie diet without further monitoring of bloods
options.B: Assess physical-health risks, including weight, glucose and lipids
options.C: Reassure that the weight gain is cosmetic and will settle with time
options.D: Stop the antipsychotic straight away and monitor for signs of relapse
options.E: Start levothyroxine for presumed drug-induced hypothyroidism

correct_answer: B. Assess physical-health risks, including weight, glucose and lipids
why_correct: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, so NICE CG178 recommends regular monitoring of weight, glucose and lipids with appropriate management.
why_wrong: A. Severe dietary restriction without monitoring is not an appropriate way to manage metabolic risk. C. Antipsychotic weight gain is linked to diabetes and dyslipidaemia and is not merely cosmetic. D. Stopping antipsychotics abruptly risks relapse and should be done only after review. E. Hypothyroidism should not be diagnosed or treated without investigation.
pearl: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, so weight, glucose, lipids and blood pressure should be monitored regularly and managed.
thinking: Patient on an antipsychotic ↓ Substantial weight gain ↓ Risk of diabetes, dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular disease ↓ Assess physical-health risks, including glucose and lipids
exam_trap: D, stopping the antipsychotic straight away — tempting as the drug is the cause, but abrupt withdrawal risks relapse; any change should follow review.
takeaway: Weight gain on antipsychotics is a metabolic risk: check weight, glucose and lipids.

stem:
A patient reports hearing a voice telling them to seriously harm another person.

What is the key next step?

options.A: Assess risk to others and self, and arrange urgent mental-health review
options.B: Reassure the patient and advise them to ignore the voice
options.C: Increase the antipsychotic dose and review their mental state in four weeks
options.D: Refer routinely to the community mental health team for follow-up next month
options.E: Arrange a routine outpatient psychiatric clinic review in about six months

correct_answer: A. Assess risk to others and self, and arrange urgent mental-health review
why_correct: Command hallucinations to harm others indicate significant risk, so the doctor should assess the immediate risk to others and the patient and arrange urgent mental-health assessment.
why_wrong: B. Reassurance without questioning fails to assess risk. C. Changing medication without assessing immediate risk, and reviewing weeks later, is unsafe. D. A routine referral is unsafe given the possible risk to others. E. Routine review is unsafe given the possible risk to others.
pearl: Command hallucinations to harm others are a risk red flag: ask about intent, plans, the potential victim and means, and arrange urgent mental-health assessment.
thinking: Voice instructing serious harm to another person ↓ Command hallucination ↓ Possible immediate risk to others and self ↓ Assess risk and arrange urgent mental-health review
exam_trap: C, increasing the antipsychotic and reviewing in four weeks — tempting as it treats the psychosis, but it ignores the immediate risk and delays assessment.
takeaway: Command hallucinations to harm: assess risk now and arrange urgent review.

stem:
A patient with OCD reports intrusive thoughts about harming a loved one and is extremely distressed by them. They have no intention of acting on the thoughts.

What is an important principle?

options.A: The thoughts suggest an emerging psychosis and need antipsychotic treatment
options.B: Reassure the patient and avoid any further assessment of risk to others
options.C: The thoughts indicate a significant risk of physical harm to the loved one
options.D: The patient should be assessed for detention under the Mental Health Act
options.E: Intrusive thoughts are common in OCD and do not indicate intent to act

correct_answer: E. Intrusive thoughts are common in OCD and do not indicate intent to act
why_correct: In OCD, intrusive harm thoughts are ego-dystonic and distressing and do not mean intent to act, so they should not be read as evidence of dangerousness, although a proportionate risk assessment is still appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Intrusive thoughts recognised as one's own are typical of OCD, not psychosis. B. Reassurance alone without appropriate assessment is not good practice. C. Ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts in OCD do not indicate intent to harm. D. Detention is not justified by OCD intrusive thoughts without other risk.
pearl: Intrusive harm thoughts in OCD are ego-dystonic: the patient finds them abhorrent and resists them. They do not signal intent, though a proportionate risk assessment is still appropriate.
thinking: Intrusive thoughts of harming a loved one ↓ Extreme distress, no intention to act ↓ Ego-dystonic obsessions typical of OCD ↓ Not a sign of intent to act
exam_trap: C, significant risk of harm to the loved one — tempting because the content is violent, but distressing, unwanted OCD thoughts do not indicate intent or dangerousness.
takeaway: Distressing, unwanted harm thoughts in OCD are obsessions, not intent.

stem:
A patient with significant OCD wants psychological treatment.

Which intervention is particularly appropriate?

options.A: Psychodynamic psychotherapy as the main treatment
options.B: Long-term benzodiazepine therapy for anxiety symptoms
options.C: CBT including exposure and response prevention

correct_answer: C. CBT including exposure and response prevention
why_correct: NICE CG31 recommends CBT including exposure and response prevention as the main psychological treatment for OCD.
why_wrong: A. Psychodynamic therapy is not recommended for OCD. B. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for OCD and carry a risk of dependence. D. Supportive counselling and relaxation do not target obsessions and compulsions and are not recommended treatments for OCD. E. ECT is not a treatment for OCD.
pearl: The key psychological treatment for OCD is CBT with exposure and response prevention: facing the feared trigger while resisting the compulsion.
thinking: Significant OCD ↓ Wants psychological treatment ↓ Therapy must target obsessions and compulsions ↓ CBT including exposure and response prevention
exam_trap: D, supportive counselling with relaxation — tempting as gentle and low-risk, but it does not target obsessions and compulsions and is not a recommended OCD treatment.
takeaway: Psychological therapy for OCD means CBT with exposure and response prevention.

stem:
A patient repeatedly avoids driving because it reminds them of a previous traumatic event.

Which symptom category does this represent?
why_correct: Avoiding reminders of a traumatic event, such as driving, is an avoidance symptom of PTSD.
why_wrong: B. Compulsions are repetitive acts to reduce anxiety, not avoidance of reminders. C. Confabulation is filling memory gaps with false memories, as seen in Korsakoff syndrome. D. Formal thought disorder is a disturbance in the form of thinking seen in psychosis. E. Mania involves elevated mood and overactivity, not avoidance of trauma reminders.
pearl: PTSD features re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance of reminders and hyperarousal; steering clear of activities linked to the trauma is avoidance.
thinking: Previous traumatic event ↓ Repeatedly avoids driving ↓ Driving is a reminder of the trauma ↓ Avoidance
exam_trap: B, compulsion — tempting because the behaviour is repeated, but compulsions are acts performed to neutralise anxiety, not avoidance of trauma reminders.
takeaway: Avoiding reminders of a trauma is an avoidance symptom of PTSD.

stem:
A young person is suspected of having an eating disorder.

What should the initial assessment include?

options.A: BMI alone, using a threshold to decide the urgency of referral
options.B: Psychological assessment, leaving physical examination to the specialist
options.C: Full assessment only once BMI has fallen below 17.5 kg/m²
options.D: Assessment of physical health, psychological health and risk
options.E: Dietary history and weight, without any physical examination

correct_answer: D. Assessment of physical health, psychological health and risk
why_correct: NICE NG69 advises assessing physical health as well as psychological health and risk in suspected eating disorders, and not using single measures such as BMI alone.
why_wrong: A. BMI alone is not a reliable measure of risk. B. Physical examination is needed at the initial assessment to detect medical complications. C. Assessment should not depend on a BMI threshold, as risk can be high at any weight. E. Physical examination is needed to detect serious medical complications.
pearl: In suspected eating disorders, assess physical health, psychological health and risk together; BMI alone is unreliable, and serious risk can exist at any weight.
thinking: Young person with suspected eating disorder ↓ Medical complications possible at any weight ↓ Single measures such as BMI miss risk ↓ Assess physical health, psychological health and risk
exam_trap: A, BMI alone to decide urgency — tempting as an objective number, but BMI misses risk from rapid weight loss, purging and cardiac complications.
takeaway: Eating disorder assessment covers body, mind and risk, never BMI alone.

stem:
A patient with a suspected eating disorder is severely medically compromised and has significant cardiovascular abnormalities.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Consider urgent medical assessment and emergency care
options.B: Arrange routine review in six months
options.C: Reassure because eating disorders are never medically dangerous
options.E: Wait until the patient's BMI falls further

correct_answer: A. Consider urgent medical assessment and emergency care
why_correct: Severe medical compromise with cardiovascular abnormalities in an eating disorder can be life-threatening, so the patient should be considered for urgent medical assessment and admission (MEED guidance).
why_wrong: B. Routine review is unsafe in a patient who is medically compromised. C. Eating disorders can be life-threatening. D. Physical complications need medical treatment alongside psychological care. E. Waiting for BMI to fall further risks death.
pearl: Eating disorders carry a high mortality; cardiovascular compromise such as bradycardia, hypotension or arrhythmia needs urgent medical assessment and possible admission.
thinking: Suspected eating disorder ↓ Severe medical compromise with cardiovascular abnormalities ↓ Risk of arrhythmia and death ↓ Urgent medical assessment and emergency care
exam_trap: D, treating only the psychological symptoms — tempting as eating disorders are psychiatric conditions, but life-threatening physical complications need urgent medical care.
takeaway: A medically compromised eating disorder is an emergency: assess and admit urgently.

stem:
A patient develops acute delirium.

What should be done?

options.A: Start regular haloperidol and continue it after discharge
options.B: Give a benzodiazepine at night to restore the sleep cycle
options.C: Arrange early discharge home, where familiar surroundings will help
options.D: Refer to the memory clinic to confirm a diagnosis of dementia
options.E: Identify and treat underlying causes while keeping the patient safe

correct_answer: E. Identify and treat underlying causes while keeping the patient safe
why_correct: Delirium is an acute and usually reversible disorder, so NICE CG103 recommends identifying and treating the underlying causes while keeping the patient safe.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics are reserved for short-term use in distressed patients and are not for routine long-term use. B. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and are not routinely used except in specific situations such as alcohol withdrawal. C. A patient with acute delirium needs assessment and treatment of the cause, not early discharge. D. Delirium is acute and often reversible and should not be assumed to be dementia.
pearl: Delirium is usually reversible: look for and treat causes such as infection, medicines, dehydration, pain, constipation and urinary retention, using non-drug measures to keep the patient safe.
thinking: Acute-onset confusion ↓ Delirium ↓ Usually has a treatable underlying cause ↓ Identify and treat causes while keeping the patient safe
exam_trap: A, regular haloperidol continued after discharge — tempting for agitation, but antipsychotics are for short-term use in distress only and do not treat the cause.
takeaway: Delirium: find and treat the cause; sedation is a short-term last resort.

stem:
A patient with dementia is being assessed before a specific medical procedure.

Which statement about capacity is correct?

options.A: A dementia diagnosis means the patient lacks capacity for medical decisions
options.B: Capacity should be formally assessed once and applied to all later decisions
options.C: The next of kin determines capacity once dementia is diagnosed
options.D: Capacity is judged by whether the MMSE score is above a set cut-off threshold
options.E: Capacity is decision-specific and assessed for this decision at this time

correct_answer: E. Capacity is decision-specific and assessed for this decision at this time
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, so it should be assessed for the particular decision at the time it needs to be made.
why_wrong: A. A diagnosis of dementia does not mean a person lacks capacity for all decisions. B. Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate, so it must be assessed at the time each decision is made. C. Family members do not decide capacity; the clinician assesses it. D. Capacity is assessed functionally under the Mental Capacity Act, not by a cognitive test score.
pearl: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision- and time-specific; a dementia diagnosis alone never proves incapacity, so assess for this decision now.
thinking: Patient with dementia ↓ Specific procedure needs consent ↓ Capacity is decision- and time-specific ↓ Assess capacity for this decision at this time
exam_trap: A, dementia means lack of capacity — tempting as cognition is impaired, but incapacity must never be assumed from a diagnosis; many people with dementia can decide.
takeaway: Capacity is assessed for each decision at the time, never assumed from a diagnosis.

stem:
A capacitous adult refuses a recommended treatment despite understanding the consequences.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Respect the refusal, provided it is informed and voluntary
options.B: Ask the next of kin to consent on their behalf
options.C: Override the refusal in the patient's best interests
options.D: Treat under the Mental Health Act to protect the patient
options.E: Declare a lack of capacity because the decision is unwise

correct_answer: A. Respect the refusal, provided it is informed and voluntary
why_correct: An adult with capacity has the right to refuse treatment, even if the decision seems unwise, as long as it is voluntary and informed (Mental Capacity Act 2005; GMC).
why_wrong: B. Family members cannot consent for, or force treatment on, an adult with capacity. C. Best-interests decisions apply only when a person lacks capacity. D. The Mental Health Act cannot be used to impose treatment for a physical condition on a capacitous adult. E. An unwise decision does not mean the patient lacks capacity.
pearl: An adult with capacity may refuse any treatment, even life-saving treatment, for any reason or none; an unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
thinking: Adult with capacity ↓ Understands the consequences of refusing ↓ Refusal is informed and voluntary ↓ Respect the refusal
exam_trap: C, overriding the refusal in best interests — tempting when refusal seems harmful, but best-interests decisions apply only to people who lack capacity.
takeaway: A capacitous adult's informed refusal must be respected, even if it seems unwise.

stem:
A competent adult asks their doctor not to disclose their diagnosis to their family.

What is the general principle?

options.A: Share the diagnosis with the next of kin, who has a right to know
options.B: Disclose to the family if they are involved in the patient's day-to-day care
options.C: Inform the family, as relatives are usually told about serious diagnoses
options.D: Disclose if a close relative asks directly, as consent can then be implied
options.E: Respect confidentiality unless disclosure is required by law or justified

correct_answer: E. Respect confidentiality unless disclosure is required by law or justified
why_correct: GMC confidentiality guidance requires doctors to respect a competent patient's wishes about disclosure unless disclosure is required by law or justified in the public interest.
why_wrong: A. Next of kin have no automatic right to an adult's medical information. B. Involvement in care does not override a competent patient's refusal of disclosure. C. Relatives are not entitled to information against a competent patient's wishes. D. A relative's request does not create consent; only the patient can consent to disclosure.
pearl: Relatives, including the next of kin, have no automatic right to an adult's health information; respect a competent patient's wishes unless law or the public interest justifies disclosure.
thinking: Competent adult ↓ Asks for diagnosis not to be shared with family ↓ Duty of confidentiality applies ↓ Respect it unless disclosure is required by law or justified
exam_trap: B, disclosing because the family is involved in care — tempting as it seems practical, but involvement in care does not override a competent patient's refusal.
takeaway: Next of kin have no automatic right to information about a competent adult.

stem:
A competent adult tells their doctor that they intend to seriously harm another identifiable person imminently.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Maintain confidentiality, as the patient has not consented to disclosure
options.B: Advise the patient against acting on the threat and arrange routine follow-up
options.C: Inform the person's employer so they can take precautions
options.D: Disclose only if the patient repeats the threat at a later GP consultation
options.E: Assess the risk and consider proportionate disclosure to protect others

correct_answer: E. Assess the risk and consider proportionate disclosure to protect others
why_correct: Confidentiality is not absolute, and GMC guidance allows disclosure in the public interest when there is a risk of serious harm to others, so the doctor should assess the risk and consider proportionate disclosure.
why_wrong: A. Confidentiality is not absolute, and disclosure without consent can be justified in the public interest to prevent serious harm. B. Routine follow-up does not address an imminent risk of serious harm. C. Any disclosure must be proportionate and to appropriate authorities such as the police, not an employer. D. Waiting for a repeated threat could allow imminent serious harm to occur.
pearl: Confidentiality is not absolute: GMC guidance permits disclosure without consent in the public interest to prevent serious harm, kept proportionate and made to an appropriate body such as the police.
thinking: Confidentiality is fundamental, but it is not absolute. Serious and imminent risk may justify proportionate disclosure through appropriate channels.
exam_trap: A, maintaining confidentiality — tempting because the patient has not consented, but an imminent risk of serious harm to an identifiable person can justify disclosure.
takeaway: Imminent serious risk to others can justify proportionate disclosure without consent.

stem:
A patient has a low bicarbonate and raised anion gap.

Which condition can cause this pattern?
why_correct: DKA causes a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis because unmeasured ketoacids accumulate.
why_wrong: A. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. B. Respiratory alkalosis causes a low CO₂ and does not raise the anion gap. C. Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis. D. Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, not a raised anion gap acidosis.
pearl: A raised anion gap metabolic acidosis means unmeasured acids: think ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure and toxins such as methanol, ethylene glycol or salicylate.
thinking: Low bicarbonate: metabolic acidosis ↓ Raised anion gap: unmeasured anions added ↓ Ketoacids accumulate in DKA ↓ Diabetic ketoacidosis
exam_trap: C, vomiting — tempting as a common cause of acid-base disturbance, but loss of gastric acid causes metabolic alkalosis with a high, not low, bicarbonate.
takeaway: Low bicarbonate with a high anion gap: think DKA, lactate, renal failure or toxins.

stem:
A patient with septic shock has a markedly raised serum lactate.

What does an elevated lactate in this context suggest?

options.A: Acute myocardial infarction as the cause of the shock
options.B: Confirmation that the infection is bacterial in origin
options.C: An expected finding with no prognostic significance
options.E: Tissue hypoperfusion and greater severity of illness

correct_answer: E. Tissue hypoperfusion and greater severity of illness
why_correct: A raised lactate in septic shock indicates tissue hypoperfusion and is associated with greater severity and mortality.
why_wrong: A. Lactate is not a marker of myocardial infarction. B. Lactate is not specific for bacterial infection. C. Raised lactate is abnormal and is associated with greater severity and mortality. D. Hypothyroidism does not cause a markedly raised lactate in this context.
pearl: Lactate is a marker of tissue hypoperfusion in sepsis; a raised level signals greater severity and higher mortality, and repeat measurement helps track the response to resuscitation.
thinking: Septic shock ↓ Markedly raised lactate ↓ Inadequate tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism ↓ Tissue hypoperfusion and greater severity of illness
exam_trap: B, confirmation of bacterial infection — tempting as lactate is part of sepsis assessment, but it reflects perfusion and severity, not the type of organism.
takeaway: Raised lactate in sepsis means hypoperfusion and higher risk, not the cause.

stem:
A patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis. Their serum potassium is initially 5.8 mmol/L.

Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: Potassium should not be added to the fluids at any point in this admission
options.B: The serum potassium accurately reflects total-body potassium stores
options.C: Total-body potassium is increased, so calcium gluconate should be given
options.D: Insulin will raise the serum potassium further, so insulin should be delayed
options.E: Total-body potassium is usually low despite a normal or high serum level

correct_answer: E. Total-body potassium is usually low despite a normal or high serum level
why_correct: In DKA, acidosis and insulin deficiency move potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis causes losses, so total-body potassium is depleted even when serum potassium is normal or raised; it falls with insulin treatment.
why_wrong: A. Potassium replacement is usually needed: once serum potassium is 5.5 mmol/L or below, potassium chloride is added to the IV fluids because insulin will drive the level down. B. Serum potassium does not reflect total-body stores in DKA. C. Total-body potassium is usually depleted, not increased, and a level of 5.8 mmol/L does not need calcium gluconate in the absence of ECG changes. D. Insulin moves potassium into cells and lowers serum potassium.
pearl: In DKA, serum potassium is often normal or high at presentation despite total-body depletion; it falls once insulin starts, so monitor it closely and replace it in the fluids as the protocol directs.
thinking: DKA with potassium 5.8 mmol/L ↓ Acidosis and insulin lack shift potassium out of cells ↓ Osmotic diuresis causes urinary losses ↓ Total-body potassium low despite high serum level
exam_trap: B, serum potassium reflects total-body stores — tempting as the number looks reassuring, but the shift out of cells masks a total-body deficit that insulin will unmask.
takeaway: In DKA, serum potassium may be high, but total-body potassium is low.

stem:
A patient with DKA has been started on appropriate fluid therapy and their potassium is safe for insulin treatment.

What is the purpose of insulin in DKA?

options.A: Suppress ketogenesis and correct the metabolic acidosis
options.B: Rapidly normalise blood glucose within the first hour
options.C: Promote renal water retention to restore volume
options.D: Stimulate glycogen breakdown to raise glucose
options.E: Lower serum potassium as the main treatment aim

correct_answer: A. Suppress ketogenesis and correct the metabolic acidosis
why_correct: Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis and increases glucose uptake, which corrects the ketoacidosis and hyperglycaemia in DKA.
why_wrong: B. Glucose should fall steadily, not be normalised rapidly, and correcting glucose is not the main aim. C. Insulin does not correct dehydration; fluid therapy does. D. Insulin inhibits glycogen breakdown and lowers blood glucose. E. Insulin lowers potassium, but this is a hazard to monitor, not the aim of treatment.
pearl: Insulin in DKA is given to switch off ketone production and clear the acidosis; glucose falls as well and should come down steadily, not abruptly.
thinking: Insulin deficiency drives lipolysis and ketogenesis ↓ Ketoacids cause the acidosis ↓ Insulin suppresses ketone production ↓ Suppress ketogenesis and correct the metabolic acidosis
exam_trap: B, rapidly normalising glucose within the first hour — tempting as hyperglycaemia is obvious, but rapid falls are unsafe and clearing ketones is the real aim.
takeaway: In DKA, insulin treats the ketoacidosis; glucose is not the main target.

stem:
An unconscious patient is found to have severe hypoglycaemia and has no safe oral route.

What is required?

options.A: Buccal glucose gel and a repeat capillary glucose after 15 minutes
options.B: An oral glucose drink given with the patient propped upright
options.C: Observation with repeated capillary glucose checks until they wake
options.D: Parenteral glucose-raising treatment suited to the clinical setting
options.E: A subcutaneous insulin correction dose according to the sliding scale

correct_answer: D. Parenteral glucose-raising treatment suited to the clinical setting
why_correct: Severe hypoglycaemia without a safe oral route needs parenteral treatment: IV glucose in hospital, or IM glucagon when IV access is not available.
why_wrong: A. Buccal or oral glucose is unsafe in an unconscious patient without a safe swallow because of aspiration risk. B. Oral fluids are unsafe in an unconscious patient because of aspiration risk. C. Severe hypoglycaemia is an emergency and must be treated, not observed. E. Additional insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Never give anything by mouth to a patient who cannot swallow safely; severe hypoglycaemia then needs IV glucose, or IM glucagon if IV access is not available.
thinking: Unconscious patient ↓ Severe hypoglycaemia ↓ No safe oral route; aspiration risk ↓ Parenteral glucose-raising treatment
exam_trap: A, buccal glucose gel — tempting as a quick hypoglycaemia remedy, but it is unsafe in an unconscious patient without a protected swallow because of aspiration risk.
takeaway: Unconscious and hypoglycaemic: IV glucose or IM glucagon, never oral treatment.

stem:
A patient with vomiting has tachycardia, postural dizziness and reduced urine output.

What should these findings prompt?

options.D: Immediate fluid restriction in every case

correct_answer: A. Assessment for dehydration and hypovolaemia
why_correct: Tachycardia, postural dizziness and reduced urine output after vomiting suggest dehydration and hypovolaemia, which need assessment and fluid replacement.
why_wrong: B. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria, not volume depletion from vomiting. C. Pulmonary oedema causes breathlessness and crackles, not features of volume loss. D. Fluid restriction would worsen hypovolaemia. E. Hyperthyroidism does not explain the dehydration features after vomiting.
pearl: Tachycardia, postural dizziness and reduced urine output after fluid losses are classic signs of hypovolaemia; assess fluid status and replace the losses.
thinking: Vomiting causes fluid loss ↓ Tachycardia and postural dizziness ↓ Reduced urine output ↓ Assess for dehydration and hypovolaemia
exam_trap: D, immediate fluid restriction — tempting if worried about fluid overload, but restriction worsens hypovolaemia after fluid losses.
takeaway: Fluid loss plus tachycardia, postural symptoms and low urine output means hypovolaemia.

stem:
A patient receiving intravenous fluids develops increasing peripheral oedema and new breathlessness with bilateral basal crackles.

What complication should be considered?
why_correct: New peripheral oedema, breathlessness and basal crackles during IV fluid therapy suggest fluid overload, so the fluids should be reviewed and the patient assessed.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis does not cause oedema and breathlessness. C. Renal colic causes loin pain, not oedema and breathlessness. D. These signs indicate fluid excess, not dehydration. E. Hypoglycaemia does not cause oedema and basal crackles.
pearl: IV fluids need regular review: new oedema, breathlessness or basal crackles during therapy suggest fluid overload, so reassess the patient and review the fluid prescription.
thinking: Patient receiving IV fluids ↓ Increasing peripheral oedema ↓ New breathlessness with bilateral basal crackles ↓ Fluid overload
exam_trap: D, severe dehydration — tempting since the patient needed IV fluids, but oedema and crackles point to fluid excess, not deficit.
takeaway: New oedema and crackles on IV fluids: suspect overload and review the prescription.

stem:
A patient requires intravenous fluids.

Which principle should guide prescribing?

options.A: Assess fluid status, electrolytes and losses, then prescribe and review
options.B: Give 3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride daily as a standard regimen
options.C: Start IV fluids whenever oral intake falls below 1 litre per day
options.D: Continue the regimen unchanged until the patient is discharged
options.E: Use Hartmann's solution for all patients, whatever their renal function

correct_answer: A. Assess fluid status, electrolytes and losses, then prescribe and review
why_correct: NICE CG174 advises assessing fluid and electrolyte needs, prescribing for maintenance, replacement or resuscitation, and reassessing regularly.
why_wrong: B. Fluid needs vary between patients, so a standard volume is not appropriate for everyone. C. IV fluids are given for clinical need after assessment, not on a fixed intake threshold. D. Fluids should be reviewed regularly and stopped when no longer needed. E. Fluid choice depends on the patient's electrolytes and renal function, which must be considered.
pearl: Prescribe IV fluids like a drug: assess fluid status, electrolytes and ongoing losses, decide whether the aim is resuscitation, replacement or maintenance, and review regularly.
thinking: Patient needs IV fluids ↓ Needs vary with fluid status, losses and electrolytes ↓ Both over- and under-prescription cause harm ↓ Assess, prescribe, then review
exam_trap: B, 3 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride daily — tempting as a familiar standard regimen, but fixed regimens ignore individual needs and risk overload and electrolyte disturbance.
takeaway: IV fluids need individual assessment, a tailored prescription and regular review.

stem:
A patient has significant hyperkalaemia requiring urgent potassium redistribution.

Which treatment can shift potassium into cells?

options.C: Furosemide in every patient regardless of renal function

why_correct: Insulin with glucose drives potassium into cells and lowers serum potassium within about 15–30 minutes; calcium only stabilises the myocardium.
why_wrong: B. Calcium protects the heart but does not lower serum potassium. C. Furosemide can increase potassium loss but depends on renal function and does not shift potassium into cells. D. Vitamin B12 has no role in treating hyperkalaemia. E. Oral iron has no effect on potassium.
pearl: In hyperkalaemia, calcium protects the heart but does not lower potassium; insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells, with blood glucose monitored for hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Significant hyperkalaemia ↓ Serum potassium must be lowered quickly ↓ Insulin drives potassium into cells ↓ Insulin with glucose
exam_trap: B, calcium alone — tempting as it is given early in hyperkalaemia, but it only stabilises the myocardium and does not shift potassium.
takeaway: Calcium protects the heart; insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells.

stem:
A patient has chronic mild hyponatraemia associated with a condition causing excess free-water retention.

Which general treatment principle may be appropriate in selected patients?
why_correct: In chronic hyponatraemia due to excess free-water retention (for example SIADH), fluid restriction is the usual first-line treatment in selected patients.
why_wrong: A. Potassium is not routinely given to correct hyponatraemia. B. Insulin does not treat dilutional hyponatraemia. C. Oral iron has no role in hyponatraemia. E. Extra water would worsen dilutional hyponatraemia.
pearl: Hyponatraemia from excess free-water retention, as in SIADH, is dilutional; fluid restriction is the usual first step in chronic, mild cases.
thinking: Chronic mild hyponatraemia ↓ Cause is excess free-water retention ↓ Sodium is diluted, not lost ↓ Fluid restriction
exam_trap: E, unlimited water intake — tempting as a general health measure, but extra water worsens dilutional hyponatraemia.
takeaway: Dilutional hyponatraemia is treated by restricting fluid, not giving more.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin has an INR of 6.5 but no clinically significant bleeding.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Manage according to the INR and guidance, not the usual warfarin dose
options.B: Continue the usual dose and recheck the INR in one week
options.C: Give IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate
options.D: Stop warfarin and start treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin instead
options.E: Give oral vitamin K today and continue the usual maintenance warfarin dose

correct_answer: A. Manage according to the INR and guidance, not the usual warfarin dose
why_correct: With an INR of 5–8 and no bleeding, BNF guidance advises withholding 1–2 doses of warfarin and reducing the subsequent maintenance dose; oral vitamin K is reserved for an INR above 8.
why_wrong: B. Continuing the same dose leaves the patient at high bleeding risk. C. IV vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding, not an INR of 6.5 without bleeding. D. Adding heparin to an already over-anticoagulated patient increases bleeding risk. E. Oral vitamin K is reserved for an INR above 8 without bleeding, and the usual dose should not be continued.
pearl: Warfarin over-anticoagulation is managed by the INR and bleeding status: without bleeding, withhold doses and adjust the maintenance dose; vitamin K is kept for higher INRs or bleeding.
thinking: INR 6.5 on warfarin ↓ No clinically significant bleeding ↓ Withhold doses and reduce maintenance as guidance directs ↓ Manage according to the INR and guidance
exam_trap: C, IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate — tempting as the INR is high, but full reversal is reserved for major bleeding, not a patient who is not bleeding.
takeaway: High INR without bleeding: withhold and adjust warfarin; full reversal is for major bleeds.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin develops major gastrointestinal bleeding.

What is the priority?

options.A: Withhold the next warfarin dose and recheck the INR the following morning
options.B: Resuscitate and manage the bleeding, reversing the anticoagulation
options.C: Give oral vitamin K and repeat the INR in 24 hours before deciding further
options.D: Transfuse platelets and continue warfarin at a reduced dose
options.E: Give tranexamic acid and continue the warfarin at the usual unchanged dose

correct_answer: B. Resuscitate and manage the bleeding, reversing the anticoagulation
why_correct: Major bleeding on warfarin needs resuscitation, stopping warfarin, and urgent reversal with IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, as the BNF advises.
why_wrong: A. Major bleeding needs immediate resuscitation and reversal, not waiting for a repeat INR. C. Oral vitamin K acts too slowly for major bleeding; IV vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate is needed. D. Platelet transfusion does not reverse warfarin, and warfarin should be stopped. E. Continuing warfarin would worsen the bleeding, and tranexamic acid does not reverse anticoagulation.
pearl: Major bleeding on warfarin: resuscitate, stop warfarin and reverse urgently with IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ Major gastrointestinal bleeding ↓ Life-threatening haemorrhage worsened by anticoagulation ↓ Resuscitate, manage the bleeding and reverse anticoagulation
exam_trap: C, oral vitamin K and repeat INR — tempting as vitamin K reverses warfarin, but the oral route is too slow for major bleeding; IV vitamin K with PCC is needed.
takeaway: Major bleed on warfarin: resuscitate and reverse with IV vitamin K and PCC.

stem:
A patient taking a direct oral anticoagulant develops significant renal impairment.

What should be done?

options.A: Continue the current dose and recheck renal function in a year's time
options.B: Increase the dose to compensate for the reduced drug absorption
options.C: Review whether the drug and dose suit the current renal function
options.D: Switch to aspirin, which needs no dose adjustment for renal function
options.E: Stop the anticoagulant permanently without considering an alternative

correct_answer: C. Review whether the drug and dose suit the current renal function
why_correct: DOACs are partly renally cleared, so declining renal function needs a review of drug choice and dose using creatinine clearance and the product information.
why_wrong: A. Declining renal function needs prompt review because DOAC accumulation increases bleeding risk. B. Renal impairment reduces clearance, so increasing the dose raises bleeding risk. D. Aspirin is not an effective substitute for anticoagulation. E. Stopping anticoagulation without considering an alternative may leave the patient at risk of thrombosis or stroke.
pearl: DOACs are partly cleared by the kidneys; when renal function falls, recalculate creatinine clearance and review whether the drug and dose are still appropriate.
thinking: Patient on a DOAC ↓ Significant renal impairment develops ↓ Reduced clearance raises drug levels and bleeding risk ↓ Review drug and dose for current renal function
exam_trap: E, stopping the anticoagulant permanently — tempting as it removes bleeding risk, but it leaves the patient exposed to thrombosis or stroke without an alternative.
takeaway: Falling renal function on a DOAC: review the drug choice and dose.

stem:
A dehydrated patient with chronic kidney disease is taking an NSAID.

Why is this important?

options.A: NSAIDs increase renal blood flow by dilating the afferent arteriole
options.B: CKD reduces NSAID absorption, so the risk of renal harm is lower
options.C: Dehydration lowers NSAID levels, so the risk of kidney injury falls
options.D: NSAIDs protect against AKI by reducing renal inflammation
options.E: NSAIDs can worsen renal function, especially with dehydration

correct_answer: E. NSAIDs can worsen renal function, especially with dehydration
why_correct: NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion by inhibiting prostaglandins, which raises the risk of acute kidney injury in people with CKD or dehydration; they should be stopped while the patient is unwell.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilatation and can reduce renal blood flow and GFR. B. CKD increases the risk of NSAID-related kidney harm. C. Dehydration increases the risk of NSAID-related acute kidney injury. D. NSAIDs can harm renal function rather than protect it.
pearl: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole dilated, so with dehydration or CKD they can precipitate AKI; stop them while the patient is unwell.
thinking: CKD reduces renal reserve ↓ Dehydration reduces renal perfusion ↓ NSAIDs block protective prostaglandin vasodilatation ↓ NSAIDs can worsen renal function
exam_trap: A, NSAIDs dilate the afferent arteriole — tempting as it names the right vessel, but NSAIDs block prostaglandin-mediated dilatation and reduce renal blood flow.
takeaway: NSAIDs plus dehydration or CKD is a recipe for acute kidney injury.

stem:
A patient taking an ACE inhibitor develops significant hyperkalaemia.

What medication-related issue should be considered?

options.A: Potassium cannot be affected by medication
options.B: The ACE inhibitor has no possible relationship to potassium
options.E: The result must be laboratory error

why_correct: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone and reduce potassium excretion, so they can cause hyperkalaemia, especially with renal impairment or other potassium-raising drugs.
why_wrong: A. Several medicines, including ACE inhibitors, affect potassium. B. ACE inhibitors are a recognised cause of hyperkalaemia. C. ACE inhibitors tend to raise potassium. E. Laboratory error such as haemolysis should be considered, but it should not be assumed when a known drug cause is present.
pearl: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and so reduce potassium excretion; the risk of hyperkalaemia rises with renal impairment and other potassium-raising drugs.
thinking: Patient on an ACE inhibitor ↓ Significant hyperkalaemia ↓ Reduced aldosterone lowers potassium excretion ↓ ACE inhibitor-associated potassium elevation
exam_trap: E, laboratory error — tempting as haemolysis can falsely raise potassium, but error should not be assumed when a recognised drug cause is present.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia on an ACE inhibitor: suspect the drug and review medicines.

stem:
A patient with suspected opioid toxicity has a respiratory rate of 6/min and oxygen saturation is falling.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give high-flow oxygen and observe until the patient wakes
options.B: Send a urine drug screen before giving any treatment
options.C: Give flumazenil to reverse the respiratory depression
options.D: Support airway and breathing; give emergency treatment
options.E: Give IV fluids and recheck observations in 30 minutes

correct_answer: D. Support airway and breathing; give emergency treatment
why_correct: Respiratory depression from opioids needs airway and breathing support (including bag-valve-mask ventilation and oxygen) and naloxone as emergency treatment.
why_wrong: A. Oxygen alone does not treat hypoventilation; ventilatory support and naloxone are needed. B. A drug screen must not delay emergency treatment. C. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and can provoke seizures. E. IV fluids do not treat opioid-induced respiratory depression, and delay is dangerous.
pearl: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is treated with airway and ventilatory support plus naloxone; watch for re-sedation, as naloxone can wear off before the opioid.
thinking: Suspected opioid toxicity ↓ Respiratory rate 6/min and falling saturation ↓ Life-threatening hypoventilation ↓ Support airway and breathing; give emergency treatment
exam_trap: C, flumazenil — tempting as a reversal agent, but it reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and can provoke seizures.
takeaway: Opioid respiratory depression: support ventilation and give naloxone.

stem:
A patient with suspected serious bacterial infection requires blood cultures.

Which principle is correct?

options.A: Blood cultures add little and can be omitted in suspected sepsis
options.B: Withhold antibiotics until culture results are reported
options.C: One culture set is enough, even in suspected endocarditis
options.D: Take cultures first unless this significantly delays antibiotics
options.E: Take cultures after the first antibiotic dose for better yield

correct_answer: D. Take cultures first unless this significantly delays antibiotics
why_correct: Blood cultures should be taken before the first dose of antibiotics because antibiotics reduce culture yield, but in suspected sepsis this must not cause a clinically significant delay to treatment (NICE NG253, suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over).
why_wrong: A. Blood cultures are valuable for identifying the organism and its sensitivities so that antibiotic therapy can be targeted. B. Antibiotics in suspected serious infection or sepsis must be given promptly, not withheld until culture results are available days later. C. The number of culture sets needed depends on the clinical context, and suspected endocarditis requires several sets. E. Antibiotics reduce culture yield, so cultures should be taken before the first dose where possible.
pearl: Take blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose where possible, as antibiotics reduce yield, but never let culture-taking delay antibiotics in suspected sepsis.
thinking: Suspected serious bacterial infection ↓ Cultures identify the organism and sensitivities ↓ Antibiotics lower yield but must not be delayed ↓ Cultures first unless this delays antibiotics
exam_trap: B, withholding antibiotics until cultures report — tempting to allow targeted treatment, but results take days and delay in serious infection increases mortality.
takeaway: Cultures before antibiotics, but never at the cost of delaying antibiotics.

stem:
A doctor takes several blood samples from a patient.

When should the samples be labelled?

options.A: At the end of the shift, using the request forms as a reference
options.B: Back at the nurses' station, using details from the electronic record
options.C: At the bedside straight after sampling, following local procedures
options.D: By the healthcare assistant who sends the samples to the laboratory
options.E: Before seeing the patient, using pre-printed addressograph labels

correct_answer: C. At the bedside straight after sampling, following local procedures
why_correct: Samples should be labelled at the patient's side, immediately after collection and before leaving the patient, after positive identification and in line with local policy, to prevent 'wrong blood in tube' errors.
why_wrong: A. Labelling later risks mislabelling and wrong blood in tube errors, which can cause serious harm such as incompatible transfusion. B. Labelling away from the patient breaks the link between positive identification and the sample. D. Labelling must be done by the person who took the sample, at the bedside. E. Pre-labelling tubes before seeing the patient is unsafe because tubes can be used for the wrong patient.
pearl: Samples should be labelled at the bedside immediately after collection, by the person who took them, after positive identification; this prevents wrong blood in tube errors.
thinking: Several samples taken ↓ Labelling away from the patient breaks the identity link ↓ Risk of wrong blood in tube ↓ Label at the bedside straight after sampling
exam_trap: E, pre-printed labels before seeing the patient — tempting as efficient, but pre-labelled tubes can end up being used for the wrong patient.
takeaway: Label samples yourself, at the bedside, straight after taking them.

stem:
A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle.

What should they do first?

options.A: Finish the procedure and report it at the end of the shift
options.B: Scrub the wound with alcohol and start oral antibiotics
options.C: Perform immediate first aid and report the exposure promptly
options.D: Wash the wound and seek testing only if symptoms develop
options.E: Apply a dressing and report it only if the source is high risk

correct_answer: C. Perform immediate first aid and report the exposure promptly
why_correct: After a needlestick injury the wound should be encouraged to bleed and washed with running water (without scrubbing or sucking), and the exposure reported immediately to occupational health or the emergency department so that the source risk can be assessed and post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV, if indicated, can be started as soon as possible.
why_wrong: A. Delaying reporting delays risk assessment and HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, which is most effective when started within hours. B. Scrubbing is not advised, and antibiotics have no role in preventing blood-borne viral infection. D. Waiting for symptoms is inappropriate because post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical. E. Every needlestick injury must be reported promptly, as the source risk is assessed by occupational health.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage bleeding and wash under running water without scrubbing, then report at once so source risk is assessed and HIV PEP started promptly if indicated.
thinking: Needlestick from a used needle ↓ Risk of blood-borne virus transmission ↓ Post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical ↓ Immediate first aid and prompt reporting
exam_trap: D, washing and testing only if symptoms develop — tempting as it seems proportionate, but post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical and needs prompt risk assessment.
takeaway: Needlestick injury: encourage bleeding, wash, report immediately.

stem:
A patient suddenly collapses and is unresponsive.

What should happen immediately?

options.A: Call for help and check for normal breathing, starting CPR if absent
options.B: Place the patient in the recovery position and recheck in 10 minutes
options.C: Wait for a doctor to arrive before assessing the patient's airway
options.D: Check capillary glucose and blood pressure before calling for help
options.E: Record a 12-lead ECG to identify the rhythm before acting

correct_answer: A. Call for help and check for normal breathing, starting CPR if absent
why_correct: A sudden collapse with unresponsiveness may be a cardiac arrest, so help should be summoned immediately and the patient assessed for normal breathing (Resuscitation Council UK ABCDE/BLS approach), starting CPR if they are not breathing normally.
why_wrong: B. The recovery position is for patients who are breathing normally; breathing must be assessed first, and a 10-minute delay could miss cardiac arrest. C. Any trained healthcare worker should assess and act immediately; waiting for a doctor delays CPR and defibrillation. D. Help must be summoned and breathing assessed first; other checks must not delay recognition of cardiac arrest. E. A 12-lead ECG must not delay recognition of cardiac arrest, CPR and defibrillation.
pearl: In sudden collapse, shout for help, open the airway and check for normal breathing; absent or abnormal breathing, including agonal gasps, means cardiac arrest, so start CPR.
thinking: Recognition and immediate action are more important than completing a prolonged assessment.
exam_trap: B, recovery position and recheck in 10 minutes — tempting for an unresponsive patient, but breathing must be checked first, and the delay could miss cardiac arrest.
takeaway: Collapse: call for help, check breathing, and start CPR if not breathing normally.

stem:
A patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally.

What is the appropriate immediate response?

options.A: Record a 12-lead ECG to confirm cardiac arrest before starting CPR
options.B: Check capillary blood glucose and give IV dextrose before starting CPR
options.C: Place in the recovery position and monitor breathing until help arrives
options.D: Give 5 rescue breaths first and reassess before starting compressions
options.E: Start CPR and attach an AED or defibrillator as soon as available

correct_answer: E. Start CPR and attach an AED or defibrillator as soon as available
why_correct: Unresponsiveness with absent or abnormal breathing should be treated as cardiac arrest: call for help, start chest compressions and attach an AED or defibrillator as soon as it is available (Resuscitation Council UK Adult Basic Life Support). Source: Resuscitation Council UK 2025 Adult Basic Life Support guidance.
why_wrong: A. CPR must not be delayed for an ECG; rhythm assessment is done via the AED or defibrillator pads once applied. B. Glucose measurement must not delay CPR; reversible causes are considered once resuscitation is under way. C. The recovery position is for unconscious patients who are breathing normally; it is inappropriate in cardiac arrest. D. Initial rescue breaths are part of paediatric, not adult, basic life support; adults should receive chest compressions straight away.
pearl: Unresponsive and not breathing normally means cardiac arrest: start chest compressions and attach an AED as soon as one is available, as early defibrillation saves lives.
thinking: Unresponsive ↓ Not breathing normally ↓ Treat as cardiac arrest ↓ Start CPR and attach an AED or defibrillator
exam_trap: D, five rescue breaths first — tempting as this is part of paediatric life support, but adults in cardiac arrest need chest compressions straight away.
takeaway: Adult unresponsive and not breathing normally: compressions and an AED now.

stem:
A patient is in cardiac arrest and an automated external defibrillator is brought to the scene.

What should be done?

options.A: Wait until a doctor arrives before switching it on
options.C: Apply the AED promptly and follow its instructions
options.D: Remove the AED because it can only be used by anaesthetists
options.E: Continue CPR indefinitely without assessing the rhythm

correct_answer: C. Apply the AED promptly and follow its instructions
why_correct: Early defibrillation improves survival, so the AED should be switched on and attached promptly while CPR continues, and its voice prompts followed (Resuscitation Council UK).
why_wrong: A. AEDs are designed to be used by anyone, and waiting for a doctor delays defibrillation and reduces the chance of survival. B. Adrenaline is given intravenously or intraosseously during advanced life support; there is no role for oral adrenaline in cardiac arrest. D. AEDs are designed for use by laypeople and all healthcare staff, not only anaesthetists. E. Rhythm assessment is essential because shockable rhythms need prompt defibrillation; CPR alone without analysis misses this.
pearl: AEDs are designed for anyone to use: switch it on, apply the pads with minimal interruption to CPR and follow the voice prompts.
thinking: Cardiac arrest ↓ AED arrives ↓ Early defibrillation of shockable rhythms improves survival ↓ Apply the AED promptly and follow its instructions
exam_trap: A, waiting for a doctor before switching it on — tempting if unsure about the device, but AEDs are built for any user and delay lowers survival.
takeaway: When an AED arrives: switch it on, apply the pads and follow the prompts.

stem:
A patient is unconscious but breathing normally and has no indication of cardiac arrest.

What is the appropriate immediate positioning?

options.A: Sit them upright in a chair and recheck their observations in 15 minutes
options.B: Lie them flat on their back with a pillow and recheck on the ward round
options.C: Recovery position, maintaining the airway and monitoring breathing
options.D: Prone with the head to one side, observed from the nurses' station desk
options.E: Start chest compressions while awaiting the defibrillator

correct_answer: C. Recovery position, maintaining the airway and monitoring breathing
why_correct: An unconscious patient who is breathing normally should be placed in the recovery position to protect the airway from obstruction and aspiration, with breathing monitored continuously in case they deteriorate into cardiac arrest.
why_wrong: A. An unconscious patient sitting upright is at risk of airway obstruction and needs continuous monitoring. B. Lying supine allows the tongue to obstruct the airway and risks aspiration, and the patient needs continuous monitoring. D. The prone position compromises airway assessment and breathing, and the patient must be closely monitored. E. Chest compressions are only indicated when the patient is unresponsive and not breathing normally; this patient is breathing normally.
pearl: An unconscious patient who is breathing normally goes in the recovery position to protect the airway, with breathing monitored continuously in case they arrest.
thinking: Unconscious ↓ Breathing normally; no cardiac arrest ↓ Airway at risk from the tongue and aspiration ↓ Recovery position with airway maintained and breathing monitored
exam_trap: E, starting chest compressions — tempting in any unconscious patient, but compressions are only for those who are not breathing normally.
takeaway: Unconscious but breathing normally: recovery position and continuous monitoring.

stem:
A patient is acutely unwell and hypoxaemic.

Which principle should guide oxygen therapy?

options.A: Give 15 L/min via reservoir mask and continue it regardless of saturation
options.B: Aim for saturations of 100% to maximise oxygen delivery to vital tissues
options.C: Withhold oxygen until an arterial blood gas result is available to guide it
options.D: Titrate oxygen to a target saturation, considering risk of hypercapnia
options.E: Target 88–92% in acutely ill patients as a default to avoid hypercapnia

correct_answer: D. Titrate oxygen to a target saturation, considering risk of hypercapnia
why_correct: Oxygen is a drug that should be prescribed to a target saturation, typically 94–98% for most acutely ill patients and 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as some patients with COPD (BTS oxygen guideline).
why_wrong: A. High-flow oxygen without titration can cause hyperoxaemia and worsen hypercapnic respiratory failure in at-risk patients. B. Aiming for 100% causes hyperoxaemia; most patients should be titrated to 94–98%. C. Hypoxaemia should be treated promptly, with an arterial blood gas taken as needed, rather than withholding oxygen. E. The 88–92% target is for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure; most acutely ill patients should be kept at 94–98%.
pearl: Oxygen is a drug prescribed to a target saturation: usually 94–98% for most acutely ill patients and 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure.
thinking: Acutely unwell and hypoxaemic ↓ Oxygen is a prescribed drug ↓ Too little or too much both harm; hypercapnia risk varies ↓ Titrate oxygen to a target saturation
exam_trap: E, 88–92% as a default for all — tempting as it avoids hypercapnia, but that lower target is only for at-risk patients; most acutely ill patients need 94–98%.
takeaway: Prescribe oxygen to a target saturation matched to the patient's hypercapnia risk.

stem:
A patient's oxygen saturation is unexpectedly low, but they are comfortable, speaking normally and have cold fingers with poor peripheral perfusion.

What should be considered?

options.A: Check the probe, signal and clinical picture before trusting the reading
options.B: Disregard the reading, as the patient looks comfortable and is speaking normally
options.C: Start high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask and arrange urgent CT pulmonary angiography
options.D: Diagnose pulmonary embolism and start treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin
options.E: Diagnose type 1 respiratory failure and refer to critical care for support

correct_answer: A. Check the probe, signal and clinical picture before trusting the reading
why_correct: Pulse oximetry depends on adequate peripheral perfusion, so cold, poorly perfused fingers can give a falsely low reading; the probe position, waveform/signal quality and the patient's clinical state should be checked, and an arterial blood gas obtained if genuine hypoxaemia remains possible.
why_wrong: B. The reading should not be disregarded; it needs to be checked and verified because genuine hypoxaemia must still be excluded. C. Investigating for PE on a possibly spurious reading in a comfortable patient is premature; the reading should be verified first. D. Pulmonary embolism cannot be diagnosed from oxygen saturation alone and requires clinical probability assessment and imaging before anticoagulation. E. Respiratory failure should not be diagnosed from a single possibly inaccurate oximetry reading in a comfortable patient.
pearl: Pulse oximetry needs a good pulsatile signal; cold, poorly perfused fingers or movement can give falsely low readings, so check the probe and treat the patient, not the number.
thinking: A monitor reading must always be interpreted alongside the patient.
exam_trap: C, high-flow oxygen and urgent CTPA — tempting as low saturation can mean PE, but a comfortable patient with poor peripheral perfusion needs the reading verified first.
takeaway: Low SpO2 in a comfortable patient with cold fingers: check the probe and signal first.

stem: Which ECG lead is normally placed at the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border?
why_correct: V1 is placed in the fourth intercostal space immediately to the right of the sternum.
why_wrong: B. V2 is placed in the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border. C. V5 is placed in the anterior axillary line at the same horizontal level as V4. D. V4 is placed in the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. E. V6 is placed in the mid-axillary line at the same horizontal level as V4.
pearl: V1 and V2 sit in the fourth intercostal space either side of the sternum (V1 right, V2 left); V4 is in the fifth space in the midclavicular line, with V5 and V6 level with it.
thinking: Lead lies in the fourth intercostal space ↓ It sits at the sternal border ↓ It is on the right side of the sternum ↓ V1
exam_trap: B, V2 — tempting as it sits in the same intercostal space, but V2 is at the left sternal border, not the right.
takeaway: V1 is right and V2 left of the sternum, both in the fourth intercostal space.

stem: Where should V4 normally be placed?

options.B: Mid-axillary line at the level of V1
