options.C: Fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
options.D: Fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border
options.E: Fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border

correct_answer: C. Fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
why_correct: V4 is placed in the fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line; correct placement matters because misplaced chest leads can alter the ECG appearance.
why_wrong: A. No standard chest lead is placed in the second intercostal space, and this would be too high for V4. B. V6, not V4, lies in the mid-axillary line, and it is placed at the horizontal level of V4 rather than V1. D. The fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border is the position for V2. E. The fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border is the position for V1.
pearl: V4 sits in the fifth intercostal space in the midclavicular line, and V5 and V6 are placed level with it in the anterior and mid-axillary lines.
thinking: V1 and V2 lie in the fourth space beside the sternum ↓ V4 is lower and more lateral ↓ V5 and V6 are placed level with it ↓ Fifth intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line
exam_trap: D, fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border — tempting as a standard chest-lead site, but that is the position for V2, not V4.
takeaway: V4: fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line; V5 and V6 level with it.

stem:
An ECG appears to show an unusual rhythm, but the patient is completely asymptomatic with a normal pulse.

What should be considered first?

options.A: Give IV amiodarone while the ECG is being repeated
options.B: Attach defibrillator pads and prepare for cardioversion
options.C: Give thrombolysis for a presumed acute coronary event
options.D: Diagnose ventricular tachycardia and call the cardiac arrest team
options.E: Check for artefact and repeat the ECG with correct lead placement

correct_answer: E. Check for artefact and repeat the ECG with correct lead placement
why_correct: An apparently abnormal rhythm in an asymptomatic patient with a normal pulse is often due to artefact (for example, movement, tremor or poor electrode contact), so the trace should be checked and repeated with correct electrode placement before acting on it, always treating the patient rather than the monitor.
why_wrong: A. Anti-arrhythmic drugs carry significant risks and should not be given on the basis of a possibly artefactual trace. B. Cardioversion is not indicated in an asymptomatic patient with a normal pulse and an unverified trace. C. Thrombolysis is not an appropriate response to an unexplained ECG appearance. D. A life-threatening arrhythmia is unlikely in an asymptomatic patient with a normal pulse, and the trace should be verified first.
pearl: Treat the patient, not the monitor: an alarming trace in an asymptomatic patient with a normal pulse is often artefact from movement, tremor or poor electrode contact.
thinking: ECG shows an unusual rhythm ↓ Patient asymptomatic with a normal pulse ↓ Clinical picture does not match the trace ↓ Check for artefact and repeat with correct lead placement
exam_trap: D, diagnosing VT and calling the arrest team — tempting if the trace looks broad and fast, but a well patient with a normal pulse makes artefact far more likely.
takeaway: Abnormal trace in a well patient: exclude artefact before acting.

stem: Before taking blood from a patient, what is essential?

options.A: Confirm identity by checking the name written on the bed or door sign
options.B: Confirm identity with appropriate identifiers and check the request
options.C: Take the sample first, then confirm the patient's details when labelling
options.D: Ask the patient to confirm the name that is read out to them from the form
options.E: Rely on recognising the patient from earlier in the same shift on the ward

correct_answer: B. Confirm identity with appropriate identifiers and check the request
why_correct: Positive patient identification, for example asking the patient to state their full name and date of birth and checking these against the wristband and request form, is essential before phlebotomy to prevent wrong blood in tube errors.
why_wrong: A. Bed or door signs are unreliable because patients move and signs may be wrong. C. Identity and request details must be checked before the sample is taken, not after. D. A closed question may be answered 'yes' by a confused or hard-of-hearing patient; the patient should state their own details. E. Recognition alone is unreliable, and formal identifiers must be checked.
pearl: Positive identification means the patient states their full name and date of birth, checked against the wristband and request form, before any sample is taken.
thinking: About to take blood ↓ Misidentification causes wrong blood in tube errors ↓ Formal identifiers must be checked before sampling ↓ Confirm identity with appropriate identifiers and check the request
exam_trap: D, asking the patient to confirm a name read out — tempting as it involves the patient, but confused or hard-of-hearing patients may simply agree; they should state their own details.
takeaway: Ask the patient to state their details and check them before taking the sample.

stem:
A blood sample has been taken correctly but is left on a clinical trolley without being labelled.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Send it unlabelled with a note explaining whose sample it probably is
options.B: Label it with the name of the patient whose blood was taken most recently
options.C: Ask the nurse which patient it most likely belongs to and label it
options.D: Label it from the likely patient's wristband and inform the laboratory
options.E: Follow local policy for unlabelled samples rather than guess its identity

correct_answer: E. Follow local policy for unlabelled samples rather than guess its identity
why_correct: An unlabelled sample cannot be safely attributed to a patient, so local policy should be followed, which usually means discarding it, reporting the incident and repeating the sample with correct identification and labelling.
why_wrong: A. Laboratories will reject unidentified samples, and a guessed identity cannot be safely attributed. B. Assuming it belongs to the most recent patient risks wrong blood in tube errors with potentially fatal consequences. C. Another person's guess cannot establish the sample's identity. D. Labelling from a wristband after the event is still guessing and risks a wrong blood in tube error.
pearl: Never label a sample after the event from memory or guesswork; an unlabelled sample is usually discarded, the incident reported and the test repeated.
thinking: Sample left unlabelled on a trolley ↓ Its identity cannot be confirmed ↓ Guessing risks a wrong blood in tube error ↓ Follow local policy rather than guess
exam_trap: D, labelling from the likely patient's wristband — tempting as it uses a formal identifier, but it is still guesswork about whose blood is in the tube.
takeaway: An unlabelled sample cannot be rescued by guessing: follow policy and repeat it.

stem:
A patient develops fever, rigors and back pain shortly after a blood transfusion begins.

What is the immediate action?

options.A: Slow the transfusion, give paracetamol and reassess in 30 minutes
options.B: Give IV chlorphenamine and continue the transfusion at the same rate
options.C: Continue the transfusion and recheck the observations in an hour
options.D: Stop the transfusion and start assessment and management of a reaction
options.E: Stop the transfusion and remove the cannula immediately

correct_answer: D. Stop the transfusion and start assessment and management of a reaction
why_correct: Fever, rigors and loin/back pain soon after starting a transfusion suggest an acute haemolytic or other serious reaction, so the transfusion must be stopped immediately, the patient assessed (ABCDE), venous access kept open and the reaction managed and investigated in line with local and SHOT/BSH guidance.
why_wrong: A. Slowing the rate is only for mild isolated fever; rigors and back pain suggest a serious reaction, so the transfusion must be stopped. B. Antihistamines do not treat a haemolytic or septic reaction, and continuing could be fatal. C. Continuing a transfusion during a suspected serious reaction could be fatal. E. Venous access should be maintained for resuscitation fluids and drugs; only the transfusion itself is stopped.
pearl: Fever with rigors and back or loin pain early in a transfusion suggests a serious reaction such as acute haemolysis: stop the transfusion, assess ABCDE and keep the venous access open.
thinking: Transfusion has just started ↓ Fever, rigors and back pain ↓ Possible acute haemolytic or other serious reaction ↓ Stop the transfusion and assess and manage the reaction
exam_trap: A, slowing the transfusion and giving paracetamol — tempting as this suits a mild isolated fever, but rigors and back pain signal a serious reaction needing it stopped.
takeaway: Serious features during transfusion: stop it, keep the cannula, assess and investigate.

stem:
A patient is unable to pass urine and has a painful, distended bladder.

What intervention may be required?
why_correct: A painful, distended bladder with inability to pass urine indicates acute urinary retention, which is relieved by urethral (or, if not possible, suprapubic) catheterisation, followed by assessment for the cause.
why_wrong: A. A nebulised bronchodilator treats bronchospasm and has no role in urinary retention. B. Colonoscopy investigates the colon and does not relieve urinary retention. C. Lumbar puncture is not a treatment for retention, although spinal causes may need urgent assessment if neurological red flags are present. D. Nasogastric feeding is used for nutritional support and is irrelevant to urinary retention.
pearl: Acute urinary retention is relieved by urethral catheterisation, or suprapubic if urethral fails, and the cause is then sought, such as outflow obstruction, medicines, constipation or infection.
thinking: Unable to pass urine ↓ Painful, distended bladder ↓ Acute urinary retention ↓ Urinary catheterisation
exam_trap: C, lumbar puncture — tempting as retention can have a neurological cause, but it has no role in relieving retention, which needs bladder drainage.
takeaway: Painful distended bladder and no urine: catheterise, then find the cause.

stem:
A urinary catheter is no longer clinically necessary.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.B: Give prophylactic antibiotics for its entire duration
options.C: Replace it every day regardless of indication
options.D: Remove it as soon as it is no longer needed

correct_answer: D. Remove it as soon as it is no longer needed
why_correct: Indwelling urinary catheters should be removed as soon as they are no longer clinically needed because the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection increases with duration (NICE guidance on healthcare-associated infections).
why_wrong: A. Permanently clamping a catheter is not a valid alternative to removal and risks retention and infection. B. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for long-term catheters because it promotes antimicrobial resistance. C. Unnecessary catheter changes increase trauma and infection risk without benefit. E. Keeping a catheter in indefinitely without an indication increases the risk of infection and other complications.
pearl: The risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection rises the longer a catheter stays in, so review the need regularly and remove it as soon as it is no longer needed.
thinking: Catheter no longer clinically needed ↓ Infection risk rises with duration ↓ No benefit from keeping it ↓ Remove it as soon as it is no longer needed
exam_trap: B, prophylactic antibiotics throughout — tempting to prevent infection, but routine prophylaxis drives resistance; removal is what reduces the risk.
takeaway: No indication, no catheter: remove it as soon as it is not needed.

stem:
A nasogastric tube has just been inserted for feeding.

Before feeding through the tube, what is essential?

options.A: Inject air down the tube and listen over the stomach
options.B: Place the end of the tube in water and check for bubbling
options.C: Confirm the tube position using the local verification method
options.D: Confirm placement because the insertion was uncomplicated
options.E: Test the aspirate with blue litmus paper to confirm acidity

correct_answer: C. Confirm the tube position using the local verification method
why_correct: Nasogastric tube placement must be confirmed before first use, usually by aspirate pH testing (pH 5.5 or below) or chest X-ray if pH testing fails, because feeding through a misplaced tube in the airway is a NHS 'Never Event'.
why_wrong: A. The 'whoosh' test is unreliable and must not be used to confirm position. B. The bubble test is unreliable and unsafe for confirming tube position. D. Uncomplicated insertion does not exclude misplacement, which can occur without obvious signs. E. Litmus paper is not sensitive enough; pH indicator strips or chest X-ray are required.
pearl: Confirm NG tube position before first use with aspirate pH indicator strips, or chest X-ray if pH testing fails; feeding through a tube misplaced in the airway is a Never Event.
thinking: New NG tube for feeding ↓ Misplacement into the airway can be silent ↓ Feeding through a misplaced tube can be fatal ↓ Confirm position using the local verification method
exam_trap: A, injecting air and listening over the stomach — tempting as a traditional bedside check, but the whoosh test is unreliable and must not be used.
takeaway: Never feed through an NG tube until its position is confirmed by pH or X-ray.

stem:
A patient has suspected meningitis but also has features suggesting raised intracranial pressure.

What is the key principle?

options.A: Perform lumbar puncture first, then give antibiotics once CSF is obtained
options.B: Arrange CT head and withhold antibiotics until the scan has been reported
options.C: Assess whether lumbar puncture is safe; do not delay antibiotics for it
options.D: Proceed to lumbar puncture if a CT head shows no mass lesion
options.E: Give oral antibiotics and observe until the features have resolved

correct_answer: C. Assess whether lumbar puncture is safe; do not delay antibiotics for it
why_correct: In suspected meningitis with signs of raised intracranial pressure, lumbar puncture may be unsafe and should be delayed until it is safe, but antibiotics must not be delayed by investigations (NICE NG240).
why_wrong: A. Lumbar puncture may be unsafe with raised intracranial pressure, and antibiotics must not wait for it. B. Antibiotics must not be delayed while imaging is arranged or reported. D. Clinical features of raised intracranial pressure contraindicate lumbar puncture even if CT shows no mass lesion. E. Suspected meningitis requires urgent parenteral antibiotics, not oral treatment.
pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, never delay antibiotics for CT or lumbar puncture; signs of raised intracranial pressure make lumbar puncture unsafe until it is reassessed.
thinking: Suspected meningitis ↓ Features of raised intracranial pressure ↓ LP may cause harm, but delaying antibiotics is dangerous ↓ Assess LP safety; do not delay antibiotics
exam_trap: B, CT head and withholding antibiotics until reported — tempting as imaging seems a sensible safety step, but delaying antibiotics worsens outcomes in meningitis.
takeaway: Suspected meningitis: antibiotics first; lumbar puncture only when safe.

stem:
A patient is severely breathless and requires an arterial blood gas.

Which principle is correct?

options.A: Delay oxygen therapy until the ABG result is available to guide it
options.B: Proceed without checking anticoagulation, as arterial puncture is low risk
options.C: Take it from the femoral artery first, as this is the easiest site
options.D: Explain, gain consent if possible, perform safely and interpret in context
options.E: Take the sample first and confirm the patient's identity afterwards

correct_answer: D. Explain, gain consent if possible, perform safely and interpret in context
why_correct: An ABG is an invasive procedure, so the patient should be identified and the procedure explained with consent obtained where possible, contraindications such as anticoagulation considered, and the result interpreted alongside the clinical picture.
why_wrong: A. Emergency treatment such as oxygen should not be delayed while awaiting an ABG result. B. Anticoagulation increases the risk of bleeding and haematoma, so it must be considered before arterial puncture. C. The radial artery is the usual first-choice site because it is safer and more accessible to compress. E. Correct patient identification is essential before every sample is taken.
pearl: An ABG is an invasive procedure: identify the patient, explain and gain consent where possible, check for anticoagulation, usually use the radial artery, and interpret the result clinically.
thinking: Severely breathless patient needs an ABG ↓ Invasive procedure with bleeding and other risks ↓ Needs consent, safe technique and contraindication checks ↓ Explain, consent, perform safely, interpret in context
exam_trap: A, delaying oxygen until the ABG result — tempting to obtain a true baseline, but emergency treatment in a severely breathless patient must not wait for results.
takeaway: ABG: identify, consent, check anticoagulation, sample safely, interpret in context.

stem:
A patient with diabetes becomes suddenly confused.

What simple bedside investigation may rapidly identify a reversible cause?
why_correct: Hypoglycaemia is a common, rapidly reversible cause of acute confusion in people with diabetes (especially those taking insulin or sulfonylureas), and a capillary glucose test identifies it within seconds at the bedside.
why_wrong: A. Fasting serum cholesterol is relevant to long-term cardiovascular risk and does not explain acute confusion. B. A bone-density (DXA) scan assesses osteoporosis and has no role in acute confusion. C. Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction and is not helpful in acute confusion. E. Urine cytology is used for suspected urothelial malignancy and is not a rapid test for confusion.
pearl: Check capillary glucose in any acutely confused patient with diabetes; hypoglycaemia, especially with insulin or sulfonylureas, is found in seconds and quickly reversed.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Sudden confusion ↓ Hypoglycaemia is common and rapidly reversible ↓ Capillary blood glucose
exam_trap: E, urine cytology — tempting only as a simple urine test, but cytology looks for urothelial cancer and cannot explain acute confusion.
takeaway: Acute confusion in diabetes: check capillary glucose straight away.

stem:
A patient presents with dysuria and urinary frequency.

Which bedside investigation may support the assessment?
why_correct: Urine dipstick testing can support the assessment of urinary symptoms by detecting nitrites and leucocyte esterase, although NICE advises against dipstick use in some groups, such as women over 65 and people with catheters.
why_wrong: A. Audiometry assesses hearing and has no role in this presentation. B. Visual acuity testing is unrelated to urinary symptoms. C. An ECG does not help assess urinary symptoms. D. Peak flow measures expiratory airflow and is not relevant to dysuria.
pearl: Urine dipstick can support a suspected UTI through nitrites and leucocyte esterase, but it is unreliable in some groups, such as women over 65 and people with catheters.
thinking: Dysuria and urinary frequency ↓ Suspected urinary tract infection ↓ Quick bedside test for nitrites and leucocytes ↓ Urine dipstick testing
exam_trap: C, ECG only — tempting as a routine bedside test, but it gives no information about urinary symptoms.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms: a dipstick supports, but does not replace, clinical judgement.

stem:
A woman of reproductive age presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.

Which investigation is particularly important early in the assessment?
why_correct: In any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, a pregnancy test is essential early because ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage must be considered, and pregnancy status changes investigation and management (NICE NG126).
why_wrong: A. Spirometry assesses lung function and is irrelevant here. C. Serum cholesterol does not help assess an acute gynaecological or pregnancy-related presentation. D. Bone-density scanning has no role in acute abdominal pain with bleeding. E. Hearing assessment is unrelated to this presentation.
pearl: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding needs an early pregnancy test, because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded even when pregnancy seems unlikely.
thinking: Pregnancy status can fundamentally alter the differential diagnosis and management of abdominal or pelvic symptoms.
exam_trap: C, serum cholesterol — tempting only as a routine blood test, but it has no role in an acute presentation where ectopic pregnancy must be excluded.
takeaway: Reproductive-age woman with pain and bleeding: pregnancy test early.

stem:
A patient's blood pressure is unexpectedly high.

What is important when repeating the measurement?

options.A: Use a correctly sized cuff and let the patient rest before measuring
options.B: Rely on the first reading, as repeat readings tend to be falsely low
options.C: Use a smaller cuff, as this improves accuracy in most adults
options.D: Measure over the shirt sleeve to keep the patient comfortable
options.E: Measure with the arm hanging down by the patient's side

correct_answer: A. Use a correctly sized cuff and let the patient rest before measuring
why_correct: Accurate blood pressure measurement requires a correctly sized cuff, a seated and rested patient with the arm supported at heart level, and repeat readings, because technique errors can falsely raise readings (NICE NG136).
why_wrong: B. Unexpectedly high readings should be repeated, and NICE recommends repeat measurement and ambulatory or home monitoring to confirm hypertension. C. A cuff that is too small overestimates blood pressure. D. Measuring over clothing reduces accuracy; the cuff should be placed on the bare upper arm. E. The arm should be supported at heart level; a dependent arm gives falsely high readings.
pearl: Measure blood pressure with a correctly sized cuff on the bare upper arm, supported at heart level, after the patient has rested; a cuff that is too small overestimates.
thinking: Unexpectedly high reading ↓ Technique errors can falsely raise blood pressure ↓ Correct cuff size and rest improve accuracy ↓ Correctly sized cuff after a period of rest
exam_trap: C, a smaller cuff — tempting as a tighter fit may seem more precise, but a cuff that is too small overestimates blood pressure.
takeaway: Accurate BP: right cuff, bare arm at heart level, rested patient.

stem:
A patient with asthma is acutely breathless.

What can peak expiratory flow provide?

options.A: A reliable way to distinguish an acute asthma attack from pulmonary embolism
options.B: An objective measure of airflow to assess severity and treatment response
options.C: A reasonable estimate of arterial oxygenation when pulse oximetry is unavailable
options.D: A measure of total lung capacity to detect a restrictive lung disease pattern
options.E: A reliable diagnosis of COPD when the measured value is below 80% of predicted

correct_answer: B. An objective measure of airflow to assess severity and treatment response
why_correct: Peak expiratory flow is a simple objective measure of airflow obstruction; expressed as a percentage of best or predicted it helps classify the severity of an acute asthma attack and monitor response to treatment (BTS/SIGN acute asthma guidance, SIGN 158).
why_wrong: A. Peak flow cannot distinguish asthma from pulmonary embolism. C. Peak flow measures airflow, not oxygenation; oxygen status needs oximetry or blood gases. D. Peak flow does not measure lung volumes. E. COPD is diagnosed by spirometry (FEV1/FVC ratio), not peak flow.
pearl: Peak flow, compared with the patient's best or predicted value, gives a quick objective measure of severity in acute asthma and tracks the response to treatment.
thinking: Acute asthma ↓ The problem is airflow obstruction ↓ Peak flow measures expiratory airflow objectively ↓ Assess severity and treatment response
exam_trap: C, estimating arterial oxygenation — tempting as both inform severity, but peak flow measures airflow, not oxygen; use oximetry or blood gases.
takeaway: Peak flow measures airflow for severity and response, not oxygenation.

stem:
A patient's spirometry shows a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio.

What does this pattern generally indicate?

options.E: A restrictive pattern in every case

why_correct: A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio (below 0.7 or below the lower limit of normal) indicates airflow obstruction, as seen in asthma and COPD.
why_wrong: A. Anaemia does not cause a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio. B. A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio is abnormal and indicates obstruction rather than normal lung function. D. Spirometry assesses lung function and cannot diagnose isolated cardiac failure. E. Restrictive disease typically gives a normal or raised FEV₁/FVC ratio with reduced FVC.
pearl: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio means airflow obstruction, as in asthma and COPD; restriction reduces FVC with a normal or raised ratio.
thinking: Spirometry ↓ FEV1 reduced relative to FVC ↓ Air cannot be exhaled quickly ↓ Obstructive ventilatory pattern
exam_trap: E, a restrictive pattern — tempting as both reduce lung function, but restriction gives a normal or high ratio with a reduced FVC.
takeaway: A low FEV1/FVC ratio is obstruction; restriction keeps the ratio normal or high.

stem:
An older patient has fallen twice in the past month.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Prescribe a night-time hypnotic to improve sleep quality and daytime alertness
options.B: Advise hip protectors alone, as some falls are expected with normal healthy ageing
options.C: Arrange a DXA scan alone and reassess only if a fracture occurs
options.D: Assess reversible risk factors, including medicines, vision, gait and home
options.E: Advise walking less until a walking aid has been provided

correct_answer: D. Assess reversible risk factors, including medicines, vision, gait and home
why_correct: Recurrent falls in an older person warrant a multifactorial falls risk assessment, including medication review, vision, gait and balance, cognition, continence, postural hypotension and home hazards, so that targeted interventions can reduce future falls (NICE guidance on falls).
why_wrong: A. Hypnotics and sedatives increase falls risk and should be reviewed and reduced rather than added. B. Falls are not an inevitable part of ageing, and many risk factors are modifiable. C. Bone health is one part of assessment, but falls risk factors should be assessed before injury occurs. E. Reducing activity can worsen strength and balance; strength and balance training is recommended instead.
pearl: Recurrent falls need multifactorial assessment: medicines, vision, gait and balance, postural hypotension, cognition, continence and home hazards, followed by targeted interventions.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Two falls in a month ↓ Falls usually have modifiable causes ↓ Assess reversible risk factors
exam_trap: C, a DXA scan alone — tempting as bone health matters in people who fall, but it ignores why the patient is falling and the chance to prevent further falls.
takeaway: Recurrent falls need multifactorial assessment, not acceptance as normal ageing.

stem:
An immobile patient is at high risk of pressure injury.

Which intervention is appropriate?

options.A: Regular skin checks, repositioning and pressure-redistributing equipment
options.B: Weekly skin inspection, with barrier cream applied to all pressure areas
options.C: Restrict fluids to reduce incontinence and moisture-related skin damage
options.D: Reposition only if the patient reports pain over a pressure area
options.E: Massage reddened pressure areas to improve the local circulation

correct_answer: A. Regular skin checks, repositioning and pressure-redistributing equipment
why_correct: Patients at high risk of pressure ulcers need regular skin assessment and a prevention plan that includes repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces and attention to nutrition and hydration (NICE CG179).
why_wrong: B. High-risk patients need more frequent skin inspection, and barrier cream alone does not relieve pressure. C. Fluid restriction worsens tissue perfusion; adequate hydration and nutrition support skin integrity. D. Repositioning should be scheduled, not dependent on pain, which many immobile patients cannot report. E. Massage of reddened skin may cause further tissue damage and is not recommended.
pearl: Pressure ulcer prevention rests on regular skin inspection, scheduled repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces and good nutrition and hydration.
thinking: Immobile patient ↓ High risk of pressure injury ↓ Sustained pressure must be relieved and skin checked ↓ Regular skin checks, repositioning and pressure-redistributing equipment
exam_trap: E, massaging reddened areas — tempting as it seems to boost circulation, but massage can further damage at-risk tissue and is not recommended.
takeaway: Prevent pressure ulcers with skin checks, repositioning and the right surface.

stem:
A healthcare worker is about to examine a patient.

When should hand hygiene be performed?

options.A: After patient contact only, to protect the next patient
options.B: Before putting gloves on, with no need after removing them
options.C: At the start and end of each shift and after meal breaks
options.D: When hands look visibly dirty after a procedure
options.E: Before and after patient contact, and at other key moments

correct_answer: E. Before and after patient contact, and at other key moments
why_correct: Hand hygiene should be performed at the WHO 'five moments': before touching a patient, before clean/aseptic procedures, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient and after touching the patient's surroundings.
why_wrong: A. Hand hygiene is needed before patient contact too, to protect the patient. B. Hand hygiene is still needed after removing gloves, which do not fully protect the hands. C. Hand hygiene is needed at the point of care around each patient contact, not just at set times in the day. D. Hands can carry pathogens even when they look clean.
pearl: Use the WHO five moments: before touching a patient, before aseptic tasks, after body-fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient and after touching their surroundings.
thinking: About to examine a patient ↓ Hands transmit pathogens in both directions ↓ Hygiene is needed at key moments around care ↓ Before and after patient contact, and at other key moments
exam_trap: A, after patient contact only — tempting as it protects the next patient, but hand hygiene before contact is needed to protect this patient.
takeaway: Hand hygiene before and after every patient contact, plus the other key moments.

stem:
A clinician is about to perform a procedure with a risk of blood or body-fluid exposure.

What should determine the appropriate PPE?

options.B: Whether the patient has a visible rash
options.E: Whether the procedure is performed before lunch

correct_answer: C. The anticipated risk of exposure
why_correct: Standard infection control precautions require PPE to be chosen according to a risk assessment of the anticipated exposure to blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin during the task.
why_wrong: A. PPE choice must be based on the risk of exposure, not personal preference. B. A visible rash is not the main determinant of PPE for a procedure with blood or body-fluid exposure risk. D. Age alone does not determine the risk of body-fluid exposure. E. The time of day has no bearing on exposure risk or the PPE required.
pearl: Under standard infection control precautions, PPE is chosen by assessing the task's anticipated exposure to blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin.
thinking: Procedure with blood or body-fluid exposure risk ↓ Standard infection control precautions apply ↓ PPE is matched to the task ↓ The anticipated risk of exposure
exam_trap: B, whether the patient has a visible rash — tempting as rashes can signal infection, but PPE for this procedure depends on the expected exposure, not visible signs.
takeaway: Choose PPE according to the anticipated exposure risk of the task.

stem:
A patient on a hospital ward develops increasing respiratory rate, falling blood pressure and new confusion.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Repeat the observations in four hours and document them in the notes
options.B: Recognise possible deterioration, assess urgently and escalate
options.C: Inform the medical team at the next scheduled ward round tomorrow
options.D: Encourage oral fluids and recheck the blood pressure later in the shift
options.E: Give a dose of haloperidol to manage the new confusion and agitation

correct_answer: B. Recognise possible deterioration, assess urgently and escalate
why_correct: A rising respiratory rate, falling blood pressure and new confusion suggest acute deterioration, possibly sepsis, so the patient needs urgent ABCDE assessment and escalation according to NEWS2 and local escalation policies.
why_wrong: A. Recording abnormal observations without acting fails to escalate care. C. Waiting for a routine ward round delays treatment in a deteriorating patient. D. Oral fluids without assessment are inadequate and potentially unsafe in a confused, hypotensive patient. E. New confusion may reflect sepsis or hypoperfusion and needs assessment of the cause, not sedation.
pearl: A rising respiratory rate, falling blood pressure and new confusion are warning signs of deterioration, possibly sepsis; assess ABCDE urgently and escalate using NEWS2 and local policy.
thinking: The key skill is recognising deterioration and acting promptly rather than simply recording abnormal observations.
exam_trap: E, haloperidol for the confusion — tempting to settle agitation, but new confusion here may reflect sepsis or hypoperfusion and needs assessment, not sedation.
takeaway: Abnormal observations with new confusion: assess urgently and escalate.

stem:
A junior doctor notices that a prescribed medication appears unsafe because of a serious documented allergy. The prescription has not yet been administered.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Raise the concern promptly so the prescription is reviewed before use
options.B: Give the medication and observe the patient closely for any reaction
options.C: Leave it, as the senior prescriber will have considered the allergy
options.D: Mention it at the next ward round once the course has started
options.E: Cross out the prescription and give an alternative without discussion

correct_answer: A. Raise the concern promptly so the prescription is reviewed before use
why_correct: A doctor of any grade has a duty to act on patient-safety concerns, so the prescriber or a senior should be contacted promptly and the prescription stopped and reviewed before the drug is given (GMC Good Medical Practice).
why_wrong: B. Giving a drug to which the patient has a documented serious allergy risks anaphylaxis, and observation does not prevent harm. C. Seniority does not override the duty to raise a credible safety concern. D. Waiting until the course has started exposes the patient to avoidable harm. E. Changing a prescription without communication can cause confusion and errors; the concern must be discussed and documented.
pearl: Every doctor, whatever their grade, must act on a patient-safety concern; a drug conflicting with a documented serious allergy should be raised and reviewed before it is given.
thinking: Professional hierarchy does not remove the duty to act when there is a credible immediate patient-safety concern.
exam_trap: C, assuming the senior prescriber has considered the allergy — tempting out of deference, but seniority does not remove the duty to raise a credible safety concern.
takeaway: Spot a safety problem: raise it promptly, whatever your grade.

stem:
A 58-year-old patient presents with unilateral calf swelling and tenderness along the deep veins. There is no alternative diagnosis that is more likely than DVT.

Which clinical assessment should be used to help determine the probability of DVT?
why_correct: NICE NG158 recommends the 2-level DVT Wells score to estimate clinical probability of DVT and guide whether to proceed to proximal leg vein ultrasound or D-dimer testing.
why_wrong: A. The Glasgow Coma Scale assesses level of consciousness. B. CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation. D. The APGAR score assesses newborns immediately after birth. E. CURB-65 assesses the severity of community-acquired pneumonia.
pearl: The 2-level DVT Wells score estimates clinical probability and decides the next step: proximal leg vein ultrasound if DVT is likely, D-dimer first if it is unlikely.
thinking: The Wells score is used to estimate the clinical probability of DVT before further investigation.
exam_trap: B, CHA₂DS₂-VASc — tempting as a familiar cardiovascular score, but it estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation, not the probability of DVT.
takeaway: Suspected DVT: score with the 2-level Wells, then ultrasound or D-dimer.

stem:
A patient has symptoms suggestive of DVT, but their 2-level DVT Wells score indicates that DVT is unlikely.

Which investigation is generally used next?
why_correct: When the 2-level DVT Wells score indicates that DVT is unlikely, NICE NG158 recommends a D-dimer test; a negative result makes DVT unlikely, whereas a positive result should lead to proximal leg vein ultrasound.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury and does not help diagnose DVT. B. Echocardiography does not diagnose DVT. C. CT head has no role in investigating suspected DVT. E. Spirometry is unrelated to the investigation of DVT.
pearl: When DVT is unlikely on the Wells score, a negative D-dimer makes DVT unlikely, while a positive result needs proximal leg vein ultrasound.
thinking: Symptoms suggest DVT ↓ 2-level Wells score: DVT unlikely ↓ A negative test can help rule DVT out ↓ D-dimer
exam_trap: B, echocardiography — tempting as an imaging test linked to thrombosis, but it does not image the leg veins and cannot diagnose DVT.
takeaway: DVT unlikely: D-dimer first; DVT likely: ultrasound first.

stem:
A patient has a 2-level PE Wells score indicating that PE is likely.

What is the appropriate next diagnostic approach?

options.A: Immediate CTPA, with interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed
options.B: D-dimer first, then proceed to CTPA only if the D-dimer is positive
options.C: Outpatient CTPA within one week without anticoagulation
options.D: Lower-limb Doppler ultrasound as the first-line investigation for PE
options.E: Echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis before any imaging of the lungs

correct_answer: A. Immediate CTPA, with interim anticoagulation if imaging is delayed
why_correct: When PE is likely on the 2-level Wells score (more than 4 points), NICE NG158 recommends an immediate CTPA, with interim therapeutic anticoagulation if there is a delay in obtaining it, where appropriate. Source: NICE NG158 recommends immediate CTPA for PE likely, with interim therapeutic anticoagulation when appropriate while awaiting imaging.
why_wrong: B. In PE-likely patients, D-dimer is not sufficient to exclude PE, and imaging is required immediately. C. A delay of up to a week without anticoagulation is unsafe when PE is likely. D. Leg ultrasound is not the first-line test for suspected PE without signs of DVT. E. Echocardiography cannot confirm or exclude PE in a stable patient and should not delay CTPA.
pearl: When PE is likely on the 2-level Wells score, arrange immediate CTPA; if imaging is delayed, give interim therapeutic anticoagulation where appropriate.
thinking: Suspected PE ↓ 2-level Wells score: PE likely ↓ A D-dimer cannot safely exclude PE ↓ Immediate CTPA, with interim anticoagulation if delayed
exam_trap: B, D-dimer first — tempting as it features in PE pathways, but when PE is likely a negative D-dimer cannot exclude it, so imaging is needed.
takeaway: PE likely: immediate CTPA; PE unlikely: D-dimer first.

stem:
A patient has a PE Wells score of 3.

What is the appropriate next investigation?

options.C: Echocardiography as the first-line diagnostic test

why_correct: A 2-level PE Wells score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely, so NICE NG158 recommends a D-dimer test, with CTPA if the result is positive.
why_wrong: B. Thrombolysis is reserved for confirmed or strongly suspected PE with haemodynamic instability and is not a diagnostic step. C. Echocardiography is not the first-line diagnostic test for suspected PE in a stable patient. D. Colonoscopy is irrelevant to suspected PE. E. Lumbar puncture has no role in investigating PE.
pearl: A 2-level PE Wells score of 4 or less means PE is unlikely: do a D-dimer, and arrange CTPA only if it is positive.
thinking: For the 2-level PE Wells score, 4 points or less = PE unlikely.
exam_trap: C, echocardiography first — tempting as it can show right heart strain, but it is not the first-line diagnostic test for suspected PE in a stable patient.
takeaway: PE unlikely on Wells: D-dimer first, with CTPA if positive.

stem:
A patient with suspected PE has a positive D-dimer.

What does this result mean?

options.A: Thrombolysis should now be considered, as PE has become likely
options.B: Further assessment is needed following the diagnostic pathway
options.C: A DVT is present, and a leg ultrasound will confirm its exact site
options.D: PE is confirmed, and anticoagulation can start without imaging
options.E: PE can still be excluded if the Wells score is 4 points or fewer

correct_answer: B. Further assessment is needed following the diagnostic pathway
why_correct: D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific, so a positive result does not confirm PE; it means imaging, usually CTPA, is needed according to the NICE NG158 pathway.
why_wrong: A. Thrombolysis is only considered for confirmed high-risk PE with haemodynamic compromise, not because of a positive D-dimer. C. A positive D-dimer does not prove DVT or any other specific thrombotic condition. D. D-dimer can be raised by infection, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy and older age, so it cannot confirm PE. E. PE can be excluded on a low Wells score only when the D-dimer is negative; a positive result needs imaging.
pearl: D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific: a negative result helps exclude PE when probability is low, but a positive result only means imaging, usually CTPA, is needed.
thinking: D-dimer is useful primarily because a negative result can help exclude VTE in appropriately selected patients; a positive result is not diagnostic of PE.
exam_trap: D, PE confirmed so anticoagulate without imaging — tempting as the test is positive, but infection, surgery, malignancy, pregnancy and older age all raise D-dimer.
takeaway: A positive D-dimer does not diagnose PE; it triggers imaging.

stem:
A patient with suspected PE has severe renal impairment.

What should be considered when selecting imaging?

options.A: CTPA is mandatory in every patient regardless of renal function
options.B: Whether an alternative such as V/Q imaging is appropriate
options.D: No imaging can ever be performed
options.E: Echocardiography always replaces all other imaging

correct_answer: B. Whether an alternative such as V/Q imaging is appropriate
why_correct: Severe renal impairment increases the risk from iodinated contrast, so NICE NG158 advises considering V/Q SPECT or planar V/Q scanning instead of CTPA in such patients.
why_wrong: A. CTPA is not mandatory; alternatives are considered when contrast is a concern, such as in severe renal impairment. C. D-dimer is non-specific and cannot confirm PE. D. Imaging can still be performed, and V/Q scanning is one alternative. E. Echocardiography may support assessment in unstable patients but does not replace definitive imaging in all cases.
pearl: When contrast for CTPA is a concern, such as in severe renal impairment, consider V/Q scanning as the alternative imaging for suspected PE.
thinking: Suspected PE ↓ Severe renal impairment ↓ Iodinated contrast for CTPA carries renal risk ↓ Consider whether V/Q imaging is appropriate
exam_trap: A, CTPA mandatory regardless of renal function — tempting as CTPA is the usual first-line test, but alternatives should be considered when contrast poses a significant risk.
takeaway: Suspected PE with severe renal impairment: consider V/Q scanning.

stem:
A patient with confirmed PE becomes profoundly hypotensive and shocked.

What is the key clinical issue?

options.A: Shock is unlikely to be due to the PE, so look for sepsis as the likely cause
options.B: Give a rapid 2-litre crystalloid bolus to correct the hypotension first
options.C: Continue anticoagulation and transfer to a general ward bed for observation
options.D: High-risk PE: urgent specialist input and consider reperfusion therapy
options.E: Repeat CTPA to confirm the diagnosis before starting any further treatment

correct_answer: D. High-risk PE: urgent specialist input and consider reperfusion therapy
why_correct: PE with shock or sustained hypotension is high-risk (massive) PE with a high mortality, needing urgent resuscitation and senior or specialist input, and reperfusion therapy (usually systemic thrombolysis) should be considered (NICE NG158).
why_wrong: A. Large PE can cause right ventricular failure and obstructive shock. B. Large fluid boluses can worsen right ventricular failure in massive PE; cautious fluid and urgent specialist care are needed. C. A shocked patient with confirmed PE is critically ill and needs urgent escalation, not ward observation. E. Repeating imaging in confirmed PE delays urgent treatment.
pearl: PE with shock or sustained hypotension is high-risk (massive) PE: resuscitate, get urgent senior or specialist input and consider reperfusion, usually systemic thrombolysis.
thinking: Confirmed PE ↓ Profound hypotension and shock ↓ Right ventricular failure with high mortality ↓ High-risk PE: urgent specialist input and consider reperfusion
exam_trap: B, a rapid 2-litre crystalloid bolus — tempting as standard shock treatment, but large fluid volumes can worsen right ventricular failure in massive PE.
takeaway: PE with shock is high-risk PE: escalate and consider thrombolysis.

stem:
A hospitalised patient has a significant rise in serum creatinine from their previous baseline.

What should this prompt?

options.C: Automatic diagnosis of chronic kidney disease
options.D: No action if the patient feels well
options.E: Assessment for acute kidney injury and its cause

correct_answer: E. Assessment for acute kidney injury and its cause
why_correct: A significant rise in serum creatinine from baseline meets KDIGO/NICE criteria for acute kidney injury and should prompt assessment of volume status, medication review, urinalysis and a search for pre-renal, renal or post-renal causes (NICE NG148).
why_wrong: A. A creatinine rise does not diagnose UTI. B. Nephrotic syndrome requires heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, and is not diagnosed from a creatinine rise alone. C. CKD requires reduced kidney function for at least 3 months and cannot be diagnosed from an acute rise. D. AKI may be asymptomatic but still needs assessment because it is associated with significant harm.
pearl: A significant creatinine rise from baseline signals AKI: assess volume status, review medicines, test the urine and look for pre-renal, renal and post-renal causes.
thinking: Hospitalised patient ↓ Significant creatinine rise from baseline ↓ Meets criteria for acute kidney injury ↓ Assess for AKI and its cause
exam_trap: C, chronic kidney disease — tempting as creatinine is raised, but CKD requires reduced function persisting for months, not an acute rise.
takeaway: Creatinine rising from baseline: think AKI and look for the cause.

stem:
An elderly patient develops AKI after several days of vomiting and diarrhoea.

What cause should be considered?

options.A: Hyperthyroidism causing increased renal blood flow
options.D: Iron-deficiency anaemia reducing renal oxygen delivery

correct_answer: E. Hypovolaemia causing reduced renal perfusion
why_correct: Prolonged vomiting and diarrhoea cause fluid loss and hypovolaemia, reducing renal perfusion and causing pre-renal AKI, particularly in older people.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism is not a typical cause of AKI after gastrointestinal fluid loss. B. Post-infectious glomerulonephritis does not follow gastrointestinal fluid loss and is not suggested by this history. C. Polycystic kidney disease causes chronic, not acute, renal impairment and does not explain this history. D. Iron deficiency does not cause AKI.
pearl: Gastrointestinal fluid loss is a classic cause of pre-renal AKI, particularly in older people, as reduced circulating volume lowers renal perfusion.
thinking: Elderly patient ↓ Several days of vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ Fluid loss reduces renal perfusion ↓ Hypovolaemia causing pre-renal AKI
exam_trap: B, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis — tempting as an infection-related cause of AKI, but it follows streptococcal infection, not gastrointestinal fluid loss.
takeaway: AKI after vomiting and diarrhoea: think hypovolaemia first.

stem:
A patient with AKI is taking an ACE inhibitor, NSAID and diuretic.

What is an important immediate consideration?

options.A: Continue all three, as stopping the ACE inhibitor causes rebound hypertension
options.B: Replace the NSAID with a different NSAID that is less nephrotoxic
options.C: Review nephrotoxic and haemodynamically relevant drugs and withhold if needed
options.D: Stop only the diuretic, continuing the ACE inhibitor and the NSAID
options.E: Stop all regular medicines permanently, including those for other conditions

correct_answer: C. Review nephrotoxic and haemodynamically relevant drugs and withhold if needed
why_correct: In AKI, medicines that impair renal perfusion or are nephrotoxic, such as ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and diuretics, should be reviewed and usually withheld temporarily, with other drug doses adjusted for renal function (NICE NG148).
why_wrong: A. Continuing these drugs would worsen renal perfusion and kidney injury. B. All NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and should be avoided in AKI. D. The ACE inhibitor and NSAID also impair renal perfusion and should be reviewed and usually withheld. E. Medicines should be reviewed individually, with essential drugs continued or restarted when appropriate, rather than all being stopped permanently.
pearl: In AKI, review and usually withhold drugs that reduce renal perfusion or are nephrotoxic, such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics, and adjust renally cleared doses.
thinking: AKI ↓ ACE inhibitor, NSAID and diuretic all impair renal perfusion ↓ Continuing them worsens the injury ↓ Review these drugs and withhold if needed
exam_trap: D, stopping only the diuretic — tempting as it addresses volume loss, but the ACE inhibitor and NSAID also impair renal perfusion and need review.
takeaway: AKI: review the drug chart and pause the nephrotoxic culprits.

stem:
A patient has suspected urinary tract obstruction causing AKI.

What is an important management principle?

options.A: Treat with IV fluids alone and monitor the creatinine
options.B: Give regular NSAIDs to relieve the associated pain
options.C: Promptly identify and relieve significant obstruction
options.D: Wait for renal function to recover before imaging the tract
options.E: Restrict fluids to 1 litre daily regardless of volume status

correct_answer: C. Promptly identify and relieve significant obstruction
why_correct: Post-renal AKI from urinary tract obstruction needs prompt relief, for example by urinary catheterisation or nephrostomy, to prevent ongoing kidney damage, with urgent urology referral where appropriate (NICE NG148).
why_wrong: A. Fluids alone ignore the cause; management must address the obstruction. B. NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and should be avoided in AKI. D. Renal function will not recover until the obstruction is relieved. E. Fluid management should be based on volume status, and post-obstructive diuresis may require fluid replacement.
pearl: Post-renal AKI recovers only when the obstruction is relieved, for example by catheter or nephrostomy; watch for post-obstructive diuresis afterwards.
thinking: AKI ↓ Suspected urinary tract obstruction ↓ Ongoing obstruction keeps damaging the kidneys ↓ Promptly identify and relieve the obstruction
exam_trap: A, IV fluids alone — tempting as fluids are often part of AKI care, but they do not address the obstruction causing the injury.
takeaway: Obstructive AKI: find and relieve the obstruction promptly.

stem:
A patient has persistently reduced kidney function over many months.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Reduced kidney function persisting for more than 3 months indicates chronic kidney disease, which is then staged by eGFR and albumin:creatinine ratio (NICE NG203).
why_wrong: A. PE does not explain persistently reduced kidney function over many months. B. Acute meningitis does not cause persistently reduced renal function. C. Acute appendicitis is an acute abdominal condition and does not explain persistently reduced kidney function. E. Recurrent hypoglycaemia is an acute metabolic disturbance and is not a cause of long-term renal impairment.
pearl: Chronic kidney disease means reduced kidney function persisting for more than 3 months; it is classified using both eGFR and the urine albumin:creatinine ratio.
thinking: The distinction between acute and chronic renal impairment depends on the time course and previous results, not simply on one abnormal creatinine.
exam_trap: E, recurrent hypoglycaemic episodes — tempting as hypoglycaemia can occur alongside CKD, but it is not a cause of persistently reduced kidney function.
takeaway: Reduced kidney function lasting over 3 months is chronic kidney disease.

stem:
A 67-year-old patient has visible painless haematuria.

What is an important consideration?
why_correct: Visible haematuria in an older adult raises concern for urological cancer, particularly bladder or kidney cancer, and NICE NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for people aged 45 and over with unexplained visible haematuria (or haematuria that persists or recurs after successful UTI treatment).
why_wrong: A. Dehydration does not cause visible haematuria, and attributing it to dehydration risks missing malignancy. C. Otitis media does not cause haematuria. D. Asthma does not cause haematuria. E. Migraine does not cause haematuria.
pearl: Unexplained visible haematuria in an adult of this age warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral to look for urological cancer, particularly bladder or kidney cancer.
thinking: Visible unexplained haematuria, particularly in an older adult, warrants appropriate investigation rather than being assumed to be a simple UTI.
exam_trap: A, simple dehydration — tempting as a benign explanation, but dehydration does not cause visible haematuria, and this label risks missing a urological cancer.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult is cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with sepsis has an infected obstructed urinary system.

Which principle is particularly important?

options.A: Antibiotics alone, with drainage only if blood cultures are positive
options.B: Source control as well as antimicrobial and supportive treatment
options.C: Delay drainage until the patient has been afebrile for at least 48 hours
options.D: Treat the fever with paracetamol and await the culture results
options.E: Oral antibiotics and outpatient urology clinic follow-up in two weeks

correct_answer: B. Source control as well as antimicrobial and supportive treatment
why_correct: An infected, obstructed urinary system is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression (for example, nephrostomy or ureteric stent) in addition to sepsis care with prompt antibiotics and supportive treatment.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics alone may not control infection behind an obstruction, so drainage is needed regardless of culture results. C. An infected obstructed system needs urgent decompression; delaying drainage risks worsening sepsis. D. Treating fever alone ignores the source, and treatment must not wait for cultures. E. Septic patients need urgent IV antibiotics and drainage, not oral treatment and outpatient follow-up.
pearl: An infected, obstructed urinary system is a urological emergency: give antibiotics and supportive care, and decompress urgently by nephrostomy or ureteric stent.
thinking: Sepsis ↓ Infected urinary system ↓ Obstruction traps infection behind it ↓ Source control as well as antimicrobial and supportive treatment
exam_trap: A, antibiotics alone with drainage only if cultures are positive — tempting as antibiotics treat infection, but they cannot clear infection trapped behind an obstruction.
takeaway: Infection plus urinary obstruction: antibiotics are not enough; drain it urgently.

stem:
A patient presents with acute central chest pain.

Which investigation should be obtained promptly as part of the initial assessment?

options.E: Urine pregnancy test as the only investigation

why_correct: A 12-lead ECG should be recorded promptly, ideally within 10 minutes of arrival, in anyone with acute chest pain to identify STEMI and other acute coronary syndromes that need immediate treatment (NICE CG95).
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy has no role in the assessment of acute chest pain. B. Spirometry is not part of the initial assessment of acute chest pain. D. CT abdomen is not routinely indicated for acute chest pain. E. A pregnancy test may be relevant in some women but cannot be the only investigation for chest pain.
pearl: Record a 12-lead ECG promptly in anyone with acute chest pain, ideally within minutes of arrival, to identify STEMI and other acute coronary syndromes needing immediate treatment.
thinking: Acute central chest pain ↓ Possible acute coronary syndrome ↓ STEMI needs immediate recognition ↓ 12-lead ECG
exam_trap: E, urine pregnancy test as the only investigation — tempting as it is relevant in some patients, but it can never replace an ECG in acute chest pain.
takeaway: Acute chest pain: record a 12-lead ECG within minutes.

stem:
A patient develops sudden severe chest pain described as tearing and radiating to the back, with unequal blood pressures between the arms.

What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back with unequal blood pressures between the arms is classic for acute aortic dissection, a surgical emergency.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis causes pleuritic, positional pain and does not cause unequal arm blood pressures. B. Oesophageal spasm does not cause tearing pain with a difference in arm blood pressures. D. Stable angina causes predictable exertional chest pain and does not cause tearing pain or a difference in arm blood pressures. E. Musculoskeletal pain does not cause a difference in arm blood pressures.
pearl: Sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back with unequal arm blood pressures is aortic dissection until proven otherwise; image urgently, usually with CT angiography.
thinking: Sudden severe tearing chest pain ↓ Radiates to the back ↓ Unequal blood pressures between the arms ↓ Acute aortic dissection
exam_trap: A, acute pericarditis — tempting as it causes severe chest pain, but it is pleuritic and positional and does not cause unequal arm blood pressures.
takeaway: Tearing pain to the back plus unequal arm pressures: think aortic dissection.

stem:
A patient has features strongly suggesting acute aortic dissection.

What is an important principle?

options.A: Give aspirin 300 mg, as ACS is far more common than aortic dissection
options.B: Give thrombolysis if the ECG shows new ST-segment elevation in two leads
options.C: Start treatment-dose low-molecular-weight heparin while awaiting the CT
options.D: Avoid anticoagulation for presumed ACS until dissection is excluded
options.E: Discharge with oral analgesia and arrange outpatient echocardiography

correct_answer: D. Avoid anticoagulation for presumed ACS until dissection is excluded
why_correct: Antiplatelets, anticoagulants and thrombolysis can be catastrophic in aortic dissection, so dissection must be actively considered and imaged, usually with CT angiography, before treating presumed ACS.
why_wrong: A. Antiplatelets can be catastrophic in aortic dissection and should not be given when it is strongly suspected. B. Thrombolysis is contraindicated in suspected aortic dissection, which can itself cause ST elevation. C. Anticoagulation is dangerous in suspected aortic dissection. E. Suspected aortic dissection is an emergency and requires urgent investigation and specialist care.
pearl: Antiplatelets, anticoagulants and thrombolysis can be catastrophic in aortic dissection, which can itself cause ST elevation, so exclude dissection before treating presumed ACS.
thinking: Features strongly suggest aortic dissection ↓ Antithrombotic drugs can worsen bleeding from the torn aorta ↓ Dissection must be excluded first ↓ Avoid anticoagulation for presumed ACS
exam_trap: B, thrombolysis for new ST elevation — tempting as it is a STEMI treatment, but dissection can cause ST elevation and thrombolysis is contraindicated.
takeaway: Suspected dissection: no antiplatelets, anticoagulants or thrombolysis until excluded.

stem:
A patient with acute pulmonary oedema is severely breathless and hypoxaemic.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give an IV fluid bolus to support the blood pressure and perfusion
options.B: Await BNP and echocardiography results before starting treatment
options.C: Give oral furosemide and arrange review in the heart failure clinic
options.D: Urgent assessment and treatment, including oxygen or ventilation
options.E: Arrange outpatient echocardiography and start an ACE inhibitor

correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment and treatment, including oxygen or ventilation
why_correct: Acute pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia is life-threatening and needs urgent assessment and treatment, including oxygen titrated to target and consideration of non-invasive ventilation, with treatment of the underlying cause (NICE CG187).
why_wrong: A. IV fluid would worsen pulmonary oedema. B. Treatment should not wait for BNP or echocardiography. C. A severely breathless, hypoxaemic patient needs urgent inpatient treatment, not oral therapy and clinic review. E. Outpatient investigation would delay treatment of an acute emergency.
pearl: Acute pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia is life-threatening: sit the patient up, titrate oxygen, consider non-invasive ventilation and treat the underlying cause without waiting for tests.
thinking: Acute pulmonary oedema ↓ Severe breathlessness and hypoxaemia ↓ Life-threatening respiratory failure ↓ Urgent assessment and treatment, including oxygen or ventilation
exam_trap: A, an IV fluid bolus — tempting if blood pressure seems low, but extra fluid worsens pulmonary oedema and hypoxaemia.
takeaway: Acute pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia: treat now; do not wait for tests.

stem:
A patient presents with symptoms that do not clearly fit a single diagnosis. There is no immediate evidence of life-threatening illness.

What is the safest approach?

options.A: Consider differentials and red flags, investigate appropriately and safety-net
options.B: Avoid mentioning the uncertainty, to prevent unnecessary anxiety for the patient
options.C: Settle on the single most likely diagnosis and treat without any further review
options.D: Reassure the patient that serious illness is excluded, as there are no red flags
options.E: Order a broad panel of investigations to exclude all possible causes at this visit

correct_answer: A. Consider differentials and red flags, investigate appropriately and safety-net
why_correct: Managing diagnostic uncertainty safely means considering important differentials, actively seeking red flags, investigating proportionately and giving clear safety-netting advice about what to do if symptoms change or worsen.
why_wrong: B. Patients should be told about uncertainty so that they understand the plan and know when to seek help. C. Premature closure on one diagnosis is a common cause of diagnostic error. D. Serious illness has not been excluded, so this reassurance is unsafe. E. Indiscriminate investigation is wasteful, may cause harm and can produce misleading incidental findings.
pearl: Diagnostic uncertainty is safe when managed: consider important differentials, seek red flags, investigate proportionately and give clear safety-netting advice.
thinking: Managing uncertainty is an explicit theme of the MLA alongside readiness for safe practice and person-centred care.
exam_trap: D, reassuring that serious illness is excluded — tempting as there are no red flags now, but their absence today does not exclude serious disease developing.
takeaway: Uncertain diagnosis: differentials, red flags, proportionate tests and safety-netting.

stem:
A patient with melaena is haemodynamically stable after initial assessment.

Which score is commonly used to assess the risk of adverse outcomes in upper GI bleeding?
why_correct: The Glasgow-Blatchford score assesses risk at first presentation in upper GI bleeding, using urea, haemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, pulse and other clinical features, and helps identify very-low-risk patients (NICE CG141).
why_wrong: A. GCS assesses consciousness level and is not a GI bleeding risk score. B. The Wells score assesses the probability of DVT or PE. D. CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation. E. CURB-65 assesses pneumonia severity.
pearl: The Glasgow-Blatchford score is used at first assessment of upper GI bleeding and helps identify very-low-risk patients who may be suitable for early discharge.
thinking: Black, tarry stools: melaena ↓ Upper GI bleeding ↓ Risk must be stratified at first presentation ↓ Glasgow-Blatchford score
exam_trap: A, Glasgow Coma Scale — tempting because of the shared 'Glasgow' name, but GCS measures consciousness level, not bleeding risk.
takeaway: Upper GI bleed at first presentation: risk-assess with the Glasgow-Blatchford score.

stem:
A patient reports passing black, tarry, offensive stools and feels light-headed.

Which source should be considered?
why_correct: Black, tarry, offensive stools (melaena) usually result from upper GI bleeding because blood is digested as it passes through the gut, and light-headedness suggests significant blood loss.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids typically cause bright red rectal bleeding, not melaena. B. Acute cystitis causes urinary symptoms, not melaena. D. Renal colic causes loin pain and haematuria, not melaena. E. Diverticular bleeding usually causes fresh or maroon rectal bleeding rather than melaena.
pearl: Melaena is black, tarry, offensive stool from blood digested in the gut, usually from an upper GI source; light-headedness suggests significant blood loss.
thinking: Black, tarry, offensive stools ↓ Melaena: digested blood ↓ Usually from the upper gastrointestinal tract ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: E, diverticular bleeding — tempting as a common cause of GI bleeding, but it usually produces fresh or maroon blood rather than melaena.
takeaway: Melaena points to upper GI bleeding; fresh red blood usually points lower.

stem: Which description is most characteristic of haematemesis?

options.A: Fresh blood passed with the urine on voiding
options.B: Black, tarry, offensive stools passed per rectum
options.C: Bright-red blood on the toilet paper after stool
options.D: Coughing up bright red blood-streaked sputum

correct_answer: E. Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material
why_correct: Haematemesis is vomiting of fresh blood or altered, coffee-ground material, indicating bleeding from the upper GI tract.
why_wrong: A. Blood in the urine is haematuria, not haematemesis. B. Black, tarry stools are melaena, not haematemesis. C. Bright red blood on toilet paper suggests anorectal bleeding, such as from haemorrhoids. D. Coughing up blood-streaked sputum is haemoptysis, not haematemesis.
pearl: Haematemesis is vomiting of fresh blood or coffee-ground material; coughed-up blood is haemoptysis and black tarry stool is melaena.
thinking: Haemat- means blood ↓ -emesis means vomiting ↓ Blood may be fresh or altered by gastric acid ↓ Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material
exam_trap: D, coughing up blood-streaked sputum — tempting as both bring blood from the mouth, but coughed-up blood is haemoptysis, not haematemesis.
takeaway: Vomited blood is haematemesis; coughed-up blood is haemoptysis.

stem:
A patient has acute pancreatitis with no history of alcohol excess.

Which cause should be actively considered?
why_correct: Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis in the UK and should be sought, usually with abdominal ultrasound, when alcohol excess is absent.
why_wrong: A. Otitis media is not a cause of acute pancreatitis. B. Asthma does not cause pancreatitis. C. Iron deficiency does not cause pancreatitis. D. Migraine does not cause pancreatitis.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol are the two commonest causes of acute pancreatitis; look for gallstones with abdominal ultrasound, especially when alcohol is not implicated.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ No history of alcohol excess ↓ Gallstones are the commonest cause in the UK ↓ Gallstones
exam_trap: C, iron deficiency — tempting only as a common incidental finding, but it has no causal link with acute pancreatitis.
takeaway: Pancreatitis without alcohol excess: look for gallstones.

stem:
A patient with suspected acute cholangitis is septic.

Which management principle is important?

options.A: Antibiotics with elective cholecystectomy after six weeks
options.B: IV fluids and analgesia, withholding antibiotics until imaging
options.C: Urgent antibiotics and assessment for biliary drainage
options.D: Oral antibiotics and outpatient MRCP within six weeks
options.E: Urgent cholecystectomy within 24 hours for source control

correct_answer: C. Urgent antibiotics and assessment for biliary drainage
why_correct: Acute cholangitis with sepsis needs urgent broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation, with prompt assessment for biliary drainage (usually ERCP) to relieve the obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Septic cholangitis needs urgent biliary drainage, not elective surgery alone. B. Antibiotics must not be delayed in sepsis. D. Oral antibiotics and outpatient imaging are inadequate for biliary sepsis. E. Source control in cholangitis is biliary drainage, usually by ERCP, not urgent cholecystectomy.
pearl: Septic cholangitis needs urgent antibiotics and resuscitation plus prompt biliary drainage, usually by ERCP, to relieve the obstructed, infected bile duct.
thinking: Suspected acute cholangitis ↓ Patient is septic ↓ Infected, obstructed bile duct needs source control ↓ Urgent antibiotics and assessment for biliary drainage
exam_trap: E, urgent cholecystectomy — tempting as gallstone-related source control, but source control in cholangitis is drainage of the obstructed bile duct, usually by ERCP.
takeaway: Septic cholangitis: antibiotics now and urgent biliary drainage.

stem:
A patient is being investigated for possible coeliac disease.

Which principle is important when testing?

options.A: Stop gluten for 6 weeks before serology to reduce symptoms
options.B: Arrange duodenal biopsy only if the serology is negative
options.C: Test for IgA tTG only after a gluten-free diet has been started
options.D: Keep eating gluten in more than one meal daily before testing
options.E: Iron deficiency explains the symptoms, so testing is not needed

correct_answer: D. Keep eating gluten in more than one meal daily before testing
why_correct: Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy are only reliable while the patient is eating gluten, so NICE NG20 advises eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing.
why_wrong: A. Excluding gluten before testing can cause false-negative serology and biopsy results. B. Positive serology is the usual indication for referral for biopsy; negative serology with no ongoing concern does not mandate biopsy. C. Testing after starting a gluten-free diet can give false-negative results. E. Iron-deficiency anaemia is an indication to test for coeliac disease, not a reason to avoid testing.
pearl: Coeliac serology and biopsy are only reliable on a gluten-containing diet, so advise eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing.
thinking: Possible coeliac disease ↓ Tests detect the immune response to gluten ↓ Avoiding gluten causes false-negative results ↓ Keep eating gluten before testing
exam_trap: A, stopping gluten before serology — tempting as it eases symptoms, but excluding gluten causes false-negative serology and biopsy results.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease while the patient is still eating gluten.

stem:
A young adult has chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss and intermittent rectal bleeding.

Which broad diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss and rectal bleeding in a young adult suggest inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis), and faecal calprotectin and specialist referral are appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Weight loss and rectal bleeding are red flags that are not explained by irritable bowel syndrome. C. The symptoms are chronic and include weight loss, so an acute infection does not explain them. D. Pancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhoea and weight loss but does not cause rectal bleeding. E. Thyrotoxicosis can cause frequent stools and weight loss but does not cause rectal bleeding.
pearl: Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss and rectal bleeding in a young adult suggests IBD; faecal calprotectin helps distinguish it from IBS, and specialist referral is needed.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Chronic diarrhoea and abdominal pain ↓ Weight loss and rectal bleeding are red flags ↓ Inflammatory bowel disease
exam_trap: A, irritable bowel syndrome — tempting as a common cause of chronic diarrhoea and pain in young adults, but weight loss and rectal bleeding are not explained by IBS.
takeaway: Chronic diarrhoea with bleeding and weight loss is not IBS: think IBD.

stem:
A patient is suspected of having C. difficile infection in hospital.

Which principle is important?

options.A: Prompt isolation and contact precautions with assessment and treatment
options.B: Isolate the patient only once stool testing has confirmed toxin production
options.C: Use alcohol hand gel before and after every single contact with the patient
options.D: Cohort with other patients who have diarrhoea in a shared bay and toilet
options.E: Continue the current broad-spectrum antibiotics to complete the planned course

correct_answer: A. Prompt isolation and contact precautions with assessment and treatment
why_correct: Suspected C. difficile infection requires prompt isolation, contact precautions and handwashing with soap and water (alcohol gel does not kill spores), alongside stool testing, review of antibiotics and acid suppression, and treatment in line with NICE NG199.
why_wrong: B. Isolation should start promptly when C. difficile is suspected, not wait for results. C. Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores; hands should be washed with soap and water. D. Sharing facilities with other patients with diarrhoea risks spreading spores; isolation with a dedicated toilet is needed. E. Unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics should be stopped where possible because they drive C. difficile infection.
pearl: Suspected C. difficile: isolate promptly with contact precautions, wash hands with soap and water because alcohol gel does not kill spores, and review antibiotics and acid suppression.
thinking: Hospital diarrhoea with suspected C. difficile ↓ Spores spread easily by contact ↓ Waiting for results allows transmission ↓ Prompt isolation and contact precautions, with assessment and treatment
exam_trap: C, alcohol hand gel at every contact — tempting as routine hand hygiene, but alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water is needed.
takeaway: Suspected C. difficile: isolate now and wash with soap and water, not gel.

stem:
A 66-year-old man has newly diagnosed iron-deficiency anaemia without an obvious explanation.

What should be considered?

options.A: Oral iron for three months, investigating only if there is no response
options.B: Check B12 and folate levels and treat any deficiency that is found
options.C: Investigation for a source, including gastrointestinal blood loss
options.D: Reassurance with a repeat full blood count in primary care in one year
options.E: Coeliac serology alone, as this is the commonest cause in older men

correct_answer: C. Investigation for a source, including gastrointestinal blood loss
why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in a man aged 60 or over can be a sign of colorectal or upper GI cancer, so the source must be investigated, including suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12).
why_wrong: A. Iron replacement without looking for the cause may mask an underlying malignancy. B. B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytic anaemia and do not explain iron deficiency. D. Iron-deficiency anaemia is not part of normal ageing and needs investigating now. E. Coeliac testing is reasonable, but unexplained iron deficiency in a man of this age needs investigation for GI cancer.
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult is a red flag for GI cancer; investigate the source, including suspected cancer pathway referral, rather than simply replacing iron.
thinking: 66-year-old man ↓ New iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ No obvious explanation; GI blood loss or cancer possible ↓ Investigate for a source, including GI blood loss
exam_trap: A, oral iron with investigation only if there is no response — tempting as it treats the anaemia, but correcting iron can mask an underlying malignancy.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult: investigate the GI tract.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy develops fever and is found to have severe neutropenia.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Oral antibiotics at home with review in the oncology clinic within 48 hours
options.B: Give G-CSF and withhold antibiotics until the blood cultures are positive
options.C: Repeat the neutrophil count in 24 hours before deciding on any treatment
options.D: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics once blood culture results are available
options.E: Treat as neutropenic sepsis, with urgent assessment and IV antibiotics

correct_answer: E. Treat as neutropenic sepsis, with urgent assessment and IV antibiotics
why_correct: Fever in a patient with chemotherapy-related neutropenia should be treated as suspected neutropenic sepsis, a medical emergency requiring immediate assessment and empirical intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour (NICE CG151).
why_wrong: A. Suspected neutropenic sepsis needs immediate hospital assessment and IV antibiotics, not delayed outpatient review. B.
