A newly diagnosed patient with type 2 diabetes asks why treatment decisions are not based solely on HbA1c.

What is an important principle of current management?

options.A: Choose drugs by HbA1c and add cardiorenal agents once the target is met
options.B: Base treatment on HbA1c, reserving kidney checks for those with symptoms
options.C: Consider cardiovascular, renal, weight and glycaemic factors together
options.D: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor once HbA1c exceeds 75 mmol/mol
options.E: Prioritise weight loss and delay drug treatment until BMI is below 30

correct_answer: C. Consider cardiovascular, renal, weight and glycaemic factors together
why_correct: NICE NG28 recommends individualised type 2 diabetes management that considers cardiovascular and renal risk, weight and glycaemic control together, for example using SGLT2 inhibitors for cardiorenal protection where indicated. Source: NICE NG28's 2026 medicines update emphasises holistic management including cardiovascular and renal risk reduction, weight management and glycaemic control.
why_wrong: A. NICE recommends considering cardiorenal protection, for example with an SGLT2 inhibitor, from the outset where indicated, not after glycaemic targets are met. B. Kidney function should be checked routinely because it influences drug choice, dosing and cardiorenal protection. D. Indications for SGLT2 inhibitors include cardiovascular disease, heart failure and CKD, independent of a particular HbA1c threshold. E. Weight management is important, but drug treatment should not be delayed until a BMI target is reached.
pearl: Type 2 diabetes management is individualised: cardiovascular and renal risk, heart failure, weight and glycaemic control all shape drug choice, not HbA1c alone.
thinking: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes ↓ Outcomes depend on cardiovascular and renal risk as well as glucose ↓ Some drugs offer cardiorenal protection ↓ Consider cardiovascular, renal, weight and glycaemic factors together
exam_trap: A, choosing drugs by HbA1c and adding cardiorenal agents later — traditional glucose-first thinking, but cardiorenal protection should be considered from the outset where indicated.
takeaway: Type 2 diabetes drug choice is guided by cardiorenal risk and weight, not HbA1c alone.

stem:
A patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor becomes acutely unwell with vomiting and poor oral intake.

What should be considered?

options.A: Temporarily stop it during the acute illness (sick-day rules)
options.B: Continue it at the usual dose to prevent stress hyperglycaemia
options.C: Double the dose because acute illness raises blood glucose
options.D: Continue it and add a sulfonylurea while the patient is unwell
options.E: Switch it to modified-release metformin for the illness

correct_answer: A. Temporarily stop it during the acute illness (sick-day rules)
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors carry a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, which can occur with near-normal glucose, during acute illness and dehydration, so 'sick day' guidance is to stop them temporarily and restart once eating and drinking normally.
why_wrong: B. Continuing an SGLT2 inhibitor during dehydration and poor intake risks ketoacidosis, which can occur with near-normal glucose. C. Increasing the dose raises the risk of ketoacidosis and volume depletion. D. Continuing the SGLT2 inhibitor keeps the DKA risk, and adding a sulfonylurea with poor intake risks hypoglycaemia. E. Metformin is also withheld during dehydrating illness because of the risk of AKI and lactic acidosis.
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors should be paused during acute illness with vomiting or poor intake because of the risk of ketoacidosis, which can occur with near-normal glucose; restart once eating and drinking.
thinking: Taking an SGLT2 inhibitor ↓ Acute illness with vomiting and poor oral intake ↓ Risk of ketoacidosis, even with near-normal glucose ↓ Temporarily stop it (sick-day rules)
exam_trap: B, continuing to prevent stress hyperglycaemia — glucose control seems important when unwell, but continuing risks ketoacidosis and volume depletion.
takeaway: SGLT2 inhibitor with vomiting or poor intake: stop temporarily, restart when eating and drinking.

stem:
A conscious patient with diabetes is sweaty, shaky and confused. Capillary glucose is 2.7 mmol/L.

What is the immediate management principle?

options.A: Give IM glucagon 1 mg before trying oral treatment
options.B: Give a slice of toast and recheck capillary glucose in one hour
options.C: Give 75 mL of 20% glucose intravenously as first-line treatment
options.D: Omit the next insulin dose and recheck glucose in 30 minutes
options.E: Give fast-acting carbohydrate orally if able to swallow safely

correct_answer: E. Give fast-acting carbohydrate orally if able to swallow safely
why_correct: A conscious patient with hypoglycaemia who can swallow safely should be given fast-acting carbohydrate (e.g. 15–20 g of glucose), then have glucose rechecked after 10–15 minutes, following JBDS guidance.
why_wrong: A. IM glucagon is for patients who cannot take oral treatment; a conscious patient who can swallow should have oral fast-acting carbohydrate first. B. Toast is a slower-acting carbohydrate that should follow, not replace, fast-acting treatment, and glucose should be rechecked after 10–15 minutes. C. IV glucose is reserved for patients who cannot swallow safely or are unconscious. D. Omitting insulin does not treat the current hypoglycaemia, which needs immediate carbohydrate.
pearl: A conscious hypoglycaemic patient who can swallow safely needs fast-acting oral carbohydrate first, a recheck after 10–15 minutes, then a longer-acting carbohydrate once recovered.
thinking: Diabetes with sweating, shaking and confusion ↓ Low capillary glucose confirms hypoglycaemia ↓ Conscious and able to swallow ↓ Fast-acting oral carbohydrate
exam_trap: A, IM glucagon first — it treats hypoglycaemia, but it is for patients who cannot take oral treatment; a patient who can swallow safely should have oral fast-acting carbohydrate.
takeaway: Hypoglycaemia in a patient able to swallow: fast-acting oral carbohydrate first, then recheck.

stem:
A patient has fatigue, weight gain, constipation and cold intolerance.

Which thyroid function pattern is most consistent with primary hypothyroidism?

options.A: High TSH with low free T4
options.B: Low TSH with high free T4
options.C: Low TSH with low free T4 in every case
options.D: Normal TSH with markedly high free T4
options.E: High TSH with high free T4

correct_answer: A. High TSH with low free T4
why_correct: In primary hypothyroidism the failing thyroid produces less T4, so the pituitary increases TSH secretion, giving a high TSH with low free T4.
why_wrong: B. Low TSH with high free T4 is the pattern of primary hyperthyroidism. C. Low TSH with low free T4 suggests secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism or non-thyroidal illness, not primary hypothyroidism. D. Normal TSH with markedly high free T4 is not the expected pattern and suggests assay interference or rare disorders. E. High TSH with high free T4 suggests rare causes such as a TSH-secreting adenoma or thyroid hormone resistance, or assay interference.
pearl: In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid fails and the pituitary responds, so TSH is high and free T4 low; a low TSH with low free T4 points instead to pituitary disease or non-thyroidal illness.
thinking: Fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance ↓ Clinical hypothyroidism ↓ Primary thyroid failure removes negative feedback ↓ High TSH with low free T4
exam_trap: C, low TSH with low free T4 — both values look underactive, but this pattern suggests secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism or non-thyroidal illness, not primary disease.
takeaway: Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH with low free T4.

stem:
A patient has weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor and palpitations.

Which thyroid function pattern is most consistent with primary hyperthyroidism?

options.A: High TSH with low free T4
options.B: High TSH with low free T3
options.C: Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
options.D: High TSH with high free T4 as the usual pattern
options.E: Normal thyroid function tests in every case

correct_answer: C. Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
why_correct: In primary hyperthyroidism excess thyroid hormone suppresses pituitary TSH, giving a low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3 (T3 toxicosis may show raised T3 only).
why_wrong: A. High TSH with low free T4 indicates primary hypothyroidism. B. High TSH with low free T3 is a hypothyroid pattern. D. High TSH with high free T4 suggests rare causes such as a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, not primary hyperthyroidism. E. Clinical hyperthyroidism is accompanied by abnormal thyroid function tests.
pearl: In primary hyperthyroidism excess thyroid hormone suppresses TSH, giving a low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3; T3 toxicosis may show a raised T3 only.
thinking: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations ↓ Clinical hyperthyroidism ↓ Excess hormone suppresses pituitary TSH ↓ Low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3
exam_trap: D, high TSH with high free T4 — high hormone levels seem to fit, but a high TSH alongside them suggests a rare TSH-secreting adenoma, not primary hyperthyroidism.
takeaway: Primary hyperthyroidism: low TSH with raised free T4 and/or free T3.

stem:
A patient taking long-term corticosteroids suddenly becomes profoundly unwell with hypotension, vomiting and abdominal pain.

What should be considered?
why_correct: Long-term corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis, so acute illness, missed doses or abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal crisis, which presents with hypotension, vomiting and abdominal pain. It needs immediate IM/IV hydrocortisone and fluids.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute collapse with hypotension and vomiting. B. The patient is hypotensive, not hypertensive. D. Indigestion does not cause profound hypotension and systemic collapse. E. Migraine does not explain hypotension and abdominal pain in a patient on long-term steroids.
pearl: Long-term steroids suppress the adrenal axis; collapse with hypotension, vomiting and abdominal pain is adrenal crisis and needs immediate hydrocortisone and IV fluids.
thinking: Long-term corticosteroids ↓ HPA axis suppression ↓ Sudden hypotension, vomiting and abdominal pain ↓ Adrenal crisis
exam_trap: D, simple indigestion — vomiting and abdominal pain suggest a gut cause, but indigestion does not cause profound hypotension, and delaying hydrocortisone can be fatal.
takeaway: Unwell and hypotensive on long-term steroids: treat as adrenal crisis with immediate hydrocortisone.

stem:
A patient has been taking systemic corticosteroids for a prolonged period.

Which statement is appropriate?

options.B: Corticosteroids never suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
options.C: Abrupt withdrawal can be dangerous because of adrenal suppression
options.D: Long-term steroids can always be stopped suddenly

correct_answer: C. Abrupt withdrawal can be dangerous because of adrenal suppression
why_correct: Prolonged systemic corticosteroids suppress the HPA axis, so abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal insufficiency or crisis; treatment should be tapered and steroid emergency guidance (including a Steroid Emergency Card) provided where indicated.
why_wrong: A. Withdrawal can cause adrenal insufficiency, which can be life-threatening. B. Exogenous corticosteroids do suppress the HPA axis. D. Stopping long-term steroids suddenly risks adrenal crisis. E. Steroid withdrawal does not cause hyperthyroidism.
pearl: Prolonged systemic steroids suppress the HPA axis, so taper rather than stop abruptly, and provide steroid emergency guidance such as a Steroid Emergency Card where indicated.
thinking: Prolonged systemic corticosteroids ↓ Exogenous steroid suppresses the HPA axis ↓ Sudden withdrawal leaves inadequate cortisol ↓ Abrupt withdrawal can be dangerous
exam_trap: D, stopping suddenly — it seems harmless once the condition has settled, but the suppressed adrenal glands cannot respond, risking adrenal insufficiency or crisis.
takeaway: Never stop long-term systemic steroids abruptly; taper and give steroid emergency advice.

stem:
A patient taking an ACE inhibitor develops a significant rise in serum potassium.

What is an appropriate response?

options.A: Continue the ACE inhibitor and recheck potassium in 3 months
options.B: Add an angiotensin receptor blocker for renal protection
options.C: Increase the ACE inhibitor dose to improve renal perfusion
options.D: Start a potassium-sparing diuretic to aid potassium excretion
options.E: Review medicines, renal function and other causes of hyperkalaemia

correct_answer: E. Review medicines, renal function and other causes of hyperkalaemia
why_correct: ACE inhibitors can raise potassium; NICE advises reviewing the drug and dose, checking renal function, and looking for other contributors such as potassium-sparing diuretics, supplements or NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. A significant rise in potassium needs prompt review, not a delayed recheck. B. Combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB increases the risk of hyperkalaemia and AKI. C. Increasing the ACE inhibitor dose may worsen hyperkalaemia. D. Potassium-sparing diuretics raise serum potassium and would worsen hyperkalaemia.
pearl: A significant potassium rise on an ACE inhibitor needs review of the drug and dose, renal function and other contributors such as potassium-sparing diuretics, supplements or NSAIDs.
thinking: Taking an ACE inhibitor ↓ Significant rise in serum potassium ↓ ACE inhibitors, other drugs and renal impairment can contribute ↓ Review medicines, renal function and other causes
exam_trap: B, adding an ARB for renal protection — it sounds kidney-friendly, but dual blockade increases the risk of hyperkalaemia and acute kidney injury.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia on an ACE inhibitor: review drugs, check renal function and seek other causes.

stem:
A patient's creatinine rises significantly from their previous baseline after several days of vomiting and poor oral intake.

What should be considered?

options.A: Acute kidney injury due to possible volume depletion
options.B: Acute interstitial nephritis caused by a newly prescribed medication
options.C: Nephrotic syndrome with acute fluid redistribution
options.D: Chronic kidney disease, as creatinine is now above normal

correct_answer: A. Acute kidney injury due to possible volume depletion
why_correct: A significant rise in creatinine from baseline after vomiting and poor intake suggests acute kidney injury from volume depletion (prerenal), as defined by KDIGO criteria used in NICE NG148.
why_wrong: B. Interstitial nephritis is usually drug-induced, and no new drug is described; vomiting and poor intake point to volume depletion. C. Nephrotic syndrome presents with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, not an acute rise in creatinine after fluid loss. D. CKD requires abnormalities persisting for more than three months, whereas this is an acute change. E. Nothing suggests immobility or muscle injury; the history points to volume depletion.
pearl: A significant creatinine rise from baseline after vomiting and poor intake suggests prerenal AKI; assess volume status and review nephrotoxic or haemodynamically active drugs.
thinking: Several days of vomiting and poor intake ↓ Volume depletion ↓ Significant creatinine rise from baseline ↓ Acute kidney injury due to volume depletion
exam_trap: D, chronic kidney disease — the creatinine is above normal, but CKD requires abnormality persisting over three months; a rise from a known baseline is acute.
takeaway: Acute creatinine rise from baseline after fluid loss: think prerenal AKI.

stem:
A patient with chronic kidney disease develops worsening renal function while taking regular NSAIDs.

What is an appropriate medication review?

options.A: Switch to a COX-2 selective inhibitor, which spares renal function
options.B: Continue the NSAID and add a proton pump inhibitor for protection
options.C: Reduce the NSAID dose and recheck renal function in a year
options.D: Increase the ACE inhibitor dose to protect the kidneys
options.E: Stop the NSAID if possible and review other nephrotoxic medicines

correct_answer: E. Stop the NSAID if possible and review other nephrotoxic medicines
why_correct: NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion and can worsen kidney function, especially in CKD, so they should be stopped where possible and other nephrotoxic or haemodynamically relevant drugs (e.g. ACE inhibitors, diuretics) reviewed.
why_wrong: A. COX-2 inhibitors are also nephrotoxic and carry similar renal risks. B. A proton pump inhibitor protects the stomach, not the kidneys. C. Worsening renal function needs prompt action and early recheck; a dose reduction with yearly review is inadequate. D. Increasing an ACE inhibitor during worsening renal function can further reduce glomerular filtration.
pearl: NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion and can worsen CKD; stop them where possible and review other nephrotoxic or haemodynamically active drugs such as ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease ↓ Regular NSAIDs ↓ NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion and worsen function ↓ Stop the NSAID and review other nephrotoxic medicines
exam_trap: A, switching to a COX-2 selective inhibitor — its gastrointestinal benefits suggest it is safer, but COX-2 inhibitors carry similar renal risks.
takeaway: Worsening renal function on NSAIDs: stop them and review all nephrotoxic drugs.

stem:
A trial reports that a treatment reduces the risk of an outcome from 2% to 1%.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: Relative risk reduction 1%; absolute risk reduction 50%
options.B: Relative risk reduction 100%; absolute risk reduction 1%
options.C: Relative risk reduction 50%; absolute risk reduction 1%
options.D: Relative risk reduction 50%; number needed to treat is 2
options.E: Absolute risk reduction 1%; number needed to treat is 50

correct_answer: C. Relative risk reduction 50%; absolute risk reduction 1%
why_correct: Relative risk is 1%/2% = 0.5, so the relative risk reduction is 50%; the absolute risk reduction is 2% − 1% = 1 percentage point (giving an NNT of 100).
why_wrong: A. The relative and absolute values are reversed: the RRR is 50% and the ARR is 1 percentage point. B. The RRR is (2 − 1)/2 = 50%, not 100%. D. The RRR is 50%, but the NNT is 1/0.01 = 100, not 2. E. The ARR is 1 percentage point, but the NNT is 100, not 50.
pearl: Relative risk reduction can make small absolute benefits look large: a fall from 2% to 1% is a 50% relative reduction but only a 1 percentage point absolute reduction.
thinking:
Relative risk = 1% / 2% = 0.5.  
Relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.5 = 50%.  
Absolute risk reduction = 2% − 1% = 1 percentage point.
exam_trap: A, RRR 1% and ARR 50% — it contains the right numbers but swaps them: 50% is the relative reduction and 1 percentage point is the absolute reduction.
takeaway: ARR = control risk minus treatment risk; RRR = ARR divided by control risk.

stem:
An older man presents with lower urinary tract symptoms and a marked rise in creatinine. Examination suggests a distended bladder.

What cause of acute kidney injury should be considered?
why_correct: Lower urinary tract symptoms, a distended bladder and rising creatinine suggest postrenal AKI from bladder outflow obstruction, an important reversible cause that is relieved by catheterisation.
why_wrong: B. Nothing suggests fluid loss, and a distended bladder points to outflow obstruction rather than a prerenal cause. C. Acute tubular necrosis follows ischaemic or toxic injury and does not explain bladder distension. D. Bilateral renal artery stenosis does not cause lower urinary tract symptoms or bladder distension. E. Rhabdomyolysis follows muscle injury and does not cause bladder distension.
pearl: Postrenal AKI from bladder outflow obstruction is an important reversible cause in older men with urinary symptoms; a distended bladder should prompt catheterisation to relieve it.
thinking: Urinary tract obstruction is an important potentially reversible cause of AKI.
exam_trap: B, prerenal hypovolaemic injury — a common cause of AKI, but nothing suggests fluid loss here, and a distended bladder points to outflow obstruction.
takeaway: AKI with a distended bladder: think postrenal obstruction and relieve it with a catheter.

stem:
A patient develops AKI after several days of vomiting and diarrhoea. They take an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and regular NSAIDs.

What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Continue the ACE inhibitor for renal protection but stop the regular NSAID
options.B: Assess volume status and withhold the NSAID, ACE inhibitor and diuretic
options.C: Give IV fluids and continue all regular medicines at their current doses
options.D: Increase the loop diuretic dose to maintain an adequate urine output overnight
options.E: Stop the NSAID and refer to the renal team for urgent haemodialysis tonight

correct_answer: B. Assess volume status and withhold the NSAID, ACE inhibitor and diuretic
why_correct: In AKI caused by volume depletion, NICE NG148 advises assessing fluid status and temporarily withholding nephrotoxic or haemodynamically relevant drugs such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics where appropriate. Source: NICE NG148 covers prevention, detection and management of AKI.
why_wrong: A. ACE inhibitors reduce glomerular perfusion in volume depletion and should be withheld temporarily in AKI. C. Continuing nephrotoxic and haemodynamically active drugs will worsen the kidney injury. D. More diuretic worsens volume depletion and the AKI. E. Dialysis is reserved for specific indications; the priority is fluid assessment and withholding all contributing drugs.
pearl: In AKI from volume depletion, assess fluid status and temporarily withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics, reviewing whether to restart them once renal function recovers.
thinking: Vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ AKI from volume depletion ↓ NSAID, ACE inhibitor and diuretic each worsen renal perfusion ↓ Assess volume status and withhold all three
exam_trap: A, continuing the ACE inhibitor for renal protection — long-term renoprotection is real, but in volume depletion ACE inhibitors reduce glomerular perfusion and should be withheld.
takeaway: AKI with volume depletion: assess fluids and withhold NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and diuretics.

stem:
A patient with diabetes has persistent protein detected on urine testing.

What is an appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeat the urine dipstick at the next annual review
options.B: Arrange a 24-hour urine collection as the first test
options.C: Diagnose nephrotic syndrome and start corticosteroids
options.D: Send a laboratory urine albumin:creatinine ratio
options.E: Refer for renal biopsy to confirm diabetic nephropathy

correct_answer: D. Send a laboratory urine albumin:creatinine ratio
why_correct: NICE NG203 recommends quantifying proteinuria with a laboratory urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) on an early-morning sample, as albuminuria indicates diabetic kidney disease and guides treatment.
why_wrong: A. Persistent proteinuria needs quantification now, not at the next annual review. B. A 24-hour collection is not needed as the first test; NICE recommends a laboratory ACR, ideally on an early-morning sample. C. Nephrotic syndrome requires heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema and cannot be diagnosed from a dipstick. E. Biopsy is not a first-line investigation; proteinuria should first be quantified with an ACR.
pearl: Quantify proteinuria in diabetes with a laboratory albumin:creatinine ratio, ideally on an early-morning sample; albuminuria signals diabetic kidney disease and shapes treatment.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Persistent protein on urine testing ↓ Dipstick cannot quantify albuminuria ↓ Send a laboratory urine albumin:creatinine ratio
exam_trap: B, 24-hour urine collection — the traditional quantification method, but it is cumbersome and not the first test; a laboratory ACR is recommended.
takeaway: Proteinuria in diabetes: quantify it with a laboratory urine albumin:creatinine ratio.

stem:
A patient with fever and flank pain is found to have hydronephrosis and an obstructing ureteric stone.

What is the important concern?

options.A: Acute pyelonephritis treatable with oral antibiotics at home
options.B: Renal colic requiring analgesia and outpatient follow-up
options.C: An uncomplicated stone likely to pass with expulsive therapy
options.D: Simple cystitis managed with three days of trimethoprim
options.E: An infected obstructed kidney needing urgent decompression

correct_answer: E. An infected obstructed kidney needing urgent decompression
why_correct: Fever with an obstructing stone and hydronephrosis indicates an infected obstructed kidney, a urological emergency needing antibiotics and urgent decompression (nephrostomy or stent) to prevent sepsis and loss of the kidney.
why_wrong: A. Fever with an obstructing stone and hydronephrosis indicates an infected obstructed system, which oral antibiotics at home will not treat. B. Fever with obstruction makes this a urological emergency, not uncomplicated colic. C. Infection with obstruction is a contraindication to waiting for spontaneous stone passage. D. Cystitis does not cause hydronephrosis with fever and an obstructing ureteric stone.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: give antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent, as antibiotics alone cannot drain it.
thinking: Fever and flank pain ↓ Hydronephrosis with an obstructing ureteric stone ↓ Infection behind an obstruction ↓ Infected obstructed kidney needing urgent decompression
exam_trap: A, pyelonephritis treated with oral antibiotics at home — fever and flank pain fit, but with obstruction antibiotics alone will not clear the infection; decompression is needed.
takeaway: Fever plus an obstructing stone: antibiotics and urgent decompression.

stem:
A patient develops sudden severe loin-to-groin pain with microscopic haematuria and vomiting.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden severe loin-to-groin colicky pain with haematuria and vomiting is classic renal colic due to a ureteric stone.
why_wrong: A. Pyelonephritis typically causes fever and loin pain, and is not present in every case of loin pain. C. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria, not acute colic. D. BPH causes gradual lower urinary tract symptoms, not acute colic. E. Testicular torsion causes testicular pain rather than loin-to-groin colic with haematuria.
pearl: Sudden severe loin-to-groin colicky pain with haematuria and vomiting is classic renal colic from a ureteric stone; always check for fever, which signals possible infected obstruction.
thinking: Sudden severe pain ↓ Radiates from loin to groin ↓ Microscopic haematuria and vomiting ↓ Ureteric stone
exam_trap: A, pyelonephritis — it also causes loin pain and urinary changes, but typically with fever rather than sudden severe loin-to-groin colic.
takeaway: Sudden loin-to-groin colic with haematuria: think ureteric stone.

stem:
A patient with a known ureteric stone develops fever, hypotension and rigors.

What is the priority?

options.A: Oral antibiotics and routine outpatient urology follow-up
options.B: Analgesia and medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin
options.C: Urgent assessment for an infected obstructed system
options.D: Arrange elective lithotripsy within the next six weeks
options.E: Encourage oral fluids and analgesia to help the stone pass

correct_answer: C. Urgent assessment for an infected obstructed system
why_correct: Fever, rigors and hypotension in a patient with a ureteric stone suggest an infected obstructed system with sepsis, which needs urgent resuscitation, antibiotics and emergency decompression.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics with outpatient follow-up are unsafe in suspected urosepsis with obstruction. B. Medical expulsive therapy is inappropriate with infection; an infected obstructed system needs urgent decompression. D. Elective lithotripsy delays decompression of an infected system in a septic patient. E. Fluids and analgesia alone do not treat an infected obstructed kidney.
pearl: Fever, rigors or hypotension with a ureteric stone means infected obstruction until proven otherwise: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange emergency decompression.
thinking: Known ureteric stone ↓ Fever, rigors and hypotension ↓ Sepsis behind an obstruction ↓ Urgent assessment for an infected obstructed system
exam_trap: B, medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin — appropriate for some uncomplicated stones, but infection with obstruction needs urgent decompression, not waiting for passage.
takeaway: Ureteric stone with signs of sepsis: urgent decompression, not expectant management.

stem:
A patient presents with black, tarry stools and postural dizziness.

Which diagnosis should be considered?

options.C: Dark stools from oral iron therapy

why_correct: Melaena (black tarry stools) with postural dizziness suggests upper GI bleeding with haemodynamic compromise, which needs urgent assessment and resuscitation.
why_wrong: B. Lower GI bleeding usually causes fresh red or maroon blood rather than black tarry melaena. C. Oral iron darkens stools but does not cause tarry melaena with postural dizziness. D. IBS does not cause melaena or haemodynamic symptoms. E. Diverticular bleeding typically presents as painless fresh rectal bleeding, not melaena.
pearl: Melaena suggests upper GI bleeding until proven otherwise; postural dizziness signals significant blood loss needing urgent resuscitation and risk assessment.
thinking: Black, tarry stools ↓ Melaena from digested blood ↓ Postural dizziness suggests haemodynamic compromise ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: C, dark stools from oral iron — iron does darken stools, but it does not cause tarry melaena with postural dizziness.
takeaway: Melaena with postural symptoms: treat as upper GI bleeding needing urgent assessment.

stem:
A patient with acute pancreatitis is found to have gallstones.

Which common cause should be considered?
why_correct: Gallstones are one of the commonest causes of acute pancreatitis in the UK, alongside alcohol, so gallstone pancreatitis should be considered and managed (e.g. cholecystectomy during the same admission where appropriate, NICE NG104).
why_wrong: A. Hypertriglyceridaemia is an uncommon cause and there is no evidence of it, whereas gallstones have been found. B. No causative drug is mentioned, and gallstones provide a common explanation. C. Autoimmune pancreatitis is rare, and gallstones provide a common explanation. D. Hypercalcaemia is a rare cause and there is no evidence of it here.
pearl: Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes of acute pancreatitis in the UK; in gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy during the same admission is recommended where appropriate.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ Gallstones identified ↓ Gallstones are a leading UK cause ↓ Gallstone-related pancreatitis
exam_trap: A, hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis — a recognised cause often tested as a rarity, but there is no evidence for it here, while gallstones have been found.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis with gallstones: think gallstone pancreatitis and plan cholecystectomy.

stem:
A patient with suspected acute cholangitis is hypotensive and confused.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: IV antibiotics on the ward with elective ERCP in six weeks
options.B: Urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy as the first step
options.C: Oral co-amoxiclav and an outpatient MRCP within two weeks
options.D: Resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage
options.E: IV fluids and analgesia, with antibiotics if fever persists

correct_answer: D. Resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage
why_correct: Cholangitis with hypotension and confusion indicates severe biliary sepsis, needing resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (usually ERCP).
why_wrong: A. Septic cholangitis with shock needs urgent biliary drainage, not elective ERCP. B. Cholecystectomy does not decompress the obstructed bile duct and is not the first step in a shocked patient. C. Oral antibiotics with outpatient imaging are unsafe in severe cholangitis. E. Antibiotics must not be delayed in a hypotensive, confused patient with biliary sepsis.
pearl: Cholangitis with hypotension or confusion is severe biliary sepsis: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP.
thinking: Suspected acute cholangitis ↓ Hypotension and confusion ↓ Severe biliary sepsis with an obstructed duct ↓ Resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage
exam_trap: B, urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy — surgery feels decisive, but removing the gallbladder does not drain the obstructed bile duct and is unsafe in a shocked patient.
takeaway: Septic cholangitis: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent biliary drainage.

stem:
A patient with intestinal obstruction develops continuous severe pain, tachycardia and increasing abdominal tenderness.

What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: In bowel obstruction, continuous severe pain, tachycardia and increasing tenderness suggest strangulation with ischaemia or perforation, which needs urgent surgical review.
why_wrong: A. Paralytic ileus is typically painless or mildly uncomfortable and does not cause increasing tenderness with tachycardia. B. Increasing pain, tenderness and tachycardia indicate worsening, not resolution. C. Simple constipation does not cause peritonism and tachycardia. E. IBS does not cause these acute findings.
pearl: In bowel obstruction, pain becoming continuous with tachycardia and increasing tenderness suggests strangulation with ischaemia or perforation and needs urgent surgical review.
thinking: Intestinal obstruction ↓ Pain becomes continuous and severe ↓ Tachycardia and increasing tenderness ↓ Bowel ischaemia or perforation
exam_trap: A, paralytic ileus — it also causes obstructive features, but it is typically painless or mildly uncomfortable and does not cause increasing tenderness with tachycardia.
takeaway: Obstruction with continuous pain, tachycardia and tenderness: suspect strangulation.

stem:
A patient has suspected C. difficile infection in hospital.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Nurse in an open bay and clean hands with alcohol gel after contact
options.B: Isolate with enteric precautions and review unnecessary antibiotics
options.C: Start loperamide to reduce diarrhoea and environmental spread
options.D: Continue current antibiotics to avoid interrupting treatment
options.E: Wait for the stool test result before starting any precautions

correct_answer: B. Isolate with enteric precautions and review unnecessary antibiotics
why_correct: Suspected C. difficile infection needs prompt isolation with enteric precautions, hand washing with soap and water, and review and stopping of unnecessary antibiotics, in line with NICE NG199 and UKHSA guidance.
why_wrong: A. Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores, and an open bay risks spread; isolation and soap-and-water hand washing are needed. C. Antimotility drugs such as loperamide should be avoided in suspected C. difficile infection. D. Continuing unnecessary antibiotics perpetuates C. difficile infection; they should be reviewed and stopped where possible. E. Precautions should start on clinical suspicion, not after results.
pearl: In suspected C. difficile infection, isolate with enteric precautions, wash hands with soap and water because alcohol gel does not kill spores, and stop unnecessary antibiotics.
thinking: Hospital patient ↓ Suspected C. difficile infection ↓ Spores spread easily and resist alcohol gel ↓ Isolate with enteric precautions and review antibiotics
exam_trap: E, waiting for the stool result — testing feels evidence-based, but precautions must start on clinical suspicion to prevent spread on the ward.
takeaway: Suspected C. difficile: isolate now, use soap and water, and stop unnecessary antibiotics.

stem:
A patient has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. Coeliac disease is suspected.

What is important before testing?

options.A: Start a gluten-free diet now to see if symptoms improve
options.B: Stop iron supplements for two weeks before serology
options.C: Continue eating gluten until testing is complete
options.D: Diagnose clinically if symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet
options.E: Reduce gluten intake to once weekly before testing

correct_answer: C. Continue eating gluten until testing is complete
why_correct: Coeliac serology and biopsy rely on an immune response to gluten, so NICE NG20 advises eating gluten in more than one meal a day for at least six weeks before testing.
why_wrong: A. A gluten-free diet before testing can give false-negative serology and histology. B. Iron supplements do not affect coeliac serology and need not be stopped. D. Response to a gluten-free diet is not diagnostic; serology, with biopsy where indicated, is needed. E. NICE advises gluten in more than one meal a day for at least six weeks before testing; once weekly is insufficient.
pearl: Coeliac serology and biopsy need ongoing gluten exposure; advise eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least six weeks before testing to avoid false negatives.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Tests depend on an immune response to gluten ↓ Removing gluten can cause false negatives ↓ Continue eating gluten until testing is complete
exam_trap: A, starting a gluten-free diet now — it feels helpful, but it can give false-negative serology and histology, making a firm diagnosis difficult.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease while the patient is still eating gluten.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy presents with fever and severe neutropenia.

What should be assumed until assessed otherwise?

options.A: Drug fever to be treated with paracetamol
options.B: Viral illness to be reviewed in 48 hours
options.C: Dehydration to be managed with oral fluids at home
options.D: Possible neutropenic sepsis needing urgent IV antibiotics
options.E: Tumour fever to be treated with naproxen

correct_answer: D. Possible neutropenic sepsis needing urgent IV antibiotics
why_correct: Fever in a patient on chemotherapy with severe neutropenia must be treated as neutropenic sepsis; NICE recommends immediate assessment and empirical IV antibiotics within one hour.
why_wrong: A. Fever with neutropenia should not be attributed to drugs; it must be treated as sepsis; antipyretics alone may mask deterioration. B. Delaying assessment risks rapid deterioration and death. C. Dehydration does not explain fever, and home management without assessment is unsafe. E. Tumour fever is a diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be assumed in a neutropenic patient.
pearl: Fever in a patient on chemotherapy with neutropenia is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; give empirical IV antibiotics within one hour without waiting for results.
thinking: Receiving chemotherapy ↓ Fever with severe neutropenia ↓ Infection can progress rapidly with few signs ↓ Possible neutropenic sepsis needing urgent IV antibiotics
exam_trap: A, drug fever treated with paracetamol — drugs can cause fever, but assuming it delays antibiotics, and antipyretics alone may mask deterioration.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy with neutropenia: treat as neutropenic sepsis with urgent IV antibiotics.

stem:
A 14-month-old child has a fever and is unusually drowsy, with reduced interaction and poor feeding.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure the parents that fever is always harmless
options.C: Give antibiotics without assessment and discharge

correct_answer: B. Assess urgently for serious illness
why_correct: Reduced responsiveness, poor interaction and poor feeding in a febrile child are amber or red features in the NICE NG143 traffic-light system, so urgent assessment for serious illness is needed.
why_wrong: A. Fever can indicate serious bacterial infection, so reassurance without assessment is unsafe. C. Antibiotics without assessment may mask serious illness and are not appropriate. D. A week's delay risks missing sepsis or meningitis. E. Teething does not explain drowsiness and poor interaction.
pearl: In a febrile young child, reduced responsiveness, poor interaction and poor feeding are worrying traffic-light features that need urgent assessment for serious illness.
thinking: Reduced responsiveness and poor interaction are concerning features in a febrile child.
exam_trap: E, teething — a common explanation offered by parents, but teething does not explain drowsiness, reduced interaction and poor feeding with fever.
takeaway: Febrile child who is drowsy or poorly interactive: assess urgently for serious illness.

stem:
A 5-month-old has coryza followed by cough, tachypnoea and wheeze during winter.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Coryza followed by cough, tachypnoea and wheeze in an infant under one year in winter is typical of bronchiolitis, usually caused by RSV (NICE NG9).
why_wrong: A. Croup causes a barking cough and stridor, typically in older children, rather than wheeze. B. Appendicitis does not cause respiratory symptoms. C. Meningitis presents with fever, irritability or drowsiness and signs of sepsis, not coryza and wheeze. E. Epiglottitis presents with drooling, stridor and toxicity, not wheeze.
pearl: Bronchiolitis typically affects infants under one year in winter: coryza followed by cough, tachypnoea and wheeze or crackles, usually caused by RSV.
thinking: 5-month-old infant ↓ Coryzal prodrome during winter ↓ Followed by cough, tachypnoea and wheeze ↓ Bronchiolitis
exam_trap: A, croup — also a viral illness that follows coryza, but it causes a barking cough and stridor, typically in older children, rather than wheeze in a young infant.
takeaway: Infant with coryza then cough, tachypnoea and wheeze in winter: bronchiolitis.

stem:
A young infant with bronchiolitis is struggling to maintain adequate oral feeds because of respiratory distress.

What is an important consideration?

options.A: Trial nebulised salbutamol and continue it if feeding improves
options.B: Assess hydration and breathing and give supportive care
options.C: Start oral amoxicillin to prevent secondary bacterial infection
options.D: Give oral prednisolone to reduce airway inflammation
options.E: Give nebulised adrenaline to reduce airway oedema

correct_answer: B. Assess hydration and breathing and give supportive care
why_correct: NICE NG9 recommends supportive management in bronchiolitis, including assessing hydration and respiratory status, and giving nasogastric or IV fluids and oxygen where needed.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol is not recommended in bronchiolitis. C. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated because bronchiolitis is viral. D. Corticosteroids are not recommended in bronchiolitis. E. NICE does not recommend nebulised adrenaline in bronchiolitis.
pearl: Bronchiolitis is managed supportively: assess hydration and breathing, give nasogastric or IV fluids if feeding is inadequate, and oxygen if needed.
thinking: Young infant with bronchiolitis ↓ Respiratory distress limiting oral feeding ↓ Viral illness with no effective drug treatment ↓ Assess hydration and breathing and give supportive care
exam_trap: A, a trial of nebulised salbutamol — wheeze makes bronchodilators tempting, but they are not recommended in bronchiolitis; fluids and oxygen are the mainstay.
takeaway: Bronchiolitis: supportive care with fluids and oxygen; no bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics.

stem:
A child develops high fever, drooling, muffled voice and severe difficulty breathing.

What is the priority?

options.A: Lie the child flat to examine the airway and give high-flow oxygen
options.B: Take a throat swab and start oral penicillin V for tonsillitis
options.C: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor to confirm the cause
options.D: Treat as an airway emergency and summon senior airway help
options.E: Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe for two hours

correct_answer: D. Treat as an airway emergency and summon senior airway help
why_correct: High fever, drooling, muffled voice and respiratory distress suggest epiglottitis or another upper airway emergency; the child should be kept calm and upright, with urgent senior anaesthetic and ENT support to secure the airway.
why_wrong: A. Lying flat can worsen airway obstruction; the child should stay upright in the position of comfort. B. These features suggest an upper airway emergency rather than tonsillitis, and a swab delays airway management. C. Examining the throat with a tongue depressor can precipitate complete airway obstruction. E. Dexamethasone and observation suit croup; drooling and high fever suggest epiglottitis needing urgent airway expertise.
pearl: In suspected epiglottitis, keep the child calm and upright, do not examine the throat, and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help to secure the airway.
thinking: High fever and drooling ↓ Muffled voice and severe breathing difficulty ↓ Suggests epiglottitis or another upper airway emergency ↓ Treat as an airway emergency and summon senior help
exam_trap: C, examining the throat with a tongue depressor — it seems the obvious way to confirm the cause, but it can precipitate complete airway obstruction.
takeaway: Suspected epiglottitis: do not examine the throat; keep the child upright and call airway experts.

stem:
A woman of reproductive age presents with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.

What simple investigation is important early in assessment?
why_correct: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding should have an early pregnancy test, because ectopic pregnancy must be excluded (NICE NG126).
why_wrong: A. HbA1c is not relevant to this acute presentation. B. Serum calcium is not a priority investigation here. D. Spirometry is irrelevant to abdominal pain and bleeding. E. An ECG does not address the possibility of pregnancy-related causes such as ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding needs an early pregnancy test, because ectopic pregnancy must be considered.
thinking: Woman of reproductive age ↓ Lower abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding ↓ Ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage must be considered ↓ Pregnancy test
exam_trap: E, ECG only — it is a quick bedside test, but it does not address pregnancy-related causes such as ectopic pregnancy.
takeaway: Pain and bleeding in a woman of reproductive age: do a pregnancy test early.

stem:
A pregnant woman has persistent vomiting with dehydration and inability to maintain oral intake.

What should be considered?

options.A: Normal pregnancy sickness to be managed with dietary advice at home
options.B: Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
options.C: Gestational diabetes requiring a glucose tolerance test
options.D: Gastroenteritis to be treated with oral rehydration at home
options.E: Diabetes insipidus requiring a water deprivation test

correct_answer: B. Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
why_correct: Persistent vomiting with dehydration and inability to keep food or fluids down suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, which needs assessment of hydration, electrolytes and ketones, and antiemetics with fluids where required (RCOG guidance).
why_wrong: A. Dehydration and inability to maintain oral intake go beyond normal nausea and vomiting of pregnancy. C. Gestational diabetes does not cause persistent vomiting with dehydration. D. Persistent vomiting with dehydration in pregnancy suggests hyperemesis gravidarum, and home oral rehydration is inadequate when intake cannot be maintained. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst, not persistent vomiting.
pearl: Hyperemesis gravidarum differs from normal pregnancy sickness by dehydration or inability to keep food and fluids down; it needs assessment, antiemetics and fluids where required.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Persistent vomiting with dehydration ↓ Unable to maintain oral intake ↓ Hyperemesis gravidarum needing hydration and nutritional assessment
exam_trap: A, normal pregnancy sickness — nausea and vomiting are common in pregnancy, but dehydration and inability to maintain intake go beyond it and need assessment.
takeaway: Vomiting in pregnancy with dehydration: hyperemesis gravidarum, not ordinary pregnancy sickness.

stem:
A pregnant woman with hypertension develops severe headache and visual disturbance.

What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia and severe complications
options.B: Reassure her that headaches are always normal in pregnancy
options.C: Give only paracetamol and discharge without assessment

correct_answer: A. Urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia and severe complications
why_correct: Severe headache and visual disturbance in a hypertensive pregnant woman are features of severe pre-eclampsia, so NICE NG133 requires urgent same-day assessment and management to prevent eclampsia and other complications.
why_wrong: B. Headache with hypertension can signal severe pre-eclampsia. C. Analgesia without assessment risks missing severe pre-eclampsia. D. Blood pressure is central to the assessment. E. A six-month delay would be dangerous.
pearl: Severe headache or visual disturbance in a hypertensive pregnant woman are features of severe pre-eclampsia and need same-day assessment to prevent eclampsia and other complications.
thinking: Pregnant with hypertension ↓ Severe headache ↓ Visual disturbance ↓ Urgent assessment for pre-eclampsia and severe complications
exam_trap: C, paracetamol and discharge — headache is common in pregnancy, but with hypertension and visual symptoms it may signal severe pre-eclampsia.
takeaway: Hypertension in pregnancy with headache or visual disturbance: urgent same-day assessment.

stem:
A pregnant woman has an eclamptic seizure.

Which treatment is central to immediate management?
why_correct: NICE NG133 recommends IV magnesium sulfate for eclampsia, to treat seizures and prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Phenytoin is less effective than magnesium sulfate for treating and preventing eclamptic seizures. B. Labetalol treats severe hypertension but does not treat or prevent eclamptic seizures. D. A benzodiazepine may be used for a prolonged seizure, but magnesium sulfate is the central treatment. E. Levetiracetam is not used for eclampsia; magnesium sulfate is recommended.
pearl: Magnesium sulfate is the central treatment in eclampsia, both to stop seizures and to prevent recurrence; severe hypertension is controlled alongside it.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Eclamptic seizure ↓ Magnesium sulfate treats and prevents eclamptic seizures ↓ Magnesium sulfate
exam_trap: B, IV labetalol — blood pressure control is part of management, but labetalol does not treat or prevent eclamptic seizures.
takeaway: Eclampsia: magnesium sulfate is the anticonvulsant of choice.

stem:
A pregnant woman reports a significant reduction in fetal movements compared with normal for her.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Advise her to count kicks at home for 24 hours
options.B: Review at the next routine antenatal appointment
options.C: Advise lying on her left side and drinking something cold
options.E: Book a growth scan for the following week

correct_answer: D. Arrange same-day maternity unit assessment
why_correct: Reduced fetal movements may indicate fetal compromise, so RCOG guidance advises prompt maternity assessment the same day, according to gestation and the local pathway.
why_wrong: A. Home kick-counting delays assessment of possible fetal compromise and is not recommended. B. Waiting for the next appointment delays assessment of possible fetal compromise. C. Trying to stimulate movements by lying down or cold drinks is not recommended and delays assessment. E. A scan next week delays assessment of possible fetal compromise.
pearl: A significant reduction in fetal movements may signal fetal compromise; advise same-day maternity unit assessment rather than home monitoring or waiting.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Significant reduction in fetal movements ↓ May indicate fetal compromise ↓ Same-day maternity unit assessment
exam_trap: C, lying on the left side and drinking something cold — a common folk remedy, but trying to stimulate movements delays assessment and is not recommended.
takeaway: Reduced fetal movements: same-day maternity assessment, not home monitoring.

stem:
A term pregnancy is found to have a persistent breech presentation.

Which option may be considered in appropriate circumstances?
why_correct: NICE recommends offering external cephalic version from 36 weeks (nulliparous) or 37 weeks (multiparous) for uncomplicated breech presentation, to increase the chance of vaginal birth.
why_wrong: A. Internal podalic version is reserved for delivery of a second twin and is not used for a singleton breech. C. McRoberts manoeuvre is used for shoulder dystocia. D. Ventouse delivery requires a cephalic presentation and is not used for breech. E. Cervical cerclage is used to prevent preterm birth and does not correct presentation.
pearl: For an uncomplicated breech presentation at term, offer external cephalic version to turn the baby and increase the chance of vaginal birth, if there are no contraindications.
thinking: Term pregnancy ↓ Persistent breech presentation ↓ Turning to cephalic increases the chance of vaginal birth ↓ External cephalic version
exam_trap: A, internal podalic version — it also changes fetal presentation, but it is reserved for delivering a second twin, not a singleton breech.
takeaway: Persistent breech at term: offer external cephalic version if there are no contraindications.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding three years after her last menstrual period. She does not take hormone replacement therapy.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Trial topical vaginal oestrogen and refer if the bleeding recurs
options.B: Arrange a routine gynaecology appointment within 18 weeks
options.C: Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for endometrial assessment
options.D: Repeat cervical screening and refer if the result is abnormal
options.E: Prescribe tranexamic acid and review in three months

correct_answer: C. Refer on the suspected cancer pathway for endometrial assessment
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding needs assessment for endometrial cancer; NICE NG12 (updated 2026) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to hormone replacement therapy (HRT), with transvaginal ultrasound and further investigation as indicated.
why_wrong: A. Atrophy cannot be assumed; postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer. B. A routine referral delays diagnosis; NICE NG12 recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding not attributable to HRT. D. Cervical screening does not assess the endometrium. E. Tranexamic acid treats the symptom and delays investigation for malignancy.
pearl: Unexplained postmenopausal bleeding not attributable to HRT in a woman aged 55 or over warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral to exclude endometrial cancer.
thinking: 62-year-old woman ↓ Vaginal bleeding three years after menopause ↓ Not taking HRT ↓ Suspected cancer pathway referral for endometrial assessment
exam_trap: A, vaginal oestrogen for presumed atrophy — atrophy is common, but it cannot be assumed; endometrial cancer must be excluded first.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding not explained by HRT: suspected cancer pathway referral.

stem:
A woman who experiences migraine with aura asks about combined hormonal contraception.

What is the important principle?

options.A: It is acceptable if a low-dose 20-microgram ethinylestradiol pill is used
options.B: It is contraindicated because of increased ischaemic stroke risk
options.C: It is suitable provided her blood pressure and BMI are both normal
options.D: It is suitable if she takes low-dose aspirin 75 mg daily alongside it
options.E: It is preferred because it reduces menstrual migraine

correct_answer: B. It is contraindicated because of increased ischaemic stroke risk
why_correct: Under UKMEC, migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk, so CHC should not be used.
why_wrong: A. A lower estrogen dose does not remove the stroke risk; migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for all combined hormonal contraception. C. Normal blood pressure and BMI do not offset the stroke risk associated with migraine with aura. D. Aspirin does not make CHC acceptable in migraine with aura. E. CHC is contraindicated in migraine with aura, whatever its effect on menstrual migraine.
pearl: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of increased ischaemic stroke risk; offer progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods instead.
thinking: Migraine with aura ↓ Request for combined hormonal contraception ↓ Oestrogen adds to ischaemic stroke risk ↓ Contraindicated (UKMEC 4)
exam_trap: A, a low-dose 20-microgram pill — lower oestrogen sounds safer, but no dose removes the stroke risk; migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for all combined methods.
takeaway: Migraine with aura: never prescribe combined hormonal contraception.

stem:
A woman requests emergency contraception after unprotected intercourse.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Offer levonorgestrel if within 24 hours, otherwise decline
options.B: Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
options.C: Arrange a pregnancy test first and offer EC if it is negative
options.D: Advise waiting for the next period before deciding on EC
options.E: Offer a copper IUD at the next routine clinic in four weeks

correct_answer: B. Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
why_correct: Emergency contraception should be offered promptly after assessing timing and cycle, with options including the copper IUD (most effective) or oral levonorgestrel or ulipristal acetate, following FSRH guidance.
why_wrong: A. Levonorgestrel can be used up to 72 hours, ulipristal up to 120 hours and a copper IUD up to 5 days, so presenting after 24 hours does not exclude emergency contraception. C. A pregnancy test cannot detect a pregnancy from this episode so soon and should not delay emergency contraception. D. Waiting for a period loses the window for emergency contraception. E. A copper IUD for emergency contraception must be fitted within 5 days of intercourse or of the earliest expected ovulation.
pearl: Emergency contraception should be offered promptly; the copper IUD is most effective, and oral ulipristal acetate or levonorgestrel are options depending on timing and circumstances.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Request for emergency contraception ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Assess timing and offer emergency contraception promptly
exam_trap: C, a pregnancy test first — it seems prudent, but it cannot detect a pregnancy from this episode so soon and only delays effective treatment.
takeaway: Emergency contraception: assess timing and offer it promptly; do not delay for tests.

stem:
A patient presents with a new sexually transmitted infection and asks whether they should have HIV testing.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Offer HIV testing if they report a partner from a high-prevalence area
options.B: Defer HIV testing for three months to cover the window period
options.C: Test for HIV with the routine bloods without discussing it
options.D: Reserve HIV testing for those with symptoms of seroconversion
options.E: Offer HIV testing with appropriate information and consent

correct_answer: E. Offer HIV testing with appropriate information and consent
why_correct: BASHH and NICE recommend offering HIV testing to everyone attending for STI assessment, with appropriate information and consent, because a new STI indicates risk of HIV.
why_wrong: A. HIV testing should be offered to everyone attending for STI assessment, not limited by partner characteristics. B. Testing should be offered now, with a repeat test after the window period if needed. C. Testing requires informed consent and should not be done covertly. D. Waiting for symptoms leads to late diagnosis and worse outcomes.
pearl: Everyone attending for STI assessment should be offered an HIV test with information and consent; a new STI indicates risk, and a repeat after the window period may be needed.
thinking: New sexually transmitted infection ↓ Shared transmission routes mean HIV risk ↓ HIV testing is offered to everyone assessed for STIs ↓ Offer testing with information and consent
exam_trap: B, deferring for three months to cover the window period — it sounds logical, but testing should happen now, with a repeat later if needed, to avoid delayed diagnosis.
takeaway: New STI: offer HIV testing now with consent; repeat after the window period if needed.

stem:
A patient privately tells a clinician that their partner has assaulted them but asks the clinician not to tell anyone.

What is an appropriate initial response?

options.A: Respect the request by not recording the disclosure in the notes
options.B: Refer to the police straight away despite the patient's objection
options.C: Arrange a joint consultation with the partner to discuss it
options.D: Advise the patient to leave the relationship as soon as possible
options.E: Respond supportively, assess safety and discuss support options

correct_answer: E. Respond supportively, assess safety and discuss support options
why_correct: A disclosure of domestic abuse needs a supportive response, assessment of immediate risk to the patient and any children, explanation of the limits of confidentiality, and signposting to specialist support, in line with NICE PH50 and GMC guidance.
why_wrong: A. The disclosure should be documented confidentially for safety and continuity of care, even if the patient declines action. B. Reporting a capacitous adult's disclosure against their wishes is not the initial step unless there is a serious risk to others, such as children, and it may increase danger. C. Involving the partner may increase the risk to the patient. D. Advising the patient to leave can increase risk and does not respect their autonomy.
pearl: After a domestic abuse disclosure, respond supportively, assess immediate risk to the patient and any children, document confidentially and signpost to specialist support.
thinking: The clinician should support the patient, consider immediate risk, maintain confidentiality within its limits, and facilitate access to appropriate specialist support.
exam_trap: B, immediate police referral — it seems protective, but for a capacitous adult it overrides autonomy and may increase danger, unless others such as children are at serious risk.
takeaway: Domestic abuse disclosure: support, assess risk, document and signpost, respecting autonomy.

stem:
A patient with depression says they have been thinking about ending their life.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Refer routinely to talking therapies and review in four weeks
options.B: Ask directly about intent, plans and immediate safety
options.C: Increase the antidepressant dose and review in two weeks
options.D: Avoid asking about plans to prevent planting the idea
options.E: Give a crisis line number and end the consultation

correct_answer: B. Ask directly about intent, plans and immediate safety
why_correct: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plans and access to means is essential in risk assessment and does not increase risk (NICE NG225).
why_wrong: A. A routine referral without assessing risk may miss serious and imminent danger. C. Changing medication without assessing suicidal intent and safety is unsafe. D. Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and is essential for assessment. E. Signposting without assessing risk is inadequate.
pearl: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plans and access to means does not increase risk and is essential to judge how urgently the patient needs help.
thinking: Direct assessment of suicidal ideation and intent is an important part of depression assessment.
exam_trap: D, avoiding questions about plans — a common fear, but asking directly does not plant the idea and is essential for assessing risk.
takeaway: Suicidal thoughts: ask directly about intent, plans and access to means.

stem:
A patient with depression says they have a specific suicide plan and intend to act on it today.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Refer to the community mental health team for a routine appointment
options.B: Agree a no-suicide contract and review the next day
options.C: Increase the antidepressant dose and arrange GP review this week
options.D: Give crisis line details and arrange review within a week
options.E: Treat as immediate risk and arrange urgent mental health assessment

correct_answer: E. Treat as immediate risk and arrange urgent mental health assessment
why_correct: A specific plan with intent to act today indicates immediate high risk, needing urgent mental health assessment and measures to keep the patient safe.
why_wrong: A. A routine referral ignores immediate high risk. B. No-suicide contracts are not effective and do not keep the patient safe. C. A dose increase does not address imminent risk. D. Signposting with delayed review is unsafe when there is a plan with intent to act today.
pearl: A specific suicide plan with intent to act today indicates immediate high risk; arrange urgent mental health assessment and keep the patient safe in the meantime.
thinking: Depression ↓ Specific suicide plan ↓ Intent to act today ↓ Immediate risk needing urgent mental health assessment
exam_trap: B, a no-suicide contract — it seems to secure commitment, but such contracts are not effective and do not keep the patient safe.
takeaway: Plan plus intent to act today: urgent mental health assessment and immediate safety measures.

stem:
A patient starts an antidepressant. Two weeks later they report increased agitation and new suicidal thoughts.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Urgently reassess suicide risk and clinical deterioration
options.B: Stop the antidepressant abruptly and review in one month
options.C: Reassure that early side effects settle and review in four weeks
options.D: Double the dose to speed up the antidepressant response
options.E: Add a benzodiazepine for agitation and continue as planned

correct_answer: A. Urgently reassess suicide risk and clinical deterioration
why_correct: Agitation and new suicidal thoughts soon after starting an antidepressant need urgent reassessment, as NICE warns of increased risk early in treatment, particularly in younger people.
why_wrong: B. Stopping abruptly can cause discontinuation symptoms and does not address the risk. C. New suicidal thoughts need urgent reassessment, not routine review. D. Increasing the dose without assessment may worsen agitation and risk. E. Treating agitation symptomatically without reassessing suicide risk is unsafe.
pearl: Agitation or new suicidal thoughts soon after starting an antidepressant need urgent reassessment, as risk can rise early in treatment, particularly in younger people.
thinking: Recently started an antidepressant ↓ Two weeks later: increased agitation ↓ New suicidal thoughts ↓ Urgently reassess suicide risk and clinical deterioration
exam_trap: C, reassurance that early side effects settle — some early effects do settle, but new suicidal thoughts need urgent reassessment, not routine review.
takeaway: New suicidal thoughts after starting an antidepressant: urgent reassessment.

stem:
A patient presenting with depression reports previous episodes of several days of markedly increased activity, reduced need for sleep and impulsive behaviour.

What should be considered?

options.A: Simple unipolar depression without further assessment

why_correct: Previous episodes of elevated activity, reduced need for sleep and impulsivity suggest hypomania or mania, so bipolar disorder should be considered; this matters because antidepressant monotherapy can trigger mania.
why_wrong: A. A history suggesting hypomania or mania should not be labelled unipolar depression without assessment. B. Generalised anxiety disorder does not explain episodes of elevated activity and reduced need for sleep. D. Dementia does not explain episodic mood elevation with reduced sleep. E. OCD is characterised by obsessions and compulsions, not manic episodes.
pearl: Always ask about past hypomanic or manic episodes before treating depression; bipolar disorder changes management, as antidepressant monotherapy can trigger mania.
thinking: Presenting with depression ↓ Past episodes of increased activity and reduced need for sleep ↓ Impulsive behaviour suggests hypomania or mania ↓ Bipolar disorder
exam_trap: A, simple unipolar depression — it fits the current presentation, but past episodes of elevated activity suggest bipolar disorder and must be assessed.
takeaway: Depression with past episodes of elevated mood or activity: consider bipolar disorder.

stem:
A patient with suspected mania is behaving dangerously and has become unable to care for themselves.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Arrange urgent specialist mental health assessment
options.B: Start a hypnotic and review in the GP surgery next week
options.C: Refer routinely to the community mental health team
options.D: Advise the family to monitor them and call if worse
options.E: Start an antidepressant for underlying low mood

correct_answer: A. Arrange urgent specialist mental health assessment
why_correct: Mania with dangerous behaviour and inability to self-care needs urgent specialist mental health assessment, which may include crisis team input or consideration of the Mental Health Act.
why_wrong: B. Treating insomnia with delayed review ignores serious risk from dangerous behaviour. C. A routine referral is unsafe given the immediate risk. D. Relying on family monitoring ignores dangerous behaviour that needs urgent action. E. Antidepressants can worsen mania and do not address the immediate risk.
pearl: Mania with dangerous behaviour or inability to self-care needs urgent specialist mental health assessment; crisis team input or a Mental Health Act assessment may be needed.
thinking: Suspected mania ↓ Dangerous behaviour ↓ Unable to care for themselves ↓ Urgent specialist mental health assessment
exam_trap: C, routine community mental health team referral — specialist input is right, but a routine timescale is unsafe given the immediate risk.
takeaway: Mania with risk to self or others: urgent specialist mental health assessment.

stem:
A young adult develops new auditory hallucinations, persecutory beliefs and marked social withdrawal.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Refer to primary care talking therapies for social anxiety
options.B: Refer promptly to early intervention in psychosis services
options.C: Start an antidepressant and review in four weeks
options.D: Arrange a routine community mental health review in three months
options.E: Start an antipsychotic in primary care and monitor response

correct_answer: B. Refer promptly to early intervention in psychosis services
why_correct: New hallucinations, persecutory beliefs and withdrawal suggest possible first-episode psychosis; NICE CG178 recommends urgent referral to early intervention in psychosis services.
why_wrong: A. Hallucinations and persecutory beliefs are not explained by social anxiety; possible psychosis needs specialist assessment. C. These features suggest psychosis rather than depression, and delayed review risks harm. D. Delayed referral worsens outcomes; NICE recommends urgent referral to early intervention in psychosis services. E. NICE advises against starting antipsychotics in primary care before specialist assessment.
pearl: Suspected first-episode psychosis should be referred urgently to early intervention in psychosis services; avoid starting antipsychotics in primary care before specialist assessment.
thinking: Young adult ↓ New auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs ↓ Marked social withdrawal ↓ Possible first-episode psychosis: refer to early intervention services
exam_trap: E, starting an antipsychotic in primary care — it seems to treat the problem early, but antipsychotics should not be started before specialist assessment.
takeaway: Possible first-episode psychosis: refer urgently to early intervention in psychosis services.

stem:
A patient receiving long-term antipsychotic treatment is attending for review.

Which area should be monitored?

options.A: Weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
options.B: Thyroid function and vitamin D levels

correct_answer: A. Weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
why_correct: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk, so NICE CG178 recommends regular monitoring of weight, BMI, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c and lipids.
why_wrong: B. Thyroid monitoring is relevant to lithium rather than routine antipsychotic monitoring, and vitamin D is not a core parameter. C. Visual acuity and intraocular pressure are not the key monitoring parameters for antipsychotics. D. Bone density and urinary calcium are not routine antipsychotic monitoring. E. Hearing and peak flow are not the parameters affected by antipsychotics.
pearl: Antipsychotics can cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, so monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose or HbA1c and lipids regularly during long-term treatment.
thinking: Long-term antipsychotic treatment ↓ Risk of weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia ↓ Increased cardiovascular risk ↓ Monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids
exam_trap: B, thyroid function — thyroid monitoring is familiar in psychiatry, but it relates to lithium, not routine antipsychotic monitoring.
takeaway: Long-term antipsychotics: monitor weight, blood pressure, glucose and lipids.

stem:
A patient repeatedly experiences intrusive thoughts of causing harm to others and is extremely distressed by the thoughts. They have no intention of acting on them.

What is an important clinical principle?

options.A: Inform the police, as the thoughts indicate a risk to others
options.B: Distinguish obsessional intrusive thoughts from intent and assess risk
options.C: Arrange urgent admission under the Mental Health Act
options.D: Advise the patient to suppress the thoughts when they occur
options.E: Diagnose psychosis and start an antipsychotic medication urgently

correct_answer: B. Distinguish obsessional intrusive thoughts from intent and assess risk
why_correct: Distressing, unwanted intrusive thoughts of harm that the patient resists are typical of OCD and are not the same as intent; risk should still be assessed appropriately, but the thoughts should not be misread as dangerousness.
why_wrong: A. Distressing intrusive thoughts that the patient resists do not indicate intent, and reporting without real risk breaches confidentiality. C. There is no indication of risk or a mental disorder that warrants detention. D. Thought suppression tends to worsen obsessions; CBT with exposure and response prevention is used. E. Intrusive thoughts recognised as one's own are not psychotic.
pearl: Unwanted, distressing intrusive thoughts of harm that the patient resists are typical of OCD and differ from intent; assess risk, but do not misread them as dangerousness.
thinking: Repeated intrusive thoughts of harming others ↓ Extremely distressed by them ↓ No intention to act ↓ Distinguish obsessional thoughts from intent and assess risk
exam_trap: A, informing the police — thoughts of harm sound alarming, but distressing intrusive thoughts the patient resists do not indicate intent, and reporting would breach confidentiality.
takeaway: Distressing, resisted thoughts of harm suggest OCD, not intent; assess risk proportionately.

stem:
A patient with an eating disorder presents with marked weakness, dizziness and abnormal observations.

What is important?

options.A: Delay physical assessment until psychological treatment is complete
options.C: Use BMI alone to determine whether treatment is required
options.D: Assume the patient is medically stable
options.E: Assess for acute physical complications and medical instability

correct_answer: E. Assess for acute physical complications and medical instability
why_correct: Weakness, dizziness and abnormal observations in an eating disorder may indicate medical instability (e.g. bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte disturbance), which needs urgent physical assessment using MEED guidance.
why_wrong: A. Physical risk must be assessed urgently, not delayed for psychological treatment. B. Discharge without observations would be unsafe. C. BMI alone does not reflect medical risk, and patients can be unstable at any BMI. D. Abnormal observations suggest instability.
pearl: Patients with eating disorders can be medically unstable at any BMI; weakness, dizziness and abnormal observations need urgent physical assessment, including electrolytes and ECG.
thinking: Eating disorder ↓ Marked weakness and dizziness ↓ Abnormal observations ↓ Assess for acute physical complications and medical instability
exam_trap: C, using BMI alone — BMI is a familiar severity marker, but it does not reflect medical risk, and patients can be unstable at any BMI.
takeaway: Eating disorder with abnormal observations: assess for medical instability, not BMI alone.

stem:
A patient develops delirium after becoming dehydrated and developing a urinary infection.

What should management include?

options.A: Start regular haloperidol and refer to memory clinic
options.B: Give regular lorazepam to manage the confusion
options.C: Treat the UTI and restrict fluids to avoid incontinence
options.D: Treat the dehydration and infection, with supportive delirium care
options.E: Use bed rails and physical restraint to prevent falls

correct_answer: D. Treat the dehydration and infection, with supportive delirium care
why_correct: Delirium management involves identifying and treating causes (here dehydration and UTI) and providing supportive care such as orientation, hydration and sleep, in line with NICE CG103.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics are reserved for distress or risk when other measures fail, and delirium is acute and often reversible rather than dementia. B. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium. C. Restricting fluids would worsen dehydration. E. Restraint and bed rails can increase agitation and injury.
pearl: Delirium is managed by treating the cause and giving supportive care: hydration, orientation and sleep, avoiding unnecessary sedation and restraint.
thinking: Acute confusion ↓ Precipitated by dehydration and urinary infection ↓ Delirium often resolves when the cause is treated ↓ Treat dehydration and infection, with supportive delirium care
exam_trap: A, regular haloperidol and memory clinic referral — antipsychotics seem to control confusion, but they are reserved for distress or risk when other measures fail, and this is delirium, not dementia.
takeaway: Delirium: treat the cause and give supportive care; avoid routine sedation.

stem:
A patient with Parkinson's disease develops new visual hallucinations.

What should be considered initially?
