correct_answer: B. To prepare for likely symptoms that may develop
why_correct: Anticipatory prescribing allows appropriate symptom-relief medicines to be available if symptoms arise.
why_wrong: A. Ongoing communication with the patient and family remains essential. C. Medicines are prescribed in advance but given only when symptoms arise, not prophylactically. D. Anticipatory prescribing supports community teams to manage symptoms promptly at home. E. Anticipatory medicines are for symptom control, not to deliberately shorten life.
pearl: Anticipatory ('just in case') medicines for pain, breathlessness, agitation, nausea and secretions are prescribed in advance so symptoms can be treated promptly, but given only when needed.
thinking: Approaching the end of life ↓ Likely symptoms: pain, breathlessness, agitation, secretions ↓ Delays in obtaining drugs cause distress ↓ Prepare for likely symptoms
exam_trap: C, treating every symptom prophylactically — prescribing in advance sounds like routine dosing, but these medicines are given only if symptoms arise.
takeaway: Anticipatory medicines are prescribed in advance and given only when symptoms arise.

stem:
A patient asks what a DNACPR decision means.

Which explanation is accurate?

options.A: It means the patient will not be admitted to the intensive care unit
options.B: It means treatment will now focus on end-of-life and comfort care
options.C: It applies to CPR in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest
options.D: It means the patient has lost the capacity to make their own decisions
options.E: It means antibiotics and IV fluids will be withheld

correct_answer: C. It applies to CPR in the event of cardiac or respiratory arrest
why_correct: DNACPR concerns CPR; it does not automatically mean that other appropriate treatments should be withheld.
why_wrong: A. Escalation to intensive care is a separate decision and is not determined by a DNACPR decision. B. DNACPR does not mean a move to end-of-life care; other appropriate treatment continues. D. DNACPR does not imply loss of capacity; patients with capacity remain involved in decisions. E. Antibiotics, fluids and other treatments may still be given where appropriate.
pearl: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other appropriate treatment, including antibiotics, fluids and escalation where suitable, continues. Not for CPR does not mean not for treatment.
thinking: Patient asks about DNACPR ↓ The decision concerns CPR only ↓ Other treatment decisions are separate ↓ Applies to CPR in cardiac or respiratory arrest
exam_trap: B, a move to end-of-life comfort care — a common misunderstanding, but DNACPR does not stop other appropriate active treatment.
takeaway: DNACPR means no CPR — it does not mean no treatment.

stem:
A patient with progressive illness wishes to discuss their preferences for future care while they have capacity.

What is the purpose of advance care planning?

options.A: To guarantee that every future treatment will be refused
options.B: To explore and document preferences for future care
options.D: To transfer decision-making automatically to relatives
options.E: To remove the patient's right to change their mind

correct_answer: B. To explore and document preferences for future care
why_correct: Advance care planning supports discussion and documentation of preferences and priorities for future care.
why_wrong: A. Advance care planning records preferences, which may include accepting as well as refusing treatments. C. Clinical assessment remains necessary when decisions are made. D. Relatives do not automatically gain decision-making authority; a Lasting Power of Attorney requires formal appointment. E. Patients can review and change their preferences at any time.
pearl: Advance care planning records a person's wishes and priorities while they have capacity; it may include an advance decision or a Lasting Power of Attorney and can be revised at any time.
thinking: Progressive illness ↓ Patient has capacity now ↓ Wants to discuss future care ↓ Advance care planning ↓ Explore and document preferences for future care
exam_trap: D, transferring decisions automatically to relatives — families are often involved, but relatives have no automatic authority; they can decide only if formally appointed, for example through a Lasting Power of Attorney.
takeaway: Advance care planning documents wishes while capacity is present, and they can be changed.

stem:
A patient receiving opioid analgesia becomes very drowsy with a markedly reduced respiratory rate.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Give oral lorazepam to settle the patient and aid sleep
options.B: Allow the patient to sleep and recheck in 4 hours
options.C: Switch to an oral opioid at the same dose and review later
options.D: Assess airway and breathing and seek urgent help
options.E: Give a further opioid dose for pain

correct_answer: D. Assess airway and breathing and seek urgent help
why_correct: Reduced consciousness and respiratory depression following opioids can be life-threatening and require immediate assessment.
why_wrong: A. A sedative would further depress consciousness and respiration. B. Leaving the patient to sleep ignores potentially life-threatening respiratory depression. C. Continuing opioid at the same dose does not address the respiratory depression. E. A further opioid dose would worsen respiratory depression.
pearl: Opioid toxicity presents with drowsiness, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils; use an ABCDE approach, call for help and give naloxone if respiratory depression is significant.
thinking: Receiving opioid analgesia ↓ Very drowsy ↓ Markedly reduced respiratory rate ↓ Opioid toxicity threatening breathing ↓ Assess airway and breathing and seek urgent help
exam_trap: B, letting the patient sleep — drowsiness may look like comfort, but with a markedly reduced respiratory rate it signals life-threatening opioid toxicity.
takeaway: Drowsy with slow breathing on opioids: ABCDE, call for help, consider naloxone.

stem:
A patient taking regular NSAIDs develops dyspepsia and then vomits a small amount of blood.

What adverse effect should be suspected?
why_correct: NSAIDs can increase the risk of gastrointestinal mucosal injury and bleeding.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs rarely cause hepatotoxicity, and it does not explain dyspepsia and haematemesis. C. NSAIDs can cause acute kidney injury, but it does not explain dyspepsia and haematemesis. D. Oesophageal candidiasis causes odynophagia and is not an NSAID adverse effect. E. NSAID sensitivity can cause bronchospasm but does not explain dyspepsia and haematemesis.
pearl: NSAIDs damage the gastric and duodenal mucosa; dyspepsia followed by haematemesis suggests peptic ulcer bleeding. Consider gastroprotection for NSAID users at higher risk.
thinking: Regular NSAID use ↓ Dyspepsia ↓ Vomiting blood ↓ Mucosal injury with bleeding ↓ Upper gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: C, NSAID-induced acute kidney injury — a genuine NSAID adverse effect, but it does not explain dyspepsia and haematemesis.
takeaway: NSAIDs plus dyspepsia and haematemesis: think upper GI bleeding from ulceration.

stem:
A patient is admitted to hospital with a medication list that differs from the medicines they report taking at home.

What should be done?

options.C: Ask the patient to choose whichever list they prefer without checking
options.E: Reconcile the medicines using reliable sources

correct_answer: E. Reconcile the medicines using reliable sources
why_correct: Medication reconciliation helps identify omissions, duplications and prescribing errors during transitions of care.
why_wrong: A. Prescribing both lists risks duplication and toxicity. B. Ignoring the discrepancy risks omissions, duplications and prescribing errors. C. Reconciliation requires verification from reliable sources such as GP records, not unchecked patient choice. D. Stopping all medicines automatically can cause harm, for example from omission of time-critical drugs.
pearl: Admission and discharge are high-risk points for medication discrepancies.
thinking: Hospital admission ↓ Listed medicines differ from those taken at home ↓ Risk of omission or duplication ↓ Verify with reliable sources ↓ Reconcile the medicines
exam_trap: C, letting the patient choose a list — the patient knows what they take, but reconciliation requires verification against reliable sources such as GP records.
takeaway: Medication discrepancies on admission: reconcile using reliable sources.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin is prescribed a new medicine. Several days later they develop unexplained bruising.

What should the clinician consider?

options.A: That warfarin cannot interact with other medicines
options.B: A possible drug interaction affecting anticoagulation
options.C: That the patient should automatically double the warfarin dose
options.D: That the new medicine is necessarily ineffective

correct_answer: B. A possible drug interaction affecting anticoagulation
why_correct: Warfarin has numerous clinically important interactions, and unexpected bleeding or bruising warrants assessment.
why_wrong: A. Warfarin has many clinically important interactions with other medicines. C. Doubling the warfarin dose would further increase bleeding risk. D. Bruising suggests an interaction affecting anticoagulation, not ineffectiveness of the new medicine. E. Bruising on warfarin suggests over-anticoagulation, not iron deficiency.
pearl: Warfarin's effect is easily altered by new drugs, such as some antibiotics and antifungals; check the INR when interacting medicines are started or stopped, and after unexplained bruising.
thinking: Taking warfarin ↓ New medicine started ↓ Unexplained bruising days later ↓ Anticoagulant effect likely increased ↓ Possible drug interaction
exam_trap: D, the new medicine being ineffective — the timing implicates the new drug, but bruising suggests increased anticoagulation from an interaction, not drug failure.
takeaway: New drug plus bruising on warfarin: suspect an interaction and check the INR.

stem:
A patient taking a direct oral anticoagulant develops significant deterioration in renal function.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Increase the dose to maintain the same anticoagulant effect
options.B: Review the dose and suitability in light of renal function
options.C: Continue the current dose and recheck renal function in 12 months
options.D: Switch to aspirin as a safer alternative
options.E: Stop the DOAC together with all of the other regular medicines

correct_answer: B. Review the dose and suitability in light of renal function
why_correct: Renal function can affect exposure to some DOACs and is important for safe prescribing.
why_wrong: A. Increasing the dose would raise drug levels and bleeding risk. C. DOACs are partly renally cleared, so significant deterioration needs prompt review rather than routine annual monitoring. D. Aspirin is not an equivalent alternative for anticoagulation and still carries bleeding risk. E. Stopping all medicines is inappropriate; individual medicines need review.
pearl: DOACs are partly renally cleared, so falling renal function raises drug levels and bleeding risk; review the dose and suitability whenever renal function deteriorates significantly.
thinking: Taking a DOAC ↓ Significant deterioration in renal function ↓ Reduced clearance raises bleeding risk ↓ Review dose and suitability
exam_trap: C, rechecking renal function in 12 months — routine annual monitoring sounds acceptable, but significant deterioration needs prompt dose review.
takeaway: DOAC with worsening renal function: review the dose and suitability promptly.

stem:
A patient taking weekly methotrexate accidentally receives instructions to take it every day.

Why is this a serious prescribing error?

options.A: Daily dosing mainly increases the risk of mild nausea
options.B: It is usually given weekly, and daily dosing can cause serious toxicity
options.C: Daily dosing reduces its efficacy by inducing hepatic enzymes over time
options.D: Daily dosing causes hypertension and fluid retention
options.E: Daily dosing increases the risk of hyperglycaemia

correct_answer: B. It is usually given weekly, and daily dosing can cause serious toxicity
why_correct: Incorrect daily administration of weekly methotrexate is a well-recognised potentially serious medication error.
why_wrong: A. Daily dosing causes serious toxicity, including bone marrow suppression, not just mild nausea. C. Methotrexate does not lose efficacy through enzyme induction; daily dosing causes cumulative toxicity. D. Methotrexate toxicity affects the bone marrow, liver, lungs and mucosa, not blood pressure. E. Hyperglycaemia is not the recognised danger; the risk is serious toxicity such as myelosuppression.
pearl: Methotrexate for inflammatory conditions is taken once weekly; daily dosing can cause potentially fatal toxicity such as bone marrow suppression. Always state the day of the week clearly.
thinking: Methotrexate prescribed weekly ↓ Instructions say daily ↓ Several-fold dose excess ↓ Cumulative toxicity ↓ Serious toxicity
exam_trap: A, mainly mild nausea — nausea is a familiar side effect, but daily dosing causes serious toxicity such as bone marrow suppression.
takeaway: Methotrexate is usually once weekly; daily dosing is a dangerous, potentially fatal error.

stem:
A patient with diabetes receives an insulin dose that is much higher than intended.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Observe without any glucose checks as long as the patient says they feel well
options.B: Omit the next meal and snack to avoid rebound hyperglycaemia later in the day
options.C: Recheck the capillary glucose at the next routine check tomorrow morning
options.D: Discharge home promptly with advice to eat a sugary snack if symptoms develop
options.E: Check glucose, assess the patient and manage the risk of hypoglycaemia

correct_answer: E. Check glucose, assess the patient and manage the risk of hypoglycaemia
why_correct: An excessive insulin dose can cause potentially serious hypoglycaemia and requires prompt assessment.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia may develop later, so a patient feeling well does not exclude risk. B. Omitting food would increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia. C. Waiting until the next day risks severe, potentially fatal hypoglycaemia. D. Discharge is unsafe until glucose has been monitored and the risk period has passed.
pearl: After an insulin overdose, check glucose immediately and frequently, ensure carbohydrate intake and keep monitoring for the full duration of the insulin's action, which may be prolonged.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Insulin dose much higher than intended ↓ Risk of severe, possibly delayed hypoglycaemia ↓ Check glucose, assess and manage the hypoglycaemia risk
exam_trap: A, observing without glucose checks because the patient feels well — reassuring now, but hypoglycaemia may develop later, so glucose must be monitored.
takeaway: Insulin overdose: check glucose now and keep monitoring for its full duration of action.

stem:
An opioid-naive patient is prescribed a strong opioid for acute pain.

Which factor is particularly important for safe prescribing?

options.A: Assess clinical status and risk factors before prescribing
options.B: Start a modified-release opioid as first-line treatment
options.C: Co-prescribe a benzodiazepine to reduce anxiety
options.D: Start at the maximum licensed dose for rapid relief
options.E: Combine two strong opioids for better pain control

correct_answer: A. Assess clinical status and risk factors before prescribing
why_correct: Opioids can cause sedation and respiratory depression, particularly in vulnerable patients or when combined with other sedatives.
why_wrong: B. Modified-release opioids are not recommended for acute pain in opioid-naive patients because of the risk of accumulation and respiratory depression. C. Combining with a benzodiazepine increases the risk of sedation and respiratory depression. D. High starting doses increase the risk of respiratory depression, particularly in opioid-naive patients. E. Combining strong opioids increases toxicity risk.
pearl: Before starting a strong opioid in an opioid-naive patient, consider age, renal and respiratory function and other sedatives; start low with immediate-release doses and monitor.
thinking: Opioid-naive patient ↓ Strong opioid for acute pain ↓ Risk of sedation and respiratory depression ↓ Risk depends on patient factors ↓ Assess clinical status and risk factors
exam_trap: B, a modified-release opioid first-line — a long-acting drug seems convenient, but in opioid-naive acute pain it risks accumulation and respiratory depression.
takeaway: Opioid-naive patient: assess risk, start low with immediate release and monitor.

stem:
A patient is discharged after hospitalisation with several high-risk medicines.

What is particularly important?

options.A: Stop blood monitoring until the GP review in 3 months
options.B: Rely on the GP to identify changes from the drug chart
options.C: Give the patient the medicines without a written list
options.D: Advise restarting the usual pre-admission medicines at home
options.E: Clear communication of medicines, doses, monitoring and follow-up

correct_answer: E. Clear communication of medicines, doses, monitoring and follow-up
why_correct: Transitions of care are a major source of medication-related harm.
why_wrong: A. Monitoring of high-risk medicines must continue after discharge. B. Changes must be clearly communicated to the GP to avoid errors. C. A medication list helps patients take medicines correctly and safely. D. Restarting pre-admission medicines may reverse changes made in hospital and cause harm.
pearl: Discharge is a high-risk transition: give the patient and GP a clear list of medicines, changes and reasons, the monitoring needed and who is responsible for follow-up.
thinking: Discharge after admission ↓ Several high-risk medicines ↓ Transitions cause medication errors ↓ Clear communication of medicines, doses, monitoring and follow-up
exam_trap: B, relying on the GP to identify changes — the GP does review medicines, but changes must be clearly communicated to prevent errors.
takeaway: At discharge, clearly communicate medicine changes, monitoring and follow-up to patient and GP.

stem:
A patient reports that a medicine caused nausea but had no rash, swelling, breathing difficulty or circulatory symptoms.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Record it accurately as a side effect rather than an allergy
options.B: Leave the reaction undocumented as it was minor
options.C: Record it as an allergy to the whole drug class
options.D: Record it as anaphylaxis to be cautious
options.E: Advise avoiding the whole drug class in future

correct_answer: A. Record it accurately as a side effect rather than an allergy
why_correct: Accurate differentiation between allergy and non-allergic adverse effects improves future prescribing decisions.
why_wrong: B. Adverse effects should still be documented to inform future prescribing. C. Nausea is not an allergic reaction, and a class allergy label may unnecessarily restrict future treatment. D. Nausea alone is not an allergic reaction and should not be labelled as anaphylaxis. E. A non-allergic side effect does not necessarily prevent future use of related medicines.
pearl: Nausea is an intolerance, not an allergy; mislabelling side effects as allergies narrows future choices and can push prescribers towards less suitable alternatives.
thinking: Medicine caused nausea ↓ No rash, swelling, breathing or circulatory features ↓ No features of allergy ↓ Record as a side effect, not an allergy
exam_trap: C, recording a class allergy — it seems cautious, but nausea is not allergic and a class label unnecessarily restricts future treatment.
takeaway: Record side effects as intolerances, not allergies, to keep future options open.

stem:
A patient is started on antibiotics while awaiting microbiological results.

The results later identify an organism susceptible to a narrower antibiotic.

What is an appropriate stewardship principle?

options.A: Continue the empirical regimen for the full course
options.B: Escalate to a broader agent to ensure full cover
options.D: Add a second agent to provide synergistic cover
options.E: Extend the course to prevent later recurrence

correct_answer: C. Narrow treatment when clinically appropriate
why_correct: Antibiotic therapy should be reviewed and narrowed where appropriate to reduce unnecessary antimicrobial exposure.
why_wrong: A. Continuing an unnecessarily broad empirical regimen ignores the microbiology result. B. Escalating to a broader agent promotes resistance and C. difficile infection. D. Adding antibiotics without indication increases adverse effects and resistance. E. Antibiotics should have a defined duration and be reviewed, not extended without reason.
pearl: Reviewing antibiotics once cultures return is a core stewardship step: switch to a narrower agent when clinically appropriate and set a clear stop or review date.
thinking: Empirical antibiotics started ↓ Microbiology identifies a susceptible organism ↓ A narrower agent will work ↓ Narrow treatment when clinically appropriate
exam_trap: A, continuing the empirical regimen — completing what was started feels safe, but staying broad ignores the result and adds resistance and C. difficile risk.
takeaway: Use microbiology results to narrow antibiotics whenever clinically appropriate.

stem:
A patient has improved substantially during treatment for a bacterial infection.

What is an important prescribing principle?

options.A: Stop antibiotics now whatever the diagnosis or recommended course length
options.B: Extend the course to 6 weeks to prevent a relapse of the infection
options.C: Increase the dose to consolidate the response
options.D: Review the need for antibiotics and use the appropriate duration
options.E: Add a second antibiotic of a different class to prevent resistance

correct_answer: D. Review the need for antibiotics and use the appropriate duration
why_correct: Antimicrobial treatment should be reviewed according to the diagnosis, clinical response and current guidance.
why_wrong: A. Stopping depends on the diagnosis and recommended course length, not improvement alone. B. Unnecessarily prolonged antibiotics increase adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. C. Clinical improvement is not a reason to increase the dose. E. Adding antibiotics without indication is poor stewardship.
pearl: Antibiotic duration should follow the diagnosis, response and current guidance, not habit; review the need regularly and avoid both premature stopping and unnecessarily long courses.
thinking: Bacterial infection being treated ↓ Substantial improvement ↓ Duration set by diagnosis, response and guidance ↓ Review the need and use the appropriate duration
exam_trap: A, stopping now whatever the diagnosis — improvement suggests treatment is done, but some infections need a defined course; duration depends on the diagnosis.
takeaway: Set antibiotic duration by diagnosis and guidance, reviewing the need regularly.

stem:
A blood culture grows an organism that is a common skin contaminant, while the patient is clinically well and other cultures are negative.

What should the clinician do?

options.C: Interpret the result in its clinical context
options.D: Assume every positive culture represents bloodstream infection

correct_answer: C. Interpret the result in its clinical context
why_correct: Some organisms commonly represent contamination, although true infection must be considered according to the organism and clinical circumstances.
why_wrong: A. Lifelong antibiotics are not indicated for a likely contaminant in a well patient. B. Endocarditis requires clinical and microbiological criteria such as multiple positive cultures, not a single probable contaminant. D. Skin contaminants commonly grow in blood cultures without true infection. E. Blood culture results are important and should not be ignored.
pearl: A single culture growing a skin commensal in a well patient with other cultures negative is often contamination; true infection is more likely with multiple positive sets or prosthetic material.
thinking: Blood culture grows a common skin contaminant ↓ Patient clinically well ↓ Other cultures negative ↓ Likely contamination, but not assumed ↓ Interpret in clinical context
exam_trap: D, assuming every positive culture is a bloodstream infection — a positive result feels definitive, but skin contaminants commonly grow without true infection.
takeaway: Interpret a positive blood culture by organism, number of sets and the clinical picture.

stem:
A patient with suspected bloodstream infection requires blood cultures.

Which principle is important when obtaining them?

options.C: Collect them from an unclean surface

why_correct: Aseptic technique reduces contamination and improves the reliability of microbiological results.
why_wrong: B. Reusing needles is unsafe and risks infection. C. Unclean surfaces increase contamination risk. D. Labelling from memory risks misidentification; samples should be labelled at the bedside. E. Touching prepared sterile equipment introduces contamination.
pearl: Contaminated blood cultures lead to unnecessary antibiotics and longer stays; use aseptic non-touch technique, clean the skin and bottle tops, and label at the bedside.
thinking: Suspected bloodstream infection ↓ Blood cultures needed ↓ Contamination gives misleading results ↓ Use appropriate aseptic technique
exam_trap: D, labelling later from memory — it seems harmless once the sample is taken, but it risks misidentification; samples should be labelled at the bedside.
takeaway: Blood cultures: aseptic non-touch technique and bedside labelling.

stem:
A healthcare worker has just examined one patient and is about to examine another.

What is an important infection-prevention measure?

options.B: Wear the same gloves for both patients
options.D: Change gloves without considering hand hygiene
options.E: Wash hands only at the end of the shift

why_correct: Hand hygiene is a fundamental measure for preventing healthcare-associated infection.
why_wrong: B. Wearing the same gloves between patients transfers microorganisms. C. Antibiotics have no role in preventing transmission between patients. D. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, which is required before and after glove use. E. Hand hygiene is needed between patients, not only at the end of a shift.
pearl: Hand hygiene between patients is the most important single measure against healthcare-associated infection; gloves must be changed between patients and never replace it.
thinking: Examined one patient ↓ About to examine another ↓ Hands may carry organisms between them ↓ Perform appropriate hand hygiene
exam_trap: D, changing gloves without hand hygiene — fresh gloves seem enough, but hands are contaminated during glove removal, so hand hygiene is still needed.
takeaway: Between patients: change gloves and clean hands, every time.

stem:
A healthcare worker is about to perform a procedure involving potential contact with body fluids.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Reuse disposable gloves if they appear intact
options.B: Re-sheath needles carefully when wearing gloves
options.C: Use gloves instead of hand hygiene
options.D: Select PPE according to the anticipated exposure
options.E: Wear gloves for all patient contact

correct_answer: D. Select PPE according to the anticipated exposure
why_correct: PPE should be selected according to the foreseeable risk of exposure.
why_wrong: A. Disposable gloves are single-use and must not be reused. B. Needles should not be re-sheathed; gloves do not remove the need for safe sharps practice. C. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. E. Gloves should be used according to risk, not for every interaction.
pearl: Choose PPE by the task: gloves and apron for contact with blood or body fluids, adding eye protection or a fluid-resistant mask if splashing is likely; gloves never replace hand hygiene.
thinking: Procedure with possible body fluid contact ↓ Standard precautions apply ↓ PPE depends on the anticipated exposure ↓ Select PPE according to risk
exam_trap: E, gloves for all patient contact — it seems safer, but unnecessary glove use is not recommended; PPE should match the anticipated exposure.
takeaway: Select PPE according to the anticipated exposure for each task.

stem:
A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a potentially contaminated needle.

What should they do?

options.A: Suck the wound, apply an alcohol-based scrub and then report the injury
options.B: Squeeze the wound hard and scrub it with a brush under hot running water
options.C: Apply a waterproof dressing and report the injury at the end of the shift
options.D: Wash the area and follow the occupational exposure pathway promptly
options.E: Wash the area and arrange a GP blood test for HIV in three months' time

correct_answer: D. Wash the area and follow the occupational exposure pathway promptly
why_correct: Prompt first aid, reporting and risk assessment are important after occupational exposure.
why_wrong: A. Sucking the wound is not recommended; it should be encouraged to bleed and washed with soap and running water. B. Scrubbing or squeezing hard may damage tissue; gentle bleeding and washing are advised. C. Delayed reporting may miss the window for post-exposure prophylaxis, which should ideally start within hours. E. Waiting 3 months misses urgent risk assessment and possible prophylaxis.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage gentle bleeding and wash with soap and running water without sucking or scrubbing, then report at once for risk assessment and possible PEP.
thinking: Needlestick from a possibly contaminated needle ↓ First aid: encourage bleeding and wash ↓ Urgent risk assessment for time-critical PEP ↓ Wash and follow the exposure pathway promptly
exam_trap: C, a dressing and reporting at the end of the shift — finishing the shift seems practical, but the delay may miss the window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
takeaway: Needlestick: bleed, wash, report immediately — never wait until the shift ends.

stem:
A patient has symptoms strongly suggestive of infectious pulmonary tuberculosis.

Which infection-control principle is important?

options.A: Admission to an open bay with standard infection-control precautions
options.B: Respiratory isolation and specialist infection-control procedures
options.C: Allow normal movement around the ward once antibiotics have been started
options.D: Treat with amoxicillin and review in 2 weeks
options.E: Nurse in a single side room with the door kept open for easy observation

correct_answer: B. Respiratory isolation and specialist infection-control procedures
why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate infection-control precautions to reduce transmission.
why_wrong: A. An open bay increases the risk of airborne transmission. C. Patients with pulmonary TB remain infectious for a period after starting treatment (usually about 2 weeks of effective therapy), so unrestricted movement around the ward increases the risk of airborne transmission. D. Amoxicillin does not treat TB and delays diagnosis. E. A side room door should be kept closed to reduce airborne spread.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs respiratory isolation in a side room with the door closed and appropriate respiratory protection, with specialist infection-control input.
thinking: Symptoms suggest infectious pulmonary TB ↓ Airborne transmission ↓ Others on the ward at risk ↓ Respiratory isolation and specialist infection-control procedures
exam_trap: E, a single room with the door open — a side room seems sufficient, but an open door allows airborne spread; the door should be kept closed.
takeaway: Suspected infectious TB: respiratory isolation with the side-room door closed.

stem:
A patient presents with fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a widespread maculopapular rash. Measles is suspected.

What is an important immediate principle?

options.A: Await measles IgM serology results before starting any infection-control measures
options.B: Isolate the patient and follow infection-control and public-health procedures
options.C: Manage in the main waiting room wearing a surgical mask
options.D: Treat as bacterial cellulitis with oral flucloxacillin and review after 48 hours
options.E: Delay notification to the health protection team until laboratory confirmation

correct_answer: B. Isolate the patient and follow infection-control and public-health procedures
why_correct: Measles is highly transmissible, so infection-control and public-health measures are important.
why_wrong: A. Infection control should start on clinical suspicion, not wait for serology. C. Measles is airborne and highly transmissible, so a shared waiting room risks spread. D. The features suggest measles, not bacterial cellulitis. E. Measles is notifiable on clinical suspicion; notification should not wait for confirmation.
pearl: Measles is highly transmissible; isolate on clinical suspicion, keep the patient out of shared waiting areas and notify the health protection team without waiting for laboratory confirmation.
thinking: Fever, cough, conjunctivitis, maculopapular rash ↓ Measles suspected ↓ Airborne, highly infectious and notifiable ↓ Isolate and follow infection-control and public-health procedures
exam_trap: E, delaying notification until laboratory confirmation — confirmation seems prudent, but measles is notifiable on clinical suspicion so public-health action can start quickly.
takeaway: Suspected measles: isolate and notify on suspicion — do not wait for results.

stem:
A patient has suspected C. difficile infection with diarrhoea.

Which measure is particularly important?

options.A: Allow use of the shared bay bathroom with cleaning at the end of each day
options.B: Transfer the patient to another ward to reduce spread on the current ward
options.C: Routine detergent cleaning of the bed space and shared equipment once daily
options.D: Prophylactic oral antibiotics for all the other patients in the same bay
options.E: Isolation and hand hygiene according to infection-control procedures

correct_answer: E. Isolation and hand hygiene according to infection-control procedures
why_correct: C. difficile spores can spread in healthcare environments, making appropriate infection-control measures essential.
why_wrong: A. Shared bathrooms increase the risk of spore transmission to vulnerable patients. B. Transfer spreads infection risk to another area and does not replace isolation. C. Spores persist on surfaces and need sporicidal cleaning, not routine detergent. D. Antibiotics do not prevent transmission and can increase C. difficile risk.
pearl: Suspected C. difficile diarrhoea needs prompt isolation, ideally with dedicated toilet facilities, soap-and-water hand washing, gloves and aprons, and sporicidal cleaning.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile ↓ Diarrhoea spreads spores ↓ Spores persist on surfaces and hands ↓ Isolation and hand hygiene per infection-control procedures
exam_trap: C, routine detergent cleaning once daily — it is the normal standard, but C. difficile spores survive detergent and need sporicidal cleaning.
takeaway: C. difficile: isolate, wash hands with soap and water, clean with sporicidal agents.

stem:
A patient with acute illness requires supplemental oxygen.

Which principle is appropriate?

options.A: Give oxygen to a target saturation range appropriate to the patient
options.B: Use oxygen in place of treating the underlying cause
options.C: Give 15 L/min via a reservoir mask throughout the hospital admission
options.D: Aim for saturations of 100% to maximise the patient's oxygen reserve
options.E: Aim for a target saturation of 88–92% in acutely ill patients by default

correct_answer: A. Give oxygen to a target saturation range appropriate to the patient
why_correct: Oxygen is a treatment that should be prescribed and monitored appropriately rather than given indiscriminately.
why_wrong: B. Oxygen supports oxygenation but does not treat the underlying cause. C. Prolonged high-concentration oxygen without titration can cause harm, e.g. hypercapnia in at-risk patients. D. Hyperoxaemia can be harmful; oxygen should be titrated to a target range. E. A target of 88–92% applies to patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, not all acutely ill patients.
pearl: Oxygen is a drug: prescribe a target range, usually 94–98% for most acutely ill patients or 88–92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, and titrate to it.
thinking: Acutely ill patient needs oxygen ↓ Both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia can harm ↓ Some patients risk hypercapnia ↓ Oxygen to a target range appropriate to the patient
exam_trap: E, 88–92% for all acutely ill patients — the figure is familiar, but it applies to those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, not to everyone by default.
takeaway: Prescribe oxygen to a patient-specific target saturation range and titrate to it.

stem:
A patient's pulse oximeter shows an unexpectedly low oxygen saturation, but the patient appears comfortable and the waveform is poor.

What should be done first?

options.A: Check the probe and signal quality and reassess the patient
options.B: Accept the reading and start high-flow oxygen
options.C: Request an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram
options.E: Arrange an arterial blood gas before checking the probe

correct_answer: A. Check the probe and signal quality and reassess the patient
why_correct: Poor probe positioning, movement, poor perfusion and other technical factors can produce unreliable readings.
why_wrong: B. A poor waveform suggests the reading may be inaccurate, so treatment should not be based on it without checking. C. Imaging is not justified on the basis of a possibly erroneous reading in a comfortable patient. D. Oxygen saturation remains an important measurement and should continue to be monitored. E. Simple checks of the probe and patient should come before an invasive test.
pearl: A low reading with a poor waveform in a comfortable patient suggests artefact from poor perfusion, movement or a misplaced probe; check the probe and the patient before acting.
thinking: Unexpectedly low saturation ↓ Patient comfortable ↓ Poor waveform ↓ Reading probably unreliable ↓ Check probe and signal and reassess the patient
exam_trap: B, starting high-flow oxygen — acting on hypoxaemia seems safe, but a poor waveform suggests a false reading; check the probe and the patient first.
takeaway: Unexpected oximeter reading: check the waveform and probe, then reassess the patient.

stem:
An ECG appears unusual and does not fit the patient's clinical presentation. The limb-lead placement may have been incorrect.

What should be done?

options.A: Check lead placement and repeat the ECG if necessary
options.B: Report the ECG as abnormal and file it in the patient notes
options.C: Discard the ECG and rely on the clinical examination alone
options.D: Treat the patient according to the current ECG findings
options.E: Diagnose myocardial infarction and start the ACS pathway

correct_answer: A. Check lead placement and repeat the ECG if necessary
why_correct: Technical errors can significantly alter ECG appearance and should be considered when the tracing is inconsistent with the clinical picture.
why_wrong: B. Filing a possibly erroneous ECG as abnormal fails to investigate the discrepancy. C. ECGs form part of the medical record and should not be discarded; the cause should be checked. D. ECG findings must be interpreted in the clinical context, particularly when lead misplacement is possible. E. Lead misplacement can mimic abnormalities; MI should not be diagnosed without checking.
pearl: Limb lead reversal can mimic pathology, such as an unexpected axis or inverted complexes in lead I; if an ECG does not fit the patient, check lead placement and repeat before acting.
thinking: ECG looks unusual ↓ Does not fit the clinical picture ↓ Limb lead placement may be wrong ↓ Check lead placement and repeat if necessary
exam_trap: E, diagnosing myocardial infarction — an abnormal-looking ECG tempts urgent action, but lead misplacement can mimic changes, so check and repeat first.
takeaway: ECG not matching the patient: check lead placement and repeat before acting.

stem:
An ECG has marked baseline wandering because the patient is moving and shivering.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Remove the electrodes and rely on the pulse
options.B: Give amiodarone for presumed ventricular tachycardia
options.C: Report the tracing as normal sinus rhythm
options.D: Start anticoagulation for presumed atrial fibrillation
options.E: Reduce artefact where possible and repeat the ECG

correct_answer: E. Reduce artefact where possible and repeat the ECG
why_correct: A technically poor ECG can obscure important abnormalities or create misleading appearances.
why_wrong: A. Electrodes are needed to record a repeat ECG, and the pulse cannot replace it. B. Artefact can mimic VT; treatment should not be based on a poor-quality tracing. C. Poor tracing quality may hide abnormalities, so it cannot be reported as normal. D. Artefact can mimic arrhythmias such as AF; it should not be diagnosed and treated on this tracing.
pearl: Movement and shivering produce artefact that can mimic arrhythmias such as AF or VT; settle and warm the patient, check the electrodes and repeat the ECG before interpreting it.
thinking: Marked baseline wander ↓ Patient moving and shivering ↓ Tracing technically poor ↓ May mimic or hide abnormalities ↓ Reduce artefact and repeat the ECG
exam_trap: D, anticoagulation for presumed AF — an irregular baseline can look like AF, but treating on an artefact-laden tracing risks unnecessary harm.
takeaway: Poor-quality ECG: reduce artefact and repeat before interpreting.

stem: When should a patient's blood sample normally be labelled?

options.A: Before sampling, using pre-printed labels prepared at the start of the shift
options.B: At the patient's side, following local identification procedures
options.C: At the nurses' station after all of the patient's samples are taken
options.D: In the laboratory reception using the request form
options.E: On return to the ward office, using the printed patient list for the bay

correct_answer: B. At the patient's side, following local identification procedures
why_correct: Correct identification and contemporaneous labelling reduce the risk of sample misidentification.
why_wrong: A. Pre-labelling before seeing the patient is unsafe and increases wrong-blood-in-tube errors. C. Delayed labelling away from the patient increases misidentification risk. D. Samples must be labelled at collection, not later by the laboratory. E. Labelling must occur at the bedside, not later away from the patient.
pearl: Wrong-blood-in-tube errors can cause fatal transfusion reactions; positively identify the patient and label each sample at the bedside straight after taking it, never in advance.
thinking: Blood sample taken ↓ Risk of misidentification ↓ Labelling must link sample to patient at collection ↓ At the patient's side, following local identification procedures
exam_trap: A, pre-printed labels prepared before sampling — it feels efficient, but pre-labelling is a classic cause of wrong-blood-in-tube errors.
takeaway: Label samples at the bedside after positive patient identification, never in advance.

stem:
A study reports a risk ratio of 1.4 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.1–1.8.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: The confidence interval shows that 95% of patients have the disease
options.B: The reported confidence interval does not include 1
options.C: The result cannot be interpreted without knowing the mean
options.E: The risk ratio must equal exactly 1.4 in every patient

correct_answer: B. The reported confidence interval does not include 1
why_correct: For a ratio measure such as a risk ratio, 1 represents no relative difference. The reported interval lies entirely above 1.
why_wrong: A. The confidence interval describes uncertainty in the estimate, not the proportion of patients with disease. C. The risk ratio can be interpreted without a mean. D. A statistically significant association does not prove causation. E. The risk ratio is a group summary estimate and does not apply exactly to each individual.
pearl: For a risk ratio, 1 means no difference; an interval lying entirely above 1 indicates a statistically significant increase in risk, but an association still does not prove causation.
thinking: Risk ratio is a ratio measure ↓ No effect = 1 ↓ 95% CI 1.1–1.8 lies entirely above 1 ↓ The confidence interval does not include 1
exam_trap: D, the study proves causation — a significant result is tempting to over-read, but excluding 1 shows only a statistically significant association.
takeaway: Ratio confidence interval entirely above 1: significant increase in risk, not proof of causation.

stem:
A treatment reduces the risk of an event from 4% to 2%.

What is the relative risk reduction?
why_correct: Relative risk = 2% ÷ 4% = 0.5, so relative risk reduction = 1 − 0.5 = 50%.
why_wrong: A. 2% is the absolute risk reduction, not the relative risk reduction. B. 25% does not correspond to the calculation (4 − 2) ÷ 4. D. 75% would require the risk to fall from 4% to 1%. E. 100% would require the risk to fall to zero.
pearl: Relative risk reduction is the absolute risk reduction divided by the baseline risk; it sounds impressive but says nothing about how common the event was to begin with.
thinking: Relative risk reduction compares the reduction with the original risk.
exam_trap: A, 2% — this is the absolute risk reduction (4% minus 2%), the figure candidates calculate first; the relative reduction expresses that 2% as a share of the 4% baseline.
takeaway: RRR = (control risk − treated risk) ÷ control risk; ARR is the simple difference.

stem:
A treatment reduces the risk of an event from 4% to 2%.

What is the absolute risk reduction?
why_correct: Absolute risk reduction = 4% − 2% = 2 percentage points.
why_wrong: A. 0.5% does not reflect the difference between 4% and 2%. B. 1% underestimates the 2-percentage-point difference. D. 4% is the baseline risk, not the reduction. E. 50% is the relative risk reduction, not the absolute reduction.
pearl: Absolute risk reduction is the plain difference in event rates between groups, and its reciprocal gives the number needed to treat, so here 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50.
thinking: Baseline risk 4%, treated risk 2% ↓ Question asks for the absolute, not relative, change ↓ Subtract: 4% − 2% ↓ ARR = 2%
exam_trap: E, 50% — it is the striking number from the same data, but it is the relative risk reduction (2% ÷ 4%), not the absolute difference in risk.
takeaway: ARR is a subtraction; RRR is a division by the baseline risk.

stem:
A highly specific screening test is applied to a population in which the target disease is extremely rare.

What problem can occur?

options.A: Sensitivity of the test falls to a low level
options.B: Most negative results will be false negatives
options.C: Specificity falls because there are few cases
options.D: Most positive results may be false positives
options.E: The test will miss most cases of the disease

correct_answer: D. Most positive results may be false positives
why_correct: When disease prevalence is very low, even a highly specific test can produce more false-positive than true-positive results among those testing positive.
why_wrong: A. Sensitivity is not altered by disease prevalence. B. In a low-prevalence population negative predictive value is high, so most negatives are true negatives. C. Specificity is not altered by disease prevalence. E. Missing cases depends on sensitivity, which is not changed by low prevalence.
pearl: Predictive values depend on prevalence: in a rare disease even a very specific test gives a low positive predictive value, because false positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives.
thinking: Disease extremely rare ↓ Almost everyone tested is disease-free ↓ A small false-positive rate across many healthy people still gives many false positives ↓ Most positive results may be false positives
exam_trap: E, the test will miss most cases — tempting because rarity feels like a detection problem, but missing cases reflects sensitivity, which prevalence does not change.
takeaway: Low prevalence lowers PPV and raises NPV; sensitivity and specificity stay fixed.

stem:
In a clinical trial, the person recruiting a participant cannot predict which treatment group the participant will enter.

What methodological feature does this describe?
why_correct: Allocation concealment prevents recruiters from knowing the upcoming allocation and reduces selection bias at enrolment.
why_wrong: B. Intention-to-treat refers to analysing participants in their allocated groups. C. External validity concerns generalisability of results to other populations. D. Blinding of outcome assessment concerns those assessing outcomes, not recruitment. E. Loss to follow-up refers to participants who drop out after enrolment.
pearl: Allocation concealment protects the randomisation sequence until the moment of enrolment, preventing selection bias; it is achievable in every trial, unlike blinding.
thinking: Recruiter cannot predict the next allocation ↓ This applies at enrolment, before treatment starts ↓ Protects the random sequence from selection bias ↓ Allocation concealment
exam_trap: D, blinding of outcome assessment — both hide group information, but blinding applies after allocation to assessors, whereas concealment hides the sequence from recruiters before enrolment.
takeaway: Concealment hides the next allocation before enrolment; blinding hides the group afterwards.

stem:
In a clinical trial, 30% of participants in one treatment group cannot be contacted for final outcome assessment.

What is a major concern?
why_correct: Differential or substantial loss to follow-up can distort the observed treatment effect.
why_wrong: A. Recall bias concerns inaccurate recall of past exposure, not loss to follow-up. B. Specificity is a diagnostic test property unrelated to loss to follow-up. C. Loss to follow-up can introduce, not eliminate, bias and imbalance. E. Loss to follow-up does not mean randomisation failed.
pearl: Substantial or unequal loss to follow-up causes attrition bias, because those who drop out often differ in prognosis from those who remain; intention-to-treat and sensitivity analyses help limit it.
thinking: 30% of one arm lost before final assessment ↓ Dropouts may differ systematically from completers ↓ Remaining groups are no longer comparable ↓ Attrition bias
exam_trap: E, guaranteed randomisation failure — loss to follow-up happens after randomisation, so allocation itself was not compromised; the problem is a biased comparison of those left.
takeaway: Large or unequal dropout after randomisation means attrition bias.

stem:
A study finds that people who drink more coffee have higher rates of a particular disease. However, smokers are also more likely to drink large amounts of coffee and smoking is associated with the disease.

What is smoking in this example?
why_correct: Smoking is associated with both the exposure and outcome and may distort the apparent association between coffee consumption and disease.
why_wrong: B. A confidence interval describes statistical uncertainty. C. Randomisation is a method of allocation, not a variable in this association. D. A placebo is an inactive comparator used in trials. E. The outcome is the disease, not smoking.
pearl: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome and is not on the causal pathway between them; it can create or hide an apparent association.
thinking: Coffee drinking associated with disease ↓ Smoking linked to coffee drinking ↓ Smoking independently linked to the disease ↓ Smoking is a confounder
exam_trap: E, the outcome — smoking is closely tied to the disease, but the outcome measured is the disease itself; smoking is a third variable distorting the coffee–disease link.
takeaway: Associated with both exposure and outcome, and not on the causal path: confounder.

stem:
An observational study finds an association between two variables.

Which conclusion is justified?

options.A: Confounding has been excluded by the study design
options.B: It may be causal, but other explanations must be considered
options.C: The association demonstrates a causal relationship
options.D: Reverse causation can be excluded by the statistical analysis
options.E: The association proves that the exposure preceded the outcome

correct_answer: B. It may be causal, but other explanations must be considered
why_correct: Observational associations can result from causation, confounding, bias or chance.
why_wrong: A. Confounding is a key limitation of observational studies and cannot be excluded by design. C. Association does not prove causation. D. Reverse causation remains possible in observational data. E. An association alone does not establish temporal sequence.
pearl: Any observed association can reflect chance, bias, confounding, reverse causation or true causation; observational designs cannot exclude the alternatives, so causal claims need cautious, cumulative evidence.
thinking: Observational design, not randomised ↓ Exposure was not allocated by investigators ↓ Chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation remain possible ↓ May be causal, but alternatives must be considered
exam_trap: C, the association demonstrates causality — tempting when the link is strong, but without randomisation confounding and bias cannot be excluded, so association never proves cause.
takeaway: Association is not causation; consider chance, bias, confounding and reverse causation.

stem:
Researchers assess blood pressure and body weight in 10,000 adults during a single health survey.

What does this study primarily measure?

options.E: Prevalence at a point or period in time

correct_answer: E. Prevalence at a point or period in time
why_correct: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at a particular time rather than following participants prospectively.
why_wrong: A. Effectiveness of an intervention requires an interventional design such as a trial. B. Incidence requires follow-up over time to identify new cases. C. Relative risk requires following exposed and unexposed groups over time, as in a cohort study. D. Survival requires a cohort followed over time.
pearl: A cross-sectional study is a single snapshot of exposure and outcome together, so it measures prevalence; it cannot establish incidence or which came first.
thinking: Single survey of 10,000 adults ↓ Measurements taken once, with no follow-up ↓ Cross-sectional design ↓ Measures prevalence at a point or period
exam_trap: B, incidence of hypertension over time — blood pressure is measured, but incidence needs a disease-free group followed for new cases; one survey only captures existing cases.
takeaway: One-off snapshot survey means cross-sectional study, which measures prevalence.

stem:
A population contains 10,000 people who are disease-free at the beginning of a year. During that year, 100 develop the disease.

What does the 100 new cases represent?
why_correct: Incidence describes new cases arising in a population over a specified period.
why_wrong: A. Specificity is a diagnostic test measure. C. Positive predictive value describes the probability of disease after a positive test. D. Prevalence includes all existing cases, not only new cases. E. Sensitivity is a diagnostic test measure.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases arising in a population at risk over a defined period; here 100 new cases among 10,000 disease-free people in a year gives an incidence of 1% per year.
thinking: 10,000 people disease-free at the start ↓ Followed for one year ↓ 100 new cases develop ↓ New cases over time define incidence
exam_trap: D, prevalence — candidates mix the two, but prevalence counts all existing cases at a time point; here the group started disease-free and only new cases were counted.
takeaway: New cases over time = incidence; all existing cases at a time = prevalence.

stem:
A survey finds that 300 of 10,000 adults currently have a particular condition.

What measure is being estimated?
why_correct: Prevalence describes the proportion of a population with a condition at a specified time or period.
why_wrong: B. Incidence measures new cases over a period, not existing cases. C. A hazard ratio compares event rates over time between groups. D. NNT describes how many patients need treating to prevent one outcome. E. Relative risk compares risk between exposed and unexposed groups.
pearl: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at a given time; it reflects both how often the condition arises and how long it lasts.
thinking: Survey at one time point ↓ Counts adults who currently have the condition ↓ Existing cases ÷ population ↓ Prevalence
exam_trap: B, incidence — tempting as the other basic frequency measure, but incidence requires counting new cases over a period of follow-up, not current cases in a survey.
takeaway: Current cases ÷ population at a point in time = prevalence.

stem:
During an outbreak, 100 people develop a particular infection and 5 of them die from it.

Which measure describes the proportion of affected patients who die from the disease?
why_correct: Case fatality describes deaths among people who have the disease.
why_wrong: B. Cumulative incidence measures new cases in an at-risk population over a period. C. Population mortality rate uses the whole population as the denominator, not only those with the disease. D. Attack rate is the proportion of an exposed population who develop the disease. E. Period prevalence measures existing cases in a population over a period.
pearl: Case fatality uses only those with the disease as the denominator, so it reflects disease severity; a mortality rate uses the whole population at risk.
thinking: 100 people develop the infection ↓ 5 of them die ↓ Denominator is affected people only ↓ Case-fatality proportion (5%)
exam_trap: C, population mortality rate — it also counts deaths, but its denominator is the whole population, not just those who developed the infection.
takeaway: Deaths among the diseased = case fatality; deaths among the population = mortality rate.

stem:
A patient has a medicine listed as requiring caution in severe renal impairment.

What does this generally mean?

options.A: It can be given at standard dose with no extra monitoring
options.B: It is contraindicated and should be stopped
options.C: The dose should be increased to overcome reduced effect
options.D: Weigh risks and benefits; dosing or monitoring may need adjustment
options.E: Renal function needs checking once a year as usual

correct_answer: D. Weigh risks and benefits; dosing or monitoring may need adjustment
why_correct: A precaution is not necessarily an absolute prohibition; it signals the need for additional consideration or monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Caution indicates potential risk, so additional consideration or monitoring is needed. B. Caution does not mean an absolute contraindication. C. Renal impairment usually requires dose reduction or monitoring, not increase. E. Severe renal impairment with a cautioned medicine needs closer monitoring than routine annual checks.
pearl: A caution is not a contraindication: the medicine may still be used after weighing risk and benefit, often with a lower dose, longer interval or closer monitoring of renal function and adverse effects.
thinking: Medicine listed with caution in severe renal impairment ↓ Caution differs from contraindication ↓ Risk of accumulation or toxicity ↓ Weigh risk and benefit and adjust dose or monitoring
exam_trap: B, contraindicated and stopped — tempting as the safe-sounding answer, but a caution is not an absolute prohibition and stopping a needed medicine can itself cause harm.
takeaway: Caution means weigh and adjust; contraindication means avoid.

stem:
A pregnant patient asks whether a medicine prescribed before pregnancy should be continued.

What is the safest general approach?

options.A: Halve the dose to reduce fetal exposure
options.B: Advise the patient to decide using information found online
options.C: Stop the medicine until the end of the first trimester
options.D: Review the medicine's risks and benefits in pregnancy before any change
options.E: Continue unchanged without reviewing the indication

correct_answer: D. Review the medicine's risks and benefits in pregnancy before any change
why_correct: Abruptly stopping some medicines can also cause harm. Decisions should consider the medicine, indication, pregnancy stage and alternatives.
why_wrong: A. Arbitrary dose reduction may cause loss of disease control and harm mother and fetus. B. Patients need balanced, reliable information from the clinician to make an informed decision. C. Abruptly stopping some medicines, e.g. antiseizure medicines, can harm mother and fetus. E. Some medicines are unsafe in pregnancy and need review or switching.
pearl: Many medicines for chronic conditions are safer continued than stopped in pregnancy; abrupt withdrawal of drugs such as antiseizure medicines can harm both mother and baby, so review before any change.
thinking: Pregnant patient on a pre-existing medicine ↓ Both continuing and stopping carry potential risk ↓ Consider drug, indication, stage of pregnancy and alternatives ↓ Review risks and benefits before any change
exam_trap: C, stop until the end of the first trimester — feels protective to the fetus, but abrupt cessation can cause relapse, such as seizures, harming mother and fetus.
takeaway: In pregnancy, review each medicine individually; never stop or halve it reflexively.

stem:
An older patient with significantly reduced kidney function is prescribed a medicine that is substantially renally cleared.

What should the prescriber consider?

options.D: Whether the dose or dosing interval needs adjustment
options.E: Giving the same dose regardless of renal function

correct_answer: D. Whether the dose or dosing interval needs adjustment
why_correct: Reduced renal clearance can increase drug exposure and toxicity for medicines that are substantially renally eliminated.
why_wrong: A. Stopping all medicines is unnecessary; individual review is required. B. Increasing the dose would increase toxicity risk in reduced clearance. C. Renal function is directly relevant for renally cleared drugs. E. The same dose may lead to accumulation and toxicity.
pearl: For substantially renally cleared drugs, reduced kidney function raises drug levels and toxicity risk; older people often have reduced clearance even when serum creatinine looks near normal.
thinking: Older patient with significantly reduced kidney function ↓ Drug is substantially renally cleared ↓ Clearance falls and the drug accumulates ↓ Consider adjusting the dose or dosing interval
exam_trap: E, give the same dose regardless of renal function — tempting if the patient seems stable, but reduced clearance causes accumulation and toxicity at standard doses.
takeaway: Renally cleared drug plus poor kidney function: reduce the dose or lengthen the interval.

stem:
A patient is taking a medicine with a narrow therapeutic index for which blood-level monitoring is recommended.

Why is monitoring used?

options.A: To replace clinical assessment of response
options.B: To confirm that the patient has taken every prescribed dose on time
options.C: To eliminate the risk of dose-related adverse effects from treatment
options.D: To remove the need for clinical review of response and toxicity
options.E: To help maintain drug exposure within an appropriate range

correct_answer: E. To help maintain drug exposure within an appropriate range
why_correct: Therapeutic drug monitoring can help balance efficacy and toxicity for selected medicines.
why_wrong: A. Drug levels complement, not replace, clinical assessment. B. Levels may suggest adherence problems but do not prove every dose was taken. C. Monitoring reduces but does not eliminate adverse effects. D. Levels must be interpreted alongside clinical review of response and toxicity.
pearl: Therapeutic drug monitoring guides dosing of narrow-therapeutic-index drugs such as lithium, digoxin, phenytoin and aminoglycosides, but levels are always interpreted with the clinical picture.
thinking: Narrow therapeutic index ↓ Small gap between effective and toxic levels ↓ Blood levels guide dose adjustment ↓ Keeps exposure within an appropriate range
exam_trap: C, to eliminate dose-related adverse effects — monitoring reduces toxicity risk but cannot remove it; toxicity can occur within range and levels need clinical interpretation.
takeaway: Drug levels guide dosing within a range; they never replace clinical review.

stem:
A doctor identifies a suspected serious adverse reaction to a medicine.

What is an important action?

options.A: Report it once causality has been proven by rechallenge
options.B: Continue the medicine and review at the next clinic
options.C: Record it in the notes, with no further reporting needed
options.D: Rechallenge the patient to confirm the reaction
options.E: Consider reporting it via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme

correct_answer: E. Consider reporting it via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme
why_correct: Reporting suspected adverse drug reactions contributes to medicine safety surveillance.
why_wrong: A. Suspected reactions should be reported; proof of causality is not required. B. A suspected serious reaction requires prompt reassessment of the medicine. C. Serious suspected reactions should be reported for safety surveillance, not only documented locally. D. Rechallenge after a serious reaction may be dangerous and is not required before reporting.
pearl: Suspected adverse drug reactions are reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme; proof of causation is not needed, and serious suspected reactions should always be reported.
thinking: Suspected serious adverse reaction ↓ Causality need not be proven ↓ National medicines safety surveillance relies on clinician reports ↓ Report via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme
exam_trap: A, report once causality is proven by rechallenge — sounds rigorous, but suspicion is enough to report, and rechallenge after a serious reaction may be dangerous.
takeaway: Suspicion is enough: report serious adverse drug reactions via Yellow Card.

stem:
A doctor notices that a prescription contains the wrong dose before the medicine reaches the patient.

What is this best described as?
why_correct: A near miss is an error that could have caused harm but was detected or prevented before reaching the patient.
why_wrong: B. The error was intercepted before reaching the patient, so no injury occurred. C. An adverse drug reaction is a harmful response to a medicine, but here no drug was given. D. A contraindication is a reason not to use a medicine, not an intercepted error. E. A diagnostic error relates to diagnosis, not prescribing.
pearl: A near miss is an error intercepted before it reaches the patient; it should still be reported through local incident systems because it exposes the same system weaknesses as harmful errors.
thinking: Wrong dose on a prescription ↓ Error spotted before the medicine reaches the patient ↓ No harm occurred, but it could have ↓ Near miss
exam_trap: C, an adverse drug reaction — tempting because a drug is involved, but an ADR is a harmful response to a medicine actually given, whereas here nothing was administered.
takeaway: Error caught before reaching the patient = near miss; still report it.

stem:
A medication error occurs despite several checks being in place.

What is the most appropriate organisational response?

options.A: Suspend the staff member involved while a disciplinary investigation is completed
options.B: Identify system and human factors and how recurrence can be prevented
options.C: Add a further independent checking step and then close the incident report
options.D: Retrain the individual and take no further action
options.E: Record the error in the individual's annual appraisal and close the incident

correct_answer: B. Identify system and human factors and how recurrence can be prevented
why_correct: Patient-safety learning should examine contributing factors and system improvements rather than focusing solely on individual blame.
why_wrong: A. A blame-focused response ignores system factors and discourages reporting. C. Adding checks without analysing why existing checks failed misses the contributing factors. D. Focusing on the individual alone ignores system factors and prevents organisational learning. E. Treating the error as an individual matter prevents system-level learning.
pearl: Patient-safety investigation focuses on learning: identify the system and human factors behind an error, because a just culture encourages reporting and prevents recurrence.
thinking: Error occurred despite several checks ↓ Points to system weaknesses, not only individual fault ↓ Analyse contributing system and human factors ↓ Prevent recurrence through organisational learning
exam_trap: C, add another checking step and close — looks like action, but adding a check without understanding why the existing checks failed misses the real contributing factors.
takeaway: Respond to errors with system learning, not individual blame.

stem:
A clinical team measures its compliance with an established guideline, compares the results with the expected standard and introduces changes.

What activity is this?
why_correct: Clinical audit assesses current practice against predefined standards and can be followed by improvement measures.
why_wrong: B. A case-control study compares exposure histories between cases and controls. C. Basic science research investigates biological mechanisms. D. An RCT tests interventions by random allocation, not compliance with standards. E. Qualitative interview studies explore experiences rather than measure against a standard.
pearl: Clinical audit measures current practice against an agreed standard, implements change, then re-audits to close the loop; it asks whether we are doing what we should, not what we should do.
thinking: Established guideline used as the standard ↓ Team measures its own compliance ↓ Compares with the expected standard and makes changes ↓ Clinical audit
exam_trap: D, randomised controlled trial — involves measuring outcomes, but an RCT generates new evidence by random allocation; audit checks practice against an existing standard.
takeaway: Audit compares practice with a set standard; research creates new knowledge.

stem:
A ward repeatedly measures the time taken to administer antibiotics, introduces a change, measures performance again and adjusts the intervention based on the results.

What does this represent?
why_correct: Quality improvement uses iterative measurement and change to improve healthcare processes or outcomes.
why_wrong: B. Randomisation is a trial allocation method, not an improvement cycle. C. Diagnostic screening identifies disease in populations. D. Surveillance monitors data but does not involve iterative change cycles. E. Case-control research compares exposures between cases and controls.
pearl: Quality improvement uses rapid repeated Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles: test a small change, measure its effect, then adapt; iteration is the core of the method.
thinking: Repeated measurement of antibiotic timing ↓ A change is introduced ↓ Performance remeasured and the intervention adjusted ↓ Iterative cycles of change ↓ Quality improvement
exam_trap: D, epidemiological surveillance only — it involves repeated measurement, but surveillance only monitors data; here changes are introduced and refined, which defines QI.
takeaway: Measure, change, remeasure, adapt: quality improvement through PDSA cycles.

stem:
A patient is invited to participate in a screening programme.

Which principle is important?

options.A: Explain that screening carries no risk of harm
options.B: Explain that a positive screening result confirms the diagnosis and treatment is needed
options.C: Explain that participation is a requirement of continued registration with the practice
options.D: Discuss the benefits but avoid mentioning false positives so as not to cause anxiety
options.E: Explain benefits, limitations and possible consequences to allow informed choice

correct_answer: E. Explain benefits, limitations and possible consequences to allow informed choice
why_correct: Screening can have benefits as well as harms such as false positives, false negatives, overdiagnosis and unnecessary investigations.
why_wrong: A. Screening can cause harms such as false positives and overdiagnosis. B. A positive screening test requires diagnostic confirmation. C. Screening is voluntary and requires informed choice. D. Patients should be informed about false positives as part of informed choice.
pearl: A screening test is not the same as a diagnostic test.
thinking: Patient invited to screening ↓ Screening is voluntary ↓ It carries harms such as false positives and overdiagnosis ↓ Explain benefits, limitations and consequences for informed choice
exam_trap: D, discuss benefits but avoid mentioning false positives — feels kind, but withholding known harms prevents informed choice and falls short of good consent practice.
takeaway: Screening is a choice: explain benefits and harms, including false positives.

stem:
A 2-day-old term baby develops mild jaundice. The baby is feeding well and is otherwise clinically well.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin for presumed neonatal sepsis
options.B: Start phototherapy on the postnatal ward before measuring bilirubin
options.C: Advise switching from breast milk to formula feeds until it settles
options.D: Measure the bilirubin according to the neonatal jaundice pathway
options.E: Reassure and advise placing the baby in sunlight at home each day

correct_answer: D. Measure the bilirubin according to the neonatal jaundice pathway
why_correct: Clinically apparent neonatal jaundice requires assessment of bilirubin according to age and gestation to determine whether treatment is required.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated in a well baby without signs of infection. B. Phototherapy decisions require measured bilirubin plotted on age-specific thresholds (NICE CG98). C. Stopping breastfeeding is not recommended for neonatal jaundice. E. Visual inspection is unreliable and sunlight is not a recommended treatment; jaundice needs measurement.
pearl: Visual assessment of jaundice is unreliable, so every baby with suspected jaundice needs a bilirubin measurement plotted on a treatment threshold graph for age and gestation.
thinking: Neonatal jaundice is assessed using age-specific bilirubin thresholds, not visual appearance alone.
exam_trap: E, reassure and advise sunlight — tempting as the baby is well and the jaundice mild, but severity cannot be judged by eye and sunlight is not a safe or recommended treatment.
takeaway: Suspected neonatal jaundice: measure the bilirubin, never judge by eye.

stem:
A newborn develops visible jaundice at 10 hours of age.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.D: Reassure the parents that this is physiological

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment for pathological jaundice
why_correct: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours is potentially pathological and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Breastfeeding should usually continue; stopping it is not indicated. C. Oral iron has no role in neonatal jaundice. D. Jaundice within 24 hours is not physiological. E. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is a red flag requiring urgent assessment with bilirubin measured within 2 hours (NICE CG98), not routine review.
pearl: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is pathological until proven otherwise, often from haemolysis such as rhesus or ABO incompatibility, and needs an urgent bilirubin measurement.
thinking: Visible jaundice at 10 hours old ↓ Onset within the first 24 hours ↓ Physiological jaundice does not appear this early ↓ Urgent assessment for pathological jaundice
exam_trap: D, reassure as physiological — physiological jaundice is common, but it appears after 24 hours; jaundice before then suggests haemolysis and needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Jaundice under 24 hours old is pathological until proven otherwise.

stem:
A newborn at increased risk of hypoglycaemia is found to have a low blood glucose concentration.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Follow the neonatal hypoglycaemia pathway, including feeding and reassessment
options.B: Delay all feeding until the glucose has been rechecked with a laboratory sample
options.C: Accept the result without further action because the baby appears clinically well
options.D: Discharge home with advice to feed on demand and to attend if the baby is unwell
options.E: Give formula top-ups and recheck the capillary blood glucose level in 24 hours

correct_answer: A. Follow the neonatal hypoglycaemia pathway, including feeding and reassessment
why_correct: At-risk neonates with low glucose require prompt assessment and management according to the clinical pathway.
why_wrong: B. Feeding is a central part of management and should not be delayed. C. Neonatal hypoglycaemia can be asymptomatic and still cause neurological harm. D. Discharge without management risks harm. E. Rechecking after 24 hours is far too late for an at-risk baby with low glucose.
pearl: Neonatal hypoglycaemia can be asymptomatic yet still cause brain injury, so at-risk babies with low glucose need prompt feeding, structured rechecks and escalation per the local pathway.
thinking: At-risk newborn ↓ Low blood glucose found ↓ Can cause neurological harm even if asymptomatic ↓ Follow the hypoglycaemia pathway with feeding and reassessment
exam_trap: C, accept the result as the baby looks well — tempting, but hypoglycaemia is often asymptomatic in neonates and can still cause lasting neurological damage.
takeaway: Low glucose in an at-risk newborn: feed, recheck and escalate, even if well.

stem:
A newborn develops grunting, nasal flaring and increased work of breathing shortly after birth.

What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Oral antibiotics and early discharge home with the mother
options.C: Assess ABC urgently and involve the neonatal team
options.D: Encourage an early breastfeed to help settle the breathing
options.E: Perform a lumbar puncture before assessing breathing

correct_answer: C. Assess ABC urgently and involve the neonatal team
why_correct: Respiratory distress in a newborn can deteriorate rapidly and requires immediate ABC assessment and appropriate neonatal support.
why_wrong: A. Oral antibiotics and discharge are unsafe for a baby with respiratory distress. B. Respiratory distress requires active assessment and management, not routine checks. D. Feeding a baby in respiratory distress risks aspiration and worsening distress. E. Airway, breathing and circulation take priority over a lumbar puncture.
pearl: Grunting, nasal flaring and increased work of breathing in a newborn signal respiratory distress, with causes from transient tachypnoea to sepsis; assess ABC and call the neonatal team early.
