exam_trap: A, aspirate both sides to exclude malignancy — aspiration is right for unexplained or atypical effusions, but typical bilateral effusions in heart failure are treated first.
takeaway: Typical bilateral effusions in heart failure: treat the heart failure first.

stem:
A patient coughs up a small amount of fresh blood.

What is the appropriate general approach?

options.A: Assess the severity and investigate the underlying cause
options.B: Reassure if the patient is under 40
options.D: Prescribe an antitussive and review if it recurs
options.E: Give oral iron and recheck in 3 months

correct_answer: A. Assess the severity and investigate the underlying cause
why_correct: Haemoptysis has a wide differential diagnosis, ranging from infection to malignancy and pulmonary vascular disease. The severity and cause need assessment.
why_wrong: B. Young patients can have serious causes such as tuberculosis or PE. C. Anticoagulation could worsen bleeding and is not given without a diagnosis such as PE. D. Haemoptysis can indicate serious disease such as cancer or pulmonary embolism and needs assessment. E. Iron without assessment ignores the underlying cause.
pearl: Haemoptysis needs assessment of volume and stability, then investigation including a chest X-ray; causes range from infection and tuberculosis to lung cancer and pulmonary embolism.
thinking: Coughing up fresh blood ↓ Wide differential from infection to cancer or PE ↓ Assess severity and stability ↓ Investigate the underlying cause
exam_trap: B, reassure if under 40 — age matters for cancer referral pathways, but younger patients can still have tuberculosis, PE or other serious causes.
takeaway: Every episode of haemoptysis needs assessment and a cause found.

stem:
A patient has chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss. Endoscopy shows areas of inflamed bowel separated by normal-looking segments.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Crohn's disease characteristically causes patchy or “skip” areas of inflammation and can affect different parts of the gastrointestinal tract.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease affects the small bowel mucosa diffusely and does not cause patchy inflamed segments. C. IBS does not cause endoscopic inflammation or weight loss. D. Ulcerative colitis causes continuous inflammation from the rectum without skip lesions. E. Diverticular disease causes outpouchings, usually in the sigmoid colon, not skip inflammation.
pearl: Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gut from mouth to anus, with skip lesions and transmural inflammation; ulcerative colitis is continuous from the rectum and mucosal.
thinking: Chronic pain, diarrhoea and weight loss ↓ Endoscopy shows inflamed segments ↓ Separated by normal bowel (skip lesions) ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: D, ulcerative colitis — the other inflammatory bowel disease with similar symptoms, but UC is continuous from the rectum without skip lesions.
takeaway: Skip lesions mean Crohn's; continuous inflammation from the rectum means UC.

stem:
A school-aged child repeatedly soils their underwear with stool and has a history of infrequent, hard bowel motions.

What is the most likely underlying problem?
why_correct: Chronic constipation can cause faecal impaction with leakage of softer stool around the impacted stool.
why_wrong: A. A history of infrequent hard stools indicates retentive constipation rather than non-retentive soiling. B. Hirschsprung disease usually presents in the neonatal period with delayed passage of meconium. D. Lactose intolerance causes diarrhoea and bloating, not hard infrequent stools. E. Coeliac disease is not suggested by hard infrequent stools with soiling.
pearl: Most childhood soiling is overflow from chronic constipation with faecal impaction; treat with disimpaction using an osmotic laxative such as macrogol, then maintenance therapy.
thinking: School-aged child soiling ↓ History of infrequent, hard stools ↓ Faecal impaction in the rectum ↓ Softer stool leaks around it ↓ Constipation with overflow soiling
exam_trap: A, behavioural soiling without constipation — soiling may look behavioural, but a history of hard infrequent stools shows retentive constipation with overflow.
takeaway: Soiling with hard infrequent stools is overflow: treat the constipation.

stem:
A 15-year-old boy has no testicular enlargement or other signs of puberty.

What should this finding prompt?

options.C: Reassurance that this is always normal

why_correct: Absence of pubertal development beyond the expected age range warrants clinical assessment for delayed puberty.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism is not diagnosed from delayed puberty. B. Antibiotics have no role in delayed puberty. C. Absent pubertal signs at 15 in a boy is outside the normal range and needs assessment. D. Absent puberty is not diagnostic of diabetes mellitus.
pearl: In boys, no testicular enlargement by around 14 years defines delayed puberty; constitutional delay is commonest, but chronic illness and hypogonadism need excluding.
thinking: 15-year-old boy ↓ No testicular enlargement ↓ No other pubertal signs ↓ Beyond the normal age range ↓ Assess for delayed puberty
exam_trap: C, reassurance that this is always normal — constitutional delay is common, but it is a diagnosis made after assessment, not assumed.
takeaway: No pubertal signs in a mid-teen boy needs assessment for delayed puberty.

stem:
A boy has recurrent painful joint swelling after minor trauma. His maternal family history includes affected male relatives.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Haemophilia A is an inherited coagulation disorder that can cause recurrent haemarthroses and has an X-linked inheritance pattern.
why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia does not cause recurrent haemarthroses. B. Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive and causes vaso-occlusion rather than haemarthroses. D. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis, not joint bleeding, and is usually autosomal dominant. E. ITP causes mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae rather than haemarthroses and is not X-linked.
pearl: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive factor VIII deficiency, so it mostly affects males via carrier mothers and causes haemarthroses and muscle bleeds with a prolonged APTT.
thinking: Boy with recurrent haemarthroses ↓ Joint bleeds after minor trauma suggest a clotting factor defect ↓ Affected male relatives on the maternal side ↓ X-linked inheritance ↓ Haemophilia A
exam_trap: E, immune thrombocytopenia — a bleeding disorder, but platelet problems cause mucocutaneous bleeding and petechiae, not haemarthroses, and ITP is not X-linked.
takeaway: Haemarthroses in a boy with affected maternal male relatives: haemophilia.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy develops a temperature of 38.5°C and feels acutely unwell.

What should be assumed until assessed appropriately?

options.A: Dehydration secondary to chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting
options.B: Drug fever as a direct reaction to the chemotherapy agents
options.C: Possible neutropenic sepsis requiring urgent assessment
options.D: Viral infection suitable for home management with paracetamol
options.E: Expected fever following the most recent chemotherapy cycle

correct_answer: C. Possible neutropenic sepsis requiring urgent assessment
why_correct: Fever or clinical deterioration in a patient who may be neutropenic is a medical emergency because infection can progress rapidly.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration does not explain fever and must not be assumed. B. Drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion and must not be assumed. D. Fever after chemotherapy must be assessed urgently as possible neutropenic sepsis. E. Fever is not a normal chemotherapy effect.
pearl: Fever or feeling unwell during chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; give empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics promptly without waiting for the neutrophil count.
thinking: Receiving chemotherapy ↓ Temperature 38.5°C and acutely unwell ↓ May be neutropenic ↓ Infection can progress rapidly ↓ Possible neutropenic sepsis
exam_trap: D, viral infection for home management — many fevers are viral, but in a patient on chemotherapy fever must be treated as neutropenic sepsis until shown otherwise.
takeaway: Fever on chemotherapy: urgent assessment and antibiotics, no waiting.

stem:
A patient develops an acute flu-like illness followed by jaundice after eating food during travel.

Which infection is a possible cause?
why_correct: Hepatitis A is transmitted mainly by the faecal–oral route and can cause an acute hepatitis syndrome with jaundice.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis C is blood-borne and usually asymptomatic acutely, not food-borne. B. Tuberculosis does not typically cause an acute food-borne hepatitis with jaundice. C. Malaria is mosquito-borne, not food-borne, although it should be considered in febrile travellers. E. HIV is not transmitted through food.
pearl: Hepatitis A spreads faeco-orally through contaminated food and water, causes acute self-limiting hepatitis and does not become chronic; vaccination is offered for travel to endemic areas.
thinking: Travel and eating local food ↓ Faeco-oral exposure ↓ Flu-like prodrome followed by jaundice ↓ Acute viral hepatitis ↓ Hepatitis A
exam_trap: C, malaria only — fever with jaundice in a traveller should always raise malaria, but it is mosquito-borne, and the food exposure points to hepatitis A.
takeaway: Jaundice after contaminated food abroad: think hepatitis A.

stem:
A patient is found incidentally to have persistently abnormal liver enzymes. They previously received a blood transfusion many years ago.

Which chronic viral infection should be considered?
why_correct: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne infection that can remain asymptomatic for years and progress to chronic liver disease.
why_wrong: A. Influenza does not cause chronic liver enzyme abnormalities. B. Hepatitis A causes acute infection only and is spread faeco-orally. D. Mumps does not cause chronic hepatitis. E. Measles does not cause chronic hepatitis.
pearl: Hepatitis C often stays silent for decades while causing chronic liver disease; transfusion before UK donor screening began is a recognised risk factor, and direct-acting antivirals now cure most cases.
thinking: Persistently abnormal liver enzymes ↓ Found incidentally, no symptoms ↓ Blood transfusion many years ago ↓ Blood-borne chronic infection ↓ Hepatitis C
exam_trap: B, hepatitis A — a familiar hepatitis virus, but it spreads faeco-orally and causes only acute infection, never chronic disease.
takeaway: Old transfusion plus abnormal LFTs: test for hepatitis C.

stem:
A patient has had a recent potential sexual exposure to HIV and asks whether a negative test immediately afterwards completely excludes infection.

What is the key concept to explain?

options.A: A test is always positive immediately
options.C: A negative test permanently excludes future infection
options.D: HIV tests have a window period after exposure
options.E: HIV can never be diagnosed by blood testing

correct_answer: D. HIV tests have a window period after exposure
why_correct: Diagnostic tests may not detect infection immediately after exposure, so the timing and type of test matter.
why_wrong: A. Tests are not immediately positive after exposure because of the window period. B. Testing is recommended after exposure regardless of symptoms. C. A negative test does not protect against future infection. E. HIV is routinely diagnosed by blood tests.
pearl: HIV tests can miss very recent infection, so a negative result soon after exposure must be repeated after the window period; post-exposure prophylaxis should be considered early.
thinking: Recent possible HIV exposure ↓ Test done immediately afterwards ↓ Antibodies and antigen not yet detectable ↓ Window period ↓ Negative result cannot yet exclude infection
exam_trap: C, a negative test permanently excludes infection — tempting reassurance, but a test soon after exposure may be falsely negative and says nothing about future exposure.
takeaway: An early negative HIV test must be repeated after the window period.

stem:
A survival analysis reports a hazard ratio of 0.70 for treatment compared with control.

What does the hazard ratio describe?

options.A: The prevalence of disease in the treated study population
options.B: The absolute number of events prevented per 100 patients treated
options.C: The sensitivity of the treatment in detecting true events
options.D: The number needed to treat over the whole follow-up period
options.E: The relative event rate over time between the groups

correct_answer: E. The relative event rate over time between the groups
why_correct: A hazard ratio compares the instantaneous event rates between groups over the follow-up period.
why_wrong: A. Prevalence is not described by a hazard ratio. B. Absolute events prevented per 100 treated are derived from the absolute risk reduction, not the hazard ratio. C. Sensitivity is a property of diagnostic tests. D. NNT is calculated from the absolute risk reduction, not the hazard ratio.
pearl: A hazard ratio of 0.70 means the event rate in the treated group is about 30% lower than in controls throughout follow-up; it is a relative, not an absolute, measure.
thinking: Survival analysis reported ↓ Hazard ratio compares event rates over time ↓ Value below 1 favours treatment ↓ Relative event rate between groups
exam_trap: B, events prevented per 100 treated — the 0.70 tempts conversion into numbers prevented, but that needs absolute risks; a hazard ratio is a relative measure.
takeaway: Hazard ratio is a relative rate over time; below 1 favours treatment.

stem:
A systematic review presents a forest plot.

What does each study's horizontal line commonly represent?

options.A: The confidence interval around its effect estimate
options.B: The number of participants in that individual study
options.C: The study's funding source and conflicts of interest
options.E: The p-value for that individual study's own comparison

correct_answer: A. The confidence interval around its effect estimate
why_correct: In a conventional forest plot, the point represents the study's effect estimate and the horizontal line represents its confidence interval.
why_wrong: B. Sample size is usually shown by the size of the box (study weight), not the horizontal line. C. Funding source and conflicts of interest are not represented on a forest plot. D. Disease prevalence is not shown by the line. E. The horizontal line shows the confidence interval, not the study's p-value.
pearl: In a forest plot each square is a study's estimate, its size reflects the study's weight, the horizontal line is the confidence interval and the diamond is the pooled result.
thinking: Systematic review forest plot ↓ Each study shows a point estimate ↓ Horizontal line spans the range of plausible values ↓ Confidence interval
exam_trap: B, number of participants — larger studies do have narrower lines, but sample size and weight are shown by the box size; the line itself is the confidence interval.
takeaway: Forest plot: the box is the estimate, the horizontal line is its confidence interval.

stem:
A meta-analysis contains studies with markedly different effect estimates and substantial statistical heterogeneity.

What does this indicate?

options.B: Results vary more than expected from chance alone
options.C: The pooled effect shows the intervention is ineffective
options.D: The fixed-effect pooled estimate is the most reliable
options.E: The studies were drawn from identical patient populations

correct_answer: B. Results vary more than expected from chance alone
why_correct: Statistical heterogeneity indicates variation between study results beyond that expected from chance alone.
why_wrong: A. Heterogeneity means the results differ, not that they are identical. C. Heterogeneity describes variability between studies; it does not indicate the intervention is ineffective. D. Substantial heterogeneity makes a fixed-effect estimate less appropriate and calls for caution and exploration of its sources. E. Heterogeneity often reflects differences in populations, interventions or methods rather than identical populations.
pearl: Substantial heterogeneity, often quantified with the I² statistic, means studies disagree beyond chance; reviewers should explore why and pool cautiously, often with a random-effects model.
thinking: Meta-analysis ↓ Markedly different effect estimates ↓ Substantial statistical heterogeneity ↓ Variation greater than chance alone
exam_trap: C, the intervention is ineffective — differing results seem to undermine the treatment, but heterogeneity describes inconsistency between studies, not lack of effect.
takeaway: Heterogeneity means studies disagree beyond chance: explore why before pooling.

stem:
A 15-year-old requests confidential medical advice and appears able to understand the nature, purpose and consequences of the proposed intervention.

What principle is relevant?
why_correct: A child under 16 may be able to consent to medical treatment if they demonstrate sufficient maturity and understanding, known as Gillick competence.
why_wrong: A. A Gillick-competent young person can consent without parental consent. B. Competence does not mean treatment is automatically refused. C. The Mental Health Act is not relevant to a routine request for confidential advice. D. Lasting power of attorney applies only to adults aged 18 or over who have lost capacity.
pearl: A young person under 16 can consent if Gillick competent, understanding the nature, purpose and consequences; their confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm.
thinking: 15-year-old requests confidential advice ↓ Under 16 ↓ Understands nature, purpose and consequences ↓ Sufficient maturity to consent ↓ Gillick competence
exam_trap: A, automatic parental consent — parents are often involved at this age, but a Gillick-competent young person can consent independently and confidentiality applies.
takeaway: Under 16 and fully understands: Gillick competent and can consent.

stem:
A competent adult tells a doctor that they intend to seriously harm another identifiable person and provides a specific plan.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Maintain confidentiality because the patient has not consented to any disclosure
options.B: Share the full consultation record with the patient's employer and the police
options.C: Inform all staff in the practice so they can be vigilant
options.D: Document the disclosure in the notes and review at the next routine appointment
options.E: Consider disclosure to protect the person at risk and seek senior advice

correct_answer: E. Consider disclosure to protect the person at risk and seek senior advice
why_correct: Confidentiality is important but not absolute. Disclosure may be justified where necessary to protect others from serious harm, using the minimum necessary information and appropriate professional/legal advice.
why_wrong: A. Confidentiality is not absolute; disclosure without consent may be justified to protect others from serious harm. B. Sharing the full record with an employer and the police is a disproportionate breach; disclosure should be the minimum necessary to appropriate people. C. Disclosure should be limited to those who need to know, not all practice staff. D. Waiting until the next appointment fails to act on a credible threat of serious harm.
pearl: Confidentiality is not absolute: a credible, specific threat of serious harm to an identifiable person can justify disclosure without consent, limited to the minimum necessary and to those who need to know.
thinking: Competent adult discloses intent to harm ↓ Specific plan and identifiable victim = credible serious risk ↓ Public interest can outweigh confidentiality ↓ Disclose minimum necessary after senior advice ↓ E
exam_trap: A, maintain confidentiality — tempting because consent is normally required, but confidentiality is not absolute when there is a credible risk of serious harm to others.
takeaway: Serious, credible risk to others can justify disclosure: proportionate, minimal and with senior advice.

stem:
A pregnant woman has been exposed to someone with suspected rubella.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Arrange urgent assessment because rubella can harm the fetus
options.B: Offer termination of pregnancy on the basis of the exposure
options.C: Reassure her, as fetal harm occurs in late pregnancy
options.E: Give a dose of MMR vaccine now to protect the pregnancy

correct_answer: A. Arrange urgent assessment because rubella can harm the fetus
why_correct: Maternal rubella infection can cause congenital rubella syndrome, so suspected exposure requires appropriate assessment. Live vaccines such as MMR are not routinely given during pregnancy.
why_wrong: B. Exposure alone does not justify termination; immunity and infection must be assessed first. C. Fetal risk from rubella is greatest in early pregnancy, not late pregnancy, so this reassurance is wrong. D. Rubella is viral, so antibiotics have no role. E. MMR is a live vaccine and is contraindicated in pregnancy.
pearl: Rubella is most dangerous to the fetus in early pregnancy; after exposure, check immunity and test for infection promptly. MMR is live and must not be given during pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant woman exposed to suspected rubella ↓ Risk of congenital rubella syndrome, greatest early in pregnancy ↓ Needs prompt immunity check and testing ↓ A, urgent assessment
exam_trap: E, MMR now — tempting as a protective step, but MMR is a live vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy; non-immune women are offered it after delivery.
takeaway: Rubella contact in pregnancy means prompt assessment; never give live vaccines during pregnancy.

stem:
A pregnant woman is exposed to a child with suspected parvovirus B19 infection.

Why is medical assessment important?

options.B: Parvovirus B19 infection can cause fetal complications
options.C: It is treated with routine antibiotics
options.E: It causes congenital deafness in every affected pregnancy

correct_answer: B. Parvovirus B19 infection can cause fetal complications
why_correct: Maternal parvovirus B19 infection can affect the fetus, including causing fetal anaemia, so appropriate assessment is required.
why_wrong: A. Exposure does not require caesarean section. C. Parvovirus is viral and is not treated with antibiotics. D. Parvovirus B19 does not usually cause maternal pneumonia; that concern relates to varicella. E. Congenital deafness is linked to rubella and CMV, not parvovirus B19.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal anaemia and hydrops, so exposure needs prompt serological assessment and, if infection is confirmed, fetal monitoring.
thinking: Pregnant woman exposed to parvovirus B19 ↓ Virus targets red-cell precursors ↓ Risk of fetal anaemia and hydrops ↓ B, fetal complications
exam_trap: E, congenital deafness — tempting as it sounds like a classic congenital infection effect, but deafness is linked to rubella and CMV; parvovirus causes fetal anaemia, and never in every pregnancy.
takeaway: Parvovirus in pregnancy risks fetal anaemia and hydrops: assess exposure promptly.

stem:
A child with sickle cell disease develops a fever and appears unwell.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.B: Manage as a viral illness with fluids and paracetamol at home
options.C: Treat as possible serious infection needing urgent assessment
options.D: Give paracetamol and seek review if fever lasts 48 hours

correct_answer: C. Treat as possible serious infection needing urgent assessment
why_correct: People with sickle cell disease are at increased risk of serious infection, particularly from encapsulated organisms.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction may precipitate a vaso-occlusive crisis. B. Fever in sickle cell disease may indicate serious bacterial infection because of hyposplenism, so home management is unsafe. D. Waiting 48 hours risks overwhelming sepsis in a hyposplenic child. E. Iron is not indicated and does not address infection.
pearl: Children with sickle cell disease are functionally hyposplenic, so fever must be treated as possible bacterial sepsis with urgent assessment rather than managed at home.
thinking: Sickle cell disease ↓ Functional hyposplenism ↓ High risk from encapsulated organisms ↓ Febrile and unwell = possible sepsis ↓ C, urgent assessment
exam_trap: B, home management as a viral illness — tempting because most childhood fevers are viral, but hyposplenism means fever in sickle cell disease may be overwhelming bacterial sepsis.
takeaway: Fever in sickle cell disease is sepsis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A young child with sickle cell disease develops sudden pallor, lethargy and abdominal enlargement. Their haemoglobin is markedly lower than usual.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Acute pooling of blood in the spleen can cause sudden splenomegaly, anaemia and cardiovascular compromise in young children with sickle cell disease.
why_wrong: B. Parvovirus-related aplastic crisis causes a sudden fall in haemoglobin with reticulocytopenia but not acute splenic enlargement. C. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria, not acute anaemia. D. Appendicitis does not cause a sudden haemoglobin drop with splenic enlargement. E. Acute chest syndrome causes chest pain, fever and new pulmonary infiltrates rather than abdominal enlargement.
pearl: Splenic sequestration causes sudden pallor, a rapidly enlarging spleen and a sharp fall in haemoglobin in young children with sickle cell disease; it can cause shock and needs urgent transfusion.
thinking: Young child with sickle cell disease ↓ Sudden pallor, lethargy and abdominal enlargement ↓ Haemoglobin well below baseline ↓ Blood pooling in an enlarging spleen ↓ A, splenic sequestration
exam_trap: B, parvovirus aplastic crisis — tempting as it also causes a sudden haemoglobin fall, but reticulocytes are low and there is no acute splenic enlargement.
takeaway: Sickle cell child with acute anaemia and an enlarging spleen: splenic sequestration.

stem:
A healthy child has intermittent aching pain in both legs at night. Examination during the day is normal, with no swelling, limp or systemic symptoms.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bilateral intermittent limb pain occurring at night with a normal daytime examination is typical of growing pains.
why_wrong: A. Osteosarcoma causes persistent localised pain and swelling, often unilateral. B. JIA causes joint swelling and morning stiffness. C. Septic arthritis causes a hot swollen joint, limp and fever. E. A fracture causes localised pain, limp and abnormal examination after trauma.
pearl: Growing pains are bilateral, nocturnal and intermittent in a well child with a normal examination; unilateral pain, limp, swelling or systemic upset point away from the diagnosis.
thinking: Healthy child ↓ Bilateral intermittent leg ache at night ↓ Normal daytime examination, no limp or systemic features ↓ D, growing pains
exam_trap: A, osteosarcoma — tempting because night pain is a bone tumour red flag, but tumour pain is persistent, localised and usually unilateral with swelling.
takeaway: Bilateral night leg pain with a normal examination in a well child: growing pains.

stem:
A teenager develops persistent localised bone pain and swelling around the knee that is progressively worsening.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent progressive bone pain with swelling in an adolescent is a red flag for a bone tumour and requires investigation.
why_wrong: A. Growing pains are bilateral and intermittent with a normal examination. B. Muscle strain does not cause progressive bone pain with swelling. C. Osgood-Schlatter causes tibial tuberosity pain related to activity, not progressive bone swelling. E. Gout is rare in teenagers and affects joints rather than bone.
pearl: Persistent, progressive, localised bone pain or swelling in a teenager, often around the knee, is a red flag for bone sarcoma and needs urgent imaging.
thinking: Teenager ↓ Persistent localised pain around the knee ↓ Progressive, with swelling ↓ Bone tumour red flags ↓ D, osteosarcoma
exam_trap: C, Osgood-Schlatter disease — tempting in a teenager with knee pain, but it causes activity-related tibial tuberosity pain, not progressive bone swelling.
takeaway: Progressive localised bone pain and swelling in a teenager needs urgent imaging for sarcoma.

stem:
A woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is planning a pregnancy.

What is the most appropriate principle?

options.B: Standard midwife-led antenatal care without extra monitoring
options.C: Stop hydroxychloroquine before conception to avoid fetal harm
options.D: Pre-pregnancy specialist assessment and medication review

correct_answer: D. Pre-pregnancy specialist assessment and medication review
why_correct: SLE can affect pregnancy and some medicines require adjustment, so pre-pregnancy planning and coordinated care are important.
why_wrong: A. Pregnancy is not absolutely contraindicated, although planning is needed. B. SLE pregnancies need additional specialist monitoring rather than standard midwife-led care. C. Hydroxychloroquine is usually continued in pregnancy, and stopping it risks a flare. E. Antenatal care is essential in SLE.
pearl: In SLE, pregnancy is best planned when disease is quiet: review medicines before conception, switching teratogenic drugs, usually continuing hydroxychloroquine, and arrange specialist-led care.
thinking: SLE planning pregnancy ↓ Risks of flare and pregnancy complications ↓ Some drugs teratogenic, others continued ↓ D, pre-pregnancy specialist review
exam_trap: C, stop hydroxychloroquine — tempting as many drugs are stopped before conception, but hydroxychloroquine is usually continued because stopping it risks a lupus flare.
takeaway: SLE and pregnancy: plan ahead, review medicines, keep hydroxychloroquine, specialist care.

stem:
A patient has difficult-to-control hypertension and persistent hypokalaemia. There is no obvious medication cause.

Which test is most appropriate to investigate suspected primary hyperaldosteronism?
why_correct: Primary hyperaldosteronism is initially investigated using the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.
why_wrong: A. D-dimer is used in suspected VTE. B. Plasma metanephrines screen for phaeochromocytoma, not primary hyperaldosteronism. C. 24-hour urinary free cortisol screens for Cushing syndrome, not primary hyperaldosteronism. D. Serum amylase and lipase assess pancreatitis.
pearl: Hypertension with hypokalaemia suggests primary hyperaldosteronism; screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which shows high aldosterone with suppressed renin.
thinking: Difficult-to-control hypertension ↓ Unexplained hypokalaemia ↓ Suspected primary hyperaldosteronism ↓ High aldosterone, suppressed renin ↓ E, aldosterone-to-renin ratio
exam_trap: B, plasma metanephrines — tempting as another screen for endocrine hypertension, but it detects phaeochromocytoma, which does not typically cause hypokalaemia.
takeaway: Hypertension plus low potassium: screen with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

stem:
A patient has persistent hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality but appears clinically euvolaemic. Urine remains inappropriately concentrated.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: SIADH causes inappropriate ADH activity, resulting in water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes dilute urine and usually hypernatraemia. C. Hyperglycaemia causes hyperosmolar hyponatraemia rather than hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine. D. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia, not euvolaemic hyponatraemia. E. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalaemia and hypertension, with normal or high sodium.
pearl: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: hypo-osmolar hyponatraemia, euvolaemia and inappropriately concentrated urine, with thyroid, adrenal and diuretic causes excluded.
thinking: Hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality ↓ Clinically euvolaemic ↓ Urine inappropriately concentrated ↓ Excess ADH action ↓ B, SIADH
exam_trap: A, diabetes insipidus — tempting as the other ADH disorder, but DI causes dilute urine and tends towards hypernatraemia, the opposite pattern.
takeaway: Euvolaemic, low-osmolality hyponatraemia with concentrated urine points to SIADH.

stem:
A patient with prolonged diarrhoea develops tremor and muscle cramps. Blood tests show low magnesium.

Which complication can occur with significant hypomagnesaemia?
why_correct: Significant magnesium deficiency can cause neuromuscular irritability and cardiac arrhythmias.
why_wrong: A. Ascites is not caused by hypomagnesaemia. B. Cataract is not an acute complication of hypomagnesaemia. D. Polycythaemia is not caused by hypomagnesaemia. E. Hypomagnesaemia is associated with hypocalcaemia rather than hypercalcaemia.
pearl: Significant hypomagnesaemia causes neuromuscular irritability and arrhythmias, including torsades de pointes, and often coexists with hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia that resist correction until magnesium is replaced.
thinking: Prolonged diarrhoea ↓ Gastrointestinal magnesium loss ↓ Tremor and cramps = neuromuscular irritability ↓ Membrane instability also affects the heart ↓ C, arrhythmias
exam_trap: E, severe hypercalcaemia — tempting as an electrolyte complication, but low magnesium impairs PTH release and action, causing hypocalcaemia instead.
takeaway: Low magnesium risks arrhythmias; replace it to correct linked low potassium and calcium.

stem:
A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops persistently raised phosphate levels.

What is a major reason for this?
why_correct: Declining kidney function reduces phosphate excretion, causing phosphate accumulation.
why_wrong: A. Bile production does not regulate serum phosphate. B. Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis rather than persistent hyperphosphataemia. D. Haemolysis can raise phosphate acutely but is not the main reason in advanced CKD. E. Insulin shifts phosphate into cells and does not cause persistent hyperphosphataemia.
pearl: The kidneys are the main route of phosphate excretion, so hyperphosphataemia is a hallmark of advanced CKD and drives secondary hyperparathyroidism.
thinking: Advanced CKD ↓ Falling GFR ↓ Less phosphate filtered and excreted ↓ Phosphate accumulates ↓ C, reduced renal excretion
exam_trap: D, increased red-cell destruction — tempting as haemolysis releases intracellular phosphate, but this is acute and not the reason for persistent hyperphosphataemia in CKD.
takeaway: Persistently high phosphate in CKD reflects failing renal excretion.

stem:
A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease develops bone pain and abnormal calcium and phosphate metabolism.

Which underlying process contributes?
correct_answer: C. Disturbed mineral and bone metabolism
why_correct: CKD causes abnormalities in phosphate, calcium, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D metabolism, contributing to mineral and bone disease.
why_wrong: A. CKD reduces renal 1-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D. B. Excess insulin production does not cause CKD mineral and bone disorder. D. CKD reduces, rather than increases, erythropoietin production. E. CKD reduces phosphate excretion.
pearl: In CKD-mineral and bone disorder, phosphate retention and reduced vitamin D activation lower calcium, driving secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease.
thinking: Advanced CKD ↓ Phosphate retained, less active vitamin D ↓ Low calcium, raised PTH ↓ Abnormal bone turnover and bone pain ↓ C, disturbed mineral and bone metabolism
exam_trap: A, increased renal vitamin D activation — tempting because vitamin D is central here, but CKD reduces 1-alpha hydroxylation, so activation falls.
takeaway: CKD causes mineral and bone disorder through phosphate retention and reduced vitamin D activation.

stem:
A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease has symptomatic anaemia after reversible causes have been assessed.

Which treatment may be considered under specialist management?
why_correct: Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents may be used in selected patients with CKD-associated anaemia under appropriate specialist management.
why_wrong: A. Levothyroxine treats hypothyroidism, not CKD anaemia. B. Anticoagulation does not treat anaemia and may worsen bleeding. C. Antibiotics are not a treatment for CKD-related anaemia. D. Insulin does not treat renal anaemia.
pearl: Anaemia of CKD is largely due to reduced erythropoietin production; correct iron deficiency and other reversible causes first, then consider an ESA under specialist care.
thinking: Advanced CKD ↓ Symptomatic anaemia, reversible causes assessed ↓ Kidneys produce less erythropoietin ↓ Replace the missing stimulus ↓ E, erythropoiesis-stimulating agent
exam_trap: A, levothyroxine — tempting because hypothyroidism can cause anaemia, but it treats thyroid disease, not erythropoietin deficiency in CKD.
takeaway: Renal anaemia: treat iron deficiency first, then consider an ESA under specialists.

stem:
A patient has a family history of kidney failure and develops hypertension. Imaging shows multiple cysts in both kidneys.

Which inherited condition is most likely?

options.A: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal arteries
options.B: Minimal change disease with nephrotic syndrome
options.E: Acute tubular injury following severe dehydration

correct_answer: D. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
why_correct: Bilateral renal cysts with a relevant family history and hypertension are characteristic of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
why_wrong: A. Fibromuscular dysplasia causes renovascular hypertension but not bilateral renal cysts. B. Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome, not renal cysts. C. Alport syndrome is inherited and causes kidney failure with haematuria and hearing loss, not multiple renal cysts. E. Acute tubular injury is acquired and does not cause multiple renal cysts.
pearl: ADPKD presents with bilateral renal cysts, hypertension and a family history of kidney failure; it may also cause flank pain, haematuria and liver cysts.
thinking: Family history of kidney failure ↓ Hypertension ↓ Multiple cysts in both kidneys ↓ Inherited cystic disease ↓ D, ADPKD
exam_trap: C, Alport syndrome — tempting as an inherited cause of kidney failure, but it presents with haematuria and sensorineural deafness, not multiple renal cysts.
takeaway: Bilateral renal cysts with family history and hypertension: think ADPKD.

stem:
A patient with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease asks about neurological complications.

Which condition is associated with ADPKD?
why_correct: ADPKD is associated with intracranial aneurysms, although screening is not routinely required for every asymptomatic patient.
why_wrong: A. Myasthenia gravis is not associated with ADPKD. B. Multiple sclerosis is not associated with ADPKD. C. Parkinson's disease is not associated with ADPKD. E. Epilepsy is not a feature of every patient with ADPKD.
pearl: ADPKD is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms, so a sudden severe headache in a patient with ADPKD should raise concern for subarachnoid haemorrhage.
thinking: ADPKD ↓ Extra-renal features include liver cysts and vascular abnormalities ↓ Berry aneurysms in the circle of Willis ↓ D, intracranial aneurysm
exam_trap: E, epilepsy in every patient — tempting if looking for any neurological link, but epilepsy is not a feature of ADPKD and the absolute wording is a giveaway.
takeaway: ADPKD carries an increased risk of intracranial berry aneurysm.

stem:
A patient with chronic kidney disease is prescribed several new medicines.

Which drug class is particularly important to review because of its potential to worsen renal function?
why_correct: NSAIDs can reduce renal perfusion and precipitate or worsen kidney injury, particularly in patients with pre-existing renal impairment.
why_wrong: A. Topical moisturisers are not nephrotoxic. B. Antacids are not the key concern for renal function, although some need caution in CKD. D. Topical emollients have no meaningful nephrotoxic effect. E. Saline nasal spray does not affect renal function.
pearl: NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow by blocking prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation; avoid or use with great caution in CKD, especially with ACE inhibitors and diuretics.
thinking: CKD with new medicines ↓ Look for nephrotoxic drugs ↓ NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole ↓ Reduced GFR and risk of AKI ↓ C, NSAIDs
exam_trap: B, antacids only — tempting because some antacids need caution in CKD, but they are not a major cause of worsening renal function; NSAIDs are.
takeaway: In CKD, always review and avoid NSAIDs where possible.

stem:
A renal transplant recipient develops deteriorating kidney function and reduced urine output.

What should this prompt?

options.A: Repeat renal function tests at the next routine clinic in a month
options.C: Reassurance that some decline in function is expected after transplant
options.D: Urgent assessment for graft dysfunction, including rejection
options.E: Stopping all immunosuppressive medication without specialist advice

correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment for graft dysfunction, including rejection
why_correct: Deterioration in renal function after transplantation requires prompt assessment for rejection, obstruction, infection, drug toxicity and other causes.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for routine review risks irreversible graft loss. B. NSAIDs are nephrotoxic and should be avoided. C. Declining graft function is not expected and needs urgent assessment. E. Stopping immunosuppression would increase rejection risk.
pearl: Rising creatinine or falling urine output in a renal transplant recipient needs urgent assessment for rejection, obstruction, infection and calcineurin inhibitor toxicity.
thinking: Renal transplant recipient ↓ Deteriorating function and falling urine output ↓ Possible rejection or other graft threat ↓ Delay risks graft loss ↓ D, urgent assessment
exam_trap: C, reassurance that decline is expected — tempting as graft function can fluctuate, but a new deterioration is never assumed benign and needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Deteriorating graft function is urgent until rejection and other causes are excluded.

stem:
A patient with nephrotic syndrome develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Nephrotic syndrome increases thrombotic risk through urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins and other changes in haemostasis.
why_wrong: A. Otitis media affects the ear. C. Migraine does not cause pleuritic chest pain or breathlessness. D. DKA causes vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul breathing rather than sudden pleuritic chest pain. E. Acute cholecystitis causes right upper-quadrant pain, not pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome is a hypercoagulable state, partly from urinary loss of antithrombin; watch for PE, DVT and renal vein thrombosis.
thinking: Nephrotic syndrome ↓ Loss of anticoagulant proteins in urine ↓ Hypercoagulable state ↓ Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness ↓ B, VTE
exam_trap: D, DKA — tempting as an acute cause of abnormal breathing, but it causes Kussmaul breathing with vomiting and abdominal pain, not sudden pleuritic chest pain.
takeaway: Nephrotic syndrome raises thrombosis risk: consider PE with new pleuritic pain.

stem:
A man presents with new lower urinary tract symptoms and is concerned about prostate cancer.

Which symptom pattern is particularly concerning for advanced disease?

options.C: Mild daytime urinary frequency on its own
options.D: Occasional nocturia, once a night, alone

correct_answer: E. New persistent unexplained bone pain
why_correct: Prostate cancer can metastasise to bone, so unexplained persistent bone pain in a man with suspected prostate cancer warrants assessment.
why_wrong: A. Temporary urgency after coffee reflects bladder irritation, not advanced cancer. B. Isolated dysuria after exercise is not a typical feature of advanced prostate cancer. C. Mild frequency alone is common in benign prostatic enlargement and does not suggest advanced disease. D. Occasional nocturia alone is non-specific and does not indicate metastatic disease.
pearl: Prostate cancer spreads to bone, so new persistent unexplained bone pain, especially back pain, in a man with urinary symptoms suggests metastatic disease and needs urgent assessment.
thinking: Man with new LUTS and prostate cancer concern ↓ Prostate cancer metastasises to bone ↓ Persistent unexplained bone pain ↓ E, concerning for advanced disease
exam_trap: C, mild daytime frequency — tempting as a urinary symptom, but on its own it is common in benign prostatic enlargement and does not suggest spread.
takeaway: New bone pain with LUTS raises concern for metastatic prostate cancer.

stem:
A young man notices a painless enlargement of one testicle.

What should be done?

options.C: Apply a cold compress and review in six months
options.D: Reassure him that painless swelling is always benign
options.E: Urgent assessment for possible testicular cancer

correct_answer: E. Urgent assessment for possible testicular cancer
why_correct: A painless testicular mass is a classic presentation of testicular cancer and requires prompt assessment.
why_wrong: A. There is no evidence of infection, and topical antibiotics have no role in managing a testicular mass. B. Epididymitis is usually painful and tender, and no diagnosis should be made without examination. C. A six-month delay risks progression of a potentially curable malignancy; NICE NG12 advises prompt ultrasound assessment. D. Painless testicular swelling is the typical presentation of testicular cancer, so it must never be assumed benign without assessment.
pearl: A painless testicular enlargement in a young man is cancer until proven otherwise; examine and refer on the suspected cancer pathway, with urgent scrotal ultrasound.
thinking: Young man ↓ Painless unilateral testicular enlargement ↓ Peak age group for testicular cancer ↓ E, urgent assessment
exam_trap: B, diagnose epididymitis — tempting as a common scrotal diagnosis, but it is usually painful and tender, and no diagnosis should be made without examination.
takeaway: Painless testicular swelling in a young man needs urgent assessment for cancer.

stem:
A postmenopausal woman has persistent itching and a new irregular lesion on the vulva.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Advise review if the lesion becomes painful or bleeds
options.B: Reassure and discharge with a soap substitute and emollients
options.C: Arrange assessment of the persistent vulval lesion
options.D: Prescribe topical clotrimazole for presumed candidiasis
options.E: Treat with a course of oral antibiotics without examination

correct_answer: C. Arrange assessment of the persistent vulval lesion
why_correct: Persistent vulval symptoms or an unexplained lesion can be features of vulval cancer and require assessment.
why_wrong: A. Vulval cancer is often painless in its early stages, so waiting for pain or bleeding is unsafe. B. A persistent vulval lesion in a postmenopausal woman warrants assessment under NICE NG12, not discharge with emollients. D. Candidiasis should not be presumed and treated in the presence of a new irregular lesion, which raises concern for vulval cancer. E. There is no evidence of bacterial infection, and antibiotics without examination would delay diagnosis of a possible malignancy.
pearl: Persistent vulval itch with a new irregular lesion in a postmenopausal woman raises concern for vulval cancer; examine and refer for assessment rather than treat empirically.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman ↓ Persistent vulval itch ↓ New irregular lesion ↓ Possible vulval cancer ↓ C, arrange assessment
exam_trap: D, clotrimazole for candidiasis — tempting because itch suggests thrush, but a new irregular lesion must be examined, not treated blindly.
takeaway: A persistent or irregular vulval lesion needs examination, not empirical treatment.

stem:
A woman has a profuse, unpleasant-smelling vaginal discharge and vulval irritation.

Which sexually transmitted infection can cause this presentation?
why_correct: Trichomoniasis can cause a profuse, malodorous vaginal discharge with vulval irritation.
why_wrong: B. HIV does not itself cause a profuse malodorous vaginal discharge, although testing is important in anyone with an STI. C. Genital herpes typically causes painful ulcers or vesicles rather than a profuse malodorous discharge. D. Hepatitis B affects the liver and does not cause vaginal discharge or vulval irritation. E. Primary syphilis usually causes a painless chancre, not a profuse offensive vaginal discharge.
pearl: Trichomonas vaginalis causes a frothy, offensive, yellow-green discharge with vulval irritation and sometimes a strawberry cervix; treat with metronidazole and treat partners.
thinking: Profuse, malodorous vaginal discharge ↓ Vulval irritation ↓ Sexually transmitted cause needed ↓ A, trichomoniasis
exam_trap: C, genital herpes — tempting as a common STI with vulval symptoms, but it causes painful vesicles and ulcers rather than a profuse offensive discharge.
takeaway: Profuse offensive discharge with vulval irritation: think trichomoniasis.

stem:
A 38-year-old develops amenorrhoea and menopausal symptoms.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Menopausal symptoms and loss of ovarian function before the usual age of menopause should prompt consideration of premature ovarian insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Menopause before the age of 40 is not a normal transition and is defined as premature ovarian insufficiency. B. Endometriosis causes cyclical pelvic pain and dysmenorrhoea rather than amenorrhoea with menopausal symptoms. C. Ovarian torsion presents with acute severe pelvic pain, not amenorrhoea and menopausal symptoms. E. Fibroids typically cause heavy menstrual bleeding or pressure symptoms, not amenorrhoea and vasomotor symptoms.
pearl: Menopausal symptoms with amenorrhoea before 40 suggest premature ovarian insufficiency; confirm with raised FSH on repeat testing and offer hormone replacement until the usual age of menopause.
thinking: Aged 38 ↓ Amenorrhoea with menopausal symptoms ↓ Loss of ovarian function before 40 ↓ D, premature ovarian insufficiency
exam_trap: A, normal perimenopausal transition — tempting as the patient is approaching 40, but loss of ovarian function before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency, not normal.
takeaway: Menopausal symptoms before 40 mean premature ovarian insufficiency until proven otherwise.

stem:
A woman develops secondary amenorrhoea and milky nipple discharge. She is not pregnant.

Which endocrine abnormality should be considered?
why_correct: Raised prolactin can suppress reproductive hormone secretion and cause amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea.
why_wrong: A. Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia symptoms and does not cause galactorrhoea. C. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia, not galactorrhoea or amenorrhoea. D. Hypocalcaemia causes paraesthesia, tetany and cramps rather than amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. E. Hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia, not amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea.
pearl: Amenorrhoea with galactorrhoea once pregnancy is excluded points to hyperprolactinaemia; consider drugs such as antipsychotics, hypothyroidism and a pituitary prolactinoma.
thinking: Secondary amenorrhoea ↓ Galactorrhoea ↓ Pregnancy excluded ↓ Prolactin suppresses GnRH ↓ B, hyperprolactinaemia
exam_trap: C, diabetes insipidus — tempting as another pituitary-related disorder, but it causes polyuria and polydipsia, not galactorrhoea or amenorrhoea.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea plus galactorrhoea, not pregnant: check prolactin.

stem:
A woman develops milk discharge from both breasts despite not being pregnant or breastfeeding.

Which term describes this symptom?
why_correct: Galactorrhoea is inappropriate milk production or milk discharge outside pregnancy and breastfeeding.
why_wrong: A. Gynaecomastia is benign enlargement of male breast glandular tissue, not milk discharge. C. Mastitis is inflammation of breast tissue causing pain, redness and swelling, usually during lactation. D. Dyspareunia refers to pain during sexual intercourse. E. Menorrhagia refers to heavy menstrual bleeding, not breast discharge.
pearl: Galactorrhoea is milky discharge outside pregnancy or breastfeeding, usually bilateral; check prolactin and review drugs, whereas bloody or single-duct discharge needs breast assessment.
thinking: Milky discharge from both breasts ↓ Not pregnant or breastfeeding ↓ Inappropriate milk production ↓ B, galactorrhoea
exam_trap: C, mastitis — tempting as a breast condition linked to lactation, but it causes a painful, red, swollen breast rather than milk discharge.
takeaway: Milky discharge outside pregnancy or breastfeeding is galactorrhoea.

stem:
A woman develops excessive coarse hair growth on the face and chest.

What is the medical term for this finding?
why_correct: Hirsutism is excessive terminal hair growth in a male-pattern distribution in women.
why_wrong: A. Telogen effluvium is diffuse hair shedding, often after physiological stress. B. Virilism describes broader masculinisation such as clitoromegaly, deepening voice and increased muscle bulk, not hair growth alone. D. Alopecia is hair loss, the opposite of the finding described. E. Hypertrichosis is generalised excess hair growth not confined to an androgen-dependent pattern.
pearl: Hirsutism is androgen-dependent, male-pattern terminal hair growth in women; rapid onset or signs of virilisation should prompt a search for an androgen-secreting tumour.
thinking: Woman with excess coarse hair ↓ Face and chest = male-pattern distribution ↓ Androgen-dependent terminal hair ↓ C, hirsutism
exam_trap: E, hypertrichosis — tempting as another term for excess hair, but it describes generalised growth not confined to an androgen-dependent pattern.
takeaway: Male-pattern coarse hair growth in women is hirsutism.

stem:
A woman undergoing assisted reproductive treatment develops abdominal pain, bloating and rapidly increasing abdominal distension.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome can cause enlarged ovaries, abdominal distension and fluid shifts following ovarian stimulation.
why_wrong: A. Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes vulval itching and discharge, not abdominal distension. B. Menopause does not cause acute abdominal pain and distension. D. IBS can cause bloating but does not cause rapidly increasing abdominal distension after ovarian stimulation. E. Endometriosis causes chronic cyclical pelvic pain and does not cause rapidly increasing distension after ovarian stimulation.
pearl: OHSS follows ovarian stimulation, causing enlarged ovaries and fluid shifts; severe cases bring ascites, haemoconcentration and thrombosis risk, needing urgent specialist assessment.
thinking: Assisted reproductive treatment ↓ Ovarian stimulation ↓ Abdominal pain, bloating, rapid distension ↓ Fluid shift into third space ↓ C, OHSS
exam_trap: D, IBS exacerbation — tempting because bloating is prominent, but IBS does not cause rapidly increasing distension after ovarian stimulation.
takeaway: Abdominal distension after fertility treatment: think ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.

stem:
A patient with severe liver disease is asked to hold their arms outstretched with wrists extended. Their hands repeatedly flap downwards.

What is this sign called?
why_correct: Asterixis is a negative myoclonus producing a characteristic flapping movement and can occur in hepatic encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Ataxia is impaired coordination of movement, not a flapping tremor. C. Fasciculations are fine spontaneous twitches of muscle fibres seen in lower motor neurone disease. D. Dysdiadochokinesia is impaired rapid alternating movement, a sign of cerebellar dysfunction. E. Chorea consists of irregular, flowing involuntary movements, not a rhythmic flap of outstretched hands.
pearl: Asterixis is a flapping tremor of outstretched, extended hands caused by negative myoclonus; it occurs in hepatic encephalopathy, CO2 retention and uraemia.
thinking: Severe liver disease ↓ Arms outstretched, wrists extended ↓ Hands repeatedly flap down ↓ Brief lapses of postural tone ↓ B, asterixis
exam_trap: E, chorea — tempting as an involuntary movement disorder, but chorea is irregular and flowing, not a repetitive flap of outstretched hands.
takeaway: Flapping tremor in liver disease is asterixis: think hepatic encephalopathy.

stem:
A patient with cirrhosis suddenly vomits a large amount of fresh blood.

Which cause is particularly important to consider?
why_correct: Portal hypertension can produce oesophageal varices, which may rupture and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes abdominal pain and does not cause haematemesis. B. Haemorrhoids cause bright red rectal bleeding, not haematemesis. C. Diverticulitis causes lower abdominal pain and fever; diverticular bleeding is rectal, not vomited. E. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
pearl: In cirrhosis, large-volume haematemesis is variceal until proven otherwise: resuscitate, give terlipressin and antibiotics, and arrange urgent endoscopy for band ligation.
thinking: Known cirrhosis ↓ Portal hypertension ↓ Oesophageal varices ↓ Sudden large fresh haematemesis ↓ D, variceal bleeding
exam_trap: B, haemorrhoids — tempting as a common bleeding source, but haemorrhoids cause bright red rectal bleeding, not vomited blood.
takeaway: Haematemesis in cirrhosis is variceal until proven otherwise.

stem: Which complication is directly associated with portal hypertension?
why_correct: Increased portal venous pressure produces collateral vessels, including oesophageal and gastric varices.
why_wrong: A. Pneumothorax is a pleural condition with no direct link to portal hypertension. B. Renal colic is caused by urinary tract stones and is unrelated to portal hypertension. C. Cataract is a lens opacity unrelated to portal venous pressure. E. Otitis externa is an infection of the ear canal unrelated to portal hypertension.
pearl: Portal hypertension opens portosystemic collaterals; oesophageal and gastric varices are the most dangerous, alongside ascites and splenomegaly as key features.
thinking: Raised portal venous pressure ↓ Blood diverts through portosystemic collaterals ↓ Gastro-oesophageal junction is a key site ↓ D, oesophageal varices
exam_trap: B, renal colic — the only other abdominal option, but it is caused by urinary stones and has no link to portal venous pressure.
takeaway: Portal hypertension causes varices, ascites and splenomegaly.

stem:
A patient with longstanding alcohol-related pancreatic disease develops recurrent abdominal pain, weight loss and bulky, oily stools.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic pancreatic damage can cause chronic pain, malabsorption and steatorrhoea because of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease can cause steatorrhoea, but the history of alcohol-related pancreatic disease points to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. B. Acute appendicitis is an acute illness and does not cause recurrent pain with steatorrhoea. C. Biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant pain without malabsorption or steatorrhoea. D. Ulcerative colitis usually causes bloody diarrhoea rather than bulky, oily stools.
pearl: Chronic pancreatitis causes recurrent epigastric pain, weight loss, steatorrhoea from exocrine failure and later diabetes; pancreatic enzyme replacement treats the malabsorption.
thinking: Longstanding alcohol-related pancreatic disease ↓ Recurrent pain and weight loss ↓ Bulky, oily stools = steatorrhoea ↓ Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency ↓ E, chronic pancreatitis
exam_trap: A, coeliac disease — tempting as a classic cause of steatorrhoea, but the alcohol-related pancreatic history points to pancreatic exocrine insufficiency.
takeaway: Alcohol, recurrent pain and steatorrhoea point to chronic pancreatitis.

stem:
A patient has jaundice, pale stools, dark urine and generalised itching.

Which pattern is most consistent with obstructive cholestasis?
correct_answer: E. Pale stools and dark urine
why_correct: Reduced bile reaching the intestine can cause pale stools, while conjugated bilirubin entering urine causes dark urine.
why_wrong: A. Black stools and haematemesis indicate upper gastrointestinal bleeding, not cholestasis. B. Red urine and dysuria suggest urinary tract pathology such as infection or stones. C. Bloody diarrhoea suggests colitis or infection rather than biliary obstruction. D. Sputum colour is unrelated to cholestasis; it is pale stools, not sputum, that are typical.
pearl: Obstructive jaundice causes pale stools, dark urine and itch because conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut; painless obstructive jaundice raises concern for pancreatic head cancer.
thinking: Jaundice with itching ↓ Bile cannot reach the intestine ↓ Pale stools ↓ Conjugated bilirubin spills into urine ↓ E, pale stools and dark urine
exam_trap: A, black stools and haematemesis — tempting as a change in stool colour, but melaena and haematemesis indicate upper GI bleeding, not cholestasis.
takeaway: Obstructive cholestasis: pale stools, dark urine and itch.

stem:
A patient with colorectal cancer develops abnormal liver tests and multiple liver lesions on imaging.

Which explanation is most likely?
why_correct: The liver is a common site of metastatic spread from colorectal cancer because of portal venous drainage from the bowel.
why_wrong: A. Gallstone ileus causes small bowel obstruction from an impacted gallstone, not multiple liver lesions. B. Renal colic is caused by urinary stones and does not produce liver lesions. C. Viral pharyngitis is a throat infection unrelated to liver lesions. D. Acute appendicitis presents with abdominal pain and does not cause multiple liver lesions.
pearl: Colorectal cancer commonly spreads to the liver via the portal venous system; liver metastases may be resectable, so staging CT matters.
thinking: Known colorectal cancer ↓ Bowel drains via the portal vein to the liver ↓ Abnormal liver tests and multiple liver lesions ↓ E, liver metastases
exam_trap: A, gallstone ileus — the only hepatobiliary-sounding option, but it causes small bowel obstruction from an impacted stone, not multiple liver lesions.
takeaway: Multiple liver lesions in colorectal cancer suggest metastases via the portal vein.

stem:
A teenager develops facial papules, pustules and comedones.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Comedones with inflammatory papules and pustules are characteristic of acne vulgaris.
why_wrong: A. Folliculitis decalvans is a scarring alopecia of the scalp, not a facial comedonal eruption. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions from bacterial infection rather than comedones. D. Rosacea typically affects older adults with flushing, erythema and telangiectasia, and lacks comedones. E. Psoriasis causes well-demarcated scaly plaques rather than comedones and pustules on the face.
pearl: Comedones are the hallmark of acne vulgaris and distinguish it from rosacea; treat according to severity, starting with topical options such as benzoyl peroxide or a topical retinoid.
thinking: Teenager ↓ Facial comedones ↓ Inflammatory papules and pustules ↓ Pilosebaceous unit disease ↓ B, acne vulgaris
exam_trap: D, rosacea — tempting as it also causes facial papules and pustules, but it affects older adults with flushing and telangiectasia and has no comedones.
takeaway: Comedones point to acne; flushing without comedones points to rosacea.

stem:
A man develops gradual hair thinning over the temples and crown.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Male-pattern hair loss typically causes gradual recession at the temples and thinning over the crown.
why_wrong: A. Tinea capitis causes scaly patches of hair loss, usually in children. B. Scarring alopecia destroys follicles with visible scarring and loss of follicular openings. C. Chronic telogen effluvium causes diffuse shedding, often after a stressor, not a patterned temporal and crown distribution. D. Alopecia areata causes well-circumscribed patches of hair loss, often sudden, rather than gradual temporal and crown thinning.
pearl: Androgenetic alopecia causes gradual, patterned thinning at the temples and crown with a normal scalp; scarring, scaling or patchy loss suggests another cause.
thinking: Man ↓ Gradual hair thinning ↓ Temples and crown pattern ↓ Non-scarring, no patches ↓ E, androgenetic alopecia
exam_trap: D, alopecia areata — tempting as a common cause of hair loss, but it causes sudden, well-circumscribed patches rather than gradual patterned thinning.
takeaway: Gradual temple and crown thinning in a man is androgenetic alopecia.

stem:
A pigmented lesion has recently changed in size and colour and has developed an irregular border.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure because all pigmented lesions are benign
options.E: Cover with a dressing and ignore it

correct_answer: B. Arrange assessment for possible melanoma
why_correct: Change in size, colour or border is an important warning feature of melanoma.
why_wrong: A. Not all pigmented lesions are benign, and change in size, shape or colour is a major warning sign of melanoma. C. Antifungal cream has no role in a changing pigmented lesion and would delay diagnosis. D. Warts are not pigmented lesions that change in colour and border, and diagnosing one without assessment is unsafe. E. Covering and ignoring a suspicious lesion would delay diagnosis of a potentially fatal melanoma.
pearl: A changing pigmented lesion is the key melanoma warning sign; assess with the weighted 7-point checklist or ABCDE features and refer on the suspected cancer pathway.
thinking: Pigmented lesion ↓ Recent change in size and colour ↓ Irregular border ↓ Major melanoma warning features ↓ B, assessment for melanoma
exam_trap: A, reassurance — tempting because most moles are benign, but change in size, colour or border is a major warning sign of melanoma.
takeaway: A changing mole needs urgent assessment for melanoma.

stem:
An older patient develops a new temporal headache and jaw pain when chewing.

What complication requires urgent consideration?

options.B: Visual loss from giant cell arteritis

correct_answer: B. Visual loss from giant cell arteritis
why_correct: Giant cell arteritis can cause permanent visual loss, so suspected disease requires urgent assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis is a superficial eye inflammation unrelated to giant cell arteritis. C. Jaw claudication and a new temporal headache in an older patient suggest giant cell arteritis rather than migraine. D. Retinal detachment is not the typical visual complication of giant cell arteritis, which causes anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. E. Cataract develops gradually and is not a complication of giant cell arteritis.
pearl: Suspected GCA needs high-dose steroids started immediately, before temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound, to prevent irreversible visual loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy.
thinking: Older patient ↓ New temporal headache ↓ Jaw pain on chewing = jaw claudication ↓ Giant cell arteritis ↓ B, risk of visual loss
exam_trap: C, migraine aura — tempting with headache and visual symptoms, but a new headache with jaw claudication in an older patient points to GCA.
takeaway: Suspected GCA: start steroids at once to protect vision.

stem:
A patient develops peripheral oedema, ascites and raised jugular venous pressure with relatively clear lungs.

Which pattern is most suggestive?
why_correct: Systemic venous congestion causing raised JVP, peripheral oedema and ascites is characteristic of right-sided heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Acute pulmonary embolism may cause raised JVP but does not typically cause established ascites and peripheral oedema. C. Asthma causes wheeze and breathlessness and does not cause systemic venous congestion. D. Pneumothorax causes acute breathlessness and chest pain, not peripheral oedema and ascites. E. Isolated left ventricular failure causes pulmonary congestion, so the lungs would not be clear.
pearl: Right heart failure causes systemic venous congestion — raised JVP, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly and ascites — with clear lungs; its commonest cause is left heart failure.
thinking: Raised JVP ↓ Peripheral oedema and ascites ↓ Clear lungs, so no pulmonary congestion ↓ Systemic venous congestion ↓ B, right-sided heart failure
exam_trap: E, left ventricular failure — tempting as the commonest form of heart failure, but isolated LVF causes pulmonary congestion, so the lungs would not be clear.
takeaway: Raised JVP, oedema and ascites with clear lungs means right heart failure.

stem:
A patient with previous occupational asbestos exposure develops progressive breathlessness and a recurrent unilateral pleural effusion.

Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Pleural mesothelioma is strongly associated with asbestos exposure and can present with breathlessness and pleural effusion.
why_wrong: A. Melanoma is linked to ultraviolet exposure, not asbestos. C. Thyroid cancer is associated with radiation exposure rather than asbestos. D. Testicular cancer is not linked to asbestos exposure. E. Prostate cancer is not associated with asbestos exposure and does not typically present with a recurrent unilateral pleural effusion.
pearl: Mesothelioma can appear decades after asbestos exposure; a recurrent unilateral effusion needs CT and pleural biopsy, as fluid cytology is often negative.
thinking: Occupational asbestos exposure ↓ Progressive breathlessness ↓ Recurrent unilateral pleural effusion ↓ Pleural malignancy ↓ B, mesothelioma
exam_trap: E, prostate cancer — tempting as a common malignancy in adults, but it is not linked to asbestos and does not typically present with a recurrent unilateral effusion.
takeaway: Asbestos exposure plus unilateral pleural effusion: think mesothelioma.

stem:
A patient with a large thoracic malignancy develops facial swelling, distended neck veins and upper-limb swelling.

Which complication should be considered?

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg

why_correct: Obstruction of the superior vena cava can cause facial and upper-limb venous congestion and distended neck veins.
why_wrong: A. Leg DVT causes unilateral leg swelling, not facial and upper-limb swelling with distended neck veins. B. Nephrotic syndrome causes generalised oedema from hypoalbuminaemia, without distended neck veins. D. Appendicitis is an abdominal condition unrelated to upper-body venous congestion. E. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain and is unrelated to SVC obstruction.
pearl: SVC obstruction, most often from lung cancer or lymphoma, causes facial swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins and breathlessness; it is an oncological emergency.
thinking: Large thoracic malignancy ↓ Facial and upper-limb swelling ↓ Distended neck veins ↓ Obstructed venous return from the upper body ↓ C, SVC obstruction
exam_trap: B, nephrotic syndrome — tempting as a cause of facial oedema, but it causes generalised oedema from low albumin, without distended neck veins.
takeaway: Facial and arm swelling with distended neck veins in thoracic cancer: SVC obstruction.

stem:
A patient develops fever, productive cough and foul-smelling sputum. Imaging shows a cavity containing an air-fluid level.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A cavitating pulmonary lesion containing an air-fluid level with foul-smelling sputum is characteristic of a lung abscess.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary oedema causes bilateral interstitial or alveolar shadowing, not a cavity with an air-fluid level. C. Pleural effusion causes a meniscus at the lung base rather than a cavity within the lung. D. Pneumothorax shows air in the pleural space without a cavitating lung lesion or foul sputum. E. Asthma causes reversible wheeze and does not cause cavitation or foul-smelling sputum.
pearl: Lung abscess classically follows aspiration and presents with swinging fever and foul sputum; imaging shows a thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level.
thinking: Fever and productive cough ↓ Foul-smelling sputum suggests anaerobes ↓ Cavity containing an air-fluid level ↓ B, lung abscess
exam_trap: C, pleural effusion — tempting because fluid is seen on imaging, but an effusion produces a basal meniscus, not a fluid level within a lung cavity.
takeaway: Foul sputum and a cavity with an air-fluid level mean lung abscess.

stem:
A patient develops fever, confusion and new focal seizures. There is no obvious extracranial source of infection.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Fever with altered mental state and seizures suggests inflammation/infection of the brain, particularly encephalitis.
why_wrong: A. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo without fever, confusion or seizures. B. Bell's palsy causes isolated facial weakness without fever, confusion or seizures. D. New focal seizures and confusion indicate brain involvement and cannot be attributed to a simple febrile illness. E. Tension headache does not cause fever, confusion or seizures.
pearl: Suspect encephalitis with fever plus confusion, altered behaviour or seizures; start IV aciclovir promptly without waiting for lumbar puncture or imaging results.
thinking: Fever ↓ Confusion and new focal seizures ↓ No extracranial source ↓ Brain parenchyma involved ↓ C, encephalitis
exam_trap: D, simple febrile illness — tempting as fever can cause mild confusion, but new focal seizures indicate brain involvement.
takeaway: Fever with confusion or seizures: think encephalitis and start aciclovir.

stem:
A patient with longstanding diabetes becomes dizzy when standing and reports early satiety and erectile dysfunction.

Which complication could explain these symptoms?
why_correct: Autonomic neuropathy can cause postural hypotension, gastrointestinal dysmotility and sexual dysfunction.
why_wrong: A. Diabetic proximal motor neuropathy (amyotrophy) causes thigh pain and proximal weakness, not autonomic symptoms. B. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable muscle weakness, not autonomic dysfunction. C. Multiple sclerosis can cause autonomic symptoms, but in longstanding diabetes this combination is best explained by autonomic neuropathy. E. Parkinson's disease can cause postural hypotension but would also cause motor features such as bradykinesia and rigidity.
pearl: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction and reduced awareness of hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ Dizziness on standing = postural hypotension ↓ Early satiety from gastroparesis ↓ Erectile dysfunction ↓ D, autonomic neuropathy
exam_trap: E, Parkinson's disease — tempting as it can cause postural hypotension, but it would also cause bradykinesia and rigidity, which are not described.
takeaway: Diabetes with postural dizziness, gastroparesis and erectile dysfunction: autonomic neuropathy.

stem:
A person with diabetes becomes sweaty, shaky and confused after accidentally taking too much insulin. They are conscious and able to swallow.

What is the immediate treatment?
why_correct: A conscious patient able to swallow should receive rapid-acting carbohydrate to correct hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia can progress to seizures, coma and death, so prompt treatment is required. C. Sulfonylureas lower blood glucose and would worsen hypoglycaemia. D. Restricting oral intake would worsen hypoglycaemia; glucose must be given. E. Further insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Treat hypoglycaemia in a conscious patient who can swallow with fast-acting glucose, recheck, then give longer-acting carbohydrate; if unable to swallow, use IM glucagon or IV glucose.
thinking: Excess insulin taken ↓ Sweaty, shaky and confused = hypoglycaemia ↓ Conscious and able to swallow ↓ B, fast-acting carbohydrate
exam_trap: A, wait for resolution — tempting if symptoms seem mild, but hypoglycaemia can progress to seizures and coma, so treat at once.
takeaway: Conscious hypoglycaemia: fast-acting carbohydrate by mouth, then recheck.

stem:
A patient is found to have a new thyroid lump.

Which feature is particularly concerning and warrants assessment for malignancy?
correct_answer: D. A rapidly enlarging thyroid mass
why_correct: Rapid enlargement of a thyroid mass is a concerning feature requiring prompt assessment.
why_wrong: A. Normal appetite is not a feature of malignancy. B. A previous common cold is irrelevant to the risk of thyroid cancer. C. Mild transient throat discomfort is non-specific and not a red flag for thyroid malignancy. E. Occasional hiccups are not a recognised feature of thyroid cancer.
pearl: Red flags in a thyroid lump include rapid enlargement, stridor, a hoarse voice and cervical lymphadenopathy; these need urgent referral for assessment.
thinking: New thyroid lump ↓ Look for features of malignancy ↓ Rapid enlargement is a red flag ↓ D, rapidly enlarging mass
exam_trap: C, mild transient throat discomfort — tempting as a local neck symptom, but it is non-specific; stridor or hoarseness, not transient discomfort, are concerning.
takeaway: A rapidly enlarging thyroid mass needs urgent assessment for malignancy.

stem:
A patient has recurrent constipation, thirst and polyuria. Blood tests show significant hypercalcaemia.

Which symptom is consistent with hypercalcaemia?
why_correct: Hypercalcaemia can impair renal concentrating ability, causing polyuria and polydipsia.
why_wrong: A. Photophobia is associated with meningism or migraine, not hypercalcaemia. C. Stridor results from upper airway obstruction and is not a feature of hypercalcaemia. D. Rhinorrhoea is not a feature of hypercalcaemia. E. Haemoptysis is not caused by hypercalcaemia, although it may occur in an underlying lung cancer.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and thirst by impairing renal concentrating ability, plus constipation, confusion and renal stones; the commonest causes are hyperparathyroidism and malignancy.
thinking: Constipation, thirst and polyuria ↓ Significant hypercalcaemia ↓ Calcium impairs renal concentrating ability ↓ B, polyuria
exam_trap: E, haemoptysis — tempting because lung cancer can cause hypercalcaemia, but haemoptysis reflects the tumour, not the high calcium itself.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and thirst by impairing urine concentration.

stem:
A patient taking a thiazide diuretic develops confusion. Blood tests show significant hyponatraemia.

Which medication is a recognised cause?
why_correct: Thiazide diuretics are a recognised cause of hyponatraemia.
why_wrong: A. Topical emollients have no systemic effect on sodium balance. B. Inhaled saline does not cause hyponatraemia. C. Simple antacids do not cause hyponatraemia. E. Vitamin D supplements may cause hypercalcaemia in excess but do not cause hyponatraemia.
pearl: Thiazide diuretics are a common cause of hyponatraemia, particularly in older people; consider the drug in any confused patient taking one and check sodium after starting.
thinking: Patient taking a thiazide ↓ New confusion ↓ Significant hyponatraemia ↓ Thiazides impair urinary dilution ↓ D, thiazide diuretic
exam_trap: C, simple antacid — tempting as another commonly used medicine, but antacids do not cause hyponatraemia.
takeaway: Always consider thiazides as a cause of hyponatraemia.

stem:
