An elderly patient with poor access to water develops marked thirst, lethargy and hypernatraemia.

What is the most likely underlying problem?
why_correct: Hypernatraemia commonly reflects a deficit of free water relative to body sodium.
why_wrong: A. Excess dietary calcium does not cause hypernatraemia. C. Potassium deficiency does not explain hypernatraemia from poor water intake. D. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes anaemia and neurological features, not hypernatraemia. E. Iron deficiency causes anaemia, not hypernatraemia.
pearl: Hypernatraemia usually reflects a free water deficit from poor intake or excess loss; older people with impaired thirst or limited access to water are at high risk. Correct it gradually.
thinking: Elderly with poor access to water ↓ Marked thirst and lethargy ↓ Raised sodium ↓ Free water deficit ↓ B
exam_trap: C, potassium deficiency alone — tempting as another electrolyte disturbance, but low potassium does not explain hypernatraemia from poor water intake.
takeaway: Hypernatraemia usually means a free water deficit.

stem:
A patient with sickle cell disease presents with severe limb and back pain without evidence of infection or acute chest syndrome.

Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Ischaemic tissue pain caused by sickling and microvascular occlusion is the typical presentation of a vaso-occlusive crisis.
why_wrong: A. Compartment syndrome follows injury and causes pain in a single tense limb compartment. B. Appendicitis causes localised right iliac fossa pain rather than limb and back pain. C. Septic arthritis causes a hot swollen joint, usually with fever, and the stem excludes infection. D. Avascular necrosis typically causes progressive localised hip pain rather than acute severe pain in the limbs and back.
pearl: Vaso-occlusive crisis is the commonest acute sickle cell presentation; give rapid, adequate analgesia, often opioids, with fluids and oxygen if hypoxic, while watching for acute chest syndrome.
thinking: Sickle cell disease ↓ Severe limb and back pain ↓ No infection or acute chest syndrome ↓ Microvascular occlusion causing ischaemia ↓ E, vaso-occlusive crisis
exam_trap: D, avascular necrosis of the hip — tempting as a sickle cell complication, but it causes progressive localised hip pain, not acute severe limb and back pain.
takeaway: Acute severe pain in sickle cell disease is a vaso-occlusive crisis: treat pain fast.

stem:
A 28-year-old has markedly elevated LDL cholesterol. His father had a myocardial infarction at 42.

Which inherited disorder should be suspected?
why_correct: Very high LDL cholesterol together with premature cardiovascular disease in a first-degree relative suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia.
why_wrong: B. Marfan syndrome causes aortic dilatation and dissection rather than hypercholesterolaemia. C. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is an inherited cardiomyopathy and does not cause markedly raised LDL cholesterol. D. Addison disease causes adrenal insufficiency and is not a cause of markedly raised LDL cholesterol. E. Haemophilia A is an X-linked bleeding disorder unrelated to cholesterol.
pearl: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is autosomal dominant: very high LDL with premature coronary disease in relatives; look for tendon xanthomas and offer cascade testing of the family.
thinking: Young adult with markedly raised LDL ↓ Father had an MI at a young age ↓ Premature CVD in a first-degree relative ↓ A, familial hypercholesterolaemia
exam_trap: C, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — tempting because of the family history of heart disease, but HCM does not raise LDL cholesterol.
takeaway: Very high LDL plus premature family heart disease: suspect FH and test relatives.

stem:
A child with Down syndrome develops new neck pain and difficulty walking after relatively minor trauma.

What complication should be considered?
why_correct: People with Down syndrome have an increased risk of atlantoaxial instability, which can cause neurological symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Perthes disease affects the hip and causes limp, not neck pain with gait disturbance after trauma. C. Scoliosis does not explain acute neck pain and new difficulty walking after trauma. D. Developmental dysplasia of the hip presents in infancy and does not cause neck pain. E. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes anterior knee pain at the tibial tuberosity.
pearl: Down syndrome carries a risk of atlantoaxial instability; new neck pain, gait change, weakness or sphincter disturbance needs urgent imaging and neurological assessment.
thinking: Down syndrome ↓ Ligamentous laxity at C1–C2 ↓ Minor trauma then neck pain and difficulty walking ↓ Possible cord compression ↓ B, atlantoaxial instability
exam_trap: A, Perthes disease — tempting in a child with difficulty walking, but it causes hip pain and limp, not neck pain after trauma.
takeaway: Down syndrome with neck pain and new gait problems: think atlantoaxial instability.

stem:
A patient has marked joint hypermobility, unusually stretchy skin and easy bruising.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility and tissue fragility are characteristic features.
why_wrong: B. Rheumatoid arthritis causes inflammatory synovitis rather than hypermobility and skin fragility. C. Systemic sclerosis causes skin tightening, the opposite of hyperextensible skin. D. Osteogenesis imperfecta causes recurrent fractures and blue sclerae rather than stretchy skin. E. Marfan syndrome causes hypermobility and tall stature but not markedly hyperextensible skin and easy bruising.
pearl: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome causes joint hypermobility, hyperextensible skin, easy bruising and poor wound healing; the vascular type risks arterial and organ rupture.
thinking: Marked joint hypermobility ↓ Stretchy skin ↓ Easy bruising = tissue fragility ↓ Connective tissue disorder ↓ A, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
exam_trap: E, Marfan syndrome — tempting as another hypermobility disorder, but it causes tall stature and aortic risk, not markedly stretchy skin and easy bruising.
takeaway: Hypermobility plus stretchy skin and easy bruising: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

stem:
A child has poor growth and bowed legs. Blood tests show evidence of impaired bone mineralisation.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Defective mineralisation of growing bone can cause skeletal deformity and impaired growth.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease of adults, not a cause of bowed legs from defective mineralisation in childhood. B. Septic arthritis causes an acutely hot swollen joint, not bowed legs. C. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a collagen disorder causing fractures and blue sclerae, with normal mineralisation biochemistry. E. Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory spondyloarthritis of young adults affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints.
pearl: Rickets is defective mineralisation of growing bone, usually from vitamin D deficiency; look for bowed legs, wrist widening and a rachitic rosary, with raised alkaline phosphatase.
thinking: Child with poor growth ↓ Bowed legs ↓ Impaired bone mineralisation on bloods ↓ Growth plates still open ↓ D, rickets
exam_trap: C, osteogenesis imperfecta — tempting as a childhood bone disorder with deformity, but it is a collagen defect with fractures and blue sclerae, not defective mineralisation.
takeaway: Bowed legs and poor mineralisation in a child: rickets.

stem:
A patient with severe malabsorption develops unexpected bleeding and a prolonged clotting time.

Which vitamin deficiency may be responsible?
why_correct: Vitamin K is required for synthesis of several clotting factors, so deficiency can cause bleeding and prolonged clotting times.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, not coagulopathy. B. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neuropathy, not prolonged clotting time. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes perifollicular and gum bleeding but does not prolong clotting times. E. Vitamin D deficiency causes osteomalacia, not bleeding.
pearl: Vitamin K is fat-soluble, so malabsorption reduces synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X, prolonging the PT; treat with vitamin K.
thinking: Severe malabsorption ↓ Fat-soluble vitamins poorly absorbed ↓ Unexpected bleeding with prolonged clotting time ↓ Clotting factor synthesis impaired ↓ D, vitamin K
exam_trap: C, vitamin C deficiency — tempting as scurvy causes bleeding, but it affects vessel integrity and gums without prolonging clotting times.
takeaway: Malabsorption with bleeding and prolonged PT: think vitamin K deficiency.

stem:
A patient with severe nutritional deficiency develops diarrhoea, a photosensitive rash and cognitive changes.

Which deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Pellagra is caused by niacin deficiency and classically causes dermatitis, diarrhoea and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin D deficiency causes bone pain and osteomalacia rather than dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. B. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding. C. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes anaemia and neurological signs but not a photosensitive rash and diarrhoea. D. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum disease and perifollicular haemorrhages, not a photosensitive dermatitis.
pearl: Pellagra from niacin deficiency causes the three Ds: dermatitis in sun-exposed areas, diarrhoea and dementia; it is seen with alcohol misuse, malnutrition and carcinoid syndrome.
thinking: Severe nutritional deficiency ↓ Diarrhoea ↓ Photosensitive dermatitis ↓ Cognitive change ↓ E, niacin deficiency (pellagra)
exam_trap: C, vitamin B12 deficiency — tempting as it causes cognitive change, but it does not produce a photosensitive rash and diarrhoea.
takeaway: Dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia mean pellagra from niacin deficiency.

stem:
A patient with severe nutritional deficiency develops peripheral neuropathy and muscle weakness.

Which vitamin deficiency is associated with this condition?
why_correct: Thiamine deficiency can cause neurological disease and peripheral neuropathy as well as cardiac manifestations.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not peripheral neuropathy. D. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not neuropathy. E. Vitamin D deficiency can cause proximal myopathy but not peripheral neuropathy.
pearl: Thiamine deficiency causes dry beriberi (peripheral neuropathy), wet beriberi (heart failure) and Wernicke encephalopathy; give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients.
thinking: Severe nutritional deficiency ↓ Peripheral neuropathy and muscle weakness ↓ B vitamin essential to nerve energy metabolism ↓ A, thiamine deficiency
exam_trap: E, vitamin D deficiency — tempting as it causes muscle weakness, but this is a proximal myopathy, not peripheral neuropathy.
takeaway: Malnutrition with peripheral neuropathy: think thiamine deficiency (dry beriberi).

stem:
A patient reports falling asleep unintentionally during the day and has loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing at night.

What is the key safety issue to address?

options.A: Risk of iron-deficiency anaemia from poor sleep
options.B: Risk of nocturnal hypoglycaemia during apnoeas
options.C: Risk of acute urinary retention during the night
options.D: Risk of accidents from daytime sleepiness
options.E: Risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma at night

correct_answer: D. Risk of accidents from daytime sleepiness
why_correct: Excessive daytime sleepiness can significantly impair driving and other safety-critical activities.
why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia is not a consequence of obstructive sleep apnoea. B. Apnoeas cause intermittent hypoxia, not hypoglycaemia, and this is not the key safety issue. C. Urinary retention is not a recognised safety issue in obstructive sleep apnoea. E. Angle-closure glaucoma is not the key safety concern in someone with excessive daytime sleepiness.
pearl: Excessive daytime sleepiness from suspected obstructive sleep apnoea impairs driving; advise not to drive while sleepy and explain DVLA notification requirements.
thinking: Unintentional daytime sleep ↓ Loud snoring with witnessed apnoeas ↓ Obstructive sleep apnoea ↓ Impaired alertness ↓ D, accident risk
exam_trap: B, nocturnal hypoglycaemia — tempting as apnoeas sound metabolically dangerous, but they cause intermittent hypoxia, not hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: Daytime sleepiness from sleep apnoea is a safety issue: always address driving.

stem:
A healthcare worker develops itchy, inflamed hands after frequent exposure to soaps and repeated handwashing.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Repeated wet work and exposure to soaps and detergents can damage the skin barrier and cause irritant contact dermatitis.
why_wrong: A. Palmoplantar pustulosis (pustular psoriasis) causes sterile pustules on the palms and soles and is not caused by wet work. C. Scabies causes intensely itchy burrows in the finger webs and is not caused by soap exposure. D. Tinea manuum is a fungal infection, usually unilateral with a scaly edge, and is not caused by soap exposure. E. Cellulitis causes a hot, spreading, tender erythema, usually unilateral, often with systemic upset.
pearl: Irritant contact dermatitis from wet work is common in healthcare workers; manage with emollients, alcohol hand rub where appropriate and occupational health input.
thinking: Healthcare worker ↓ Frequent handwashing and soap exposure ↓ Itchy, inflamed hands ↓ Skin barrier damage from wet work ↓ B, irritant contact dermatitis
exam_trap: D, tinea manuum — tempting as a cause of an itchy hand rash, but it is usually unilateral with a scaly edge and is not caused by wet work.
takeaway: Hand dermatitis from repeated washing is irritant contact dermatitis.

stem:
A patient develops an itchy rash precisely where a new adhesive dressing has been applied.

Which mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: A delayed itchy eczematous reaction at the site of contact with an allergen is typical of allergic contact dermatitis.
why_wrong: A. A fixed drug eruption is caused by a systemic medicine and recurs at the same site, not at a site of adhesive contact. C. Erysipelas is a superficial bacterial infection with a raised, well-demarcated edge and fever. D. Cellulitis is a spreading bacterial infection, not an itchy reaction confined to the site of contact. E. Urticaria causes transient wheals that are not typically confined precisely to a contact site.
pearl: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed type IV reaction appearing hours to days after contact and sharply confined to the contact site; patch testing identifies the allergen.
thinking: New adhesive dressing ↓ Itchy rash exactly at the contact site ↓ Delayed sensitisation reaction ↓ B, allergic contact dermatitis
exam_trap: E, acute urticaria — tempting as an itchy allergic rash, but wheals are transient and not typically confined precisely to the contact site.
takeaway: A rash precisely matching a contact site suggests allergic contact dermatitis.

stem:
A patient develops localised swelling several hours after prolonged pressure from tight clothing.

Which condition could cause this?
why_correct: Pressure can trigger a form of physical urticaria, producing delayed localised swelling.
why_wrong: B. Psoriasis, including Koebner lesions, causes scaly plaques rather than delayed swelling after pressure. C. Cellulitis is a bacterial infection with spreading erythema, not swelling triggered by pressure. D. Scabies causes itchy burrows from mite infestation, not pressure-induced swelling. E. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender cord along a vein, not swelling after sustained pressure.
pearl: Delayed pressure urticaria causes deep, often painful swelling hours after sustained pressure, such as from tight waistbands, straps or prolonged standing.
thinking: Prolonged pressure from tight clothing ↓ Localised swelling hours later ↓ Physical trigger for urticaria ↓ A, pressure urticaria
exam_trap: C, cellulitis — tempting as a cause of localised swelling, but it is an infection with spreading erythema, not swelling triggered by pressure.
takeaway: Swelling hours after sustained pressure suggests delayed pressure urticaria.

stem:
A patient develops marked weakness raising the arm after a fall. There is difficulty actively abducting the shoulder.

Which injury should be considered?
why_correct: Trauma followed by shoulder weakness, particularly difficulty with active elevation, suggests rotator cuff injury.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms in the hand, not shoulder weakness. B. De Quervain tenosynovitis causes pain at the radial side of the wrist. C. Tennis elbow causes lateral elbow pain on gripping. D. Dupuytren contracture causes progressive finger flexion contractures.
pearl: After a fall, weakness of active shoulder abduction with preserved passive movement suggests a rotator cuff tear, typically supraspinatus; ultrasound or MRI confirms it.
thinking: Fall ↓ Marked weakness raising the arm ↓ Difficulty with active abduction ↓ Cuff tendon disruption ↓ E, rotator cuff tear
exam_trap: C, tennis elbow — tempting as a common upper-limb tendon problem, but it causes lateral elbow pain on gripping, not shoulder weakness.
takeaway: Weak active shoulder abduction after a fall: suspect a rotator cuff tear.

stem:
An older adult has chronic pain and stiffness at the base of the great toe that worsens with walking.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic mechanical pain and stiffness of a weight-bearing joint are typical of osteoarthritis.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is an acute skin infection, not a chronic joint problem. B. Gout causes acute episodic attacks of a hot, red, swollen joint rather than chronic mechanical pain and stiffness. C. Septic arthritis is an acute, hot, swollen joint, usually with fever. D. Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes symmetrical small-joint synovitis with morning stiffness, not isolated first MTP mechanical pain.
pearl: Osteoarthritis of the first MTP joint (hallux rigidus) causes chronic pain and stiffness on walking, especially at push-off; gout instead causes acute hot, swollen attacks.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Chronic pain and stiffness at the base of the great toe ↓ Worse with walking = mechanical ↓ No acute inflammation ↓ E, osteoarthritis
exam_trap: B, gout — tempting because the first MTP joint is its classic site, but gout causes acute attacks of a hot, red, swollen joint, not chronic mechanical pain.
takeaway: Chronic mechanical big-toe pain is osteoarthritis; an acute hot big toe is gout.

stem:
A patient has recurrent sneezing, nasal itching, watery rhinorrhoea and itchy eyes during the pollen season.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Sneezing, nasal itching and watery rhinorrhoea with seasonal variation are characteristic of allergic rhinitis.
why_wrong: A. A nasal foreign body usually causes unilateral foul-smelling discharge, typically in children. B. Epistaxis is nasal bleeding, which is not described. D. Bacterial sinusitis causes facial pain and purulent discharge rather than seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes. E. Nasal septal haematoma follows trauma and causes nasal obstruction.
pearl: Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, itch, watery rhinorrhoea and often itchy eyes; first-line care includes allergen avoidance, non-sedating antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids.
thinking: Sneezing and nasal itching ↓ Watery rhinorrhoea and itchy eyes ↓ Pollen season ↓ IgE-mediated response ↓ C, allergic rhinitis
exam_trap: D, bacterial sinusitis — tempting because of nasal discharge, but it causes facial pain and purulent discharge, not seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes.
takeaway: Seasonal sneezing, itch and watery rhinorrhoea mean allergic rhinitis.

stem:
A patient develops sudden unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness. They cannot fully close the affected eye.

What complication requires particular attention?
why_correct: Incomplete eye closure can expose the cornea to drying and injury, so eye protection is important.
why_wrong: B. Optic neuritis is not caused by facial nerve palsy. C. Acute glaucoma is unrelated to facial nerve palsy. D. Cataract is not a complication of incomplete eye closure. E. Retinal detachment is not a complication of facial nerve palsy.
pearl: In facial nerve palsy with incomplete eye closure, protect the cornea with lubricating drops, ointment and taping the eye closed at night; refer urgently if the eye becomes painful or red.
thinking: Sudden unilateral LMN facial weakness ↓ Orbicularis oculi weak ↓ Eye cannot close fully ↓ Cornea dries and is exposed ↓ A, corneal exposure
exam_trap: C, acute glaucoma — tempting as an eye emergency, but it is unrelated to facial nerve palsy; the real risk is exposure keratopathy.
takeaway: Facial palsy with incomplete eye closure: protect the cornea.

stem:
A patient with frequent headaches takes simple analgesics on most days. The headaches have gradually become more frequent.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Frequent use of acute headache medication can contribute to increasingly frequent or chronic headaches.
why_wrong: A. Giant cell arteritis occurs in older people with temporal tenderness and jaw claudication. C. Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a sudden thunderclap headache, not gradually increasing frequency. D. Temporal lobe epilepsy causes focal seizures rather than frequent headaches linked to analgesic use. E. Cluster headache causes short, severe unilateral orbital attacks with autonomic features rather than daily worsening headache with analgesic use.
pearl: Medication-overuse headache develops with regular use of simple analgesics, triptans or opioids; management is withdrawal of the overused drug, which may briefly worsen headache.
thinking: Frequent headaches ↓ Simple analgesics on most days ↓ Headaches becoming more frequent ↓ Analgesic use driving headache ↓ B, medication-overuse headache
exam_trap: E, chronic cluster headache — tempting as a frequent headache disorder, but it causes short, severe unilateral orbital attacks with autonomic features.
takeaway: Frequent headache with analgesics on most days: think medication overuse.

stem:
A young woman develops painful loss of vision in one eye over several days. She has previously had an episode of limb weakness that resolved.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Episodes separated in time affecting different neurological sites are characteristic of a relapsing demyelinating disorder such as MS.
why_wrong: B. Bell's palsy causes facial weakness, not visual loss. C. Migraine aura is transient and does not cause painful visual loss over several days. D. Retinal detachment is painless and would not explain a previous episode of limb weakness. E. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye with haloes and would not explain the previous limb weakness.
pearl: Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss over days, often worse on eye movement; with a previous separate neurological episode, it points to multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Painful monocular visual loss over days = optic neuritis ↓ Previous resolved limb weakness ↓ Episodes separated in time and place ↓ A, multiple sclerosis
exam_trap: E, acute glaucoma — tempting with a painful eye and visual loss, but it causes a red eye with haloes and cannot explain the earlier limb weakness.
takeaway: Optic neuritis plus a prior separate neurological episode suggests MS.

stem:
A patient with long-term alcohol misuse develops symmetrical numbness and burning in both feet.

Which pattern is most consistent with peripheral neuropathy?
why_correct: Peripheral polyneuropathy commonly produces length-dependent, symmetrical distal sensory symptoms.
why_wrong: B. Isolated visual loss is not a feature of peripheral polyneuropathy. C. A dermatomal rash suggests herpes zoster. D. Sudden unilateral facial weakness suggests Bell's palsy or stroke, not peripheral neuropathy. E. Single-joint swelling suggests arthritis, not neuropathy.
pearl: Alcohol-related peripheral neuropathy is length-dependent, causing a symmetrical glove-and-stocking pattern starting in the feet; nutritional deficiency, especially thiamine, contributes.
thinking: Long-term alcohol misuse ↓ Symmetrical numbness and burning in both feet ↓ Longest nerves affected first ↓ A, distal symmetrical sensory symptoms
exam_trap: C, dermatomal rash — tempting as a sensory-related finding, but it suggests herpes zoster in a single nerve root, not a symmetrical polyneuropathy.
takeaway: Peripheral neuropathy is distal, symmetrical and starts in the feet.

stem:
A patient develops shooting pain from the lower back down the lateral leg to the foot. The pain is worsened by coughing.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Radiating leg pain in a dermatomal distribution that is aggravated by increased intrathecal pressure suggests nerve-root irritation.
why_wrong: B. Polymyalgia rheumatica causes bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness in older people. C. Hip osteoarthritis causes groin and thigh pain rather than radiating pain to the foot worsened by coughing. D. Peripheral vascular disease causes exertional calf pain relieved by rest, not pain worsened by coughing. E. Septic arthritis causes a hot swollen joint, not radiating dermatomal pain.
pearl: Sciatica from lumbar nerve-root compression causes radiating leg pain below the knee, often worse than the back pain and aggravated by coughing; always screen for cauda equina red flags.
thinking: Shooting pain from back down lateral leg to foot ↓ Dermatomal radiation ↓ Worse with coughing (raised intrathecal pressure) ↓ Nerve-root irritation ↓ A, lumbar radiculopathy
exam_trap: D, peripheral vascular disease — tempting as a cause of leg pain, but claudication is exertional calf pain relieved by rest, not worsened by coughing.
takeaway: Radiating dermatomal leg pain worsened by coughing means lumbar radiculopathy.

stem:
A patient has persistently elevated haemoglobin and haematocrit with headaches and facial plethora.

Which broad diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistently increased red-cell mass can cause headache, plethora and increased blood viscosity.
why_wrong: A. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia with low haemoglobin. B. Thrombocytopenia refers to a low platelet count and does not cause plethora. D. Iron-deficiency anaemia causes low haemoglobin, not elevated haemoglobin. E. Neutropenia refers to a low neutrophil count, not raised haemoglobin.
pearl: Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit mean polycythaemia; distinguish primary polycythaemia vera (JAK2) from secondary causes such as chronic hypoxia, and exclude dehydration.
thinking: Persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Headache from hyperviscosity ↓ Facial plethora ↓ Increased red-cell mass ↓ C, polycythaemia
exam_trap: D, iron-deficiency anaemia — tempting because haemoglobin is abnormal, but iron deficiency lowers haemoglobin, whereas here it is raised.
takeaway: Raised haemoglobin with plethora means polycythaemia: look for primary or secondary cause.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy develops a markedly reduced neutrophil count but is currently afebrile.

What is the key clinical concern?
why_correct: Neutropenia substantially increases susceptibility to bacterial and fungal infection, and fever requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: B. Iron deficiency is not a consequence of neutropenia. C. Hypercalcaemia is not caused by neutropenia. D. Cataract formation is not the immediate concern with neutropenia. E. Osteoarthritis is unrelated to neutropenia.
pearl: Neutropenic patients may show few signs of infection; advise them to seek urgent help for any fever or feeling unwell, as neutropenic sepsis can deteriorate rapidly.
thinking: Chemotherapy ↓ Markedly reduced neutrophil count ↓ Impaired defence against bacteria and fungi ↓ A, serious infection risk
exam_trap: B, iron deficiency — tempting as a blood-count problem, but neutropenia affects white cells and does not cause iron deficiency.
takeaway: Neutropenia means high infection risk: any fever needs urgent action.

stem:
A pregnant woman is exposed to cat faeces and is concerned about infection.

Which organism is associated with this exposure?
why_correct: Toxoplasma gondii can be transmitted through exposure to contaminated cat faeces and undercooked meat and is important in pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Clostridioides difficile causes antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and is not linked to cat faeces. B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is sexually transmitted. D. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough and is spread by respiratory droplets. E. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis and is sexually transmitted, not acquired from cat faeces.
pearl: Toxoplasmosis is acquired from cat faeces, soil and undercooked meat; in pregnancy advise gloves for gardening and litter trays, hand washing and thorough cooking of meat.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Exposure to cat faeces ↓ Cats shed infective oocysts in faeces ↓ Risk of congenital infection ↓ C, Toxoplasma gondii
exam_trap: A, Clostridioides difficile — tempting as a faecally spread organism, but it causes antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and is not linked to cats.
takeaway: Cat faeces or undercooked meat in pregnancy: think toxoplasmosis.

stem:
A newborn has a persistent nasal discharge and later develops characteristic skeletal and dental abnormalities.

Which maternal infection can cause this?
why_correct: Untreated maternal syphilis can cross the placenta and cause congenital infection.
why_wrong: B. Cystitis does not cause congenital infection. C. Influenza does not cause congenital skeletal and dental abnormalities. D. Chickenpox after childhood is not a congenital infection and does not cause snuffles or dental abnormalities. E. Otitis media does not cause congenital infection.
pearl: Congenital syphilis causes snuffles and rash early, then Hutchinson teeth, saddle nose and sabre shins; antenatal screening allows maternal treatment to prevent it.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Persistent nasal discharge (snuffles) ↓ Later skeletal and dental abnormalities ↓ Transplacental infection ↓ A, syphilis
exam_trap: D, chickenpox — tempting as an infection linked to congenital problems, but fetal varicella causes limb and skin scarring, not snuffles or dental defects.
takeaway: Snuffles followed by dental and bone abnormalities: congenital syphilis.

stem:
A baby is born with sensorineural hearing loss and congenital heart disease after maternal infection during early pregnancy.

Which infection is classically associated with this combination?
why_correct: Congenital rubella can cause sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease and ocular abnormalities.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A does not cause congenital malformations. B. Cystitis does not cause congenital infection. D. Influenza is not associated with congenital deafness and heart disease. E. Tonsillitis does not cause congenital infection.
pearl: Congenital rubella classically causes sensorineural deafness, cataracts and congenital heart disease such as PDA; risk is highest with infection early in pregnancy.
thinking: Maternal infection in early pregnancy ↓ Sensorineural hearing loss ↓ Congenital heart disease ↓ Classic triad with cataracts ↓ C, rubella
exam_trap: D, influenza — tempting as a common viral infection in pregnancy, but it is not associated with congenital deafness and heart disease.
takeaway: Deafness, cataracts and heart defects: congenital rubella.

stem:
A pregnant woman is exposed to a child with a febrile rash illness. The child has a characteristic “slapped-cheek” appearance.

Which infection is involved?
why_correct: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum, classically producing a slapped-cheek rash.
why_wrong: A. Varicella-zoster virus causes a vesicular rash. C. Rubella causes a maculopapular rash starting on the face with lymphadenopathy, not a slapped-cheek appearance. D. Mumps causes parotitis rather than a rash. E. Measles causes coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots and a maculopapular rash, not slapped cheeks.
pearl: Slapped cheek (erythema infectiosum) is parvovirus B19; children are no longer infectious once the rash appears, but pregnant contacts need assessment because of fetal anaemia risk.
thinking: Child with febrile rash illness ↓ Slapped-cheek appearance ↓ Erythema infectiosum ↓ B, parvovirus B19
exam_trap: C, rubella — tempting as the classic rash concern in pregnancy, but the rubella rash spreads from the face with lymphadenopathy, not slapped cheeks.
takeaway: Slapped cheek is parvovirus B19: assess any pregnant contacts.

stem:
A pregnant woman who is uncertain whether she has had chickenpox reports significant contact with a person with chickenpox.

What is the important first step?

options.A: Reassure her that pregnancy has no relevance
options.B: Give live varicella vaccine immediately without assessment
options.E: Establish her immunity status and seek prompt clinical advice

correct_answer: E. Establish her immunity status and seek prompt clinical advice
why_correct: Varicella exposure during pregnancy requires prompt assessment of immunity and appropriate management.
why_wrong: A. Varicella in pregnancy can cause severe maternal pneumonia and fetal varicella syndrome, so exposure is highly relevant. B. Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. C. A cervical smear is irrelevant to chickenpox exposure. D. Antibiotics have no role in varicella exposure; post-exposure management depends on immunity.
pearl: After significant chickenpox contact in pregnancy with uncertain immunity, check VZV IgG promptly; non-immune women may need post-exposure prophylaxis and should report any rash.
thinking: Pregnant ↓ Uncertain chickenpox history ↓ Significant contact ↓ Risk of maternal pneumonia and fetal varicella ↓ E, establish immunity promptly
exam_trap: B, live varicella vaccine — tempting as a preventive step, but it is a live vaccine and contraindicated in pregnancy.
takeaway: Chickenpox contact in pregnancy: check immunity urgently, then decide on prophylaxis.

stem:
A patient presents with a contaminated puncture wound. Their vaccination history is uncertain.

What is the key issue to assess?

options.A: Hearing threshold on formal pure-tone audiometry
options.B: Tetanus immunisation status and wound risk
options.D: Blood group and the need for urgent cross-matching
options.E: Peak expiratory flow and oxygen saturations

correct_answer: B. Tetanus immunisation status and wound risk
why_correct: Tetanus prevention after injury depends on the wound characteristics and the person's vaccination history.
why_wrong: A. Hearing threshold is not relevant to tetanus risk. C. Visual acuity is not relevant to a puncture wound. D. Blood group and cross-matching are irrelevant to tetanus prevention after a puncture wound. E. Respiratory measurements are not relevant to tetanus risk.
pearl: Tetanus prevention depends on wound risk and vaccination status: clean the wound, give a vaccine dose if immunisation is incomplete or uncertain, and add human tetanus immunoglobulin for tetanus-prone wounds when immunisation is absent or uncertain, as here.
thinking: Contaminated puncture wound ↓ Tetanus-prone injury ↓ Vaccination history uncertain ↓ B, assess immunisation status and wound risk
exam_trap: D, blood group and cross-match — tempting as a reflex for any injury, but a puncture wound needs tetanus prevention, not transfusion planning.
takeaway: For every tetanus-prone wound, check vaccination status and wound risk.

stem:
A patient presents after being bitten by a cat. The wound is small but puncture-like and located on the hand.

Why is this clinically important?

options.B: Cat bites have a significant risk of infection
options.C: Cat bites never require medical assessment

correct_answer: B. Cat bites have a significant risk of infection
why_correct: Cat teeth can inoculate bacteria deeply, and bites to the hand are particularly important because infection can involve deeper structures.
why_wrong: A. NICE recommends prophylactic antibiotics for cat bites that have broken the skin. C. Cat bites, especially to the hand, frequently need assessment because of high infection risk. D. Tetanus status should be checked after any bite that breaks the skin. E. Small puncture wounds are high-risk because bacteria are inoculated deeply and the wound seals over.
pearl: Cat bites cause deep punctures with a high infection risk, often from Pasteurella; prophylactic antibiotics, usually co-amoxiclav, are advised when the skin is broken, especially on the hand.
thinking: Cat bite ↓ Small but deep puncture ↓ Bacteria inoculated deep and wound seals over ↓ Hand involves tendons and joints ↓ B, significant infection risk
exam_trap: E, small punctures cannot become infected — tempting because the wound looks minor, but deep punctures are high-risk as bacteria are sealed in.
takeaway: Cat bites look small but carry a high infection risk, especially on the hand.

stem:
A patient punches another person in the mouth and sustains a wound over the knuckle.

Which injury should be treated as particularly high risk?
correct_answer: D. Human bite to the hand
why_correct: Human bites to the hand can introduce oral bacteria into tendons and joints and may cause serious infection.
why_wrong: A. A superficial forearm scratch carries low infection risk. B. An uncomplicated blister is low risk. C. A minor bruise does not breach the skin. E. A closed ankle sprain has no wound and no infection risk.
pearl: A knuckle wound from punching someone in the mouth is a human bite (fight bite); it can seed the joint and tendons, needing exploration, antibiotics and often hand surgery review.
thinking: Punch to the mouth ↓ Wound over the knuckle ↓ Tooth penetrates skin = human bite ↓ Oral bacteria seeded into joint and tendon ↓ D
exam_trap: A, superficial forearm scratch — tempting if judging risk by wound size, but the small knuckle fight bite carries far greater infection risk.
takeaway: A knuckle wound after a punch is a fight bite: treat it as high-risk.

stem:
Several residents of a care home develop intensely itchy rashes, particularly worse at night.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Treat the most symptomatic resident and review the others next week
options.B: Wait for spontaneous resolution and review all residents in four weeks
options.C: Apply topical antibiotics to the excoriated areas on all of the residents
options.D: Assess for scabies and treat affected residents and their contacts
options.E: Prescribe emollients and topical steroids for presumed asteatotic eczema

correct_answer: D. Assess for scabies and treat affected residents and their contacts
why_correct: Scabies spreads readily through close contact, so management of cases and appropriate contacts is important in institutional outbreaks.
why_wrong: A. Treating one resident and delaying the others allows ongoing transmission; cases and contacts should be treated together. B. Scabies does not resolve spontaneously and will continue to spread while awaiting review. C. Topical antibiotics do not treat scabies. E. Clustering of nocturnal itch in a care home suggests scabies rather than eczema, and topical steroids may mask or worsen it.
pearl: In scabies outbreaks, treat all affected people and close contacts at the same time, usually with permethrin, and wash bedding and clothing; itch may persist for weeks after treatment.
thinking: Several care home residents ↓ Intense itch, worse at night ↓ Clustering suggests a contagious cause ↓ Scabies ↓ D, treat cases and contacts
exam_trap: A, treat only the most symptomatic resident — tempting as a targeted approach, but treating cases one at a time allows ongoing spread and reinfection.
takeaway: Scabies outbreak: treat all cases and contacts at the same time.

stem:
A patient with prolonged fever develops painless linear haemorrhages beneath several fingernails.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Splinter haemorrhages can occur as a peripheral manifestation of infective endocarditis.
why_wrong: A. Psoriasis can cause splinter haemorrhages, but prolonged fever points to endocarditis. C. Iron deficiency causes spoon-shaped nails, not splinter haemorrhages with fever. D. Cellulitis does not cause splinter haemorrhages. E. Raynaud phenomenon causes colour changes of the digits, not splinter haemorrhages with fever.
pearl: Splinter haemorrhages with prolonged fever should prompt suspicion of infective endocarditis: take multiple sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and arrange echocardiography.
thinking: Prolonged fever ↓ Painless linear haemorrhages under several nails ↓ Splinter haemorrhages ↓ Peripheral sign of endocarditis ↓ B, infective endocarditis
exam_trap: A, psoriasis — tempting as it can also cause splinter haemorrhages, but it does not explain a prolonged fever.
takeaway: Fever plus splinter haemorrhages: suspect endocarditis and take blood cultures.

stem:
A 34-year-old develops persistent amenorrhoea, hot flushes and vaginal dryness.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Menopausal symptoms and ovarian failure occurring before the usual age of menopause suggest premature ovarian insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis causes cyclical pelvic pain rather than amenorrhoea with menopausal symptoms. B. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea from intrauterine adhesions, but ovarian function is preserved, so hot flushes and vaginal dryness do not occur. C. PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes oligomenorrhoea with hyperandrogenism, but not hot flushes and vaginal dryness from oestrogen deficiency. E. Bacterial vaginosis causes fishy-smelling discharge, not amenorrhoea or hot flushes.
pearl: Premature ovarian insufficiency causes oestrogen-deficiency symptoms before 40; hormone replacement is advised until the usual age of menopause to protect bone and cardiovascular health.
thinking: Aged 34 ↓ Persistent amenorrhoea ↓ Hot flushes and vaginal dryness = oestrogen deficiency ↓ Ovarian failure before 40 ↓ D, premature ovarian insufficiency
exam_trap: B, Asherman syndrome — tempting as a cause of secondary amenorrhoea, but ovarian function is preserved, so there are no hot flushes or vaginal dryness.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea with oestrogen-deficiency symptoms before 40: premature ovarian insufficiency.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman reports bilateral breast discomfort and nodularity that become more noticeable before menstruation and improve afterwards.

Which diagnosis is most consistent?
why_correct: Cyclical breast pain and nodularity are typical of benign fibrocystic breast changes.
why_wrong: A. Paget disease of the breast causes an eczematous change of the nipple. B. Breast abscess causes a painful, red, fluctuant swelling, often with fever. C. Fibroadenoma is a discrete, mobile lump rather than bilateral cyclical nodularity. D. Breast cancer usually presents as a persistent discrete lump that does not fluctuate with the menstrual cycle.
pearl: Fibrocystic change causes bilateral cyclical breast pain and lumpiness that eases after menstruation; a discrete or persistent lump still needs assessment.
thinking: 32-year-old woman ↓ Bilateral breast discomfort and nodularity ↓ Worse before menstruation, better after ↓ Hormonally responsive benign change ↓ E, fibrocystic change
exam_trap: C, fibroadenoma — tempting in a young woman with breast lumps, but it is a discrete, mobile lump rather than bilateral cyclical nodularity.
takeaway: Bilateral cyclical nodularity that settles after periods suggests fibrocystic change.

stem:
A woman develops rapid enlargement of one breast with diffuse redness, oedema and a peau d'orange appearance.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Rapid breast enlargement with diffuse erythema, oedema and peau d'orange is concerning for inflammatory breast cancer.
why_wrong: A. Fibrocystic change causes cyclical nodularity without skin changes. C. A giant fibroadenoma is a discrete mobile mass without skin changes such as peau d'orange. D. Galactocele is a painless milk cyst in lactating women without peau d'orange. E. Mastitis may cause erythema, but rapid enlargement with peau d'orange, especially outside lactation or without response to antibiotics, suggests inflammatory cancer.
pearl: Inflammatory breast cancer mimics mastitis with rapid diffuse redness, oedema and peau d'orange; suspect it outside lactation or when there is no response to antibiotics, and refer urgently.
thinking: Rapid enlargement of one breast ↓ Diffuse redness and oedema ↓ Peau d'orange from lymphatic obstruction ↓ B, inflammatory breast cancer
exam_trap: E, simple lactational mastitis — tempting because of the redness, but rapid enlargement with peau d'orange suggests inflammatory cancer.
takeaway: Peau d'orange with diffuse redness is inflammatory breast cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A breastfeeding woman develops a painless, soft, fluctuant breast lump without fever or systemic illness. Aspiration yields milky fluid.

Which benign condition can cause this?
why_correct: A galactocele is a milk-filled cyst that can occur during lactation.
why_wrong: A. Inflammatory breast cancer causes diffuse redness, oedema and peau d'orange, not a painless lump yielding milk. C. Mastitis causes breast pain, redness and often fever. D. Breast abscess is painful and usually accompanied by fever or systemic upset. E. Fibroadenoma is a firm, mobile, solid lump and would not yield milky fluid on aspiration.
pearl: A galactocele is a milk-retention cyst during or soon after lactation; it is painless and aspiration yields milk, unlike an abscess, which is painful with systemic upset.
thinking: Breastfeeding woman ↓ Painless, soft, fluctuant lump ↓ No fever or systemic upset ↓ Aspiration yields milky fluid ↓ B, galactocele
exam_trap: D, breast abscess — tempting as a fluctuant lump in lactation, but it is painful, usually with fever, and yields pus rather than milk.
takeaway: A painless fluctuant lump yielding milk during lactation is a galactocele.

stem:
A woman notices a new breast lump associated with dimpling of the overlying skin.

What does this finding suggest?
why_correct: Skin tethering or dimpling can occur when a breast tumour involves structures beneath the skin.
why_wrong: B. Simple cysts are smooth and mobile and do not tether the skin. C. Fibrocystic change causes cyclical nodularity without skin tethering. D. Galactocele is a milk-filled cyst during lactation without skin dimpling. E. Mastitis causes pain and erythema rather than a new lump with skin dimpling.
pearl: Skin dimpling or tethering over a breast lump suggests malignancy involving the suspensory ligaments or skin; refer urgently for triple assessment.
thinking: New breast lump ↓ Overlying skin dimpling ↓ Tumour tethering to deeper structures and skin ↓ A, possible malignancy
exam_trap: B, simple breast cyst — tempting as a common breast lump, but cysts are smooth and mobile and do not tether the skin.
takeaway: A breast lump with skin dimpling needs urgent triple assessment.

stem:
A woman develops new unilateral inversion of a previously normal nipple.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.B: It is a normal involutional change with ageing
options.C: It suggests a fibroadenoma behind the nipple
options.D: It needs assessment for possible malignancy

correct_answer: D. It needs assessment for possible malignancy
why_correct: New unilateral nipple retraction can be associated with an underlying breast tumour.
why_wrong: A. New nipple inversion requires assessment to exclude malignancy. B. New unilateral nipple inversion is not a normal age-related change and must be assessed. C. Fibroadenomas do not usually cause nipple inversion. E. Mastitis does not typically cause new nipple inversion and cannot be confirmed from this sign.
pearl: New unilateral nipple inversion needs breast assessment for cancer, whereas long-standing or bilateral inversion is usually benign.
thinking: Previously normal nipple ↓ New inversion ↓ Unilateral change ↓ Possible tethering by an underlying tumour ↓ D, assess for malignancy
exam_trap: B, normal involutional change — tempting because nipple changes can occur with age, but new unilateral inversion must be assessed.
takeaway: New unilateral nipple inversion needs assessment for breast cancer.

stem:
A young woman reports bleeding after intercourse. Examination shows an area of red glandular tissue around the cervical os.

Which benign condition can cause this appearance?
why_correct: Cervical ectropion exposes delicate glandular epithelium and can cause contact bleeding, particularly in younger women.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer can cause postcoital bleeding, but the question asks for a benign cause of red glandular tissue around the os. C. Vulval cancer affects the vulva, not the cervix. D. Endometrial cancer typically causes postmenopausal bleeding and is not visible on the cervix. E. Ovarian cancer does not produce visible cervical changes.
pearl: Cervical ectropion is common in young women, in pregnancy and with the combined pill, and can cause postcoital bleeding; check screening is up to date and the cervix looks benign.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Postcoital bleeding ↓ Red glandular tissue around the os ↓ Benign cause asked for ↓ B, cervical ectropion
exam_trap: A, cervical cancer — tempting as postcoital bleeding is a red flag, but the question asks for a benign cause of red glandular tissue around the os.
takeaway: Red glandular tissue around the os with contact bleeding suggests cervical ectropion.

stem:
A woman has intermittent postcoital spotting. Examination identifies a small smooth lesion protruding from the cervical os.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Cervical polyps can protrude through the cervical os and cause intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain, not a lesion at the cervical os. C. Vulval cancer affects the vulva, not the cervical os. D. Endometriosis causes cyclical pelvic pain rather than a protruding cervical lesion. E. Fibroids are uterine muscle tumours and rarely protrude through the os as a small smooth lesion.
pearl: Cervical polyps are usually benign and can cause postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding; they are typically removed and sent for histology.
thinking: Intermittent postcoital spotting ↓ Small smooth lesion protruding from the os ↓ Benign growth of the cervical canal ↓ B, cervical polyp
exam_trap: E, fibroid — tempting as a benign uterine growth, but fibroids rarely protrude through the os as a small smooth lesion.
takeaway: A smooth lesion protruding from the os with postcoital spotting is a cervical polyp.

stem:
A woman has previously had untreated chlamydial infection and now has difficulty conceiving.

Which complication is particularly important?
why_correct: Untreated chlamydia can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and subsequent tubal damage.
why_wrong: A. Cervical ectropion is a benign variant and not a complication of chlamydia. B. Premature ovarian insufficiency is not a recognised complication of chlamydia. D. Fibroadenoma is a benign breast lump unrelated to chlamydia. E. Vulval cancer is not linked to chlamydia infection.
pearl: Untreated chlamydia can ascend to cause PID, leading to tubal damage, infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain; infection is often asymptomatic, so testing matters.
thinking: Previous untreated chlamydia ↓ Ascending infection causes PID ↓ Fallopian tube scarring ↓ Difficulty conceiving ↓ C, tubal factor infertility
exam_trap: B, premature ovarian insufficiency — tempting as a cause of infertility, but chlamydia damages the tubes, not the ovaries.
takeaway: Untreated chlamydia causes tubal infertility and raises ectopic risk.

stem:
A postmenopausal woman develops vaginal dryness, discomfort during intercourse and urinary symptoms.

Which condition can explain these symptoms?

options.E: Ectopic pregnancy in the fallopian tube

why_correct: Reduced oestrogen after menopause can cause vaginal and urinary symptoms through changes in the genitourinary tissues.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian torsion causes acute severe pain. B. Hyperemesis gravidarum occurs in early pregnancy. C. Endometriosis typically regresses after menopause and does not explain these urogenital symptoms. E. Ectopic pregnancy does not occur after menopause.
pearl: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause causes vaginal dryness, dyspareunia and urinary symptoms; vaginal oestrogen is effective and can be used alongside systemic HRT.
thinking: Postmenopausal ↓ Vaginal dryness and painful intercourse ↓ Urinary symptoms ↓ Oestrogen-deficient genitourinary tissues ↓ D
exam_trap: C, rectovaginal endometriosis — tempting as a cause of dyspareunia, but it typically regresses after menopause and does not explain the urinary symptoms.
takeaway: Postmenopausal dryness, dyspareunia and urinary symptoms: genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

stem:
A woman with prolonged unopposed oestrogen exposure develops abnormal uterine bleeding.

Which condition can precede endometrial cancer?
why_correct: Endometrial hyperplasia, particularly atypical hyperplasia, can be associated with progression to endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: B. Cervical ectropion is a benign cervical change and does not precede endometrial cancer. C. Vulvovaginal candidiasis is not premalignant. D. Bartholin cyst is a benign vulval cyst unrelated to endometrial cancer. E. Ovarian torsion is not a premalignant endometrial condition.
pearl: Unopposed oestrogen, for example from obesity, anovulation or oestrogen-only HRT with a uterus, drives endometrial hyperplasia; atypical hyperplasia carries a significant risk of progression to cancer.
thinking: Prolonged unopposed oestrogen ↓ Endometrial proliferation ↓ Abnormal uterine bleeding ↓ Hyperplasia, especially atypical ↓ A, endometrial hyperplasia
exam_trap: B, cervical ectropion — tempting as a cause of abnormal bleeding, but it is a benign cervical change and does not precede endometrial cancer.
takeaway: Unopposed oestrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia, a precursor of endometrial cancer.

stem:
A young woman notices a painless lump near the vaginal opening. It is located at the posterolateral aspect of the vaginal introitus.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bartholin cysts occur near the posterolateral vaginal opening and may be painless unless infected.
why_wrong: A. Cervical polyps arise from the cervix and are seen at the os, not the introitus. B. Fibroids are uterine and not located at the introitus. C. Ovarian cysts are pelvic and not palpable at the vaginal introitus. D. Vulval carcinoma is uncommon in young women and usually presents as an ulcer or plaque rather than a smooth cyst at the gland site.
pearl: Bartholin glands lie at the posterolateral vaginal introitus; cysts are painless unless infected, and a new lump at this site in an older woman needs assessment to exclude cancer.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Painless lump near the vaginal opening ↓ Posterolateral introitus = Bartholin gland site ↓ E, Bartholin cyst
exam_trap: D, vulval carcinoma — tempting for any vulval lump, but it is uncommon in young women and usually presents as an ulcer or plaque.
takeaway: A painless posterolateral introital lump in a young woman is a Bartholin cyst.

stem:
A woman develops a very painful swelling near the vaginal opening with difficulty sitting and walking.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Infection of a Bartholin gland cyst can produce a very painful vulval swelling.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian cysts are pelvic and do not cause a vulval swelling. B. An uninfected Bartholin cyst is usually painless. C. Fibroids are uterine and do not cause a vulval swelling. D. A cervical polyp is not palpable near the vaginal opening and is not painful.
pearl: A Bartholin abscess is an acutely painful, tender swelling at the introitus that makes sitting and walking difficult; treat with drainage, for example Word catheter or marsupialisation.
thinking: Very painful swelling ↓ Near the vaginal opening ↓ Difficulty sitting and walking ↓ Infected Bartholin gland ↓ E, Bartholin abscess
exam_trap: B, uninfected Bartholin cyst — tempting as it occurs at the same site, but uninfected cysts are usually painless; severe pain means abscess.
takeaway: A very painful swelling at the vaginal opening is a Bartholin abscess.

stem:
A woman develops a persistent itchy or irregular pigmented lesion on the vulva.

What is the appropriate concern?

options.E: Recurrent bacterial cystitis with vulval irritation

correct_answer: D. Vulval intraepithelial neoplasia or cancer
why_correct: Persistent, atypical, pigmented or changing vulval lesions require assessment for neoplasia.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis causes cyclical pelvic pain rather than a persistent vulval lesion. B. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain. C. Candidiasis causes itch and discharge but not a persistent irregular pigmented lesion, which needs assessment for neoplasia. E. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms, not a persistent irregular pigmented vulval lesion.
pearl: Any persistent, itchy, irregular or pigmented vulval lesion needs examination and biopsy to exclude VIN, vulval cancer or melanoma.
thinking: Persistent itchy vulval lesion ↓ Irregular and pigmented ↓ Possible premalignant or malignant change ↓ D, VIN or cancer
exam_trap: C, candidiasis with excoriation — tempting because of the itch, but thrush does not cause a persistent irregular pigmented lesion.
takeaway: A persistent irregular or pigmented vulval lesion needs assessment for neoplasia.

stem:
A pregnant woman is found to have hyperglycaemia during routine antenatal testing despite having no symptoms.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Hyperglycaemia first recognised during pregnancy may represent gestational diabetes.
why_wrong: A. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic hypertension and is rare. B. Addison disease tends to cause hypoglycaemia, not hyperglycaemia. D. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria with normal blood glucose. E. Hyperglycaemia first detected in pregnancy is most likely gestational diabetes, not necessarily type 1 diabetes.
pearl: Gestational diabetes is often asymptomatic and found on testing; it raises risks of macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycaemia and needs glucose testing after birth.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Hyperglycaemia on routine antenatal testing ↓ No symptoms ↓ First recognised in pregnancy ↓ C, gestational diabetes
exam_trap: E, type 1 diabetes only — tempting as a cause of hyperglycaemia, but asymptomatic hyperglycaemia found on antenatal testing most likely reflects gestational diabetes.
takeaway: Hyperglycaemia first found in pregnancy is usually gestational diabetes.

stem:
A toddler sustains a scald from a cup of hot tea.

Which household intervention helps reduce the risk of similar injuries?

options.A: Cool the room below 10°C so that hot drinks cool more quickly
options.B: Cover hot drinks with a tablecloth to hide them from view
options.C: Place hot drinks on the floor, well away from the table edges
options.D: Keep hot drinks out of reach, away from table edges
options.E: Add salt to hot drinks so that they cool down more quickly

correct_answer: D. Keep hot drinks out of reach, away from table edges
why_correct: Young children are particularly vulnerable to scalds from hot drinks, making safe positioning an important preventive measure.
why_wrong: A. Room temperature does not meaningfully affect the temperature of a freshly made hot drink and cooling a room below 10°C is unsafe for a young child. B. Tablecloths can be pulled by a child, bringing hot drinks down on them. C. Placing hot drinks on the floor puts them within easy reach of a toddler and increases scald risk. E. Adding salt to drinks does not lower their temperature or reduce scald risk.
pearl: Hot-drink scalds are a common, preventable injury in toddlers; keep hot drinks out of reach and away from table edges, and avoid holding a hot drink while holding a child.
thinking: Toddler scalded by hot tea ↓ Toddlers reach for and pull at objects ↓ Prevention depends on removing access ↓ Keep hot drinks out of reach, away from edges
exam_trap: C, place hot drinks on the floor — it sounds like moving them away from the table edge, but the floor is exactly where a toddler can reach them.
takeaway: Prevent scalds by removing access: hot drinks high up and back from edges.

stem:
A patient with a recent dental infection develops bilateral submandibular swelling, a raised tongue and difficulty swallowing.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis of the floor of the mouth and submandibular spaces, often originating from a dental infection.
why_wrong: B. Viral pharyngitis causes sore throat but not bilateral submandibular swelling with tongue elevation after dental infection. C. Aphthous ulcers are small painful mucosal ulcers and do not cause bilateral submandibular swelling with an elevated tongue. D. A parotid tumour typically causes a slowly growing preauricular mass, not acute bilateral submandibular swelling. E. Gingivitis is a localised gum inflammation and does not spread to the submandibular spaces or elevate the tongue.
pearl: Ludwig's angina is bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, usually from a lower molar infection; airway protection takes priority alongside IV antibiotics.
thinking: Recent dental infection ↓ Bilateral submandibular swelling ↓ Raised tongue and dysphagia ↓ Spreading floor-of-mouth cellulitis ↓ Ludwig's angina
exam_trap: C, peritonsillar aphthous ulcer — 'peritonsillar' echoes quinsy, but aphthous ulcers are small mucosal lesions and do not cause bilateral submandibular swelling.
takeaway: Dental infection plus bilateral submandibular swelling and a raised tongue = Ludwig's angina.

stem:
A patient develops painful swelling in front of the ear that becomes worse when eating.

Which salivary gland is most likely affected?
why_correct: Parotid inflammation causes painful preauricular swelling, which can become more noticeable during eating.
why_wrong: A. The thyroid lies in the anterior neck, is not a salivary gland and does not swell in front of the ear with eating. B. The tonsil is lymphoid tissue in the oropharynx and does not cause preauricular swelling with eating. C. The submandibular area is below the jaw and a lymph node is not a salivary gland. E. The lacrimal gland lies in the superolateral orbit and produces tears, not saliva.
pearl: The parotid lies in front of the ear; parotid inflammation or duct obstruction causes preauricular swelling that is often worse with eating as saliva production rises.
thinking: Painful swelling in front of the ear ↓ Worse when eating ↓ Salivary gland stimulated by meals ↓ Preauricular site ↓ Parotid gland
exam_trap: C, submandibular lymph node — meal-related swelling suggests salivary disease, but the submandibular area is below the jaw and a lymph node is not a salivary gland.
takeaway: Preauricular salivary swelling = parotid; swelling below the jaw = submandibular.

stem:
A patient repeatedly develops painful swelling beneath the jaw during meals, which settles afterwards.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.E: Periapical dental abscess of a molar

why_correct: Meal-related swelling and pain are typical of obstruction of a salivary gland duct by a stone.
why_wrong: A. A parotid tumour usually presents as a persistent preauricular mass that does not fluctuate with meals. C. Thyroiditis causes anterior neck pain and swelling unrelated to eating. D. Reactive cervical lymphadenitis causes tender nodes that do not swell and settle with each meal. E. A dental abscess causes persistent localised pain and swelling that does not come and go with meals.
pearl: Most salivary stones form in the submandibular gland; pain and swelling at mealtimes that settle afterwards is the classic history.
thinking: Swelling beneath the jaw ↓ Comes on with meals ↓ Settles afterwards ↓ Intermittent duct obstruction ↓ Submandibular salivary stone
exam_trap: D, reactive cervical lymphadenitis — tender nodes below the jaw are common, but they do not swell and settle with each meal.
takeaway: Meal-related swelling below the jaw = submandibular stone.

stem:
A healthy young adult develops a small, painful, shallow ulcer inside the mouth that resolves spontaneously.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Aphthous ulcers are common, painful, shallow oral ulcers that usually heal spontaneously.
why_wrong: A. Ludwig's angina is a spreading floor-of-mouth cellulitis with systemic illness, not a small self-limiting ulcer. B. A dental abscess causes toothache and localised swelling, not a shallow mucosal ulcer. C. Oral squamous cell carcinoma typically causes a persistent, non-healing ulcer, often in older smokers or drinkers, not one that resolves spontaneously. D. Herpes zoster causes a painful unilateral vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution rather than a single shallow ulcer.
pearl: Aphthous ulcers are small, painful, shallow and self-limiting; any mouth ulcer that fails to heal should prompt review for malignancy.
thinking: Healthy young adult ↓ Small, painful, shallow oral ulcer ↓ Heals by itself ↓ Aphthous ulcer
exam_trap: C, oral squamous cell carcinoma — candidates fear missing cancer, but malignant ulcers persist and do not resolve spontaneously.
takeaway: Painful, shallow and healing = aphthous; persistent = exclude cancer.

stem:
A patient has a persistent ulcer on the side of the tongue that has not healed after several weeks.

What is the most appropriate concern?
why_correct: A persistent non-healing oral ulcer, particularly on the lateral tongue, requires assessment for malignancy.
why_wrong: A. A salivary stone causes meal-related glandular swelling, not a non-healing ulcer on the tongue. B. Viral gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea and does not produce a persistent tongue ulcer. C. Aphthous ulcers usually heal within about two weeks, so persistence for several weeks should not be attributed to them without excluding malignancy. E. Otitis media is a middle-ear infection unrelated to a tongue ulcer.
pearl: An unexplained oral ulcer that persists beyond about three weeks warrants a suspected cancer referral; the lateral tongue is a classic site for squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Ulcer on the side of the tongue ↓ Not healed after several weeks ↓ Benign ulcers usually heal sooner ↓ Oral malignancy
exam_trap: C, aphthous ulcer only — aphthous ulcers are common, but they usually heal within a couple of weeks; persistence must not be attributed to them.
takeaway: A non-healing tongue ulcer is cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A child has recurrent toothache and visible cavities in several teeth.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Dental caries results from progressive destruction of tooth tissue and commonly causes toothache and visible cavities.
why_wrong: A. Aphthous ulcers affect the oral mucosa and do not cause cavities in teeth. B. Peritonsillar abscess causes severe unilateral sore throat and trismus, not toothache with cavities. C. Sialolithiasis causes meal-related salivary gland swelling, not dental cavities. E. Parotitis causes painful preauricular swelling, not toothache or visible cavities.
pearl: Dental caries is largely preventable: reducing how often sugary food and drink are taken, fluoride toothpaste and regular dental review are the core measures.
thinking: Child with recurrent toothache ↓ Visible cavities in several teeth ↓ Progressive destruction of tooth tissue ↓ Dental caries
exam_trap: A, aphthous ulcers — they cause oral pain in children, but they affect the mucosa, not the teeth, and never cause cavities.
takeaway: Toothache with visible cavities = dental caries.

stem:
A pregnant woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. Urine testing suggests a urinary tract infection.

Why is treatment particularly important?

options.A: UTI in pregnancy usually resolves without treatment
options.B: Pregnancy increases the risk of pyelonephritis
options.C: Untreated UTI commonly causes fetal neural tube defects
options.E: Pregnancy protects against urinary tract infection

correct_answer: B. Pregnancy increases the risk of pyelonephritis
why_correct: Urinary infection during pregnancy can progress to upper urinary tract infection and requires appropriate assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. UTI in pregnancy should be treated, as untreated infection risks pyelonephritis and preterm labour. C. Neural tube defects relate to folate deficiency or first-trimester folate antagonists, not untreated UTI. D. Ovarian torsion is not a complication of urinary infection. E. Pregnancy increases rather than protects against urinary infection because of urinary stasis and ureteric dilatation.
pearl: Treat UTI in pregnancy promptly with an antibiotic suitable for pregnancy and send a urine culture; untreated infection can ascend to pyelonephritis and is linked to preterm labour.
thinking: Pregnant woman with dysuria and frequency ↓ Urine test suggests UTI ↓ Urinary stasis and ureteric dilatation in pregnancy ↓ Pregnancy increases the risk of pyelonephritis
exam_trap: A, UTI usually resolves without treatment — some uncomplicated UTIs settle outside pregnancy, but in pregnancy treatment is needed because of the risk of ascending infection.
takeaway: UTI in pregnancy always needs treatment and a urine culture.

stem:
A pregnant woman with severe prolonged vomiting has poor oral intake and develops confusion and unsteadiness.

Which nutritional deficiency is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Prolonged vomiting and poor intake can cause thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency causes a bleeding tendency rather than confusion and unsteadiness. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with gum bleeding and poor wound healing, not acute confusion and ataxia. D. Iron deficiency causes anaemia and fatigue but does not explain acute confusion and ataxia suggestive of Wernicke encephalopathy. E. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, not acute encephalopathy.
pearl: Wernicke encephalopathy can complicate severe vomiting in pregnancy; give thiamine before glucose-containing fluids in at-risk patients.
thinking: Pregnant with prolonged severe vomiting ↓ Poor oral intake ↓ Confusion and unsteadiness ↓ Wernicke encephalopathy ↓ Thiamine deficiency
exam_trap: D, iron deficiency only — common in pregnancy and causes fatigue, but it does not cause acute confusion and ataxia.
takeaway: Severe vomiting in pregnancy plus confusion or ataxia: think thiamine and Wernicke's.

stem:
A newborn has a low temperature and is lethargic and feeding poorly.

Which underlying problem should be considered?
why_correct: Hypothermia, lethargy and poor feeding can be signs of serious neonatal infection.
why_wrong: A. Migraine is not a recognised cause of hypothermia and lethargy in a newborn. B. Teething does not cause hypothermia, lethargy or poor feeding in a newborn. C. Irritable bowel syndrome is not a neonatal diagnosis and does not cause hypothermia or lethargy. D. Hay fever does not occur in newborns and does not cause systemic illness.
pearl: Newborns often show infection through non-specific signs; a low temperature, lethargy and poor feeding can all indicate sepsis and need urgent assessment.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Low temperature ↓ Lethargy and poor feeding ↓ Non-specific signs of sepsis ↓ Neonatal infection
exam_trap: B, simple teething — parents often blame teething, but it does not cause hypothermia, lethargy or poor feeding in a newborn.
takeaway: A cold, lethargic, poorly feeding newborn has sepsis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A young infant becomes pale, lethargic and difficult to wake.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Give an oral sedating antihistamine and observe at home
options.B: Encourage oral fluids and arrange GP review the next day
options.C: Allow the infant to sleep and reassess in the morning
options.D: Treat as an emergency with immediate ABC assessment
options.E: Assume infant colic and give reassurance advice to the parents

correct_answer: D. Treat as an emergency with immediate ABC assessment
why_correct: Reduced responsiveness and pallor in an infant may indicate serious illness and require immediate assessment.
why_wrong: A. An antihistamine is inappropriate and may worsen drowsiness; it does not address the possible underlying serious illness. B. Reduced consciousness is a red-flag feature in NICE fever and sepsis guidance and requires immediate assessment, not review the next day. C. Allowing a pale infant who is difficult to rouse to sleep risks missing serious illness such as sepsis or hypoglycaemia. E. Colic causes crying in an otherwise well infant and does not explain pallor and reduced responsiveness.
pearl: Pallor and being difficult to wake are red-flag features in an infant; manage as an emergency with structured ABC assessment and check blood glucose.
thinking: Young infant ↓ Pale and lethargic ↓ Difficult to wake = reduced consciousness ↓ Red flag for serious illness ↓ Emergency ABC assessment
exam_trap: C, allow the infant to sleep — tiredness seems a benign explanation, but difficulty rousing is reduced consciousness and may signal sepsis or hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: An infant who is hard to wake needs immediate emergency assessment.

stem:
A febrile child develops a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash and becomes increasingly unwell.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Acute urticaria from a drug reaction, managed with antihistamines
options.B: Possible meningococcal disease needing emergency treatment
options.C: Viral exanthem suitable for home care with safety-netting advice
options.D: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) needing urinalysis and BP checks
options.E: Flare of atopic eczema needing topical steroids and emollients

correct_answer: B. Possible meningococcal disease needing emergency treatment
why_correct: A non-blanching rash in an acutely unwell febrile child is a major red flag for invasive meningococcal disease.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria causes transient blanching wheals rather than a non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash. C. A non-blanching rash in an unwell febrile child must not be managed as a viral exanthem at home; meningococcal disease must be treated first. D. IgA vasculitis causes a palpable purpuric rash over the legs and buttocks in a usually well child, not rapid deterioration with fever. E. Atopic eczema is a chronic itchy rash that blanches and does not present with fever and rapid deterioration.
pearl: Fever with a non-blanching rash in an unwell child is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; give parenteral antibiotics without delay and arrange emergency transfer.
thinking: Febrile child ↓ Rapidly spreading non-blanching rash ↓ Increasingly unwell ↓ Possible meningococcal disease needing emergency treatment
exam_trap: D, IgA vasculitis — it does cause a non-blanching rash, but the child is usually well; fever with rapid deterioration points to meningococcal disease.
takeaway: Fever plus non-blanching rash in an unwell child: treat as meningococcal now.

stem:
A child develops sudden severe stridor and difficulty breathing after eating peanuts.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Sudden onset of respiratory distress and stridor during eating strongly suggests inhalation of a foreign body.
why_wrong: A. Cystitis is a bladder infection and has no relationship to stridor. B. Croup develops over a day or two with coryza and a barking cough, not suddenly while eating. C. Migraine causes headache and does not produce stridor or respiratory distress. E. Gastroenteritis causes vomiting and diarrhoea, not sudden stridor during eating.
pearl: Sudden choking, stridor or respiratory distress while eating, particularly nuts, suggests an inhaled foreign body; young children are especially vulnerable.
thinking: Child eating peanuts ↓ Sudden onset ↓ Severe stridor and breathing difficulty ↓ Foreign-body airway obstruction
exam_trap: B, croup — stridor in a child prompts croup, but croup builds over a day or two with coryza and a barking cough, not suddenly during eating.
takeaway: Sudden stridor during eating = inhaled foreign body until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with sarcoidosis develops polyuria and thirst. Blood tests show hypercalcaemia.

What is the mechanism?

options.C: Vitamin D activation by granulomatous tissue
options.D: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption in the small bowel
options.E: Increased calcitonin secretion by thyroid C cells

correct_answer: C. Vitamin D activation by granulomatous tissue
why_correct: Activated macrophages within granulomas can increase conversion of vitamin D to its active form, increasing calcium absorption.
why_wrong: A. PTHrP is produced by some malignancies; in sarcoidosis PTH and PTHrP are suppressed, and hypercalcaemia is driven by calcitriol. B. Renal calcium wasting would lower serum calcium; hypercalciuria in sarcoidosis is a consequence of increased absorption, not the cause of hypercalcaemia. D. Granulomatous calcitriol production increases rather than reduces intestinal calcium absorption. E. Calcitonin lowers serum calcium, and increased secretion would not cause hypercalcaemia.
pearl: Granuloma macrophages convert vitamin D to active calcitriol independently of PTH, so PTH is suppressed; sarcoid hypercalcaemia typically responds to corticosteroids.
thinking: Sarcoidosis ↓ Polyuria, thirst and hypercalcaemia ↓ Granulomas activate vitamin D ↓ More intestinal calcium absorption ↓ Vitamin D activation by granulomatous tissue
exam_trap: A, PTHrP from granulomas — PTHrP is a familiar cause of hypercalcaemia, but it comes from malignancy; in sarcoidosis the driver is calcitriol.
takeaway: Sarcoid hypercalcaemia is driven by granuloma-derived calcitriol, with PTH suppressed.

stem:
A patient with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis presents with a persistent cough.

Which infection-control measure is particularly important?

options.D: No precautions until treatment is completed
options.E: Standard precautions are sufficient in all circumstances

why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate airborne/respiratory infection-control measures to reduce transmission.
why_wrong: A. Reverse isolation protects immunocompromised patients from infection and does not prevent onward spread of TB. C. Contact precautions alone do not prevent airborne transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. D. Patients with suspected infectious pulmonary TB should be isolated from the outset, not only after treatment. E. Standard precautions alone are insufficient for suspected infectious pulmonary TB, which requires airborne precautions.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs airborne precautions from the outset: a single room, with negative pressure where indicated, and respirator masks for staff.
thinking: Suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Persistent cough ↓ Spread by the airborne route ↓ Appropriate respiratory isolation
exam_trap: E, standard precautions are sufficient — they cover routine care, but TB is airborne and needs respiratory isolation from the point of suspicion.
takeaway: Suspected infectious TB: isolate with airborne precautions straight away.

stem:
A patient with known sarcoidosis develops a painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Sarcoidosis can cause ocular inflammation, including uveitis.
