A pregnant patient repeatedly eats non-food substances such as soil and has no cultural explanation for the behaviour.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Pica involves persistent eating of substances that are not normally considered food.
why_wrong: A. Binge-eating disorder involves recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food, not non-food substances. B. Anorexia nervosa involves restricted intake and a distorted body image, not eating non-food substances. D. Bulimia nervosa involves binge eating with compensatory behaviours, not eating non-food substances. E. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions rather than eating non-food substances.
pearl: Pica is persistent eating of non-food substances; in pregnancy it is associated with iron deficiency, so check a full blood count and ferritin.
thinking: Pregnant patient ↓ Repeatedly eats soil ↓ Non-food substance ↓ No cultural explanation ↓ Pica
exam_trap: E, OCD — repetitive behaviour suggests compulsions, but OCD involves obsessions and compulsions, not eating non-food substances.
takeaway: Persistent eating of non-food items = pica; check for iron deficiency.

stem:
A patient presents with haematemesis and melaena.

Which investigation is usually required to identify the source of an upper gastrointestinal bleed?
why_correct: Upper GI endoscopy can identify the bleeding source and allows endoscopic treatment when indicated.
why_wrong: A. MRI brain has no role in locating a gastrointestinal bleed. B. Abdominal ultrasound cannot visualise mucosal bleeding sources and does not allow endoscopic treatment. C. Flexible sigmoidoscopy only examines the distal colon and is irrelevant to haematemesis. E. Colonoscopy examines the colon and cannot identify a source proximal to the ligament of Treitz.
pearl: Upper GI endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic in upper GI bleeding; resuscitate first, and in unstable patients perform endoscopy immediately after resuscitation.
thinking: Haematemesis ↓ Melaena ↓ Source in the upper GI tract ↓ Need to see and treat the lesion ↓ Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
exam_trap: E, colonoscopy with bowel preparation — melaena is passed rectally, which tempts, but it reflects upper GI bleeding that colonoscopy cannot reach.
takeaway: Haematemesis or melaena: resuscitate, then upper GI endoscopy.

stem:
A patient with long-standing gastro-oesophageal reflux disease undergoes endoscopy.

Which condition is associated with chronic GORD?
why_correct: Chronic reflux can cause metaplastic change in the distal oesophageal epithelium known as Barrett oesophagus.
why_wrong: A. Diverticulitis is a colonic condition unrelated to reflux. B. Appendicitis is not a complication of gastro-oesophageal reflux. D. Ulcerative colitis is an inflammatory bowel disease of the colon and is not caused by GORD. E. Haemorrhoids are anorectal vascular cushions unrelated to reflux disease.
pearl: Barrett oesophagus is metaplasia from squamous to columnar epithelium caused by chronic reflux; it is a precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma and may warrant endoscopic surveillance.
thinking: Long-standing GORD ↓ Chronic acid exposure of the distal oesophagus ↓ Squamous to columnar metaplasia ↓ Barrett oesophagus
exam_trap: D, ulcerative colitis — a chronic inflammatory GI condition seen at endoscopy, but it affects the colon and is not caused by reflux.
takeaway: Chronic GORD can cause Barrett oesophagus, a precursor of adenocarcinoma.

stem:
A patient being treated for diverticulitis remains febrile and develops a tender palpable mass in the left lower abdomen.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Persistent sepsis with a localised tender mass following diverticulitis suggests an intra-abdominal abscess.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain and is not a complication of diverticulitis. B. Coeliac disease is a chronic malabsorptive condition and does not cause a tender mass with persistent fever. C. Haemorrhoids cause rectal bleeding and perianal symptoms, not a febrile abdominal mass. E. Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea, not sepsis with a palpable mass.
pearl: Persistent fever or a tender mass despite treatment for diverticulitis suggests an abscess; CT confirms it, and larger collections may need drainage.
thinking: Diverticulitis on treatment ↓ Persistent fever ↓ Tender palpable left lower abdominal mass ↓ Localised collection ↓ Diverticular abscess
exam_trap: C, haemorrhoids — a familiar lower GI problem, but they cause rectal bleeding and perianal symptoms, not fever with an abdominal mass.
takeaway: Diverticulitis not settling, with a tender mass = abscess; arrange CT.

stem:
An older patient with chronic constipation develops marked abdominal distension, abdominal pain and inability to pass stool or flatus.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Sigmoid volvulus causes large-bowel obstruction and is particularly associated with older adults and chronic constipation.
why_wrong: A. Acute hepatitis causes jaundice and malaise, not marked distension with failure to pass flatus. B. Coeliac disease causes malabsorption rather than acute obstruction with absolute constipation. C. Gastric ulcer causes epigastric pain and bleeding rather than large-bowel obstruction. E. Biliary colic causes right upper quadrant pain and does not cause large-bowel obstruction.
pearl: Sigmoid volvulus typically affects older, chronically constipated patients and causes marked distension; uncomplicated cases are often decompressed endoscopically.
thinking: Older adult with chronic constipation ↓ Marked distension and pain ↓ No stool or flatus ↓ Large-bowel obstruction ↓ Sigmoid volvulus
exam_trap: C, gastric ulcer — it causes abdominal pain, but not marked distension with failure to pass stool or flatus.
takeaway: Older constipated patient with massive distension and absolute constipation: sigmoid volvulus.

stem:
A child with known Hirschsprung disease develops sudden abdominal distension, fever and profuse diarrhoea.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever, abdominal distension and diarrhoea in a child with Hirschsprung disease are red flags for Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric stenosis presents in early infancy with projectile non-bilious vomiting, not fever and diarrhoea. B. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorption rather than an acute febrile illness. D. Lactose intolerance does not cause fever or acute systemic illness. E. Biliary colic is rare in children and does not cause fever with profuse diarrhoea and distension.
pearl: Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can occur before or after surgery and may progress to sepsis and perforation; fever, distension and diarrhoea need urgent assessment.
thinking: Known Hirschsprung disease ↓ Sudden abdominal distension ↓ Fever and profuse diarrhoea ↓ Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis
exam_trap: D, lactose intolerance — it causes diarrhoea and distension, but not fever or acute systemic illness.
takeaway: Hirschsprung disease plus fever and diarrhoea = enterocolitis, an emergency.

stem:
A patient develops extensive painful epidermal detachment involving a large proportion of the body surface after starting a medicine.

Which condition represents the severe end of the Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis spectrum?
why_correct: TEN is the severe end of the SJS/TEN spectrum and involves extensive epidermal detachment.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals without epidermal detachment. B. Psoriasis is a chronic scaly inflammatory dermatosis, not an acute drug-induced detachment. D. Cellulitis is a localised bacterial infection, not widespread drug-induced epidermal detachment. E. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is toxin-mediated superficial blistering, usually in young children, and is not part of the SJS/TEN spectrum.
pearl: SJS and TEN are severe drug reactions graded by the extent of epidermal detachment, TEN being the more extensive; stop the culprit drug immediately and involve specialist care.
thinking: New medicine started ↓ Painful epidermal detachment ↓ Large body surface area involved ↓ Severe end of SJS/TEN spectrum ↓ Toxic epidermal necrolysis
exam_trap: E, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome — it also causes widespread skin peeling, but it is toxin-mediated, usually in young children, and not drug-induced.
takeaway: Extensive drug-induced epidermal detachment = TEN; stop the drug.

stem:
A postmenopausal woman develops chronic vulval itching with pale, thin skin and architectural changes.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Lichen sclerosus commonly causes pruritus and pale, thin vulval skin and is associated with an increased risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Genital herpes causes painful vesicles and ulcers rather than chronic pale atrophic skin. B. Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes itch with thick white discharge and erythema rather than pale thin skin with architectural change. C. A Bartholin cyst is a swelling at the vaginal introitus, not chronic itch with pale skin. D. Bacterial vaginosis causes a thin fishy-smelling discharge, not vulval skin changes.
pearl: Lichen sclerosus gives itchy, white, thin 'cigarette-paper' vulval skin with loss of normal architecture; treat with a potent topical steroid and keep under review because of the small risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma.
thinking: Postmenopausal woman with chronic vulval itch ↓ Skin is pale and thin, not red or ulcerated ↓ Architectural change (labial fusion or resorption) points to a chronic scarring dermatosis ↓ Lichen sclerosus
exam_trap: B, vulvovaginal candidiasis — itch makes it tempting, but thrush gives red, inflamed skin with thick white discharge and does not cause pale atrophic skin or architectural change.
takeaway: Chronic vulval itch plus pale, thin skin and scarring means lichen sclerosus until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops new neck pain and neurological symptoms.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause atlantoaxial instability, which may threaten the spinal cord.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms in the hand and does not explain new neck pain. B. Lumbar disc prolapse would not explain neck pain, and the word 'only' ignores cervical involvement in rheumatoid arthritis. C. Gout rarely affects the cervical spine and is not the classic complication here. D. Osteoarthritis of the hip does not cause neck pain or neurological symptoms.
pearl: In long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, new neck pain or neurological signs suggest atlantoaxial subluxation; take care with neck manipulation, including at intubation, and seek urgent imaging and specialist review.
thinking: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Synovitis can erode the transverse ligament and odontoid peg ↓ New neck pain with neurological symptoms suggests cord compromise ↓ Cervical spine instability
exam_trap: A, carpal tunnel syndrome only — a well-known RA complication, but it causes median nerve symptoms in the hand and cannot explain new neck pain; 'only' ignores a threat to the spinal cord.
takeaway: RA plus new neck pain or neurological signs: think atlantoaxial instability and protect the cervical spine.

stem: Which patient has an important risk factor for osteoporosis?

options.A: An adult with isolated, recurrent bacterial otitis externa
options.B: A patient with uncomplicated myopia wearing contact lenses
options.C: A postmenopausal woman on long-term oral prednisolone
options.D: A healthy child with normal growth
options.E: A young adult using a steroid nasal spray for hay fever

correct_answer: C. A postmenopausal woman on long-term oral prednisolone
why_correct: Increasing age, menopause and prolonged systemic corticosteroid use are important osteoporosis risk factors.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa, even when recurrent, has no relationship with bone density. B. Myopia and contact lens use have no association with osteoporosis. D. A healthy child with normal growth has no osteoporosis risk factor. E. Intranasal corticosteroids for allergic rhinitis have minimal systemic absorption and are not a meaningful osteoporosis risk factor.
pearl: Long-term oral glucocorticoids are one of the commonest secondary causes of osteoporosis; consider fracture risk assessment and bone protection when prolonged systemic steroid treatment is started, especially after the menopause.
thinking: Look for established osteoporosis risk factors ↓ Postmenopausal oestrogen loss accelerates bone loss ↓ Long-term oral prednisolone adds systemic steroid-induced bone loss ↓ Postmenopausal woman on long-term oral prednisolone
exam_trap: E, a young adult using a steroid nasal spray — the word 'steroid' tempts, but intranasal steroids have minimal systemic absorption and are not a meaningful osteoporosis risk factor.
takeaway: Systemic, prolonged glucocorticoids plus menopause is a classic high-risk combination for osteoporosis.

stem:
A young adult with inflammatory back pain develops a painful red eye with photophobia.

Which ocular condition should be suspected?
why_correct: A painful photophobic red eye in a patient with an inflammatory systemic condition is characteristic of anterior uveitis.
why_wrong: A. Conjunctivitis causes a red, gritty eye with discharge but not significant pain and photophobia, and is not linked to inflammatory back pain. B. Cataract causes gradual painless blurring without a red eye. D. Subconjunctival haemorrhage is painless and does not cause photophobia. E. A chalazion is a painless eyelid lump and does not cause photophobia.
pearl: Acute anterior uveitis is the commonest extra-articular feature of axial spondyloarthritis: a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision need same-day ophthalmology review.
thinking: Young adult with inflammatory back pain suggests axial spondyloarthritis ↓ Painful red eye with photophobia, not just discomfort ↓ This is the classic associated eye inflammation ↓ Acute anterior uveitis
exam_trap: A, conjunctivitis — the commonest red eye, but it causes grittiness and discharge, not significant pain and photophobia; missing uveitis risks sight-threatening complications.
takeaway: Inflammatory back pain plus a painful, photophobic red eye equals anterior uveitis: refer urgently.

stem:
A patient has chronic irritation, crusting around the eyelashes and burning eyes.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Blepharitis causes chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins, often with crusting and irritation.
why_wrong: A. Orbital cellulitis is an acute infection with fever, lid swelling and painful eye movements, not chronic crusting. B. Cataract causes gradual painless blurring without lid irritation. C. Acute anterior uveitis causes a painful photophobic red eye rather than eyelid margin crusting. E. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a field defect, not eyelid crusting.
pearl: Blepharitis is chronic eyelid-margin inflammation causing burning, grittiness and crusting at the lashes; mainstay treatment is daily lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid cleaning, usually long term.
thinking: Chronic rather than acute symptoms ↓ Crusting localised to the eyelashes and lid margins ↓ Burning, irritated eyes without red flags ↓ Blepharitis
exam_trap: C, acute anterior uveitis — a cause of eye discomfort, but it presents acutely with pain, photophobia and reduced vision, not chronic crusting of the lash line.
takeaway: Chronic crusty lid margins with burning eyes is blepharitis; treat with regular lid hygiene.

stem:
A patient reports a gritty sensation and intermittent blurred vision that improves after blinking.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Grittiness, irritation and fluctuating vision that improves with blinking are typical of dry eye disease.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment causes flashes, floaters and a curtain-like field loss rather than grittiness relieved by blinking. C. Optic neuritis causes painful eye movements and reduced vision that does not improve with blinking. D. Cataract causes gradual, persistent blurring that does not improve with blinking. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye, haloes and systemic upset.
pearl: Dry eye disease causes gritty, burning eyes with vision that blurs and then clears on blinking as the tear film is restored; first-line treatment is lubricating eye drops and addressing contributing factors.
thinking: Gritty, irritated eyes ↓ Blurring is intermittent, not persistent ↓ Vision clears after blinking, so the tear film is the problem ↓ Dry eye disease
exam_trap: D, cataract — causes blurred vision, but it is gradual, painless and constant; blinking does not clear it and it does not cause grittiness.
takeaway: Blurring that clears with blinking plus grittiness points to the tear film: dry eye disease.

stem:
A patient develops sudden unilateral hearing loss over several hours. Otoscopy is normal.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.B: Reassure and review in six months

why_correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is time-sensitive and requires urgent specialist assessment.
why_wrong: B. Sudden sensorineural hearing loss needs same-day assessment because treatment is time-dependent, so delayed review is unsafe. C. Routine audiology alone would delay the urgent ENT assessment needed for sudden hearing loss. D. Ear drops do not treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss and would delay urgent assessment. E. Otitis externa causes ear canal inflammation visible on otoscopy, which is normal here.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss with a normal ear on otoscopy is an ENT emergency; urgent referral allows audiometry, steroid treatment where appropriate and investigation for causes such as a vestibular schwannoma.
thinking: Hearing loss developing over hours ↓ Normal otoscopy rules out wax, effusion and canal causes ↓ Likely sudden sensorineural hearing loss ↓ Time-sensitive, so arrange urgent ENT assessment
exam_trap: C, routine audiology only — a hearing test is part of work-up, but a routine referral wastes the short window in which treatment is most likely to help.
takeaway: Sudden unilateral hearing loss with normal otoscopy needs urgent, same-day ENT referral.

stem:
A patient develops ear pain after frequent swimming. Movement of the tragus markedly worsens the pain.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Pain aggravated by movement of the tragus is characteristic of inflammation of the external ear canal.
why_wrong: A. Cholesteatoma typically causes painless offensive discharge and hearing loss. B. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss rather than ear pain. C. Acute otitis media causes deep ear pain with a bulging tympanic membrane, not pain on tragal movement. D. Otosclerosis causes painless progressive conductive hearing loss.
pearl: Otitis externa is typical in swimmers: canal pain worsened by moving the tragus or pinna, often with discharge; topical treatment and keeping the ear dry are the mainstay.
thinking: Frequent swimming keeps the ear canal moist ↓ Ear pain localised to the canal ↓ Tragal movement markedly worsens pain ↓ Otitis externa
exam_trap: C, acute otitis media — a common cause of ear pain, but it arises in the middle ear, so moving the tragus does not typically worsen it and swimming is not the classic trigger.
takeaway: Ear pain worse on tragal pressure after swimming is otitis externa, not otitis media.

stem:
A patient has persistent offensive ear discharge and conductive hearing loss.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent offensive otorrhoea with conductive hearing loss is characteristic of cholesteatoma.
why_wrong: A. Acute otitis externa causes painful otorrhoea of short duration rather than persistent offensive discharge with conductive loss. B. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo with no hearing loss or discharge. D. Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss but no ear discharge. E. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss, not offensive discharge.
pearl: Cholesteatoma is a destructive keratinising growth in the middle ear: persistent foul-smelling discharge with conductive hearing loss needs ENT referral, as it can erode the ossicles and beyond.
thinking: Persistent rather than acute discharge ↓ Discharge is offensive ↓ Conductive hearing loss suggests middle-ear involvement ↓ Cholesteatoma
exam_trap: A, acute otitis externa — causes ear discharge, but it is acute and painful with tragal tenderness, and does not explain chronic foul discharge with conductive loss.
takeaway: Chronic foul-smelling otorrhoea plus conductive hearing loss: refer for suspected cholesteatoma.

stem:
A patient experiences repeated episodes of jerking of the right hand followed by brief confusion. The episodes are stereotyped.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent stereotyped motor episodes affecting one body region are characteristic of focal seizures.
why_wrong: A. Syncope causes brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, not focal motor jerking. B. Panic attacks cause anxiety, palpitations and hyperventilation rather than stereotyped focal jerking. D. TIA causes sudden negative symptoms such as weakness or numbness, not jerking followed by confusion. E. Migraine aura evolves gradually over minutes and does not usually cause stereotyped limb jerking with post-event confusion.
pearl: Focal seizures are stereotyped and arise from one area of cortex; motor jerking of one limb followed by post-event confusion suggests seizure activity, and new episodes warrant specialist neurology assessment.
thinking: Recurrent episodes that are stereotyped ↓ Positive motor symptom: jerking of one hand ↓ Followed by brief confusion, a post-ictal feature ↓ Focal seizure
exam_trap: D, TIA — a sudden focal neurological event tempts, but TIAs cause negative symptoms such as weakness or numbness, not rhythmic jerking followed by confusion.
takeaway: Stereotyped positive motor episodes with post-event confusion suggest focal seizures, not TIA.

stem:
A patient develops fever, confusion and altered behaviour followed by a focal seizure.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever accompanied by altered mental state and seizures suggests inflammation of the brain, including viral encephalitis.
why_wrong: A. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo with no fever or altered mental state. B. Bell's palsy causes isolated facial weakness without encephalopathy. C. Migraine without aura does not cause fever, behavioural change or seizures. D. Tension-type headache does not cause fever, altered behaviour or seizures.
pearl: Fever with confusion, behavioural change or seizures suggests encephalitis; start intravenous aciclovir promptly for possible herpes simplex encephalitis while arranging imaging and lumbar puncture when safe.
thinking: Fever indicates infection or inflammation ↓ Confusion and altered behaviour mean brain parenchymal involvement ↓ New focal seizure supports this ↓ Encephalitis
exam_trap: C, migraine without aura — can cause headache and nausea, but does not cause fever, altered behaviour or seizures.
takeaway: Fever plus altered mental state or seizures is encephalitis until proven otherwise: start aciclovir.

stem:
A patient is clinically stable but infective endocarditis is suspected.

Which investigation is important before antibiotics when this can be done without delaying urgent treatment?
why_correct: Blood cultures are essential for identifying the causative organism and guiding antimicrobial therapy.
why_wrong: B. Spirometry assesses airway function and has no role in suspected endocarditis. C. Stool culture does not identify the organism in infective endocarditis. D. D-dimer is used in suspected venous thromboembolism and does not help diagnose endocarditis. E. A pregnancy test may be relevant before some treatments but does not identify the causative organism.
pearl: In suspected infective endocarditis, take several sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics when the patient is stable, as identifying the organism guides weeks of targeted treatment.
thinking: Suspected infective endocarditis ↓ Patient is stable, so cultures will not delay urgent treatment ↓ Organism identification guides prolonged therapy ↓ Multiple blood culture sets before antibiotics
exam_trap: D, D-dimer — tempting as a common acute blood test, but it is non-specific and has no role in diagnosing endocarditis or guiding antibiotics.
takeaway: Suspected endocarditis in a stable patient: multiple blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

stem:
A young child has fever lasting several days together with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, changes in the mouth and a widespread rash.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent fever with mucocutaneous features is characteristic of Kawasaki disease, which carries a risk of coronary complications.
why_wrong: A. Measles causes coryza, cough and conjunctivitis with Koplik spots and a descending rash, usually with an unvaccinated history. B. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue, typically with tonsillitis, rather than non-purulent conjunctivitis with prolonged fever. C. Viral conjunctivitis does not explain prolonged fever with mouth changes and a widespread rash. E. Chickenpox causes crops of vesicles rather than conjunctivitis with mucosal changes.
pearl: Kawasaki disease should be suspected in a child with several days of fever plus non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral changes, rash, extremity changes or cervical lymphadenopathy; early IV immunoglobulin reduces coronary aneurysm risk.
thinking: Young child with prolonged fever ↓ Bilateral conjunctivitis without pus ↓ Mouth changes and widespread rash, all mucocutaneous ↓ Kawasaki disease
exam_trap: A, measles — fever, conjunctivitis and rash overlap, but measles gives coryza, cough and Koplik spots; persistent fever with non-purulent conjunctivitis and oral changes fits Kawasaki.
takeaway: Prolonged fever plus mucocutaneous signs in a young child: think Kawasaki and protect the coronaries.

stem:
A boy has recurrent painful swelling of his knees and ankles caused by bleeding into the joints.

Which inherited bleeding disorder is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent haemarthroses are characteristic of haemophilia.
why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia is not a bleeding disorder. C. Sickle cell disease causes painful vaso-occlusive crises, not bleeding into joints. D. Immune thrombocytopenia is acquired and causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, not joint bleeds. E. Von Willebrand disease usually causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as epistaxis and menorrhagia rather than recurrent haemarthroses.
pearl: Haemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency, so it mainly affects males; spontaneous or minor-trauma bleeds into joints and muscles are typical, with a prolonged APTT and normal platelet count.
thinking: Boy, so consider an X-linked disorder ↓ Recurrent bleeding into joints (haemarthroses) ↓ Deep tissue bleeding suggests a clotting factor deficiency ↓ Haemophilia A
exam_trap: E, von Willebrand disease — the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, but it typically causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as nosebleeds and menorrhagia rather than recurrent haemarthroses.
takeaway: Recurrent haemarthroses in a boy point to haemophilia, not platelet or von Willebrand problems.

stem:
A child with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia develops complications after many years of regular blood transfusions.

Which problem is an important long-term complication?
why_correct: Repeated transfusions can cause significant iron accumulation, potentially damaging multiple organs.
why_wrong: A. Acute appendicitis is unrelated to transfusion therapy. B. Gout is not a characteristic complication of long-term transfusion in thalassaemia. C. Vitamin C deficiency is not a complication of regular transfusion. E. Hyperthyroidism is not a recognised complication of transfusion; iron overload more often causes hypothyroidism.
pearl: Each unit of transfused blood adds iron the body cannot excrete, so regularly transfused patients need monitoring and iron chelation to protect the heart, liver and endocrine glands.
thinking: Transfusion-dependent thalassaemia ↓ Many years of regular red-cell transfusions ↓ The body has no active route to excrete iron ↓ Iron overload
exam_trap: E, hyperthyroidism in every case — endocrine damage does occur with iron overload, but hypothyroidism is the recognised pattern and 'in every case' makes this wrong.
takeaway: Long-term regular transfusions mean iron overload: monitor and chelate.

stem:
A young adult has markedly elevated LDL cholesterol and a strong family history of premature cardiovascular disease.

Which inherited condition should be considered?
why_correct: Markedly elevated LDL cholesterol with premature cardiovascular disease in close relatives suggests familial hypercholesterolaemia.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism is a secondary cause of raised cholesterol but does not explain a strong inherited pattern of premature cardiovascular disease. B. Iron-deficiency anaemia does not cause hypercholesterolaemia. C. Cystic fibrosis is not associated with markedly raised LDL cholesterol. D. Type 1 diabetes does not characteristically cause markedly raised LDL cholesterol with a family history of premature cardiovascular disease.
pearl: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is a common, usually autosomal dominant cause of very high LDL cholesterol and early cardiovascular disease; diagnosis should prompt treatment and cascade testing of relatives.
thinking: Young adult, so markedly high LDL is unusual ↓ Strong family history of premature cardiovascular disease ↓ Suggests an inherited lipid disorder ↓ Familial hypercholesterolaemia
exam_trap: A, primary hypothyroidism with dyslipidaemia — a real secondary cause of raised cholesterol worth checking, but it does not explain a strong family history of premature cardiovascular disease.
takeaway: Very high LDL plus premature cardiovascular disease in relatives: think familial hypercholesterolaemia and test the family.

stem:
A patient taking lithium regularly starts taking ibuprofen for back pain.

What is the important potential consequence?

options.D: Reduced lithium levels and loss of efficacy

correct_answer: A. Raised lithium levels and toxicity
why_correct: NSAIDs can reduce renal lithium clearance and increase the risk of lithium toxicity.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with metformin and PPIs, not lithium with NSAIDs. C. Hypoglycaemia is not a recognised consequence of combining lithium with ibuprofen. D. NSAIDs increase rather than reduce lithium concentrations. E. Agranulocytosis is associated with drugs such as clozapine and carbimazole, not this combination.
pearl: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics can all raise lithium levels by reducing renal clearance; avoid the combination where possible or monitor levels closely and warn about toxicity symptoms.
thinking: Patient on lithium, a narrow therapeutic index drug ↓ Lithium is renally cleared ↓ NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance ↓ Raised lithium levels and toxicity
exam_trap: D, reduced lithium levels and loss of efficacy — tempting if you know there is an interaction but forget the direction; NSAIDs increase, not reduce, lithium levels.
takeaway: NSAIDs push lithium levels up: avoid, or monitor closely for toxicity.

stem:
A woman taking sodium valproate is planning a pregnancy.

What is the key issue?

options.A: Valproate is completely contraindicated in all adults
options.B: Valproate causes maternal diabetes in all pregnancies

correct_answer: D. Valproate carries significant fetal risk
why_correct: Valproate is associated with major fetal risks and requires strict pregnancy-prevention and specialist prescribing considerations.
why_wrong: A. Valproate is not contraindicated in all adults; it is restricted in people who could become pregnant and requires specialist review. B. Valproate does not cause diabetes in pregnancy. C. Valproate does not cause ectopic pregnancy. E. Valproate does not cause permanent anovulation.
pearl: Valproate carries a high risk of birth defects and neurodevelopmental disorders; in anyone who could become pregnant it needs specialist review, and a woman planning pregnancy should be referred promptly without stopping it abruptly herself.
thinking: Woman taking sodium valproate ↓ Planning a pregnancy ↓ Valproate is highly teratogenic and affects neurodevelopment ↓ Valproate carries significant fetal risk
exam_trap: A, valproate is completely contraindicated in all adults — overstates the restriction; valproate is still used in some adults, but it is tightly controlled in anyone who could become pregnant.
takeaway: Valproate and pregnancy plans: significant fetal risk, so urgent specialist review of treatment.

stem:
A patient taking metformin long term develops numbness and macrocytosis.

Which deficiency should be considered?
why_correct: Long-term metformin treatment can be associated with vitamin B12 deficiency, which can cause neurological symptoms and megaloblastic anaemia.
why_wrong: B. Thiamine deficiency can cause neuropathy but is not linked to metformin and does not cause macrocytosis. C. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not macrocytosis, and is not linked to metformin. D. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness and is not associated with metformin. E. Vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not numbness and macrocytosis.
pearl: Long-term metformin can reduce vitamin B12 absorption; consider checking B12 if a patient on metformin develops neuropathy or macrocytic anaemia, as neuropathy may otherwise be wrongly blamed on diabetes.
thinking: Long-term metformin use ↓ New numbness suggests neuropathy ↓ Macrocytosis points to B12 or folate deficiency ↓ Vitamin B12
exam_trap: B, vitamin B1 (thiamine) — deficiency can cause neuropathy, but it is linked to alcohol and malnutrition rather than metformin, and does not cause macrocytosis.
takeaway: Metformin plus neuropathy or macrocytosis: check vitamin B12.

stem:
A patient taking long-term oral corticosteroids develops a significant acute illness.

Why is steroid management important?

options.C: Steroids commonly cause hypoglycaemia during illness
options.D: Steroids treat infection, so antibiotics can be omitted
options.E: Adrenal suppression impairs the cortisol stress response

correct_answer: E. Adrenal suppression impairs the cortisol stress response
why_correct: Long-term corticosteroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so the patient cannot mount a cortisol stress response; sick-day rules (Society for Endocrinology guidance and the NatPSA Steroid Emergency Card) mean doubling the oral glucocorticoid dose during significant illness and never stopping it abruptly. If vomiting or acutely unwell, IM/IV hydrocortisone is needed to prevent adrenal crisis.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids cause hyperglycaemia by increasing insulin resistance; they do not permanently suppress insulin production. B. Steroids may blunt fever, but this is not why dose management matters in an HPA-suppressed patient. C. Corticosteroids typically cause hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia. D. Steroids do not treat infection and do not remove the need for antibiotics.
pearl: Patients on long-term steroids have a suppressed adrenal axis, so they need sick-day rules during significant illness and parenteral hydrocortisone if vomiting or very unwell; never stop long-term steroids abruptly.
thinking: Long-term oral corticosteroids ↓ HPA axis is suppressed, so the adrenals cannot respond ↓ Significant illness needs a cortisol stress response ↓ Adrenal suppression impairs the cortisol stress response
exam_trap: D, steroids treat infection so antibiotics can be omitted — wrong: steroids suppress immunity and can mask infection; the real danger is adrenal crisis without extra steroid cover.
takeaway: Long-term steroids plus acute illness: increase steroid cover to prevent adrenal crisis.

stem:
A patient is prescribed an oral bisphosphonate.

Which instruction helps reduce oesophageal irritation?

options.A: Crush the tablet and take it in a warm drink at bedtime
options.B: Take it with a large meal
options.C: Take it with an antacid to protect the oesophagus
options.D: Take it at night, immediately before lying down to sleep
options.E: Take with a full glass of water and stay upright

correct_answer: E. Take with a full glass of water and stay upright
why_correct: Oral bisphosphonates can cause oesophageal irritation and should be taken with water while remaining upright according to the specific product instructions.
why_wrong: A. Crushing the tablet or taking it at bedtime increases oesophageal irritation and reduces absorption. B. Food markedly reduces bisphosphonate absorption, so it must be taken on an empty stomach. C. Antacids and calcium bind bisphosphonates and reduce their absorption. D. Taking it before lying down increases the risk of oesophagitis.
pearl: Oral bisphosphonates are taken on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, staying upright for a set time before food or other medicines, to reduce oesophagitis and allow absorption.
thinking: Oral bisphosphonate prescribed ↓ Main risk is oesophageal irritation and ulceration ↓ Tablet must reach the stomach quickly and not reflux ↓ Full glass of water and stay upright
exam_trap: C, take it with an antacid to protect the oesophagus — sounds protective, but calcium and other antacids block bisphosphonate absorption and do not prevent oesophageal injury.
takeaway: Bisphosphonate tablets: plain water, empty stomach, and stay upright afterwards.

stem:
A patient taking several medicines is prescribed clarithromycin. The pharmacist identifies a potentially serious interaction.

Why can clarithromycin cause clinically important drug interactions?
why_correct: Clarithromycin is a CYP3A4 inhibitor and can increase concentrations of several medicines metabolised by this pathway.
why_wrong: A. Chelation is a mechanism of tetracyclines and quinolones with metal ions, not of clarithromycin. C. Clarithromycin does not permanently inhibit glomerular filtration. D. Clarithromycin does not block vitamin B12 absorption. E. Clarithromycin does not induce insulin secretion.
pearl: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, raising levels of drugs such as some statins, so combinations can cause toxicity; check interactions before prescribing and pause or switch medicines where needed.
thinking: Patient on several medicines ↓ Clarithromycin added ↓ It inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that metabolises many drugs ↓ Inhibits CYP3A4, raising other drug levels
exam_trap: A, it chelates all oral medicines — chelation is a real mechanism for tetracyclines and quinolones with metal ions, but it is not how clarithromycin interacts.
takeaway: Clarithromycin is a CYP3A4 inhibitor: expect raised levels of co-prescribed drugs.

stem:
A healthcare worker has a significant occupational exposure to blood potentially containing HIV.

What determines whether HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is indicated?

options.B: The presence of a fever in the worker
options.C: Whether the worker has received influenza vaccination
options.E: Assessment of the exposure and source risk

correct_answer: E. Assessment of the exposure and source risk
why_correct: PEP decisions depend on the type of exposure and the likelihood that the source has transmissible HIV.
why_wrong: A. The source patient's age alone does not determine HIV risk. B. Fever in the worker does not determine whether PEP is needed after exposure. C. Influenza vaccination status is irrelevant to HIV PEP. D. Blood group has no bearing on HIV transmission risk or the need for PEP.
pearl: After a sharps or blood exposure, first aid comes first, then urgent risk assessment of the exposure type and the source's HIV status; PEP, if indicated, should start as soon as possible.
thinking: Significant occupational blood exposure ↓ HIV transmission risk depends on the injury and the source ↓ PEP is given only when that combined risk warrants it ↓ Assessment of the exposure and source risk
exam_trap: B, fever in the worker — tempting as a sign of infection, but early symptoms play no part in the PEP decision, which is made urgently on exposure and source risk.
takeaway: HIV PEP decisions rest on exposure type and source risk, assessed urgently.

stem:
After using a needle, a healthcare worker is about to recap it before disposal.

What is the appropriate action?

options.A: Place it unrecapped into a yellow clinical-waste bag
options.C: Do not recap; place it directly in a sharps container
options.E: Leave it on the trolley and dispose of it afterwards

correct_answer: C. Do not recap; place it directly in a sharps container
why_correct: Recapping increases needlestick risk. Used sharps should be disposed of immediately in an appropriate sharps container.
why_wrong: A. Clinical-waste bags can be punctured, so sharps must go in a rigid sharps container. B. Bending needles increases the risk of injury and is not permitted. D. Recapping, especially two-handed, is a major cause of needlestick injury. E. Leaving a used needle on a trolley, even temporarily, exposes others to needlestick injury.
pearl: Never recap used needles; dispose of sharps immediately at the point of use into a sharps container, which is the user's own responsibility.
thinking: Used needle in hand ↓ Recapping is a leading cause of needlestick injury ↓ Immediate disposal removes the hazard ↓ Do not recap; place it directly in a sharps container
exam_trap: A, place it unrecapped into a yellow clinical-waste bag — avoids recapping, but bags are easily pierced and put others handling the waste at risk; sharps go in a rigid sharps bin.
takeaway: Never recap: used needles go straight into a sharps container.

stem:
A doctor is handing over a deteriorating patient to the on-call team.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Ask the receiving doctor to read the entire medical record first
options.B: Give a structured handover, such as SBAR, with clear actions
options.C: Focus on confirmed facts and leave out diagnostic uncertainties
options.D: Hand over by email after the shift so that it is fully documented

correct_answer: B. Give a structured handover, such as SBAR, with clear actions
why_correct: Structured communication reduces omissions and ensures the receiving team understands what needs to happen.
why_wrong: A. Expecting the receiving doctor to read the entire record is inefficient and risks key issues being missed. C. Uncertainties should be highlighted, as they are often the most important information for the receiving team. D. Handing over by email after the shift leaves a deteriorating patient without clear, timely ownership. E. Giving only the name omits the clinical information needed for safe care.
pearl: A structured handover such as SBAR covers situation, background, assessment and recommendation, making the deterioration and the actions needed explicit, and it should be face to face or verbal for unwell patients.
thinking: Deteriorating patient needs timely action ↓ Unstructured handovers miss key information ↓ A structured format with clear actions closes gaps ↓ Structured handover such as SBAR
exam_trap: C, focus on confirmed facts and leave out diagnostic uncertainties — sounds tidy, but uncertainties are exactly what the on-call team needs to know to act safely.
takeaway: Hand over deteriorating patients verbally with a structured tool such as SBAR and explicit actions.

stem:
A patient is undergoing an intimate examination.

What should the clinician do?

options.C: Offer a chaperone and respect the patient's wishes
options.E: Require a family member to be present as chaperone

correct_answer: C. Offer a chaperone and respect the patient's wishes
why_correct: Chaperones help protect patient dignity and both patient and clinician during intimate examinations.
why_wrong: A. Intimate examinations require explanation and consent before proceeding. B. Another patient is not an appropriate chaperone and would breach confidentiality. D. Refusing to examine is not appropriate; the examination should be offered with a chaperone and the patient's wishes respected. E. A family member should not be required to chaperone; a chaperone should usually be a trained impartial observer.
pearl: Before any intimate examination, explain what is involved, get consent and offer a chaperone regardless of the clinician's or patient's gender; record the offer and the patient's decision.
thinking: Intimate examination planned ↓ Patient dignity and consent are paramount ↓ A chaperone protects both patient and clinician ↓ Offer a chaperone and respect the patient's wishes
exam_trap: E, require a family member to be present as chaperone — a relative is not an impartial chaperone, and the patient's wishes about who is present must be respected.
takeaway: Always offer a chaperone for intimate examinations and record the patient's choice.

stem:
A child presents with injuries that do not fit the history provided by the accompanying adult.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Ask the child to investigate the cause
options.B: Confront the adult directly about the suspected abuse
options.C: Discharge and ask the health visitor to review next month
options.D: Consider safeguarding and follow local procedures

correct_answer: D. Consider safeguarding and follow local procedures
why_correct: An inconsistent history and unexplained injuries should raise safeguarding concerns and prompt appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. A child should never be asked to investigate the cause of their injuries. B. Confronting the adult may escalate risk to the child and is not part of safeguarding procedure. C. Discharging with delayed review could leave the child at risk; concerns must be acted on now. E. Ignoring an unexplained discrepancy could leave a child at risk of further harm.
pearl: Injuries inconsistent with the history given are a safeguarding red flag; record findings carefully, discuss with a senior or the safeguarding lead, and follow local child protection procedures without delay.
thinking: Child with injuries ↓ History from the adult does not fit the injuries ↓ This raises concern for non-accidental injury ↓ Consider safeguarding and follow local procedures
exam_trap: B, confront the adult directly about the suspected abuse — feels proactive, but accusing the adult may put the child at further risk; concerns go through safeguarding procedures.
takeaway: An injury that does not fit the history triggers safeguarding procedures, not confrontation.

stem:
A patient attends repeatedly with injuries and their partner insists on staying in the consultation.

What is an appropriate step?

options.B: Tell the partner that abuse has definitely occurred
options.D: Ask the partner to answer all questions
options.E: Seek an opportunity to speak with the patient privately

correct_answer: E. Seek an opportunity to speak with the patient privately
why_correct: Private consultation allows the clinician to assess safety and possible abuse without the potential perpetrator being present.
why_wrong: A. Discharging without assessment ignores injuries and possible safeguarding concerns. B. Accusing the partner without evidence may increase risk to the patient. C. Assuming the injuries are accidental risks missing domestic abuse. D. Allowing the partner to answer may silence a patient who is experiencing domestic abuse.
pearl: Repeated injuries with a partner who will not leave the room should raise concern about domestic abuse; find a way to see the patient alone, ask directly and sensitively, and signpost support.
thinking: Repeated attendances with injuries ↓ Partner insists on staying, a possible controlling behaviour ↓ The patient cannot disclose safely in front of them ↓ Seek an opportunity to speak with the patient privately
exam_trap: B, tell the partner that abuse has definitely occurred — confronting the suspected perpetrator without evidence may escalate risk to the patient; the priority is a safe private conversation.
takeaway: Suspected domestic abuse: see the patient alone before asking about safety.

stem:
An adult patient lacks capacity to make one particular treatment decision but can make other decisions independently.

Which principle applies?

options.C: Incapacity for one decision means incapacity for all decisions
options.D: The doctor automatically becomes the legal decision-maker
options.E: Family members automatically make every decision

why_correct: Mental capacity is assessed for the specific decision at the specific time. A person may lack capacity for one decision while retaining capacity for others.
why_wrong: A. Capacity can fluctuate and should be reassessed when relevant. C. Under the Mental Capacity Act, lacking capacity for one decision does not mean lacking capacity for all. D. The doctor makes best-interests decisions but does not automatically become the legal decision-maker for everything. E. Family members do not automatically make decisions unless they hold a valid lasting power of attorney or deputyship.
pearl: Under the Mental Capacity Act, capacity is assessed for a specific decision at a specific time; someone may lack capacity for a complex decision but still make simpler ones themselves.
thinking: Adult lacks capacity for one treatment decision ↓ Yet can make other decisions independently ↓ Capacity is judged decision by decision ↓ Capacity is decision-specific
exam_trap: C, incapacity for one decision means incapacity for all decisions — a common misconception; the Mental Capacity Act requires capacity to be assessed for each decision.
takeaway: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, never all or nothing.

stem:
An adult patient makes a decision that the doctor considers unwise but understands the relevant information and consequences.

What should the clinician do?

options.A: Respect the decision if the patient has capacity
options.B: Override the decision because it is unwise
options.E: Ask the patient's family to make the decision

correct_answer: A. Respect the decision if the patient has capacity
why_correct: An unwise decision does not, by itself, demonstrate lack of capacity.
why_wrong: B. The Mental Capacity Act states that an unwise decision does not by itself mean a person lacks capacity. C. Detention has no basis when a patient with capacity makes an unwise decision. D. Capacity must be presumed unless shown otherwise, and an unwise choice is not evidence of incapacity. E. Family members cannot make decisions for an adult who has capacity.
pearl: An adult with capacity may make a decision others consider unwise; the clinician should explain risks clearly and document the discussion, but must respect the decision.
thinking: Doctor considers the decision unwise ↓ Patient understands the information and consequences ↓ An unwise decision alone does not show incapacity ↓ Respect the decision if the patient has capacity
exam_trap: D, assume the patient lacks capacity — tempting when a choice seems harmful, but capacity is presumed and an unwise decision alone is not evidence of incapacity.
takeaway: An unwise decision is not proof of incapacity: respect choices made with capacity.

stem:
A patient with capacity has previously made a valid and applicable advance decision refusing a specific life-sustaining treatment.

What is the key principle?

options.A: It applies to every possible treatment
options.B: Family members can automatically override it
options.C: It is invalid because the patient is currently unconscious
options.D: A valid and applicable advance decision should be respected

correct_answer: D. A valid and applicable advance decision should be respected
why_correct: A valid and applicable advance decision can be legally binding and may refuse specified treatment, including life-sustaining treatment, subject to the relevant legal requirements.
why_wrong: A. An advance decision applies only to the specified treatments and circumstances. B. Family members cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision. C. An advance decision applies precisely when the patient lacks capacity, such as when unconscious. E. Doctors must follow a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment.
pearl: A valid and applicable advance decision refusing life-sustaining treatment must be in writing, signed and witnessed, and state that it applies even if life is at risk; if valid, it must be respected.
thinking: Advance decision made when the patient had capacity ↓ Refuses a specific life-sustaining treatment ↓ It is valid and applicable to the situation ↓ It should be respected
exam_trap: B, family members can automatically override it — relatives often feel they should decide, but they cannot override a valid and applicable advance decision.
takeaway: A valid and applicable advance decision is legally binding, even for life-sustaining treatment.

stem:
A patient with metastatic breast cancer develops constipation, thirst and polyuria.

Which electrolyte abnormality explains these symptoms?
why_correct: Hypercalcaemia can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, thirst and polyuria due to impaired renal concentrating ability.
why_wrong: B. Hypermagnesaemia causes weakness, hyporeflexia and hypotension rather than thirst and polyuria. C. Hypocalcaemia causes paraesthesia, tetany and cramps rather than constipation and polyuria. D. Hyperkalaemia causes arrhythmias and weakness, not thirst and polyuria. E. Hypophosphataemia causes weakness and haemolysis rather than this triad.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is common with breast cancer and bone metastases; constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion should prompt a calcium check, with IV fluids first-line if raised.
thinking: Metastatic breast cancer, often spreading to bone ↓ Constipation suggests a GI effect ↓ Thirst and polyuria suggest impaired renal concentration ↓ Hypercalcaemia
exam_trap: C, hypocalcaemia — the right electrolyte but the wrong direction; low calcium causes tingling, cramps and tetany, not constipation, thirst and polyuria.
takeaway: Malignancy plus constipation, thirst and polyuria: check calcium for hypercalcaemia.

stem:
A patient with hyperthyroidism develops bilateral eye prominence and a gritty sensation.

Which condition is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Graves' disease can cause thyroid eye disease, with orbital inflammation and tissue expansion producing proptosis and ocular discomfort.
why_wrong: B. Cataract causes blurred vision, not proptosis or grittiness. C. Retinal detachment causes flashes and field loss, not proptosis. D. Orbital cellulitis is usually unilateral and acutely painful with fever. E. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes a painful red eye with reduced vision, not bilateral proptosis.
pearl: Thyroid eye disease in Graves' disease causes grittiness, proptosis and lid retraction; reduced vision, colour loss or painful eye movements suggest optic nerve compromise and need urgent ophthalmology review.
thinking: Hyperthyroidism, most often due to Graves' disease ↓ Bilateral eye prominence (proptosis) ↓ Gritty discomfort from exposure ↓ Thyroid eye disease
exam_trap: D, orbital cellulitis — causes proptosis, but it is usually unilateral, acute and painful with fever, not bilateral prominence linked to hyperthyroidism.
takeaway: Bilateral proptosis with grittiness in hyperthyroidism is thyroid eye disease.

stem:
A pregnant woman is diagnosed with gestational diabetes.

Which complication is particularly associated with diabetes in pregnancy?
why_correct: Maternal hyperglycaemia can increase fetal growth and the risk of a large-for-gestational-age infant.
why_wrong: A. Gestational diabetes is not associated with microcephaly, and certainly not in every pregnancy. B. Gestational diabetes does not cause ectopic pregnancy, which occurs in early pregnancy. C. Gestational diabetes does not cause cleft palate in every pregnancy. E. Neonatal appendicitis is not a complication of gestational diabetes.
pearl: Maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal growth, so gestational diabetes increases the risk of macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and neonatal hypoglycaemia; good glucose control reduces these risks.
thinking: Gestational diabetes means maternal hyperglycaemia ↓ Glucose crosses the placenta ↓ Fetal hyperinsulinaemia promotes growth ↓ Fetal macrosomia
exam_trap: C, cleft palate in every pregnancy — pre-existing diabetes around conception can raise the risk of congenital anomalies, but the hallmark complication of gestational diabetes is macrosomia, and 'in every pregnancy' is wrong.
takeaway: Diabetes in pregnancy: the classic fetal complication is macrosomia.

stem:
A newborn of a mother with diabetes is found to have low blood glucose.

Why is this baby at increased risk?

options.A: Fetal pancreatic beta-cell failure from maternal hyperglycaemia
options.B: Maternal hypothyroidism reducing fetal hepatic glycogen
options.C: Reduced fetal red-cell production from maternal hyperglycaemia
options.E: Excess fetal glucagon secretion from maternal hyperglycaemia

correct_answer: D. Fetal hyperinsulinaemia from maternal hyperglycaemia
why_correct: Maternal hyperglycaemia can lead to increased fetal insulin production. After birth, the maternal glucose supply stops while insulin remains elevated, predisposing to neonatal hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: A. Infants of diabetic mothers have beta-cell hyperplasia with high, not absent, insulin production. B. Maternal hypothyroidism does not deplete fetal glycogen stores and does not explain neonatal hypoglycaemia in this setting. C. Maternal hyperglycaemia tends to increase fetal red-cell production (polycythaemia), which does not cause hypoglycaemia. E. Fetal glucagon is not increased, and excess glucagon would raise, not lower, blood glucose.
pearl: Babies of mothers with diabetes are at risk of early hypoglycaemia because their own insulin stays high after the maternal glucose supply stops; feed early and monitor blood glucose.
thinking: Maternal hyperglycaemia crosses the placenta ↓ Fetal pancreas responds with high insulin ↓ At birth glucose supply stops but insulin remains high ↓ Fetal hyperinsulinaemia
exam_trap: A, fetal pancreatic beta-cell failure — sounds plausible because of the hyperglycaemia, but the fetal beta cells are overactive, not failing; that is why insulin is high.
takeaway: Infant of a diabetic mother: hyperinsulinaemia causes neonatal hypoglycaemia.

stem:
A child develops prolonged fever, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucosal changes and cervical lymphadenopathy.

Why is prompt recognition important?

options.A: It can cause coronary artery aneurysms
options.B: It commonly causes acute kidney injury later
options.C: It frequently leads to bacterial meningitis
options.D: It often progresses to childhood epilepsy
options.E: It causes structural congenital heart disease

correct_answer: A. It can cause coronary artery aneurysms
why_correct: Kawasaki disease is an inflammatory vasculitis in childhood with potentially serious coronary artery complications.
why_wrong: B. Acute kidney injury is not a characteristic complication of Kawasaki disease. C. Kawasaki disease is not a cause of bacterial meningitis. D. Kawasaki disease does not progress to epilepsy. E. Kawasaki disease is acquired and causes coronary aneurysms, not congenital heart disease.
pearl: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis whose key danger is coronary artery aneurysm; prompt IV immunoglobulin, aspirin under specialist guidance and echocardiography are central to management.
thinking: Prolonged fever in a child ↓ Non-purulent conjunctivitis, mucosal changes and lymphadenopathy ↓ This is Kawasaki disease, a vasculitis ↓ It can cause coronary artery aneurysms
exam_trap: E, structural congenital heart disease — the heart link tempts, but Kawasaki is acquired; the damage is to the coronary arteries, not a congenital structural defect.
takeaway: Kawasaki disease matters because of coronary aneurysms: recognise and treat early.

stem:
A traveller is bitten by a potentially rabid mammal while abroad.

What is the appropriate principle?

options.B: Clean the wound and seek medical advice if symptoms develop later
options.D: Seek urgent assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
options.E: Suture the wound primarily and give a tetanus booster dose today

correct_answer: D. Seek urgent assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
why_correct: Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical symptoms develop, so potentially significant exposures require urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Corticosteroids have no role and may impair the response to rabies vaccination. B. Rabies cannot be reliably treated once symptoms develop, so waiting for symptoms is unsafe. C. Antibiotics do not prevent rabies, which requires vaccine with or without immunoglobulin. E. Primary closure and tetanus cover do not address the need for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis.
pearl: After a possible rabies exposure, wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water straight away and seek urgent medical assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis; do not wait for symptoms.
thinking: Bite from a potentially rabid mammal abroad ↓ Rabies is almost always fatal once symptomatic ↓ Prophylaxis works only before symptoms develop ↓ Seek urgent assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
exam_trap: B, clean the wound and seek advice if symptoms develop later — wound cleaning is correct, but waiting for symptoms is fatal; prophylaxis must be assessed urgently.
takeaway: Possible rabies exposure: wash the wound and get urgent PEP assessment, never wait for symptoms.

stem:
A woman with asthma becomes pregnant and asks whether she should stop her inhaled corticosteroid.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Continue her inhaled corticosteroid as prescribed
options.B: Replace all her inhalers with a course of antibiotics
options.C: Stop all inhalers immediately to protect the fetus
options.D: Use only oral corticosteroids throughout pregnancy
options.E: Avoid all asthma treatment until after the delivery

correct_answer: A. Continue her inhaled corticosteroid as prescribed
why_correct: Maintaining good asthma control during pregnancy is important for both mother and fetus. Effective treatment should not be stopped without appropriate clinical advice.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics do not treat asthma. C. Stopping inhalers risks poor control and exacerbations, which pose a greater risk to mother and fetus. D. Long-term oral corticosteroids are not routine; inhaled therapy should continue. E. Delaying treatment until after delivery risks uncontrolled asthma during pregnancy.
pearl: Asthma medicines, including inhaled corticosteroids, should be continued in pregnancy; poorly controlled asthma poses a greater risk to mother and baby than the treatment.
thinking: Pregnant woman with asthma ↓ Worried about inhaled steroid safety ↓ Uncontrolled asthma is the greater risk to mother and fetus ↓ Continue her inhaled corticosteroid as prescribed
exam_trap: C, stop all inhalers immediately to protect the fetus — reflects common anxiety, but stopping treatment risks exacerbations and fetal hypoxia.
takeaway: In pregnancy, keep asthma controlled: continue inhaled corticosteroids.

stem:
A patient with suspected obstructive sleep apnoea reports falling asleep while driving.

What is the key immediate issue?
why_correct: Excessive sleepiness while driving creates a significant road-safety risk. Patients should receive appropriate advice regarding driving and medical assessment.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction does not address the driving risk. B. Iron supplementation is irrelevant to sleepiness while driving. C. Anticoagulation is not indicated for obstructive sleep apnoea. D. Antibiotics have no role in obstructive sleep apnoea.
pearl: Excessive sleepiness affecting driving in suspected sleep apnoea is a safety issue: advise the patient not to drive until symptoms are satisfactorily controlled, explain their legal duty to notify the DVLA where required, and refer for sleep assessment.
thinking: Suspected obstructive sleep apnoea ↓ Falling asleep at the wheel ↓ Immediate risk to the patient and the public ↓ Driving safety
exam_trap: C, anticoagulation — tempting if thinking of cardiovascular associations of sleep apnoea, but there is no indication here and the immediate concern is road safety.
takeaway: Sleepiness at the wheel in suspected OSA: address driving safety first.

stem:
A former coal miner develops progressive breathlessness and an abnormal chest radiograph showing diffuse pulmonary changes.

Which occupational disease should be considered?
why_correct: Prolonged occupational exposure to coal dust can cause pneumoconiosis.
why_wrong: A. Isocyanate-induced occupational asthma causes variable airflow obstruction rather than diffuse radiographic changes, and is unrelated to coal mining. C. Mesothelioma is caused by asbestos exposure and typically causes a pleural mass or effusion. D. Byssinosis is caused by cotton dust, not coal dust. E. Farmer's lung is hypersensitivity pneumonitis from mouldy hay, not coal dust.
pearl: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis follows long-term coal dust inhalation and causes nodular lung changes and progressive breathlessness; a full occupational history is key to diagnosis.
thinking: Former coal miner, so long-term coal dust exposure ↓ Progressive breathlessness ↓ Diffuse changes on chest radiograph ↓ Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
exam_trap: C, malignant pleural mesothelioma — a classic occupational lung disease, but it follows asbestos exposure and typically causes pleural thickening or effusion, not diffuse coal-dust changes.
takeaway: Coal miner with diffuse lung changes and breathlessness: coal workers' pneumoconiosis.

stem:
A woman notices a new persistent inversion of one nipple.

Which condition should be excluded?
why_correct: New unilateral nipple inversion can be a sign of underlying breast malignancy and warrants appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Fibroadenomas are mobile lumps and do not typically cause nipple inversion. C. Lipomas are soft fatty lumps that do not cause nipple inversion. D. Mastitis does not occur in every case of nipple inversion, and new inversion must not be assumed benign. E. A simple cyst does not usually cause new persistent nipple inversion.
pearl: New unilateral nipple inversion can be caused by an underlying cancer tethering the ductal tissue; it needs breast assessment, whereas long-standing inversion is usually benign.
thinking: Change is new, not long-standing ↓ Persistent and affecting one nipple ↓ Suggests tethering from an underlying lesion ↓ Breast cancer must be excluded
exam_trap: A, fibroadenoma — a common benign breast lump, but it is mobile and does not tether tissue to cause new nipple inversion.
takeaway: New persistent nipple inversion: exclude breast cancer.

stem:
A young woman has dysuria and increased vaginal discharge but minimal systemic symptoms.

Which sexually transmitted infection is commonly asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic in women?
why_correct: Chlamydia is frequently asymptomatic, particularly in women, but can cause cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease.
why_wrong: B. Genital warts cause visible warty lesions rather than discharge. C. Gonorrhoea is often asymptomatic in women, so 'in every case' makes this statement incorrect. D. Syphilis causes a painless chancre and is not the classic minimally symptomatic cause of discharge in women. E. Genital herpes typically causes painful vesicles and ulcers.
pearl: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK and is often asymptomatic, especially in women; untreated infection can cause pelvic inflammatory disease and tubal infertility, so test with NAAT.
thinking: Young woman with dysuria and increased discharge ↓ Minimal systemic upset ↓ The question asks for the STI that is often silent or only mildly symptomatic in women ↓ Chlamydia
exam_trap: C, gonorrhoea in every case — gonorrhoea can also be silent in women, but 'in every case' is wrong and chlamydia is the classic commonly asymptomatic STI.
takeaway: Chlamydia is often silent in women: test sexually active patients with genital symptoms.

stem:
A patient with recurrent genital herpes asks why the lesions keep returning.

Which explanation is correct?

options.A: The virus remains only on the skin surface
options.B: Recurrences are caused by a new bacterial infection
options.C: Herpes simplex virus remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia
options.D: The infection is completely eradicated after the first episode
options.E: Recurrences occur only after reinfection from another person

correct_answer: C. Herpes simplex virus remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia
why_correct: HSV establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia and can reactivate periodically.
why_wrong: A. HSV becomes latent in sensory ganglia, not on the skin surface. B. Recurrences are caused by viral reactivation, not bacterial infection. D. HSV is not eradicated after the first episode. E. Recurrences usually reflect reactivation of latent virus, not reinfection.
pearl: Herpes simplex virus travels along sensory nerves and stays latent in the ganglia for life; reactivation causes recurrences, which are usually milder and shorter than the first episode.
thinking: Recurrent genital herpes ↓ After the first infection HSV travels up sensory nerves ↓ It lies latent in the ganglia and reactivates ↓ HSV remains latent in sensory nerve ganglia
exam_trap: E, recurrences occur only after reinfection — tempting because herpes is sexually transmitted, but recurrences come from the patient's own latent virus, not new exposure.
takeaway: Herpes recurrences are reactivation from latent virus in sensory ganglia.

stem:
A woman with migraine asks about starting a combined hormonal contraceptive. Her migraines are associated with transient visual and sensory neurological symptoms.

What is the important consideration?

options.A: Migraine with aura prevents ovulation permanently
options.C: Migraine with aura makes combined contraception unsuitable
options.E: Combined contraception treats migraine with aura

correct_answer: C. Migraine with aura makes combined contraception unsuitable
why_correct: Migraine with aura is an important contraindication/eligibility consideration for combined hormonal contraception because of increased cerebrovascular risk.
why_wrong: A. Migraine with aura does not cause permanent anovulation. B. There is a clinically important association with increased stroke risk. D. Migraine with aura has no bearing on fertility or pregnancy. E. Combined hormonal contraception does not treat migraine with aura and is generally contraindicated (UKMEC 4).
pearl: Migraine with aura increases ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception adds to it; offer progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods instead.
thinking: Migraine with transient visual and sensory symptoms ↓ This is migraine with aura ↓ Oestrogen-containing methods add to ischaemic stroke risk ↓ Combined contraception is unsuitable
exam_trap: B, there is no relevant association — migraine without aura carries fewer restrictions, but aura is a recognised contraindication to combined hormonal contraception because of the added ischaemic stroke risk.
takeaway: Migraine with aura rules out combined hormonal contraception: use progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods.

stem:
A woman asks why emergency contraception is used after unprotected intercourse.

What is its primary purpose?

options.D: To terminate an established ectopic pregnancy

correct_answer: A. To prevent pregnancy following intercourse
why_correct: Emergency contraception is used after unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure to reduce the chance of pregnancy.
why_wrong: B. Emergency contraception is not a treatment for endometriosis. C. Emergency contraception does not induce menopause. D. Emergency contraception does not treat ectopic pregnancy. E. Emergency contraception does not treat sexually transmitted infections.
pearl: Emergency contraception reduces the chance of pregnancy after unprotected sex or contraceptive failure; the copper IUD is the most effective option, with oral methods as alternatives.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse or contraceptive failure ↓ Risk of pregnancy ↓ Emergency contraception acts before pregnancy is established ↓ To prevent pregnancy following intercourse
exam_trap: E, to treat sexually transmitted infections — STI risk is assessed at the same visit, but emergency contraception has no effect on infection.
takeaway: Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy; it does not treat STIs or end an established pregnancy.

stem:
A woman using a copper intrauterine device develops heavier and more painful periods.

Which adverse effect is recognised with copper IUDs?
why_correct: Copper IUDs can increase menstrual bleeding and period pain, particularly after insertion.
why_wrong: B. Copper IUDs do not cause ovarian failure. C. Copper IUDs do not cause hyperthyroidism. D. Copper IUDs do not cause amenorrhoea; they tend to make periods heavier. E. Copper IUDs do not cause hypoglycaemia.
pearl: The copper IUD is non-hormonal and can make periods heavier, longer and more painful, especially in the first months; this is a common reason for removal.
thinking: Woman using a copper IUD ↓ Heavier and more painful periods ↓ A recognised effect of the copper device ↓ Heavier, more painful periods
exam_trap: D, permanent amenorrhoea — confuses the copper IUD with the hormonal intrauterine system, which can reduce or stop bleeding; the copper coil tends to increase it.
takeaway: Copper IUD: periods often heavier and more painful; the hormonal IUS tends to lighten them.

stem:
A woman wants contraception but has a medical reason why oestrogen-containing contraception is unsuitable.

Which contraceptive option does not contain oestrogen?
why_correct: The progestogen-only pill contains progestogen without oestrogen.
why_wrong: A. The combined transdermal patch contains oestrogen. B. The combined vaginal ring contains oestrogen. C. The combined oral contraceptive pill contains oestrogen. E. This is incorrect because the progestogen-only pill is oestrogen-free.
pearl: When oestrogen is unsuitable, progestogen-only methods such as the pill, implant, injection and hormonal IUS, or a copper IUD, remain options.
thinking: Oestrogen must be avoided ↓ The patch, ring and combined pill all contain oestrogen ↓ The progestogen-only pill contains none ↓ Progestogen-only pill
exam_trap: B, combined vaginal ring — easy to mistake for a progestogen-only device, but the ring contains both oestrogen and progestogen.
takeaway: No oestrogen allowed: choose progestogen-only or copper methods; avoid the patch, ring and combined pill.

stem:
A woman has a contraceptive implant inserted into her upper arm.

Which hormone does the commonly used UK implant release?
why_correct: The contraceptive implant used in the UK releases the progestogen etonogestrel.
why_wrong: A. The implant releases a progestogen, not oestrogen. C. The implant releases synthetic progestogen; it does not involve ovarian progesterone. D. Thyroxine has no contraceptive role. E. Testosterone is not used in contraceptive implants.
pearl: The contraceptive implant releases etonogestrel, a progestogen, as a long-acting reversible method; irregular bleeding is the commonest side effect.
thinking: Implant in the upper arm ↓ It is a progestogen-only method ↓ The UK device releases a synthetic progestogen ↓ Etonogestrel
exam_trap: C, progesterone only from the ovary — sounds close, but the implant delivers synthetic etonogestrel itself and does not act by stimulating ovarian progesterone.
takeaway: The UK contraceptive implant is progestogen-only and releases etonogestrel.

stem:
A couple have been trying to conceive without success. The initial assessment of the male partner is required.

Which investigation is commonly used to assess male fertility?
why_correct: Semen analysis assesses sperm concentration, motility and morphology and is a key investigation in male infertility.
why_wrong: A. A chest radiograph does not assess male fertility. C. D-dimer is used in suspected thrombosis and has no role in infertility assessment. D. Colonoscopy has no role in assessing male fertility. E. Echocardiography is irrelevant to male fertility.
pearl: Semen analysis is the first-line test for the male partner in subfertility; if abnormal, it is usually repeated to confirm before further investigation.
thinking: Couple unable to conceive ↓ Male partner needs initial assessment ↓ Sperm count, motility and morphology must be checked ↓ Semen analysis
exam_trap: E, echocardiogram — may tempt as a thorough-sounding specialist test, but it assesses the heart, not sperm production; semen analysis is the first-line test for the male partner.
takeaway: First-line male fertility test: semen analysis.

stem:
A man with infertility has a soft, tortuous mass above the testis that becomes more prominent when standing.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A varicocele is dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus and is classically described as a "bag of worms."
why_wrong: A. Epididymitis causes a tender, swollen epididymis with infective symptoms. B. Testicular cancer usually presents as a firm, painless mass within the testis. C. Testicular torsion causes acute severe pain, not a chronic soft mass. D. A hydrocele is a fluid collection around the testis that transilluminates.
pearl: A varicocele feels like a 'bag of worms' above the testis, is more prominent when standing and usually left-sided; it can be associated with subfertility.
thinking: Man with infertility ↓ Soft, tortuous mass above the testis ↓ Enlarges on standing as the veins fill ↓ Varicocele
exam_trap: D, hydrocele — a common painless scrotal swelling, but it surrounds the testis, transilluminates and is not a tortuous mass that changes with posture.
takeaway: Bag-of-worms swelling above the testis that fills on standing is a varicocele.

stem:
A teenage boy develops sudden severe unilateral testicular pain and nausea.

Why is urgent treatment important?

options.B: It is self-limiting in most cases
options.C: Testicular blood supply can be compromised
options.D: It is usually caused by urinary infection
options.E: It always causes infertility within minutes

correct_answer: C. Testicular blood supply can be compromised
why_correct: Spermatic cord torsion can obstruct testicular blood flow, risking irreversible ischaemic damage.
why_wrong: A. Testicular torsion does not cause renal failure. B. Torsion is not self-limiting and needs urgent surgical exploration to save the testis. D. Sudden severe testicular pain in a teenager suggests torsion, not urinary infection. E. Infertility is not an immediate consequence within minutes; the urgent risk is testicular loss from ischaemia.
pearl: Testicular torsion twists the spermatic cord and cuts off blood supply; suspected torsion needs immediate surgical exploration, as testicular salvage falls sharply within hours.
thinking: Teenage boy ↓ Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain with nausea ↓ Suspected torsion cutting off the blood supply ↓ Testicular blood supply can be compromised
