pearl: CML causes splenomegaly and a very high white count; the Philadelphia chromosome creates BCR-ABL1, the target of tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.
thinking: Fatigue, weight loss, splenomegaly ↓ markedly raised white-cell count ↓ chronic myeloid leukaemia ↓ Philadelphia chromosome translocation ↓ BCR-ABL1 fusion
exam_trap: C, factor VIII deficiency — a haematological abnormality, but it causes haemophilia A, a bleeding disorder, not leukaemia.
takeaway: CML equals the Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR-ABL1 fusion.

stem:
A 70-year-old man has iron-deficiency anaemia without an obvious source of blood loss.

What should be considered?
why_correct: New iron-deficiency anaemia in an older man requires investigation for possible gastrointestinal blood loss, including gastrointestinal malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin D deficiency and osteomalacia do not cause iron-deficiency anaemia. C. Mild haemophilia A causes bleeding after trauma or surgery and does not explain new iron deficiency in a 70-year-old without a bleeding history. D. Iron-deficiency anaemia should not be attributed simply to ageing. E. Dehydration can concentrate haemoglobin rather than cause iron deficiency.
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult is gastrointestinal cancer until proven otherwise; investigate both the upper and lower GI tract.
thinking: 70-year-old man ↓ iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ no obvious blood loss ↓ occult gastrointestinal bleeding, including malignancy ↓ gastrointestinal blood loss
exam_trap: D, normal age-related marrow decline — ageing is a tempting explanation, but iron deficiency always has a cause that must be found.
takeaway: Iron deficiency in an older man means occult GI loss until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient has headaches, dizziness and a persistently raised haemoglobin concentration.

Which broad abnormality is present?
why_correct: Polycythaemia refers to an increased red-cell mass, reflected by an elevated haemoglobin or haematocrit.
why_wrong: A. Neutropenia means a low neutrophil count. B. Anaemia means reduced haemoglobin. C. Pancytopenia means reduction of red cells, white cells and platelets. E. Thrombocytopenia means a low platelet count.
pearl: A persistently raised haemoglobin is polycythaemia; distinguish primary polycythaemia vera from secondary causes such as hypoxia, smoking or EPO-secreting tumours.
thinking: Headaches and dizziness ↓ possible hyperviscosity symptoms ↓ persistently raised haemoglobin ↓ increased red-cell mass ↓ polycythaemia
exam_trap: B, anaemia — headaches and dizziness are classic anaemic symptoms, but anaemia means a low haemoglobin, not a raised one.
takeaway: Raised haemoglobin is polycythaemia; then look for primary or secondary causes.

stem:
A patient with multiple myeloma develops thirst, constipation and confusion.

Which metabolic complication is particularly likely?
why_correct: Bone destruction in multiple myeloma can release calcium and cause hypercalcaemia, producing thirst, constipation and confusion.
why_wrong: B. Hypoglycaemia is not a characteristic direct complication of myeloma. C. Myeloma-associated bone destruction more commonly causes hypercalcaemia. D. Hypokalaemia is not the characteristic electrolyte abnormality. E. Diabetes insipidus is unrelated to the typical myeloma complication pattern.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia gives 'bones, stones, groans and psychic moans'; treat with IV fluids first, then a bisphosphonate. Myeloma is remembered by its CRAB features.
thinking: Known multiple myeloma ↓ thirst, constipation and confusion ↓ lytic bone destruction releases calcium ↓ classic hypercalcaemia picture ↓ hypercalcaemia
exam_trap: E, hypernatraemia from diabetes insipidus — thirst and confusion tempt, but it does not explain constipation or fit the myeloma pattern.
takeaway: Myeloma with thirst, constipation or confusion: check calcium.

stem:
A young child with sickle cell disease becomes suddenly pale and lethargic and develops abdominal distension. The spleen is enlarged.

Which complication is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden pooling of blood in the spleen can cause acute anaemia, splenomegaly and circulatory compromise in young children with sickle cell disease.
why_wrong: B. Renal colic causes flank pain rather than splenomegaly and acute anaemia. C. Haemophilia causes bleeding due to factor deficiency. D. Iron deficiency develops more gradually. E. A vaso-occlusive crisis causes severe pain, typically in bones, without acute splenic enlargement and sudden severe anaemia.
pearl: Splenic sequestration is a sickle emergency in young children: rapid haemoglobin fall, enlarging spleen and shock; resuscitate and transfuse urgently.
thinking: Young child with sickle cell disease ↓ sudden pallor and lethargy ↓ abdominal distension with enlarged spleen ↓ blood pooling in the spleen ↓ splenic sequestration crisis
exam_trap: E, vaso-occlusive crisis — the commonest sickle crisis, but it causes pain without sudden severe anaemia and acute splenic enlargement.
takeaway: Sickle cell child with sudden pallor and a big spleen: splenic sequestration.

stem:
A young adult has hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon.

Which inherited condition is most likely?
why_correct: FAP is an inherited polyposis syndrome characterised by numerous adenomatous colorectal polyps and a very high colorectal cancer risk if untreated.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome) increases colorectal cancer risk but causes few adenomas rather than hundreds of polyps. B. Ulcerative colitis causes continuous mucosal inflammation rather than a classic hundreds-of-adenomas phenotype. C. IBS does not cause colorectal polyps. D. Diverticular disease causes diverticula rather than hundreds of adenomatous polyps.
pearl: FAP is autosomal dominant (APC gene); polyps carpet the colon from adolescence and cancer is near-inevitable, so prophylactic colectomy is offered.
thinking: Young adult ↓ hundreds of colonic polyps ↓ adenomatous type ↓ inherited polyposis syndrome ↓ familial adenomatous polyposis
exam_trap: A, HNPCC (Lynch syndrome) — also an inherited colorectal cancer syndrome, but it causes few adenomas, not hundreds of polyps.
takeaway: Hundreds of adenomas in a young adult means FAP.

stem:
A young adult develops colorectal cancer and has several relatives with colorectal and endometrial cancers at relatively young ages.

Which inherited syndrome should be considered?
why_correct: Lynch syndrome is an inherited mismatch-repair disorder associated with colorectal cancer and several other cancers, particularly endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune small-bowel disorder. B. IBS does not cause inherited colorectal cancer syndromes. D. FAP typically causes hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps. E. Diverticular disease is not an inherited colorectal cancer syndrome.
pearl: Lynch syndrome is an autosomal dominant mismatch-repair defect causing early colorectal and endometrial cancers; colorectal cancers are routinely tested for it.
thinking: Young adult with colorectal cancer ↓ relatives with colorectal and endometrial cancers ↓ young ages of onset ↓ inherited mismatch-repair defect ↓ Lynch syndrome
exam_trap: D, familial adenomatous polyposis — an inherited colorectal cancer syndrome, but it shows hundreds of polyps and is not linked to endometrial cancer.
takeaway: Familial colorectal plus endometrial cancer at young ages suggests Lynch syndrome.

stem: A 46-year-old woman is found to have a solitary thyroid nodule on examination. She has no compressive symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_correct: Thyroid function tests, particularly TSH, are part of the initial assessment of a thyroid nodule. The result helps determine subsequent investigation.
why_wrong: A. Most thyroid nodules do not require immediate surgery. B. Thyroglobulin is not a routine initial diagnostic test for a thyroid nodule. C. CT is not the routine first investigation of a thyroid nodule. E. FNA is guided by ultrasound appearances and clinical assessment rather than performed immediately in every nodule.
pearl: A thyroid nodule is assessed with TSH and ultrasound; a low TSH suggests a hyperfunctioning nodule, which is rarely malignant.
thinking: Solitary thyroid nodule ↓ no compressive symptoms ↓ start by assessing thyroid function ↓ result shapes next steps such as ultrasound ↓ serum TSH
exam_trap: E, immediate fine-needle aspiration — it gives cytology, but FNA is guided by ultrasound features and thyroid function, not done first.
takeaway: First step for a thyroid nodule: check TSH, then image and sample as indicated.

stem: A patient develops tingling around the mouth and carpopedal spasm several hours after total thyroidectomy. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Accidental damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery can cause acute hypocalcaemia, producing perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm.
why_wrong: A. Hyperkalaemia does not typically cause this characteristic neuromuscular presentation. B. Hypermagnesaemia tends to cause neuromuscular depression rather than tetany. C. Thyrotoxicosis does not explain acute postoperative tetany. D. Adrenal insufficiency has a different clinical and biochemical presentation.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy reflects parathyroid injury; check calcium, look for Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs and give IV calcium gluconate if severe.
thinking: Total thyroidectomy ↓ hours later perioral tingling ↓ carpopedal spasm means tetany ↓ hypocalcaemia from parathyroid damage ↓ hypoparathyroidism
exam_trap: C, hyperthyroidism — thyroid storm after thyroid surgery may come to mind, but it causes fever and tachycardia, not tetany.
takeaway: Tetany after thyroidectomy is hypocalcaemia from parathyroid damage.

stem: A patient with longstanding vitamin B12 deficiency develops numbness in both feet and difficulty walking. Which neurological complication is characteristic?

options.A: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

correct_answer: A. Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can damage the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord, producing sensory disturbance and gait problems.
why_wrong: B. Bell's palsy causes an acute unilateral facial nerve palsy. C. Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of lumbosacral nerve roots. D. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy is an immune-mediated neuropathy and is not the characteristic neurological complication of vitamin B12 deficiency. E. Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.
pearl: Subacute combined degeneration hits the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts: lost vibration and joint position sense, positive Romberg's, and extensor plantars with absent ankle jerks.
thinking: Longstanding B12 deficiency ↓ numbness in both feet ↓ difficulty walking ↓ posterior and lateral column damage ↓ subacute combined degeneration of the cord
exam_trap: D, CIDP — it causes symmetrical sensory and motor deficits, but it is immune-mediated, not the characteristic B12 complication.
takeaway: B12 deficiency with sensory ataxia: subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

stem: A patient has pernicious anaemia. Which other condition is associated with this disorder?
why_correct: Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune condition and is associated with other autoimmune diseases, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease.
why_wrong: A. Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder caused by FBN1 mutations. C. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive CFTR disorder. D. Haemophilia A is an X-linked clotting-factor deficiency. E. Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited red-cell membrane disorder.
pearl: Autoimmune conditions cluster: pernicious anaemia is linked with autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes and vitiligo, so check thyroid function.
thinking: Pernicious anaemia ↓ autoimmune attack on parietal cells ↓ autoimmune diseases cluster together ↓ only one autoimmune option ↓ autoimmune thyroid disease
exam_trap: E, hereditary spherocytosis — another anaemia, so it tempts by association, but it is an inherited membrane defect, not autoimmune.
takeaway: Pernicious anaemia travels with other autoimmune disease, especially thyroid.

stem: A traveller develops fever, malaise, anorexia and jaundice after eating contaminated food. Which virus is most characteristically transmitted by the faecal–oral route?
why_correct: Hepatitis A is classically transmitted by the faecal–oral route through contaminated food or water and causes an acute, self-limiting hepatitis with jaundice in travellers; it is the only enterically transmitted virus among the options.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis C is primarily blood-borne, for example through shared injecting equipment. C. Cytomegalovirus is spread by saliva, sexual contact, transplacentally and through transplants or transfusion, not characteristically by the faecal–oral route. D. Hepatitis D only occurs with hepatitis B co-infection or superinfection and is transmitted by blood and body fluids. E. Hepatitis B is primarily transmitted through blood, sexual contact and vertically, not by contaminated food.
pearl: Hepatitis A spreads faecal–orally, causes an acute self-limiting hepatitis and does not become chronic; vaccination protects travellers.
thinking: Traveller ↓ contaminated food ↓ fever, malaise, anorexia then jaundice ↓ enterically transmitted hepatitis ↓ hepatitis A
exam_trap: E, hepatitis B — a well-known cause of acute hepatitis in travellers, but it spreads through blood, sex and vertically, not via food.
takeaway: Hepatitis after contaminated food or water is hepatitis A.

stem: A young woman has dysuria and increased vaginal discharge but no obvious genital ulceration. Which sexually transmitted infection is commonly asymptomatic but can cause pelvic inflammatory disease?
why_correct: Chlamydia is frequently asymptomatic but can cause cervicitis and ascending infection leading to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A is not a cause of PID. C. HPV causes genital warts and cervical precancer rather than typical cervicitis/PID. D. Herpes typically causes painful vesicles or ulcers. E. Syphilis has a different clinical progression, beginning classically with a painless chancre.
pearl: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK and is often silent; untreated it can cause PID, ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility. Test with NAAT.
thinking: Young woman ↓ dysuria and increased discharge ↓ no genital ulceration ↓ often asymptomatic STI that ascends to cause PID ↓ chlamydia
exam_trap: C, genital warts — HPV is common and often silent, but it causes warts and cervical precancer, not cervicitis or PID.
takeaway: Silent STI that causes PID and infertility: think chlamydia.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with gestational diabetes during pregnancy. Which complication is particularly associated with diabetes in pregnancy?
why_correct: Maternal hyperglycaemia crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal insulin secretion, which drives excess fetal growth, so gestational diabetes is particularly associated with macrosomia and a large-for-gestational-age baby (NICE NG3).
why_wrong: A. Diabetes in pregnancy is associated with polyhydramnios (from fetal polyuria), not oligohydramnios. C. Diabetes in pregnancy does not cause maternal hyperthyroidism. D. Congenital anomalies such as neural tube defects are associated with pre-existing (pregestational) diabetes, not gestational diabetes, which develops after organogenesis. E. Gestational diabetes is associated with excessive rather than restricted fetal growth.
pearl: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta but insulin does not; fetal hyperinsulinaemia drives macrosomia, shoulder dystocia risk and neonatal hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Gestational diabetes ↓ maternal glucose crosses the placenta ↓ fetal hyperinsulinaemia ↓ excess fetal growth ↓ macrosomia
exam_trap: D, neural tube defect — linked to diabetes in pregnancy, but with pre-existing diabetes; gestational diabetes arises after organogenesis.
takeaway: Gestational diabetes means a big baby: macrosomia and its delivery risks.

stem: A 34-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has new hypertension and proteinuria. She has no previous history of hypertension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: New hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy together with proteinuria is characteristic of pre-eclampsia.
why_wrong: A. Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy or is identified before 20 weeks. B. Placenta praevia typically presents with painless vaginal bleeding. C. Hyperemesis causes severe nausea and vomiting, usually earlier in pregnancy. D. Gestational diabetes causes hyperglycaemia rather than this characteristic hypertensive presentation.
pearl: Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or other organ dysfunction; ask about headache, visual disturbance and epigastric pain.
thinking: 34 weeks' gestation ↓ new hypertension ↓ proteinuria ↓ no previous hypertension, onset after 20 weeks ↓ pre-eclampsia
exam_trap: A, chronic hypertension — raised blood pressure fits, but chronic hypertension predates pregnancy or is found before 20 weeks.
takeaway: New hypertension plus proteinuria after 20 weeks is pre-eclampsia.

stem: During labour, a woman reports feeling something in the vagina after spontaneous rupture of membranes. Examination reveals the umbilical cord below the presenting part. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Descent of the umbilical cord below or alongside the presenting part after membrane rupture is cord prolapse and can cause acute fetal compromise.
why_wrong: A. Placenta praevia concerns placental location. B. Shoulder dystocia occurs after delivery of the fetal head. D. Vasa praevia involves fetal vessels crossing near the internal cervical os. E. Uterine rupture causes maternal and fetal compromise but does not mean the cord has prolapsed.
pearl: In cord prolapse, call for help, relieve pressure on the cord by elevating the presenting part or using the knee–chest position, and expedite delivery.
thinking: Labour after membrane rupture ↓ feels something in the vagina ↓ cord found below the presenting part ↓ risk of cord compression ↓ cord prolapse
exam_trap: D, vasa praevia — it also involves fetal vessels near membrane rupture, but those vessels run in the membranes over the os, not a prolapsed cord.
takeaway: Cord below the presenting part after membrane rupture is cord prolapse: an obstetric emergency.

stem: A 58-year-old woman discovers a hard, irregular breast lump that appears fixed to surrounding tissue. Which feature makes malignancy particularly concerning?

options.A: Smooth mobile lump in a young woman

why_correct: A hard, irregular or fixed breast mass is a red-flag feature for breast malignancy and requires appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. A smooth mobile lump in a young woman is typical of fibroadenoma. B. Bilateral cyclical tenderness is commonly benign. C. Cyclical discomfort is commonly associated with benign hormonal breast changes. D. Symmetrical enlargement alone is not a typical breast cancer presentation.
pearl: A hard, irregular or fixed breast lump warrants a suspected cancer referral for triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging and biopsy.
thinking: 58-year-old woman ↓ breast lump ↓ hard and irregular ↓ fixed to surrounding tissue ↓ hard, irregular, fixed lump
exam_trap: A, smooth mobile lump in a young woman — a lump is a lump, but these reassuring features describe a fibroadenoma, not malignancy.
takeaway: Hard, irregular, fixed breast lump: refer urgently for triple assessment.

stem: A 67-year-old woman has persistent abdominal bloating, early satiety and urinary frequency. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent bloating, early satiety and urinary or abdominal symptoms can be features of ovarian cancer, particularly in an older woman.
why_wrong: A. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms but does not typically explain persistent abdominal bloating and early satiety. B. Gastroenteritis usually causes acute diarrhoea and/or vomiting. D. Renal colic typically causes severe colicky flank pain. E. Appendicitis usually causes acute abdominal pain and systemic symptoms.
pearl: Ovarian cancer presents vaguely; persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain or urinary frequency in an older woman warrant CA125, with ultrasound if raised.
thinking: 67-year-old woman ↓ persistent abdominal bloating ↓ early satiety ↓ urinary frequency ↓ ovarian cancer
exam_trap: A, cystitis — urinary frequency tempts, but cystitis does not explain persistent bloating and early satiety.
takeaway: Persistent bloating and early satiety in an older woman: think ovarian cancer, check CA125.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding three years after menopause. What diagnosis must be excluded?
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding must be assumed to be endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, and NICE NG12 (updated 2026) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for women aged 55 or over with unexplained postmenopausal bleeding that cannot be attributed to hormone replacement therapy (HRT).
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis is oestrogen-dependent and generally affects premenopausal women; it does not need to be excluded as the priority here. B. PMOS (formerly PCOS) is a reproductive-age endocrine disorder and does not explain new postmenopausal bleeding. C. Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle ovulation pain and cannot occur after menopause. D. Ectopic pregnancy is not a plausible explanation three years after menopause.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding needs a suspected cancer referral; transvaginal ultrasound assesses endometrial thickness and hysteroscopy with biopsy confirms the cause.
thinking: 62-year-old woman ↓ three years after menopause ↓ vaginal bleeding ↓ postmenopausal bleeding ↓ exclude endometrial cancer
exam_trap: A, endometriosis — a gynaecological cause of bleeding and pain, but it is oestrogen-driven and typically affects premenopausal women.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has severe cyclical pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia and pain during bowel movements, particularly around menstruation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cyclical pelvic pain with deep dyspareunia and cyclical bowel symptoms is characteristic of endometriosis.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy occurs in pregnancy and does not cause recurrent menstrual-cycle symptoms. B. Appendicitis generally causes acute, progressive abdominal pain rather than cyclical symptoms. C. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms and is not characteristically cyclical. D. Ovarian torsion usually presents with sudden severe acute pain.
pearl: Endometriosis causes cyclical pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, painful defecation and subfertility; examination and ultrasound can be normal, and laparoscopy is definitive.
thinking: 29-year-old woman ↓ severe cyclical pelvic pain ↓ deep dyspareunia ↓ painful bowel movements around menstruation ↓ endometriosis
exam_trap: D, ovarian torsion — severe pelvic pain in a young woman tempts, but torsion is sudden and acute, not recurrent and cyclical.
takeaway: Cyclical pelvic pain with deep dyspareunia and painful defecation means endometriosis.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has progressively painful, heavy periods. Examination reveals a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Adenomyosis commonly causes heavy, painful periods and a diffusely enlarged, tender uterus.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy presents in early pregnancy. C. Ovarian torsion causes acute unilateral pelvic pain. D. A cervical polyp may cause intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding but does not cause a uniformly enlarged uterus. E. Endometrial cancer may cause abnormal bleeding but does not typically produce a uniformly tender, enlarged uterus in this pattern.
pearl: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium, typically in later reproductive years; transvaginal ultrasound is the usual first imaging test.
thinking: 43-year-old woman ↓ progressively heavy, painful periods ↓ uniformly enlarged uterus ↓ tender on examination ↓ adenomyosis
exam_trap: E, endometrial cancer — abnormal bleeding at 43 raises concern, but it does not produce a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus with painful periods.
takeaway: Heavy painful periods with a bulky, tender uterus suggests adenomyosis.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has not menstruated for 14 months and reports hot flushes and night sweats. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Menopause is diagnosed clinically in women over 45 based on 12 months of amenorrhoea with typical symptoms, when there is no other explanation.
why_wrong: A. Pregnancy should be considered with amenorrhoea when appropriate, but 14 months of amenorrhoea with vasomotor symptoms at 52 is characteristic of menopause. B. PMOS (formerly PCOS) is generally associated with irregular ovulation from reproductive age rather than new-onset amenorrhoea with vasomotor symptoms at 52. C. Hyperprolactinaemia can cause amenorrhoea but does not typically cause this classic vasomotor symptom pattern. D. Ectopic pregnancy presents with pain and/or bleeding in early pregnancy, not prolonged amenorrhoea with hot flushes.
pearl: In women over 45 with typical symptoms, menopause is a clinical diagnosis after 12 months without a period; FSH testing is not needed.
thinking: 52-year-old woman ↓ 14 months without periods ↓ hot flushes and night sweats ↓ over 45 with 12 months' amenorrhoea ↓ menopause
exam_trap: C, hyperprolactinaemia — a recognised cause of amenorrhoea, but it does not explain typical vasomotor symptoms in a 52-year-old.
takeaway: Over 45 with 12 months' amenorrhoea and vasomotor symptoms: menopause, no tests needed.

stem: A 6-year-old child develops small superficial skin lesions around the nose and mouth that rupture and leave golden-yellow crusts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection classically producing vesicles or pustules that rupture to form honey-coloured crusts.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes deeper, diffuse erythema, warmth and swelling. B. Scabies causes intense itching, often worse at night, with typical distribution. D. Psoriasis causes well-demarcated scaly plaques rather than honey-coloured crusts. E. Eczema herpeticum causes widespread painful vesicles in someone with eczema.
pearl: Impetigo is a contagious superficial infection, often Staphylococcus aureus; localised non-bullous disease is treated topically, for example with hydrogen peroxide cream.
thinking: 6-year-old child ↓ superficial lesions around nose and mouth ↓ rupture easily ↓ golden-yellow crusts ↓ impetigo
exam_trap: E, eczema herpeticum — crusted facial lesions may tempt, but it causes widespread painful punched-out vesicles in a child with eczema.
takeaway: Golden, honey-coloured crusts around the nose and mouth mean impetigo.

stem: Which change in a pigmented skin lesion is particularly concerning for melanoma?

options.A: Uniform mid-brown colour throughout the lesion
options.B: Recent change in size, shape or colour
options.C: Stable appearance over many years of follow-up
options.D: Diameter below 6 mm with a regular border

correct_answer: B. Recent change in size, shape or colour
why_correct: Evolution or recent change in a pigmented lesion is an important warning feature for melanoma.
why_wrong: A. Uniform pigmentation is generally less concerning than marked colour variation. C. Long-term stability is less suggestive of a newly developing melanoma. D. A diameter below 6 mm with a regular border is less suspicious, although size alone does not exclude melanoma. E. Symmetry is generally reassuring rather than a classic melanoma feature.
pearl: Change in size, irregular shape and irregular colour are the three major features of the weighted 7-point checklist; any evolving pigmented lesion needs assessment for melanoma.
thinking: Pigmented skin lesion ↓ which feature is worrying ↓ evolution is the key melanoma sign ↓ the other options are reassuring ↓ recent change in size, shape or colour
exam_trap: D, diameter below 6 mm with a regular border — it echoes the ABCDE rule, but it is reassuring, and small lesions can still be melanoma.
takeaway: A changing pigmented lesion is melanoma until proven otherwise.

stem: A 76-year-old man develops a rapidly enlarging, rough, scaly lesion on chronically sun-damaged skin. It occasionally bleeds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: SCC commonly presents as a scaly, keratotic or ulcerated lesion on sun-damaged skin and may grow relatively quickly.
why_wrong: A. Actinic keratoses are flat, rough, scaly patches that do not usually enlarge rapidly or bleed; such change suggests progression to SCC. B. Melanoma usually involves a pigmented lesion with concerning asymmetry or evolution. C. Seborrhoeic keratoses, even when irritated, are benign stuck-on warty lesions that do not grow rapidly on sun-damaged skin. D. BCC is typically slower growing and often has a pearly appearance with telangiectasia.
pearl: SCC is a rapidly growing keratotic or ulcerated lesion on sun-damaged skin in older people; it can metastasise, so refer on a suspected cancer pathway.
thinking: 76-year-old man ↓ chronically sun-damaged skin ↓ rough, scaly lesion ↓ rapidly enlarging and bleeding ↓ squamous cell carcinoma
exam_trap: A, actinic keratosis — rough, scaly and on sun-damaged skin, but it does not enlarge rapidly or bleed; such change suggests SCC.
takeaway: Rapidly growing scaly or bleeding lesion on sun-damaged skin: squamous cell carcinoma.

stem: A woman with longstanding iron deficiency develops diffuse hair shedding rather than discrete bald patches. Which description best fits this pattern?
why_correct: Nutritional deficiencies, including iron deficiency, can contribute to diffuse non-scarring hair shedding.
why_wrong: A. Vesicles indicate a different dermatological process. B. Depigmented patches suggest vitiligo. D. Annular scaling lesions suggest dermatophyte infection. E. Scarring plaques suggest a scarring inflammatory or infectious alopecia.
pearl: Diffuse hair shedding without scarring should prompt checks of ferritin and thyroid function; correcting iron deficiency can help regrowth.
thinking: Longstanding iron deficiency ↓ diffuse shedding ↓ no discrete bald patches ↓ follicles intact, no scarring ↓ diffuse non-scarring hair loss
exam_trap: E, scarring plaques — hair loss may suggest this, but scarring alopecia destroys follicles in patches, unlike diffuse nutritional shedding.
takeaway: Iron deficiency causes diffuse, non-scarring hair shedding.

stem: A patient develops painful vesicles over the forehead and tip of the nose on one side. What complication requires urgent ophthalmological assessment?
why_correct: Ophthalmic division trigeminal involvement can threaten the eye. Vesicles involving the forehead and particularly the nose should prompt assessment for ocular involvement.
why_wrong: B. Periorbital cellulitis causes eyelid swelling and erythema without grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. C. Bullous impetigo causes flaccid blisters and honey-coloured crusts, not a unilateral dermatomal eruption. D. Herpes simplex labialis affects the lip border rather than the forehead and nasal tip. E. Psoriasis causes scaly plaques rather than grouped dermatomal vesicles.
pearl: Hutchinson's sign, vesicles on the tip of the nose, signals nasociliary nerve involvement and a high risk of eye disease; start antivirals and refer urgently.
thinking: Painful unilateral vesicles ↓ forehead distribution ↓ tip of the nose involved ↓ ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ herpes zoster ophthalmicus
exam_trap: D, herpes simplex labialis — another herpes vesicular eruption, but it affects the lip border, not the forehead and nasal tip.
takeaway: Shingles on the forehead and nasal tip needs urgent eye assessment.

stem: A child has recurrent fractures after minor trauma and unusually blue sclerae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Osteogenesis imperfecta is an inherited connective-tissue disorder causing bone fragility and classically blue sclerae.
why_wrong: A. Rickets causes defective bone mineralisation, often associated with vitamin D deficiency. C. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature, long limbs and connective-tissue features rather than recurrent fractures with blue sclerae. D. Duchenne muscular dystrophy causes progressive muscle weakness. E. Achondroplasia causes disproportionate short stature.
pearl: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen disorder with fragile bones, blue sclerae and sometimes hearing loss; it must be considered alongside non-accidental injury.
thinking: Child with recurrent fractures ↓ after only minor trauma, so fragile bone ↓ unusually blue sclerae ↓ osteogenesis imperfecta
exam_trap: A, rickets — it weakens bone in children, but causes bowing and metaphyseal changes, not blue sclerae.
takeaway: Fractures after minor trauma plus blue sclerae means osteogenesis imperfecta.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty running and climbing stairs. He uses his hands to push himself up from the floor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Progressive proximal muscle weakness and Gowers' sign are characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
why_wrong: A. Cerebral palsy, including spastic diplegia, results from non-progressive brain injury and causes spasticity rather than progressive proximal weakness. B. Osteogenesis imperfecta type I causes fractures and bone fragility rather than progressive proximal weakness with Gowers' sign. D. Juvenile myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, often with ptosis, but is uncommon at this age and does not characteristically cause Gowers' sign. E. Spina bifida causes neurological deficits related to spinal dysraphism.
pearl: Gowers' sign in a young boy suggests Duchenne muscular dystrophy; creatine kinase is markedly raised, and inheritance is X-linked recessive.
thinking: 4-year-old boy ↓ difficulty running and climbing stairs ↓ proximal weakness ↓ pushes up from the floor with hands, Gowers' sign ↓ Duchenne muscular dystrophy
exam_trap: A, spastic diplegic cerebral palsy — it causes motor difficulty in young children, but it is non-progressive spasticity, not proximal weakness.
takeaway: Gowers' sign in a young boy: Duchenne, check creatine kinase.

stem: A newborn has a positive Ortolani test during examination. What condition is this test used to detect?
correct_answer: E. Developmental dysplasia of the hip
why_correct: The Ortolani manoeuvre is used in newborn hip examination to detect a dislocated hip that can be reduced.
why_wrong: A. Osteogenesis imperfecta causes bone fragility. B. SUFE occurs later, typically during adolescence. C. Cerebral palsy is a neurological diagnosis. D. Club foot is diagnosed by examination of the foot.
pearl: Ortolani relocates a dislocated hip and Barlow dislocates an unstable one; risk factors such as breech presentation or family history prompt hip ultrasound.
thinking: Newborn examination ↓ Ortolani manoeuvre ↓ dislocated hip clunks back into the socket ↓ hip instability at birth ↓ developmental dysplasia of the hip
exam_trap: B, SUFE — it is a hip disorder, but it occurs in adolescents, not newborns.
takeaway: Positive Ortolani or Barlow test in a newborn means DDH.

stem: A 14-year-old boy who plays football has gradually worsening pain and tenderness over the bony prominence just below the knee. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Osgood-Schlatter disease causes activity-related pain and tenderness at the tibial tubercle in growing adolescents.
why_wrong: A. SUFE is a hip disorder that may refer pain to the knee. B. Perthes disease affects the femoral head and occurs in younger children. C. Septic arthritis causes an acutely painful, swollen joint with systemic features. E. A meniscal tear usually follows knee injury and causes joint-line pain and mechanical symptoms.
pearl: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in active adolescents; it is self-limiting and managed with rest, ice and activity modification.
thinking: 14-year-old footballer ↓ gradual onset ↓ pain over the bony prominence below the knee ↓ tibial tubercle traction injury ↓ Osgood-Schlatter disease
exam_trap: A, SUFE — knee pain in a teenager should prompt hip examination, but SUFE does not cause tibial tubercle tenderness.
takeaway: Teenage athlete with a tender tibial tubercle: Osgood-Schlatter disease.

stem: A man with longstanding lower urinary tract symptoms has a markedly enlarged, painless bladder and overflow dribbling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic retention may produce a large, relatively painless bladder with overflow incontinence or dribbling.
why_wrong: A. Acute urinary retention is typically painful with sudden inability to void, unlike this painless enlarged bladder with overflow. B. Overactive bladder causes urgency and frequency without a markedly enlarged bladder. C. Renal colic causes severe flank pain. D. Epididymitis causes painful, inflamed scrotal structures.
pearl: Chronic retention is painless with a large residual volume and overflow; high-pressure retention can impair renal function, so check U&Es.
thinking: Longstanding lower urinary tract symptoms ↓ markedly enlarged bladder ↓ painless ↓ overflow dribbling ↓ chronic urinary retention
exam_trap: A, acute urinary retention — a distended bladder tempts, but acute retention is painful with a sudden inability to void.
takeaway: Painless distended bladder with overflow dribbling is chronic retention.

stem: A 64-year-old man has painless visible haematuria without dysuria or urinary frequency. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Painless visible haematuria is an important warning symptom of urinary tract malignancy, including renal cell carcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Cystitis commonly causes dysuria, frequency and urgency. B. Epididymitis causes painful scrotal symptoms. C. Benign prostatic enlargement causes lower urinary tract symptoms rather than typically painless haematuria. E. Renal colic causes severe colicky flank pain.
pearl: Unexplained painless visible haematuria in an older adult warrants a suspected urological cancer referral to exclude bladder and renal cancer.
thinking: 64-year-old man ↓ painless visible haematuria ↓ no dysuria or frequency, so infection unlikely ↓ urological malignancy until proven otherwise ↓ renal cell carcinoma
exam_trap: C, benign prostatic enlargement — common in older men and can bleed, but it presents with urinary symptoms, and painless haematuria demands cancer exclusion.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult is urological cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A man has a groin swelling that becomes more prominent on coughing and can be pushed back when lying down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A reducible groin swelling that becomes more prominent with increased intra-abdominal pressure is characteristic of an inguinal hernia.
why_wrong: A. Varicocele produces a characteristic scrotal venous swelling. B. Epididymitis causes painful scrotal inflammation. D. Hydrocele is a scrotal fluid collection. E. Testicular cancer produces an intratesticular mass.
pearl: An inguinal hernia has a cough impulse and reduces; you cannot get above it, unlike a true scrotal swelling such as a hydrocele.
thinking: Groin swelling ↓ more prominent on coughing ↓ reduces when lying down ↓ abdominal contents through the inguinal canal ↓ inguinal hernia
exam_trap: D, hydrocele — a common swelling in men, but it is scrotal, transilluminates and has no cough impulse.
takeaway: Reducible groin swelling with a cough impulse is an inguinal hernia.

stem: A patient with a known inguinal hernia develops severe constant pain. The swelling is tender, irreducible and associated with vomiting. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: A painful, irreducible hernia with systemic or obstructive symptoms raises concern for compromised blood supply and strangulation.
why_wrong: A. Hydrocele is a fluid collection and does not cause bowel obstruction. C. A reducible hernia is not typically acutely painful and irreducible. D. Epididymitis does not cause an irreducible groin swelling with vomiting. E. Varicocele is a venous scrotal swelling.
pearl: A tender, irreducible hernia with vomiting suggests strangulation; it needs emergency surgical review because ischaemic bowel can perforate.
thinking: Known inguinal hernia ↓ severe constant pain ↓ tender and irreducible ↓ vomiting suggests obstruction ↓ strangulation
exam_trap: C, simple reducible hernia — the patient does have a hernia, but it is now tender and irreducible with vomiting.
takeaway: Painful, tender, irreducible hernia with vomiting: strangulation, emergency surgery.

stem: Which hernia is more common in women and has a relatively high risk of strangulation?
why_correct: Femoral hernias are more common in women and have a relatively narrow neck, increasing the risk of incarceration and strangulation.
why_wrong: A. Incisional hernias occur through previous surgical wounds. C. Umbilical hernias occur around the umbilicus and have different epidemiological characteristics. D. Epigastric hernias occur through the linea alba above the umbilicus. E. Hiatus hernia occurs at the oesophageal hiatus and is internal rather than a groin hernia.
pearl: Femoral hernias lie below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and are more common in women; their narrow neck means repair is advised.
thinking: Hernia commoner in women ↓ high strangulation risk ↓ narrow, rigid femoral canal ↓ neck below the inguinal ligament ↓ femoral hernia
exam_trap: C, umbilical hernia — it is also seen in women, but it lacks the narrow-necked, high-strangulation profile of a femoral hernia.
takeaway: Femoral hernias: commoner in women, high strangulation risk, so repair.

stem: A 2-year-old child has a small, painless swelling at the umbilicus that becomes more obvious when crying. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Umbilical hernias are common in children and typically become more prominent with crying or straining.
why_wrong: A. Femoral hernias occur in the groin below the inguinal ligament. B. Hydrocele causes scrotal swelling. D. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting rather than an umbilical swelling. E. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain.
pearl: Most umbilical hernias in young children close spontaneously; surgery is considered only if they persist into later childhood or become complicated.
thinking: 2-year-old child ↓ small painless swelling ↓ at the umbilicus ↓ more obvious when crying ↓ umbilical hernia
exam_trap: A, femoral hernia — a hernia that bulges with straining tempts, but femoral hernias lie in the groin, not at the umbilicus.
takeaway: Painless umbilical swelling on crying in a toddler is an umbilical hernia; most close.

stem: A patient develops foot drop after prolonged compression around the fibular head. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck and is vulnerable to compression. Injury can cause foot drop.
why_wrong: B. Tibial nerve injury primarily affects plantarflexion and intrinsic foot function. C. Sciatic nerve injury can cause broader deficits and is not specifically associated with the fibular head. D. The superficial fibular nerve supplies the foot evertors; isolated injury does not cause foot drop, and it is the common fibular nerve that is compressed at the fibular head. E. Femoral nerve injury causes weakness of knee extension.
pearl: Common fibular (peroneal) nerve palsy causes foot drop with weak eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot; inversion is preserved.
thinking: Prolonged compression ↓ around the fibular head ↓ nerve winds superficially round the fibular neck ↓ weak dorsiflexion, foot drop ↓ common fibular nerve
exam_trap: D, superficial fibular nerve — a branch near the fibula, but it supplies the evertors only; isolated injury does not cause foot drop.
takeaway: Foot drop after pressure at the fibular head: common fibular nerve palsy.

stem: A patient sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation and subsequently has difficulty abducting the arm. Which nerve is most likely injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid, which is important for shoulder abduction, and is vulnerable in shoulder dislocation.
why_wrong: A. Median nerve injury mainly affects forearm/hand function. B. Radial nerve injury affects extension of the wrist and fingers. C. Femoral nerve supplies the lower limb. D. Ulnar nerve injury affects intrinsic hand function and ulnar-sided sensation.
pearl: After an anterior shoulder dislocation, test sensation over the regimental badge area before and after reduction; numbness signals axillary nerve injury.
thinking: Anterior shoulder dislocation ↓ axillary nerve runs round the surgical neck of humerus ↓ it supplies deltoid ↓ weak abduction ↓ axillary nerve
exam_trap: B, radial nerve — a classic upper-limb nerve injury with humeral shaft fractures, but it causes wrist drop, not weak shoulder abduction.
takeaway: Shoulder dislocation with weak abduction or badge-area numbness: axillary nerve.

stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes develops symmetrical numbness and burning pain in both feet, extending gradually upwards. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Longstanding diabetes can cause a symmetrical length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, typically beginning in the feet.
why_wrong: A. Motor neurone disease is predominantly motor and does not typically cause distal sensory loss or burning pain. C. Guillain–Barré is acute or subacute and causes progressive weakness with reduced reflexes. D. Myasthenia causes fatigable motor weakness without sensory loss. E. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis causes focal central neurological episodes rather than a gradually ascending stocking distribution.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy is a length-dependent stocking-and-glove loss; regular foot checks with monofilament testing aim to prevent ulcers and amputation.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ symmetrical numbness and burning pain ↓ starts in the feet ↓ spreads gradually upwards, stocking pattern ↓ diabetic peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: C, Guillain–Barré syndrome — ascending symptoms tempt, but GBS is acute with progressive weakness and lost reflexes, not gradual painful sensory loss.
takeaway: Gradual symmetrical burning numbness in the feet in diabetes is peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 32-year-old man has a persistent cough, night sweats and unintentional weight loss. A chest X-ray shows upper-lobe cavitation. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats and upper-lobe cavitation are characteristic features of pulmonary tuberculosis.
why_wrong: A. Asthma causes variable wheeze and breathlessness, not cavitation. C. Pneumothorax causes acute pleuritic pain and breathlessness. D. Pneumonia usually has a more acute presentation with fever and focal consolidation. E. Pulmonary oedema causes bilateral respiratory symptoms and characteristic radiographic changes rather than upper-lobe cavitation.
pearl: Suspected pulmonary TB: send several sputum samples for microscopy and culture, take infection control precautions, and notify the case to public health.
thinking: Persistent cough ↓ night sweats ↓ unintentional weight loss ↓ upper-lobe cavitation on chest X-ray ↓ pulmonary tuberculosis
exam_trap: D, community-acquired pneumonia — cough fits, but pneumonia is acute with consolidation, not chronic with upper-lobe cavitation.
takeaway: Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss and upper-lobe cavitation: pulmonary TB.

stem: A patient has confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis. Which household contact is particularly important to assess for possible infection?

options.A: A shop assistant who served the patient once
options.B: A neighbour seen once a month
options.C: A young child living in the same household
options.D: A colleague working in another building
options.E: A person who lives in another city

correct_answer: C. A young child living in the same household
why_correct: Close household contacts have significant exposure risk, and young children are particularly important to identify and assess following exposure to infectious TB.
why_wrong: A. A single brief retail interaction is not comparable with household exposure. B. Occasional contact generally represents substantially less exposure. D. Working in another building does not usually represent close exposure. E. Living separately without close exposure does not constitute a typical household contact.
pearl: TB contact tracing prioritises household and close contacts; young children are at high risk of progressing to severe disease such as TB meningitis.
thinking: Infectious pulmonary TB ↓ transmission needs prolonged close contact ↓ household members most exposed ↓ young children progress more often to severe disease ↓ young child in the same household
exam_trap: B, a neighbour seen monthly — a regular contact may seem relevant, but occasional exposure carries far less risk than living together.
takeaway: TB contact tracing: household contacts first, especially young children.

stem: A patient develops severe toothache, facial swelling and fever. Examination shows a tender tooth with surrounding gingival swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe localised dental pain with swelling and systemic features is characteristic of a dental abscess.
why_wrong: A. Aphthous ulcers are small mucosal ulcers and do not cause facial swelling. B. Oral candidiasis causes mucosal plaques. C. Temporomandibular disorders cause jaw pain or dysfunction rather than fever and dental swelling. D. Viral pharyngitis causes sore throat rather than a localised painful tooth and facial swelling.
pearl: A dental abscess needs drainage by a dentist; antibiotics are an adjunct for spreading infection or systemic features, and floor-of-mouth swelling threatens the airway.
thinking: Severe toothache ↓ tender tooth with gingival swelling ↓ facial swelling ↓ fever ↓ dental abscess
exam_trap: C, temporomandibular disorder — jaw and facial pain tempt, but it does not cause fever or swelling around a tender tooth.
takeaway: Tender tooth with swelling and fever is a dental abscess: it needs drainage.

stem: A patient with infective endocarditis develops painless erythematous lesions on the palms and soles. What are these called?
why_correct: Janeway lesions are painless erythematous or haemorrhagic lesions on the palms and soles associated with infective endocarditis.
why_wrong: A. Koplik spots occur on the buccal mucosa in measles. B. Vesicles are fluid-filled skin lesions and are not the characteristic finding here. C. Erythema nodosum causes tender subcutaneous nodules, usually on the shins. D. Osler nodes are typically painful or tender.
pearl: Janeway lesions are painless macules on the palms and soles; Osler nodes are painful nodules on finger and toe pads. Both point to infective endocarditis.
thinking: Infective endocarditis ↓ lesions on palms and soles ↓ erythematous ↓ painless, not tender ↓ Janeway lesions
exam_trap: D, Osler nodes — also a peripheral sign of endocarditis, but they are painful nodules on the finger and toe pads.
takeaway: Janeway painless, Osler painful: both are signs of endocarditis.

stem: A child develops involuntary, irregular movements several weeks after a streptococcal throat infection. What manifestation of acute rheumatic fever is this?
why_correct: Sydenham chorea is a neurological manifestation of acute rheumatic fever and causes involuntary, purposeless movements.
why_wrong: A. Parkinsonism causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor. C. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than choreiform movements. D. Bell's palsy causes unilateral facial weakness. E. Essential tremor is predominantly an action or postural tremor.
pearl: Sydenham chorea can appear weeks to months after a streptococcal throat infection and may be the only sign of rheumatic fever; it is a major Jones criterion.
thinking: Child ↓ preceding streptococcal throat infection ↓ weeks later ↓ involuntary, irregular, purposeless movements ↓ Sydenham chorea
exam_trap: E, essential tremor — involuntary movement tempts, but it is a regular action tremor, not irregular chorea after infection.
takeaway: Chorea weeks after a strep throat is Sydenham chorea of rheumatic fever.

stem: A traveller develops fever, agitation and difficulty swallowing several weeks after being bitten by a potentially rabid animal. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Rabies can cause an encephalitic illness with agitation, dysphagia and characteristic hydrophobia after an infected animal bite.
why_wrong: A. Lyme disease has a different clinical spectrum and exposure pattern. C. Infectious mononucleosis causes fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy and fatigue. D. Botulism causes descending flaccid paralysis. E. Tetanus causes rigidity and muscle spasms following wound contamination.
pearl: Once rabies symptoms appear it is almost always fatal; prompt wound cleaning and post-exposure vaccine, with immunoglobulin when indicated, prevent disease after a bite.
thinking: Bitten by a potentially rabid animal ↓ weeks of incubation ↓ fever and agitation suggest encephalitis ↓ difficulty swallowing from pharyngeal spasm ↓ rabies
exam_trap: E, tetanus — it follows bite wounds and can affect swallowing, but it causes rigidity and spasms, not an agitated encephalitis.
takeaway: Agitation and dysphagia weeks after an animal bite abroad: rabies.

stem: A patient develops blurred vision, difficulty swallowing and progressive descending weakness after eating home-preserved food. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Foodborne botulism causes cranial nerve dysfunction followed by descending flaccid paralysis due to botulinum neurotoxin.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus causes rigidity and spasms. B. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness but is not characteristically linked to contaminated preserved food. C. Meningitis causes systemic and meningeal features rather than descending paralysis. E. Guillain–Barré usually causes ascending weakness.
pearl: Botulism causes symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis starting with the cranial nerves, with sensation intact; give antitoxin early and monitor respiratory function.
thinking: Home-preserved food ↓ blurred vision and dysphagia, cranial nerves first ↓ weakness descends ↓ toxin-mediated flaccid paralysis ↓ botulism
exam_trap: E, Guillain–Barré syndrome — acute flaccid weakness tempts, but GBS usually ascends from the legs; botulism descends from the cranial nerves.
takeaway: Descending paralysis after home-preserved food is botulism.

stem: A pregnant woman asks about the infection associated with undercooked meat and cat faeces that can cause congenital disease. Which infection is this?
why_correct: Toxoplasma gondii can be acquired from undercooked meat and exposure to cat faeces and can cause congenital infection.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis A is primarily transmitted by the faecal–oral route. C. Rubella is transmitted mainly through respiratory droplets. D. Varicella spreads mainly through respiratory droplets and direct contact with vesicular fluid. E. Parvovirus B19 spreads through respiratory secretions.
pearl: Advise pregnant women to avoid undercooked meat, wash hands after gardening and avoid cleaning cat litter to reduce toxoplasmosis risk.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ infection from undercooked meat and cat faeces ↓ causes congenital disease ↓ toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: E, parvovirus B19 — it is a congenital infection risk, but it spreads by respiratory secretions, not via meat or cat faeces.
takeaway: Undercooked meat and cat faeces in pregnancy: toxoplasmosis.

stem: A pregnant woman with no history of chickenpox has been exposed to a child with confirmed varicella. What is the key issue?

options.A: Development of maternal hypothyroidism in every case
options.B: Development of congenital hearing loss in every case
options.D: Risk of maternal and fetal complications from varicella

correct_answer: D. Risk of maternal and fetal complications from varicella
why_correct: Varicella infection during pregnancy can cause significant maternal illness and, depending on gestational timing, fetal complications.
why_wrong: A. It does not inevitably cause hypothyroidism. B. Congenital hearing loss is not the defining fetal complication. C. Varicella does not inevitably cause diabetes. E. Exposure in a non-immune pregnant woman requires appropriate assessment.
pearl: A pregnant woman with uncertain chickenpox immunity exposed to varicella needs urgent VZV IgG testing; if non-immune, post-exposure prophylaxis is offered.
thinking: Pregnant ↓ no history of chickenpox, possibly non-immune ↓ significant varicella exposure ↓ risk of maternal pneumonia and fetal varicella ↓ maternal and fetal complications
exam_trap: E, no clinical significance — chickenpox seems a mild childhood illness, but in a non-immune pregnant woman it can cause serious harm.
takeaway: Non-immune pregnant woman exposed to chickenpox: check immunity and offer prophylaxis urgently.

stem: A young adult develops headache, photophobia and neck stiffness but remains alert and haemodynamically stable. There is no focal neurological deficit. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Viral meningitis can present with headache, photophobia and neck stiffness, often with a less severe systemic presentation than bacterial meningitis.
why_wrong: A. Subarachnoid haemorrhage classically causes a sudden thunderclap headache. B. Temporal arteritis occurs predominantly in older adults and has a different clinical pattern. C. Brain tumour usually has a more progressive course. D. Migraine can cause photophobia but does not typically cause true neck stiffness with meningeal irritation.
pearl: Viral meningitis is usually milder and self-limiting, but bacterial meningitis cannot be excluded clinically; lumbar puncture and CSF analysis distinguish them.
thinking: Young adult ↓ headache, photophobia, neck stiffness: meningism ↓ alert and haemodynamically stable ↓ no focal deficit ↓ viral meningitis
exam_trap: A, subarachnoid haemorrhage — it also causes meningism, but presents with a sudden thunderclap headache.
takeaway: Meningism in an alert, stable young adult is most often viral meningitis.

stem: A patient develops fever, confusion, personality change and seizures. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Altered mental state, seizures and behavioural or personality changes with fever are characteristic features of encephalitis.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa causes local ear symptoms. C. Migraine aura causes transient neurological symptoms but does not explain fever and altered consciousness. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. E. Tension headache does not cause fever, confusion or seizures.
pearl: In suspected encephalitis, start IV aciclovir promptly without waiting for results, because herpes simplex encephalitis is treatable and devastating if missed.
thinking: Fever ↓ confusion ↓ personality change ↓ seizures, so brain parenchyma involved ↓ encephalitis
exam_trap: C, migraine aura — it causes transient neurological symptoms, but not fever, confusion and seizures.
takeaway: Fever with altered behaviour or seizures: encephalitis, give IV aciclovir.

stem: A patient with a history of chronic otitis media develops headache, fever and a new focal neurological deficit. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: A focal intracranial infection can arise from contiguous ear infection and present with headache, systemic features and focal neurological signs.
why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy causes isolated peripheral facial weakness. C. Migraine does not explain persistent fever and a new focal neurological deficit. D. Essential tremor causes an action tremor rather than focal neurological deficits and fever. E. Tension headache does not cause fever or focal neurological signs.
pearl: Ear, sinus or dental infection can spread to form a brain abscess; the triad of headache, fever and focal deficit is often incomplete, so image early.
thinking: Chronic otitis media ↓ contiguous spread of infection ↓ headache and fever ↓ new focal neurological deficit ↓ brain abscess
exam_trap: A, Bell's palsy — ear disease and a facial deficit may tempt, but Bell's palsy is an isolated facial weakness without fever or headache.
takeaway: Ear infection plus fever, headache and focal signs: think brain abscess.

stem: A patient with an intracranial mass develops headache that is worse in the morning and vomiting without nausea. What mechanism may explain these symptoms?
why_correct: Intracranial mass lesions can raise intracranial pressure, causing headache and vomiting, sometimes particularly prominent in the morning.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy does not cause raised intracranial pressure symptoms. C. Cervical spondylosis may cause occipital headache with neck movement but does not explain early-morning headache with vomiting from an intracranial mass. D. Nocturnal hypoglycaemia causes sweating, confusion or seizures but does not explain vomiting due to an intracranial mass. E. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms.
pearl: Headache worse on waking, with vomiting, or worse on coughing or bending suggests raised intracranial pressure; look for papilloedema.
thinking: Intracranial mass ↓ headache worse in the morning ↓ vomiting ↓ lying flat overnight raises pressure ↓ raised intracranial pressure
exam_trap: D, early-morning hypoglycaemia — morning symptoms tempt, but it causes sweating and confusion, not headache with vomiting from a mass.
takeaway: Morning headache with vomiting points to raised intracranial pressure.

stem: An older patient develops progressive gait difficulty, urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment. Brain imaging shows enlarged ventricles. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: The combination of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence with ventriculomegaly is the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus.
why_wrong: B. Guillain–Barré causes acute progressive peripheral weakness. C. Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor but does not produce this classic triad. D. Lambert–Eaton syndrome causes proximal weakness and autonomic features but not cognitive impairment or ventricular enlargement. E. Multiple sclerosis usually presents with focal neurological episodes.
pearl: Normal pressure hydrocephalus is 'wet, wacky and wobbly' and potentially reversible with CSF shunting; gait disturbance is usually the first feature.
thinking: Older patient with gait difficulty ↓ urinary incontinence and cognitive impairment ↓ enlarged ventricles on imaging ↓ normal pressure hydrocephalus
exam_trap: C, Parkinson's disease — gait disturbance and later cognitive decline tempt, but it does not cause this triad with enlarged ventricles.
takeaway: Gait, continence and cognition problems with big ventricles: normal pressure hydrocephalus.

stem: An 82-year-old man develops gradually worsening headache and confusion several weeks after a minor head injury. He takes anticoagulant medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Older adults, particularly those taking anticoagulants, are at increased risk of subdural haematoma after relatively minor trauma. Symptoms may develop gradually.
why_wrong: A. Tension headache does not explain progressive confusion after head trauma. B. Bell's palsy causes facial weakness rather than progressive headache and confusion. C. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief paroxysmal facial pain. D. Migraine is not typically associated with progressive cognitive deterioration after trauma.
pearl: Chronic subdural haematoma affects older, anticoagulated or alcohol-dependent patients, with fluctuating confusion after minor trauma; request a CT head.
thinking: 82-year-old man ↓ takes anticoagulant ↓ minor head injury weeks ago ↓ gradually worsening headache and confusion ↓ subdural haematoma
exam_trap: A, tension headache — a common headache diagnosis, but it does not explain progressive confusion after trauma.
takeaway: Elderly, anticoagulated, minor head injury and slow confusion: chronic subdural, get a CT.

stem: A patient with longstanding inflammatory disease has a mild anaemia. Ferritin is normal or raised, while serum iron is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: In chronic inflammation, iron becomes sequestered in storage sites; serum iron is low while ferritin is often normal or raised.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency usually produces a low ferritin. C. Acute blood loss does not produce this characteristic chronic inflammatory iron profile. D. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis rather than this iron pattern. E. B12 deficiency is typically macrocytic.
pearl: Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so in inflammation it may be normal or raised; anaemia of chronic disease shows low serum iron with low TIBC.
thinking: Longstanding inflammatory disease ↓ mild anaemia ↓ low serum iron ↓ normal or raised ferritin, iron locked in stores ↓ anaemia of chronic disease
exam_trap: A, iron deficiency anaemia — low serum iron tempts, but iron deficiency gives a low ferritin, not a normal or raised one.
takeaway: Low iron with normal or high ferritin in chronic inflammation: anaemia of chronic disease.

stem: A boy has recurrent deep muscle and joint bleeding. His maternal grandfather had a similar bleeding disorder. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Haemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing recurrent deep bleeding, particularly haemarthroses.
why_wrong: A. Sickle cell disease causes vaso-occlusive and haemolytic complications. B. Von Willebrand disease commonly causes mucosal bleeding rather than recurrent haemarthroses. C. Iron deficiency causes anaemia rather than abnormal bleeding. D. Immune thrombocytopenia causes thrombocytopenic bleeding, often mucocutaneous.
pearl: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive, so boys are affected through carrier mothers; expect a prolonged APTT with normal PT and platelets.
thinking: Boy ↓ recurrent deep muscle and joint bleeds ↓ maternal grandfather affected ↓ X-linked inheritance ↓ haemophilia A
exam_trap: B, von Willebrand disease — the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, but it causes mucosal bleeding rather than recurrent haemarthroses.
takeaway: Haemarthroses in a boy with a maternal-line family history: haemophilia A.

stem: A teenager develops fatigue, recurrent infections, bruising and bone pain. Blood tests show anaemia, thrombocytopenia and abnormal white cells. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Acute leukaemia can cause bone-marrow failure, producing anaemia, thrombocytopenia, abnormal white-cell counts, infections and bone pain.
why_wrong: B. Iron deficiency does not explain pancytopenia-type abnormalities and bone pain. C. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolytic anaemia rather than abnormal white cells and thrombocytopenia. D. Von Willebrand disease causes bleeding but not marrow failure. E. Thalassaemia trait causes mild chronic microcytosis.
pearl: Bone marrow failure features with bone pain in a young person need an urgent full blood count and blood film; blasts mean immediate specialist referral.
thinking: Teenager ↓ fatigue, infections, bruising ↓ anaemia, thrombocytopenia, abnormal white cells ↓ marrow failure plus bone pain ↓ acute leukaemia
exam_trap: D, von Willebrand disease — bruising tempts, but it does not cause anaemia, infections, abnormal white cells or bone pain.
takeaway: Marrow failure with bone pain in a young person: acute leukaemia until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient develops rapidly enlarging, painless lymph nodes together with weight loss and fever. Which broad diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present with painless lymphadenopathy and systemic "B" symptoms such as fever and weight loss.
why_wrong: A. Tension headache does not cause lymphadenopathy. B. Osteoarthritis causes joint symptoms. C. Iron-deficiency anaemia causes fatigue and pallor rather than rapidly enlarging lymph nodes. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms.
pearl: Unexplained enlarging lymph nodes with B symptoms need urgent referral; lymphoma is diagnosed on excision or core biopsy, not fine-needle aspiration.
thinking: Rapidly enlarging lymph nodes ↓ painless ↓ fever and weight loss, B symptoms ↓ lymphoid malignancy ↓ non-Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: C, iron-deficiency anaemia — fatigue and weight loss may overlap, but it never causes rapidly enlarging lymph nodes.
takeaway: Painless enlarging nodes with B symptoms: think lymphoma, arrange biopsy.

stem: A woman has recurrent miscarriages and a previous unprovoked venous thrombosis. Which autoimmune condition should be considered?
why_correct: Antiphospholipid syndrome is associated with thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity, including recurrent pregnancy loss.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not cause thrombosis or recurrent miscarriage. B. Myasthenia causes fatigable muscle weakness. C. Primary Sjögren's syndrome causes dry eyes and mouth and is not characteristically associated with recurrent miscarriage and unprovoked thrombosis. D. Coeliac disease primarily affects the gastrointestinal system and may cause malabsorption.
pearl: Antiphospholipid syndrome links thrombosis and pregnancy loss with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies; in pregnancy, aspirin plus LMWH reduces risk.
thinking: Woman ↓ recurrent miscarriages ↓ previous unprovoked venous thrombosis ↓ autoimmune prothrombotic state ↓ antiphospholipid syndrome
exam_trap: C, primary Sjögren's syndrome — an autoimmune condition common in women, but it causes dry eyes and mouth, not thrombosis with miscarriage.
takeaway: Recurrent miscarriage plus unprovoked thrombosis: test for antiphospholipid syndrome.

stem: A patient with persistent dry mouth develops frequent dental caries. Which mechanism best explains the increased dental problems?
why_correct: Saliva protects teeth and oral mucosa; reduced salivary production increases the risk of dental caries and oral discomfort.
why_wrong: A. Renal calcium handling does not directly explain the oral findings. C. Insulin secretion is unrelated. D. Gastric acid does not explain the characteristic dry-mouth-associated pattern. E. Bile production is unrelated to salivary protection.
pearl: Saliva buffers acid, clears food debris and is antibacterial; dry mouth from drugs, radiotherapy or Sjögren's syndrome raises caries risk.
thinking: Persistent dry mouth ↓ frequent dental caries ↓ saliva normally buffers and cleanses teeth ↓ that protection is lost ↓ reduced saliva production
exam_trap: D, increased gastric acid — acid erodes teeth in reflux, but it does not explain caries linked to a dry mouth.
takeaway: Dry mouth causes caries because saliva protects the teeth.

stem: An older patient has persistent localised bone pain. Imaging shows abnormal thickening and remodelling of a single bone. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Paget disease causes abnormal bone remodelling and may affect one or several bones, particularly in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis primarily affects articular joints. B. Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone. C. Osteoporosis causes reduced bone density without the characteristic abnormal remodelling pattern. E. Rheumatoid arthritis primarily affects synovial joints.
pearl: Paget disease: older patient, bone pain and deformity, raised ALP with normal calcium; bisphosphonates treat the bone pain.
thinking: Older patient ↓ persistent localised bone pain ↓ single bone affected ↓ thickening and remodelling on imaging ↓ Paget disease of bone
exam_trap: B, osteomyelitis — persistent localised bone pain tempts, but it is a bone infection, not chronic thickening and disordered remodelling.
takeaway: Thickened, remodelled bone with pain in an older person: Paget disease.

stem: A patient with diabetes develops a chronic ulcer on the foot. The ulcer reaches bone and the patient develops persistent local pain and fever. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: A chronic diabetic foot ulcer extending to bone can become complicated by infection of the underlying bone.
why_wrong: A. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without local bone infection. B. Gout causes crystal-induced inflammatory arthritis. C. Osteoarthritis is degenerative joint disease. D. Osteoporosis causes bone fragility rather than infection.
pearl: If a diabetic foot ulcer reaches bone, assume osteomyelitis; MRI helps confirm it, and urgent multidisciplinary foot team review is needed.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ chronic foot ulcer ↓ ulcer reaches bone ↓ persistent local pain and fever ↓ osteomyelitis
exam_trap: B, gout — a hot, painful foot tempts, but gout is crystal arthritis, not infection beneath an ulcer that reaches bone.
takeaway: Diabetic foot ulcer down to bone: osteomyelitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient falls onto a flexed wrist and develops a distal radius fracture with volar displacement. Which fracture is this?
why_correct: A Smith fracture is a distal radius fracture with volar displacement, typically following a fall onto a flexed wrist.
why_wrong: A. A boxer’s fracture affects the neck of the fifth metacarpal. B. A Colles fracture has dorsal displacement of the distal radius. C. A Monteggia injury involves an ulna fracture with radial-head dislocation. E. A scaphoid fracture involves the scaphoid and typically causes anatomical snuffbox tenderness.
pearl: A Smith fracture is the reverse Colles: a fall on a flexed wrist with volar displacement of the distal radius, giving a garden-spade deformity.
thinking: Fall onto a flexed wrist ↓ distal radius fracture ↓ fragment displaced volarly ↓ the opposite of a Colles fracture ↓ Smith fracture
exam_trap: B, Colles fracture — the commonest distal radius fracture, but it follows a fall on an outstretched hand with dorsal displacement.
takeaway: Distal radius fracture with volar displacement after a flexed-wrist fall is a Smith fracture.

stem: A man punches a wall and develops pain and swelling over the ulnar side of the hand. X-ray shows a fracture of the fifth metacarpal neck. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: A fracture of the fifth metacarpal neck following punching is classically called a boxer’s fracture.
why_wrong: A. Colles fractures involve the distal radius with dorsal displacement. B. Smith fractures involve the distal radius with volar displacement. D. Scaphoid fractures involve the wrist. E. A radial-head fracture occurs at the elbow.
pearl: A boxer's fracture is a fifth metacarpal neck fracture after punching; check for rotational deformity and look for a fight bite over the knuckle.
thinking: Punched a wall ↓ ulnar-sided hand pain and swelling ↓ X-ray: fifth metacarpal neck fracture ↓ classic punching injury ↓ boxer’s fracture
exam_trap: D, scaphoid fracture — a common wrist fracture, but it follows a fall on an outstretched hand with anatomical snuffbox tenderness.
takeaway: Fifth metacarpal neck fracture after a punch is a boxer’s fracture.

stem: A cyclist falls directly onto their shoulder and develops pain and swelling over the middle of the clavicle. What is the most likely injury?
why_correct: Direct trauma to the shoulder commonly causes a clavicular fracture, particularly through the middle third.
why_wrong: A. Humeral shaft fracture causes pain and swelling along the upper arm. B. Shoulder dislocation causes deformity and marked restriction of shoulder movement. C. Olecranon fracture causes elbow pain. E. Scaphoid fracture causes wrist and anatomical snuffbox tenderness.
pearl: Clavicle fractures usually involve the middle third and most are managed conservatively in a broad arm sling; always check skin integrity and distal neurovascular status.
thinking: Fall directly onto the shoulder ↓ Pain and swelling over the mid-clavicle ↓ Classic mechanism for a middle-third clavicle fracture ↓ Clavicle fracture
exam_trap: B, shoulder dislocation — the injury is around the shoulder, but dislocation causes loss of shoulder contour and marked restriction; localised mid-clavicular swelling points to the clavicle.
takeaway: Direct shoulder impact with mid-clavicular tenderness means a clavicle fracture until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient develops respiratory distress, confusion and a petechial rash 48 hours after a major long-bone fracture. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Fat embolism syndrome can occur after long-bone fractures and classically involves respiratory, neurological and petechial manifestations.
why_wrong: A. Tuberculosis has a chronic presentation. C. Asthma causes wheeze and variable airflow obstruction. D. Tension pneumothorax causes acute respiratory compromise but not the characteristic petechial rash. E. Pulmonary oedema does not explain the post-fracture neurological and petechial features.
pearl: Fat embolism syndrome classically appears a day or two after a long-bone or pelvic fracture with hypoxia, confusion and petechiae (often axillae and conjunctivae); early fracture fixation reduces the risk.
thinking: Major long-bone fracture ↓ 48 hours later: respiratory distress ↓ Plus confusion and petechial rash ↓ Lungs, brain and skin involved ↓ Fat embolism syndrome
exam_trap: E, pulmonary oedema — explains breathlessness in an unwell trauma patient, but cannot account for the confusion and petechial rash that complete the fat-embolism triad.
takeaway: Hypoxia, confusion and petechiae after a long-bone fracture mean fat embolism syndrome.

stem: An older woman has pain at the base of her thumb that worsens when opening jars. Examination shows bony enlargement around the thumb base. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Thumb-base osteoarthritis commonly causes activity-related pain and bony enlargement at the first carpometacarpal joint.
why_wrong: A. De Quervain tenosynovitis causes pain over the radial wrist, particularly with thumb movement. B. Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes inflammatory polyarthritis with soft-tissue swelling. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-nerve sensory symptoms. E. Gout usually presents as an acute inflammatory attack.
pearl: First carpometacarpal joint osteoarthritis is common in older women; look for squaring of the thumb base, pain on pinch and grip, and a positive grind test.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Thumb-base pain worse with gripping (opening jars) ↓ Bony enlargement around the thumb base ↓ Degenerative first CMC joint ↓ Osteoarthritis
exam_trap: A, De Quervain tenosynovitis — also causes radial-sided thumb pain, but it affects the tendons over the radial styloid (positive Finkelstein test) and causes no bony enlargement.
takeaway: Bony swelling at the thumb base with pain on gripping is first CMC osteoarthritis.

stem: A tennis player develops pain over the outside of the elbow that worsens when gripping objects. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Lateral epicondylitis, commonly called tennis elbow, causes pain around the lateral elbow associated with gripping and wrist extension.
