why_wrong: B. Generalised tonic-clonic movements suggest a generalised seizure. C. Progressive memory loss is not cataplexy. D. Prolonged confusion after loss of consciousness suggests another neurological event. E. Persistent unilateral weakness suggests a focal neurological disorder.
pearl: Cataplexy, a sudden emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone with retained awareness, is highly specific for narcolepsy type 1, alongside excessive daytime sleepiness.
thinking: Cataplexy ↓ Triggered by strong emotion such as laughter ↓ Sudden transient loss of muscle tone ↓ Consciousness preserved ↓ Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
exam_trap: D, Loss of consciousness with prolonged confusion — collapse suggests a seizure, but cataplexy preserves awareness and has no post-ictal confusion.
takeaway: Cataplexy is emotion-triggered loss of tone with full consciousness: think narcolepsy.

stem: A patient becomes markedly unsteady when standing with their feet together and eyes closed, after being relatively stable with their eyes open. What does a positive Romberg test suggest?
why_correct: A positive Romberg test indicates impaired proprioceptive input or vestibular function, with vision compensating while the eyes are open.
why_wrong: B. Aphasia is a language disorder. C. Isolated weakness does not produce the characteristic test finding. D. Facial nerve palsy affects facial movement. E. Lower motor neurone disease is characterised by weakness, wasting and reduced reflexes.
pearl: Romberg tests position sense, not cerebellar function: a patient with cerebellar ataxia is unsteady even with eyes open, whereas sensory ataxia worsens markedly when the eyes close.
thinking: Stable with eyes open ↓ Unsteady when eyes close ↓ Vision was compensating for lost position sense ↓ Positive Romberg ↓ Impaired proprioception
exam_trap: C, Isolated motor weakness — unsteadiness may suggest weakness, but weakness does not worsen specifically when the eyes are closed.
takeaway: A positive Romberg points to sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia, not cerebellar disease.

stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes develops reduced sensation in both feet extending upwards in a symmetrical stocking distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy commonly produces symmetrical distal sensory loss in a stocking distribution.
why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome causes saddle sensory disturbance and bladder or bowel dysfunction. B. Stroke usually causes an acute focal neurological deficit. D. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than sensory loss. E. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis typically produces focal or multifocal neurological episodes rather than a symmetrical stocking distribution.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy begins distally and ascends in a stocking distribution; loss of protective sensation raises ulcer risk, so regular foot review with monofilament testing matters.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ Symmetrical sensory loss in both feet ↓ Length-dependent stocking distribution ↓ Peripheral diabetic neuropathy
exam_trap: A, Cauda equina syndrome — bilateral lower-limb sensory change tempts, but it causes saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction.
takeaway: Symmetrical stocking sensory loss in diabetes is peripheral neuropathy; protect the feet.

stem: Which nerve root predominantly contributes to knee extension?
why_correct: Knee extension via the quadriceps is predominantly supplied by the femoral nerve, with major contributions from L3 and L4.
why_wrong: A. C5–C6 contributes to upper-limb movements. B. S1–S2 contributes mainly to plantarflexion and other lower-limb functions. C. T1–T2 is associated with upper thoracic and upper-limb innervation. D. L5–S1 is not the principal root contribution to knee extension.
pearl: The knee jerk tests L3–L4 via the femoral nerve, while the ankle jerk tests S1. Quadriceps weakness with a reduced knee jerk points to an L3–L4 root or femoral nerve lesion.
thinking: Knee extension is the movement tested ↓ Performed by quadriceps femoris ↓ Supplied by the femoral nerve ↓ Main root contribution is L3–L4
exam_trap: D, L5–S1 — the familiar lumbar roots of sciatica questions, but they serve ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, not knee extension.
takeaway: Knee extension and the knee jerk: L3–L4 via the femoral nerve.

stem: A patient has difficulty lifting the front of the foot while walking. Which movement is impaired?
why_correct: Foot drop refers to weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, causing difficulty clearing the foot during walking.
why_wrong: A. Foot drop involves dorsiflexion rather than isolated toe flexion. C. Hip extension is unrelated to the characteristic gait abnormality. D. Plantarflexion weakness is a different motor deficit. E. Knee flexion is not the defining movement affected.
pearl: Foot drop, or weak ankle dorsiflexion, produces a high-stepping gait; common causes include common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular neck and L5 radiculopathy.
thinking: Cannot lift the front of the foot ↓ Toes catch while walking ↓ Tibialis anterior weakness ↓ Ankle dorsiflexion
exam_trap: D, Ankle plantarflexion — the opposite ankle movement and easily confused; plantarflexion weakness affects push-off, not lifting the forefoot.
takeaway: Foot drop means weak ankle dorsiflexion: think common peroneal nerve or L5.

stem: Which finding is most characteristic of a lower motor neurone lesion?
correct_answer: D. Muscle wasting with reduced reflexes
why_correct: Lower motor neurone lesions cause weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations and reduced or absent reflexes.
why_wrong: A. An extensor plantar response indicates an upper motor neurone lesion. B. Spasticity is an upper motor neurone sign. C. Increased tone and brisk reflexes are upper motor neurone features. E. Clonus is associated with hyperreflexia and upper motor neurone lesions.
pearl: LMN lesions give weakness, wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone and reduced or absent reflexes; UMN lesions give spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus and extensor plantars.
thinking: Lower motor neurone damaged ↓ Muscle loses its nerve supply ↓ Wasting and a broken reflex arc ↓ Muscle wasting with reduced reflexes
exam_trap: C, Increased tone and brisk reflexes — often mixed up, but these are upper motor neurone signs; LMN lesions reduce tone and reflexes.
takeaway: LMN: wasting, fasciculation, low tone, reduced reflexes; UMN: the opposite.

stem: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome develops increasing difficulty breathing and a weak cough. What complication is the greatest immediate concern?
why_correct: Guillain–Barré syndrome can progress to respiratory muscle paralysis, making respiratory function an immediate priority.
why_wrong: A. Thyrotoxicosis does not explain progressive respiratory muscle weakness with a weak cough. B. Asthma causes wheeze and bronchospasm and does not explain progressive weakness with a weak cough. C. Hyperventilation should not be assumed; increasing breathlessness with a weak cough in Guillain–Barré syndrome indicates respiratory muscle weakness. D. Functional dyspnoea should not be assumed in Guillain–Barré syndrome, where breathlessness and a weak cough signal impending respiratory failure.
pearl: In Guillain–Barré syndrome, monitor forced vital capacity regularly; oxygen saturation falls late, and a falling FVC or weak cough needs urgent critical care review.
thinking: Guillain–Barré syndrome ↓ Ascending weakness can reach respiratory muscles ↓ Increasing breathlessness with a weak cough ↓ Neuromuscular respiratory failure
exam_trap: C, Psychogenic hyperventilation — anxiety is common in acute illness, but a weak cough signals respiratory muscle weakness, and blaming anxiety is dangerous.
takeaway: Breathlessness in Guillain–Barré: measure FVC and escalate early.

stem: A previously well older adult suddenly becomes unable to form new memories, repeatedly asking the same questions, while remaining alert and otherwise neurologically intact. The episode resolves within several hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Transient global amnesia causes sudden temporary anterograde memory impairment with repetitive questioning while other neurological functions are relatively preserved.
why_wrong: A. Delirium causes broader disturbance of attention and awareness. B. A generalised seizure would usually involve impaired consciousness and other seizure features. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically causes sudden severe headache and may cause neurological deterioration. E. Dementia causes persistent rather than transient cognitive impairment.
pearl: Transient global amnesia causes sudden anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning but preserved identity and alertness, resolving within 24 hours; recurrence is uncommon.
thinking: Older adult, sudden onset ↓ Cannot form new memories, repeats questions ↓ Alert and otherwise neurologically intact ↓ Resolves within hours ↓ Transient global amnesia
exam_trap: A, Delirium — acute confusion in an older adult tempts, but delirium impairs attention and awareness, whereas here alertness is preserved and only memory fails.
takeaway: Sudden isolated amnesia with repetitive questions, resolving within a day: transient global amnesia.

stem: An elderly hospital patient becomes acutely confused over one day. Their attention fluctuates and they cannot maintain a conversation. What feature most strongly supports delirium?
correct_answer: D. Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention
why_correct: Delirium is characterised by an acute disturbance in attention and awareness that often fluctuates.
why_wrong: A. Long-term personality change suggests another chronic neurological or psychiatric process. B. Gradual decline over years is more consistent with dementia. C. Isolated stable amnesia does not capture the fluctuating attentional disturbance of delirium. E. Lifelong learning difficulty suggests a developmental condition.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention; screen at-risk older inpatients with a tool such as the 4AT and seek causes like infection, drugs, dehydration, pain, constipation and urinary retention.
thinking: Elderly inpatient ↓ Acute onset over one day ↓ Fluctuating attention, cannot hold a conversation ↓ Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention
exam_trap: B, Gradual memory decline over years — memory problems in older patients suggest dementia, but delirium is acute and fluctuating.
takeaway: Acute onset with fluctuating inattention is the hallmark of delirium.

stem: A 72-year-old develops gradually progressive difficulty remembering recent events, followed by deterioration in other cognitive functions. There is no prominent early movement disorder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Alzheimer's disease typically causes gradually progressive cognitive decline, with memory impairment often prominent early in the illness.
why_wrong: A. Multiple sclerosis causes focal or multifocal neurological dysfunction rather than this typical progressive dementia pattern. B. Huntington disease causes chorea and behavioural/cognitive changes, usually with a family history. C. Parkinson disease is primarily a movement disorder. E. Delirium develops acutely and fluctuates.
pearl: Alzheimer's disease classically begins with recent memory loss, then affects language, visuospatial skills and executive function; early parkinsonism or visual hallucinations suggest Lewy body dementia.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Gradually progressive recent memory loss ↓ Other cognitive domains then decline ↓ No early movement disorder ↓ Alzheimer's disease
exam_trap: E, Delirium — cognitive impairment in an older adult tempts, but delirium is acute and fluctuating, not gradually progressive.
takeaway: Slowly progressive memory loss first, then wider decline: Alzheimer's disease.

stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of a limb. Neurological examination shows findings that are inconsistent with recognised neuroanatomical patterns, and investigations do not demonstrate a structural lesion. What diagnosis may explain the presentation?

options.A: Acute ischaemic stroke in the internal capsule

why_correct: Functional neurological disorder can cause genuine neurological symptoms associated with abnormal nervous-system functioning without an explanatory structural lesion; diagnosis is based on positive clinical features of inconsistency or incongruence.
why_wrong: A. Stroke produces a neurological deficit corresponding to a vascular territory or recognised syndrome. B. Motor neurone disease causes progressive upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction. C. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis produces deficits corresponding to demyelinating lesions, usually visible on MRI. E. A peripheral mononeuropathy follows a recognised nerve-distribution pattern.
pearl: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed on positive signs such as Hoover sign, not simply by excluding disease; explain the diagnosis clearly, as symptoms are genuine, and consider specialist physiotherapy.
thinking: Sudden limb weakness ↓ Signs inconsistent with neuroanatomy ↓ No structural lesion on investigation ↓ Genuine symptoms from altered nervous-system function ↓ Functional neurological disorder
exam_trap: C, Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis — tempting because MS signs vary, but its deficits follow anatomy and usually show lesions on MRI.
takeaway: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis based on internal inconsistency.

stem: A patient develops ipsilateral facial weakness together with weakness and sensory abnormalities affecting the opposite side of the body. Where is the lesion most likely located?
why_correct: Crossed neurological signs involving cranial nerve findings on one side and long-tract body findings on the opposite side suggest a brainstem lesion.
why_wrong: A. A lumbar spinal cord lesion cannot produce ipsilateral cranial nerve findings. C. A peripheral nerve lesion does not produce contralateral body weakness. D. Neuromuscular-junction disorders do not produce crossed neurological deficits. E. A purely cerebellar lesion causes coordination abnormalities rather than this classic crossed pattern.
pearl: Crossed signs, a cranial nerve deficit on one side with limb weakness or sensory loss on the other, localise to the brainstem, where cranial nerve nuclei lie beside long tracts serving the opposite side of the body.
thinking: Ipsilateral facial weakness: cranial nerve ↓ Contralateral body weakness and sensory change: long tracts ↓ Crossed signs ↓ Brainstem
exam_trap: E, Cerebellar hemisphere only — the posterior fossa location tempts, but cerebellar lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia, not crossed weakness and sensory loss.
takeaway: Crossed cranial nerve and body signs localise to the brainstem.

stem: A patient develops sudden severe vertigo, inability to walk and marked limb ataxia. Which diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: Sudden severe vertigo accompanied by inability to walk or marked neurological signs is concerning for a central cause such as cerebellar stroke.
why_wrong: A. BPPV causes brief positional vertigo without persistent severe neurological deficits. B. Tension headache does not cause acute cerebellar signs. C. Peripheral neuropathy develops differently and does not cause sudden severe vertigo. D. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than acute vertigo and ataxia.
pearl: Acute vertigo with inability to walk, limb ataxia or other neurological signs suggests a central cause such as cerebellar stroke; urgent imaging is needed, as swelling can compress the brainstem.
thinking: Sudden severe vertigo ↓ Unable to walk ↓ Marked limb ataxia ↓ Central rather than peripheral cause ↓ Cerebellar stroke
exam_trap: A, Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — the commonest cause of vertigo, but it is brief and positional and does not cause limb ataxia or inability to walk.
takeaway: Vertigo with ataxia or inability to walk is central until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance. Which vascular territory should be considered?
why_correct: Brainstem and posterior-circulation ischaemia can produce symptoms such as diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia.
why_wrong: A. Renal circulation does not cause these neurological symptoms. B. Coronary circulation supplies the heart. C. Middle cerebral artery syndromes more typically affect the lateral cerebral hemisphere. E. Anterior cerebral artery disease predominantly affects medial frontal/parietal regions and the leg.
pearl: Posterior circulation TIA or stroke causes diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo, ataxia and visual field loss; these need the same urgent stroke assessment as anterior circulation events.
thinking: Recurrent transient episodes ↓ Diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance ↓ Brainstem and cerebellar features ↓ Posterior circulation ↓ Vertebrobasilar circulation
exam_trap: C, Middle cerebral artery only — the most familiar stroke territory, but MCA events cause contralateral weakness, sensory loss and aphasia, not diplopia with imbalance.
takeaway: Diplopia, dysarthria and imbalance point to vertebrobasilar ischaemia.

stem: A patient has continuous generalised convulsive activity without returning to consciousness. What emergency should be suspected?
why_correct: Continuous or recurrent seizure activity without recovery of consciousness constitutes status epilepticus and requires urgent treatment.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause continuous generalised convulsive activity. B. Transient global amnesia causes temporary memory impairment rather than convulsions. D. Syncope causes transient loss of consciousness rather than ongoing convulsions. E. Absence seizures are brief and do not produce continuous convulsive activity.
pearl: Treat a convulsive seizure lasting five minutes or more as status epilepticus: give a benzodiazepine first (buccal midazolam, rectal diazepam or IV lorazepam), then escalate if seizures continue.
thinking: Continuous generalised convulsions ↓ No recovery of consciousness ↓ Prolonged seizure activity ↓ Status epilepticus
exam_trap: E, Absence seizure — another seizure type, but absences are brief non-convulsive lapses, never continuous convulsive activity.
takeaway: Continuous convulsions without recovery are status epilepticus: give a benzodiazepine early.

stem: A patient collapses suddenly while exercising, without any warning symptoms, and rapidly regains consciousness. Which cause requires particular consideration?
why_correct: Syncope occurring during exertion or without a prodrome raises concern for a cardiac cause, including arrhythmia or structural heart disease.
why_wrong: A. Orthostatic hypotension is associated with standing and postural change. C. Migraine does not typically cause abrupt exertional syncope. D. Tension headache does not cause syncope. E. Vasovagal syncope usually has a prodrome.
pearl: Syncope during exertion, or without any prodrome, is a red flag for cardiac causes such as arrhythmia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or aortic stenosis; arrange an ECG and urgent specialist assessment.
thinking: Collapse during exercise ↓ No warning symptoms ↓ Rapid recovery, so syncope ↓ Exertional and without prodrome suggests arrhythmia or outflow obstruction ↓ Cardiac syncope
exam_trap: E, Vasovagal syncope — the commonest cause of fainting, but it has a prodrome and is not typically triggered during exertion.
takeaway: Exertional syncope, or syncope without warning, is cardiac until proven otherwise.

stem: An older patient repeatedly becomes dizzy or faints when turning their head or when a tight collar is worn. What condition may explain this?

options.E: Temporal lobe epilepsy with drop attacks

why_correct: Stimulation of the carotid sinus can trigger an exaggerated reflex response in susceptible patients, causing bradycardia and/or hypotension.
why_wrong: B. Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo causes brief vertigo with head position changes but not fainting or symptoms triggered by a tight collar. C. Cranial diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia, not reproducible fainting triggered by neck pressure. D. Migraine causes headache rather than reproducible syncope from neck stimulation. E. Temporal lobe epilepsy is not typically triggered by head turning or a tight collar.
pearl: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity causes syncope in older adults with head turning or neck pressure; carotid sinus massage under monitoring can confirm it, and pacing helps the cardioinhibitory type.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Dizziness or fainting on head turning ↓ Also with a tight collar ↓ Carotid sinus stimulation causes bradycardia or hypotension ↓ Carotid sinus hypersensitivity
exam_trap: B, Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo — triggered by head movement, but it causes brief spinning vertigo, not fainting, and a tight collar does not provoke it.
takeaway: Syncope with head turning or a tight collar in an older adult: carotid sinus hypersensitivity.

stem: A young person has unexplained exertional syncope and a family history of sudden cardiac death. Which inherited electrical disorder should be considered?
why_correct: Long QT syndrome is an inherited cardiac electrical disorder that can predispose to malignant ventricular arrhythmias and syncope.
why_wrong: A. Essential hypertension does not usually cause sudden exertional syncope. C. Pericarditis causes pleuritic chest pain rather than inherited arrhythmic syncope. D. Stable angina causes exertional chest discomfort rather than typically unexplained syncope. E. Mitral stenosis has a different structural and clinical presentation.
pearl: In a young person with exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death, check the ECG for a prolonged QTc, pre-excitation, Brugada pattern or hypertrophy, and refer urgently to cardiology.
thinking: Young person ↓ Unexplained exertional syncope ↓ Family history of sudden cardiac death ↓ Inherited arrhythmia risk ↓ Long QT syndrome
exam_trap: E, Mitral stenosis — a valve lesion could cause collapse, but it is not an inherited electrical disorder and does not fit a family history of sudden death.
takeaway: Exertional syncope with family sudden death: get an ECG and consider long QT syndrome.

stem: An ECG shows progressive prolongation of the PR interval followed by a dropped QRS complex. What is the diagnosis?
correct_answer: B. Second-degree AV block Mobitz I
why_correct: Mobitz I, or Wenckebach phenomenon, is characterised by progressive PR prolongation followed by a non-conducted P wave.
why_wrong: A. Sinus arrest involves failure of sinus node activity rather than progressive AV conduction delay. C. Complete heart block causes complete AV dissociation. D. Mobitz II has sudden dropped beats without progressive PR prolongation. E. First-degree AV block has a prolonged but constant PR interval with no dropped beats.
pearl: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) is usually benign and arises in the AV node, whereas Mobitz II and complete heart block carry a higher risk of asystole and often need pacing.
thinking: PR interval lengthens beat by beat ↓ Then a P wave fails to conduct ↓ The cycle repeats ↓ Wenckebach pattern ↓ Second-degree AV block Mobitz I
exam_trap: D, Mobitz II — also has dropped beats, but its PR interval stays constant before the dropped QRS, with no progressive lengthening.
takeaway: Progressive PR lengthening then a dropped beat is Mobitz I (Wenckebach).

stem: An ECG shows intermittent dropped QRS complexes without progressive prolongation of the PR interval. What is the diagnosis?
correct_answer: E. Second-degree AV block Mobitz II
why_correct: Mobitz II causes intermittent failure of AV conduction without the preceding progressive PR prolongation seen in Mobitz I.
why_wrong: A. Third-degree AV block causes complete AV dissociation. B. First-degree block has no dropped beats. C. Sinus tachycardia is a sinus rhythm with an increased rate. D. Mobitz I (Wenckebach) has progressive PR prolongation before the dropped beat.
pearl: Mobitz II signals conduction disease below the AV node and can progress suddenly to complete heart block, so it usually warrants referral for permanent pacing.
thinking: Intermittent dropped QRS complexes ↓ PR interval constant before the drop ↓ No Wenckebach progression ↓ Second-degree AV block Mobitz II
exam_trap: D, Mobitz I — also second-degree block with dropped beats, but Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation before each dropped beat.
takeaway: Dropped beats with a fixed PR interval are Mobitz II; consider pacing.

stem: A patient with previous myocardial infarction develops a rapid broad-complex tachycardia with hypotension. What rhythm should be presumed until proven otherwise?
why_correct: A broad-complex tachycardia, particularly in a patient with structural heart disease, should be treated as ventricular tachycardia unless there is strong evidence otherwise.
why_wrong: A. Sinus bradycardia is a slow sinus rhythm. B. Sinus tachycardia is usually narrow-complex unless there is an existing conduction abnormality. C. First-degree AV block causes PR prolongation rather than a rapid broad-complex rhythm. E. Atrial fibrillation is classically irregularly irregular.
pearl: Treat a broad-complex tachycardia as VT, especially after MI; with adverse features such as shock, Resuscitation Council UK guidance advises synchronised DC cardioversion.
thinking: Previous myocardial infarction leaves scar ↓ Rapid broad-complex tachycardia ↓ Hypotension ↓ Presume ventricular origin ↓ Ventricular tachycardia
exam_trap: E, Atrial fibrillation — AF with bundle branch block can look broad, but presuming it in a hypotensive patient after MI risks missing VT.
takeaway: Broad-complex tachycardia after MI is VT until proven otherwise.

stem: An ECG shows a regular rhythm with normal P waves before every QRS complex, but the heart rate is 48 beats per minute. What is the rhythm?
why_correct: Sinus bradycardia is a sinus rhythm with a rate below 60 beats per minute.
why_wrong: B. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular and lacks organised sinus P waves. C. Atrial flutter produces characteristic flutter waves. D. Complete heart block produces AV dissociation. E. Ventricular tachycardia is a rapid ventricular rhythm, usually broad-complex.
pearl: Sinus bradycardia is common in athletes and during sleep; consider beta-blockers, hypothyroidism, hypothermia and raised intracranial pressure, and treat only if symptomatic or with adverse features.
thinking: Regular rhythm ↓ Normal P wave before every QRS ↓ Sinus origin ↓ Rate below 60 ↓ Sinus bradycardia
exam_trap: D, Complete heart block — the slow rate tempts, but heart block shows P waves dissociated from QRS complexes, not a P wave before every QRS.
takeaway: A normal P wave before every QRS at a rate below 60 is sinus bradycardia.

stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of haemolytic anaemia and a family history of similar illness. Which inherited condition causes red cells to become spherical and prone to haemolysis?
why_correct: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited red-cell membrane disorder causing spherical erythrocytes and haemolytic anaemia.
why_wrong: A. von Willebrand disease causes impaired primary haemostasis. B. Haemophilia A is a coagulation-factor deficiency. C. Thalassaemia involves impaired globin-chain production. E. Sickle cell disease causes abnormal haemoglobin and sickling.
pearl: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant and causes haemolysis, jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones; spherocytes on the film with a negative direct antiglobulin test support it.
thinking: Recurrent haemolytic anaemia ↓ Family history ↓ Inherited red-cell membrane defect ↓ Spherical red cells ↓ Hereditary spherocytosis
exam_trap: E, Sickle cell disease — inherited and haemolytic, but the defect is an abnormal haemoglobin causing sickled cells, not spherical cells.
takeaway: Inherited haemolysis with spherical red cells is hereditary spherocytosis.

stem: A boy has recurrent haemarthroses and prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Which clotting-factor deficiency is most likely?
why_correct: Haemophilia A is caused by factor VIII deficiency and classically causes deep bleeding such as haemarthroses.
why_wrong: B. Factor XIII deficiency has a different presentation and routine clotting tests may be normal. C. Factor IX deficiency causes haemophilia B. D. Factor X deficiency is a different, rare inherited bleeding disorder. E. Factor VII deficiency primarily affects the extrinsic pathway.
pearl: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked and mainly affect males; both prolong the APTT with a normal PT and platelet count, and only factor assays separate factor VIII from factor IX deficiency.
thinking: Boy, fitting X-linked inheritance ↓ Recurrent haemarthroses, a deep bleeding pattern ↓ Prolonged APTT ↓ Haemophilia, most commonly type A ↓ Factor VIII
exam_trap: C, Factor IX — also X-linked with haemarthroses and a prolonged APTT, but haemophilia B is less common, so factor VIII deficiency is the most likely.
takeaway: Boy with haemarthroses and a prolonged APTT: haemophilia A, factor VIII.

stem: A patient has an inherited bleeding disorder caused by factor IX deficiency. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Haemophilia B is caused by factor IX deficiency.
why_wrong: A. DIC causes widespread coagulation activation and consumption of clotting factors and platelets. C. Immune thrombocytopenia causes isolated thrombocytopenia. D. von Willebrand disease involves von Willebrand factor deficiency or dysfunction. E. Haemophilia A is caused by factor VIII deficiency.
pearl: Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) is factor IX deficiency and haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency; both are X-linked and cause deep bleeding into joints and muscles.
thinking: Inherited bleeding disorder ↓ Factor IX is deficient ↓ Clinically identical to haemophilia A but a different factor ↓ Haemophilia B
exam_trap: E, Haemophilia A — the more familiar haemophilia, but it is factor VIII deficiency; factor IX deficiency is haemophilia B.
takeaway: Factor IX deficiency is haemophilia B; factor VIII deficiency is haemophilia A.

stem: A young adult presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and reports drenching night sweats. Which malignancy should be considered?
why_correct: Hodgkin lymphoma commonly presents in younger adults with painless lymphadenopathy and may cause systemic symptoms such as night sweats.
why_wrong: A. Multiple myeloma predominantly affects older adults and causes bone, renal and calcium abnormalities. B. Iron deficiency causes anaemia rather than persistent lymphadenopathy. C. Immune thrombocytopenia causes thrombocytopenia rather than persistent lymphadenopathy. D. Haemophilia causes bleeding.
pearl: Hodgkin lymphoma often affects young adults; B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss) and alcohol-induced node pain are classic clues, and Reed–Sternberg cells on biopsy confirm it.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Painless cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ Drenching night sweats, a B symptom ↓ Lymphoma typical of this age group ↓ Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: A, Multiple myeloma — a haematological malignancy, but it affects older adults with bone pain, renal impairment and hypercalcaemia, not painless nodes.
takeaway: Young adult with painless nodes and B symptoms: think Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: An older adult develops progressively enlarging, painless lymph nodes in several non-contiguous regions. What broad diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present with painless lymphadenopathy involving multiple lymph-node regions.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolytic anaemia. B. Iron deficiency causes anaemia. D. G6PD deficiency causes episodic haemolysis. E. Haemophilia causes abnormal bleeding.
pearl: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is commoner in older adults and often involves multiple non-contiguous node groups and extranodal sites; diagnosis needs excision or core biopsy, not fine-needle aspiration alone.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Progressively enlarging painless nodes ↓ Several non-contiguous regions ↓ Non-Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: B, Iron-deficiency anaemia — anaemia often accompanies malignancy, but iron deficiency itself does not cause enlarging lymph nodes.
takeaway: Painless enlarging nodes in several non-contiguous regions in an older adult: non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: A patient has a painless cervical lymph node that has progressively enlarged over several weeks. What feature makes malignancy particularly concerning?

options.A: A small mobile node that is shrinking
options.B: Recent mild sore throat that has resolved
options.D: Generalised itch after using a new soap

why_correct: Persistent, progressive, unexplained lymphadenopathy warrants assessment for malignancy among other causes.
why_wrong: A. A shrinking node is less concerning than progressive enlargement. B. A resolving sore throat can cause reactive lymphadenopathy. C. Tenderness may occur with an acute inflammatory process. D. Local skin irritation does not explain progressive lymph-node enlargement.
pearl: Unexplained lymphadenopathy that persists or keeps enlarging, especially if painless, hard or fixed, or with night sweats or weight loss, warrants urgent assessment for malignancy.
thinking: Painless cervical node ↓ Progressively enlarging over weeks ↓ Not explained by recent infection ↓ Malignancy concern ↓ Persistent progressive enlargement
exam_trap: B, Recent sore throat that has resolved — this explains reactive nodes, which settle; it is persistent growth over weeks that raises concern.
takeaway: A painless node that keeps growing needs assessment for malignancy.

stem: A patient has persistent unexplained thrombocytosis and no evidence of a reactive cause. Which myeloproliferative neoplasm should be considered?
why_correct: Essential thrombocythaemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by persistent elevated platelet production.
why_wrong: A. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causes a low platelet count. C. Haemophilia A causes a clotting-factor deficiency. D. Aplastic anaemia causes reduced production of blood-cell lines. E. Iron deficiency can sometimes cause reactive thrombocytosis but does not itself constitute essential thrombocythaemia.
pearl: Essential thrombocythaemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm often driven by JAK2, CALR or MPL mutations; it risks both thrombosis and bleeding, so exclude reactive causes such as iron deficiency or infection first.
thinking: Persistently raised platelets ↓ Reactive causes excluded ↓ Clonal marrow overproduction ↓ Myeloproliferative neoplasm ↓ Essential thrombocythaemia
exam_trap: E, Iron-deficiency anaemia — a recognised cause of a raised platelet count, but that is reactive thrombocytosis, which the stem has excluded.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained thrombocytosis with no reactive cause suggests essential thrombocythaemia.

stem: Which clinical situation is a recognised trigger for disseminated intravascular coagulation?
why_correct: Severe infection, particularly sepsis, can trigger widespread activation of coagulation and DIC.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause DIC. C. Osteoarthritis does not typically cause DIC. D. Allergic rhinitis does not cause DIC. E. Myopia does not cause systemic coagulation activation.
pearl: DIC is always secondary to a trigger such as sepsis, trauma, malignancy or obstetric complications; expect low platelets, prolonged clotting times, low fibrinogen and raised D-dimer. Treat the cause.
thinking: DIC needs a systemic trigger ↓ Widespread activation of coagulation ↓ Sepsis is a leading cause ↓ Severe sepsis
exam_trap: C, Stable osteoarthritis — a chronic disease, but it causes no systemic coagulation activation; DIC needs an acute systemic insult.
takeaway: DIC always has a trigger: sepsis, trauma, malignancy or an obstetric emergency.

stem: A patient develops wheeze, allergic symptoms and a raised eosinophil count. Which broad category of condition commonly causes eosinophilia?
why_correct: Eosinophilia is commonly associated with allergic/atopic disease and can also occur with parasitic infection and some haematological disorders.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency does not characteristically cause eosinophilia. B. Osteoarthritis does not cause eosinophilia. D. Dehydration may concentrate blood measurements but does not specifically cause eosinophilia. E. Acute blood loss does not typically produce eosinophilia.
pearl: Common causes of eosinophilia include allergy and atopy (asthma, eczema, hay fever), parasitic infection and drug reactions; in a returning traveller, consider helminth infection.
thinking: Wheeze ↓ Allergic symptoms ↓ Raised eosinophil count ↓ Atopic, allergic process ↓ Allergic disease
exam_trap: E, Acute blood loss — it does change the blood count, but it causes anaemia and sometimes neutrophilia, not eosinophilia.
takeaway: Eosinophilia: think allergy first, then parasites and drugs.

stem: A patient receiving cytotoxic chemotherapy develops a markedly reduced neutrophil count. What is the term for this abnormality?
why_correct: Neutropenia means a reduced circulating neutrophil count and is a common consequence of some cytotoxic chemotherapy.
why_wrong: A. Neutrophilia is an increased neutrophil count. B. Polycythaemia involves increased red-cell mass. D. Lymphocytosis is an increased lymphocyte count. E. Thrombocytosis is an increased platelet count.
pearl: Neutropenic sepsis is an emergency in patients on chemotherapy: fever or feeling unwell needs urgent assessment and empirical IV antibiotics within an hour, without waiting for the count.
thinking: Cytotoxic chemotherapy ↓ Bone marrow suppression ↓ Markedly reduced neutrophil count ↓ Neutropenia
exam_trap: D, Lymphocytosis — another white-cell term, but it describes a raised lymphocyte count; a low neutrophil count is neutropenia.
takeaway: Low neutrophils after chemotherapy is neutropenia; fever then means neutropenic sepsis.

stem: A patient has anaemia and a markedly increased reticulocyte count. What does this generally indicate?

options.A: Reduced erythropoietin from chronic kidney disease
options.C: Increased marrow output due to red-cell loss or destruction
options.D: Vitamin B12 deficiency with megaloblastic change

correct_answer: C. Increased marrow output due to red-cell loss or destruction
why_correct: Reticulocytosis generally indicates that the bone marrow is responding appropriately to increased red-cell loss or destruction, such as haemolysis or recent blood loss.
why_wrong: A. Reduced erythropoietin in chronic kidney disease lowers red-cell production and causes a low reticulocyte count. B. Marrow infiltration impairs production and usually produces an inadequate reticulocyte response. D. B12 deficiency causes ineffective erythropoiesis with a low rather than markedly increased reticulocyte count. E. Suppressed erythropoiesis produces a low rather than high reticulocyte response.
pearl: The reticulocyte count shows whether the marrow is responding: high in haemolysis or bleeding, low in production failure such as haematinic deficiency, CKD or marrow infiltration.
thinking: Anaemia ↓ Markedly raised reticulocytes ↓ Marrow is responding appropriately ↓ Red cells are being lost or destroyed ↓ Increased marrow output due to loss or destruction
exam_trap: D, B12 deficiency with megaloblastic change — a common anaemia, but ineffective erythropoiesis gives a low, not raised, reticulocyte count.
takeaway: High reticulocytes in anaemia point to haemolysis or bleeding, not underproduction.

stem: A 19-year-old develops fever, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy and marked fatigue. Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Infectious mononucleosis is classically caused by Epstein–Barr virus and commonly causes fever, pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy and prolonged fatigue.
why_wrong: A. Influenza usually causes an acute influenza-like illness with prominent systemic symptoms. B. Hepatitis A primarily causes an acute hepatitis syndrome. C. Pneumococcal infection does not typically cause this mononucleosis syndrome. E. Varicella-zoster virus causes chickenpox or shingles rather than this typical presentation.
pearl: Avoid amoxicillin in suspected glandular fever, as it commonly causes a rash, and advise avoiding contact sports for several weeks because of the risk of splenic rupture.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Fever and sore throat ↓ Cervical lymphadenopathy ↓ Marked fatigue ↓ Infectious mononucleosis from Epstein–Barr virus
exam_trap: A, Influenza A — fever and fatigue fit, but influenza is an abrupt systemic illness without the prominent cervical lymphadenopathy of glandular fever.
takeaway: Young adult with sore throat, nodes and marked fatigue: think EBV glandular fever.

stem: A patient develops painful grouped vesicles and shallow ulcers around the genital area. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Genital herpes typically causes painful grouped vesicles that rupture to form painful ulcers.
why_wrong: A. Gonorrhoea commonly causes purulent urethral or cervical discharge. C. Primary syphilis typically causes a painless chancre. D. Chlamydia commonly causes urethritis or cervicitis and does not typically produce grouped vesicles. E. HPV commonly causes genital warts.
pearl: Genital herpes causes painful vesicles and ulcers, whereas a painless ulcer suggests primary syphilis; swab the lesion for HSV PCR and offer full sexual health screening.
thinking: Genital lesions ↓ Painful ↓ Grouped vesicles breaking down into shallow ulcers ↓ Herpes simplex virus
exam_trap: C, Treponema pallidum — a classic cause of genital ulcers, but the primary chancre is typically single and painless, not painful grouped vesicles.
takeaway: Painful grouped genital vesicles and ulcers: herpes simplex; painless ulcer: syphilis.

stem: A patient with untreated syphilis develops a widespread rash involving the palms and soles. What stage is most consistent with this presentation?
why_correct: Secondary syphilis can cause a widespread rash that characteristically includes the palms and soles.
why_wrong: B. Latent syphilis has no clinical manifestations. C. Primary syphilis is characterised by a chancre. D. Genital herpes causes painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions. E. Tertiary syphilis occurs later and can cause neurological, cardiovascular and gummatous disease.
pearl: Secondary syphilis is systemic: rash including the palms and soles, lymphadenopathy, mucous patches and condylomata lata. Serology confirms it, and benzathine penicillin is first-line treatment.
thinking: Untreated syphilis ↓ Primary chancre stage has passed ↓ Widespread rash involving palms and soles ↓ Haematogenous spread ↓ Secondary syphilis
exam_trap: E, Tertiary syphilis — later and more severe, but it causes gummas and neurological or cardiovascular disease, not a palm-and-sole rash.
takeaway: A rash on the palms and soles in syphilis means the secondary stage.

stem: A young adult has dysuria and urethral discharge, but the discharge is less prominent than typically seen with gonorrhoea. Which sexually transmitted infection is a common cause?
why_correct: Chlamydia is a common cause of urethritis and may produce mild or absent symptoms, particularly compared with gonorrhoea.
why_wrong: A. Herpes causes painful vesicular or ulcerative lesions. B. HPV causes genital warts or asymptomatic infection. C. Syphilis classically causes a painless chancre initially. D. Hepatitis C primarily affects the liver.
pearl: Chlamydia is the most commonly diagnosed bacterial STI in the UK and is often asymptomatic; NAAT testing confirms it, and partner notification is essential.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Dysuria and urethral discharge ↓ Discharge milder than in gonorrhoea ↓ Common, often mild urethritis ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis
exam_trap: A, Herpes simplex virus — it can cause dysuria, but it presents with painful vesicles or ulcers rather than urethral discharge.
takeaway: Mild urethritis with scant discharge in a young adult: think chlamydia and test by NAAT.

stem: Which route is particularly important in the transmission of hepatitis C virus?
why_correct: Hepatitis C is primarily transmitted through exposure to infected blood.
why_wrong: A. Casual physical contact does not transmit hepatitis C. B. Food is not a typical transmission route. D. Mosquito transmission is not an established route. E. Hepatitis C is not spread by respiratory droplets.
pearl: Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood, most often via shared injecting equipment; there is no vaccine, but direct-acting antivirals now cure most patients.
thinking: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne virus ↓ Main UK risk is shared injecting equipment ↓ Transmission needs blood exposure ↓ Blood-to-blood exposure
exam_trap: B, Sharing cooked food — food-borne spread fits hepatitis A and E, not hepatitis C, which needs exposure to infected blood.
takeaway: Hepatitis C is blood-borne: think injecting drug use and blood exposure.

stem: A traveller develops acute hepatitis after consuming contaminated food and water. Which virus is classically transmitted by the faecal–oral route?
why_correct: Hepatitis A is classically transmitted by the faecal–oral route, often through contaminated food or water.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis D requires hepatitis B infection and is transmitted through infected blood or body fluids. C. Hepatitis B is mainly transmitted through infected blood and body fluids. D. Hepatitis C is primarily blood-borne. E. HIV is transmitted through infected body fluids, not by the faecal–oral route.
pearl: Hepatitis A and E spread by the faecal–oral route and cause acute hepatitis; hepatitis A does not become chronic, and vaccination is advised for travellers to higher-risk areas.
thinking: Traveller ↓ Contaminated food and water ↓ Faecal–oral transmission ↓ Acute hepatitis ↓ Hepatitis A virus
exam_trap: C, Hepatitis B virus — a common hepatitis in travel advice, but it spreads through blood and body fluids, not food or water.
takeaway: Food- and water-borne hepatitis: think hepatitis A (and E).

stem: A patient develops painful muscle spasms and trismus after a contaminated wound. Which organism causes tetanus?
why_correct: Clostridium tetani produces a neurotoxin that causes muscle rigidity and spasms, classically including trismus.
why_wrong: B. S. pyogenes causes infections including pharyngitis and cellulitis. C. S. aureus causes a wide range of skin and systemic infections. D. C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and colitis. E. C. diphtheriae causes diphtheria.
pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds need an assessment of immunisation status; give a booster as needed and consider human tetanus immunoglobulin for high-risk wounds when immunisation is incomplete or uncertain.
thinking: Contaminated wound ↓ Painful muscle spasms ↓ Trismus (lockjaw) ↓ Toxin-mediated rigidity ↓ Clostridium tetani
exam_trap: D, Clostridium difficile — the same genus, but C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, not spasms after a wound.
takeaway: Trismus and spasms after a dirty wound: tetanus from Clostridium tetani.

stem: A child develops a sore throat with a thick grey-white membrane over the pharynx. Which infection should be suspected?
why_correct: Diphtheria classically causes an adherent grey-white pharyngeal pseudomembrane and can cause serious systemic toxin-mediated complications.
why_wrong: B. Herpes simplex does not typically cause this presentation. C. Scarlet fever causes streptococcal pharyngitis with a characteristic rash. D. Candida causes oral plaques rather than a characteristic pharyngeal pseudomembrane. E. EBV causes exudative pharyngitis but not the classic adherent diphtheritic membrane.
pearl: Diphtheria toxin can cause myocarditis and neuropathy; suspected cases need urgent public health notification, antitoxin and antibiotics. Vaccination has made it rare in the UK.
thinking: Child with sore throat ↓ Thick grey-white membrane over the pharynx ↓ Adherent pseudomembrane ↓ Diphtheria
exam_trap: E, Infectious mononucleosis — also causes exudative tonsillitis, but its exudate is not the thick, adherent grey pseudomembrane of diphtheria.
takeaway: Grey adherent pharyngeal membrane: think diphtheria and check vaccination status.

stem: A patient has had a persistent cough for several weeks, weight loss and night sweats. Which infection should be considered?
why_correct: Pulmonary tuberculosis can present with a persistent cough, constitutional symptoms, weight loss and night sweats.
why_wrong: A. Influenza usually presents acutely. C. Cystitis causes urinary rather than respiratory symptoms. D. Infectious mononucleosis causes an acute febrile illness with pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy. E. Sinusitis does not typically cause this prolonged systemic illness.
pearl: A persistent cough with weight loss, night sweats or haemoptysis needs a chest X-ray and sputum testing for TB; ask about country of birth, travel, contacts and immunosuppression.
thinking: Cough for several weeks ↓ Weight loss ↓ Night sweats ↓ Chronic infection with constitutional symptoms ↓ Tuberculosis
exam_trap: A, Influenza — causes cough and fever, but it is acute and self-limiting, not weeks of cough with weight loss.
takeaway: Weeks of cough with weight loss and night sweats: think TB.

stem: How is pulmonary tuberculosis most commonly transmitted?
why_correct: Pulmonary TB is transmitted through inhalation of airborne particles containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
why_wrong: A. TB is not transmitted by mosquitoes. B. Contaminated water is not the usual route of pulmonary TB transmission. D. Food is not the usual route of pulmonary TB transmission. E. Faecal–oral transmission is associated with infections such as hepatitis A.
pearl: Pulmonary TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei from people with active pulmonary disease; infectious inpatients need respiratory isolation, and close contacts are traced and screened.
thinking: Pulmonary TB ↓ Coughing releases infectious particles ↓ Inhaled by close contacts ↓ Airborne particles
exam_trap: D, Contaminated food — unpasteurised milk can transmit bovine TB, but pulmonary TB in people spreads by inhalation, not food.
takeaway: Pulmonary TB spreads through the air: isolate infectious patients and trace contacts.

stem: A person has evidence of previous exposure to tuberculosis but has no symptoms and no evidence of active disease. What is this state called?
why_correct: Latent TB infection describes infection with M. tuberculosis without clinical evidence of active disease.
why_wrong: B. Miliary TB is disseminated active TB. C. Active pulmonary TB causes clinical disease. D. Tuberculous meningitis is active infection involving the central nervous system. E. Multidrug resistance describes antimicrobial resistance, not simply asymptomatic infection.
pearl: Latent TB is asymptomatic and not infectious; it is detected by a tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, and treatment reduces the risk of later reactivation.
thinking: Evidence of previous TB exposure ↓ No symptoms ↓ No active disease ↓ Infected but contained ↓ Latent tuberculosis infection
exam_trap: C, Active pulmonary tuberculosis — evidence of exposure tempts, but active disease needs clinical or radiological features, which are absent here.
takeaway: Infected, asymptomatic and not infectious: latent TB.

stem: A patient with tuberculosis develops fever, weight loss and widespread abnormalities involving several organs. What term describes disseminated tuberculosis?
why_correct: Miliary TB occurs when tuberculosis disseminates through the bloodstream to multiple organs.
why_wrong: A. Bronchitis is an airway infection and does not describe disseminated TB. B. Latent TB has no active clinical disease. D. Viral pneumonia does not describe disseminated mycobacterial infection. E. Pulmonary embolism is a vascular condition rather than an infection.
pearl: Miliary TB results from bloodstream spread, giving numerous tiny nodules on chest X-ray; it is commoner in the immunosuppressed and can involve the meninges, liver and bone marrow.
thinking: Known tuberculosis ↓ Fever and weight loss ↓ Several organs involved ↓ Bloodstream dissemination ↓ Miliary tuberculosis
exam_trap: B, Latent tuberculosis — also a TB term, but latent infection is asymptomatic; multi-organ illness is active disseminated TB.
takeaway: Disseminated, bloodstream-spread TB is miliary TB.

stem: A previously healthy adult develops severe pneumonia, diarrhoea and confusion after staying in a hotel with a poorly maintained water system. Which infection should be considered?
why_correct: Legionella infection can cause severe pneumonia with systemic features including diarrhoea and confusion and is associated with contaminated water systems.
why_wrong: B. Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia, usually milder, and spreads person to person rather than via water systems. C. Influenza commonly causes fever, myalgia and respiratory symptoms but this exposure pattern is less characteristic. D. Croup is an acute upper-airway illness in children. E. TB generally has a more prolonged course.
pearl: Legionella comes from contaminated water systems such as those in hotels, cooling towers and spas; a urinary antigen test aids diagnosis, and hyponatraemia and deranged LFTs are classic clues.
thinking: Recent hotel stay ↓ Poorly maintained water system ↓ Severe pneumonia with diarrhoea and confusion ↓ Legionnaires' disease
exam_trap: B, Mycoplasma pneumoniae — another atypical pneumonia, but it is usually milder, spreads person to person and is not linked to water systems.
takeaway: Severe pneumonia with GI and neurological features after a hotel stay: Legionella.

stem: An older adult develops fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. Which organism is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia?
why_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
why_wrong: B. T. pallidum causes syphilis. C. C. tetani causes tetanus. D. Streptococcus agalactiae (group B streptococcus) mainly causes neonatal and peripartum infection, not common community-acquired pneumonia. E. HPV causes papillomavirus infection.
pearl: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia; assess severity with CRB-65 in the community or CURB-65 in hospital to guide management.
thinking: Fever and productive cough ↓ Pleuritic chest pain ↓ Community-acquired pneumonia ↓ Commonest bacterial cause ↓ Streptococcus pneumoniae
exam_trap: D, Streptococcus agalactiae — a streptococcus, so it tempts, but group B streptococcus mainly causes neonatal and peripartum infection.
takeaway: Typical community-acquired pneumonia: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: A patient develops an expanding red rash after a recent tick bite while walking in woodland. The rash is not particularly painful or itchy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Erythema migrans is an expanding skin lesion that can occur following infection with Borrelia transmitted by ticks.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria produces transient raised wheals. B. Cellulitis is typically painful, warm and tender. D. Herpes zoster causes painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. E. Impetigo produces superficial infected lesions, often with crusting.
pearl: Erythema migrans after a tick bite is diagnostic of Lyme disease; NICE advises treating it clinically without waiting for serology, which is often negative early on.
thinking: Recent tick bite in woodland ↓ Expanding red rash ↓ Not particularly painful or itchy ↓ Erythema migrans ↓ Lyme disease
exam_trap: B, Cellulitis — spreading redness tempts, but cellulitis is painful, hot and tender, unlike erythema migrans.
takeaway: An expanding painless rash after a tick bite is erythema migrans: treat as Lyme disease.

stem: A patient previously treated for a tick-borne illness develops facial weakness. Which infection can cause a facial nerve palsy?
why_correct: Lyme disease can cause neurological manifestations including cranial nerve palsies, particularly facial nerve palsy.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis A primarily causes acute hepatitis. C. Influenza is not a typical cause of this neurological manifestation. D. Candidiasis does not characteristically cause facial nerve palsy. E. Scarlet fever does not characteristically cause facial nerve palsy.
pearl: Lyme disease can cause facial nerve palsy, sometimes bilateral; ask about tick exposure in any patient with facial palsy, especially after time in woodland or heathland.
thinking: Previous tick-borne illness ↓ New facial weakness ↓ Neurological spread of Borrelia ↓ Cranial nerve palsy ↓ Lyme disease
exam_trap: C, Influenza — a viral illness can precede facial palsy, but influenza is not a typical cause, and the tick history points to Lyme disease.
takeaway: Facial palsy after a tick-borne illness: think Lyme neuroborreliosis.

stem: A traveller returns from sub-Saharan Africa with fever, confusion and severe systemic illness. Which malaria species is particularly associated with severe disease?
why_correct: P. falciparum is the species most strongly associated with severe and potentially life-threatening malaria.
why_wrong: B. P. knowlesi can cause severe malaria, but the classic PLAB 1 association with severe malaria is P. falciparum. C. P. ovale is generally less severe. D. P. malariae usually causes less severe disease. E. P. vivax can cause significant illness but is less strongly associated with severe disease.
pearl: Fever in a traveller returning from a malaria area is malaria until proven otherwise; P. falciparum causes most severe and fatal cases, so urgent blood films are essential.
thinking: Returned from sub-Saharan Africa ↓ Fever ↓ Confusion and severe systemic illness ↓ Severe malaria ↓ Plasmodium falciparum
exam_trap: E, Plasmodium vivax — a common species that can cause significant illness, but severe and cerebral malaria are most strongly linked to falciparum.
takeaway: Severe malaria after sub-Saharan Africa is falciparum until proven otherwise.

stem: A traveller develops fever followed by abnormal sensations around a previous animal bite and then difficulty swallowing and fear of water. Which infection is most likely?
why_correct: Rabies can cause encephalitis with characteristic hydrophobia and neurological symptoms after exposure to an infected animal.
why_wrong: B. Tetanus causes rigidity and muscle spasms but not typical hydrophobia. C. Malaria causes febrile illness rather than this progressive encephalitic syndrome. D. Lyme disease has different neurological manifestations and exposure history. E. Dengue typically causes an acute febrile illness with systemic symptoms.
pearl: Rabies has a variable incubation, often begins with paraesthesia at the bite site, then progresses to encephalitis with hydrophobia; once symptoms appear it is almost always fatal.
thinking: Previous animal bite while travelling ↓ Fever, then abnormal sensation at the bite site ↓ Difficulty swallowing and fear of water ↓ Encephalitis ↓ Rabies
exam_trap: B, Tetanus — follows wounds and causes spasms with swallowing difficulty, but not paraesthesia at the bite site or hydrophobia.
takeaway: Bite-site paraesthesia followed by hydrophobia means rabies.

stem: A person is bitten by an animal in a region where rabies is endemic. What should they do?

options.A: Apply topical steroid cream and observe
options.B: Wash the wound and seek care if symptoms develop
options.D: Seek urgent assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
options.E: Arrange rabies vaccination at a routine travel clinic visit

correct_answer: D. Seek urgent assessment for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
why_correct: Rabies is almost invariably fatal once clinical disease develops, so potentially exposed people require urgent assessment for appropriate post-exposure measures.
why_wrong: A. Topical steroid treatment does not provide rabies prophylaxis. B. Wound washing is important, but waiting for symptoms is unsafe because clinical rabies is almost always fatal. C. Rehydration does not prevent rabies. E. Post-exposure prophylaxis is time-critical and must not wait for a routine appointment.
pearl: After a possible rabies exposure, wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water at once, then seek urgent risk assessment; post-exposure prophylaxis may include vaccine and immunoglobulin.
thinking: Animal bite ↓ Rabies-endemic region ↓ Clinical rabies is almost always fatal ↓ Prophylaxis must start before symptoms ↓ Urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis
exam_trap: B, Wash the wound and seek care if symptoms develop — washing is right, but waiting for symptoms is fatal; prophylaxis must be given before disease appears.
takeaway: Possible rabies exposure: wash the wound and seek urgent PEP assessment; never wait for symptoms.

stem: A child develops a small papule after a cat scratch followed by regional lymph-node enlargement. Which organism is the typical cause?
why_correct: Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae and typically causes regional lymphadenopathy following a cat scratch.
why_wrong: A. T. pallidum causes syphilis. B. P. falciparum causes malaria. D. C. tetani causes tetanus. E. Borrelia causes Lyme disease.
pearl: Cat-scratch disease is usually a self-limiting regional lymphadenopathy after a cat scratch or bite; it is a recognised cause of persistent nodes in children, and immunocompromised patients may need antibiotics.
thinking: Child ↓ Cat scratch ↓ Papule at the inoculation site ↓ Regional lymphadenopathy ↓ Bartonella henselae
exam_trap: E, Borrelia burgdorferi — another zoonosis with a skin lesion, but it is tick-borne and causes erythema migrans, not cat-scratch lymphadenopathy.
takeaway: Regional lymphadenopathy after a cat scratch: Bartonella henselae.

stem: A pregnant woman is concerned after exposure to cat faeces. Which infection is particularly relevant because primary infection during pregnancy can affect the fetus?
why_correct: Toxoplasma gondii infection acquired during pregnancy can cause congenital toxoplasmosis.
why_wrong: B. Tetanus is not specifically associated with cat-faeces exposure. C. Scarlet fever is caused by group A Streptococcus. D. Influenza is respiratory. E. Gonorrhoea is sexually transmitted.
pearl: Pregnant women should avoid handling cat litter, wear gloves when gardening and avoid undercooked meat to reduce toxoplasmosis risk; congenital infection can affect the eyes and brain.
thinking: Pregnancy ↓ Exposure to cat faeces ↓ Cats shed Toxoplasma oocysts ↓ Primary infection can cross the placenta ↓ Toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: B, Tetanus — soil and animal contamination tempts, but tetanus is not linked to cat faeces or to congenital infection.
takeaway: Cat faeces exposure in pregnancy: think toxoplasmosis.

stem: A patient develops profuse watery diarrhoea after drinking contaminated water while travelling. Which protozoal infection can cause this?
why_correct: Cryptosporidium can cause watery diarrhoea and is transmitted through contaminated water and other faecal–oral routes.
why_wrong: A. Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes respiratory infection. B. C. tetani causes tetanus. C. S. pyogenes causes infections such as pharyngitis and cellulitis. D. T. pallidum causes syphilis.
pearl: Cryptosporidium is a chlorine-resistant waterborne protozoan; it causes self-limiting watery diarrhoea in healthy people but can be severe and prolonged in immunosuppression.
thinking: Contaminated water ↓ Profuse watery diarrhoea ↓ Protozoal cause asked for ↓ Cryptosporidium
exam_trap: A, Mycoplasma pneumoniae — an unusual organism candidates may misplace, but it is a respiratory bacterium, not a waterborne protozoan.
takeaway: Watery diarrhoea from contaminated water with a protozoal cause: Cryptosporidium.

stem: A traveller develops abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea after exposure to contaminated food or water. Which protozoan is a possible cause?
why_correct: Entamoeba histolytica can cause amoebic dysentery with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea.
why_wrong: A. P. falciparum causes malaria. B. Cryptosporidium commonly causes watery diarrhoea. C. Toxoplasma is not a typical cause of dysentery. D. Giardia typically causes non-bloody diarrhoea and malabsorption.
pearl: Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery and can spread to cause an amoebic liver abscess; stool testing confirms it, and metronidazole is used in treatment.
thinking: Traveller ↓ Contaminated food or water ↓ Abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea ↓ Protozoal dysentery ↓ Entamoeba histolytica
exam_trap: D, Giardia lamblia — a common traveller's protozoan, but it causes non-bloody diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption, not dysentery.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea from a protozoan: Entamoeba; non-bloody with bloating: Giardia.

stem: Several people develop sudden nausea and vomiting a few hours after eating contaminated food. Which organism can cause food poisoning through a preformed toxin?
why_correct: S. aureus can produce preformed enterotoxin in food, causing rapid-onset nausea and vomiting.
why_wrong: A. B. burgdorferi causes Lyme disease. B. C. tetani causes tetanus. D. TB causes a chronic infectious disease. E. T. pallidum causes syphilis.
pearl: Preformed-toxin food poisoning, from S. aureus or B. cereus, causes vomiting within hours of eating; S. aureus classically follows handled foods such as cold meats, cream and pastries.
thinking: Several people affected ↓ Same contaminated food ↓ Vomiting within a few hours ↓ Short incubation means preformed toxin ↓ Staphylococcus aureus
exam_trap: B, Clostridium tetani — a toxin-producing bacterium, but its toxin causes muscle spasms after wounds, not food poisoning.
takeaway: Vomiting within hours of a shared meal suggests a preformed toxin, classically S. aureus.

stem: Several people develop vomiting shortly after eating reheated rice that had been stored improperly. Which organism is classically associated with this presentation?
why_correct: Bacillus cereus can cause rapid-onset vomiting after consumption of contaminated foods, classically associated with improperly stored cooked rice.
why_wrong: A. T. pallidum causes syphilis. B. C. tetani causes tetanus. C. M. tuberculosis causes tuberculosis. E. B. burgdorferi causes Lyme disease.
pearl: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking; if rice is left warm they germinate and produce a heat-stable toxin that reheating does not destroy, causing vomiting within hours.
thinking: Several people affected ↓ Reheated rice stored improperly ↓ Rapid-onset vomiting ↓ Heat-stable preformed toxin ↓ Bacillus cereus
exam_trap: B, Clostridium tetani — a spore-forming bacterium, which tempts, but it causes tetanus, not food poisoning.
takeaway: Vomiting after reheated rice: Bacillus cereus.

stem: A patient develops fever, abdominal pain and diarrhoea, which becomes bloody. They recently ate undercooked poultry. Which organism is a common cause?
why_correct: Campylobacter is commonly associated with undercooked poultry and can cause fever, abdominal pain and inflammatory, sometimes bloody, diarrhoea.
why_wrong: A. C. tetani causes tetanus. C. Cholera classically causes profuse watery diarrhoea. D. Giardia causes prolonged diarrhoea and malabsorption. E. T. pallidum causes syphilis.
pearl: Campylobacter is the commonest bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in the UK and is linked to undercooked poultry; Guillain–Barré syndrome is a recognised later complication.
thinking: Undercooked poultry ↓ Fever and abdominal pain ↓ Diarrhoea becoming bloody ↓ Inflammatory gastroenteritis ↓ Campylobacter
exam_trap: D, Giardia lamblia — a gut pathogen, but it causes prolonged non-bloody diarrhoea and malabsorption, not acute bloody diarrhoea after poultry.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea after undercooked poultry: Campylobacter; watch for later Guillain–Barré.

stem: A patient develops fever, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea after eating contaminated food. Which organism is a common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis?
why_correct: Salmonella can cause acute gastroenteritis with diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and fever.
why_wrong: A. B. burgdorferi causes Lyme disease. B. M. tuberculosis causes tuberculosis. C. C. tetani causes tetanus. E. T. pallidum causes syphilis.
pearl: Salmonella gastroenteritis follows contaminated eggs, poultry or meat; most cases settle with fluids, and antibiotics are reserved for severe illness or high-risk patients.
thinking: Contaminated food ↓ Fever ↓ Abdominal cramps and diarrhoea ↓ Bacterial gastroenteritis ↓ Salmonella
exam_trap: B, Mycobacterium tuberculosis — abdominal TB exists, but it is chronic with weight loss, not an acute food-borne gastroenteritis.
takeaway: Acute fever, cramps and diarrhoea after contaminated food: think Salmonella.

stem: A traveller develops sudden profuse watery diarrhoea described as "rice-water" stools. Which organism is the classic cause?
why_correct: Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea that can rapidly lead to severe dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Giardia typically causes prolonged diarrhoea and malabsorption. C. Salmonella commonly causes fever and diarrhoea. D. Shigella can cause dysentery with blood and mucus. E. Campylobacter commonly causes inflammatory diarrhoea with abdominal pain and fever.
pearl: Cholera causes painless, profuse rice-water diarrhoea that can kill through dehydration within hours; rapid oral or IV rehydration is the key treatment.
thinking: Traveller ↓ Sudden profuse watery diarrhoea ↓ Rice-water stools ↓ Toxin-mediated secretory diarrhoea ↓ Vibrio cholerae
exam_trap: A, Giardia lamblia — a traveller's pathogen causing watery stools, but its diarrhoea is prolonged with bloating, not sudden rice-water stools.
takeaway: Rice-water stools in a traveller: cholera; rehydrate urgently.

stem: A patient develops fever, abdominal cramps and frequent small-volume stools containing blood and mucus. Which organism is a classic cause of bacillary dysentery?
why_correct: Shigella can cause dysentery with fever, abdominal cramps and frequent bloody or mucoid stools.
why_wrong: B. Cryptosporidium usually causes watery diarrhoea. C. Giardia causes prolonged, typically non-bloody diarrhoea. D. Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea. E. B. cereus can cause acute vomiting or diarrhoeal food poisoning but not this classic dysentery syndrome.
pearl: Bloody, mucoid, small-volume stools with fever and cramps mean dysentery, which points to an invasive colonic pathogen such as Shigella rather than a toxin-mediated or small-bowel organism.
thinking: Fever, cramps and frequent small stools ↓ Blood and mucus = colonic mucosal invasion ↓ Bacillary (bacterial) dysentery ↓ Classic organism: Shigella
exam_trap: D, Vibrio cholerae — a famous diarrhoeal pathogen, but cholera is toxin-mediated and causes profuse rice-water stools without blood or mucus.
takeaway: Blood and mucus with fever means invasive dysentery; Shigella is the classic bacterial cause.

stem: A patient develops mild diarrhoea shortly after starting an antibiotic but has no fever, abdominal tenderness or systemic illness. What is a common explanation?
why_correct: Antibiotics can alter the normal intestinal microbiota and cause diarrhoea without necessarily causing C. difficile infection.
why_wrong: A. Amoebic dysentery commonly causes inflammatory or bloody diarrhoea. C. Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth causes chronic bloating and diarrhoea, often with predisposing anatomy, and is treated with antibiotics rather than caused by them. D. Cholera causes profuse watery diarrhoea and significant fluid loss. E. Tuberculous intestinal disease is uncommon and usually has a more chronic presentation.
pearl: Mild diarrhoea soon after starting an antibiotic, in a well patient, is usually simple antibiotic-associated diarrhoea from disrupted gut flora; think C. difficile if there is fever, pain or systemic illness.
thinking: Diarrhoea shortly after starting antibiotic ↓ Mild, no fever, no tenderness, no systemic upset ↓ Altered gut microbiota, not invasive infection ↓ Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea
exam_trap: C, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth — sounds like a flora disturbance, but it is a chronic bloating syndrome with predisposing anatomy and is treated with antibiotics, not caused by them.
takeaway: Mild diarrhoea after antibiotics in a well patient is usually simple antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

stem: A patient with infective endocarditis develops small, painful nodules on the pads of several fingers. What are these lesions called?
why_correct: Osler nodes are painful, tender nodules that can occur on the fingers or toes in infective endocarditis.
why_wrong: A. Vesicles are small fluid-filled skin lesions and are not the characteristic lesion described. B. Koplik spots are associated with measles. C. Janeway lesions are classically painless erythematous lesions on the palms or soles. D. Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with pale centres.
pearl: Osler nodes are painful and on the finger or toe pads; Janeway lesions are painless and on the palms or soles. Remember 'Osler = Ouch'.
thinking: Known infective endocarditis ↓ Small nodules on the finger pads ↓ Painful and tender, so immune-mediated nodules ↓ Osler nodes
exam_trap: C, Janeway lesions — also a peripheral sign of endocarditis, but they are painless macules on the palms and soles rather than painful finger-pad nodules.
takeaway: Painful finger-pad nodules in endocarditis are Osler nodes; painless palm or sole lesions are Janeway.

stem: A patient with suspected infective endocarditis is found to have retinal haemorrhages with pale centres. What are these lesions called?
why_correct: Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with pale or white centres and can occur in infective endocarditis.
why_wrong: A. Vesicles are fluid-filled skin lesions. B. Osler nodes are painful peripheral nodules. D. Koplik spots are oral lesions associated with measles. E. Janeway lesions occur on the palms and soles.
pearl: Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with pale centres; they are a recognised but non-specific sign of infective endocarditis, so look for them on fundoscopy.
thinking: Suspected infective endocarditis ↓ Lesion found in the retina ↓ Haemorrhage with a pale centre ↓ Roth spots
exam_trap: E, Janeway lesions — another vascular sign of endocarditis, but these are painless macules on the palms and soles, not retinal haemorrhages.
takeaway: Pale-centred retinal haemorrhages in endocarditis are Roth spots.

stem: Which factor increases the risk of infective endocarditis involving the tricuspid valve?
why_correct: Intravenous drug use is an important risk factor for right-sided infective endocarditis, particularly tricuspid valve infection.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not increase the risk. B. Osteoarthritis does not predispose to infective endocarditis. D. Allergic rhinitis does not predispose to endocarditis. E. Myopia does not increase the risk.
pearl: Intravenous drug use is the classic risk factor for right-sided endocarditis; the tricuspid valve is typically affected and septic pulmonary emboli may follow.
thinking: Tricuspid valve endocarditis = right-sided ↓ Organisms reach the right heart via the venous system ↓ Repeated non-sterile venous injection ↓ Intravenous drug use
exam_trap: B, osteoarthritis — chronic conditions can sound like general risk factors, but osteoarthritis creates no route for bacteraemia and does not predispose to endocarditis.
takeaway: Tricuspid valve endocarditis should make you think of intravenous drug use.

stem: Which cardiac condition can result from rheumatic fever?
why_correct: Rheumatic fever can cause inflammatory valvular damage, with the mitral valve particularly commonly affected.
why_wrong: A. Ventricular fibrillation is a malignant cardiac rhythm. C. A bicuspid aortic valve is a congenital abnormality, not a consequence of rheumatic fever. D. Aortic dissection is an aortic wall disorder. E. Myocardial infarction results from coronary artery occlusion.
pearl: Rheumatic fever causes long-term valve damage, most often to the mitral valve, and mitral stenosis is the classic late result.
thinking: Rheumatic fever ↓ Immune-mediated pancarditis ↓ Valvular scarring, mitral valve most often affected ↓ Rheumatic mitral valve disease
exam_trap: C, congenital bicuspid aortic valve disease — also a valve disease, but it is a congenital anomaly present from birth, not acquired after rheumatic fever.
takeaway: Rheumatic fever leads to chronic valve disease, classically affecting the mitral valve.

stem: A patient develops persistent localised bone pain and fever. Blood tests show evidence of inflammation, and imaging suggests infection of the bone. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone and can cause persistent local pain and systemic inflammatory features.
why_wrong: A. Osteoporosis causes reduced bone strength rather than infection. B. Rheumatoid arthritis primarily causes inflammatory synovitis. C. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without focal bone infection. D. Osteoarthritis affects joints.
pearl: Persistent focal bone pain with fever and raised inflammatory markers suggests osteomyelitis; MRI is sensitive early, and bone or blood cultures guide prolonged antibiotics.
thinking: Localised persistent bone pain ↓ Fever and raised inflammatory markers ↓ Imaging shows bone infection ↓ Osteomyelitis
exam_trap: B, rheumatoid arthritis — an inflammatory condition with raised markers, but it causes symmetrical synovitis of joints, not a focal bone infection with fever.
takeaway: Focal bone pain with fever and inflammation is osteomyelitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient is suspected of having necrotising fasciitis. What is the key management priority?

options.C: Delaying treatment until skin culture results return

correct_answer: D. Urgent surgical assessment and treatment
why_correct: Necrotising fasciitis is a rapidly progressive surgical emergency requiring urgent assessment, source control and appropriate antimicrobial treatment.
why_wrong: A. Antihistamines do not treat necrotising infection. B. Emollients do not treat deep soft-tissue infection. C. Treatment should not be delayed while waiting for microbiological results. E. Delay can result in rapid deterioration.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to visible skin changes with rapid spread and systemic toxicity suggests necrotising fasciitis; urgent surgical debridement plus IV antibiotics saves life and limb.
thinking: Suspected necrotising fasciitis ↓ Rapidly spreading deep tissue necrosis ↓ Antibiotics alone cannot reach dead tissue ↓ Urgent surgical assessment and debridement
exam_trap: C, delaying treatment until culture results return — sounds like careful practice, but waiting allows rapid spread; antibiotics and surgery must not wait for microbiology.
takeaway: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency: urgent debridement plus antibiotics, never a delay.

stem: A child has a rough, hyperkeratotic papule on the hand. Which infection commonly causes this lesion?
why_correct: Common warts are caused by infection with human papillomavirus.
why_wrong: A. HSV causes vesicular and ulcerative lesions. B. VZV causes chickenpox and shingles. C. Candida commonly causes mucosal or superficial fungal infections. E. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis and other associated conditions.
pearl: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are rough, hyperkeratotic papules caused by human papillomavirus and often resolve spontaneously in children.
thinking: Child with a rough papule on the hand ↓ Hyperkeratotic surface ↓ Common wart ↓ Human papillomavirus
