why_wrong: A. Endometrial cancer is a different pathological process. B. PID is not a typical direct cause of ovarian cancer. C. Fibroadenoma affects breast tissue. D. PID does not typically cause early menopause (premature ovarian insufficiency).
pearl: Each episode of PID raises the risk of tubal scarring, causing tubal factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain; prompt treatment and partner management reduce this.
thinking: Recurrent PID ↓ Repeated inflammation of the fallopian tubes ↓ Scarring and blockage ↓ Difficulty conceiving ↓ Tubal factor infertility
exam_trap: D, early menopause — infertility tempts thoughts of ovarian failure, but PID damages the tubes, not ovarian reserve, so ovulation and menopause timing are unaffected.
takeaway: Recurrent PID causes tubal scarring: infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.

stem:
A 20-year-old woman has dysuria and mucopurulent cervical discharge. She has a new sexual partner.

Which infection is an important possibility?
why_correct: Chlamydia commonly causes cervicitis, which may present with dysuria and mucopurulent discharge, although many infections are asymptomatic.
why_wrong: A. Varicella-zoster causes chickenpox or shingles. B. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis. D. Influenza causes respiratory illness. E. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis.
pearl: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK and is often asymptomatic; test with a nucleic acid amplification test (vulvovaginal swab in women) and treat first line with doxycycline.
thinking: Young woman with a new sexual partner ↓ Dysuria ↓ Mucopurulent cervical discharge = cervicitis ↓ Commonest bacterial STI ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis
exam_trap: B, hepatitis A — it can be sexually transmitted, which tempts, but it causes acute hepatitis with jaundice, not cervicitis with mucopurulent discharge.
takeaway: Young woman, new partner, cervicitis: test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea with NAAT.

stem:
A young adult develops marked purulent genital discharge and dysuria shortly after a new sexual contact.

Which infection is particularly associated with this presentation?
why_correct: Gonorrhoea commonly causes a prominent purulent genital discharge and dysuria.
why_wrong: A. Bacterial vaginosis typically causes a thin, malodorous discharge. B. Genital herpes causes painful vesicles or ulcers. D. Candidiasis typically causes itching and thick vaginal discharge. E. Trichomoniasis can cause discharge but the marked purulent urethral/cervical presentation is particularly characteristic of gonorrhoea.
pearl: Gonorrhoea typically causes purulent discharge and dysuria; take a culture before treatment for sensitivities because antibiotic resistance is rising, and treat with ceftriaxone per BASHH guidance.
thinking: New sexual contact ↓ Short incubation period ↓ Marked purulent genital discharge with dysuria ↓ Classic purulent STI ↓ Gonorrhoea
exam_trap: E, trichomoniasis — another discharge-causing STI, but it typically gives frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge with itch; marked purulent discharge is classic for gonorrhoea.
takeaway: Profuse purulent discharge after a new contact: gonorrhoea; culture before treatment.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman has had absent periods for several months with hot flushes. Investigations confirm ovarian failure.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Premature ovarian insufficiency is loss of ovarian function before the age of 40, presenting with amenorrhoea, menopausal symptoms and raised FSH (NICE NG23).
why_wrong: A. Pregnancy is not the explanation when ovarian failure has been confirmed and does not cause hot flushes. B. Natural menopause occurs on average at about 51; ovarian failure at 35 is premature ovarian insufficiency. C. PMOS (formerly PCOS) is associated with ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism, not ovarian failure with hot flushes. D. Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea causes low rather than raised gonadotrophins and is not primary ovarian failure.
pearl: Premature ovarian insufficiency is ovarian failure before 40, with raised FSH on two samples weeks apart; offer hormone replacement until at least the usual age of menopause to protect bone and heart.
thinking: Woman aged 35 ↓ Months of amenorrhoea with hot flushes ↓ Ovarian failure confirmed ↓ Ovarian failure before 40 ↓ Premature ovarian insufficiency
exam_trap: B, physiological menopause — the symptoms are identical, which tempts, but ovarian failure at 35 is premature by definition; this is premature ovarian insufficiency.
takeaway: Menopausal symptoms with ovarian failure before 40 = POI; replace hormones.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman develops vaginal bleeding three years after her periods stopped.

What is the most important condition to exclude?
why_correct: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment because endometrial cancer is an important potential cause.
why_wrong: A. Hyperemesis is a pregnancy-related vomiting disorder. B. Ectopic pregnancy is not a typical explanation in a postmenopausal woman. D. Dysmenorrhoea refers to painful menstruation. E. Normal ovulation does not explain postmenopausal bleeding.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment to exclude endometrial cancer: transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness, then hysteroscopy and biopsy as indicated.
thinking: Woman aged 61 ↓ Periods stopped three years ago ↓ New vaginal bleeding = postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Must exclude endometrial malignancy ↓ Endometrial cancer
exam_trap: B, ectopic pregnancy — the exclude-the-dangerous reflex tempts with any bleeding, but pregnancy is not plausible three years after menopause; endometrial cancer is the concern.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A woman with PMOS (formerly PCOS) has excess facial hair and acne.

Which hormone group is primarily responsible for these clinical features?
why_correct: Hyperandrogenism, from increased ovarian androgen production and reduced sex hormone-binding globulin, causes hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS).
why_wrong: B. Thyroid hormone abnormalities are not the mechanism of hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS). C. Prolactin deficiency does not cause hirsutism or acne. D. Cortisol deficiency causes adrenal insufficiency rather than the androgenic features of PMOS (formerly PCOS). E. Oestrogens do not cause hirsutism or acne; these are androgenic features.
pearl: Hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS) reflect hyperandrogenism from raised ovarian androgens and low SHBG; insulin resistance contributes, so weight reduction can improve symptoms.
thinking: PMOS (formerly PCOS) ↓ Excess facial hair and acne ↓ Both are androgen-dependent features ↓ Raised ovarian androgens and low SHBG ↓ Androgens
exam_trap: E, oestrogens only — ovarian hormones are the obvious guess, but oestrogens do not cause hirsutism or acne; these signs come from androgen excess.
takeaway: Hirsutism and acne mean androgen excess; in PMOS it is ovarian hyperandrogenism.

stem:
A couple has been trying to conceive. The woman has very irregular menstrual cycles.

Which factor is particularly important to assess?
why_correct: Irregular cycles can indicate ovulatory dysfunction, which is an important cause of female infertility.
why_wrong: A. Visual acuity is unrelated. B. Skin pigmentation is not an assessment of ovulatory function. D. Lung volume is not a routine initial fertility assessment. E. Hearing threshold is not a routine cause of infertility.
pearl: Irregular cycles in a woman trying to conceive suggest anovulation; assess ovulation and look for causes such as PMOS (formerly PCOS), thyroid disease and hyperprolactinaemia.
thinking: Couple trying to conceive ↓ Very irregular menstrual cycles ↓ Irregular cycles imply ovulatory dysfunction ↓ Ovulation
exam_trap: B, skin pigmentation — skin signs such as acanthosis nigricans can hint at an endocrine cause, which tempts, but pigmentation does not assess fertility; ovulation does.
takeaway: Subfertility with irregular cycles: assess ovulation first.

stem:
A 58-year-old man develops persistent difficulty achieving erections. He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension.

Which condition is an important possible underlying contributor?
why_correct: Erectile dysfunction is commonly associated with vascular disease and cardiovascular risk factors such as diabetes and hypertension.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa is unrelated. C. Appendicitis does not explain chronic erectile dysfunction. D. Cystitis is not a typical cause of persistent erectile dysfunction. E. Migraine does not explain this presentation.
pearl: Erectile dysfunction in a man with diabetes and hypertension is usually vasculogenic; assess cardiovascular risk, including glucose control, lipids and blood pressure.
thinking: Persistent erectile dysfunction ↓ Type 2 diabetes and hypertension ↓ Both damage endothelium and penile arteries ↓ Reduced penile blood flow ↓ Vascular disease
exam_trap: D, cystitis only — it tempts as a genitourinary condition, but cystitis causes dysuria and frequency, not persistent erectile dysfunction.
takeaway: ED with diabetes or hypertension is usually vascular; assess cardiovascular risk.

stem:
A man presents with new erectile dysfunction and has several cardiovascular risk factors.

Why is this clinically important?

options.A: It suggests a primarily psychogenic or relationship cause
options.B: It may indicate underlying cardiovascular disease
options.C: It suggests a recent episode of testicular torsion
options.D: It is a recognised early sign of localised prostate cancer
options.E: It is most often caused by testosterone deficiency

correct_answer: B. It may indicate underlying cardiovascular disease
why_correct: Erectile dysfunction can be associated with endothelial and vascular disease and may coexist with cardiovascular risk.
why_wrong: A. With several vascular risk factors, an organic vascular cause is more likely than a primarily psychogenic one. C. Testicular torsion causes acute testicular pain. D. Erectile dysfunction is not an early sign of prostate cancer. E. Vascular disease is the commonest organic cause; testosterone deficiency accounts for a minority of cases.
pearl: Erectile dysfunction can precede symptomatic coronary disease by several years because penile arteries are small; new ED should prompt a cardiovascular risk assessment.
thinking: New erectile dysfunction ↓ Several cardiovascular risk factors ↓ Small penile arteries show endothelial disease early ↓ ED may be the first sign ↓ May indicate underlying cardiovascular disease
exam_trap: E, testosterone deficiency — hormones seem a natural cause, but hypogonadism explains only a minority; with vascular risk factors, vascular disease is likelier.
takeaway: New ED with vascular risk factors is a cardiovascular warning sign.

stem:
A man develops erectile dysfunction after starting a new medication. He asks whether medication can contribute.

Which statement is correct?

options.C: Erectile dysfunction cannot have psychological contributors
options.D: Some medicines can contribute to erectile dysfunction

correct_answer: D. Some medicines can contribute to erectile dysfunction
why_correct: Several medicines can contribute to erectile dysfunction, so medication history is relevant.
why_wrong: A. Medication effects are a recognised contributor. B. Erectile dysfunction has multiple possible causes. C. Psychological factors can contribute, although organic causes should also be considered. E. Erectile dysfunction does not mean cancer is present.
pearl: Common drug causes of erectile dysfunction include thiazides, beta-blockers, antidepressants (especially SSRIs), antipsychotics and antiandrogens; always take a medication history.
thinking: New ED after starting a medicine ↓ Temporal link suggests a drug effect ↓ Many drugs affect vascular, neural or hormonal pathways ↓ Some medicines can contribute to erectile dysfunction
exam_trap: B, always indicates hypogonadism — low testosterone is a recognised cause, which tempts, but ED has vascular, neurogenic, psychological and drug causes; always is wrong.
takeaway: New ED after a new medicine: review the drug list; thiazides, beta-blockers and SSRIs are common.

stem:
An older man with benign prostatic enlargement reports urgency, frequency and nocturia.

What type of lower urinary tract symptoms are these?
why_correct: Urgency, frequency and nocturia are storage symptoms.
why_wrong: A. They are urinary storage symptoms rather than sexual symptoms. B. These are urinary symptoms rather than neurological deficits. C. Renal colic causes acute flank-to-groin pain. D. They do not involve the gastrointestinal tract.
pearl: LUTS divide into storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence), voiding (hesitancy, poor stream, straining) and post-micturition (dribbling, incomplete emptying), which guides treatment.
thinking: Older man with benign prostatic enlargement ↓ Urgency, frequency and nocturia ↓ Symptoms arise during bladder filling ↓ Storage symptoms
exam_trap: C, renal colic — a urological problem, but renal colic is acute loin-to-groin pain from a stone, not chronic urgency, frequency and nocturia.
takeaway: Frequency, urgency and nocturia = storage symptoms; hesitancy and poor stream = voiding.

stem:
An older man reports hesitancy, poor urinary stream and straining to begin urination.

What type of lower urinary tract symptoms are these?
why_correct: Hesitancy, weak stream and straining are typical voiding symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Storage symptoms include urgency, frequency and nocturia. B. These symptoms arise from the lower urinary tract. C. They are not seizure symptoms. E. They do not involve the respiratory system.
pearl: Voiding symptoms such as hesitancy, weak stream, straining and intermittency suggest bladder outlet obstruction, commonly from benign prostatic enlargement in older men.
thinking: Older man ↓ Hesitancy, poor stream and straining ↓ Difficulty emptying the bladder, as in outlet obstruction ↓ Voiding symptoms
exam_trap: A, storage symptoms — both groups occur in prostatic disease, which tempts, but storage symptoms are frequency, urgency and nocturia; emptying problems are voiding symptoms.
takeaway: Hesitancy, weak stream and straining = voiding (obstructive) symptoms.

stem:
A man with advanced prostate cancer develops persistent lower back and hip pain.

Which site is commonly involved when prostate cancer metastasises?
why_correct: Prostate cancer commonly metastasises to bone and can cause bone pain.
why_wrong: A. The appendix is not a typical site. C. The external ear is not a typical metastatic site. D. Corneal metastasis is not a typical pattern. E. The thyroid is not a characteristic primary metastatic site.
pearl: Prostate cancer spreads preferentially to bone, especially the axial skeleton; new back pain in prostate cancer needs urgent assessment for metastatic spinal cord compression.
thinking: Advanced prostate cancer ↓ Persistent lower back and hip pain ↓ Axial skeleton involvement ↓ Typically sclerotic metastases ↓ Bone
exam_trap: E, thyroid only — thyroid cancer is itself a classic bone-metastasising cancer, which confuses, but the thyroid is not a typical metastatic site for prostate cancer.
takeaway: Prostate cancer with back pain: think bone metastases and watch for cord compression.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy develops sudden severe unilateral testicular pain and vomiting. There is no preceding urinary infection.

Which diagnosis should be treated as the emergency?
why_correct: Sudden severe testicular pain with vomiting is highly concerning for torsion, which threatens testicular viability and requires urgent surgical assessment.
why_wrong: A. Hydrocele is generally painless. B. Testicular cancer usually presents as a painless mass. C. Epididymitis more often develops gradually and may have urinary or infective symptoms. D. Varicocele is usually chronic and painless.
pearl: Suspected testicular torsion needs immediate surgical exploration; do not delay for ultrasound, as testicular viability falls with every hour of ischaemia.
thinking: Adolescent boy ↓ Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain ↓ Vomiting ↓ No preceding urinary infection ↓ Testicular torsion
exam_trap: C, epididymitis — it also causes a painful testis, but it usually comes on gradually with urinary or sexually transmitted infective features, which are absent here.
takeaway: Sudden testicular pain in a young male: torsion until proven otherwise; explore urgently.

stem:
An older man with untreated urinary retention develops bilateral hydronephrosis and worsening renal function.

What is the mechanism of the kidney injury?
why_correct: Urinary outflow obstruction raises pressure within the urinary tract and can impair renal function, producing postrenal AKI.
why_wrong: B. Renal artery embolism causes vascular renal injury rather than bilateral urinary obstruction. C. Prerenal AKI results from reduced renal perfusion. D. Tubular toxins cause intrinsic AKI. E. Autoimmune glomerular disease causes intrinsic renal injury.
pearl: Bilateral hydronephrosis with AKI points to bladder outflow obstruction; catheterise to relieve it, and watch for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte disturbance afterwards.
thinking: Older man with untreated urinary retention ↓ Bilateral hydronephrosis ↓ Back-pressure impairs filtration ↓ Obstruction below the kidneys ↓ Postrenal obstruction
exam_trap: D, tubular toxin exposure — intrinsic tubular injury is a common AKI cause, which tempts, but hydronephrosis with retention points to an outflow problem, i.e. postrenal.
takeaway: AKI with bilateral hydronephrosis and retention: postrenal obstruction; catheterise.

stem:
A patient has haematuria with significant proteinuria and hypertension. The urine microscopy suggests dysmorphic red cells.

What is the most likely source of the bleeding?
why_correct: Dysmorphic red cells with proteinuria and hypertension suggest glomerular bleeding.
why_wrong: A. External bleeding does not produce true glomerular haematuria. C. Bladder bleeding usually does not produce dysmorphic red cells. D. Prostatic bleeding does not explain a glomerular urine sediment. E. Urethral bleeding is not typically associated with significant proteinuria.
pearl: Dysmorphic red cells and red-cell casts on urine microscopy point to glomerular bleeding; with proteinuria and hypertension this suggests glomerulonephritis needing renal referral.
thinking: Haematuria with significant proteinuria ↓ Hypertension ↓ Red cells deformed passing through the glomerular basement membrane ↓ Glomeruli
exam_trap: C, bladder only — the bladder is a common source of haematuria, but lower tract bleeding gives normally shaped red cells and no significant proteinuria.
takeaway: Haematuria with dysmorphic red cells and proteinuria = glomerular source.

stem:
A child with suspected intussusception develops stool containing blood and mucus.

What is this classically described as?
why_correct: Blood and mucus mixed with stool in intussusception can produce the classic "redcurrant jelly" appearance.
why_wrong: A. Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, fatty stool. B. Pale acholic stool suggests reduced bile reaching the intestine. C. Rice-water stool is classically associated with cholera. D. Melaena is black, tarry stool from upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
pearl: Intussusception typically affects infants and toddlers, with paroxysmal colicky pain and pallor; redcurrant jelly stool is a late sign, so do not wait for it before arranging urgent ultrasound.
thinking: Suspected intussusception ↓ Telescoping bowel causes venous congestion ↓ Mucosal ischaemia releases blood and mucus ↓ Redcurrant jelly stool
exam_trap: D, melaena — the other named bloody stool, but melaena is black tarry stool from upper GI bleeding; intussusception gives dark red blood mixed with mucus.
takeaway: Intussusception gives redcurrant jelly stool, but it is a late sign.

stem:
A 2-week-old infant develops sudden green vomiting and abdominal distension.

Which diagnosis is particularly important to consider?
why_correct: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is an emergency because it may indicate intestinal obstruction, including malrotation with volvulus.
why_wrong: A. Lactose intolerance does not cause acute bilious vomiting. C. Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious vomiting. D. Reflux usually causes uncomplicated regurgitation rather than acute bilious vomiting. E. Coeliac disease does not present as neonatal intestinal obstruction.
pearl: Bilious (green) vomiting in a neonate is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; malrotation with volvulus can cause bowel ischaemia within hours, so seek urgent surgical review.
thinking: 2-week-old infant ↓ Sudden green (bilious) vomiting ↓ Obstruction distal to the ampulla ↓ Abdominal distension ↓ Malrotation with volvulus
exam_trap: C, pyloric stenosis — the classic vomiting infant at this age, but the obstruction is proximal to bile entry, so vomit is non-bilious and projectile.
takeaway: Bilious vomiting in a neonate = malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

stem: What is the underlying abnormality in Hirschsprung disease?

options.A: Hypertrophy of the pyloric smooth muscle

correct_answer: B. Aganglionic segment of distal bowel
why_correct: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cells to populate part of the intestine, producing an aganglionic segment.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric smooth-muscle hypertrophy causes infantile pyloric stenosis. C. Excess gastric acid is not the underlying problem. D. Villous atrophy occurs in coeliac disease. E. Pancreatic insufficiency is a different disorder.
pearl: In Hirschsprung disease ganglion cells are absent from the distal bowel, so it cannot relax; it presents with delayed passage of meconium and is confirmed by rectal suction biopsy.
thinking: Hirschsprung disease ↓ Neural crest cells fail to migrate fully ↓ Distal segment lacks ganglion cells ↓ Bowel cannot relax, causing functional obstruction ↓ Aganglionic segment of distal bowel
exam_trap: A, hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle — a classic infant obstruction, but that is pyloric stenosis; Hirschsprung disease is a nerve defect in the distal bowel.
takeaway: Hirschsprung = aganglionic distal bowel; confirm with rectal suction biopsy.

stem:
A 3-year-old child develops chronic diarrhoea, abdominal distension and poor weight gain after introduction of a gluten-containing diet.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chronic gastrointestinal symptoms with poor growth following gluten exposure are typical of coeliac disease.
why_wrong: A. Pyloric stenosis presents in early infancy with projectile vomiting. B. Hirschsprung disease causes constipation and obstruction. C. Intussusception causes acute episodic abdominal pain. D. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain rather than chronic malabsorption.
pearl: Test for coeliac disease with tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA while the child is still eating gluten; faltering growth, diarrhoea and distension are classic in young children.
thinking: 3-year-old with chronic diarrhoea ↓ Abdominal distension and poor weight gain ↓ Began after gluten was introduced ↓ Gluten-driven enteropathy ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: B, Hirschsprung disease — distension and poor growth tempt, but Hirschsprung causes constipation and obstruction from early life, not diarrhoea after gluten.
takeaway: Faltering growth with diarrhoea after gluten: test for coeliac on a gluten-containing diet.

stem:
A child with type 1 diabetes is being assessed for other autoimmune conditions.

Which condition is associated with type 1 diabetes?
why_correct: Type 1 diabetes is associated with other autoimmune diseases, including coeliac disease.
why_wrong: B. Renal colic is usually caused by urinary tract stones. C. Gout is caused by urate crystal deposition. D. Emphysema is a chronic lung disorder. E. Osteoarthritis is degenerative joint disease.
pearl: Children with type 1 diabetes are at higher risk of autoimmune thyroid disease and coeliac disease; screening for both is part of routine diabetes care.
thinking: Child with type 1 diabetes ↓ Autoimmune destruction of beta cells ↓ Autoimmune conditions cluster together ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: C, gout — a metabolic condition that tempts in a diabetes question, but gout is urate crystal arthritis with no autoimmune link to type 1 diabetes.
takeaway: Type 1 diabetes: screen for coeliac disease and autoimmune thyroid disease.

stem:
A boy develops progressive proximal muscle weakness and has difficulty climbing stairs.

Which inheritance pattern is characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
why_correct: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene and is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.
why_wrong: A. Mitochondrial disorders are transmitted through the maternal line. B. Y-linked disorders are transmitted from father to son. C. Autosomal recessive conditions require pathogenic variants on both autosomes. E. Autosomal dominant inheritance gives transmission through either sex.
pearl: Duchenne muscular dystrophy affects boys, with proximal weakness, Gowers sign and calf pseudohypertrophy; creatine kinase is markedly raised, and carrier mothers pass it to half their sons.
thinking: Boy with progressive proximal weakness ↓ Difficulty climbing stairs ↓ Duchenne muscular dystrophy ↓ Dystrophin gene lies on the X chromosome ↓ X-linked recessive
exam_trap: C, autosomal recessive — many childhood muscle disorders are autosomal recessive, which tempts, but Duchenne affects boys through a dystrophin mutation on the X chromosome.
takeaway: Duchenne = X-linked recessive dystrophin defect: affected boys, high CK, Gowers sign.

stem:
A child develops persistent abnormal muscle tone and movement following a perinatal brain injury. The symptoms are non-progressive.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Cerebral palsy describes a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by a non-progressive disturbance of the developing brain.
why_wrong: A. Duchenne causes progressive muscular weakness. B. Parkinson disease is primarily an adult neurodegenerative condition. C. Huntington disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. E. Multiple sclerosis is uncommon in young children and has a different clinical pattern.
pearl: Cerebral palsy is a permanent, non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from injury to the developing brain; loss of acquired skills suggests a different, progressive condition.
thinking: Abnormal tone and movement ↓ Follows perinatal brain injury ↓ Non-progressive course ↓ Disorder of the developing brain ↓ Cerebral palsy
exam_trap: A, Duchenne muscular dystrophy — a childhood motor disorder, but it is a progressive muscle disease, not a non-progressive problem after perinatal brain injury.
takeaway: Non-progressive motor disorder after perinatal brain injury = cerebral palsy.

stem:
A healthy young child has flexible flat feet without pain or functional limitation.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: It suggests tarsal coalition requiring imaging
options.B: It is often a normal developmental variant
options.C: It suggests an early-onset form of muscular dystrophy
options.D: It suggests underlying spastic cerebral palsy
options.E: It requires referral for custom-made orthotics

correct_answer: B. It is often a normal developmental variant
why_correct: Flexible flat feet are common in children and may be a normal developmental variant when painless and functionally normal.
why_wrong: A. Tarsal coalition causes a rigid, often painful flat foot rather than a flexible painless one. C. Flat feet do not suggest muscular dystrophy. D. Flat feet alone do not suggest cerebral palsy. E. Orthotics are not routinely needed for asymptomatic flexible flat feet.
pearl: Flexible flat feet are common in young children; the arch reappears on tiptoe and most need only reassurance. A rigid or painful flat foot needs further assessment.
thinking: Healthy young child ↓ Flat feet that are flexible ↓ No pain or functional limitation ↓ Arch develops through childhood ↓ Often a normal developmental variant
exam_trap: E, custom orthotics — parents often want treatment, which tempts, but orthotics are not needed for painless flexible flat feet; reassurance is enough.
takeaway: Painless, flexible flat feet in a child: reassure; rigid or painful feet need review.

stem:
A child has bowed legs, poor growth and widened wrists. Dietary history suggests inadequate vitamin D intake.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Vitamin D deficiency in children can impair bone mineralisation, causing rickets with features such as bowed legs and widened wrists.
why_wrong: B. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint condition. C. Scoliosis is abnormal spinal curvature. D. Septic arthritis causes acute painful joint inflammation. E. Gout is caused by urate crystal deposition.
pearl: Rickets causes bowed legs, widened wrists, a rachitic rosary and poor growth; check calcium, phosphate, ALP, vitamin D and PTH, and treat with vitamin D and adequate calcium.
thinking: Child with bowed legs and widened wrists ↓ Poor growth ↓ Inadequate vitamin D intake ↓ Defective mineralisation of growing bone ↓ Rickets
exam_trap: C, scoliosis — a childhood skeletal deformity that tempts, but it is curvature of the spine and does not explain bowed legs, widened wrists and low vitamin D intake.
takeaway: Bowed legs and widened wrists with poor vitamin D intake: rickets.

stem:
A child has persistent fever and a widespread non-blanching rash. The child is drowsy and clinically very unwell.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Await blood culture results before giving antibiotics
options.D: Review again in 24 hours if the rash fades

correct_answer: C. Urgently treat possible bacterial sepsis
why_correct: A febrile, seriously unwell child with a non-blanching rash may have invasive meningococcal disease or another serious infection and requires urgent assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics should not be delayed while awaiting culture results. B. Routine dermatology review is inappropriate for a potentially life-threatening illness. D. Delaying review could be dangerous even if the rash fades. E. Antihistamines do not treat invasive bacterial infection.
pearl: A febrile, unwell child with a non-blanching rash needs immediate treatment for suspected meningococcal sepsis; give parenteral antibiotics at the earliest opportunity without delaying transfer.
thinking: Child with persistent fever ↓ Widespread non-blanching rash ↓ Drowsy and very unwell ↓ Possible invasive meningococcal disease ↓ Urgently treat possible bacterial sepsis
exam_trap: A, await blood culture results — taking cultures is good practice, which tempts, but waiting for results delays antibiotics in a child who can deteriorate within hours.
takeaway: Fever plus non-blanching rash in an unwell child: antibiotics now, do not wait.

stem: A 12-hour-old baby develops visible jaundice. The baby is otherwise well and feeding adequately. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.E: Reassure the parents that this is physiological jaundice

why_correct: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is potentially pathological and requires prompt assessment of bilirubin.
why_wrong: B. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. C. Breastfeeding should generally continue. D. Phototherapy depends on the bilirubin level and the baby's age/gestation. E. Physiological jaundice generally develops after the first 24 hours.
pearl: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is pathological until proven otherwise; measure serum bilirubin urgently and look for haemolysis or infection.
thinking: 12-hour-old baby ↓ Visible jaundice ↓ Onset within the first 24 hours ↓ Potentially pathological, e.g. haemolysis ↓ Arrange urgent bilirubin measurement
exam_trap: E, reassure as physiological jaundice — the baby is well and feeding, which tempts, but physiological jaundice does not appear within the first 24 hours.
takeaway: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never assumed physiological: measure bilirubin urgently.

stem: A 4-week-old breastfed infant remains visibly jaundiced. The baby is otherwise well. Which finding would particularly suggest pathological cholestasis?

options.C: Jaundice that began on day 3 of life

why_correct: Pale or acholic stools suggest reduced bile flow and cholestasis and require investigation.
why_wrong: A. Mild early weight loss can be physiological. B. Frequent breastfeeding is not a sign of cholestasis. C. Jaundice beginning after 24 hours can be physiological. D. Normal stool colour is reassuring.
pearl: Prolonged jaundice in a term infant (beyond two weeks) needs a split bilirubin; pale stools or dark urine suggest biliary atresia, where early surgery improves outcome.
thinking: 4-week-old with persistent jaundice ↓ Prolonged neonatal jaundice ↓ Consider conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia ↓ Bile not reaching the gut ↓ Pale, chalky stools
exam_trap: C, jaundice beginning on day 3 — the timing sounds abnormal, which tempts, but onset after 24 hours fits physiological jaundice; pale stools are the cholestatic warning sign.
takeaway: Prolonged jaundice with pale stools: check conjugated bilirubin and exclude biliary atresia.

stem: A newborn has a raised bilirubin concentration. What determines whether phototherapy is required?

options.A: Bilirubin level against the treatment threshold
options.B: Whether the parents are worried about the baby's skin colour
options.C: Whether the baby is exclusively breastfed or formula-fed
options.D: The baby's birth weight and current feeding pattern
options.E: The extent of visible jaundice on skin inspection

correct_answer: A. Bilirubin level against the treatment threshold
why_correct: Management is based on the measured bilirubin level interpreted against the appropriate age- and gestation-specific treatment threshold.
why_wrong: B. Parental concern about skin colour does not determine treatment. C. Feeding method does not itself determine the phototherapy threshold. D. Birth weight and feeding pattern do not determine the treatment threshold. E. Visual assessment of jaundice is unreliable; a measured bilirubin is needed.
pearl: Phototherapy decisions use the measured bilirubin plotted on a treatment threshold chart for the baby's gestation and age in hours; visual inspection alone is unreliable.
thinking: Newborn with raised bilirubin ↓ Needs an objective decision on phototherapy ↓ Threshold depends on age in hours and gestation ↓ Bilirubin level against the treatment threshold
exam_trap: E, extent of visible jaundice — clinicians do inspect the skin, which tempts, but visual assessment is unreliable; a measured bilirubin against the threshold decides.
takeaway: Phototherapy is decided by measured bilirubin on gestation- and age-specific charts.

stem: A 2-year-old child with known congenital heart disease becomes acutely cyanosed while crying. Which congenital lesion is classically associated with these episodes?
why_correct: Children with Tetralogy of Fallot can develop hypercyanotic ("Tet") spells, often triggered by crying or exertion.
why_wrong: A. Coarctation primarily causes systemic outflow obstruction. B. PDA usually causes increased pulmonary blood flow. D. ASD is generally not associated with episodic severe cyanosis in childhood. E. An isolated VSD usually causes left-to-right shunting.
pearl: Hypercyanotic (Tet) spells occur in Tetralogy of Fallot when crying or exertion increases right-to-left shunting; knee-chest positioning and oxygen are first steps.
thinking: Child with congenital heart disease ↓ Acute cyanosis while crying ↓ Right ventricular outflow obstruction worsens ↓ Increased right-to-left shunt across the VSD ↓ Tetralogy of Fallot
exam_trap: E, ventricular septal defect — Fallot includes a VSD, which tempts, but an isolated VSD shunts left to right and does not cause episodic cyanotic spells.
takeaway: Cyanotic spells on crying in a child with congenital heart disease: Tetralogy of Fallot.

stem: A 4-year-old child has dysuria, urinary frequency and suprapubic discomfort. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort are typical lower urinary tract symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis typically causes abdominal pain progressing to right iliac fossa tenderness. B. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia. C. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria. E. Gastroenteritis causes gastrointestinal symptoms rather than dysuria and frequency.
pearl: Dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain in a child suggest cystitis; send a urine sample before antibiotics, and remember that younger children often present non-specifically.
thinking: 4-year-old child ↓ Dysuria and urinary frequency ↓ Suprapubic discomfort ↓ Lower urinary tract infection ↓ Cystitis
exam_trap: A, appendicitis — it causes lower abdominal pain in children and a pelvic appendix can irritate the bladder, but dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain point to cystitis.
takeaway: Dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain in a child: cystitis; get urine before antibiotics.

stem: A 2-year-old with suspected UTI is about to receive antibiotics. What should generally be done before starting antibiotics if possible?
correct_answer: A. Obtain an appropriate urine sample
why_correct: Obtaining a urine sample before antibiotics improves the ability to confirm the diagnosis microbiologically.
why_wrong: B. Renal biopsy is not part of routine initial assessment. C. Cystoscopy is not an initial investigation. D. Prophylaxis is not routinely started for a first suspected UTI. E. Lumbar puncture is not routine for suspected UTI.
pearl: In a young child with suspected UTI, collect a clean-catch urine sample before starting antibiotics where possible, as culture confirms the diagnosis and guides treatment and further investigation.
thinking: 2-year-old with suspected UTI ↓ Antibiotics about to start ↓ Antibiotics can sterilise the urine ↓ Culture needed to confirm the diagnosis ↓ Obtain an appropriate urine sample
exam_trap: D, start long-term prophylaxis — it is used in some recurrent UTIs, which tempts, but it is not routine after a first UTI and does not replace a pre-treatment sample.
takeaway: Suspected UTI in a child: clean-catch urine before antibiotics where possible.

stem: An otherwise healthy 7-year-old wets the bed most nights but has no daytime urinary symptoms, constipation or other abnormalities. What is an appropriate first-line treatment option?
why_correct: A bedwetting alarm is an important treatment option for children with uncomplicated nocturnal enuresis and has a good long-term success rate.
why_wrong: A. Imaging is not routinely required for uncomplicated bedwetting. B. Renal biopsy is unnecessary. D. Antibiotics are not indicated. E. Catheterisation is inappropriate.
pearl: For uncomplicated bedwetting with no daytime symptoms, an enuresis alarm is first-line; desmopressin is used when rapid or short-term control is needed or an alarm is unsuitable.
thinking: Healthy 7-year-old ↓ Wets the bed most nights ↓ No daytime symptoms or constipation ↓ Uncomplicated nocturnal enuresis ↓ Bedwetting alarm
exam_trap: A, immediate renal ultrasound — investigating seems thorough, but uncomplicated bedwetting without daytime symptoms needs no imaging; an enuresis alarm is first-line.
takeaway: Uncomplicated bedwetting: no investigations; enuresis alarm first, desmopressin if needed.

stem: A 6-year-old with longstanding bedwetting also has infrequent, hard stools and soiling. What should be addressed?
why_correct: Constipation can contribute to urinary symptoms and bedwetting and should be identified and managed.
why_wrong: A. Coarctation is unrelated to these urinary symptoms. B. Renal stones are not suggested by this presentation. D. Glomerulonephritis causes haematuria, oedema and/or hypertension. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia.
pearl: Constipation commonly coexists with bedwetting and daytime wetting; treat it first, as a loaded rectum presses on the bladder and reduces its functional capacity.
thinking: 6-year-old with longstanding bedwetting ↓ Infrequent hard stools ↓ Soiling suggests faecal loading ↓ Loaded rectum reduces bladder capacity ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: E, diabetes insipidus — wetting tempts a polyuria cause, but diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia, not hard stools and soiling.
takeaway: Bedwetting with hard stools or soiling: treat constipation first.

stem: An 8-year-old has persistent difficulty sustaining attention, excessive activity and impulsive behaviour, causing problems at school and home. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent developmentally inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity and/or impulsivity causing impairment are characteristic of ADHD.
why_wrong: A. Specific phobia causes marked fear associated with a particular object or situation. C. Conduct disorder involves persistent patterns of serious behavioural disturbance. D. Absence seizures cause brief episodes of impaired awareness rather than persistent behavioural symptoms. E. Autism is primarily characterised by social-communication differences and restricted/repetitive patterns.
pearl: ADHD requires persistent inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity causing impairment in more than one setting, such as home and school; diagnosis is made by a specialist.
thinking: 8-year-old ↓ Persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity ↓ Problems at school and at home ↓ Impairment across settings ↓ ADHD
exam_trap: C, conduct disorder — behavioural problems at school tempt, but conduct disorder involves persistent aggression or serious rule-breaking, not core inattention and hyperactivity.
takeaway: Inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity across settings with impairment: think ADHD.

stem: A teacher suspects ADHD in a 9-year-old because of poor concentration in class. What is most appropriate regarding diagnosis?

options.A: Diagnose ADHD from standardised parent and teacher rating scales
options.B: Diagnose ADHD from a brain scan
options.C: Full assessment of symptoms and impairment across settings
options.D: Start a trial of stimulant medication to confirm the diagnosis
options.E: Diagnose ADHD from a single blood test

correct_answer: C. Full assessment of symptoms and impairment across settings
why_correct: ADHD diagnosis requires a comprehensive assessment, including symptoms, development, functioning and information from relevant settings.
why_wrong: A. Rating scales can support but cannot replace a full clinical assessment. B. There is no diagnostic brain scan for ADHD. D. Response to stimulant medication does not confirm the diagnosis; medication follows diagnosis. E. There is no diagnostic blood test.
pearl: ADHD is diagnosed by a specialist after full clinical assessment of symptoms, development and impairment in more than one setting; rating scales help but cannot diagnose alone.
thinking: Teacher suspects ADHD ↓ Concern reported from one setting only ↓ No single scale, scan or test diagnoses ADHD ↓ Needs specialist assessment across settings ↓ Full assessment of symptoms and impairment
exam_trap: A, diagnose from rating scales — scales are widely used and feel objective, but they only support assessment; diagnosis needs a full clinical evaluation across settings.
takeaway: ADHD needs full specialist assessment across settings; no scale, scan or blood test diagnoses it.

stem: A 10-year-old has repeated involuntary eye blinking, facial grimacing and shoulder shrugging, together with throat-clearing sounds. The tics have persisted for more than a year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Tourette syndrome is characterised by multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic persisting for more than a year.
why_wrong: A. Absence seizures cause brief episodes of impaired awareness rather than persistent motor and vocal tics. C. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness, including ptosis, rather than involuntary tics. D. Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor in older adults, not motor and vocal tics in a child. E. Cerebral palsy causes a non-progressive motor impairment from early brain injury, present from infancy, not motor and vocal tics.
pearl: Tourette syndrome needs multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic for over a year, starting in childhood; tics wax and wane, can be briefly suppressed, and ADHD and OCD often coexist.
thinking: 10-year-old ↓ Multiple motor tics: blinking, grimacing, shrugging ↓ Vocal tic: throat-clearing ↓ Persisting over a year ↓ Tourette syndrome
exam_trap: A, absence epilepsy — repetitive eye blinking in a school-age child tempts, but absences cause brief lapses of awareness, not motor and vocal tics.
takeaway: Multiple motor tics plus a vocal tic for over a year: Tourette syndrome.

stem: A 9-year-old boy is much shorter than his classmates. His height has progressively fallen across several centile lines over the last three years. What is the most important interpretation?

options.A: Growth assessment is unnecessary before puberty
options.B: Crossing down multiple height centiles warrants assessment
options.C: Short stature always indicates growth hormone deficiency
options.D: Height is irrelevant if weight is normal
options.E: This is definitely familial short stature

correct_answer: B. Crossing down multiple height centiles warrants assessment
why_correct: A significant change in growth trajectory is more concerning than simply being short while following an established centile.
why_wrong: A. Growth should be assessed throughout childhood. C. Many causes of short stature are unrelated to growth hormone deficiency. D. Height trajectory remains clinically important. E. Familial short stature usually follows an appropriate growth trajectory.
pearl: A child crossing down height centiles needs assessment for causes such as hypothyroidism, coeliac disease, growth hormone deficiency or chronic illness; plot serial measurements against parental heights.
thinking: 9-year-old boy shorter than peers ↓ Height falling across several centiles ↓ Growth velocity has slowed ↓ A change in trajectory signals pathology ↓ Warrants assessment
exam_trap: E, familial short stature — short children often have short parents, which tempts, but familial short stature tracks a centile; falling across centiles is not familial.
takeaway: Shortness on a steady centile may be normal; falling across centiles needs assessment.

stem: A 14-year-old boy is short compared with classmates and has no signs of puberty. His father reports that he also entered puberty late. What is the most likely explanation?

options.D: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

correct_answer: D. Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
why_correct: Delayed puberty with a family history of late puberty is characteristic of constitutional delay.
why_wrong: A. Non-classical CAH causes androgen excess with early pubic hair and accelerated growth, not familial delayed puberty. B. Precocious puberty involves unusually early pubertal development. C. Hyperthyroidism does not typically produce this classic pattern. E. Cushing syndrome causes characteristic systemic features and impaired growth.
pearl: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is commonest in boys, often with a family history of late puberty; bone age is delayed and final height is usually normal.
thinking: 14-year-old boy ↓ Short with no signs of puberty ↓ Father also entered puberty late ↓ Familial pattern of late development ↓ Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
exam_trap: C, hyperthyroidism — thyroid disease affects growth, but it is hypothyroidism that slows growth and puberty, and neither explains a familial late-puberty pattern.
takeaway: Short, late-developing boy with a parent who was also late: constitutional delay.

stem: A 15-year-old boy has no testicular enlargement and no other signs of puberty. Which finding is most useful in assessing whether puberty has started?
why_correct: Testicular enlargement is the first clear sign of true male puberty.
why_wrong: B. BMI centile is not a marker of pubertal onset. C. A single height and weight centile cannot establish the onset of puberty. D. Head circumference is not a marker of puberty in this age group. E. Shoe size is not a marker of pubertal onset.
pearl: In boys the first sign of puberty is testicular enlargement, measured with an orchidometer; absent testicular enlargement by around 14 suggests delayed puberty and warrants assessment.
thinking: 15-year-old boy ↓ No signs of puberty ↓ Need a marker of true pubertal onset ↓ First sign in boys is testicular growth ↓ Testicular enlargement
exam_trap: C, current height and weight centile — growth is linked to puberty, which tempts, but a single centile cannot show pubertal onset; testicular enlargement does.
takeaway: First sign of puberty in boys is testicular enlargement; in girls it is breast budding.

stem: A 7-year-old girl develops breast enlargement and pubic hair. What does this represent?
why_correct: Pubertal development beginning unusually early in childhood is considered precocious puberty and warrants assessment.
why_wrong: A. Premature ovarian insufficiency causes impaired ovarian function rather than early puberty. B. Delayed puberty involves absent or insufficient development beyond the expected age. D. The timing is earlier than expected. E. Menopause occurs after cessation of ovarian function later in life.
pearl: Precocious puberty in girls is usually central and idiopathic, but needs assessment of growth, bone age and the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to exclude an underlying cause.
thinking: 7-year-old girl ↓ Breast enlargement and pubic hair ↓ Pubertal signs earlier than expected ↓ Precocious puberty
exam_trap: D, normal puberty — breast budding then pubic hair is the normal sequence, which tempts, but at 7 this is earlier than expected and needs assessment.
takeaway: Breast development and pubic hair in a 7-year-old girl = precocious puberty; assess.

stem: A 10-month-old has poor weight gain over several months. Height is relatively preserved, but weight has crossed down several centile lines. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Growth charts are unnecessary after infancy
options.B: Failure to gain weight is only significant if the child is below the 0.4th centile
options.E: This is always normal in breastfed infants

correct_answer: D. The weight trajectory requires assessment
why_correct: Crossing down centiles can indicate faltering growth and should prompt assessment of feeding, health and social factors.
why_wrong: A. Growth monitoring remains important during childhood. B. A concerning trajectory can occur before reaching an extreme centile. C. Preserved height does not exclude nutritional or feeding problems. E. Poor weight gain should not automatically be attributed to breastfeeding.
pearl: Faltering growth is judged by weight crossing down centiles, not just a low centile; assess feeding, illness, absorption and psychosocial factors, including observing a feed.
thinking: 10-month-old with poor weight gain ↓ Weight crossing down several centiles ↓ Preserved height suggests a nutritional problem ↓ Faltering growth ↓ Weight trajectory requires assessment
exam_trap: E, always normal in breastfed infants — breastfed babies can follow slightly different patterns, which tempts, but crossing several centiles is never automatically normal.
takeaway: Weight crossing down centiles signals faltering growth and needs assessment.

stem: Which infections are prevented by the MMR vaccine?
why_correct: MMR protects against measles, mumps and rubella.
why_wrong: A. Meningitis and rabies are not components of MMR. C. Diphtheria is not included in MMR. D. Tetanus is not included in MMR. E. Malaria is not vaccine-prevented by MMR.
pearl: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella, given as two doses in the UK schedule; as a live vaccine it is avoided in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression.
thinking: MMR is a combined live vaccine ↓ First M = measles ↓ Second M = mumps ↓ R = rubella ↓ Measles, mumps and rubella
exam_trap: A, measles, meningitis and rabies — meningitis starts with M and sounds like a vaccine target, but MMR covers measles, mumps and rubella only.
takeaway: MMR covers measles, mumps and rubella; it is live, so avoid in pregnancy and immunosuppression.

stem: A previously healthy adolescent develops painful swelling of both parotid glands. Which complication is particularly important in a post-pubertal male?
why_correct: Mumps can cause orchitis, particularly in post-pubertal males.
why_wrong: A. Hirschsprung disease is a congenital disorder of intestinal innervation. B. Appendicitis is unrelated to the characteristic complication of mumps. D. Intussusception is an acute intestinal obstruction in young children. E. Pyloric stenosis presents in early infancy.
pearl: Mumps causes painful parotitis; after puberty, orchitis is the commonest complication in males, usually unilateral, and can occasionally reduce fertility. Mumps is notifiable.
thinking: Painful bilateral parotid swelling ↓ Mumps ↓ Post-pubertal male ↓ Virus can infect the testes ↓ Orchitis
exam_trap: B, appendicitis — mumps can cause pancreatitis, which tempts thoughts of abdominal complications, but appendicitis is unrelated; orchitis is the key complication.
takeaway: Mumps in a post-pubertal male: watch for orchitis.

stem: Which condition is routinely screened for using the newborn blood spot test?
why_correct: Phenylketonuria is included in the UK newborn blood spot screening programme.
why_wrong: A. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is not a newborn screening condition. B. Asthma is not screened for in newborns. D. Type 1 diabetes is not routinely screened for by the newborn blood spot test. E. Appendicitis is diagnosed clinically when suspected.
pearl: The UK newborn blood spot test, usually taken around day 5, screens for conditions including phenylketonuria, congenital hypothyroidism, sickle cell disease and cystic fibrosis.
thinking: Newborn blood spot test ↓ Targets treatable conditions where early detection prevents harm ↓ Untreated PKU causes intellectual disability ↓ Phenylketonuria
exam_trap: D, type 1 diabetes — a serious childhood condition that sounds blood-test based, but it is not part of the newborn blood spot screening programme.
takeaway: Blood spot screening covers PKU, hypothyroidism, sickle cell disease, CF and other metabolic disorders.

stem: Why is congenital hypothyroidism detected through newborn screening?

options.B: To prevent prolonged neonatal jaundice and kernicterus
options.C: To allow early treatment to protect brain development
options.D: To diagnose early-onset neonatal sepsis before symptoms develop
options.E: To identify any associated congenital heart disease early

correct_answer: C. To allow early treatment to protect brain development
why_correct: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism can impair brain development; early treatment substantially reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. It does not prevent asthma. B. Prolonged jaundice can occur in congenital hypothyroidism, but preventing kernicterus is not the purpose of this screening. D. It is not a test for early-onset neonatal sepsis. E. Congenital heart disease is not the target of this screening test.
pearl: Congenital hypothyroidism is often clinically silent at birth; detection by blood spot screening allows early levothyroxine, which prevents the intellectual impairment of untreated disease.
thinking: Congenital hypothyroidism ↓ Few signs at birth ↓ Thyroid hormone is essential for brain development ↓ Early levothyroxine prevents impairment ↓ Early treatment protects brain development
exam_trap: B, to prevent prolonged jaundice and kernicterus — prolonged jaundice is a feature, which tempts, but the goal of screening is protecting neurodevelopment.
takeaway: Screen for congenital hypothyroidism to start levothyroxine early and protect the brain.

stem: A newborn screening test identifies a baby as likely to have sickle cell disease. What is the main reason for early diagnosis?

options.A: To predict whether the baby will develop asthma later on
options.B: To confirm the carrier status of both of the baby's parents
options.C: To start early specialist care to reduce complications
options.D: To arrange early exchange transfusion in the neonatal period
options.E: To diagnose and treat neonatal jaundice at an early stage

correct_answer: C. To start early specialist care to reduce complications
why_correct: Early identification allows appropriate follow-up and preventive management, reducing serious complications.
why_wrong: A. Sickle cell disease screening does not predict asthma. B. Parental carrier testing is not the main reason for early diagnosis of the baby. D. Exchange transfusion is not routine neonatal management; early diagnosis allows prophylaxis and specialist follow-up. E. It is not a jaundice test; early diagnosis allows prophylaxis and specialist follow-up.
pearl: Babies with sickle cell disease identified by screening start penicillin prophylaxis and specialist care early, reducing deaths from pneumococcal infection and splenic sequestration.
thinking: Newborn screen suggests sickle cell disease ↓ High early-childhood risk of overwhelming infection ↓ Prophylaxis and parental education reduce complications ↓ Start early specialist care
exam_trap: B, confirm parental carrier status — parents are offered testing, which tempts, but the main purpose of diagnosing the baby is early care for the baby.
takeaway: Newborn sickle screening allows early penicillin and specialist care, reducing deaths.

stem: Which test is used as part of newborn screening for cystic fibrosis in the UK?
why_correct: Cystic fibrosis is included in the UK newborn blood spot screening programme.
why_wrong: A. Flexible bronchoscopy is invasive and inappropriate for screening. B. Lumbar puncture assesses cerebrospinal fluid. D. Echocardiography assesses the heart. E. Otoacoustic emission testing is newborn hearing screening, not CF screening.
pearl: Cystic fibrosis is screened through the newborn blood spot test by measuring immunoreactive trypsinogen, followed by DNA analysis; a positive screen is confirmed by sweat testing.
thinking: UK newborn CF screening ↓ Part of the blood spot programme ↓ Raised immunoreactive trypsinogen, then genetic testing ↓ Newborn blood spot test
exam_trap: E, otoacoustic emission test — it is also a routine newborn screen, which tempts, but it screens hearing, not cystic fibrosis.
takeaway: CF is screened by blood spot IRT and confirmed with a sweat test.

stem: Which symptom can indicate hypoglycaemia in a newborn?
why_correct: Jitteriness, poor feeding and lethargy can occur with neonatal hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: B. Chronic stridor suggests an airway problem. C. Jaundice has many causes and is not a typical specific sign of hypoglycaemia. D. Clubbing is not a neonatal presentation of hypoglycaemia. E. Joint swelling is unrelated.
pearl: Neonatal hypoglycaemia may be silent or cause jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy, hypotonia, apnoea or seizures; at-risk babies need early feeding and glucose monitoring.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Low glucose deprives the brain of fuel ↓ Sympathetic and neurological irritability ↓ Jitteriness
exam_trap: C, isolated jaundice — very common in newborns, which tempts, but jaundice reflects bilirubin, not glucose; jitteriness is the classic hypoglycaemia sign.
takeaway: Jittery, poorly feeding newborn: check blood glucose.

stem: A very premature infant requires prolonged respiratory support and later develops ongoing oxygen dependency. Which chronic respiratory condition can occur following prematurity?
why_correct: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is a chronic lung condition associated particularly with very premature infants requiring prolonged respiratory support.
why_wrong: B. Silicosis is an occupational lung disease. C. Pulmonary embolism is not the typical chronic complication described. D. Mesothelioma is a malignancy associated with asbestos exposure. E. Congenital lobar emphysema is a developmental malformation, not a consequence of prematurity and prolonged respiratory support.
pearl: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is the chronic lung disease of prematurity, caused by injury to immature lungs from ventilation and oxygen; it shows as an ongoing oxygen requirement.
thinking: Very premature infant ↓ Prolonged respiratory support ↓ Injury to immature developing lungs ↓ Ongoing oxygen dependency ↓ Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
exam_trap: E, congenital lobar emphysema — a neonatal lung disorder, which tempts, but it is a developmental malformation, not a consequence of prematurity and ventilation.
takeaway: Premature baby with ongoing oxygen need after ventilation: bronchopulmonary dysplasia.

stem: A newborn develops intestinal obstruction due to thick, sticky meconium that is difficult to pass. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Meconium ileus is strongly associated with cystic fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. Intussusception usually occurs later in infancy or childhood. C. Hirschsprung disease can cause delayed passage of meconium but is a different mechanism. D. Pyloric stenosis presents with vomiting, typically after the neonatal period. E. Coeliac disease does not cause neonatal meconium ileus.
pearl: Meconium ileus is often the earliest presentation of cystic fibrosis; any newborn with it should be tested for CF, even if newborn screening results are awaited.
thinking: Newborn with intestinal obstruction ↓ Thick, sticky meconium ↓ Viscid secretions from CFTR dysfunction ↓ Meconium ileus ↓ Cystic fibrosis
exam_trap: C, Hirschsprung disease — it also causes delayed meconium and neonatal obstruction, but the problem is aganglionic bowel, not thick, sticky meconium.
takeaway: Meconium ileus means cystic fibrosis until proven otherwise.

stem: A child has recurrent chest infections, poor growth and features suggestive of cystic fibrosis. Which test can help confirm the diagnosis?
why_correct: Measurement of sweat chloride is an established diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. Faecal occult blood testing does not diagnose CF. B. A Mantoux test assesses tuberculosis exposure rather than CF. C. D-dimer assesses coagulation activation. E. Troponin assesses myocardial injury.
pearl: Suspect cystic fibrosis in any child with recurrent chest infections and faltering growth; a raised sweat chloride confirms it, even when newborn screening has already flagged the child.
thinking: Recurrent chest infections ↓ Poor growth suggesting malabsorption ↓ Multisystem picture points to cystic fibrosis ↓ CFTR defect raises chloride in sweat ↓ Sweat chloride test
exam_trap: B, Mantoux test alone — recurrent chest infections with poor growth can suggest tuberculosis, but a Mantoux test only shows TB exposure and says nothing about CF.
takeaway: Chest infections plus faltering growth in a child: think CF and confirm with a sweat test.

stem: A child with croup develops increasing respiratory distress and stridor at rest. What does this indicate?

options.D: Chronic asthma with poor inhaler technique

why_correct: Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway obstruction and requires urgent assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Gastroenteritis with dehydration does not cause stridor. B. Stridor at rest with increasing distress is not normal sleep-related breathing. C. Stridor at rest represents deterioration, not resolution. D. Asthma causes lower-airway wheeze rather than upper-airway stridor, whatever the inhaler technique.
pearl: In croup, stridor at rest, rising work of breathing, agitation or drowsiness signal worsening airway obstruction; this needs urgent hospital treatment with steroids and nebulised adrenaline.
thinking: Child with croup ↓ Stridor now present at rest ↓ Increasing respiratory distress ↓ Upper airway narrowing is worsening ↓ More severe airway obstruction
exam_trap: C, expected resolution of the illness — croup usually settles within days, but stridor at rest with rising distress shows deterioration, not recovery.
takeaway: Stridor at rest in croup means severe obstruction, so escalate urgently.

stem: Which child is most likely to develop bronchiolitis?
why_correct: Bronchiolitis predominantly affects infants, particularly during the first year of life.
why_wrong: B. Bronchiolitis is not the typical diagnosis in an adolescent. C. Same reason. D. Viral-induced wheeze or asthma would be more relevant. E. Bronchiolitis is not typical at this age.
pearl: Bronchiolitis is a viral lower respiratory tract infection, mostly caused by RSV, that mainly affects children under 2, with the peak incidence between 3 and 6 months of age.
thinking: Bronchiolitis is a disease of infancy ↓ Peak age is in the first year of life ↓ Older children with wheeze have other diagnoses ↓ A 3-month-old infant
exam_trap: D, a 10-year-old child — older children do get viral wheeze, but bronchiolitis is defined by infancy and is not the diagnosis at this age.
takeaway: Bronchiolitis affects children under 2, most often in the first months of life.

stem: A 4-month-old with bronchiolitis is breathing rapidly and taking much less milk than usual. What is the principal concern?
why_correct: Infants with bronchiolitis may struggle to feed because of respiratory effort, increasing the risk of dehydration and deterioration.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria. B. Pyloric stenosis presents with projectile vomiting and does not explain the respiratory presentation. C. Acute glaucoma is not relevant. E. Diabetes insipidus causes excessive urination and thirst.
pearl: In bronchiolitis, poor feeding is a key severity marker: an infant breathing hard cannot feed well, so dehydration and respiratory failure can develop together.
thinking: Infant with bronchiolitis ↓ Rapid breathing shows increased work of breathing ↓ Much reduced milk intake ↓ Risk of dehydration and tiring ↓ Dehydration and respiratory deterioration
exam_trap: B, pyloric stenosis with projectile vomiting — it causes feeding problems in young infants, but there is no vomiting here and it does not explain the tachypnoea.
takeaway: In bronchiolitis, reduced feeding plus tachypnoea is a red flag for dehydration and deterioration.

stem: A 5-year-old has fever, cough, tachypnoea and focal crackles on chest examination. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, cough, tachypnoea and focal chest findings strongly support pneumonia.
why_wrong: B. Eczema is a skin disorder. C. Otitis externa causes ear canal symptoms. D. Migraine causes headache and neurological symptoms. E. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms.
pearl: In children, fever with tachypnoea and focal crackles is pneumonia until proven otherwise; raised respiratory rate is among the most useful signs of lower respiratory infection.
thinking: Fever and cough ↓ Tachypnoea shows lower respiratory involvement ↓ Focal crackles localise disease to one area of lung ↓ Pneumonia
exam_trap: C, otitis externa — febrile children often have ear infections, but otitis externa affects the ear canal and cannot explain tachypnoea or chest crackles.
takeaway: Fever, tachypnoea and focal crackles in a child point to pneumonia.

stem: A 3-year-old develops fever, painful mouth ulcers and small vesicular lesions on the hands and feet. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Oral ulcers accompanied by lesions on the hands and feet are characteristic of hand-foot-and-mouth disease.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo causes superficial crusted lesions. B. Scabies causes intensely itchy burrows and papules. C. Scarlet fever causes a diffuse fine sandpaper-like rash and strawberry tongue, not vesicles. D. Erythema nodosum causes tender subcutaneous nodules.
pearl: Hand, foot and mouth disease, usually caused by coxsackievirus, gives mouth ulcers plus vesicles on the hands and feet in young children; it is self-limiting and needs supportive care only.
thinking: Young child with fever ↓ Painful mouth ulcers ↓ Vesicles on the hands and feet ↓ Classic distribution of an enteroviral rash ↓ Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
exam_trap: C, scarlet fever with strawberry tongue — it also causes fever and oral changes, but its rash is fine and sandpaper-like, not vesicular on the hands and feet.
takeaway: Mouth ulcers plus vesicles on hands and feet in a toddler mean hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

stem: A 1-year-old develops vomiting followed by frequent watery diarrhoea. What is the most important immediate clinical assessment?
why_correct: Young children with gastroenteritis can deteriorate rapidly from dehydration, making hydration status a priority.
why_wrong: A. Pubertal stage is irrelevant. B. Hearing assessment is not an acute priority. C. Hip stability is not the immediate concern. E. Visual acuity is unrelated to the acute presentation.
pearl: In infant gastroenteritis the first priority is the hydration assessment: alertness, mucous membranes, skin turgor, capillary refill, urine output and heart rate guide how to rehydrate.
thinking: Infant with vomiting and watery diarrhoea ↓ Young children lose fluid quickly ↓ Dehydration is the main acute danger ↓ Hydration status
exam_trap: C, hip stability — hip checks are part of routine infant examination, but they are irrelevant to an acute illness where fluid loss is the threat.
takeaway: In acute gastroenteritis in a young child, assess hydration first.

stem: A child with mild dehydration from gastroenteritis is alert and able to drink. What is generally the preferred initial approach to rehydration?
why_correct: Oral rehydration solution is effective for children who can drink and is preferred for most mild-to-moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis.
why_wrong: A. Dialysis is not indicated for simple dehydration. B. Blood transfusion is not a treatment for dehydration. C. Parenteral nutrition is unnecessary. E. Antibiotics are not routinely required for uncomplicated gastroenteritis.
pearl: Children with gastroenteritis who are alert and able to drink should be rehydrated with oral rehydration solution; IV fluids are kept for shock, red-flag signs or failure of oral rehydration.
thinking: Gastroenteritis with mild dehydration ↓ Child is alert ↓ Child is able to drink ↓ Oral route is effective and safest ↓ Oral rehydration solution
exam_trap: E, intramuscular antibiotics — infection causes the illness, but most gastroenteritis is viral and antibiotics do nothing to correct dehydration.
takeaway: Alert child who can drink with mild dehydration: oral rehydration solution first.

stem: A 3-year-old with diarrhoea develops marked lethargy, sunken eyes and very reduced urine output. What does this suggest?
why_correct: Marked lethargy, sunken eyes and reduced urine output are concerning features of significant dehydration.
why_wrong: B. Migraine does not explain reduced urine output and dehydration signs. C. The clinical signs indicate more than mild dehydration. D. Otitis externa does not explain the systemic features. E. Hay fever does not cause these findings.
pearl: Lethargy, sunken eyes and markedly reduced urine output in a child with diarrhoea are red-flag signs of significant dehydration and need urgent assessment for shock and fluid replacement.
thinking: Child with diarrhoea ↓ Marked lethargy shows altered responsiveness ↓ Sunken eyes and low urine output show fluid loss ↓ Significant dehydration
exam_trap: C, mild gastroenteritis without dehydration — diarrhoea fits gastroenteritis, but lethargy, sunken eyes and oliguria show the dehydration is significant.
takeaway: Lethargy, sunken eyes and oliguria in diarrhoea mean significant dehydration.

stem: At approximately what age would a normally developing infant usually be expected to sit without support?
why_correct: Sitting without support is generally achieved around 6 months.
why_wrong: A. Too early for independent sitting. B. Some infants may sit with support, but independent sitting is usually later. D. Most infants should achieve this well before 12 months. E. This would be significantly delayed.
pearl: Most infants sit without support at around 6 months; failure to sit unsupported by about 9 months is a gross motor red flag that needs developmental assessment.
thinking: Gross motor milestone ↓ Head control comes first, then sitting with support ↓ Independent sitting follows ↓ Achieved at around 6 months
exam_trap: B, 4 months — infants may sit propped or with support at this age, but sitting without support usually comes later, at around 6 months.
takeaway: Independent sitting is expected at around 6 months.

stem: At approximately what age do most children begin to walk independently?
why_correct: Independent walking is commonly achieved around 12–15 months.
why_wrong: A. Far too early. B. Most infants are not independently walking at this age. C. Some may walk at 9 months, but this is earlier than usual. E. This is well beyond the normal range; inability to walk by 18 months warrants assessment.
pearl: Most children walk independently at around 12–15 months; a child not walking by 18 months needs assessment, including checking creatine kinase in boys to look for muscular dystrophy.
thinking: Gross motor milestone ↓ Sitting, then crawling and cruising ↓ Independent walking follows ↓ Usually 12–15 months
exam_trap: C, 9 months — some infants walk this early, which makes it tempting, but it is earlier than usual and is not the typical age.
takeaway: Independent walking typically starts at 12–15 months; not walking by 18 months needs review.

stem: At approximately what age does a child commonly begin saying meaningful single words?
why_correct: Meaningful single words commonly emerge around the end of the first year.
why_wrong: A. Too early. B. Single words should have developed much earlier. C. Babbling may occur, but meaningful words are usually later. E. Two-word phrases are more typical around this stage.
pearl: Meaningful single words usually appear at around 12 months, after babbling; two-word phrases follow at around 2 years. Concern about speech delay should always prompt a hearing test.
thinking: Speech milestone question ↓ Babbling comes in the middle of the first year ↓ First meaningful words come at the end of the first year ↓ 12 months
exam_trap: C, 6 months — babbling such as 'ba-ba' appears around then and can sound like words, but it is not meaningful speech.
takeaway: First meaningful words at about 12 months; two-word phrases at about 2 years.

stem: A normally developing 2-year-old should generally be beginning to combine words into simple phrases. Which example best demonstrates this?
why_correct: Combining two meaningful words is an expected language milestone around 2 years.
why_wrong: B. Lack of vocalisation at this age is concerning. C. Repeated sounds are more characteristic of earlier development. D. This is not a meaningful two-word phrase. E. A single word is less advanced than a two-word phrase.
pearl: By about 2 years a child should join two meaningful words, such as 'Mummy gone'; no word combinations at this age is a language red flag and needs hearing and developmental review.
thinking: Expected milestone at 2 years ↓ Two meaningful words combined ↓ Babble and single sounds are earlier stages ↓ 'Mummy gone'
exam_trap: C, 'Ba-ba' — it sounds like early speech, but it is repetitive babble from the first year, not two meaningful words joined together.
takeaway: Two-word phrases such as 'Mummy gone' are expected at around 2 years.

stem: A 4-month-old infant does not smile responsively at parents or carers. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.B: It is normal until 6 months of age

why_correct: Absence of expected social interaction such as responsive smiling can be a developmental red flag and warrants assessment.
why_wrong: A. One developmental finding cannot establish autism. B. Responsive smiling is expected by about 6–8 weeks, so its absence at 4 months is not normal. D. Hearing impairment is one possible consideration but is not established by this finding alone. E. It does not indicate cerebral palsy.
pearl: Responsive (social) smiling is expected by about 6–8 weeks; its absence at 4 months is a red flag needing developmental assessment, including vision and hearing, without jumping to a diagnosis.
thinking: Social smiling is expected by 6–8 weeks ↓ Infant is now 4 months old ↓ Milestone is clearly missed ↓ Cause not yet known ↓ It needs developmental assessment
exam_trap: A, it indicates autism spectrum disorder — poor social responsiveness raises the idea, but one missed milestone cannot establish any single diagnosis.
takeaway: No responsive smile at 4 months is a red flag that needs developmental assessment, not a label.

stem: A toddler who previously used several words stops using them and becomes less socially interactive. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Wait until the child starts school

why_correct: Regression of previously acquired skills is a significant developmental concern requiring assessment.
why_wrong: A. Assessment should not be unnecessarily delayed. B. Treatment should follow appropriate assessment of the cause. C. Antibiotics have no role without evidence of bacterial infection. E. Regression should not be dismissed.
pearl: Loss of previously acquired skills, such as words or social interaction, is always a red flag in child development and needs prompt specialist assessment, never reassurance.
thinking: Toddler had several words ↓ Words now lost ↓ Social interaction also reduced ↓ This is regression, not delay ↓ Arrange prompt developmental assessment
exam_trap: E, reassure the parents — language develops at different rates, but losing skills already gained is never normal variation.
takeaway: Developmental regression at any age needs prompt assessment.

stem: A 3-year-old has a persistent inward deviation of one eye. Why is timely assessment important?
why_correct: Persistent childhood strabismus can interfere with normal visual development and lead to amblyopia.
why_wrong: A. It does not directly cause scoliosis. B. There is no relationship with appendicitis. C. It does not cause otitis externa. E. Strabismus does not cause asthma.
pearl: A persistent squint in a child needs prompt orthoptic and ophthalmology assessment, because the brain suppresses the deviating eye's image and amblyopia can become permanent if treated late.
thinking: Persistent inward deviation of one eye ↓ Squint in a young child ↓ Brain suppresses the image from the deviating eye ↓ Visual development is still plastic ↓ To prevent amblyopia
exam_trap: A, to prevent scoliosis — a head tilt can accompany some squints, but a squint does not cause spinal deformity; the risk is lasting visual loss.
takeaway: Any persistent squint in a child needs prompt referral to prevent amblyopia.

stem: A child has reduced visual acuity in one eye despite having an otherwise normal-looking eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Amblyopia is reduced vision due to abnormal visual development, often associated with strabismus or unequal refractive error.
why_wrong: A. Amblyopia does not require a visible cataract. B. Retinal detachment is uncommon in this typical childhood presentation. C. Optic neuritis is an inflammatory optic nerve disorder. E. Acute glaucoma presents differently.
