pearl: Amblyopia is reduced vision in a structurally normal eye due to abnormal visual development, usually from squint or unequal refraction; it is treated by glasses and patching while the visual system is still developing.
thinking: Child with reduced acuity in one eye ↓ The eye looks normal ↓ No structural disease to explain it ↓ Abnormal visual development ↓ Amblyopia
exam_trap: A, cataract in every case — cataract does cause reduced vision in childhood, but the eye here looks normal and amblyopia needs no visible abnormality.
takeaway: Reduced vision in one normal-looking eye in a child suggests amblyopia.

stem: A parent notices a white reflection from their child's pupil in photographs. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: It is usually a flash artefact needing no action
options.B: It needs a routine optician review in 6 months

correct_answer: E. It needs urgent ophthalmology referral
why_correct: Leukocoria can indicate serious intraocular disease, including retinoblastoma, and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. A white pupil reflex should not be assumed to be an artefact, as it can indicate retinoblastoma. B. Routine review causes unsafe delay; urgent referral is needed. C. Conjunctivitis does not characteristically cause leukocoria. D. Myopia does not cause a white pupillary reflex.
pearl: A white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in a child must be referred urgently to ophthalmology because it can be retinoblastoma; never dismiss it as a camera artefact.
thinking: White reflection from the pupil in photos ↓ This is leukocoria ↓ Retinoblastoma must be excluded ↓ Serious and time-critical ↓ It needs urgent ophthalmology referral
exam_trap: A, flash artefact needing no action — photos can give odd reflections, but a white reflex must be treated as retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Leukocoria in a child means urgent referral to exclude retinoblastoma.

stem: A newborn is found to have a dense opacity of the lens. What is the main concern?
why_correct: Congenital cataracts can interfere with visual development and require timely specialist management.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus is unrelated. B. Hearing loss is not an inevitable consequence. C. Nephrotic syndrome is unrelated. D. There is no relationship with appendicitis.
pearl: A dense congenital cataract blocks the visual pathway during a critical period, so it needs early specialist surgery to prevent permanent amblyopia; the red reflex check at newborn examination detects it.
thinking: Newborn with dense lens opacity ↓ Light cannot reach the retina normally ↓ Visual development needs clear input early in life ↓ Impaired visual development
exam_trap: B, hearing loss in every case — some causes such as congenital rubella link cataract and deafness, but hearing loss is not inevitable; the core risk is to vision.
takeaway: Congenital cataract threatens visual development and needs early specialist care.

stem: A newborn has excessive tearing, marked sensitivity to light and enlarged cloudy corneas. Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Congenital glaucoma can present with tearing, photophobia and enlarged or cloudy corneas.
why_wrong: B. Conjunctivitis does not typically cause enlarged cloudy corneas. C. Amblyopia does not produce these ocular signs. D. Myopia does not cause this presentation. E. Otitis media is unrelated.
pearl: Congenital glaucoma presents with watering eyes, photophobia and large, cloudy corneas (buphthalmos); it needs urgent ophthalmology referral because raised pressure damages the optic nerve.
thinking: Newborn with excessive tearing ↓ Photophobia ↓ Enlarged cloudy corneas ↓ Raised intraocular pressure stretching the infant eye ↓ Congenital glaucoma
exam_trap: B, conjunctivitis — watering eyes in a newborn often prompt this diagnosis, but conjunctivitis does not cause enlarged cloudy corneas or marked photophobia.
takeaway: Watering, photophobia and large cloudy corneas in a baby suggest congenital glaucoma.

stem: A child develops persistent headaches with vomiting and new visual disturbance. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Diagnose migraine and start regular simple analgesia
options.B: Urgent assessment for raised intracranial pressure
options.C: Routine optician review for the visual symptoms only
options.D: Diagnose tension-type headache without a full examination
options.E: Treat with antihistamines for presumed allergic rhinitis

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment for raised intracranial pressure
why_correct: Headache with vomiting and new visual disturbance can indicate raised intracranial pressure and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Migraine should not be assumed in the presence of red-flag features. C. Routine review delays assessment of a potentially serious cause. D. A serious secondary cause must first be considered. E. Antihistamines for presumed rhinitis do not address possible intracranial pathology.
pearl: Headache with vomiting and new visual disturbance in a child are red flags for raised intracranial pressure, such as from a brain tumour, and need urgent assessment including fundoscopy and imaging.
thinking: Persistent headaches in a child ↓ Vomiting ↓ New visual disturbance ↓ Red flags for a space-occupying lesion ↓ Urgent assessment for raised intracranial pressure
exam_trap: A, diagnose migraine and start simple analgesia — migraine is the commonest cause of headache in children, but red flags must be investigated first.
takeaway: Headache plus vomiting plus visual change in a child: assess urgently for raised ICP.

stem: A teenager with a restrictive eating disorder becomes faint and has marked bradycardia. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.C: An expected athletic adaptation needing no action
options.E: Simple dehydration managed with oral fluids at home

correct_answer: D. Medical instability needing urgent assessment
why_correct: Significant bradycardia and syncope in an adolescent with an eating disorder can indicate serious physiological compromise.
why_wrong: A. Asthma does not explain marked bradycardia and syncope. B. There is insufficient evidence for epilepsy. C. Marked bradycardia with syncope in an eating disorder should not be attributed to fitness and can be medically serious. E. Dehydration may contribute, but oral fluids at home do not address possible medical instability.
pearl: In restrictive eating disorders, marked bradycardia, syncope, hypotension or electrolyte disturbance mean medical instability; these patients need urgent medical assessment and may need admission.
thinking: Teenager with restrictive eating disorder ↓ Faintness ↓ Marked bradycardia ↓ Signs of physiological compromise from starvation ↓ Medical instability needing urgent assessment
exam_trap: C, athletic adaptation needing no action — fit young people can have a slow pulse, but bradycardia with syncope in an eating disorder is dangerous.
takeaway: Bradycardia with fainting in an eating disorder means medical instability: assess urgently.

stem: A 15-year-old has never menstruated but has normal breast development and normal height. What is this termed?
why_correct: Primary amenorrhoea refers to failure to have the first menstrual period by the expected age.
why_wrong: A. Menorrhagia refers to heavy menstrual bleeding. C. Dysmenorrhoea means painful periods. D. Menopause occurs after established reproductive function later in life. E. Secondary amenorrhoea occurs when menstruation has previously occurred and then stops.
pearl: Primary amenorrhoea means periods have never started; with normal secondary sexual characteristics it is usually investigated from around age 15, looking for outflow, ovarian and pituitary causes.
thinking: 15-year-old ↓ Has never menstruated ↓ Normal breast development and height ↓ No prior periods to lose ↓ Primary amenorrhoea
exam_trap: E, secondary amenorrhoea — both describe absent periods, but secondary means periods have started and then stopped; here they never began.
takeaway: Never menstruated means primary amenorrhoea; periods that stopped mean secondary.

stem: A 16-year-old experiences cramping lower abdominal pain during the first two days of otherwise regular periods. There are no other symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Cramping menstrual pain without features suggesting another pelvic disorder is typical of primary dysmenorrhoea.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis is a possible cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea but is not established here. C. PID usually causes pelvic pain with other infectious features. D. Ovarian torsion causes acute severe pelvic pain rather than predictable menstrual cramps. E. Ectopic pregnancy would require pregnancy to be possible and has a different presentation.
pearl: Primary dysmenorrhoea is cramping lower abdominal pain starting with menstruation in young people with otherwise normal periods; NSAIDs are first-line, and red flags suggest a secondary cause.
thinking: 16-year-old with regular periods ↓ Cramping pain in the first days of bleeding ↓ No other symptoms or red flags ↓ No underlying pelvic disease suggested ↓ Primary dysmenorrhoea
exam_trap: A, endometriosis in every case — it causes painful periods, but with no other features it is not established and simple cramps are far more common.
takeaway: Predictable period cramps with no other features mean primary dysmenorrhoea.

stem: A 14-year-old demonstrates a clear understanding of the nature, benefits, risks and alternatives of a proposed treatment. What concept is most relevant?

options.C: Mental capacity assessment for an adult

why_correct: Gillick competence concerns whether a child under 16 has sufficient understanding and intelligence to consent to a particular medical intervention.
why_wrong: A. DNACPR concerns cardiopulmonary resuscitation. B. An advance decision is not the relevant concept. C. Adult mental capacity legislation is not the defining concept here. D. A lasting power of attorney is a different legal mechanism.
pearl: A young person under 16 who fully understands the nature, benefits, risks and alternatives of a treatment can be Gillick competent to consent to it; competence is decision-specific.
thinking: 14-year-old patient ↓ Under 16 so adult capacity law is not the defining test ↓ Shows full understanding of the treatment ↓ Can consent if mature enough ↓ Gillick competence
exam_trap: C, mental capacity assessment for an adult — understanding is also central there, but the key concept for consent under 16 is Gillick competence.
takeaway: Under 16 with full understanding of a treatment: think Gillick competence.

stem: A 4-month-old infant is brought with a large unexplained bruise. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Discharge with advice if the infant is otherwise well
options.C: Reassure the parents that bruising is normal
options.E: Assess as a possible safeguarding concern

correct_answer: E. Assess as a possible safeguarding concern
why_correct: Bruising is unusual in a non-mobile infant and requires careful assessment, including consideration of safeguarding.
why_wrong: A. A well appearance does not exclude a safeguarding concern. B. Bleeding disorders are a differential diagnosis, not an automatic diagnosis. C. Bruising is not considered routine in a non-mobile infant. D. A non-mobile infant cannot normally sustain a fall independently.
pearl: Bruising in a non-mobile infant is rare and must be treated as a possible safeguarding concern: take a full history, examine fully and follow local child protection procedures.
thinking: 4-month-old infant ↓ Not yet mobile ↓ Large unexplained bruise ↓ Bruising in non-mobile infants is rarely accidental ↓ Assess as a possible safeguarding concern
exam_trap: A, discharge with advice if well — a well-looking infant can seem reassuring, but appearance never excludes abuse in a non-mobile baby with bruising.
takeaway: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant needs safeguarding assessment.

stem: A child presents with a significant injury. The explanation given by the carer is inconsistent with the child's developmental abilities and the physical findings. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Record the explanation and review at the next visit
options.D: Tell the child they are responsible
options.E: Discharge once the injury has been treated

correct_answer: C. Consider safeguarding and arrange assessment
why_correct: An inconsistent history that does not fit the child's developmental abilities or injuries is a safeguarding red flag.
why_wrong: A. Deferring action until a later visit may leave the child at risk. B. The inconsistency requires further assessment. D. Blaming the child is inappropriate. E. Discharge without safeguarding assessment may place the child at risk.
pearl: An injury that does not match the stated mechanism or the child's developmental stage is a key safeguarding red flag; document carefully and act on it the same day.
thinking: Significant injury in a child ↓ Carer's explanation is inconsistent ↓ Does not fit developmental ability or findings ↓ Red flag for non-accidental injury ↓ Consider safeguarding and arrange assessment
exam_trap: A, record and review at the next visit — documentation matters, but delaying action can leave the child at continued risk of harm.
takeaway: An injury that does not fit the history or development: act on safeguarding now.

stem: A young child has an unexplained metaphyseal fracture. Why is this finding important?

options.A: It most often reflects osteogenesis imperfecta
options.B: It is a common accidental toddler injury
options.D: It is usually caused by vitamin D deficiency

correct_answer: E. It may indicate non-accidental injury
why_correct: Certain fracture patterns, including metaphyseal injuries in young children, can raise significant safeguarding concerns.
why_wrong: A. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a differential but not the most common explanation. B. Metaphyseal fractures are not typical accidental injuries in young children. C. It raises rather than lowers concern about abuse. D. Vitamin D deficiency is only one possible differential.
pearl: Metaphyseal (corner or bucket-handle) fractures in young children are highly specific for non-accidental injury from shaking or twisting forces and should trigger safeguarding assessment.
thinking: Young child ↓ Metaphyseal fracture ↓ No explanation given ↓ Pattern linked to shaking or twisting forces ↓ It may indicate non-accidental injury
exam_trap: A, mostly osteogenesis imperfecta — bone fragility is a real differential to exclude, but it is far less common than abuse in this situation.
takeaway: Unexplained metaphyseal fractures in young children raise concern for abuse.

stem: A child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis requires regular ophthalmological monitoring. What complication is particularly important?
why_correct: JIA can be associated with chronic anterior uveitis, which may be asymptomatic and therefore requires screening.
why_wrong: A. Simple conjunctivitis is not the important JIA-associated ocular disease. B. Cataract can occur secondary to inflammation or treatment but is not the primary screening concern. C. Retinal detachment is not the characteristic complication. E. Acute glaucoma is not the typical complication.
pearl: JIA, especially the oligoarticular ANA-positive type, can cause chronic anterior uveitis that is often painless and silent, so children need regular slit-lamp screening.
thinking: Child with JIA ↓ Regular eye checks are needed ↓ Uveitis linked to JIA may cause no symptoms ↓ Can cause lasting visual damage if missed ↓ Uveitis
exam_trap: B, cataract from trauma — cataract can occur in JIA, but as a result of uveitis or steroids, not trauma; uveitis is the condition screening aims to find.
takeaway: Children with JIA need regular eye screening for silent uveitis.

stem: A child with IgA vasculitis develops colicky abdominal pain and vomiting. Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: IgA vasculitis can cause bowel-wall oedema and is associated with intussusception.
why_wrong: A. Hirschsprung disease is congenital and presents much earlier. C. Appendicitis is not the characteristic complication of IgA vasculitis. D. Coeliac disease causes chronic gastrointestinal symptoms rather than this acute complication. E. Pyloric stenosis typically affects young infants.
pearl: In IgA vasculitis, colicky abdominal pain with vomiting should prompt consideration of intussusception, which is usually ileo-ileal and best assessed with ultrasound.
thinking: Child with IgA vasculitis ↓ Vasculitis can cause bowel wall oedema ↓ Colicky abdominal pain with vomiting ↓ Suggests telescoping bowel ↓ Intussusception
exam_trap: C, appendicitis in every case — abdominal pain and vomiting suggest it, but colicky pain in IgA vasculitis characteristically points to intussusception.
takeaway: Colicky abdominal pain in IgA vasculitis: consider intussusception.

stem: A child has IgA vasculitis with purpura and abdominal pain but initially normal renal function. What complication should still be monitored for?
why_correct: IgA vasculitis can cause renal involvement, including haematuria and proteinuria, which may develop after the initial presentation.
why_wrong: B. Asthma is unrelated. C. Congenital heart disease is unrelated. D. Pyloric stenosis is unrelated. E. Cataracts are not a characteristic complication.
pearl: Renal involvement in IgA vasculitis can appear weeks after the rash, so children need follow-up urinalysis and blood pressure checks even when initial renal function is normal.
thinking: Child with IgA vasculitis ↓ Purpura and abdominal pain ↓ Kidneys normal at first ↓ Nephritis can develop later ↓ Renal involvement
exam_trap: D, pyloric stenosis — it is a gastrointestinal condition that may come to mind with abdominal pain, but it is a disease of young infants and unrelated to vasculitis.
takeaway: Monitor urine and blood pressure in IgA vasculitis even if kidneys start normal.

stem: A child is suspected of having Kawasaki disease. What is the key reason for prompt treatment?

options.A: To prevent long-term rheumatic valve disease
options.B: To reduce the risk of coronary aneurysms
options.C: To prevent appendicitis from mesenteric adenitis
options.D: To prevent cerebral palsy from febrile seizures
options.E: To prevent later development of childhood asthma

correct_answer: B. To reduce the risk of coronary aneurysms
why_correct: Kawasaki disease can cause coronary artery abnormalities, and prompt treatment reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatic valve disease follows group A streptococcal infection, not Kawasaki disease. C. Kawasaki disease does not cause appendicitis, and preventing it is not the aim of treatment. D. It is not a cause of cerebral palsy, and preventing this is not the aim of treatment. E. It does not cause asthma later in childhood.
pearl: Kawasaki disease can cause coronary artery aneurysms; prompt IV immunoglobulin and aspirin reduce this risk, and echocardiography is needed to assess the coronary arteries.
thinking: Suspected Kawasaki disease ↓ Medium-vessel vasculitis ↓ Coronary arteries can be involved ↓ Early IV immunoglobulin lowers aneurysm risk ↓ To reduce the risk of coronary aneurysms
exam_trap: A, to prevent rheumatic valve disease — both are childhood febrile conditions with heart effects, but rheumatic heart disease follows streptococcal infection.
takeaway: Treat Kawasaki disease promptly to protect the coronary arteries.

stem: A patient with suspected appendicitis experiences right iliac fossa pain when the left iliac fossa is palpated. What is this finding called?
why_correct: Rovsing sign is pain in the right lower quadrant elicited by palpation of the left lower quadrant.
why_wrong: A. Kernig sign is associated with meningeal irritation. C. Murphy sign is associated with acute cholecystitis. D. Tinel sign is associated with nerve irritation, such as carpal tunnel syndrome. E. Babinski sign assesses the plantar response.
pearl: Rovsing sign is pain in the right iliac fossa on palpating the left iliac fossa; it supports appendicitis but no single sign confirms or excludes it.
thinking: Suspected appendicitis ↓ Palpation of the left iliac fossa ↓ Pain felt in the right iliac fossa ↓ Rovsing sign
exam_trap: C, Murphy sign — it is also an abdominal examination sign, but it is pain-induced arrest of inspiration under the right costal margin, pointing to cholecystitis.
takeaway: Left-sided pressure causing right iliac fossa pain is Rovsing sign.

stem: An older adult develops progressive abdominal distension, constipation and vomiting. What underlying cause should be considered?
why_correct: Colorectal cancer is an important cause of large bowel obstruction, particularly in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause mechanical bowel obstruction. B. Conjunctivitis is unrelated. C. Asthma is unrelated. E. IBS does not cause progressive distension with vomiting in an older adult, and new symptoms at this age require exclusion of malignancy.
pearl: Progressive distension, constipation and vomiting in an older adult suggest large bowel obstruction, and colorectal cancer is the leading cause; urgent CT of abdomen and pelvis is the usual first imaging.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Progressive abdominal distension ↓ Constipation then vomiting ↓ Picture of large bowel obstruction ↓ Colorectal cancer
exam_trap: E, irritable bowel syndrome — it causes bloating and altered bowel habit, but new progressive obstructive symptoms in older age demand exclusion of cancer.
takeaway: New obstructive bowel symptoms in an older adult: exclude colorectal cancer.

stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of left-sided abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habit but no systemic inflammatory features. What condition may explain these symptoms?
why_correct: Diverticular disease can cause intermittent abdominal symptoms and altered bowel habit without the systemic features of acute diverticulitis.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis is usually an acute inflammatory presentation. C. Acute mesenteric ischaemia causes severe acute pain out of proportion to signs, not recurrent mild symptoms. D. Cholangitis causes systemic illness and biliary symptoms. E. Meningitis causes neurological/systemic features.
pearl: Symptomatic diverticular disease causes intermittent left lower abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habit without fever or raised inflammatory markers, unlike acute diverticulitis.
thinking: Recurrent left-sided abdominal discomfort ↓ Altered bowel habit ↓ No systemic inflammation ↓ Chronic symptoms rather than acute infection ↓ Diverticular disease
exam_trap: C, acute mesenteric ischaemia — it causes abdominal pain, but it is sudden and severe, out of proportion to signs, not recurrent mild discomfort.
takeaway: Recurrent left-sided pain and altered bowel habit without fever suggest diverticular disease.

stem: A patient reports that food initially sticks behind the sternum. What symptom is this?
why_correct: A sensation of food sticking after swallowing, particularly behind the sternum, suggests oesophageal dysphagia.
why_wrong: A. Oropharyngeal dysphagia causes difficulty initiating a swallow, often with coughing, rather than food sticking behind the sternum. B. Odynophagia is pain on swallowing, not a sensation of food sticking. C. Dyspnoea means breathlessness. D. Expressive dysphasia means impaired language production.
pearl: Food sticking behind the sternum after swallowing is oesophageal dysphagia; new dysphagia is a red flag and usually warrants urgent upper GI endoscopy to exclude cancer.
thinking: Food sticks after swallowing ↓ Felt behind the sternum ↓ Problem is beyond the pharynx ↓ Oesophageal dysphagia
exam_trap: A, oropharyngeal dysphagia — both involve swallowing difficulty, but oropharyngeal dysphagia affects starting the swallow, often with coughing or choking.
takeaway: Food sticking behind the sternum means oesophageal dysphagia.

stem: A patient passes a large amount of bright red blood per rectum. Which term describes this?
why_correct: Haematochezia refers to the passage of fresh or bright red blood per rectum.
why_wrong: A. Dyspepsia describes upper gastrointestinal discomfort. B. Steatorrhoea refers to fatty stools. C. Haematemesis is vomiting blood. E. Melaena refers to black, tarry stool.
pearl: Haematochezia is fresh red blood per rectum, usually from a lower GI source; a brisk upper GI bleed can also cause it, so check haemodynamic stability.
thinking: Passage of blood per rectum ↓ Blood is bright red ↓ Fresh rather than digested, altered blood ↓ Haematochezia
exam_trap: E, melaena — both describe blood passed rectally, but melaena is black, tarry stool from digested blood, usually from an upper GI source.
takeaway: Bright red rectal blood is haematochezia; black tarry stool is melaena.

stem: A patient with psoriasis develops multiple small pits in the fingernails. What is this finding called?
why_correct: Nail pitting is a recognised manifestation of psoriasis.
why_wrong: A. Koilonychia refers to spoon-shaped nails. B. Beau lines are transverse depressions caused by interruption of nail growth. C. Clubbing is enlargement of the distal digits and nail curvature. E. Trauma can cause nail changes but does not explain classic multiple pits associated with psoriasis.
pearl: Nail pitting is a classic sign of psoriasis, often with onycholysis and subungual hyperkeratosis; nail disease is linked with a higher risk of psoriatic arthritis.
thinking: Patient with known psoriasis ↓ New nail changes ↓ Multiple small pits on the nail plate surface ↓ Nail pitting
exam_trap: E, onycholysis due to trauma — onycholysis does occur in psoriasis, but it is separation of the nail plate, not small pits, and trauma adds nothing here.
takeaway: Small pits in the nails of a patient with psoriasis are psoriatic nail pitting.

stem: A patient reports that a longstanding mole has recently increased in size and developed irregular colour and shape. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.C: It can be safely monitored if painless
options.D: It is a benign change associated with age
options.E: It is typical of a wart

correct_answer: B. It needs assessment for melanoma
why_correct: A changing pigmented lesion, particularly with changes in size, colour or shape, is a warning sign requiring assessment.
why_wrong: A. A changing mole with irregular colour and shape should not be assumed to be a seborrhoeic keratosis. C. Melanoma is often painless, and monitoring delays diagnosis. D. A changing lesion should not be assumed to be benign age-related change. E. Warts have a different appearance.
pearl: A mole that changes in size, shape or colour is the most important warning sign of melanoma and needs urgent assessment on a suspected cancer pathway, not watchful waiting.
thinking: Longstanding mole ↓ Recently increasing in size ↓ Irregular colour and shape ↓ Change is the key warning sign ↓ It needs assessment for melanoma
exam_trap: C, safely monitored if painless — absence of pain feels reassuring, but melanoma is usually painless and delay worsens the prognosis.
takeaway: A changing mole needs urgent assessment for melanoma, even if painless.

stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes has peripheral neuropathy and develops a painless ulcer beneath the first metatarsal head. What is the most likely explanation?

options.C: Acute gout of the first MTP

why_correct: Loss of protective sensation and repetitive pressure can produce painless ulcers on weight-bearing areas in diabetes.
why_wrong: B. Venous ulcers typically occur around the medial gaiter region, not the forefoot. C. Gout causes painful inflammatory arthritis. D. Melanoma is not the typical cause of a plantar pressure ulcer. E. Cellulitis may coexist but does not explain the characteristic painless pressure ulcer.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathic ulcers form painlessly over pressure points such as the metatarsal heads; patients need urgent multidisciplinary foot care, offloading and assessment for infection and ischaemia.
thinking: Longstanding diabetes ↓ Peripheral neuropathy so no protective sensation ↓ Painless ulcer ↓ Under a weight-bearing pressure point ↓ Neuropathic foot ulcer
exam_trap: E, cellulitis of the forefoot — infection often complicates diabetic foot ulcers, but cellulitis does not explain a painless ulcer at a pressure point.
takeaway: Painless ulcer over a pressure point in diabetes with neuropathy is neuropathic.

stem: Which feature helps distinguish folate deficiency from vitamin B12 deficiency?

options.A: Folate deficiency causes a marked reactive thrombocytosis
options.C: Folate deficiency causes a microcytic hypochromic anaemia
options.D: Folate deficiency seldom causes neurological features
options.E: Folate deficiency causes raised methylmalonic acid levels

correct_answer: D. Folate deficiency seldom causes neurological features
why_correct: Both deficiencies can cause megaloblastic anaemia, but neurological manifestations are characteristic of vitamin B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Thrombocytosis is not the characteristic finding. B. It causes anaemia rather than polycythaemia. C. Folate deficiency causes macrocytic/megaloblastic anaemia. E. Raised methylmalonic acid is characteristic of B12 deficiency and is typically normal in folate deficiency.
pearl: Both B12 and folate deficiency cause megaloblastic anaemia, but neurological features point to B12 deficiency; check B12 and give replacement before folic acid when B12 status is unknown.
thinking: Both cause megaloblastic anaemia ↓ Need a feature that separates them ↓ B12 is needed for nerve function ↓ Folate deficiency spares the nervous system ↓ Folate deficiency seldom causes neurological features
exam_trap: E, raised methylmalonic acid — it is a real distinguishing test, but it is raised in B12 deficiency and typically normal in folate deficiency.
takeaway: Neurological features suggest B12, not folate, deficiency.

stem: A patient has vitamin B12 deficiency due to autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells. What is the underlying diagnosis?
why_correct: Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune cause of vitamin B12 deficiency due to impaired intrinsic-factor-mediated absorption.
why_wrong: A. Thalassaemia is an inherited haemoglobin disorder. B. Iron deficiency results from depleted iron stores. D. Sickle cell disease is an inherited haemoglobinopathy. E. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolytic anaemia.
pearl: Pernicious anaemia is autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, causing loss of intrinsic factor and B12 malabsorption; intrinsic factor antibodies support the diagnosis.
thinking: Vitamin B12 deficiency ↓ Autoimmune attack on gastric parietal cells ↓ Loss of intrinsic factor ↓ B12 cannot be absorbed ↓ Pernicious anaemia
exam_trap: B, iron deficiency anaemia — atrophic gastritis can also impair iron absorption, but the stem names B12 deficiency, which defines pernicious anaemia.
takeaway: Autoimmune parietal cell loss causing B12 deficiency is pernicious anaemia.

stem: A patient with longstanding inflammatory disease has anaemia. Which pattern is most consistent with anaemia of chronic disease?

options.A: Macrocytosis caused by vitamin B12 deficiency
options.B: Low ferritin with severe iron depletion
options.D: Low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin

correct_answer: D. Low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin
why_correct: Inflammation increases hepcidin, reducing circulating iron while iron stores are often preserved or increased.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 deficiency is a separate cause of macrocytic anaemia. B. Low ferritin is characteristic of iron deficiency. C. Anaemia means haemoglobin is reduced. E. Increased B12 does not explain the typical pattern.
pearl: In anaemia of chronic disease, inflammation raises hepcidin, trapping iron in stores; serum iron is low but ferritin is normal or high, unlike iron deficiency.
thinking: Longstanding inflammatory disease ↓ Inflammation raises hepcidin ↓ Iron trapped in stores ↓ Serum iron falls, stores preserved ↓ Low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin
exam_trap: B, low ferritin with severe iron depletion — both share low serum iron, but low ferritin means absent stores, which defines iron deficiency.
takeaway: Low iron with normal or high ferritin suggests anaemia of chronic disease.

stem: A young adult has painless cervical lymphadenopathy. Which diagnosis is an important consideration?
why_correct: Painless lymphadenopathy, particularly in the cervical region of a young adult, is a classic presentation of Hodgkin lymphoma.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency causes anaemia rather than lymphadenopathy. C. Tinea pedis causes a superficial fungal infection of the feet. D. Osteoarthritis affects joints. E. Migraine does not cause persistent lymphadenopathy.
pearl: Hodgkin lymphoma typically presents in young adults with painless cervical lymphadenopathy; persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy needs urgent assessment for lymphoma.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Painless lymph nodes ↓ Cervical region ↓ Classic age and site for lymphoma ↓ Hodgkin lymphoma
exam_trap: A, iron deficiency anaemia — anaemia can accompany lymphoma, but iron deficiency itself never causes lymphadenopathy.
takeaway: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy in a young adult: consider Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: Which symptom is classically considered a systemic “B symptom” in lymphoma?
why_correct: B symptoms include unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and significant unexplained weight loss.
why_wrong: A. Pruritus can occur in Hodgkin lymphoma but is not a B symptom. B. Tinnitus is unrelated. D. Alcohol-induced nodal pain is a recognised but uncommon Hodgkin feature, not a B symptom. E. Sneezing is not a lymphoma B symptom.
pearl: Lymphoma B symptoms are unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and significant weight loss; they are recorded as a "B" suffix in staging and indicate a worse prognosis.
thinking: B symptoms are systemic symptoms in lymphoma ↓ The three are fever, night sweats and weight loss ↓ Only one is listed ↓ Drenching night sweats
exam_trap: A, generalised pruritus without rash — it is a recognised Hodgkin symptom, but it is not one of the three B symptoms.
takeaway: B symptoms are fever, drenching night sweats and weight loss.

stem: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops a temperature of 38.5°C and is clinically unwell. What serious diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: Fever or clinical deterioration during a period of possible chemotherapy-induced neutropenia is a medical emergency because infection may progress rapidly.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not explain the febrile illness. B. Stable eczema does not explain fever and systemic deterioration. C. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy causes confusion, thirst and constipation rather than fever with systemic illness. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute fever and systemic illness.
pearl: Fever or being unwell during chemotherapy is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise; give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics urgently without waiting for the neutrophil count.
thinking: Patient on chemotherapy ↓ Possible bone marrow suppression ↓ Fever and clinically unwell ↓ Infection can progress very quickly ↓ Neutropenic sepsis
exam_trap: C, hypercalcaemia — it is a common oncological emergency, but it causes confusion, thirst and constipation, not fever with systemic illness.
takeaway: Fever during chemotherapy: treat as neutropenic sepsis with urgent IV antibiotics.

stem: A patient has jaundice, anaemia and evidence of increased red-cell destruction. Which blood-film finding is associated with haemolysis?
why_correct: Increased red-cell destruction stimulates the bone marrow to release more reticulocytes as it attempts to compensate.
why_wrong: A. Isolated thrombocytopenia does not indicate haemolysis. C. Rouleaux can occur in conditions such as paraproteinaemia but is not the defining feature of haemolysis. D. Pancytopenia suggests a broader marrow problem. E. Neutropenia is not the typical compensatory response to haemolysis.
pearl: In haemolysis the marrow compensates by releasing reticulocytes; with raised bilirubin, raised LDH and low haptoglobin this confirms increased red-cell destruction.
thinking: Jaundice and anaemia ↓ Increased red-cell destruction ↓ Marrow responds by making more red cells ↓ Immature cells appear in blood ↓ Reticulocytosis
exam_trap: C, rouleaux as the defining feature — it is a familiar blood film finding, but it reflects paraproteins or inflammation and is not the marker of haemolysis.
takeaway: Haemolysis causes a raised reticulocyte count as the marrow compensates.

stem: A patient with anaemia has a raised reticulocyte count. What does this generally indicate?

options.B: The bone marrow has completely stopped producing red cells
options.C: The bone marrow is responding to red-cell loss or destruction
options.E: There is always vitamin B12 deficiency

correct_answer: C. The bone marrow is responding to red-cell loss or destruction
why_correct: Reticulocytes are immature red cells, and their increase generally indicates an appropriate marrow response to anaemia caused by blood loss or haemolysis.
why_wrong: A. It does not by itself diagnose leukaemia. B. Marrow failure generally produces an inadequate reticulocyte response. D. Reticulocytosis does not indicate iron overload. E. B12 deficiency usually causes ineffective erythropoiesis.
pearl: A high reticulocyte count shows the marrow is working and suggests bleeding or haemolysis; a low count in anaemia points to reduced production, such as deficiency or marrow failure.
thinking: Anaemia present ↓ Reticulocytes are young red cells ↓ High count means increased production ↓ Marrow compensating for loss or destruction ↓ The bone marrow is responding to red-cell loss or destruction
exam_trap: B, marrow has stopped producing red cells — this is the opposite: marrow failure gives a low reticulocyte count, not a raised one.
takeaway: Raised reticulocytes mean the marrow is replacing lost or destroyed red cells.

stem: A patient develops acute blood loss after trauma. Initially, which type of anaemia is most likely?
why_correct: Acute blood loss initially produces loss of red cells and plasma proportionally, so the remaining red cells are generally normocytic.
why_wrong: A. Megaloblastic anaemia is usually due to impaired DNA synthesis. C. Sideroblastic anaemia is a different disorder of haem synthesis. D. Microcytosis develops with iron deficiency over time. E. Macrocytosis is associated with conditions such as B12/folate deficiency.
pearl: Acute blood loss gives a normocytic anaemia, and haemoglobin may not fall until fluid shifts or resuscitation dilute the blood; microcytosis appears only with ongoing loss and iron depletion.
thinking: Acute blood loss after trauma ↓ Whole blood lost, so cells unchanged ↓ No time for iron stores to run down ↓ Remaining red cells are normal-sized ↓ Normocytic anaemia
exam_trap: D, microcytic anaemia — blood loss is a classic cause of microcytosis, but only chronic loss causing iron deficiency, not an acute bleed.
takeaway: Acute haemorrhage causes normocytic anaemia; chronic loss causes microcytosis.

stem: A patient develops fever, chills and back pain shortly after a blood transfusion. What serious complication should be suspected?

options.A: Acute flare of lumbar spine osteoarthritis
options.C: Iron deficiency from ongoing blood loss

why_correct: Fever, chills and back pain shortly after transfusion can indicate an acute haemolytic reaction, often due to ABO incompatibility.
why_wrong: A. An osteoarthritis flare does not cause fever and chills during transfusion. C. Iron deficiency does not cause an acute reaction during transfusion. D. A delayed haemolytic reaction occurs days to weeks after transfusion, not shortly after it. E. TACO causes breathlessness, hypertension and pulmonary oedema rather than fever, chills and back pain.
pearl: Fever, chills and back pain soon after starting a transfusion suggest an acute haemolytic reaction, usually ABO incompatibility; stop the transfusion immediately and recheck patient and unit identity.
thinking: Blood transfusion just given ↓ Fever and chills ↓ Back pain ↓ Onset shortly after starting ↓ Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction
exam_trap: D, delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction — it is also haemolytic, but it occurs days to weeks later, not shortly after transfusion.
takeaway: Fever, rigors and back pain early in a transfusion: stop it and suspect ABO incompatibility.

stem: An adult with little sunlight exposure develops diffuse bone discomfort and proximal muscle weakness. Which deficiency should be considered?
why_correct: Vitamin D deficiency can cause osteomalacia, presenting with bone pain and proximal muscle weakness.
why_wrong: A. B12 deficiency is associated particularly with megaloblastic anaemia and neurological dysfunction. B. Vitamin A deficiency is associated with visual and epithelial problems. C. Thiamine deficiency causes neurological and cardiac syndromes. D. Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired coagulation.
pearl: Vitamin D deficiency in adults causes osteomalacia, with bone pain, tenderness and proximal myopathy; limited sun exposure and darker skin are key risk factors.
thinking: Little sunlight exposure ↓ Reduced vitamin D synthesis in skin ↓ Diffuse bone discomfort ↓ Proximal muscle weakness ↓ Vitamin D deficiency
exam_trap: A, vitamin B12 deficiency — it can cause weakness and neurological symptoms, but it does not explain bone pain or a link with low sunlight.
takeaway: Bone pain and proximal weakness with low sun exposure suggest vitamin D deficiency.

stem: What is the main underlying problem in osteomalacia?
why_correct: Osteomalacia results from inadequate mineralisation of newly formed bone, commonly due to vitamin D deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Haemolysis is unrelated. C. Cartilage formation is not the primary abnormality. D. Thyroid hormone excess does not define osteomalacia. E. Muscle destruction is not the defining process.
pearl: Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation of bone matrix, usually from vitamin D deficiency; osteoporosis is reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation.
thinking: Osteomalacia means soft bone ↓ Bone matrix is laid down ↓ It is not properly mineralised ↓ Often due to low vitamin D ↓ Defective mineralisation of bone
exam_trap: E, acute destruction of skeletal muscle — osteomalacia causes muscle weakness, but that is myopathy, not rhabdomyolysis, and the core defect is in bone.
takeaway: Osteomalacia means poorly mineralised bone; osteoporosis means reduced bone mass.

stem: Which factor increases the risk of osteoporosis?

options.A: Maintaining a normal healthy body weight
options.E: Adequate dietary calcium and vitamin D intake

why_correct: Prolonged systemic corticosteroid treatment increases bone loss and fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Low body weight is a recognised risk factor; a normal healthy weight is not. B. Weight-bearing exercise generally supports bone health. D. Sunlight exposure supports vitamin D production. E. Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake supports bone health.
pearl: Long-term oral corticosteroids are a major cause of secondary osteoporosis; patients on prolonged courses should have their fracture risk assessed and bone protection considered.
thinking: Osteoporosis risk factors needed ↓ Healthy weight, exercise, sunlight and calcium all protect bone ↓ Steroids increase bone loss ↓ Long-term oral corticosteroid use
exam_trap: A, maintaining a normal healthy body weight — weight is a real osteoporosis risk factor, but low body weight raises risk; normal weight does not.
takeaway: Long-term oral steroids are a major cause of osteoporosis.

stem: A patient with known Addison's disease presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, severe hypotension and confusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute adrenal insufficiency can cause severe hypotension, gastrointestinal symptoms, electrolyte abnormalities and altered consciousness.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis can cause abdominal pain and systemic illness but does not explain the characteristic adrenal-insufficiency context. B. HHS causes severe hyperglycaemia and dehydration. C. Myxoedema coma is severe hypothyroidism. D. Thyroid storm occurs with severe thyrotoxicosis.
pearl: Addisonian crisis is a life-threatening emergency: give IV or IM hydrocortisone immediately with IV fluids; do not delay treatment for test results.
thinking: Known Addison's disease ↓ Vomiting and abdominal pain ↓ Severe hypotension ↓ Confusion ↓ Addisonian crisis
exam_trap: A, acute pancreatitis — it causes abdominal pain, vomiting and shock, but in known Addison's this picture is an adrenal crisis until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Shock with vomiting in Addison's disease: give hydrocortisone immediately.

stem: A patient with acromegaly develops headaches and loss of peripheral vision. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: A pituitary macroadenoma can compress the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal visual-field loss.
why_wrong: B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes painful red eye and visual disturbance. C. Cataract causes gradual visual blurring. D. Retinal detachment causes a field defect or visual phenomena from retinal separation. E. Optic neuritis commonly causes painful visual loss rather than the classic field defect from a pituitary mass.
pearl: A pituitary macroadenoma, such as in acromegaly, can press on the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia; formal visual field testing is part of assessment.
thinking: Acromegaly means a pituitary adenoma ↓ Headache suggests a mass effect ↓ Loss of peripheral vision ↓ Chiasm sits just above the pituitary ↓ Optic chiasm compression
exam_trap: E, demyelinating optic neuritis — it also causes visual loss, but usually painful central loss in one eye, not peripheral field loss from a pituitary mass.
takeaway: Pituitary tumour with peripheral visual loss: think chiasmal compression.

stem: What is the name given to primary hyperaldosteronism caused by an adrenal aldosterone-producing adenoma?
why_correct: Conn syndrome refers to primary hyperaldosteronism, classically due to an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma.
why_wrong: B. Addison's disease is primary adrenal insufficiency. C. Cushing syndrome results from cortisol excess. D. Sheehan syndrome is postpartum hypopituitarism. E. Graves' disease causes autoimmune hyperthyroidism.
pearl: Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism from an adrenal adenoma, typically causing hypertension with hypokalaemia; a raised aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the screening test.
thinking: Primary hyperaldosteronism ↓ Caused by an adrenal adenoma ↓ Makes aldosterone autonomously ↓ Has a named eponym ↓ Conn syndrome
exam_trap: C, Cushing syndrome — it is also an adrenal hormone-excess syndrome, but from cortisol, not aldosterone.
takeaway: Aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma is Conn syndrome.

stem: A patient develops muscle weakness and an irregular heartbeat. Blood tests show significant hypokalaemia. Which ECG abnormality can occur?

options.A: Shortened QT interval as the defining feature
options.D: Persistent complete heart block in every case

why_correct: Hypokalaemia can cause ECG changes including flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves.
why_wrong: A. Hypokalaemia does not characteristically cause a shortened QT interval. B. ST elevation is associated with acute myocardial injury and is not the characteristic finding of hypokalaemia. C. Delta waves are associated with ventricular pre-excitation such as WPW syndrome. D. Complete heart block is not an inevitable feature.
pearl: Hypokalaemia causes flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves, and increases arrhythmia risk, especially with digoxin.
thinking: Muscle weakness ↓ Irregular heartbeat ↓ Significant hypokalaemia ↓ Low potassium affects repolarisation ↓ Flattened T waves
exam_trap: A, shortened QT interval — it tempts because electrolytes alter QT, but hypokalaemia does not shorten it; a short QT is typical of hypercalcaemia.
takeaway: Hypokalaemia: flat T waves, ST depression and U waves.

stem: A patient has severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. Which treatment protects the myocardium rapidly while definitive potassium-lowering treatment is arranged?

options.E: Subcutaneous insulin without glucose in every patient

why_correct: Intravenous calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. It does not remove potassium, so additional potassium-lowering treatment is required.
why_wrong: B. Oral calcium does not provide the required rapid cardiac membrane stabilisation. C. Iron has no role in acute hyperkalaemia. D. Vitamin B12 has no role. E. Insulin can shift potassium intracellularly, but giving insulin without appropriate glucose consideration is unsafe; it also does not directly stabilise the myocardium.
pearl: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium stabilises the myocardium within minutes but does not lower potassium; follow it with insulin and glucose and treat the cause.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ ECG changes show cardiac risk ↓ Need rapid membrane stabilisation ↓ Calcium works within minutes ↓ Intravenous calcium
exam_trap: E, subcutaneous insulin without glucose — insulin does lower potassium, but it does not protect the heart, and without glucose it risks hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first to protect the heart.

stem: A patient is suspected of having meningococcal disease in the community. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Take blood cultures and start antibiotics once results return
options.B: Give emergency antibiotics; arrange urgent hospital review
options.C: Arrange a routine dermatology appointment to assess the rash
options.D: Give oral amoxicillin and review at the surgery in 48 hours

correct_answer: B. Give emergency antibiotics; arrange urgent hospital review
why_correct: Suspected invasive meningococcal disease is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment and urgent hospital assessment.
why_wrong: A. Treatment should not wait for microbiological confirmation. C. Dermatology review is inappropriate for a potentially life-threatening infection. D. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are inadequate and unsafe for suspected invasive meningococcal disease. E. Topical treatment is inadequate for invasive infection.
pearl: In suspected meningococcal disease in the community, give parenteral benzylpenicillin straight away if it does not delay transfer, and arrange emergency hospital admission.
thinking: Suspected meningococcal disease ↓ Patient is in the community ↓ Can deteriorate within hours ↓ Antibiotics must not wait ↓ Give emergency antibiotics; arrange urgent hospital review
exam_trap: A, take blood cultures first and wait for results — cultures help, but waiting for results before treating is unsafe in meningococcal disease.
takeaway: Suspected meningococcal disease: give antibiotics now and admit urgently.

stem: A patient with advanced HIV develops headache, confusion and focal neurological deficits. Brain imaging shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which opportunistic infection is an important consideration?
why_correct: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an important opportunistic infection in advanced HIV and can produce multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions.
why_wrong: A. Tinea capitis affects the scalp. B. Impetigo is a superficial skin infection. D. Otitis externa affects the external ear. E. Viral conjunctivitis does not cause multiple intracranial lesions.
pearl: In advanced HIV, multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions suggest cerebral toxoplasmosis, with primary CNS lymphoma as the main differential.
thinking: Advanced HIV ↓ Headache, confusion, focal deficits ↓ Multiple ring-enhancing lesions on imaging ↓ Classic opportunistic infection ↓ Cerebral toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: A, tinea capitis — it is an infection of the head, but it affects the scalp and hair, not the brain.
takeaway: Advanced HIV with multiple ring-enhancing lesions: think toxoplasmosis.

stem: A clinically stable patient is suspected of having infective endocarditis. Which investigation is important before starting antibiotics where this can be done without unsafe delay?
why_correct: Blood cultures are important for identifying the causative organism and guiding antibiotic treatment.
why_wrong: B. Pregnancy testing may be relevant in some clinical situations but does not diagnose endocarditis. C. Bone-density scanning assesses fracture risk. D. Skin prick testing assesses allergy. E. Peak flow assesses airflow limitation.
pearl: In suspected infective endocarditis, take several sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics if the patient is stable; identifying the organism guides prolonged treatment.
thinking: Suspected infective endocarditis ↓ Patient is stable ↓ Organism identity guides prolonged treatment ↓ Antibiotics first may sterilise cultures ↓ Blood cultures
exam_trap: B, urine pregnancy test only — it may be relevant before some treatments, but it does not help diagnose endocarditis or guide antibiotics.
takeaway: Stable suspected endocarditis: take blood cultures before antibiotics.

stem: A patient develops hydrophobia and progressive neurological symptoms after being bitten by a potentially rabid animal. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Hydrophobia and progressive encephalitic neurological symptoms following an animal exposure are classic features of rabies.
why_wrong: A. Parkinson's disease causes chronic movement abnormalities. C. Migraine does not cause progressive encephalitis. D. Multiple sclerosis has a different pattern of neurological episodes. E. Tetanus causes rigidity and spasms rather than hydrophobia.
pearl: Clinical rabies after an animal bite causes encephalitis with hydrophobia and is almost always fatal, so prompt post-exposure care after a bite from a possibly rabid animal is essential.
thinking: Bite from a possibly rabid animal ↓ Hydrophobia ↓ Progressive neurological symptoms ↓ Viral encephalitis ↓ Rabies
exam_trap: E, tetanus — it also follows wounds and causes neurological symptoms, but it gives rigidity and spasms, not hydrophobia.
takeaway: Hydrophobia with progressive neurology after an animal bite means rabies.

stem: A patient has chronic hepatitis C infection. Which important long-term complication can occur?
why_correct: Chronic hepatitis C can cause progressive liver fibrosis and cirrhosis and increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Primary sclerosing cholangitis is associated with inflammatory bowel disease rather than hepatitis C virus infection. B. Osteoarthritis is unrelated. D. Cataract is unrelated. E. Otitis externa is unrelated.
pearl: Chronic hepatitis C can progress silently to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; direct-acting antiviral treatment is highly effective, so diagnose and refer.
thinking: Chronic hepatitis C infection ↓ Ongoing liver inflammation ↓ Progressive fibrosis ↓ Cirrhosis develops ↓ Cirrhosis and liver cancer
exam_trap: A, primary sclerosing cholangitis — it is a chronic liver disease, but it is linked to inflammatory bowel disease, not hepatitis C.
takeaway: Chronic hepatitis C can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

stem: Which group is routinely offered hepatitis B vaccination as part of occupational protection?

options.B: All adults with seasonal allergic rhinitis

correct_answer: A. Healthcare workers at occupational risk
why_correct: Healthcare workers with occupational exposure risk to blood and body fluids are an important group for hepatitis B vaccination.
why_wrong: B. Allergic rhinitis does not itself create a hepatitis B vaccination indication. C. Osteoarthritis is unrelated. D. Myopia does not create a hepatitis B risk. E. Migraine does not create a hepatitis B risk.
pearl: Healthcare workers at risk of exposure to blood and body fluids should be vaccinated against hepatitis B, with a check of antibody response after the course.
thinking: Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids ↓ Healthcare workers have occupational exposure ↓ Vaccination protects them ↓ Healthcare workers at occupational risk
exam_trap: C, patients with osteoarthritis only — a chronic condition may sound like a reason to vaccinate, but osteoarthritis carries no blood-borne virus risk.
takeaway: Healthcare workers exposed to blood should be vaccinated against hepatitis B.

stem: A hospitalised patient develops frequent watery diarrhoea after a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Antibiotic exposure can disrupt normal bowel flora and allow C. difficile to cause diarrhoea and colitis.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease causes chronic malabsorption rather than typically acute post-antibiotic diarrhoea. B. IBS does not cause an acute antibiotic-associated inflammatory diarrhoeal illness. C. UC is chronic inflammatory bowel disease and is not specifically associated with recent antibiotic exposure. E. Crohn disease is chronic inflammatory bowel disease.
pearl: New diarrhoea after broad-spectrum antibiotics in hospital suggests C. difficile infection; send a stool sample, isolate the patient and stop or review the antibiotic if possible.
thinking: Hospitalised patient ↓ Recent broad-spectrum antibiotics ↓ Normal gut flora disrupted ↓ Frequent watery diarrhoea ↓ C. difficile infection
exam_trap: C, ulcerative colitis — it causes diarrhoea and colitis, but it is chronic and not specifically triggered by recent antibiotics.
takeaway: Diarrhoea after antibiotics in hospital: suspect C. difficile.

stem: A patient with suspected C. difficile diarrhoea is admitted to hospital. Which infection-control measure is particularly important?

options.A: Sharing a bathroom with other patients
options.C: No hand hygiene if gloves are worn

correct_answer: D. Appropriate isolation and contact precautions
why_correct: C. difficile can spread through contaminated environments and spores, so appropriate isolation and infection-control measures are important.
why_wrong: A. Shared bathroom facilities increase transmission risk. B. Airborne isolation alone is not the relevant precaution. C. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. E. Contaminated equipment can facilitate transmission.
pearl: C. difficile spores survive on surfaces and are not killed by alcohol gel; isolate patients and use gloves, aprons and soap-and-water handwashing.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile diarrhoea ↓ Spores contaminate the environment ↓ Spread by contact ↓ Alcohol gel does not kill spores ↓ Appropriate isolation and contact precautions
exam_trap: B, routine airborne isolation only — isolation is right, but C. difficile spreads by contact, so airborne precautions alone miss the main route.
takeaway: C. difficile: isolate, use contact precautions and wash hands with soap and water.

stem: An older adult develops a painful unilateral band of grouped vesicles on the trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Painful grouped vesicles in a unilateral dermatomal distribution are characteristic of herpes zoster.
why_wrong: A. Molluscum causes chronic umbilicated papules. B. Impetigo produces superficial infected lesions and crusting. C. Urticaria causes transient wheals. D. Tinea corporis causes annular scaly lesions.
pearl: Herpes zoster is reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in a dermatome, giving painful grouped vesicles on one side; antivirals work best when started early.
thinking: Older adult with a painful rash ↓ Grouped vesicles ↓ Unilateral band on the trunk ↓ Dermatomal pattern ↓ Herpes zoster
exam_trap: D, tinea corporis — it is a common rash on the trunk, but it is an annular scaly patch, not painful vesicles in one dermatome.
takeaway: Painful unilateral dermatomal vesicles mean herpes zoster.

stem: A patient develops a painful vesicular rash involving the forehead and tip of the nose. What complication should be particularly considered?

options.A: Ramsay Hunt syndrome of the ear
options.C: Tinea pedis of the toe webs

why_correct: Involvement of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve can threaten the eye and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves the facial nerve with vesicles in or around the ear, not the forehead and nasal tip. C. Tinea pedis affects the feet. D. Cellulitis of the leg is unrelated. E. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes scaly erythema, not a painful dermatomal vesicular eruption.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) suggest nasociliary nerve involvement and a high risk of eye involvement in shingles; start antivirals and arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment.
thinking: Painful vesicular rash ↓ Forehead involvement ↓ Tip of the nose involved ↓ Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
exam_trap: A, Ramsay Hunt syndrome — it is also facial shingles, but it involves the facial nerve with vesicles in or around the ear.
takeaway: Shingles on the forehead or nose tip: think ophthalmic involvement and refer urgently.

stem: Which group is routinely targeted for shingles vaccination because the risk of herpes zoster increases with age?

options.B: Children with simple viral upper respiratory infections
options.C: All patients with uncomplicated hay fever
options.D: Older adults eligible under the UK programme

correct_answer: D. Older adults eligible under the UK programme
why_correct: The UK shingles vaccination programme targets eligible older adults because the risk and complications of shingles increase with age.
why_wrong: A. Newborns are not the routine target group for shingles vaccination. B. A simple viral respiratory infection is not an indication. C. Hay fever does not create a shingles vaccination indication. E. Myopia is unrelated.
pearl: The UK shingles vaccination programme targets eligible older adults, and some severely immunosuppressed people, because the risk of shingles and postherpetic neuralgia rises with age.
thinking: Shingles risk rises with age ↓ Complications worse in older people ↓ Vaccine offered to reduce this ↓ Older adults eligible under the UK programme
exam_trap: A, newborn babies — infants do get routine vaccines, but they are not the target for shingles vaccination, which focuses on older age.
takeaway: Shingles vaccination in the UK targets eligible older adults.

stem: A patient develops recurrent small, painful grouped vesicles at the border of the lip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent grouped painful vesicles around the lips are typical of herpes simplex infection.
why_wrong: A. Molluscum produces painless umbilicated papules. B. Impetigo typically produces superficial crusted lesions. C. Psoriasis produces chronic scaly plaques. E. Tinea produces annular scaly lesions.
pearl: Recurrent painful grouped vesicles on the lip border are herpes simplex labialis (cold sores), often triggered by stress, illness or sunlight.
thinking: Recurrent lesions ↓ Small painful grouped vesicles ↓ At the lip border ↓ HSV reactivation ↓ Herpes simplex labialis
exam_trap: B, impetigo — it often affects the face around the mouth, but it gives honey-crusted lesions, not recurrent painful grouped vesicles.
takeaway: Recurrent grouped vesicles on the lip are cold sores from herpes simplex.

stem: A child develops painful clusters of vesicles and ulcers throughout the mouth with fever and difficulty eating. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Primary HSV infection in children can cause fever with widespread painful oral vesicles and ulcers, often involving the gums.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo is a superficial bacterial skin infection with honey-crusted lesions, not widespread intraoral vesicles. B. Candidiasis produces white plaques rather than widespread painful vesicular ulcers. C. Leukoplakia is a persistent white mucosal patch rather than an acute febrile illness. D. Recurrent aphthous ulcers are discrete ulcers without a febrile vesicular illness.
pearl: Primary HSV infection in young children causes herpetic gingivostomatitis: fever, swollen gums and many painful oral ulcers; the main risk is dehydration from poor intake.
thinking: Child with fever and difficulty eating ↓ Painful vesicles and ulcers throughout the mouth ↓ Typical of primary HSV infection ↓ Herpetic gingivostomatitis
exam_trap: D, recurrent minor aphthous ulcers — they are painful mouth ulcers, but they are few and discrete, without fever or widespread vesicles.
takeaway: Fever with widespread painful oral vesicles in a child: herpetic gingivostomatitis.

stem: A young woman develops painful loss of vision in one eye. Colour vision is reduced and the symptoms develop over several days. Which diagnosis is an important consideration?
why_correct: Painful subacute visual loss, particularly with impaired colour vision, is characteristic of optic neuritis and may be associated with multiple sclerosis.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment commonly causes flashes, floaters or a curtain-like visual field defect. B. Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe painful red eye and markedly raised intraocular pressure. C. Conjunctivitis causes red eye and discharge rather than this pattern of visual loss. E. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment.
pearl: Optic neuritis causes subacute visual loss with pain on eye movement and reduced colour vision, often with a relative afferent pupillary defect; it can be the first sign of multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Painful loss of vision in one eye ↓ Reduced colour vision ↓ Develops over days ↓ Optic nerve inflammation ↓ Optic neuritis
exam_trap: B, acute angle-closure glaucoma — it causes painful visual loss, but onset is sudden with a red eye, haloes and a hard eye, not reduced colour vision over days.
takeaway: Painful subacute monocular visual loss with poor colour vision: optic neuritis.

stem: A patient with motor neurone disease develops progressive difficulty speaking and swallowing. What is this most consistent with?
why_correct: Motor neurone disease can affect the bulbar muscles responsible for speech and swallowing.
why_wrong: B. Cerebellar stroke can cause coordination problems but does not explain the progressive pattern in established MND. C. Peripheral vascular disease affects circulation. D. Optic neuritis causes visual symptoms. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-nerve symptoms in the hand.
pearl: Bulbar involvement in motor neurone disease causes dysarthria and dysphagia, with risk of aspiration and malnutrition; it needs early speech, swallowing and nutrition planning.
thinking: Motor neurone disease ↓ Progressive speech difficulty ↓ Progressive swallowing difficulty ↓ Brainstem motor nuclei affected ↓ Bulbar involvement
exam_trap: B, cerebellar stroke — it can cause slurred speech, but it is sudden, and progressive speech and swallowing loss in MND reflects bulbar disease.
takeaway: Progressive speech and swallowing problems in MND mean bulbar involvement.

stem: A patient has an unsteady gait that becomes markedly worse when their eyes are closed. Which neurological deficit is most likely contributing?
why_correct: Sensory ataxia due to impaired proprioception becomes worse when visual compensation is removed by closing the eyes.
why_wrong: A. Hallucinations do not explain the gait disturbance. B. Hearing loss does not cause this characteristic pattern. D. Loss of smell does not cause ataxia. E. Facial weakness does not cause sensory ataxia.
pearl: Sensory ataxia from loss of proprioception worsens when the eyes are closed, giving a positive Romberg test; causes include B12 deficiency and peripheral neuropathy.
thinking: Unsteady gait ↓ Markedly worse with eyes closed ↓ Vision was compensating ↓ Position sense is lost ↓ Loss of proprioception
exam_trap: B, isolated hearing loss — inner ear problems can affect balance, but hearing loss alone does not cause gait that worsens with eyes closed.
takeaway: Gait much worse with eyes closed means proprioceptive loss.

stem: Which is a recognised non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease?
why_correct: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease and may occur before prominent motor symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria for a different reason. B. Haemoptysis is respiratory tract bleeding. D. Urticaria is an allergic skin condition. E. Haematemesis indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
pearl: Parkinson's disease has important non-motor features, including constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression and dementia; some can come years before tremor.
thinking: Non-motor feature of Parkinson's needed ↓ Autonomic involvement affects the gut ↓ Slowed bowel motility ↓ Can precede motor signs ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: A, polyuria from diabetes insipidus — urinary symptoms are common in Parkinson's, but they reflect bladder dysfunction, not diabetes insipidus.
takeaway: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease.

stem: A patient experiences an electric-shock sensation travelling down the spine and into the limbs when flexing the neck. What is this called?
why_correct: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock-like sensation triggered by neck flexion and can occur with cervical cord pathology, including multiple sclerosis.
why_wrong: A. Murphy sign is associated with acute cholecystitis. B. Babinski sign assesses corticospinal tract function. C. Romberg sign assesses proprioception and balance. D. Tinel sign is used to elicit nerve irritation, often at the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.
pearl: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock sensation down the spine and limbs on neck flexion, suggesting cervical cord disease such as multiple sclerosis.
thinking: Electric-shock sensation ↓ Travels down the spine into the limbs ↓ Triggered by neck flexion ↓ Cervical cord pathology ↓ Lhermitte sign
exam_trap: D, Tinel sign — it also produces tingling, but by tapping over a peripheral nerve such as the median nerve at the wrist.
takeaway: Electric shocks down the spine on neck flexion are Lhermitte sign.

stem: A patient develops sudden weakness and loss of sensation affecting the right side of the body. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely responsible?

options.C: Peripheral nerves of the right leg only

why_correct: The cerebral hemispheres predominantly control the opposite side of the body, so a left hemispheric lesion can cause right-sided weakness and sensory loss.
why_wrong: A. A right hemispheric lesion would typically produce left-sided deficits. B. A spinal lesion would depend on its level and pattern. C. A peripheral nerve lesion would not usually affect an entire side of the body. D. Cerebellar lesions mainly cause coordination problems.
pearl: Each cerebral hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, so sudden right-sided weakness and numbness point to a left hemisphere lesion, which may also affect language.
thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness ↓ Right-sided sensory loss ↓ Motor and sensory pathways cross over ↓ Lesion is on the opposite side ↓ Left hemisphere
exam_trap: A, right hemisphere — candidates may link the deficit to the same side, but motor and sensory pathways cross, so right-sided signs mean a left-sided lesion.
takeaway: Right-sided weakness and sensory loss point to a left hemisphere lesion.

stem: A patient develops loss of vision in the outer halves of both visual fields. What is this visual-field defect called?
why_correct: Loss of the temporal visual fields of both eyes is bitemporal hemianopia and can result from optic chiasm compression.
why_wrong: A. Monocular blindness affects one eye. C. A central scotoma affects central vision. D. Homonymous hemianopia affects the same side of the visual field in both eyes. E. Diplopia means double vision rather than loss of a visual field.
pearl: Bitemporal hemianopia is loss of the outer (temporal) halves of both visual fields, caused by optic chiasm compression, most often by a pituitary tumour.
thinking: Loss of the outer halves ↓ Both visual fields affected ↓ Temporal fields lost in each eye ↓ Crossing nasal fibres at the chiasm ↓ Bitemporal hemianopia
exam_trap: D, homonymous hemianopia — it also affects both eyes, but it is loss of the same side of the field in each eye from a lesion behind the chiasm.
takeaway: Loss of both outer visual fields is bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression.

stem: Which joint is commonly affected in rheumatoid arthritis but is usually spared in osteoarthritis of the hands?

options.A: Interphalangeal joint of the great toe

why_correct: Rheumatoid arthritis commonly affects the MCP and PIP joints, whereas DIP involvement is less typical.
why_wrong: A. This is not a typical distinguishing hand-joint pattern. B. The first CMC joint is commonly affected by osteoarthritis. D. DIP involvement is characteristic of hand osteoarthritis. E. Distal interphalangeal disease is more typical of osteoarthritis.
pearl: Rheumatoid arthritis affects the MCP and PIP joints and spares the DIPs, while hand osteoarthritis affects the DIPs, PIPs and thumb base.
thinking: Need a joint typical of RA ↓ RA affects MCP and PIP joints ↓ Hand OA hits DIPs and thumb base ↓ MCPs usually spared in OA ↓ Metacarpophalangeal joint
exam_trap: D, distal interphalangeal joint — it is a classic hand-arthritis joint, but DIP disease is typical of osteoarthritis and is usually spared in RA.
takeaway: MCP involvement suggests RA; DIP and thumb-base involvement suggests OA.

stem: Which is a recognised extra-articular feature of rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Rheumatoid nodules are a recognised extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis, particularly in established disease.
why_wrong: A. Café-au-lait spots are pigmented skin lesions with different associations. B. Koplik spots occur in measles. D. Xanthelasma is associated with lipid deposition. E. Erythema migrans occurs in Lyme disease.
pearl: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, painless lumps over pressure areas such as the extensor forearm, more common in seropositive, established rheumatoid arthritis.
thinking: Extra-articular feature of RA needed ↓ RA is systemic ↓ Firm subcutaneous lumps at pressure points ↓ Rheumatoid nodules
exam_trap: E, erythema migrans — Lyme disease can also cause arthritis, but erythema migrans is its expanding rash, not a feature of RA.
takeaway: Rheumatoid nodules are a classic extra-articular feature of RA.

stem: Why is septic arthritis treated as a medical emergency?

options.A: It causes persistent hyperuricaemia and gout
options.B: It can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis
options.C: It usually resolves without treatment within days
options.D: It often progresses to rheumatoid arthritis

correct_answer: B. It can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis
why_correct: Infection within a joint can rapidly damage cartilage and may lead to bacteraemia and sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Hyperuricaemia is associated with gout, not septic arthritis. C. Untreated septic arthritis does not resolve spontaneously and can cause severe complications. D. It does not cause rheumatoid arthritis. E. Septic arthritis does not cause generalised osteoporosis.
pearl: Septic arthritis can destroy cartilage within days and cause sepsis; a hot, swollen joint needs urgent aspiration and cultures before IV antibiotics where safe.
thinking: Bacteria in the joint space ↓ Cartilage can be destroyed rapidly ↓ Infection can spread to the blood ↓ Delay worsens outcome ↓ It can rapidly destroy the joint and cause sepsis
exam_trap: A, causes persistent hyperuricaemia and gout — gout is the main differential for a hot joint, but septic arthritis does not cause hyperuricaemia.
takeaway: A hot swollen joint is septic arthritis until aspirated: treat as an emergency.

stem: Which symptom is particularly suggestive of giant cell arteritis?
why_correct: Jaw claudication is a characteristic symptom of giant cell arteritis and reflects vascular insufficiency affecting the muscles of mastication.
why_wrong: A. Pain triggered by swallowing cold drinks is not characteristic of GCA. B. Fatty-food-related pain suggests biliary disease. C. Jaw clicking may occur with temporomandibular joint disorders. D. Tooth sensitivity suggests dental pathology.
pearl: Jaw claudication is one of the most specific symptoms of giant cell arteritis; start high-dose steroids promptly to protect vision while confirming the diagnosis.
thinking: Possible giant cell arteritis ↓ Arteries to the jaw muscles inflamed ↓ Reduced blood flow when chewing ↓ Pain with use of muscles ↓ Jaw pain on chewing
exam_trap: C, jaw clicking only — it involves the jaw, but clicking points to temporomandibular joint disorder, not ischaemic pain on chewing.
takeaway: Jaw pain on chewing is jaw claudication, suggesting giant cell arteritis.

stem: Which medication is an important risk factor for osteoporosis when used long term?
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy increases bone loss and fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Topical antibiotics do not cause osteoporosis. C. Topical emollients do not cause significant systemic bone loss. D. Inhaled salbutamol is not a major osteoporosis risk factor. E. Paracetamol is not a major cause of osteoporosis.
pearl: Long-term oral corticosteroids are the commonest drug cause of osteoporosis; assess fracture risk and consider bone protection for patients on prolonged courses.
thinking: Medication causing osteoporosis ↓ Taken long term ↓ Must have systemic effect ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation ↓ Oral corticosteroids
exam_trap: D, inhaled salbutamol therapy — long-term inhaler use in asthma may suggest steroids, but salbutamol is a bronchodilator and not a major bone risk.
takeaway: Long-term oral steroids are the classic drug cause of osteoporosis.

stem: Which person is at increased risk of vitamin D deficiency?

options.A: A person with very limited exposure to sunlight
options.C: A person with a balanced diet and adequate sunlight
options.D: A person who regularly spends time outdoors
options.E: A person with isolated seasonal rhinitis

correct_answer: A. A person with very limited exposure to sunlight
why_correct: Reduced exposure to sunlight reduces cutaneous vitamin D synthesis and increases the risk of deficiency.
why_wrong: B. Paracetamol does not cause vitamin D deficiency. C. Adequate dietary intake and sunlight reduce deficiency risk. D. Regular outdoor exposure generally supports vitamin D synthesis. E. Seasonal rhinitis does not itself cause vitamin D deficiency.
pearl: Most vitamin D comes from skin synthesis in sunlight, so people with little sun exposure, such as the housebound, are at risk; supplements may be advised for at-risk groups.
thinking: Vitamin D mostly made in skin ↓ Needs sunlight ↓ Very limited sun exposure ↓ Reduced synthesis ↓ A person with very limited exposure to sunlight
exam_trap: C, balanced diet and adequate sunlight — it mentions the right factors, but describes protection, not risk.
takeaway: Limited sunlight exposure is a key risk factor for vitamin D deficiency.

stem: A young woman develops photosensitive facial erythema over the cheeks and bridge of the nose, sparing the nasolabial folds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A photosensitive malar rash that characteristically spares the nasolabial folds is associated with systemic lupus erythematosus.
why_wrong: A. Rosacea commonly affects the central face with flushing and papules but has a different pattern and does not spare the nasolabial folds. B.
