why_wrong: A. NSAIDs do not permanently inactivate lithium. B. The clinically important interaction is increased rather than reduced lithium exposure. C. Lithium does not prevent NSAID absorption. D. The interaction is clinically relevant.
pearl: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range; NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazides reduce its renal clearance, as do dehydration and renal impairment, so levels need close monitoring.
thinking: Patient on lithium ↓ Starts an NSAID ↓ Renal lithium clearance falls ↓ Level rises into the toxic range ↓ NSAIDs can increase lithium concentrations
exam_trap: B, NSAIDs always reduce lithium concentrations — recognises that an interaction exists but reverses its direction; NSAIDs raise lithium levels and cause toxicity.
takeaway: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides raise lithium levels.

stem: A patient taking low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis accidentally takes it every day instead of once weekly. What serious complication can occur?
why_correct: Accidental daily administration of weekly methotrexate can cause severe toxicity, including bone marrow suppression and mucosal injury.
why_wrong: A. Retroperitoneal fibrosis is not a recognised methotrexate toxicity. B. Methotrexate does not cause acute angle-closure glaucoma as a characteristic toxicity. D. It does not cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. E. Cataract is not the characteristic acute toxicity.
pearl: Methotrexate for inflammatory disease is taken once weekly, on a named day; daily dosing errors cause marrow suppression and mucositis, and need urgent specialist management including folinic acid.
thinking: Weekly methotrexate ↓ Taken daily by mistake ↓ Several-fold overdose ↓ Antifolate damage to dividing cells ↓ Bone marrow suppression
exam_trap: A, retroperitoneal fibrosis — tempting because methotrexate can cause liver and lung fibrosis, but retroperitoneal fibrosis is not a recognised methotrexate toxicity.
takeaway: Weekly methotrexate taken daily can cause life-threatening marrow suppression.

stem: A patient taking methotrexate for an inflammatory condition becomes pregnant. What is the key concern?

options.A: Methotrexate is a treatment for ectopic pregnancy in every circumstance
options.B: Methotrexate is routinely continued throughout pregnancy

correct_answer: C. Methotrexate can cause fetal harm
why_correct: Methotrexate is teratogenic and should not be used during pregnancy for inflammatory conditions.
why_wrong: A. Methotrexate has a specific role in selected ectopic pregnancies but this does not make it appropriate for inflammatory disease during pregnancy. B. Routine continuation during pregnancy is inappropriate. D. Methotrexate has important reproductive effects. E. It does not protect against congenital abnormalities.
pearl: Methotrexate is teratogenic: patients need effective contraception during treatment, it is stopped before planned conception, and specialist advice is needed urgently if pregnancy occurs.
thinking: On methotrexate for inflammatory disease ↓ Becomes pregnant ↓ Antifolate disrupts fetal development ↓ Methotrexate can cause fetal harm
exam_trap: A, treatment for ectopic pregnancy — true that methotrexate treats selected ectopic pregnancies, but that effect on pregnancy tissue is exactly why it harms a continuing pregnancy.
takeaway: Methotrexate is teratogenic: contraception during treatment, urgent review if pregnant.

stem: A patient taking an ACE inhibitor develops sudden swelling of the lips and tongue. What adverse effect should be suspected?
why_correct: ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema, which may involve the lips, tongue and upper airway.
why_wrong: B. Digoxin toxicity has gastrointestinal, neurological and cardiac manifestations. C. Hypoglycaemia causes adrenergic and neuroglycopenic symptoms. D. Serotonin syndrome produces neuromuscular, autonomic and mental-state abnormalities. E. Cholestatic liver injury produces jaundice and abnormal liver tests.
pearl: ACE inhibitor angioedema is bradykinin-mediated, can occur at any point during treatment and threatens the airway; assess the airway immediately and stop the drug permanently.
thinking: Taking an ACE inhibitor ↓ Sudden lip and tongue swelling ↓ Bradykinin accumulation ↓ Airway at risk ↓ Angioedema
exam_trap: D, serotonin syndrome — an adverse drug reaction often tested, but it causes clonus, agitation and autonomic instability, not lip and tongue swelling.
takeaway: Lip or tongue swelling on an ACE inhibitor is angioedema: protect the airway, stop the drug.

stem: A patient taking a statin develops new symmetrical muscle aches and weakness. Which adverse effect should be considered?
why_correct: Statins can cause muscle symptoms, ranging from myalgia to rare severe myopathy.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory condition, not a drug adverse effect, and typically causes stiffness rather than weakness. C. Ménière disease causes vertigo and auditory symptoms. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria and oedema. E. Appendicitis causes abdominal symptoms.
pearl: Statin muscle effects range from myalgia to rare rhabdomyolysis; check creatine kinase when muscle symptoms occur, and remember interacting drugs such as clarithromycin raise the risk.
thinking: Taking a statin ↓ New symmetrical muscle aches ↓ Weakness ↓ Drug-related muscle toxicity ↓ Statin myopathy
exam_trap: A, polymyalgia rheumatica — it also causes symmetrical proximal aching, but stiffness predominates over weakness and it is not a drug adverse effect.
takeaway: New muscle pain or weakness on a statin: check CK and consider myopathy.

stem: A patient is taking warfarin for long-term anticoagulation. Which blood test is routinely used to monitor its anticoagulant effect?
why_correct: The international normalised ratio (INR) is used to monitor the anticoagulant effect of warfarin.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin assesses iron stores and can be altered by inflammation. B. HbA1c assesses longer-term glycaemic control. C. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. D. Amylase is used in assessment of pancreatic injury.
pearl: Warfarin is monitored by the INR against an indication-specific target range; many drugs, including several antibiotics, alter the INR, so recheck it after starting or stopping medicines.
thinking: Long-term warfarin ↓ Reduces vitamin K-dependent clotting factors ↓ Prolongs the prothrombin time ↓ Standardised as INR ↓ INR
exam_trap: C, troponin — a common test in patients with heart disease who may be anticoagulated, but it measures myocardial injury, not anticoagulant effect.
takeaway: Warfarin's anticoagulant effect is monitored routinely with the INR.

stem: A patient taking warfarin develops excessive anticoagulation. Which vitamin is central to the mechanism of warfarin?
why_correct: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing activation of several vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin D is important in calcium and bone metabolism. C. Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant. D. Vitamin C is involved in collagen synthesis and other functions. E. Vitamin B12 is important for DNA synthesis and neurological function.
pearl: Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase, lowering active factors II, VII, IX and X; vitamin K reverses it, with prothrombin complex concentrate added for major bleeding.
thinking: Excessive warfarin anticoagulation ↓ Drug blocks vitamin K recycling ↓ Factors II, VII, IX and X fall ↓ Vitamin K
exam_trap: E, vitamin B12 — a vitamin linked to blood disorders, but deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neuropathy, not altered clotting factor activation.
takeaway: Warfarin antagonises vitamin K; vitamin K reverses it.

stem: A patient takes a large overdose of a beta-blocker and develops marked bradycardia and hypotension. Which medication is commonly used in severe beta-blocker poisoning?
why_correct: Glucagon can increase intracellular cyclic AMP independently of beta-adrenergic receptors and is used in significant beta-blocker poisoning.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity. C. Flumazenil antagonises benzodiazepines. D. Vitamin K reverses vitamin-K-dependent anticoagulation. E. N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning.
pearl: In beta-blocker poisoning, bradycardia and hypotension may respond to atropine, then glucagon, which raises cyclic AMP independently of beta-receptors; seek TOXBASE or poisons advice early.
thinking: Beta-blocker overdose ↓ Bradycardia and hypotension ↓ Beta-receptors blocked ↓ Raise cAMP by another route ↓ Glucagon
exam_trap: E, N-acetylcysteine — the most famous overdose antidote, but it is specific to paracetamol poisoning and does nothing for beta-blockade.
takeaway: Glucagon bypasses blocked beta-receptors in beta-blocker poisoning.

stem: A patient presents with severe hypotension and bradycardia after taking a large amount of a calcium-channel blocker. Which treatment can be used in significant toxicity?
why_correct: Intravenous calcium is used as part of the management of significant calcium-channel blocker poisoning.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K reverses vitamin-K-dependent anticoagulation. B. N-acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity. D. Naloxone treats opioid toxicity. E. Atropine may be considered for bradycardia but is not sufficient treatment for all severe calcium-channel blocker poisoning.
pearl: Calcium-channel blocker poisoning causes bradycardia, hypotension and often hyperglycaemia; IV calcium is used alongside high-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy, with specialist poisons advice.
thinking: Calcium-channel blocker overdose ↓ Hypotension and bradycardia ↓ Calcium entry into cells blocked ↓ Raise extracellular calcium ↓ Intravenous calcium
exam_trap: E, atropine alone in every case — bradycardia makes atropine tempting, but it is often insufficient alone in significant toxicity; 'every case' signals a wrong answer.
takeaway: Calcium-channel blocker overdose: give IV calcium and seek poisons advice.

stem:
An 82-year-old inpatient becomes intermittently confused over several hours. He is unable to maintain attention and is disorientated at times. His family says this is a new change from his usual state.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and cognition.
why_wrong: A. Schizophrenia is not characterised by an acute fluctuating disturbance in attention. B. Depression does not typically cause acute fluctuating inattention. D. Dementia is usually chronic and progressive rather than developing over hours. E. Mild cognitive impairment is chronic and does not usually cause acute fluctuating confusion.
pearl: Delirium is acute in onset, fluctuating and marked by inattention; screen with a tool such as the 4AT, then search for causes including infection, drugs, urinary retention, constipation and metabolic upset.
thinking: Elderly inpatient ↓ Confusion developing over hours ↓ Fluctuating with inattention ↓ New change from baseline ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: D, dementia — common at this age and causes disorientation, but it develops over months to years; acute fluctuating inattention over hours is delirium.
takeaway: Acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention is delirium until proven otherwise.

stem:
An 85-year-old patient develops acute confusion following admission to hospital. He has dysuria and a temperature of 38.1°C.

Which is the most likely precipitating factor for his delirium?
why_correct: Infection is a common precipitant of delirium in older people.
why_wrong: A. Hearing impairment may increase vulnerability but is not the likely trigger here. B. Chronic osteoarthritis is not a typical acute precipitant. D. Visual impairment can increase vulnerability but does not explain the acute change here. E. Older age increases susceptibility but is not itself an acute precipitant.
pearl: Infection, especially urinary and chest, is a leading trigger of delirium in older people; also look for drugs, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.
thinking: 85-year-old ↓ Acute confusion after admission ↓ Dysuria and fever ↓ Infective precipitant ↓ Urinary tract infection
exam_trap: E, age alone — older age does raise delirium risk, but it is a predisposing factor, not an acute precipitant; fever and dysuria identify the trigger.
takeaway: Always look for a precipitant in delirium; infection is among the commonest.

stem:
A 79-year-old woman has experienced gradually worsening short-term memory over three years. Her family reports increasing difficulty managing finances and medications. There has been no acute fluctuation in her cognition.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Progressive cognitive impairment affecting everyday functioning over years is characteristic of dementia.
why_wrong: A. Dissociative disorders do not typically produce this pattern of progressive cognitive impairment. B. Panic disorder causes recurrent panic attacks rather than progressive cognitive decline. C. Delirium is acute and fluctuating. E. Acute psychosis does not typically cause a progressive decline in memory and function over years.
pearl: Dementia is progressive cognitive decline affecting daily function without the fluctuation of delirium; check reversible contributors such as B12, folate, thyroid function and medication before memory clinic referral.
thinking: 79-year-old ↓ Memory decline over three years ↓ Struggling with finances and medicines ↓ No acute fluctuation ↓ Dementia
exam_trap: C, delirium — it causes confusion in older people, but it is acute and fluctuating; steady decline over years without fluctuation is dementia.
takeaway: Gradual cognitive decline over years affecting daily life suggests dementia.

stem:
An 80-year-old patient reports repeated dizziness when standing and has fallen twice. His blood pressure is 138/78 mmHg lying down and 112/64 mmHg after standing.

What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: A significant fall in blood pressure after standing, associated with postural symptoms, indicates orthostatic hypotension.
why_wrong: A. Hypertension does not explain the postural fall. B. Hyperthyroidism is not the characteristic explanation for this finding. D. Raised intracranial pressure does not cause this pattern. E. Vasovagal syncope is not typically demonstrated by a reproducible postural blood-pressure fall.
pearl: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic on standing; in older fallers, review culprit drugs such as antihypertensives, diuretics and alpha-blockers.
thinking: 80-year-old with falls ↓ Dizziness on standing ↓ Systolic falls by 26 mmHg on standing ↓ Symptomatic postural drop ↓ Orthostatic hypotension
exam_trap: E, vasovagal syncope — a common cause of collapse, but it is not demonstrated by a reproducible postural fall in blood pressure, and it does not occur as described while supine.
takeaway: Symptomatic BP fall on standing in a faller is orthostatic hypotension: review the drugs.

stem:
An older patient has recurrent falls shortly after starting a new sedative medication at night.

What is the most appropriate first step in reducing this medication-related falls risk?

options.A: Review and reduce or stop the sedative
options.C: Add melatonin and continue the sedative
options.D: Increase the dose to improve sleep continuity

correct_answer: A. Review and reduce or stop the sedative
why_correct: Medicines causing sedation or postural hypotension should be reviewed in patients with falls.
why_wrong: B. Restricting activity does not address the medication cause. C. Continuing the sedative leaves the cause unaddressed, and adding another hypnotic may increase risk further. D. Increasing sedation may worsen falls risk. E. Antibiotics have no role in preventing medication-related falls.
pearl: Sedatives such as hypnotics and benzodiazepines are major falls-risk drugs in older people; a structured medication review to reduce or stop them is a core part of falls prevention.
thinking: Older patient ↓ New night-time sedative ↓ Recurrent falls since starting it ↓ Drug is the likely cause ↓ Review and reduce or stop the sedative
exam_trap: C, add melatonin and continue the sedative — sounds like better sleep management, but it leaves the cause in place and adds another hypnotic.
takeaway: New falls after a new sedative: review and deprescribe it first.

stem:
An older inpatient has unintentionally lost weight and is eating very little.

What should be undertaken to identify whether he is at risk of malnutrition?
why_correct: Patients at risk should undergo nutritional screening to identify malnutrition and guide management.
why_wrong: A. CT abdomen is not a routine nutritional screening test. C. Echocardiography assesses cardiac structure and function. D. Bone marrow biopsy does not assess nutritional status. E. Lumbar puncture is unrelated to nutritional screening.
pearl: Hospital inpatients should be screened for malnutrition on admission with a validated tool such as MUST, which combines BMI, unintentional weight loss and the effect of acute illness on intake.
thinking: Older inpatient ↓ Unintentional weight loss ↓ Eating very little ↓ Identify malnutrition risk ↓ Nutritional screening
exam_trap: A, routine CT of the abdomen — weight loss can prompt a search for cancer, but CT does not assess nutritional risk; screening identifies malnutrition.
takeaway: Weight loss and poor intake in an inpatient: screen for malnutrition with a tool such as MUST.

stem:
An older patient has reduced mobility, weakness, weight loss and reduced physiological reserve. A minor infection causes a marked deterioration in his function.

What does this most closely describe?
why_correct: Frailty is characterised by reduced physiological reserve and increased vulnerability to relatively minor stressors.
why_wrong: A. Hypertension alone does not produce this syndrome. B. Psychosis is a mental-health syndrome rather than reduced physiological reserve. C. Asthma is an obstructive airway disease. D. Hyperthyroidism does not explain this overall pattern.
pearl: Frailty is loss of physiological reserve, so minor stressors cause major functional decline; it often presents with falls, immobility, delirium or fluctuating disability and should shape care planning.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Weakness, weight loss, reduced mobility ↓ Low physiological reserve ↓ Minor infection causes major decline ↓ Frailty
exam_trap: D, hyperthyroidism — it can cause weight loss and weakness, but it does not explain the overall syndrome of low reserve and disproportionate decline after minor illness.
takeaway: Disproportionate decline after a minor stressor is the hallmark of frailty.

stem:
A patient with advanced cancer is approaching the end of life and has troublesome symptoms despite treatment of the underlying disease.

What is a central aim of palliative care?

options.A: Further curative treatment of the primary cancer
options.B: Mandatory admission to an acute hospital ward
options.C: Symptom relief and better quality of life
options.E: Routine admission to intensive care when unwell

correct_answer: C. Symptom relief and better quality of life
why_correct: Palliative care focuses on quality of life and relief of physical, psychological, social and spiritual problems associated with serious illness.
why_wrong: A. Palliative care is not primarily curative treatment. B. Palliative care can be delivered in different settings, including the patient's home, and admission is not mandatory. D. Medications may be essential for symptom control. E. Intensive care is not a routine component of palliative care.
pearl: Palliative care improves quality of life by addressing physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs; it can run alongside disease treatment and be delivered at home, in a hospice or in hospital.
thinking: Advanced cancer ↓ Approaching the end of life ↓ Troublesome symptoms ↓ Focus on comfort and quality ↓ Symptom relief and better quality of life
exam_trap: A, further curative treatment — tempting to keep targeting the cancer, but cure is no longer the aim at this stage; palliative care focuses on symptoms and quality of life.
takeaway: Palliative care aims at symptom relief and quality of life, not cure.

stem:
A patient with advanced disease is deteriorating and is likely to develop pain, breathlessness, agitation and secretions near the end of life.

What is the purpose of anticipatory medicines?

options.A: To replace regular oral analgesia with a syringe driver now
options.B: To slow progression of the underlying disease
options.C: To provide continuous sedation from the point of prescription
options.D: To make further discussions with the family unnecessary
options.E: To treat predictable end-of-life symptoms promptly

correct_answer: E. To treat predictable end-of-life symptoms promptly
why_correct: Anticipatory medicines can be prescribed in advance so that common symptoms can be treated promptly if they occur.
why_wrong: A. Anticipatory medicines are prescribed in advance for use if symptoms arise, not started routinely in place of current analgesia. B. They are for symptom management, not disease modification. C. They are not intended to sedate routinely; their purpose is symptom relief when needed. D. Medication does not replace communication and care planning.
pearl: Anticipatory ('just in case') medicines usually cover pain, breathlessness, agitation, nausea and respiratory secretions, prescribed for the subcutaneous route so they can be given promptly when needed.
thinking: Advanced, deteriorating disease ↓ Pain, breathlessness, agitation and secretions likely ↓ Prescribe in advance ↓ Treat symptoms without delay ↓ Treat predictable end-of-life symptoms promptly
exam_trap: C, continuous sedation from prescription — anticipatory drugs include sedatives such as midazolam, but they are given only if symptoms arise, not to sedate routinely.
takeaway: Anticipatory medicines are prescribed in advance so expected end-of-life symptoms are treated promptly.

stem:
A DNACPR decision is documented for a patient with advanced disease.

What does a DNACPR decision specifically concern?

options.A: Withdrawal of all active treatment and ward escalation plans
options.B: Withholding of opioid analgesia in the last days of life
options.C: Stopping antibiotics for any new infection
options.D: Attempted CPR in the event of cardiorespiratory arrest
options.E: Withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition and hydration

correct_answer: D. Attempted CPR in the event of cardiorespiratory arrest
why_correct: DNACPR relates specifically to attempted cardiopulmonary resuscitation following cardiac or respiratory arrest.
why_wrong: A. Other appropriate treatments, including escalation where agreed, can continue; DNACPR concerns CPR only. B. Analgesia can still be provided. C. A DNACPR decision does not automatically prohibit antibiotics. E. Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration decisions are separate considerations.
pearl: A DNACPR decision applies only to CPR; all other treatment, including antibiotics, fluids, analgesia and ward-level escalation, should still be considered on its own merits.
thinking: DNACPR documented ↓ Covers resuscitation only ↓ Other care continues as appropriate ↓ Attempted CPR in cardiorespiratory arrest
exam_trap: A, withdrawal of all active treatment — a common misunderstanding of DNACPR, but it concerns CPR alone; other treatment and escalation decisions are made separately.
takeaway: DNACPR means no CPR, not no treatment; all other care is decided separately.

stem:
A patient with progressive disease wishes to discuss his preferences for future care should he later become unable to communicate.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Refer him to intensive care for a future escalation plan
options.B: Defer the discussion until his condition deteriorates further
options.C: Ask his next of kin to make the decisions on his behalf
options.D: Discuss and record his preferences while he can take part
options.E: Advise that preferences cannot be recorded in advance

correct_answer: D. Discuss and record his preferences while he can take part
why_correct: Advance care planning allows patients to discuss and document preferences for future care while they are able to participate.
why_wrong: A. Intensive care referral is not automatically appropriate and does not explore his own preferences. B. Delaying discussion may mean preferences are not known when needed. C. The patient's own views should be sought where possible. E. Preferences can and should be documented, for example as an advance statement, to communicate agreed plans.
pearl: Advance care planning records a patient's wishes while they can take part; it may include an advance statement, an advance decision to refuse treatment, or a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare.
thinking: Progressive disease ↓ May later be unable to communicate ↓ Wants to discuss future care now ↓ Act while he can take part ↓ Discuss and record his preferences
exam_trap: C, ask his next of kin to decide — family seems the natural choice, but they cannot decide for him unless legally appointed, and he can state his own wishes now.
takeaway: Record future care wishes while the patient can still take part.

stem: Before taking blood from a hospital patient, which action is essential?

options.A: Leave the tubes unlabelled until the laboratory receives them
options.B: Confirm the patient's identity using appropriate identifiers
options.C: Use the bed number as the sole identifier
options.D: Ask another patient to confirm the identity
options.E: Label the samples at the end of the ward round

correct_answer: B. Confirm the patient's identity using appropriate identifiers
why_correct: Correct patient identification is essential to prevent wrong-patient investigations and treatment.
why_wrong: A. Samples must be appropriately identified according to local procedures. C. Bed numbers can change and should not be the sole identifier. D. Another patient is not an appropriate source of identity confirmation. E. Delayed labelling increases the risk of identification errors.
pearl: Positive identification means asking the patient to state their full name and date of birth where possible and checking these against the wristband and request; label samples at the bedside.
thinking: Taking blood ↓ Wrong-patient samples cause harm ↓ Positively identify the patient ↓ Label at the bedside ↓ Confirm identity using appropriate identifiers
exam_trap: C, bed number as the sole identifier — convenient on a busy ward, but patients move beds; identity must be confirmed with personal identifiers such as name and date of birth.
takeaway: Positively identify the patient and label samples at the bedside.

stem:
Immediately before starting a blood transfusion, the patient's identity does not match the details on the blood component.

What should be done?

options.A: Start the transfusion if the ABO group on the bag matches
options.B: Give the unit to the next compatible patient on the ward
options.C: Reprint the wristband to match the blood component details
options.D: Start the transfusion and complete the checks afterwards
options.E: Do not start the transfusion and resolve the discrepancy

correct_answer: E. Do not start the transfusion and resolve the discrepancy
why_correct: Any identification discrepancy must be resolved before a blood component is administered.
why_wrong: A. Any identification discrepancy must be resolved first; a matching ABO group on the bag does not confirm the right patient. B. Blood must only be given to the intended recipient after full bedside checks. C. The wristband should not simply be changed to match the blood. D. Starting an incorrectly identified transfusion could cause a serious or fatal reaction.
pearl: The bedside check of patient identity against the blood component is the final barrier against a wrong-blood transfusion; any mismatch means the unit is not given until the discrepancy is resolved.
thinking: About to start a transfusion ↓ Patient details do not match the component ↓ Risk of a wrong-blood incident ↓ Stop and resolve ↓ Do not start the transfusion
exam_trap: A, start if the ABO group matches — feels safe on compatibility grounds, but a matching group does not prove this unit is for this patient; any identity mismatch stops it.
takeaway: Any identification mismatch at the bedside: do not transfuse until it is resolved.

stem: Where is the V1 chest electrode placed when recording a standard 12-lead ECG?

options.A: Second intercostal space, right sternal edge
options.B: Fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
options.C: Fourth intercostal space, left sternal edge
options.D: Fifth intercostal space level, left anterior axillary line
options.E: Fourth intercostal space, right sternal edge

correct_answer: E. Fourth intercostal space, right sternal edge
why_correct: V1 is placed in the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal edge, with V2 at the same level on the left sternal edge; incorrect high placement alters the right precordial QRS and ST morphology.
why_wrong: A. The second intercostal space at the right sternal edge is too high and is not a standard 12-lead electrode position. B. The fifth intercostal space in the left midclavicular line is the position for V4. C. The fourth intercostal space at the left sternal edge is the position for V2. D. The left anterior axillary line at the level of V4 is the position for V5.
pearl: V1 and V2 sit in the fourth intercostal space either side of the sternum and V4 in the fifth space at the midclavicular line; placing V1 and V2 too high distorts right precordial QRS and ST appearances.
thinking: Standard 12-lead ECG ↓ Locate the sternal angle at the second rib ↓ Count down to the fourth intercostal space ↓ Right sternal edge ↓ Fourth intercostal space, right sternal edge
exam_trap: C, fourth intercostal space, left sternal edge — the correct level but the wrong side; that is V2, whereas V1 lies at the right sternal edge.
takeaway: V1 is the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal edge; V2 mirrors it on the left.

stem:
A patient with asthma is learning to measure peak expiratory flow.

Which instruction is appropriate?

options.A: Breathe out slowly and steadily into the device for 30 seconds
options.B: Seal lips on the mouthpiece and exhale gently after a normal breath
options.C: Take several small breaths, then record the average of the readings
options.D: Inhale fully, seal lips on the mouthpiece and blow hard and fast
options.E: Breathe in fully, hold for ten seconds, then blow out slowly

correct_answer: D. Inhale fully, seal lips on the mouthpiece and blow hard and fast
why_correct: Peak flow measures the maximum speed of expiration after a full inspiration.
why_wrong: A. Peak flow requires a forceful, rapid expiration. B. Peak flow requires a full inspiration followed by a forceful expiration, not a gentle one. C. The manoeuvre starts with a full inspiration, and the best of three readings is recorded rather than an average. E. Expiration must be forceful and rapid; a slow blow after breath-holding underestimates peak flow.
pearl: For peak flow, sit or stand upright, take a full breath in, seal the lips around the mouthpiece and blow as hard and fast as possible; record the best of three attempts.
thinking: Peak flow measures maximum expiratory speed ↓ Full inspiration first ↓ Tight seal on the mouthpiece ↓ Short, forceful blow ↓ Inhale fully, seal lips, blow hard and fast
exam_trap: A, breathe out slowly and steadily — confuses peak flow with a slow vital capacity effort; peak flow needs a short maximal blast, and slow blowing underestimates it.
takeaway: Peak flow: full breath in, tight seal, short hard blast, best of three.

stem:
A patient with dysuria has a urine dipstick positive for nitrites.

What does this finding most strongly suggest?
correct_answer: D. Bacterial UTI with nitrate-reducing organisms
why_correct: Some urinary bacteria reduce nitrate to nitrite, making a positive nitrite test supportive of bacterial UTI.
why_wrong: A. Nitrites do not indicate renal stones. B. Diabetes is suggested by glycosuria, not urinary nitrites. C. Nephrotic syndrome is associated with heavy proteinuria. E. Glomerulonephritis is more associated with haematuria and proteinuria.
pearl: Nitrites form when Gram-negative organisms such as E. coli reduce urinary nitrate, making them more specific for UTI than leucocytes; in adults over 65, dipsticks are unreliable and should not guide diagnosis.
thinking: Dysuria ↓ Dipstick positive for nitrites ↓ Bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite ↓ Bacterial UTI with nitrate-reducing organisms
exam_trap: A, renal calculus — stones cause urinary symptoms and abnormal dipsticks, but they cause haematuria; nitrites reflect bacterial metabolism.
takeaway: Positive nitrites with dysuria strongly support a bacterial UTI.

stem:
A woman of reproductive age presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy status is initially unknown.

Which test should be performed promptly?
why_correct: Establishing pregnancy status is important because ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage must be considered in this presentation.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. B. Amylase does not establish pregnancy status. D. D-dimer does not establish pregnancy status. E. Thyroid antibodies are not an initial test for this presentation.
pearl: Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain or vaginal bleeding needs a pregnancy test; a positive result raises concern for ectopic pregnancy until an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed.
thinking: Reproductive age ↓ Abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding ↓ Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage must be considered ↓ Establish pregnancy status ↓ Pregnancy test for β-hCG
exam_trap: B, serum amylase only — a standard test in abdominal pain, but it cannot establish pregnancy status, which must be checked promptly to consider ectopic pregnancy.
takeaway: Abdominal pain or bleeding in a woman of reproductive age: pregnancy test first.

stem:
A diagnostic test has a positive predictive value of 80%.

What does this mean?

options.A: 80% of people with the disease test positive
options.B: 80% of people with a positive test actually have the disease
options.D: 80% of people with a negative test do not have the disease
options.E: 80% of people without the disease test negative

correct_answer: B. 80% of people with a positive test actually have the disease
why_correct: Positive predictive value is the proportion of positive test results that are true positives.
why_wrong: A. This is sensitivity. C. Predictive value is not the same as prevalence. D. This is negative predictive value. E. This is specificity.
pearl: Predictive values answer the patient's question about their own result and change with disease prevalence, whereas sensitivity and specificity describe the test itself.
thinking: PPV of 80% ↓ Start from those who test positive ↓ Proportion who truly have the disease ↓ 80% of people with a positive test have the disease
exam_trap: A, 80% of people with the disease test positive — reverses the direction; that is sensitivity, which starts from the diseased rather than from positive results.
takeaway: PPV is true positives divided by all positive results.

stem:
A diagnostic test has a negative predictive value of 95%.

What does this mean?

options.A: 95% of the whole tested population are free of the disease
options.B: 95% of those testing negative do not have the disease
options.C: 95% of people with a positive test truly have the disease
options.D: 95% of people who truly have the disease test positive
options.E: 95% of people without the disease correctly test negative

correct_answer: B. 95% of those testing negative do not have the disease
why_correct: Negative predictive value is the proportion of negative results that are true negatives.
why_wrong: A. Predictive value is not the same as the proportion free of disease, which reflects prevalence. C. This is positive predictive value. D. This is sensitivity. E. This is specificity.
pearl: Negative predictive value is true negatives divided by all negative results; like PPV it depends on disease prevalence, so the same test can perform differently in high- and low-risk groups.
thinking: NPV of 95% ↓ Start from those who test negative ↓ Proportion truly free of disease ↓ 95% of those testing negative do not have the disease
exam_trap: E, 95% of people without the disease test negative — starts from the disease-free group; that is specificity, not negative predictive value.
takeaway: NPV is true negatives divided by all negative results.

stem:
A survey measures how many people in a community currently have asthma on a particular date.

Which epidemiological measure is being assessed?
why_correct: Point prevalence measures the proportion of a population with a condition at a particular point in time.
why_wrong: A. Case fatality rate measures deaths among affected patients. B. Sensitivity describes diagnostic test performance. C. Incidence measures new cases occurring over time. D. Relative risk compares risk between groups.
pearl: Prevalence counts existing cases at a point or over a period, whereas incidence counts new cases arising over time; long-lasting conditions accumulate a high prevalence relative to incidence.
thinking: Survey of current asthma cases ↓ Existing cases, not new ones ↓ Counted on one particular date ↓ Point prevalence
exam_trap: C, incidence — a core epidemiological measure, but it counts new cases over a period; a snapshot of current cases on one date is point prevalence.
takeaway: Existing cases at one time is prevalence; new cases over time is incidence.

stem:
In a randomised trial, participants do not know whether they have received the active treatment or placebo.

What is the main purpose of this blinding?

options.A: Reduce expectation effects on reported outcomes
options.B: Balance known and unknown confounders between groups
options.C: Prevent selection bias when participants are allocated
options.D: Reduce loss to follow-up in the treatment arm
options.E: Increase statistical power to detect a true effect

correct_answer: A. Reduce expectation effects on reported outcomes
why_correct: Blinding participants can reduce expectation-related effects and some forms of measurement or reporting bias.
why_wrong: B. Balancing confounders is the role of randomisation, not blinding. C. Selection bias at allocation is prevented by allocation concealment, not by blinding participants. D. Blinding is not mainly aimed at reducing attrition. E. Power depends mainly on sample size and effect size, not blinding.
pearl: Randomisation balances confounders, allocation concealment prevents selection bias, and blinding reduces performance and detection bias, including placebo and expectation effects.
thinking: Participants unaware of their allocation ↓ Beliefs could alter reported outcomes ↓ Blinding removes that influence ↓ Reduce expectation effects on reported outcomes
exam_trap: B, balance known and unknown confounders — a key trial safeguard, but that is the job of randomisation; blinding protects against expectation and reporting bias.
takeaway: Randomisation balances the groups; blinding protects outcomes from expectation bias.

stem:
A participant in a randomised controlled trial stops taking the assigned treatment because of side effects but remains in the study analysis.

Which analytical principle is being used?
why_correct: Intention-to-treat analysis generally analyses participants according to their original randomised groups, regardless of whether they completed the assigned treatment.
why_wrong: A. Ecological studies analyse groups or populations rather than individual randomised participants. B. Nested case-control studies begin with outcome status and look retrospectively for exposures. D. Per-protocol analysis focuses on participants who adhered to the protocol. E. Cross-sectional studies assess exposure and outcome at a point in time.
pearl: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone in the group they were randomised to, preserving the benefits of randomisation and reflecting real-world use; per-protocol analysis risks bias by excluding non-adherers.
thinking: Randomised participant ↓ Stops treatment because of side effects ↓ Still analysed in the original group ↓ Intention-to-treat analysis
exam_trap: D, per-protocol analysis of adherers — also used in trials, but it analyses only those who followed the protocol; keeping non-adherers in their randomised group is intention-to-treat.
takeaway: Analysed as randomised, whatever happened next: intention-to-treat.

stem:
A study reports a treatment effect with a 95% confidence interval.

What does the confidence interval primarily communicate?

options.A: The precision of the estimated treatment effect
options.B: The probability that a repeat study would give the same result
options.C: The prevalence of the disease in the study population
options.D: The sensitivity of the diagnostic test
options.E: The probability that the null hypothesis is false

correct_answer: A. The precision of the estimated treatment effect
why_correct: A confidence interval communicates the precision and uncertainty around an estimated effect.
why_wrong: B. It does not predict that a repeat study will give the same result. C. It is not a measure of disease prevalence. D. It is not a measure of diagnostic sensitivity. E. A confidence interval does not give the probability that a hypothesis is true or false.
pearl: A narrow confidence interval means a precise estimate; for a ratio such as relative risk an interval crossing 1, or for a difference an interval crossing 0, means the result is not statistically significant.
thinking: Treatment effect reported with a 95% CI ↓ Range of plausible true values ↓ Width reflects uncertainty ↓ Precision of the estimated treatment effect
exam_trap: E, probability that the null hypothesis is false — a common misreading of statistics, but neither a confidence interval nor a p-value gives the probability that a hypothesis is true.
takeaway: Confidence intervals show precision: the narrower, the more precise.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman who is 18 weeks pregnant presents with right-sided abdominal pain, fever and vomiting. Appendicitis is suspected.

Which imaging modality is generally preferred initially when imaging is required?
why_correct: Ultrasound is generally preferred initially in pregnancy because it avoids ionising radiation.
why_wrong: A. Barium enema is not an appropriate initial investigation for suspected appendicitis. B. PET-CT involves substantial radiation and is inappropriate for routine assessment. C. Plain abdominal radiography is not the preferred investigation. E. CT involves ionising radiation and is not usually the first imaging choice in pregnancy.
pearl: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging for suspected appendicitis in pregnancy; if it is inconclusive, MRI is preferred over CT where available, to avoid ionising radiation.
thinking: 18 weeks pregnant ↓ Suspected appendicitis ↓ Avoid ionising radiation ↓ Safe, accessible first test ↓ Ultrasound
exam_trap: E, CT abdomen and pelvis — the usual test for appendicitis in non-pregnant adults, but it uses ionising radiation, so ultrasound comes first in pregnancy.
takeaway: Suspected appendicitis in pregnancy: ultrasound first, MRI if inconclusive.

stem:
A drain is placed during abdominal surgery to allow postoperative fluid to leave the operative area.

What is the primary purpose of the drain?

options.A: Drainage of fluid from the operative site
options.B: Guarantee absence of an anastomotic leak

correct_answer: A. Drainage of fluid from the operative site
why_correct: Surgical drains are used selectively to allow drainage of fluid such as blood, pus or other collections.
why_wrong: B. A drain cannot guarantee that an anastomotic leak will not occur. C. It does not replace appropriate antimicrobial treatment. D. A drain does not prevent all infections. E. Drains do not prevent venous thromboembolism.
pearl: Surgical drains remove blood, pus, bile or other fluid and may give early warning of bleeding or a leak, but a quiet drain does not exclude a complication.
thinking: Drain placed at surgery ↓ Fluid may collect after the operation ↓ The tube provides an exit ↓ Drainage of fluid from the operative site
exam_trap: B, guarantee absence of an anastomotic leak — drains can signal a leak, but they cannot prevent or exclude one; their primary role is drainage.
takeaway: Drains remove fluid; they do not prevent leaks or infection.

stem:
A patient rescued from a house fire has facial burns, soot around the mouth and a hoarse voice.

What complication requires urgent attention?
why_correct: Facial burns, soot exposure and hoarseness following a fire raise concern for inhalational injury and evolving airway oedema.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic does not explain the presentation. B. DVT is not the immediate life-threatening concern. D. Otitis media is unrelated. E. There is no evidence of appendicitis.
pearl: Inhalational injury is suggested by facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness and stridor; airway oedema can progress rapidly, so involve an anaesthetist early.
thinking: House fire ↓ Facial burns and soot around the mouth ↓ Hoarse voice ↓ Inhalational injury with evolving oedema ↓ Airway compromise
exam_trap: B, deep-vein thrombosis — burns patients are immobile and at VTE risk, but that is a later concern; soot and hoarseness mean the airway is threatened now.
takeaway: Soot, facial burns and hoarseness after a fire: secure the airway early.

stem:
A patient with a large burn has increasing thirst, tachycardia and hypotension.

What is a major early physiological consequence of extensive burns?
why_correct: Extensive burns cause increased capillary permeability and movement of fluid into tissues, contributing to hypovolaemia.
why_wrong: A. Capillary permeability increases rather than decreases. B. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated. D. Increased red-cell production is not an immediate response. E. Plasma oncotic pressure does not increase as the primary response.
pearl: Extensive burns increase capillary permeability, shifting plasma into the tissues and causing burn shock; fluid needs are estimated from burn area and weight, for example with the Parkland formula, and titrated to urine output.
thinking: Large burn ↓ Capillaries become leaky ↓ Plasma moves into the tissues ↓ Thirst, tachycardia, hypotension ↓ Loss of intravascular fluid
exam_trap: A, reduced capillary permeability — rightly links burns to capillary change but gets the direction wrong; permeability rises, driving fluid out of the circulation.
takeaway: Large burns cause leaky capillaries and hypovolaemia: replace fluid early.

stem:
A patient has sustained a displaced limb fracture.

Which assessment should be performed routinely before and after manipulation or immobilisation?
why_correct: Fractures and their treatment can compromise distal circulation and nerve function, so neurovascular status should be assessed.
why_wrong: A. Visual acuity is unrelated to the injured limb. B. Thyroid examination is unrelated. C. Hearing is unrelated. D. Abdominal examination does not assess limb neurovascular compromise.
pearl: Check and document distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation and movement before and after any reduction or splintage; a new deficit needs urgent senior review.
thinking: Displaced limb fracture ↓ Vessels and nerves at risk ↓ Manipulation can worsen compromise ↓ Check before and after ↓ Distal neurovascular status
exam_trap: D, abdominal examination only — part of a full trauma assessment, but it does not assess the injured limb; neurovascular checks before and after manipulation are essential.
takeaway: Document distal neurovascular status before and after any fracture manipulation.

stem:
A patient has a lower-leg fracture with a wound communicating with the fracture site.

What type of fracture is this?
why_correct: An open fracture communicates with the external environment through a wound.
why_wrong: A. A greenstick fracture is an incomplete fracture commonly seen in children. B. A stress fracture results from repetitive loading. C. A pathological fracture occurs through abnormal bone. E. An impacted fracture involves one fracture fragment being driven into another.
pearl: Open fractures need prompt IV antibiotics, tetanus cover, photography of the wound and a saline-soaked dressing, followed by urgent surgical debridement, ideally by combined orthopaedic and plastic surgery teams.
thinking: Lower-leg fracture ↓ Overlying wound ↓ Wound communicates with the fracture ↓ Bone exposed to the environment ↓ Open fracture
exam_trap: C, pathological fracture — another fracture category, but it describes a break through abnormal bone such as a metastasis; communication with a wound makes it open.
takeaway: A wound communicating with a fracture makes it open: antibiotics and urgent debridement.

stem:
A patient involved in a high-speed road traffic collision has severe pelvic pain and haemodynamic instability.

What complication is a major immediate concern?
why_correct: Pelvic fractures can cause substantial internal haemorrhage and haemodynamic instability.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not explain traumatic haemodynamic instability. B. Otitis externa is unrelated. C. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated. D. Peptic ulcer disease does not explain the traumatic presentation.
pearl: In an unstable patient with a suspected pelvic fracture, apply a pelvic binder early and activate the major haemorrhage protocol; avoid repeatedly springing the pelvis.
thinking: High-speed collision ↓ Severe pelvic pain ↓ Haemodynamic instability ↓ Pelvic fracture bleeding internally ↓ Major haemorrhage
exam_trap: D, peptic ulcer disease — a recognised cause of haemorrhagic shock elsewhere, but it has no link to blunt pelvic trauma; pelvic fractures bleed heavily.
takeaway: Pelvic injury with shock: assume major haemorrhage and apply a pelvic binder.

stem:
A patient presents with sudden severe leg pain and absent pedal pulses. Acute limb ischaemia is suspected.

What is the appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Apply a compression stocking and discharge

why_correct: Acute limb ischaemia threatens limb viability and requires urgent vascular assessment and treatment.
why_wrong: B. Compression is not appropriate for acute arterial occlusion. C. Dermatology referral is unrelated. D. Physiotherapy is inappropriate during acute limb ischaemia. E. Delay risks irreversible tissue damage.
pearl: Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency; the 6 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishingly cold, paraesthesia, paralysis) guide assessment, and heparin is usually started while urgent vascular review is arranged.
thinking: Sudden severe leg pain ↓ Absent pedal pulses ↓ Acute arterial occlusion ↓ Limb viability at risk ↓ Urgent vascular assessment
exam_trap: B, compression stocking and discharge — fits venous problems, but compression worsens arterial ischaemia; a painful pulseless limb needs urgent vascular review.
takeaway: A sudden painful pulseless limb is an emergency: urgent vascular referral.

stem: Which of the following is a live attenuated vaccine?
why_correct: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus vaccine is a toxoid vaccine. C. Hepatitis B vaccine is a recombinant subunit vaccine. D. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine is not a live vaccine. E. The standard injected influenza vaccine is inactivated.
pearl: UK live vaccines include MMR, BCG, rotavirus, varicella and the nasal flu spray; tetanus, hepatitis B, pneumococcal and injected influenza vaccines are non-live.
thinking: Which vaccine contains live weakened organisms? ↓ Toxoid, recombinant, conjugate and inactivated vaccines are non-live ↓ Measles, mumps and rubella are attenuated ↓ MMR
exam_trap: E, inactivated influenza vaccine — tempting because the nasal spray flu vaccine is live, but the standard injected influenza vaccine is inactivated.
takeaway: MMR is live; toxoid, subunit, conjugate and inactivated vaccines are not.

stem:
A woman is pregnant and asks whether she should receive a routine live attenuated vaccine.

What is the general principle?

options.A: All vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy
options.B: Live vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy
options.C: Live vaccines are always mandatory during pregnancy
options.D: Pregnancy has no relevance to vaccine choice
options.E: Pregnancy makes live vaccines more effective

correct_answer: B. Live vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy
why_correct: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy because of theoretical fetal risk.
why_wrong: A. Some non-live vaccines are recommended or may be indicated during pregnancy. C. Live vaccines are not routinely mandatory during pregnancy. D. Pregnancy is an important consideration when selecting vaccines. E. Pregnancy does not make live vaccines more effective.
pearl: Live vaccines such as MMR are generally avoided in pregnancy, and pregnancy should be avoided for a short time after MMR; inactivated vaccines such as pertussis and influenza are offered during pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Asks about a live attenuated vaccine ↓ Theoretical risk of fetal infection ↓ Live vaccines generally avoided during pregnancy
exam_trap: A, all vaccines are contraindicated — overgeneralises; inactivated vaccines such as pertussis and influenza are actively recommended in pregnancy.
takeaway: Avoid live vaccines in pregnancy; inactivated vaccines can be given.

stem:
A child developed anaphylaxis immediately after a previous dose of a particular vaccine.

What is the most appropriate principle regarding another dose of the same vaccine?

options.A: Give the dose as two half-doses 30 minutes apart
options.B: Give it after an oral antihistamine as a premedication
options.C: Give it with oral prednisolone cover in general practice
options.D: Give the next dose as scheduled with routine observation
options.E: Withhold further doses pending specialist assessment

correct_answer: E. Withhold further doses pending specialist assessment
why_correct: A previous serious allergic reaction to a vaccine or its components requires careful assessment before further doses.
why_wrong: A. Split dosing does not make re-exposure safe and is no substitute for specialist assessment. B. Antihistamine premedication does not prevent anaphylaxis. C. Corticosteroid cover does not prevent anaphylaxis, and re-exposure needs specialist assessment. D. Routine re-exposure without assessment could cause another severe reaction.
pearl: Confirmed anaphylaxis to a previous dose of a vaccine or one of its components contraindicates further doses until specialist assessment; every vaccination setting must be equipped to treat anaphylaxis with adrenaline.
thinking: Child had anaphylaxis ↓ Immediately after a previous dose ↓ Re-exposure risks a repeat reaction ↓ Specialist assessment needed ↓ Withhold further doses pending assessment
exam_trap: B, oral antihistamine premedication — seems a sensible safety net, but antihistamines do not prevent anaphylaxis; further doses need specialist assessment first.
takeaway: Previous vaccine anaphylaxis: withhold further doses until specialist assessment.

stem:
A high proportion of a population becomes immune to an infectious disease through vaccination.

What is a major population-level effect?

options.B: Prevention of every infection in vaccinated individuals

correct_answer: A. Reduced transmission of the infection
why_correct: High population immunity can reduce transmission and provide indirect protection to susceptible people.
why_wrong: B. Vaccination does not guarantee that every vaccinated individual will never become infected. C. Increased immunity generally reduces transmission. D. Herd immunity relates to infectious diseases. E. It does not directly cause antibiotic resistance.
pearl: Herd immunity reduces transmission so that unvaccinated and immunocompromised people are indirectly protected; the coverage needed rises with how transmissible the infection is, being highest for measles.
thinking: High population immunity ↓ Fewer susceptible hosts ↓ Chains of transmission broken ↓ Indirect protection ↓ Reduced transmission of the infection
exam_trap: B, prevention of every infection in vaccinated individuals — vaccines are effective, but none protects every individual completely; the population effect is reduced transmission.
takeaway: High vaccine coverage reduces transmission and protects the unvaccinated.

stem:
A patient asks why unnecessary antibiotic use is discouraged.

What is a major public-health reason?

options.A: It permanently increases immunity to bacteria

why_correct: Antibiotic exposure creates selection pressure favouring resistant organisms.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotic treatment does not provide permanent immunity. B. Antibiotics can cause allergic reactions but do not guarantee future allergy. C. Antibiotics do not cause viral infections. E. Antibiotic use does not prevent vaccination.
pearl: Every antibiotic course selects for resistant organisms and risks harms such as C. difficile infection; avoid antibiotics for self-limiting viral illness and use delayed prescribing where appropriate.
thinking: Unnecessary antibiotic use ↓ Selection pressure on bacteria ↓ Resistant strains survive and spread ↓ Promotes antimicrobial resistance
exam_trap: B, guarantees future allergy — antibiotics can cause allergic reactions, but not inevitably; the major public-health concern is antimicrobial resistance.
takeaway: Unnecessary antibiotics drive antimicrobial resistance.

stem:
A patient suffers significant harm because of an error in their care.

What professional principle requires openness with the patient about what happened?
why_correct: The duty of candour requires healthcare professionals and organisations to be open and honest with patients when things go wrong and cause harm.
why_wrong: A. Confidentiality concerns protecting patient information. C. Clinical negligence is a legal concept, not the professional communication duty itself. D. Informed refusal concerns declining treatment. E. Gillick competence concerns a young person's ability to consent.
pearl: The professional duty of candour, set out in joint GMC and NMC guidance, means telling the patient when something has gone wrong, apologising, offering a remedy and explaining the likely effects.
thinking: Error in care ↓ Significant harm to the patient ↓ Obligation to be open and honest about it ↓ Duty of candour
exam_trap: C, clinical negligence itself — it relates to harm from errors, but it is a legal concept about breach of duty; the obligation to be open with the patient is candour.
takeaway: When care causes harm, the duty of candour requires openness and an apology.

stem: Following a significant clinical incident causing harm, which communication approach is appropriate?

options.A: Be open and honest with the patient about what happened
options.D: Hide the incident unless the patient discovers it
options.E: Blame another member of staff without investigation

correct_answer: A. Be open and honest with the patient about what happened
why_correct: Open and honest communication is central to the duty of candour.
why_wrong: B. Clinical incidents should be appropriately documented and reported. C. Altering records is inappropriate and unsafe. D. Concealing an incident is inconsistent with openness. E. Responsibility should not be assigned without appropriate investigation.
pearl: After harm, tell the patient promptly what happened, apologise, explain what will be done, and record and report the incident; an apology is not an admission of legal liability.
thinking: Clinical incident causes harm ↓ Patient is entitled to know ↓ Duty of candour applies ↓ Be open and honest with the patient
exam_trap: D, hide the incident unless discovered — may seem to avoid distress or complaint, but concealment breaches the duty of candour and undermines trust.
takeaway: After harm: be open, apologise, explain, document and report.

stem:
A patient has a groin swelling that disappears when lying down and can be gently pushed back into the abdomen.

How is the hernia described?
why_correct: A reducible hernia can be returned to the abdominal cavity.
why_wrong: A. An irreducible hernia cannot be reduced. C. Perforation is not the defining feature of a hernia. D. Strangulation involves compromised blood supply. E. An obstructed hernia causes bowel obstruction.
pearl: A hernia that disappears on lying down and can be pushed back is reducible; once a hernia becomes irreducible, tender or painful, think incarceration or strangulation and escalate.
thinking: Swelling disappears when lying flat ↓ Contents return to the abdomen with gentle pressure ↓ The hernia can be reduced ↓ Reducible hernia
exam_trap: A, incarcerated and irreducible — the word incarcerated sounds like a standard descriptor, but by definition an incarcerated hernia cannot be pushed back, which is the opposite of this stem.
takeaway: Goes back in easily = reducible; will not go back = irreducible (incarcerated).

stem:
A patient with a previously reducible groin hernia develops severe constant pain. The swelling becomes tender and cannot be reduced.

What serious complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Severe pain and an irreducible tender hernia raise concern for compromised blood supply and strangulation.
why_wrong: A. Constipation does not explain the acutely painful irreducible swelling. B. The hernia is no longer reducible. D. Haemorrhoids do not cause a painful groin swelling. E. Reflux is unrelated.
pearl: A previously reducible hernia that becomes tense, tender, irreducible and constantly painful is strangulated until proven otherwise; it needs urgent surgical review because bowel viability is at risk.
thinking: Previously reducible groin hernia ↓ Now irreducible and tender ↓ Severe constant pain suggests ischaemia ↓ Blood supply compromised ↓ Strangulation
exam_trap: B, simple reducibility — it tempts because the hernia was reducible before, but the stem says it can no longer be reduced, so this describes the past, not the current emergency.
takeaway: New irreducibility plus severe constant pain and tenderness in a hernia = strangulation, an emergency.

stem:
A patient develops a reducible abdominal-wall swelling directly beneath a previous laparotomy scar.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An incisional hernia occurs through a weakness at a previous surgical incision.
why_wrong: A. A lipoma is a soft mass that is not reducible. B. A femoral hernia emerges through the femoral canal in the groin, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, not beneath a laparotomy scar. D. Inguinal hernias occur through the inguinal canal. E. A varicocele is dilatation of the pampiniform venous plexus.
pearl: A reducible swelling under or along a previous surgical scar is an incisional hernia; it arises through a weakness in the healed fascial closure.
thinking: Reducible abdominal-wall swelling ↓ Lies directly beneath a laparotomy scar ↓ Weakness at the old incision site ↓ Incisional hernia
exam_trap: D, indirect inguinal hernia — it tempts as the most common hernia, but it arises through the inguinal canal in the groin, not beneath a laparotomy scar.
takeaway: Hernia at the site of a previous operation scar = incisional hernia.

stem:
A patient develops severe throbbing perianal pain with a tender fluctuant swelling adjacent to the anus.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Severe local pain with a tender fluctuant perianal swelling is characteristic of an abscess.
why_wrong: A. Rectal prolapse is protrusion of rectal tissue. C. Anal fissure causes severe pain associated with defaecation but not usually a fluctuant abscess. D. Haemorrhoids cause vascular swellings and may bleed or cause discomfort. E. A pilonidal sinus occurs in the natal cleft rather than adjacent to the anus.
pearl: Severe throbbing perianal pain with a tender fluctuant swelling is a perianal abscess; the mainstay of treatment is surgical incision and drainage rather than antibiotics alone.
thinking: Severe throbbing perianal pain ↓ Tender, fluctuant swelling beside the anus ↓ Localised collection of pus ↓ Perianal abscess
exam_trap: C, anal fissure — it tempts because it causes severe anal pain, but a fissure gives sharp pain on defaecation and a visible tear, not a fluctuant swelling.
takeaway: Fluctuant, tender, throbbing perianal swelling = abscess, which needs drainage.

stem:
An older patient develops intensely itchy, tense fluid-filled blisters on otherwise relatively normal skin.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bullous pemphigoid typically causes tense, pruritic blisters in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Scabies causes intense pruritus and burrows rather than large tense bullae. B. Pemphigus vulgaris typically causes fragile flaccid blisters and mucosal involvement. D. Herpes zoster causes painful grouped vesicles in a dermatomal distribution. E. Impetigo causes superficial lesions and characteristic crusting.
pearl: Tense, itchy blisters in an older person suggest bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal split); flaccid, fragile blisters with mouth ulcers suggest pemphigus vulgaris (intraepidermal split).
thinking: Older patient ↓ Intensely itchy blisters ↓ Blisters are tense, so the split is deep (subepidermal) ↓ Bullous pemphigoid
exam_trap: B, pemphigus vulgaris — another autoimmune blistering disease, but its blisters are flaccid and rupture easily, often with mucosal involvement, not tense and itchy.
takeaway: Tense and itchy in the elderly = pemphigoid; flaccid with mucosal ulcers = pemphigus.

stem:
A woman has amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and headaches. Blood tests show markedly raised prolactin.

What type of tumour can cause this presentation?
why_correct: A prolactinoma is a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma and can cause galactorrhoea and menstrual disturbance.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid carcinoma does not typically cause marked hyperprolactinaemia. B. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma does not characteristically cause this syndrome. C. Renal cell carcinoma is not a typical cause of hyperprolactinaemia. D. An adrenal adenoma can cause cortisol or aldosterone excess but does not typically produce this pattern.
pearl: Amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and a markedly raised prolactin point to a prolactinoma; headache or visual field loss suggests a larger adenoma, and dopamine agonists are first-line treatment.
thinking: Amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea ↓ Markedly raised prolactin ↓ Headache suggests a pituitary mass ↓ Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma ↓ Prolactinoma
exam_trap: D, adrenal adenoma — it tempts as a common hormone-secreting tumour, but adrenal adenomas produce cortisol or aldosterone excess, not hyperprolactinaemia.
takeaway: Galactorrhoea + amenorrhoea + high prolactin = think pituitary prolactinoma.

stem: Why are people with diabetes offered regular retinal screening?

options.A: To measure intraocular pressure for early glaucoma
options.B: To monitor refractive error caused by fluctuating glucose
options.C: To detect diabetic retinopathy before sight is threatened
options.D: To detect cataract so surgery can be planned early
options.E: To grade hypertensive retinopathy and adjust BP treatment

correct_answer: C. To detect diabetic retinopathy before sight is threatened
why_correct: Regular retinal screening aims to detect diabetic retinopathy early and reduce the risk of visual loss.
why_wrong: A. Measuring intraocular pressure is not the purpose of diabetic eye screening. B. Refractive changes are not the target of retinal screening. D. Cataracts may occur in diabetes but are not the purpose of diabetic retinal screening. E. The programme targets diabetic retinopathy, not hypertensive retinopathy.
pearl: Diabetic retinopathy can threaten sight before any symptoms appear, so people with diabetes are offered regular retinal photography screening to detect and treat it early.
thinking: Screening offered to everyone with diabetes ↓ Retinopathy is often asymptomatic until advanced ↓ Early detection allows treatment ↓ Detect retinopathy before sight is threatened
exam_trap: A, measuring intraocular pressure for glaucoma — it tempts because eye pressure checks are familiar, but diabetic eye screening photographs the retina; it does not measure pressure.
takeaway: Diabetic eye screening exists to catch retinopathy early, before vision is lost.

stem:
A patient with diabetes develops worsening central vision due to retinal changes involving the macula.

Which visual function is particularly affected?
why_correct: Macular disease can impair detailed central vision.
why_wrong: A. Macular disease is not restricted to colour perception. C. Balance is not controlled by the macula. D. Hearing is unrelated to macular disease. E. Smell is unrelated.
pearl: The macula is responsible for detailed central vision, so diabetic maculopathy causes blurred central vision and difficulty reading or recognising faces while peripheral vision is preserved.
thinking: Diabetic retinal changes ↓ Macula is involved ↓ Macula serves fine, detailed vision ↓ Central vision is affected
exam_trap: A, colour perception only — it tempts because colour vision can be affected by macular disease, but the defining loss is central detailed vision, not colour alone.
takeaway: Macular disease = loss of central vision; peripheral vision is spared.

stem:
A contact-lens wearer develops severe eye pain, photophobia and reduced vision.

Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Painful photophobic red eye with reduced vision, particularly in a contact-lens wearer, raises concern for corneal infection.
why_wrong: A. Allergic conjunctivitis is usually itchy rather than severely painful with reduced vision. B. Hypermetropia is a refractive error and does not cause acute pain. C. Presbyopia causes difficulty with near vision and is painless. D. Cataract causes gradual painless visual impairment.
pearl: A contact-lens wearer with a painful, photophobic red eye and reduced vision has microbial keratitis until proven otherwise; stop lens wear and arrange same-day ophthalmology assessment.
thinking: Contact-lens wearer ↓ Severe eye pain and photophobia ↓ Reduced vision implies corneal involvement ↓ Sight-threatening corneal infection ↓ Keratitis
exam_trap: A, simple allergic conjunctivitis — a common red eye, but it is itchy with normal vision; severe pain, photophobia and reduced vision point to corneal disease.
takeaway: Painful red eye + reduced vision in a contact-lens wearer = urgent keratitis referral.

stem:
A woman with a known ectopic pregnancy develops sudden severe abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness and hypotension.

What complication is most likely?

options.A: Torsion of a corpus luteum cyst

why_correct: Sudden pain, haemodynamic compromise and shoulder-tip pain suggest intraperitoneal bleeding from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian torsion causes acute pain but does not explain haemorrhagic shock with shoulder-tip pain in a known ectopic. C. Vaginal infection does not explain the presentation. D. Endometriosis is a chronic condition and does not usually cause acute haemorrhagic shock. E. Red degeneration of a fibroid does not typically cause haemoperitoneum and shock.
pearl: A ruptured ectopic causes haemoperitoneum: sudden pain, shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation, and shock. Resuscitate and take the patient to theatre urgently.
thinking: Known ectopic pregnancy ↓ Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Shoulder-tip pain suggests blood under the diaphragm ↓ Dizziness and hypotension indicate haemorrhage ↓ Ruptured ectopic
exam_trap: A, torsion of a corpus luteum cyst — it causes sudden pelvic pain in early pregnancy, but does not explain shoulder-tip pain and haemorrhagic shock in a known ectopic.
takeaway: Known ectopic + shoulder-tip pain + hypotension = rupture; resuscitate and operate.

stem:
A woman develops fever, lower abdominal pain and offensive lochia three days after giving birth.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, uterine/lower abdominal pain and offensive lochia after delivery are characteristic of postpartum endometritis.
why_wrong: A. Ovarian cancer does not present acutely after delivery in this way. B. Urinary retention does not cause fever and offensive lochia. C. Mastitis causes breast pain, erythema and systemic symptoms. E. Endometriosis is a chronic condition and does not explain postpartum fever with offensive lochia.
pearl: Fever, lower abdominal or uterine tenderness and offensive lochia after delivery suggest postpartum endometritis, a common cause of maternal sepsis that needs prompt intravenous antibiotics.
thinking: A few days after birth ↓ Fever and lower abdominal pain ↓ Offensive lochia points to the uterus as the source ↓ Infection of the endometrium ↓ Postpartum endometritis
exam_trap: C, lactational infective mastitis — a common cause of postpartum fever, but it causes breast pain and redness, not lower abdominal pain or offensive lochia.
takeaway: Postpartum fever + uterine pain + offensive lochia = endometritis; treat as possible sepsis.

stem:
A newborn has a temperature of 35.5°C and feels cold to touch.

What is an important concern?
why_correct: A low temperature in a newborn is abnormal and may reflect environmental exposure or illness, including infection.
why_wrong: A. Teething is irrelevant in a newborn. B. 35.5°C is below the normal neonatal temperature range. D. Hyperthyroidism does not explain acute neonatal hypothermia. E. Jaundice does not cause this temperature abnormality.
pearl: Newborns lose heat quickly; a low temperature is abnormal and may be the only sign of sepsis or hypoglycaemia, so warm the baby, check glucose and look for infection.
thinking: Newborn feels cold ↓ Temperature 35.5°C is below the normal range ↓ Low temperature in a neonate is abnormal ↓ Neonatal hypothermia
exam_trap: B, normal neonatal temperature — tempting because newborn temperatures vary slightly, but 35.5°C is below normal and must be acted on rather than accepted.
takeaway: A cold newborn is a sick newborn until proven otherwise: warm, check glucose, consider sepsis.

stem:
A newborn develops tachypnoea, grunting and subcostal recession shortly after birth.

What do these findings indicate?
why_correct: Tachypnoea, grunting and chest recession are signs of respiratory distress in a newborn.
why_wrong: A. These signs should not be regarded as normal. B. Jaundice does not cause respiratory distress. C. Gastroenteritis does not explain immediate respiratory signs after birth. E. Otitis media does not cause this presentation.
pearl: Tachypnoea, grunting, nasal flaring and chest recession are the cardinal signs of respiratory distress in a newborn and need prompt assessment, oxygen as required and a search for the cause.
thinking: Newborn shortly after birth ↓ Tachypnoea ↓ Grunting and subcostal recession show increased work of breathing ↓ Neonatal respiratory distress
exam_trap: A, normal transitional breathing — tempting because breathing can be irregular after birth, but grunting and recession are never normal and signal respiratory distress.
takeaway: Grunting + recession + tachypnoea in a newborn = respiratory distress, not normal transition.

stem:
A premature newborn develops increasing respiratory distress shortly after birth due to inadequate pulmonary surfactant.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Prematurity predisposes to surfactant deficiency and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Croup is a childhood upper-airway infection. B. Pulmonary embolism is not the typical cause in this setting. C. Transient tachypnoea is due to delayed clearance of lung fluid, not surfactant deficiency. E. Bronchiectasis is a chronic airway condition.
pearl: Respiratory distress syndrome results from surfactant deficiency in premature lungs; antenatal corticosteroids reduce its risk and exogenous surfactant is used in treatment.
thinking: Premature newborn ↓ Worsening respiratory distress soon after birth ↓ Inadequate surfactant causes alveolar collapse ↓ Respiratory distress syndrome
exam_trap: C, transient tachypnoea of the newborn — also causes early tachypnoea, but it is due to delayed clearance of lung fluid, classically after caesarean section, not surfactant deficiency.
takeaway: Prematurity + surfactant deficiency = respiratory distress syndrome.

stem:
A newborn develops green (bilious) vomiting.

What should this be considered until proven otherwise?
why_correct: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a red flag for intestinal obstruction, including malrotation with volvulus.
why_wrong: A. Teething is not relevant to a newborn. B. Jaundice does not cause bilious vomiting. C. Simple reflux is generally non-bilious. D. Colic does not cause bilious vomiting.
pearl: Bilious (green) vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise; malrotation with volvulus must be excluded urgently because the bowel can infarct within hours.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Green vomit means bile ↓ Obstruction lies distal to the ampulla ↓ Risk of malrotation with volvulus ↓ Intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: C, infant reflux — tempting because reflux and possetting are common, but reflux is non-bilious; green vomit indicates obstruction.
takeaway: Green vomit in a baby = intestinal obstruction (think malrotation) until proven otherwise.

stem:
A newborn develops persistent central cyanosis that does not improve with simple warming.

What should be considered?

options.B: Benign acrocyanosis of the hands and feet

why_correct: Persistent central cyanosis in a newborn requires urgent assessment for serious cardiopulmonary disease, including cyanotic congenital heart disease.
why_wrong: B. Acrocyanosis is peripheral and benign, not persistent central cyanosis. C. Jaundice causes yellow rather than blue discoloration. D. Constipation does not cause persistent central cyanosis. E. Colic, even with breath-holding, does not cause persistent central cyanosis.
pearl: Peripheral blueness of the hands and feet (acrocyanosis) is common and benign in newborns, but persistent central cyanosis of the lips and tongue needs urgent assessment for cyanotic heart or lung disease.
thinking: Newborn with central cyanosis ↓ Persists despite warming ↓ Not peripheral acrocyanosis ↓ Serious cardiopulmonary cause needed ↓ Cyanotic congenital heart disease
exam_trap: B, benign acrocyanosis — common in newborns and improves with warming, but it is peripheral; persistent central cyanosis is never benign.
takeaway: Central cyanosis in a newborn is never normal; consider cyanotic congenital heart disease.

stem:
A patient with fever, cough and focal chest signs develops sharp chest pain that worsens with inspiration.

What type of pain is this?
why_correct: Pain arising from the pleura is typically sharp and worsened by inspiration or coughing.
why_wrong: A. Neuropathic pain arises from nerve dysfunction. B. Colicky pain classically fluctuates in severity, as in renal or biliary colic. C. Mechanical joint pain is associated with movement of a joint. E. Ischaemic limb pain relates to impaired arterial blood supply.
pearl: Pleuritic pain is sharp, well localised and worse on deep inspiration or coughing; in a patient with fever and focal chest signs it suggests pneumonia involving the pleura.
