why_correct: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (46,XY) causes primary amenorrhoea with normal breast development, from peripheral aromatisation of testicular testosterone, but scant pubic and axillary hair because androgen-dependent hair growth fails; there are testes rather than functional ovaries and no uterus.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis presents with pelvic pain and/or subfertility in women who menstruate, not primary amenorrhoea. B. Turner syndrome causes ovarian failure with absent or poor breast development and usually normal pubic hair from adrenal androgens, the opposite of this picture. C. Pregnancy should be considered in sexually active adolescents but does not explain primary amenorrhoea with scant pubic hair and absent ovaries. E. PMOS (formerly PCOS) causes irregular or absent ovulation with hyperandrogenism, not absent ovaries with scant body hair.
pearl: Complete androgen insensitivity: 46,XY with testes, normal breasts from aromatised testosterone, scant pubic and axillary hair and no uterus, presenting as primary amenorrhoea.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea at 16 ↓ Normal breast development ↓ Scant pubic and axillary hair ↓ No functional ovaries ↓ Androgen insensitivity syndrome
exam_trap: B, Turner syndrome — classic for primary amenorrhoea with ovarian failure, but it gives poor breast development and usually normal pubic hair, the reverse of this picture.
takeaway: Breasts present, body hair scant and primary amenorrhoea: think androgen insensitivity.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy has no testicular enlargement and has not developed other expected pubertal changes. His height is below that of most peers but his growth pattern has remained consistent.

What is an important initial consideration?
why_correct: Absence of expected pubertal development by this age warrants assessment for delayed puberty.
why_wrong: A. Cushing syndrome has a different clinical pattern and does not specifically cause absent testicular development. C. Precocious puberty involves unusually early pubertal development. D. Acromegaly occurs after growth plates have largely fused. E. Hyperthyroidism does not explain absent testicular enlargement.
pearl: In boys, absent testicular enlargement by about 14 years defines delayed puberty; constitutional delay with steady growth is commonest, but hypogonadism and chronic illness must be excluded.
thinking: Boy aged 16 ↓ No testicular enlargement ↓ No other pubertal changes ↓ Short but growing consistently ↓ Delayed puberty
exam_trap: C, precocious puberty — the other puberty-timing option, but it means unusually early development, whereas this boy has none at 16.
takeaway: No testicular enlargement by around 14 years in a boy means delayed puberty.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman presents with a painful, red area of breast tissue three weeks after starting breastfeeding. She has a temperature of 38.5°C.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Breastfeeding-associated breast pain, erythema and systemic symptoms are typical of lactational mastitis.
why_wrong: A. Intraductal papilloma commonly causes nipple discharge. C. Fibrocystic change can cause cyclical breast discomfort but not an acute febrile presentation. D. Breast cancer does not typically present with an acute febrile inflammatory illness. E. Fibroadenoma is usually a painless discrete lump.
pearl: In lactational mastitis, continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected breast; add flucloxacillin if infection is likely or symptoms fail to settle, and look for an abscess if not improving.
thinking: Three weeks into breastfeeding ↓ Painful red area of breast ↓ Fever of 38.5°C ↓ Inflammation of the lactating breast ↓ Lactational mastitis
exam_trap: D, breast cancer — inflammatory cancer can mimic infection, but an acute febrile illness in early breastfeeding is mastitis; cancer is considered if it fails to resolve.
takeaway: A painful, red, febrile breast while breastfeeding is mastitis; keep feeding.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman notices spontaneous blood-stained discharge from one nipple. There is no fever or breast inflammation.

Which lesion is a recognised cause of this presentation?
why_correct: An intraductal papilloma can cause spontaneous, often blood-stained, unilateral nipple discharge.
why_wrong: A. A galactocele is a milk-retention cyst associated with lactation. C. Fat necrosis typically follows trauma and presents as a firm lump, not spontaneous bloody discharge. D. A breast abscess is painful and inflammatory. E. Fibroadenoma typically presents as a painless breast lump.
pearl: Spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct most often comes from an intraductal papilloma near the areola; assessment is still needed because ductal carcinoma can present similarly.
thinking: Spontaneous nipple discharge ↓ From one nipple ↓ Blood-stained ↓ No fever or inflammation ↓ Intraductal papilloma
exam_trap: D, subareolar breast abscess — near the nipple and may discharge, but it is painful and inflamed, and this woman has no fever or inflammation.
takeaway: Spontaneous bloody discharge from one nipple is classically an intraductal papilloma.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman presents with a new breast lump. It is hard, irregular and poorly mobile. There is associated skin tethering.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: The features are suspicious for breast malignancy
options.B: No assessment is required if there is no pain
options.C: The features are diagnostic of fibroadenoma
options.D: The lump is necessarily a cyst
options.E: The lump is necessarily an abscess

correct_answer: A. The features are suspicious for breast malignancy
why_correct: A new hard, irregular, poorly mobile breast lump with skin tethering has suspicious features and requires urgent breast assessment.
why_wrong: B. Breast cancer can be painless. C. Fibroadenomas are typically smooth and mobile. D. A simple cyst is typically smooth and fluctuant. E. Abscesses usually cause pain and inflammatory changes.
pearl: Hard, irregular, fixed lumps with skin tethering, nipple change or axillary nodes are suspicious; refer on a suspected cancer pathway for triple assessment: examination, imaging and biopsy.
thinking: New breast lump at 52 ↓ Hard and irregular ↓ Poorly mobile ↓ Skin tethering ↓ Suspicious for breast malignancy
exam_trap: C, diagnostic of fibroadenoma — a common breast lump, but fibroadenomas are smooth, rubbery and mobile, typically in younger women, not hard and tethered.
takeaway: A hard, irregular, tethered breast lump is cancer until triple assessment says otherwise.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman develops severe loin pain and fever. She has rigors and appears unwell. Imaging shows a ureteric stone with proximal urinary tract dilatation.

What is the most important concern?
why_correct: Infection proximal to an obstructed urinary tract can rapidly become life-threatening and requires urgent urological management.
why_wrong: B. Obstruction makes this complicated; infection behind an obstruction needs urgent decompression. C. Fever and systemic illness make uncomplicated renal colic inappropriate as the diagnosis. D. Asymptomatic bacteriuria does not cause this clinical picture. E. Cystitis does not explain an obstructed upper urinary tract with systemic illness.
pearl: An infected obstructed kidney is a urological emergency: resuscitate, give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent; antibiotics alone are not enough.
thinking: Ureteric stone ↓ Proximal dilatation means obstruction ↓ Fever and rigors mean infection ↓ Infection behind obstruction risks urosepsis ↓ Infected obstructed urinary tract
exam_trap: B, uncomplicated pyelonephritis — fever and loin pain fit, but obstruction makes it complicated; without decompression it can rapidly progress to septic shock.
takeaway: Fever plus an obstructing stone needs urgent decompression, not antibiotics alone.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no vaginal discharge, flank pain or systemic symptoms.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria and frequency without systemic or upper urinary tract features are typical of a lower UTI.
why_wrong: A. Glomerulonephritis causes renal findings such as haematuria and proteinuria rather than isolated dysuria. B. Pyelonephritis usually causes fever, systemic illness and flank pain. C. PID is usually associated with pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness and/or abnormal vaginal discharge. D. Renal colic causes severe colicky pain.
pearl: In a non-pregnant woman with typical lower UTI symptoms and no upper tract or systemic features, the diagnosis is clinical, and a short course of nitrofurantoin is the usual UK first-line choice.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Dysuria and frequency ↓ No vaginal discharge, so vaginitis less likely ↓ No flank pain or systemic features ↓ Lower urinary tract infection
exam_trap: B, acute pyelonephritis — also a UTI, but it needs fever, systemic upset or flank pain, all absent here.
takeaway: Dysuria and frequency without fever or flank pain mean lower UTI.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman has dysuria, urinary frequency and fever. She also has marked tenderness in the costovertebral angle.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, urinary symptoms and flank or costovertebral-angle tenderness suggest infection of the kidney.
why_wrong: B. Stress incontinence causes leakage. C. Cystitis usually lacks systemic illness and flank tenderness. D. Stones cause colicky pain but do not by themselves explain fever and infection. E. Candidiasis causes vulvovaginal itching and discharge rather than renal-angle tenderness.
pearl: Acute pyelonephritis needs an antibiotic that reaches renal tissue, so nitrofurantoin is unsuitable; send urine for culture, and admit if septic, vomiting or not improving.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency ↓ Fever adds systemic features ↓ Costovertebral angle tenderness ↓ Upper urinary tract infection ↓ Acute pyelonephritis
exam_trap: C, uncomplicated cystitis — shares the dysuria and frequency, but fever and renal-angle tenderness show the infection has reached the kidney.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms plus fever and loin tenderness mean pyelonephritis.

stem:
A 67-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops persistent nausea, itching and increasing confusion despite appropriate medical management.

Which complication may indicate the need to consider renal replacement therapy?
why_correct: Significant uraemic complications are among the situations in which renal replacement therapy may need to be considered.
why_wrong: A. Mild oedema can often be managed medically. B. An isolated creatinine value is not by itself an indication for dialysis. D. Controlled hypertension is not an indication. E. Chronic anaemia alone does not automatically require renal replacement therapy.
pearl: Reasons to consider dialysis in CKD include uraemic complications such as encephalopathy, pericarditis or intractable symptoms, plus refractory fluid overload, hyperkalaemia or acidosis.
thinking: CKD ↓ Persistent nausea and itching ↓ Increasing confusion ↓ Despite appropriate medical management, so refractory ↓ Uraemic complications
exam_trap: B, mild isolated creatinine elevation — a number feels decisive, but dialysis decisions rest on symptoms and complications, not a single mild creatinine rise.
takeaway: Refractory uraemic complications are a reason to consider renal replacement therapy.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman develops severe abdominal pain and diarrhoea several days after returning from abroad. She is drinking normally and has no signs of dehydration.

What is the most important initial management principle?
why_correct: Maintaining hydration is central to management of acute diarrhoeal illness when there is no evidence of severe dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Fluid restriction increases the risk of dehydration. B. There is no evidence of a surgical abdomen. C. Corticosteroids are not routine treatment for infectious diarrhoea. E. Insulin has no role.
pearl: Most traveller's diarrhoea is self-limiting; maintaining oral fluid intake is the mainstay, with oral rehydration solution for those at risk, and stool culture if bloody, severe or persistent.
thinking: Diarrhoea after travel abroad ↓ Likely infective ↓ Drinking normally, not dehydrated ↓ Ongoing losses must be replaced ↓ Maintain adequate fluid intake
exam_trap: B, immediate emergency surgery — the severe pain tempts, but nothing described suggests a surgical abdomen; this is a diarrhoeal illness managed medically.
takeaway: Acute infective diarrhoea is managed first by keeping the patient hydrated.

stem:
A 29-year-old man develops profuse watery diarrhoea after returning from a tropical region. He is thirsty and has dry mucous membranes.

What complication is the immediate concern?
why_correct: Profuse diarrhoea with thirst and dry mucous membranes indicates fluid loss and dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Osteoporosis is unrelated. B. Cataract is unrelated. C. There is no evidence of liver failure. E. Hyperthyroidism does not explain acute diarrhoeal fluid loss.
pearl: Profuse watery diarrhoea after tropical travel, as in cholera, can cause rapid fluid and electrolyte loss; oral rehydration solution is first line, with IV fluids if severe or unable to drink.
thinking: Recent tropical travel ↓ Profuse watery diarrhoea causes large fluid losses ↓ Thirst ↓ Dry mucous membranes ↓ Dehydration
exam_trap: E, hyperthyroidism — can cause loose stools, but it does not cause sudden profuse watery diarrhoea after travel; fluid loss is the immediate danger.
takeaway: Profuse watery diarrhoea with thirst and dry mucosa means dehydration: rehydrate.

stem:
A 31-year-old man develops fever, abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea after eating inadequately cooked food.

Which feature should prompt particular concern?
correct_answer: D. Systemic illness with bloody diarrhoea
why_correct: Bloody diarrhoea with systemic illness can indicate invasive intestinal infection and warrants appropriate clinical assessment.
why_wrong: A. Cramps relieved by defecation are non-specific and not a marker of invasive infection. B. Bloating and flatus are not markers of invasive infection. C. Belching is nonspecific. E. Heartburn does not suggest invasive diarrhoeal illness.
pearl: Bloody diarrhoea with fever suggests invasive infection such as Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella or E. coli O157; send stool culture and avoid antimotility drugs.
thinking: Undercooked food ↓ Fever and abdominal cramps ↓ Bloody diarrhoea ↓ Mucosal invasion with systemic upset ↓ Systemic illness with bloody diarrhoea
exam_trap: A, cramps relieved by defecation — sounds clinically relevant, but it is a non-specific, IBS-like feature; blood with systemic illness is the real red flag.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea with fever signals invasive infection: send stool culture.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has intensely itchy linear burrows between her fingers. Her partner has similar symptoms.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Prescribe oral antibiotics for household members
options.B: Treat her and close contacts at the same time
options.C: Treat her now and her partner if symptoms persist
options.D: Wash bedding at high temperature as the main treatment
options.E: Treat symptomatic contacts and observe the others

correct_answer: B. Treat her and close contacts at the same time
why_correct: Scabies spreads readily through close contact, so appropriate close contacts require simultaneous management to reduce reinfestation.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not eradicate scabies mites. C. Delaying treatment of contacts allows reinfestation. D. Environmental measures alone do not treat infestation. E. Asymptomatic contacts may still be infested.
pearl: Treat scabies with permethrin cream applied to the whole body as directed and repeated after one week, for the patient and all close contacts at the same time; itch can persist for weeks after cure.
thinking: Itchy linear burrows between fingers ↓ Scabies ↓ Partner has similar symptoms ↓ Spread by close contact ↓ Treat her and close contacts at the same time
exam_trap: E, treat symptomatic contacts and observe the others — seems proportionate, but contacts may be infested before itch starts, so untreated contacts cause reinfestation.
takeaway: Scabies: treat the patient and all close contacts simultaneously.

stem:
A 23-year-old man develops a sharply demarcated, itchy rash in the groin with scaling at the edge. He has recently been using communal changing facilities.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: An itchy, scaly, sharply demarcated rash with an advancing edge in a moist area is characteristic of dermatophyte infection.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is usually painful, warm and acutely inflamed. B. Psoriasis can affect the groin but the described advancing scaly edge and exposure favour tinea. C. Urticaria produces transient wheals rather than persistent scaling. D. Melanoma presents as a pigmented lesion rather than a spreading scaly rash.
pearl: Tinea cruris is an itchy, well-demarcated groin rash with a scaly active edge; treat with a topical antifungal such as terbinafine, and avoid topical steroids alone, which can worsen it.
thinking: Young man ↓ Itchy groin rash ↓ Sharply demarcated with a scaly edge ↓ Use of communal changing facilities ↓ Tinea infection
exam_trap: B, psoriasis only — flexural psoriasis can affect the groin, but the scaly advancing edge and exposure history favour dermatophyte infection.
takeaway: An itchy groin rash with a scaly active edge is tinea; treat with a topical antifungal.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman has a sharply demarcated, bright-red, painful rash on her cheek. The edge is raised and clearly defined, and she has fever.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Erysipelas is a superficial bacterial skin infection producing a sharply demarcated, raised, erythematous area with systemic symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals. C. Vitiligo causes depigmented patches. D. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes chronic scaling in seborrhoeic areas. E. Tinea is a superficial fungal infection with scaling.
pearl: Erysipelas affects the upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, giving a raised, sharply demarcated edge, whereas cellulitis is deeper with less defined margins; streptococci are the usual cause.
thinking: Bright-red painful rash on the cheek ↓ Raised, clearly defined edge ↓ Fever indicates systemic infection ↓ Superficial dermal bacterial infection ↓ Erysipelas
exam_trap: E, tinea corporis — also has a defined edge, but it is itchy and scaly without fever, not painful, bright red and systemically unwell.
takeaway: A raised, sharply demarcated, painful red rash with fever is erysipelas.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman develops sudden swelling of her lips and tongue shortly after eating a food she has not previously tolerated.

What is the most concerning associated complication?
why_correct: Angioedema involving the tongue or upper airway can rapidly compromise the airway and may form part of anaphylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Cataract is unrelated. C. Urinary retention is unrelated. D. Renal colic is unrelated. E. Osteoarthritis is unrelated.
pearl: Lip and tongue swelling after a food trigger can herald anaphylaxis; assess airway, breathing and circulation and give IM adrenaline promptly if any of these is compromised.
thinking: Exposure to a new food ↓ Sudden lip and tongue swelling ↓ Angioedema ↓ Tongue and upper airway at risk ↓ Airway obstruction
exam_trap: C, acute urinary retention — nothing in the stem points to it; the real danger is the swelling spreading to obstruct the upper airway.
takeaway: Tongue swelling after an allergen threatens the airway: think anaphylaxis.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman develops sudden widespread itching, wheeze, dizziness and facial swelling after receiving an antibiotic.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rapid onset of airway/respiratory or circulatory compromise with skin or mucosal features after exposure to a likely trigger is characteristic of anaphylaxis.
why_wrong: B. Panic attacks do not explain objective facial swelling, widespread itching and wheeze. C. Vasovagal episodes do not cause widespread itching, wheeze and facial swelling. D. Urticaria alone does not explain wheeze and dizziness indicating systemic involvement. E. Viral exanthems do not typically cause this sudden post-exposure presentation.
pearl: In adult anaphylaxis give IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 in 1000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeating after 5 minutes if needed; antihistamines are not first line.
thinking: Antibiotic just given ↓ Sudden widespread itch and facial swelling ↓ Wheeze shows airway involvement ↓ Dizziness suggests circulatory compromise ↓ Anaphylaxis
exam_trap: D, simple urticaria — the itch and swelling fit, but wheeze and dizziness show respiratory and circulatory involvement, which makes this anaphylaxis.
takeaway: Skin signs plus breathing or circulation problems after a trigger mean anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline.

stem:
A 59-year-old woman develops central chest pain at rest lasting 30 minutes. Her ECG shows ST-segment depression and troponin is elevated.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Myocardial ischaemic symptoms with raised troponin but without ST elevation are consistent with NSTEMI.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis usually produces diffuse ST elevation and PR changes. B. Unstable angina does not cause a troponin rise. D. Reflux does not cause myocardial injury. E. Costochondritis causes musculoskeletal chest-wall pain.
pearl: Troponin separates NSTEMI from unstable angina: both present with ischaemic pain without ST elevation, but only NSTEMI shows myocardial injury with a raised troponin.
thinking: Central chest pain at rest for 30 minutes ↓ ST depression, not elevation ↓ Troponin raised, so myocardial injury ↓ ACS without ST elevation ↓ Non-ST-elevation MI
exam_trap: B, unstable angina — shares the rest pain and ST depression, but by definition troponin is not raised; a raised troponin makes this NSTEMI.
takeaway: Ischaemic pain, no ST elevation and a raised troponin mean NSTEMI.

stem:
A 67-year-old man with heart failure develops increasing breathlessness and cannot lie flat because he feels unable to breathe.

What symptom is he describing?
why_correct: Orthopnoea is breathlessness that occurs when lying flat and is commonly associated with heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Claudication is exertional limb pain caused by arterial insufficiency. B. Pleuritic pain is pain associated with breathing. D. Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion. E. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
pearl: Orthopnoea occurs because lying flat increases venous return to a failing left ventricle; ask how many pillows the patient needs, and distinguish it from paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea.
thinking: Heart failure ↓ Increasing breathlessness ↓ Cannot lie flat ↓ Breathlessness provoked by lying down ↓ Orthopnoea
exam_trap: B, pleuritic pain — also linked to breathing, but it is sharp chest pain on inspiration, not breathlessness provoked by lying flat.
takeaway: Breathlessness on lying flat is orthopnoea, a classic heart failure symptom.

stem:
A 45-year-old man has episodic wheeze and cough that are worse when he is exposed to house dust. Between episodes, his respiratory examination is normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Variable respiratory symptoms triggered by environmental exposure with normal findings between episodes are characteristic of asthma.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary fibrosis causes persistent rather than highly variable symptoms. B. Pleural effusion causes persistent breathlessness and reduced breath sounds. C. Bronchiectasis usually causes chronic productive cough. D. Lung cancer commonly causes persistent respiratory symptoms.
pearl: Asthma is diagnosed from variable symptoms supported by objective evidence of airway inflammation or variable obstruction, such as FeNO, bronchodilator reversibility or peak flow variability.
thinking: Episodic wheeze and cough ↓ Triggered by house dust ↓ Normal examination between episodes ↓ Variable, reversible airway obstruction ↓ Asthma
exam_trap: C, bronchiectasis — a chronic airway disease with cough, but it causes persistent daily productive sputum rather than episodic, trigger-driven wheeze.
takeaway: Episodic, trigger-driven wheeze with normal findings between attacks suggests asthma.

stem:
A 23-year-old man develops sudden severe pain and swelling of the left side of his scrotum. He has no urinary symptoms and the pain began abruptly while he was asleep.

What is the most important diagnosis to exclude?
why_correct: Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain without urinary symptoms is highly concerning for testicular torsion, a time-critical surgical emergency.
why_wrong: A. An inguinal hernia may cause groin or scrotal swelling but the abrupt severe testicular presentation requires torsion to be excluded. B. Hydrocele is generally painless. C. An epididymal cyst is usually painless. E. Varicocele usually develops gradually and causes a dragging discomfort.
pearl: Testicular torsion is a clinical diagnosis needing urgent surgical exploration; do not delay for ultrasound, as the chance of saving the testis falls sharply within hours.
thinking: Young man ↓ Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain ↓ Onset during sleep ↓ No urinary symptoms to suggest infection ↓ Testicular torsion
exam_trap: E, varicocele — another left-sided scrotal swelling, but it develops gradually with a dragging ache, not sudden severe pain.
takeaway: Sudden severe testicular pain is torsion until surgery proves otherwise.

stem:
A 66-year-old man has a history of peripheral arterial disease and asks about smoking cessation.

Why is stopping smoking particularly important?

options.C: Smoking improves collateral blood flow to the legs

why_correct: Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular and peripheral arterial disease.
why_wrong: A. Smoking promotes rather than prevents atherosclerosis. C. Smoking causes vasoconstriction and does not improve collateral flow. D. Smoking does not reverse established atherosclerotic plaque. E. Smoking increases rather than prevents vascular risk.
pearl: In peripheral arterial disease, smoking cessation, an antiplatelet, a statin and supervised exercise are core; stopping smoking slows progression and lowers amputation and cardiovascular risk.
thinking: Peripheral arterial disease ↓ Caused by atherosclerosis ↓ Smoking damages endothelium and promotes plaque ↓ Major modifiable risk factor ↓ Smoking accelerates atherosclerosis
exam_trap: C, smoking improves collateral blood flow — sounds plausible, but smoking causes vasoconstriction and endothelial damage, worsening limb perfusion.
takeaway: Stopping smoking is a cornerstone of managing peripheral arterial disease.

stem:
A 65-year-old man has swelling and pain in his right calf following several weeks of reduced mobility.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Unilateral calf swelling and pain with a provoking factor such as immobility are characteristic features that should raise suspicion of DVT.
why_wrong: A. Gout typically causes acute inflammatory arthritis. C. Osteoarthritis causes joint-related mechanical pain. D. Varicose eczema causes chronic inflammatory skin changes. E. Cellulitis can cause unilateral swelling and erythema but does not explain the thrombotic risk context by itself.
pearl: For suspected DVT use the two-level Wells score: if likely, arrange proximal leg vein ultrasound, with interim anticoagulation if it is delayed; if unlikely, start with a D-dimer.
thinking: Older man ↓ Several weeks of reduced mobility ↓ Unilateral calf pain and swelling ↓ Venous stasis as a provoking factor ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: E, cellulitis — can cause unilateral leg swelling and pain, but no erythema or fever is described, and recent immobility points to venous thrombosis.
takeaway: Unilateral calf swelling after immobility is DVT until excluded.

stem:
A 56-year-old man presents with sudden onset of weakness affecting his right face and arm. His speech is slurred.

What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.C: Activate the local acute stroke pathway
options.D: Reassure him that symptoms are likely migraine

correct_answer: C. Activate the local acute stroke pathway
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms are highly concerning for acute stroke and require immediate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Routine referral would delay time-critical assessment. B. There is no evidence of bacterial infection. D. Stroke must be considered urgently rather than assumed to be migraine. E. Rehabilitation may be required later but is not the initial priority.
pearl: Sudden facial and arm weakness with speech disturbance is FAST-positive: activate the stroke pathway at once because reperfusion treatments are time-dependent, and check glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Right face and arm weakness ↓ Slurred speech ↓ FAST-positive, likely stroke ↓ Activate the local acute stroke pathway
exam_trap: D, reassure that it is likely migraine — migraine aura can cause focal symptoms, but sudden focal weakness must be treated as stroke; delay loses the treatment window.
takeaway: FAST-positive symptoms: activate the stroke pathway immediately.

stem:
A 68-year-old man develops sudden loss of vision in his right eye lasting 10 minutes. His vision then returns completely to normal.

What is this episode commonly called?
why_correct: Transient monocular visual loss due to retinal or optic circulation is termed amaurosis fugax and can be a manifestation of transient ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. Retinal detachment generally causes persistent visual symptoms. C. Optic neuritis typically causes subacute painful visual loss. D. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment. E. Conjunctivitis causes redness and discharge.
pearl: Amaurosis fugax is a TIA affecting the eye, often from carotid emboli; arrange urgent specialist TIA assessment with carotid imaging and start aspirin unless contraindicated.
thinking: Older man ↓ Sudden monocular visual loss ↓ Lasts 10 minutes ↓ Complete recovery suggests transient ischaemia ↓ Amaurosis fugax
exam_trap: A, retinal detachment — causes sudden monocular loss, but it is usually preceded by floaters and flashes and persists rather than resolving completely.
takeaway: Transient monocular blindness is amaurosis fugax: manage as a TIA.

stem:
A 35-year-old woman develops weakness that becomes worse after repeated movements but improves after resting. Examination is otherwise normal.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fatigable weakness that improves with rest is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.
why_wrong: A. Parkinson's causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor. B. Peripheral arterial disease causes exertional limb pain rather than fatigable muscle weakness. C. MS produces neurological deficits separated in time and space. D. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness with UMN/LMN signs.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis classically causes fatigable ptosis, diplopia and proximal weakness; check acetylcholine receptor antibodies and image the chest for thymoma.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Weakness worsens with repeated movement ↓ Improves after rest ↓ Examination otherwise normal ↓ Myasthenia gravis
exam_trap: C, multiple sclerosis — common in young women and causes fatigue, but it produces deficits separated in time and space, not fatigable weakness that recovers with rest.
takeaway: Weakness that worsens with use and recovers with rest is myasthenia gravis.

stem: A 74-year-old man suddenly develops difficulty speaking and weakness of his right arm. Which clinical feature would make a stroke particularly likely?

options.A: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
options.B: Gradual onset of symptoms over several months
options.C: Bilateral chronic joint pain and morning stiffness

correct_answer: A. Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
why_correct: Stroke classically presents with sudden focal neurological dysfunction.
why_wrong: B. Gradual progression is not typical of acute stroke. C. Chronic joint pain and stiffness are unrelated. D. Itching is unrelated. E. Constipation and bloating do not indicate acute focal cerebral ischaemia.
pearl: Stroke is a sudden focal loss of neurological function; always check capillary glucose because hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke, and image urgently to exclude haemorrhage.
thinking: Older man ↓ Speech difficulty and right arm weakness ↓ Abrupt onset ↓ Focal deficit fitting a vascular territory ↓ Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
exam_trap: B, gradual onset over several months — a neurological history, but slow progression suggests a tumour or degenerative disease rather than stroke.
takeaway: Sudden onset of a focal neurological deficit is the hallmark of stroke.

stem:
A 60-year-old man suddenly develops weakness and sensory loss affecting the left side of his body. He also has left-sided visual field loss.

Which vascular territory is most likely involved?
correct_answer: A. Right middle cerebral artery territory
why_correct: A right hemispheric lesion can produce contralateral weakness, sensory loss and visual field deficit, commonly within the MCA territory.
why_wrong: B. A left MCA lesion would usually produce right-sided deficits. C. Basilar artery disease produces a different brainstem pattern. D. The radial artery is a peripheral vessel and cannot produce these neurological deficits. E. An optic nerve lesion would not cause hemiparesis.
pearl: MCA strokes cause contralateral weakness and sensory loss, face and arm more than leg, with homonymous hemianopia; a dominant-side lesion adds aphasia, a non-dominant one neglect.
thinking: Left-sided weakness and sensory loss ↓ Left visual field loss ↓ Contralateral deficits localise to the right hemisphere ↓ Classic MCA pattern ↓ Right middle cerebral artery territory
exam_trap: B, left MCA territory — tempting because the symptoms are left-sided, but hemispheric lesions cause contralateral deficits, so the lesion is on the right.
takeaway: Hemispheric stroke signs are contralateral: left-sided deficits mean right MCA.

stem:
A 70-year-old man develops abdominal distension, vomiting and absolute constipation. Imaging suggests a large bowel obstruction.

Which underlying condition should be considered particularly in an older adult?
why_correct: Colorectal malignancy is an important cause of large bowel obstruction, particularly in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease does not cause mechanical large bowel obstruction. B. Appendicitis does not typically cause large bowel obstruction. C. Cataract affects the lens of the eye. D. Asthma affects the airways.
pearl: Colorectal cancer is the commonest cause of large bowel obstruction in adults, ahead of volvulus and diverticular stricture; CT abdomen and pelvis confirms the level and cause.
thinking: Older man ↓ Distension, vomiting and absolute constipation ↓ Imaging suggests large bowel obstruction ↓ Commonest cause in older adults ↓ Colorectal cancer
exam_trap: B, appendicitis — an abdominal surgical emergency, but it presents with right iliac fossa pain and does not typically cause mechanical large bowel obstruction.
takeaway: Large bowel obstruction in an older adult is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule and biochemical evidence of hyperthyroidism.

Which imaging investigation can help determine whether the nodule is functioning?

options.B: Plain radiograph of the thoracic inlet
options.D: MRI of the neck and thyroid

why_correct: A radionuclide thyroid scan can demonstrate whether a thyroid nodule is functioning autonomously.
why_wrong: A. CT shows anatomy, not function, and iodinated contrast can interfere with later radionuclide imaging. B. A thoracic inlet radiograph shows tracheal deviation or retrosternal extension, not nodule function. C. CT colonography examines the large bowel. D. MRI shows anatomy, not iodine uptake, so it cannot show whether the nodule is functioning.
pearl: A hot nodule takes up tracer and is rarely malignant, whereas a cold nodule does not; in hyperthyroidism, radionuclide scanning separates a toxic nodule from Graves disease.
thinking: Thyroid nodule ↓ Biochemical hyperthyroidism ↓ Question is whether the nodule makes hormone ↓ Functional imaging needed ↓ Radionuclide thyroid scan
exam_trap: D, MRI of the neck and thyroid — gives detailed anatomy, but it shows structure, not iodine uptake, so it cannot show whether the nodule is functioning.
takeaway: Function needs a functional test: a radionuclide scan shows hot versus cold nodules.

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. The leg is visibly larger than the other leg.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Unilateral leg swelling and tenderness are typical features that should raise suspicion of DVT.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis of the hand cannot explain unilateral calf swelling. B. Asthma does not cause unilateral calf swelling. C. Migraine does not cause leg swelling. D. Osteoarthritis does not typically cause acute unilateral calf swelling.
pearl: Acute unilateral leg swelling in an adult is DVT until proven otherwise; bilateral swelling points instead to systemic causes such as heart failure, low albumin or drugs.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Unilateral calf swelling ↓ Calf tenderness ↓ Leg visibly larger than the other ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: D, osteoarthritis — a common cause of leg pain at this age, but it causes joint pain and stiffness, not acute unilateral calf swelling.
takeaway: Acute unilateral calf swelling needs DVT excluded.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman develops unilateral leg swelling several days after hip replacement surgery.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Recent major orthopaedic surgery is a major risk factor for venous thromboembolism, and unilateral leg swelling is a typical presentation of DVT.
why_wrong: A. Acute limb ischaemia causes a pale, cold, pulseless limb rather than swelling. B. Otitis externa affects the ear. D. Migraine does not cause leg swelling. E. Appendicitis causes abdominal symptoms.
pearl: Hip and knee replacement carry a high VTE risk, so extended pharmacological thromboprophylaxis is usual after surgery; new unilateral leg swelling still needs DVT excluded.
thinking: Recent hip replacement ↓ Major orthopaedic surgery and reduced mobility ↓ High VTE risk ↓ New unilateral leg swelling ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: A, peripheral arterial embolism — a post-operative vascular event, but it causes a pale, cold, painful, pulseless limb rather than swelling.
takeaway: Unilateral leg swelling after joint replacement is DVT until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman presents with a painful groin swelling that is irreducible. She is vomiting and has abdominal distension.

What is the most concerning diagnosis?
why_correct: An irreducible painful hernia associated with vomiting and obstruction raises concern for strangulation and compromised bowel.
why_wrong: A. Lymphadenitis causes tender nodes but not bowel obstruction. B. A reducible inguinal hernia can be returned to the abdomen. D. A lipoma is usually a soft benign mass and does not cause bowel obstruction. E. A varicocele is dilated scrotal veins and does not cause bowel obstruction.
pearl: A tender, irreducible hernia with obstructive symptoms suggests strangulation: keep nil by mouth, resuscitate and arrange emergency surgery, as delay risks bowel necrosis.
thinking: Painful groin swelling ↓ Irreducible ↓ Vomiting and distension mean bowel obstruction ↓ Blood supply likely compromised ↓ Strangulated hernia
exam_trap: A, inguinal lymphadenitis — a tender groin lump, but nodes do not cause vomiting and abdominal distension; obstruction points to trapped bowel.
takeaway: A painful irreducible hernia with obstruction is strangulation: emergency surgery.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents with a new breast lump that is hard, irregular and fixed to surrounding tissue.

What diagnosis must be considered?
why_correct: A new hard, irregular or fixed breast lump is suspicious for malignancy and requires appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: B. Fibroadenomas are typically smooth and mobile. C. Lipomas are generally soft and mobile. D. Mastitis produces painful inflammatory changes rather than a persistent suspicious lump. E. Simple cysts are usually smooth and fluctuant.
pearl: A new breast lump in an older woman is cancer until proven otherwise; refer on a suspected cancer pathway, where triple assessment of examination, imaging and biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
thinking: Older woman ↓ New breast lump ↓ Hard and irregular texture ↓ Fixed to surrounding tissue ↓ Breast cancer
exam_trap: B, fibroadenoma — the commonest benign breast lump, but it is smooth, rubbery and mobile, usually in younger women, not hard and fixed at 68.
takeaway: A new hard, fixed breast lump in an older woman is cancer until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 63-year-old man develops progressive difficulty swallowing and a persistent sore throat. He has a long history of smoking.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent throat symptoms and dysphagia, particularly in a smoker, can be features of head and neck malignancy and require appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa affects the external ear. C. Tension headache does not explain progressive swallowing difficulty. D. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms rather than progressive dysphagia. E. IBS does not cause dysphagia.
pearl: Persistent unexplained sore throat, dysphagia, hoarseness or a neck lump in a smoker should prompt suspected head and neck cancer referral; tobacco and alcohol act synergistically.
thinking: Long smoking history ↓ Persistent sore throat ↓ Progressive dysphagia ↓ Possible upper aerodigestive tract malignancy ↓ Head and neck cancer
exam_trap: D, allergic rhinitis — postnasal drip can cause a sore throat, but it does not cause progressive dysphagia, and persistent symptoms in a smoker need cancer excluded.
takeaway: Persistent throat symptoms with dysphagia in a smoker need head and neck cancer excluded.

stem:
A 55-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the side of his tongue that has persisted for six weeks.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: It requires assessment for oral malignancy
options.B: It is most likely a traumatic ulcer from teeth
options.C: It is caused by referred chronic otitis media
options.D: It is typical of a recent viral gastroenteritis
options.E: It is likely aphthous and can be observed for now

correct_answer: A. It requires assessment for oral malignancy
why_correct: A persistent oral ulcer, particularly lasting more than a few weeks, is a red flag for possible oral cancer.
why_wrong: B. Trauma is possible but should not be assumed when an ulcer persists. C. Otitis media does not cause persistent oral ulceration. D. Gastroenteritis does not explain a persistent tongue ulcer. E. Aphthous ulcers are painful and heal within about two weeks; a persistent painless ulcer needs assessment.
pearl: An oral ulcer persisting beyond about three weeks needs urgent assessment for oral cancer; the lateral tongue is a common site, and smoking and alcohol are key risk factors.
thinking: Middle-aged man ↓ Tongue ulcer for six weeks ↓ Painless and persistent ↓ Lateral tongue is a high-risk site ↓ Requires assessment for oral malignancy
exam_trap: B, traumatic ulcer from teeth — common on the lateral tongue, but a trauma ulcer should heal once the cause is removed; persistence demands cancer assessment.
takeaway: Never attribute a persistent mouth ulcer to trauma without excluding cancer.

stem:
A 40-year-old woman has a white patch on the side of her tongue that cannot be scraped away.

What is this lesion called?
why_correct: Leukoplakia is a persistent white oral patch that cannot be scraped off and may require assessment because of its association with oral malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Herpes labialis causes vesicular lesions, usually around the lips. C. Gingivitis causes inflamed gums. D. Candidal plaques can generally be scraped away, often leaving an erythematous surface. E. An aphthous ulcer is an ulcer rather than a persistent white patch.
pearl: Leukoplakia is a white patch that cannot be wiped off and is not explained by another diagnosis; it is potentially premalignant, so persistent patches need specialist review and often biopsy.
thinking: White patch on the side of the tongue ↓ Cannot be scraped away ↓ Candidal plaques usually wipe off ↓ Persistent keratotic lesion ↓ Leukoplakia
exam_trap: D, oral candidiasis — the classic white oral lesion, but candidal plaques can usually be wiped off, leaving a red base, whereas this patch cannot.
takeaway: A white oral patch that will not scrape off is leukoplakia and potentially premalignant.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman develops widespread itchy wheals together with swelling of her lips shortly after eating peanuts.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute widespread wheals accompanied by lip swelling following an allergen exposure are typical of urticaria with angioedema.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary angioedema causes angioedema without urticarial wheals. B. Cellulitis is a local bacterial skin infection. C. Contact dermatitis is eczematous at the site of contact rather than causing widespread wheals and lip swelling. D. Erythema multiforme causes target lesions rather than acute wheals after an allergen.
pearl: Allergic angioedema usually comes with urticaria and a clear trigger; hereditary angioedema causes swelling without wheals and responds poorly to antihistamines and adrenaline.
thinking: Peanut exposure ↓ Rapid onset ↓ Widespread itchy wheals ↓ Lip swelling from deeper tissue oedema ↓ Urticaria with angioedema
exam_trap: A, hereditary angioedema — causes lip swelling, but without wheals or itch and not allergen-triggered; wheals after peanuts indicate allergic urticaria.
takeaway: Wheals plus lip swelling after an allergen is urticaria with angioedema; watch for anaphylaxis.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman develops a widespread itchy rash and wheezing shortly after receiving an antibiotic.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute allergic symptoms involving the skin and respiratory system after drug exposure are characteristic of anaphylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Viral exanthems do not usually cause sudden wheezing immediately after a drug. B. Tinea causes localised fungal infection. D. Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition. E. Cellulitis is usually localised.
pearl: After anaphylaxis, record the suspected drug clearly as an allergy, take mast cell tryptase samples and refer to a specialist allergy service for assessment.
thinking: Antibiotic just given ↓ Rapid widespread itchy rash ↓ Wheeze shows airway involvement ↓ Skin plus respiratory features after a trigger ↓ Anaphylaxis
exam_trap: A, viral exanthem — a widespread rash is typical, but it develops with a viral illness and does not cause sudden wheeze straight after a drug.
takeaway: Rash plus wheeze shortly after a drug is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 58-year-old man develops jaundice, pale stools and dark urine. His serum alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin are markedly elevated.

Which type of liver-test pattern is most likely?
why_correct: Jaundice with pale stools and dark urine, together with prominent alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin elevation, suggests cholestasis.
why_wrong: A. The liver tests are clearly abnormal. B. Haemolysis causes unconjugated bilirubin elevation but does not produce this cholestatic pattern. C. A hepatocellular pattern is characterised predominantly by elevated transaminases. D. Endocrine is not a liver-test pattern.
pearl: Read liver tests by pattern: raised ALP and GGT with bilirubin suggests cholestasis, while transaminases far exceeding ALP suggest hepatocellular injury; ultrasound then looks for duct dilatation.
thinking: Jaundice ↓ Pale stools and dark urine ↓ Markedly raised ALP and bilirubin ↓ Impaired bile flow ↓ Cholestatic
exam_trap: B, haemolytic — tempting because bilirubin is high, but haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which does not reach the urine, and it does not cause pale stools or a marked ALP rise.
takeaway: Jaundice with pale stools, dark urine and high ALP means cholestasis.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman with acute kidney injury has a urinary catheter inserted. Her urine output remains very low, and ultrasound demonstrates bilateral hydronephrosis.

What is the most likely underlying problem?
why_correct: Bilateral hydronephrosis indicates obstruction to urinary drainage and can cause post-renal AKI.
why_wrong: B. Prerenal AKI does not cause bilateral hydronephrosis. C. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes proteinuria and oedema. E. Simple cystitis does not usually cause bilateral hydronephrosis.
pearl: Ultrasound the renal tract early in unexplained AKI: bilateral hydronephrosis means post-renal obstruction, relieved by catheter if at the bladder outlet or by nephrostomy or stent if higher.
thinking: AKI ↓ Catheter inserted yet output stays very low ↓ Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis ↓ Urinary drainage is blocked ↓ Urinary tract obstruction
exam_trap: B, prerenal AKI from hypovolaemia — the commonest AKI cause and gives low urine output, but it does not dilate the collecting systems.
takeaway: Bilateral hydronephrosis in AKI means post-renal obstruction.

stem:
A 76-year-old man with acute kidney injury develops severe breathlessness. Examination suggests pulmonary oedema despite appropriate initial management.

Which complication of AKI is this?
why_correct: Reduced renal excretion of fluid can result in significant fluid overload and pulmonary oedema.
why_wrong: B. Iron deficiency does not cause acute pulmonary oedema. C. Neutropenia does not cause fluid overload. D. Hypoglycaemia is unrelated to fluid accumulation. E. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated to this acute renal complication.
pearl: Pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics in AKI is an indication for renal replacement therapy, alongside refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis and uraemic complications.
thinking: AKI with reduced fluid excretion ↓ Severe breathlessness ↓ Signs of pulmonary oedema ↓ Persists despite initial management ↓ Fluid overload
exam_trap: B, iron deficiency — anaemia can cause breathlessness on exertion, but it does not cause acute pulmonary oedema; retained fluid from failing kidneys does.
takeaway: AKI can cause fluid overload and pulmonary oedema; refractory cases may need dialysis.

stem:
A 63-year-old man with AKI develops persistent severe hyperkalaemia despite initial medical treatment.

Which treatment may be required if the hyperkalaemia remains refractory?
why_correct: Refractory severe hyperkalaemia is an indication to consider renal replacement therapy in AKI.
why_wrong: A. Inhaled corticosteroids do not treat severe hyperkalaemia. C. Colonoscopy is unrelated. D. Ipratropium does not shift potassium; it is salbutamol that lowers serum potassium. E. Iron does not correct hyperkalaemia.
pearl: In severe hyperkalaemia give IV calcium to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol to shift potassium; if it remains refractory in AKI, dialysis is needed.
thinking: AKI ↓ Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ Initial medical treatment fails ↓ Kidneys cannot clear potassium ↓ Renal replacement therapy
exam_trap: D, nebulised ipratropium — tempting as a nebuliser like salbutamol, but ipratropium does not shift potassium into cells.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia refractory to medical therapy in AKI needs renal replacement therapy.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has persistent proteinuria and haematuria. Urine microscopy shows red-cell casts.

What does this finding suggest?
why_correct: Red-cell casts are strongly suggestive of glomerular bleeding and inflammation.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration does not cause red-cell casts. C. Lower UTI does not typically produce red-cell casts. D. Renal stones can cause haematuria but not typically red-cell casts. E. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria rather than glomerular haematuria.
pearl: Red-cell casts form in the renal tubules and indicate glomerular bleeding; with proteinuria they point to glomerulonephritis, which may need urgent renal referral.
thinking: Persistent proteinuria ↓ Haematuria ↓ Red-cell casts on microscopy ↓ Bleeding originates in the glomerulus ↓ Glomerular inflammation
exam_trap: D, renal stone alone — a common cause of haematuria, but stones bleed into the collecting system and do not form red-cell casts.
takeaway: Red-cell casts mean glomerular disease, not lower urinary tract bleeding.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops bone pain and biochemical abnormalities involving calcium and phosphate.

Which complication should be considered?

options.B: Iron overload from IV iron therapy
options.E: Paget disease of the pelvis and skull

why_correct: CKD can disrupt phosphate, calcium, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone regulation, producing mineral and bone abnormalities.
why_wrong: B. Iron overload is not the characteristic complication described. C. Primary hyperparathyroidism from an adenoma is not a complication of CKD; CKD causes secondary hyperparathyroidism within CKD-MBD. D. Appendicitis is unrelated to CKD and to calcium and phosphate abnormalities. E. Paget disease is not a complication of CKD.
pearl: In CKD, phosphate retention and reduced renal activation of vitamin D lower calcium and drive secondary hyperparathyroidism, causing renal bone disease and vascular calcification.
thinking: CKD ↓ Bone pain ↓ Abnormal calcium and phosphate ↓ Phosphate retention and low active vitamin D raise PTH ↓ CKD-mineral and bone disorder
exam_trap: C, primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma) — bone pain with calcium changes suggests parathyroid disease, but CKD drives secondary, not primary, hyperparathyroidism.
takeaway: Bone pain with calcium and phosphate disturbance in CKD is CKD-MBD.

stem:
A 59-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops persistent metabolic acidosis despite appropriate medical management.

Which renal replacement indication is being illustrated?
why_correct: Severe metabolic acidosis that remains refractory to medical management can be an indication for renal replacement therapy.
why_wrong: A. Microscopic haematuria alone is not an indication. B. Anaemia alone is not an indication for renal replacement therapy. C. Controlled hypertension is not an indication. D. Stable proteinuria alone is not an indication.
pearl: Remember dialysis indications as AEIOU: Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload and Uraemia, each meaning refractory to medical treatment.
thinking: CKD ↓ Persistent metabolic acidosis ↓ Despite appropriate medical management ↓ Refractory acidosis meets dialysis criteria ↓ Refractory metabolic acidosis
exam_trap: B, mild isolated anaemia — anaemia is common in CKD, but it is treated with iron and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, not by starting dialysis.
takeaway: Dialysis is for refractory acidosis, potassium, overload, uraemia or certain toxins.

stem:
A 42-year-old man develops severe loin-to-groin pain with microscopic haematuria. The pain comes in waves and he cannot keep still.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Severe colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria is characteristic of a ureteric stone.
why_wrong: A. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain. B. Peptic ulcer disease causes upper abdominal symptoms. D. Diverticulitis usually causes left lower abdominal pain. E. Appendicitis usually progresses towards right lower quadrant pain.
pearl: In renal colic, give an NSAID first line if not contraindicated and arrange a non-contrast CT KUB; fever with an obstructing stone is an emergency needing urgent decompression.
thinking: Severe loin-to-groin pain ↓ Pain in waves, colicky ↓ Cannot keep still ↓ Microscopic haematuria ↓ Renal colic
exam_trap: D, diverticulitis — lower abdominal pain in middle age, but it is constant left iliac fossa pain, not colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria.
takeaway: Colicky loin-to-groin pain, restlessness and haematuria mean renal colic.

stem:
A 25-year-old man develops a single painless genital ulcer. He has no systemic symptoms.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Primary syphilis classically presents with a painless genital ulcer or chancre.
why_wrong: B. Genital herpes typically causes painful grouped vesicles or ulcers. C. Bacterial vaginosis affects the vagina and causes discharge. D. Candidiasis is not a cause of genital ulcers in men. E. Genital warts cause painless wart-like lesions rather than ulcers.
pearl: A painless indurated chancre is primary syphilis; refer to sexual health for testing, partner notification and treatment, usually with benzathine penicillin.
thinking: Young man ↓ Single genital ulcer ↓ Painless, suggesting a chancre ↓ No systemic symptoms ↓ Primary syphilis
exam_trap: B, genital herpes — the commonest cause of genital ulceration in the UK, but it causes multiple painful vesicles or ulcers, not a single painless one.
takeaway: Single painless genital ulcer suggests syphilis; multiple painful ulcers suggest herpes.

stem:
A 23-year-old woman has lower abdominal pain following a recent new sexual partner. She has abnormal vaginal discharge and cervical motion tenderness.

Which sexually transmitted infection is an important cause of PID?
why_correct: Chlamydia trachomatis is a major sexually transmitted cause of PID.
why_wrong: A. Dermatophytes cause superficial fungal skin infections. B. Candida causes vulvovaginal candidiasis rather than typical PID. C. Influenza does not cause PID. D. Varicella-zoster virus does not cause typical PID.
pearl: PID is often polymicrobial, but Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are key causes; treat empirically on clinical suspicion, as delay increases the risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
thinking: Young woman with a new partner ↓ Lower abdominal pain ↓ Abnormal vaginal discharge ↓ Cervical motion tenderness suggests PID ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis
exam_trap: B, Candida albicans — a common cause of abnormal discharge, but it causes vulvovaginitis and does not ascend to cause typical PID.
takeaway: Chlamydia is a leading cause of PID; treat on clinical suspicion.

stem:
A 72-year-old man is found to have iron-deficiency anaemia. He has no obvious history of blood loss.

Why is gastrointestinal investigation important?

options.B: Iron deficiency is always caused by dietary deficiency in older adults
options.C: Colonoscopy is unnecessary in asymptomatic patients
options.D: Occult gastrointestinal blood loss may be present
options.E: Iron deficiency always indicates coeliac disease

correct_answer: D. Occult gastrointestinal blood loss may be present
why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult can result from occult gastrointestinal bleeding, including gastrointestinal malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency can occur with gastrointestinal malignancy. B. Dietary deficiency is not the only explanation. C. Lack of gastrointestinal symptoms does not exclude significant pathology. E. Coeliac disease is one possible cause but not the only one.
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult needs GI investigation, usually lower and upper GI endoscopy plus coeliac serology, as right-sided colon cancer can bleed silently.
thinking: Older man ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ No obvious blood loss ↓ Occult GI bleeding, including cancer, possible ↓ Occult gastrointestinal blood loss may be present
exam_trap: B, always dietary deficiency in older adults — poor diet does occur, but assuming it misses occult GI bleeding and malignancy.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult means investigate the GI tract.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman has macrocytic anaemia but no neurological symptoms. Her diet contains very little fresh fruit and vegetables.

Which deficiency should be considered?
why_correct: Folate deficiency can cause macrocytic anaemia and may occur with poor dietary intake.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired clotting. C. Iron deficiency causes microcytic anaemia. D. Calcium deficiency does not typically cause macrocytic anaemia. E. Vitamin D deficiency affects bone mineralisation.
pearl: Folate deficiency follows poor diet, alcohol excess, pregnancy or malabsorption; always check B12 as well, and replace B12 before folate if both are low to avoid neurological harm.
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia ↓ No neurological symptoms ↓ Diet very low in fresh fruit and vegetables ↓ Folate comes largely from fresh produce ↓ Folate
exam_trap: C, iron — the commonest dietary deficiency causing anaemia, but iron deficiency gives a microcytic picture, not macrocytosis.
takeaway: Macrocytic anaemia with poor fruit and vegetable intake suggests folate deficiency.

stem:
A 25-year-old man develops severe pain and swelling of his knee after a minor injury. He has haemophilia A.

What is the most likely cause of the joint swelling?
why_correct: Haemophilia commonly causes bleeding into large joints, producing painful swelling and restricted movement.
why_wrong: A. Bursitis affects a bursa rather than causing typical haemarthrosis. B. Cellulitis affects skin and subcutaneous tissue. D. Osteoarthritis usually causes chronic mechanical joint pain. E. Gout can cause acute arthritis but is not the characteristic bleeding complication of haemophilia.
pearl: Haemarthrosis is the hallmark bleed of severe haemophilia; give prompt factor VIII replacement as directed by the haemophilia centre, and avoid aspiration without factor cover.
thinking: Haemophilia A ↓ Minor injury ↓ Severe pain and swelling of the knee ↓ Factor VIII deficiency causes bleeding into large joints ↓ Haemarthrosis
exam_trap: E, gout — causes acute painful joint swelling, but it is unusual at 25 and haemophilia makes bleeding into the joint the expected cause.
takeaway: Acute joint swelling in haemophilia is haemarthrosis: replace factor promptly.

stem:
A 45-year-old man has recurrent attacks of severe pain and swelling at the base of his big toe. Joint aspiration demonstrates needle-shaped crystals with negative birefringence.

What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis causes a chronic inflammatory polyarthritis rather than monosodium urate crystal deposition. C. CPPD produces rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals. D. Septic arthritis is caused by infection rather than urate crystals. E. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease.
pearl: Gout shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent urate crystals; pseudogout shows rhomboid, positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Treat acute gout with an NSAID or colchicine.
thinking: Recurrent attacks ↓ Base of the big toe ↓ Joint aspirate examined ↓ Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals ↓ Gout
exam_trap: C, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease — the other crystal arthritis, but its crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, and it favours the knee.
takeaway: Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals mean gout.

stem:
A 79-year-old woman is admitted after a fall and is found to have a fractured neck of femur.

Which complication is particularly important to prevent during her hospital admission?
why_correct: Hip fracture and reduced mobility increase the risk of venous thromboembolism, so appropriate VTE prevention is important.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa is unrelated. B. Reflux is not a specific risk of a hip fracture admission. D. Migraine is unrelated. E. Cataract is unrelated to the acute admission.
pearl: Hip fracture combines trauma, surgery and immobility, so assess VTE risk on admission, give pharmacological prophylaxis unless contraindicated and mobilise early after surgery.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Fractured neck of femur ↓ Surgery and reduced mobility ↓ High risk of venous thrombosis ↓ Venous thromboembolism
exam_trap: B, oesophageal reflux — a common inpatient complaint, but it is not a specific risk of hip fracture; VTE is a major preventable complication.
takeaway: Hip fracture patients need VTE prophylaxis and early mobilisation.

stem:
A 19-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy asks why he should avoid strenuous competitive exercise.

What is the main concern?
why_correct: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is associated with ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, particularly during exertion.
why_wrong: A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy does not cause pulmonary fibrosis. B. It does not primarily cause chronic kidney disease. C. Exercise does not specifically cause iron deficiency. D. It has no characteristic association with peptic ulcer disease.
pearl: HCM is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes; screen first-degree relatives, and individualise exercise advice with a cardiologist based on risk assessment.
thinking: Young man ↓ Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy ↓ Hypertrophied myocardium is prone to ventricular arrhythmia ↓ Risk heightened by strenuous exertion ↓ Sudden cardiac death
exam_trap: C, development of iron-deficiency anaemia — sport-related but irrelevant to HCM; the danger of exertion in HCM is ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death.
takeaway: The major exercise risk in HCM is sudden cardiac death from arrhythmia.

stem:
A 27-year-old man develops chest pain and breathlessness following a recent viral illness. ECG shows widespread ST-segment changes and troponin is elevated.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Myocarditis can follow a viral infection and cause chest pain, ECG abnormalities and elevated cardiac troponin.
why_wrong: B. DVT causes limb symptoms rather than this cardiac presentation. C. Peripheral arterial disease affects limb circulation. D. Stable angina causes predictable exertional chest pain and is less likely in this context. E. Mitral stenosis does not typically cause an acute troponin-positive presentation after a viral illness.
pearl: Myocarditis after a viral illness can mimic ACS with chest pain, ECG changes and raised troponin in a young person; cardiac MRI helps confirm it, and strenuous exercise is avoided during recovery.
thinking: Young man ↓ Recent viral illness ↓ Chest pain and breathlessness ↓ Widespread ST changes and raised troponin ↓ Myocarditis
exam_trap: D, stable angina — chest pain with ECG changes, but it is predictable exertional pain without a troponin rise, and unlikely at 27 after a viral illness.
takeaway: Chest pain with raised troponin after a viral illness in a young adult suggests myocarditis.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman develops chest pain after a recent viral illness. Troponin is elevated and echocardiography shows impaired ventricular function.

Which cardiac complication of myocarditis is particularly important?
why_correct: Myocarditis can impair myocardial contractility and lead to acute or chronic heart failure.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic is unrelated. B. Myocarditis does not directly cause chronic liver failure. D. Osteoporosis is unrelated. E. Peptic ulcer disease is unrelated.
pearl: Suspect myocarditis when chest pain and a raised troponin follow a viral illness; impaired ventricular function signals the risk of heart failure and arrhythmia, so these patients need cardiology input and monitoring.
thinking: Recent viral illness ↓ Chest pain with raised troponin ↓ Echo shows impaired ventricular function ↓ Inflamed myocardium contracts poorly ↓ Heart failure
exam_trap: B, chronic liver failure — severe heart failure can cause congestive liver changes, which may make it tempting, but myocarditis does not directly cause chronic liver failure; the question asks for the cardiac complication, which is heart failure.
takeaway: Myocarditis with impaired ventricular function means watching for heart failure and arrhythmia.

stem:
A 30-year-old man taking a new medication develops palpitations. ECG demonstrates QT prolongation.

Which adverse effect should be recognised as potentially serious?
why_correct: Drug-induced QT prolongation can predispose to torsades de pointes and potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias.
why_wrong: B. QT prolongation does not cause a hypertensive crisis. C. Constipation does not explain the significance of QT prolongation. D. First-degree heart block is benign PR prolongation and not the danger of QT prolongation. E. It does not directly cause cataracts.
pearl: A prolonged QT interval matters because it predisposes to torsades de pointes and fatal ventricular arrhythmia; always review the drug list and correct potassium and magnesium.
thinking: New medication ↓ Palpitations ↓ ECG shows QT prolongation ↓ Delayed repolarisation predisposes to torsades de pointes ↓ Ventricular arrhythmia
exam_trap: D, first-degree heart block — it sounds like the ECG-related answer, but it is benign PR prolongation, not the danger of a long QT interval.
takeaway: Long QT is dangerous because of torsades de pointes and sudden ventricular arrhythmia.

stem:
A 46-year-old man has fever, weight loss and a new heart murmur. He has a history of injecting drugs.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever, a new murmur and intravenous drug use are important features suggesting infective endocarditis.
why_wrong: A. Stable angina does not cause fever and a new murmur. B. Osteoarthritis does not cause systemic infection. D. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is chronic, causes a diastolic murmur and does not explain fever and weight loss. E. Nephrotic syndrome causes protein loss and oedema rather than this presentation.
pearl: Fever plus a new murmur is infective endocarditis until proven otherwise, especially in people who inject drugs, who are prone to right-sided (tricuspid) involvement.
thinking: Fever and weight loss ↓ New heart murmur ↓ Injecting drug use gives venous bacteraemia ↓ Infection of the heart valves ↓ Infective endocarditis
exam_trap: D, rheumatic mitral stenosis — it explains a murmur, but it is chronic, gives a diastolic murmur and does not account for fever and weight loss.
takeaway: Fever with a new murmur in someone who injects drugs is endocarditis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A patient is suspected of having infective endocarditis but is haemodynamically stable and has not yet received antibiotics.

What should generally be obtained before starting antibiotics?
why_correct: In suspected infective endocarditis, blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics where this can be done without compromising urgent treatment.
why_wrong: A. Stool culture does not establish infective endocarditis. B. Pregnancy testing may be relevant to prescribing but does not diagnose endocarditis. C. Sputum cytology is not the relevant investigation. D. Skin biopsy is not routinely used to diagnose endocarditis.
pearl: In suspected endocarditis in a stable patient, take multiple sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics; one dose of antibiotic can render cultures negative.
thinking: Suspected infective endocarditis ↓ Stable, no antibiotics yet ↓ Need to identify the organism to guide prolonged therapy ↓ Antibiotics first would sterilise cultures ↓ Blood cultures
exam_trap: C, sputum cytology — it sounds like a reasonable infection workup sample, but endocarditis is an intravascular infection identified on blood culture, not sputum.
takeaway: Blood cultures before antibiotics in suspected endocarditis, provided treatment is not dangerously delayed.

stem:
A 40-year-old man has severe chest pain after repeated vomiting. Imaging demonstrates air in the mediastinum.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Forceful vomiting followed by severe chest pain and pneumomediastinum suggests spontaneous oesophageal rupture.
why_wrong: A. Costochondritis causes chest-wall pain without pneumomediastinum. B. A Mallory-Weiss tear is mucosal, causes haematemesis and does not produce pneumomediastinum. C. GORD does not cause oesophageal rupture. D. Stable angina is exertional rather than vomiting-associated.
pearl: Severe chest pain after forceful vomiting with mediastinal air is Boerhaave syndrome, a full-thickness oesophageal rupture and surgical emergency with high mortality if missed.
thinking: Repeated forceful vomiting ↓ Sudden severe chest pain ↓ Air in the mediastinum ↓ Full-thickness oesophageal tear ↓ Boerhaave syndrome
exam_trap: B, Mallory-Weiss tear — it also follows vomiting, but it is a mucosal tear that causes haematemesis and cannot let air into the mediastinum.
takeaway: Vomiting then chest pain with pneumomediastinum means oesophageal rupture, not a Mallory-Weiss tear.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with chronic cough undergoes spirometry. The FEV₁/FVC ratio is reduced.

What type of ventilatory defect does this indicate?
why_correct: A reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio indicates airflow obstruction, as seen in conditions such as COPD and asthma.
why_wrong: A. Restrictive disease generally has a preserved or increased FEV₁/FVC ratio. B. A reduced ratio is abnormal. C. Neuromuscular junction disorders are not diagnosed by this spirometric pattern. E. Anaemia does not cause an obstructive spirometric pattern.
pearl: A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio defines airflow obstruction (COPD, asthma); restrictive disease reduces both volumes, so the ratio is normal or raised.
thinking: Chronic cough ↓ Spirometry performed ↓ FEV1 falls more than FVC ↓ Reduced FEV1/FVC ratio ↓ Obstructive defect
exam_trap: A, restrictive — candidates mix up the two patterns; restriction lowers FEV1 and FVC together, preserving or raising the ratio rather than reducing it.
takeaway: Low FEV1/FVC ratio means obstruction; a preserved ratio with low volumes suggests restriction.

stem:
A 54-year-old woman has been taking prednisolone at a moderate dose for several months. She stops it suddenly without medical advice.

What is the main concern?
why_correct: Prolonged systemic corticosteroid treatment suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, so abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. Steroid withdrawal does not directly cause iron deficiency. B. It does not characteristically cause hypercalcaemia. C. Steroid withdrawal does not cause hyperthyroidism. D. Acute pancreatitis is not a recognised consequence of stopping steroids; the danger is adrenal crisis from HPA-axis suppression.
pearl: Months of systemic steroids suppress the HPA axis; stopping abruptly risks adrenal crisis, so prolonged courses are tapered and patients should carry a steroid card.
thinking: Months of moderate-dose prednisolone ↓ HPA axis suppressed ↓ Adrenals cannot produce cortisol on demand ↓ Abrupt stop removes steroid cover ↓ Adrenal insufficiency
exam_trap: D, acute pancreatitis — steroids are linked with pancreatitis, so it can seem plausible, but the danger of sudden withdrawal is adrenal crisis.
takeaway: Never stop long-term steroids abruptly: the risk is adrenal insufficiency and adrenal crisis.

stem: A patient has been taking long-term prednisolone. Which complication is associated with prolonged systemic corticosteroid treatment?
why_correct: Long-term systemic corticosteroids increase bone loss and the risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures.
why_wrong: A. They do not cause appendicitis. B. They do not cause Parkinson disease. C. Corticosteroids do not characteristically cause iron-deficiency anaemia. E. They do not directly cause primary hypothyroidism.
pearl: Long-term systemic steroids accelerate bone loss and raise fracture risk; assess fracture risk and consider bone protection for patients on prolonged courses.
thinking: Long-term prednisolone ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and increase resorption ↓ Bone mineral density falls ↓ Fragility fracture risk rises ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: E, hypothyroidism — steroids affect many endocrine axes, so a hormonal answer tempts, but they do not cause primary hypothyroidism; bone loss is the classic complication.
takeaway: Prolonged systemic steroids cause osteoporosis: think bone protection early.

stem:
A patient taking long-term prednisolone develops blurred vision. Examination reveals lens opacity.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Long-term corticosteroid treatment is associated with cataract formation, particularly posterior subcapsular cataracts.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis is associated with inflammatory/demyelinating disease. B. Corneal abrasion causes acute painful surface injury. D. Retinal detachment is not the characteristic steroid-related lens complication. E. Conjunctivitis affects the conjunctiva rather than producing lens opacity.
pearl: Chronic corticosteroid use classically causes posterior subcapsular cataract and can also raise intraocular pressure; ask about steroid use in any patient with lens opacity.
thinking: Long-term prednisolone ↓ Blurred vision ↓ Lens opacity on examination ↓ Steroids cause posterior subcapsular lens changes ↓ Cataract
exam_trap: A, optic neuritis — it causes blurred vision, but it affects the optic nerve with pain on eye movement, not an opacity in the lens.
takeaway: Steroids plus lens opacity means steroid-induced (posterior subcapsular) cataract.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman starts a combined oral contraceptive pill. She asks when contraceptive protection begins.

Which factor is most important in determining when additional contraception is required?

options.B: Whether she has been pregnant before
options.E: Cycle day on which the pill was started

correct_answer: E. Cycle day on which the pill was started
why_correct: The timing of initiation determines whether contraceptive protection is immediate or whether additional precautions are required.
why_wrong: A. Childhood vaccination history does not determine onset of contraceptive efficacy. B. Previous pregnancy does not determine when protection starts. C. Smoking affects COC safety, not the onset of protection. D. BMI affects COC eligibility, not the onset of protection.
pearl: Starting the combined pill on day 1 to 5 of the cycle gives immediate protection; starting at any other time needs extra precautions such as condoms for the first 7 days.
thinking: New combined pill ↓ Asks when protection begins ↓ Ovulation suppression depends on when in the cycle she starts ↓ Early-cycle start covers it, later start does not ↓ Cycle day of starting
exam_trap: D, body mass index — it is relevant to COC prescribing, but it affects eligibility and risk, not when contraceptive protection begins.
takeaway: The start day of the cycle decides whether extra contraception is needed with a new combined pill.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive develops a severe migraine for the first time, associated with visual disturbances immediately before the headache.

What type of migraine is this?
why_correct: Transient focal neurological symptoms such as visual disturbances preceding the headache indicate migraine with aura.
why_wrong: A. Medication-overuse headache is associated with frequent analgesic use. C. Tension headache is usually bilateral and pressing. D. Cluster headache typically causes severe unilateral orbital pain with autonomic symptoms. E. Migraine without aura lacks these transient focal neurological symptoms.
