why_wrong: B. Thrombocytopenia means a low platelet count. C. Haemophilia causes bleeding due to clotting-factor deficiency. D. Iron deficiency causes low haemoglobin. E. Aplastic anaemia causes bone-marrow failure and cytopenias.
pearl: Persistently raised haemoglobin and haematocrit with itching after a warm bath or shower should prompt consideration of polycythaemia vera, usually confirmed by JAK2 mutation testing.
thinking: Persistently high haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Headaches suggest hyperviscosity ↓ Aquagenic pruritus is a classic myeloproliferative clue ↓ Polycythaemia
exam_trap: E, aplastic anaemia — a marrow disorder that may tempt, but it causes low counts across all cell lines, the opposite of a raised haemoglobin and haematocrit.
takeaway: High haemoglobin and haematocrit plus aquagenic itch: think polycythaemia vera.

stem:
A patient with severe neutropenia develops fever but has no obvious focal source of infection.

Why may infection be difficult to localise?

options.B: Infections are usually viral in neutropenia

correct_answer: D. Neutropenia blunts the inflammatory response
why_correct: A reduced neutrophil response can mean that typical localising signs of infection are absent or less pronounced.
why_wrong: A. Fever in neutropenia should be assumed to be infective until proven otherwise. B. Bacterial infections predominate in neutropenic fever. C. Neutrophils, not lymphocytes, form the key local response; lymphocyte migration is not the issue. E. Neutropenic fever must be treated as infection rather than attributed to drugs.
pearl: Without neutrophils there is little pus, swelling or consolidation, so fever may be the only sign; treat fever in a neutropenic patient as infection until proven otherwise.
thinking: Severe neutropenia ↓ Neutrophils produce pus, swelling and localising signs ↓ A blunted inflammatory response hides the source ↓ Neutropenia blunts the inflammatory response
exam_trap: A, neutropenia causes fever without infection — tempting because no source is found, but fever in neutropenia must be assumed infective; absent signs reflect a muted response.
takeaway: Neutropenia hides the signs of infection, not the infection itself.

stem:
A pregnant woman has concerns after handling cat litter.

Which infection is of particular relevance?
why_correct: Toxoplasma gondii can be transmitted through exposure to infected cat faeces or contaminated soil and is important during pregnancy because congenital infection can occur.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa is an external ear infection. B. Tetanus is not specifically associated with cat litter. D. Influenza is transmitted primarily through respiratory exposure. E. Scabies is caused by mites and spreads mainly through close skin contact.
pearl: Toxoplasmosis is caught from cat faeces, soil and undercooked meat; pregnant women should avoid emptying cat litter or wear gloves and wash hands, and eat meat well cooked.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Exposure to cat litter (cat faeces) ↓ Toxoplasma gondii is shed in cat faeces and can cross the placenta ↓ Toxoplasmosis
exam_trap: B, tetanus — dirt and soil exposure can bring tetanus to mind, but tetanus needs a contaminated wound and is not specifically linked to cat litter or congenital infection.
takeaway: Cat litter in pregnancy means toxoplasmosis risk: gloves and hand hygiene.

stem:
A pregnant woman who is not known to be immune is exposed to rubella.

What is the major concern?
why_correct: Maternal rubella infection, particularly early in pregnancy, can cause congenital rubella syndrome with serious fetal consequences.
why_wrong: A. Rubella is not a cause of peptic ulcer disease. B. Renal colic is unrelated. C. Rubella does not cause congenital appendicitis. D. Scabies is a mite infestation unrelated to congenital rubella.
pearl: Rubella in early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome with deafness, cataracts and heart defects; MMR is live, so non-immune women are vaccinated after delivery, not during pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant, not known to be immune ↓ Exposed to rubella ↓ Virus crosses the placenta, with greatest risk early in pregnancy ↓ Congenital rubella syndrome
exam_trap: D, neonatal scabies — the only other infection-sounding option, but scabies is a mite infestation spread by skin contact and has no link to rubella.
takeaway: The danger of rubella in pregnancy is to the fetus: congenital rubella syndrome.

stem:
A pregnant woman asks whether seasonal influenza vaccination is appropriate.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
options.C: Only women with diabetes should be vaccinated
options.D: All vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy
options.E: Vaccination must always be delayed until after delivery

correct_answer: A. Influenza vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
why_correct: Seasonal influenza vaccination is offered during pregnancy because pregnant women have increased risk of complications from influenza and vaccination also provides protection to the infant after birth.
why_wrong: B. The recommended influenza vaccines do not cause influenza infection. C. The recommendation is not restricted to women with diabetes. D. Some vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy, but not all. E. Vaccination should not routinely be postponed until after delivery.
pearl: Inactivated influenza vaccine is offered to all pregnant women during flu season at any stage of pregnancy; it protects the mother and passes antibodies that protect the baby in early infancy.
thinking: Pregnant woman asks about flu vaccine ↓ Pregnancy raises the risk of severe influenza ↓ Inactivated vaccine is safe at any gestation ↓ Vaccination is recommended during pregnancy
exam_trap: D, all vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy — tempting caution, but only live vaccines are avoided; inactivated influenza vaccine is actively recommended.
takeaway: Offer inactivated flu vaccine to every pregnant woman in flu season.

stem: Which vaccine type is generally avoided during pregnancy because it contains live attenuated organisms?
why_correct: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy as a precaution because of theoretical fetal risk.
why_wrong: B. Toxoid vaccines use inactivated toxins. C. Inactivated vaccines do not contain replicating live organisms. D. Recombinant subunit vaccines contain selected antigenic components. E. Conjugate vaccines contain antigen linked to a carrier protein.
pearl: Live vaccines such as MMR, varicella and BCG are generally avoided in pregnancy; inactivated, toxoid and subunit vaccines can be given when indicated.
thinking: Pregnancy ↓ Concern is a vaccine organism that can replicate ↓ Only live attenuated vaccines contain replicating organisms ↓ Live attenuated vaccine
exam_trap: B, toxoid vaccine — 'toxin' sounds risky in pregnancy, but toxoids are inactivated toxins that cannot replicate and are not routinely avoided.
takeaway: In pregnancy avoid live vaccines; inactivated vaccines are generally acceptable.

stem:
A child develops an itchy rash consisting of crops of vesicles and crusted lesions at different stages.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox characteristically causes successive crops of itchy vesicles, pustules and crusted lesions at different stages.
why_wrong: B. Scarlet fever produces a fine, sandpaper-like rash. C. Measles causes a maculopapular rash rather than crops of vesicles. D. Rubella causes a maculopapular rash. E. Impetigo causes superficial bacterial skin lesions, often with honey-coloured crusts.
pearl: Chickenpox lesions appear in successive crops, so papules, vesicles and crusts are seen together; a child remains infectious until all lesions have crusted over.
thinking: Child with itchy rash ↓ Vesicles and crusts present together ↓ Lesions at different stages = successive crops ↓ Varicella
exam_trap: E, impetigo — also causes crusting, but it gives localised honey-coloured crusts rather than widespread itchy crops of vesicles at different stages.
takeaway: Itchy vesicles in crops at different stages = chickenpox.

stem:
A new screening test is being assessed for a disease. Of 100 people who definitely have the disease, 95 test positive.

What does this result primarily describe?
why_correct: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive: true positives ÷ all people with the disease.
why_wrong: A. Positive predictive value is the probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease. B. Specificity measures correctly identified people without the disease. C. Prevalence is the proportion of the population with the disease. E. Negative predictive value is the probability that a person with a negative test does not have the disease.
pearl: Sensitivity is calculated only among people who truly have the disease; a highly sensitive test rarely misses disease, so a negative result helps rule it out.
thinking: Group studied = 100 people who definitely have the disease ↓ 95 test positive ↓ True positives ÷ all with disease ↓ Sensitivity
exam_trap: A, positive predictive value — also involves positive tests, but PPV starts from those who test positive and asks how many truly have the disease; here the starting group is the diseased.
takeaway: Start with the diseased: sensitivity. Start with positive tests: PPV.

stem:
A GP practice records 20 new cases of type 2 diabetes during one calendar year among its registered population.

Which epidemiological measure is being described?
why_correct: Incidence measures new cases occurring in a population over a specified period.
why_wrong: A. Prevalence describes existing cases at a particular time or over a period. B. Case fatality describes deaths among people with a particular disease. C. Specificity describes diagnostic test performance. E. Sensitivity describes diagnostic test performance.
pearl: Incidence counts new cases over a defined period in a population at risk; prevalence counts all existing cases. In chronic diseases prevalence builds up as new cases accumulate.
thinking: 20 cases recorded ↓ They are new diagnoses ↓ Over a defined period of one calendar year ↓ Incidence
exam_trap: A, prevalence — the commonest confusion, but prevalence includes all existing cases, old and new; counting only new diagnoses over a year is incidence.
takeaway: New cases over time = incidence; all current cases = prevalence.

stem:
A survey finds that 8% of adults in a town currently have asthma.

Which epidemiological measure is being reported?
why_correct: Prevalence describes the proportion of a population with a condition at a specified time or during a specified period.
why_wrong: A. Sensitivity concerns detection of people with disease. B. Relative risk compares disease risk between groups. C. Specificity concerns correctly identifying people without disease. E. Incidence measures new cases.
pearl: Prevalence is a snapshot of everyone with the condition at a point or period, regardless of when it began; cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence, not incidence.
thinking: Survey of a town population ↓ 8% currently have asthma ↓ Existing cases as a proportion at one time ↓ Prevalence
exam_trap: E, incidence — tempting because it is also a measure of disease frequency, but incidence counts only new cases over time; 'currently have' signals existing cases.
takeaway: 'Currently have' a condition signals prevalence.

stem:
A cohort study compares two groups. The risk of developing a disease is 10% in the exposed group and 5% in the unexposed group.

What is the relative risk?
why_correct: Relative risk = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed = 10% ÷ 5% = 2.
why_wrong: A. This would represent the reverse ratio. B. A relative risk of 1 indicates equal risk. D. This is not the ratio of the two risks. E. This is also not the ratio.
pearl: Relative risk compares risk in the exposed with risk in the unexposed: above 1 means higher risk with exposure, 1 means no difference, below 1 means lower risk.
thinking: Cohort study ↓ Risk 10% in exposed, 5% in unexposed ↓ RR = exposed ÷ unexposed ↓ 10 ÷ 5 = 2
exam_trap: A, 0.5 — the result of dividing the wrong way round (unexposed ÷ exposed); the exposed group always goes on top.
takeaway: Relative risk = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed.

stem:
A treatment produces an absolute risk reduction of 10%.

What is the approximate number needed to treat to prevent one additional event?
why_correct: NNT = 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction. An ARR of 0.10 gives an NNT of 10.
why_wrong: A. Would require an ARR of 100%. B. Would correspond to an ARR of 20%. D. Would correspond to an ARR of 5%. E. Would correspond to an ARR of 1%.
pearl: NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction; express the ARR as a decimal first, and round any fractional NNT up to the next whole patient.
thinking: Absolute risk reduction given as 10% ↓ Convert the percentage to a decimal: 0.10 ↓ NNT = 1 ÷ ARR = 1 ÷ 0.10 ↓ 10
exam_trap: E, 100 — the result of treating 10% as if it were 1% when converting the percentage; 1 ÷ 0.10 gives 10, not 100.
takeaway: NNT = 1 ÷ ARR, with the ARR written as a decimal.

stem:
A case-control study reports an odds ratio of 3 for exposure to a particular factor and development of a disease.

What does this indicate?

options.A: 3% of exposed people develop the disease
options.B: The relative risk of disease in the exposed group is 3
options.C: Three people must be exposed for one extra case of the disease
options.D: The exposure is proven to cause the disease
options.E: The odds of disease are 3 times higher in the exposed

correct_answer: E. The odds of disease are 3 times higher in the exposed
why_correct: An odds ratio of 3 indicates that the odds of the outcome are three times as high in the exposed group relative to the comparison group.
why_wrong: A. An odds ratio is not an absolute risk or prevalence. B. A case-control study cannot directly estimate relative risk; the odds ratio approximates it only when the disease is rare. C. This describes a number needed to harm. D. An association does not by itself establish causation.
pearl: Case-control studies start from the outcome and look back at exposure, so they yield odds ratios; the odds ratio approximates relative risk only when the disease is rare.
thinking: Case-control design ↓ Groups chosen by outcome, so risk cannot be measured directly ↓ Odds ratio compares odds by exposure ↓ Odds of disease 3 times higher in the exposed
exam_trap: B, relative risk of 3 — tempting because the OR often approximates the RR, but a case-control study cannot measure risk directly and the approximation holds only for rare diseases.
takeaway: Case-control studies give an odds ratio, not a relative risk or proof of causation.

stem:
A study reports a relative risk of 1.4 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.9–2.1.

Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The exposure significantly increases the risk by 40%
options.B: The study proves there is no difference between the groups
options.C: The p-value for this result is below the 0.05 threshold
options.D: It is not statistically significant at the 5% level
options.E: The interval shows a clinically important harm from exposure

correct_answer: D. It is not statistically significant at the 5% level
why_correct: For a relative risk, a 95% confidence interval that includes 1 is compatible with no association at the conventional 5% significance level.
why_wrong: A. The interval includes 1, so the increase is not statistically significant. B. Failure to demonstrate statistical significance does not prove the null hypothesis. C. An interval including 1 corresponds to p above 0.05. E. The interval includes a range of possible effects, including no effect.
pearl: For ratios such as relative risk or odds ratio, the value of no effect is 1; if the 95% confidence interval includes 1, the result is not statistically significant at the 5% level.
thinking: Relative risk 1.4 ↓ 95% CI 0.9 to 2.1 ↓ Interval includes 1, the value of no effect ↓ Not statistically significant at the 5% level
exam_trap: A, a significant 40% increase — the point estimate does suggest a 40% rise, but the interval includes 1, so the result is compatible with no effect and is not significant.
takeaway: Ratio CI including 1, or difference CI including 0: not significant.

stem:
A researcher concludes that a new treatment is effective when in reality there is no true treatment effect.

What type of error has occurred?
why_correct: A Type I error is a false-positive conclusion: rejecting a true null hypothesis.
why_wrong: B. Recall bias concerns inaccurate recollection of past exposures or events. C. Type II error is failing to detect a true effect. D. Selection bias results from systematic differences in who enters or remains in a study. E. Confounding occurs when another factor distorts an observed association.
pearl: A type I error is a false positive: finding an effect that is not really there, with its probability set by alpha. A type II error is a false negative, often from too small a sample.
thinking: Conclusion: the treatment works ↓ Reality: no true effect ↓ A true null hypothesis has been rejected ↓ Type I error
exam_trap: C, type II error — the other statistical error, but type II means missing a real effect (false negative); here a non-existent effect was claimed (false positive).
takeaway: Type I error = false positive; type II error = false negative.

stem: What does increasing the statistical power of a study primarily do?

options.A: Increases the chance of detecting a true effect
options.B: Reduces the probability of a type I error
options.D: Increases the true effect size of the treatment being tested
options.E: Lowers the significance level required for a result

correct_answer: A. Increases the chance of detecting a true effect
why_correct: Statistical power is the probability of detecting a specified true effect, commonly expressed as 1 − β.
why_wrong: B. The type I error rate is set by the chosen alpha, not by power. C. Confounding requires appropriate study design or analysis. D. Power does not change the true effect size. E. The significance level is chosen independently of power.
pearl: Power (1 − β) is the chance of detecting a true effect of a given size; it rises mainly with larger sample size, larger effect size and less variability.
thinking: Power = 1 − β ↓ β is the chance of missing a true effect ↓ Higher power means fewer false negatives ↓ Increases the chance of detecting a true effect
exam_trap: B, reduces type I error — tempting because power and error rates are linked, but the type I error rate is fixed by the chosen alpha; power reduces type II error.
takeaway: More power means fewer type II errors, not fewer type I errors.

stem: What is the main purpose of randomisation in a clinical trial?

options.A: To keep participants and assessors blind to allocation
options.B: To make results generalisable to the wider population
options.C: To balance known and unknown confounders between groups
options.D: To increase the statistical power of the trial
options.E: To reduce loss to follow-up in each group

correct_answer: C. To balance known and unknown confounders between groups
why_correct: Random allocation helps create comparable groups and reduces confounding by indication and other baseline differences.
why_wrong: A. Keeping participants and assessors unaware of allocation is blinding, a separate methodological feature. B. Generalisability depends on who is recruited, not on randomisation. D. Power depends mainly on sample size and effect size. E. Randomisation does not reduce loss to follow-up.
pearl: Randomisation is the only method that balances unknown as well as known confounders between groups; allocation concealment protects it, and blinding is a separate safeguard.
thinking: Purpose of random allocation ↓ Chance alone decides group membership ↓ Known and unknown baseline factors spread evenly ↓ Balances confounders between groups
exam_trap: A, keeping participants and assessors blind — randomisation and blinding often appear together, but blinding hides allocation once made; randomisation decides allocation and balances confounders.
takeaway: Randomisation balances confounders; blinding protects against bias after allocation.

stem:
In a randomised trial, participants and investigators are unaware of which treatment each participant receives.

What methodological feature is being used?
why_correct: Blinding prevents participants and/or investigators from knowing treatment allocation and can reduce certain forms of bias.
why_wrong: A. Matching pairs participants according to selected characteristics. B. Intention-to-treat concerns how trial participants are analysed after allocation. D. Randomisation determines how participants are allocated. E. Stratification involves dividing participants according to important characteristics before analysis or allocation.
pearl: Blinding stops knowledge of allocation influencing behaviour, care or outcome assessment; when both participants and investigators are unaware, the trial is double-blind.
thinking: Randomised trial ↓ Participants and investigators do not know who receives which treatment ↓ Knowledge of the treatment received is hidden after allocation ↓ Blinding
exam_trap: D, randomisation — present in every RCT, but randomisation determines how allocation is made; keeping people unaware of that allocation is blinding.
takeaway: Unaware of treatment received = blinding; chance allocation = randomisation.

stem:
A study finds that coffee drinking is associated with lung cancer. Further analysis shows that smokers are much more likely to drink coffee.

What concept may explain part of the observed association?
why_correct: Smoking is associated with both the exposure and outcome and may distort the observed relationship between coffee consumption and lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Randomisation is a method used to reduce confounding in trials. B. Sensitivity concerns diagnostic testing. C. Specificity concerns diagnostic testing. D. Blinding concerns knowledge of treatment allocation.
pearl: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome without lying on the causal pathway; it can be handled by randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification or multivariable analysis.
thinking: Coffee associated with lung cancer ↓ Smokers drink more coffee ↓ Smoking itself causes lung cancer ↓ A third factor distorts the association: confounding
exam_trap: A, randomisation — it is the best tool against confounding, so it tempts, but it is a method of prevention, not the concept that explains this distorted association.
takeaway: A factor linked to both exposure and outcome is a confounder.

stem:
Researchers randomly allocate patients with hypertension to receive either a new drug or standard treatment and compare blood pressure after six months.

What type of study is this?
why_correct: Participants are randomly allocated to intervention and comparison groups and outcomes are subsequently compared.
why_wrong: B. In a cohort study the investigators observe rather than allocate the exposure. C. Case-control studies start with outcome status. D. Cross-sectional studies assess exposure and outcome at a single time point. E. Allocation here was random, so it is not a non-randomised trial.
pearl: The defining feature of an RCT is that investigators allocate the intervention by chance; in observational studies such as cohorts, exposure is not assigned by the investigator.
thinking: Investigators assign the treatment ↓ Allocation is random ↓ Outcomes compared after follow-up ↓ Randomised controlled trial
exam_trap: B, prospective cohort study — it also follows groups forward over time, but in a cohort the exposure is observed, not allocated by the investigators.
takeaway: Investigator randomly allocates the intervention = RCT.

stem:
A hospital measures compliance with a clinical standard and introduces a change to improve performance.

What is the next step to complete the audit cycle?

options.A: Publish the results before implementing change

why_correct: The audit cycle is completed by re-audit: measuring practice again against the same standard after implementing change, to determine whether improvement has occurred.
why_wrong: A. Publication is not a required step in completing an audit cycle, and the change has already been implemented. B. Randomisation is a feature of research trials, not clinical audit. D. Audit findings do not automatically replace guidelines; audit measures practice against an existing standard. E. Stopping data collection prevents assessment of whether the change has improved practice and leaves the cycle incomplete.
pearl: Audit measures practice against an agreed standard, implements change, then re-audits; without re-audit there is no evidence the change improved care. Audit is not research.
thinking: Practice measured against a standard ↓ A change has been introduced ↓ The effect must be checked against the same standard ↓ Re-audit
exam_trap: A, publish the results — sharing findings feels like good practice, but publication is not a step of the audit cycle; the loop is closed only by re-auditing.
takeaway: The audit cycle is closed by re-audit against the same standard.

stem:
A clinical team uses repeated measurements to test small changes intended to improve waiting times and adjusts the intervention according to the results.

What type of activity is this?
why_correct: Quality improvement uses structured, iterative changes and measurement to improve healthcare processes or outcomes.
why_wrong: A. Case-control research compares previous exposures between groups defined by outcome. B. A case report describes an individual clinical case. C. An RCT randomly allocates participants to interventions. E. Diagnostic accuracy studies evaluate tests against a reference standard.
pearl: Quality improvement tests small changes in rapid cycles, such as Plan-Do-Study-Act, using repeated measurement to see whether each change is an improvement.
thinking: Repeated measurements ↓ Small changes tested and adjusted ↓ Aim is to improve a service process ↓ Quality improvement
exam_trap: C, randomised controlled trial — it also tests an intervention, but there is no random allocation or comparison group here, only iterative change and measurement.
takeaway: Small iterative changes with repeated measurement = quality improvement (PDSA).

stem:
A doctor realises that an entry in a patient's paper medical record contains an incorrect factual statement.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Correct it transparently so the original entry remains identifiable
options.C: Leave a known significant error uncorrected
options.D: Ask another doctor to sign a replacement entry without explanation

correct_answer: A. Correct it transparently so the original entry remains identifiable
why_correct: Corrections should preserve the integrity and auditability of the clinical record.
why_wrong: B. Removing pages is inappropriate and compromises the record. C. Known clinically significant errors should be corrected appropriately. D. Another clinician should not be asked to conceal or retrospectively replace an entry. E. Erasing the original entry destroys the audit trail.
pearl: Never erase, remove or obscure a record entry; strike through the error with a single line so it stays legible, then add the correction with date, time, name and signature.
thinking: Factual error in a paper record ↓ Records must stay accurate and auditable ↓ Original must remain readable alongside the correction ↓ Correct it transparently
exam_trap: E, completely erasing the entry — feels like a clean fix, but it destroys the audit trail and can look like falsification; the original must remain identifiable.
takeaway: Correct errors openly: single line through, dated and signed, original still legible.

stem:
A doctor is handing over a deteriorating patient to the on-call team.

Which information is particularly important to include?

options.A: Full admission history and complete past medical history
options.B: Diagnosis, drug chart and next of kin details
options.C: Admission diagnosis and planned discharge date
options.D: Current status, outstanding tasks and escalation plan

correct_answer: D. Current status, outstanding tasks and escalation plan
why_correct: Safe handover should communicate the information required for continuity of care, including current concerns, pending tasks and what to do if the patient deteriorates.
why_wrong: A. Extensive background can obscure the important handover points. B. These details do not convey current risk or what to do if the patient deteriorates. C. The original diagnosis may not describe the current risk. E. Identification alone is insufficient.
pearl: A safe handover focuses on what the next team needs: current condition, outstanding jobs and what to do if things worsen. Structured tools such as SBAR help.
thinking: Deteriorating patient ↓ On-call team must act after handover ↓ They need current state, pending tasks and an escalation plan ↓ Current status, outstanding tasks and escalation plan
exam_trap: A, full admission and past medical history — feels thorough, but excessive background buries the critical points; the team needs current risk and clear actions.
takeaway: Hand over the present and the plan: status, jobs, escalation.

stem:
A junior doctor is caring for a patient whose condition is deteriorating despite initial management. The doctor is unsure what to do next.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Wait until the next routine ward round
options.D: Ignore the deterioration if the initial diagnosis was benign
options.E: Manage the patient alone despite uncertainty

correct_answer: B. Seek senior clinical help promptly
why_correct: Doctors should recognise the limits of their competence and escalate promptly when a patient's condition is deteriorating or when additional expertise is required.
why_wrong: A. Waiting may delay necessary treatment. C. Discharge is inappropriate for an unexplained deterioration. D. A previous diagnosis does not override new clinical deterioration. E. Continuing beyond one's competence can place the patient at risk.
pearl: Recognising the limits of your competence and escalating early is a core professional duty; delay in seeking help for a deteriorating patient is a common cause of avoidable harm.
thinking: Patient deteriorating ↓ Initial management not working ↓ Doctor unsure what to do next ↓ Seek senior clinical help promptly
exam_trap: A, wait for the next routine ward round — feels less disruptive, but deterioration needs action now; waiting delays treatment and puts the patient at risk.
takeaway: Deteriorating patient and unsure what to do: escalate to a senior now.

stem:
A 22-year-old is brought to the emergency department several hours after deliberately taking a large quantity of paracetamol tablets.

Which investigation is particularly important in assessing the risk of hepatotoxicity?

options.E: Serum calcium, phosphate and magnesium levels

why_correct: After a potentially toxic paracetamol ingestion, the plasma paracetamol concentration is interpreted according to the time since ingestion using the appropriate treatment nomogram.
why_wrong: B. Salicylate levels assess aspirin poisoning, not paracetamol hepatotoxicity risk. C. Creatine kinase assesses muscle injury. D. A qualitative urine toxicology screen does not quantify paracetamol toxicity risk. E. Calcium, phosphate and magnesium do not determine paracetamol toxicity.
pearl: A paracetamol level taken earlier than 4 hours after ingestion cannot be interpreted; the timed level is plotted on the treatment nomogram to decide on acetylcysteine.
thinking: Deliberate paracetamol overdose ↓ Ingestion several hours ago ↓ Level must be interpreted against time since ingestion ↓ Timed plasma paracetamol concentration
exam_trap: D, qualitative urine toxicology screen — tempting in any overdose, but it only shows that a drug is present and cannot quantify paracetamol hepatotoxicity risk.
takeaway: Paracetamol overdose: a timed level on the nomogram guides acetylcysteine.

stem:
A patient receiving unfractionated heparin develops serious bleeding.

Which drug can reverse the anticoagulant effect of unfractionated heparin?
why_correct: Protamine binds to and neutralises unfractionated heparin.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids. B. Idarucizumab specifically reverses dabigatran. C. N-acetylcysteine is used for paracetamol toxicity. D. Vitamin K is used to reverse vitamin K antagonists.
pearl: Protamine fully reverses unfractionated heparin but only partially reverses low molecular weight heparin; vitamin K reverses warfarin and idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
thinking: Unfractionated heparin ↓ Serious bleeding ↓ Need an agent that binds and neutralises heparin ↓ Protamine sulfate
exam_trap: D, vitamin K — the best-known anticoagulant reversal agent, but it works only for vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin, not heparin.
takeaway: Heparin reversal = protamine; warfarin reversal = vitamin K.

stem:
A patient taking warfarin develops significant bleeding with a markedly raised INR.

Which vitamin is central to reversal of warfarin's anticoagulant effect?
why_correct: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting-factor activation; vitamin K is therefore used in its reversal, alongside other measures when clinically indicated.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 is important for normal red-cell production and neurological function. B. Vitamin E is not used to reverse warfarin. C. Vitamin C is important for collagen synthesis. E. Vitamin D is important for calcium and bone metabolism.
pearl: For major bleeding on warfarin, stop warfarin and give IV vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate; vitamin K alone acts too slowly for immediate reversal.
thinking: Warfarin with markedly raised INR ↓ Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting-factor activation ↓ Giving vitamin K restores factor activity ↓ Vitamin K
exam_trap: A, vitamin B12 — a vitamin often given by injection, so it may tempt, but it relates to red-cell production and nerve function, not clotting-factor activation.
takeaway: Warfarin antagonises vitamin K; vitamin K is central to its reversal.

stem:
A patient taking digoxin develops nausea, confusion and yellow-green visual disturbances.

Which drug toxicity should be suspected?
why_correct: Gastrointestinal symptoms, neurological disturbance and visual changes are recognised features of digoxin toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Amoxicillin does not characteristically produce this toxidrome. B. Metformin toxicity is associated with lactic acidosis in severe toxicity. C. Lithium toxicity can cause neurological and gastrointestinal symptoms but does not characteristically cause yellow-green vision. E. Salbutamol toxicity may cause tremor, tachycardia and hypokalaemia.
pearl: Digoxin toxicity is more likely with hypokalaemia, renal impairment and interacting drugs; check potassium, renal function and ECG, and consider digoxin-specific antibody fragments if severe.
thinking: Patient taking digoxin ↓ Nausea and confusion ↓ Yellow-green visual disturbance (xanthopsia) ↓ Digoxin toxicity
exam_trap: C, lithium — another narrow-therapeutic-index drug causing nausea and confusion, but lithium toxicity gives tremor and ataxia, not yellow-green vision.
takeaway: Nausea, confusion and yellow-green vision on digoxin = digoxin toxicity.

stem:
A patient with type 2 diabetes taking metformin develops severe illness with metabolic acidosis and raised lactate in the context of significant renal impairment.

Which medication may contribute?
why_correct: Metformin accumulation, particularly in severe renal impairment or significant acute illness, can be associated with lactic acidosis.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol toxicity primarily causes hepatic injury. B. Amoxicillin is not a characteristic cause of lactic acidosis. C. Cetirizine is an antihistamine and does not characteristically cause this metabolic disturbance. D. Salbutamol can cause hypokalaemia and tremor.
pearl: Metformin can accumulate in severe renal impairment or acute illness with dehydration or hypoxia; sick-day advice is to pause it during dehydrating illness.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes on metformin ↓ Significant renal impairment ↓ Metabolic acidosis with raised lactate ↓ Metformin
exam_trap: A, paracetamol — a common culprit in drug-toxicity questions, but its principal toxicity is liver injury; renal impairment in a patient on metformin points to metformin.
takeaway: Metformin plus renal impairment plus lactic acidosis: suspect metformin.

stem:
A patient with type 2 diabetes taking a sulfonylurea develops recurrent episodes of hypoglycaemia.

What is a recognised effect of sulfonylureas?

options.E: Reduced glucose absorption by the intestine only

why_correct: Sulfonylureas stimulate pancreatic beta cells to release insulin and can therefore cause hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: A. They stimulate rather than suppress insulin secretion. C. They do not destroy pancreatic beta cells. D. Increased urinary glucose excretion is characteristic of SGLT2 inhibitors. E. This is not the principal mechanism of sulfonylureas.
pearl: Sulfonylureas such as gliclazide cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain; risk is higher in older people, renal impairment and missed meals. Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycaemia.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea ↓ Recurrent hypoglycaemia ↓ Sulfonylureas close beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels ↓ Increased insulin secretion
exam_trap: D, increased urinary glucose excretion — another oral glucose-lowering mechanism, but it belongs to SGLT2 inhibitors, which seldom cause hypoglycaemia on their own.
takeaway: Sulfonylureas push insulin out, so they cause hypoglycaemia.

stem:
A patient with type 2 diabetes is prescribed a drug that lowers blood glucose by increasing urinary glucose excretion.

Which drug class works in this way?
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce renal glucose reabsorption, increasing urinary glucose excretion.
why_wrong: B. DPP-4 inhibitors enhance incretin activity. C. Metformin, the principal biguanide, reduces hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity. D. Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion. E. Thiazolidinediones improve insulin sensitivity.
pearl: SGLT2 inhibitors (the flozins) cause glycosuria, so watch for genital fungal infection, volume depletion and euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis, especially during acute illness.
thinking: Glucose lowered via the urine ↓ Kidney normally reabsorbs filtered glucose ↓ Blocking SGLT2 in the proximal tubule causes glycosuria ↓ SGLT2 inhibitors
exam_trap: B, DPP-4 inhibitors — also oral agents with a similar-sounding name, but they prolong incretin action to raise insulin and lower glucagon, not increase urinary glucose.
takeaway: Glucose lost in the urine = SGLT2 inhibitor (flozin).

stem: Which class of medication used in type 2 diabetes can reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying through incretin-related effects?
why_correct: GLP-1 receptor agonists enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion and can reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying.
why_wrong: A. Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors delay carbohydrate digestion in the intestine. B. SGLT2 inhibitors act primarily in the renal proximal tubule. D. Thiazolidinediones improve insulin sensitivity. E. Sulfonylureas stimulate insulin secretion independently of glucose to a greater extent and do not characteristically slow gastric emptying.
pearl: GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide and liraglutide promote weight loss by reducing appetite and slowing gastric emptying; nausea and other GI side effects are common.
thinking: Reduced appetite ↓ Slowed gastric emptying ↓ Incretin-related action ↓ GLP-1 receptor agonists
exam_trap: B, SGLT2 inhibitors — also linked to weight loss, but through urinary glucose and calorie loss, not appetite reduction or slower gastric emptying.
takeaway: Appetite down, stomach slower, weight loss: GLP-1 receptor agonist.

stem:
A woman taking a combined oral contraceptive pill forgets to take one active pill and remembers the following day.

What is generally appropriate?

options.A: Use condoms for 7 days and omit the missed pill
options.B: Take the missed pill now and continue the pack
options.C: Stop and take a 7-day pill-free interval now
options.D: Take two pills daily until the pack ends
options.E: Take emergency contraception and continue the pack

correct_answer: B. Take the missed pill now and continue the pack
why_correct: Management of a single missed combined pill generally involves taking it when remembered and continuing the pack.
why_wrong: A. The missed pill should be taken, and additional precautions are not needed after a single missed pill. C. Starting a pill-free interval early increases the risk of contraceptive failure. D. Doubling pills for the rest of the pack is not recommended. E. Emergency contraception is not required after a single missed pill.
pearl: For one missed combined pill, take it as soon as remembered, even if that means two in one day, and continue the pack; extra precautions and emergency contraception are not needed.
thinking: Combined pill ↓ Only one active pill missed ↓ Contraceptive cover is maintained ↓ Take the missed pill now and continue the pack
exam_trap: E, emergency contraception — feels safest after any missed pill, but a single missed combined pill does not reduce protection enough to need it.
takeaway: One missed combined pill: take it now, carry on, no extra cover needed.

stem:
A woman has had unprotected sexual intercourse and wants to reduce the risk of pregnancy.

Which is a recognised form of emergency contraception?
why_correct: The copper IUD is an effective form of emergency contraception and can also provide ongoing contraception.
why_wrong: B. Antipsychotics have no contraceptive role. C. Barrier cream alone is not a recognised emergency contraceptive method. D. Routine combined contraception is not itself an emergency method after intercourse. E. Methotrexate is not an emergency contraceptive.
pearl: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraceptive and also provides ongoing contraception; the oral options are levonorgestrel and ulipristal acetate.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Wants to reduce pregnancy risk now ↓ Needs a recognised emergency method ↓ Copper intrauterine device
exam_trap: E, methotrexate — associated with ending an early pregnancy, so it may tempt, but it is used for ectopic pregnancy and is not an emergency contraceptive.
takeaway: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception.

stem: Which emergency contraceptive works primarily by delaying or preventing ovulation?

options.D: Progesterone pessary used for luteal support

why_correct: Levonorgestrel is an emergency contraceptive that acts mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation.
why_wrong: A. The copper IUD prevents pregnancy through intrauterine effects and is not primarily an ovulation-delaying oral drug. B. Methotrexate is an antimetabolite. C. Misoprostol is a prostaglandin analogue with different clinical uses. D. A progesterone pessary used for luteal support is not emergency contraception.
pearl: Oral emergency contraceptives such as levonorgestrel act mainly by delaying ovulation, so they are ineffective once ovulation has occurred; the copper IUD does not rely on delaying ovulation.
thinking: Emergency contraception ↓ Mechanism asked: delaying or preventing ovulation ↓ Oral hormonal method ↓ Levonorgestrel
exam_trap: A, copper IUD — the most effective emergency method, but it works mainly through intrauterine effects on fertilisation and implantation, not by delaying ovulation.
takeaway: Levonorgestrel delays ovulation; the copper IUD acts locally in the uterus.

stem:
A woman reports menstrual bleeding that is significantly heavier than usual and interferes with her daily activities.

Which term is commonly used for this problem?
why_correct: Heavy menstrual bleeding refers to excessive menstrual bleeding that affects a woman's physical, social, emotional or material quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Irregular bleeding refers to variable cycle timing rather than volume. B. Dysmenorrhoea, primary or secondary, means painful menstruation. D. Intermenstrual bleeding occurs between periods. E. Amenorrhoea means absence of menstruation.
pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on quality of life rather than measured blood loss; ask about flooding, clots and changing protection, and check a full blood count.
thinking: Periods much heavier than usual ↓ Interferes with daily activities ↓ The problem is volume, not pain or timing ↓ Heavy menstrual bleeding
exam_trap: D, intermenstrual bleeding — another abnormal bleeding pattern, but it means bleeding between periods; here the periods themselves are heavier.
takeaway: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on the woman's life.

stem:
A 24-year-old who previously had regular periods has had no menstruation for four months.

What should be excluded first?
why_correct: Pregnancy is the commonest and most important initial cause to exclude in a person with secondary amenorrhoea who could become pregnant.
why_wrong: A. Cataract does not cause amenorrhoea. B. Otitis externa is unrelated. C. Iron overload is not the initial consideration in this presentation. D. Appendicitis does not explain persistent amenorrhoea.
pearl: In anyone with secondary amenorrhoea who could be pregnant, do a pregnancy test first, before investigating causes such as PCOS, thyroid disease or hyperprolactinaemia.
thinking: Previously regular periods ↓ No menstruation for four months: secondary amenorrhoea ↓ The commonest cause must be ruled out first ↓ Pregnancy
exam_trap: C, iron overload — haemochromatosis can rarely cause hypogonadism and amenorrhoea, but it is uncommon and never the first thing to exclude.
takeaway: Secondary amenorrhoea: always exclude pregnancy first.

stem:
A woman who is 9 weeks pregnant develops vaginal bleeding and cramping. Ultrasound confirms that the pregnancy is no longer viable.

What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Pregnancy loss before fetal viability is classified as miscarriage.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterine cavity. B. Placenta praevia concerns placental location in later pregnancy. C. Placental abruption occurs later in pregnancy, usually with placental separation. E. Postpartum haemorrhage occurs after delivery.
pearl: Miscarriage is loss of a pregnancy before viability; in early pregnancy bleeding, ultrasound establishes viability and location, which also helps exclude ectopic pregnancy.
thinking: 9 weeks pregnant ↓ Vaginal bleeding and cramping ↓ Ultrasound confirms the pregnancy is no longer viable ↓ Miscarriage
exam_trap: A, ectopic pregnancy — the key alternative in early pregnancy bleeding and pain, but it means implantation outside the uterus; the stem describes an ultrasound-confirmed non-viable pregnancy.
takeaway: Pregnancy lost before viability = miscarriage.

stem:
A patient receiving chemotherapy presents with a temperature of 38.5°C and neutrophil count of 0.3 × 10⁹/L.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Start G-CSF alone and review the patient in 24 hours
options.B: Platelet transfusion and regular oral paracetamol for fever
options.C: Await blood culture results before starting antibiotics
options.D: Oral antibiotics and a next-day haematology review
options.E: Empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour of arrival

correct_answer: E. Empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour of arrival
why_correct: Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency. Empirical antibiotics should be started promptly after appropriate cultures, without waiting for culture results.
why_wrong: A. G-CSF does not replace urgent empirical antibiotics. B. Platelet transfusion and antipyretics do not treat neutropenic sepsis. C. Waiting for cultures delays potentially life-saving treatment. D. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are inappropriate for suspected neutropenic sepsis.
pearl: Suspected neutropenic sepsis is an emergency: give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as piperacillin with tazobactam, immediately, without waiting for the neutrophil count or cultures.
thinking: Receiving chemotherapy ↓ Fever with neutrophils 0.3 × 10⁹/L ↓ Neutropenic sepsis can be fatal within hours ↓ Empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour
exam_trap: C, await blood culture results — cultures matter, but they should be taken without delaying antibiotics; waiting for results costs time a neutropenic patient may not have.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy: IV antibiotics within the hour, no waiting.

stem:
A patient with chemotherapy-induced neutropenia presents with fever and suspected neutropenic sepsis.

Which investigation should be performed before antibiotics if this does not cause a clinically significant delay?
why_correct: Blood cultures help identify the causative organism and should be obtained promptly, while ensuring that antibiotic treatment is not unnecessarily delayed.
why_wrong: A. DXA assesses bone mineral density. B. Skin-prick testing assesses IgE-mediated allergy. D. An exercise ECG is unrelated to the acute presentation. E. Colonoscopy is not an initial investigation for neutropenic sepsis.
pearl: Take blood cultures, including from any central line, before the first antibiotic dose in suspected neutropenic sepsis, but never let sampling delay antibiotics.
thinking: Suspected neutropenic sepsis ↓ Antibiotics are urgent ↓ Need to identify the organism without delaying treatment ↓ Blood cultures
exam_trap: E, colonoscopy — may tempt if a gut source is suspected, but it is invasive, risky in neutropenia and has no place in the initial work-up.
takeaway: Blood cultures first, but never at the cost of delaying antibiotics.

stem:
A 61-year-old has headaches, facial plethora and itching after a hot shower. Blood tests show an elevated haemoglobin and haematocrit.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative disorder causing increased red-cell production; aquagenic pruritus is a recognised symptom.
why_wrong: A. Acute leukaemia commonly causes marrow failure and blasts. B. Iron deficiency causes reduced haemoglobin. D. Thalassaemia trait typically causes microcytosis rather than this acquired erythrocytosis. E. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia.
pearl: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm usually driven by a JAK2 mutation; it raises thrombosis risk and is managed with venesection and low-dose aspirin, sometimes cytoreduction.
thinking: Headaches and facial plethora ↓ Itching after a hot shower ↓ Raised haemoglobin and haematocrit ↓ Polycythaemia vera
exam_trap: A, acute leukaemia — another marrow malignancy, but it causes marrow failure with anaemia, infection and bleeding, not raised haemoglobin with plethora.
takeaway: Plethora, aquagenic itch and high haematocrit: polycythaemia vera.

stem:
A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anaemia. Reticulocyte count is very low.

Which infection is classically associated with this presentation?
why_correct: Parvovirus B19 temporarily suppresses erythropoiesis and can cause an aplastic crisis in people with chronic haemolytic anaemia such as sickle cell disease.
why_wrong: B. EBV causes infectious mononucleosis. C. Varicella-zoster causes chickenpox and shingles. D. Rhinovirus commonly causes the common cold. E. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 briefly halts red-cell production; in chronic haemolysis this causes a sudden aplastic crisis with a very low reticulocyte count, which may need transfusion.
thinking: Sickle cell disease ↓ Sudden severe anaemia ↓ Very low reticulocytes = marrow not responding ↓ Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
exam_trap: B, Epstein–Barr virus — a familiar childhood viral infection with blood changes, but it causes infectious mononucleosis, not selective red-cell aplasia in haemolytic anaemia.
takeaway: Sickle cell plus sudden anaemia plus low reticulocytes = parvovirus B19.

stem:
A patient with long-term heavy alcohol consumption develops jaundice and abnormal liver tests.

Which pattern is classically associated with alcohol-related hepatitis?

options.A: ALT greater than AST in every case

why_correct: Alcohol-related liver injury commonly produces an AST-predominant transaminase elevation.
why_wrong: A. ALT does not characteristically predominate in alcohol-related hepatitis. B. Significant alcohol-related liver injury can produce abnormal liver tests. C. This is not the typical pattern. D. Alcohol-related liver disease is not characterised solely by unconjugated bilirubin elevation.
pearl: In alcohol-related liver injury AST usually exceeds ALT, often with raised GGT and macrocytosis; ALT-predominant rises point more towards viral or other hepatocellular causes.
thinking: Long-term heavy alcohol use ↓ Jaundice and abnormal liver tests ↓ Alcohol injury characteristically raises AST more than ALT ↓ AST greater than ALT
exam_trap: A, ALT greater than AST in every case — ALT is the usual hepatocellular marker, but alcohol typically gives an AST-predominant pattern, and 'in every case' is absolute.
takeaway: AST greater than ALT points to alcohol-related liver injury.

stem:
A patient with cirrhosis becomes confused. Examination reveals asterixis. He has recently developed constipation.

Which factor may have precipitated the deterioration?
why_correct: Constipation is a recognised precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy, alongside factors such as infection, gastrointestinal bleeding and certain medications.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa is unrelated. B. Myopia does not precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. C. A stable cataract is unrelated. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute encephalopathy.
pearl: Always look for precipitants of hepatic encephalopathy, such as constipation, infection, GI bleeding, dehydration and sedatives; lactulose is used to ensure regular soft stools.
thinking: Cirrhosis ↓ Confusion with asterixis = hepatic encephalopathy ↓ New constipation increases gut ammonia absorption ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: D, osteoarthritis — may tempt if you think of the analgesics used for it, but osteoarthritis itself does not precipitate encephalopathy; the stem flags new constipation.
takeaway: Hepatic encephalopathy: find the trigger; constipation is a classic one.

stem:
A patient with cirrhosis and ascites develops fever and abdominal pain.

What investigation is particularly important to diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?

options.A: Liver function tests and INR measurement

why_correct: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid analysis is required when spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is suspected.
why_wrong: A. Liver function tests and INR assess liver function but cannot diagnose peritoneal infection. B. CT does not diagnose SBP, which requires ascitic neutrophil count and culture. C. Endoscopy assesses varices and upper GI bleeding, not ascitic infection. D. Amylase and lipase assess pancreatitis.
pearl: Any patient with cirrhosis and ascites who has fever, abdominal pain or unexplained deterioration needs a diagnostic ascitic tap; a raised ascitic neutrophil count confirms SBP.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites ↓ Fever and abdominal pain ↓ Suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis ↓ Diagnostic ascitic fluid sampling
exam_trap: B, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen — feels thorough for abdominal pain, but SBP is diagnosed on ascitic neutrophil count and culture, which only a tap provides.
takeaway: Suspected SBP: diagnostic paracentesis, not imaging.

stem:
A patient with advanced cirrhosis develops progressive renal dysfunction without another clear structural renal cause.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: Hepatorenal syndrome is a form of renal dysfunction occurring in advanced liver disease, in the absence of another sufficient explanation for the renal failure.
why_wrong: B. Cystitis causes lower urinary tract symptoms rather than this pattern. C. Polycystic kidney disease is a chronic inherited structural disorder. D. Renal cell carcinoma usually presents as a renal mass, haematuria or incidental imaging finding. E. Nephrolithiasis typically causes renal colic.
pearl: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal failure from renal vasoconstriction in advanced liver disease; diagnose it only after excluding hypovolaemia, nephrotoxins and structural kidney disease.
thinking: Advanced cirrhosis ↓ Progressive renal dysfunction ↓ No structural renal cause found ↓ Hepatorenal syndrome
exam_trap: C, polycystic kidney disease — can coexist with liver cysts, but it is a chronic inherited structural disorder, whereas the stem excludes a structural renal cause.
takeaway: Cirrhosis with unexplained renal failure and normal kidney structure: hepatorenal syndrome.

stem:
A newborn is found to have prolonged jaundice, poor feeding and hypotonia. Screening suggests thyroid hormone deficiency.

Why is early treatment important?
why_correct: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism can cause irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment, so early detection and treatment are important.
why_wrong: A. Congenital cataracts have different causes. B. Hypoglycaemic seizures are not the key complication of congenital hypothyroidism. C. Prolonged jaundice is a feature but kernicterus is not the reason early thyroxine is critical. E. Adrenal crisis relates to congenital adrenal hyperplasia, not thyroid hormone deficiency.
pearl: Congenital hypothyroidism is picked up on the newborn blood spot test; prompt levothyroxine prevents irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment. Prolonged jaundice is a recognised clue.
thinking: Newborn with prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, hypotonia ↓ Screening suggests thyroid hormone deficiency ↓ Thyroid hormone is essential for early brain development ↓ Prevent impaired neurodevelopment
exam_trap: C, preventing kernicterus — tempting because jaundice is in the stem, but kernicterus is not the reason early thyroxine is critical; untreated hypothyroidism harms brain development.
takeaway: Congenital hypothyroidism: early levothyroxine protects neurodevelopment.

stem:
A newborn screening programme identifies an infant with persistently elevated phenylalanine.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Phenylketonuria is caused by impaired metabolism of phenylalanine, resulting in elevated blood phenylalanine concentrations.
why_wrong: A. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia involves inherited adrenal steroid synthesis defects. B. Congenital hypothyroidism involves deficient thyroid hormone production. C. Cystic fibrosis is caused by CFTR dysfunction. E. Down syndrome is caused by chromosome 21 abnormalities.
pearl: Phenylketonuria is detected on the newborn blood spot screen; a low-phenylalanine diet from early infancy prevents intellectual disability, with tight control needed before and during pregnancy.
thinking: Newborn screening ↓ Persistently raised phenylalanine ↓ Impaired phenylalanine metabolism ↓ Phenylketonuria
exam_trap: B, congenital hypothyroidism — also detected on the newborn blood spot, but it is picked up through raised TSH, not raised phenylalanine.
takeaway: Raised phenylalanine on newborn screening = phenylketonuria.

stem:
A girl has short stature, delayed puberty and a broad chest with widely spaced nipples.

Which chromosomal abnormality is classically associated with Turner syndrome?
why_correct: Turner syndrome classically results from complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, commonly represented as 45,X.
why_wrong: A. 47,XXX is triple-X syndrome. B. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome. D. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome. E. Trisomy 18 causes Edwards syndrome.
pearl: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature and ovarian insufficiency with delayed puberty; look for coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve.
thinking: Girl with short stature ↓ Delayed puberty ↓ Broad chest with widely spaced nipples ↓ Turner syndrome: 45,X
exam_trap: A, 47,XXX — also a sex chromosome abnormality in females, but triple X syndrome is often associated with tall stature and usually normal puberty, unlike Turner syndrome.
takeaway: Short girl, delayed puberty, broad chest = 45,X Turner syndrome.

stem:
A tall young man has small testes, reduced facial hair and infertility.

Which chromosomal pattern is classically associated with Klinefelter syndrome?
why_correct: Klinefelter syndrome is classically associated with an additional X chromosome, giving a 47,XXY karyotype.
why_wrong: A. 47,XXX is triple-X syndrome. B. A typical 46,XY karyotype does not explain classic Klinefelter syndrome. C. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome. E. 45,X is Turner syndrome.
pearl: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes primary testicular failure: small firm testes, raised gonadotrophins, low testosterone and infertility; it is often diagnosed late.
thinking: Tall young man ↓ Small testes and reduced facial hair ↓ Infertility from testicular failure ↓ Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY
exam_trap: E, 45,X — another classic sex chromosome karyotype, but it is Turner syndrome in females with short stature, not a tall man with small testes.
takeaway: Tall male, small testes, infertility = 47,XXY Klinefelter syndrome.

stem:
A newborn has severe developmental abnormalities, clenched hands with overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet.

Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely?
why_correct: Edwards syndrome is caused by trisomy 18 and is associated with severe congenital abnormalities including clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet.
why_wrong: A. Trisomy 13 causes Patau syndrome. B. 47,XXY causes Klinefelter syndrome. D. 45,X causes Turner syndrome. E. Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome.
pearl: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18): clenched hands with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia and heart defects; Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) gives cleft lip and palate and polydactyly.
thinking: Newborn with severe abnormalities ↓ Clenched hands with overlapping fingers ↓ Rocker-bottom feet ↓ Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)
exam_trap: A, trisomy 13 — the other severe autosomal trisomy with multiple anomalies, but Patau syndrome is classically marked by cleft lip and palate, polydactyly and midline defects.
takeaway: Overlapping clenched fingers plus rocker-bottom feet = Edwards syndrome, trisomy 18.

stem:
A child has seizures, developmental difficulties and multiple hypopigmented skin lesions.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with seizures, developmental difficulties and characteristic hypomelanotic skin lesions.
why_wrong: B. Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder. C. NF1 classically causes café-au-lait patches and neurofibromas. D. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune gastrointestinal disorder. E. Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder affecting females.
pearl: Tuberous sclerosis: ash-leaf hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas and shagreen patches, with seizures, including infantile spasms, and learning difficulties; a Wood's lamp helps show the macules.
thinking: Child with seizures ↓ Developmental difficulties ↓ Multiple hypopigmented (ash-leaf) patches ↓ Tuberous sclerosis
exam_trap: C, neurofibromatosis type 1 — the other classic neurocutaneous syndrome, but its skin lesions are pigmented café-au-lait patches and neurofibromas, not hypopigmented macules.
takeaway: Seizures plus hypopigmented ash-leaf macules = tuberous sclerosis.

stem:
A boy has developmental delay. His mother is clinically well but has several male relatives with similar difficulties.

Which inheritance pattern is characteristic of Fragile X syndrome?

options.A: Simple autosomal dominant inheritance without anticipation
options.C: Autosomal recessive inheritance without repeat expansion

why_correct: Fragile X is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene and demonstrates anticipation, particularly with maternal transmission.
why_wrong: A. Its inheritance is not simple autosomal dominant inheritance. B. It is not mitochondrial. C. It is not a conventional autosomal recessive disorder. E. It is not Y-linked.
pearl: Fragile X is a leading inherited cause of learning disability; CGG repeats in FMR1 expand through maternal transmission, and features include a long face, large ears and macro-orchidism after puberty.
thinking: Boy with developmental delay ↓ Well mother, several affected male relatives ↓ X-linked pattern through female carriers ↓ Repeat expansion causes anticipation ↓ X-linked inheritance with anticipation
exam_trap: A, simple autosomal dominant — tempting because the condition runs through several generations, but autosomal dominant traits affect both sexes and pass from an affected parent; here affected males are linked through a clinically well mother, an X-linked pattern, and repeat expansion gives anticipation.
takeaway: Affected males, carrier mothers, worsening over generations: fragile X.

stem:
A 42-year-old develops progressive involuntary jerking movements, personality changes and cognitive decline. His father had a similar illness.

Which inheritance pattern is characteristic?
why_correct: Huntington disease is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion.
why_wrong: B. It is not mitochondrial. C. It is not Y-linked. D. It is not X-linked recessive. E. It is not autosomal recessive.
pearl: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk; predictive testing should be offered only with genetic counselling.
thinking: Adult with progressive involuntary jerking movements ↓ Personality change and cognitive decline ↓ Affected father points to Huntington disease ↓ Autosomal dominant
exam_trap: D, X-linked recessive — may tempt when an affected father and son are seen, but father-to-son transmission rules out X-linked inheritance.
takeaway: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant: 50% risk to each child.

stem:
A family with Huntington disease has a pattern in which symptoms occur at progressively younger ages in successive generations.

What phenomenon does this illustrate?
why_correct: Anticipation describes earlier onset or increased severity in successive generations, classically seen with trinucleotide repeat disorders such as Huntington disease.
why_wrong: A. Mosaicism means genetically distinct cell populations within an individual. C. Codominance means both alleles are expressed. D. Genomic imprinting involves parent-of-origin effects and is not the defining phenomenon here. E. Genetic drift refers to random changes in allele frequencies in populations.
pearl: Anticipation occurs in trinucleotide repeat disorders because repeats expand between generations; in Huntington disease expansion is more marked with paternal transmission.
thinking: Family with Huntington disease ↓ Onset at younger ages in each generation ↓ Unstable CAG repeat expands when passed on ↓ Anticipation
exam_trap: D, genomic imprinting — parent-of-origin effects sound relevant, but earlier onset in successive generations is, by definition, anticipation.
takeaway: Earlier or more severe disease each generation = anticipation (repeat expansion).

stem:
A parent is heterozygous for an autosomal dominant condition.

What is the probability that each pregnancy will inherit the condition?
why_correct: A heterozygous affected parent has a 50% chance of transmitting the pathogenic allele in each pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. This is not the expected Mendelian probability. B. 25% applies to a different inheritance scenario, such as two carrier parents for an autosomal recessive condition. D. This is not the expected probability for a heterozygous affected parent. E. A heterozygous parent does not transmit the allele to every child.
pearl: Each child of a heterozygous parent with an autosomal dominant condition has a 50% chance of inheriting it, independent of what happened in previous pregnancies.
thinking: Autosomal dominant condition ↓ Parent heterozygous: one affected allele ↓ Each pregnancy receives one of the two alleles ↓ 50%
exam_trap: B, 25% — the familiar figure for two carrier parents of an autosomal recessive condition, but one heterozygous dominant parent gives 50% per pregnancy.
takeaway: Autosomal dominant, one affected parent: 50% risk each pregnancy.

stem:
A woman is a carrier of an X-linked recessive condition and her partner is unaffected.

What is the probability that each male child will be affected?
why_correct: Each son receives his X chromosome from his mother. A carrier mother has a 50% chance of transmitting the affected X chromosome to each son.
why_wrong: A. There is no standard 10% probability here. B. This does not represent the probability for an individual male child. D. The probability is not 75%. E. A carrier mother will not transmit the affected X chromosome to every son.
pearl: A carrier mother of an X-linked recessive condition passes it to half her sons (affected) and half her daughters (carriers); affected fathers never pass it to sons.
thinking: X-linked recessive, carrier mother ↓ Unaffected father gives his Y to every son ↓ Each son gets either maternal X with equal chance ↓ 50%
exam_trap: B, 25% — the chance that any one child, before its sex is known, is an affected boy, but the question asks about each male child, for whom the risk is 50%.
takeaway: Carrier mother: each son 50% affected, each daughter 50% carrier.

stem:
A woman has a mitochondrial genetic disorder.

Which statement about transmission is correct?

options.A: Affected fathers transmit it to all their daughters
options.B: Affected mothers can transmit it to their children
options.C: It follows an autosomal dominant pattern
options.D: Each child has a 25% risk if both parents carry it
options.E: Affected fathers transmit it to half their children

correct_answer: B. Affected mothers can transmit it to their children
why_correct: Mitochondria are transmitted through the ovum, so mitochondrial disorders are maternally inherited.
why_wrong: A. Transmission from fathers to all daughters describes X-linked dominant inheritance; fathers do not normally transmit mitochondrial DNA. C. Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal, not autosomal dominant. D. A 25% risk with carrier parents describes autosomal recessive inheritance. E. Fathers do not normally transmit mitochondrial DNA to their children.
pearl: Mitochondrial disorders are maternally inherited and can affect children of either sex; affected fathers do not normally transmit them. Severity varies because of heteroplasmy.
thinking: Mitochondrial disorder ↓ Mitochondria come from the ovum, not the sperm ↓ Inheritance is maternal ↓ Affected mothers can transmit it to their children
exam_trap: A, affected fathers transmit to all daughters — a familiar sex-linked pattern, but that is X-linked dominant inheritance; fathers do not normally pass on mitochondrial DNA.
takeaway: Mitochondrial inheritance is maternal; affected fathers do not pass it on.

stem:
A couple has a child with a known inherited disorder and wants to understand the risk to future pregnancies.

What service is most appropriate?
why_correct: Genetic counselling provides information about inheritance, recurrence risk, testing options and reproductive choices.
why_wrong: A. Occupational health assesses workplace-related health issues. B. Dermatology is unrelated unless the disorder specifically requires it. D. Physiotherapy does not assess inheritance risk. E. Vaccination clinics do not provide formal genetic risk assessment.
pearl: Genetic counselling explains the diagnosis, inheritance and recurrence risk, and options such as carrier testing, prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation testing, supporting the couple's own decisions.
thinking: Child with a known inherited disorder ↓ Couple asks about future pregnancies ↓ They need recurrence risk and reproductive options ↓ Genetic counselling
exam_trap: B, dermatology review — may tempt if the disorder has skin features, but a specialty review does not provide formal recurrence risk or reproductive counselling.
takeaway: Recurrence risk and reproductive options: refer for genetic counselling.

stem:
A competent adult is offered a procedure. The clinician explains the purpose, important risks and alternatives, and the patient agrees voluntarily.

What principle is being demonstrated?
why_correct: Valid consent requires capacity, sufficient information and voluntariness.
why_wrong: B. Emergency treatment without consent is relevant only in specific circumstances where valid consent cannot be obtained. C. Implied consent is not the appropriate description when explicit consent has been obtained for a significant procedure. D. Best-interests decisions apply when an adult lacks capacity for the relevant decision. E. Deprivation of liberty concerns restrictions on a person's freedom.
pearl: Valid consent needs three things: capacity, enough information (including material risks and alternatives) and a voluntary decision; it is a process, not just a signature.
thinking: Competent adult ↓ Purpose, risks and alternatives explained ↓ Agrees freely ↓ Valid informed consent
exam_trap: C, implied consent only — patients do imply consent for simple acts, but here a procedure was explained and explicitly agreed, which is valid informed consent.
takeaway: Valid consent = capacity + adequate information + voluntariness.

stem:
A competent patient agrees to an operation only after their partner threatens to leave them if they refuse.

What is the key concern?
why_correct: Consent must be voluntary and free from coercion. Significant pressure from another person can undermine valid consent.
why_wrong: B. Renal function does not determine voluntariness. C. Blood group does not determine whether consent is voluntary. D. Vaccination status does not determine whether consent is voluntary. E. Visual acuity is unrelated to voluntariness.
pearl: Consent given under pressure from a partner or family may not be valid; speak to the patient alone, explore their own wishes and make sure the decision is genuinely theirs.
thinking: Competent patient ↓ Agrees only after a threat from their partner ↓ Coercion undermines free choice ↓ The voluntariness of consent
exam_trap: B, renal function — a routine preoperative check that may seem relevant to surgery, but it has nothing to do with whether consent is valid; the issue is coercion.
takeaway: Consent given under pressure may not be valid: check voluntariness.

stem:
A competent adult tells their doctor about a sensitive medical problem and asks that the information not be shared with their family.

What should the doctor generally do?

options.C: Tell all members of the clinical team regardless of relevance

why_correct: Competent adults are entitled to confidentiality. Information should only be shared where there is an appropriate justification.
why_wrong: A. A spouse has no automatic right to confidential medical information. B. Employers do not automatically have access to confidential clinical information. C. Information should be shared only with those who need it for appropriate care. D. Public disclosure would breach confidentiality.
pearl: Confidentiality applies to family and spouses too; disclosure without consent needs a clear justification, such as a legal requirement or a serious risk of harm to others.
thinking: Competent adult ↓ Shares sensitive information ↓ Asks that family are not told ↓ No justification to disclose: respect confidentiality
exam_trap: A, tell the patient's spouse — feels natural for a close family member, but spouses have no automatic right to a competent adult's medical information.
takeaway: Family have no automatic right to a competent patient's information.

stem:
A woman attends alone and tells her doctor that her partner controls her finances and prevents her from seeing friends. She asks whether this counts as abuse.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Recommend couples counselling with her partner as a first step
options.B: Explain that abuse requires physical or sexual violence
options.C: Explain this may be domestic abuse and offer support
options.D: Advise her to leave the relationship today for her own safety
options.E: Document it and review if injuries occur

correct_answer: C. Explain this may be domestic abuse and offer support
why_correct: Domestic abuse can include controlling or coercive behaviour, emotional and financial abuse, as well as physical or sexual abuse.
why_wrong: A. Couples counselling is not recommended in domestic abuse and may increase risk. B. Domestic abuse includes coercive control and financial abuse, not only physical or sexual violence. D. The clinician should support her and discuss safe options rather than instructing her what to do. E. Absence of physical injury does not exclude abuse, and support should not be delayed.
pearl: Domestic abuse includes coercive control and financial and emotional abuse, not just violence; listen, validate, assess risk, document and offer referral to specialist support.
thinking: Partner controls her finances ↓ Prevents her seeing friends ↓ This is coercive and controlling behaviour ↓ Explain this may be domestic abuse and offer support
exam_trap: D, advise her to leave today — feels protective, but leaving can be a high-risk time; she should be supported to make her own safe plan, not instructed.
takeaway: Coercive control and financial abuse are domestic abuse, even without violence.

stem:
A competent adult is being assessed for capacity to make a particular medical decision.

Which ability is required?

options.A: Ability to have no mental health diagnosis
options.B: Ability to make the decision the doctor considers sensible
options.C: Ability to agree with the doctor's recommendation
options.D: Ability to remember every detail of their medical history
options.E: Ability to understand the relevant information

correct_answer: E. Ability to understand the relevant information
why_correct: Capacity requires the person to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information, and communicate the decision.
why_wrong: A. Having a mental health diagnosis does not automatically mean lack of capacity. B. Capacity is not determined by whether the decision appears sensible. C. A person can have capacity while making a decision the clinician disagrees with. D. Remembering every detail is unnecessary.
pearl: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific; the functional test asks whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh the relevant information, and communicate a decision.
thinking: Capacity assessment for one decision ↓ Decision-specific functional test ↓ Understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate ↓ Ability to understand the relevant information
exam_trap: B, making a decision the doctor considers sensible — tempting when a choice seems risky, but an unwise decision does not on its own mean a lack of capacity.
takeaway: Capacity: understand, retain, use or weigh, and communicate.

stem:
A patient understands the information about a proposed procedure but cannot retain the information long enough to make the decision.

Which element of capacity is impaired?
why_correct: The ability to retain relevant information long enough to make the decision is one of the functional elements of capacity.
