why_correct: Upper-airway disease, pulmonary involvement and glomerulonephritis are characteristic of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
why_wrong: A. Polyarteritis nodosa does not typically cause glomerulonephritis. C. IgA vasculitis classically causes palpable purpura, abdominal pain, arthralgia and renal involvement. D. Microscopic polyangiitis can cause pulmonary-renal disease but usually lacks the prominent ENT involvement. E. Goodpasture syndrome causes pulmonary haemorrhage and glomerulonephritis but not chronic destructive ENT disease.
pearl: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis affects the upper airway, lungs and kidneys and is usually PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) positive; blood and protein in the urine need urgent renal assessment.
thinking: Chronic sinusitis and nosebleeds = upper airway ↓ Haemoptysis = lung ↓ Haematuria and proteinuria = glomerulonephritis ↓ Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
exam_trap: E, anti-GBM disease — a pulmonary–renal syndrome, which tempts, but it does not cause chronic sinusitis or nosebleeds; upper airway disease points to GPA.
takeaway: Upper airway, lung and kidney involvement together suggest GPA.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with asthma develops chronic sinusitis, nasal polyps and recurrent episodes of worsening asthma. Her blood count shows marked eosinophilia. Which diagnosis should be suspected?

options.C: Polyarteritis nodosa associated with hepatitis B
options.E: Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis with lung disease

why_correct: Asthma, eosinophilia and systemic small-vessel vasculitis are characteristic of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
why_wrong: A. Goodpasture syndrome causes pulmonary-renal disease without asthma or eosinophilia. C. PAN is a medium-vessel vasculitis and does not typically cause asthma or eosinophilia. D. GPA commonly affects the upper respiratory tract but is not characteristically associated with asthma and marked eosinophilia. E. Systemic sclerosis causes skin thickening and systemic fibrosis rather than eosinophilic asthma-associated vasculitis.
pearl: Suspect EGPA when asthma worsens with nasal polyps and marked eosinophilia; it may be MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) positive, but many patients are ANCA-negative.
thinking: Asthma ↓ Nasal polyps and sinusitis ↓ Marked eosinophilia ↓ Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
exam_trap: D, granulomatosis with polyangiitis — shares sinus disease, but lacks the asthma and eosinophilia that define EGPA.
takeaway: Asthma, eosinophilia and vasculitis mean EGPA.

stem: A 48-year-old woman develops progressive proximal muscle weakness. She struggles to climb stairs and lift objects above her head. Which investigation is most appropriate initially?
why_correct: Creatine kinase is typically raised in inflammatory myopathies causing proximal muscle weakness.
why_wrong: B. D-dimer is used in assessment of venous thromboembolism. C. Calcium abnormalities can cause weakness but do not provide the appropriate initial assessment for suspected inflammatory myopathy. D. Amylase is mainly used in the assessment of pancreatic disease. E. Troponin is primarily a marker of myocardial injury.
pearl: Check CK early in proximal muscle weakness to look for myositis; also check thyroid function, as hypothyroidism and other metabolic causes can mimic inflammatory myopathy.
thinking: Progressive proximal weakness ↓ Difficulty climbing stairs and lifting overhead ↓ Suspect a myopathy such as myositis ↓ Creatine kinase
exam_trap: C, serum calcium only — metabolic causes of weakness exist, but calcium alone does not assess muscle damage; CK is the initial marker.
takeaway: Proximal muscle weakness: check CK first.

stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes has reduced visual acuity. Examination shows retinal microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages and new vessels. Which complication is present?
why_correct: Retinal neovascularisation defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
why_wrong: A. Retinal vein occlusion causes retinal haemorrhages and venous abnormalities but does not define diabetic proliferative disease. B. Cataract causes lens opacity. D. Retinal detachment causes separation of the neurosensory retina and typically presents with flashes, floaters or a visual field defect. E. AMD affects the macula and is associated with ageing.
pearl: New vessel formation defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy; these fragile vessels bleed and scar, so urgent ophthalmology referral for treatment such as laser is needed.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes ↓ Microaneurysms and haemorrhages = diabetic retinal damage ↓ New vessels = neovascularisation ↓ Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
exam_trap: A, central retinal vein occlusion — also causes widespread retinal haemorrhages, but microaneurysms and new vessels in a diabetic fit proliferative retinopathy.
takeaway: New vessels in diabetic retinopathy mean proliferative disease: refer urgently.

stem: A patient with long-standing type 1 diabetes has persistent albuminuria but normal renal function. Which complication is most likely developing?
why_correct: Persistent albuminuria is an early marker of diabetic kidney disease.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic presents with acute severe loin-to-groin pain. B. Acute interstitial nephritis is usually associated with drugs or systemic inflammatory reactions. C. Acute glomerulonephritis usually presents with haematuria, proteinuria and acute renal dysfunction. D. Polycystic kidney disease is an inherited structural renal disorder.
pearl: Persistent albuminuria is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic kidney disease; screen with urine albumin:creatinine ratio and offer ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy for renal protection.
thinking: Long-standing type 1 diabetes ↓ Persistent albuminuria ↓ Renal function still normal ↓ Early diabetic nephropathy
exam_trap: C, acute glomerulonephritis — proteinuria tempts, but it is an acute nephritic illness with haematuria and hypertension, not silent albuminuria in long-standing diabetes.
takeaway: Albuminuria in diabetes means early nephropathy: start renal protection.

stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes becomes unwell with vomiting and fever. He is eating very little. Which advice is most appropriate regarding his insulin?

options.A: Omit all insulin if capillary glucose is below 10 mmol/L
options.B: Continue basal insulin; check glucose and ketones often
options.C: Halve all insulin doses, including basal, while eating less
options.D: Stop basal insulin and give rapid-acting doses with meals
options.E: Stop insulin until eating normally again

correct_answer: B. Continue basal insulin; check glucose and ketones often
why_correct: During acute illness, people with type 1 diabetes generally need to continue basal insulin because stopping it can precipitate DKA.
why_wrong: A. Basal insulin should not be withheld because glucose is below a particular threshold. C. Insulin requirements often rise in illness, so halving doses risks DKA. D. Stopping basal insulin can precipitate DKA. E. Stopping insulin can precipitate DKA.
pearl: Sick day rules in type 1 diabetes: never stop basal insulin, monitor glucose and ketones frequently, keep hydrated and seek urgent help if ketones rise or vomiting persists.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes, unwell and vomiting ↓ Illness raises stress hormones and insulin needs ↓ Stopping insulin risks ketoacidosis ↓ Continue basal insulin; monitor glucose and ketones
exam_trap: E, stop insulin until eating normally — seems logical when intake is poor, but insulin deficiency rapidly leads to DKA.
takeaway: Type 1 diabetes sick day rule: never stop basal insulin.

stem: A pregnant woman who is rhesus D-negative gives birth to a rhesus D-positive baby. What is the purpose of anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.A: Treat haemolytic disease in this newborn baby
options.C: Reduce maternal haemolysis in the days after delivery
options.D: Prevent neonatal jaundice in this newborn baby

correct_answer: E. Prevent maternal anti-D antibody formation
why_correct: Anti-D reduces the risk of maternal antibody formation against rhesus D-positive fetal red cells.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D is prophylaxis for future pregnancies, not treatment of the current baby. B. It has no role in preventing haemorrhage. C. It does not treat maternal haemolysis. D. Neonatal jaundice requires assessment and treatment according to bilirubin levels and cause.
pearl: Anti-D works by preventing sensitisation of an RhD-negative mother; once she has formed anti-D antibodies it cannot help, which is why timely doses after delivery and sensitising events matter.
thinking: RhD-negative mother ↓ RhD-positive baby; fetal cells enter her circulation ↓ Sensitisation would threaten future RhD-positive pregnancies ↓ Anti-D prevents maternal antibody formation
exam_trap: A, treat haemolytic disease in this newborn — tempting because HDFN is the concern, but anti-D is given to the mother to protect future pregnancies.
takeaway: Anti-D is maternal prophylaxis that protects future pregnancies.

stem: A newborn develops jaundice at 12 hours of age. Which feature makes this jaundice particularly concerning?
correct_answer: D. Onset within the first 24 hours
why_correct: Jaundice appearing during the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise and requires assessment.
why_wrong: A. Breastfeeding itself is not an indication that jaundice is pathological. B. Rapid resolution is reassuring rather than concerning. C. Normal feeding and behaviour are reassuring features. E. Mild jaundice developing after the first 24 hours can be physiological.
pearl: Jaundice within the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise, often from haemolysis or infection; measure serum bilirubin urgently rather than relying on visual assessment.
thinking: Jaundice at 12 hours of age ↓ Physiological jaundice appears after the first day ↓ Early onset suggests haemolysis or sepsis ↓ Onset within the first 24 hours
exam_trap: A, breastfeeding — associated with neonatal jaundice, but breast milk jaundice appears later and is benign; early onset is the warning sign.
takeaway: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological until proven otherwise.

stem: A newborn becomes increasingly lethargic, feeds poorly and develops temperature instability. What is the most appropriate concern?
why_correct: Poor feeding, lethargy and temperature instability are important clinical features of neonatal infection.
why_wrong: A. Colic causes crying but not lethargy and temperature instability. B. Reflux may cause feeding symptoms but not systemic deterioration. C. These findings should not be considered normal neonatal behaviour. D. Physiological jaundice does not explain this systemic deterioration.
pearl: Neonatal sepsis presents non-specifically with lethargy, poor feeding and temperature instability; take blood cultures and start IV antibiotics promptly rather than waiting for a fever.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Increasing lethargy and poor feeding ↓ Temperature instability ↓ Neonatal sepsis
exam_trap: C, normal neonatal behaviour — newborns sleep and feed variably, but increasing lethargy with temperature instability is never normal.
takeaway: Lethargic, poorly feeding newborn with unstable temperature: treat as sepsis.

stem: A patient with asthma uses a salbutamol inhaler several times every day. Which medication is generally required to address the underlying airway inflammation?
why_correct: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation and are a key anti-inflammatory treatment in asthma.
why_wrong: B. Antihistamines may help allergic rhinitis but are not the main anti-inflammatory treatment for asthma. C. Antibiotics do not treat the underlying airway inflammation of asthma. D. Morphine has no role in routine asthma management. E. A PPI does not treat airway inflammation.
pearl: Frequent reliever use signals poorly controlled asthma; inhaled corticosteroid-containing treatment controls airway inflammation and reduces attacks, whereas a short-acting reliever alone does not.
thinking: Salbutamol several times daily ↓ Asthma poorly controlled ↓ Underlying airway inflammation untreated ↓ Inhaled corticosteroid
exam_trap: B, antihistamine alone — allergy is linked to asthma, but antihistamines do not control airway inflammation and are not asthma maintenance therapy.
takeaway: Frequent reliever use means anti-inflammatory inhaled steroid treatment is needed.

stem: A patient with COPD has increased breathlessness, increased sputum volume and new purulent sputum. Which treatment may be indicated depending on the overall clinical assessment?
why_correct: Increased sputum purulence, particularly with increased volume and breathlessness, can indicate a bacterial infective exacerbation where antibiotics may be appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Insulin does not treat a COPD exacerbation. B. COPD alone is not an indication for long-term anticoagulation. D. Routine antifungal treatment is not indicated. E. Thrombolysis is not routine treatment for COPD exacerbation.
pearl: In a COPD exacerbation, purulent sputum is the main pointer to bacterial infection and the need for antibiotics; also increase bronchodilator use and consider a short course of oral steroid.
thinking: COPD ↓ More breathlessness and more sputum ↓ New purulent sputum suggests bacterial infection ↓ Antibiotics
exam_trap: B, long-term anticoagulation — breathlessness may raise thoughts of thromboembolism, but nothing suggests it; the clues point to infection.
takeaway: COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum: consider antibiotics.

stem: A patient with chronic COPD is prescribed oxygen during an acute exacerbation. Why should oxygen therapy be carefully controlled?

options.A: Oxygen toxicity causes acute pulmonary fibrosis within hours
options.B: High oxygen concentrations worsen bronchospasm in COPD
options.C: Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in some patients
options.D: Excess oxygen causes a primary respiratory alkalosis in COPD
options.E: Oxygen dries airway secretions and so causes secondary pneumonia

correct_answer: C. Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in some patients
why_correct: Some patients with severe COPD are vulnerable to worsening hypercapnia when given excessive oxygen, so controlled oxygen therapy is used.
why_wrong: A. Therapeutic oxygen does not cause acute pulmonary fibrosis. B. Oxygen does not cause bronchospasm. D. Excess oxygen in susceptible COPD patients causes respiratory acidosis, not alkalosis. E. Oxygen does not cause pneumonia.
pearl: In COPD at risk of hypercapnia, give controlled oxygen via a Venturi mask aiming for saturations of 88–92% and check blood gases; never withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient.
thinking: COPD exacerbation ↓ Some patients retain CO2 ↓ Excess oxygen worsens V/Q mismatch and reduces ventilation ↓ Risk of worsening hypercapnia
exam_trap: B, high oxygen worsens bronchospasm — sounds plausible in airways disease, but oxygen does not cause bronchospasm; the danger is CO2 retention.
takeaway: COPD: controlled oxygen, target 88–92%, to avoid hypercapnia.

stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis asks which antibody is relatively specific for the disease and can help support the diagnosis. Which is the best answer?
why_correct: Anti-CCP antibodies are relatively specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
why_wrong: B. Anti-centromere antibodies are associated particularly with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. C. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are strongly associated with SLE. D. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are associated with primary biliary cholangitis. E. Anti-GBM antibodies are associated with anti-GBM disease.
pearl: Anti-CCP is more specific for rheumatoid arthritis than rheumatoid factor and predicts more erosive disease; a negative result does not exclude RA.
thinking: Rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Need a relatively specific antibody ↓ Rheumatoid factor is less specific ↓ Anti-CCP antibody
exam_trap: C, anti-dsDNA — a well-known specific autoantibody, but for SLE, not rheumatoid arthritis.
takeaway: Anti-CCP is the relatively specific antibody for RA.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has a positive ANA test but no symptoms or clinical signs of autoimmune disease. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: A positive ANA alone does not diagnose SLE
options.B: She has early seronegative rheumatoid arthritis
options.C: She has early drug-induced lupus erythematosus

correct_answer: A. A positive ANA alone does not diagnose SLE
why_correct: ANA can be positive in healthy people and in several autoimmune conditions; it must be interpreted in the clinical context.
why_wrong: B. ANA is not diagnostic of rheumatoid arthritis, and she has no joint symptoms. C. There is no drug history or clinical features of drug-induced lupus. D. Treatment should not be started on the basis of a positive ANA alone. E. Corticosteroids should not be started solely because ANA is positive.
pearl: ANA is sensitive but not specific and is positive in many healthy people, so test only when clinical features suggest autoimmune disease, and never treat a result alone.
thinking: Positive ANA ↓ No symptoms or signs ↓ ANA occurs in healthy people ↓ A positive ANA alone does not diagnose SLE
exam_trap: D, start hydroxychloroquine — the familiar lupus drug tempts, but treatment is for disease, not for a laboratory result in someone with no clinical features.
takeaway: Treat the patient, not the ANA: a positive test alone is not a diagnosis.

stem: A 68-year-old man has progressive difficulty swallowing, first with solid foods and later with liquids. What mechanism best explains this pattern?

options.E: Failure of oesophageal peristalsis from the outset

why_correct: Dysphagia that begins with solids and later affects liquids suggests a progressively narrowing mechanical obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Excessive LES relaxation does not cause this pattern. C. Pharyngeal weakness produces oropharyngeal swallowing difficulty rather than progressive oesophageal obstruction. D. Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting rather than oesophageal dysphagia. E. Motility disorders such as achalasia typically cause dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids in an older adult suggests oesophageal cancer and needs urgent upper GI endoscopy; achalasia classically affects solids and liquids from the start.
thinking: Older man ↓ Dysphagia to solids first, then liquids ↓ Progressive narrowing of the lumen ↓ Mechanical obstruction
exam_trap: E, failure of peristalsis from the outset — the motility pattern of achalasia, which affects solids and liquids together from the start, unlike here.
takeaway: Solids then liquids suggests mechanical; both from the start suggests motility.

stem: A patient develops a sudden painful, red eye with photophobia. There is a hazy cornea and reduced vision. Which condition requires urgent ophthalmological assessment?
why_correct: Pain, photophobia, corneal abnormality and reduced vision are red flags for keratitis and possible corneal ulceration.
why_wrong: A. Subconjunctival haemorrhage causes a sharply demarcated red area but usually no pain or visual loss. B. Blepharitis primarily affects the eyelid margins. C. Dry eye usually causes irritation rather than an acutely painful red eye with reduced vision. D. Simple conjunctivitis generally causes irritation and discharge without significant corneal involvement or visual loss.
pearl: A painful red eye with photophobia, reduced vision and corneal haze is a red flag; contact lens wearers are at particular risk of microbial keratitis and need same-day ophthalmology review.
thinking: Sudden painful red eye ↓ Photophobia and reduced vision ↓ Hazy cornea = corneal involvement ↓ Keratitis
exam_trap: D, simple conjunctivitis — the commonest red eye, but it does not reduce vision or cloud the cornea and is rarely painful.
takeaway: Red eye with pain, photophobia and reduced vision needs urgent ophthalmology.

stem: A patient develops a painful vesicular rash over one side of the forehead and the tip of the nose. What complication is particularly important to consider?

options.A: Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy

why_correct: Ophthalmic division trigeminal involvement, particularly with lesions on the forehead and nose, can involve the eye and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves the facial nerve with vesicles in the ear and facial palsy. B. Molluscum causes small umbilicated papules. C. Kaposi varicelliform eruption (eczema herpeticum) occurs on eczematous skin rather than in a dermatome. E. Bullous impetigo causes superficial bullae rather than a unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) indicate nasociliary involvement and a high risk of eye disease in shingles; start oral antivirals and arrange urgent ophthalmology review.
thinking: Unilateral vesicular rash on the forehead ↓ Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ Nasal tip involved: Hutchinson sign ↓ Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
exam_trap: A, Ramsay Hunt syndrome — also zoster of a cranial nerve, but it involves the ear and facial nerve, not the forehead and nose.
takeaway: Zoster on the tip of the nose: assume eye involvement and refer.

stem: A 72-year-old man develops recurrent falls. His medications include an opioid, a benzodiazepine and several antihypertensives. Which medication-related factor should be specifically considered?
correct_answer: D. Polypharmacy causing adverse drug effects
why_correct: Multiple medications, particularly sedatives and blood-pressure-lowering drugs, can increase the risk of falls through sedation, impaired balance and postural hypotension.
why_wrong: A. None of his medicines commonly cause B12 deficiency. B. Constipation does not explain recurrent falls. C. Dependence is not the mechanism by which benzodiazepines cause falls. E. He is not taking antibiotics, and diarrhoea does not explain this pattern.
pearl: Falls in older adults should prompt a structured medication review, particularly of sedatives, opioids and antihypertensives, as part of a multifactorial falls assessment.
thinking: 72-year-old with recurrent falls ↓ Opioid and benzodiazepine cause sedation ↓ Antihypertensives cause postural hypotension ↓ Polypharmacy causing adverse drug effects
exam_trap: C, benzodiazepine dependence syndrome — the benzodiazepine is relevant, but dependence is not the falls mechanism; sedation and combined drug effects are.
takeaway: Recurrent falls in older people: review sedatives and antihypertensives.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of wheeze, cough and chest tightness. Symptoms vary considerably from day to day and are worse after exercise. Which feature most strongly supports asthma?
why_correct: Asthma is characterised by variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation.
why_wrong: A. Persistent unilateral wheeze raises concern about a local airway lesion or foreign body. B. Clubbing is not a typical feature of asthma. D. Fixed exercise limitation is less characteristic of asthma. E. Persistent productive cough suggests another chronic respiratory disorder.
pearl: Variability is the hallmark of asthma: symptoms come and go, worsen at night or with triggers, and objective testing shows variable airflow obstruction.
thinking: Recurrent wheeze, cough and chest tightness ↓ Symptoms vary day to day ↓ Worse after exercise ↓ Variable respiratory symptoms
exam_trap: E, persistent daily productive cough — a respiratory symptom, but its persistence suggests COPD or bronchiectasis rather than variable asthma.
takeaway: Variability of symptoms and airflow is the hallmark of asthma.

stem: A 67-year-old smoker has persistent cough, weight loss and blood-streaked sputum. Which diagnosis should be considered particularly important?
why_correct: Persistent respiratory symptoms with haemoptysis and unexplained weight loss in an older smoker are concerning for lung cancer.
why_wrong: B. A viral infection would usually be self-limiting. C. Asthma does not typically cause unexplained weight loss and haemoptysis. D. Acute bronchitis is generally short-lived and does not explain persistent constitutional symptoms. E. Allergic rhinitis does not explain haemoptysis and weight loss.
pearl: An older smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss needs urgent assessment on a suspected lung cancer pathway; a normal chest X-ray does not exclude cancer if suspicion remains.
thinking: 67-year-old smoker ↓ Persistent cough and weight loss ↓ Blood-streaked sputum ↓ Lung cancer
exam_trap: D, acute bronchitis only — explains cough and streaky sputum, but not persistent symptoms with weight loss in a high-risk smoker.
takeaway: Haemoptysis and weight loss in a smoker: lung cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient with suspected lung cancer has a chest X-ray showing a central lung mass. Which symptom may result from obstruction of a main bronchus?
why_correct: A central airway tumour can cause localised airway narrowing and persistent or focal wheeze.
why_wrong: A. Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is associated with lung cancer but is not caused by bronchial obstruction. B. Bilateral crackles suggest pulmonary oedema or fibrosis. D. Pleuritic pain suggests pleural involvement rather than bronchial obstruction. E. Ankle oedema is not caused by bronchial obstruction.
pearl: A fixed, monophonic wheeze heard over one area suggests partial obstruction of a large airway by tumour or foreign body, unlike the diffuse polyphonic wheeze of asthma.
thinking: Central lung mass ↓ Main bronchus partly obstructed ↓ Narrowing at one fixed site ↓ Persistent focal wheeze
exam_trap: A, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy — a real lung cancer feature, but it is paraneoplastic, not a result of bronchial obstruction.
takeaway: Fixed focal wheeze suggests localised airway obstruction such as a tumour.

stem: A patient with recurrent abdominal pain from acute intermittent porphyria asks about a possible precipitating factor. Which is a recognised trigger?
why_correct: Various medicines can precipitate acute porphyria attacks, so medication review is important.
why_wrong: A. Exercise alone is not the classic medication-related trigger. B. Normal water intake is not a typical trigger. C. Dietary fibre is not a characteristic precipitant. D. Contact lenses have no relevant association.
pearl: Acute porphyria attacks can be triggered by many drugs, alcohol, fasting, hormonal changes and infection; always check a medicine's porphyria safety before prescribing.
thinking: Acute intermittent porphyria ↓ Attacks follow increased demand on haem synthesis ↓ Many drugs induce hepatic haem pathways ↓ Certain medications
exam_trap: A, regular exercise alone — a lifestyle factor sounds plausible, but it is not a recognised trigger; drugs, alcohol and fasting are.
takeaway: Acute porphyria: check every drug for safety.

stem: A patient has recurrent nosebleeds originating from the anterior nasal septum. Which anatomical site is the commonest source of anterior epistaxis?
why_correct: Little's area on the anterior nasal septum contains a vascular network and is the commonest site of anterior epistaxis.
why_wrong: A. The middle ear is not a usual source of anterior epistaxis. B. The maxillary sinus is not the commonest source. D. The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear with the nasopharynx. E. The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the nose and is not the typical source.
pearl: Most nosebleeds arise from Little's area; first aid is to sit forward and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10–15 minutes without releasing.
thinking: Anterior epistaxis ↓ Source on the anterior nasal septum ↓ Plexus of anastomosing vessels ↓ Little's area
exam_trap: B, maxillary sinus — sits next to the nasal cavity, but it is not the source of anterior septal bleeding.
takeaway: Anterior epistaxis usually comes from Little's area.

stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation is being assessed for stroke prevention. Which factor is relevant to the decision about anticoagulation?
why_correct: Stroke risk in atrial fibrillation is assessed from recognised thromboembolic risk factors (age, sex, heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease) using the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score recommended by NICE NG196, and this guides the anticoagulation decision alongside bleeding-risk assessment.
why_wrong: A. CURB-65 assesses the severity of community-acquired pneumonia. B. The Wells score estimates the clinical probability of pulmonary embolism, not stroke risk in AF. C. QRISK3 estimates 10-year cardiovascular risk for statin decisions, not AF stroke risk. D. ABCD2 was used to stratify TIA risk and is not used in AF anticoagulation decisions.
pearl: In atrial fibrillation, CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates stroke risk to guide anticoagulation, while bleeding risk is assessed alongside; bleeding risk should prompt correction of modifiable factors rather than automatically stopping anticoagulation.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation ↓ Decision about stroke prevention ↓ Need the AF stroke-risk score ↓ CHA₂DS₂-VASc
exam_trap: D, ABCD2 score — another stroke-related score, which tempts, but it was designed for TIA, not stroke prevention in AF.
takeaway: AF anticoagulation: CHA₂DS₂-VASc for stroke risk, with bleeding risk assessed too.

stem: A patient taking warfarin is prescribed a new medication. Why is medication review important?

options.A: Warfarin blocks absorption of most oral drugs
options.B: Warfarin is renally cleared and accumulates
options.C: Interacting drugs can alter the INR
options.D: Warfarin is a potent enzyme inducer
options.E: Warfarin increases the clearance of other drugs

correct_answer: C. Interacting drugs can alter the INR
why_correct: Numerous medicines can alter warfarin's effect, increasing either bleeding or thrombosis risk.
why_wrong: A. Warfarin does not block absorption of other drugs. B. Warfarin is hepatically metabolised, not renally cleared. D. Warfarin is not an enzyme inducer; its metabolism is affected by inducers and inhibitors. E. Warfarin does not increase clearance of other drugs.
pearl: Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic range and many interactions: enzyme inhibitors such as clarithromycin raise the INR and bleeding risk, while enzyme inducers lower it. Check the INR when interacting drugs start or stop.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ Narrow therapeutic range, hepatic metabolism ↓ New drugs can inhibit or induce its metabolism ↓ Interacting drugs can alter the INR
exam_trap: D, warfarin is a potent enzyme inducer — interactions do involve liver enzymes, but warfarin is affected by inducers and inhibitors rather than being one.
takeaway: Any new drug with warfarin: check interactions and monitor the INR.

stem: A patient with diabetes has reduced sensation in both feet. Which intervention is particularly important to reduce the risk of foot ulceration?

options.A: Walking barefoot at home to improve sensation
options.B: Soaking the feet in hot water every evening
options.C: Regular foot checks and protective foot care
options.E: Cutting calluses with a blade at home

correct_answer: C. Regular foot checks and protective foot care
why_correct: Neuropathy increases the risk of unnoticed injury, so regular assessment and protective foot care are important.
why_wrong: A. Walking barefoot increases injury risk. B. Hot water risks unnoticed burns and soaking macerates the skin. D. Corn plasters contain acids that can cause ulceration. E. Cutting calluses at home can cause injury and infection.
pearl: Loss of protective sensation is a key risk for diabetic foot ulcers; daily self-inspection, well-fitting footwear and regular foot assessment with podiatry input prevent ulcers and amputations.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Reduced sensation in both feet ↓ Injuries go unnoticed ↓ Regular foot checks and protective foot care
exam_trap: D, corn plasters on calluses — look like simple self-care, but their acid can ulcerate insensate diabetic skin.
takeaway: Neuropathic diabetic feet need daily checks and professional foot care.

stem: A patient develops a sharply demarcated, itchy, scaly plaque on the scalp, elbows and knees. The nails have small pits. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Extensor plaques with scale and nail pitting are characteristic of psoriasis.
why_wrong: B. Atopic eczema commonly affects flexures and has different morphology. C. Cellulitis is an acute bacterial infection. D. Tinea corporis usually produces annular lesions with peripheral scale. E. Urticaria causes transient wheals.
pearl: Psoriasis gives well-demarcated scaly plaques on extensor surfaces and the scalp; nail pitting and onycholysis are clues, and nail disease is linked with psoriatic arthritis.
thinking: Sharply demarcated scaly plaques ↓ Scalp, elbows and knees = extensor sites ↓ Nail pitting ↓ Psoriasis
exam_trap: B, atopic eczema — itchy and can be scaly, but it favours the flexures and lacks the sharp demarcation and extensor distribution of psoriasis.
takeaway: Extensor plaques with nail pitting mean psoriasis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has itchy flexural eczema. She also has asthma and allergic rhinitis. Which diagnosis best explains the combination?
why_correct: Atopic eczema commonly occurs in association with other atopic conditions such as asthma and allergic rhinitis.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is a bacterial infection. C. Tinea corporis causes fungal annular lesions. D. Scabies causes intense itching and characteristic burrows. E. Psoriasis is not characteristically associated with asthma and allergic rhinitis.
pearl: Atopic eczema typically affects the flexures in older children and adults and clusters with asthma and allergic rhinitis; emollients are the foundation of treatment, with topical steroids for flares.
thinking: Itchy rash in the flexures ↓ Personal history of asthma ↓ And allergic rhinitis = atopic tendency ↓ Atopic eczema
exam_trap: E, psoriasis — a chronic scaly rash, but it favours extensor surfaces and lacks the atopic association.
takeaway: Flexural eczema with asthma and hay fever is the atopic triad.

stem: A doctor realises that they have made a significant error in a patient's clinical record. What is the appropriate way to correct the entry?

options.A: Ask a colleague to countersign the original entry
options.B: Delete the original entry and enter the correction
options.C: Add a dated correction, keeping the original visible
options.D: Use correction fluid and rewrite the entry neatly
options.E: Amend the entry without noting the change

correct_answer: C. Add a dated correction, keeping the original visible
why_correct: Clinical records should remain an accurate and transparent account of events, with amendments identifiable rather than concealed.
why_wrong: A. Another doctor should not authenticate an entry they did not make. B. Deleting the original record undermines the integrity of the record. D. Obscuring the original entry is inappropriate. E. Undocumented alteration is inappropriate.
pearl: Never delete or obscure a record entry; correct errors with a clear, dated, timed and signed addition so the original remains readable and the record stays transparent.
thinking: Significant error in the record ↓ Records must be accurate and transparent ↓ Any change must be traceable ↓ Add a dated correction, keeping the original visible
exam_trap: B, delete and re-enter — produces a tidy record, but erasing the original conceals what happened and may be viewed as falsification.
takeaway: Correct records by dated addition; never erase.

stem: A doctor receives a critical laboratory result for a patient but is approaching the end of their shift. What is the safest action?

options.A: Leave it for the next shift to find in the system
options.B: Document it in the notes and go home
options.C: Hand over the result and required action
options.D: Ask the ward clerk to pass it on
options.E: Assume the laboratory will phone the team

correct_answer: C. Hand over the result and required action
why_correct: Clinically important information must be communicated reliably to the person responsible for ongoing care.
why_wrong: A. Relying on others to find the result is unsafe. B. Documentation without communication may delay action. D. Non-clinical staff should not be relied on to communicate critical results. E. Laboratories do not replace the treating team's responsibility for follow-up.
pearl: Responsibility for a result you have received continues until it is safely handed over; give a direct handover of the result and the action needed, and document it.
thinking: Critical result received ↓ Shift ending ↓ Action still needed for patient safety ↓ Hand over the result and required action
exam_trap: B, document it in the notes and go home — documentation feels responsible, but nobody may read it in time; the result must be actively handed over.
takeaway: Critical results must be actively handed over, not left in the notes.

stem: A doctor is asked to perform a procedure that they have never been trained to perform and that is outside their current competence. What should they do?

options.A: Seek supervision or a competent colleague
options.B: Watch a video tutorial and then perform it
options.C: Delegate it to a medical student
options.D: Attempt it and call for help if difficulty arises
options.E: Ask the patient to consent to a trainee attempt

correct_answer: A. Seek supervision or a competent colleague
why_correct: Doctors should work within the limits of their competence and seek appropriate help when necessary.
why_wrong: B. A video does not provide competence for an untrained procedure. C. Delegation does not remove the requirement for appropriate competence and supervision. D. Attempting an unfamiliar procedure without support creates avoidable risk. E. Consent does not make an unsupervised, untrained attempt appropriate.
pearl: GMC guidance requires doctors to recognise and work within the limits of their competence; if asked to perform an unfamiliar procedure, seek supervision or a competent colleague.
thinking: Procedure never trained in ↓ Outside current competence ↓ Patient safety comes first ↓ Seek supervision or a competent colleague
exam_trap: D, attempt it and call for help if difficulty arises — sounds proactive, but it exposes the patient to avoidable harm from an untrained operator.
takeaway: Outside your competence: seek help before acting, not after.

stem: A patient with ulcerative colitis develops severe abdominal distension, abdominal pain, fever and systemic toxicity. Abdominal imaging shows marked colonic dilatation. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Severe colitis with systemic toxicity and marked colonic dilatation is characteristic of toxic megacolon.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain. B. Appendicitis does not cause diffuse colonic dilatation in this setting. C. Biliary colic causes episodic right upper abdominal pain. D. Pyloric stenosis occurs in infants.
pearl: Toxic megacolon is a life-threatening complication of severe colitis; manage jointly with surgeons, with IV steroids, fluids and close monitoring, as the risk of perforation is high.
thinking: Ulcerative colitis ↓ Severe pain, distension, fever and toxicity ↓ Marked colonic dilatation on imaging ↓ Toxic megacolon
exam_trap: B, appendicitis — causes fever and abdominal pain, but not marked colonic dilatation in a patient with active colitis.
takeaway: Colitis with systemic toxicity and a dilated colon means toxic megacolon.

stem: A patient with chronic diarrhoea has evidence of malabsorption. Which deficiency is particularly associated with steatorrhoea?
why_correct: Fat malabsorption can lead to deficiencies of vitamins A, D, E and K.
why_wrong: A. Water-soluble vitamins are not specifically affected by fat malabsorption. B. B12 deficiency can occur in some malabsorptive disorders but is not the general consequence of fat malabsorption. C. Iron and folate deficiency may occur in several gastrointestinal disorders but are not specifically consequences of impaired fat absorption. E. Vitamin C is water-soluble.
pearl: Steatorrhoea means fat malabsorption and with it loss of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; vitamin K deficiency can prolong the clotting time.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea with malabsorption ↓ Steatorrhoea = fat not absorbed ↓ Vitamins absorbed with fat are lost ↓ Fat-soluble vitamins
exam_trap: B, vitamin B12 — a classic malabsorption deficiency, but it reflects gastric or terminal ileal disease rather than fat malabsorption.
takeaway: Steatorrhoea: think vitamin A, D, E and K deficiency.

stem: A patient with meningitis develops a reduced level of consciousness and a new focal neurological deficit. Why might lumbar puncture need to be delayed?

options.A: Risk of introducing infection into the CSF
options.B: Risk of a traumatic tap affecting the cell count
options.C: Focal signs mean the diagnosis is encephalitis
options.D: Risk of herniation from raised intracranial pressure

correct_answer: D. Risk of herniation from raised intracranial pressure
why_correct: Reduced consciousness or focal neurological signs may indicate raised intracranial pressure or another intracranial complication, requiring appropriate assessment before LP.
why_wrong: A. Infection risk is not the reason to delay LP here. B. A traumatic tap is not a reason to delay LP. C. Focal signs can occur in complicated meningitis and do not establish encephalitis. E. Post-dural puncture headache is not a reason to delay LP.
pearl: Never delay antibiotics for an LP; reduced consciousness, focal signs, seizures or papilloedema suggest raised intracranial pressure, so treat first and assess before any LP.
thinking: Meningitis ↓ Reduced consciousness and new focal deficit ↓ Possible raised ICP or mass effect ↓ LP risks herniation
exam_trap: A, risk of introducing infection — LP is invasive, but infection risk is not why it is delayed here; the danger is herniation.
takeaway: Focal signs or reduced consciousness: treat first, delay LP.

stem: A 21-year-old student develops fever, severe headache and a non-blanching rash. Which organism is an important cause of this presentation?
why_correct: Meningococcal disease can cause rapidly progressive meningitis and meningococcal septicaemia with a non-blanching rash.
why_wrong: A. Streptococcus pyogenes causes pharyngitis, scarlet fever and cellulitis rather than meningitis with a non-blanching rash. B. Listeria causes meningitis mainly in neonates, older adults and the immunocompromised. C. Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia. E. E. coli is an important cause of neonatal meningitis but not of this presentation in a young adult.
pearl: Fever with a non-blanching rash suggests meningococcal disease; outside hospital give IM or IV benzylpenicillin if it does not delay urgent transfer.
thinking: Young adult with fever and severe headache ↓ Non-blanching rash = petechiae or purpura ↓ Meningitis with septicaemia ↓ Neisseria meningitidis
exam_trap: A, Streptococcus pyogenes — causes fever with rash, but its scarlatiniform rash blanches; a non-blanching rash points to meningococcus.
takeaway: Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient has a painful unilateral vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution. Which virus causes this condition?
why_correct: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in a sensory ganglion causes herpes zoster.
why_wrong: A. Parvovirus B19 causes conditions including erythema infectiosum. B. CMV causes congenital and opportunistic infections. D. Hepatitis B primarily infects the liver. E. EBV is associated with infectious mononucleosis.
pearl: Shingles is reactivation of latent varicella-zoster virus in a sensory ganglion; oral antivirals started early, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, reduce severity.
thinking: Painful vesicular rash ↓ Unilateral, dermatomal distribution ↓ Reactivation from a sensory ganglion ↓ Varicella-zoster virus
exam_trap: E, Epstein–Barr virus — another herpesvirus, but it causes glandular fever, not a dermatomal vesicular rash.
takeaway: A dermatomal vesicular rash is shingles from VZV reactivation.

stem: A patient with herpes zoster develops a painful rash around the ear accompanied by facial weakness. Which complication should be considered?

options.E: Bell's palsy from idiopathic facial nerve palsy

why_correct: Herpes zoster involving the geniculate ganglion can cause an ear vesicular eruption with ipsilateral facial nerve palsy.
why_wrong: A. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus. B. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief facial pain rather than facial weakness. D. Otitis externa does not explain facial nerve palsy with vesicles. E. Bell's palsy does not characteristically cause vesicles around the ear.
pearl: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is zoster of the geniculate ganglion: ear pain, vesicles in or around the ear and ipsilateral LMN facial palsy, with a poorer outlook than Bell's palsy.
thinking: Herpes zoster ↓ Painful rash around the ear = geniculate ganglion ↓ Ipsilateral facial weakness ↓ Ramsay Hunt syndrome
exam_trap: E, Bell's palsy — causes LMN facial weakness, but it is idiopathic with no vesicular rash.
takeaway: Facial palsy with ear vesicles means Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

stem: A patient develops a widespread itchy rash several days after starting a new medication. There are no blisters or mucosal lesions. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A widespread maculopapular rash occurring after a medication is a common presentation of a morbilliform drug eruption.
why_wrong: A. SJS usually involves mucosal lesions and systemic illness. B. Herpes zoster follows a dermatomal distribution. C. Eczema herpeticum causes painful vesicles and erosions. D. TEN causes extensive epidermal detachment and severe systemic illness.
pearl: Morbilliform drug eruptions appear days after starting a drug; look for warning signs such as mucosal involvement, blistering, skin pain, fever or facial swelling that suggest SJS/TEN or DRESS.
thinking: New medication ↓ Widespread itchy rash days later ↓ No blisters or mucosal lesions ↓ Morbilliform drug eruption
exam_trap: A, Stevens–Johnson syndrome — a feared drug reaction, but it involves mucosal erosions and blistering, both absent here.
takeaway: A drug rash without mucosal or blistering features is usually morbilliform.

stem: A patient develops recurrent episodes of facial swelling and abdominal pain. There is no urticaria. Several family members have experienced similar episodes. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria, particularly with a family history and abdominal attacks, suggests hereditary angioedema.
why_wrong: B. Eczema causes inflammatory skin lesions. C. Contact dermatitis causes localised inflammatory skin reactions following exposure. D. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is characterised by transient wheals, often with histaminergic angioedema; there is no urticaria here. E. Cellulitis is a local bacterial infection with fever and erythema, and does not cause abdominal pain or run in families.
pearl: Hereditary angioedema is a C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency causing recurrent swelling without urticaria, often with abdominal attacks; complement C4 is a useful screening test.
thinking: Recurrent facial swelling ↓ Episodes of abdominal pain ↓ No urticaria, positive family history ↓ Hereditary angioedema
exam_trap: D, chronic spontaneous urticaria — can come with angioedema, but it features weals and has no family pattern or abdominal attacks.
takeaway: Angioedema without urticaria plus family history suggests HAE.

stem: A patient with hereditary angioedema develops swelling of the tongue and difficulty breathing. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Oral antihistamine and observation for 4 hours
options.C: Oral prednisolone and outpatient clinic review
options.D: Nebulised salbutamol and an urgent chest X-ray

correct_answer: E. Urgent airway assessment and management
why_correct: Tongue or upper-airway swelling can rapidly compromise the airway and is a medical emergency.
why_wrong: A. Hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated and does not respond to antihistamines; the airway is the priority. B. Airway compromise cannot safely be managed with reassurance alone. C. Corticosteroids are ineffective in hereditary angioedema and outpatient review is unsafe with airway swelling. D. Salbutamol treats bronchospasm, not upper-airway oedema, and investigation should not delay airway management.
pearl: Airway swelling in hereditary angioedema can progress rapidly; secure the airway early and give C1-esterase inhibitor or icatibant, as antihistamines, steroids and adrenaline are largely ineffective.
thinking: Hereditary angioedema ↓ Tongue swelling ↓ Difficulty breathing ↓ Urgent airway assessment and management
exam_trap: A, oral antihistamine and observation — reasonable for mild allergic swelling, but HAE is bradykinin-mediated, will not respond, and the airway is threatened.
takeaway: Tongue swelling with breathing difficulty: airway first.

stem: A patient with suspected septic arthritis has a joint aspirate sent for analysis. Which finding supports bacterial infection?

options.A: Low inflammatory-cell count with no clinical symptoms
options.B: Normal clear synovial fluid appearance with no cells
options.D: Heavily bloodstained fluid with a normal white-cell count
options.E: High synovial white-cell count, mainly neutrophils

correct_answer: E. High synovial white-cell count, mainly neutrophils
why_correct: Acute bacterial septic arthritis typically produces a markedly inflammatory synovial fluid with neutrophil predominance.
why_wrong: A. A low inflammatory-cell count is less consistent with acute bacterial infection. B. Normal fluid findings do not support septic arthritis. C. Absence of inflammatory cells argues against acute bacterial infection. D. Bloodstained fluid with a normal white-cell count suggests haemarthrosis rather than bacterial infection.
pearl: A septic joint aspirate is turbid with a high white-cell count, mainly neutrophils; send for Gram stain and culture, aspirating before antibiotics where possible without delaying treatment.
thinking: Suspected septic arthritis ↓ Bacteria provoke intense inflammation ↓ Neutrophils flood the joint ↓ High synovial white-cell count, mainly neutrophils
exam_trap: D, heavily bloodstained fluid with a normal white-cell count — an abnormal aspirate, but haemarthrosis suggests trauma or a bleeding disorder, not infection.
takeaway: Septic joint fluid: turbid with a high neutrophil count.

stem: A patient with acute gout has severe pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Which crystal appearance is characteristic?
why_correct: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent under polarised light.
why_wrong: A. Demonstrating crystals supports the diagnosis when present. C. Rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals are characteristic of CPPD. D. Cholesterol crystals are not the typical finding. E. Urate crystals are needle-shaped but negatively, not positively, birefringent.
pearl: Gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent; pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate) crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent.
thinking: Acute arthritis of the first MTP joint ↓ Classic site for gout ↓ Monosodium urate crystals ↓ Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent
exam_trap: C, rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals — the pseudogout pattern, which is commonly swapped with gout.
takeaway: Gout: needles, negative. Pseudogout: rhomboids, positive.

stem: A patient develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm 24 hours after a total thyroidectomy. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely?
why_correct: Inadvertent damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands during total thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcaemia, which increases neuromuscular excitability and produces perioral paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm (tetany).
why_wrong: A. Hypernatraemia mainly causes thirst, lethargy and confusion from cellular dehydration, not tetany. B. Hypermagnesaemia causes neuromuscular depression with hyporeflexia, the opposite of tetany. C. Hyperchloraemia is not a recognised complication of thyroidectomy and does not cause tetany. E. Hyperkalaemia mainly causes muscle weakness and cardiac conduction abnormalities rather than tetany.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy reflects parathyroid injury; check calcium, look for Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and give IV calcium gluconate for severe symptoms.
thinking: Total thyroidectomy ↓ Parathyroids injured or removed ↓ Parathyroid hormone falls ↓ Perioral tingling and tetany: hypocalcaemia
exam_trap: B, hypermagnesaemia — magnesium affects neuromuscular function, but excess causes weakness and reduced reflexes, not tetany.
takeaway: Tingling and tetany after thyroidectomy: check calcium.

stem: A patient has persistent diarrhoea and develops a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Which mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: Diarrhoea causes gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, producing a hyperchloraemic normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
why_wrong: A. Lactic acidosis produces a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. B. Tissue hypoxia causes lactic acidosis. C. Ketones cause a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. D. Toxic alcohol metabolites (e.g. from methanol) cause a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
pearl: Diarrhoea causes a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis through bicarbonate loss; a raised gap points instead to added acids such as lactate, ketones or toxins.
thinking: Persistent diarrhoea ↓ Intestinal fluid is rich in bicarbonate ↓ Bicarbonate lost, chloride retained ↓ Gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss
exam_trap: A, lactic acid accumulation — common in unwell patients, but lactic acidosis raises the anion gap.
takeaway: Normal anion gap acidosis with diarrhoea means GI bicarbonate loss.

stem: A patient presents with vomiting and develops metabolic alkalosis. Which renal response contributes to maintenance of the alkalosis?

options.E: Complete cessation of hydrogen ion secretion

why_correct: Volume and chloride depletion associated with vomiting promote renal retention of bicarbonate and maintenance of metabolic alkalosis.
why_wrong: A. Ketone production causes high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. B. Lactate production causes metabolic acidosis. D. Increased bicarbonate excretion would help correct alkalosis. E. Hydrogen ion handling is more complex and is not completely abolished.
pearl: Vomiting causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis maintained by volume and chloride depletion; correction needs saline with potassium replacement.
thinking: Vomiting loses gastric acid ↓ Volume and chloride depletion ↓ Kidneys retain sodium and bicarbonate ↓ Increased renal bicarbonate retention
exam_trap: D, increased bicarbonate excretion — the normal renal response to alkalosis, but volume and chloride depletion prevent it, so the alkalosis persists.
takeaway: Vomiting alkalosis is sustained by volume depletion: give saline and potassium.

stem: A patient has severe diarrhoea and develops dehydration. Which clinical finding most strongly suggests significant volume depletion?

options.C: A raised jugular venous pressure at 45°

why_correct: Orthostatic symptoms and a fall in blood pressure suggest reduced circulating volume.
why_wrong: B. Ascites represents fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity. C. Raised JVP suggests increased venous pressure rather than simple volume depletion. D. Pulmonary crackles in this context suggest pulmonary congestion. E. Peripheral oedema suggests fluid accumulation.
pearl: Postural hypotension, tachycardia, reduced urine output and prolonged capillary refill indicate significant hypovolaemia; rehydrate and reassess.
thinking: Severe diarrhoea ↓ Fluid loss reduces circulating volume ↓ Blood pressure falls on standing ↓ Postural hypotension with dizziness
exam_trap: C, raised jugular venous pressure — an important volume sign, but a raised JVP reflects overload; in dehydration it is low.
takeaway: Postural hypotension is a key sign of volume depletion.

stem: A patient with severe dehydration has reduced urine output. Which renal mechanism helps conserve water?

options.C: Complete inhibition of renal water reabsorption

why_correct: Dehydration stimulates ADH release, increasing renal water reabsorption and concentrating the urine.
why_wrong: A. Thirst is stimulated rather than suppressed. B. Reduced ADH would increase free-water loss. C. This would worsen dehydration. D. Increased urinary water loss is the opposite of the physiological response.
pearl: Dehydration raises plasma osmolality and stimulates ADH, which increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts to concentrate the urine and conserve water.
thinking: Severe dehydration ↓ Rising osmolality and falling volume ↓ Pituitary releases more ADH ↓ Increased ADH secretion
exam_trap: B, reduced ADH secretion — the right hormone, but the wrong direction; less ADH would increase water loss.
takeaway: Dehydration increases ADH, concentrating urine and conserving water.

stem: A patient develops polyuria after treatment with lithium. Urine remains dilute despite dehydration. Which mechanism is most likely?
why_correct: Lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by reducing the kidney's response to ADH.
why_wrong: A. Excess thyroid hormone causes thyrotoxicosis. B. Reduced pituitary ADH secretion causes cranial diabetes insipidus; lithium causes the nephrogenic form. D. Excess insulin causes hypoglycaemia. E. Excess aldosterone causes hypertension and hypokalaemia.
pearl: Lithium is a classic cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; the kidney fails to respond to ADH, so desmopressin is ineffective, unlike in cranial diabetes insipidus.
thinking: Lithium therapy ↓ Polyuria ↓ Dilute urine despite dehydration ↓ Renal resistance to ADH: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
exam_trap: B, reduced pituitary ADH secretion — also causes dilute polyuria, but lithium acts on the kidney, so the cause is nephrogenic, not cranial.
takeaway: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

stem: A patient develops weakness and palpitations after several days of persistent vomiting. Blood tests show hypokalaemia. Which additional electrolyte abnormality commonly accompanies significant potassium depletion?
why_correct: Magnesium deficiency commonly accompanies potassium depletion and can make hypokalaemia difficult to correct.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia is not the expected accompanying abnormality. B. Hyperphosphataemia is not typical. D. Vomiting more commonly causes chloride depletion. E. Hypernatraemia is not a characteristic consequence of potassium depletion.
pearl: Hypokalaemia that does not correct with potassium replacement should prompt a magnesium check, because hypomagnesaemia drives ongoing renal potassium loss.
thinking: Persistent vomiting ↓ Hypokalaemia ↓ Magnesium is often depleted alongside potassium ↓ Hypomagnesaemia
exam_trap: D, hyperchloraemia — vomiting does disturb chloride, but it causes chloride loss (hypochloraemia), not excess.
takeaway: Refractory hypokalaemia: check and replace magnesium.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is found to have a positive pregnancy test. She is unsure when her last menstrual period occurred. What is the most appropriate way to establish gestational age?
why_correct: Ultrasound provides an objective assessment of gestational age, particularly when the menstrual history is uncertain.
why_wrong: A. Cervical screening does not determine gestational age. B. Blood group provides no information about gestational age. C. Urinalysis does not date pregnancy. E. Progesterone does not accurately establish gestational age.
pearl: A first-trimester ultrasound measuring crown–rump length is the most accurate way to date a pregnancy and is routinely offered to all pregnant women.
thinking: Positive pregnancy test ↓ Uncertain last menstrual period ↓ Need an objective gestational age ↓ Ultrasound dating scan
exam_trap: E, serum progesterone alone — a pregnancy-related blood test, but it does not establish gestational age.
takeaway: Date pregnancies by ultrasound, especially when the LMP is uncertain.

stem: A pregnant woman attends for routine antenatal care. Which blood test is routinely performed early in pregnancy to determine her ABO and rhesus blood group?
correct_answer: D. Blood group and antibody screen
why_correct: Maternal blood grouping and antibody screening are part of routine antenatal assessment.
why_wrong: A. A full blood count and ferritin assess anaemia and iron stores, not blood group. B. Haemoglobin electrophoresis screens for haemoglobinopathies, not ABO or rhesus group. C. The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody bound to red cells and does not determine blood group. E. The Kleihauer–Betke test quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage, not maternal blood group.
pearl: All pregnant women have a blood group and antibody screen at booking and again later in pregnancy to identify RhD-negative women and red-cell antibodies that could cause fetal haemolysis.
thinking: Routine antenatal care ↓ Need ABO and RhD group ↓ Also screen for red-cell antibodies ↓ Blood group and antibody screen
exam_trap: C, direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — linked with haemolytic disease, but it detects antibody bound to red cells, usually the baby's; it does not give the maternal group.
takeaway: Booking bloods include a blood group and antibody screen.

stem: A woman is found to have anti-D antibodies during pregnancy. Why is this clinically important?

options.A: It indicates a raised risk of fetal neural tube defect
options.C: It predicts maternal thrombocytopenia later in pregnancy
options.D: It risks haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

correct_answer: D. It risks haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
why_correct: Maternal red-cell antibodies can cross the placenta and cause fetal or neonatal haemolysis.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D antibodies do not indicate a risk of neural tube defects. B. Anti-D antibodies do not diagnose iron deficiency. C. Anti-D antibodies target fetal red cells and do not predict maternal thrombocytopenia. E. Gestational diabetes is diagnosed using glucose testing.
pearl: Once maternal anti-D antibodies are present, prophylactic anti-D no longer helps; the pregnancy needs specialist fetal medicine monitoring for fetal anaemia.
thinking: Maternal anti-D antibodies ↓ IgG crosses the placenta ↓ Destroys RhD-positive fetal red cells ↓ Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
exam_trap: C, maternal thrombocytopenia — antibodies in pregnancy may suggest immune thrombocytopenia, but anti-D targets red cells and the fetus is at risk.
takeaway: Maternal anti-D antibodies threaten the fetus with haemolysis.

stem: A pregnant woman asks why folic acid is recommended before conception and during early pregnancy. What is the principal reason?

options.A: To prevent gestational hypertension in pregnancy
options.B: To reduce the risk of neural tube defects
options.D: To reduce the risk of fetal growth restriction

correct_answer: B. To reduce the risk of neural tube defects
why_correct: Adequate folic acid around conception reduces the risk of neural tube defects.
why_wrong: A. Folic acid is not primarily used to prevent gestational hypertension. C. Rhesus sensitisation is prevented with appropriate anti-D prophylaxis. D. Folic acid is not given principally to prevent fetal growth restriction. E. It does not prevent neonatal jaundice.
pearl: Folic acid is advised from before conception until 12 weeks to reduce neural tube defects; higher-risk women, such as those with a previous affected pregnancy, need a higher dose.
thinking: Pregnancy planned ↓ Neural tube closes in the first weeks ↓ Folate supports neural tube development ↓ Reduce the risk of neural tube defects
exam_trap: D, reduce fetal growth restriction — a plausible pregnancy benefit, but the established reason is neural tube defect prevention.
takeaway: Folic acid before conception prevents neural tube defects.

stem: A woman is taking a medication known to cause fetal harm and is planning pregnancy. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Arrange pre-conception medication review and advice
options.B: Continue unchanged and start folic acid 5 mg daily
options.D: Stop the medication as soon as she stops contraception
options.E: Defer discussion until the first antenatal booking visit

correct_answer: A. Arrange pre-conception medication review and advice
why_correct: Potentially teratogenic medicines should be reviewed before conception, balancing maternal treatment needs against fetal risk.
why_wrong: B. Folic acid does not address the teratogenic risk; the medicine itself needs review. C. Continuing a potentially harmful medicine without review is unsafe. D. Stopping without assessment may harm the mother by leaving her condition untreated. E. Booking occurs after organogenesis has begun, so review should happen before conception.
pearl: Women planning pregnancy on teratogenic drugs such as valproate need pre-conception specialist review, balancing maternal disease control against fetal risk; they should not stop abruptly without advice.
thinking: Teratogenic medication ↓ Planning pregnancy ↓ Organogenesis happens early, often before booking ↓ Pre-conception medication review and advice
exam_trap: D, stop the medication as soon as she stops contraception — seems cautious, but abrupt stopping can destabilise her condition; changes need planned specialist advice.
takeaway: Teratogenic drug and planning pregnancy: review before conception.

stem: A newborn has central cyanosis that does not improve adequately with oxygen. Which category of disease should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent central cyanosis in a newborn raises concern for significant congenital cardiac or pulmonary disease, particularly cyanotic congenital heart disease.
why_wrong: A. Jaundice does not cause central cyanosis. B. Transient tachypnoea usually responds to oxygen and does not cause refractory central cyanosis. C. Pyloric stenosis causes vomiting rather than cyanosis. E. Colic does not cause cyanosis.
pearl: Cyanosis from lung disease usually improves with oxygen, whereas cyanotic heart disease does not; suspected duct-dependent lesions need prostaglandin to keep the duct open and urgent cardiology input.
thinking: Newborn with central cyanosis ↓ Little improvement with oxygen ↓ Right-to-left shunt bypasses the lungs ↓ Cyanotic congenital heart disease
exam_trap: B, transient tachypnoea of the newborn — a common cause of neonatal respiratory distress, but its hypoxaemia responds to oxygen.
takeaway: Cyanosis that does not correct with oxygen suggests cyanotic heart disease.

stem: A child develops a barking cough and stridor. Which feature would make epiglottitis more likely than croup?

options.A: Gradual onset over several days with coryza
options.B: Barking, seal-like cough worse at night
options.E: Hoarse voice with a low-grade fever

why_correct: Drooling and marked dysphagia are concerning features of epiglottitis.
why_wrong: A. A gradual coryzal prodrome is typical of croup, whereas epiglottitis is usually abrupt. B. A barking cough worse at night is characteristic of croup. C. Stridor occurs in both conditions. E. Hoarseness with low-grade fever is typical of croup.
pearl: Epiglottitis presents with rapid onset, high fever, drooling and a toxic child sitting forward; do not examine the throat, keep the child calm and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help.
thinking: Child with barking cough and stridor ↓ Barking cough and stridor alone fit croup ↓ Drooling and difficulty swallowing suggest supraglottic swelling ↓ Epiglottitis more likely
exam_trap: B, barking, seal-like cough worse at night — echoes the stem, but it is the hallmark of croup, not epiglottitis.
takeaway: Drooling, dysphagia and toxicity point to epiglottitis, not croup.

stem: A 7-year-old child has recurrent abdominal pain associated with school-related stress. Growth, examination and investigations are normal. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Recurrent abdominal pain without red flags, with normal growth and examination and a clear functional context, is consistent with functional abdominal pain.
why_wrong: A. IBD may cause weight loss, diarrhoea or other inflammatory features. B. Appendicitis is usually an acute illness. C. Intussusception typically causes episodic severe abdominal pain and may cause vomiting or bloody stool. E. Obstruction causes vomiting, distension and other acute obstructive features.
pearl: Functional abdominal pain is common in school-age children; with normal growth, examination and no red flags, explain, reassure, address stressors and avoid unnecessary investigation.
thinking: Recurrent abdominal pain ↓ Linked to school stress ↓ Normal growth, examination and tests ↓ Functional abdominal pain
exam_trap: A, inflammatory bowel disease — causes recurrent pain in children, but expect weight loss, poor growth, bloody diarrhoea or abnormal tests.
takeaway: Recurrent pain with normal growth and no red flags is usually functional.

stem: A 10-year-old child has excessive thirst and frequent urination. Which initial test is particularly appropriate?
why_correct: Urinalysis can rapidly identify glycosuria, ketones and evidence of urinary infection in a child with polyuria and polydipsia.
why_wrong: A. Chest X-ray is not an appropriate initial investigation. B. Spirometry assesses lung function. C. Audiometry assesses hearing. E. ECG does not investigate polyuria.
pearl: Thirst and polyuria in a child should prompt same-day testing for type 1 diabetes, with glucose and ketones checked, and same-day specialist referral if diabetes is suspected.
thinking: Child with excessive thirst ↓ Frequent urination ↓ Suspect diabetes mellitus ↓ Urinalysis for glucose and ketones
exam_trap: E, ECG — sometimes reached for in an unwell child, but it does not address the cause of polyuria and polydipsia.
takeaway: Thirsty child passing lots of urine: test for diabetes the same day.

stem: A child with congenital adrenal hyperplasia develops acute vomiting, hypotension and severe weakness during an intercurrent illness. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Adrenal insufficiency can decompensate during illness, causing hypotension, vomiting and circulatory collapse.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary oedema causes respiratory distress rather than this characteristic endocrine presentation. C. Thyroid storm occurs with severe thyrotoxicosis. D. HHS occurs with severe hyperglycaemia and hyperosmolality. E. DKA is associated with insulin deficiency and hyperglycaemia.
pearl: Children with CAH need increased steroid doses during illness and an emergency hydrocortisone kit; adrenal crisis requires immediate IM or IV hydrocortisone and fluid resuscitation.
thinking: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia ↓ Cortisol deficiency ↓ Intercurrent illness raises demand ↓ Vomiting and hypotension: adrenal crisis
exam_trap: E, diabetic ketoacidosis — vomiting and collapse in an ill child tempt this, but nothing suggests diabetes; CAH predisposes to adrenal crisis.
takeaway: Steroid-dependent child collapsing during illness: give hydrocortisone.

stem: A 5-year-old child has recurrent infections, eczema and low platelet counts. Which primary immunodeficiency is classically associated with this combination?
why_correct: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome classically causes recurrent infections, eczema and thrombocytopenia.
why_wrong: A. DiGeorge syndrome causes T-cell deficiency with hypocalcaemia and cardiac defects, not eczema with thrombocytopenia. C. SCID causes severe early infections but not the classic eczema-thrombocytopenia combination. D. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia causes recurrent bacterial infections without eczema or thrombocytopenia. E. Hyper-IgE syndrome causes eczema and recurrent infections but not thrombocytopenia.
pearl: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked disorder causing the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets and recurrent infections.
thinking: Child with recurrent infections ↓ Eczema ↓ Low platelet counts ↓ Classic triad of an X-linked immunodeficiency ↓ Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome
exam_trap: E, hyper-IgE syndrome — also combines eczema with recurrent infections, but it does not cause thrombocytopenia.
takeaway: Eczema, thrombocytopenia and infections mean Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome.

stem: A child has recurrent bacterial infections and very low immunoglobulin levels. Which type of immune deficiency is primarily affected?
why_correct: Immunoglobulins are produced by B cells and are central to humoral immunity.
why_wrong: A. Platelet production occurs through megakaryocytes. C. Red-cell production occurs primarily in bone marrow. D. Clotting factors are separate from immunoglobulin-mediated immunity. E. Thyroid hormone synthesis is an endocrine process.
pearl: Recurrent bacterial infections, especially with encapsulated organisms, plus low immunoglobulins point to an antibody (humoral) deficiency such as X-linked agammaglobulinaemia.
thinking: Recurrent bacterial infections ↓ Very low immunoglobulins ↓ Immunoglobulins are made by B cells ↓ Humoral immunity
exam_trap: D, complement-independent clotting — sounds immunological, but clotting is not an immune function and does not explain low immunoglobulins.
takeaway: Low immunoglobulins mean a humoral (B-cell) immune deficiency.

stem: A child has recurrent severe infections with catalase-positive organisms. Which disorder should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic granulomatous disease causes impaired phagocyte oxidative killing and susceptibility to recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms.
why_wrong: A. Selective IgA deficiency is often asymptomatic or causes mucosal infections, not catalase-positive infections. B. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia causes recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections from antibody deficiency. C. Leucocyte adhesion deficiency impairs neutrophil migration, with delayed cord separation and pus-free infections, rather than a specific catalase-positive pattern. D. Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infection.
pearl: Chronic granulomatous disease is an NADPH oxidase defect: phagocytes cannot mount a respiratory burst, so catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus cause recurrent abscesses.
thinking: Recurrent severe infections in a child ↓ Organisms are catalase-positive ↓ Points to failed phagocyte oxidative killing ↓ Chronic granulomatous disease
exam_trap: C, leucocyte adhesion deficiency — also a phagocyte disorder, but it causes delayed cord separation and pus-free infections, not a catalase-positive pattern.
takeaway: Catalase-positive infections in a child = phagocyte oxidative burst defect = CGD.

stem: A 3-year-old child has developmental delay, recurrent chest infections and characteristic coarse facial features. Which investigation is most appropriate when an inherited metabolic disorder is suspected?

options.A: Specialist metabolic assessment and targeted testing
options.B: Sweat chloride testing to exclude suspected cystic fibrosis
options.C: Chest X-ray and sputum culture for the recurrent infections
options.D: Serum immunoglobulins and specific vaccine antibody levels
options.E: Hearing assessment and community paediatric developmental review

correct_answer: A. Specialist metabolic assessment and targeted testing
why_correct: Suspected inherited metabolic disease requires appropriate specialist assessment followed by targeted biochemical and/or genetic investigation.
why_wrong: B. A sweat test assesses cystic fibrosis, which does not cause coarse facial features. C. Chest imaging and sputum culture address the infections but not the suspected metabolic disorder. D. Immunodeficiency screening does not investigate a suspected inherited metabolic disorder. E. Hearing assessment and developmental review do not establish a metabolic diagnosis.
pearl: Developmental delay with coarse facial features and recurrent chest infections suggests a storage disorder such as a mucopolysaccharidosis; diagnosis rests on specialist metabolic input with targeted tests.
thinking: Developmental delay plus coarse facial features ↓ Suggests an inherited metabolic (storage) disorder ↓ Infections are a feature, not the diagnosis ↓ Specialist metabolic assessment and targeted testing
exam_trap: C, chest X-ray and sputum culture — tempting because infections recur, but it addresses the symptom and leaves the suspected metabolic disorder uninvestigated.
takeaway: Coarse facies with developmental delay: think metabolic and refer for specialist targeted testing.

stem: A patient with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anaemia with a low reticulocyte count after a febrile illness. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Parvovirus B19 can temporarily suppress erythropoiesis, causing an aplastic crisis with severe anaemia and a low reticulocyte count.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency develops more gradually and does not characteristically cause an abrupt reticulocyte fall. B. Vaso-occlusive crisis causes pain rather than isolated severe reticulocytopenic anaemia. C. Splenic sequestration causes acute anaemia with splenic enlargement and is a different mechanism. E. Acute chest syndrome involves new pulmonary symptoms and infiltrates.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 halts red-cell production; in sickle cell disease, where red-cell survival is short, this causes an abrupt fall in haemoglobin with reticulocytopenia that may need transfusion.
thinking: Sickle cell disease ↓ Sudden severe anaemia after a febrile illness ↓ Low reticulocytes, so the marrow is not responding ↓ Aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19)
exam_trap: C, splenic sequestration — also causes sudden severe anaemia, but the marrow keeps responding, so reticulocytes are high and the spleen enlarges.
takeaway: Sickle cell with acute anaemia: low reticulocytes = aplastic crisis; high = sequestration or haemolysis.

stem: A patient taking an ACE inhibitor develops persistent dry cough. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: ACE inhibition reduces bradykinin breakdown, contributing to the characteristic dry cough.
why_wrong: A. Insulin secretion is unrelated. B. ACE inhibitors generally reduce aldosterone production. C. Histamine deficiency does not explain ACE-inhibitor cough. D. Dopamine depletion is not involved.
pearl: ACE inhibitor cough is dry and persistent; if it is troublesome, switch to an angiotensin II receptor blocker, which does not cause bradykinin accumulation.
thinking: ACE inhibitor started ↓ Persistent dry cough ↓ ACE also breaks down bradykinin ↓ Bradykinin accumulates in the airways ↓ Bradykinin accumulation
exam_trap: C, histamine deficiency — tempting because histamine is linked with airway symptoms, but ACE inhibitors do not deplete histamine; the cause is unbroken-down bradykinin.
takeaway: ACE inhibitor dry cough = bradykinin accumulation; switch to an ARB.

stem: A patient develops wheeze and hypotension shortly after receiving intravenous penicillin. Which mechanism best explains the reaction?
why_correct: Rapid-onset anaphylaxis following drug exposure is commonly mediated by IgE-dependent mast-cell activation.
