why_wrong: A. Immune-complex reactions such as serum sickness develop over days, not minutes. C. Bacterial infection does not explain the immediate drug-associated reaction. D. Type IV reactions are delayed, typically occurring days after exposure. E. Vitamin deficiency is irrelevant.
pearl: Wheeze and hypotension within minutes of a drug is anaphylaxis, an IgE-mediated type I reaction; stop the drug, give IM adrenaline and document the allergy clearly.
thinking: IV penicillin given ↓ Wheeze and hypotension shortly afterwards ↓ Immediate onset means mast-cell degranulation ↓ IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity
exam_trap: D, type IV T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity — tempting because many drug allergies are type IV, but these are delayed by days and do not cause immediate collapse.
takeaway: Minutes after exposure = type I IgE; days later = type III or IV.

stem: A patient is prescribed methotrexate for an inflammatory condition. Which dosing schedule is characteristic of methotrexate for many rheumatological indications?
why_correct: Methotrexate for many inflammatory diseases is administered once weekly; accidental daily dosing can cause serious toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Twice-daily dosing is inappropriate. B. Hourly dosing would be dangerously excessive. C. Methotrexate is not administered every five years. E. It is a disease-modifying treatment, not an as-required analgesic.
pearl: Methotrexate for inflammatory disease is taken once weekly on a fixed day, with folic acid on a different day; accidental daily dosing can cause fatal bone marrow suppression.
thinking: Methotrexate for an inflammatory condition ↓ Low-dose DMARD regimen ↓ Daily dosing causes serious toxicity ↓ Once weekly
exam_trap: A, twice daily indefinitely — tempting because most regular tablets are taken daily, but daily methotrexate is a recognised cause of fatal prescribing errors.
takeaway: Methotrexate for inflammatory disease: once weekly, never daily.

stem: A patient taking an NSAID develops epigastric pain and melaena. Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: NSAIDs can damage the gastric or duodenal mucosa and cause ulceration and bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back but not melaena. B. Biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant pain without gastrointestinal bleeding. C. A Mallory–Weiss tear follows forceful retching and typically presents with haematemesis. E. Acute cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain and fever, not melaena.
pearl: NSAIDs inhibit protective mucosal prostaglandins; melaena signals upper GI bleeding, so resuscitate, assess risk, stop the NSAID and arrange endoscopy.
thinking: NSAID use ↓ Epigastric pain ↓ Melaena indicates upper GI bleeding ↓ Bleeding peptic ulcer
exam_trap: C, Mallory–Weiss tear — also an upper GI bleed, but it follows forceful retching and typically presents with haematemesis rather than NSAID-related melaena.
takeaway: NSAID plus epigastric pain plus melaena = bleeding peptic ulcer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease is started on donepezil and develops marked diarrhoea. Which mechanism best explains this adverse effect?

options.A: Stimulation of opioid receptors in the gut
options.B: Increased cholinergic stimulation of the gut
options.E: Blockade of muscarinic receptors in the gut

correct_answer: B. Increased cholinergic stimulation of the gut
why_correct: Donepezil is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; raised acetylcholine increases muscarinic stimulation of gut smooth muscle and secretions, increasing motility and causing diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting.
why_wrong: A. Opioid receptor stimulation slows gut transit and causes constipation. C. Prostaglandin inhibition is the action of NSAIDs and is linked to gastric mucosal injury rather than this effect. D. D2 blockade is the mechanism of antiemetics and antipsychotics and does not explain donepezil-induced diarrhoea. E. Muscarinic blockade (anticholinergic effect) reduces gut motility and causes constipation, not diarrhoea.
pearl: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil cause cholinergic effects, notably diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting and bradycardia; watch for bradycardia and syncope during treatment.
thinking: Donepezil started ↓ Acetylcholinesterase inhibited ↓ More acetylcholine at gut muscarinic receptors ↓ Increased motility and secretion ↓ Increased cholinergic stimulation
exam_trap: E, blockade of muscarinic receptors — the right receptor in the wrong direction: anticholinergic blockade slows the gut and causes constipation.
takeaway: Donepezil raises acetylcholine: expect diarrhoea, nausea and bradycardia.

stem: A patient is prescribed an antibiotic for a confirmed bacterial infection. After several days, they develop frequent watery diarrhoea and abdominal cramping. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Antibiotic exposure followed by significant diarrhoea is a classic setting for C. difficile infection.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes focal abdominal pain rather than this typical diarrhoeal illness. B. Post-infectious IBS follows gastroenteritis and causes chronic symptoms, not acute watery diarrhoea after recent antibiotics. C. Secondary lactose intolerance follows gut mucosal injury and produces symptoms after lactose ingestion, not after antibiotics. E. SIBO causes chronic bloating and diarrhoea and is treated, rather than typically triggered, by antibiotics.
pearl: New diarrhoea after recent antibiotics should prompt stool testing for C. difficile toxin, isolation of the patient and review or stopping of the causative antibiotic.
thinking: Recent antibiotic course ↓ Days later, frequent watery diarrhoea and cramps ↓ Disrupted gut flora allows toxin-producing overgrowth ↓ C. difficile infection
exam_trap: C, secondary lactose intolerance — tempting as diarrhoea can follow gut upset, but it follows mucosal injury and relates to lactose intake, not antibiotics.
takeaway: New diarrhoea after antibiotics: test for C. difficile and isolate.

stem: A patient with suspected C. difficile infection asks why unnecessary antibiotics should be avoided. What is the main reason?

options.B: Antibiotics directly cause inflammatory bowel disease in every patient
options.C: Antibiotics can disrupt normal gut flora and promote C. difficile overgrowth
options.E: Antibiotics permanently eliminate all intestinal bacteria

correct_answer: C. Antibiotics can disrupt normal gut flora and promote C. difficile overgrowth
why_correct: Antibiotic exposure can disrupt protective intestinal microbiota, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not cause appendicitis. B. They do not invariably cause inflammatory bowel disease. D. Antibiotics can themselves cause diarrhoea. E. They do not permanently eliminate all intestinal bacteria.
pearl: Antibiotic stewardship is central to C. difficile prevention; broad-spectrum agents such as clindamycin, cephalosporins and quinolones carry particular risk.
thinking: Normal gut flora resists C. difficile ↓ Antibiotics disrupt this protective microbiota ↓ C. difficile proliferates and produces toxin ↓ Antibiotics can disrupt normal gut flora and promote C. difficile overgrowth
exam_trap: E, antibiotics permanently eliminate all intestinal bacteria — close to the truth but overstated: the flora is disrupted, not permanently wiped out.
takeaway: Antibiotics disrupt protective gut flora; stewardship prevents C. difficile.

stem: A patient develops fever, diarrhoea and abdominal pain after returning from overseas travel. Several other travellers developed similar symptoms. What is the most likely broad category of illness?
why_correct: Acute diarrhoea with fever following travel and clustering among travellers strongly suggests infectious gastroenteritis.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis causes chronic joint symptoms. B. IBD does not cause an acute illness clustering among fellow travellers. C. Acute glaucoma causes painful visual symptoms. D. Migraine does not cause this gastrointestinal outbreak pattern.
pearl: Fever and diarrhoea clustering among fellow travellers points to a shared infectious source; send stool samples and involve public health when an outbreak is suspected.
thinking: Acute fever and diarrhoea ↓ Onset after overseas travel ↓ Several fellow travellers similarly affected ↓ Infectious gastroenteritis
exam_trap: B, inflammatory bowel disease — the only other bowel diagnosis offered, but IBD does not start acutely in a cluster of fellow travellers.
takeaway: Acute diarrhoea clustering in a group = shared infectious source.

stem: A traveller develops profuse watery diarrhoea without blood or significant fever after visiting an area with limited access to clean water. Which organism is classically associated with this presentation?
why_correct: Cholera classically causes profuse watery diarrhoea with substantial fluid loss.
why_wrong: A. Syphilis causes sexually transmitted infection with characteristic clinical stages. B. Meningococcus causes invasive meningococcal disease. C. Falciparum malaria causes febrile systemic illness. E. TB causes chronic infection rather than profuse acute watery diarrhoea.
pearl: Cholera causes profuse rice-water diarrhoea with little fever; the danger is rapid dehydration, so oral or intravenous rehydration is the cornerstone of treatment.
thinking: Travel to an area with poor clean water ↓ Profuse watery diarrhoea ↓ No blood and little fever, so toxin-mediated, not invasive ↓ Vibrio cholerae
exam_trap: C, Plasmodium falciparum — the reflex answer for any unwell traveller, but malaria is a febrile systemic illness, not afebrile profuse watery diarrhoea.
takeaway: Profuse afebrile rice-water diarrhoea after poor water exposure = cholera; rehydrate.

stem: A patient develops bloody diarrhoea after eating undercooked minced beef. Which complication is particularly associated with some Shiga toxin-producing strains of E. coli?
why_correct: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli can cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome, particularly in children.
why_wrong: A. Guillain–Barré syndrome is classically associated with Campylobacter rather than STEC. B. Reactive arthritis follows Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia rather than being the characteristic STEC complication. D. Toxic shock syndrome is caused by staphylococcal or streptococcal toxins. E. Acute glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency.
pearl: In suspected Shiga toxin-producing E. coli such as O157, antibiotics and antimotility drugs are generally avoided, and blood count and renal function are monitored for HUS, especially in children.
thinking: Undercooked minced beef ↓ Bloody diarrhoea ↓ Shiga toxin-producing E. coli ↓ Toxin damages endothelium, notably in the kidney ↓ Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
exam_trap: A, Guillain–Barré syndrome — a famous post-diarrhoeal complication, but its classic trigger is Campylobacter, not Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea after undercooked beef: watch for haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

stem: A child develops bloody diarrhoea after a suspected Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection. Which combination suggests haemolytic uraemic syndrome?

options.C: Anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury

correct_answer: C. Anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
why_correct: HUS is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury.
why_wrong: A. This combination does not indicate HUS. B. These findings are not the characteristic triad. D. This does not represent HUS. E. These findings are unrelated to HUS.
pearl: HUS is a thrombotic microangiopathy: fragmented red cells on the blood film, low platelets and rising creatinine; some children need dialysis, so monitor counts and renal function closely.
thinking: Recent STEC bloody diarrhoea ↓ Toxin injures endothelium, especially in the kidney ↓ Red-cell fragmentation, platelet consumption and renal damage ↓ Anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI
exam_trap: A, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia and asthma — hyperkalaemia can accompany AKI, but this set misses the haemolytic anaemia and low platelets that define HUS.
takeaway: HUS triad: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury.

stem: A traveller returns from sub-Saharan Africa with fever, rigors and confusion. Which diagnosis must be urgently considered?
why_correct: Fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area, particularly with neurological features, requires urgent assessment for potentially severe falciparum malaria.
why_wrong: B. Labyrinthitis causes vertigo, not fever, rigors and confusion. C. Hay fever does not cause fever and confusion. D. Tension-type headache does not cause fever and confusion. E. An osteoarthritis flare is not an acute febrile illness.
pearl: Fever after travel to a malaria area is malaria until proven otherwise; confusion suggests severe falciparum malaria needing same-day blood films and urgent intravenous artesunate.
thinking: Returned from sub-Saharan Africa ↓ Fever and rigors ↓ Confusion suggests cerebral involvement ↓ Severe falciparum malaria
exam_trap: B, viral labyrinthitis — the only other option with a neurological flavour, but it causes vertigo, not fever, rigors and confusion.
takeaway: Fever plus confusion after African travel = severe falciparum malaria until excluded.

stem: A patient develops fever after returning from a malaria-endemic region. Which part of the history is particularly important?
correct_answer: D. Exact travel destinations and dates
why_correct: Malaria risk varies geographically and according to timing of travel, so destination and travel dates are important.
why_wrong: A. Hair colour is irrelevant. B. Hand dominance does not affect malaria risk. C. Shoe size is irrelevant. E. Handwriting preference is irrelevant.
pearl: A travel history should cover exact destinations, dates, prophylaxis and adherence; falciparum usually presents within weeks of return, but other species can appear months later.
thinking: Fever after malaria-endemic travel ↓ Risk depends on where and when ↓ Timing defines the incubation window ↓ Exact destinations and dates
exam_trap: B, dominant hand — distractors like this test discipline; hand dominance has no bearing on malaria risk, which depends on geography and timing.
takeaway: Febrile traveller: document where, when and whether prophylaxis was taken.

stem: A patient has fever, headache and myalgia after returning from an area where dengue is prevalent. Which medication should generally be avoided until a bleeding risk has been considered?
why_correct: Dengue can cause thrombocytopenia and bleeding, so aspirin and other NSAIDs may increase bleeding risk.
why_wrong: A. Appropriate antiemetic treatment can be used when clinically indicated. B. Paracetamol can be used appropriately for symptomatic treatment, subject to normal precautions. C. Maintaining hydration is important. D. Oral rehydration is supportive treatment.
pearl: Dengue can cause thrombocytopenia and plasma leakage; manage symptoms with paracetamol and fluids, and avoid aspirin and NSAIDs until bleeding risk is clear.
thinking: Fever, headache and myalgia after dengue-area travel ↓ Dengue can cause low platelets and bleeding ↓ Antiplatelet effect would add to this ↓ Avoid aspirin
exam_trap: B, paracetamol — tempting if all analgesics seem risky, but paracetamol is the preferred antipyretic in dengue; it is aspirin and NSAIDs that are avoided.
takeaway: Suspected dengue: paracetamol yes, aspirin and NSAIDs no.

stem: A patient develops fever, headache and a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash. What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Wait for the rash to disappear
options.E: Reassure the patient that the rash is viral

correct_answer: D. Treat suspected meningococcal disease urgently
why_correct: A rapidly progressive febrile illness with a non-blanching rash is a medical emergency because meningococcal disease can deteriorate rapidly.
why_wrong: A. Waiting risks dangerous delay. B. Topical treatment does not address invasive infection. C. Routine dermatology review is inappropriate for a potentially life-threatening infection. E. The presentation cannot safely be assumed to be benign viral illness.
pearl: Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; in the community give IM or IV benzylpenicillin if it will not delay transfer, and admit urgently.
thinking: Fever and headache ↓ Rapidly spreading non-blanching rash ↓ Suggests meningococcal septicaemia ↓ Treat urgently without waiting
exam_trap: E, reassure that the rash is viral — viral illnesses can cause petechiae, but a spreading non-blanching rash with fever cannot safely be assumed benign.
takeaway: Fever plus non-blanching rash: treat as meningococcal now, investigate after.

stem: A patient with suspected bacterial meningitis has already received appropriate empiric antibiotics. Why should treatment not be unnecessarily delayed while waiting for diagnostic investigations?

options.A: Antibiotics prevent all diagnostic information from being obtained
options.B: Antibiotics become ineffective after lumbar puncture
options.C: Delay can increase the risk of serious complications and death
options.D: CSF testing cannot be performed after antibiotics

correct_answer: C. Delay can increase the risk of serious complications and death
why_correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires prompt treatment; diagnostic procedures should not cause an unsafe delay in antibiotics.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics can affect culture yield but do not eliminate all diagnostic information. B. Lumbar puncture does not make antibiotics ineffective. D. CSF may still provide useful diagnostic information after treatment. E. Bacterial meningitis can be rapidly life-threatening.
pearl: In suspected bacterial meningitis, antibiotics must not wait for lumbar puncture or imaging; blood cultures and CSF, including PCR, can still be informative after treatment starts.
thinking: Suspected bacterial meningitis ↓ Can deteriorate within hours ↓ Delay raises risk of death and complications ↓ Treat promptly; investigations follow
exam_trap: D, CSF testing cannot be performed after antibiotics — tempting because culture yield falls, but CSF still gives useful cell counts, biochemistry and PCR.
takeaway: Never delay antibiotics in suspected meningitis for investigations.

stem: A patient is being assessed for suspected tuberculosis. Which symptom combination is particularly suggestive of pulmonary TB?

options.A: Persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats
options.B: Acute productive cough, fever and pleuritic pain
options.C: Episodic wheeze, nocturnal cough and chest tightness

correct_answer: A. Persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats
why_correct: Persistent cough with constitutional symptoms such as weight loss and night sweats is a classic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis.
why_wrong: B. Acute cough with fever and pleuritic pain suggests community-acquired pneumonia. C. Episodic wheeze with nocturnal cough and chest tightness suggests asthma. D. Dysuria and frequency suggest urinary tract pathology. E. Sudden monocular visual loss suggests an acute ophthalmic disorder.
pearl: Pulmonary TB typically causes a prolonged cough with weight loss, night sweats, fever or haemoptysis; obtain a chest X-ray and send sputum for microscopy and culture.
thinking: Cough is persistent, not acute ↓ Constitutional features: weight loss and night sweats ↓ Chronic infection pattern ↓ Pulmonary tuberculosis
exam_trap: B, acute productive cough, fever and pleuritic pain — infective and respiratory, but the acute course fits community-acquired pneumonia rather than TB.
takeaway: Persistent cough plus weight loss and night sweats: think TB.

stem: A patient has a macrocytic anaemia. Which additional feature would point to vitamin B12 deficiency rather than folate deficiency?
why_correct: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause neurological disease (peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord, with loss of vibration and proprioception), whereas folate deficiency does not typically cause this neurological syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Macrocytosis occurs in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it does not discriminate. B. Mildly raised bilirubin from ineffective erythropoiesis occurs with either deficiency. C. Both deficiencies cause megaloblastic anaemia. D. Fatigue is a non-specific feature of anaemia from either cause.
pearl: B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord; never give folic acid alone in megaloblastic anaemia until B12 deficiency is excluded or treated.
thinking: Macrocytic anaemia ↓ B12 and folate deficiency share the blood picture ↓ Only B12 deficiency damages myelin ↓ Neurological symptoms point to B12
exam_trap: B, raised serum bilirubin — tempting as a sign of ineffective erythropoiesis, but it occurs in folate deficiency too and does not discriminate.
takeaway: Macrocytosis plus neurological signs = B12; replace B12 before folate.

stem: A 72-year-old man has iron-deficiency anaemia without an obvious dietary explanation. What should be considered particularly important in the investigation of an older adult?
why_correct: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult requires assessment for potential gastrointestinal blood loss, including malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Thalassaemia trait causes microcytosis without iron deficiency. C. Anaemia of chronic kidney disease is a different pattern and does not explain true iron deficiency. D. Autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) can impair iron absorption, but in an older adult gastrointestinal blood loss, including malignancy, must be excluded first. E. Sideroblastic anaemia is a disorder of iron utilisation rather than iron deficiency.
pearl: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult needs upper and lower GI investigation for occult blood loss, including gastric and colorectal cancer, plus coeliac serology.
thinking: Iron-deficiency anaemia ↓ No dietary explanation ↓ Older adult, so occult malignancy is a real risk ↓ Look for gastrointestinal blood loss
exam_trap: D, pernicious anaemia — autoimmune gastritis can impair iron absorption, but GI blood loss, including cancer, is the priority to exclude in an older adult.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older adult: investigate the GI tract.

stem: A woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and develops microcytic anaemia. Which laboratory finding is most consistent with iron deficiency?
why_correct: Low ferritin indicates depleted iron stores and is characteristic of iron deficiency.
why_wrong: B. Ferritin is generally reduced in uncomplicated iron deficiency. C. Vitamin B12 does not assess iron stores. D. Calcium is unrelated to iron stores. E. Folate does not assess iron stores.
pearl: Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency, but ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so a normal or raised level can mask iron deficiency when inflammation is present.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding ↓ Chronic blood loss depletes iron ↓ Microcytic anaemia ↓ Iron stores are reflected by ferritin ↓ Low ferritin
exam_trap: B, high ferritin — tempting if ferritin is confused with transferrin or iron-binding capacity, which rise in iron deficiency; ferritin itself falls.
takeaway: Low ferritin = depleted iron stores; inflammation can falsely normalise it.

stem: A patient develops petechiae and easy bruising. Blood tests show an isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise normal blood counts. Which diagnosis is a possible cause?
why_correct: Immune thrombocytopenia typically causes isolated thrombocytopenia and may present with petechiae or mucosal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency primarily causes anaemia. B. Hyperthyroidism does not characteristically cause isolated severe thrombocytopenia. C. Polycythaemia is an increased red-cell disorder. E. Osteoarthritis does not cause thrombocytopenia.
pearl: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion: isolated thrombocytopenia with otherwise normal counts; a blood film is essential to exclude clumping artefact and marrow disease.
thinking: Petechiae and easy bruising ↓ Platelets low ↓ Other counts normal, so the marrow is likely working ↓ Immune platelet destruction: ITP
exam_trap: A, iron-deficiency anaemia alone — a common blood disorder, but it causes anaemia, which is absent here, and does not cause isolated thrombocytopenia.
takeaway: Isolated low platelets with bruising and petechiae: think ITP and check a film.

stem: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis develops jaundice and splenomegaly. What type of anaemia is present?

options.C: Anaemia of acute blood loss only

why_correct: Hereditary spherocytosis causes premature destruction of abnormal red blood cells, producing haemolytic anaemia.
why_wrong: A. Megaloblastic anaemia results from impaired DNA synthesis. C. The process is chronic red-cell destruction rather than acute external blood loss. D. Aplastic anaemia involves bone-marrow failure. E. Iron deficiency is caused by inadequate iron availability or loss.
pearl: Hereditary spherocytosis is usually autosomal dominant: rigid spherocytes are destroyed in the spleen, causing anaemia, jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones.
thinking: Hereditary spherocytosis ↓ Abnormal rigid red-cell membrane ↓ Cells destroyed early in the spleen ↓ Jaundice and splenomegaly ↓ Haemolytic anaemia
exam_trap: D, aplastic anaemia — spherocytosis can have parvovirus-triggered aplastic crises, but jaundice with splenomegaly reflects haemolysis, not marrow failure.
takeaway: Spherocytes, jaundice and splenomegaly = haemolytic anaemia.

stem: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis has recurrent episodes of jaundice. Which blood-test pattern supports haemolysis?

options.A: Raised conjugated bilirubin and raised ALP
options.B: Raised ferritin and low reticulocyte count
options.C: Raised bilirubin and LDH with low haptoglobin

correct_answer: C. Raised bilirubin and LDH with low haptoglobin
why_correct: Haemolysis typically produces increased unconjugated bilirubin and LDH with consumption of haptoglobin.
why_wrong: A. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with raised ALP suggests cholestasis rather than haemolysis. B. Raised ferritin and a low reticulocyte count do not indicate haemolysis. D. This is not the typical haemolysis pattern. E. In haemolysis haptoglobin is consumed (low) and reticulocytes usually rise.
pearl: A haemolysis screen shows raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH, low haptoglobin and raised reticulocytes; a blood film and direct antiglobulin test help find the cause.
thinking: Recurrent jaundice in hereditary spherocytosis ↓ Red-cell breakdown releases haemoglobin and LDH ↓ Free haemoglobin binds and depletes haptoglobin ↓ Raised bilirubin and LDH, low haptoglobin
exam_trap: A, raised conjugated bilirubin and ALP — tempting as a jaundice pattern, but it signals cholestasis; haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin.
takeaway: Haemolysis: bilirubin and LDH up, haptoglobin down, reticulocytes up.

stem: A patient develops dark urine and jaundice several days after receiving a blood transfusion. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Haemolysis following transfusion can cause jaundice and dark urine and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. TACO causes breathlessness and fluid overload, not jaundice and dark urine. B. Febrile non-haemolytic reactions cause fever during transfusion without haemolysis. D. Hepatitis B has an incubation period of weeks to months, so jaundice after several days is not explained. E. TRALI causes acute respiratory distress within hours of transfusion.
pearl: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions appear days later as red-cell antibodies re-emerge; check a direct antiglobulin test, haemolysis screen and repeat antibody screen, and inform the transfusion lab.
thinking: Recent blood transfusion ↓ Dark urine and jaundice ↓ Onset several days later ↓ Antibody-mediated red-cell destruction ↓ Haemolytic transfusion reaction
exam_trap: D, transfusion-transmitted hepatitis B — tempting because jaundice follows transfusion, but its incubation is weeks to months, not days.
takeaway: Jaundice and dark urine days after transfusion = delayed haemolytic reaction.

stem: A patient with lymphoma has painless enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Which feature is particularly concerning for malignancy?

options.C: A lymph node that disappears within 24 hours
options.D: Mild transient tenderness during a common cold

why_correct: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy warrants assessment for serious causes, including malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Headache alone does not indicate lymph-node pathology. C. Rapid resolution is less concerning for malignancy. D. Tender lymphadenopathy during an acute infection is commonly reactive. E. A bruise does not represent lymphadenopathy.
pearl: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy, especially painless, firm or enlarging nodes or nodes with B symptoms, warrants prompt assessment for lymphoma or other malignancy.
thinking: Painless enlarged cervical nodes ↓ Reactive nodes are tender and settle with infection ↓ Persistence without a cause is the warning feature ↓ Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy
exam_trap: D, mild transient tenderness during a common cold — it involves the nodes, but tender nodes that settle with infection are typically reactive and reassuring.
takeaway: Lymph nodes that persist without a cause need investigation for malignancy.

stem: A patient with lymphoma develops painless generalised lymphadenopathy. Which additional symptom is classically described as a B symptom?
why_correct: B symptoms include unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and significant unexplained weight loss.
why_wrong: A. Earwax is unrelated. B. Hiccups are not a B symptom. D. Sneezing is not a lymphoma B symptom. E. Mild thirst is nonspecific.
pearl: B symptoms are unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and significant weight loss; they reflect systemic disease and inform lymphoma staging and prognosis.
thinking: Painless generalised lymphadenopathy ↓ Lymphoma ↓ B symptoms are fever, night sweats and weight loss ↓ Drenching night sweats
exam_trap: E, mild thirst — tempting as a vague systemic symptom, but it is non-specific and not one of the defined B symptoms.
takeaway: B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss.

stem: A patient has a persistently enlarged lymph node. Which finding is generally more concerning for lymphoma than a tender node associated with an acute infection?

options.A: Recent minor trauma to the area

why_correct: Persistent, painless lymphadenopathy is a recognised presentation of lymphoma and warrants appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Minor trauma does not by itself indicate lymphoma. B. Rapid resolution is reassuring. C. Tender nodes can occur with acute infection. D. Local skin infection can cause reactive lymphadenopathy.
pearl: Reactive nodes are usually tender, follow an infection and settle; painless, persistent or enlarging nodes, particularly if hard or matted, need assessment for lymphoma.
thinking: Persistently enlarged node ↓ Infective nodes are tender and transient ↓ Painless persistence suggests infiltration ↓ Painless persistent enlargement
exam_trap: C, tenderness during a sore throat — tenderness feels worrying, but tender nodes with an acute infection are usually reactive and benign.
takeaway: Painless and persistent is more sinister than tender and transient.

stem: A patient presents with recurrent infections and a low white-cell count. Which blood cell type is particularly important in protecting against many bacterial infections?
why_correct: Neutrophils are an important component of innate immune defence against bacterial and fungal infections.
why_wrong: A. Osteoblasts form bone. B. Erythrocytes are another name for red blood cells. C. Platelets are mainly involved in haemostasis. E. Red blood cells primarily transport oxygen.
pearl: Neutrophils are the front line against bacterial and fungal infection; neutropenic patients may show few signs of infection, so fever alone must be taken seriously.
thinking: Recurrent infections ↓ Low white-cell count ↓ Innate bacterial defence relies on phagocytes ↓ Neutrophils
exam_trap: C, platelets — part of the full blood count, but their role is haemostasis; low platelets cause bleeding, not recurrent bacterial infection.
takeaway: Neutrophils defend against bacteria and fungi; neutropenia means infection risk.

stem: A patient has a white-cell count of 1.0 × 10⁹/L with a neutrophil count of 0.3 × 10⁹/L. What is the principal concern?

options.A: Increased bleeding risk from a low platelet count
options.B: Secondary iron overload from previous transfusions
options.D: Severe neutropenia with high infection risk

correct_answer: D. Severe neutropenia with high infection risk
why_correct: A very low neutrophil count substantially increases susceptibility to serious infection.
why_wrong: A. No platelet count is given, so bleeding risk is not the concern shown. B. Iron overload is unrelated to the neutrophil count. C. The result concerns neutrophils, not platelet production. E. The result concerns white cells; haemoglobin is not reported.
pearl: Severe neutropenia carries a high risk of rapidly progressive sepsis; fever in a neutropenic patient is an emergency needing immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics without waiting for results.
thinking: Very low white-cell count ↓ Neutrophils markedly reduced ↓ Innate bacterial defence is lost ↓ Severe neutropenia with high infection risk
exam_trap: A, increased bleeding risk — tempting because low counts often coexist, but no platelet count is given; the result shown concerns neutrophils.
takeaway: Neutropenia plus fever = neutropenic sepsis; treat immediately.

stem: A patient develops severe back pain after lifting a heavy object. There is no neurological deficit and no red-flag symptom. What is an appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine
options.B: Start gabapentin and review in 2 weeks
options.C: Prolonged complete bed rest for several weeks
options.D: Advise staying active with suitable analgesia

correct_answer: D. Advise staying active with suitable analgesia
why_correct: Most uncomplicated acute low back pain is managed conservatively, with advice to remain active and appropriate analgesia.
why_wrong: A. Imaging is not indicated for acute back pain without red flags or neurological deficit. B. Gabapentinoids are not recommended for managing low back pain. C. Prolonged bed rest is not recommended. E. Spinal injections are not recommended for non-specific low back pain.
pearl: Acute non-specific low back pain usually settles within weeks; advise staying active, use simple analgesia such as an NSAID if suitable, and avoid imaging without red flags.
thinking: Back pain after lifting ↓ No neurological deficit ↓ No red flags ↓ Non-specific mechanical low back pain ↓ Stay active with suitable analgesia
exam_trap: A, urgent MRI of the lumbar spine — feels thorough, but imaging without red flags or neurological deficit does not change management and is not recommended.
takeaway: Non-specific back pain without red flags: stay active, analgesia, no imaging.

stem: A patient has chronic low back pain and is found to have osteoporosis. Which symptom would particularly raise concern for a vertebral compression fracture?

options.A: Gradual morning stiffness easing with exercise
options.B: Pain radiating below the knee with paraesthesia
options.C: Sudden severe back pain after minor trauma
options.D: Chronic aching worse after prolonged standing

correct_answer: C. Sudden severe back pain after minor trauma
why_correct: Osteoporosis increases fracture risk, and vertebral compression fractures may occur after relatively minor trauma.
why_wrong: A. Morning stiffness easing with exercise suggests inflammatory back pain. B. Radiating pain below the knee with paraesthesia suggests nerve root irritation. D. Chronic aching with prolonged standing suggests mechanical back pain. E. Relief on sitting forward suggests lumbar spinal stenosis.
pearl: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures can follow trivial trauma, or none, causing sudden severe localised back pain; they may also be silent, presenting as height loss or kyphosis.
thinking: Known osteoporosis ↓ Fragile vertebrae ↓ Sudden severe pain after minor trauma ↓ Vertebral compression fracture
exam_trap: B, pain radiating below the knee with paraesthesia — sounds serious, but it suggests nerve root irritation, not a vertebral compression fracture.
takeaway: Osteoporosis plus sudden back pain after minor trauma = vertebral fracture.

stem: A 78-year-old patient falls and sustains a hip fracture. Which complication is particularly important to prevent during hospital admission?
why_correct: Hip fracture and immobility substantially increase VTE risk, so appropriate thromboprophylaxis and mobilisation are important.
why_wrong: B. Hypercalcaemia is not a typical complication of hip fracture admission. C. Myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossification) is not a key preventable complication during admission for hip fracture. D. Acute gout is not a characteristic complication of hip fracture. E. Compartment syndrome is not a typical complication of hip fracture.
pearl: Hip fracture combines trauma, surgery and immobility, so assess VTE risk and give thromboprophylaxis with early mobilisation unless contraindicated.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Hip fracture ↓ Trauma, surgery and immobility raise clot risk ↓ Venous thromboembolism
exam_trap: E, compartment syndrome — a feared fracture complication, but it is classically linked to tibial and forearm fractures, not hip fracture.
takeaway: Hip fracture admissions need VTE prophylaxis and early mobilisation.

stem: An older patient with a hip fracture becomes acutely confused and disorientated after admission. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Acute onset of fluctuating confusion during an acute illness or hospital admission is characteristic of delirium.
why_wrong: A. Dementia generally develops gradually rather than suddenly. B. Personality disorder does not cause acute fluctuating cognition. C. Schizophrenia does not typically present as acute fluctuating confusion in an older patient with acute illness. E. Dyslexia is a longstanding learning difficulty.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention and confusion; after hip fracture look for pain, infection, hypoxia, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation and drugs.
thinking: Older patient with hip fracture ↓ Confusion begins after admission ↓ Acute onset during illness ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: A, dementia developing overnight — tempting in an older confused patient, but dementia is gradual; acute confusion is delirium, though both can coexist.
takeaway: New acute confusion in hospital is delirium until proven otherwise.

stem: An older inpatient with delirium is distressed and repeatedly trying to climb out of bed. What is an important initial non-drug intervention?

options.B: Move to a side room with lights dimmed all day
options.C: Apply bed rails to prevent climbing out

correct_answer: E. Reassure, reorientate and address triggers
why_correct: Non-pharmacological measures include reassurance, orientation, familiar surroundings, appropriate lighting and addressing contributing factors.
why_wrong: A. Clocks and calendars can assist orientation. B. Isolation and constant dim lighting can worsen disorientation. C. Bed rails can increase the risk of injury in an agitated patient trying to climb out. D. Familiar visitors usually help orientation and reduce distress.
pearl: First-line delirium care is non-drug: reassure, reorientate, involve family, correct sensory deficits and treat triggers; reserve short-term medication for severe distress or risk.
thinking: Delirium with distress ↓ Climbing out of bed risks falls ↓ First line is non-pharmacological ↓ Reassure, reorientate and address triggers
exam_trap: C, bed rails — seem a safe way to stop climbing, but in an agitated patient they can lead to falls from a greater height and injury.
takeaway: Delirium: reorientate, reassure and treat the cause before any sedation.

stem: A patient with achalasia has difficulty swallowing and regurgitates undigested food, particularly at night. What is the underlying abnormality?

options.B: Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation

correct_answer: B. Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation
why_correct: Achalasia results from impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter with loss of normal oesophageal peristalsis.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatic enzyme deficiency causes maldigestion. C. Bile production does not explain achalasia. D. Gastric acid excess causes acid-related disease, not achalasia. E. Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations cause reflux, not achalasia.
pearl: Achalasia causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids with regurgitation; manometry confirms the diagnosis, and endoscopy is needed to exclude malignancy.
thinking: Dysphagia ↓ Regurgitation of undigested food, worse at night ↓ Food retained above a closed sphincter ↓ Failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation
exam_trap: E, transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations — tempting as it involves the same sphincter, but these cause reflux; achalasia is failure to relax.
takeaway: Achalasia = LOS fails to relax with loss of peristalsis; confirm with manometry.

stem: A patient with cirrhosis and known oesophageal varices presents with haematemesis. Which medication is commonly used to reduce portal pressure during suspected variceal bleeding?
why_correct: Terlipressin reduces portal venous pressure and is used in the acute management of suspected variceal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Metformin treats type 2 diabetes. B. Ibuprofen increases gastrointestinal bleeding risk. D. Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone. E. Salbutamol is a bronchodilator.
pearl: In suspected variceal bleeding, give terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics at presentation alongside resuscitation, then proceed to endoscopic band ligation.
thinking: Cirrhosis with known varices ↓ Haematemesis ↓ Suspected variceal bleed ↓ Vasoconstrictor lowers portal pressure ↓ Terlipressin
exam_trap: B, ibuprofen — tempting only as analgesia, but NSAIDs worsen GI bleeding and are best avoided in cirrhosis.
takeaway: Variceal bleed: terlipressin plus antibiotics, then band ligation.

stem: A patient with recurrent oesophageal variceal bleeding undergoes endoscopic treatment. Which technique is commonly used to control oesophageal varices?
why_correct: Endoscopic variceal band ligation is a standard endoscopic treatment for bleeding oesophageal varices.
why_wrong: B. Appendicectomy treats appendicitis. C. ERCP sphincterotomy is used for selected biliary/pancreatic indications. D. Colonoscopic polypectomy treats colonic polyps. E. Gastric lavage does not definitively control oesophageal variceal bleeding.
pearl: Band ligation is the endoscopic treatment of choice for oesophageal varices; gastric varices are usually treated by injecting tissue adhesive instead.
thinking: Recurrent oesophageal variceal bleeding ↓ Endoscopic control needed ↓ Bands strangulate the varix ↓ Endoscopic band ligation
exam_trap: E, gastric lavage alone — tempting as it clears the stomach for endoscopy, but it neither treats varices nor stops the bleeding.
takeaway: Oesophageal varices are banded at endoscopy.

stem: A patient with cirrhosis is started on a non-selective beta-blocker to reduce the risk of variceal bleeding. What is the intended effect?
why_correct: Non-selective beta-blockers reduce portal pressure and can reduce the risk of variceal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. They do not increase gastric acid secretion. B. Beta-blockers generally reduce heart rate. C. They do not increase bile production. D. They do not directly increase red-cell production.
pearl: Non-selective beta-blockers such as propranolol or carvedilol lower portal pressure by reducing cardiac output and splanchnic blood flow.
thinking: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension ↓ Varices at risk of bleeding ↓ Non-selective beta-blockade reduces splanchnic inflow ↓ Reduction of portal hypertension
exam_trap: B, increased heart rate — the reverse of the true effect; beta-blockers slow the heart, which is part of how they lower portal pressure.
takeaway: Non-selective beta-blockers prevent variceal bleeding by lowering portal pressure.

stem: A patient has recurrent painless visible haematuria. Which investigation is commonly used to directly examine the bladder?
why_correct: Cystoscopy allows direct visualisation of the urethra and bladder and is an important investigation for suspected bladder pathology.
why_wrong: A. Gastroscopy examines the upper gastrointestinal tract. B. Bronchoscopy examines the airways. C. Lumbar puncture assesses cerebrospinal fluid. E. Colonoscopy examines the large bowel.
pearl: Visible haematuria in adults needs urological assessment with cystoscopy for the bladder and imaging of the upper tract; bladder cancer is the key concern.
thinking: Painless visible haematuria ↓ Bladder cancer must be excluded ↓ The bladder needs direct inspection ↓ Cystoscopy
exam_trap: E, colonoscopy — another lower-body endoscopy, but it examines the large bowel and cannot visualise the bladder.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria: cystoscopy plus upper-tract imaging.

stem: A 70-year-old man has progressive difficulty passing urine, poor urinary stream and nocturia. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive lower urinary tract symptoms in an older man are characteristic of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes abdominal pain. C. Chronic bacterial prostatitis causes pelvic pain and recurrent urinary infection rather than progressive obstructive symptoms in an older man. D. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma may cause haematuria or systemic symptoms but does not typically cause progressive lower urinary tract symptoms. E. Membranous nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome with proteinuria and oedema, not obstructive urinary symptoms.
pearl: BPH causes voiding symptoms such as hesitancy and poor stream, plus storage symptoms such as nocturia; assess with abdominal and digital rectal examination, urinalysis and a frequency-volume chart.
thinking: Older man ↓ Hesitancy and poor stream ↓ Progressive, with nocturia ↓ Bladder outflow obstruction ↓ Benign prostatic hyperplasia
exam_trap: C, chronic bacterial prostatitis — also prostatic, but it causes pelvic pain and recurrent UTI rather than gradually progressive obstructive symptoms.
takeaway: Progressive voiding symptoms in an older man suggest BPH; examine the prostate.

stem: A man with acute urinary retention has a palpable distended bladder. Why can urinary retention cause acute kidney injury?

options.A: It reduces renal blood flow by causing hypovolaemia
options.B: It triggers immune-mediated glomerular injury in both kidneys
options.C: It causes back-pressure obstructing renal drainage
options.D: It causes pulmonary embolism that reduces cardiac output

correct_answer: C. It causes back-pressure obstructing renal drainage
why_correct: Significant urinary tract obstruction can impair renal drainage and lead to post-renal acute kidney injury.
why_wrong: A. Retention is a post-renal cause and does not cause AKI through hypovolaemia. B. Retention does not cause glomerulonephritis. D. It does not directly cause PE. E. It does not cause haemolysis.
pearl: Bladder outlet obstruction is a post-renal cause of AKI; catheterise, then watch for post-obstructive diuresis with fluid and electrolyte losses.
thinking: Acute retention with a distended bladder ↓ Urine cannot drain ↓ Pressure transmits back to the kidneys ↓ Post-renal AKI from back-pressure
exam_trap: A, hypovolaemia reducing renal blood flow — a common AKI cause, but that is pre-renal; retention causes AKI by post-renal obstruction.
takeaway: Urinary retention causes post-renal AKI; relieve it with a catheter.

stem: A man has a testicular swelling that allows light to pass through it on examination. What is this finding called?
why_correct: Transillumination occurs when light passes through a fluid-filled swelling and can support the diagnosis of a hydrocele.
why_wrong: A. Fluctuation assesses fluid movement within a swelling. B. Shifting dullness assesses ascites. C. Rebound tenderness is a sign of peritoneal irritation. D. Crepitus refers to a crackling sensation.
pearl: A scrotal swelling that transilluminates, can be got above and surrounds the testis suggests a hydrocele; ultrasound helps exclude an underlying testicular tumour.
thinking: Testicular swelling ↓ Light passes through it ↓ Swelling contains clear fluid ↓ Transillumination
exam_trap: A, fluctuation — also a sign of a fluid-filled swelling, but it describes transmitted pressure on palpation, not light passing through.
takeaway: Transillumination = clear fluid, as in a hydrocele.

stem: A patient has a painful, swollen, erythematous joint and fever. Septic arthritis is suspected. What is the key diagnostic investigation?
why_correct: Synovial fluid aspiration is essential for diagnosing septic arthritis and allows microscopy, culture and crystal analysis.
why_wrong: B. Urine dipstick does not establish the diagnosis. C. Spirometry assesses lung function. D. ECG assesses cardiac electrical activity. E. Chest X-ray does not diagnose septic arthritis.
pearl: Suspected septic arthritis needs synovial fluid for Gram stain, culture and crystals, ideally before antibiotics if this causes no delay, plus blood cultures.
thinking: Hot, swollen, painful joint ↓ Fever ↓ Septic arthritis must be confirmed or excluded ↓ Synovial fluid analysis ↓ Joint aspiration
exam_trap: E, chest X-ray only — a common part of a sepsis screen, but it looks for a source elsewhere and cannot diagnose infection within a joint.
takeaway: Hot swollen joint: aspirate before antibiotics where possible.

stem: A patient with fibromyalgia asks why their symptoms may fluctuate. Which factor commonly contributes to worsening symptoms?
why_correct: Fibromyalgia symptoms commonly fluctuate and can be exacerbated by poor sleep, stress and physical or psychological strain.
why_wrong: A. Bile production is unrelated. B. Appropriate graded physical activity is generally part of management rather than a typical trigger of worsening symptoms. C. Cataract does not cause fibromyalgia symptoms. E. Bone density does not explain symptom fluctuation.
pearl: Fibromyalgia is managed with explanation, graded exercise and support; poor sleep, stress and overexertion are common triggers for flares.
thinking: Fibromyalgia: chronic widespread pain ↓ Symptoms fluctuate ↓ Linked with sleep and psychological strain ↓ Poor sleep and stress
exam_trap: B, improved physical conditioning — tempting as activity can cause short-term discomfort, but graded exercise is a core treatment, not a cause of worsening.
takeaway: Fibromyalgia flares with poor sleep and stress; graded exercise helps.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She has noticed that symptoms are worse after eating and improve after opening her bowels. There is no weight loss, rectal bleeding or nocturnal diarrhoea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent abdominal pain associated with defaecation and altered bowel habit, without alarm features, is typical of IBS.
why_wrong: A. Crohn disease is an inflammatory bowel disease and may cause weight loss, inflammatory markers or other complications. B. Ulcerative colitis commonly causes persistent bloody diarrhoea. D. Colorectal cancer is more concerning with features such as persistent rectal bleeding, weight loss or altered bowel habit with other red flags. E. SIBO typically causes bloating and diarrhoea with predisposing factors, rather than pain relieved by defaecation in a young woman without risk factors.
pearl: IBS is a positive diagnosis in the absence of red flags; in primary care check a full blood count, inflammatory markers and coeliac serology before confirming it.
thinking: Young adult with recurrent pain and diarrhoea ↓ Worse after eating, relieved by defaecation ↓ No weight loss, bleeding or nocturnal symptoms ↓ Irritable bowel syndrome
exam_trap: A, terminal ileal Crohn disease — also causes pain and diarrhoea in young adults, but no weight loss, bleeding or nocturnal symptoms argues against it.
takeaway: Pain eased by defaecation with no red flags = IBS; still test for coeliac disease.

stem: A patient with irritable bowel syndrome asks whether the condition causes structural damage to the intestine. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: It causes mucosal changes that raise colorectal cancer risk
options.B: It is a functional disorder without structural damage
options.C: It causes gradual fibrotic narrowing of the colon over time
options.D: It causes patchy transmural inflammation of the bowel wall
options.E: It causes mucosal ulceration that may bleed intermittently

correct_answer: B. It is a functional disorder without structural damage
why_correct: IBS is characterised by gastrointestinal symptoms without the structural inflammatory damage seen in diseases such as Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause mucosal changes that increase colorectal cancer risk. C. Progressive narrowing or obstruction is not a feature of IBS. D. Patchy transmural inflammation is characteristic of Crohn disease, not IBS. E. Mucosal ulceration and bleeding suggest another diagnosis.
pearl: IBS is a disorder of gut–brain interaction: symptoms are real, but there is no inflammation, ulceration or raised cancer risk, which is reassuring to explain.
thinking: Patient with IBS ↓ Worried about bowel damage ↓ IBS has no structural or inflammatory pathology ↓ Functional disorder without structural damage
exam_trap: A, mucosal changes raising cancer risk — a common fear, but IBS does not increase colorectal cancer risk; that concern applies to long-standing colitis.
takeaway: IBS is functional: real symptoms without structural damage or cancer risk.

stem: A patient with chronic diarrhoea has normal inflammatory markers and no weight loss. The symptoms are associated with bloating and improve after defaecation. Which feature would most strongly suggest an alternative organic diagnosis rather than uncomplicated IBS?
why_correct: Unexplained weight loss is an alarm feature that should prompt assessment for organic disease rather than assuming IBS.
why_wrong: A. Meal-related symptoms can occur in IBS. B. Pain related to defaecation is characteristic of IBS. D. Bloating commonly occurs in IBS. E. Altered bowel habit is part of the typical IBS presentation.
pearl: Red flags against IBS include unexplained weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, an abdominal or rectal mass and a family history of bowel or ovarian cancer.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea with bloating, relieved by defaecation ↓ These features fit IBS ↓ Look for the alarm feature ↓ Unexplained weight loss
exam_trap: A, symptoms associated with meals — may seem to suggest organic disease, but meal-related symptoms are common in IBS and are not an alarm feature.
takeaway: Unexplained weight loss is a red flag; do not label it IBS.

stem: A 48-year-old man has recurrent heartburn and acid regurgitation. Which lifestyle measure may help reduce gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms?
correct_answer: A. Avoiding meals close to bedtime
why_correct: Avoiding food shortly before lying down can reduce nocturnal reflux symptoms.
why_wrong: B. Late meals can worsen nocturnal reflux. C. Smoking can aggravate reflux and has additional health risks. D. Alcohol can aggravate reflux symptoms. E. Lying down after eating can promote reflux.
pearl: Reflux lifestyle advice: avoid late meals, raise the head of the bed, lose weight if overweight, stop smoking and cut down trigger foods and alcohol.
thinking: Heartburn and regurgitation ↓ Reflux is worse lying down with a full stomach ↓ Reduce nocturnal acid exposure ↓ Avoid meals close to bedtime
exam_trap: E, lying flat immediately after eating — may seem restful, but gravity then favours reflux; patients should stay upright after meals.
takeaway: Reflux: eat earlier, raise the bed head, lose weight, stop smoking.

stem: A patient with reflux symptoms develops difficulty swallowing. Which feature requires particular attention because it may indicate significant oesophageal pathology?
why_correct: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom in a patient with reflux and warrants appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: B. Mild intermittent heartburn is common in uncomplicated reflux. C. Bloating is nonspecific. D. Occasional hiccups are not a typical alarm feature. E. Belching is nonspecific.
pearl: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom needing urgent upper GI endoscopy to look for stricture or oesophageal cancer, whatever the patient's age.
thinking: Background reflux ↓ New difficulty swallowing ↓ May reflect stricture or cancer ↓ Dysphagia is the alarm feature
exam_trap: B, occasional mild heartburn — the cardinal reflux symptom, but on its own it is common and not an alarm feature.
takeaway: Dysphagia at any age needs urgent endoscopy.

stem: A patient with carcinoid syndrome develops persistent diarrhoea and flushing. Which cardiac complication can occur?

options.D: Complete heart block in every patient

why_correct: Carcinoid heart disease characteristically causes fibrotic involvement of the right-sided valves.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis is not the characteristic cardiac complication. B. Rheumatic mitral stenosis has a different cause. D. Complete heart block is not an inevitable consequence. E. Aortic dissection is unrelated to carcinoid syndrome.
pearl: Carcinoid syndrome usually implies liver metastases; vasoactive substances reaching the right heart cause tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis, while the lungs largely protect the left side.
thinking: Carcinoid syndrome: flushing and diarrhoea ↓ Serotonin reaches the right heart ↓ Fibrotic plaques on right-sided valves ↓ Right-sided valvular heart disease
exam_trap: B, mitral stenosis — the valve lesion candidates know best, but carcinoid targets right-sided valves; mitral stenosis is classically rheumatic.
takeaway: Carcinoid heart disease hits the right side: tricuspid and pulmonary valves.

stem: A patient presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, constipation and abdominal distension. A CT scan demonstrates multiple diverticula in the sigmoid colon. What is the underlying condition?
why_correct: In NICE NG147 terms, diverticulosis is the presence of diverticula without symptoms, diverticular disease is diverticula causing symptoms (such as intermittent lower abdominal pain, altered bowel habit and bloating), and diverticulitis is inflammation or infection of diverticula; this symptomatic patient with sigmoid diverticula therefore has diverticular disease.
why_wrong: A. Ulcerative colitis causes continuous mucosal inflammation with bloody diarrhoea, not diverticula on CT. C. Crohn disease causes patchy transmural inflammation, often with diarrhoea and weight loss, not sigmoid diverticula. D. Appendicitis is an acute illness involving the appendix, not recurrent symptoms from sigmoid diverticula. E. Coeliac disease is a small-bowel enteropathy and does not produce colonic diverticula.
pearl: Diverticulosis means diverticula without symptoms, diverticular disease means diverticula causing symptoms, and diverticulitis means inflamed or infected diverticula.
thinking: Sigmoid diverticula on CT ↓ Recurrent pain, constipation and distension ↓ Symptomatic, with no infection described ↓ Diverticular disease
exam_trap: C, colonic Crohn disease — another cause of recurrent abdominal pain, but it causes patchy transmural inflammation, not sigmoid diverticula on CT.
takeaway: Symptomatic diverticula without inflammation = diverticular disease.

stem: A patient with diverticular disease develops sudden large-volume painless rectal bleeding. What is a possible cause?
why_correct: Diverticular disease can cause significant painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Anal fissures typically cause painful bright-red bleeding associated with defaecation. B. Oesophageal varices cause upper gastrointestinal bleeding. C. Gastric ulcers cause upper gastrointestinal bleeding. D. Ischaemic colitis typically causes abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea rather than painless large-volume bleeding.
pearl: Diverticular bleeding is a common cause of large painless lower GI bleeding; it often stops spontaneously but can be heavy enough to need resuscitation and transfusion.
thinking: Known diverticular disease ↓ Sudden large-volume rectal bleeding ↓ Painless ↓ Vessel erosion at a diverticulum ↓ Diverticular bleeding
exam_trap: D, ischaemic colitis — another colonic bleed, but it usually causes abdominal pain with bloody diarrhoea, not painless large-volume bleeding.
takeaway: Painless large-volume rectal bleeding with diverticula = diverticular bleed.

stem: A patient with chronic constipation asks about simple dietary measures. Which intervention can help improve bowel regularity?

options.A: Complete avoidance of fruit and vegetables
options.B: Adequate dietary fibre and fluid intake

correct_answer: B. Adequate dietary fibre and fluid intake
why_correct: Adequate fibre and fluid intake can help improve bowel habit in appropriate patients with constipation.
why_wrong: A. Avoiding fruit and vegetables reduces fibre intake. C. Fluid restriction can worsen constipation unless medically indicated. D. Alcohol is not an appropriate treatment. E. Fasting is not a treatment for constipation.
pearl: First-line constipation care is diet and lifestyle: more fibre, adequate fluids and activity; if this fails, a bulk-forming laxative is usually tried, then an osmotic laxative.
thinking: Chronic constipation ↓ Stool bulk and water content matter ↓ Fibre adds bulk and fluid softens stool ↓ Adequate fibre and fluid intake
exam_trap: A, complete avoidance of fruit and vegetables — tempting if foods seem to cause bloating, but it removes the fibre that promotes regular bowels.
takeaway: Constipation first line: fibre, fluids and activity.

stem: A patient has chronic constipation and regularly uses stimulant laxatives. They ask how these medicines work. What is the principal effect?
why_correct: Stimulant laxatives promote bowel movement by increasing intestinal motility.
why_wrong: A. They do not reduce bile production. C. Acid suppression is the action of medicines such as proton-pump inhibitors. D. Stimulant laxatives do not treat diabetes. E. Their effect is to promote, not paralyse, intestinal movement.
pearl: Stimulant laxatives such as senna and bisacodyl increase intestinal motility; they can cause cramping and are useful in opioid-induced constipation.
thinking: Chronic constipation ↓ Regular stimulant laxative use ↓ Stimulates colonic nerves and smooth muscle ↓ Increased intestinal motility
exam_trap: E, they paralyse the colon — the opposite of their action; stimulant laxatives increase peristalsis, which is why they can cause cramps.
takeaway: Stimulant laxatives such as senna work by increasing gut motility.

stem: A patient with chronic diarrhoea develops perianal soreness. Which simple measure can reduce irritation?

options.A: Vigorous scrubbing after every bowel movement
options.B: Reducing fluid intake to firm the stool
options.E: Gentle cleansing and a barrier cream

correct_answer: E. Gentle cleansing and a barrier cream
why_correct: Gentle hygiene and a protective barrier can reduce irritant dermatitis caused by frequent stool exposure.
why_wrong: A. Vigorous scrubbing can worsen skin damage. B. Fluid restriction risks dehydration and does not protect the skin. C. Strong antiseptics may further irritate damaged skin. D. Abrasive wipes can worsen irritation.
pearl: Perianal irritant dermatitis from frequent stools is prevented by gentle cleansing with water, patting dry and a barrier product, while the cause of the diarrhoea is treated.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea ↓ Frequent stool contact irritates perianal skin ↓ Protect rather than damage the skin ↓ Gentle cleansing and a barrier cream
exam_trap: C, concentrated antiseptic — seems hygienic, but strong antiseptics further irritate inflamed skin and worsen the dermatitis.
takeaway: Perianal soreness: gentle cleansing and barrier cream, not scrubbing.

stem: A patient with acute colonic pseudo-obstruction develops severe abdominal pain and peritonism. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Severe distension can compromise the bowel wall and lead to ischaemia or perforation, particularly when the patient deteriorates with peritonism.
why_wrong: B. Sigmoid volvulus is a mechanical twist rather than a complication of pseudo-obstruction causing peritonism. C. Mesenteric adenitis is a self-limiting cause of abdominal pain, mainly in children. D. Biliary pancreatitis is caused by gallstones and does not explain peritonism in pseudo-obstruction. E. Renal colic causes loin-to-groin pain without peritonism.
pearl: In acute colonic pseudo-obstruction, marked caecal distension risks ischaemia and perforation; new peritonism means suspected perforation and urgent surgical assessment.
thinking: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction ↓ Progressive colonic distension ↓ Bowel wall ischaemia ↓ Severe pain with peritonism ↓ Colonic perforation
exam_trap: B, sigmoid volvulus — another cause of a grossly distended colon, but it is a separate mechanical twist, not a complication of pseudo-obstruction.
takeaway: Pseudo-obstruction plus peritonism = perforation until proven otherwise.

stem: A patient presents with acute severe abdominal pain and rigid abdominal muscles. Which finding most strongly suggests peritonitis?
why_correct: Involuntary guarding is a sign of peritoneal irritation and may indicate serious intra-abdominal pathology.
why_wrong: A. Hyperactive bowel sounds suggest obstruction or gastroenteritis; peritonitis tends to produce a quiet abdomen. B. Voluntary guarding can occur with anxiety and is not specific. D. Mild bloating is nonspecific. E. Writhing suggests colic; patients with peritonitis typically lie still.
pearl: Patients with peritonitis lie still because movement hurts; involuntary guarding and rigidity reflect reflex muscle spasm over inflamed peritoneum.
thinking: Acute severe abdominal pain ↓ Rigid abdominal muscles ↓ Spasm not under voluntary control ↓ Involuntary guarding: peritonitis
exam_trap: B, voluntary guarding when anxious — looks like guarding, but voluntary tensing is non-specific; only involuntary guarding indicates peritoneal irritation.
takeaway: Involuntary guarding and lying still = peritonitis; writhing = colic.

stem: A 76-year-old patient with atrial fibrillation develops sudden severe abdominal pain and vomiting. Which mechanism could cause acute mesenteric ischaemia?
correct_answer: B. Embolism to the mesenteric arteries
why_correct: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of arterial emboli, which can occlude mesenteric vessels.
why_wrong: A. Gallbladder contraction does not cause mesenteric arterial embolism. C. Middle-ear infection is unrelated. D. Hypothyroidism does not produce this acute arterial occlusion. E. Gastric acid does not cause arterial occlusion.
pearl: Acute mesenteric ischaemia classically causes pain out of proportion to examination findings; AF is a major embolic risk factor, so suspect it early and arrange urgent CT angiography.
thinking: Older patient with AF ↓ Thrombus forms in the left atrium ↓ Embolus lodges in a mesenteric artery ↓ Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Mesenteric embolism
exam_trap: A, gallbladder contraction alone — a familiar cause of abdominal pain, but biliary colic does not occlude mesenteric arteries or cause bowel ischaemia.
takeaway: AF plus sudden severe abdominal pain: think mesenteric embolism.

stem: A patient develops sudden severe abdominal pain with metabolic acidosis and elevated lactate. Which diagnosis should be considered urgently?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain with metabolic acidosis and raised lactate can indicate tissue hypoperfusion and bowel ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. Rhinitis is unrelated. B. Haemorrhoids do not cause bowel ischaemia. D. IBS does not cause bowel ischaemia or significant lactic acidosis. E. Functional dyspepsia does not cause this systemic disturbance.
pearl: Raised lactate with metabolic acidosis in acute abdominal pain suggests bowel ischaemia, but a normal lactate does not exclude it, so urgent CT angiography should not be delayed.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Metabolic acidosis ↓ Raised lactate indicating hypoperfusion ↓ Bowel ischaemia
exam_trap: D, uncomplicated IBS — a stock answer for abdominal pain, but IBS never causes metabolic acidosis or a raised lactate.
takeaway: Severe abdominal pain plus raised lactate: suspect bowel ischaemia.

stem: A patient with an abdominal stoma notices that the stoma has become dark purple and painful. What should be suspected?
why_correct: A healthy intestinal stoma should generally appear pink or red. A dark, dusky or black stoma can indicate compromised blood supply.
why_wrong: A. A dark painful stoma is not a normal appearance. B. Gastritis does not affect stoma colour. C. Haemorrhoids do not cause stoma ischaemia. D. Constipation alone does not explain a dusky stoma.
pearl: A dusky, dark or black stoma suggests ischaemia or necrosis, most often early after surgery; it needs urgent surgical review to judge how deep the ischaemia extends.
thinking: Abdominal stoma ↓ Becomes dark purple and painful ↓ Healthy mucosa should be pink or red ↓ Compromised blood supply ↓ Stoma ischaemia
exam_trap: D, simple constipation — could explain discomfort, but it does not change the colour of the stoma mucosa.
takeaway: Dark or dusky stoma = ischaemia; get urgent surgical review.

stem: A patient with a new ileostomy has high-volume watery output and becomes dizzy. What complication should be considered?

options.D: Vasovagal reaction to the stoma care
options.E: Small bowel obstruction at the stoma

why_correct: High-output ileostomies can result in substantial fluid and electrolyte losses.
why_wrong: A. Stoma retraction causes leakage and skin problems rather than high output with dizziness. C. A parastomal hernia causes a bulge around the stoma, not high-volume output. D. A vasovagal reaction does not explain persistent high-volume output. E. Obstruction reduces stoma output rather than causing high-volume watery output.
pearl: High-output ileostomy losses are rich in sodium and water, risking dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and AKI; oral rehydration solution and limiting hypotonic drinks are key.
thinking: New ileostomy ↓ Colon bypassed ↓ High-volume watery output ↓ Dizziness indicates volume depletion ↓ Dehydration and electrolyte loss
exam_trap: E, small bowel obstruction at the stoma — a recognised early stoma problem, but obstruction reduces output; here output is high.
takeaway: High-output ileostomy with dizziness = dehydration; replace salt and water.

stem: A patient with a colostomy asks about the normal appearance of their stoma. What colour should a healthy stoma normally be?
why_correct: A healthy intestinal stoma is generally moist and pink or red because of its blood supply.
why_wrong: A. Black discoloration may indicate necrosis. B. Blue-grey discoloration may indicate impaired perfusion. C. Pale yellow is not the normal appearance of viable bowel mucosa. E. White is not a normal stoma colour.
pearl: A healthy stoma is moist and pink to red; dusky, blue-grey or black mucosa suggests poor perfusion or necrosis and needs prompt review.
thinking: Question about stoma colour ↓ A stoma is viable bowel mucosa ↓ Good blood supply gives a moist red appearance ↓ Pink or red
exam_trap: B, blue-grey — tempting if some discoloration seems normal after surgery, but blue-grey suggests impaired perfusion and needs review.
takeaway: Healthy stoma: moist and pink-red; dark means poor blood supply.

stem: A patient with an ileostomy asks why they have been advised to maintain adequate fluid intake. What is the main reason?

options.A: The colon no longer absorbs water from the stool
options.B: Ileostomies impair the kidneys' ability to concentrate urine
options.C: The stomach secretes more fluid after surgery
options.D: Ileostomies raise the body's metabolic rate
options.E: Fluids are needed to prevent the stoma retracting

correct_answer: A. The colon no longer absorbs water from the stool
why_correct: The colon normally absorbs substantial amounts of water and electrolytes; an ileostomy can therefore result in greater fluid losses.
why_wrong: B. Renal concentrating ability is not impaired by an ileostomy. C. Increased gastric secretion is not the main reason. D. Ileostomy does not raise the metabolic rate. E. Fluid intake does not prevent stoma retraction.
pearl: With an ileostomy, colonic absorption of water and sodium is lost, so output is liquid and the risk of dehydration rises, especially in hot weather or intercurrent illness.
thinking: Ileostomy diverts output before the colon ↓ The colon normally absorbs water and electrolytes ↓ This absorption is lost, so fluid losses rise ↓ The colon no longer absorbs water from the stool
exam_trap: B, impaired renal concentrating ability — tempting because dehydration affects the kidneys, but the kidneys work normally; the problem is gut losses.
takeaway: An ileostomy bypasses colonic water absorption, so fluid losses rise.

stem: A patient with a parastomal hernia develops severe pain, vomiting and a non-reducible swelling. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Pain, irreducibility and vomiting raise concern for obstruction or compromised blood supply.
why_wrong: A. Pyoderma gangrenosum causes painful peristomal ulceration, not an irreducible swelling with vomiting. B. An uncomplicated reducible hernia would not cause this acute deterioration. D. Mucocutaneous separation is a wound problem at the stoma edge and does not cause vomiting. E. Contact dermatitis causes skin irritation, not an irreducible painful swelling.
pearl: A painful, tense, irreducible parastomal hernia with vomiting suggests obstruction or strangulation and needs emergency surgical assessment.
thinking: Known parastomal hernia ↓ Becomes painful and irreducible ↓ Vomiting suggests bowel obstruction ↓ Blood supply at risk ↓ Obstruction or strangulation
exam_trap: B, uncomplicated reducible parastomal hernia — the baseline diagnosis, but irreducibility with pain and vomiting signals a complication.
takeaway: Irreducible painful hernia with vomiting = obstruction or strangulation.

stem: A patient with a colostomy reports no stoma output, increasing abdominal pain and vomiting. What should be considered?
why_correct: Absence of stoma output accompanied by pain and vomiting can indicate obstruction and requires assessment.
why_wrong: A. Peristomal skin irritation does not explain absent output with pain and vomiting. B. Reflux does not explain absent stoma output with abdominal pain and vomiting. C. Complete cessation of output with symptoms is not normal. D. A skin infection does not explain absent output with vomiting.
pearl: Absent stoma output with abdominal pain, distension or vomiting suggests obstruction, from adhesions, hernia or blockage at the stoma, and needs prompt surgical assessment.
thinking: Colostomy ↓ Output has stopped ↓ Abdominal pain and vomiting ↓ Mechanical obstruction pattern ↓ Stoma or bowel obstruction
exam_trap: C, normal stoma function — colostomy output can be infrequent, but complete cessation with pain and vomiting is not normal.
takeaway: No stoma output plus pain and vomiting = obstruction.

stem: A patient with a new colostomy is distressed about the change in body image. What is an appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure them most patients adapt and arrange review at 6 months
options.B: Start an SSRI antidepressant and make a referral to liaison psychiatry
options.C: Defer any detailed discussion of body image until the stoma is reversed
options.D: Explore concerns; offer stoma nurse and psychological support
options.E: Tell the patient that adjustment should occur immediately after surgery

correct_answer: D. Explore concerns; offer stoma nurse and psychological support
why_correct: Stoma formation can affect body image, intimacy and emotional wellbeing. Support should address both practical stoma management and psychological concerns.
why_wrong: A. Reassurance with delayed review does not address current distress. B. Antidepressants and psychiatric referral are not automatically indicated. C. Deferring discussion does not provide support, and many stomas are not reversed. E. Adjustment varies between individuals and should not be assumed to be immediate.
pearl: Body-image distress after stoma formation is common; explore concerns, involve the stoma care nurse early and offer psychological support where needed.
thinking: New colostomy ↓ Distress about body image ↓ Needs practical and emotional support ↓ Explore concerns; offer stoma nurse and psychological support
exam_trap: B, start an SSRI and refer to liaison psychiatry — feels proactive, but adjustment distress is not automatically depression and should be explored first.
takeaway: Stoma body-image distress: listen, involve the stoma nurse, offer support.

stem:
A 2-day-old baby develops green vomiting and abdominal distension.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: This is physiological reflux; reduce feed volumes and review
options.B: This is likely bile-stained swallowed amniotic fluid; observe
options.C: It may be intestinal obstruction needing urgent review
options.D: This is likely cow's milk protein allergy; change formula
options.E: This is typical of pyloric stenosis; arrange an ultrasound

correct_answer: C. It may be intestinal obstruction needing urgent review
why_correct: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is a red flag for intestinal obstruction, including malrotation with volvulus.
why_wrong: A. Physiological reflux does not normally produce green/bilious vomit. B. Bilious vomiting should not be attributed to swallowed fluid and observed; it is a red flag. D. Milk allergy does not explain bilious vomiting with abdominal distension. E. Pyloric stenosis causes non-bilious projectile vomiting, usually from a few weeks of age.
pearl: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise; it needs urgent surgical review and an upper GI contrast study.
thinking: Two-day-old baby ↓ Green, bilious vomiting ↓ Abdominal distension ↓ Obstruction beyond the ampulla ↓ Urgent review for intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: E, pyloric stenosis — the classic infant vomiting answer, but it causes non-bilious projectile vomiting, usually after a few weeks of life.
takeaway: Green vomit in a newborn is a surgical emergency.

stem:
A child with IgA vasculitis is reviewed in primary care.

Which investigation is particularly important because of a possible renal complication?
why_correct: IgA vasculitis can cause renal involvement, including haematuria and proteinuria, so urine should be checked.
why_wrong: B. Spirometry assesses lung function. C. ECG assesses cardiac electrical activity. D. Faecal calprotectin is used when assessing intestinal inflammation. E. Peak flow assesses variable airflow obstruction.
