exam_trap: B, polycythaemia with hyperviscosity — another blood count abnormality, but neutropenia does not raise red cell mass.
takeaway: Severe neutropenia means high risk of serious bacterial infection.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman develops sudden painless swelling of one leg. The leg is warm and tender compared with the other side.

Which investigation is commonly used when DVT is suspected and imaging is indicated?

options.A: Plain radiograph of the lower leg
options.E: Nerve conduction studies of the leg

why_correct: Ultrasound is commonly used to assess suspected lower-limb DVT when indicated by the clinical assessment.
why_wrong: A. A plain radiograph cannot detect venous thrombosis. C. CT pulmonary angiography is used for suspected pulmonary embolism, not DVT. D. The ABPI assesses peripheral arterial disease, not venous thrombosis. E. Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerve function, not venous thrombosis.
pearl: If DVT is likely on the Wells score, arrange proximal leg vein ultrasound; if it cannot be done promptly, take a D-dimer and start interim anticoagulation.
thinking: Sudden swelling of one leg ↓ warm and tender compared with the other ↓ suspected DVT ↓ imaging indicated ↓ compression duplex ultrasound
exam_trap: C, CT pulmonary angiography — familiar VTE imaging, but it looks for pulmonary embolism, not clot in the leg veins.
takeaway: Suspected DVT needing imaging: compression duplex ultrasound.

stem:
A 33-year-old man develops unilateral leg swelling after a long-haul flight. His Wells assessment indicates that DVT is unlikely.

Which blood test may be used as part of the diagnostic pathway?
why_correct: In patients assessed as unlikely to have DVT, D-dimer can be used as part of the diagnostic pathway to help exclude venous thromboembolism.
why_wrong: A. HbA1c assesses longer-term glycaemic control. B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. C. PSA is associated with prostate assessment. E. Amylase is associated with pancreatic injury but is not a DVT test.
pearl: When the Wells score shows DVT is unlikely, a negative D-dimer effectively excludes it; a positive D-dimer is non-specific and needs proximal leg vein ultrasound.
thinking: Unilateral leg swelling after a long flight ↓ Wells score: DVT unlikely ↓ need a sensitive rule-out test ↓ D-dimer
exam_trap: B, troponin — a familiar emergency blood test that can rise in PE, but it has no role in diagnosing DVT.
takeaway: DVT unlikely on Wells: D-dimer, and a negative result rules it out.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman has recurrent falls. Her medication list includes several drugs that can cause dizziness and sedation.

What is an appropriate intervention?

options.E: Stop all medicines immediately without assessment

why_correct: Polypharmacy and medicines causing sedation or postural symptoms can contribute to falls, so medication review is an important component of assessment.
why_wrong: A. Additional sedation may increase falls risk. C. Prolonged bed rest can worsen frailty and mobility. D. Unnecessary fluid restriction may worsen dehydration and postural symptoms. E. Medicines should not be stopped indiscriminately without assessing their indications and risks.
pearl: In recurrent falls, a structured medication review should reduce or stop sedating, hypotensive and anticholinergic drugs where possible, weighing each drug's indication.
thinking: Recurrent falls ↓ several drugs causing dizziness and sedation ↓ modifiable risk factor ↓ medication review
exam_trap: E, stop all medicines immediately — removes the culprit drugs, but abrupt stopping without assessment risks withdrawal effects and loss of needed treatment.
takeaway: Falls on sedating drugs: review medicines carefully, do not stop them all.

stem:
A 36-year-old woman has palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. Blood tests show a suppressed TSH and raised free T4.

Which symptom is also commonly associated with hyperthyroidism?
why_correct: Hyperthyroidism commonly causes tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance and weight loss.
why_wrong: A. Weight loss is more typical. B. Heat intolerance, rather than cold intolerance, is typical. C. Constipation is more characteristic of hypothyroidism. D. Hyperthyroidism usually causes tachycardia.
pearl: Hyperthyroidism causes adrenergic features such as fine tremor, tachycardia and sweating; a beta-blocker such as propranolol relieves these while definitive treatment takes effect.
thinking: Palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance ↓ suppressed TSH with raised free T4 ↓ hyperthyroidism ↓ excess sympathetic activity ↓ fine tremor
exam_trap: B, cold intolerance — a classic thyroid symptom, but it occurs in hypothyroidism; hyperthyroidism causes heat intolerance.
takeaway: Hyperthyroidism: fine tremor, tachycardia, heat intolerance and weight loss.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is found to have persistent albumin in his urine.

Which complication of diabetes does this finding suggest?
why_correct: Persistent albuminuria is an important marker of diabetic kidney disease.
why_wrong: A. PE does not cause persistent albuminuria. B. Retinopathy is a microvascular complication of diabetes, but albuminuria specifically indicates renal involvement. C. Autonomic neuropathy does not cause albuminuria. E. Appendicitis does not cause persistent albuminuria.
pearl: Persistent albuminuria in diabetes is the earliest practical marker of diabetic kidney disease and also flags raised cardiovascular risk; it is screened for with a urine albumin:creatinine ratio.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes ↓ Persistent albumin in the urine ↓ Glomerular damage from microvascular disease ↓ Diabetic kidney disease
exam_trap: B, proliferative diabetic retinopathy — another microvascular complication that often coexists, but albuminuria is a renal finding and points to the kidney, not the eye.
takeaway: Persistent albuminuria in a diabetic patient means diabetic kidney disease until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has reduced sensation in both feet. She does not notice a small blister on her heel.

What complication is most likely responsible for her reduced sensation?

options.B: Acute lacunar stroke of the thalamus
options.D: Peripheral arterial disease of the legs

why_correct: Long-standing diabetes can cause distal symmetrical peripheral neuropathy, reducing protective sensation in the feet.
why_wrong: A. Tarsal tunnel syndrome is an uncommon focal entrapment and is far less likely than diabetic neuropathy to cause symmetrical sensory loss in both feet. B. A thalamic lacunar stroke causes unilateral sensory loss rather than symmetrical loss in both feet. C. Ménière disease affects the vestibular and auditory systems. D. Peripheral arterial disease causes claudication and ischaemic changes rather than symmetrical sensory loss.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy causes symmetrical glove-and-stocking loss of protective sensation, so minor foot injuries go unnoticed; every diabetic foot needs regular inspection and foot risk assessment.
thinking: Type 2 diabetes ↓ Symmetrical reduced sensation in both feet ↓ Unnoticed heel blister = loss of protective sensation ↓ Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: D, peripheral arterial disease — common in diabetes and also threatens the foot, but it causes claudication and ischaemic changes, not symmetrical sensory loss.
takeaway: Bilateral distal sensory loss in diabetes is peripheral neuropathy; unnoticed foot injury is the danger.

stem:
A 15-year-old boy has delayed puberty. Examination shows small testes and little facial or body hair.

Which finding would be most suggestive of hypogonadism?
why_correct: Testosterone deficiency causes impaired male pubertal development.
why_wrong: A. Hyponatraemia has many causes but is not a defining feature. B. Amylase relates mainly to pancreatic pathology. D. Raised bilirubin suggests hepatobiliary or haemolytic pathology. E. Hyperglycaemia does not specifically indicate hypogonadism.
pearl: In a boy with delayed puberty, low testosterone confirms hypogonadism; LH and FSH then separate primary testicular failure (high) from central causes or constitutional delay (low or normal).
thinking: 15-year-old boy with delayed puberty ↓ Small testes, little facial or body hair ↓ Deficient androgen effect ↓ Low testosterone
exam_trap: E, high blood glucose — sounds endocrine and familiar, but hyperglycaemia says nothing about gonadal function; hypogonadism is shown by low sex hormone.
takeaway: Male hypogonadism is shown by low testosterone; check LH and FSH to locate the problem.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman is found to have a serum calcium concentration of 2.9 mmol/L. She has constipation and increased thirst.

Which symptom is consistent with hypercalcaemia?
why_correct: Hypercalcaemia can cause constipation, thirst, polyuria, abdominal symptoms and neurocognitive changes.
why_wrong: B. Bradycardia is not the defining clinical feature. C. Constipation rather than diarrhoea is more typical. D. Carpopedal spasm is associated with hypocalcaemia. E. Stridor is an upper-airway symptom.
pearl: Hypercalcaemia causes bones, stones, abdominal groans and psychic moans: constipation, thirst and polyuria, renal stones, abdominal pain, and confusion or low mood.
thinking: Calcium 2.9 mmol/L = raised ↓ Thirst plus constipation ↓ High calcium slows gut smooth muscle ↓ Constipation
exam_trap: D, carpopedal spasm — a classic calcium-related sign, but it reflects neuromuscular irritability from low calcium, the opposite of this picture.
takeaway: High calcium slows things down (constipation, lethargy); low calcium makes nerves irritable (tetany).

stem:
A 64-year-old man has chronic kidney disease. His blood tests show persistently raised phosphate and reduced calcium.

Which complication of chronic kidney disease is this pattern associated with?
why_correct: Chronic kidney disease causes phosphate retention and impaired vitamin D activation, contributing to hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
why_wrong: A. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus concerns water balance and does not explain this calcium-phosphate pattern. B. Primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from an adenoma, causes hypercalcaemia with low or normal phosphate. C. Addison disease causes adrenal hormone deficiency. D. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism (including after transplant), whereas calcium is low here.
pearl: In CKD, phosphate retention and reduced renal activation of vitamin D lower calcium and drive the parathyroids to overwork: secondary hyperparathyroidism, part of CKD mineral and bone disease.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease ↓ High phosphate, low calcium ↓ Reduced activated vitamin D ↓ PTH rises in response ↓ Secondary hyperparathyroidism
exam_trap: D, tertiary hyperparathyroidism — also linked to CKD and transplant, but it follows long-standing secondary disease and causes high calcium, not the low calcium seen here.
takeaway: CKD with low calcium and high phosphate is secondary hyperparathyroidism; high calcium suggests tertiary.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman has chronic kidney disease and is advised to avoid NSAIDs.

Why can NSAIDs be particularly harmful in patients with chronic kidney disease?

options.B: They cause dehydration through a potent diuretic effect
options.E: They reduce renal blood flow, worsening kidney function

correct_answer: E. They reduce renal blood flow, worsening kidney function
why_correct: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which can reduce renal blood flow and precipitate or worsen kidney injury, particularly in susceptible patients.
why_wrong: A. Increased B12 absorption is unrelated. B. NSAIDs cause sodium and fluid retention rather than a diuretic effect. C. Cataracts are not their characteristic renal adverse effect. D. They do not increase haemoglobin.
pearl: In CKD the kidney relies on prostaglandin-mediated afferent vasodilatation to maintain filtration; NSAIDs block this and can precipitate acute kidney injury, especially with dehydration, ACE inhibitors or diuretics.
thinking: CKD patient told to avoid NSAIDs ↓ NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis ↓ Loss of afferent arteriolar dilatation ↓ Reduced renal blood flow, worsening kidney function
exam_trap: B, dehydration through a diuretic effect — sounds renal and plausible, but NSAIDs cause sodium and fluid retention, not diuresis; the harm comes from reduced renal perfusion.
takeaway: NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow by blocking prostaglandins, so avoid them in CKD.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is found to have blood group RhD negative during pregnancy.

Which test is used to identify clinically significant red-cell antibodies in pregnancy?
why_correct: Antenatal antibody screening identifies maternal red-cell antibodies that may cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. B. The Kleihauer test quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage rather than detecting maternal red-cell antibodies. D. D-dimer is associated with thromboembolic assessment. E. HbA1c assesses longer-term glycaemic control.
pearl: All pregnant women have blood group and red-cell antibody screening at booking and again around 28 weeks; RhD-negative women without anti-D antibodies are offered routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis.
thinking: RhD-negative pregnant woman ↓ Risk of maternal red-cell antibodies ↓ Antibodies can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn ↓ Antibody screening
exam_trap: B, Kleihauer–Betke test — closely linked with RhD-negative pregnancy, but it measures the volume of fetomaternal haemorrhage to guide anti-D dosing; it does not detect maternal antibodies.
takeaway: Antibody screening detects red-cell antibodies; Kleihauer measures fetal cells in maternal blood.

stem:
A 30-year-old pregnant woman is found to have iron-deficiency anaemia at routine antenatal testing.

Which dietary advice is appropriate?

options.C: Stop eating foods containing vitamin C

correct_answer: B. Increase intake of iron-rich foods
why_correct: Iron-rich foods contribute to maintaining iron stores and are appropriate dietary advice in iron deficiency.
why_wrong: A. Protein restriction is not appropriate. C. Vitamin C can enhance iron absorption. D. Fruit juice alone cannot correct iron deficiency. E. Vegetables should not generally be avoided.
pearl: Antenatal iron deficiency is treated with oral iron, with dietary advice alongside: iron-rich foods such as red meat, pulses and fortified cereals, ideally with vitamin C and away from tea or coffee.
thinking: Pregnant woman ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia on routine testing ↓ Iron stores need replenishing ↓ Increase intake of iron-rich foods
exam_trap: C, stop eating foods containing vitamin C — reflects a muddled link between vitamin C and iron, but vitamin C actually enhances non-haem iron absorption.
takeaway: In iron deficiency, advise iron-rich foods; vitamin C helps absorption while tea and coffee hinder it.

stem:
A woman who is 10 weeks pregnant asks whether she should continue taking folic acid.

What is the usual advice regarding folic acid supplementation?

options.A: Stop now, as the neural tube has already fully closed
options.B: Continue throughout pregnancy at a dose of 5 mg daily
options.C: Continue through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy
options.D: Avoid it now, as it may mask vitamin B12 deficiency

correct_answer: C. Continue through the first 12 weeks of pregnancy
why_correct: Folic acid supplementation around conception and during the first trimester reduces the risk of neural tube defects.
why_wrong: A. Although the neural tube closes early, folic acid is advised until 12 weeks of pregnancy. B. The 5 mg dose is reserved for women at higher risk, and standard advice is 400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks. D. Folic acid is routinely recommended in early pregnancy, and concern about masking B12 deficiency is not a reason to avoid it. E. Stopping immediately after conception misses the key period of neural tube development.
pearl: Standard advice is folic acid 400 micrograms daily from before conception until 12 weeks; a 5 mg dose is reserved for higher-risk women, such as those with a previous neural tube defect, diabetes or antiepileptic use.
thinking: 10 weeks pregnant ↓ Still in the first trimester ↓ Folic acid reduces neural tube defect risk ↓ Continue until 12 weeks
exam_trap: B, continue throughout pregnancy at 5 mg daily — the high dose is real but only for higher-risk women, and routine supplementation stops at 12 weeks.
takeaway: Folic acid: 400 micrograms daily from preconception to 12 weeks; 5 mg only if higher risk.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman is 36 weeks pregnant. She notices a sudden gush of clear fluid from the vagina followed by continuous leakage.

What does this suggest?
why_correct: A sudden gush followed by continued leakage of clear fluid at this stage of pregnancy is typical of rupture of the membranes.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy occurs outside the uterine cavity, usually early in pregnancy. B. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain. D. Hyperemesis causes severe vomiting. E. Abruption usually presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain.
pearl: Suspected rupture of membranes is confirmed by history and sterile speculum examination showing pooling of liquor; avoid digital vaginal examination if she is not in labour because of infection risk.
thinking: 36 weeks pregnant ↓ Sudden gush of clear fluid ↓ Continuous leakage afterwards ↓ Amniotic fluid loss ↓ Rupture of membranes
exam_trap: E, placental abruption — a third-trimester emergency, but it presents with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, not a gush of clear fluid followed by continuous leakage.
takeaway: A gush then continuous clear fluid leak in late pregnancy is rupture of membranes.

stem:
A 4-month-old infant has frequent effortless regurgitation after feeds but remains well and continues to gain weight.

What is the most likely explanation?

options.E: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in early infancy

why_correct: Regurgitation is common in otherwise well infants and usually resolves as the gastrointestinal tract matures.
why_wrong: B. Intussusception causes episodic severe abdominal pain and may cause blood/mucus in stool. C. GORD implies reflux causing complications such as faltering growth, feeding difficulty or distress, which are absent here. D. Hirschsprung disease typically presents with delayed meconium passage and obstructive symptoms. E. Pyloric stenosis causes forceful projectile vomiting, typically in early infancy.
pearl: Effortless regurgitation in a thriving infant is physiological reflux; it is very common in the first months and usually settles by about one year, so reassurance is the mainstay.
thinking: 4-month-old infant ↓ Effortless regurgitation after feeds ↓ Well and gaining weight ↓ No complications ↓ Physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux
exam_trap: C, GORD — the same reflux process, but GORD requires complications such as faltering growth, feeding difficulty or distress, none of which are present.
takeaway: A happy, thriving infant who regurgitates has physiological reflux, not GORD.

stem:
A 9-month-old infant has not yet started crawling or pulling to stand. He has otherwise normal social interaction and language development.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.D: Diagnose cerebral palsy and start physiotherapy
options.E: Review overall development and arrange assessment

correct_answer: E. Review overall development and arrange assessment
why_correct: Motor development should be assessed in the context of the child's overall development rather than making an immediate diagnosis from one milestone alone.
why_wrong: A. There is no indication for antiepileptic therapy. B. Social interaction and language are normal, so there is no indication for autism assessment. C. Developmental concerns should be assessed rather than dismissed. D. Cerebral palsy cannot be diagnosed from this information alone.
pearl: A single delayed milestone is judged in context: review gross motor, fine motor, language and social skills, tone and growth; isolated motor delay may be normal variation but must not be dismissed without assessment.
thinking: 9-month-old not crawling or pulling to stand ↓ Social and language development normal ↓ Possible isolated motor delay ↓ Review overall development and arrange assessment
exam_trap: C, reassure without assessing development — tempting because many infants crawl late, but reassurance is only safe after a proper developmental assessment.
takeaway: Never diagnose or dismiss from one milestone; assess development across all domains.

stem:
A 59-year-old man presents with recurrent nosebleeds. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation.

Which medication-related factor may contribute to prolonged bleeding?
why_correct: Excessive anticoagulation with warfarin can increase bleeding risk and should be assessed in a patient with recurrent bleeding.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin B12 supplementation does not increase anticoagulation. C. Hypoglycaemia does not cause excessive anticoagulation. D. Hypothyroidism alone does not explain warfarin-related bleeding. E. Inhaled saline does not cause systemic anticoagulation.
pearl: Bleeding on warfarin should prompt an urgent INR check; over-anticoagulation is often caused by interacting drugs such as antibiotics, intercurrent illness or dietary change.
thinking: Recurrent nosebleeds ↓ Taking warfarin for AF ↓ Bleeding risk rises with the INR ↓ Excessive anticoagulation
exam_trap: D, hypothyroidism alone — sounds like a systemic medical cause, but it does not explain warfarin-related bleeding; the immediate suspect is over-anticoagulation shown by a raised INR.
takeaway: Bleeding on warfarin: check the INR and look for over-anticoagulation.

stem:
A 75-year-old woman taking apixaban develops black, tarry stools and feels faint.

What should be suspected?
why_correct: Melaena indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and anticoagulation can increase bleeding severity.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding. B. Haemorrhoids generally cause fresh rectal bleeding rather than melaena. D. Coeliac disease does not typically cause acute melaena. E. Constipation does not cause melaena.
pearl: Melaena means upper GI bleeding until proven otherwise; with faintness on an anticoagulant, resuscitate, risk-stratify with a score such as Glasgow-Blatchford and arrange urgent endoscopy.
thinking: Black, tarry stools = melaena ↓ Feels faint = haemodynamic compromise ↓ Apixaban increases bleeding ↓ Gastrointestinal bleeding
exam_trap: B, haemorrhoids without bleeding — haemorrhoids are common in older adults, but they cause fresh red blood, not black tarry stools, and this option excludes bleeding anyway.
takeaway: Black tarry stools plus faintness on an anticoagulant is a GI bleed until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 58-year-old man taking aspirin develops epigastric discomfort. He has no haematemesis or melaena.

Which medication can increase the risk of peptic ulceration when taken regularly?
why_correct: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis and can increase the risk of gastric and duodenal ulceration, particularly with other risk factors such as aspirin.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol is not a typical cause of peptic ulceration. B. Amoxicillin is an antibiotic and is not a typical cause of peptic ulceration. C. Loratadine is an antihistamine. D. Salbutamol is a bronchodilator.
pearl: NSAIDs, including aspirin, block prostaglandin-mediated gastric protection; ulcer risk rises with age, previous ulcer, steroids, anticoagulants and combined use, so consider PPI gastroprotection.
thinking: Taking aspirin with epigastric discomfort ↓ Aspirin and other NSAIDs inhibit protective prostaglandins ↓ Mucosal injury and ulceration ↓ NSAIDs
exam_trap: A, paracetamol — a common analgesic people associate with drug harm, but it does not damage the gastric mucosa and is the stomach-safe analgesic choice.
takeaway: NSAIDs and aspirin cause peptic ulcers; paracetamol does not.

stem:
A 40-year-old man has recurrent upper abdominal discomfort. Testing confirms *Helicobacter pylori* infection.

Why is eradication treatment important?

options.B: It eliminates the risk of colorectal cancer
options.D: It reduces peptic ulcer risk and recurrence

correct_answer: D. It reduces peptic ulcer risk and recurrence
why_correct: *H. pylori* is strongly associated with peptic ulcer disease, and eradication reduces ulcer recurrence.
why_wrong: A. It does not dissolve gallstones. B. Eradication reduces gastric cancer risk but has no established role in colorectal cancer prevention. C. It does not prevent appendicitis. E. It does not cure inflammatory bowel disease.
pearl: H. pylori causes most duodenal and many gastric ulcers; eradication with a PPI plus two antibiotics heals ulcers and sharply reduces recurrence.
thinking: Recurrent upper abdominal discomfort ↓ H. pylori confirmed ↓ H. pylori drives peptic ulcer disease ↓ Eradication reduces ulcer risk and recurrence
exam_trap: B, eliminates colorectal cancer risk — sounds plausible because eradication lowers gastric cancer risk, but it has no established role in colorectal cancer prevention.
takeaway: Eradicating H. pylori reduces peptic ulcer recurrence and lowers gastric, not colorectal, cancer risk.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with known abdominal aortic aneurysm develops sudden severe abdominal pain and becomes hypotensive.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Arrange a CT angiogram as an outpatient
options.C: Give fluids to a normal BP before referral

correct_answer: B. Activate an emergency vascular pathway
why_correct: Suspected ruptured AAA is a life-threatening vascular emergency requiring immediate specialist management.
why_wrong: A. Outpatient imaging would dangerously delay treatment of a suspected rupture. C. Fluid resuscitation to a normal blood pressure is not advised (permissive hypotension) and must not delay emergency vascular referral. D. Routine review is inappropriate. E. Physiotherapy is irrelevant.
pearl: Known AAA with sudden pain and hypotension is rupture until proven otherwise: call the vascular team immediately and use permissive hypotension rather than chasing a normal blood pressure.
thinking: Known AAA ↓ Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ Hypotension ↓ Suspected rupture ↓ Activate emergency vascular pathway
exam_trap: C, give fluids to a normal BP before referral — resuscitation feels instinctive, but aggressive fluids can worsen bleeding and any delay to the vascular team costs lives.
takeaway: Suspected ruptured AAA: immediate vascular referral with permissive hypotension.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has symmetrical pain and swelling affecting the small joints of both hands. Morning stiffness lasts over an hour.

Which investigation is particularly useful when rheumatoid arthritis is suspected?
correct_answer: B. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies
why_correct: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies support the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis when considered alongside the clinical picture.
why_wrong: A. ANA and complement are used when SLE is suspected and are not specific for rheumatoid arthritis. C. HLA-B27 is associated with spondyloarthritis rather than rheumatoid arthritis. D. Serum urate is used in suspected gout. E. Amylase assesses pancreatic pathology.
pearl: Anti-CCP antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor for RA and predict erosive disease; seronegative RA still occurs, so persistent synovitis needs urgent rheumatology referral regardless.
thinking: Symmetrical small-joint swelling of both hands ↓ Morning stiffness over an hour ↓ Inflammatory polyarthritis ↓ Suspected rheumatoid arthritis ↓ Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP
exam_trap: A, antinuclear antibodies and complement — also used in inflammatory arthritis work-up, but they point towards SLE and are not specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
takeaway: Suspected RA: request rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP; anti-CCP is the more specific.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman has chronic widespread pain, fatigue and poor sleep. She asks whether she should remain completely inactive to avoid worsening her symptoms.

What is an appropriate general management principle?

options.B: Start regular long-term strong opioid analgesia
options.C: Rest until the pain has fully settled

correct_answer: D. Encourage regular graded physical activity
why_correct: Regular appropriately paced physical activity is an important component of management for chronic widespread pain such as fibromyalgia.
why_wrong: A. Prolonged bed rest can worsen deconditioning. B. Opioids are not recommended for chronic widespread pain because of harms without clear benefit. C. Waiting for pain to settle before resuming activity worsens deconditioning. E. Fluid restriction is unrelated.
pearl: In fibromyalgia, regular graded exercise is the best-supported intervention; explain the condition, address sleep and mood, and avoid strong opioids.
thinking: Chronic widespread pain ↓ Fatigue and poor sleep ↓ Likely fibromyalgia ↓ Inactivity worsens deconditioning ↓ Encourage regular graded physical activity
exam_trap: C, rest until the pain has fully settled — feels kind and protective, but the pain may never fully settle and waiting causes deconditioning that worsens symptoms.
takeaway: Chronic widespread pain: keep moving with graded activity, not rest or strong opioids.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with osteoporosis asks about vitamin D and calcium.

Which statement is most appropriate?

options.A: Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake supports bone health
options.B: Calcium intake should be reduced to prevent kidney stones
options.C: Vitamin D supplements accelerate bone loss in osteoporosis
options.D: Vitamin D mainly matters for bone growth in childhood
options.E: Calcium has little effect on adult bone health

correct_answer: A. Adequate calcium and vitamin D intake supports bone health
why_correct: Adequate calcium and vitamin D are important for maintaining normal bone health.
why_wrong: B. Adequate calcium intake is important in osteoporosis and should not be reduced. C. Vitamin D deficiency, rather than supplementation, impairs bone health. D. Vitamin D is relevant across the lifespan, including in older adults. E. Calcium is an important component of adult bone.
pearl: Calcium and vitamin D underpin osteoporosis care and should be optimised, often as supplements, alongside bone-protective drugs such as bisphosphonates in those at high fracture risk.
thinking: Man with osteoporosis ↓ Calcium is the main bone mineral ↓ Vitamin D enables calcium absorption ↓ Adequate intake supports bone health
exam_trap: B, reduce calcium to prevent kidney stones — sounds cautious, but restricting calcium worsens bone health and is not advised in osteoporosis.
takeaway: In osteoporosis, ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D alongside fracture-prevention treatment.

stem:
A 31-year-old man develops sudden severe pain and swelling in the ankle after twisting it while playing football. He cannot bear weight.

Which initial imaging investigation is most appropriate when a fracture is suspected?
why_correct: Plain radiography is the usual initial imaging investigation when a clinically significant fracture is suspected.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy is unrelated. C. Abdominal ultrasound does not assess an ankle fracture. D. Echocardiography assesses the heart. E. Brain MRI is unrelated.
pearl: Plain X-ray is the first-line imaging for a suspected fracture; always request two views at right angles and include the adjacent joints where relevant.
thinking: Twisting ankle injury ↓ Severe pain and swelling ↓ Unable to bear weight ↓ Suspected fracture ↓ X-ray
exam_trap: E, MRI of the brain — MRI sounds like the most detailed imaging, but this images the wrong region entirely; a suspected ankle fracture needs a plain X-ray first.
takeaway: Suspected fracture: plain X-ray first, with two views.

stem:
A 24-year-old man injures his ankle while playing football. There is localised bony tenderness and he cannot take four steps.

What does this indicate?

options.A: An MRI of the ankle is needed before any plain X-ray is taken
options.B: A simple sprain is likely, so no imaging is needed at this stage
options.C: Reassess after 1 week of rest before considering an X-ray
options.D: Antibiotics are required to prevent infection of the joint
options.E: Possible fracture: Ottawa rules indicate an ankle X-ray

correct_answer: E. Possible fracture: Ottawa rules indicate an ankle X-ray
why_correct: Inability to bear weight and significant bony tenderness are important features used when deciding whether ankle radiography is required.
why_wrong: A. MRI is not the first-line investigation; when Ottawa criteria are met a plain ankle X-ray is indicated. B. Bony tenderness with inability to weight-bear meets the Ottawa criteria for X-ray, so a simple sprain cannot be assumed. C. Delaying appropriate imaging is unsafe when Ottawa criteria are met. D. Antibiotics are not routinely indicated for a closed injury.
pearl: Ottawa ankle rules: X-ray if there is malleolar pain plus bony tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps both immediately and in the department.
thinking: Football ankle injury ↓ Localised bony tenderness ↓ Cannot take four steps ↓ Ottawa criteria met ↓ Ankle X-ray for possible fracture
exam_trap: B, simple sprain likely, no imaging — sprains are far more common than fractures, but bony tenderness with inability to weight-bear meets Ottawa criteria and demands an X-ray.
takeaway: After an ankle injury, malleolar bony tenderness or inability to take four steps means an X-ray under the Ottawa rules.

stem:
A 52-year-old man presents with a painful swollen ankle following an injury. There is a visible deformity.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Encourage early weight-bearing to reduce stiffness
options.B: Apply heat and discharge without assessment
options.C: Immobilise the limb and arrange urgent assessment
options.D: Arrange outpatient fracture clinic review next week

correct_answer: C. Immobilise the limb and arrange urgent assessment
why_correct: A visibly deformed injured limb may represent a fracture or dislocation and requires urgent assessment and appropriate immobilisation.
why_wrong: A. Weight-bearing on a deformed injured ankle could worsen the injury. B. Heat and discharge without assessment are inappropriate. D. Visible deformity needs urgent assessment and immobilisation, not delayed outpatient review. E. Forceful manipulation without appropriate expertise is unsafe.
pearl: A deformed injured limb needs urgent assessment of neurovascular status and skin; immobilise, give analgesia and X-ray, and reduce promptly if the circulation or skin is threatened.
thinking: Ankle injury ↓ Painful swelling ↓ Visible deformity ↓ Fracture or dislocation likely ↓ Immobilise and arrange urgent assessment
exam_trap: D, outpatient fracture clinic next week — a real pathway, but a visibly deformed limb risks neurovascular and skin compromise and needs same-day assessment.
takeaway: Deformity after injury: immobilise, check neurovascular status and assess urgently.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, bloating and diarrhoea. She reports that symptoms are worse after eating bread and pasta. She has lost 4 kg over the past 6 months. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
why_correct: Coeliac disease should be investigated with coeliac serology while the patient is still eating gluten.
why_wrong: A. CT is not an appropriate first-line test. C. Colonoscopy is not the initial investigation for suspected coeliac disease. D. Faecal occult blood testing does not diagnose coeliac disease. E. Faecal calprotectin is mainly used to assess possible intestinal inflammation.
pearl: Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA) is the first test for suspected coeliac disease, done while still eating gluten; positive results lead to duodenal biopsy referral in adults.
thinking: Abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhoea ↓ Worse with bread and pasta ↓ Weight loss ↓ Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Coeliac serology
exam_trap: E, faecal calprotectin — a sensible test for chronic diarrhoea when inflammatory bowel disease is in question, but the gluten link points to coeliac disease, tested by serology.
takeaway: Gluten-related symptoms: start with coeliac serology while the patient still eats gluten.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents with gradual difficulty swallowing. Initially she struggled with solid food, but she now has difficulty swallowing liquids as well. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia starting with solids and later involving liquids in an older adult indicates a progressively narrowing mechanical obstruction, which is oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise; NICE NG12 (recs 1.2.1 and 1.2.7, amended 2025) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for anyone with dysphagia.
why_wrong: A. Globus is a sensation of a lump in the throat without true swallowing impairment. C. Achalasia typically causes dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset, often with regurgitation, usually in younger patients. D. Oropharyngeal dysphagia causes difficulty initiating swallowing with coughing, choking or nasal regurgitation. E. A peptic stricture can cause progressive solid dysphagia but usually with long-standing reflux, and malignancy is the more likely and more important diagnosis at this age.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia, solids first then liquids, in an older adult is oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise; dysphagia warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for urgent endoscopy.
thinking: 72-year-old ↓ Gradual dysphagia ↓ Solids first, now liquids ↓ Progressive mechanical narrowing ↓ Oesophageal cancer
exam_trap: C, achalasia — a classic cause of dysphagia to liquids, but it affects solids and liquids from the outset, usually in younger patients, rather than progressing from solids.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia, solids then liquids, in an older adult: oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 35-year-old man has recurrent episodes of painful oral ulcers. Examination reveals ulcers with a grey-white base and surrounding erythema. He is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent painful shallow oral ulcers with a pale base and erythematous margin are typical of aphthous ulcers.
why_wrong: A. Leukoplakia is a persistent white patch that cannot be scraped off. B. Candidiasis usually produces removable white plaques. C. Herpes commonly produces grouped vesicles and ulcers, often affecting the lips or keratinised mucosa. E. Lichen planus commonly produces a characteristic white lacy pattern.
pearl: Aphthous ulcers are shallow, round and recurrent with a grey-white base and red halo; any single mouth ulcer persisting beyond about three weeks needs urgent referral to exclude oral cancer.
thinking: Recurrent painful oral ulcers ↓ Grey-white base with erythematous halo ↓ Otherwise well ↓ Aphthous ulcers
exam_trap: C, oral herpes simplex — also causes recurrent painful mouth lesions, but typically grouped vesicles that ulcerate, often on the lips or keratinised mucosa.
takeaway: Recurrent shallow ulcers with a grey-white base and red halo in a well adult are aphthous.

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain, constipation and feeling unusually cold. Which thyroid function test pattern is most consistent with primary hypothyroidism?
why_correct: In primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid produces insufficient hormone, causing low FT4 and compensatory elevation of TSH.
why_wrong: B. May occur in inappropriate TSH secretion rather than primary hypothyroidism. C. Does not indicate primary hypothyroidism. D. Suggests central hypothyroidism. E. Consistent with hyperthyroidism.
pearl: TSH is the best single test for primary thyroid disease: high TSH with low FT4 means primary hypothyroidism, while low TSH with low FT4 points to pituitary or hypothalamic disease.
thinking: Fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance ↓ Hypothyroid features ↓ Primary disease = failing gland, low FT4 ↓ Loss of negative feedback raises TSH ↓ High TSH, low FT4
exam_trap: D, low TSH, low FT4 — also hypothyroidism, which makes it tempting, but this is the central pattern from pituitary failure, not primary thyroid failure.
takeaway: Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH, low FT4; low TSH with low FT4 is central.

stem: A 19-year-old student develops sudden severe unilateral headache associated with photophobia and vomiting. He reports that he has had identical attacks several times previously. Between attacks he is completely well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent stereotyped attacks of headache with photophobia and vomiting, with complete recovery between episodes, are typical of migraine.
why_wrong: A. Meningitis usually causes systemic illness with fever and meningeal features. B. Brain tumours usually produce progressive or persistent symptoms. D. Temporal arteritis predominantly affects older adults. E. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically causes a sudden thunderclap headache and requires urgent assessment.
pearl: Migraine is recurrent and stereotyped, often unilateral with photophobia and vomiting, and fully resolves between attacks; a first or worst-ever thunderclap headache needs subarachnoid haemorrhage excluded.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Unilateral headache with photophobia and vomiting ↓ Several identical previous attacks ↓ Completely well between attacks ↓ Migraine
exam_trap: E, subarachnoid haemorrhage — sudden severe headache with vomiting tempts, but identical recurrent attacks with full recovery fit migraine rather than a single thunderclap event.
takeaway: Recurrent identical headaches with full recovery are migraine; a new thunderclap is SAH until excluded.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with a new persistent cough and coughing up small amounts of blood. He has smoked for 40 years. What diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
why_correct: Haemoptysis with a persistent cough in a long-term smoker is a red-flag presentation for lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. Asthma causes variable wheeze and breathlessness rather than unexplained haemoptysis. B. Viral infections can cause cough but do not adequately explain persistent haemoptysis in this context. C. Reflux may cause chronic cough but does not explain haemoptysis. E. Allergic rhinitis does not usually cause haemoptysis.
pearl: Unexplained haemoptysis at 40 or over warrants a suspected lung cancer pathway referral; a long smoking history makes lung cancer the diagnosis to exclude first.
thinking: 68-year-old with 40-year smoking history ↓ New persistent cough ↓ Haemoptysis ↓ Red flags for malignancy ↓ Lung cancer
exam_trap: B, viral upper respiratory infection — a common cause of cough and minor blood-streaking, but it is self-limiting and cannot explain persistent cough with haemoptysis in a long-term smoker.
takeaway: Haemoptysis in an older smoker is lung cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with a painful, swollen, red calf. Which feature would most strongly support cellulitis rather than DVT?

options.B: Calf tenderness along the deep venous system
options.C: Unilateral calf swelling of more than 3 cm
options.D: Previous proximal DVT in the same leg last year
options.E: Well-demarcated warm erythema of the skin

correct_answer: E. Well-demarcated warm erythema of the skin
why_correct: Prominent superficial erythema and warmth favour cellulitis.
why_wrong: A. Recent immobility increases the risk of DVT. B. Localised tenderness along the deep venous system is a Wells criterion favouring DVT. C. Unilateral swelling occurs in both conditions, and calf swelling of more than 3 cm is a Wells criterion for DVT. D. Previous DVT increases the likelihood of recurrent DVT.
pearl: Cellulitis is a skin infection, so it shows spreading warm erythema of the skin itself; DVT causes deep swelling and tenderness, and when doubt remains use the Wells score and ultrasound.
thinking: Painful, swollen, red calf ↓ Cellulitis versus DVT ↓ Cellulitis involves the skin itself ↓ Well-demarcated warm erythema
exam_trap: C, unilateral calf swelling of more than 3 cm — a striking finding that sounds decisive, but it is a Wells criterion for DVT, not a feature favouring cellulitis.
takeaway: Superficial warm erythema favours cellulitis; deep venous tenderness and calf swelling favour DVT.

stem: A 42-year-old woman develops proximal muscle weakness. She finds it difficult to climb stairs and lift objects above her head. Sensation is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Predominantly proximal weakness with preserved sensation is characteristic of a muscle disorder.
why_wrong: A. MS can cause weakness but does not characteristically present as isolated symmetrical proximal weakness. B. Peripheral neuropathy commonly causes distal weakness and sensory abnormalities. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve distribution in the hand. E. Radiculopathy follows a nerve-root distribution and often causes pain or sensory changes.
pearl: Proximal symmetrical weakness (stairs, lifting overhead) with normal sensation suggests myopathy; check creatine kinase, thyroid function and drugs such as statins or steroids, and consider inflammatory myositis.
thinking: Difficulty climbing stairs ↓ Difficulty lifting above the head ↓ Proximal weakness ↓ Sensation normal ↓ Myopathy
exam_trap: B, peripheral neuropathy — weakness makes a nerve cause tempting, but neuropathy is usually distal with sensory loss, whereas here weakness is proximal with normal sensation.
takeaway: Proximal weakness with intact sensation points to muscle disease.

stem: A 34-year-old man develops severe pain and swelling in his calf following a long-distance flight. Which investigation is commonly used to assess suspected DVT?

options.A: Plain radiograph of the lower leg
options.D: Plain chest X-ray in the PA view

why_correct: Compression ultrasound is the standard imaging investigation for suspected lower-limb DVT.
why_wrong: A. A plain radiograph cannot detect venous thrombosis. C. CT pulmonary angiography is used for suspected pulmonary embolism, not DVT. D. Chest X-ray does not diagnose DVT. E. Spirometry and gas transfer assess lung function.
pearl: Suspected DVT is assessed with the two-level Wells score and proximal leg compression ultrasound; D-dimer helps rule out DVT when clinical probability is low.
thinking: Calf pain and swelling ↓ Long-distance flight = immobility risk ↓ Suspected DVT ↓ Image the deep veins ↓ Compression duplex ultrasound
exam_trap: C, CT pulmonary angiography — a key test in venous thromboembolism, but it images the pulmonary arteries for PE; DVT is shown on leg ultrasound.
takeaway: Suspected DVT: leg compression ultrasound; suspected PE: CTPA.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding. She is otherwise well and has no pelvic mass or significant pain. Which complication should be specifically considered?
why_correct: Chronic heavy menstrual bleeding can cause iron depletion and iron-deficiency anaemia.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism is not a typical direct complication. B. Chronic blood loss is more likely to cause anaemia than polycythaemia. C. Respiratory alkalosis is unrelated to chronic menstrual blood loss. D. Heavy menstrual bleeding does not typically cause hypercalcaemia.
pearl: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count; iron deficiency is common and should be treated alongside management of the bleeding itself.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding ↓ Repeated chronic blood loss ↓ Iron stores depleted ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia
exam_trap: A, hyperthyroidism — thyroid disorders can disturb menstruation, so it sounds linked, but it is not a complication of heavy bleeding; chronic blood loss causes iron deficiency.
takeaway: Heavy menstrual bleeding: check a full blood count for iron-deficiency anaemia.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with painless enlargement of a cervical lymph node that has persisted for 6 weeks. He has no evidence of an acute infection. What should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy, particularly in an adult, requires assessment for malignancy among other causes.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not cause cervical lymphadenopathy. B. Migraine does not cause lymph node enlargement. C. Muscle strain does not cause persistent cervical lymphadenopathy. D. Gastroenteritis does not explain a persistent cervical node.
pearl: A painless cervical node persisting for weeks without infection in an adult needs urgent assessment for lymphoma or metastatic head and neck cancer.
thinking: 58-year-old ↓ Painless cervical lymph node ↓ Persisting 6 weeks ↓ No infective cause ↓ Malignancy
exam_trap: C, simple muscle strain — a neck lump can be mistaken for a strained muscle, but a strain does not produce a persistent enlarged lymph node.
takeaway: A painless persistent neck node in an adult needs malignancy excluded.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with a painless swelling in his neck. Examination reveals multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes. He reports night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent lymphadenopathy with systemic symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss is concerning for lymphoma.
why_wrong: A. Tension headache does not cause lymphadenopathy. B. Osteoarthritis does not cause enlarged lymph nodes. C. Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal skin infection and does not explain this presentation. E. IBS does not cause persistent cervical lymphadenopathy or systemic weight loss.
pearl: Painless lymphadenopathy with B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss) is classic for lymphoma, with Hodgkin lymphoma peaking in young adults; it needs urgent referral and tissue biopsy.
thinking: Young adult ↓ Multiple painless cervical nodes ↓ Night sweats and weight loss = B symptoms ↓ Lymphoma
exam_trap: C, tinea corporis — a skin infection can cause regional reactive nodes, but it does not explain night sweats, weight loss and multiple painless cervical nodes.
takeaway: Painless nodes plus B symptoms means lymphoma until proven otherwise.

stem: A 70-year-old man has been taking prednisolone for several months. Which adverse effect is particularly associated with prolonged corticosteroid treatment?
why_correct: Long-term corticosteroid treatment increases the risk of osteoporosis and fragility fractures.
why_wrong: A. Steroids can cause potassium loss, but adrenal suppression itself does not cause hypokalaemia. B. Severe neutropenia is not a typical complication of corticosteroid therapy. D. Bradycardia is not a characteristic adverse effect. E. Corticosteroids can increase blood glucose.
pearl: Anyone on long-term oral corticosteroids, typically three months or more, should have fracture risk assessed and bone protection considered, often a bisphosphonate with calcium and vitamin D.
thinking: Prednisolone for several months ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and increase resorption ↓ Loss of bone mineral density ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: A, hypokalaemia caused by adrenal suppression — steroids can lower potassium, but adrenal suppression is not the mechanism; osteoporosis is the hallmark long-term risk.
takeaway: Long-term steroids cause osteoporosis: assess fracture risk and give bone protection.

stem: A 45-year-old woman taking methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis develops a persistent dry cough and increasing breathlessness. What adverse effect should be considered?

options.A: Pulmonary embolism caused directly by methotrexate

why_correct: Methotrexate can rarely cause pneumonitis, presenting with cough, dyspnoea and systemic symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Methotrexate is not a typical direct cause of pulmonary embolism. B. Lung cancer is possible in general but the medication-related complication is particularly relevant here. C. Pneumothorax usually causes sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness. D. Pulmonary oedema usually has clinical features of heart failure.
pearl: New cough and breathlessness on methotrexate suggests pneumonitis, which can be life-threatening: withhold methotrexate and arrange urgent assessment with chest imaging.
thinking: Methotrexate for RA ↓ Persistent dry cough ↓ Increasing breathlessness ↓ Drug-induced lung toxicity ↓ Methotrexate-associated pneumonitis
exam_trap: B, lung cancer — always worth considering with a persistent cough, but the drug history makes methotrexate pneumonitis the key adverse effect to recognise.
takeaway: Cough and breathlessness on methotrexate: think pneumonitis and stop the drug pending review.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is 8 weeks pregnant and has severe vomiting. She is unable to keep fluids down and feels dizzy when standing. What complication is most concerning?
why_correct: Severe vomiting with poor oral intake and postural dizziness suggests significant dehydration.
why_wrong: A. COPD does not explain the presentation. C. Vomiting does not specifically cause polycythaemia. D. Hypothermia is unrelated. E. Hypercalcaemia is not the expected complication.
pearl: Hyperemesis gravidarum is protracted vomiting with dehydration, weight loss or electrolyte imbalance; inability to keep fluids down needs assessment, IV fluids and antiemetics, with ketones and electrolytes checked.
thinking: 8 weeks pregnant ↓ Severe vomiting, cannot keep fluids down ↓ Postural dizziness ↓ Fluid depletion ↓ Dehydration
exam_trap: C, polycythaemia — dehydration can raise the haematocrit, which tempts, but that is relative haemoconcentration, not polycythaemia; the real danger is fluid depletion.
takeaway: Severe pregnancy vomiting with postural symptoms means dehydration needing IV fluids.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has vaginal bleeding 3 years after her last menstrual period. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.B: Arrange review only if bleeding becomes painful
options.C: Reassure her that this is normal

correct_answer: D. Investigate for possible endometrial cancer
why_correct: Any postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment because endometrial cancer is an important cause.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. B. Investigation should not be delayed until pain develops. C. Postmenopausal bleeding is not considered normal. E. Combined contraception is not an appropriate response.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; refer urgently, usually on a suspected cancer pathway, with transvaginal ultrasound to assess endometrial thickness.
thinking: 55-year-old ↓ Last period 3 years ago ↓ Vaginal bleeding = postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Endometrial cancer must be excluded ↓ Investigate
exam_trap: C, reassure her that this is normal — tempting if bleeding is light or atrophy seems likely, but postmenopausal bleeding is never normal and needs urgent investigation.
takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer.

stem: A 60-year-old man with COPD becomes increasingly drowsy and confused. He has severe breathlessness and reduced oxygen saturation. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Severe COPD with worsening drowsiness and confusion can indicate carbon dioxide retention and hypercapnic respiratory failure.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis, even with sepsis, does not explain this respiratory presentation in COPD. B. Migraine does not explain severe respiratory compromise. D. Otitis externa is unrelated to this respiratory deterioration. E. There is no history of liver disease, and hepatic encephalopathy does not explain the respiratory deterioration.
pearl: In COPD, drowsiness and confusion signal rising carbon dioxide; obtain an arterial blood gas, give controlled oxygen targeting 88–92%, and consider non-invasive ventilation for respiratory acidosis.
thinking: COPD ↓ Severe breathlessness and low saturation ↓ Increasing drowsiness and confusion ↓ CO2 retention ↓ Hypercapnic respiratory failure
exam_trap: E, hepatic encephalopathy — also causes drowsiness and confusion, but there is no liver history and it does not explain the respiratory deterioration in COPD.
takeaway: Drowsy, confused COPD patient: suspect CO2 retention and check an ABG.

stem: A 62-year-old man with diabetes becomes sweaty, shaky and confused. His capillary blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L. What is the immediate priority?
why_correct: A glucose of 2.4 mmol/L with symptoms represents clinically significant hypoglycaemia requiring immediate treatment.
why_wrong: B. Insulin would worsen the hypoglycaemia. C. A statin has no role in acute management. D. Colonoscopy is unrelated. E. Carbohydrate restriction is inappropriate during hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia is glucose below 4 mmol/L; if conscious and able to swallow give fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck after 10–15 minutes, then give longer-acting carbohydrate.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Sweaty, shaky, confused ↓ Capillary glucose 2.4 mmol/L ↓ Symptomatic hypoglycaemia ↓ Treat immediately
exam_trap: B, start insulin — insulin is linked with diabetes care, but giving it now would drive glucose lower and could be fatal.
takeaway: Symptomatic low glucose in diabetes: give fast-acting glucose first.

stem: A 73-year-old man has progressive memory impairment. His wife reports that he repeatedly asks the same questions and struggles with familiar tasks. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive cognitive decline affecting memory and everyday functioning is characteristic of dementia.
why_wrong: A. Delirium develops acutely and fluctuates. B. Psychosis is characterised by disturbances such as delusions or hallucinations. C. Syncope is transient loss of consciousness rather than progressive cognitive decline. E. Panic disorder causes recurrent episodes of intense anxiety.
pearl: Dementia is a gradual, progressive decline in memory and other cognition that impairs daily function; screen for reversible contributors such as thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, depression and medicines.
thinking: 73-year-old ↓ Progressive memory impairment ↓ Repetitive questions, struggles with familiar tasks ↓ Gradual decline affecting function ↓ Dementia
exam_trap: A, delirium — also causes confusion in older adults, but delirium is acute and fluctuating, whereas this decline is gradual and progressive.
takeaway: Gradual progressive cognitive decline is dementia; acute fluctuating confusion is delirium.

stem: A 45-year-old man reports persistent low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities, poor sleep and reduced energy for 2 months. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent low mood and anhedonia with associated biological and psychological symptoms over several weeks are typical of depression.
why_wrong: A. Generalised anxiety disorder causes persistent excessive worry; low mood with anhedonia is the core feature here. B. Specific phobia causes marked fear of a particular object or situation. D. Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition. E. Hypomania involves elevated or irritable mood with increased energy and activity.
pearl: Core features of depression are persistent low mood and anhedonia for at least two weeks, with biological symptoms such as poor sleep, low energy and appetite change; always assess suicide risk.
thinking: Persistent low mood ↓ Loss of interest = anhedonia ↓ Poor sleep, reduced energy ↓ Lasting 2 months ↓ Major depressive episode
exam_trap: A, generalised anxiety disorder — often coexists and disturbs sleep, but its core is excessive worry; low mood with anhedonia defines depression.
takeaway: Low mood plus anhedonia for over two weeks is a depressive episode; always ask about suicide.

stem: A 35-year-old man reports hearing voices when nobody is present. He believes that strangers are sending him secret messages through television programmes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Hallucinations and delusional beliefs are characteristic features of psychosis.
why_wrong: A. Specific phobia causes fear of a particular stimulus. B. OCD involves intrusive thoughts and compulsions, with preserved reality testing usually. C. Panic disorder causes episodic intense anxiety. E. Generalised anxiety causes excessive worry.
pearl: Hallucinations (voices) and delusions (messages sent through the television) define psychosis; refer a first episode urgently to early intervention in psychosis services and assess risk.
thinking: Hears voices when nobody is present = hallucinations ↓ Believes TV sends him messages = delusion of reference ↓ Loss of reality testing ↓ Psychosis
exam_trap: B, OCD — intrusive unwanted thoughts can sound bizarre, but in OCD insight is usually preserved and the thoughts are recognised as the person's own.
takeaway: Hallucinations plus delusions mean psychosis; OCD thoughts are recognised as one's own.

stem: A 30-year-old man is found unconscious with very slow breathing and pinpoint pupils. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
why_correct: The combination of reduced consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils is characteristic of opioid toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotic overdose has different characteristic toxic effects. B. Stimulant toxicity typically causes agitation, tachycardia and hypertension. D. Beta-blocker overdose may cause bradycardia and hypotension but not this classic toxidrome. E. SSRI overdose does not typically cause profound respiratory depression with pinpoint pupils.
pearl: Reduced consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils is opioid toxicity: support airway and breathing and give naloxone, repeated as needed because it is shorter-acting than many opioids.
thinking: Unconscious young man ↓ Very slow breathing ↓ Pinpoint pupils ↓ Classic opioid toxidrome ↓ Opioids
exam_trap: D, beta-blockers — overdose can also cause reduced consciousness and bradycardia, but pinpoint pupils with slow breathing is the classic opioid toxidrome.
takeaway: Coma, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils: opioid toxicity, treat with naloxone.

stem: A 36-year-old man presents with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. Examination reveals a painful irreducible groin swelling. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: An irreducible painful hernia with abdominal pain and vomiting raises concern for obstruction and strangulation.
why_wrong: A. The swelling is irreducible and painful, so this is not an uncomplicated reducible hernia. B. Ureteric colic causes loin-to-groin pain without an irreducible groin swelling. C. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain and a high-riding testis rather than an irreducible groin swelling. E. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms.
pearl: A painful, irreducible hernia with abdominal pain and vomiting suggests obstruction and strangulation; this is a surgical emergency needing urgent surgical review and operation to save the bowel.
thinking: Groin swelling ↓ Painful and irreducible ↓ Abdominal pain and vomiting = obstruction ↓ Compromised blood supply ↓ Strangulated inguinal hernia
exam_trap: C, torsion of the spermatic cord — an acute emergency in the same region, but it causes scrotal pain with a high-riding testis, not an irreducible groin swelling with obstruction.
takeaway: Painful irreducible hernia with vomiting is strangulation until proven otherwise: emergency surgery.

stem: A 61-year-old man has chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms. He develops increasing difficulty swallowing. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_correct: New dysphagia in a patient with reflux is an alarm symptom requiring prompt investigation.
why_wrong: A. Physiotherapy has no role. B. Fluid restriction is inappropriate. C. New dysphagia is an alarm symptom; an empirical PPI trial delays urgent investigation. D. Dental assessment does not investigate oesophageal dysphagia.
pearl: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom that needs urgent endoscopy; in long-standing reflux it may signal peptic stricture, Barrett's oesophagus or adenocarcinoma.
thinking: Chronic reflux ↓ New, increasing dysphagia ↓ Alarm symptom ↓ Possible stricture or cancer ↓ Urgent upper GI assessment
exam_trap: C, double-dose PPI trial — sensible for reflux symptoms alone, but new dysphagia is an alarm feature and a PPI trial only delays urgent investigation.
takeaway: Reflux plus new dysphagia: urgent endoscopy, not a PPI trial.

stem: A 74-year-old man presents with severe central abdominal pain and vomiting. His abdomen is distended and bowel sounds are high-pitched. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Abdominal distension, vomiting and high-pitched bowel sounds in the context of severe abdominal pain are typical features of intestinal obstruction.
why_wrong: A. GORD causes upper gastrointestinal reflux symptoms. B. Simple constipation generally does not cause this acute obstructive presentation. C. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms rather than bowel obstruction.
pearl: Bowel obstruction presents with colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation, with tinkling bowel sounds; adhesions and hernias are common small-bowel causes and cancer a key large-bowel cause.
thinking: Severe central abdominal pain ↓ Vomiting ↓ Distension ↓ High-pitched bowel sounds ↓ Intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, uncomplicated constipation — common in older adults and can cause distension, but not severe pain, vomiting and high-pitched obstructive bowel sounds.
takeaway: Pain, vomiting, distension and tinkling bowel sounds mean bowel obstruction.

stem: A 22-year-old man notices a painless, firm lump within his right testis. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassurance and review in one year

why_correct: A new painless testicular mass requires urgent assessment for testicular malignancy, with ultrasound forming a key part of evaluation.
why_wrong: A. A persistent testicular mass should not simply be observed. C. A painless firm intratesticular lump without infective features should not be treated as epididymitis. D. Compression stockings are unrelated. E. Massage has no diagnostic or therapeutic role.
pearl: A painless firm lump within the testis is cancer until proven otherwise; testicular cancer peaks in young men, and urgent ultrasound with tumour markers precedes urological management.
thinking: Young man ↓ Painless lump ↓ Firm and within the testis ↓ Possible testicular cancer ↓ Urgent testicular ultrasound
exam_trap: C, antibiotics for presumed epididymitis — a common scrotal diagnosis in young men, but epididymitis is painful and tender; a painless intratesticular lump needs imaging, not antibiotics.
takeaway: Painless intratesticular lump in a young man: urgent ultrasound to exclude cancer.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a weak urinary stream, hesitancy and a feeling of incomplete bladder emptying. Which symptom is most characteristic of bladder outlet obstruction?
why_correct: Hesitancy is a typical voiding symptom associated with bladder outlet obstruction, commonly due to prostatic enlargement.
why_wrong: B. Loin-to-groin colicky pain suggests ureteric colic rather than bladder outlet obstruction. C. Photophobia and headache are neurological symptoms. D. Tinnitus is an auditory symptom. E. Dysphagia to solids concerns swallowing.
pearl: Lower urinary tract symptoms divide into voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, straining, incomplete emptying) and storage (frequency, urgency, nocturia); voiding symptoms point to bladder outlet obstruction.
thinking: 58-year-old man ↓ Weak stream, incomplete emptying ↓ Voiding symptoms ↓ Bladder outlet obstruction ↓ Urinary hesitancy
exam_trap: B, loin-to-groin colicky pain — a urological symptom, but it reflects ureteric colic from a stone, not obstruction at the bladder outlet.
takeaway: Hesitancy, weak stream and incomplete emptying are voiding symptoms of outlet obstruction.

stem: A 25-year-old man is diagnosed with chlamydia. He asks why his recent sexual partners need to be contacted. What is the main reason?

options.A: To check his partners' hepatitis B vaccination status
options.B: To record his partners' blood groups for antenatal screening
options.C: To treat infected partners and reduce transmission
options.E: To arrange routine fertility testing for his partners

correct_answer: C. To treat infected partners and reduce transmission
why_correct: Partner notification helps identify and treat infections in contacts and reduces onward transmission and reinfection.
why_wrong: A. Checking vaccination status is not the purpose of chlamydia partner notification. B. Blood group testing is irrelevant to chlamydia partner notification. D. Chlamydia partner notification is not a diabetes-screening strategy. E. Fertility assessment is not the immediate purpose of partner notification.
pearl: Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so partner notification finds and treats infected contacts, prevents reinfection of the index patient and reduces complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease.
thinking: Chlamydia diagnosed ↓ Partners often asymptomatic ↓ Untreated partners transmit and reinfect ↓ Treat infected partners and reduce transmission
exam_trap: E, routine fertility testing for partners — chlamydia can affect fertility, which tempts, but notification exists to test and treat contacts, not for fertility work-up.
takeaway: Partner notification exists to treat contacts and break the chain of transmission.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with painful, swollen joints and a new skin rash several days after developing a sore throat. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Migratory inflammatory arthritis following a recent streptococcal throat infection is a classic feature of acute rheumatic fever.
why_wrong: A. Polymyalgia rheumatica affects older adults with proximal girdle pain and stiffness, not post-pharyngitis arthritis with rash. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without inflammatory arthritis. D. Gout usually causes an acute monoarthritis in older adults and is not triggered by a sore throat. E. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and not triggered by a recent throat infection.
pearl: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and causes migratory polyarthritis, carditis and rashes such as erythema marginatum; diagnosis uses the Jones criteria with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.
thinking: Recent sore throat ↓ Possible streptococcal infection ↓ Painful swollen joints plus new rash ↓ Post-streptococcal immune reaction ↓ Acute rheumatic fever
exam_trap: D, acute polyarticular gout — swollen painful joints suggest crystal arthritis, but gout is unusual in a young woman, is not triggered by a sore throat and does not cause a rash.
takeaway: Arthritis and rash after a sore throat: think acute rheumatic fever.

stem: A 45-year-old man has painful, red nodules over both shins. He recently developed diarrhoea after travelling abroad. What skin manifestation should be considered?
why_correct: Tender erythematous nodules over the shins are characteristic of erythema nodosum, which can occur after infections and with inflammatory diseases.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals. B. Psoriasis causes scaly plaques. C. Tinea corporis causes annular scaly lesions. D. Lichen planus causes itchy violaceous flat-topped papules, not acute tender nodules.
pearl: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis causing tender red shin nodules; triggers include streptococcal and gastrointestinal infections, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, TB, pregnancy and drugs.
thinking: Painful red nodules ↓ Over both shins ↓ Recent diarrhoea after travel ↓ Reactive panniculitis after infection ↓ Erythema nodosum
exam_trap: A, urticaria — a red rash after a gut infection can suggest an allergic reaction, but urticarial wheals are transient and itchy, not persistent tender shin nodules.
takeaway: Tender red shin nodules are erythema nodosum; look for the trigger.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has a photosensitive facial rash across her cheeks and nose. She also reports joint pains and fatigue. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: A photosensitive malar rash with arthralgia and systemic symptoms is suggestive of SLE.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis causes mechanical joint symptoms and not a photosensitive rash. C. Psoriatic arthritis is associated with scaly psoriatic plaques, not a photosensitive malar rash. D. Cellulitis is an acute localised bacterial skin infection. E. Facial seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy scale involving the nasolabial folds and is not photosensitive or associated with arthralgia.
pearl: A photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, with arthralgia and fatigue, suggests SLE; ANA is a sensitive screening test, while anti-dsDNA is more specific.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Photosensitive rash over cheeks and nose ↓ Joint pain and fatigue ↓ Multisystem autoimmune picture ↓ Systemic lupus erythematosus
exam_trap: E, seborrhoeic dermatitis — another common rash in the same facial area, but it is greasy and scaly, involves the nasolabial folds and causes no joint pain or fatigue.
takeaway: Photosensitive malar rash plus arthralgia and fatigue: think SLE and check ANA.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has a painless ulcer beneath the ball of his foot. Examination reveals reduced sensation to light touch. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: A painless plantar ulcer in a person with diabetes and loss of protective sensation is characteristic of a neuropathic foot ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Arterial ulcers are typically painful and associated with poor perfusion. C. Venous ulcers usually occur around the gaiter region. D. A sacral pressure ulcer would occur over the sacrum, not the plantar foot. E. Cellulitis causes inflammatory skin changes rather than a chronic painless plantar ulcer.
pearl: Neuropathic diabetic ulcers form painlessly over pressure points such as the metatarsal heads; any diabetic foot ulcer needs urgent referral to the multidisciplinary foot service.
thinking: Diabetes ↓ Painless ulcer under ball of foot = pressure point ↓ Reduced sensation ↓ Loss of protective sensation ↓ Diabetic neuropathic ulcer
exam_trap: A, arterial ulcer — also common on the diabetic foot, but arterial ulcers are typically painful with signs of poor perfusion, not painless with sensory loss.
takeaway: A painless plantar ulcer with sensory loss in diabetes is neuropathic; refer to the foot team.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has severe pain in her hip after a minor fall. X-ray confirms a fracture. Which factor is most likely to have contributed?
why_correct: A low-trauma fracture in an older adult is strongly suggestive of underlying osteoporosis or reduced bone strength.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause fragility fractures. C. Asthma itself does not directly explain a low-trauma fracture. D. Hyperthyroidism can affect bone health, but osteoporosis is the direct condition associated with fragility fracture. E. Otitis media is unrelated.
pearl: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less is a fragility fracture and suggests osteoporosis; after hip fracture, assess bone health and falls risk to prevent the next fracture.
thinking: 72-year-old woman ↓ Minor fall ↓ Hip fracture = low-trauma fracture ↓ Reduced bone strength ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: D, hyperthyroidism alone — a genuine risk factor for bone loss, but it acts through reduced bone density; the direct explanation for a fragility fracture is osteoporosis.
takeaway: Low-trauma fracture in an older adult means osteoporosis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is found to have a vertebral compression fracture after minimal trauma. Which investigation may be used to assess bone mineral density?
why_correct: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry is used to assess bone mineral density.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy assesses the gastrointestinal tract. C. Audiometry assesses hearing. D. Spirometry assesses lung function. E. ECG assesses cardiac electrical activity.
pearl: DXA measures bone mineral density, reported as a T-score; a T-score of −2.5 or below defines osteoporosis, and a vertebral fragility fracture should prompt bone health assessment.
thinking: 70-year-old woman ↓ Vertebral compression fracture ↓ Minimal trauma = fragility fracture ↓ Suspected osteoporosis ↓ DXA scan
exam_trap: D, spirometry — a familiar routine test in older adults, but it measures lung function; bone mineral density is measured by DXA.
takeaway: Bone mineral density is measured by DXA; a fragility fracture should trigger it.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with persistent fatigue and widespread muscle aches. Examination is normal and inflammatory markers are normal. She has poor sleep and feels exhausted despite resting. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Widespread pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance and absence of objective inflammatory findings are typical of fibromyalgia.
why_wrong: B. Septic arthritis causes an acutely inflamed joint and systemic illness. C. Giant cell arteritis occurs mainly in older adults and causes headache and vascular symptoms. D. Osteomyelitis is an infection of bone and may cause local or systemic inflammatory features. E. Gout causes an acute inflamed joint.
pearl: Fibromyalgia is a clinical diagnosis of chronic widespread pain with fatigue and unrefreshing sleep; a normal examination and normal blood tests, including inflammatory markers, support it.
thinking: Widespread muscle aches ↓ Fatigue and poor sleep ↓ Normal examination ↓ Normal inflammatory markers ↓ Fibromyalgia
exam_trap: C, giant cell arteritis — aches and fatigue may suggest it, but it affects older adults, causes headache and raises inflammatory markers, which are normal here.
takeaway: Widespread pain, fatigue and poor sleep with normal tests suggests fibromyalgia.

stem: A 48-year-old man develops jaundice, dark urine and pale stools. Blood tests show a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase. What type of jaundice is suggested?
why_correct: Pale stools, dark urine and markedly raised alkaline phosphatase indicate impaired bile flow.
why_wrong: B. Neonatal jaundice occurs in newborns. C. Haemolysis predominantly causes unconjugated bilirubin elevation and does not typically produce pale stools. D. Anaemia alone does not explain cholestatic liver tests. E. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without cholestatic features.
pearl: Pale stools and dark urine mean conjugated bilirubin is not reaching the gut; with a markedly raised ALP, think obstruction such as gallstones or pancreatic head cancer and arrange ultrasound first.
thinking: Jaundice ↓ Dark urine and pale stools ↓ Bile not reaching the gut ↓ Markedly raised ALP ↓ Cholestatic/obstructive jaundice
exam_trap: C, haemolytic jaundice — a classic jaundice category, but haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, so there is no bilirubin in the urine and stools are not pale.
takeaway: Dark urine, pale stools and high ALP mean obstructive jaundice; ultrasound first.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. Which public-health measure is particularly important?
why_correct: Tuberculosis can be transmitted to close contacts, so contact tracing and appropriate assessment are important.
