stem: A 48-year-old man develops severe central abdominal pain followed by rigid abdominal muscles and marked tenderness. What condition should be suspected?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain with guarding and rigidity suggests peritoneal inflammation.
why_wrong: A. Biliary colic does not typically cause generalized rigidity. C. IBS does not cause peritonism. D. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. E. Functional dyspepsia does not cause peritoneal signs.
pearl: Board-like rigidity, guarding and marked tenderness indicate peritonitis, often from a perforated viscus; resuscitate, give analgesia and seek urgent surgical review.
thinking: Severe central abdominal pain ↓ Followed by rigid abdominal muscles ↓ Marked tenderness ↓ Signs of peritoneal irritation ↓ Peritonitis
exam_trap: A, biliary colic — it causes severe abdominal pain, but it is right upper quadrant pain without generalised rigidity; rigidity signals peritoneal inflammation.
takeaway: Abdominal rigidity and guarding mean peritonitis and need urgent surgical review.

stem: A 26-year-old man twists his knee while playing football. He subsequently develops locking of the knee and pain along the joint line. What injury should be considered?
why_correct: Joint-line pain with mechanical locking after a twisting injury is typical of a meniscal tear.
why_wrong: A. Plantar fasciitis affects the plantar heel. B. Achilles rupture affects the ankle. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the wrist and hand. D. Tennis elbow affects the lateral elbow.
pearl: A twisting injury on a weight-bearing knee followed by locking and joint-line tenderness suggests a meniscal tear; MRI confirms it when needed.
thinking: Twisting knee injury playing football ↓ Mechanical locking ↓ Joint-line pain ↓ Torn meniscal fragment blocking movement ↓ Meniscal tear
exam_trap: B, Achilles rupture — a common sports injury in young adults, but it affects the heel and ankle and causes loss of push-off power, not knee locking.
takeaway: Twisting injury plus locking and joint-line pain means meniscal tear.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has gradually increasing shoulder pain and marked difficulty moving her shoulder in several directions. Passive and active movement are both restricted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Frozen shoulder causes painful restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes acute inflammatory joint attacks. B. Tennis elbow affects the lateral elbow. D. Achilles tendinopathy affects the ankle. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median-nerve symptoms in the hand.
pearl: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) restricts both active and passive movement, especially external rotation; it is more common in middle age and in people with diabetes.
thinking: 58-year-old with gradually worsening shoulder pain ↓ Restriction in several directions ↓ Active and passive movement both limited ↓ Capsular stiffening ↓ Frozen shoulder
exam_trap: A, gout — it may tempt as a cause of joint pain and stiffness, but it causes acute, intensely inflamed attacks, not gradual global loss of shoulder movement.
takeaway: Loss of both active and passive shoulder movement suggests frozen shoulder.

stem: A 42-year-old man develops shoulder pain after repeatedly lifting heavy objects. There is painful movement of the shoulder, particularly when lifting the arm. What type of problem is most likely?
why_correct: Shoulder pain associated with overhead or lifting activities commonly results from rotator cuff pathology.
why_wrong: B. Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain. C. Achilles rupture affects the lower leg and ankle. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand. E. Meniscal injury affects the knee.
pearl: Rotator cuff disorders cause pain on lifting or abducting the arm, often with a painful arc, while passive range is largely preserved, which helps distinguish them from frozen shoulder.
thinking: Shoulder pain after repetitive heavy lifting ↓ Pain worse on raising the arm ↓ Overloaded cuff tendons under the acromion ↓ Rotator cuff disorder
exam_trap: E, meniscal tear — like cuff disease it is an overuse or sports soft-tissue injury, but it occurs in the knee, so it cannot explain shoulder pain on lifting.
takeaway: Shoulder pain on lifting or abduction after overuse suggests rotator cuff pathology.

stem: A 74-year-old man has severe back pain following a minor fall. An X-ray shows a vertebral compression fracture. Which condition is an important underlying risk factor?
why_correct: Osteoporosis weakens bone and can cause vertebral compression fractures after minimal trauma.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a peripheral nerve disorder. B. IBS does not cause bone fragility. C. Migraine does not cause vertebral fractures. D. Gout does not typically cause fragility fractures.
pearl: A vertebral compression fracture after minimal trauma is a fragility fracture; treat the pain, assess bone health and consider whether causes such as myeloma or metastases need excluding.
thinking: 74-year-old man ↓ Severe back pain after a minor fall ↓ Vertebral compression fracture on X-ray ↓ Minimal trauma suggests fragile bone ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: D, gout — a common metabolic condition in older men, but it causes inflammatory arthritis, not bone fragility or compression fractures.
takeaway: Vertebral fracture from minor trauma signals osteoporosis, in men as well as women.

stem: A 76-year-old woman develops a new unilateral headache and pain when chewing. She also reports transient visual blurring. What complication of giant cell arteritis is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Giant cell arteritis can compromise the ophthalmic circulation and cause permanent visual loss, making urgent recognition and treatment essential.
why_wrong: A. Cataracts do not develop within hours from GCA. B. Corneal abrasion is unrelated to the underlying vasculitis. D. Retinal detachment is not the characteristic complication. E. Otitis externa is unrelated to GCA.
pearl: Visual symptoms in suspected giant cell arteritis are an emergency: give high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and refer urgently to ophthalmology, as visual loss is often irreversible.
thinking: 76-year-old with new unilateral headache ↓ Jaw claudication ↓ Transient visual blurring ↓ Ischaemia of the optic nerve circulation ↓ Permanent visual loss
exam_trap: D, retinal detachment from trauma — it is a sight-threatening emergency, but it follows flashes and floaters and is not a complication of the arteritis in GCA.
takeaway: GCA with visual symptoms needs immediate steroids to prevent permanent blindness.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting several seconds, triggered by turning over in bed. She has no hearing loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Brief, position-triggered episodes of vertigo without hearing loss are characteristic of BPPV.
why_wrong: A. Vestibular migraine can cause longer episodes and is associated with migraine features. B. Vestibular schwannoma usually causes progressive unilateral hearing loss. D. Ménière disease causes longer episodes with hearing symptoms and tinnitus. E. Labyrinthitis causes prolonged vertigo, often with hearing symptoms.
pearl: BPPV causes brief vertigo provoked by head movement; confirm with the Dix-Hallpike test and treat with the Epley manoeuvre rather than vestibular sedatives.
thinking: Recurrent vertigo lasting seconds ↓ Triggered by turning over in bed ↓ No hearing loss ↓ Positional inner-ear cause ↓ Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
exam_trap: D, Ménière disease — also recurrent vertigo, but attacks last minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, which are absent here.
takeaway: Seconds-long positional vertigo without hearing loss is BPPV.

stem: A 43-year-old man develops sudden unilateral hearing loss over several hours. There is no earwax or other obvious external-ear cause. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Wait several months before seeking help

why_correct: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a time-sensitive condition requiring prompt assessment.
why_wrong: A. Delaying assessment can delay potentially beneficial treatment. B. The cause must be assessed rather than assumed to be benign. C. Ear drops do not treat sensorineural hearing loss. E. Sudden hearing loss is not normal ageing.
pearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency; once wax and external causes are excluded, refer urgently, as early steroid treatment may improve recovery.
thinking: Sudden unilateral hearing loss over hours ↓ No wax or external-ear cause ↓ Likely sensorineural ↓ Time-sensitive treatment window ↓ Urgent assessment is required
exam_trap: C, treat routinely with ear drops — drops suit wax or otitis externa, but these have been excluded; sudden sensorineural loss needs urgent ENT assessment.
takeaway: Sudden unexplained hearing loss needs urgent same-day ENT assessment.

stem: A 4-month-old infant with bronchiolitis is feeding poorly and has increasing respiratory effort. Which finding is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Apnoea is a serious feature in an infant with bronchiolitis and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Cough is expected in bronchiolitis. B. Nasal congestion is common. D. Rhinorrhoea is common in viral respiratory infections. E. Some reduction in feeding can occur, although significant feeding difficulty is concerning.
pearl: In bronchiolitis, apnoea, severe respiratory distress, central cyanosis or persistently low oxygen saturations are red flags needing emergency referral; young infants are most at risk.
thinking: 4-month-old with bronchiolitis ↓ Poor feeding and rising work of breathing ↓ Look for red-flag features ↓ Apnoea signals exhaustion ↓ Apnoeic episodes
exam_trap: E, slight reduction in appetite — feeding matters in bronchiolitis, but a mild drop is expected; markedly reduced intake or apnoea is what signals danger.
takeaway: Apnoea in an infant with bronchiolitis is a red flag for emergency care.

stem: A 2-year-old child develops sudden severe coughing and wheezing while playing with small toys. What is the most important initial consideration?
why_correct: Sudden respiratory symptoms during play with small objects should raise immediate concern about foreign-body aspiration.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis does not cause sudden wheezing after playing with an object. B. Croup produces characteristic barking cough and stridor. C. Bronchiolitis usually follows viral symptoms. D. Asthma is not typically triggered by a sudden choking event.
pearl: Sudden choking, coughing or wheeze in a toddler, especially while playing with small objects, suggests an inhaled foreign body; bronchoscopy may be needed even if symptoms settle.
thinking: 2-year-old ↓ Sudden onset of coughing and wheeze ↓ Playing with small toys at the time ↓ Choking-type event ↓ Inhaled foreign body
exam_trap: B, croup — common at this age with noisy breathing, but it follows a coryzal illness with barking cough and stridor, not a sudden onset during play.
takeaway: Sudden cough and wheeze while playing with small objects means foreign body.

stem: A 2-year-old child has a seizure during a fever. The seizure lasts 25 minutes. What is the most appropriate classification?
why_correct: A febrile seizure lasting more than 5 minutes requires emergency management because of the risk of status epilepticus.
why_wrong: A. A simple febrile seizure is brief (under 15 minutes) and generalised. B. Syncope is not a prolonged convulsive state. C. Rigors with febrile delirium are not a seizure and do not explain a 25-minute convulsion. E. Breath-holding episodes occur in specific circumstances and do not explain a prolonged convulsion.
pearl: Any febrile seizure lasting more than 5 minutes needs emergency treatment as for status epilepticus; a seizure this long is never classed as a simple febrile seizure.
thinking: 2-year-old ↓ Seizure during a fever ↓ Lasts 25 minutes ↓ Far beyond a brief simple febrile seizure ↓ Prolonged febrile seizure
exam_trap: A, typical simple febrile seizure — the age and fever fit, but simple seizures are brief and generalised; 25 minutes makes it prolonged and an emergency.
takeaway: A long febrile seizure is not simple; over 5 minutes needs emergency treatment.

stem: A 10-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain. He is growing normally, has no weight loss or rectal bleeding, and examination is normal. Which feature would be a red flag requiring further assessment?
why_correct: Weight loss is an alarm feature in a child with recurrent abdominal pain.
why_wrong: A. Mild intermittent pain alone is not necessarily a red flag. B. Stress-related symptoms can occur in functional abdominal pain. C. Symptoms associated with school can occur with functional disorders. E. Normal growth is reassuring.
pearl: Most recurrent abdominal pain in children is functional, but weight loss, faltering growth, rectal bleeding, nocturnal symptoms or persistent vomiting suggest organic disease.
thinking: Child with recurrent abdominal pain ↓ Growing well with normal examination ↓ Which feature would change this ↓ Weight loss suggests organic disease ↓ Unintentional weight loss
exam_trap: B, symptoms associated with stress — it may seem worrying, but a link to stress is typical of functional abdominal pain and is not an alarm feature.
takeaway: Weight loss turns childhood recurrent abdominal pain into a red-flag presentation.

stem: A 3-year-old child has diarrhoea and vomiting. He is thirsty and has dry mucous membranes but remains alert and is drinking. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
why_correct: Oral rehydration is appropriate for children with mild-to-moderate dehydration who can drink.
why_wrong: A. Restricting fluids would worsen dehydration. B. Antidiarrhoeal medicines are generally not appropriate in young children. C. Antibiotics are not routinely required for uncomplicated gastroenteritis. E. Insulin does not treat dehydration from gastroenteritis.
pearl: Children with gastroenteritis and clinical dehydration who are alert and can drink should have oral rehydration solution, given little and often; IV fluids are for shock or ORS failure.
thinking: 3-year-old with diarrhoea and vomiting ↓ Thirst and dry mucous membranes ↓ Alert and drinking, no shock ↓ Mild-to-moderate dehydration ↓ Oral rehydration solution
exam_trap: C, immediate IV antibiotics — an unwell child may seem to need urgent intervention, but most gastroenteritis is viral and the priority is oral rehydration.
takeaway: Alert, drinking, dehydrated child: oral rehydration solution first.

stem: A 4-year-old child with gastroenteritis becomes lethargic, has markedly reduced urine output and cannot keep fluids down. What is the main concern?
why_correct: Lethargy, oliguria and inability to maintain oral intake are concerning features of significant dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Post-infective lactose intolerance causes ongoing loose stools, not acute lethargy and oliguria. C. Allergic rhinitis does not cause oliguria. D. Otitis externa does not explain the presentation. E. Constipation does not explain the acute systemic findings.
pearl: Red-flag signs in a dehydrated child include lethargy or altered responsiveness, reduced urine output, tachycardia and sunken eyes; inability to keep fluids down needs urgent escalation.
thinking: Child with gastroenteritis ↓ Lethargy ↓ Markedly reduced urine output ↓ Cannot keep fluids down ↓ Significant dehydration
exam_trap: A, post-infective lactose intolerance — it does follow gastroenteritis, but it causes persistent loose stools, not acute lethargy, oliguria and inability to keep fluids down.
takeaway: Lethargy and oliguria in gastroenteritis signal significant dehydration.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has had constipation for 8 months, starting around the time of toilet training. He withholds stool, passes large, hard stools and frequently soils his underwear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: A. Functional constipation with overflow soiling
why_correct: Constipation starting around toilet training with withholding behaviour and large hard stools is functional constipation; faecal impaction lets softer stool leak around it, causing overflow soiling (NICE CG99).
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease can cause gastrointestinal symptoms and faltering growth but does not best explain withholding and overflow soiling. C. Hirschsprung disease usually presents from birth with delayed meconium, and soiling is uncommon. D. Intussusception is an acute obstructive emergency with colicky pain and vomiting. E. Appendicitis is an acute illness with abdominal pain and fever, not months of constipation.
pearl: Overflow soiling in a constipated child is not deliberate: loose stool leaks around an impacted mass. Disimpaction with macrogol, then maintenance laxatives and toileting, is the mainstay.
thinking: Constipation for 8 months ↓ Began around toilet training ↓ Withholding with large hard stools ↓ Soiling from leakage around impacted stool ↓ Functional constipation with overflow soiling
exam_trap: C, Hirschsprung disease — it causes chronic constipation, but usually presents from birth with delayed meconium; onset at toilet training with withholding is functional.
takeaway: Constipation starting at toilet training with withholding and soiling is functional.

stem: A 6-year-old child has constipation and abdominal pain. He is otherwise well and growing normally. Which initial management is most appropriate?

options.D: Arrange urgent abdominal X-ray and blood tests
options.E: Dietary fibre changes alone without a laxative

correct_answer: A. Regular toileting and laxative treatment
why_correct: Behavioural measures, regular toileting and appropriate laxative treatment form the basis of management of childhood constipation.
why_wrong: B. Chemotherapy has no role. C. Fluid restriction can worsen constipation. D. Investigations are not needed for idiopathic constipation in a well, normally growing child. E. Dietary measures alone are not recommended as first-line treatment.
pearl: In idiopathic childhood constipation, start a laxative (macrogol first line) with behavioural measures such as scheduled toileting and a reward system; diet changes alone are not enough.
thinking: 6-year-old with constipation and abdominal pain ↓ Otherwise well and growing normally ↓ No red flags, so idiopathic ↓ Laxatives plus behavioural measures ↓ Regular toileting and laxative treatment
exam_trap: E, dietary fibre changes alone — diet advice feels gentler and is part of care, but it is not recommended as sole first-line treatment; a laxative is needed.
takeaway: Treat childhood constipation with laxatives plus toileting, not diet alone.

stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after accidentally swallowing a button battery. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Give an antacid and review the child again in 48 hours
options.B: Discharge and check stools for the battery passing
options.C: Give an antidiarrhoeal and observe for passage at home
options.D: Urgent X-ray to look for oesophageal impaction
options.E: Induce vomiting with ipecacuanha to expel the battery

correct_answer: D. Urgent X-ray to look for oesophageal impaction
why_correct: Button batteries can cause serious tissue injury, particularly when lodged in the oesophagus, and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Antacids do not prevent battery-related tissue damage, and delay is dangerous. B. Discharge without imaging can miss oesophageal impaction and severe injury. C. Antidiarrhoeals have no role. E. Inducing vomiting is unsafe.
pearl: A swallowed button battery can cause severe oesophageal burns within hours; get an urgent X-ray, and a battery lodged in the oesophagus needs emergency endoscopic removal.
thinking: Child has swallowed a button battery ↓ A lodged battery causes rapid tissue injury ↓ Its position determines management ↓ Imaging needed now ↓ Urgent X-ray to look for oesophageal impaction
exam_trap: B, discharge and check stools — reasonable for many harmless swallowed objects, but a battery stuck in the oesophagus can perforate within hours; it must be imaged.
takeaway: A swallowed button battery needs an urgent X-ray, never watchful waiting.

stem: A 7-year-old child develops a widespread rash consisting of small, itchy, fluid-filled blisters. Several lesions have already crusted. What is an appropriate infection-control measure?

options.A: Return to school as soon as some lesions crust
options.B: Give the siblings oral aciclovir to prevent them catching it
options.C: Isolate until the fever has settled
options.E: Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts

correct_answer: E. Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts
why_correct: Chickenpox can cause serious complications in susceptible pregnant people and immunocompromised individuals.
why_wrong: A. The child remains infectious until all lesions have crusted. B. Routine antiviral prophylaxis is not given to healthy siblings. C. Infectivity continues until all lesions crust, not just until fever settles. D. Shared personal items can facilitate transmission.
pearl: Chickenpox is infectious until all lesions have crusted over; keep the child off school until then and away from susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised people, who risk severe disease.
thinking: Child with itchy vesicular rash ↓ Lesions at different stages, some crusted ↓ Chickenpox ↓ Serious risk to vulnerable contacts ↓ Avoid susceptible pregnant or immunocompromised contacts
exam_trap: A, return when some lesions crust — crusting does mark the end of infectivity, but only once all lesions have crusted, not just some.
takeaway: Chickenpox is infectious until every lesion has crusted; protect vulnerable contacts.

stem: A 6-year-old child develops a bright-red rash on both cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the limbs. The child is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A slapped-cheek facial rash followed by a lacy body rash is characteristic of parvovirus B19 infection.
why_wrong: A. Meningococcal disease causes acute systemic illness and a non-blanching rash. C. Cellulitis is usually localized. D. Impetigo produces crusted superficial lesions. E. Measles usually causes fever with a widespread maculopapular rash and respiratory symptoms.
pearl: Parvovirus B19 (slapped cheek) is usually mild, and children are no longer infectious once the rash appears; it matters most in pregnancy and in people with haemolytic anaemias.
thinking: 6-year-old, otherwise well ↓ Bright-red rash on both cheeks ↓ Followed by lacy rash on the limbs ↓ Classic parvovirus B19 pattern ↓ Slapped cheek syndrome
exam_trap: E, measles — also a childhood viral rash, but it causes a febrile, unwell child with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis and a spreading maculopapular rash.
takeaway: Slapped cheeks then a lacy limb rash in a well child means parvovirus B19.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has recurrent urinary tract infections and dysuria. Which advice can help reduce the risk of recurrent lower urinary tract infections?

options.B: Restrict fluid intake to reduce voiding
options.C: Void promptly when the bladder is full

correct_answer: C. Void promptly when the bladder is full
why_correct: Regularly emptying the bladder and avoiding prolonged urinary retention can form part of advice for preventing recurrent UTIs.
why_wrong: A. Unnecessary catheterisation increases infection risk. B. Fluid restriction is inappropriate. D. Unsupervised antibiotics promote adverse effects and antimicrobial resistance. E. Deliberately avoiding urination does not reduce UTI risk.
pearl: Self-care advice for recurrent UTIs includes good hydration and not delaying voiding; these measures come before considering preventive antibiotics.
thinking: Recurrent lower UTIs ↓ Bacteria multiply in urine held in the bladder ↓ Regular emptying flushes them out ↓ Void promptly when the bladder is full
exam_trap: B, restrict fluid intake — fewer voids may sound like less irritation, but concentrated urine and infrequent emptying favour bacterial growth; good hydration is advised.
takeaway: Prevent recurrent UTIs with good hydration and prompt, regular bladder emptying.

stem: A 67-year-old man has urinary hesitancy, weak urinary stream and difficulty starting urination. What is the most likely underlying problem?
why_correct: Hesitancy and weak urinary flow are typical lower urinary tract symptoms caused by bladder outlet obstruction, commonly from benign prostatic enlargement.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and polydipsia. B. Overactive bladder causes storage symptoms such as urgency and frequency rather than hesitancy and a weak stream. C. Appendicitis does not cause chronic obstructive urinary symptoms. D. Renal colic causes acute flank pain.
pearl: Lower urinary tract symptoms divide into voiding (hesitancy, weak stream, straining) and storage (urgency, frequency, nocturia); voiding symptoms in older men usually reflect benign prostatic enlargement.
thinking: 67-year-old man ↓ Hesitancy and weak stream ↓ Voiding symptoms of outlet obstruction ↓ Commonest cause in older men ↓ Benign prostatic enlargement
exam_trap: B, overactive bladder — a common cause of urinary symptoms in older people, but it causes storage symptoms such as urgency and frequency, not hesitancy or a weak stream.
takeaway: Hesitancy and a weak stream in an older man point to benign prostatic enlargement.

stem: A 63-year-old man with diabetes attends his annual review. His feet are intact with no ulceration. What is an important routine preventive measure?

options.E: Cutting calluses with a blade at home

why_correct: NICE NG19 recommends regular (at least annual) diabetic foot assessment to detect neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease and deformity, so that risk can be stratified and ulceration prevented.
why_wrong: A. Walking barefoot increases the risk of unnoticed injury in a neuropathic foot. B. Poorly fitting footwear increases pressure and the risk of ulceration. C. Minor foot injuries may progress to ulceration and infection and need prompt attention. E. Self-cutting calluses can cause wounds and infection and should be done by a podiatrist.
pearl: Every person with diabetes needs at least annual foot assessment for neuropathy, ischaemia and deformity, with risk stratification; an active ulcer or infection needs urgent referral.
thinking: Diabetes at annual review ↓ Feet currently intact ↓ Neuropathy and ischaemia can develop silently ↓ Detect risk before ulceration ↓ Regular diabetic foot assessment
exam_trap: E, cutting calluses at home — removing callus does reduce pressure, but self-cutting with a blade risks wounds and infection; callus should be managed by a podiatrist.
takeaway: Examine diabetic feet at least annually to prevent ulceration.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has dysuria but also develops vaginal discharge and pelvic discomfort. What diagnosis should be considered?

options.A: Renal colic from a ureteric stone

why_correct: Dysuria accompanied by vaginal discharge and pelvic symptoms should prompt consideration of an STI rather than assuming a simple UTI.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes severe flank pain. C. Uncomplicated UTI does not usually cause vaginal discharge. D. Interstitial cystitis causes chronic bladder pain and urgency but not vaginal discharge. E. Osteoarthritis is unrelated.
pearl: Dysuria with vaginal discharge or pelvic pain should prompt STI testing (chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT) and consideration of PID, not just a urine dipstick for UTI.
thinking: 23-year-old with dysuria ↓ Also vaginal discharge ↓ Pelvic discomfort ↓ Features beyond simple cystitis ↓ Sexually transmitted infection
exam_trap: C, uncomplicated lower UTI — dysuria fits, but simple cystitis does not cause vaginal discharge; discharge with pelvic pain suggests an STI and possible PID.
takeaway: Dysuria with vaginal discharge means testing for STIs, not assuming a UTI.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with chlamydia. She has a regular sexual partner who has no symptoms. What is an important part of management?

options.A: Treat the partner if symptoms develop
options.B: Test the partner in 6 months if still asymptomatic
options.C: Advise abstinence for six months after treatment

correct_answer: D. Partner notification, testing and treatment
why_correct: Sexual partners should be appropriately notified and tested, and treated where indicated, to reduce reinfection and onward transmission.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for symptoms risks ongoing transmission. B. Chlamydia is often asymptomatic, so delayed testing risks reinfection and onward transmission. C. Prolonged abstinence is unnecessary; sex is avoided only until treatment is completed. E. Emollients do not treat chlamydia.
pearl: In chlamydia, partner notification is essential: current partners should be tested and treated without waiting for their results, and sex avoided until both have completed treatment.
thinking: Confirmed chlamydia ↓ Regular partner without symptoms ↓ Chlamydia is often asymptomatic ↓ An untreated partner means reinfection ↓ Partner notification, testing and treatment
exam_trap: A, treat the partner if symptoms develop — the partner looks well, but chlamydia is usually silent, so waiting for symptoms allows reinfection and onward spread.
takeaway: Treat chlamydia partners regardless of symptoms to prevent reinfection.

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops tingling in her fingers and around her mouth. She has carpopedal spasm. Which ECG change may occur with significant hypocalcaemia?

options.A: Complete heart block in every case
options.B: Absent P waves in every case
options.C: Persistent atrial fibrillation in every case

why_correct: Hypocalcaemia can prolong the QT interval.
why_wrong: A. Complete heart block is not an inevitable consequence. B. Absent P waves are not characteristic of hypocalcaemia. C. Atrial fibrillation is not the characteristic ECG finding. E. Hypocalcaemia classically prolongs rather than shortens the QT interval.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia causes perioral and peripheral tingling, carpopedal spasm and QT prolongation; Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs are classic, and severe cases need IV calcium gluconate.
thinking: Perioral and finger tingling ↓ Carpopedal spasm ↓ Hypocalcaemia ↓ Low calcium lengthens ventricular repolarisation ↓ Prolonged QT interval
exam_trap: E, shortened QT interval — it is the calcium-related ECG change many recall, but it occurs with hypercalcaemia; low calcium prolongs the QT.
takeaway: Low calcium lengthens the QT; high calcium shortens it.

stem: A 48-year-old man develops severe weakness after taking a new medication. Blood tests show a markedly raised potassium level. Which cardiac complication is the major immediate concern?
why_correct: Severe hyperkalaemia can cause dangerous cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias.
why_wrong: A. Pericarditis is inflammatory and not caused by hyperkalaemia. C. Endocarditis is an infective valvular disease unrelated to potassium. D. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a structural inherited condition, not an effect of hyperkalaemia. E. Aortic dissection is a vascular emergency unrelated to hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Severe hyperkalaemia is a cardiac emergency: get an ECG, give IV calcium to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells.
thinking: Weakness after a new medicine ↓ Markedly raised potassium ↓ Disturbed myocardial membrane potential ↓ Risk of conduction block and ventricular arrhythmia ↓ Life-threatening arrhythmia
exam_trap: A, acute pericarditis — it can cause ECG changes, but it is an inflammatory condition; hyperkalaemia threatens the heart through conduction failure and arrhythmia.
takeaway: Severe hyperkalaemia kills through arrhythmia: ECG, IV calcium, then shift potassium.

stem: A 73-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has persistent nausea, reduced appetite and increasing fatigue. His renal function has deteriorated significantly. Which complication of advanced kidney disease can contribute to these symptoms?
why_correct: Accumulation of uraemic toxins in advanced kidney failure can cause nausea, anorexia, fatigue and other systemic symptoms.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa causes local ear symptoms. B. Hyperthyroidism produces a different systemic pattern. C. Iron overload does not explain the typical uraemic syndrome. E. Acute glaucoma causes a painful red eye.
pearl: Symptomatic uraemia (nausea, anorexia, fatigue, pruritus, confusion) in advanced CKD is a key trigger to discuss dialysis or conservative kidney management.
thinking: CKD with significant deterioration ↓ Nausea, poor appetite and fatigue ↓ Retained nitrogenous waste ↓ Uraemic syndrome ↓ Uraemia
exam_trap: C, iron overload — it may tempt because iron is part of anaemia care in CKD, but overload does not cause this picture; uraemic toxins explain the symptoms.
takeaway: Nausea, anorexia and fatigue in advanced CKD suggest uraemia.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with asthma uses her salbutamol inhaler several times every day. She is otherwise stable. What does this suggest?

options.A: Salbutamol should replace all preventer treatment
options.B: She no longer needs asthma review
options.D: Her asthma control may be inadequate

correct_answer: D. Her asthma control may be inadequate
why_correct: Frequent reliance on a reliever inhaler suggests poor asthma control and should prompt review of treatment and adherence.
why_wrong: A. Reliever treatment does not replace appropriate anti-inflammatory treatment. B. Frequent symptoms are a reason for review, not discharge from follow-up. C. Salbutamol use does not diagnose diabetes. E. Frequent reliever use suggests ongoing symptoms.
pearl: Needing a short-acting reliever several times a day indicates uncontrolled asthma; check inhaler technique, adherence and triggers before stepping up anti-inflammatory treatment.
thinking: Asthma ↓ Salbutamol used several times every day ↓ Frequent reliever use reflects ongoing symptoms ↓ Review technique, adherence and treatment ↓ Her asthma control may be inadequate
exam_trap: A, salbutamol should replace preventer treatment — it relieves symptoms quickly, but relying on it alone leaves airway inflammation untreated and increases attack risk.
takeaway: Frequent reliever use means poor asthma control and needs review.

stem: A 29-year-old man presents with fever, headache and a new cardiac murmur. Infective endocarditis is suspected. Which investigation is particularly important before antibiotics when clinically safe?
why_correct: Multiple blood cultures should be obtained before antibiotics when possible in suspected infective endocarditis because they help identify the causative organism.
why_wrong: B. A pregnancy test does not diagnose infective endocarditis. C. Colonoscopy does not diagnose infective endocarditis. D. DXA assesses bone density. E. Spirometry assesses airflow.
pearl: In suspected infective endocarditis, take several sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics when clinically safe, then arrange echocardiography.
thinking: Fever and headache ↓ New cardiac murmur ↓ Suspected infective endocarditis ↓ Identifying the organism guides treatment ↓ Blood cultures
exam_trap: C, colonoscopy — it can become relevant later if Streptococcus gallolyticus is grown, but it does not diagnose endocarditis and has no role before antibiotics.
takeaway: Suspected endocarditis: multiple blood cultures before antibiotics.

stem: A 64-year-old woman taking warfarin presents with unexplained bruising. Her INR is significantly above her therapeutic range. What is the most appropriate principle?

options.A: Continue warfarin and recheck the INR next month
options.B: Review anticoagulation and assess for bleeding
options.C: Start low-dose aspirin 75 mg once daily routinely
options.D: Increase the warfarin dose and recheck the INR in a week

correct_answer: B. Review anticoagulation and assess for bleeding
why_correct: A markedly elevated INR increases bleeding risk and requires assessment and appropriate adjustment of anticoagulation.
why_wrong: A. A significantly elevated INR with bruising should not be left for a month. C. Aspirin can further increase bleeding risk and is not routinely added. D. Increasing warfarin would further increase anticoagulation. E. Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding, not bruising alone.
pearl: With a high INR, management depends on bleeding: minor bleeding may need warfarin withheld and vitamin K, while major bleeding needs prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ Unexplained bruising ↓ INR well above range ↓ Assess bleeding severity and adjust treatment ↓ Review anticoagulation and assess for bleeding
exam_trap: E, give prothrombin complex concentrate immediately — it rapidly reverses warfarin, but it is reserved for major bleeding; bruising alone does not justify it.
takeaway: High INR: assess bleeding first, then withhold warfarin or reverse accordingly.

stem: A 35-year-old woman develops widespread itchy wheals shortly after eating a food. She has no breathing difficulty, dizziness or swelling of the tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Transient itchy wheals without airway, breathing or circulatory compromise are characteristic of urticaria.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis causes localized painful erythema. B. Erysipelas is a localized bacterial skin infection. C. Anaphylaxis requires features of significant airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. D. Contact eczema causes eczematous change at the site of contact rather than widespread transient wheals.
pearl: Acute urticaria presents with transient itchy wheals; check for airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, which would mean anaphylaxis. Uncomplicated cases need a non-sedating antihistamine.
thinking: Itchy widespread wheals ↓ Shortly after eating a food ↓ No breathing difficulty, dizziness or tongue swelling ↓ Skin-only allergic reaction ↓ Acute urticaria
exam_trap: C, anaphylaxis — the food trigger and rapid onset fit, but anaphylaxis requires airway, breathing or circulation problems, which are absent here.
takeaway: Wheals without airway, breathing or circulation compromise is urticaria, not anaphylaxis.

stem: An 81-year-old woman with dementia is asked to consent to a proposed procedure. What should be assessed before deciding whether she can consent?

options.A: Whether she agrees with the doctor's recommendation
options.B: Whether she can understand, retain and weigh relevant information and communicate a choice
options.C: Whether her Mini-Mental State Examination score is above the cut-off of 24/30
options.D: Whether she can correctly recall today's date, the name of the hospital and the doctor's name
options.E: Whether her next of kin agrees with the procedure that is being proposed

correct_answer: B. Whether she can understand, retain and weigh relevant information and communicate a choice
why_correct: Mental capacity is decision-specific and requires assessment of the person's ability to understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information, and communicate a decision.
why_wrong: A. Capacity does not depend on agreeing with the clinician. C. A cognitive screening score does not determine decision-specific capacity. D. Orientation and recall of names are not the capacity test. E. Relatives do not automatically make the decision for an adult who has capacity.
pearl: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, capacity is decision-specific: assume capacity, then assess whether the person can understand, retain, use or weigh information and communicate a decision.
thinking: Dementia does not remove capacity automatically ↓ Capacity is decision-specific ↓ Apply the functional test ↓ Whether she can understand, retain and weigh relevant information and communicate a choice
exam_trap: C, an MMSE score above the cut-off — a cognitive score feels objective, but no screening score determines capacity; the decision-specific functional test does.
takeaway: Capacity is tested per decision: understand, retain, weigh, communicate.

stem: A doctor realises that they have made an error in a patient's prescription. The medication has not yet been administered. What should they do?

options.A: Correct it at the next routine ward round
options.B: Correct the error promptly and inform the team
options.D: Take no action because no harm has occurred
options.E: Ask the pharmacist to amend it quietly

correct_answer: B. Correct the error promptly and inform the team
why_correct: Prompt recognition and correction of errors reduces the risk of harm and supports safe clinical practice.
why_wrong: A. Delaying action could allow the medication to be administered. C. Deleting evidence without appropriate documentation is unsafe. D. An error still requires appropriate action even if harm has not yet occurred. E. The prescriber should correct the error and the team must be informed so the incident is handled openly.
pearl: When you find a prescribing error, correct it immediately, inform the team, document it and report it through local incident reporting even if no harm occurred, as near misses drive learning.
thinking: Prescribing error found ↓ Drug not yet given ↓ Risk remains until corrected ↓ Act now and be open with the team ↓ Correct the error promptly and inform the team
exam_trap: D, take no action because no harm occurred — no patient was hurt, but the error remains live; it must be corrected and handled openly as a near miss.
takeaway: Correct errors immediately and be open, even when no harm has occurred.

stem: A patient is unconscious and requires an urgent life-saving procedure. There is no available advance decision refusing treatment. What principle generally applies?

options.A: Consent should first be obtained from an IMCA
options.B: Treatment requires written consent from the next of kin
options.C: Emergency treatment may be given in their best interests
options.D: Treatment should wait until a relative can consent
options.E: A court order is needed before the procedure can proceed

correct_answer: C. Emergency treatment may be given in their best interests
why_correct: Necessary emergency treatment can be provided when the patient lacks capacity and delay would put them at significant risk, subject to relevant legal and clinical requirements.
why_wrong: A. An IMCA does not give consent, and waiting would cause dangerous delay. B. Relatives cannot consent for an adult and written consent is not required in an emergency. D. Waiting for relatives may cause dangerous delay. E. A court order is not needed for necessary emergency treatment.
pearl: In an emergency, an adult who lacks capacity can be given necessary treatment in their best interests without consent; relatives cannot consent for them unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
thinking: Unconscious patient lacks capacity ↓ Urgent life-saving treatment needed ↓ No advance decision refusing it ↓ Delay would cause serious harm ↓ Emergency treatment may be given in their best interests
exam_trap: B, written consent from the next of kin — involving family feels proper, but relatives cannot consent for an adult, and seeking it must not delay emergency treatment.
takeaway: Treat incapacitated patients in emergencies in their best interests; relatives cannot consent.

stem: A patient asks the doctor not to disclose their diagnosis to their adult daughter. The patient has capacity. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Ask another patient to tell the daughter
options.B: Tell the daughter because she is a close relative
options.C: Disclose the diagnosis automatically because the daughter is next of kin
options.E: Post the diagnosis in the family group chat

why_correct: Confidential patient information should not be disclosed to relatives without appropriate consent or another valid justification.
why_wrong: A. This would still breach confidentiality. B. Being a relative does not automatically provide access to confidential information. C. Next-of-kin status does not automatically override a capacitous patient's confidentiality. E. Electronic disclosure to a group would be inappropriate.
pearl: A patient with capacity decides who is told about their health; next-of-kin status gives relatives no automatic right to confidential information.
thinking: Patient has capacity ↓ Asks for the diagnosis to be kept from the daughter ↓ No overriding justification described ↓ Respect the patient's confidentiality
exam_trap: C, disclose because the daughter is next of kin — next of kin sounds like a legal right, but it gives no entitlement to confidential information without consent.
takeaway: Next of kin has no automatic right to a capacitous patient's information.

stem: A 78-year-old inpatient is at high risk of pressure injury because she is immobile and has poor nutritional intake. What is an important preventive measure?

options.D: Keeping her in one position to rest the skin
options.E: Massaging reddened skin over bony prominences

correct_answer: B. Regular repositioning and pressure relief
why_correct: Reducing prolonged pressure through repositioning and appropriate pressure-relieving equipment is central to pressure injury prevention.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration may worsen vulnerability. C. Regular skin inspection is important for early detection. D. Prolonged immobility increases pressure injury risk. E. Massage of damaged or vulnerable tissue can cause further injury.
pearl: Pressure ulcer prevention rests on risk assessment, regular skin inspection, repositioning, pressure-redistributing surfaces and optimising nutrition and hydration.
thinking: Immobile older inpatient ↓ Poor nutrition increases vulnerability ↓ Sustained pressure over bony prominences ↓ Relieve pressure regularly ↓ Regular repositioning and pressure relief
exam_trap: E, massaging reddened skin — it sounds as if it would improve circulation, but rubbing at-risk skin can cause further tissue damage and is not recommended.
takeaway: Prevent pressure injury by regular repositioning and pressure relief.

stem: An 84-year-old man has fallen twice since starting several new medicines. He reports dizziness when standing. What should be considered?

options.A: Medication review and assessment for postural hypotension
options.C: Ignoring the falls because they are common in older people
options.D: Stopping every medication immediately without review

correct_answer: A. Medication review and assessment for postural hypotension
why_correct: Falls with postural dizziness in an older person taking multiple medicines should prompt assessment for medication-related adverse effects and postural hypotension.
why_wrong: B. Prolonged bed rest can increase deconditioning and falls risk. C. Falls warrant assessment because they may have preventable causes. D. Medicines should be reviewed systematically rather than all stopped indiscriminately. E. Increasing doses could worsen adverse effects.
pearl: Falls with postural dizziness after new medicines should prompt lying and standing blood pressure and a structured medication review, targeting antihypertensives, diuretics and sedatives.
thinking: 84-year-old with two falls ↓ Several new medicines started ↓ Dizziness on standing ↓ Possible drug-related postural hypotension ↓ Medication review and assessment for postural hypotension
exam_trap: D, stop every medication immediately — it removes possible culprits, but abrupt stopping can cause harm; medicines should be reviewed and adjusted systematically.
takeaway: Falls with postural dizziness: check lying and standing BP and review medicines.

stem: A 79-year-old woman has unintentionally lost 8 kg over six months and reports reduced appetite. What is an appropriate initial approach?

options.B: Assess for medical, psychological and social causes
options.C: Prescribe an appetite stimulant such as megestrol
options.D: Start oral supplements and review in a year

correct_answer: B. Assess for medical, psychological and social causes
why_correct: Significant unintentional weight loss requires assessment for causes including disease, medication effects, depression, nutritional problems and social factors.
why_wrong: A. Restricting food would worsen nutritional risk. C. Prescribing without assessing the cause is inappropriate. D. Supplements without assessment and a year's delay risk missing serious disease. E. Significant weight loss should not automatically be attributed to ageing.
pearl: Unintentional weight loss in an older adult needs a structured search for cancer and other organic disease, depression, dementia, medication effects, dental or swallowing problems and social factors.
thinking: 79-year-old ↓ 8 kg lost over six months unintentionally ↓ Reduced appetite ↓ Many possible causes ↓ Assess for medical, psychological and social causes
exam_trap: D, start supplements and review in a year — supplements may help nutrition, but without assessment and with a year's delay they risk missing cancer or treatable disease.
takeaway: Unintentional weight loss in older people needs a cause found, not just supplements.

stem: A 70-year-old man coughs repeatedly while drinking water and has a wet-sounding voice afterwards. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Coughing during swallowing and a wet voice afterwards are features that may indicate swallowing dysfunction with aspiration risk.
why_wrong: A. DVT causes limb swelling and pain. B. Otitis externa causes ear pain and canal inflammation. C. Renal colic causes flank pain. E. Migraine causes headache and associated neurological symptoms.
pearl: Coughing while drinking and a wet-sounding voice afterwards suggest oropharyngeal dysphagia with aspiration; arrange a speech and language therapy swallow assessment.
thinking: 70-year-old ↓ Repeated coughing while drinking ↓ Wet-sounding voice afterwards ↓ Fluid entering the airway ↓ Aspiration
exam_trap: E, migraine — it may come to mind as a neurological cause, but it does not cause coughing on swallowing or a wet voice; these signs point to aspiration.
takeaway: Coughing on drinking with a wet voice means aspiration risk: get a swallow assessment.

stem: A hospital inpatient has been prescribed a medicine to which they have a documented severe allergy. What should the doctor do?

options.A: Avoid the medicine and select an appropriate alternative
options.B: Give it and observe for a reaction
options.C: Ignore the allergy because the patient is in hospital
options.D: Give it with an antihistamine routinely
options.E: Give it at half the dose

correct_answer: A. Avoid the medicine and select an appropriate alternative
why_correct: A documented severe drug allergy should be taken seriously and the offending medicine avoided unless there is an exceptional specialist reason to use it.
why_wrong: B. Deliberately exposing the patient to a known severe allergen is unsafe. C. Hospitalisation does not remove allergy risk. D. An antihistamine does not make administration of a contraindicated drug safe. E. Dose reduction does not reliably prevent an allergic reaction.
pearl: Check allergy status, including the nature of the reaction, before prescribing; a documented severe allergy means the drug, and often related drugs, should be avoided.
thinking: Inpatient prescribed a drug ↓ Documented severe allergy to it ↓ Re-exposure risks anaphylaxis ↓ Avoid the medicine and select an appropriate alternative
exam_trap: D, give it with an antihistamine — premedication sounds protective, but it does not prevent a severe allergic reaction; the drug should be avoided.
takeaway: Never give a drug with a documented severe allergy; choose an alternative.

stem: A patient receiving a blood transfusion develops fever, chills and back pain. What is the immediate action?
why_correct: A suspected acute transfusion reaction requires the transfusion to be stopped immediately and the patient assessed according to the local transfusion-reaction protocol.
why_wrong: A. Further blood should not be administered until the reaction has been assessed. B. Increasing the rate could worsen a serious reaction. C. These symptoms may indicate a significant transfusion reaction. E. Intravenous access is needed for ongoing assessment and treatment.
pearl: In an acute transfusion reaction, stop the transfusion, keep the line open, assess ABCDE and recheck patient and unit identity; fever with back pain raises concern for ABO incompatibility.
thinking: Transfusion in progress ↓ Fever, chills and back pain ↓ Possible acute haemolytic reaction ↓ Stop further exposure first ↓ Stop the transfusion
exam_trap: E, remove all intravenous access — removing the source seems logical, but the cannula is needed for fluids and treatment; stop the blood, keep the line.
takeaway: Transfusion reaction: stop the transfusion, keep IV access, assess urgently.

stem: Before administering a unit of blood, which information is particularly important to check against the patient and blood component?

options.B: The patient's ward name and bed number
options.C: The patient's next of kin details

correct_answer: A. Patient identity and compatibility details
why_correct: Correct patient identification and compatibility checks are essential to prevent potentially fatal transfusion errors.
why_wrong: B. Ward and bed number are not reliable patient identifiers. C. Next-of-kin details do not confirm identity or compatibility. D. Occupation is irrelevant to transfusion identification. E. Food preference is irrelevant.
pearl: Wrong blood in the patient is a leading cause of serious transfusion harm; positive bedside identity checks against the wristband and blood component prevent ABO-incompatible transfusion.
thinking: Unit of blood ready ↓ Biggest risk is giving the wrong blood ↓ Bedside check against the patient ↓ Patient identity and compatibility details
exam_trap: B, ward name and bed number — commonly used to locate patients, but patients move beds; they are not reliable identifiers for transfusion.
takeaway: Positive patient identification at the bedside prevents fatal transfusion errors.

stem: A patient has a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding. Before using it for feeding, what is important?

options.A: Ask the patient whether the tube feels correctly positioned
options.B: Check position by testing aspirate with litmus paper
options.C: Confirm position with the air 'whoosh' test
options.D: Confirm position by aspirate pH testing or X-ray
options.E: Use the tube without checking because it was inserted by a doctor

correct_answer: D. Confirm position by aspirate pH testing or X-ray
why_correct: Incorrectly positioned feeding tubes can cause serious harm, including pulmonary aspiration. Position must be confirmed according to the relevant protocol before use.
why_wrong: A. Patient sensation cannot reliably confirm tube position. B. Litmus paper is not a safe method for confirming tube position. C. Auscultation of injected air is unreliable and should not be used. E. Professional status does not remove the need for safety checks.
pearl: Confirm nasogastric tube position before first use with aspirate pH testing, using X-ray if no suitable aspirate is obtained; never rely on litmus paper or the air whoosh test.
thinking: NG tube inserted for feeding ↓ Misplacement in the lung can be fatal ↓ Reliable confirmation needed ↓ Confirm position by aspirate pH testing or X-ray
exam_trap: C, the air whoosh test — it is a traditional bedside check, but auscultation is unreliable and is no longer acceptable for confirming tube position.
takeaway: Confirm NG tube position by aspirate pH or X-ray before feeding.

stem: A 55-year-old man has persistent heartburn and difficulty swallowing. Which symptom represents an important alarm feature?
why_correct: Dysphagia associated with upper gastrointestinal symptoms is an alarm feature requiring appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Hunger is not an alarm symptom. B. Occasional hiccups are usually benign. C. Belching is common and nonspecific. E. Flatulence is nonspecific.
pearl: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom at any age and needs urgent upper GI endoscopy to exclude oesophageal cancer.
thinking: 55-year-old with persistent heartburn ↓ Now difficulty swallowing ↓ Possible stricture or malignancy ↓ Alarm feature identified ↓ Dysphagia
exam_trap: C, mild belching — it accompanies reflux, so may seem relevant, but it is nonspecific and benign; dysphagia is the red flag.
takeaway: Dysphagia is always an alarm symptom requiring urgent endoscopy.

stem: A patient with advanced terminal illness is approaching the end of life. Which approach is appropriate when discussing future care?

options.A: Explore the patient's preferences and goals of care
options.B: Discuss only treatment that can cure the illness
options.C: Wait until the patient becomes unconscious before discussing care
options.D: Make all decisions without involving the patient
options.E: Avoid discussing deterioration because it may upset the patient

correct_answer: A. Explore the patient's preferences and goals of care
why_correct: Advance care planning should explore what matters to the patient and their preferences for future treatment and care.
why_wrong: B. End-of-life care includes symptom control and treatment preferences, not only curative treatment. C. Planning should ideally occur while the patient can participate. D. Patients should be involved in decisions when they have capacity. E. Avoiding important discussions can prevent appropriate planning.
pearl: Advance care planning should start while the patient can take part, exploring their values, preferred place of care and treatment wishes, and recording them for the team.
thinking: Terminal illness nearing end of life ↓ Future care decisions approaching ↓ Patient can still take part ↓ Explore the patient's preferences and goals of care
exam_trap: E, avoid discussing deterioration — it seems kind, but avoidance denies the patient the chance to shape their care; most want honest, sensitive discussion.
takeaway: Plan end-of-life care with the patient, early, around their own goals.

stem: A patient receiving palliative care develops distressing breathlessness despite treatment of the underlying cause. What is an important general principle?

options.B: Withhold treatment because the illness is terminal
options.D: Stop regular medications to reduce burden
options.E: Treat reversible causes and relieve symptoms

correct_answer: E. Treat reversible causes and relieve symptoms
why_correct: Palliative care includes identifying potentially reversible causes while managing distressing symptoms according to the patient's goals.
why_wrong: A. Communication remains important. B. Terminal illness does not mean symptoms should be untreated. C. Antibiotics are not routinely appropriate. D. Medication should be reviewed individually rather than stopped indiscriminately.
pearl: In palliative breathlessness, treat reversible causes where appropriate, then use non-drug measures such as a fan and positioning, and low-dose opioids for symptom relief.
thinking: Palliative patient ↓ Distressing breathlessness ↓ Underlying cause already treated ↓ Address other reversible factors and relieve symptoms ↓ Treat reversible causes and relieve symptoms
exam_trap: D, stop regular medications to reduce burden — deprescribing has a place, but stopping everything is indiscriminate and does not relieve breathlessness.
takeaway: Palliative care: treat what is reversible and always relieve symptoms.

stem: A healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a patient whose blood-borne virus status is unknown. What should they do first?

options.B: Encourage bleeding, wash it and report promptly
options.C: Continue working without reporting the minor incident
options.D: Suck the wound clean, cover it and report it later
options.E: Finish the shift and report it if symptoms develop

correct_answer: B. Encourage bleeding, wash it and report promptly
why_correct: Immediate first aid and prompt occupational-health assessment are important because post-exposure management may be time-sensitive.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics have no role in preventing blood-borne viral infection. C. Even an apparently minor incident should be reported and assessed appropriately. D. The wound should not be sucked, and delayed reporting risks missing time-sensitive prophylaxis. E. Blood-borne infections may initially be asymptomatic and prophylaxis is time-sensitive.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage bleeding, wash with soap and running water without scrubbing or sucking, and report immediately to occupational health or the emergency department.
thinking: Needlestick injury ↓ Source blood-borne virus status unknown ↓ First aid limits exposure ↓ Prophylaxis is time-sensitive ↓ Encourage bleeding, wash it and report promptly
exam_trap: E, finish the shift and report if symptoms develop — it seems minor, but blood-borne infection may be silent and HIV PEP works best when started within hours.
takeaway: Needlestick: bleed it, wash it, report it immediately.

stem: A healthcare worker has a needlestick injury potentially involving HIV exposure. Why is urgent assessment important?

options.A: A tetanus vaccine booster effectively treats HIV exposure
options.B: PEP should wait until the source patient's result is back
options.C: Seroconversion symptoms typically appear within 24 hours

correct_answer: E. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive
why_correct: Significant occupational exposure may require urgent assessment for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus vaccination does not prevent HIV. B. PEP should not be delayed while awaiting source testing when the exposure is significant. C. Acute HIV infection may be asymptomatic and seroconversion illness occurs weeks later. D. Antibiotics do not prevent HIV.
pearl: HIV PEP should start as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure; do not wait for source test results when the exposure is significant.
thinking: Needlestick with possible HIV exposure ↓ PEP works best when started early ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is time-sensitive
exam_trap: B, PEP should wait for the source result — it seems to avoid unnecessary drugs, but delay reduces effectiveness; start PEP and stop it if the source tests negative.
takeaway: Start HIV PEP as early as possible; do not wait for source results.

stem: A doctor suspects that an older patient may be experiencing financial abuse by a relative. What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Take no action unless there are visible injuries or bruising
options.B: Tell other patients on the ward so that they can stay vigilant
options.C: Confront the relative on the ward with the patient present
options.D: Speak privately with the patient about safety and wishes
options.E: Discharge the patient home with the relative as originally planned

correct_answer: D. Speak privately with the patient about safety and wishes
why_correct: Safeguarding concerns require sensitive assessment, ideally in private, with attention to immediate safety and the patient's wishes.
why_wrong: A. Financial abuse does not require physical injuries. B. Patient information must remain confidential. C. Confrontation may increase risk. E. Discharge without assessing safety may increase risk.
pearl: When abuse of an adult at risk is suspected, speak to the person alone, ensure immediate safety, explore their wishes and follow local safeguarding procedures.
thinking: Older patient ↓ Suspected financial abuse by a relative ↓ Need the patient's own account and wishes ↓ Relative must not be present ↓ Speak privately with the patient about safety and wishes
exam_trap: C, confront the relative — tackling the suspected abuser feels decisive, but it may escalate risk and silence the patient; speak to the patient privately first.
takeaway: Suspected abuse: speak to the patient alone first, then follow safeguarding procedures.

stem: A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is admitted with a persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats. What infection-control principle is particularly important?

options.A: Routine contact with other patients on the ward
options.B: Sharing a room with other vulnerable patients
options.C: No precautions until the diagnosis is confirmed
options.E: Turning off the ventilation in the patient's room

correct_answer: D. Respiratory isolation and infection control
why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires appropriate isolation and infection-control measures because transmission can occur through airborne particles.
why_wrong: A. Unrestricted contact increases transmission risk. B. Vulnerable patients may be at greater risk. C. Precautions may be necessary while diagnosis is being established. E. Appropriate ventilation is an important infection-control measure.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs a single room with respiratory precautions until infectivity is assessed; suspected multidrug-resistant TB needs a negative-pressure room.
thinking: Persistent cough, weight loss and night sweats ↓ Suspected pulmonary TB ↓ Airborne transmission risk ↓ Protect other patients and staff ↓ Respiratory isolation and infection control
exam_trap: C, no precautions until confirmed — waiting for proof seems proportionate, but confirmation takes time and transmission occurs meanwhile; isolate on suspicion.
takeaway: Isolate suspected pulmonary TB on suspicion, not confirmation.

stem: A patient is diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis. What is an important public-health action?

options.A: Advise the patient to avoid dairy products
options.C: Notify TB services for contact tracing
options.D: Prescribe an antitussive for the cough
options.E: Advise the patient that household contacts do not need assessment

correct_answer: C. Notify TB services for contact tracing
why_correct: Active TB requires coordinated public-health management, including assessment of relevant contacts.
why_wrong: A. Dairy avoidance is not the central public-health intervention. B. TB treatment requires an appropriate course rather than stopping when symptoms improve. D. Treatment addresses the infection, not simply the cough. E. Household and other relevant contacts may require assessment.
pearl: TB is a notifiable disease in the UK; notification triggers contact tracing, and treatment requires a full multi-drug course with adherence support.
thinking: Active pulmonary TB ↓ Infectious to close contacts ↓ Notifiable disease ↓ Contacts need screening ↓ Notify TB services for contact tracing
exam_trap: E, household contacts do not need assessment — they may be well, but close contacts are at highest risk and may have latent or active TB needing screening.
takeaway: Active TB is notifiable and needs contact tracing.

stem: A patient with a new sexually transmitted infection asks whether their recent sexual partners need to know. What is an important principle?

options.A: Partners need informing if they develop symptoms
options.B: Partners will be told the patient's identity by the clinic
options.C: Partner notification helps reduce onward transmission
options.D: The patient has to tell partners personally
options.E: Partner notification is unnecessary if symptoms have resolved

correct_answer: C. Partner notification helps reduce onward transmission
why_correct: Partner notification is an important part of STI management and helps prevent onward transmission and complications.
why_wrong: A. Many STIs are asymptomatic, so notification should not depend on symptoms. B. Provider-led notification can be anonymous and protects the patient's confidentiality. D. Partners can also be notified by the clinic, so the patient does not have to do it personally. E. Resolution of symptoms does not necessarily mean the infection has cleared or that partners are safe.
pearl: Partner notification is a routine part of STI care; it can be patient-led or provider-led, and provider-led notification keeps the index patient anonymous.
thinking: New STI diagnosis ↓ Partners may be infected without symptoms ↓ Untreated partners transmit and reinfect ↓ Partner notification helps reduce onward transmission
exam_trap: A, inform partners if they develop symptoms — it seems proportionate, but many STIs are asymptomatic, so waiting allows onward spread and complications.
takeaway: Notify STI partners regardless of symptoms; anonymity can be preserved.

stem: A 17-year-old develops a painful blistering rash and extensive skin peeling shortly after starting a new medicine. What serious condition should be considered?
why_correct: Acute widespread blistering and epidermal detachment following a medication exposure is characteristic of severe drug-related epidermal necrolysis.
why_wrong: A. Tinea corporis causes annular scaly lesions rather than blistering and skin peeling. B. Pompholyx causes itchy vesicles on the hands and feet, not widespread painful skin peeling. C. Vitiligo causes painless depigmentation. D. An acneiform drug eruption causes papules and pustules, not blistering and skin peeling.
pearl: SJS/TEN is a dermatological emergency: stop the suspected drug immediately and refer urgently; mucosal involvement and painful skin detachment are key features.
thinking: 17-year-old starts a new medicine ↓ Painful blistering rash soon after ↓ Extensive skin peeling ↓ Severe drug-induced epidermal necrolysis ↓ Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN
exam_trap: B, acute pompholyx — it also causes blisters, but itchy vesicles confined to the hands and feet; widespread painful peeling after a new drug suggests SJS/TEN.
takeaway: Painful blistering and skin peeling after a new drug is SJS/TEN until proven otherwise.

stem: A 32-year-old woman develops a widespread itchy rash after staying in a hotel. Several people sharing her accommodation are also affected. What is an important consideration?

options.A: The rash is likely an autoimmune reaction
options.B: The rash suggests a shared food allergy
options.D: Infection is excluded as she has no fever

correct_answer: C. Consider scabies or another infestation
why_correct: A pruritic rash affecting multiple close contacts suggests a transmissible infestation such as scabies.
why_wrong: A. Shared exposure makes an infectious or infestive cause important to consider. B. Shared exposure does not establish food allergy. D. Infestations such as scabies do not cause fever. E. There is no basis for avoiding vaccination.
pearl: Scabies spreads through close contact; treat the patient and all household and close contacts at the same time, and wash bedding and clothing, to prevent reinfestation.
thinking: Widespread itchy rash ↓ Others sharing accommodation also affected ↓ Transmissible cause likely ↓ Intense itch suggests infestation ↓ Consider scabies or another infestation
exam_trap: B, shared food allergy — people living together seems to fit a shared trigger, but a shared exposure with intense itch points to infestation such as scabies or bedbugs.
takeaway: An itchy rash shared by close contacts suggests scabies or another infestation.

stem: A traveller develops severe watery diarrhoea during a holiday abroad but remains alert and able to drink. What is an important initial management measure?
why_correct: Replacing water and electrolytes is the key initial treatment for uncomplicated diarrhoeal illness when the patient can drink safely.
why_wrong: A. Prolonged fasting is unnecessary. C. Antibiotics are not routinely required for uncomplicated diarrhoea. D. Chemotherapy has no role in routine infectious diarrhoea. E. Fluid restriction increases dehydration risk.
pearl: Rehydration is the cornerstone of managing travellers' diarrhoea; oral rehydration solution replaces water and electrolytes, and most cases are self-limiting.
thinking: Traveller with watery diarrhoea ↓ Large fluid and electrolyte losses ↓ Alert and able to drink ↓ Oral route is safe ↓ Oral rehydration solution
exam_trap: C, routine intravenous antibiotics — severe diarrhoea abroad may feel infective and serious, but most cases are self-limiting and rehydration is the priority.
takeaway: Rehydrate first in travellers' diarrhoea; use ORS if the patient can drink.

stem: A patient is suspected of having meningococcal meningitis and is rapidly deteriorating. What is the key principle?

options.A: Discharge if the patient remains conscious
options.B: Wait for lumbar puncture results before antibiotics
options.C: Delay antibiotics until a CT head is reported
options.D: Give oral amoxicillin and review next day
options.E: Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations

correct_answer: E. Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations
why_correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and treatment should not be unnecessarily delayed.
why_wrong: A. Consciousness does not exclude serious meningitis. B. Waiting for lumbar puncture results can cause dangerous treatment delay. C. Imaging should not delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease. D. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are inadequate for suspected meningococcal disease.
pearl: In suspected meningococcal disease, give parenteral antibiotics immediately; in primary care, give IM or IV benzylpenicillin before urgent transfer if this does not delay it.
thinking: Suspected meningococcal meningitis ↓ Rapid deterioration ↓ Delay increases mortality ↓ Investigations must not hold up treatment ↓ Give antibiotics without waiting for investigations
exam_trap: B, wait for lumbar puncture results — LP helps confirm the diagnosis, but it must never delay antibiotics in suspected meningococcal disease.
takeaway: Suspected meningococcal disease: give antibiotics immediately; never wait for tests.

stem: A patient has a deep contaminated wound after stepping on a dirty metal object. What factor is particularly important when assessing the need for tetanus prevention?

options.A: Whether the patient has a penicillin allergy
options.B: Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
options.C: The patient's eye colour and skin complexion
options.D: Whether the patient ate breakfast that morning
options.E: The patient's ABO blood group and rhesus status

correct_answer: B. Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
why_correct: Tetanus prevention depends on the type of wound and the patient's previous immunisation status.
why_wrong: A. Penicillin allergy affects antibiotic choice, not tetanus prophylaxis. C. Eye colour and complexion are irrelevant. D. Food intake is irrelevant. E. Blood group does not determine tetanus prophylaxis.
pearl: Tetanus-prone wounds include deep, puncture or soil-contaminated wounds; the need for a vaccine booster and human tetanus immunoglobulin depends on wound risk and vaccination history.
thinking: Deep wound from a dirty metal object ↓ Contaminated, so tetanus-prone ↓ Protection depends on prior immunity ↓ Tetanus vaccination history and wound type
exam_trap: A, penicillin allergy — it seems relevant to antibiotic cover for dirty wounds, but it does not determine the need for tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin.
takeaway: Tetanus prophylaxis depends on wound risk and vaccination history.

stem: A patient presents after an animal bite. What is an important initial principle?

options.A: Prescribe co-amoxiclav and discharge without examination
options.B: Leave small wounds unassessed if they are not bleeding
options.C: Assess the wound, infection risk and tetanus status
options.D: Close the wound primarily with tight interrupted sutures
options.E: Avoid documenting the type of animal involved in the bite

correct_answer: C. Assess the wound, infection risk and tetanus status
why_correct: Animal bites require assessment of wound severity, infection risk, tetanus status and, depending on circumstances, other risks such as rabies.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotic decisions depend on wound assessment and circumstances. B. Even small bites can become infected. D. Primary closure is not automatically appropriate for bites. E. Details of the animal and circumstances can be clinically important.
pearl: Animal bites need thorough irrigation, assessment of depth and infection risk, tetanus review, rabies risk where relevant, and often prophylactic co-amoxiclav for higher-risk wounds.
thinking: Animal bite ↓ High infection risk from mouth flora ↓ Wound depth and site matter ↓ Tetanus and rabies may apply ↓ Assess the wound, infection risk and tetanus status
exam_trap: A, prescribe co-amoxiclav and discharge — co-amoxiclav is the usual choice, but prescribing without examining the wound misses depth, damage and tetanus or rabies risk.
takeaway: Every bite needs assessment of the wound, infection risk and tetanus status.

stem: A hospital ward has several patients with diarrhoea caused by *Clostridioides difficile*. Which measure is particularly important for reducing transmission?

options.A: Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
options.B: Using alcohol hand gel as the only measure in every circumstance
options.C: Allowing unrestricted movement between affected patients and vulnerable patients
options.D: Sharing equipment between affected and unaffected patients without cleaning

correct_answer: A. Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
why_correct: *C. difficile* spores can persist in the environment, so appropriate hand hygiene and effective environmental cleaning are important infection-control measures.
why_wrong: B. Alcohol hand rub is not reliably sporicidal against *C. difficile* spores. C. Unrestricted contact can increase transmission. D. Shared contaminated equipment can facilitate transmission. E. Appropriate infection-control precautions should be maintained.
pearl: Alcohol gel does not kill C. difficile spores; use soap and water handwashing, isolation, gloves and aprons and sporicidal (chlorine-based) cleaning, alongside antibiotic review.
thinking: Ward outbreak of C. difficile diarrhoea ↓ The organism forms resistant spores ↓ Spores survive alcohol and persist on surfaces ↓ Appropriate hand hygiene and environmental cleaning with suitable sporicidal methods
exam_trap: B, alcohol gel as the only measure — it is standard ward hand hygiene, but it does not kill C. difficile spores; soap and water and sporicidal cleaning are needed.
takeaway: C. difficile: soap and water, not alcohol gel, plus sporicidal cleaning.

stem: A 26-year-old woman wants to start a combined oral contraceptive pill. Which factor is an important contraindication?
why_correct: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in women with migraine with aura because of the increased risk of ischaemic stroke.
why_wrong: A. Dysmenorrhoea is not a contraindication. C. Previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery is not a contraindication. D. Age 26 alone is not a contraindication. E. Mild acne is not a contraindication.
pearl: Migraine with aura is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk; progestogen-only methods or a copper IUD are suitable alternatives.
thinking: Wants the combined pill ↓ Oestrogen raises thrombotic risk ↓ Migraine with aura already raises stroke risk ↓ Combined risk unacceptable ↓ Migraine with aura
exam_trap: A, dysmenorrhoea — painful periods may seem a reason for caution, but the combined pill is often used to treat dysmenorrhoea and is not contraindicated.
