why_correct: Pregnancy requires prompt review of medication safety so that harmful exposure can be minimised while avoiding unsafe abrupt withdrawal of essential medicines.
why_wrong: A. Abruptly stopping essential medicines can cause harm. B. Delay prolongs potentially harmful fetal exposure. C. Exposure alone does not mandate termination; the risk needs specialist assessment and counselling. D. Folic acid does not offset the harm of a teratogenic medicine.
pearl: When pregnancy is confirmed on a potentially harmful medicine, review it urgently: some drugs need switching, but stopping essential treatment abruptly, such as antiepileptics, can harm mother and fetus.
thinking: Positive pregnancy test ↓ Taking a medicine known to be harmful in pregnancy ↓ Minimise fetal exposure without unsafe abrupt withdrawal ↓ Urgently review the medication's pregnancy safety
exam_trap: A, stop all regular medicines — it seems the safest instinct, but abrupt withdrawal of essential drugs can cause serious harm, such as seizures.
takeaway: Pregnancy on a risky drug: urgent medicine review, not blanket stopping or waiting.

stem: A pregnant woman is found to have blood group O RhD-negative status. Why is this clinically important?

options.A: She must have a caesarean section
options.B: She cannot carry a pregnancy safely
options.C: She cannot receive any blood products
options.D: She may require assessment for anti-D prophylaxis

correct_answer: D. She may require assessment for anti-D prophylaxis
why_correct: RhD-negative pregnant women may require anti-D prophylaxis to prevent maternal sensitisation and haemolytic disease in a future/current pregnancy where appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Blood group does not determine mode of delivery. B. RhD-negative women can have normal pregnancies. C. RhD-negative patients can receive appropriate blood products when required. E. Blood group does not diagnose iron deficiency.
pearl: RhD-negative women are assessed for antenatal anti-D prophylaxis and given anti-D after sensitising events, to prevent sensitisation and haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
thinking: RhD-negative mother ↓ An RhD-positive fetus could sensitise her immune system ↓ Anti-D antibodies threaten this or later pregnancies ↓ Assessment for anti-D prophylaxis
exam_trap: C, cannot receive any blood products — her group does matter for transfusion, but she can receive compatible products; the key issue in pregnancy is sensitisation.
takeaway: RhD-negative in pregnancy: think anti-D prophylaxis to prevent haemolytic disease.

stem: A pregnant woman has a routine antenatal blood test showing antibodies that could affect the fetus. What is the main concern?
correct_answer: C. Fetal and neonatal haemolytic disease
why_correct: Maternal red-cell antibodies can cross the placenta and cause fetal or neonatal haemolysis.
why_wrong: A. Red-cell antibodies do not cause gestational diabetes. B. Obstetric cholestasis is diagnosed by itch and raised bile acids, not antibody screening. D. Antibody positivity does not by itself diagnose placental abruption. E. Pre-eclampsia is defined by hypertension with proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
pearl: Maternal red-cell antibodies such as anti-D can cross the placenta and haemolyse fetal red cells, so their detection needs monitoring for fetal anaemia and neonatal jaundice.
thinking: Routine antenatal antibody screen ↓ Antibodies found that could affect the fetus ↓ IgG red-cell antibodies cross the placenta ↓ Fetal and neonatal haemolytic disease
exam_trap: E, pre-eclampsia — it is a major antenatal concern, but it is diagnosed by hypertension with proteinuria or organ dysfunction, not by red-cell antibodies.
takeaway: Red-cell antibodies in pregnancy mean risk of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.

stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman develops vaginal bleeding and severe abdominal pain. She feels faint and has a rapid pulse. What is the immediate concern?
why_correct: Pregnancy-associated bleeding with severe pain, faintness and tachycardia requires urgent assessment and resuscitation for possible significant haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Vasovagal syncope does not explain bleeding and severe abdominal pain. B. Supine hypotension resolves on lateral positioning and does not cause bleeding. C. Threatened miscarriage involves bleeding without haemodynamic compromise. E. Hyperemesis causes vomiting and dehydration, not vaginal bleeding with severe pain.
pearl: Bleeding, severe pain, faintness and tachycardia in pregnancy signal haemorrhagic shock, for example from a ruptured ectopic or abruption; resuscitate with ABCDE and call senior help immediately.
thinking: Pregnant with vaginal bleeding ↓ Severe abdominal pain ↓ Feels faint with a rapid pulse ↓ Hypovolaemic shock from haemorrhage
exam_trap: C, threatened miscarriage — bleeding in pregnancy suggests it, but threatened miscarriage involves a stable patient, not severe pain with signs of shock.
takeaway: Pregnancy bleeding plus tachycardia and faintness: treat as haemorrhagic shock.

stem: A 67-year-old woman develops new constipation and abdominal bloating. She has no vomiting and continues to pass flatus. What is the most appropriate initial consideration?
correct_answer: A. New change in bowel habit
why_correct: A new persistent change in bowel habit, particularly in an older adult, warrants assessment for an underlying cause.
why_wrong: B. Complete obstruction usually causes marked distension, vomiting and inability to pass stool or flatus. C. Volvulus causes acute pain, gross distension and absolute constipation. D. New bowel symptoms after the age of 60 should not be attributed to IBS without assessment. E. Appendicitis usually causes acute abdominal pain.
pearl: A new change in bowel habit in an older adult needs assessment for colorectal cancer; new bowel symptoms after 60 should not be attributed to IBS.
thinking: Woman in her late sixties ↓ New constipation and bloating ↓ Still passing flatus with no vomiting, so not obstructed ↓ New change in bowel habit
exam_trap: D, IBS with constipation — the symptoms resemble IBS-C, but new bowel symptoms in older adults must be investigated before IBS is considered.
takeaway: A new change in bowel habit in later life is investigated, not labelled IBS.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has painless bright-red rectal bleeding. She has no abdominal pain and feels otherwise well. Which common anorectal condition can cause this presentation?
why_correct: Haemorrhoids commonly cause painless bright-red rectal bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis causes severe upper abdominal pain. B. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain. C. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain. E. Gastric ulcer bleeding may cause melaena or haematemesis rather than typical painless fresh rectal blood.
pearl: Haemorrhoids classically cause painless bright-red blood on the paper or coating the stool; persistent or atypical bleeding still needs examination, including rectal examination and proctoscopy.
thinking: Bright-red rectal blood ↓ Painless and otherwise well ↓ Common anorectal source ↓ Haemorrhoids
exam_trap: E, gastric ulcer — the only other option that bleeds into the gut, but upper GI bleeding usually causes melaena or haematemesis, not fresh red rectal blood.
takeaway: Painless bright-red rectal bleeding suggests haemorrhoids, but still examine.

stem: A 61-year-old man develops painless progressive jaundice with weight loss. What serious underlying cause should be considered?
why_correct: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice with weight loss can be caused by malignancy obstructing the biliary system, including pancreatic cancer.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not cause jaundice. B. Tension headache is unrelated. C. IBS does not cause obstructive jaundice. E. Osteoarthritis does not cause jaundice.
pearl: Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss suggests pancreatic head cancer; a palpable gallbladder with painless jaundice (Courvoisier's law) makes gallstones less likely.
thinking: Older man ↓ Painless progressive jaundice ↓ Weight loss suggests malignancy ↓ Pancreatic malignancy
exam_trap: C, irritable bowel syndrome — the only other gut option, but IBS does not cause jaundice or significant weight loss.
takeaway: Painless jaundice plus weight loss: pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise.

stem: A 45-year-old man with acute pancreatitis becomes hypotensive and confused. What complication should be suspected?

options.A: Pancreatic pseudocyst formation in the lesser sac
options.D: Gallstone ileus from a cholecystoenteric fistula

correct_answer: B. Systemic inflammation with organ failure
why_correct: Severe acute pancreatitis can cause systemic inflammation and organ failure, with hypotension and altered mental state being concerning features.
why_wrong: A. Pseudocysts develop weeks later and do not explain acute shock. C. Chronic pancreatitis causes long-term pain and malabsorption, not acute hypotension and confusion. D. Gallstone ileus is small-bowel obstruction from a fistulating gallstone. E. Exocrine insufficiency causes malabsorption rather than acute circulatory compromise.
pearl: Hypotension or confusion in acute pancreatitis signals severe disease with systemic inflammation and organ failure; resuscitate promptly and involve critical care early.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis ↓ New hypotension and confusion ↓ Systemic inflammatory response causing circulatory and cerebral dysfunction ↓ Systemic inflammation with organ failure
exam_trap: A, pancreatic pseudocyst — a well-known complication, but pseudocysts develop weeks later and do not cause acute shock and confusion.
takeaway: Shock or confusion in acute pancreatitis means severe disease with organ failure.

stem: A 64-year-old man develops severe abdominal pain and abdominal distension. He has persistent vomiting and cannot pass flatus. What complication of bowel obstruction is particularly important to identify?
why_correct: Prolonged or strangulated obstruction can compromise the blood supply to the bowel, causing ischaemia and potentially perforation.
why_wrong: A. Otitis externa affects the ear. C. Vitiligo causes depigmentation. D. Migraine is unrelated. E. Cataract affects the lens.
pearl: In bowel obstruction, constant severe pain, peritonism, fever, tachycardia or raised lactate suggest strangulation and ischaemia, which needs urgent surgical review.
thinking: Severe pain, distension and vomiting ↓ Cannot pass flatus ↓ Obstruction can compromise the bowel blood supply ↓ Bowel ischaemia
exam_trap: D, migraine — it can cause vomiting, the one overlapping feature, but it does not cause abdominal distension or absolute constipation.
takeaway: In obstruction, look actively for ischaemia: strangulated bowel needs urgent surgery.

stem: A 43-year-old man develops severe abdominal pain and fever. His abdomen is rigid and extremely tender. What does this suggest?
why_correct: Severe abdominal tenderness with rigidity and systemic illness suggests inflammation of the peritoneum.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause rigidity. B. Simple constipation does not typically cause peritonism and fever. C. Migraine does not cause abdominal rigidity. E. Biliary colic causes episodic upper abdominal pain without generalized peritonism.
pearl: A rigid, board-like abdomen with fever indicates generalised peritonitis, often from perforation; resuscitate, give antibiotics and seek urgent surgical review.
thinking: Severe abdominal pain with fever ↓ Rigid, extremely tender abdomen ↓ Signs of peritoneal inflammation ↓ Peritonitis
exam_trap: E, biliary colic — it causes severe abdominal pain, but it is episodic upper abdominal pain without fever or generalised rigidity.
takeaway: Rigidity plus fever means peritonitis: an emergency surgical abdomen.

stem: A 37-year-old man develops severe epigastric pain after taking large amounts of NSAIDs. What gastrointestinal complication is a recognised risk?
why_correct: NSAIDs impair gastric mucosal protection and increase the risk of peptic ulcer disease.
why_wrong: A. Gallstone pancreatitis is caused by gallstones rather than NSAID use. B. Biliary colic results from gallstones. C. NSAIDs are not a recognised cause of gastric adenocarcinoma. E. Varices result from portal hypertension.
pearl: NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection and cause peptic ulcers; stop the NSAID and consider PPI protection in higher-risk patients who need ongoing NSAIDs.
thinking: Large NSAID intake ↓ Loss of prostaglandin mucosal protection ↓ Severe epigastric pain ↓ Peptic ulcer disease
exam_trap: A, acute gallstone pancreatitis — it also causes severe epigastric pain, but it is caused by gallstones, not NSAID use.
takeaway: NSAIDs plus epigastric pain: think peptic ulcer and watch for bleeding or perforation.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with haematemesis and dizziness. Her blood pressure is low and pulse is rapid. What is the immediate priority?

options.D: Oral omeprazole and observation on the ward

why_correct: Haematemesis with haemodynamic compromise represents a potentially life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleed requiring immediate resuscitation.
why_wrong: A. Risk scores support later decisions but do not take priority over resuscitation. B. Endoscopy follows resuscitation. D. PPIs before endoscopy are not recommended, and ward observation alone is unsafe in shock. E. Tranexamic acid is not recommended for upper GI bleeding and does not replace resuscitation.
pearl: In upper GI bleeding with shock, resuscitate first: large-bore access, bloods including crossmatch, fluids and blood as needed, with endoscopy immediately after resuscitation.
thinking: Haematemesis ↓ Dizzy, hypotensive and tachycardic ↓ Haemodynamically unstable upper GI bleed ↓ ABCDE assessment and resuscitation
exam_trap: B, urgent endoscopy — endoscopy is the definitive step for an unstable bleed, but it follows resuscitation rather than replacing it.
takeaway: Unstable GI bleed: ABCDE and resuscitate first, endoscopy after.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has long-standing reflux symptoms. Which complication of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux can predispose to oesophageal adenocarcinoma?
why_correct: Barrett's oesophagus is associated with chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux and carries an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Peptic strictures cause dysphagia but are not premalignant. C. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is an allergic condition rather than a complication of reflux. D. Candidiasis is an infection associated with immunosuppression or inhaled steroids. E. A hiatus hernia predisposes to reflux rather than being a premalignant complication of it.
pearl: Barrett's oesophagus is columnar metaplasia of the lower oesophagus caused by chronic reflux; it is the precursor of oesophageal adenocarcinoma and is kept under endoscopic surveillance.
thinking: Long-standing reflux ↓ Chronic acid exposure changes the lower oesophageal lining ↓ Columnar metaplasia is premalignant ↓ Barrett's oesophagus
exam_trap: A, peptic oesophageal stricture — a genuine complication of chronic reflux, but it causes dysphagia and is not premalignant.
takeaway: Reflux leads to Barrett's, which predisposes to adenocarcinoma.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids. Symptoms vary considerably from day to day. Which broad mechanism is most consistent with this pattern?
why_correct: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from an early stage, particularly when intermittent, suggests a motility disorder.
why_wrong: A. Fixed mechanical obstruction usually causes solids-first dysphagia. B. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. C. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain. D. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms.
pearl: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests a mechanical stricture or tumour.
thinking: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids ↓ Intermittent and variable from day to day ↓ Abnormal oesophageal motility rather than fixed narrowing ↓ Oesophageal motility disorder
exam_trap: A, fixed mechanical obstruction — the only other oesophageal mechanism, but it causes progressive solids-first dysphagia rather than variable symptoms.
takeaway: Solids and liquids from the start: motility. Solids first, then liquids: mechanical.

stem: A 63-year-old man has chronic cough and hoarseness. He also reports longstanding heartburn. Which condition can cause extra-oesophageal symptoms in association with reflux?
why_correct: Reflux can be associated with upper airway or respiratory symptoms in some patients.
why_wrong: A. Eosinophilic oesophagitis typically causes dysphagia and food bolus obstruction. B. Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food. D. Candidiasis causes odynophagia, usually in immunosuppressed patients. E. Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes chest pain and intermittent dysphagia.
pearl: Reflux can cause extra-oesophageal symptoms such as chronic cough, hoarseness and throat clearing; persistent hoarseness in an older adult still needs ENT assessment to exclude laryngeal cancer.
thinking: Chronic cough and hoarseness ↓ Longstanding heartburn ↓ Refluxed acid can irritate the larynx and airways ↓ Gastro-oesophageal reflux
exam_trap: B, achalasia — it can cause regurgitation and aspiration cough, but it presents with progressive dysphagia rather than heartburn with hoarseness.
takeaway: Reflux can present with cough and hoarseness, but persistent hoarseness needs cancer excluded.

stem: A patient with suspected C. difficile infection asks how transmission can be reduced in hospital. Which measure is particularly important?

options.A: Effective hand hygiene and appropriate infection-control measures
options.C: Encouraging unnecessary contact between symptomatic patients

correct_answer: A. Effective hand hygiene and appropriate infection-control measures
why_correct: C. difficile spores can spread in healthcare settings, making appropriate infection-control measures essential.
why_wrong: B. Sharing towels can facilitate transmission. C. Contact between symptomatic patients can facilitate spread. D. Environmental cleaning is important. E. Unnecessary antibiotics increase the risk of C. difficile.
pearl: C. difficile spores are not killed by alcohol gel, so control relies on soap-and-water handwashing, isolation, gloves and aprons, and chlorine-based environmental cleaning.
thinking: Suspected C. difficile in hospital ↓ Spread by spores via hands and the environment ↓ Spores resist alcohol and persist on surfaces ↓ Effective hand hygiene and infection-control measures
exam_trap: E, indiscriminate antibiotics — antibiotics treat C. difficile, but broad, unnecessary antibiotic use is the main risk factor for acquiring it.
takeaway: C. difficile: soap and water, isolation, cleaning and antibiotic stewardship.

stem: A 39-year-old woman has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and recurrent mouth ulcers. Which inflammatory bowel disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract?
why_correct: Crohn's disease can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus and may cause weight loss and extraintestinal manifestations.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause inflammatory disease or weight loss as a typical feature. B. Coeliac disease primarily affects the small intestine and has a different mechanism. D. Haemorrhoids do not cause chronic inflammatory diarrhoea. E. Ulcerative colitis is confined to the colon and rectum.
pearl: Crohn's disease is transmural and can affect anywhere from mouth to anus with skip lesions; mouth ulcers, perianal disease and weight loss are useful clues.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss ↓ Recurrent mouth ulcers ↓ Inflammatory disease beyond the colon ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: E, ulcerative colitis — the other main IBD, but it is confined to the colon and rectum and does not affect the whole gut.
takeaway: Mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural: Crohn's. Colon only, continuous: UC.

stem: A patient with suspected infectious mononucleosis is prescribed an antibiotic and subsequently develops a widespread rash. Which antibiotic classically causes this reaction in infectious mononucleosis?
why_correct: A widespread maculopapular rash can occur after aminopenicillin treatment in infectious mononucleosis.
why_wrong: A. Tetracyclines do not cause the classic infectious-mononucleosis-associated rash. B. Metronidazole is not the classic association. C. Nitrofurantoin is not the classic association. D. Macrolides are not classically associated with this characteristic reaction.
pearl: Amoxicillin or ampicillin given during glandular fever commonly causes a widespread maculopapular rash, so avoid aminopenicillins when a sore throat could be EBV.
thinking: Suspected infectious mononucleosis ↓ Antibiotic given, often for presumed tonsillitis ↓ Widespread rash follows ↓ Aminopenicillin
exam_trap: D, macrolide — a common sore throat antibiotic, especially in penicillin allergy, but it is not the classic cause of the glandular fever rash.
takeaway: Glandular fever plus amoxicillin often means a widespread rash.

stem: A 52-year-old man has a painful swollen eyelid with localised tenderness near the eyelashes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A painful, localised inflammatory swelling at the eyelid margin is typical of a stye.
why_wrong: A. Optic neuritis causes visual loss and pain with eye movement. B. Glaucoma affects intraocular pressure and the optic nerve. D. Retinal detachment affects the retina. E. Cataract affects the lens and causes painless visual impairment.
pearl: A stye is an acute infection of a lash follicle or associated gland at the lid margin; warm compresses usually suffice and antibiotics are rarely needed.
thinking: Painful swollen eyelid ↓ Localised tenderness at the lash line ↓ Acute infection of a lash follicle ↓ Stye
exam_trap: A, optic neuritis — it also causes eye pain, but it presents with visual loss and pain on eye movement, not a tender eyelid swelling.
takeaway: Tender lump at the lash line is a stye; a firm painless lump within the lid is a chalazion.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has chronic irritation and crusting around both eyelid margins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Chronic inflammation and crusting of the eyelid margins are characteristic of blepharitis.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment. B. Acute angle closure causes severe painful red eye and visual disturbance. C. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss. E. Retinal detachment causes visual-field symptoms.
pearl: Blepharitis is chronic lid-margin inflammation causing gritty, sore eyes and crusting; it is managed long term with lid hygiene and warm compresses.
thinking: Chronic irritation ↓ Crusting along both eyelid margins ↓ Bilateral lid-margin inflammation ↓ Blepharitis
exam_trap: B, acute angle-closure glaucoma — an irritable eye may suggest it, but it is acute, severely painful and affects vision, unlike chronic crusted lids.
takeaway: Chronic bilateral crusting of the lid margins is blepharitis; treat with lid hygiene.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has viral conjunctivitis and notices a tender lump just in front of her ear. Which lymph node group is most likely enlarged?
why_correct: The pre-auricular lymph nodes drain the eyelids, conjunctiva, temporal scalp and anterior ear, and tender pre-auricular lymphadenopathy is typical of viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis.
why_wrong: A. Epitrochlear nodes drain the medial forearm and hand. C. Popliteal nodes drain parts of the leg and foot. D. Inguinal nodes drain the lower limb, perineum and external genitalia. E. Supraclavicular nodes drain the thorax and abdomen and are not the regional nodes for the eye.
pearl: Tender pre-auricular lymphadenopathy with a red, watery eye points to adenoviral conjunctivitis, which is highly contagious, so advise strict hand hygiene.
thinking: Viral conjunctivitis ↓ Tender lump just in front of the ear ↓ Conjunctiva and eyelids drain to the pre-auricular nodes ↓ Pre-auricular lymph node
exam_trap: E, supraclavicular node — a well-known, clinically important node, but it drains the thorax and abdomen, not the eye.
takeaway: Viral conjunctivitis with a tender pre-auricular node suggests adenovirus.

stem: A 20-year-old man has a painless enlarged lymph node in the neck that has persisted for several weeks. He has no obvious local infection. What is an important consideration?
why_correct: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy requires assessment for causes including infection, inflammatory disease and malignancy.
why_wrong: B. A thyroglossal cyst is midline and moves with tongue protrusion rather than being a lymph node. C. Submandibular stones cause meal-related swelling and pain. D. A pharyngeal pouch causes dysphagia, regurgitation and halitosis. E. A node persisting for several weeks without explanation requires assessment.
pearl: Painless neck lymphadenopathy persisting for weeks without an infective cause needs assessment for lymphoma and other malignancy; in young adults Hodgkin lymphoma is a key consideration.
thinking: Young man with a painless neck node ↓ Persisting for several weeks ↓ No local infection to explain it ↓ Lymphadenopathy needing assessment
exam_trap: E, normal finding — reactive nodes are common in young people, but a node persisting for weeks without an infective cause needs assessment.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained painless lymphadenopathy must be assessed, not dismissed.

stem: A 36-year-old man develops a painful swelling under his jaw that becomes worse when eating. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Pain and swelling of a salivary gland triggered by eating are characteristic of salivary gland stones causing obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Pleomorphic adenoma is a slow-growing painless parotid swelling. C. Mumps causes parotid swelling with systemic symptoms rather than recurrent meal-related pain. D. Lymphadenitis is not provoked by eating. E. A dental abscess causes toothache and localised swelling unrelated to meals.
pearl: Salivary stones occur most often in the submandibular gland; pain and swelling at mealtimes from duct obstruction is the classic history.
thinking: Painful swelling under the jaw ↓ Worse when eating ↓ Salivary flow blocked during meals ↓ Submandibular gland stone
exam_trap: D, reactive cervical lymphadenitis — a tender lump under the jaw fits, but node swelling is not triggered by eating.
takeaway: Meal-related salivary swelling and pain means duct obstruction, usually a submandibular stone.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has recurrent swelling and pain near the angle of her jaw. The symptoms worsen during meals. What anatomical structure is most likely involved?
why_correct: The parotid glands lie near the angle of the jaw and can become painful and swollen when their ducts are obstructed.
why_wrong: B. The appendix is in the abdomen. C. The pancreas is in the upper abdomen. D. The thyroid is in the anterior neck. E. The kidneys are retroperitoneal.
pearl: Swelling at the angle of the jaw is parotid territory; recurrent pain and swelling with meals suggest obstruction of the parotid duct by a stone or stricture.
thinking: Swelling near the angle of the jaw ↓ Recurrent and worse with meals ↓ Salivary duct obstruction ↓ Parotid gland
exam_trap: D, thyroid gland — the only other neck structure offered, but it lies in the anterior neck and its swelling is not meal-related.
takeaway: Angle-of-jaw swelling is parotid; meal-related pain points to a salivary cause.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has a thyroid swelling and develops hoarseness of her voice. Which nearby nerve can be affected by thyroid pathology?
why_correct: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply the intrinsic muscles of the larynx and can be affected by thyroid disease or surgery, causing voice changes.
why_wrong: A. The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles. B. The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm. C. The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. D. The marginal mandibular nerve supplies muscles of the lower lip.
pearl: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the thyroid; hoarseness with a thyroid swelling raises concern for malignant infiltration and needs urgent assessment including laryngoscopy.
thinking: Thyroid swelling ↓ New hoarseness ↓ Nerve supplying the intrinsic laryngeal muscles lies beside the thyroid ↓ Recurrent laryngeal nerve
exam_trap: A, hypoglossal nerve — a neck nerve linked to speech, but it supplies the tongue, so damage causes dysarthria rather than hoarseness.
takeaway: Thyroid lump plus hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement, so suspect malignancy.

stem: A 32-year-old woman has a thyroid swelling and develops symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Which symptom would support hyperthyroidism?
why_correct: Heat intolerance is a typical symptom of increased thyroid hormone activity.
why_wrong: A. Hyperthyroidism more commonly causes tachycardia. C. Constipation is more typical of hypothyroidism. D. Cold intolerance is more characteristic of hypothyroidism. E. Weight gain is more typical of hypothyroidism.
pearl: Hyperthyroidism raises the metabolic rate: heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss despite good appetite, tremor, palpitations and loose stools.
thinking: Thyroid swelling ↓ Symptoms of hyperthyroidism ↓ Increased metabolic rate generates excess heat ↓ Heat intolerance
exam_trap: D, cold intolerance — a classic, easily recalled thyroid symptom, but it belongs to hypothyroidism.
takeaway: Hyperthyroid: hot, thin and fast. Hypothyroid: cold, heavy and slow.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has episodes of palpitations, sweating and tremor. Her pulse is persistently fast. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Palpitations, sweating and tremor are typical features of increased thyroid hormone activity.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism is more associated with fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance. B. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. C. Osteoarthritis causes joint symptoms. E. Cataract causes visual impairment.
pearl: Palpitations, sweating, tremor and persistent tachycardia suggest hyperthyroidism; check TSH and free T4, and a beta-blocker can control symptoms meanwhile.
thinking: Palpitations, sweating and tremor ↓ Persistently fast pulse ↓ Excess thyroid hormone drives adrenergic-type features ↓ Hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: A, hypothyroidism — it is the other thyroid diagnosis, but it causes bradycardia, cold intolerance and weight gain, the opposite picture.
takeaway: Persistent tachycardia with tremor and sweating: check thyroid function.

stem: A 23-year-old man is found unconscious after taking an unknown quantity of tablets. His respiratory rate is 6/min and his pupils are pinpoint. Which drug class is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Opioid toxicity classically causes reduced consciousness, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils.
why_wrong: B. Amphetamines typically cause agitation, tachycardia and hypertension. C. Cocaine usually causes sympathetic overactivity. D. Tricyclic overdose can cause coma, arrhythmias and broad QRS complexes. E. Benzodiazepines cause CNS depression but do not typically cause marked pinpoint pupils and profound respiratory depression alone.
pearl: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and reduced consciousness form the opioid toxidrome; give titrated naloxone and support breathing, watching for re-sedation as naloxone wears off.
thinking: Unconscious after an unknown quantity of tablets ↓ Respiratory rate 6/min ↓ Pinpoint pupils ↓ Classic opioid toxidrome ↓ Opioids
exam_trap: E, benzodiazepines — they cause drowsiness, but on their own they rarely cause pinpoint pupils with profound respiratory depression.
takeaway: Pinpoint pupils plus slow breathing: opioid toxicity, give naloxone.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is found drowsy after taking an excessive amount of diazepam. Which drug can specifically reverse benzodiazepine effects?
why_correct: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist.
why_wrong: B. Vitamin K reverses warfarin anticoagulation. C. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity. D. Glucagon is used in specific situations including severe beta-blocker toxicity. E. Adrenaline is used in emergencies including anaphylaxis.
pearl: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but is not used routinely because it can provoke seizures, especially in mixed overdoses or dependence; supportive care is usually enough.
thinking: Drowsy after excess diazepam ↓ Diazepam is a benzodiazepine ↓ Needs a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: C, naloxone — the familiar overdose antidote, but it reverses opioids and has no effect on benzodiazepines.
takeaway: Benzodiazepines: flumazenil, used with caution. Opioids: naloxone.

stem: A 76-year-old woman taking a direct oral anticoagulant develops a major gastrointestinal haemorrhage. Her medication is identified as dabigatran. Which specific reversal agent is available?
why_correct: Idarucizumab is a specific reversal agent for dabigatran.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids. B. Vitamin K reverses warfarin. C. Protamine reverses heparin. D. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
pearl: Idarucizumab is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran; vitamin K reverses warfarin but has no effect on direct oral anticoagulants.
thinking: Major haemorrhage on a DOAC ↓ Drug identified as dabigatran ↓ Dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor with its own antibody antidote ↓ Idarucizumab
exam_trap: B, vitamin K — the best-known anticoagulant reversal, but it works only for warfarin and does nothing for dabigatran.
takeaway: Dabigatran bleed: idarucizumab. Warfarin bleed: vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes is found unconscious. His capillary glucose is very low and he cannot safely swallow. What is appropriate treatment?
why_correct: Severe hypoglycaemia with impaired consciousness requires parenteral glucose when intravenous access is available.
why_wrong: B. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia. C. Metformin does not rapidly correct hypoglycaemia. D. Oral treatment is unsafe in an unconscious patient. E. Iron has no role.
pearl: Hypoglycaemia with impaired consciousness or an unsafe swallow needs IV glucose, or IM glucagon if there is no IV access; never give oral glucose to an unconscious patient.
thinking: Person with diabetes found unconscious ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Cannot swallow safely, so the oral route is unsafe ↓ Intravenous glucose
exam_trap: D, oral glucose tablets — standard first-line for mild hypoglycaemia, but unsafe in an unconscious patient who cannot protect the airway.
takeaway: Hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness: IV glucose or IM glucagon, never oral.

stem: A 72-year-old man develops muscle weakness after taking a new medication. Blood tests show a markedly elevated potassium concentration. Which cardiac complication is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Severe hyperkalaemia can cause dangerous cardiac conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias.
why_wrong: B. Pericarditis is inflammatory and not caused by hyperkalaemia. C. Aortic dissection is a structural vascular emergency unrelated to potassium. D. Endocarditis is an infection of the heart valves. E. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is stress-induced and not a recognised effect of hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Severe hyperkalaemia can cause peaked T waves, broad QRS complexes and fatal arrhythmias; get an ECG immediately and review culprit drugs such as ACE inhibitors and potassium-sparing diuretics.
thinking: New medication ↓ Muscle weakness ↓ Markedly raised potassium disrupts cardiac conduction ↓ Cardiac arrhythmia
exam_trap: E, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy — an acute cardiac complication with a recognised trigger, but it is stress-induced and not caused by hyperkalaemia, which acts on conduction.
takeaway: Severe hyperkalaemia: the danger is arrhythmia, so get an ECG straight away.

stem: A patient with severe hyperkalaemia develops ECG changes. Which treatment is used to protect the myocardium while definitive measures lower potassium?
why_correct: IV calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG abnormalities.
why_wrong: B. Magnesium does not stabilise the myocardium in hyperkalaemia. C. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate is a potassium binder that lowers potassium over hours and does not protect the myocardium. D. Salbutamol shifts potassium into cells but does not stabilise the cardiac membrane. E. Furosemide increases renal potassium loss slowly and does not protect the myocardium.
pearl: IV calcium (gluconate or chloride) stabilises the myocardium within minutes but does not lower potassium, so insulin with glucose and definitive measures must follow.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ ECG changes present ↓ Myocardium needs immediate membrane stabilisation ↓ Intravenous calcium
exam_trap: D, nebulised salbutamol — a genuine hyperkalaemia treatment, but it lowers potassium by shifting it into cells and does not protect the heart.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first to protect the heart.

stem: A 45-year-old man with severe hyperkalaemia requires a rapid temporary reduction in serum potassium. Which treatment shifts potassium into cells?
why_correct: Insulin promotes cellular uptake of potassium; glucose is given to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia.
why_wrong: B. Calcium stabilises the myocardium but does not lower potassium. C. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate removes potassium via the gut over hours rather than shifting it into cells. D. Furosemide increases renal excretion rather than shifting potassium into cells. E. Haemodialysis removes potassium from the body rather than shifting it into cells.
pearl: Insulin with glucose drives potassium into cells quickly but only temporarily; monitor capillary glucose afterwards because hypoglycaemia is a common complication.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ Needs rapid temporary lowering ↓ Insulin stimulates cellular potassium uptake ↓ Insulin with glucose
exam_trap: B, IV calcium gluconate — it is given early in severe hyperkalaemia, but it only stabilises the myocardium and does not lower potassium.
takeaway: Calcium protects; insulin–glucose and salbutamol shift; binders and dialysis remove.

stem: A 40-year-old man develops severe muscle cramps and tingling around his mouth after prolonged vomiting. Blood tests show low calcium. Which symptom is characteristic of hypocalcaemia?
why_correct: Hypocalcaemia can cause perioral tingling, paraesthesia and muscle spasms.
why_wrong: B. Productive cough suggests respiratory infection. C. Jaundice indicates bilirubin accumulation. D. Polyuria is associated with disorders such as diabetes insipidus. E. Haematuria indicates urinary tract pathology.
pearl: Hypocalcaemia causes perioral and peripheral tingling, cramps and tetany; Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs are classic, and severe symptoms need IV calcium gluconate.
thinking: Prolonged vomiting ↓ Low calcium on blood tests ↓ Increased neuromuscular excitability ↓ Perioral paraesthesia
exam_trap: D, polyuria from diabetes insipidus — an electrolyte-linked symptom, but calcium-related polyuria is a feature of hypercalcaemia, not hypocalcaemia.
takeaway: Tingling around the mouth, cramps and tetany: check the calcium.

stem: A 63-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has a markedly raised phosphate concentration. Which abnormality commonly accompanies this?
why_correct: Chronic kidney disease commonly causes phosphate retention and reduced calcium availability, contributing to secondary hyperparathyroidism.
why_wrong: B. Hyperglycaemia is not a direct consequence of phosphate retention. C. CKD more commonly causes anaemia. D. Bilirubin is not directly related. E. Sodium is not characteristically increased.
pearl: CKD causes phosphate retention and reduced activation of vitamin D, lowering calcium and driving secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease ↓ Phosphate retained and less active vitamin D ↓ Calcium falls ↓ Reduced serum calcium
exam_trap: C, increased haemoglobin — kidneys do regulate red cell production, but CKD reduces erythropoietin and causes anaemia, not a raised haemoglobin.
takeaway: CKD: high phosphate, low calcium, high PTH.

stem: A 27-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of one side of her body while taking a combined oral contraceptive. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficit is a medical emergency and may represent acute stroke.
why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment. B. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause sudden hemiparesis. E. Tension headache does not typically cause sudden focal neurological deficit.
pearl: Sudden focal neurology is stroke until proven otherwise, even in young adults; oestrogen-containing contraception adds to thrombotic risk.
thinking: Sudden one-sided weakness ↓ Focal neurological deficit ↓ Combined pill adds thrombotic risk ↓ Stroke
exam_trap: E, tension headache — it is common in young adults, but it does not cause sudden hemiparesis.
takeaway: Sudden focal weakness at any age needs urgent stroke assessment.

stem: A 74-year-old man develops sudden unilateral weakness and speech difficulty. What should happen first?
correct_answer: D. Activate the acute stroke pathway
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms require urgent stroke assessment because time-sensitive treatment may be appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Iron does not treat acute neurological deficit. B. Discharge would risk missing an acute stroke. C. Cataract surgery is unrelated. E. Physiotherapy is not the immediate priority.
pearl: Sudden weakness with speech disturbance needs immediate stroke-pathway activation and urgent brain imaging, because thrombolysis and thrombectomy are time-critical.
thinking: Sudden unilateral weakness ↓ Speech difficulty ↓ Acute stroke likely and treatment is time-dependent ↓ Activate the acute stroke pathway
exam_trap: E, outpatient physiotherapy — rehabilitation matters after stroke, but delaying acute assessment loses the window for reperfusion treatment.
takeaway: Time is brain: suspected stroke means the acute stroke pathway now.

stem: A 56-year-old man develops sudden monocular loss of vision that he describes as a curtain descending over the eye. What should be suspected?
correct_answer: A. Retinal detachment or vascular occlusion
why_correct: Sudden monocular visual loss is an ocular emergency and requires urgent assessment; a curtain-like field defect is particularly concerning for retinal detachment.
why_wrong: B. Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes without a curtain-like field loss. C. Angle closure causes a painful red eye with haloes. D. Migraine aura is usually binocular, positive and transient. E. Age-related macular degeneration causes gradual central visual loss.
pearl: A curtain or shadow across the vision of one eye suggests retinal detachment and needs same-day ophthalmology; sudden monocular loss may also be a retinal vascular occlusion.
thinking: Sudden monocular visual loss ↓ Described as a curtain descending ↓ Field loss from retinal pathology ↓ Retinal detachment or vascular occlusion
exam_trap: B, posterior vitreous detachment — it often precedes retinal detachment, but it causes flashes and floaters without a curtain-like field defect.
takeaway: Curtain over one eye: urgent same-day eye assessment for retinal detachment.

stem: A 61-year-old man has sudden painless monocular visual loss. The eye is not red or painful. Which diagnosis is an important consideration?
why_correct: Sudden, profound, painless monocular visual loss is characteristic of retinal artery occlusion and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Corneal abrasion causes pain and photophobia. C. Anterior uveitis causes a painful photophobic red eye. D. Conjunctivitis generally preserves vision. E. Acute angle closure causes severe pain and a red eye.
pearl: Sudden painless profound monocular loss suggests central retinal artery occlusion, a stroke equivalent; refer immediately and in older patients consider giant cell arteritis.
thinking: Sudden monocular visual loss ↓ Painless, eye not red ↓ Vascular cause in the retina ↓ Retinal artery occlusion
exam_trap: E, acute angle-closure glaucoma — a sudden sight-threatening emergency, but it causes a painful red eye, which this patient does not have.
takeaway: Sudden painless monocular loss in a quiet eye: think retinal artery occlusion.

stem: A 47-year-old woman develops transient episodes of weakness and numbness affecting one side of the body. Each episode lasts several minutes and is followed by complete recovery. Which investigation is particularly important to identify a possible vascular cause?
correct_answer: C. Urgent brain and vascular assessment
why_correct: Recurrent transient focal neurological symptoms require urgent assessment for cerebrovascular disease.
why_wrong: A. EEG is for suspected seizures and does not identify a vascular cause. B. Delayed investigation is inappropriate after a suspected TIA; assessment should be urgent. D. Lumbar puncture does not identify a vascular cause. E. Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves.
pearl: Transient focal deficits with full recovery suggest TIA; start antiplatelet treatment and arrange urgent specialist assessment with brain and carotid imaging.
thinking: Brief episodes of one-sided weakness and numbness ↓ Complete recovery each time ↓ Recurrent TIAs carry a high early stroke risk ↓ Urgent brain and vascular assessment
exam_trap: A, EEG — recurrent transient episodes may suggest seizures, but sudden negative symptoms such as weakness and numbness with full recovery point to TIA.
takeaway: TIA is a stroke warning: urgent specialist and vascular assessment.

stem: A hospital patient becomes acutely confused overnight. He is pulling at his intravenous line and is unable to maintain attention during conversation. What should be done first?

options.A: Prescribe regular oral haloperidol at night
options.B: Identify and treat causes of delirium
options.C: Apply wrist restraints to protect the line
options.D: Start a cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil

correct_answer: B. Identify and treat causes of delirium
why_correct: Delirium requires assessment for reversible precipitants such as infection, medication effects, pain, dehydration and metabolic disturbance.
why_wrong: A. Antipsychotics are reserved for severe distress or risk after non-drug measures and do not treat the cause. C. Restraints increase agitation and injury risk. D. Cholinesterase inhibitors treat dementia, not delirium. E. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium unless treating alcohol withdrawal.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating inattention; look first for causes such as infection, drugs, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration and metabolic upset, alongside non-drug measures.
thinking: Acute confusion overnight ↓ Inattention and agitation ↓ Delirium ↓ Identify and treat causes of delirium
exam_trap: A, regular haloperidol — it is used in delirium, but only short-term for severe distress or risk after non-drug measures, and it does not treat the cause.
takeaway: Delirium: find and treat the cause first; sedation is a last resort.

stem: A 82-year-old patient with dementia becomes increasingly agitated in hospital. Which environmental measure may help reduce distress and confusion?

options.A: Remove hearing aids to reduce background noise
options.B: Move to a busier ward for closer observation
options.C: Keep the room dark during the day to encourage sleep

why_correct: Familiar surroundings, orientation and appropriate sensory aids can reduce confusion and distress.
why_wrong: A. Removing sensory aids impairs communication and worsens confusion. B. Moving ward increases disorientation. C. Darkness can worsen disorientation. E. Antipsychotics are not first-line and carry stroke and mortality risks in dementia.
pearl: Agitation in dementia often eases with orientation, familiar objects and people, sensory aids, consistent staff and a calm, well-lit environment; antipsychotics are a last resort.
thinking: Dementia with agitation in hospital ↓ Unfamiliar setting drives confusion ↓ Non-drug measures come first ↓ Familiar surroundings and orientation
exam_trap: E, regular low-dose antipsychotic — it can calm agitation, but it is not first-line and increases stroke and mortality risk in dementia.
takeaway: Agitation in dementia: environment and orientation first, drugs last.

stem: A 75-year-old man taking several medicines develops a new fall and dizziness. What should be considered as part of the assessment?
why_correct: Polypharmacy and adverse drug effects can contribute to falls and dizziness, so medication review is important.
why_wrong: A. Dental treatment does not address the immediate issue. B. Cataract surgery may be relevant only if visual impairment is identified. C. Antibiotics are not indicated simply because a fall occurred. D. Parkinson's disease cannot be diagnosed from a single fall.
pearl: Falls in older adults are often drug-related: antihypertensives, sedatives, anticholinergics and psychotropics cause dizziness and postural hypotension, so review medicines after every fall.
thinking: Older man on several medicines ↓ New fall with dizziness ↓ Polypharmacy is a common reversible cause ↓ Medication review
exam_trap: D, immediate Parkinson's diagnosis — falls occur in Parkinson's disease, but the diagnosis needs characteristic clinical features, not a single fall.
takeaway: A fall with dizziness on multiple medicines needs a medication review.

stem: A 71-year-old woman taking a medicine with strong anticholinergic effects develops dry mouth, constipation and blurred vision. Which explanation is most likely?

options.C: Primary Sjögren's syndrome with dry eyes

why_correct: Dry mouth, constipation and blurred vision are typical anticholinergic effects.
why_wrong: B. Autonomic neuropathy occurs in long-standing diabetes and is not linked to a new drug. C. Sjögren's syndrome causes dry eyes and mouth but does not explain drug-related constipation and blurred vision. D. Hypothyroidism can cause constipation but does not explain dry mouth and blurred vision after starting an anticholinergic drug. E. Serotonin syndrome causes hyperthermia, clonus and agitation.
pearl: Anticholinergics cause dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention and confusion; older adults are especially vulnerable, so review the total anticholinergic burden.
thinking: Older woman on a strongly anticholinergic drug ↓ Dry mouth, constipation and blurred vision ↓ Classic muscarinic blockade pattern ↓ Anticholinergic side effects
exam_trap: C, Sjögren's syndrome — it causes dryness, but it does not explain constipation and blurred vision after starting an anticholinergic drug.
takeaway: Dry mouth, constipation and blurred vision on a new drug: think anticholinergic effects.

stem: A 79-year-old man has difficulty swallowing and has lost weight because eating has become difficult. What is an important immediate management principle?

options.A: Arrange PEG feeding tube insertion first
options.D: Start an appetite stimulant such as megestrol
options.E: Advise a soft diet and review in 3 months

correct_answer: B. Assess swallow safety and nutrition
why_correct: Dysphagia can lead to aspiration and malnutrition, so swallowing safety and adequate nutrition require assessment.
why_wrong: A. Tube feeding is considered only after swallowing and nutritional assessment. C. Oral supplements may be unsafe before swallowing safety is known. D. The problem is difficulty swallowing, not appetite. E. Delayed review risks aspiration and further malnutrition, and new dysphagia also needs investigation.
pearl: In dysphagia with weight loss, assess swallow safety, often with speech and language therapy, and nutritional status, and investigate the cause; new dysphagia warrants urgent endoscopy.
thinking: Older man with difficulty swallowing ↓ Weight loss from reduced intake ↓ Risks of aspiration and malnutrition ↓ Assess swallow safety and nutrition
exam_trap: C, high-calorie sip feeds alone — they address weight loss, but liquids may be aspirated before swallow safety is known, and the cause is left uninvestigated.
takeaway: Dysphagia with weight loss: assess swallow and nutrition, and investigate the cause.

stem: A 66-year-old woman is admitted after a fall. She is found to have poor appetite and has unintentionally lost 8 kg over the previous six months. Which assessment is particularly appropriate?
why_correct: Significant unintentional weight loss and poor intake indicate risk of malnutrition and warrant nutritional assessment.
why_wrong: B. Hearing assessment may be useful for other reasons but does not address the primary concern. C. Allergy testing is not indicated by this presentation. D. Visual-field testing does not assess nutritional status. E. Spirometry assesses respiratory function.
pearl: Unintentional weight loss with poor intake signals malnutrition risk; screen with a validated tool such as MUST, involve dietitians and look for the underlying cause.
thinking: Admitted after a fall ↓ Poor appetite ↓ Significant unintentional weight loss over months ↓ Nutritional assessment
exam_trap: D, visual-field testing only — vision is relevant to falls, but it ignores the weight loss and poor intake, which are the main concern here.
takeaway: Unintentional weight loss in an older patient: assess nutrition and seek the cause.

stem: A 60-year-old man taking an NSAID develops epigastric discomfort and black stools. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: NSAIDs increase the risk of peptic ulceration and GI bleeding; black tarry stools indicate melaena.
why_wrong: A. Diverticular bleeding causes fresh red rectal blood rather than black stools. B. Reflux does not cause melaena. D. Pancreatitis causes severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, not black stools. E. Cholecystitis causes right upper quadrant pain and fever.
pearl: Melaena means upper GI bleeding until proven otherwise; on an NSAID think peptic ulcer, assess with ABCDE and the Glasgow–Blatchford score, and arrange endoscopy.
thinking: Taking an NSAID ↓ Epigastric discomfort suggests peptic ulceration ↓ Black stools indicate melaena ↓ Upper GI bleeding
exam_trap: A, diverticular bleeding — a common cause of GI bleeding in older adults, but it produces fresh red rectal blood, not black stools.
takeaway: Black tarry stools mean an upper GI bleed; NSAIDs point to a peptic ulcer.

stem: A patient taking an NSAID develops wheeze shortly after taking the medication. He has previously experienced similar episodes after aspirin. What should be considered?
why_correct: Some patients with asthma or related airway disease develop bronchospasm after aspirin or other NSAIDs.
why_wrong: A. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction is triggered by exertion, not by NSAIDs. B. Pulmonary oedema causes breathlessness with crackles and is not triggered by aspirin. D. Nothing in the stem suggests beta-blocker use, and the episodes are consistently triggered by NSAIDs and aspirin. E. ABPA is a chronic hypersensitivity to Aspergillus rather than an acute drug-triggered reaction.
pearl: Some people with asthma develop bronchospasm after aspirin and other NSAIDs, often with nasal polyps; they should avoid NSAIDs, and the reaction should be clearly recorded.
thinking: Wheeze shortly after an NSAID ↓ Similar episodes after aspirin ↓ Cyclo-oxygenase inhibition triggers bronchospasm ↓ NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease
exam_trap: D, beta-blocker-induced bronchospasm — a classic drug cause of wheeze, but nothing suggests beta-blocker use and the trigger is consistently aspirin or NSAIDs.
takeaway: Wheeze after aspirin and NSAIDs: avoid all NSAIDs and document the reaction.

stem: A 35-year-old woman taking methotrexate for an inflammatory condition develops a sore throat and fever. Which complication requires consideration?
why_correct: Methotrexate can cause bone marrow suppression, increasing susceptibility to infection.
why_wrong: A. Methotrexate pneumonitis presents with breathlessness and dry cough rather than sore throat. B. Hepatotoxicity causes deranged liver tests rather than sore throat and fever. C. Acute kidney injury does not explain sore throat and fever. E. Osteoarthritis does not cause this presentation.
pearl: Sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers on methotrexate suggest neutropenia; check an urgent full blood count, and patients should be told to report such symptoms promptly.
thinking: Taking methotrexate ↓ New sore throat and fever ↓ Possible infection from low white cells ↓ Bone marrow suppression
exam_trap: A, methotrexate pneumonitis — a serious methotrexate toxicity, but it presents with dry cough and breathlessness rather than sore throat and fever.
takeaway: Methotrexate plus sore throat or fever: urgent full blood count for marrow suppression.

stem: A patient taking a new antibiotic develops widespread itching and raised transient wheals but has normal breathing and blood pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Transient itchy wheals are characteristic of urticaria.
why_wrong: A. Scabies typically causes persistent intense itching with characteristic distribution and contact history. B. Stevens–Johnson syndrome causes severe mucocutaneous disease and blistering. C. Cellulitis causes localised painful erythema. E. Psoriasis causes persistent scaly plaques.
pearl: Urticaria is transient itchy wheals that individually fade within hours; with normal airway, breathing and circulation it is not anaphylaxis, and a non-sedating antihistamine is first-line.
thinking: New antibiotic ↓ Widespread itch with raised transient wheals ↓ Breathing and blood pressure normal ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: B, Stevens–Johnson syndrome — a feared drug rash, but it causes blistering and mucosal involvement, not transient itchy wheals.
takeaway: Transient itchy wheals with stable ABC: urticaria, not anaphylaxis.

stem: A 45-year-old man develops a widespread rash after starting a medication. He has blistering skin and painful mouth ulcers. What is the key concern?
why_correct: Blistering skin with mucosal involvement following a medication is concerning for a severe cutaneous adverse reaction such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Bullous pemphigoid usually spares the mucosae and is not an acute reaction to a new drug. B. Urticaria causes wheals rather than blistering mucosal disease. D. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes oral ulcers with small vesicles on the hands and feet, not widespread blistering after a drug. E. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome mainly affects young children and spares the mucous membranes.
pearl: Blistering with painful mucosal ulcers after a new drug suggests Stevens–Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis; stop the culprit drug immediately and arrange urgent specialist care.
thinking: Rash after starting a medication ↓ Blistering skin ↓ Painful mouth ulcers showing mucosal involvement ↓ Severe cutaneous drug reaction
exam_trap: A, bullous pemphigoid — it also causes blisters, but it affects older adults, usually spares the mucosae and is not an acute drug reaction.
takeaway: Drug rash with blisters and mucosal involvement: think SJS/TEN and stop the drug.

stem: A 54-year-old man taking allopurinol develops a widespread rash, fever and facial swelling shortly after starting treatment. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Continue allopurinol with an oral antihistamine
options.B: Switch to febuxostat and review in two weeks
options.C: Stop allopurinol and seek urgent assessment
options.D: Halve the allopurinol dose and review

correct_answer: C. Stop allopurinol and seek urgent assessment
why_correct: A systemic drug reaction with rash and facial swelling can be serious and requires prompt assessment and withdrawal of the suspected medicine.
why_wrong: A. Continuing the drug risks progression of a serious reaction such as DRESS or Stevens–Johnson syndrome. B. Systemic features need urgent assessment rather than a routine switch. D. Dose reduction does not stop a hypersensitivity reaction progressing. E. Colchicine treats gout flares, not drug hypersensitivity.
pearl: Allopurinol is a common trigger of severe cutaneous reactions such as DRESS and Stevens–Johnson syndrome, usually early in treatment; stop it at the first sign of rash with systemic features.
thinking: Recently started allopurinol ↓ Widespread rash, fever and facial swelling ↓ Systemic drug hypersensitivity such as DRESS ↓ Stop allopurinol and seek urgent assessment
exam_trap: B, switch to febuxostat — an alternative urate-lowering drug seems sensible, but systemic features need urgent assessment first, not a routine switch.
takeaway: Rash with fever on new allopurinol: stop it and assess urgently.

stem: A 73-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has increasing difficulty initiating movement and frequent falls. Which symptom is typical of Parkinson's disease?
why_correct: Bradykinesia is a core motor feature of Parkinson's disease.
why_wrong: A. Haematemesis indicates upper GI bleeding. C. Polyuria has numerous urinary and metabolic causes. D. Hyperreflexia is not the defining motor feature. E. Sudden monocular blindness suggests an ocular vascular emergency.
pearl: Parkinson's disease is defined by bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity; postural instability and falls tend to develop later.
thinking: Parkinson's disease ↓ Difficulty initiating movement ↓ Slowness and progressive reduction of movement ↓ Bradykinesia
exam_trap: D, hyperreflexia — it is a motor sign, but it reflects upper motor neuron disease and is not the core feature of Parkinson's disease.
takeaway: Bradykinesia is essential for a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has episodes of involuntary muscle contractions in her neck that produce abnormal sustained postures. What term describes this movement disorder?
why_correct: Dystonia causes sustained or intermittent muscle contractions producing abnormal movements or postures.
why_wrong: A. Tremor is rhythmic involuntary movement. B. Aphasia is impaired language. C. Ataxia is impaired coordination. E. Paraesthesia is an abnormal sensation.
pearl: Dystonia is sustained or intermittent muscle contraction causing twisting movements or abnormal postures; cervical dystonia (torticollis) is the commonest focal form.
thinking: Involuntary neck muscle contractions ↓ Abnormal sustained postures ↓ Not rhythmic and not incoordination ↓ Dystonia
exam_trap: A, tremor — also an involuntary movement disorder, but tremor is a rhythmic oscillation, not a sustained abnormal posture.
takeaway: Sustained involuntary contraction with abnormal posture is dystonia.

stem: A 70-year-old woman has a rhythmic shaking of both hands that is most noticeable when she holds her arms out. There is no rigidity or bradykinesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Essential tremor commonly produces an action or postural tremor without the cardinal features of Parkinson's disease.
why_wrong: A. Cerebellar stroke usually causes acute coordination problems. B. Dystonia produces abnormal sustained postures or movements. C. Parkinsonian tremor is typically associated with other parkinsonian features. D. Myoclonus consists of sudden brief jerks rather than a rhythmic tremor.
pearl: Essential tremor is a bilateral postural and action tremor, often familial and eased by alcohol; propranolol is first-line when it is troublesome.
thinking: Rhythmic shaking of both hands ↓ Most noticeable with arms outstretched ↓ No rigidity or bradykinesia ↓ Essential tremor
exam_trap: C, Parkinson's disease — the best-known tremor, but parkinsonian tremor is typically asymmetric at rest and accompanied by bradykinesia and rigidity.
takeaway: Bilateral postural tremor without parkinsonism: essential tremor.

stem: A 33-year-old man has progressive difficulty coordinating his movements, slurred speech and an unsteady gait. Which neurological structure is particularly associated with these findings?
why_correct: The cerebellum is important for coordination, balance and smooth movement; dysfunction can cause ataxia and dysarthria.
why_wrong: A. Optic nerve disease causes visual impairment. B. Anterior horn disease produces lower motor neuron weakness. C. Peripheral sensory neuropathy does not typically produce this classic cerebellar syndrome. D. Frontal motor cortex lesions primarily cause weakness and upper motor neuron signs.
pearl: Cerebellar signs include ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia; a cerebellar hemisphere lesion causes signs on the same side.
thinking: Progressive difficulty coordinating movements ↓ Slurred speech (dysarthria) ↓ Unsteady gait ↓ Cerebellum
exam_trap: C, peripheral sensory nerve — sensory loss can cause an unsteady gait, but it does not cause slurred speech or cerebellar-type limb incoordination.
takeaway: Ataxia plus dysarthria localises to the cerebellum.

stem: A 47-year-old woman develops weakness that is worse when she repeatedly uses the affected muscles. Sensation is normal. Which anatomical site is primarily affected in myasthenia gravis?
why_correct: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder affecting neuromuscular transmission at the neuromuscular junction.
why_wrong: A. Cerebellar disease causes coordination problems. B. Optic nerve disease causes visual impairment. C. Kidney disease does not explain fatigable skeletal muscle weakness. D. Posterior column disease primarily affects proprioception and vibration.
pearl: Myasthenia gravis is antibody-mediated, usually against acetylcholine receptors, at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable weakness, often with ptosis and diplopia, and normal sensation.
thinking: Weakness worse with repeated use ↓ Fatigability ↓ Sensation normal ↓ Neuromuscular junction
exam_trap: D, spinal cord posterior columns — a neurological site, but posterior column disease causes loss of proprioception and vibration sense, not fatigable weakness.
takeaway: Fatigable weakness with normal sensation: neuromuscular junction, think myasthenia.

stem: A 34-year-old man reports numbness and tingling in both feet. Examination shows reduced vibration sensation and reduced ankle reflexes. What type of problem is most likely?
why_correct: Distal sensory loss with reduced ankle reflexes is typical of peripheral neuropathy.
why_wrong: B. Upper motor neuron lesions usually produce brisk reflexes. C. Migraine does not cause persistent distal sensory loss. D. Myasthenia affects motor transmission without sensory loss. E. Cerebellar disease causes incoordination rather than a distal sensory neuropathy pattern.
pearl: Length-dependent peripheral neuropathy starts in the feet with reduced vibration sense and depressed ankle reflexes; common causes include diabetes, alcohol and B12 deficiency.
thinking: Numbness and tingling in both feet ↓ Reduced vibration sensation ↓ Reduced ankle reflexes ↓ Peripheral neuropathy
exam_trap: B, upper motor neuron lesion — it can cause bilateral leg symptoms, but it produces brisk reflexes, not reduced ankle reflexes.
takeaway: Distal sensory loss with reduced ankle reflexes: peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has recurrent attacks of acute arthritis and is found to have hard nodules around several finger joints. What are these nodules most likely to represent?
why_correct: Tophi are deposits of monosodium urate associated with longstanding gout.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid nodules are associated with rheumatoid arthritis rather than chronic urate deposition. B. Ganglia are fluid-filled structures commonly found around joints and tendons. D. Sebaceous cysts are skin-associated cysts. E. Lipomas are benign fatty tissue lumps.
pearl: Tophi are urate deposits of chronic gout, often around finger joints, the ears and elbows; they indicate the need for long-term urate-lowering therapy.
thinking: Recurrent acute arthritis ↓ Hard nodules around finger joints ↓ Chronic urate crystal deposition ↓ Tophi
exam_trap: A, rheumatoid nodules — firm nodules near joints are a recognised RA feature, but recurrent acute arthritis attacks point to gout.
takeaway: Recurrent acute arthritis with hard periarticular nodules: tophaceous gout.

stem: A 67-year-old man has a painful swollen big toe following several days of heavy alcohol intake and dietary excess. What mechanism underlies gout?

options.C: Bacterial invasion of the joint in every case

correct_answer: E. Deposition of monosodium urate crystals
why_correct: Gout results from inflammatory responses to monosodium urate crystal deposition.
why_wrong: A. Cholesterol deposition is not the mechanism of gout. B. Calcium oxalate is not the usual cause of gout. C. Bacterial infection causes septic arthritis. D. Autoimmune mechanisms are important in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis.
pearl: Gout is inflammation triggered by monosodium urate crystals, which are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent; alcohol and dietary excess can precipitate attacks.
thinking: Painful swollen big toe ↓ Heavy alcohol and dietary excess ↓ Urate precipitates in the joint ↓ Deposition of monosodium urate crystals
exam_trap: C, bacterial invasion of the joint — septic arthritis must be excluded in a hot joint, but it is not the mechanism of gout.
takeaway: Gout: monosodium urate crystals, needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

stem: A 69-year-old man has acute pain and swelling of the knee. Synovial fluid contains calcium pyrophosphate crystals. What is the diagnosis?
why_correct: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease causes acute inflammatory arthritis known as pseudogout.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory arthritis. C. Bursitis affects a bursa rather than the joint itself. D. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals. E. Osteoarthritis does not cause calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis.
pearl: Pseudogout is acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis, classically of an older adult's knee; crystals are rhomboid and positively birefringent, often with chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.
thinking: Older man with acute knee pain and swelling ↓ Joint aspirated ↓ Calcium pyrophosphate crystals seen ↓ Pseudogout
exam_trap: D, gout — it is the other crystal arthritis, but it is caused by monosodium urate, not calcium pyrophosphate.
takeaway: Pyrophosphate crystals mean pseudogout; urate crystals mean gout.

stem: A 41-year-old man has recurrent episodes of painful swelling of several fingers, with sausage-like swelling of entire digits. What is this finding called?
why_correct: Dactylitis is diffuse swelling of an entire digit and is associated with conditions including psoriatic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Erythema nodosum causes tender subcutaneous nodules, usually on the shins. B. Clubbing is enlargement of the distal fingers with altered nail curvature. C. Koilonychia refers to spoon-shaped nails. D. Cyanosis is bluish discoloration from increased deoxygenated haemoglobin.
pearl: Dactylitis, sausage-like swelling of a whole digit, is typical of spondyloarthritis, especially psoriatic arthritis, so look for psoriasis and nail pitting.
thinking: Painful swelling of several fingers ↓ Whole digits swollen like sausages ↓ Inflammation of joints and tendon sheaths together ↓ Dactylitis
exam_trap: B, clubbing — another finger sign, but it is painless bulbous enlargement of the fingertip with nail changes, not whole-digit swelling.
takeaway: Sausage digit means dactylitis: think psoriatic arthritis.

stem: A patient with suspected acute intermittent porphyria asks why the urine becomes darker after standing. What substance is responsible for the characteristic colour change?

options.C: Haemoglobin from haemolysis in every case

why_correct: Urinary porphyrin precursors can oxidise and produce a dark or reddish colour, particularly after standing.
why_wrong: A. Ketones do not cause the characteristic porphyria colour change. C. Haemoglobinuria has different causes and is not the defining mechanism here. D. Glucose does not produce this characteristic colour change. E. Bilirubin can darken urine in cholestasis but does not explain the classic porphyria presentation.
pearl: In acute intermittent porphyria, urine may look normal when passed but darkens to red-brown on standing as porphobilinogen oxidises; raised urinary porphobilinogen confirms an attack.
thinking: Suspected acute intermittent porphyria ↓ Excess porphyrin precursors excreted in urine ↓ Porphobilinogen oxidises on standing ↓ Porphobilinogen-related pigments
exam_trap: E, bilirubin only — a familiar cause of dark urine, but it reflects liver or biliary disease and does not explain urine darkening on standing in porphyria.
takeaway: Urine that darkens on standing: think acute porphyria and check porphobilinogen.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, vomiting and neurological symptoms. Her older brother has similar episodes. Which type of trigger can precipitate an acute intermittent porphyria attack?

options.A: Mild exercise alone in every case

why_correct: Several medicines can precipitate acute porphyria attacks by increasing hepatic haem synthesis.
why_wrong: A. Exercise is not the defining trigger. C. Sleep is not a typical precipitant. D. Water does not precipitate attacks. E. Wearing glasses is unrelated.
pearl: Acute porphyria attacks are triggered by drugs that induce haem synthesis, alcohol, fasting, infection and hormonal changes; check drug safety in a porphyria resource before prescribing.
thinking: Recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting and neurological symptoms ↓ Affected sibling suggests an inherited cause ↓ Acute intermittent porphyria ↓ Certain medicines
exam_trap: A, mild exercise — it sounds like a plausible lifestyle trigger, but it is not a recognised precipitant; drugs, alcohol and fasting are.
takeaway: Acute porphyria: check every prescribed drug for safety.

stem: A 46-year-old man develops severe abdominal pain. Examination reveals marked tenderness, but imaging shows no clear surgical cause. He also has peripheral neuropathy and confusion. What diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Severe abdominal pain with neurological and psychiatric features without an obvious abdominal cause should raise consideration of acute porphyria.
why_wrong: B. Cataract causes visual impairment. C. Constipation does not explain the neurological features. D. Osteoarthritis causes joint symptoms. E. Otitis externa causes ear canal inflammation.
pearl: Severe abdominal pain without a surgical cause, combined with neuropathy, confusion or psychiatric symptoms, should prompt urine porphobilinogen testing for acute porphyria.
thinking: Severe abdominal pain ↓ Imaging shows no clear surgical cause ↓ Peripheral neuropathy and confusion ↓ Acute porphyria
exam_trap: C, simple constipation — it can cause abdominal pain with a negative surgical work-up, but it does not explain neuropathy and confusion.
takeaway: Unexplained abdominal pain plus neuropsychiatric features: test for acute porphyria.

stem: A 24-year-old man develops severe abdominal pain and vomiting after returning from a holiday abroad. Several friends who ate the same meal have similar symptoms. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Multiple people developing acute gastrointestinal symptoms after sharing food strongly suggests foodborne illness.
why_wrong: B. Migraine does not explain a cluster of gastrointestinal illness. C. Appendicitis would not typically affect several people who ate the same meal. D. Renal colic is not a foodborne illness. E. Testicular torsion causes acute scrotal pain.
pearl: Several people falling ill after a shared meal indicates foodborne illness; suspected food poisoning is notifiable in England, so inform the local health protection team.
thinking: Abdominal pain and vomiting ↓ After a shared meal ↓ Several companions affected at the same time ↓ Food poisoning
exam_trap: C, appendicitis — severe abdominal pain in a young man suggests it, but a cluster of people ill after the same meal points to a shared food source.
takeaway: A cluster of gastrointestinal illness after a shared meal means food poisoning: notify.

stem: A 30-year-old woman develops acute diarrhoea and vomiting after eating undercooked poultry. What is an important bacterial cause?
why_correct: Campylobacter is a common cause of bacterial gastroenteritis and is associated with undercooked poultry.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus causes muscle rigidity and spasms. B. Syphilis is sexually transmitted. C. Tuberculosis usually causes chronic disease rather than acute foodborne diarrhoea. D. Pertussis causes prolonged cough.
pearl: Campylobacter is a leading cause of bacterial gastroenteritis in the UK and is linked to undercooked poultry; it can be followed by Guillain–Barré syndrome.
thinking: Acute diarrhoea and vomiting ↓ After undercooked poultry ↓ Commonest bacterial cause linked to chicken ↓ Campylobacter
exam_trap: C, Mycobacterium tuberculosis — it can affect the gut, but intestinal TB is chronic and is not an acute foodborne illness after poultry.
takeaway: Undercooked chicken and diarrhoea: Campylobacter, and remember Guillain–Barré.

stem: A child develops bloody diarrhoea after a suspected foodborne infection. Several days later, he becomes pale, tired and passes very little urine. What complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Bloody diarrhoea followed by anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury is characteristic of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency from blood loss develops gradually and does not cause reduced urine output. B. Henoch–Schönlein purpura causes a purpuric rash, joint and abdominal pain rather than this post-diarrhoeal picture. D. Intussusception causes colicky pain and redcurrant-jelly stool rather than pallor and oliguria days later. E. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follows a throat or skin infection, not bloody diarrhoea.
pearl: HUS typically follows bloody diarrhoea from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli such as O157; antibiotics and antimotility agents are generally avoided in suspected cases.
thinking: Bloody diarrhoea after foodborne infection ↓ Days later, pale and tired from anaemia ↓ Very little urine from acute kidney injury ↓ Haemolytic uraemic syndrome
exam_trap: A, iron deficiency from blood loss — pallor after bloody diarrhoea seems to fit, but it develops slowly and does not explain reduced urine output.
takeaway: Bloody diarrhoea followed by pallor and oliguria in a child: HUS.

stem: A child recovering from bloody diarrhoea develops pallor, bruising and reduced urine output. Which three abnormalities characterise haemolytic uraemic syndrome?

options.A: Aplastic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
options.B: Haemolytic anaemia, neutropenia and acute kidney injury
options.C: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
options.D: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytosis and acute kidney injury
options.E: Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute liver failure

correct_answer: C. Haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
why_correct: This triad is characteristic of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
why_wrong: A. The anaemia in HUS is haemolytic, not aplastic. B. Neutropenia is not part of the triad. D. Platelets are low, not raised, in HUS. E. The organ injury in HUS is renal, not hepatic.
