options.B: Prescribe coenzyme Q10 and continue the statin
options.C: Switch to the maximum dose of atorvastatin
options.D: Reassure that statins do not cause muscle pain
options.E: Start an NSAID and review in three months

correct_answer: A. Assess symptoms and measure creatine kinase
why_correct: New muscle symptoms in a patient taking a statin should prompt clinical assessment, including consideration of creatine kinase testing when indicated and review of other causes or interacting medicines.
why_wrong: B. NICE does not recommend coenzyme Q10 for statin-associated muscle symptoms. C. Increasing statin intensity could worsen muscle symptoms. D. Statins can cause myalgia and, rarely, myositis or rhabdomyolysis. E. Masking pain with NSAIDs delays assessment and may harm renal function.
pearl: New muscle symptoms on a statin need assessment, a CK and a look for other causes such as hypothyroidism or interacting drugs; a markedly raised CK means stopping the statin.
thinking: Statin started weeks ago ↓ new unexplained muscle aches ↓ possible statin-associated myopathy ↓ assess symptoms and measure creatine kinase
exam_trap: D, Reassure that statins do not cause muscle pain — statin aches are often non-specific, but statins can cause myalgia and rarely rhabdomyolysis, so assessment is needed.
takeaway: New muscle symptoms on a statin: assess and check CK.

stem: A 64-year-old man taking warfarin has an INR of 7.2 but no bleeding. What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.A: Give 10 mg intravenous vitamin K as an immediate bolus
options.B: Give prothrombin complex concentrate to reverse the INR
options.C: Withhold warfarin and manage by INR and bleeding risk
options.D: Transfuse fresh frozen plasma to correct the raised INR
options.E: Continue the current dose and repeat the INR in one week

correct_answer: C. Withhold warfarin and manage by INR and bleeding risk
why_correct: A markedly raised INR without bleeding requires withholding/reviewing anticoagulation and management according to the INR and clinical circumstances.
why_wrong: A. High-dose intravenous vitamin K is for major bleeding and can cause prolonged warfarin resistance. B. Prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding. D. Fresh frozen plasma is not indicated in the absence of bleeding. E. Continuing warfarin at a markedly elevated INR increases bleeding risk.
pearl: A high INR without bleeding is managed by withholding warfarin, adding oral vitamin K at higher INRs; IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate are for bleeding.
thinking: Warfarin with INR 7.2 ↓ no bleeding ↓ action depends on INR and bleeding risk ↓ withhold warfarin and manage by INR and bleeding risk
exam_trap: B, Prothrombin complex concentrate — it reverses the INR rapidly, but it is reserved for major bleeding and carries thrombotic risk; this patient is not bleeding.
takeaway: High INR without bleeding: withhold warfarin; urgent reversal is for bleeding.

stem: A patient taking warfarin presents with severe gastrointestinal bleeding and haemodynamic instability. What is the priority?

options.A: Withhold the next dose and recheck INR tomorrow
options.B: Give oral vitamin K and observe on the ward
options.C: Resuscitate, reverse warfarin and control bleeding
options.E: Give tranexamic acid and arrange routine endoscopy

correct_answer: C. Resuscitate, reverse warfarin and control bleeding
why_correct: Life-threatening bleeding requires immediate resuscitation and urgent reversal/management of anticoagulation alongside definitive haemorrhage control.
why_wrong: A. An unstable patient needs immediate treatment rather than delay. B. Oral vitamin K acts too slowly and ward observation is inadequate in major bleeding. D. Resuscitation precedes endoscopy. E. Tranexamic acid is not recommended for GI bleeding, and routine endoscopy is inappropriate in an unstable patient.
pearl: Major bleeding on warfarin: resuscitate, stop warfarin, give IV vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate, then arrange urgent endoscopy once stabilised.
thinking: Severe GI bleed ↓ haemodynamically unstable ↓ warfarin is worsening the haemorrhage ↓ resuscitate, reverse warfarin and control bleeding
exam_trap: D, Urgent endoscopy before fluid resuscitation — endoscopy gives definitive control, but an unstable patient must be resuscitated first.
takeaway: Unstable bleed on warfarin: resuscitate, IV vitamin K plus PCC, then endoscopy.

stem: A 70-year-old man taking apixaban develops significant gastrointestinal bleeding. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Apixaban needs urgent review during bleed management
options.B: Vitamin K will rapidly reverse the effect of apixaban
options.C: INR reliably measures the anticoagulant effect of apixaban
options.D: Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent of choice for apixaban
options.E: Apixaban can continue if the initial haemoglobin is normal

correct_answer: A. Apixaban needs urgent review during bleed management
why_correct: Significant bleeding in a patient taking a DOAC requires urgent assessment, resuscitation and review of anticoagulant therapy.
why_wrong: B. Apixaban does not act via vitamin K, so vitamin K does not reverse it. C. INR is not a reliable measure of apixaban activity. D. Protamine reverses heparin; andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate are used for apixaban-associated bleeding. E. A normal initial haemoglobin does not exclude significant acute blood loss.
pearl: Apixaban is a factor Xa inhibitor: vitamin K does not reverse it and INR does not reliably measure it; in significant bleeding, stop it and seek urgent haematology advice.
thinking: Taking apixaban ↓ significant GI bleed ↓ direct factor Xa inhibitor, not a vitamin K antagonist ↓ apixaban needs urgent review during bleed management
exam_trap: B, Vitamin K will rapidly reverse apixaban — tempting by analogy with warfarin, but apixaban acts on factor Xa directly and is unaffected by vitamin K.
takeaway: Apixaban: no vitamin K reversal and INR is unreliable; stop it and get urgent advice.

stem: A 58-year-old woman develops widespread bruising after starting a new medication. Her platelet count is normal. What broad mechanism should be considered?
correct_answer: D. Coagulation defect or drug effect
why_correct: Easy bruising with a normal platelet count can result from impaired coagulation, medication effects or other causes affecting haemostasis.
why_wrong: A. ITP causes a low platelet count. B. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia causes a fall in platelet count and thrombosis. C. Essential thrombocythaemia causes a raised platelet count. E. Aplastic anaemia causes pancytopenia, including a low platelet count.
pearl: Bruising with a normal platelet count suggests a coagulation problem or a drug effect, such as anticoagulants, antiplatelets or corticosteroids; check a clotting screen and review medicines.
thinking: Widespread bruising ↓ began after a new medication ↓ platelet count is normal ↓ coagulation defect or drug effect
exam_trap: A, Immune thrombocytopenic purpura — a classic cause of new bruising, but ITP produces a low platelet count, which is normal here.
takeaway: Bruising with normal platelets: think coagulation or drug effect, not thrombocytopenia.

stem: A 66-year-old man develops sudden severe abdominal pain and abdominal distension. He has repeated vomiting and cannot pass stool or flatus. What syndrome is most likely?
why_correct: Abdominal pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation are characteristic features of intestinal obstruction.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause acute complete obstruction. B. Chronic constipation does not explain this acute obstructive syndrome. C. Functional dyspepsia causes upper gastrointestinal symptoms. D. GORD causes reflux symptoms rather than intestinal obstruction.
pearl: Bowel obstruction causes colicky pain, distension, vomiting and absolute constipation; manage with drip and suck, imaging (usually CT) and urgent surgical review.
thinking: Sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ distension and repeated vomiting ↓ no stool or flatus passed ↓ acute intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, Chronic constipation — failure to pass stool tempts it, but absolute constipation with vomiting, distension and acute pain is obstruction, not constipation.
takeaway: Pain, distension, vomiting and no flatus = intestinal obstruction until proven otherwise.

stem: A 70-year-old man with abdominal distension and vomiting has a CT scan showing a transition point in the small bowel. What does the transition point indicate?

options.A: Change from dilated to collapsed bowel
options.B: The site of a localised bowel perforation
options.C: The normal position of the ileocaecal valve
options.D: A segment of bowel wall thickening from colitis
options.E: A region of adynamic ileus without obstruction

correct_answer: A. Change from dilated to collapsed bowel
why_correct: A transition point is where dilated bowel proximally changes to relatively collapsed bowel distally, supporting mechanical obstruction.
why_wrong: B. Perforation is shown by free gas rather than a change in bowel calibre. C. The ileocaecal valve is a normal anatomical structure and is not synonymous with a transition point. D. Bowel wall thickening is not defined by a change in calibre. E. Ileus causes diffuse dilatation without a transition point.
pearl: A transition point on CT, with dilated bowel proximally and collapsed bowel distally, confirms mechanical obstruction and localises the cause, such as adhesions or a hernia.
thinking: Distension and vomiting ↓ CT shows a transition point ↓ calibre changes from dilated to collapsed bowel ↓ mechanical obstruction at that site
exam_trap: E, A region of adynamic ileus without obstruction — ileus also causes distension and vomiting, but it produces diffuse dilatation without a transition point.
takeaway: Transition point = dilated to collapsed bowel, marking mechanical obstruction.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has chronic constipation. She opens her bowels every few days and passes hard stools with straining. There are no alarm symptoms. Which initial measure is appropriate?

options.A: Daily phosphate enemas as first-line treatment
options.B: Urgent colonoscopy to exclude colorectal cancer
options.C: Increase fibre, fluids and physical activity
options.D: Prescribe loperamide to help regulate her stools
options.E: Switch to a low-fibre, low-residue diet for 4 weeks

correct_answer: C. Increase fibre, fluids and physical activity
why_correct: Lifestyle measures are an important initial approach to uncomplicated constipation.
why_wrong: A. Enemas are not first-line for uncomplicated chronic constipation. B. Colonoscopy is not required without alarm features. D. Loperamide is an antidiarrhoeal and would worsen constipation. E. Reducing fibre would usually worsen constipation.
pearl: Uncomplicated chronic constipation: start with fibre, fluids and activity, then a bulk-forming laxative, then an osmotic laxative such as a macrogol if needed.
thinking: Infrequent hard stools with straining ↓ chronic course ↓ no alarm symptoms ↓ increase fibre, fluids and physical activity
exam_trap: B, Urgent colonoscopy — cancer worries make it tempting, but without alarm features investigation is not needed; lifestyle measures come first.
takeaway: Constipation without red flags: lifestyle first, then laxatives stepwise.

stem: A 48-year-old man has chronic constipation and suddenly develops severe abdominal pain, vomiting and marked distension. What should this change in symptoms suggest?
why_correct: Sudden severe pain, vomiting and marked distension are red flags for an acute obstructive or other surgical abdominal process.
why_wrong: A. Reflux does not explain the symptoms. B. Sudden severe pain, vomiting and marked distension are not features of uncomplicated constipation. C. Functional dyspepsia does not cause this acute obstructive picture. E. IBS does not cause acute severe obstruction.
pearl: A sudden change from chronic constipation to severe pain, vomiting and distension is a red flag for obstruction, for example from tumour or volvulus, and needs urgent surgical assessment.
thinking: Background chronic constipation ↓ sudden severe abdominal pain ↓ vomiting and marked distension ↓ acute intestinal obstruction
exam_trap: B, Exacerbation of simple constipation — the background history tempts it, but acute severe pain with vomiting and marked distension is not simple constipation.
takeaway: New vomiting, distension and severe pain in a constipated patient: think obstruction.

stem: A 54-year-old woman develops severe abdominal pain with guarding and rebound tenderness. What does this examination finding suggest?
why_correct: Guarding and rebound tenderness indicate irritation of the peritoneum and can occur with serious intra-abdominal pathology.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not produce abdominal guarding. C. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms rather than generalized peritoneal signs. D. Simple constipation does not usually cause peritoneal signs. E. Reflux does not cause guarding and rebound tenderness.
pearl: Guarding and rebound tenderness signal peritonitis, from causes such as perforation or appendicitis, and the patient needs urgent surgical assessment.
thinking: Severe abdominal pain ↓ guarding on palpation ↓ rebound tenderness ↓ inflamed peritoneum = peritoneal irritation
exam_trap: D, Simple constipation — common and can be painful, but it does not produce guarding or rebound; these signs mean peritoneal irritation.
takeaway: Guarding plus rebound tenderness = peritonism: get urgent surgical review.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with acute flank pain and visible blood in her urine. She has no fever. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Acute severe flank pain with haematuria and no evidence of infection is typical of a ureteric stone.
why_wrong: A. Pyelonephritis usually causes fever and systemic illness. B. Polycystic kidney disease causes chronic renal manifestations rather than typical acute colic. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes proteinuria and oedema. E. Cystitis usually causes dysuria, frequency and urgency rather than severe colicky flank pain.
pearl: Renal colic causes sudden severe loin-to-groin pain with haematuria; NSAIDs are first-line analgesia and non-contrast CT KUB confirms the stone.
thinking: Acute, severe flank pain ↓ visible blood in the urine ↓ no fever, so infection less likely ↓ ureteric stone
exam_trap: A, Acute pyelonephritis — flank pain with abnormal urine tempts it, but pyelonephritis usually brings fever and systemic illness, which are absent.
takeaway: Acute flank pain plus haematuria without fever = ureteric stone.

stem: A woman develops heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery. The placenta has been delivered but appears incomplete. What cause of postpartum haemorrhage should be considered?
why_correct: Retained placental tissue can prevent effective uterine contraction and cause postpartum haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy occurs outside the uterus in early pregnancy. C. Amniotic fluid embolism presents with sudden collapse, hypoxia and coagulopathy. D. Gestational thrombocytopenia is mild and does not cause significant postpartum haemorrhage. E. Hyperemesis causes severe vomiting during pregnancy.
pearl: Postpartum haemorrhage causes follow the 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin; an incomplete placenta means retained tissue that must be removed.
thinking: Heavy bleeding after delivery ↓ placenta delivered but incomplete ↓ retained fragments stop the uterus contracting well ↓ retained placental tissue
exam_trap: C, Amniotic fluid embolism — a dramatic obstetric emergency with bleeding, but it presents with sudden collapse, hypoxia and coagulopathy, not an incomplete placenta.
takeaway: Postpartum haemorrhage with an incomplete placenta: retained tissue, the Tissue of the 4 Ts.

stem: A 5-day-old newborn is feeding poorly and has a temperature of 38.2°C. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
why_correct: Fever and poor feeding in a neonate are important signs of possible serious infection and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Fever in a neonate should not be attributed to overwrapping; serious infection must be excluded. B. Fever is not a normal neonatal finding. C. Colic does not cause fever. E. Breastfeeding does not normally cause fever and poor feeding.
pearl: Any fever in a baby under 3 months is a red flag for serious bacterial infection; a febrile, poorly feeding neonate needs urgent assessment and a full septic screen.
thinking: 5-day-old neonate ↓ temperature of 38.2°C, a fever ↓ feeding poorly ↓ possible serious neonatal infection
exam_trap: A, Overheating from excessive wrapping — a common reassuring explanation, but fever in a neonate must never be put down to wrapping before infection is excluded.
takeaway: Fever in a baby under 3 months is serious infection until proven otherwise.

stem: A child with a barking cough develops increasing stridor at rest and difficulty breathing. What does this indicate?

options.A: Mild croup suitable for home care

why_correct: Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway obstruction and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Stridor at rest indicates at least moderate croup and is not suitable for home management. B. Bronchiolitis affects infants and causes wheeze and crackles rather than stridor. C. Asthma causes expiratory wheeze rather than inspiratory stridor. D. Allergic rhinitis does not cause stridor.
pearl: In croup, stridor at rest with increasing work of breathing signals significant airway narrowing; give oral dexamethasone and, if severe, nebulised adrenaline with senior help.
thinking: Barking cough suggests croup ↓ stridor now present at rest ↓ increasing difficulty breathing ↓ severe upper-airway obstruction
exam_trap: A, Mild croup suitable for home care — the barking cough suggests croup, but stridor at rest with breathing difficulty is not mild and needs hospital assessment.
takeaway: Croup with stridor at rest is not mild: assess urgently in hospital.

stem: A 74-year-old woman suddenly develops difficulty producing speech. She understands what is being said to her but can only produce a few words. What type of aphasia is most likely?
why_correct: Difficulty producing language despite relatively preserved comprehension is characteristic of expressive aphasia.
why_wrong: A. Dysphonia is a disorder of voice quality. B. Receptive aphasia primarily impairs understanding of language. C. Dysarthria is impaired articulation rather than impaired language formulation. D. Amnesia concerns memory rather than language production.
pearl: Expressive (Broca's) aphasia gives non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension, typically from a dominant frontal lobe lesion such as stroke.
thinking: Sudden onset of speech difficulty ↓ can produce only a few words ↓ understands what is said ↓ expressive aphasia
exam_trap: C, Dysarthria — also limits speech output, but dysarthria is impaired articulation with intact language; she cannot produce language, which is aphasia.
takeaway: Non-fluent speech with preserved understanding = expressive (Broca's) aphasia.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of flushing, diarrhoea and wheezing. Investigations suggest carcinoid syndrome. Which tumour is a common source of the syndrome?
why_correct: Small-intestinal neuroendocrine tumours are an important cause of carcinoid syndrome, particularly when metastatic disease allows secreted mediators to reach the systemic circulation.
why_wrong: A. Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension, headache and sweating. B. Pancreatic adenocarcinoma presents with painless jaundice, weight loss and pain. D. Colonic adenocarcinoma causes change in bowel habit and bleeding. E. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a primary liver cancer and does not cause carcinoid syndrome.
pearl: Carcinoid syndrome usually needs liver metastases from a small-bowel NET, so mediators escape hepatic breakdown; urinary 5-HIAA supports the diagnosis.
thinking: Flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze ↓ carcinoid syndrome suspected ↓ vasoactive mediators from a neuroendocrine tumour ↓ small-bowel NET is a common source
exam_trap: A, Adrenal phaeochromocytoma — also an episodic hormone-secreting tumour, but it causes hypertension, headache and sweating, not flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze.
takeaway: Flushing, diarrhoea and wheeze: carcinoid from a small-bowel NET, usually with liver metastases.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has recurrent unilateral headaches accompanied by transient visual disturbance. What feature would be particularly concerning for a secondary headache disorder?

options.B: Previous identical headaches over many years
options.C: Photophobia and phonophobia during each episode
options.E: Improvement after a period of sleep or rest

correct_answer: A. Sudden onset peaking within seconds
why_correct: A thunderclap headache is a red flag for serious secondary causes such as subarachnoid haemorrhage.
why_wrong: B. A stable recurrent pattern is more suggestive of a primary headache disorder. C. Photophobia and phonophobia are common in migraine. D. Nausea commonly accompanies migraine. E. Improvement with sleep or rest can occur with migraine.
pearl: A thunderclap headache, reaching maximum intensity almost instantly, needs emergency assessment for subarachnoid haemorrhage, whatever the previous headache history.
thinking: Recurrent unilateral headache with visual aura suggests migraine ↓ look for features that break the pattern ↓ sudden onset peaking within seconds ↓ red flag for a secondary cause
exam_trap: C, Photophobia and phonophobia — they sound worrying, but they are typical migraine features; the red flag is the speed of onset.
takeaway: Thunderclap onset is a red flag even in someone with known migraine.

stem: A 24-year-old man suddenly loses consciousness, becomes stiff and then develops rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. He is confused afterwards. What is the most likely seizure type?
why_correct: Loss of consciousness followed by tonic stiffening, clonic jerking and a postictal period is characteristic of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure.
why_wrong: A. Focal impaired awareness seizures cause altered awareness with automatisms rather than generalised stiffening and jerking of all limbs. B. Atonic seizures involve sudden loss of tone. C. Myoclonic seizures consist primarily of brief jerks. E. Absence seizures are brief and lack tonic-clonic activity.
pearl: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures cause sudden loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening then clonic jerking, often with tongue biting, followed by postictal confusion.
thinking: Sudden loss of consciousness ↓ tonic stiffening ↓ rhythmic jerking of all four limbs ↓ postictal confusion ↓ generalised tonic-clonic seizure
exam_trap: C, Myoclonic seizure — also produces jerking, but myoclonic jerks are brief, often with preserved awareness, without prior stiffening or postictal confusion.
takeaway: Stiffening, then jerking of all limbs, then confusion = generalised tonic-clonic seizure.

stem: A 20-year-old man has a seizure for the first time. He has now recovered fully and is alert. What is an important next step?

options.B: Diagnose epilepsy on the basis of this event
options.C: Arrange GP review if a second seizure occurs
options.E: Advise he may continue driving meanwhile

correct_answer: D. Refer for specialist first-seizure review
why_correct: A first suspected seizure requires appropriate assessment to determine the cause and risk of recurrence before a definitive diagnosis or long-term treatment decision.
why_wrong: A. Antiseizure medication is not usually started before specialist assessment. B. A single seizure does not automatically establish epilepsy. C. A first seizure needs prompt specialist assessment rather than waiting for recurrence. E. He must stop driving and inform the DVLA after a first seizure.
pearl: After a first suspected seizure, refer urgently to a first-seizure specialist and advise the patient to stop driving and inform the DVLA; drug treatment is a specialist decision.
thinking: First seizure ↓ now fully recovered ↓ cause and recurrence risk not yet known ↓ refer for specialist first-seizure review
exam_trap: A, Start levetiracetam before discharge — seems protective, but antiseizure drugs are not usually started after one seizure before specialist assessment.
takeaway: First seizure: urgent specialist referral and driving advice, not immediate drugs.

stem: A 19-year-old woman reports brief episodes of sudden muscle jerks shortly after waking. She remains conscious throughout. What seizure type is most likely?
why_correct: Myoclonic seizures cause brief, sudden muscle jerks with preserved awareness.
why_wrong: A. Focal impaired-awareness seizures involve impaired awareness. B. Absence seizures primarily cause brief impaired awareness. C. Tonic-clonic seizures involve loss of consciousness and sustained motor activity. E. Atonic seizures cause sudden loss of muscle tone.
pearl: Morning myoclonic jerks in a young person suggest juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; sodium valproate is generally avoided in anyone who could become pregnant.
thinking: Young woman ↓ brief sudden muscle jerks ↓ occur shortly after waking ↓ consciousness preserved ↓ myoclonic seizure
exam_trap: C, Generalised tonic-clonic seizure — the jerking tempts it, but GTCS involves loss of consciousness and sustained activity; brief jerks with awareness are myoclonic.
takeaway: Brief jerks soon after waking with preserved awareness = myoclonic seizures.

stem: A 42-year-old woman develops weakness of one side of the body after a seizure. The weakness resolves over several hours. What is this phenomenon called?
why_correct: Temporary focal weakness following a seizure is known as Todd's paresis.
why_wrong: B. Multiple sclerosis causes neurological episodes separated in time and space rather than a typical immediate postictal weakness. C. Bell's palsy causes isolated facial weakness. D. Myasthenia causes fluctuating fatigable weakness rather than a postictal focal deficit. E. Guillain-Barré causes progressive peripheral weakness.
pearl: Todd's paresis is temporary focal weakness after a seizure that usually resolves within hours, occasionally longer; a persisting deficit needs assessment for stroke.
thinking: Seizure first ↓ then weakness of one side of the body ↓ resolves over several hours ↓ Todd's paresis
exam_trap: B, Multiple sclerosis — causes transient focal deficits, but they are not tied to a seizure; one-sided weakness immediately after a seizure is Todd's paresis.
takeaway: Transient one-sided weakness after a seizure = Todd's paresis.

stem: A 67-year-old man suddenly becomes unable to understand spoken language. He speaks fluently but his words make little sense. What type of aphasia is most likely?
why_correct: Fluent but meaningless speech accompanied by impaired comprehension is characteristic of receptive aphasia.
why_wrong: A. Dysphonia is impaired voice quality. B. Expressive aphasia primarily impairs speech production with relatively preserved comprehension. C. Dysarthria is impaired articulation. D. Mutism is absence of speech rather than fluent but impaired language.
pearl: Receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia gives fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension, often without awareness of errors; it localises to the dominant temporal lobe.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ cannot understand spoken language ↓ speech fluent but makes little sense ↓ receptive aphasia
exam_trap: B, Expressive aphasia — also an aphasia after stroke, but it causes non-fluent speech with preserved comprehension, the reverse of this picture.
takeaway: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor understanding = receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia.

stem: A 71-year-old man develops difficulty swallowing after a stroke. He coughs repeatedly while drinking water. What complication is he at increased risk of?
why_correct: Dysphagia with coughing during swallowing suggests aspiration risk, which can lead to aspiration pneumonia.
why_wrong: B. Dysphagia does not directly cause renal failure. C. Otitis externa is unrelated. D. Stroke can increase DVT risk through immobility, but coughing with swallowing specifically indicates aspiration risk. E. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: After a stroke, screen swallowing before giving oral food, fluids or medicines; coughing on drinking suggests aspiration and needs speech and language therapy assessment.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ new difficulty swallowing ↓ coughing while drinking water ↓ fluid entering the airway ↓ aspiration pneumonia risk
exam_trap: D, Deep vein thrombosis only — immobility after stroke does raise DVT risk, but coughing on swallowing specifically signals aspiration.
takeaway: Post-stroke dysphagia with coughing on drinking = aspiration risk: swallow screen first.

stem: A 69-year-old woman develops sudden difficulty walking, slurred speech and severe unsteadiness. Limb coordination is impaired. Which part of the brain is particularly associated with coordination?
why_correct: The cerebellum is important for coordination, balance and smooth execution of movement.
why_wrong: A. The hypothalamus regulates autonomic and endocrine functions. B. The medulla contains important autonomic centres but is not the principal site for coordination. C. The pituitary is an endocrine gland. E. The frontal lobes are involved in executive function and voluntary motor control but are not the principal coordination centre.
pearl: Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus, slurred speech and past-pointing; sudden onset suggests a posterior circulation stroke.
thinking: Sudden difficulty walking and severe unsteadiness ↓ slurred speech ↓ impaired limb coordination ↓ cerebellum
exam_trap: B, Medulla only — brainstem strokes can also cause unsteadiness and slurred speech, but the structure principally responsible for coordination is the cerebellum.
takeaway: Ataxia, slurred speech and incoordination point to the cerebellum.

stem: A 76-year-old man has gradually worsening memory loss and difficulty managing finances. His symptoms have progressed over several years. What broad diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Progressive cognitive decline affecting everyday functioning over years is characteristic of dementia.
why_wrong: A. Delirium is acute and fluctuating. C. Acute psychosis primarily involves disturbances such as delusions and hallucinations. D. Panic disorder causes recurrent panic attacks. E. Syncope is transient loss of consciousness.
pearl: Dementia is progressive cognitive decline that affects daily function, such as managing money; check for reversible contributors such as B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and depression.
thinking: Gradually worsening memory ↓ difficulty managing finances ↓ progression over several years ↓ dementia
exam_trap: A, Delirium — also causes cognitive problems in older people, but delirium is acute and fluctuating; slow decline over years is dementia.
takeaway: Slowly progressive cognitive decline affecting daily life = dementia.

stem: A 78-year-old woman has gradually progressive memory impairment and difficulty finding words. Which cognitive domain is particularly affected by difficulty remembering recent events?
why_correct: Difficulty retaining or recalling information is impairment of memory.
why_wrong: A. Motor coordination concerns movement control. C. Peripheral sensation concerns detection of touch, pain and related stimuli. D. Visual acuity concerns clarity of vision. E. Hearing concerns auditory perception.
pearl: Early Alzheimer's disease typically affects recent memory first, with difficulty recalling recent events, while older memories are relatively preserved.
thinking: Gradually progressive cognitive impairment ↓ difficulty remembering recent events ↓ problem retaining and recalling information ↓ memory
exam_trap: E, Hearing — poor hearing can mimic memory problems because information is never heard, but forgetting recent events is a memory deficit.
takeaway: Trouble recalling recent events is a memory deficit.

stem: A 74-year-old man with cognitive impairment becomes lost in a familiar area and struggles to recognise familiar objects. Which cognitive function may be affected?
why_correct: Getting lost in familiar surroundings and difficulty recognising objects can reflect impairment of visuospatial and higher cortical recognition functions.
why_wrong: A. Expressive language problems cause word-finding difficulty rather than getting lost or failing to recognise objects. B. Apraxia impairs skilled movements rather than recognition. D. Changes in social cognition cause disinhibition and altered behaviour. E. Receptive language problems affect understanding of speech.
pearl: Getting lost in familiar places and failing to recognise objects reflect visuospatial and perceptual impairment, functions of the parietal and temporal cortex.
thinking: Cognitive impairment ↓ lost in a familiar area ↓ cannot recognise familiar objects ↓ visuospatial and recognition skills
exam_trap: A, Expressive language and word-finding — failing to name an object can look like failed recognition, but getting lost and not recognising objects are visuospatial problems.
takeaway: Getting lost and failing to recognise objects = visuospatial and recognition impairment.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with dementia has difficulty recognising her daughter despite being able to see her clearly. What is this symptom called?
why_correct: Agnosia is inability to recognise or identify sensory information despite adequate basic sensory function.
why_wrong: A. Dysarthria is impaired speech articulation. B. Ataxia is impaired coordination. C. Apraxia is difficulty performing learned purposeful movements despite adequate strength and comprehension. D. Aphasia is impaired language.
pearl: Agnosia is failure to recognise despite intact senses; prosopagnosia, the inability to recognise familiar faces, can occur in dementia.
thinking: Known dementia ↓ cannot recognise her own daughter ↓ vision is adequate ↓ failure of recognition = agnosia
exam_trap: D, Aphasia — she may struggle to name her daughter, but aphasia is a language deficit; failing to recognise someone despite clear vision is agnosia.
takeaway: Failure to recognise a familiar person or object despite intact senses = agnosia.

stem: A 73-year-old man with cognitive impairment understands a request but cannot carry out a familiar learned task, despite having adequate strength and coordination. What is this called?
why_correct: Apraxia is the inability to perform a learned purposeful movement despite preserved basic motor function and understanding.
why_wrong: A. Ataxia is impaired coordination. B. Aphasia is impaired language. C. Dysphonia is impaired voice quality. D. Agnosia is impaired recognition.
pearl: Apraxia is inability to perform learned purposeful movements, such as dressing or using a toothbrush, despite intact strength, coordination and understanding.
thinking: Understands the request ↓ strength and coordination adequate ↓ still cannot perform a familiar learned task ↓ apraxia
exam_trap: A, Ataxia — also disrupts carrying out movements, but ataxia is poor coordination, which is intact here; failing a learned task despite intact function is apraxia.
takeaway: Understands and has normal power and coordination, but cannot do learned tasks = apraxia.

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of both legs with loss of sensation below the umbilicus. She also has difficulty passing urine. What is the most appropriate concern?
why_correct: Bilateral weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction suggest spinal cord involvement and require urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy affects the facial nerve. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve in the hand. C. Migraine does not cause a sensory level and urinary retention. E. Tension headache does not cause spinal neurological deficits.
pearl: Bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level and bladder dysfunction indicate a spinal cord lesion; arrange urgent MRI of the spine and specialist assessment.
thinking: Sudden weakness of both legs ↓ sensory loss below the umbilicus (a sensory level) ↓ difficulty passing urine ↓ spinal cord compression
exam_trap: C, Migraine — can cause transient neurological symptoms, but never a sensory level with bilateral leg weakness and urinary difficulty.
takeaway: Bilateral leg weakness plus sensory level plus bladder change = cord lesion: urgent MRI.

stem: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic prostate cancer develops severe back pain followed by weakness in both legs. What is the most important diagnosis to exclude urgently?
why_correct: New severe back pain and neurological symptoms in a patient with cancer are red flags for metastatic spinal cord compression.
why_wrong: A. Spinal stenosis causes chronic neurogenic claudication rather than acute leg weakness in a patient with metastatic cancer. C. Guillain–Barré syndrome causes ascending, areflexic weakness, often after an infection; back pain can occur, but in a man with metastatic prostate cancer, MSCC must be excluded first. D. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, constipation and generalised weakness rather than back pain followed by bilateral leg weakness. E. A ruptured aneurysm causes back or abdominal pain with collapse and shock rather than progressive leg weakness.
pearl: In known cancer, new back pain with neurological symptoms suggests metastatic spinal cord compression: urgent whole-spine MRI, corticosteroids and oncology input.
thinking: Metastatic prostate cancer ↓ new severe back pain ↓ followed by weakness of both legs ↓ metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: C, Guillain–Barré syndrome — causes bilateral leg weakness and sometimes back pain, but with metastatic cancer MSCC must be excluded first.
takeaway: Cancer plus back pain plus leg weakness = MSCC until proven otherwise.

stem: A 41-year-old woman develops weakness of both legs several days after a viral illness. Examination shows reduced reflexes. What neurological pattern is most characteristic of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
why_correct: Guillain-Barré classically causes progressive symmetrical weakness that may ascend from the legs.
why_wrong: B. Brief impaired awareness suggests a seizure disorder. C. Resting tremor is associated with Parkinson's disease. D. Unilateral painful visual loss can occur with optic neuritis. E. Isolated facial weakness suggests a facial nerve disorder.
pearl: Guillain–Barré syndrome causes progressive, symmetrical, ascending weakness with reduced reflexes after an infection; monitor FVC because respiratory muscles can fail.
thinking: Recent viral illness ↓ weakness of both legs ↓ reduced reflexes ↓ ascending symmetrical weakness of Guillain–Barré
exam_trap: E, Isolated facial weakness — facial weakness can occur in GBS, but alone it suggests a facial nerve disorder; the hallmark is ascending symmetrical limb weakness.
takeaway: Post-infective ascending symmetrical weakness with reduced reflexes = Guillain–Barré.

stem: A patient diagnosed with scabies asks why household members may also need treatment. What is the main reason?

options.B: Scabies is transmitted only through blood
options.C: Close contacts may be infected even before symptoms develop
options.D: Treatment is needed only to prevent bacterial infection
options.E: Scabies is caused by contaminated food

correct_answer: C. Close contacts may be infected even before symptoms develop
why_correct: Close contacts can acquire scabies and may initially have few or no symptoms, so appropriate contact management helps prevent reinfestation.
why_wrong: A. Scabies is acquired through transmission, not inheritance. B. It is not primarily a blood-borne infection. D. Treatment targets the mite infestation itself. E. Scabies is not food-borne.
pearl: Scabies itching can take weeks to appear after a first infestation, so all household and close contacts are treated at the same time, even without symptoms.
thinking: Scabies spreads by close skin contact ↓ symptoms can lag weeks behind infestation ↓ contacts may be infected yet symptom-free ↓ treat household members together
exam_trap: D, Treatment is needed only to prevent bacterial infection — secondary infection can occur, but contacts are treated to eradicate mites and prevent reinfestation.
takeaway: Treat all close contacts of scabies at the same time, even if asymptomatic.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with inflammatory bowel disease develops a painful swollen knee. What is this most likely to represent?

options.A: Acute gouty arthritis of the knee

why_correct: Peripheral arthritis is a recognised extra-intestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease.
why_wrong: A. Gout is uncommon in young women and usually affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint. B. Osteoarthritis is degenerative and unlikely at 29 without risk factors. C. Rheumatic fever follows streptococcal infection with carditis and migratory arthritis. D. Haemarthrosis follows trauma or occurs with a bleeding disorder.
pearl: Enteropathic arthritis in IBD may affect large peripheral joints, often in step with bowel activity, or the spine and sacroiliac joints independently of gut disease.
thinking: Known inflammatory bowel disease ↓ painful swollen knee ↓ peripheral arthritis is an extra-intestinal manifestation of IBD ↓ enteropathic arthritis
exam_trap: A, Acute gouty arthritis — a common cause of an acutely swollen joint, but it is uncommon in a young woman and usually affects the big toe; IBD links to enteropathic arthritis.
takeaway: Swollen joint in IBD: think enteropathic arthritis, an extra-intestinal manifestation.

stem: A 31-year-old woman with coeliac disease asks why gluten must be avoided long term. What is the main reason?

options.A: Gluten is directly toxic to the liver
options.C: Gluten is poorly digested by pancreatic enzymes
options.E: Gluten triggers immune damage to the small bowel

correct_answer: E. Gluten triggers immune damage to the small bowel
why_correct: In coeliac disease, gluten triggers an immune-mediated injury to the small intestinal mucosa.
why_wrong: A. Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy, not direct hepatotoxicity. B. IgE-mediated reactions describe wheat allergy rather than coeliac disease. C. Coeliac disease is not caused by pancreatic insufficiency. D. Coeliac disease is immune-mediated, not driven by colonic bacterial overgrowth.
pearl: Coeliac disease is a lifelong immune enteropathy triggered by gluten, causing villous atrophy; strict gluten avoidance allows mucosal healing and reduces complications.
thinking: Coeliac disease ↓ gluten triggers an immune response ↓ small-bowel mucosa is damaged (villous atrophy) ↓ lifelong avoidance prevents ongoing injury
exam_trap: B, Gluten causes IgE-mediated anaphylaxis — tempting as a food reaction, but that describes wheat allergy; coeliac disease is a T-cell-mediated enteropathy.
takeaway: Coeliac disease: gluten drives immune small-bowel damage, so avoidance is lifelong.

stem: A 70-year-old man with COPD becomes acutely confused and increasingly breathless. His oxygen saturation is low. What complication should be considered?
why_correct: Acute worsening breathlessness, hypoxaemia and confusion in severe respiratory disease may indicate respiratory failure.
why_wrong: B. Wernicke's encephalopathy causes confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency and does not explain hypoxaemia. C. Hepatic encephalopathy occurs in liver failure. D. Stroke causes focal deficits rather than hypoxaemia with breathlessness. E. Hyponatraemia can cause confusion but does not explain low oxygen saturation and breathlessness.
pearl: Confusion, worsening breathlessness and hypoxaemia in COPD suggest acute respiratory failure; check arterial blood gases and give controlled oxygen, targeting 88–92%.
thinking: COPD patient ↓ increasingly breathless ↓ low oxygen saturation ↓ new confusion from hypoxaemia or hypercapnia ↓ acute respiratory failure
exam_trap: D, Acute ischaemic stroke — new confusion in an older man tempts it, but stroke causes focal deficits and does not explain hypoxaemia and breathlessness.
takeaway: Confused, breathless, hypoxic COPD patient: think respiratory failure and get an ABG.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. His leg is swollen and painful on the same side. What underlying condition is particularly relevant?
why_correct: A painful swollen leg can indicate DVT, which is an important source of pulmonary emboli.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis does not explain acute unilateral leg swelling with possible embolic symptoms. B. Hand cellulitis is unrelated. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand. D. Cataract affects the eye.
pearl: Most pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein thrombosis in the leg; a swollen, painful leg with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain strongly supports PE.
thinking: Sudden breathlessness ↓ pleuritic chest pain ↓ swollen, painful leg ↓ DVT as the source of pulmonary embolism
exam_trap: B, Cellulitis of the hand — infection causes swelling and pain, but the hand is irrelevant here; a swollen leg with chest symptoms points to DVT.
takeaway: Pleuritic pain and breathlessness with a swollen leg: think DVT with PE.

stem: A 73-year-old woman develops sudden weakness and difficulty speaking. She is assessed in the emergency department shortly after symptom onset. What should be considered immediately?
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficits require urgent assessment for acute stroke.
why_wrong: A. Sinusitis does not explain sudden focal neurological symptoms. B. Dementia causes progressive cognitive decline rather than sudden focal neurological deficit. C. Migraine can mimic stroke but must not be assumed without assessment. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute speech disturbance.
pearl: Sudden focal neurological deficit is stroke until proven otherwise; urgent brain imaging decides eligibility for time-critical thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ weakness and difficulty speaking ↓ seen shortly after onset ↓ acute stroke, a time-critical emergency
exam_trap: C, Migraine prophylaxis only — migraine with aura can mimic stroke, but sudden weakness and speech difficulty must be treated as stroke until proven otherwise.
takeaway: Sudden focal deficit: treat as acute stroke and image urgently.

stem: A 59-year-old woman develops sudden monocular loss of vision lasting 10 minutes before completely resolving. What vascular event should be considered?
why_correct: Transient monocular visual loss can result from retinal ischaemia and may be a vascular warning symptom.
why_wrong: A. Posterior vitreous detachment causes flashes and floaters rather than a transient complete loss of vision. B. Chronic open-angle glaucoma causes gradual, painless peripheral field loss. C. Optic neuritis causes painful visual loss evolving over days rather than a 10-minute episode. D. Allergic conjunctivitis causes itchy red eyes without loss of vision.
pearl: Transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) is a TIA equivalent, often from carotid emboli; it needs urgent TIA assessment including carotid imaging.
thinking: Sudden loss of vision in one eye ↓ lasts about 10 minutes ↓ resolves completely ↓ transient retinal ischaemia
exam_trap: C, Acute demyelinating optic neuritis — causes monocular visual loss, but it is painful and evolves over days rather than resolving within minutes.
takeaway: Brief monocular visual loss = amaurosis fugax: manage as a TIA.

stem: A 46-year-old man develops sudden weakness of the right side of his face, arm and leg. He also has difficulty speaking. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden unilateral weakness involving the face, arm and leg together with speech disturbance strongly suggests an acute stroke.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy does not typically cause sudden hemiparesis with aphasia. C. Bell's palsy causes isolated lower motor neuron facial weakness. D. Migraine can cause neurological symptoms but stroke must be urgently considered. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve distribution in the hand.
pearl: Sudden one-sided face, arm and leg weakness with speech disturbance fits a stroke; a positive FAST screen means emergency transfer to a stroke unit.
thinking: Sudden onset in a 46-year-old ↓ weakness of the right face, arm and leg together ↓ difficulty speaking ↓ stroke
exam_trap: C, Bell's palsy — the facial weakness tempts it, but Bell's affects the face alone; arm and leg weakness with speech difficulty means stroke.
takeaway: Sudden face, arm and leg weakness with speech change = stroke.

stem: A 23-year-old woman experiences recurrent attacks of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and wheezing after eating certain foods. She has no fever and feels completely well between attacks. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent symptoms involving the gastrointestinal and respiratory systems after food exposure suggest food allergy.
why_wrong: A. Acute cholecystitis causes persistent right upper quadrant pain and systemic inflammation. B. Renal colic causes acute flank-to-groin pain. C. Peptic ulcer disease does not typically cause episodic wheeze after food. E. Appendicitis is usually an acute progressive illness.
pearl: Food allergy can cause reproducible gastrointestinal, skin and respiratory symptoms soon after a trigger food; wheeze signals a risk of anaphylaxis and needs allergy assessment.
thinking: Recurrent attacks after certain foods ↓ abdominal pain, diarrhoea and wheeze ↓ well between attacks, no fever ↓ food allergy
exam_trap: C, Peptic ulcer disease — food-related abdominal pain tempts it, but peptic ulcers do not cause diarrhoea and wheeze after eating.
takeaway: Recurrent GI plus respiratory symptoms after specific foods: think food allergy.

stem: A 10-year-old boy develops widespread itchy wheals shortly after eating a food. He is otherwise well, with no breathing difficulty or circulatory symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.C: Intramuscular adrenaline immediately in every case

why_correct: Isolated urticaria without features of anaphylaxis can be treated symptomatically with an antihistamine.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not treat allergic urticaria. B. Insulin has no role. C. Adrenaline is required for anaphylaxis, not uncomplicated isolated urticaria. D. Antifungal treatment is inappropriate.
pearl: Isolated urticaria without airway, breathing or circulation problems is treated with a non-sedating oral antihistamine; adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis.
thinking: Itchy wheals after a food ↓ no breathing difficulty ↓ no circulatory symptoms ↓ isolated urticaria, not anaphylaxis ↓ antihistamine
exam_trap: C, Intramuscular adrenaline immediately in every case — lifesaving in anaphylaxis, but isolated urticaria without airway, breathing or circulation involvement does not need it.
takeaway: Urticaria alone = antihistamine; airway, breathing or circulation compromise = adrenaline.

stem: A 17-year-old girl develops recurrent episodes of wheeze after exposure to cats. Which mechanism best explains asthma?

options.A: Pulmonary arterial obstruction by thromboembolism causing V/Q mismatch
options.B: Air in the pleural space causing partial lung collapse
options.C: Irreversible destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil
options.D: Interstitial fibrosis reducing lung compliance and gas transfer
options.E: Variable airway narrowing due to inflammation and hyperresponsiveness

correct_answer: E. Variable airway narrowing due to inflammation and hyperresponsiveness
why_correct: Asthma involves airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness producing variable airflow obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Pulmonary arterial obstruction by thromboembolism describes pulmonary embolism. B. Air in the pleural space describes pneumothorax. C. Irreversible alveolar destruction with loss of elastic recoil is characteristic of emphysema. D. Interstitial fibrosis describes interstitial lung disease, which causes a restrictive rather than variable obstructive pattern.
pearl: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with hyperresponsiveness, causing variable, reversible airflow obstruction that can be triggered by allergens such as cat dander.
thinking: Recurrent episodes of wheeze ↓ triggered by exposure to cats ↓ allergic airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness ↓ variable airway narrowing
exam_trap: C, Irreversible destruction of alveolar walls — another obstructive process, but this describes emphysema; asthmatic narrowing is variable and reversible.
takeaway: Asthma = variable, reversible airway narrowing from inflammation and hyperresponsiveness.

stem: A 59-year-old woman has a persistent cough, recurrent chest infections and coughing up blood. She has a long smoking history. What diagnosis requires investigation?
why_correct: Haemoptysis with persistent respiratory symptoms in a smoker is a red flag for lung cancer.
why_wrong: A. IBS causes gastrointestinal symptoms. B. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand. C. Osteoarthritis affects joints. D. Migraine does not cause haemoptysis.
pearl: Haemoptysis in a smoker, or a persistent cough with recurrent chest infections, warrants an urgent chest X-ray or a suspected lung cancer pathway referral.
thinking: Long smoking history ↓ persistent cough and recurrent chest infections ↓ coughing up blood ↓ lung cancer must be investigated
exam_trap: D, Migraine — has no link to cough or haemoptysis; the real danger is attributing recurrent chest infections to simple infection, when haemoptysis in a smoker needs cancer investigation.
takeaway: Haemoptysis in a smoker is a lung cancer red flag: investigate urgently.

stem: A 76-year-old man develops fever, cough and increasing confusion. He has low blood pressure and a fast respiratory rate. What serious complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Infection accompanied by systemic deterioration, hypotension, tachypnoea and altered mental state is concerning for sepsis.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome is unrelated. B. Cataract does not cause acute systemic deterioration. D. Tension headache does not explain fever and hypotension. E. Stable angina does not cause systemic infection.
pearl: Infection with new confusion, hypotension and a raised respiratory rate signals sepsis; escalate early and start the sepsis bundle, including cultures, antibiotics and fluids.
thinking: Fever and cough suggest infection ↓ increasing confusion ↓ low blood pressure and fast respiratory rate ↓ sepsis
exam_trap: E, Stable angina — cardiovascular disease is common at his age, but angina does not cause fever, confusion and hypotension with tachypnoea.
takeaway: Infection plus confusion, hypotension or tachypnoea = suspect sepsis.

stem: A 19-year-old student develops fever, headache and a rapidly spreading non-blanching rash. What diagnosis requires urgent consideration?
why_correct: Fever with acute systemic illness and a non-blanching rash is a major warning pattern for meningococcal disease.
why_wrong: A. Urticaria produces blanching itchy wheals, with or without angioedema. B. Guttate psoriasis produces small scaly plaques, often after a sore throat, and does not cause a non-blanching rash. D. Pityriasis rosea causes a herald patch and oval scaly lesions without systemic illness. E. Contact dermatitis usually corresponds to an area of exposure and does not cause a non-blanching rash with fever.
pearl: Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal disease until proven otherwise; outside hospital, give parenteral benzylpenicillin if it will not delay transfer.
thinking: Young adult with fever and headache ↓ rapidly spreading rash ↓ rash is non-blanching ↓ meningococcal disease
exam_trap: A, Acute urticaria with angioedema — an acute widespread rash, but urticarial wheals blanch and do not come with fever and systemic illness.
takeaway: Fever plus non-blanching rash: treat as meningococcal disease immediately.

stem: A 34-year-old man has fever, cough and a painful swollen knee. Joint aspiration produces purulent fluid. What diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: An acutely hot, swollen joint with systemic infection and purulent aspirate is characteristic of septic arthritis.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome does not cause purulent arthritis. B. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without a hot, infected joint. C. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative condition and does not produce purulent joint fluid. D. Migraine does not cause septic joint inflammation.
pearl: A hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise; aspirate before antibiotics if this causes no delay, sending fluid for Gram stain and culture.
thinking: Fever and cough ↓ painful, swollen knee ↓ purulent fluid on joint aspiration ↓ infected joint ↓ septic arthritis
exam_trap: C, Osteoarthritis — a common cause of knee pain and swelling, but it is degenerative and does not produce purulent joint fluid with fever.
takeaway: Hot swollen joint with pus on aspiration = septic arthritis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman develops diarrhoea and abdominal cramps after returning from travelling abroad. Several other people on the trip have similar symptoms. What is the most likely broad diagnosis?
why_correct: Acute diarrhoea and abdominal cramps affecting several people after travel strongly suggest an infectious cause.
why_wrong: A. Bowel cancer does not typically cause an acute cluster of diarrhoeal illness. C. Coeliac disease is a chronic immune-mediated condition. D. IBS is a chronic functional disorder. E. Appendicitis does not usually cause an outbreak affecting several people.
pearl: Acute diarrhoea in several travel companions points to infective gastroenteritis; most cases are self-limiting and oral rehydration is the mainstay of treatment.
thinking: Recent travel abroad ↓ acute diarrhoea and cramps ↓ several fellow travellers affected ↓ infective gastroenteritis
exam_trap: D, Irritable bowel syndrome — causes cramps and diarrhoea, but it is chronic and does not strike a group of travellers at the same time.
takeaway: Acute diarrhoea in a cluster after travel = infective gastroenteritis.

stem: A 32-year-old man has acute diarrhoea and vomiting for 24 hours. He is thirsty and passing very little urine. What complication is most likely?
why_correct: Thirst and reduced urine output during acute gastrointestinal fluid loss are features of dehydration.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis causes chronic inflammatory joint disease. B. Gout causes inflammatory arthritis. D. Hyperthyroidism does not explain acute fluid loss. E. Cataract affects vision.
pearl: Thirst and reduced urine output signal dehydration from gastrointestinal losses; oral rehydration is first-line, with IV fluids if severe or unable to drink.
thinking: 24 hours of diarrhoea and vomiting ↓ thirsty ↓ passing very little urine ↓ fluid losses exceed intake ↓ dehydration
exam_trap: B, Gout — dehydration can precipitate gout, but nothing in the stem suggests joint inflammation; thirst and low urine output mean dehydration.
takeaway: Gut fluid loss with thirst and low urine output = dehydration.

stem: A 68-year-old man notices that he has become increasingly constipated and has lost weight without trying. What diagnosis requires consideration?
why_correct: A new change in bowel habit accompanied by unexplained weight loss is a warning pattern requiring assessment for colorectal cancer.
why_wrong: B. IBS is less likely when significant alarm features are present. C. GORD causes upper gastrointestinal symptoms. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the hand. E. Migraine does not explain the bowel changes.
pearl: A new change in bowel habit with unexplained weight loss in an older adult is a red flag for colorectal cancer; assess urgently, including a FIT, on the suspected cancer pathway.
thinking: Older man ↓ new change in bowel habit (constipation) ↓ unintentional weight loss ↓ colorectal cancer must be considered
exam_trap: B, Irritable bowel syndrome — causes altered bowel habit, but new symptoms at 68 with weight loss are alarm features that must not be labelled IBS.
takeaway: New bowel habit change plus weight loss in older age: investigate for colorectal cancer.

stem: A 47-year-old woman develops severe right upper abdominal pain and fever. The pain is worse when she takes a deep breath during palpation of the right upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Right upper quadrant pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign are characteristic of acute cholecystitis.
why_wrong: B. Appendicitis classically causes right lower quadrant pain after initial central pain. C. Pancreatitis usually causes severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back. D. Renal colic typically causes flank pain radiating towards the groin. E. IBS does not cause fever or focal peritoneal inflammation.
pearl: Murphy's sign, arrest of inspiration on right upper quadrant palpation, with fever suggests acute cholecystitis; ultrasound is the first-line imaging.
thinking: Severe right upper quadrant pain ↓ fever ↓ pain catches on deep inspiration during RUQ palpation (Murphy's sign) ↓ acute cholecystitis
exam_trap: C, Acute pancreatitis — severe upper abdominal pain tempts it, but pancreatitis is epigastric and radiates to the back; RUQ pain with Murphy's sign is cholecystitis.
takeaway: RUQ pain, fever and a positive Murphy's sign = acute cholecystitis.

stem: A 61-year-old man develops yellowing of the skin, dark urine and pale stools. What does this pattern suggest?
why_correct: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stools suggests conjugated bilirubin and impaired bile flow.
why_wrong: A. Iron-deficiency anaemia does not cause this pattern. B. Dehydration does not cause obstructive jaundice. C. Haemolysis causes predominantly unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and does not typically cause pale stools. D. Gilbert syndrome causes mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without pale stools.
pearl: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated bilirubin is not reaching the gut; obstructive jaundice in an older adult raises concern for pancreatic or biliary cancer as well as stones.
thinking: Jaundice ↓ dark urine from conjugated bilirubin ↓ pale stools from absent bile in the gut ↓ obstructive jaundice
exam_trap: C, Uncomplicated haemolysis — causes jaundice, but the bilirubin is unconjugated, so the urine does not contain bilirubin and stools are not pale.
takeaway: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stools = obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice.

stem: A 58-year-old woman develops fever, flank pain and dysuria. She has tenderness over the renal angle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Fever, flank pain, dysuria and renal-angle tenderness indicate an upper urinary tract infection.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes severe colicky pain and may cause haematuria but not typically fever and dysuria together. B. Candidiasis causes vulvovaginal symptoms rather than renal-angle tenderness and fever. C. IBS does not cause urinary infection. D. Cystitis usually causes lower urinary tract symptoms without systemic illness or renal-angle tenderness.
pearl: Pyelonephritis causes fever, loin pain and renal-angle tenderness, with or without lower urinary symptoms; send a urine culture and start antibiotics promptly.
thinking: Fever ↓ flank pain and dysuria ↓ renal-angle tenderness ↓ upper urinary tract infection = pyelonephritis
exam_trap: D, Uncomplicated cystitis — explains the dysuria, but cystitis lacks fever, flank pain and renal-angle tenderness, which mark upper tract infection.
takeaway: UTI plus fever and loin tenderness = pyelonephritis, not cystitis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman develops facial and ankle swelling. Urinalysis shows blood and protein, and her blood pressure is markedly elevated. What renal syndrome should be suspected?
why_correct: Haematuria, proteinuria, hypertension and renal impairment are characteristic features of nephritic disease.
why_wrong: A. Diabetes insipidus causes polyuria and thirst. B. Renal colic causes severe colicky pain. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms rather than glomerular haematuria and hypertension. E. Nephrotic syndrome is dominated by heavy proteinuria and oedema.
pearl: Nephritic syndrome brings haematuria, hypertension, oedema and variable proteinuria, often with reduced kidney function; nephrotic syndrome is dominated by heavy proteinuria.
thinking: Facial and ankle swelling ↓ blood and protein in the urine ↓ markedly raised blood pressure ↓ haematuria with hypertension = nephritic syndrome
exam_trap: E, Nephrotic syndrome — oedema and proteinuria tempt it, but nephrotic syndrome is dominated by heavy proteinuria; haematuria and hypertension point to nephritic.
takeaway: Haematuria plus hypertension = nephritic; heavy proteinuria plus oedema = nephrotic.

stem: A 56-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease develops persistent itching without a primary skin rash. What is a possible cause?

options.A: Seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp and face
options.D: Psoriasis with chronic scaly extensor plaques

correct_answer: E. Uraemia from advanced kidney disease
why_correct: Pruritus can occur in advanced chronic kidney disease and is associated with uraemic and metabolic disturbances.
why_wrong: A. Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a primary skin rash, which is absent here. B. Atopic eczema produces a visible primary rash, which is absent here. C. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal symptoms. D. Psoriasis produces visible scaly plaques, which are absent here.
pearl: Itch without a primary rash in advanced CKD suggests uraemic pruritus; also consider other systemic causes such as cholestasis, iron deficiency and thyroid disease.
thinking: Advanced chronic kidney disease ↓ persistent itching ↓ no primary skin rash to explain it ↓ uraemic pruritus
exam_trap: B, Atopic eczema — a common cause of itch, but it produces a visible primary rash with lichenified plaques, which is absent here.
takeaway: Itch without a rash in advanced CKD: think uraemic pruritus.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with hyperthyroidism has prominent, staring eyes and difficulty closing her eyelids. What condition is associated with these findings?
why_correct: Graves' disease can cause thyroid eye disease, including prominence of the eyes.
why_wrong: A. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism. B. Phaeochromocytoma causes catecholamine excess. C. Diabetes insipidus affects water regulation. E. Addison's disease affects the adrenal glands.
pearl: Graves' disease is the common cause of hyperthyroidism with eye disease; lid lag can occur in any thyrotoxicosis, but proptosis and poor lid closure point to Graves' orbitopathy, which smoking worsens.
thinking: Hyperthyroidism in a young woman ↓ Prominent staring eyes with poor lid closure ↓ Autoimmune orbitopathy ↓ Graves' disease
exam_trap: A, Hashimoto's thyroiditis — it is also autoimmune thyroid disease, which tempts, but it typically causes hypothyroidism rather than this hyperthyroid picture with proptosis.
takeaway: Hyperthyroidism plus proptosis means Graves' disease until proven otherwise.

stem: A 68-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has persistently high blood glucose despite taking his prescribed medication. What is an important long-term complication of poorly controlled diabetes?
why_correct: Persistent hyperglycaemia can cause microvascular complications affecting the eyes, kidneys and nerves.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic is not an inevitable diabetic complication. C. Appendicitis is not a typical diabetic complication. D. Cataracts are not inevitable in every person with diabetes. E. Otitis externa is not a characteristic diabetic microvascular complication.
pearl: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages small vessels, causing retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy; this is why people with diabetes have regular eye screening, urine albumin checks and foot reviews.
thinking: Long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes ↓ Sustained hyperglycaemia injures small vessels ↓ Eyes, kidneys and nerves affected ↓ Microvascular damage
exam_trap: D, cataract in every patient — diabetes does increase cataract risk, which tempts, but the word 'every' makes it false; cataract is not inevitable.
takeaway: Poor glycaemic control drives microvascular disease: eyes, kidneys and nerves.

stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetes develops a painless wound on the sole of his foot. He has reduced sensation in both feet. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Venous ulcer from chronic venous insufficiency
options.C: Acute gout of the first MTP joint

why_correct: A painless plantar ulcer in a patient with diabetic peripheral neuropathy is characteristic of a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Venous ulcers typically occur in the gaiter area of the lower leg rather than on the sole. C. Gout causes acute painful inflammation of a joint rather than a painless wound. D. A plantar wart is a hyperkeratotic viral lesion rather than an open wound. E. Tinea pedis causes itchy scaling and maceration between the toes rather than a painless plantar ulcer.
pearl: Loss of protective sensation lets repeated pressure injure the sole unnoticed, so neuropathic ulcers form over pressure points; any active diabetic foot ulcer needs prompt specialist foot team review.
thinking: Diabetes with reduced sensation in both feet ↓ Painless wound on the weight-bearing sole ↓ Unnoticed repetitive pressure trauma ↓ Neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer
exam_trap: A, venous ulcer — chronic ulcers are common at this age, but venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area with oedema and pigmentation, not on the sole of the foot.
takeaway: Painless plantar ulcer plus numb feet in diabetes is a neuropathic ulcer.

stem: A 67-year-old man with diabetes has gradually worsening vision. Which diabetic complication should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic diabetes can damage retinal blood vessels and cause diabetic retinopathy with progressive visual impairment.
why_wrong: B. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain. C. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal symptoms. D. Otitis externa affects the ear canal. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes hand symptoms.
pearl: Diabetic retinopathy is often symptomless until advanced, which is why people with diabetes are offered regular retinal screening; any worsening vision warrants prompt eye assessment.
thinking: Patient with diabetes ↓ Gradual visual deterioration ↓ Microvascular damage to retinal vessels ↓ Diabetic retinopathy
exam_trap: E, carpal tunnel syndrome — it is genuinely more common in diabetes, which makes it feel linked, but it causes hand numbness, not visual loss.
takeaway: Visual decline in a patient with diabetes: think retinopathy first.

stem: A 25-year-old woman develops a painful round ulcer inside her mouth. She has no fever or other systemic symptoms. It heals spontaneously after several days. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A small, painful oral ulcer that heals spontaneously is typical of an aphthous ulcer.
why_wrong: A. Leukoplakia causes persistent white patches. B. Candidiasis usually causes white plaques rather than a solitary ulcer. D. Melanoma is not the typical cause of a short-lived painful oral ulcer. E. Oral cancer should be considered for persistent or suspicious lesions.
pearl: Aphthous ulcers are small, painful, round ulcers with a yellow-grey base and red halo that heal on their own; any mouth ulcer persisting beyond three weeks needs referral to exclude cancer.
thinking: Young adult, no systemic features ↓ Single painful round oral ulcer ↓ Heals spontaneously within days ↓ Aphthous ulcer
exam_trap: E, oral squamous cell carcinoma — any mouth ulcer prompts cancer worry, but malignant ulcers persist and are often painless rather than healing within days.
takeaway: A painful, self-healing oral ulcer is aphthous; a persistent one needs referral.

stem: A 48-year-old man develops recurrent painful blisters around the lips. They begin with tingling and then form small grouped vesicles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Recurrent grouped vesicles preceded by tingling around the lips are characteristic of herpes simplex.
why_wrong: B. Scabies causes widespread intense itching with burrows. C. Cellulitis causes spreading painful erythema rather than grouped vesicles. D. Angular cheilitis causes fissuring at the corners of the mouth rather than grouped vesicles. E. Aphthous ulcers occur inside the mouth and are not preceded by tingling vesicles on the lips.
pearl: Cold sores are reactivations of herpes simplex from the trigeminal ganglion, typically heralded by tingling before grouped vesicles appear; triggers include sunlight, stress and intercurrent illness.
thinking: Recurrent lip lesions ↓ Prodromal tingling ↓ Grouped painful vesicles ↓ Herpes simplex infection
exam_trap: D, angular cheilitis — it also affects the lips and recurs, but it causes fissuring at the corners of the mouth without a tingling prodrome or vesicles.
takeaway: Tingling followed by recurrent grouped lip vesicles equals herpes labialis.

stem: A 69-year-old woman develops a painful vesicular rash on her forehead and the tip of her nose. She also has eye discomfort. What complication is particularly concerning?

options.A: Allergic contact dermatitis of the face
options.B: Seborrhoeic dermatitis of the face and scalp
options.C: Rosacea flare affecting the nose and cheeks
options.D: Alopecia areata affecting the eyebrow hair

correct_answer: E. Ocular involvement from herpes zoster
why_correct: Herpes zoster affecting the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve can involve the eye and threaten vision, requiring urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy eczematous rash at the site of exposure rather than a painful dermatomal vesicular rash. B. Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes greasy scaling rather than painful vesicles. C. Rosacea causes facial flushing and papules without vesicles or a dermatomal pattern. D. Alopecia areata causes patchy hair loss.
pearl: Vesicles on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson's sign) indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and a higher risk of eye involvement in shingles; start antivirals and arrange urgent ophthalmology assessment.
thinking: Painful vesicles on the forehead in an older adult ↓ Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve ↓ Nose tip involved plus eye discomfort ↓ Ocular involvement from herpes zoster
exam_trap: A, allergic contact dermatitis of the face — a facial rash with eye irritation is common, but contact dermatitis is itchy and eczematous at the exposure site, not painful dermatomal vesicles.
takeaway: Shingles on the nose tip warns of eye involvement: assess the eye urgently.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has pain and stiffness affecting both shoulders and hips. Her symptoms are particularly severe in the morning. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: New bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and prolonged morning stiffness in an older adult are characteristic of polymyalgia rheumatica.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis causes predominantly mechanical symptoms. B. Rheumatoid arthritis more typically causes inflammatory peripheral joint disease. C. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain but not this characteristic inflammatory pattern. E. Gout usually causes acute monoarthritis.
pearl: Polymyalgia rheumatica causes bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain with prolonged morning stiffness in people over 50, with raised inflammatory markers and a rapid response to low-dose steroids; always ask about GCA symptoms.
thinking: Older adult ↓ Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain ↓ Marked morning stiffness ↓ Polymyalgia rheumatica
exam_trap: B, rheumatoid arthritis — it also causes morning stiffness, but it mainly affects small peripheral joints of the hands and feet rather than the shoulder and hip girdles.
takeaway: Older patient with girdle pain and morning stiffness: think PMR and screen for GCA.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis after a low-trauma vertebral fracture. What does osteoporosis primarily involve?

options.A: Reduced bone strength and increased fracture risk
options.B: Loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with ageing
options.D: Defective mineralisation of osteoid from vitamin D deficiency
options.E: Bacterial infection of bone and marrow

correct_answer: A. Reduced bone strength and increased fracture risk
why_correct: Osteoporosis is characterised by reduced bone strength, resulting in increased susceptibility to fragility fractures.
why_wrong: B. Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength is sarcopenia. C. Autoimmune synovial inflammation is characteristic of inflammatory arthritis. D. Defective osteoid mineralisation describes osteomalacia. E. Bone infection is osteomyelitis.
pearl: Osteoporosis is low bone mass with microarchitectural deterioration causing fragility fractures; a low-trauma vertebral fracture should prompt fracture risk assessment and bone-protective treatment such as a bisphosphonate.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Low-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ Bone too weak for normal loads ↓ Reduced bone strength and increased fracture risk
exam_trap: D, defective mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency — osteomalacia also weakens bone and causes fractures, but it is a mineralisation defect, not reduced bone mass.
takeaway: Osteoporosis is low bone strength; osteomalacia is poor mineralisation.

stem: A 66-year-old man suddenly develops weakness of his right arm and leg with difficulty speaking. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic investigation for suspected acute stroke?
why_correct: Urgent brain imaging is required to distinguish intracranial haemorrhage from ischaemic stroke and guide acute management.
why_wrong: B. Cardiac investigation may be needed later but does not replace urgent brain imaging. C. Lumbar puncture is not required routinely for suspected acute stroke. D. Abdominal ultrasound does not assess the acute neurological event. E. Colonoscopy is unrelated to acute stroke assessment.
pearl: Brain imaging, usually non-contrast CT, is done immediately in suspected acute stroke because thrombolysis or thrombectomy cannot be considered until haemorrhage has been excluded.
thinking: Sudden right arm and leg weakness with speech difficulty ↓ Suspected acute stroke ↓ Haemorrhage must be excluded before treatment ↓ Urgent brain imaging
exam_trap: B, echocardiography — a cardiac embolic source is often sought, which tempts, but this belongs to later work-up and must never delay brain imaging.
takeaway: Suspected stroke: image the brain first, because time is brain.

stem: A 72-year-old man suddenly develops difficulty producing speech while his comprehension appears relatively preserved. Which neurological deficit is this?
why_correct: Difficulty producing language with relatively preserved comprehension is characteristic of expressive aphasia.
why_wrong: B. Cerebellar truncal ataxia is impaired coordination of balance and gait. C. Receptive (Wernicke) aphasia impairs comprehension, which is relatively preserved here. D. Homonymous hemianopia is loss of part of the visual field. E. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing.
pearl: Expressive (Broca's) aphasia gives slow, effortful, non-fluent speech with relatively preserved comprehension; it usually reflects a lesion in the dominant frontal lobe.
thinking: Sudden-onset speech problem ↓ Difficulty producing words ↓ Comprehension relatively preserved ↓ Expressive aphasia
