exam_trap: C, receptive (Wernicke) aphasia — it is the other major aphasia, but it impairs comprehension with fluent, meaningless speech; here comprehension is preserved.
takeaway: Broca's aphasia breaks output; Wernicke's breaks understanding.

stem: A 65-year-old man with heart failure notices increasing ankle swelling and breathlessness after several days of missing his medication. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Fluid overload due to worsening heart failure

correct_answer: A. Fluid overload due to worsening heart failure
why_correct: Increasing peripheral oedema and breathlessness in a patient with heart failure suggest worsening congestion and fluid overload.
why_wrong: B. Pneumonia can cause breathlessness but does not explain increasing ankle swelling after stopping heart failure medication. C. Venous insufficiency causes chronic ankle swelling but not acute breathlessness. D. He has missed his medication, and drug-induced ankle oedema does not cause breathlessness. E. A COPD exacerbation does not explain the combination of fluid retention and missed heart failure treatment.
pearl: Missing diuretics and other heart failure medicines is a common precipitant of decompensation; weight gain, worsening oedema and breathlessness signal fluid overload.
thinking: Known heart failure ↓ Missed medication for several days ↓ Increasing ankle oedema and breathlessness ↓ Fluid overload due to worsening heart failure
exam_trap: B, community-acquired pneumonia — it is a common trigger of decompensation and causes breathlessness, but it does not explain rising ankle swelling after stopping treatment.
takeaway: Heart failure plus missed tablets plus new oedema means decompensation.

stem: A 58-year-old man has intermittent calf pain when walking that reliably settles after a few minutes of rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Sciatica from lumbar disc herniation and L5 root compression
options.B: Cellulitis of the lower leg with ascending lymphangitis
options.C: Ruptured Baker's cyst tracking down into the calf
options.D: Deep vein thrombosis in the soleal and calf veins
options.E: Claudication due to peripheral arterial disease

correct_answer: E. Claudication due to peripheral arterial disease
why_correct: Predictable exertional calf pain relieved by rest is characteristic of intermittent claudication caused by peripheral arterial disease.
why_wrong: A. Sciatica causes radiating radicular pain rather than predictable exertional calf pain relieved by rest. B. Cellulitis causes inflammatory skin changes. C. A ruptured Baker's cyst causes sudden calf pain and swelling rather than recurrent exertional pain. D. DVT usually causes persistent swelling and pain rather than predictable exertional symptoms.
pearl: Intermittent claudication is reproducible exertional calf pain relieved within minutes by rest; check pulses and ankle brachial pressure index, and address cardiovascular risk, including smoking.
thinking: Middle-aged man ↓ Calf pain on walking ↓ Reliably relieved by rest ↓ Claudication due to peripheral arterial disease
exam_trap: A, sciatica — lumbar spine disease can cause walking-related leg pain, but sciatica gives radiating radicular pain that does not reliably settle within minutes of standing still.
takeaway: Calf pain that comes with walking and goes with rest is arterial claudication.

stem: A 52-year-old man develops sudden swelling and pain in his left calf. The leg is more swollen than the right. What diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Acute unilateral leg swelling and pain are typical features of DVT.
why_wrong: B. Intermittent claudication causes exertional arterial pain rather than acute unilateral swelling. C. Osteoarthritis affects joints. D. Bell's palsy causes facial weakness. E. Migraine causes headache.
pearl: Acute unilateral calf pain and swelling should be assessed with the two-level Wells score, followed by D-dimer or proximal leg vein ultrasound according to the result.
thinking: Sudden left calf pain ↓ Unilateral leg swelling ↓ Suspected venous obstruction ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: B, intermittent claudication — it also causes calf pain, but it is exertional, relieved by rest and does not cause leg swelling.
takeaway: An acutely swollen, painful single calf is DVT until excluded.

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops a widespread itchy rash after taking a new antibiotic. There is no breathing difficulty, facial swelling or circulatory compromise. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: An acute itchy wheal-and-flare rash following a medicine, without systemic airway or circulatory compromise, is consistent with urticaria.
why_wrong: A. Scabies causes persistent infestation-related itching rather than an acute drug-associated eruption. B. Herpes zoster produces painful dermatomal vesicles. C. Pityriasis rosea causes a herald patch and oval scaly lesions unrelated to a new medicine. E. Anaphylaxis involves systemic features such as airway, breathing or circulation problems, which are absent.
pearl: Drug-induced urticaria causes itchy wheals soon after a new medicine; stop the culprit, give a non-sedating antihistamine, record the reaction and check for airway, breathing or circulation problems.
thinking: New antibiotic ↓ Widespread itchy rash ↓ No airway, breathing or circulatory compromise ↓ Drug-induced urticaria
exam_trap: E, anaphylaxis to the antibiotic — the same drug trigger can cause both, but anaphylaxis needs airway, breathing or circulatory compromise, which is absent here.
takeaway: Skin-only drug reaction is urticaria; add ABC compromise and it is anaphylaxis.

stem: A 67-year-old man with longstanding reflux develops progressive difficulty swallowing. Which investigation is most appropriate to assess suspected oesophageal pathology?

options.B: Transabdominal ultrasound of the upper abdomen
options.C: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
options.D: Erect chest and plain abdominal X-ray

why_correct: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom requiring assessment of the oesophagus, and upper GI endoscopy allows direct visualisation and biopsy when indicated.
why_wrong: A. Spirometry assesses lung function. B. Abdominal ultrasound does not assess the oesophagus. C. CT may be used later for staging but does not allow direct visualisation and biopsy of the oesophagus. D. Plain X-rays do not adequately assess the oesophagus.
pearl: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom; upper GI endoscopy is the investigation of choice because it allows direct visualisation and biopsy, which matters after long-standing reflux where Barrett's and adenocarcinoma are concerns.
thinking: Long-standing reflux ↓ Progressive dysphagia ↓ Possible stricture or oesophageal cancer ↓ Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
exam_trap: C, CT of the abdomen and pelvis — CT is used in oesophageal cancer, which tempts, but for staging after diagnosis; it cannot visualise the mucosa or take biopsies.
takeaway: Dysphagia needs a camera: upper GI endoscopy with biopsy.

stem: A patient is being investigated for suspected coeliac disease. Which initial blood test is most appropriate?
why_correct: Coeliac serology is used in the initial investigation of suspected coeliac disease.
why_wrong: A. Faecal calprotectin is used to assess intestinal inflammation such as inflammatory bowel disease, not coeliac disease. B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. D. Amylase may be used in the assessment of pancreatitis. E. Antinuclear antibodies are used in the assessment of connective tissue disease.
pearl: First-line coeliac testing is IgA tissue transglutaminase with total IgA, done while the patient is still eating gluten; positive serology leads to gastroenterology referral.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Non-invasive first-line test needed ↓ IgA tTG with total IgA ↓ Coeliac serology
exam_trap: A, faecal calprotectin — it is used to investigate diarrhoea and bowel symptoms, but it detects intestinal inflammation such as IBD rather than coeliac disease.
takeaway: Suspected coeliac disease: serology first, while still eating gluten.

stem: A 58-year-old woman who has been through menopause develops vaginal bleeding. What diagnosis requires assessment?
why_correct: Vaginal bleeding after menopause is abnormal and requires assessment for causes including endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: A. Ovulation does not normally occur after menopause. B. Dysmenorrhoea is menstrual pain. C. Bleeding after menopause has occurred is not part of the normal menopause. E. Mittelschmerz is ovulation-related mid-cycle pain.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; it warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral, and transvaginal ultrasound of endometrial thickness is usually the first investigation.
thinking: Woman after menopause ↓ New vaginal bleeding ↓ Abnormal at this stage of life ↓ Possible endometrial pathology
exam_trap: C, normal menopausal transition — irregular bleeding is normal around the menopause, but once menopause has occurred any bleeding is abnormal.
takeaway: Any bleeding after menopause needs urgent endometrial assessment.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a previous ectopic pregnancy becomes pregnant again. Why is she at increased risk of another ectopic pregnancy?

options.A: Pregnancy always occurs in both fallopian tubes
options.B: Previous ectopic pregnancy eliminates future risk
options.C: Ectopic pregnancy occurs only in women with fibroids
options.D: Previous ectopic pregnancy increases recurrence risk
options.E: Ectopic pregnancy is caused only by menopause

correct_answer: D. Previous ectopic pregnancy increases recurrence risk
why_correct: A previous ectopic pregnancy is an established risk factor for another ectopic pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Pregnancy normally implants in the uterus, not both tubes. B. Previous ectopic pregnancy increases rather than eliminates risk. C. Fibroids are not the sole cause. E. Menopause is not a cause of ectopic pregnancy.
pearl: After a previous ectopic pregnancy, an early transvaginal ultrasound is offered in later pregnancies to confirm an intrauterine location, because the recurrence risk is increased.
thinking: Previous ectopic pregnancy ↓ Tubal damage or underlying risk persists ↓ Higher chance of recurrence ↓ Previous ectopic pregnancy increases recurrence risk
exam_trap: C, ectopic pregnancy only with fibroids — it names a plausible gynaecological condition, but ectopic risk relates mainly to tubal damage, and 'only' makes it false.
takeaway: A past ectopic raises recurrence risk: confirm the pregnancy site early next time.

stem: A 34-year-old pregnant woman asks why she should avoid certain medicines during pregnancy. What is the most appropriate general principle?

options.A: Topical medicines carry the main risk of fetal harm
options.B: Most medicines are broken down by the placenta before reaching the fetus
options.C: Some medicines can cross the placenta and affect the fetus
options.D: Medicines affect the fetus mainly after 36 weeks of gestation
options.E: Fetal drug effects depend mainly on the mother's body weight

correct_answer: C. Some medicines can cross the placenta and affect the fetus
why_correct: Many medicines can cross the placenta, and fetal effects depend on the drug and stage of pregnancy.
why_wrong: A. Fetal exposure mainly follows systemic maternal absorption; topical use is not the principal risk. B. Many medicines cross the placenta and reach the fetus. D. The first trimester, during organogenesis, carries the greatest teratogenic risk. E. Fetal effects depend mainly on the specific drug, dose and stage of pregnancy.
pearl: Teratogenic risk is greatest in the first trimester during organogenesis; in pregnancy, prescribe only when benefit outweighs risk, at the lowest effective dose, checking the BNF.
thinking: Pregnant woman asking about medicine safety ↓ Many drugs cross the placenta ↓ Fetal effect depends on drug and gestation ↓ Some medicines can cross the placenta and affect the fetus
exam_trap: B, medicines broken down by the placenta — it sounds reassuring and plausible, but the placenta is not a reliable barrier and many drugs reach the fetus.
takeaway: The placenta is not a barrier: check every drug in pregnancy.

stem: A woman develops heavy postpartum bleeding and examination suggests that placental tissue remains inside the uterus. What is a recognised cause of postpartum haemorrhage?
why_correct: Retained placental tissue is a recognised cause of postpartum haemorrhage.
why_wrong: A. Hyperemesis gravidarum causes severe vomiting in early pregnancy. B. Migraine causes headache. D. Otitis externa affects the external ear. E. Symphysis pubis dysfunction causes pelvic girdle pain.
pearl: Causes of postpartum haemorrhage are remembered as the 4 Ts: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin; retained placental tissue is the tissue cause and stops the uterus contracting effectively.
thinking: Heavy bleeding after delivery ↓ Placental tissue remains in the uterus ↓ Uterus cannot contract fully ↓ Retained placenta
exam_trap: E, symphysis pubis dysfunction — it is a pregnancy-related condition so feels relevant, but it causes pelvic girdle pain, not bleeding.
takeaway: Postpartum haemorrhage causes: tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin.

stem: A newborn develops jaundice at 8 hours of age. What is the significance of this finding?

options.B: It is diagnostic of biliary atresia
options.D: It is caused by breast milk in every case
options.E: It is likely to be pathological

correct_answer: E. It is likely to be pathological
why_correct: Jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life is considered pathological and requires assessment.
why_wrong: A. Teething does not cause neonatal jaundice. B. Early jaundice has many possible causes and is not diagnostic of biliary atresia. C. Physiological neonatal jaundice usually develops after the first 24 hours. D. Breast milk jaundice is not the explanation for jaundice appearing within hours of birth.
pearl: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is pathological, often from haemolysis or infection; measure serum bilirubin urgently rather than relying on visual assessment.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Jaundice appears at 8 hours ↓ Onset before 24 hours of age ↓ Likely to be pathological
exam_trap: C, always physiological — neonatal jaundice is very common and usually benign, but physiological jaundice does not appear within the first 24 hours.
takeaway: Jaundice in a baby under 24 hours old is pathological until proven otherwise.

stem: A 2-year-old child is choking and can no longer cough, speak or breathe effectively. What is the appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts
options.B: Give sips of water to help dislodge the object
options.C: Encourage the child to keep trying to cough
options.D: Observe and wait for the ambulance before acting
options.E: Perform a blind finger sweep of the mouth

correct_answer: A. Give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts
why_correct: An ineffective cough with inability to breathe or speak indicates severe airway obstruction requiring immediate choking first aid.
why_wrong: B. Water cannot relieve an airway obstruction and may worsen it. C. Encouraging coughing is appropriate only while the cough is effective; this child's cough is ineffective. D. Severe airway obstruction can rapidly become fatal, so first aid must not be delayed. E. Blind finger sweeps may push the object further into the airway.
pearl: In a choking child over 1 year with an ineffective cough, give up to 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts and repeat; infants under 1 receive chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.
thinking: 2-year-old choking ↓ Cannot cough, speak or breathe effectively ↓ Severe obstruction in a conscious child ↓ Back blows, then abdominal thrusts
exam_trap: C, encourage coughing — this is right while the cough is effective, but once it is ineffective, waiting wastes time and active manoeuvres are needed.
takeaway: Ineffective cough in a choking child means back blows then thrusts.

stem: A child with cystic fibrosis has bulky, greasy stools and poor weight gain. What is the likely explanation?
why_correct: Cystic fibrosis can cause pancreatic insufficiency, leading to malabsorption and steatorrhoea.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome causes proteinuria and oedema. B. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain. C. Pyloric stenosis causes projectile vomiting. E. Lactose intolerance does not explain the characteristic cystic fibrosis presentation.
pearl: Most people with cystic fibrosis have exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, causing fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea; it is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamins.
thinking: Cystic fibrosis ↓ Thick secretions block pancreatic ducts ↓ Fat malabsorption with bulky greasy stools ↓ Pancreatic insufficiency
exam_trap: E, lactose intolerance in every case — it causes diarrhoea in children, but not greasy steatorrhoea with poor growth, and 'in every case' is never right.
takeaway: CF with steatorrhoea and poor growth means pancreatic insufficiency.

stem: A 9-year-old child has suspected cystic fibrosis. Which investigation is commonly used to support the diagnosis?
why_correct: Measurement of sweat chloride is an established diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis.
why_wrong: A. Serum immunoglobulins assess immunodeficiency rather than cystic fibrosis. B. A chest X-ray may show lung changes but does not support the diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. D. Faecal calprotectin assesses intestinal inflammation. E. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is measured for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, not cystic fibrosis.
pearl: The sweat test is the established diagnostic test for cystic fibrosis; most UK cases are now first identified through newborn blood spot screening.
thinking: Suspected cystic fibrosis ↓ Defective CFTR chloride transport ↓ Raised chloride in sweat ↓ Sweat chloride testing
exam_trap: B, chest X-ray — it may show bronchiectatic changes in CF, which tempts, but these are non-specific and cannot establish the diagnosis.
takeaway: Suspected CF: confirm with a sweat chloride test.

stem: A 23-year-old woman asks about contraception and wants a method that also helps protect against sexually transmitted infections. Which method provides this protection?
why_correct: Condoms reduce the risk of transmission of many sexually transmitted infections as well as providing contraception.
why_wrong: A. The combined pill does not protect against STIs. B. The levonorgestrel IUS does not protect against STIs. C. The implant does not protect against STIs. E. Copper IUDs do not protect against STIs.
pearl: Condoms are the only contraceptive method that also reduces STI transmission; combining them with a more effective method gives the best protection against both pregnancy and infection.
thinking: Wants contraception ↓ Also wants STI protection ↓ Only barrier methods reduce transmission ↓ Condoms
exam_trap: B, levonorgestrel IUS — it is highly effective contraception, which tempts, but it offers no protection against STIs.
takeaway: Only condoms give both contraception and STI protection.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has missed her period and has developed nausea and breast tenderness. What is the most appropriate initial test if pregnancy is possible?
why_correct: A pregnancy test is the appropriate initial investigation when pregnancy is possible in a woman with a missed period.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. B. Pelvic CT is not used to diagnose pregnancy and involves radiation exposure. C. Thyroid function tests do not confirm pregnancy. D. D-dimer assesses selected thromboembolic presentations.
pearl: Do a pregnancy test in any woman of reproductive age with a missed period, and before imaging, prescribing or procedures where pregnancy would change management.
thinking: Missed period in a young woman ↓ Nausea and breast tenderness ↓ Pregnancy is possible ↓ Pregnancy test
exam_trap: C, thyroid function tests — thyroid disease can disturb periods, but nausea and breast tenderness point to pregnancy, which must be excluded first with a simple test.
takeaway: Missed period with possible pregnancy: do a pregnancy test first.

stem: A pregnant woman is found to be rhesus D negative. Why may anti-D immunoglobulin be required?

options.A: To treat hyperemesis gravidarum in the first trimester
options.B: To prevent haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
options.C: To reduce the risk of group B streptococcal infection
options.D: To lower the risk of pre-eclampsia in later pregnancy

correct_answer: B. To prevent haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
why_correct: Anti-D immunoglobulin reduces maternal sensitisation to rhesus D antigen and therefore reduces the risk of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D does not treat vomiting in pregnancy. C. Anti-D does not prevent group B streptococcal infection. D. Anti-D does not reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D does not treat iron-deficiency anaemia.
pearl: Anti-D prevents an RhD-negative mother forming anti-D antibodies that could cross the placenta in a later pregnancy and destroy RhD-positive fetal red cells.
thinking: RhD-negative mother ↓ RhD-positive fetal cells may enter her circulation ↓ Sensitisation produces maternal antibodies ↓ Anti-D prevents haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
exam_trap: E, correct iron-deficiency anaemia — anaemia is a common antenatal blood problem, but anti-D does not affect iron or haemoglobin; it only prevents RhD sensitisation.
takeaway: Anti-D protects future babies from haemolytic disease.

stem: A pregnant woman has a significant sensitising event and is known to be rhesus D negative. What is the purpose of giving anti-D immunoglobulin?
why_correct: Anti-D binds fetal rhesus-positive red cells that enter the maternal circulation, reducing the risk of maternal antibody formation.
why_wrong: A. It does not treat iron-deficiency or other maternal anaemia. B. It does not prevent pre-eclampsia. C. It does not treat gestational diabetes. E. It does not directly increase fetal haemoglobin.
pearl: After a potentially sensitising event in an RhD-negative woman, anti-D is given as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours; a Kleihauer test estimates the size of any fetomaternal haemorrhage.
thinking: RhD-negative pregnant woman ↓ Sensitising event lets fetal cells enter her blood ↓ Anti-D clears them before antibodies form ↓ Prevent maternal rhesus sensitisation
exam_trap: E, increase fetal haemoglobin directly — it links anti-D to the fetus, but anti-D acts on the mother's immune response and does not raise fetal haemoglobin.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents maternal sensitisation; it is prophylaxis, not treatment.

stem: A 35-year-old pregnant woman develops sudden vaginal bleeding with severe abdominal pain and becomes hypotensive. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Perform a vaginal examination to assess the cervix
options.B: ABCDE assessment and resuscitation of the mother
options.C: Start continuous CTG monitoring before other steps
options.D: Give oral analgesia and reassess in an hour
options.E: Arrange an ultrasound scan in the antenatal clinic

correct_answer: B. ABCDE assessment and resuscitation of the mother
why_correct: Maternal haemodynamic compromise is an emergency; immediate resuscitation and stabilisation take priority.
why_wrong: A. Vaginal examination does not address maternal shock and may be dangerous if placenta praevia is present. C. Fetal monitoring must not delay maternal resuscitation. D. Oral analgesia and delayed review are unsafe in a hypotensive patient. E. A clinic scan would delay emergency resuscitation.
pearl: In antepartum haemorrhage with shock, resuscitate the mother first with ABCDE, large-bore access and blood; maternal stabilisation is also the best treatment for the fetus.
thinking: Pregnant woman with sudden bleeding and severe pain ↓ Hypotension indicates haemorrhagic shock ↓ Mother's life is the priority ↓ ABCDE assessment and resuscitation
exam_trap: C, continuous CTG monitoring — fetal wellbeing matters, which tempts, but monitoring must never delay resuscitation of a shocked mother.
takeaway: Shocked pregnant woman: resuscitate the mother first.

stem: A 68-year-old man develops sudden severe pain in his calf after walking a long distance. The pain improves after several minutes of rest. There is no swelling or redness. What is the most likely cause?

options.B: Cellulitis of the calf and shin
options.C: Deep vein thrombosis of the calf

why_correct: Predictable exertional calf pain relieved by rest is characteristic of intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease.
why_wrong: A. Septic arthritis affects a joint and causes acute inflammation. B. Cellulitis causes inflammatory skin changes. C. DVT generally causes persistent pain and swelling. E. Achilles rupture causes sudden posterior ankle/calf pain and functional impairment.
pearl: Claudication pain comes on at a predictable walking distance and settles within minutes of rest; the absence of swelling and redness helps exclude DVT and cellulitis.
thinking: Older man with calf pain on walking ↓ Relieved after minutes of rest ↓ No swelling or redness ↓ Peripheral arterial disease
exam_trap: C, deep vein thrombosis of the calf — calf pain in an older man suggests it, but DVT causes persistent pain with swelling and is not relieved by rest.
takeaway: Exertional calf pain eased by rest without swelling: think PAD.

stem: A 58-year-old man has a painless ulcer on his lower leg that has been present for several months. He has chronic ankle swelling and brownish skin around the ulcer. What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A chronic lower-leg ulcer associated with oedema and skin pigmentation is characteristic of venous disease.
why_wrong: A. Arterial ulcers are typically painful and associated with poor perfusion. B. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis. C. DVT is an acute venous thrombotic condition. E. Cellulitis is an acute skin infection.
pearl: Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area with oedema, haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis; check the ankle brachial pressure index before compression to exclude arterial disease.
thinking: Chronic lower-leg ulcer for months ↓ Ankle swelling ↓ Brown haemosiderin pigmentation ↓ Chronic venous insufficiency
exam_trap: A, peripheral arterial disease — it also causes chronic leg ulcers, but arterial ulcers are painful, punched-out and often on the foot, without oedema or pigmentation.
takeaway: Leg ulcer plus oedema plus brown staining is venous.

stem: A 45-year-old woman notices that her fingers become white and then blue when exposed to cold, followed by redness when they warm up. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Episodic colour changes of the fingers triggered by cold are characteristic of Raynaud's phenomenon.
why_wrong: A. An arterial embolus causes acute persistent limb ischaemia. B. Osteoarthritis causes joint pain and stiffness. C. DVT affects veins and usually causes swelling and pain. E. Cellulitis causes local inflammatory skin changes.
pearl: Raynaud's phenomenon gives white, then blue, then red finger colour change on cold exposure; new onset in an adult should prompt a search for secondary causes such as connective tissue disease.
thinking: Episodes triggered by cold exposure ↓ Fingers turn white then blue ↓ Red on rewarming ↓ Raynaud's phenomenon
exam_trap: A, peripheral arterial embolism — it also makes digits pale and ischaemic, but embolism is sudden and persistent, not episodic and triggered by cold.
takeaway: Cold-triggered white-blue-red fingers is Raynaud's phenomenon.

stem: A 64-year-old man with atrial fibrillation suddenly develops severe pain and numbness in one leg. What is a possible cause?
why_correct: Atrial fibrillation can produce cardiac thromboembolism, which may acutely occlude a peripheral artery.
why_wrong: A. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis rather than limb ischaemia. C. Osteoarthritis causes chronic joint symptoms. D. Venous insufficiency does not cause sudden arterial occlusion. E. Cellulitis causes an inflammatory skin infection.
pearl: Acute limb ischaemia presents with the 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, perishing cold and paralysis; it is an emergency needing heparin and urgent vascular review.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation ↓ Atrial thrombus can embolise ↓ Sudden severe leg pain and numbness ↓ Arterial embolism
exam_trap: D, venous insufficiency — it is a common leg problem in older adults, but it is chronic and causes swelling, not sudden painful numb ischaemia.
takeaway: AF plus a sudden painful, numb limb means arterial embolism.

stem: A 17-year-old girl has primary amenorrhoea and is significantly shorter than her peers. Examination shows features suggestive of gonadal dysgenesis. Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Short stature, primary amenorrhoea and gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries) are characteristic of Turner syndrome (45,X).
why_wrong: A. PMOS (formerly PCOS) presents after puberty with irregular periods and androgen excess, not short stature and gonadal dysgenesis. C. Endometriosis causes pelvic pain and subfertility, not primary amenorrhoea with short stature. D. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature and connective-tissue features. E. Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism with anosmia, usually with normal height.
pearl: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature and primary amenorrhoea from streak ovaries, with associations including coarctation of the aorta and bicuspid aortic valve.
thinking: Primary amenorrhoea at 17 ↓ Significantly short stature ↓ Features of gonadal dysgenesis ↓ Turner syndrome
exam_trap: E, Kallmann syndrome — it also causes primary amenorrhoea, but it is hypogonadotrophic with anosmia and usually normal height, without gonadal dysgenesis.
takeaway: Short stature plus primary amenorrhoea: think Turner syndrome.

stem: A 20-year-old man is unusually tall and has long fingers. Several family members have died suddenly from aortic disease. Which inherited disorder should be suspected?
why_correct: Tall stature, long fingers and a family history of aortic disease are characteristic clues to Marfan syndrome.
why_wrong: A. Turner syndrome causes short stature in affected females. B. Huntington disease is a neurodegenerative disorder. C. Cystic fibrosis mainly affects the respiratory and gastrointestinal systems. D. Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadism and impaired smell.
pearl: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 disorder; aortic root dilatation and dissection are the main threats to life, so regular echocardiographic surveillance is essential.
thinking: Tall stature with long fingers ↓ Family deaths from aortic disease ↓ Inherited connective tissue disorder ↓ Marfan syndrome
exam_trap: D, Kallmann syndrome — hypogonadism can produce long limbs, which tempts, but Kallmann syndrome does not cause familial aortic disease.
takeaway: Tall, long fingers and family aortic deaths: Marfan syndrome.

stem: A 26-year-old woman has marked joint hypermobility and recurrent unexplained bruising. Her mother has similar features. Which type of disorder should be considered?
why_correct: Generalised joint hypermobility with easy bruising and a family history suggests an inherited connective tissue disorder.
why_wrong: A. Acute leukaemia can cause bruising but does not explain familial generalised hypermobility. B. Polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis causes joint inflammation rather than hypermobility. D. ITP can cause bruising but does not explain joint hypermobility or a similar family history. E. Scurvy causes bruising and gum disease from dietary deficiency, not inherited hypermobility.
pearl: Joint hypermobility with easy bruising and an affected parent suggests an inherited connective tissue disorder such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
thinking: Marked joint hypermobility ↓ Recurrent unexplained bruising ↓ Mother has similar features ↓ Heritable connective tissue disorder
exam_trap: D, immune thrombocytopenic purpura — it explains unexplained bruising, but not joint hypermobility or the matching family history.
takeaway: Hypermobility plus bruising running in a family suggests a connective tissue disorder.

stem: A couple are found to carry the same autosomal recessive genetic condition. They are considering having another child. What is an appropriate next step?

options.A: Tell them the next child will definitely be unaffected
options.B: Advise them that inheritance cannot be assessed
options.C: Recommend avoiding all medical care during pregnancy
options.E: Tell them the next child will definitely be affected

why_correct: Genetic counselling can explain inheritance, recurrence risks and available reproductive options.
why_wrong: A. The recurrence risk is not zero. B. Mendelian inheritance can be assessed. C. This is inappropriate and unsafe advice. E. The recurrence risk is not 100%.
pearl: When both parents carry the same autosomal recessive condition, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child; genetic counselling covers this and reproductive options such as prenatal testing.
thinking: Both parents carry the same recessive condition ↓ Every pregnancy carries a recurrence risk ↓ They need information on risk and options ↓ Offer genetic counselling
exam_trap: A, next child will definitely be unaffected — it sounds reassuring, but each pregnancy carries the same risk regardless of previous outcomes.
takeaway: Two carriers of a recessive condition: 1 in 4 risk each pregnancy; offer counselling.

stem: A 43-year-old woman has several close relatives who developed breast cancer at young ages. She asks whether she may have an inherited cancer predisposition. What is an appropriate response?

options.A: Reassure her and advise routine NHS breast screening from age 50
options.B: Make a suspected cancer pathway referral to the breast clinic today
options.C: Arrange a CA 15-3 tumour marker test to estimate her inherited risk
options.D: Take a detailed family history and consider genetics referral
options.E: Advise bilateral prophylactic mastectomy as the first management step

correct_answer: D. Take a detailed family history and consider genetics referral
why_correct: A strong pattern of early-onset cancers in close relatives may indicate an inherited cancer predisposition and warrants appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Several close relatives with early-onset breast cancer may warrant assessment beyond routine screening. B. An urgent suspected cancer referral is for symptoms, not asymptomatic family-history concerns. C. Tumour markers are not used to assess inherited cancer risk. E. Risk-reducing surgery is considered only after formal genetic and risk assessment.
pearl: Familial cancer risk is judged by the number of affected relatives, how closely related they are and their age at diagnosis; people with a possible inherited predisposition are referred for genetics assessment.
thinking: Several close relatives affected ↓ Breast cancers at young ages ↓ Pattern suggests inherited predisposition ↓ Detailed family history and consider genetics referral
exam_trap: B, suspected cancer pathway referral — breast cancer worry tempts urgent referral, but she has no symptoms; that pathway is for suspicious findings, not family history.
takeaway: Strong family history without symptoms: take a pedigree and consider genetics referral.

stem: A screening test for a disease returns a positive result in an otherwise asymptomatic patient. What does this result generally mean?

options.A: No further action is needed if the patient is well
options.B: Treatment should start before any confirmatory tests
options.C: The result is most likely a laboratory error
options.D: The patient has the disease and needs treatment

correct_answer: E. Confirmatory diagnostic testing is needed
why_correct: Screening tests identify people who may have a condition; a positive result does not necessarily establish a diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Screening is performed in well people, so a positive result still needs follow-up. B. Treatment should generally follow diagnostic confirmation. C. A positive screening result is not usually a laboratory error, although false positives occur. D. Screening tests can produce false-positive results and do not establish the diagnosis.
pearl: Screening identifies people at higher risk rather than diagnosing disease; positive results need confirmatory diagnostic testing because false positives occur, especially when prevalence is low.
thinking: Asymptomatic person ↓ Positive screening test ↓ Screening identifies risk, not diagnosis ↓ Confirmatory diagnostic testing needed
exam_trap: D, has the disease and needs treatment — a positive result feels conclusive, but screening tests produce false positives and do not establish the diagnosis.
takeaway: A positive screening test leads to a diagnostic test, not straight to treatment.

stem: A pregnant woman has a positive prenatal screening test for a chromosomal condition. What should she be told?

options.A: A termination of pregnancy should be arranged
options.B: It indicates a higher chance but is not a diagnosis
options.C: It confirms that the fetus has the condition
options.D: It is likely a false positive and can be disregarded
options.E: Diagnostic testing is not possible until after birth

correct_answer: B. It indicates a higher chance but is not a diagnosis
why_correct: Prenatal screening estimates the likelihood of a condition; diagnostic testing may be offered when appropriate.
why_wrong: A. A positive screening result does not dictate a particular pregnancy outcome. C. Screening is not diagnostic. D. The result can be clinically important and requires further discussion. E. Diagnostic testing such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis may be offered during pregnancy.
pearl: Prenatal screening gives a chance result; a higher-chance result leads to an offer of further testing, such as NIPT or diagnostic CVS or amniocentesis, and every decision remains the woman's.
thinking: Positive prenatal screening result ↓ Screening estimates likelihood ↓ Diagnosis needs CVS or amniocentesis ↓ Higher chance but not a diagnosis
exam_trap: C, confirms the fetus has the condition — the word 'positive' sounds definitive, but screening only shows a higher chance; only diagnostic testing confirms it.
takeaway: Prenatal screening gives a chance, not a diagnosis.

stem: A 76-year-old man with intestinal obstruction develops worsening constant abdominal pain, fever and increasing tenderness. What serious complication should be suspected?
why_correct: Increasing constant pain, fever and tenderness in an obstructed patient raise concern for compromised bowel blood supply.
why_wrong: A. GORD does not cause bowel obstruction complications. C. Haemorrhoids do not cause this abdominal presentation. D. Functional constipation does not explain systemic deterioration. E. IBS does not cause bowel ischaemia.
pearl: In bowel obstruction, pain turning constant, with fever, tachycardia, peritonism or rising lactate, suggests strangulation or ischaemia and needs urgent surgical review rather than continued conservative care.
thinking: Known intestinal obstruction ↓ Pain becomes constant ↓ Fever and increasing tenderness ↓ Bowel ischaemia
exam_trap: D, functional constipation — it is common in older adults and causes abdominal discomfort, but it cannot explain fever and worsening tenderness.
takeaway: Obstruction with constant pain, fever and tenderness means ischaemia.

stem:
A 30-year-old man has felt persistently low in mood and has lost interest in activities he previously enjoyed. He has poor concentration and disturbed sleep. These symptoms have been present most days for 3 weeks.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Regular diazepam to improve sleep and agitation
options.C: No treatment because symptoms have lasted less than 6 weeks
options.D: CBT or an antidepressant, guided by severity and preference

correct_answer: D. CBT or an antidepressant, guided by severity and preference
why_correct: Persistent depressive symptoms affecting functioning require assessment and treatment. Management depends on severity, risk, preference and previous history.
why_wrong: A. Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for depression. B. Antipsychotics are not routine first-line treatment for uncomplicated depression. C. Treatment should not be withheld simply because symptoms have lasted less than 6 weeks. E. ECT is reserved for selected severe or treatment-resistant cases, particularly where rapid response is needed.
pearl: Depression is managed according to severity, risk and patient preference, with options including psychological therapy such as CBT or an SSRI; suicide risk should always be assessed.
thinking: Low mood and loss of interest most days ↓ Poor concentration and disturbed sleep ↓ More than two weeks indicates a depressive episode ↓ CBT or antidepressant by severity and preference
exam_trap: C, no treatment because under 6 weeks — it sounds cautious, but a depressive episode is diagnosed after two weeks, and treatment should not wait for an arbitrary duration.
takeaway: Depressive episode: treat by severity and preference, and always assess risk.

stem:
A 42-year-old man reports hearing voices speaking about him when nobody is present. He has become socially withdrawn and increasingly suspicious over several months. There is no evidence of substance misuse or an acute medical illness.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent hallucinations and persecutory symptoms with social withdrawal over months are characteristic of schizophrenia.
why_wrong: A. Panic disorder causes recurrent panic attacks, not persistent psychotic symptoms. B. Bipolar disorder requires episodes of mania or hypomania, usually with prominent mood disturbance. C. Adjustment disorder follows an identifiable stressor and does not typically cause persistent psychosis. D. Delirium is acute and associated with impaired attention and fluctuating consciousness.
pearl: Persistent psychotic symptoms such as third-person auditory hallucinations and persecutory ideas, without a substance or organic cause, suggest schizophrenia; refer to early intervention in psychosis services.
thinking: Voices talking about him ↓ Suspicion and social withdrawal over months ↓ No substance misuse or medical cause ↓ Schizophrenia
exam_trap: D, delirium — it also causes hallucinations, but it is acute and fluctuating with impaired attention, unlike this months-long course in clear consciousness.
takeaway: Months of psychotic symptoms in clear consciousness suggests schizophrenia.

stem:
A 19-year-old student has become increasingly withdrawn over the past year. His academic performance has deteriorated and he has stopped seeing friends. His family reports that he has neglected his personal hygiene.

Which feature is particularly characteristic of schizophrenia?
why_correct: Thought insertion is a first-rank psychotic symptom in which a person experiences thoughts as being put into their mind by an external source.
why_wrong: B. Flight of ideas is associated particularly with mania. C. Increased need for sleep is not characteristic of schizophrenia. D. Obsessions are intrusive unwanted thoughts characteristic of OCD. E. Panic attacks are episodes of acute anxiety.
pearl: Schneider's first-rank symptoms include thought insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting, third-person auditory hallucinations, passivity phenomena and delusional perception; they strongly suggest schizophrenia.
thinking: Young man with withdrawal and self-neglect ↓ Suggests negative or prodromal symptoms ↓ Question asks for a characteristic schizophrenic symptom ↓ Thought insertion
exam_trap: B, flight of ideas — it is a formal thought disorder and feels psychotic, but it is typical of mania rather than schizophrenia.
takeaway: Thought insertion is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman is convinced that her neighbours are monitoring her through hidden cameras. She has no evidence to support this belief but remains completely convinced despite reassurance.

What is this symptom called?
why_correct: A fixed false belief that is held despite evidence to the contrary is a delusion.
why_wrong: A. Confabulation involves producing false memories, often unintentionally. C. An obsession is an intrusive, unwanted thought recognised as originating from the person's own mind. D. An illusion is a misinterpretation of a real external stimulus. E. A hallucination is a perception without an external stimulus.
pearl: A delusion is a fixed, false belief held with conviction despite contrary evidence and out of keeping with the person's cultural background; persecutory delusions are the most common type.
thinking: Belief she is watched by neighbours ↓ No supporting evidence ↓ Unshaken by reassurance ↓ Delusion
exam_trap: E, hallucination — psychotic symptoms are often grouped together, but a hallucination is a false perception, whereas this is a false belief.
takeaway: False belief is a delusion; false perception is a hallucination.

stem:
A 26-year-old man with depression says, “My life isn't worth living.” When asked directly, he says he has been thinking about taking an overdose and has tablets at home.

What is the most important immediate priority?

options.A: Reassure him that suicidal thoughts are common
options.B: Ask him to return in 6 months
options.C: Assess and manage his immediate suicide risk

correct_answer: C. Assess and manage his immediate suicide risk
why_correct: Active suicidal thoughts with a specific method and access to means require urgent assessment and appropriate safety measures.
why_wrong: A. Reassurance alone is unsafe. B. Routine long-term follow-up is inappropriate when there is immediate risk. D. Benzodiazepines do not treat the underlying problem and may increase risk in overdose. E. Psychological therapy may be required but does not replace immediate risk management.
pearl: Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk; a specific plan, access to means and hopelessness indicate high risk requiring urgent assessment, safety planning and reducing access to means.
thinking: Depression with life not worth living ↓ Specific plan to overdose ↓ Tablets available at home ↓ Assess and manage immediate suicide risk
exam_trap: E, routine psychological therapy — it may be part of later care, but a routine referral ignores the immediate danger of a plan with available means.
takeaway: A suicide plan with access to means needs urgent risk assessment today.

stem:
A patient with delirium is found to be dehydrated and has recently developed a urinary infection.

What is the most appropriate management principle?

options.A: Reassure the patient that the confusion is imaginary
options.B: Give long-term antipsychotic treatment to all patients
options.C: Keep the patient in a dark room
options.E: Treat the underlying cause and provide supportive care

correct_answer: E. Treat the underlying cause and provide supportive care
why_correct: Delirium management focuses on identifying and treating precipitating factors while providing appropriate environmental and supportive measures.
why_wrong: A. The confusion is a genuine medical syndrome. B. Antipsychotics are not routinely required for all patients. C. A calm, well-lit and orientating environment is preferable. D. Dehydration should be corrected, not worsened.
pearl: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention; manage it by treating causes such as infection, dehydration, drugs, pain, constipation and urinary retention, in a calm, orientating environment.
thinking: Acute confusion ↓ Dehydration and urinary infection ↓ Reversible precipitants identified ↓ Treat the underlying cause and provide supportive care
exam_trap: B, long-term antipsychotic treatment — antipsychotics are sometimes used briefly for severe distress, but they are not routine and do not treat the cause.
takeaway: Delirium: find and treat the cause, and support orientation.

stem:
A 68-year-old man develops a tremor predominantly when his hands are at rest. He also has bradykinesia and a shuffling gait.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rest tremor, bradykinesia and a shuffling gait are characteristic features of Parkinson's disease.
why_wrong: A. Essential tremor is usually an action or postural tremor. B. Cerebellar disease typically causes intention tremor and ataxia. C. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness and wasting rather than this typical movement disorder. E. Huntington's disease is characterised predominantly by choreiform movements and cognitive/psychiatric features.
pearl: Parkinson's disease is diagnosed clinically by bradykinesia with rest tremor, rigidity or both; the tremor is often asymmetrical and pill-rolling, and suspected cases are referred to a specialist before treatment.
thinking: Older man ↓ Tremor mainly at rest ↓ Bradykinesia with shuffling gait ↓ Parkinson's disease
exam_trap: A, essential tremor — it is the commonest tremor in older adults, but it is postural or action-related and does not cause bradykinesia.
takeaway: Rest tremor with bradykinesia is Parkinson's; action tremor suggests essential tremor.

stem:
A 72-year-old man suddenly loses consciousness while standing. He recovers completely within seconds and has no confusion afterwards. He recalls feeling light-headed immediately beforehand.

What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Transient loss of consciousness with a prodrome of light-headedness and rapid complete recovery is typical of syncope.
why_wrong: A. Migraine does not usually cause transient loss of consciousness. B. Seizures may have tonic-clonic activity, tongue biting, incontinence or postictal confusion. C. Stroke does not usually cause brief isolated loss of consciousness with rapid recovery. E. Delirium causes persistent fluctuating confusion.
pearl: Syncope causes brief loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion, usually with a prodrome and rapid full recovery; everyone with transient loss of consciousness needs a 12-lead ECG.
thinking: Sudden loss of consciousness while standing ↓ Light-headed prodrome ↓ Full recovery in seconds without confusion ↓ Syncope
exam_trap: B, epileptic seizure — sudden collapse suggests it, but seizures usually leave postictal confusion, whereas recovery here was rapid and complete.
takeaway: Prodrome and rapid full recovery suggest syncope; postictal confusion suggests seizure.

stem:
A 29-year-old man has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. He is now drowsy and confused.

What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Protect his airway in the recovery position and observe
options.B: Give sweet oral fluids straight away to aid his recovery
options.C: Give buccal midazolam now to prevent a further seizure occurring
options.D: Gently restrain his limbs to prevent further injury occurring
options.E: Insert a bite block to protect his tongue

correct_answer: A. Protect his airway in the recovery position and observe
why_correct: During and immediately after a seizure, priorities are safety, airway support, monitoring and allowing recovery.
why_wrong: B. Food and drink should be withheld until he is fully recovered and able to swallow safely. C. The seizure has stopped after 2 minutes, so emergency rescue medication is not indicated. D. Physical restraint can cause injury. E. Nothing should be placed in the mouth.
pearl: Once a seizure stops, place the person in the recovery position, protect the airway and observe until recovered; emergency benzodiazepines are for seizures lasting 5 minutes or more.
thinking: Tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes ↓ Seizure has stopped ↓ Postictal drowsiness and confusion ↓ Recovery position, protect airway and observe
exam_trap: C, buccal midazolam — rescue medication tempts in any seizure, but it is for prolonged or repeated seizures, not one that has already stopped.
takeaway: Seizure over: recovery position, protect the airway and observe.

stem:
A 58-year-old man develops sudden severe pain and swelling in his right calf after a long-haul flight. He has no chest symptoms.

Which investigation is most appropriate for suspected deep vein thrombosis?

options.A: ECG to look for right heart strain
options.B: Chest X-ray to look for evidence of pulmonary embolism first
options.C: CT pulmonary angiogram as the first-line test to exclude PE
options.D: Contrast venography of the affected leg as the first-line test
options.E: Two-level Wells score to guide D-dimer and leg ultrasound

correct_answer: E. Two-level Wells score to guide D-dimer and leg ultrasound
why_correct: Suspected DVT is assessed using clinical probability, with D-dimer and/or proximal leg vein ultrasound according to the clinical pathway.
why_wrong: A. ECG does not diagnose DVT. B. Chest X-ray does not diagnose DVT or pulmonary embolism. C. CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism, and he has no chest symptoms. D. Contrast venography is not the first-line investigation for suspected DVT.
pearl: For suspected DVT, use the two-level Wells score: if DVT is likely, arrange proximal leg vein ultrasound; if unlikely, request a D-dimer and scan only if it is positive.
thinking: Calf pain and swelling after a long-haul flight ↓ Suspected DVT, no chest symptoms ↓ Clinical probability guides testing ↓ Two-level Wells score to guide D-dimer and ultrasound
exam_trap: C, CT pulmonary angiogram — travel-related thrombosis brings PE to mind, but he has no chest symptoms and CTPA does not image the leg veins.
takeaway: Suspected DVT: Wells score first, then D-dimer or proximal leg ultrasound.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman has painful swelling and redness around one lower leg. She is febrile and the affected area is warm and tender.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Gout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint

why_correct: A hot, painful, erythematous area of skin with systemic features is typical of cellulitis.
why_wrong: A. Gout classically affects a joint, especially the first MTP joint. B. Varicose veins may cause chronic venous symptoms but not typically acute fever and spreading erythema. C. Osteoarthritis causes joint pain and stiffness rather than acute skin inflammation. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes sensory or motor symptoms.
pearl: Cellulitis is usually unilateral; bilateral red legs suggest an alternative such as venous eczema. Mark the margin, treat with antibiotics and escalate if systemically unwell.
thinking: Painful swelling of one lower leg ↓ Red, warm and tender skin ↓ Febrile, suggesting infection ↓ Cellulitis
exam_trap: B, varicose veins — they cause leg discomfort and skin changes, but not acute fever with hot, spreading erythema.
takeaway: Hot, red, tender single leg with fever is cellulitis.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman presents with acute lower back pain after lifting a heavy object. She has no neurological deficit, no bladder or bowel symptoms and no red flags.

What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Regular codeine with paracetamol for several months
options.B: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine within 24 hours
options.C: Strict bed rest for two weeks until pain settles
options.D: Referral for an early spinal surgical opinion
options.E: Advise staying active, with simple analgesia

correct_answer: E. Advise staying active, with simple analgesia
why_correct: Most uncomplicated acute low back pain is managed conservatively, with advice to remain active and appropriate analgesia.
why_wrong: A. Prolonged opioid treatment is not appropriate routine management of acute low back pain. B. Imaging is not routinely required when there are no red flags. C. Prolonged bed rest can delay recovery. D. Surgical referral is not indicated without significant neurological compromise or another serious cause.
pearl: Acute low back pain without red flags is managed with reassurance, advice to stay active and simple analgesia; imaging is not routinely needed.
thinking: Back pain after lifting ↓ No neurological deficit or sphincter symptoms ↓ No red flags ↓ Stay active with simple analgesia
exam_trap: B, urgent MRI of the lumbar spine — it feels thorough, but imaging without red flags does not change management and may reveal incidental findings.
takeaway: Non-specific back pain without red flags: stay active, analgesia, no imaging.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman develops shoulder pain and progressive restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement. There was no significant injury.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Progressive painful restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement is characteristic of adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder).
why_wrong: B. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms in the hand. C. Lateral epicondylitis affects the elbow. D. Olecranon bursitis causes swelling around the elbow. E. Cervical radiculopathy may cause radiating pain and neurological symptoms but does not characteristically restrict passive shoulder movement.
pearl: Frozen shoulder causes painful global restriction of both active and passive movement, especially external rotation; it is more common in diabetes and usually resolves slowly over months to years.
thinking: Shoulder pain without injury ↓ Progressive restriction ↓ Both active and passive movement limited ↓ Frozen shoulder
exam_trap: E, cervical radiculopathy — neck disease can refer pain to the shoulder, but it does not restrict passive shoulder movement.
takeaway: Loss of both active and passive shoulder movement suggests frozen shoulder.

stem:
A 19-year-old man presents with excessive thirst, frequent urination and weight loss. He is vomiting and has abdominal pain. He has a fruity smell to his breath.

What complication of diabetes is most likely?
why_correct: Vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration and fruity breath in a young person with diabetes are characteristic of diabetic ketoacidosis.
why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia causes sweating, tremor and altered consciousness rather than this presentation. C. HHS generally occurs with severe hyperglycaemia and marked dehydration, usually without significant ketoacidosis. D. Peripheral neuropathy is also a chronic complication. E. Nephropathy develops as a chronic complication.
pearl: DKA combines hyperglycaemia or known diabetes, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis; vomiting, abdominal pain and ketotic breath should prompt urgent blood ketone and blood gas testing.
thinking: Young man with thirst, polyuria and weight loss ↓ Vomiting and abdominal pain ↓ Fruity ketotic breath ↓ Diabetic ketoacidosis
exam_trap: C, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — it also causes severe hyperglycaemia and dehydration, but typically in older people with type 2 diabetes, without significant ketosis.
takeaway: Young person with vomiting, abdominal pain and fruity breath: DKA.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with longstanding type 2 diabetes has persistent protein detected on urine testing. His blood pressure is also elevated.

Which chronic complication is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent albuminuria/proteinuria in a patient with longstanding diabetes is suggestive of diabetic kidney disease.
why_wrong: A. Diabetic retinopathy is a different microvascular complication. C. DKA is an acute metabolic emergency. D. Hypoglycaemia is an acute complication of treatment. E. Peripheral arterial embolism is not a typical direct chronic complication of diabetes.
pearl: Diabetic kidney disease is detected by a raised urine albumin to creatinine ratio; an ACE inhibitor or ARB, with blood pressure and glucose control, slows progression.
thinking: Long-standing type 2 diabetes ↓ Persistent proteinuria ↓ Raised blood pressure ↓ Diabetic nephropathy
exam_trap: A, retinal detachment — eye disease is a classic diabetic complication, which tempts, but detachment is not the typical microvascular lesion and does not explain proteinuria.
takeaway: Diabetes with persistent proteinuria and hypertension means nephropathy.

stem:
A 70-year-old man has persistent back pain and is diagnosed with multiple myeloma.

Which blood abnormality is commonly associated with this condition?
why_correct: Myeloma can cause increased bone resorption and hypercalcaemia.
why_wrong: A. Marrow infiltration can cause cytopenias, but isolated severe neutropenia is not the characteristic finding. B. Paraprotein production commonly increases serum protein. C. Inflammatory markers are often raised rather than characteristically low. E. Hypoglycaemia is not a typical feature.
pearl: Myeloma features are summarised as CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions; persistent bone pain in an older adult should prompt protein electrophoresis.
thinking: Older man with persistent back pain ↓ Multiple myeloma ↓ Osteolytic bone resorption releases calcium ↓ Hypercalcaemia
exam_trap: C, low ESR — myeloma is classically linked with the ESR, which tempts, but the paraprotein raises the ESR rather than lowering it.
takeaway: Myeloma is CRAB: calcium high, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions.

stem:
A 56-year-old man notices a painless lump in his neck that has gradually increased in size over several weeks. He has no obvious local infection.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure and arrange review if the lump becomes painful
options.B: Prescribe a 2-week course of oral antibiotics and review
options.C: Prescribe an NSAID and review the lump in 3 months
options.D: Arrange routine ENT review in 6 months

correct_answer: E. Urgent assessment for unexplained lymphadenopathy
why_correct: Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy, particularly in an adult, requires assessment for malignancy and other causes.
why_wrong: A. Painless lymphadenopathy can occur with malignancy, so pain is not required before assessment. B. There is no evidence of infection, and empirical antibiotics could delay diagnosis. C. Anti-inflammatory treatment could delay diagnosis. D. A routine review in 6 months would delay assessment of a progressively enlarging node.
pearl: An enlarging, painless neck lump in an adult needs urgent assessment for lymphoma or head and neck cancer; it should not be attributed to infection without evidence.
thinking: Middle-aged man ↓ Painless neck lump ↓ Enlarging over weeks without infection ↓ Urgent assessment for unexplained lymphadenopathy
exam_trap: B, oral antibiotics — reactive nodes are common, which tempts, but there is no infection and empirical antibiotics only delay diagnosis of malignancy.
takeaway: A painless, enlarging neck lump in an adult needs urgent assessment.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman has intermittent difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids from the beginning. Investigation shows no obvious obstructing lesion.

Which disorder is most consistent with this presentation?
why_correct: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the outset suggests impaired oesophageal motility rather than a progressively narrowing mechanical obstruction.
why_wrong: B. A peptic stricture is an obstructing lesion causing mainly solid-food dysphagia. C. Oesophageal cancer more typically produces progressive solid-food dysphagia and would be seen as an obstructing lesion. D. Gastric outlet obstruction causes vomiting and early satiety. E. Peptic ulcer disease does not typically cause this dysphagia pattern.
pearl: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset suggests a motility disorder such as achalasia; progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids suggests mechanical obstruction from a stricture or cancer.
thinking: Dysphagia to both solids and liquids ↓ Present from the start and intermittent ↓ No obstructing lesion found ↓ Oesophageal motility disorder
exam_trap: C, distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma — dysphagia always raises cancer concern, but it causes progressive solid-food dysphagia and an obstructing lesion would be seen.
takeaway: Solids and liquids from the start: motility; solids then liquids: obstruction.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman has chronic heartburn and develops difficulty swallowing. She has not previously been investigated.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Arrange assessment for an upper GI cause of dysphagia
options.B: Increase her PPI dose and review in 8 weeks
options.C: Test and treat for Helicobacter pylori first
options.D: Reassure her and advise reflux lifestyle measures
options.E: Attribute the dysphagia to reflux and add an alginate

correct_answer: A. Arrange assessment for an upper GI cause of dysphagia
why_correct: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom requiring assessment rather than simple treatment as uncomplicated reflux.
why_wrong: B. Escalating acid suppression without investigation could delay diagnosis of an alarm symptom. C. H. pylori testing does not investigate dysphagia. D. Dysphagia is an alarm symptom requiring investigation rather than reassurance. E. Dysphagia should not be attributed automatically to uncomplicated reflux.
pearl: Dysphagia is an alarm symptom at any age, even in someone with known reflux; it must be investigated rather than treated empirically with acid suppression.
thinking: Chronic heartburn ↓ New difficulty swallowing ↓ Alarm symptom, not uncomplicated reflux ↓ Assess for an upper GI cause of dysphagia
exam_trap: B, increase her PPI dose — reflux can cause a stricture, so treating it seems logical, but escalating treatment without investigation may delay a cancer diagnosis.
takeaway: Dysphagia always needs investigation, never just more PPI.

stem:
A 43-year-old woman has had epigastric discomfort and early satiety for 2 months.

Which additional feature in her history would warrant a suspected cancer pathway referral for upper GI cancer?
why_correct: NICE NG12 (recs 1.2.1 and 1.2.7, amended 2025) recommends a suspected cancer pathway referral for anyone with dysphagia, regardless of age, to assess for oesophageal or stomach cancer. The 2025 update replaced the previous urgent direct-access endoscopy route.
why_wrong: A. Symptoms relieved by antacids suggest acid-related dyspepsia and are not an alarm feature. B. Belching is a non-specific dyspeptic symptom without alarm significance. D. Heartburn after large meals suggests reflux and does not on its own warrant a suspected cancer pathway referral at this age. E. Bloating is a common dyspeptic symptom and is not an alarm feature.
pearl: Dysphagia warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for upper GI cancer at any age, whereas dyspeptic symptoms alone in a younger adult usually do not and are managed in primary care.
thinking: 43-year-old with dyspepsia and early satiety ↓ Uncomplicated dyspepsia does not need urgent referral ↓ Dysphagia is an alarm symptom at any age ↓ Dysphagia
exam_trap: D, heartburn after large meals — it sounds like a significant upper GI symptom, but it is typical reflux and is not an alarm feature at this age.
takeaway: Dysphagia at any age warrants urgent upper GI cancer assessment.

stem:
A 67-year-old man has urinary hesitancy and a weak stream. His symptoms have gradually worsened over several years.

Which symptom is particularly suggestive of bladder outlet obstruction?
why_correct: Hesitancy is a typical voiding symptom associated with bladder outlet obstruction.
why_wrong: A. Haemoptysis is coughing blood. B. Haematemesis is vomiting blood. D. Dysuria with fever suggests urinary tract infection rather than bladder outlet obstruction. E. Photophobia is sensitivity to light.
pearl: Bladder outlet obstruction, often from benign prostatic enlargement, causes voiding symptoms such as hesitancy, weak stream, straining and terminal dribbling; frequency, urgency and nocturia are storage symptoms.
thinking: Older man ↓ Gradually worsening weak stream ↓ Voiding rather than storage symptoms ↓ Urinary hesitancy
exam_trap: D, febrile dysuria — it is a urinary symptom, which tempts, but it points to infection such as prostatitis rather than outlet obstruction.
takeaway: Hesitancy and weak stream are voiding symptoms of outlet obstruction.

stem:
A 36-year-old woman has a screening cervical sample that is reported as positive for high-risk HPV.

What does this result mean?

options.A: She has an active genital herpes infection needing aciclovir
options.B: She has cervical cancer and needs urgent referral to oncology
options.C: She can return to routine screening recall with no further tests
options.D: She needs follow-up for possible cervical cell changes
options.E: She needs a CA-125 test for ovarian cancer

correct_answer: D. She needs follow-up for possible cervical cell changes
why_correct: High-risk HPV is associated with cervical precancerous changes but does not itself mean that cancer is present.
why_wrong: A. HPV and herpes are different viruses. B. HPV positivity does not diagnose cervical cancer. C. HPV-positive results require triage within the screening programme rather than routine recall. E. High-risk HPV is not related to ovarian cancer testing.
pearl: UK cervical screening tests for high-risk HPV first; a positive sample is then examined by cytology, with abnormal cells leading to colposcopy and normal cells to an earlier repeat test.
thinking: Screening sample positive for high-risk HPV ↓ HPV causes most cervical cell changes ↓ Infection is not cancer ↓ Follow-up for possible cell changes
exam_trap: B, cervical cancer needing urgent oncology referral — HPV causes cervical cancer, so it alarms, but a positive test shows infection, not cancer.
takeaway: HPV-positive screening means triage for cell changes, not a cancer diagnosis.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman has a cervical screening result showing abnormal cells. She asks whether this means she has cervical cancer.

What is the most accurate explanation?

options.A: They are caused by a genital herpes infection
options.B: They can be precancerous changes needing follow-up
options.C: They indicate cancer spreading from the ovaries
options.D: They confirm invasive cancer needing treatment
options.E: They usually resolve, so no further follow-up is required

correct_answer: B. They can be precancerous changes needing follow-up
why_correct: Cervical screening is designed to identify HPV-related abnormalities and precancerous changes before invasive cancer develops.
why_wrong: A. Herpes is not the usual cause of cervical screening abnormalities; high-risk HPV is. C. Cervical screening does not diagnose ovarian cancer. D. Most cervical abnormalities are not invasive cancer. E. Some low-grade changes regress, but appropriate follow-up is essential.
pearl: Abnormal cervical cells (dyskaryosis) usually reflect precancerous change (CIN), which colposcopy can assess and treat before cancer develops.
thinking: Abnormal cells on cervical screening ↓ Screening detects precancerous change ↓ Most are not invasive cancer ↓ Precancerous changes needing follow-up
exam_trap: E, usually resolve so no follow-up needed — low-grade changes often regress, which tempts, but follow-up is still needed to catch those that progress.
takeaway: Abnormal cervical cells mean possible precancer needing follow-up, not cancer.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman wants contraception and also wants protection against sexually transmitted infections.

Which method provides both contraception and STI protection?
why_correct: Condoms provide contraception and reduce the transmission of many sexually transmitted infections.
why_wrong: A. The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but does not protect against STIs. B. The progestogen-only pill does not protect against STIs. D. The implant does not protect against STIs. E. The combined pill does not protect against STIs.
pearl: Condoms are the only method listed that reduces STI transmission; using them alongside a highly effective method gives the best protection against pregnancy and infection.
thinking: Wants contraception ↓ Also wants STI protection ↓ Only barrier methods reduce transmission ↓ Condom
exam_trap: A, copper intrauterine device — it is highly effective and hormone-free, which appeals, but it offers no protection against STIs.
takeaway: For contraception plus STI protection, the answer is condoms.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman wants a highly effective long-acting contraceptive method but does not want hormones.

Which option is most appropriate?
why_correct: The copper IUD is a highly effective long-acting, non-hormonal contraceptive method.
why_wrong: A. The implant releases a progestogen. B. The injection is a hormonal contraceptive. D. The combined pill contains hormones and requires daily use. E. The progestogen-only pill contains a hormone and requires regular dosing.
pearl: The copper IUD is the only long-acting reversible contraceptive that is hormone-free; it is also the most effective method of emergency contraception.
thinking: Wants highly effective contraception ↓ Long-acting ↓ Must be hormone-free ↓ Copper intrauterine device
exam_trap: A, contraceptive implant — it is a highly effective long-acting method, but it releases a progestogen, so it fails her non-hormonal requirement.
takeaway: Long-acting and hormone-free contraception: copper IUD.

stem:
A 25-year-old woman has taken the combined oral contraceptive pill correctly but has recently started a medication that she is told may interact with it.

What is the most appropriate general advice?

options.A: Take two pills each day until the end of the current pill packet
options.B: Switch to a desogestrel progestogen-only pill straight away instead
options.C: Stop the pill until the course of the new medication is finished
options.D: Continue as normal, as drug interactions with the pill are rare
options.E: Check the interaction and advise extra contraception if needed

correct_answer: E. Check the interaction and advise extra contraception if needed
why_correct: Contraceptive effectiveness can be affected by some medicines, so the specific interaction should be checked and additional precautions advised where necessary.
why_wrong: A. Doubling doses is not an appropriate strategy. B. A desogestrel progestogen pill may be affected by the same interaction and does not replace checking it. C. Stopping the pill leaves her without contraception. D. Some interactions, such as with enzyme inducers, are clinically important and must be checked.
pearl: Enzyme-inducing drugs such as rifampicin and carbamazepine reduce the effectiveness of the combined pill, whereas most non-enzyme-inducing antibiotics need no extra precautions.
thinking: Correct combined pill use ↓ New medicine with possible interaction ↓ Effect depends on the specific drug ↓ Check interaction and advise extra contraception if needed
exam_trap: D, continue as normal — most antibiotics no longer need extra precautions, which tempts, but enzyme inducers do reduce effectiveness, so the interaction must be checked.
takeaway: Check each drug against the pill; enzyme inducers are the ones that matter.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents with pelvic pain and abnormal vaginal discharge. She is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease.

Why is early treatment important?

options.A: To reduce the long-term risk of cervical cancer
options.B: To prevent the development of bacterial vaginosis
options.C: To reduce the risk of endometriosis developing later
options.D: To prevent complications such as infertility and pelvic pain
options.E: To reduce the risk of ovarian cancer in later life

correct_answer: D. To prevent complications such as infertility and pelvic pain
why_correct: Prompt treatment of PID reduces the risk of reproductive complications, including infertility and chronic pelvic pain.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer is caused by high-risk HPV, not the organisms causing PID. B. Bacterial vaginosis is a separate condition not prevented by PID treatment. C. PID treatment does not prevent endometriosis. E. PID treatment is not given to reduce ovarian cancer risk.
pearl: PID is often caused by chlamydia or gonorrhoea; prompt antibiotics, partner notification and STI screening reduce tubal damage, infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain.
thinking: Pelvic pain with abnormal discharge ↓ Pelvic inflammatory disease ↓ Infection can scar the fallopian tubes ↓ Early treatment prevents infertility and pelvic pain
exam_trap: A, reduce cervical cancer risk — STIs and cervical cancer both relate to sexual health, but cervical cancer is caused by high-risk HPV, not PID organisms.
takeaway: Treat PID early to protect fertility and prevent chronic pain.

stem:
A 72-year-old man develops sudden weakness of his right arm and difficulty speaking. The symptoms began 30 minutes ago.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficits such as unilateral weakness and speech disturbance are characteristic of acute stroke.
why_wrong: B. Migraine can cause neurological symptoms but the sudden focal deficit in this context requires stroke assessment. C. Peripheral neuropathy does not usually cause sudden unilateral arm weakness with aphasia. D. Bell's palsy causes isolated lower motor neurone facial weakness. E. Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke but requires glucose assessment rather than being assumed from this presentation.
pearl: Use FAST in the community and ROSIER in the emergency department to recognise stroke, and always check capillary glucose, because hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke.
thinking: Sudden weakness of the right arm ↓ Speech disturbance ↓ Onset 30 minutes ago in an older man ↓ Acute stroke
exam_trap: E, hypoglycaemia — it is a classic stroke mimic that must be checked, but it is not the most likely diagnosis from a sudden focal deficit alone.
takeaway: Sudden focal deficit is stroke until proven otherwise, but always check glucose.

stem:
A 74-year-old man suddenly develops weakness and numbness affecting the right side of his body. He is also unable to understand spoken language.

Which part of the brain is most likely affected?
why_correct: Right-sided weakness and sensory loss with receptive aphasia indicate a lesion of the left (dominant) cerebral hemisphere, as in a left middle cerebral artery stroke.
why_wrong: A. Spinal cord disease does not cause aphasia. B. Cerebellar disease causes ataxia and incoordination, not hemiparesis with aphasia. D. Neuromuscular junction disorders cause fatigable weakness without sensory loss or aphasia. E. A peripheral nerve lesion causes a restricted deficit in that nerve's territory and no aphasia.
pearl: Hemiparesis and sensory loss with aphasia indicate a cortical lesion of the dominant hemisphere, typically in the left middle cerebral artery territory.
thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness and numbness ↓ Cannot understand spoken language ↓ Aphasia localises to the dominant cortex ↓ Cerebral hemisphere
exam_trap: A, spinal cord — it can cause weakness and sensory loss, but never aphasia, which localises to the cerebral cortex.
takeaway: Hemiparesis plus aphasia localises to the dominant cerebral hemisphere.

stem:
A 65-year-old woman has a brief episode of right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking lasting 15 minutes. She has now completely recovered.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Bell's palsy of the facial nerve

why_correct: A transient focal neurological deficit caused by cerebral ischaemia, with complete recovery, is characteristic of a TIA.
why_wrong: B. Syncope is transient loss of consciousness rather than focal neurological dysfunction. C.
