stem: A 74-year-old woman develops sudden unilateral weakness and speech disturbance. Which feature should prompt immediate assessment for acute stroke?

options.A: Long-standing bilateral knee pain on walking

correct_answer: E. Sudden onset focal neurological deficit
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological impairment is a key warning sign of acute stroke and requires emergency assessment.
why_wrong: A. Long-standing knee pain does not indicate acute neurological disease. B. Gradual high-frequency hearing loss is age-related presbycusis. C. Recurrent heartburn is a gastrointestinal symptom. D. Chronic constipation is not a stroke presentation.
pearl: Any sudden focal neurological deficit, such as face, arm or leg weakness or speech disturbance, is a stroke until proven otherwise and needs emergency assessment.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Sudden unilateral weakness ↓ Speech disturbance ↓ Abrupt focal neurological loss ↓ Sudden onset focal neurological deficit
exam_trap: B, gradual bilateral high-frequency hearing loss — a neurological-sounding symptom, but gradual and bilateral describes age-related presbycusis, not acute stroke.
takeaway: A sudden focal deficit is a stroke until proven otherwise.

stem: A 67-year-old man notices painless blood in his urine on several occasions. There is no dysuria or fever. What diagnosis must be excluded?
why_correct: Unexplained visible haematuria, particularly in an older adult, is an important warning sign of urinary tract malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration: Concentrates urine but does not explain true haematuria. B. Benign prostatic enlargement: Causes lower urinary tract symptoms rather than unexplained visible haematuria as its typical presentation. D. Renal colic: Usually causes severe colicky flank pain. E. Acute cystitis: Usually causes dysuria, frequency and urgency.
pearl: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult is bladder or kidney cancer until proven otherwise and warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral to urology.
thinking: Older man ↓ Recurrent visible haematuria ↓ Painless ↓ No dysuria or fever, so infection unlikely ↓ Urinary tract malignancy
exam_trap: B, benign prostatic enlargement — common in older men and can bleed, but it typically causes urinary symptoms; painless visible haematuria must first exclude cancer.
takeaway: Painless visible haematuria in an older adult: exclude urological cancer.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has increasingly heavy menstrual bleeding and an enlarged irregular uterus. Ultrasound shows several well-defined masses within the uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Heavy menstrual bleeding with an enlarged irregular uterus and discrete uterine masses is characteristic of fibroids.
why_wrong: A. Endometriosis: Causes pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea and subfertility rather than multiple uterine masses. B. Ovarian torsion: Causes acute unilateral pelvic pain. C. Pelvic inflammatory disease: Causes pelvic pain, discharge and cervical motion tenderness. D. Vulvovaginal candidiasis: Causes vulval itching and discharge.
pearl: Fibroids are benign smooth-muscle tumours causing heavy menstrual bleeding, pressure symptoms and an enlarged, irregular uterus; ultrasound confirms them.
thinking: Heavy menstrual bleeding ↓ Enlarged irregular uterus ↓ Several well-defined uterine masses ↓ Benign myometrial tumours ↓ Uterine fibroids
exam_trap: A, endometriosis — a common gynaecological diagnosis at this age, but it presents with pain and subfertility, not discrete uterine masses.
takeaway: Heavy periods with a bulky, irregular uterus: fibroids.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding two years after her last menstrual period. What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Reassure her that this is normal
options.C: Prescribe contraception and review in one year

why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding requires assessment because it can be a presenting symptom of endometrial cancer.
why_wrong: A. Reassure: Postmenopausal bleeding is not considered normal. B. Endometriosis treatment: Is inappropriate for new postmenopausal bleeding. C. Contraception: Does not address the cause. E. Cystitis treatment: Does not explain vaginal bleeding.
pearl: Bleeding a year or more after the last period is postmenopausal bleeding; it needs prompt assessment, usually starting with transvaginal ultrasound, to exclude endometrial cancer.
thinking: Vaginal bleeding ↓ Two years after the last period ↓ Postmenopausal bleeding ↓ Endometrial cancer must be excluded ↓ Investigate the postmenopausal bleeding
exam_trap: A, reassure her that this is normal — irregular bleeding is common around the menopause, but bleeding after a year without periods is never normal.
takeaway: Postmenopausal bleeding always needs investigation.

stem: A 33-year-old woman has irregular menstrual cycles, acne and increased facial hair. Which hormone is commonly associated with the androgen excess seen in PMOS (formerly PCOS)?
why_correct: PMOS (formerly PCOS) is characterised by ovarian androgen excess, and raised testosterone is the main circulating androgen responsible for hirsutism and acne.
why_wrong: A. Erythropoietin stimulates red-cell production. B. Calcitonin is involved in calcium regulation. C. Insulin resistance is common in PMOS (formerly PCOS) and drives ovarian androgen production, but insulin is not itself the androgen. E. Prolactin excess can cause menstrual disturbance but does not explain androgenic features.
pearl: In PMOS (formerly PCOS), raised ovarian androgens, chiefly testosterone, cause hirsutism and acne, while insulin resistance helps drive the androgen excess.
thinking: Irregular cycles ↓ Acne and facial hair = hyperandrogenism ↓ Ovarian androgen excess in PMOS (formerly PCOS) ↓ Main circulating androgen ↓ Testosterone
exam_trap: C, insulin — insulin resistance is central to PMOS (formerly PCOS) and drives androgen production, but insulin is not an androgen; testosterone causes the features.
takeaway: Hirsutism and acne in PMOS (formerly PCOS) reflect raised testosterone.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has irregular periods, hot flushes and night sweats. Her symptoms have become increasingly frequent over the past year. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Irregular menstrual cycles accompanied by vasomotor symptoms such as hot flushes and night sweats are typical of the perimenopausal transition.
why_wrong: A. Ectopic pregnancy: Requires pregnancy and usually causes pain and/or vaginal bleeding. C. Ovarian torsion: Causes acute severe unilateral pelvic pain. D. Vulvovaginal candidiasis: Causes vulval itching and abnormal discharge. E. Acute pelvic inflammatory disease: Causes pelvic pain, fever and abnormal discharge.
pearl: Perimenopause is usually diagnosed clinically from vasomotor symptoms and a change in the menstrual cycle; in a woman younger than the usual menopausal age, as here, an FSH test may be considered to support the diagnosis.
thinking: Woman in her forties ↓ Irregular periods ↓ Hot flushes and night sweats ↓ Vasomotor symptoms increasing over a year ↓ Perimenopause
exam_trap: A, ectopic pregnancy — irregular periods prompt thoughts of pregnancy, but ectopic presents with pain or bleeding, not a year of hot flushes and night sweats.
takeaway: Irregular cycles plus hot flushes and night sweats in the forties: perimenopause.

stem:
A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of dysuria and urinary frequency. She has no vaginal discharge, flank pain or fever. Urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leukocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Dysuria and frequency without systemic illness or upper urinary tract symptoms are typical of acute cystitis.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes severe intermittent flank pain rather than isolated dysuria and frequency. B. Pyelonephritis usually causes fever, flank pain and systemic illness. D. PID usually causes pelvic/lower abdominal pain and may have abnormal vaginal discharge. E. Urethritis is commonly associated with sexually transmitted infection and may cause urethral discharge.
pearl: Lower UTI presents with dysuria and frequency without fever or loin pain; positive nitrites and leucocytes on dipstick support the diagnosis.
thinking: Dysuria and frequency ↓ No fever or flank pain ↓ No vaginal discharge ↓ Nitrites and leucocytes positive ↓ Acute cystitis
exam_trap: E, urethritis — dysuria fits, but urethritis is typically STI-related with discharge, whereas nitrite-positive urine without discharge points to bacterial cystitis.
takeaway: Dysuria, frequency and positive nitrites without systemic upset: cystitis.

stem:
A 29-year-old man develops profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting 24 hours after several people at a wedding became unwell.

Which mode of transmission is most likely?
why_correct: Acute outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea are commonly caused by organisms spread through contaminated food, water or hands via the faeco-oral route.
why_wrong: A. Vector-borne infections are transmitted by organisms such as mosquitoes or ticks. B. Sexual transmission is relevant to infections such as gonorrhoea and HIV. C. Vertical transmission occurs from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding. E. Blood-borne infections include hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
pearl: Outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea after a shared event point to food-borne or person-to-person faeco-oral spread; suspected food poisoning is notifiable.
thinking: Profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting ↓ Onset within a day ↓ Several wedding guests affected ↓ Common source: shared food or close contact ↓ Faeco-oral transmission
exam_trap: A, vector-borne transmission — a cluster at one event suggests a shared exposure, but vector-borne infections do not cause rapid outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea.
takeaway: Clustered vomiting and diarrhoea after a shared meal: faeco-oral spread.

stem:
A 42-year-old man develops jaundice and dark urine. Blood tests show a markedly raised ALT and AST with only a modest increase in alkaline phosphatase.

Which pattern of liver injury is present?
why_correct: Predominant elevation of ALT and AST indicates hepatocellular injury.
why_wrong: A. Synthetic dysfunction is assessed using markers such as INR and albumin. B. Renal disease does not produce this characteristic liver enzyme pattern. D. Cholestatic injury predominantly raises alkaline phosphatase and GGT. E. Haemolysis causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia rather than a transaminase-predominant pattern.
pearl: Read LFTs by pattern: transaminases rising out of proportion to ALP mean hepatocellular injury, as in viral, drug-induced, alcoholic or ischaemic hepatitis.
thinking: Jaundice and dark urine ↓ Liver enzymes abnormal ↓ ALT and AST markedly raised ↓ ALP only modestly raised ↓ Hepatocellular
exam_trap: D, cholestatic — jaundice with dark urine tempts it, but cholestasis is ALP- and GGT-predominant; here the transaminases dominate.
takeaway: Transaminase-predominant LFTs mean hepatocellular injury; ALP-predominant mean cholestasis.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman has persistently raised alkaline phosphatase. ALT is only mildly elevated. She has no symptoms.

Which additional blood test is most useful to establish whether the alkaline phosphatase is of hepatobiliary origin?
why_correct: A raised GGT alongside alkaline phosphatase supports a hepatobiliary source.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin and iron studies assess iron status; ferritin is also an acute-phase reactant. B. CK is mainly used to assess muscle injury. C. Amylase and lipase are associated with pancreatic injury. D. Vitamin D is relevant to bone causes of a raised ALP but does not establish a hepatobiliary origin.
pearl: ALP comes mainly from liver and bone; a raised GGT alongside it supports a hepatobiliary source, while a normal GGT points towards bone.
thinking: Persistently raised ALP ↓ ALP can be hepatic or bony in origin ↓ Need a marker specific to the biliary tree ↓ GGT rises with hepatobiliary ALP ↓ Gamma-glutamyl transferase
exam_trap: D, serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D — relevant if bone disease is the cause, but it cannot confirm a hepatobiliary origin; GGT can.
takeaway: Raised ALP: check GGT to separate liver from bone.

stem:
A 71-year-old man is found to have a low serum sodium concentration. He is clinically euvolaemic. His serum osmolality is low and urine osmolality is inappropriately high.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine is characteristic of SIADH.
why_wrong: A. Dehydration usually produces clinical signs of volume depletion. B. HHS causes marked hyperglycaemia and increased plasma osmolality. C. Diabetes insipidus causes excessive free-water loss and typically hypernatraemia. D. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia.
pearl: SIADH is euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine; exclude hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diuretics first.
thinking: Low sodium ↓ Clinically euvolaemic ↓ Low serum osmolality ↓ Urine inappropriately concentrated ↓ SIADH
exam_trap: C, diabetes insipidus — the other ADH disorder, but DI loses free water, giving dilute urine and usually high sodium, the reverse of this picture.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine: SIADH.

stem:
A patient with severe vomiting has a serum potassium concentration of 2.7 mmol/L.

Which ECG abnormality is most associated with hypokalaemia?

options.B: Widened QRS complexes as the characteristic early finding

why_correct: Hypokalaemia can produce flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves.
why_wrong: A. Delta waves indicate ventricular pre-excitation, as in WPW syndrome. B. Markedly widened QRS complexes are more characteristic of severe hyperkalaemia. D. Complete heart block is not the typical ECG finding of hypokalaemia. E. ST elevation suggests acute myocardial injury or other causes such as pericarditis.
pearl: Hypokalaemia on ECG causes flattened T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves; correct potassium and check magnesium, as low magnesium hinders correction.
thinking: Severe vomiting ↓ Potassium loss ↓ Low serum potassium ↓ Delayed ventricular repolarisation ↓ Prominent U waves
exam_trap: B, widened QRS complexes — QRS widening is a classic potassium-related ECG change, but it belongs to severe hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia.
takeaway: Low potassium: flat T waves and U waves. High potassium: peaked T waves and wide QRS.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has a serum potassium concentration of 6.8 mmol/L. ECG shows tall, peaked T waves.

What is the immediate treatment that stabilises the cardiac membrane?
why_correct: In significant hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, intravenous calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane and reduces the immediate risk of arrhythmia.
why_wrong: A. Furosemide may increase potassium excretion but does not immediately stabilise the myocardium. C. Sodium bicarbonate is not routinely required for every case of hyperkalaemia. D. Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly but does not directly stabilise the cardiac membrane. E. Potassium would worsen hyperkalaemia.
pearl: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, give IV calcium first to protect the heart, then insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells, then remove potassium from the body.
thinking: Markedly raised potassium ↓ Tall peaked T waves on ECG ↓ Risk of arrhythmia ↓ Myocardium needs immediate protection ↓ Intravenous calcium gluconate
exam_trap: D, insulin alone — insulin with glucose lowers serum potassium quickly, but it shifts potassium rather than stabilising the cardiac membrane.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first, then shift and remove potassium.

stem:
A 73-year-old woman becomes confused after starting a new medication. Her sodium is 121 mmol/L and she is euvolaemic.

Which drug is a recognised cause of SIADH?
why_correct: Carbamazepine is a recognised cause of SIADH and can produce significant hyponatraemia.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol is not a typical cause of SIADH. B. Amoxicillin is not a typical cause of SIADH. C. Thyroxine is not a cause of SIADH. E. Allopurinol is not a recognised cause of SIADH.
pearl: Drug causes of SIADH include carbamazepine, SSRIs, tricyclics, antipsychotics and some chemotherapy; check sodium in older patients who become confused after starting them.
thinking: New medication ↓ Confusion with hyponatraemia ↓ Euvolaemic ↓ Pattern of drug-induced SIADH ↓ Carbamazepine
exam_trap: C, thyroxine — hypothyroidism can cause hyponatraemia, which makes thyroid drugs feel linked, but thyroxine treats that cause rather than causing SIADH.
takeaway: Carbamazepine is a classic drug cause of SIADH and hyponatraemia.

stem:
A 64-year-old man with chronic kidney disease develops metabolic acidosis.

Which blood gas finding is most likely?

options.D: Reduced hydrogen ion concentration with alkalosis

why_correct: Metabolic acidosis is characterised by a primary reduction in bicarbonate.
why_wrong: B. Metabolic acidosis lowers pH unless fully compensated. C. Base excess is reduced in metabolic acidosis. D. This describes alkalosis rather than acidosis. E. Increased bicarbonate is associated with metabolic alkalosis or compensation for respiratory acidosis.
pearl: Metabolic acidosis is a primary fall in bicarbonate with a low pH and negative base excess; CKD causes it through reduced renal acid excretion.
thinking: Chronic kidney disease ↓ Kidneys fail to excrete acid ↓ Bicarbonate consumed by buffering ↓ Primary metabolic acidosis ↓ Reduced bicarbonate
exam_trap: E, increased bicarbonate — raised bicarbonate appears in compensated respiratory acidosis, but a primary metabolic acidosis lowers bicarbonate.
takeaway: Metabolic acidosis: low pH, low bicarbonate, negative base excess.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Her blood film shows small, pale red cells.

Which term describes these red cells?
why_correct: Small red cells with reduced haemoglobin content appear microcytic and hypochromic.
why_wrong: A. Target cells have a characteristic bull's-eye appearance. B. Fragmented red cells are schistocytes. D. Macrocytic cells are larger than normal. E. Spherocytes are round red cells lacking the normal central pallor.
pearl: Small, pale red cells are microcytic and hypochromic; in a young woman the commonest cause is iron deficiency, so check ferritin and ask about menstrual loss.
thinking: Fatigue and pallor ↓ Small red cells = microcytic ↓ Pale red cells = hypochromic ↓ Reduced haemoglobin content ↓ Microcytic hypochromic
exam_trap: E, spherocytic — spherocytes look small, but they are dense and lack central pallor rather than pale; small and pale means microcytic hypochromic.
takeaway: Small, pale red cells: microcytic hypochromic, usually iron deficiency.

stem: A 44-year-old woman develops bloating and diarrhoea after drinking milk. Which enzyme deficiency causes lactose intolerance?
why_correct: Lactase breaks down lactose into glucose and galactose in the small intestine.
why_wrong: A. Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach. B. Trypsin is a pancreatic protease. C. Amylase digests starch. E. Lipase digests fats.
pearl: Brush-border lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose; without it, undigested lactose is fermented in the colon, causing bloating and diarrhoea.
thinking: Bloating and diarrhoea after milk ↓ Milk sugar is lactose ↓ Needs a brush-border enzyme to be digested ↓ Deficiency leaves lactose unabsorbed ↓ Lactase
exam_trap: C, amylase — a carbohydrate-digesting enzyme, so it seems plausible, but amylase breaks down starch; lactose needs lactase.
takeaway: Lactose intolerance is lactase deficiency.

stem:
A 4-year-old child suddenly develops coughing and choking while eating peanuts. He remains conscious and is coughing forcefully.

What should you advise him to do?
correct_answer: B. Encourage him to keep coughing
why_correct: An effective cough can expel a foreign body. The child should be encouraged to continue coughing while being closely observed.
why_wrong: A. Abdominal thrusts are used when a person has an ineffective cough and severe airway obstruction. C. Chest compressions are used if the patient becomes unresponsive and is not breathing normally. D. Giving water does not treat airway obstruction. E. Lying flat is inappropriate and may worsen the situation.
pearl: A choking child with an effective cough should be encouraged to cough and watched closely; if the cough becomes ineffective, give back blows, then abdominal thrusts in a child over one year.
thinking: Child choking on peanuts ↓ Conscious ↓ Coughing forcefully = effective cough ↓ Coughing is the best clearance mechanism ↓ Encourage him to keep coughing
exam_trap: A, perform abdominal thrusts immediately — feels decisive, but thrusts are for an ineffective cough; with a strong cough, intervention can cause harm.
takeaway: Effective cough: encourage coughing. Ineffective cough: back blows then thrusts.

stem:
A 61-year-old man with COPD is receiving oxygen during an acute exacerbation. His oxygen saturation target is specified by the clinical team as 88–92%.

Why is controlled oxygen therapy important in some patients with COPD?

options.A: High-concentration oxygen rapidly causes lung fibrosis
options.B: Oxygen increases the risk of venous thromboembolism
options.C: Excessive oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention
options.D: Oxygen triggers bronchospasm in reactive airways
options.E: High-flow oxygen tends to cause respiratory alkalosis

correct_answer: C. Excessive oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention
why_correct: Some patients with severe COPD are vulnerable to worsening hypercapnia during uncontrolled oxygen administration, so controlled oxygen therapy may be required.
why_wrong: A. Short-term oxygen therapy does not cause pulmonary fibrosis. B. Oxygen does not increase the risk of venous thromboembolism. D. Oxygen does not trigger bronchospasm. E. Excess oxygen in susceptible COPD patients tends to cause respiratory acidosis, not alkalosis.
pearl: In COPD patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, give controlled oxygen, for example via a Venturi mask, to the target range and check an arterial blood gas.
thinking: COPD exacerbation ↓ Some patients are prone to hypercapnia ↓ Uncontrolled oxygen raises CO2 further ↓ Risk of respiratory acidosis ↓ Excessive oxygen can worsen carbon dioxide retention
exam_trap: E, high-flow oxygen tends to cause respiratory alkalosis — it names the right system, but CO2 retention causes respiratory acidosis, not alkalosis.
takeaway: At-risk COPD: titrate oxygen to the target range to avoid worsening hypercapnia.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman develops intensely itchy lesions that appear within minutes and disappear from one area before appearing elsewhere. Individual lesions last less than 24 hours.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Transient, migratory, itchy wheals that resolve within 24 hours are characteristic of urticaria.
why_wrong: A. Psoriatic plaques persist and are scaly. C. Eczema herpeticum causes painful grouped vesicles and systemic illness. D. Cellulitis causes persistent painful erythema. E. Scabies causes persistent intense itching, often worse at night, with characteristic distribution.
pearl: Urticarial wheals are itchy and each fades within 24 hours without marking; lesions lasting longer or leaving bruising suggest urticarial vasculitis. Non-sedating antihistamines are first line.
thinking: Intensely itchy lesions ↓ Appear within minutes ↓ Move from one area to another ↓ Each lasts under 24 hours ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: E, scabies — intense itch tempts it, but scabies lesions persist, often with burrows in typical sites; transient, migratory wheals are urticaria.
takeaway: Itchy wheals that come and go within 24 hours: urticaria.

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on the side of his tongue that has persisted for 4 weeks. He is a smoker.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Urgent assessment for possible oral cancer
options.C: Start antifungal treatment without further assessment
options.D: Reassure and review in one year

correct_answer: A. Urgent assessment for possible oral cancer
why_correct: A persistent unexplained oral ulcer, particularly in a person with risk factors such as smoking, requires assessment for malignancy.
why_wrong: B. Antihistamines do not treat a persistent ulcer of this type. C. Empirical antifungal treatment should not delay assessment of a suspicious persistent lesion. D. Persistent unexplained oral ulcers should not simply be observed for a year. E. Hydration does not address the underlying concern.
pearl: An unexplained oral ulcer persisting beyond about three weeks needs urgent suspected cancer assessment, particularly in smokers; the lateral tongue is a typical site.
thinking: Smoker ↓ Painless ulcer on the side of the tongue ↓ Persisting for 4 weeks ↓ Persistent unexplained oral ulcer = red flag ↓ Urgent assessment for possible oral cancer
exam_trap: C, start antifungal treatment — empirical treatment seems reasonable, but it delays assessment of a persistent ulcer in a smoker, which must be assessed urgently.
takeaway: A persistent unexplained oral ulcer in a smoker needs urgent cancer assessment.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman reports a new breast lump. Examination confirms a discrete, persistent lump.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Review in 6 weeks, after her next menstrual period
options.B: Prescribe antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
options.C: Reassure because most breast lumps are benign
options.D: Refer on the suspected breast cancer pathway
options.E: Arrange a routine NHS breast screening mammogram

correct_answer: D. Refer on the suspected breast cancer pathway
why_correct: A new unexplained breast lump requires appropriate breast assessment, even though many breast lumps are benign.
why_wrong: A. Delaying review is inappropriate for a discrete persistent lump in a woman of this age. B. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. C. The possibility of benign disease does not remove the need for assessment. E. Screening mammography is not the route for assessing a symptomatic breast lump.
pearl: A discrete, persistent breast lump in an adult woman should be referred on the suspected breast cancer pathway for triple assessment: examination, imaging and biopsy.
thinking: Woman in her forties ↓ New breast lump ↓ Discrete and persistent on examination ↓ Cancer must be excluded ↓ Refer on the suspected breast cancer pathway
exam_trap: A, review in 6 weeks after her next period — sometimes used for cyclical lumpiness in younger women, but a discrete persistent lump at this age needs referral now.
takeaway: Discrete breast lump in an adult woman: suspected cancer referral and triple assessment.

stem:
A 59-year-old man notices a new, painless lump in his neck that has persisted for 5 weeks. He has no obvious recent infection.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Review if the lump becomes painful or grows
options.B: Reassure, as painless nodes are usually reactive
options.C: Re-examine the neck at a routine review in 6 months
options.D: Urgent assessment of persistent unexplained neck nodes
options.E: Prescribe a 2-week antibiotic course and review

correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment of persistent unexplained neck nodes
why_correct: Persistent unexplained cervical lymphadenopathy in an adult requires assessment for potentially serious causes, including malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Pain is not required for clinically significant lymphadenopathy. B. Persistent painless lymphadenopathy can occur with malignancy. C. A persistent unexplained node should not be left for months without assessment. E. Empirical antibiotics without evidence of infection are inappropriate and could delay diagnosis.
pearl: A persistent, unexplained neck lump in an adult, with no infective cause, needs urgent assessment for head and neck cancer or lymphoma.
thinking: Man in his fifties ↓ New painless neck lump ↓ Persisting for 5 weeks ↓ No infective cause ↓ Urgent assessment of persistent unexplained neck nodes
exam_trap: E, a 2-week antibiotic course — feels like a sensible trial, but there is no infection and delay risks missing malignancy; persistent nodes need urgent assessment.
takeaway: Persistent unexplained neck lump in an adult: urgent assessment, not antibiotics.

stem:
A 74-year-old man becomes dizzy when standing after starting treatment for hypertension. His blood pressure falls significantly on standing.

Which drug is particularly associated with postural hypotension?
why_correct: Alpha-1 blockers such as doxazosin can cause postural hypotension, particularly when treatment is initiated.
why_wrong: B. Paracetamol does not characteristically cause postural hypotension. C. Metformin does not characteristically cause orthostatic hypotension. D. Amoxicillin is not a typical cause. E. Omeprazole is not a typical cause.
pearl: Alpha-blockers such as doxazosin cause first-dose and postural hypotension, so they are started at a low dose; warn older patients about dizziness on standing.
thinking: New antihypertensive treatment ↓ Dizziness on standing ↓ Significant postural BP fall ↓ Alpha-1 blockade causes vasodilatation ↓ Doxazosin
exam_trap: C, metformin — commonly prescribed in older adults with cardiovascular risk, but it does not lower blood pressure or cause postural hypotension.
takeaway: Alpha-blockers such as doxazosin are a classic cause of postural hypotension.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman taking warfarin develops an unexpectedly high INR after starting an antibiotic.

Which antibiotic is particularly associated with increasing the anticoagulant effect of warfarin?
why_correct: Metronidazole can significantly increase the anticoagulant effect of warfarin, increasing the INR and bleeding risk.
why_wrong: A. Nitrofurantoin is not the characteristic answer. B. Flucloxacillin is not the classic interaction tested here. C. Phenoxymethylpenicillin is not a classic major warfarin interaction. E. Topical fusidic acid has minimal systemic exposure.
pearl: Metronidazole inhibits warfarin metabolism and can sharply raise the INR; monitor the INR closely when any antibiotic is started in a patient on warfarin.
thinking: Patient on warfarin ↓ New antibiotic ↓ INR unexpectedly high ↓ Enzyme inhibition reduces warfarin clearance ↓ Metronidazole
exam_trap: B, flucloxacillin — a commonly prescribed antibiotic, but it is not the classic warfarin potentiator; metronidazole markedly raises the INR.
takeaway: Warfarin plus metronidazole: expect a rising INR and monitor closely.

stem:
A woman taking the combined oral contraceptive pill asks whether it protects against sexually transmitted infections.

What is the correct advice?

options.A: It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections
options.B: It reduces viral STIs but not bacterial infections
options.C: It protects against HIV but not other infections
options.D: It gives protection against STIs similar to condoms
options.E: It protects against gonorrhoea but not chlamydia

correct_answer: A. It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections
why_correct: Combined hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy but does not provide STI protection.
why_wrong: B. It does not protect against viral STIs. C. It does not provide protection against HIV. D. Condoms provide a degree of protection against many STIs; the combined pill does not. E. It does not specifically protect against gonorrhoea or chlamydia.
pearl: Hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy but gives no STI protection; advise condoms for STI protection, especially with new or multiple partners.
thinking: Combined pill user ↓ The pill works hormonally to prevent ovulation ↓ No barrier to pathogens ↓ No STI protection ↓ It does not protect against sexually transmitted infections
exam_trap: D, protection similar to condoms — both are contraceptives so they seem equivalent, but only barrier methods reduce STI transmission.
takeaway: The pill prevents pregnancy, not STIs: use condoms as well.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman has missed two consecutive periods. She is sexually active and uses no contraception.

What should be excluded first?
why_correct: Pregnancy is the commonest cause of secondary amenorrhoea and must be excluded first, with a pregnancy test, in any sexually active woman of reproductive age.
why_wrong: B. Thyroid disease can cause menstrual disturbance but is not the first exclusion. C. PMOS (formerly PCOS) can cause oligomenorrhoea, but pregnancy must be excluded first. D. Menopause is unlikely at 32 and would be considered only after pregnancy is excluded. E. Prolactinoma can cause amenorrhoea but pregnancy must be excluded first.
pearl: Always exclude pregnancy first in secondary amenorrhoea in a sexually active woman of reproductive age, before investigating thyroid, prolactin or ovarian causes.
thinking: Woman of reproductive age ↓ Two missed periods ↓ Sexually active ↓ No contraception ↓ Pregnancy
exam_trap: C, PMOS (formerly PCOS) — a common cause of irregular periods at this age, but pregnancy is commoner and must be excluded first with a pregnancy test.
takeaway: Secondary amenorrhoea: do a pregnancy test first.

stem:
A 23-year-old man presents with urethral discharge and dysuria. A sexually transmitted infection is suspected.

Which organism is a common cause of urethritis?
why_correct: Chlamydia is a common cause of sexually transmitted urethritis.
why_wrong: A. C. difficile causes antibiotic-associated diarrhoea. B. H. pylori is associated with gastric disease. C. Candida commonly causes mucosal fungal infection rather than typical STI-associated urethritis. E. Giardia causes gastrointestinal infection.
pearl: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea are the key causes of urethritis; refer to sexual health for NAAT testing, treatment, partner notification and screening for other STIs.
thinking: Young man ↓ Urethral discharge and dysuria ↓ Suspected STI ↓ Common sexually transmitted cause of urethritis ↓ Chlamydia trachomatis
exam_trap: C, Candida albicans — it causes genital infection, but candida typically causes balanitis and itch rather than sexually transmitted urethritis with discharge.
takeaway: Urethritis with discharge: think chlamydia and gonorrhoea.

stem:
A 29-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on his penis. He has no fever and no significant pain.

Which sexually transmitted infection should be considered?
why_correct: A painless genital ulcer is characteristic of primary syphilis.
why_wrong: A. Genital herpes typically causes painful vesicles or ulcers. B. Genital warts produce papillary lesions rather than ulcers. C. Bacterial vaginosis is a vaginal condition and does not cause a penile ulcer. E. Candidiasis does not typically cause a painless genital ulcer.
pearl: A painless genital ulcer is primary syphilis until proven otherwise; the chancre heals on its own, so untreated infection can silently progress to later stages.
thinking: Young man with a penile ulcer ↓ Ulcer is painless, unlike herpes ↓ No fever or systemic illness ↓ Painless genital ulcer = chancre ↓ Syphilis
exam_trap: A, genital herpes — the commonest cause of genital ulceration, but herpetic lesions are painful; a painless ulcer points to syphilis.
takeaway: Painless genital ulcer: syphilis. Painful: herpes.

stem:
A 76-year-old man develops urinary retention. Examination suggests significant prostatic enlargement.

Which symptom is most characteristic of bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic enlargement?
why_correct: Hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency and incomplete emptying are typical lower urinary tract symptoms associated with bladder outlet obstruction from BPE.
why_wrong: A. Polyuria and polydipsia suggest disorders such as diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus. B. Severe loin pain suggests renal or ureteric pathology. D. Faecal urgency is a gastrointestinal symptom. E. Haemoptysis is a respiratory symptom.
pearl: Benign prostatic enlargement causes voiding symptoms such as hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency and incomplete emptying, and can progress to urinary retention.
thinking: Older man ↓ Urinary retention ↓ Enlarged prostate ↓ Bladder outlet obstruction ↓ Weak urinary stream
exam_trap: A, polyuria with polydipsia — urinary symptoms in an older man tempt it, but that pair points to diabetes; outlet obstruction gives voiding symptoms like a weak stream.
takeaway: Bladder outlet obstruction: hesitancy, weak stream and incomplete emptying.

stem:
A 48-year-old man with long-standing reflux develops progressive difficulty swallowing solid food.

Which symptom is considered an alarm feature requiring further assessment?

options.A: Early satiety after a large meal only

why_correct: Progressive dysphagia is an alarm feature that requires investigation for significant oesophageal pathology, including malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Early satiety after a large meal alone is not equivalent to progressive dysphagia. C. Belching is common and nonspecific. D. Intermittent hiccups are usually nonspecific. E. Mild bloating is nonspecific.
pearl: Dysphagia is a red flag for oesophageal cancer and warrants urgent upper GI endoscopy; long-standing reflux adds risk through Barrett's oesophagus.
thinking: Long-standing reflux ↓ Difficulty swallowing solids ↓ Progressive course ↓ Suggests structural narrowing ↓ Progressive dysphagia
exam_trap: A, early satiety after a large meal only — early satiety can be a warning sign, but after a large meal it is normal; progressive dysphagia is the alarm feature.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia is an alarm symptom: urgent endoscopy.

stem:
A 35-year-old man has recurrent epigastric discomfort that improves after eating. He frequently uses ibuprofen for headaches.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Epigastric pain that may improve temporarily with food is a classic presentation of duodenal ulcer disease, with NSAID use being an important risk factor.
why_wrong: B. Biliary colic typically causes right upper quadrant or epigastric pain after meals. C. Crohn's disease usually causes chronic gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea and abdominal pain. D. Appendicitis causes acute progressive abdominal pain. E. Renal colic causes severe flank pain radiating to the groin.
pearl: Duodenal ulcer pain is classically epigastric, eased by eating and may wake the patient at night; H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes.
thinking: Recurrent epigastric discomfort ↓ Improves after eating ↓ Frequent ibuprofen use ↓ NSAID-related peptic ulcer ↓ Duodenal ulcer
exam_trap: B, biliary colic — it also causes epigastric pain, but biliary pain is brought on after meals; pain relieved by food points to a duodenal ulcer.
takeaway: Epigastric pain eased by food, plus NSAIDs: duodenal ulcer.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman develops painful swelling of a single joint over several hours. The joint is hot and she has a temperature of 38.5°C.

What diagnosis must be excluded urgently?
why_correct: An acutely hot, swollen, painful joint with fever should be treated as possible septic arthritis until excluded.
why_wrong: A. Osteoarthritis usually causes chronic mechanical joint pain. B. Reactive arthritis can cause an inflamed joint but is not the diagnosis that must be urgently excluded in a febrile hot joint. C. Tendinopathy causes local tendon pain rather than a hot swollen joint with fever. E. Osteoporosis usually causes no symptoms until a fracture occurs and does not fit a 29-year-old with a hot joint.
pearl: A hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise; aspirate for Gram stain and culture before antibiotics, provided this does not delay treatment.
thinking: Single joint affected ↓ Painful swelling developing over hours ↓ Hot joint with fever of 38.5°C ↓ Infection must be assumed until excluded ↓ Septic arthritis
exam_trap: B, reactive arthritis — a young adult with an inflamed joint fits, but a hot joint with fever must be treated as septic until joint aspiration excludes it.
takeaway: Acute hot joint with fever: exclude septic arthritis urgently by aspiration.

stem:
A 67-year-old man has fatigue and bone pain. Blood tests show anaemia, and serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates a monoclonal protein.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Anaemia, bone pain and a monoclonal protein are characteristic features suggesting multiple myeloma.
why_wrong: A. Iron deficiency causes microcytic anaemia but not a monoclonal protein. B. Appendicitis is an acute abdominal condition. D. Haemophilia causes bleeding due to clotting-factor deficiency. E. Hyperthyroidism does not produce a monoclonal protein with this clinical picture.
pearl: Think myeloma in older patients with bone pain, anaemia, hypercalcaemia or renal impairment; serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains detect the paraprotein.
thinking: Older man ↓ Bone pain and fatigue ↓ Anaemia ↓ Monoclonal protein on electrophoresis ↓ Multiple myeloma
exam_trap: A, iron deficiency anaemia — anaemia with fatigue is common, but it does not cause bone pain or a monoclonal protein.
takeaway: Bone pain, anaemia and a paraprotein: multiple myeloma.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman has fatigue and recurrent mouth ulcers. Blood tests show a neutrophil count of 0.4 × 10⁹/L.

What does this result indicate?
why_correct: A markedly reduced neutrophil count represents severe neutropenia and increases susceptibility to serious infection.
why_wrong: A. Mild neutropenia is a neutrophil count of 1.0–1.5 × 10⁹/L. B. Neutrophilia is a raised neutrophil count; this count is markedly low. C. Polycythaemia refers to increased red-cell mass. D. Lymphocytosis is an increased lymphocyte count.
pearl: A neutrophil count below 0.5 × 10⁹/L is severe neutropenia; any fever in such a patient is a medical emergency needing immediate antibiotics.
thinking: Fatigue and mouth ulcers ↓ Neutrophils 0.4 × 10⁹/L ↓ Far below normal ↓ Below the severe threshold ↓ Severe neutropenia
exam_trap: A, mild neutropenia — it correctly identifies a low count, but mild neutropenia is 1.0–1.5 × 10⁹/L; 0.4 is well into the severe range.
takeaway: Neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L: severe neutropenia and high infection risk.

stem:
A 64-year-old man has an enlarged spleen and persistent fatigue. His blood count shows a very high white-cell count with a range of granulocyte precursors.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: CML can cause marked leukocytosis, splenomegaly and the presence of multiple stages of granulocyte maturation.
why_wrong: A. Haemophilia A causes impaired clotting and bleeding. B. Sickle cell trait is usually asymptomatic and does not cause this blood-count pattern. D. ITP causes isolated thrombocytopenia. E. Iron deficiency causes microcytic anaemia.
pearl: CML causes a very high white count with granulocytes at every stage of maturation and marked splenomegaly; it is driven by the BCR-ABL (Philadelphia) translocation.
thinking: Persistent fatigue ↓ Splenomegaly ↓ Very high white-cell count ↓ Full range of granulocyte precursors ↓ Chronic myeloid leukaemia
exam_trap: D, immune thrombocytopenia — a haematological disorder that tempts, but ITP causes isolated low platelets, not leukocytosis with splenomegaly.
takeaway: Very high white count, granulocyte precursors and a big spleen: CML.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain. Her mother has had similar episodes. During attacks she develops muscle weakness.

Which type of inheritance is typical of acute intermittent porphyria?
why_correct: Acute intermittent porphyria is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, although penetrance is variable.
why_wrong: A. Mitochondrial inheritance is transmitted through the maternal line. B. Y-linked disorders affect only males and pass from father to son. D. Autosomal recessive conditions require two pathogenic alleles. E. X-linked recessive conditions have characteristic sex-linked transmission.
pearl: Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance; attacks bring abdominal pain, neuropathy and psychiatric features, often triggered by drugs.
thinking: Recurrent severe abdominal pain ↓ Muscle weakness during attacks ↓ Mother similarly affected ↓ Passed vertically, one copy is enough ↓ Autosomal dominant
exam_trap: A, mitochondrial only — mother-to-daughter transmission tempts it, but AIP is autosomal dominant and can be inherited from either parent.
takeaway: Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance.

stem:
A 67-year-old man suddenly develops weakness of the right side of his body and difficulty speaking.

Which investigation should be performed urgently to distinguish ischaemic stroke from intracranial haemorrhage?
why_correct: Urgent brain imaging is required to distinguish haemorrhage from ischaemia and guide acute stroke management.
why_wrong: A. A chest X-ray does not diagnose the type of stroke. C. Abdominal ultrasound is irrelevant to the acute neurological presentation. D. DXA assesses bone mineral density. E. ECG may identify associated cardiac conditions but cannot distinguish haemorrhage from infarction.
pearl: Suspected acute stroke needs immediate non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage before thrombolysis; CT angiography is added if thrombectomy is being considered.
thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness ↓ Difficulty speaking ↓ Acute stroke ↓ Ischaemia and haemorrhage look alike clinically ↓ Non-contrast CT head
exam_trap: E, ECG only — an ECG is part of the stroke work-up and may show AF, but it cannot tell haemorrhage from infarction; brain imaging can.
takeaway: Acute stroke: urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude haemorrhage.

stem:
A 4-month-old infant is brought to clinic because he has not yet started smiling responsively and has poor head control.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.B: Reassure that this is always normal at 4 months

why_correct: Lack of expected early developmental milestones, particularly poor head control, warrants assessment rather than simple reassurance.
why_wrong: B. Developmental delay should be assessed when important milestones are absent. C. There is no history of seizures. D. There is no evidence of bacterial infection. E. Nothing in the presentation suggests cataract.
pearl: Most infants smile responsively within the first two months and are gaining head control by around 3–4 months; absence of both at 4 months needs developmental assessment.
thinking: Infant aged 4 months ↓ No responsive smile ↓ Poor head control ↓ Two expected milestones missed ↓ Arrange developmental assessment
exam_trap: B, reassure that this is always normal at 4 months — development varies, but missing both social smiling and head control is a red flag, not a normal variant.
takeaway: Missed early milestones need developmental assessment, not reassurance.

stem:
A 2-year-old child is not yet using any meaningful words and rarely makes eye contact. His parents are concerned about his development.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Significant language delay together with reduced social communication and eye contact should prompt consideration of autism spectrum disorder and developmental assessment.
why_wrong: A. Nephrotic syndrome causes oedema and proteinuria. B. Developmental coordination disorder affects motor skills rather than language and social communication. C. Croup causes acute upper-airway symptoms. E. Otitis media may temporarily affect hearing but does not explain this overall social-communication pattern by itself.
pearl: Autism presents with persistent differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviour; refer early for specialist assessment and check hearing.
thinking: Child aged 2 ↓ No meaningful words ↓ Rarely makes eye contact ↓ Language delay plus social-communication difficulty ↓ Autism spectrum disorder
exam_trap: E, recurrent acute otitis media — hearing loss can delay speech, so check hearing, but it does not explain poor eye contact and reduced social communication.
takeaway: Speech delay with poor eye contact: consider autism and refer for assessment.

stem:
A 6-year-old child has significant difficulty reading despite having normal intelligence and adequate schooling.

Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Dyslexia is a specific learning difficulty primarily affecting reading and language processing.
why_wrong: A. Cerebral palsy causes permanent disorders of movement and posture. B. ADHD primarily affects attention and impulse control. C. Epilepsy is characterised by recurrent seizures. D. Autism primarily affects social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviours.
pearl: Dyslexia is a specific learning difficulty affecting reading and spelling despite normal intelligence and adequate teaching; it does not reflect general cognitive ability.
thinking: Child aged 6 ↓ Marked difficulty with reading ↓ Normal intelligence ↓ Adequate schooling ↓ Dyslexia
exam_trap: B, ADHD — inattention can disrupt learning to read, but ADHD affects attention and impulse control broadly; a selective reading problem points to dyslexia.
takeaway: Specific reading difficulty with normal intelligence and teaching: dyslexia.

stem:
A 6-year-old child presents with fever and severe pain in the thigh. He refuses to walk. Blood tests show raised inflammatory markers.

Which diagnosis should be urgently considered?
why_correct: Bone pain with fever, inability to weight-bear and raised inflammatory markers suggests osteomyelitis.
why_wrong: A. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes activity-related tibial tubercle pain. C. Flat feet do not cause acute febrile bone pain. D. Scoliosis does not cause this acute presentation. E. Growing pains are typically bilateral, occur at night and do not cause fever or inflammatory markers.
pearl: Acute osteomyelitis in children often affects long-bone metaphyses; fever, bone pain, refusal to bear weight and raised inflammatory markers need urgent assessment, cultures and imaging.
thinking: Child with fever ↓ Severe thigh pain ↓ Refuses to walk ↓ Raised inflammatory markers ↓ Osteomyelitis
exam_trap: E, growing pains — common in children with leg pain, but they are typically bilateral and nocturnal, and do not cause fever, refusal to walk or raised inflammatory markers.
takeaway: Febrile child with bone pain who refuses to walk: think osteomyelitis.

stem:
A newborn develops jaundice at 12 hours of life.

What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: It is likely breast milk jaundice and needs no action
options.B: Urgent assessment, as jaundice under 24 hours is pathological
options.C: It is physiological if it resolves by 2 weeks of age
options.D: Repeat the bilirubin at the routine day 5 midwife visit
options.E: Home monitoring by the midwife if the baby feeds well

correct_answer: B. Urgent assessment, as jaundice under 24 hours is pathological
why_correct: Jaundice appearing during the first 24 hours of life is abnormal and requires prompt assessment.
why_wrong: A. Breast milk jaundice does not explain jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours. C. Jaundice in the first 24 hours is not physiological regardless of later course. D. Delaying measurement to day 5 is unsafe when jaundice appears in the first 24 hours. E. Good feeding does not exclude significant neonatal jaundice requiring urgent assessment.
pearl: Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is always pathological, often from haemolysis or sepsis; measure bilirubin urgently, within hours, and assess the baby.
thinking: Newborn ↓ Jaundice at 12 hours of age ↓ Onset within the first 24 hours ↓ Pathological, often haemolytic ↓ Urgent assessment, as jaundice under 24 hours is pathological
exam_trap: C, physiological if it resolves by 2 weeks — physiological jaundice is common, but it appears after the first day; early-onset jaundice is pathological regardless of course.
takeaway: Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life is pathological until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 3-day-old newborn becomes visibly jaundiced but is otherwise feeding well and clinically stable.

Which blood test is used to quantify the severity of neonatal jaundice?
why_correct: Measurement of bilirubin is used to assess the severity of neonatal jaundice and determine whether treatment is required.
why_wrong: A. HbA1c assesses longer-term glucose control. C. Amylase is associated with pancreatic disease. D. Troponin assesses myocardial injury. E. CK is associated with muscle injury.
pearl: Visual inspection is unreliable for judging neonatal jaundice; measure bilirubin and plot it on a gestation-specific treatment threshold chart.
thinking: Newborn aged 3 days ↓ Visible jaundice ↓ Clinically well ↓ Severity must be measured, not judged by eye ↓ Serum bilirubin
exam_trap: E, creatine kinase — a familiar blood test, but it reflects muscle injury and cannot quantify jaundice; bilirubin is the measure.
takeaway: Quantify neonatal jaundice with a bilirubin level against treatment thresholds.

stem:
A 9-month-old infant presents with episodic abdominal pain and vomiting. During painful episodes the child becomes pale and draws the knees towards the chest.

What complication of intussusception is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Telescoping of bowel can compromise its blood supply, leading to ischaemia and perforation.
why_wrong: B. Hypertension is unrelated to the mechanism. C. Cataracts are unrelated. D. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated. E. Otitis externa is unrelated to intestinal obstruction.
pearl: Intussusception compromises the blood supply to the telescoped bowel; redcurrant jelly stool is a late sign of ischaemia, so do not wait for it before acting.
thinking: Infant aged 9 months ↓ Episodic pain with pallor and knees drawn up ↓ Intussusception ↓ Telescoped bowel compresses its own vessels ↓ Bowel ischaemia
exam_trap: B, chronic hypertension — the infant looks pale and distressed, but intussusception threatens the bowel wall, not blood pressure; ischaemia and perforation are the dangers.
takeaway: Intussusception is an emergency because the bowel can become ischaemic.

stem:
A 5-year-old child has a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor. The symptoms are mild and occur mainly when the child is upset.

Which medication is commonly used to reduce airway swelling in croup?
why_correct: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone reduce upper-airway oedema in croup.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol is primarily used for lower-airway bronchospasm. B. Croup is usually viral, so routine antibiotics are not appropriate. C. Furosemide is a diuretic and does not treat croup. E. Omeprazole has no role in treating croup.
pearl: A single oral dose of dexamethasone is given for croup of any severity; nebulised adrenaline is added for severe croup with significant stridor at rest.
thinking: Barking cough and hoarse voice ↓ Inspiratory stridor ↓ Croup ↓ Subglottic airway oedema ↓ Dexamethasone
exam_trap: A, salbutamol tablets — a familiar treatment for noisy breathing, but it acts on lower-airway bronchospasm, not the subglottic swelling of croup.
takeaway: Croup: oral dexamethasone to reduce airway swelling.

stem:
A 3-year-old child has fever, drooling, muffled speech and difficulty swallowing. He sits leaning forward and looks severely unwell.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A toxic-looking child with drooling, dysphagia and a characteristic forward-leaning posture has features strongly suggestive of epiglottitis.
why_wrong: A. Croup causes barking cough and stridor rather than prominent drooling and dysphagia. B. Otitis media causes ear pain and fever rather than acute upper-airway obstruction. D. Viral pharyngitis is generally less severe and does not typically cause this airway presentation. E. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms.
pearl: Suspected epiglottitis is an airway emergency: keep the child calm and upright, do not examine the throat, and call senior anaesthetic and ENT help.
thinking: Febrile, toxic-looking child ↓ Drooling and difficulty swallowing ↓ Muffled speech ↓ Sitting forward to protect the airway ↓ Epiglottitis
exam_trap: A, croup — another cause of upper-airway obstruction in children, but croup has a barking cough and a less toxic child; drooling and dysphagia suggest epiglottitis.
takeaway: Toxic child drooling and leaning forward: epiglottitis; do not examine the throat.

stem:
A 2-month-old infant has cough, tachypnoea and difficulty feeding. Examination reveals widespread fine crackles and wheeze during a winter viral outbreak.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bronchiolitis commonly affects infants and causes cough, tachypnoea, wheeze and feeding difficulty following a viral infection.
why_wrong: B. Croup causes upper-airway symptoms including barking cough and stridor. C. Asthma is much less typical at this age and is generally characterised by recurrent variable symptoms. D. Pulmonary embolism is exceptionally unusual in this presentation and age group. E. Epiglottitis causes severe upper-airway obstruction and drooling.
pearl: Bronchiolitis, usually caused by RSV, affects infants in winter with coryza, cough, tachypnoea, wheeze and fine crackles; management is mainly supportive.
thinking: Infant aged 2 months ↓ Winter viral outbreak ↓ Cough, tachypnoea and feeding difficulty ↓ Widespread fine crackles and wheeze ↓ Bronchiolitis
exam_trap: C, asthma — wheeze tempts it, but asthma is not diagnosed in young infants; wheeze and crackles in an infant during a winter outbreak is bronchiolitis.
takeaway: Infant with winter cough, wheeze and fine crackles: bronchiolitis.

stem:
A 4-month-old infant with bronchiolitis has increased work of breathing and is taking much less fluid than usual.

Which feature is particularly concerning?

options.A: Occasional dry cough between and after feeds
options.B: Clear nasal discharge for the past several days
options.C: Reduced feeding with signs of dehydration
options.D: Nasal congestion that improves with suction
options.E: Low-grade fever of 37.8°C lasting for one day

correct_answer: C. Reduced feeding with signs of dehydration
why_correct: Young infants with bronchiolitis can deteriorate through respiratory compromise and inadequate fluid intake.
why_wrong: A. Cough is expected in bronchiolitis. B. Rhinorrhoea is common and usually mild. D. Nasal congestion is common and responsive congestion is reassuring. E. A low-grade fever alone does not indicate severe bronchiolitis.
pearl: In bronchiolitis, inadequate feeding or dehydration, apnoea, severe work of breathing or persistently low saturations are reasons to admit; most other infants can be managed at home.
thinking: Infant with bronchiolitis ↓ Increased work of breathing ↓ Taking much less fluid ↓ Dehydration develops ↓ Reduced feeding with signs of dehydration
exam_trap: E, low-grade fever — fever worries parents, but a mild fever is common in bronchiolitis; poor intake with dehydration signals severe disease.
takeaway: Bronchiolitis: poor feeding and dehydration are red flags.

stem:
A 15-year-old girl has severe lower abdominal pain associated with menstruation. The pain has been present for several years and is affecting school attendance.

Which diagnosis should be considered if symptoms are persistent and significantly impairing?
why_correct: Persistent, significant dysmenorrhoea affecting daily activities should raise consideration of endometriosis.
why_wrong: A. Gastroenteritis causes acute gastrointestinal symptoms. B. Pyelonephritis causes fever and flank pain. C. Appendicitis causes an acute progressive illness rather than recurrent menstrual-associated pain. E. Cystitis causes dysuria and urinary frequency.
pearl: Severe dysmenorrhoea that disrupts school or daily life should prompt consideration of endometriosis, even in adolescents, to reduce diagnostic delay.
thinking: Teenage girl ↓ Severe pain with periods ↓ Present for years ↓ Impairs school attendance ↓ Endometriosis
exam_trap: C, acute appendicitis — lower abdominal pain in a young person tempts it, but appendicitis is a single acute illness, not years of cyclical pain.
takeaway: Severe, disabling period pain, even in teenagers: consider endometriosis.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman has increasingly heavy periods and bleeding between periods. Pregnancy testing is negative.

What is the most appropriate principle of management?

options.A: Prescribe antibiotics for presumed endometritis and review
options.B: Reassure her and review if bleeding continues
options.C: Attribute it to the perimenopause and observe
options.D: Investigate for the cause of her abnormal bleeding
options.E: Start the combined pill to regulate her cycle

correct_answer: D. Investigate for the cause of her abnormal bleeding
why_correct: New or changing abnormal uterine bleeding requires assessment for structural, hormonal and other causes, including significant pathology.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. B. New intermenstrual or increasingly heavy bleeding should be assessed rather than observed. C. Perimenopause can alter bleeding patterns but should not explain new abnormal bleeding without assessment. E. Hormonal treatment should not be started before the cause has been assessed.
pearl: New intermenstrual or worsening heavy bleeding needs examination and investigation, which may include pelvic ultrasound and endometrial sampling, before it is blamed on age.
thinking: Woman in her late forties ↓ Increasingly heavy periods ↓ New intermenstrual bleeding ↓ Pregnancy excluded ↓ Investigate for the cause of her abnormal bleeding
exam_trap: C, attribute it to the perimenopause — her age makes cycle change plausible, but new intermenstrual bleeding must be investigated before blaming hormones.
takeaway: New abnormal uterine bleeding needs investigation, not attribution to age.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman has a painful lump in the lower abdomen. She has severe constipation and has never passed stool normally since birth. Her parents report that she required rectal stimulation as a newborn to pass stool.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Lifelong severe constipation with neonatal difficulty passing stool suggests congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells, as occurs in Hirschsprung disease.
why_wrong: A. Lactose intolerance causes symptoms after dairy ingestion. C. IBS does not typically cause severe constipation dating from the neonatal period. D. GORD affects the upper gastrointestinal tract. E. Coeliac disease can cause gastrointestinal symptoms but does not produce this characteristic lifelong obstruction pattern.
pearl: Hirschsprung disease is absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel; it classically presents in the neonatal period, but milder cases can present later. Rectal biopsy confirms it.
thinking: Lifelong severe constipation ↓ Needed rectal stimulation as a newborn ↓ Problem present from birth ↓ Aganglionic segment cannot relax ↓ Hirschsprung disease
exam_trap: C, irritable bowel syndrome — a common cause of constipation and pain in young adults, but IBS does not begin at birth or need neonatal rectal stimulation.
takeaway: Constipation dating from the neonatal period: think Hirschsprung disease.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman is being investigated for possible coeliac disease. She has already stopped eating gluten for several months.

Why can this make the initial testing less reliable?

options.A: It causes a false-positive anti-tTG IgA antibody test result
options.B: It raises antibody levels above the laboratory's detection range
options.C: It causes villous atrophy that mimics active coeliac disease
options.D: It causes iron deficiency that interferes with the serology
options.E: It can reduce the antibody response that testing detects

correct_answer: E. It can reduce the antibody response that testing detects
why_correct: Coeliac serology and intestinal findings may become less abnormal after gluten is removed, potentially reducing diagnostic sensitivity.
why_wrong: A. Gluten avoidance tends to cause false-negative, not false-positive, serology. B. Gluten avoidance lowers rather than raises coeliac antibody levels. C. Gluten avoidance allows villous atrophy to improve rather than causing it. D. Gluten avoidance does not cause iron deficiency that interferes with serology.
pearl: Coeliac serology and biopsy are reliable only while gluten is being eaten; advise gluten in more than one meal a day for at least 6 weeks before testing.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Already gluten-free for months ↓ Immune response to gluten subsides ↓ Antibodies fall and villi recover ↓ It can reduce the antibody response that testing detects
exam_trap: A, false-positive anti-tTG — testing is less reliable, but gluten avoidance causes false negatives, not false positives.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease only while the patient is eating gluten.

stem:
A 23-year-old man reports hearing voices discussing his actions. He has become socially withdrawn and has stopped attending university.

Which symptom is most characteristic of psychosis?
why_correct: Hearing voices in the absence of an external stimulus is an auditory hallucination and is a psychotic symptom.
why_wrong: A. Panic attacks are episodes of intense anxiety. C. Obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts recognised as one's own rather than hallucinations. D. Initial insomnia is nonspecific. E. Anhedonia and low energy are particularly associated with depression.
pearl: Voices discussing or commenting on the patient are a classic psychotic symptom; a first episode of psychosis needs urgent referral to early intervention services.
thinking: Young man hears voices ↓ Voices discuss his actions ↓ No external source ↓ Perception without a stimulus ↓ Auditory hallucinations
exam_trap: C, intrusive obsessional thoughts — both feel unwelcome, but obsessions are recognised as one's own thoughts; voices perceived as heard are hallucinations.
takeaway: Hearing voices discussing oneself is an auditory hallucination and a psychotic symptom.

stem:
A 19-year-old student says he has been feeling hopeless and has recently started thinking that he would be better off dead.

What is the most important immediate consideration?
why_correct: Thoughts of death or suicide require direct assessment of immediate risk, intent, plans, access to means and protective factors.
why_wrong: A. Dental assessment is unrelated to the immediate risk. B. There is no evidence of hyperthyroidism. D. Reassurance without risk assessment is unsafe. E. Hearing assessment does not address the immediate concern.
pearl: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and access to means; asking does not increase risk, and a safety plan follows the assessment.
thinking: Hopelessness ↓ Thinks he would be better off dead ↓ Suicidal ideation ↓ Immediate safety comes first ↓ Assess suicide risk
exam_trap: D, reassure without further assessment — reassurance feels kind, but it skips the essential step; suicidal thoughts always need direct risk assessment.
takeaway: Thoughts of being better off dead: ask directly and assess suicide risk.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman taking several medications develops dizziness and falls. Her blood pressure drops substantially when she stands.

What is the most appropriate initial step?

options.A: Reassure her that postural drops are common in older age
options.B: Review her medications and assess for reversible causes
options.C: Add an alpha-blocker to improve her blood pressure control
options.D: Restrict her daily fluid intake to 1.5 litres to reduce oedema
options.E: Start a night-time hypnotic to improve sleep and reduce falls

correct_answer: B. Review her medications and assess for reversible causes
why_correct: Medication-related hypotension is common in older adults, and potentially causative drugs should be reviewed alongside other causes.
why_wrong: A. A significant postural blood-pressure fall is clinically relevant and needs assessment. C. Additional antihypertensive treatment could worsen hypotension. D. Fluid restriction could worsen volume depletion and postural hypotension. E. Hypnotics increase falls risk.
pearl: In older people with falls and postural hypotension, review medicines first: antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, nitrates and psychotropics are common culprits.
thinking: Older woman on several medicines ↓ Dizziness and falls ↓ Substantial postural BP drop ↓ Polypharmacy is a common reversible cause ↓ Review her medications and assess for reversible causes
exam_trap: A, reassure her that postural drops are common — they are common in older age, but a symptomatic drop causing falls needs active assessment and medication review.
takeaway: Postural hypotension with falls: review medications and look for reversible causes.

stem:
A 78-year-old man has recurrent falls. He takes a sedating medication at night and reports daytime drowsiness.

Which adverse effect is most relevant?
why_correct: Sedation and impaired alertness can increase falls risk, particularly in older adults.
why_wrong: A. Sedation does not improve visual acuity. B. Sedative effects do not reduce bleeding risk. C. Sedating medicines do not improve bone density. E. They do not reduce infection risk.
pearl: Sedating drugs such as hypnotics, benzodiazepines and sedating antihistamines are major falls risks in older people; reduce or stop them where possible.
thinking: Older man with recurrent falls ↓ Sedating medicine at night ↓ Daytime drowsiness ↓ Impaired alertness and balance ↓ Increased falls risk
exam_trap: C, improved bone density — bone health matters in people who fall, but sedating medicines do not improve bone density; their key harm is increased falls.
takeaway: Sedating medicines increase falls risk in older people.

stem:
A 81-year-old woman develops a painful fracture after a minor fall. A DXA scan subsequently confirms low bone mineral density.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Low bone mineral density with a fragility fracture is characteristic of osteoporosis.
why_wrong: A. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory joint disease. B. Osteoarthritis affects joints but does not characteristically cause fragility fractures. D. Gout causes acute crystal arthritis. E. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain without reduced bone density as its defining feature.
pearl: Osteoporosis is defined on DXA by a T-score of −2.5 or lower; a fragility fracture should prompt bone health assessment and treatment.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Fracture after a minor fall ↓ Fragility fracture ↓ DXA confirms low bone mineral density ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: B, osteoarthritis — common in older women and painful, but it affects joints and does not cause fragility fractures or low bone density.
takeaway: Fragility fracture with low bone density on DXA: osteoporosis.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman is prescribed an oral bisphosphonate for osteoporosis.

Which instruction is appropriate?

options.A: Take it together with an antacid to improve absorption
options.C: Take it immediately before going to bed
options.D: Take it with water and remain upright afterwards
options.E: Take it with a large glass of milk

correct_answer: D. Take it with water and remain upright afterwards
why_correct: Oral bisphosphonates can irritate the oesophagus, so they should be taken correctly with water while following the specific product instructions, including remaining upright.
why_wrong: A. Antacids can interfere with absorption. B. Tablets should not routinely be crushed unless the specific formulation permits it. C. Taking it immediately before lying down increases oesophageal exposure. E. Calcium-containing drinks can interfere with absorption.
pearl: Counsel on oral bisphosphonates: swallow whole on an empty stomach with plain water, stay upright, and delay food, other drinks and medicines as directed.
thinking: Oral bisphosphonate ↓ Poorly absorbed and irritant to the oesophagus ↓ Needs plain water on an empty stomach ↓ Upright posture prevents oesophageal irritation ↓ Take it with water and remain upright afterwards
exam_trap: E, take it with a large glass of milk — milk seems good for bones, but its calcium binds the bisphosphonate and blocks absorption; use plain water.
takeaway: Bisphosphonates: plain water, empty stomach, stay upright.

stem:
A 58-year-old man develops sudden weakness and difficulty speaking. His symptoms began 90 minutes ago.

Which information is particularly important when assessing him for acute reperfusion treatment?

options.B: Time he was last known to be well
options.C: What he had for breakfast this morning
options.D: His shoe size and usual type of footwear

correct_answer: B. Time he was last known to be well
why_correct: The time of symptom onset or last known well is crucial when determining eligibility for time-dependent acute stroke treatments.
why_wrong: A. Dental history is irrelevant to the acute decision. C. Breakfast history does not determine the timing of stroke treatment. D. Shoe size and footwear are irrelevant. E. Vaccination history does not determine immediate reperfusion eligibility.
pearl: Thrombolysis and thrombectomy are time-critical; when onset is unwitnessed or unclear, use the time the patient was last known to be well.
thinking: Sudden weakness and speech difficulty ↓ Acute stroke likely ↓ Reperfusion treatment is time-dependent ↓ Eligibility depends on onset time ↓ Time he was last known to be well
exam_trap: C, what he had for breakfast — recent food intake can matter before some procedures, but it does not decide reperfusion eligibility; onset time does.
takeaway: In acute stroke, establish the time last known well: it drives reperfusion decisions.

stem:
A 67-year-old man presents with gradually worsening difficulty swallowing. Initially, solid food caused difficulty, but he now struggles with liquids as well. He has lost 7 kg unintentionally.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor

why_correct: Progressive dysphagia, particularly with weight loss, is an alarm feature requiring urgent investigation for structural disease, including oesophageal malignancy.
why_wrong: A. Swallow assessment is for oropharyngeal dysphagia and does not investigate progressive oesophageal dysphagia with weight loss. B. A routine delayed test is inappropriate for alarm symptoms. D. An empirical PPI trial would delay investigation of alarm symptoms. E. Alarm symptoms should not be managed with delayed review.
pearl: Progressive dysphagia from solids to liquids with weight loss suggests oesophageal cancer; refer for urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy.
thinking: Older man ↓ Progressive dysphagia, solids then liquids ↓ Unintentional weight loss ↓ Alarm features for oesophageal cancer ↓ Urgent upper gastrointestinal investigation
exam_trap: A, speech and language therapy assessment — a swallow assessment sounds fitting, but it suits oropharyngeal problems; progressive dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent endoscopy.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss: urgent upper GI endoscopy.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman has intermittent difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Her symptoms are not progressive and investigations show no structural obstruction.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Achalasia can cause dysphagia to both solids and liquids because of impaired relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer disease primarily causes upper abdominal pain. B. Haemorrhoids cause anorectal symptoms. C. Gallstones cause biliary symptoms rather than oesophageal dysphagia. D. Appendicitis causes acute abdominal pain.
pearl: Achalasia is failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter to relax with loss of peristalsis, causing dysphagia to both solids and liquids; manometry confirms it.
thinking: Dysphagia ↓ Both solids and liquids ↓ Not progressive ↓ No structural obstruction ↓ Achalasia
exam_trap: A, peptic ulcer disease — an upper GI condition, so it tempts, but it causes epigastric pain, not dysphagia to both solids and liquids.
takeaway: Dysphagia to solids and liquids without a structural block: think achalasia.

stem:
A 73-year-old woman develops jaundice, fever and right upper abdominal pain. She is hypotensive and confused.

What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.A: Outpatient ultrasound of the biliary tree next week
options.C: Oral antibiotics at home and review in 48 hours
options.E: Urgent treatment of suspected biliary sepsis

correct_answer: E. Urgent treatment of suspected biliary sepsis
why_correct: Fever, jaundice, abdominal pain and systemic deterioration suggest severe acute cholangitis with sepsis and require urgent management.
why_wrong: A. Outpatient imaging is inappropriate in a septic, hypotensive patient. B. Elective surgery does not address the immediate septic emergency. C. Oral antibiotics with delayed review are inadequate for severe sepsis with shock. D. Imaging must not delay resuscitation and antibiotics.
pearl: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot's triad) mean cholangitis; with hypotension and confusion it is septic shock needing resuscitation, IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage.
thinking: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain = Charcot's triad ↓ Suggests acute cholangitis ↓ Hypotension and confusion ↓ Septic shock ↓ Urgent treatment of suspected biliary sepsis
exam_trap: D, MRCP before starting any treatment — imaging seems needed to find the obstruction, but delaying resuscitation and antibiotics in septic shock is dangerous.
takeaway: Cholangitis with shock: treat sepsis now, then drain the biliary tree.

stem:
A 59-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. She has had no bleeding for 8 years.

What is the appropriate approach?

options.A: Ignore the bleeding unless it becomes painful
options.B: Treat empirically with antibiotics without assessment
options.D: Urgent assessment for possible endometrial pathology
options.E: Reassurance that this is normal after menopause

correct_answer: D. Urgent assessment for possible endometrial pathology
why_correct: Postmenopausal bleeding is an important symptom requiring assessment because endometrial cancer is an important possible cause.
why_wrong: A. Pain is not required for significant endometrial pathology. B. Antibiotics do not address the important differential diagnosis. C. Cervical screening does not replace assessment of postmenopausal bleeding. E. Vaginal bleeding after menopause is not considered normal.
pearl: Postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer, usually starting with transvaginal ultrasound to measure endometrial thickness.
thinking: Woman aged 59 ↓ No periods for 8 years ↓ New vaginal bleeding ↓ Endometrial cancer must be excluded ↓ Urgent assessment for possible endometrial pathology
exam_trap: C, routine cervical smear only — the cervix can bleed, but cervical screening does not assess the endometrium; this needs urgent assessment.
takeaway: Any postmenopausal bleeding needs urgent assessment for endometrial cancer.

stem:
A 20-year-old woman presents with fever, sore throat and tender anterior cervical lymph nodes. She has tonsillar exudate and no cough.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy and absence of cough are features supporting streptococcal pharyngitis.
