why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis usually causes sneezing, nasal symptoms and itching. B. Otitis externa causes ear-canal pain and discharge rather than an exudative sore throat. C. Migraine causes headache rather than an exudative sore throat. D. Gastroenteritis causes gastrointestinal rather than pharyngeal symptoms.
pearl: FeverPAIN or Centor scores estimate the likelihood of streptococcal infection; fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes and absent cough favour it.
thinking: Fever and sore throat ↓ Tonsillar exudate ↓ Tender anterior cervical nodes ↓ No cough ↓ Streptococcal pharyngitis
exam_trap: B, acute bacterial otitis externa — sore throats can cause referred ear pain, but otitis externa affects the ear canal and does not cause exudative tonsillitis.
takeaway: Fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes and no cough: streptococcal pharyngitis.

stem:
A 7-year-old child has a widespread itchy rash with small vesicles and crusted lesions. New lesions continue to appear over several days.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Crops of itchy vesicular lesions at different stages of development are characteristic of chickenpox.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo causes superficial crusted lesions, typically without widespread crops of vesicles. B. Scarlet fever causes a fine, rough-textured rash. D. Measles causes a widespread maculopapular rash with systemic symptoms rather than crops of vesicles. E. Meningococcal disease classically causes a non-blanching rash with systemic illness.
pearl: Chickenpox erupts in crops, so papules, vesicles and crusts coexist; children remain infectious until all lesions have crusted over.
thinking: Child with a widespread itchy vesicular rash ↓ New lesions keep appearing over several days ↓ Lesions at different stages at once ↓ Chickenpox
exam_trap: A, impetigo — the crusted lesions tempt, but impetigo gives localised honey-coloured crusting, not widespread itchy vesicles erupting in successive crops.
takeaway: Itchy vesicles in crops at different stages in a child = chickenpox.

stem:
A 2-year-old child has a high fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a widespread maculopapular rash. The parents report that the child has not received routine vaccinations.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, cough, conjunctivitis and a widespread maculopapular rash are characteristic of measles.
why_wrong: B. Impetigo produces localised superficial skin lesions. C. Scarlet fever is associated with streptococcal pharyngitis and a fine rough rash. D. Scabies causes intense pruritus and characteristic burrows. E. Chickenpox produces vesicles.
pearl: Measles starts with high fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, followed by a maculopapular rash spreading from behind the ears; it is a notifiable disease in the UK.
thinking: Unvaccinated toddler ↓ High fever with cough and conjunctivitis ↓ Widespread maculopapular rash ↓ Measles
exam_trap: C, scarlet fever — fever and a widespread rash tempt, but scarlet fever follows a sore throat with a fine sandpaper rash, not cough and conjunctivitis.
takeaway: Unvaccinated child with fever, cough, conjunctivitis and maculopapular rash = measles.

stem:
A 5-year-old child has persistent nasal discharge, facial discomfort and a cough that has lasted more than 10 days without improvement.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent upper-respiratory symptoms beyond the expected uncomplicated viral course can suggest acute sinusitis.
why_wrong: A. Croup causes barking cough and stridor. C. Otitis externa causes ear-canal symptoms. D. Migraine does not cause persistent purulent nasal symptoms. E. Gastroenteritis causes gastrointestinal symptoms.
pearl: Most colds settle within about 10 days; nasal discharge, facial pain and cough persisting beyond this without improvement suggest acute sinusitis.
thinking: Child with nasal discharge and cough ↓ Facial discomfort ↓ No improvement beyond 10 days, longer than a simple cold ↓ Acute sinusitis
exam_trap: A, croup — a cough in a young child tempts, but croup is an acute barking cough with stridor, not persistent nasal discharge with facial pain.
takeaway: Cold symptoms failing to improve beyond about 10 days with facial pain suggest sinusitis.

stem:
A 3-year-old child has a painful, swollen area behind the ear. The pinna appears pushed forwards and the child has fever.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, post-auricular swelling and displacement of the pinna are characteristic warning features of mastoiditis.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms. B. Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and hearing symptoms rather than acute post-auricular inflammation. C. Otitis externa affects the external ear canal. D. Wax impaction causes conductive hearing symptoms without systemic illness.
pearl: Acute mastoiditis usually complicates acute otitis media; post-auricular swelling with a pushed-forward pinna in a febrile child needs urgent ENT admission for IV antibiotics.
thinking: Febrile three-year-old child ↓ Painful swelling behind the ear ↓ Pinna pushed forwards by the swelling ↓ Acute mastoiditis
exam_trap: C, otitis externa — ear pain tempts, but otitis externa affects the ear canal; it does not cause post-auricular swelling that pushes the pinna forwards.
takeaway: Fever with post-auricular swelling and a protruding pinna = mastoiditis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman has progressive hearing loss. Otoscopy is normal. She has no history of recurrent ear infections.

Which type of hearing loss is most likely with age-related hearing impairment?

options.A: Hearing loss from a perforated tympanic membrane in every case
options.C: Conductive hearing loss from otitis externa

why_correct: Age-related hearing loss is typically sensorineural due to degeneration of the auditory system.
why_wrong: A. A perforated tympanic membrane causes conductive hearing loss. C. Otitis externa causes conductive impairment through canal inflammation or obstruction. D. Middle-ear effusion causes conductive hearing loss. E. Wax causes conductive hearing loss.
pearl: Presbycusis is gradual, bilateral sensorineural loss, typically affecting high frequencies first, so speech in background noise suffers early; otoscopy is normal.
thinking: Older woman with progressive hearing loss ↓ Normal otoscopy excludes wax, effusion and perforation ↓ No history of ear infections ↓ Age-related sensorineural loss
exam_trap: E, conductive loss from wax — wax is common in older adults, which tempts, but it would be visible on otoscopy, and here otoscopy is normal.
takeaway: Gradual hearing loss in an older adult with normal otoscopy is sensorineural.

stem:
A 36-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of wheezing, chest tightness and cough. Symptoms are worse after exposure to cat dander.

Which investigation can help demonstrate variable airflow obstruction?

options.A: Chest X-ray with lateral and frontal views
options.C: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air at rest
options.D: Pulse oximetry at rest and on formal exertion

why_correct: Spirometry, including assessment of bronchodilator reversibility where appropriate, can help demonstrate variable airflow obstruction in suspected asthma.
why_wrong: A. A chest X-ray does not demonstrate variable airflow obstruction. B. Echocardiography assesses cardiac structure and function. C. Arterial blood gases assess gas exchange rather than variable airflow obstruction. D. Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, not airflow.
pearl: Asthma needs objective confirmation; spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility is a core test for variable airflow obstruction, alongside FeNO and peak flow variability.
thinking: Recurrent wheeze, chest tightness and cough ↓ Triggered by cat dander, suggesting allergic asthma ↓ Need to show variable airflow obstruction ↓ Spirometry with bronchodilator assessment
exam_trap: A, chest X-ray — a reflex respiratory test, but it is usually normal in asthma and cannot demonstrate variable airflow obstruction.
takeaway: Suspected asthma needs objective testing; spirometry with reversibility shows variable obstruction.

stem:
A 69-year-old smoker has chronic cough, sputum production and progressive exertional breathlessness. He has a long history of cigarette smoking.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Acute bronchiolitis following a viral infection
options.D: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from heart failure

why_correct: Persistent respiratory symptoms in an older smoker, particularly chronic cough, sputum and exertional breathlessness, are characteristic of COPD.
why_wrong: A. Bronchiolitis is predominantly an acute illness of young children. B. Epiglottitis causes acute upper-airway obstruction. D. Pulmonary oedema has a different acute presentation and is not established by smoking history alone. E. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis typically causes a dry cough rather than chronic sputum production.
pearl: Suspect COPD in anyone over 35 with a risk factor such as smoking who has exertional breathlessness, chronic cough or regular sputum; confirm with post-bronchodilator spirometry.
thinking: Older man with a long smoking history ↓ Chronic cough with sputum ↓ Progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ COPD
exam_trap: E, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — progressive breathlessness in an older adult tempts, but IPF gives a dry cough and fine crackles, not chronic sputum.
takeaway: Smoker over 35 with chronic productive cough and exertional breathlessness: think COPD.

stem:
A 72-year-old man with COPD becomes increasingly breathless and produces more purulent sputum than usual. His symptoms have worsened over several days.

What does this represent?
why_correct: An acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond the usual day-to-day variation is characteristic of an acute COPD exacerbation.
why_wrong: A. BPPV causes positional vertigo. B. Stable COPD does not involve an acute deterioration. C. Otitis externa affects the ear canal. D. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms.
pearl: A COPD exacerbation is a sustained worsening beyond normal day-to-day variation; more breathlessness with more purulent sputum suggests a bacterial trigger.
thinking: Known COPD ↓ Increasing breathlessness over several days ↓ Sputum more purulent than usual ↓ Acute exacerbation of COPD
exam_trap: B, stable COPD — the underlying diagnosis is right, but 'stable' ignores the sustained worsening over days that defines an exacerbation.
takeaway: Sustained worsening of breathlessness and sputum in COPD = acute exacerbation.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. She is haemodynamically stable and has a low clinical probability of pulmonary embolism.

Which test may be used to help exclude PE when appropriate?
why_correct: In patients with sufficiently low clinical probability, a negative D-dimer can help exclude venous thromboembolism.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin assesses iron stores. B. Troponin assesses myocardial injury and is not a stand-alone rule-out test for PE. C. HbA1c assesses long-term glucose control. D. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury.
pearl: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: a negative result helps exclude PE only when clinical probability is low, such as a Wells score of PE unlikely; a positive result needs imaging.
thinking: Pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness ↓ Haemodynamically stable with low clinical probability ↓ Need a sensitive rule-out test ↓ D-dimer
exam_trap: B, troponin alone — chest pain and breathlessness prompt a troponin, but it assesses myocardial injury and cannot rule out PE.
takeaway: Low pre-test probability of PE: a negative D-dimer helps exclude it; a positive one means imaging.

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with acute chest pain. His ECG shows ST-segment elevation in a regional distribution consistent with acute myocardial infarction.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Acute chest pain with a characteristic regional ST-elevation pattern is consistent with STEMI.
why_wrong: A. PE can produce ECG abnormalities but does not typically cause this regional STEMI pattern. B. Pericarditis typically produces widespread rather than regional ST changes. C. Stable angina does not cause an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction pattern. D. GORD does not cause myocardial ST elevation.
pearl: Regional ST elevation in a coronary territory with acute chest pain means STEMI; act on the ECG immediately for reperfusion rather than waiting for troponin.
thinking: Acute chest pain ↓ ST elevation confined to one coronary territory ↓ Pattern of acute infarction ↓ STEMI
exam_trap: B, acute pericarditis — it also causes chest pain with ST elevation, but the elevation is widespread and saddle-shaped, not confined to one territory.
takeaway: Regional ST elevation with chest pain is STEMI; widespread saddle-shaped elevation suggests pericarditis.

stem:
A 70-year-old man with heart failure develops worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and bilateral ankle swelling over several days.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.B: Bilateral cellulitis of the lower legs

why_correct: Worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and peripheral oedema in a patient with heart failure indicate fluid congestion and possible acute decompensation.
why_wrong: B. Cellulitis causes localised skin and soft-tissue inflammation and is rarely bilateral. C. Pneumonia does not explain orthopnoea with bilateral ankle swelling. D. Renal colic causes acute flank-to-groin pain. E. Asthma does not cause orthopnoea with peripheral oedema in this context.
pearl: Worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea and peripheral oedema in known heart failure indicate fluid congestion; IV loop diuretics are the mainstay of decongestion.
thinking: Known heart failure ↓ Worsening breathlessness and orthopnoea over days ↓ Bilateral ankle swelling = fluid congestion ↓ Acute decompensated heart failure
exam_trap: C, community-acquired pneumonia — it causes worsening breathlessness and can trigger decompensation, but it does not explain orthopnoea with bilateral ankle oedema.
takeaway: Orthopnoea, bilateral oedema and worsening breathlessness in heart failure = decompensation.

stem:
A 58-year-old man has persistent tiredness and blood tests show an elevated serum creatinine. Repeat testing several months later confirms reduced kidney function.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Persistent reduction in kidney function over time is characteristic of chronic kidney disease.
why_wrong: A. Appendicitis causes an acute abdominal presentation. B. Reduced kidney function persisting over several months indicates a chronic rather than acute process. C. Migraine causes recurrent headaches. E. Hypothyroidism causes tiredness but does not explain persistently reduced kidney function.
pearl: CKD means reduced kidney function or kidney damage persisting for more than 3 months; always repeat an abnormal result to confirm chronicity before labelling it CKD.
thinking: Persistent tiredness ↓ Raised serum creatinine ↓ Still reduced on repeat testing months later ↓ Chronic kidney disease
exam_trap: B, acute kidney injury — a raised creatinine tempts, but AKI develops over hours to days; reduction persisting for months is chronic.
takeaway: Reduced kidney function persisting beyond 3 months = CKD, not AKI.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease has blood tests showing a persistently raised potassium concentration.

Which complication of chronic kidney disease is this?
why_correct: Reduced renal potassium excretion can cause hyperkalaemia, particularly in advanced CKD.
why_wrong: B. CKD does not characteristically cause hypoglycaemia. C. Sodium abnormalities are not inevitably hypernatraemic. D. Hyperbilirubinaemia is not a typical direct consequence of CKD. E. CKD more commonly causes anaemia than polycythaemia.
pearl: Falling GFR reduces potassium excretion, so hyperkalaemia is common in advanced CKD; ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing diuretics can worsen it.
thinking: Known chronic kidney disease ↓ Persistently raised potassium ↓ Kidneys excrete less potassium ↓ Hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: E, polycythaemia — CKD does affect red cells, which tempts, but reduced erythropoietin causes anaemia, and the stem describes a raised potassium.
takeaway: Raised potassium in CKD is hyperkalaemia from reduced renal excretion.

stem:
A 67-year-old man with severe hyperkalaemia develops muscle weakness and ECG abnormalities.

Which treatment is used urgently to protect the heart?
why_correct: Intravenous calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.
why_wrong: A. Vitamin B12 is unrelated. B. Iron does not treat hyperkalaemia. C. Oral calcium is not the appropriate emergency cardiac stabilisation treatment. E. Fluid restriction does not rapidly stabilise the myocardium.
pearl: In hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, IV calcium stabilises the myocardium within minutes but does not lower potassium; insulin with glucose then shifts potassium into cells.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ ECG abnormalities = arrhythmia risk ↓ First protect the myocardium ↓ Intravenous calcium
exam_trap: C, oral calcium supplements only — calcium is the right agent, but the oral route is far too slow; emergency cardiac protection needs IV calcium.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium first to protect the heart.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman becomes confused after developing severe hyponatraemia. Blood tests suggest inappropriate retention of water without evidence of dehydration or oedema.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.D: Cranial diabetes insipidus after head injury

why_correct: SIAD causes inappropriate water retention leading to dilutional hyponatraemia.
why_wrong: A. Hyperparathyroidism primarily affects calcium regulation; confusion would reflect hypercalcaemia, not hyponatraemia. B. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and hypokalaemia. C. Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia involves dehydration, which is absent here. D. Diabetes insipidus causes excessive water loss and tends towards hypernatraemia.
pearl: SIAD is euvolaemic hyponatraemia from inappropriate water retention; confirm euvolaemia and exclude hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency before diagnosing it.
thinking: Confusion with severe hyponatraemia ↓ Neither dehydrated nor oedematous = euvolaemic ↓ Inappropriate water retention ↓ SIAD
exam_trap: C, hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from diuretics — diuretics commonly cause hyponatraemia in older adults, but the stem excludes dehydration.
takeaway: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia from inappropriate water retention = SIAD.

stem:
A 48-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of severe unilateral headaches associated with tearing of one eye and nasal congestion on the same side.

Which class of headache is this pattern characteristic of?
why_correct: Severe unilateral headache accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic features such as lacrimation and nasal congestion is characteristic of a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, including cluster headache.
why_wrong: B. Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief stabbing facial pain without prominent autonomic features. C. Sinus disease does not account for this characteristic recurrent autonomic pattern. D. Tension headache is usually bilateral and pressing. E. Medication-overuse headache is associated with frequent analgesic use and chronic headache.
pearl: Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, with cluster headache the commonest, combine severe unilateral pain with same-side autonomic features such as tearing, red eye and nasal congestion.
thinking: Recurrent severe unilateral headache ↓ Same-side tearing ↓ Same-side nasal congestion = autonomic features ↓ Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia
exam_trap: B, trigeminal neuralgia — severe unilateral facial pain tempts, but it causes brief electric-shock pains without prominent autonomic features.
takeaway: Unilateral headache with same-side autonomic features = trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia.

stem:
A 65-year-old man develops sudden difficulty speaking and weakness of his right arm and leg. He is brought to hospital shortly after symptom onset.

What is the key initial brain imaging investigation for suspected acute stroke?
why_correct: Urgent brain imaging is required in suspected acute stroke, with non-contrast CT commonly used initially to distinguish haemorrhage from ischaemia.
why_wrong: A. CT colonography does not assess acute stroke. B. Abdominal imaging is unrelated. D. Knee MRI is irrelevant. E. Renal ultrasound is unrelated.
pearl: Non-contrast CT head is the first imaging in suspected acute stroke to exclude haemorrhage before reperfusion treatment; it may look normal in early ischaemic stroke.
thinking: Sudden speech difficulty and right-sided weakness ↓ Suspected acute stroke ↓ Must exclude haemorrhage before reperfusion ↓ Non-contrast CT head
exam_trap: A, CT colonography — the word CT can catch a hurried candidate, but it images the bowel, not the brain.
takeaway: Suspected acute stroke: urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude bleeding.

stem:
A 52-year-old man develops lower back pain after lifting a heavy object. He has no neurological deficit, fever, weight loss or bladder symptoms.

Which initial management is generally appropriate?

options.A: Emergency spinal MRI for every patient
options.C: Encourage continued normal activity as tolerated
options.D: Long-term opioid treatment as first-line therapy

correct_answer: C. Encourage continued normal activity as tolerated
why_correct: Uncomplicated acute mechanical low back pain is generally managed conservatively, including maintaining activity where possible.
why_wrong: A. Routine emergency imaging is unnecessary without red flags. B. Prolonged bed rest can delay recovery. D. Long-term opioids are not first-line treatment. E. Surgery is not routinely required for uncomplicated mechanical back pain.
pearl: Acute mechanical low back pain without red flags needs no imaging; advise staying active and continuing normal activities, with simple analgesia if needed.
thinking: Back pain after lifting ↓ No neurological deficit, fever, weight loss or bladder symptoms ↓ No red flags = mechanical pain ↓ Encourage normal activity
exam_trap: B, prolonged bed rest — it feels intuitive after a strain, but bed rest delays recovery; staying active is the advice.
takeaway: Uncomplicated mechanical back pain: no imaging, stay active.

stem:
A 61-year-old man with a history of cancer develops new severe back pain and progressive leg weakness.

What diagnosis should be considered urgently?

options.A: Mechanical lumbar muscle strain from lifting

why_correct: New severe back pain with neurological deficits in a patient with cancer is a red flag for metastatic spinal cord compression.
why_wrong: A. A muscular strain does not explain progressive neurological weakness. B. Spondylosis does not typically produce this acute progressive neurological picture. D. Chemotherapy neuropathy is mainly sensory and does not explain new severe back pain. E. Facet joint arthropathy causes mechanical back pain without progressive weakness.
pearl: Suspect metastatic spinal cord compression in anyone with cancer who develops back pain with neurological symptoms; arrange urgent whole-spine MRI.
thinking: History of cancer ↓ New severe back pain ↓ Progressive leg weakness ↓ Metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: D, chemotherapy-induced neuropathy — weakness in a patient with cancer tempts, but it is mainly sensory and does not cause new severe back pain.
takeaway: Cancer with new back pain and neurology = spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 73-year-old woman falls and sustains a fracture after minimal trauma. Her bone density is reduced.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: A fragility fracture with reduced bone mineral density is characteristic of osteoporosis.
why_wrong: B. Rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory joint disease. C. Fibromyalgia does not cause reduced bone density. D. Osteomalacia involves defective bone mineralisation and has a different underlying mechanism. E. Osteoarthritis affects joints rather than causing fragility fractures.
pearl: A fragility fracture follows trauma no greater than a fall from standing height; it should prompt fracture risk assessment and consideration of bone-protective treatment.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Fracture after minimal trauma = fragility fracture ↓ Reduced bone density ↓ Osteoporosis
exam_trap: D, osteomalacia — it also weakens bone, but it is defective mineralisation, usually from vitamin D deficiency, not the usual cause of fragility fracture with low bone density.
takeaway: Fragility fracture with reduced bone density = osteoporosis.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has a painful swollen joint in her right hand. She has prolonged morning stiffness and several other small joints are also affected symmetrically.

Which blood test is commonly associated with rheumatoid arthritis?
why_correct: Anti-CCP antibodies are strongly associated with rheumatoid arthritis and can support the diagnosis.
why_wrong: A. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus. C. D-dimer is used in selected assessment of venous thromboembolism. D. HbA1c assesses longer-term glucose control. E. Amylase and lipase are associated with pancreatic injury.
pearl: Anti-CCP antibody is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis and supports the diagnosis alongside rheumatoid factor; refer persistent synovitis urgently whatever the blood results.
thinking: Symmetrical small-joint swelling ↓ Prolonged morning stiffness ↓ Inflammatory polyarthritis suggesting RA ↓ Anti-CCP antibody
exam_trap: A, anti-dsDNA antibody — autoantibodies with joint pain tempt, but anti-dsDNA is associated with SLE, not rheumatoid arthritis.
takeaway: Anti-CCP is the most specific antibody test for rheumatoid arthritis.

stem:
A 55-year-old man presents with painless rectal bleeding. The blood is bright red and appears on the toilet paper after defecation.

Which diagnosis is a common cause?
why_correct: Bright-red blood associated with defecation is commonly caused by haemorrhoids, although persistent or unexplained rectal bleeding requires appropriate assessment.
why_wrong: A. Peptic ulcer disease more commonly causes melaena or upper GI bleeding. B. Cholecystitis causes right upper abdominal pain. D. Pancreatitis causes abdominal pain and vomiting. E. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain.
pearl: Bright-red blood on the paper after defecation suggests haemorrhoids, but persistent or unexplained rectal bleeding in an older adult still needs assessment for colorectal cancer.
thinking: Painless rectal bleeding ↓ Bright red, seen on the toilet paper ↓ After defecation = anal canal source ↓ Haemorrhoids
exam_trap: A, peptic ulcer disease — a common cause of GI bleeding, but an upper source usually gives melaena, not bright-red blood on the paper.
takeaway: Painless bright-red blood on the paper suggests haemorrhoids; still assess persistent bleeding.

stem:
A 40-year-old woman is being investigated for suspected coeliac disease. She has already stopped eating gluten for several weeks.

What is the main problem with testing while she remains gluten-free?

options.A: It makes routine blood tests unreliable
options.B: It tends to cause false-positive coeliac serology
options.C: It increases the chance of a false-positive biopsy
options.D: It can reduce the sensitivity of coeliac testing
options.E: It makes Crohn's disease harder to exclude

correct_answer: D. It can reduce the sensitivity of coeliac testing
why_correct: Avoiding gluten before assessment can reduce the immune response and make coeliac serology and subsequent testing less sensitive.
why_wrong: A. Gluten avoidance does not affect routine blood tests. B. Gluten avoidance causes false-negative rather than false-positive serology. C. Gluten avoidance allows the mucosa to recover, making a false-negative biopsy more likely. E. Gluten avoidance does not affect the assessment of Crohn's disease.
pearl: Coeliac serology and biopsy depend on gluten exposure; advise eating gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before testing.
thinking: Suspected coeliac disease ↓ Already gluten-free for several weeks ↓ Antibodies fall and the mucosa heals ↓ Testing loses sensitivity
exam_trap: B, false-positive serology — candidates know diet affects results, but gluten avoidance lowers antibody levels, giving false negatives, not positives.
takeaway: Test for coeliac disease only while the patient is eating gluten.

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis develops a sudden marked increase in bloody diarrhoea, fever, tachycardia and abdominal tenderness.

Which complication should be considered?
why_correct: A marked acute deterioration with frequent bloody diarrhoea and systemic toxicity in a patient with ulcerative colitis suggests acute severe disease.
why_wrong: A. Faecal impaction does not cause bloody diarrhoea with fever and tachycardia. C. IBS does not cause systemic toxicity or significant bloody diarrhoea. D. Haemorrhoids do not explain the systemic deterioration and diarrhoeal illness. E. Lactose intolerance does not cause systemic inflammatory illness.
pearl: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is a medical emergency: frequent bloody stools with systemic toxicity such as fever or tachycardia need admission, IV corticosteroids and surgical review.
thinking: Known ulcerative colitis ↓ Marked increase in bloody diarrhoea ↓ Fever, tachycardia and tenderness = systemic toxicity ↓ Acute severe ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: D, bleeding haemorrhoids — the bleeding tempts, but haemorrhoids do not cause diarrhoea, fever and tachycardia.
takeaway: UC with bloody diarrhoea plus fever or tachycardia = acute severe colitis; admit.

stem:
A 24-year-old man with Crohn's disease develops a painful lump near the anus associated with fever.

Which complication should be suspected?
why_correct: A painful perianal swelling with fever in someone with Crohn's disease is concerning for an abscess.
why_wrong: A. GORD affects the upper gastrointestinal tract. C. Haemorrhoids do not usually cause fever and a painful inflammatory mass. D. An anal fissure causes severe pain with defecation but does not typically produce a febrile perianal mass. E. Diverticulosis affects the colon and does not explain this perianal presentation.
pearl: Perianal abscesses and fistulae are common in Crohn's disease; a painful perianal swelling with fever needs surgical drainage, not antibiotics alone.
thinking: Known Crohn's disease ↓ Painful lump near the anus ↓ Fever suggests a collection of pus ↓ Perianal abscess
exam_trap: D, anal fissure alone — fissures are common in Crohn's and painful, but a fissure is a split in the anal skin, not a febrile swelling.
takeaway: Painful perianal lump with fever, especially in Crohn's = perianal abscess.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman has absent periods, low body weight and a history of intense exercise. Pregnancy testing is negative.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Low energy availability, low body weight and excessive exercise can suppress hypothalamic reproductive function and cause amenorrhoea.
why_wrong: A. PID causes pelvic pain and genital tract symptoms. B. Fibroids more commonly cause heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms. D. Ectopic pregnancy requires pregnancy, which a negative test makes unlikely, and usually causes pain and/or bleeding. E. Endometrial cancer is much less likely in this young patient and would not explain this characteristic history.
pearl: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea results from low energy availability; low weight, excessive exercise or stress suppress GnRH, causing low oestrogen and a risk to bone density.
thinking: Amenorrhoea with a negative pregnancy test ↓ Low body weight ↓ Intense exercise = low energy availability ↓ Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea
exam_trap: D, early tubal ectopic pregnancy — amenorrhoea always raises pregnancy, but the negative test and absence of pain or bleeding make it unlikely.
takeaway: Amenorrhoea with low weight and heavy exercise = functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman develops dysuria and urinary frequency. She also has new vaginal discharge and lower abdominal discomfort.

What is the most appropriate consideration?
why_correct: Urinary symptoms accompanied by new vaginal discharge and pelvic discomfort should prompt consideration of an STI and appropriate sexual-health assessment.
why_wrong: B. Otitis externa affects the external ear; aural discharge is unrelated to vaginal discharge or dysuria. C. IBS causes bowel symptoms rather than dysuria and vaginal discharge. D. A ureteric stone causes colicky loin-to-groin pain and does not explain vaginal discharge. E. Migraine does not explain dysuria or vaginal discharge.
pearl: Dysuria in a young woman is not always cystitis; new vaginal discharge or pelvic discomfort should prompt STI testing, including for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.
thinking: Young woman with dysuria and frequency ↓ New vaginal discharge ↓ Lower abdominal discomfort ↓ Consider a sexually transmitted infection
exam_trap: D, ureteric stone — urinary symptoms with abdominal pain tempt, but a stone causes colicky loin-to-groin pain and does not explain vaginal discharge.
takeaway: Urinary symptoms plus new vaginal discharge: think STI, not just UTI.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman develops a widespread itchy rash after taking amoxicillin. She has no breathing difficulty, facial swelling or circulatory problems.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Urticaria causes transient, itchy, raised wheals and can occur following exposure to a medication.
why_wrong: A. Stevens–Johnson syndrome causes painful blistering and mucosal involvement. C. Cellulitis causes a localised, painful, erythematous skin infection. D. Scabies causes intensely itchy lesions, often worse at night, with characteristic distribution. E. Psoriasis causes persistent scaly plaques.
pearl: Drug-induced urticaria without airway, breathing or circulatory problems is not anaphylaxis; stop the drug, give a non-sedating antihistamine and record the allergy.
thinking: Widespread itchy rash ↓ After taking amoxicillin ↓ No breathing difficulty, facial swelling or circulatory problems ↓ Urticaria
exam_trap: A, Stevens–Johnson syndrome — a serious drug rash tempts, but SJS is painful with blistering and mucosal involvement, not an itchy wheal rash.
takeaway: Itchy drug rash without ABC compromise = urticaria, not anaphylaxis.

stem:
A 17-year-old boy has multiple inflammatory spots and blackheads across his face and upper back.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Comedones with inflammatory papules and pustules are characteristic of acne vulgaris.
why_wrong: A. Bullous impetigo causes superficial blisters and crusted lesions without comedones. B. Cellulitis is a localised bacterial skin infection. C. Rosacea typically causes facial flushing and persistent central facial erythema without comedones. D. Guttate psoriasis causes small scaly plaques without comedones.
pearl: Comedones (blackheads and whiteheads) are the hallmark of acne vulgaris and distinguish it from rosacea, which causes flushing and papulopustules without comedones.
thinking: Teenage boy ↓ Multiple inflammatory spots on the face and upper back ↓ Blackheads = comedones ↓ Acne vulgaris
exam_trap: C, rosacea — inflammatory facial spots tempt, but rosacea typically affects older adults, causes flushing and has no comedones or back involvement.
takeaway: Comedones plus inflammatory papules = acne vulgaris.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman develops a painful unilateral rash involving the tip of her nose, followed by a red painful eye.

What complication of herpes zoster is particularly concerning?
why_correct: Herpes zoster affecting the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve can involve the eye and requires urgent assessment.
why_wrong: A. Allergic rhinitis causes nasal symptoms and is not a complication of zoster. B. Gout causes acute inflammatory arthritis. C. Otitis externa affects the external ear canal. D. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain.
pearl: Hutchinson's sign, zoster on the tip of the nose, signals nasociliary nerve involvement and a high risk of eye disease; arrange urgent same-day ophthalmology review.
thinking: Painful unilateral rash ↓ Involving the tip of the nose = nasociliary branch ↓ Followed by a red painful eye ↓ Ocular involvement
exam_trap: A, allergic rhinitis — the nasal location tempts, but it is not a complication of zoster and does not cause a painful unilateral rash.
takeaway: Zoster on the nasal tip predicts eye involvement: urgent ophthalmology.

stem:
A 42-year-old man presents with severe pain in his lower leg after a minor injury. The skin is swollen and increasingly discoloured, and he is systemically unwell. The pain is much greater than expected from the appearance.

Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?

options.E: Tinea corporis of the lower leg

why_correct: Severe pain out of proportion to skin findings with systemic toxicity is a major warning sign of necrotising fasciitis.
why_wrong: A. Superficial thrombophlebitis causes a tender cord along a vein without systemic toxicity. B. Urticaria causes transient itchy wheals. D. Vitiligo causes depigmentation without acute systemic illness. E. Tinea corporis is a superficial fungal infection.
pearl: Pain out of proportion to skin findings with systemic toxicity suggests necrotising fasciitis; it needs urgent surgical debridement plus IV antibiotics without delay.
thinking: Minor leg injury ↓ Pain far greater than the appearance suggests ↓ Swelling, spreading discolouration and systemic illness ↓ Necrotising fasciitis
exam_trap: A, superficial thrombophlebitis — a painful swollen leg tempts, but it causes a tender cord along a vein without systemic toxicity.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion plus systemic illness after minor injury = necrotising fasciitis.

stem:
A 71-year-old woman develops sudden painless swelling of one leg. She has recently returned from a long-haul flight.

What condition should be considered?
why_correct: Prolonged immobility during long-haul travel increases the risk of venous thrombosis, which can present with unilateral leg swelling.
why_wrong: A. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the upper limb. B. Gout causes acute joint inflammation rather than diffuse leg swelling. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause acute unilateral leg swelling from prolonged travel. E. Fibromyalgia does not cause acute unilateral swelling.
pearl: Unilateral leg swelling after prolonged immobility suggests DVT; assess with the two-level Wells score, then arrange proximal leg vein ultrasound or D-dimer accordingly.
thinking: Older woman ↓ Sudden unilateral leg swelling ↓ Recent long-haul flight = immobility ↓ Deep vein thrombosis
exam_trap: B, gout — acute lower-limb swelling tempts, but gout causes a hot, painful inflamed joint, not diffuse painless swelling of the leg.
takeaway: Unilateral leg swelling after long travel = DVT until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 67-year-old man taking warfarin presents with unexplained bruising. His INR is markedly above his therapeutic range, but he has no significant bleeding.

What is the most appropriate general approach?

options.B: Continue warfarin and recheck the INR in 4 weeks' time
options.C: Switch to a direct oral anticoagulant from today onwards
options.D: Give IV prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K
options.E: Manage according to the INR level and bleeding risk

correct_answer: E. Manage according to the INR level and bleeding risk
why_correct: Management of excessive anticoagulation depends on the INR level, presence of bleeding and individual clinical circumstances.
why_wrong: A. Increasing warfarin would worsen anticoagulation. B. A markedly elevated INR requires prompt action rather than routine recheck. C. Switching anticoagulants without addressing the raised INR is inappropriate. D. IV prothrombin complex concentrate is reserved for major bleeding, which is absent.
pearl: Warfarin over-anticoagulation is managed by INR level and bleeding: without major bleeding, withhold warfarin and give vitamin K according to the INR and any minor bleeding; PCC is reserved for major bleeding.
thinking: On warfarin with a markedly raised INR ↓ Bruising but no significant bleeding ↓ Response scales with INR and bleeding ↓ Manage according to INR and bleeding risk
exam_trap: D, IV prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K — a very high INR tempts full reversal, but PCC is reserved for major bleeding, which is absent.
takeaway: High INR without major bleeding: tailor action to the INR; PCC only for major bleeds.

stem:
A 74-year-old woman taking apixaban presents with significant gastrointestinal bleeding.

What is the most important immediate priority?

options.A: Give the next dose of apixaban

correct_answer: B. Assess and stabilise the patient
why_correct: Significant bleeding requires immediate assessment of airway, breathing, circulation and haemodynamic status, alongside management of the anticoagulant.
why_wrong: A. Continuing anticoagulation during significant bleeding may worsen haemorrhage. C. Anticoagulant use is clinically important. D. Aspirin would increase bleeding risk. E. Significant GI bleeding requires urgent assessment.
pearl: In any significant bleed on an anticoagulant, ABCDE assessment and resuscitation come first; then withhold the anticoagulant and consider specific reversal.
thinking: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding ↓ On apixaban, so bleeding may be brisk ↓ Haemodynamic compromise is the immediate threat ↓ Assess and stabilise
exam_trap: A, give the next dose of apixaban — continuing to prevent stroke tempts, but anticoagulation during active haemorrhage worsens bleeding.
takeaway: Bleeding on an anticoagulant: ABCDE and stabilise first, then manage the drug.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of visible blood in her urine. She has no pain or urinary symptoms.

Which investigation is particularly important in the initial assessment?
why_correct: Urinalysis is an important initial investigation for haematuria and can identify blood and other urinary abnormalities.
why_wrong: A. An ECG does not investigate haematuria. B. Amylase assesses pancreatic injury. D. Spirometry assesses lung function. E. Peak flow assesses airway obstruction.
pearl: Haematuria assessment starts with urinalysis to confirm blood and look for infection or proteinuria; unexplained visible haematuria then needs further assessment, including for urological causes.
thinking: Recurrent visible blood in the urine ↓ No pain or urinary symptoms ↓ First confirm blood and check for infection or protein ↓ Urinalysis
exam_trap: A, ECG only — a routine baseline test that tempts by habit, but it gives no information about the urinary tract or the source of bleeding.
takeaway: Haematuria: start with urinalysis to confirm blood and look for infection or proteinuria.

stem:
A 71-year-old man with Parkinson's disease develops increasing difficulty swallowing and coughing when drinking fluids.

What complication is particularly important to recognise?
why_correct: Parkinson's disease can cause dysphagia, increasing the risk of aspiration and aspiration pneumonia.
why_wrong: A. DVT does not explain coughing during swallowing. B. Renal colic is unrelated to swallowing difficulty. C. Otitis externa affects the external ear canal. D. Peptic ulcer disease does not typically cause aspiration.
pearl: Dysphagia in Parkinson's disease raises the risk of aspiration pneumonia, a common cause of death; arrange speech and language therapy swallow assessment.
thinking: Parkinson's disease ↓ Increasing difficulty swallowing ↓ Coughing when drinking = unsafe swallow ↓ Aspiration
exam_trap: D, peptic ulcer disease — a GI problem in an older adult tempts, but it does not cause coughing on drinking or aspiration.
takeaway: Coughing on drinking in Parkinson's = aspiration risk; arrange swallow assessment.

stem:
A 58-year-old man suddenly develops weakness of the left arm and leg. He is also unable to see objects in the left half of his visual field.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficits involving motor and visual function strongly suggests an acute cerebrovascular event.
why_wrong: A. Peripheral neuropathy does not explain simultaneous hemiparesis and visual field loss. B. Bell's palsy causes isolated unilateral facial weakness. C. Migraine may cause neurological symptoms but sudden focal deficits require urgent stroke assessment. D. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve.
pearl: Hemiparesis with a same-sided homonymous hemianopia points to a stroke in the opposite cerebral hemisphere; use FAST in the community and ROSIER in the emergency department.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Weakness of left arm and leg ↓ Loss of the left visual field = right hemisphere lesion ↓ Acute stroke
exam_trap: C, migraine — it can cause transient visual and focal symptoms, but sudden hemiparesis with field loss must be managed as stroke.
takeaway: Sudden hemiparesis plus hemianopia = acute stroke until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 73-year-old woman develops acute confusion, fever and urinary symptoms. Her family reports that she was functioning normally until the previous day.

Which diagnosis best describes her acute cognitive change?
why_correct: Acute onset and fluctuating cognitive disturbance associated with an underlying physical illness are characteristic of delirium.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety does not explain acute fluctuating confusion. C. Dementia usually develops gradually and is not typically an acute change over one day. D. Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric disorder. E. Depression does not usually cause this abrupt fluctuating state.
pearl: Delirium is acute, fluctuating confusion with inattention triggered by illness such as infection or drugs; a sudden change from baseline is the key clue.
thinking: Functioning normally until the day before ↓ Acute confusion ↓ Fever and urinary symptoms = precipitating infection ↓ Delirium
exam_trap: C, dementia — confusion in an older woman tempts, but dementia develops gradually; a change within a day is delirium.
takeaway: Acute confusion over hours to days with an illness = delirium.

stem:
A 79-year-old man with dementia becomes suddenly more confused after developing a chest infection.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.C: Look for and treat the acute precipitating cause
options.D: Assume his dementia has permanently progressed

correct_answer: C. Look for and treat the acute precipitating cause
why_correct: Sudden deterioration in cognition in a person with dementia should prompt assessment for delirium and an underlying acute cause.
why_wrong: A. An antidepressant does not treat acute delirium. B. An acute change requires clinical assessment. D. Sudden deterioration is not necessarily permanent progression of dementia. E. Medication changes should be individualised rather than stopping everything automatically.
pearl: People with dementia are at high risk of delirium; sudden worsening should trigger a search for causes such as infection, drugs, urinary retention, constipation or dehydration.
thinking: Known dementia ↓ Sudden increase in confusion ↓ New chest infection as a trigger ↓ Delirium: look for and treat the cause
exam_trap: D, assume his dementia has permanently progressed — the dementia history tempts, but dementia worsens gradually; sudden change suggests reversible delirium.
takeaway: Sudden worsening in dementia is delirium until proven otherwise; treat the cause.

stem:
A 24-year-old man reports hearing voices commenting on his actions. He has become socially withdrawn and his behaviour has changed over several months.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Persistent hallucinations with social and behavioural deterioration are characteristic features of schizophrenia.
why_wrong: A. OCD causes obsessions and/or compulsions. B. Generalised anxiety disorder causes excessive persistent worry. C. Panic disorder causes recurrent episodes of intense anxiety. D. A specific phobia causes marked fear related to a particular object or situation.
pearl: Voices commenting on a person's actions are a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia; refer suspected first-episode psychosis urgently to an early intervention in psychosis service.
thinking: Young man ↓ Voices commenting on his actions ↓ Social withdrawal and behaviour change over months ↓ Schizophrenia
exam_trap: A, obsessive-compulsive disorder — intrusive experiences tempt, but obsessional thoughts are recognised as the person's own, not external voices.
takeaway: Running-commentary voices with functional decline in a young adult = schizophrenia.

stem:
A 29-year-old man has slept only 2 hours a night for a week but does not feel tired. He is unusually energetic, talks rapidly and has started several unrealistic business projects.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Reduced need for sleep, increased energy, rapid speech and increased goal-directed activity are characteristic features of mania.
why_wrong: B. Panic disorder involves recurrent panic attacks. C. GAD is characterised by excessive worry. D. Depression is characterised by low mood and/or loss of interest with associated symptoms. E. OCD involves obsessions and compulsions.
pearl: Mania brings elevated or irritable mood with reduced need for sleep, increased energy, pressured speech and grandiose plans; hypomania is milder without severe impairment or psychosis.
thinking: Sleeping 2 hours a night for a week ↓ Not tired, unusually energetic ↓ Rapid speech and unrealistic business projects ↓ Mania
exam_trap: C, generalised anxiety disorder — poor sleep and restlessness tempt, but anxiety brings worry and fatigue, not reduced need for sleep with grandiosity.
takeaway: Reduced need for sleep without tiredness plus grandiose plans = mania.

stem:
A 52-year-old man presents with persistent depressive symptoms and says, “I don't see the point in being alive anymore.”

What should be assessed directly?
why_correct: Expressions of hopelessness or wanting to die require direct assessment of suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and immediate safety.
why_wrong: A. Thyroid tests may be relevant later but do not address the immediate safety concern. B. Blood glucose does not assess suicide risk. D. Cognitive testing does not address the immediate safety concern. E. Peak flow is unrelated to the presentation.
pearl: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and intent does not increase risk and is essential in anyone expressing hopelessness or a wish to die.
thinking: Persistent depressive symptoms ↓ Says he sees no point being alive ↓ Possible suicidal ideation ↓ Assess suicidal thoughts and intent directly
exam_trap: A, thyroid function tests — hypothyroidism can mimic depression, but testing does not address the immediate safety concern.
takeaway: Hopelessness or a wish to die: ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and intent.

stem:
A 68-year-old man taking several medications has recurrent dizziness and falls. His blood pressure is low when standing.

What is an appropriate initial step?

options.D: Ignore the postural blood pressure change

why_correct: Medication-related hypotension is common in older adults, so a medication review is an important part of assessment.
why_wrong: A. Sedatives may increase falls risk. C. Increasing antihypertensives could worsen hypotension. D. The postural blood pressure change is clinically relevant. E. Medication changes should be targeted rather than stopping everything automatically.
pearl: Postural hypotension in older adults is often drug-related, for example antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers and antipsychotics; a targeted medication review comes first.
thinking: Older man on several medications ↓ Recurrent dizziness and falls ↓ Low blood pressure on standing ↓ Review his medications
exam_trap: E, automatically stop every medication — the drugs are a likely cause, which tempts, but blanket withdrawal is unsafe; changes should be targeted.
takeaway: Postural hypotension with falls on several drugs: targeted medication review.

stem:
A 78-year-old woman has fallen twice in the past month. She takes several medications and reports difficulty seeing obstacles clearly.

Which approach is appropriate?

options.A: Refer for hip protectors without further assessment
options.B: Multifactorial assessment of modifiable falls risks
options.C: Advise bed rest until her confidence improves
options.D: Prescribe a hypnotic to improve her sleep
options.E: Advise her that falls are expected at her age

correct_answer: B. Multifactorial assessment of modifiable falls risks
why_correct: Falls assessment should consider factors such as medication, vision, balance, gait and environmental hazards.
why_wrong: A. Hip protectors do not replace assessment of modifiable risk factors such as medication and vision. C. Bed rest can worsen strength and mobility. D. Hypnotics can increase falls risk. E. Falls should be assessed for modifiable causes rather than accepted as inevitable.
pearl: Older people with recurrent falls need a multifactorial risk assessment covering gait, balance, medication, vision, continence, cognition and home hazards.
thinking: Two falls in a month ↓ Several medications ↓ Difficulty seeing obstacles ↓ Multiple modifiable risks: multifactorial falls assessment
exam_trap: A, hip protectors without further assessment — they may reduce fracture risk, which tempts, but they do nothing about why she is falling.
takeaway: Recurrent falls in older people need multifactorial assessment of modifiable risks.

stem:
A 69-year-old man with several chronic conditions asks why his doctor wants to review all his regular medicines.

What is a key purpose of a medication review?

options.A: Switch his medicines to cheaper generic brands where possible
options.B: Find unneeded medicines, interactions and adverse effects
options.C: Add preventive medicines for each guideline condition he has
options.D: Reduce the frequency of his GP appointments
options.E: Confirm that all his medicines continue unchanged long term

correct_answer: B. Find unneeded medicines, interactions and adverse effects
why_correct: Medication review aims to ensure medicines remain appropriate, effective and safe, including identifying adverse effects and interactions.
why_wrong: A. Cost is not the key purpose of a clinical medication review. C. The aim is appropriate prescribing, not increasing medication burden. D. Medication review is not intended to reduce appointment frequency. E. Medicines should be reviewed rather than automatically continued.
pearl: A structured medication review checks each medicine is still needed, effective and safe, reducing harm from interactions, adverse effects and inappropriate polypharmacy.
thinking: Several chronic conditions ↓ Multiple regular medicines ↓ Risk of interactions, adverse effects and unneeded drugs ↓ Review to keep prescribing appropriate
exam_trap: C, add preventive medicines for each condition — it sounds guideline-driven, but adding drugs increases burden and harm; review aims at appropriate prescribing.
takeaway: Medication review: stop what isn't needed and catch interactions and side effects.

stem:
A 28-year-old man has urethral discharge and dysuria following unprotected sex. He has no testicular pain.

Which infection is an important possibility?
why_correct: Gonorrhoea commonly causes urethral discharge and dysuria in men.
why_wrong: A. Candidiasis does not typically cause purulent urethral discharge in men. B. Genital warts cause visible lesions rather than urethral discharge. C. Molluscum causes umbilicated papules. E. Bacterial vaginosis affects the vagina.
pearl: Purulent urethral discharge with dysuria in a man suggests gonorrhoea; test for gonorrhoea and chlamydia, and take a culture before treatment because of antibiotic resistance.
thinking: Young man after unprotected sex ↓ Urethral discharge ↓ Dysuria without testicular pain = urethritis ↓ Gonorrhoea
exam_trap: A, candidiasis — genital symptoms tempt, but candida in men typically causes balanitis, not purulent urethral discharge.
takeaway: Urethral discharge and dysuria after unprotected sex: think gonorrhoea, and test for chlamydia too.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman has vaginal discharge following unprotected sex. She has mild lower abdominal discomfort but no fever.

Which infection should be considered particularly in this context?
why_correct: Chlamydia is a common sexually transmitted infection that may cause vaginal or cervical symptoms and can be asymptomatic.
why_wrong: A. Impetigo causes superficial skin infection. B. Tinea corporis causes annular skin lesions. D. Otitis externa affects the external ear. E. Influenza causes a systemic respiratory illness.
pearl: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial STI in the UK and is often asymptomatic; untreated, it can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Vaginal discharge after unprotected sex ↓ Mild lower abdominal discomfort, no fever ↓ Chlamydia
exam_trap: B, tinea corporis — an infection spread by close contact, which may tempt, but it causes annular skin lesions, not vaginal discharge.
takeaway: Vaginal discharge after unprotected sex in a young woman: test for chlamydia.

stem:
A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed with chlamydia. She asks whether her recent sexual partner should also be assessed.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Recent partners should be notified and offered assessment
options.B: Asymptomatic chlamydia is unlikely to be passed to partners
options.C: Partners do not require assessment if they are asymptomatic
options.D: Partners need assessment if they develop visible genital lesions
options.E: Partner notification is reserved for HIV and infectious syphilis

correct_answer: A. Recent partners should be notified and offered assessment
why_correct: Partner notification is an important part of STI management to reduce ongoing transmission and reinfection.
why_wrong: B. Asymptomatic infection can still be transmitted. C. Many STIs, including chlamydia, are asymptomatic. D. Chlamydia does not usually cause visible lesions. E. Partner notification applies to chlamydia and other transmissible STIs.
pearl: Partner notification is central to chlamydia management: recent partners are tested and treated even if asymptomatic, to prevent reinfection and onward spread.
thinking: Chlamydia diagnosed ↓ Often asymptomatic yet transmissible ↓ An untreated partner risks reinfection ↓ Notify and assess recent partners
exam_trap: C, partners need no assessment if asymptomatic — sounds pragmatic, but chlamydia is usually silent, so asymptomatic partners still need assessment.
takeaway: Every chlamydia diagnosis needs partner notification, symptoms or not.

stem:
A 35-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He feels well and asks why treatment is recommended despite having no symptoms.

What is the key reason?

options.A: Treatment is started once the CD4 count falls below 350
options.B: Treatment is mainly needed during opportunistic infections
options.C: HIV is often cleared by the immune system without treatment
options.D: A short antiretroviral course can eradicate HIV
options.E: Antiretrovirals suppress HIV and slow disease progression

correct_answer: E. Antiretrovirals suppress HIV and slow disease progression
why_correct: Effective antiretroviral therapy suppresses viral replication, preserves immune function and reduces HIV-related morbidity.
why_wrong: A. Current guidance recommends treatment for all people with HIV regardless of CD4 count. B. HIV treatment is lifelong rather than limited to opportunistic infections. C. Untreated HIV does not clear spontaneously. D. Antiretroviral therapy suppresses but does not eradicate HIV.
pearl: Antiretroviral therapy is offered to everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count; a sustained undetectable viral load preserves immunity and prevents sexual transmission.
thinking: New HIV diagnosis ↓ Asymptomatic but the virus is still replicating ↓ ART suppresses the virus and preserves CD4 cells ↓ Slows disease progression
exam_trap: A, start once CD4 falls below 350 — this reflects older practice, but treatment is now recommended for all, whatever the CD4 count.
takeaway: Treat HIV at diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count or symptoms.

stem:
A patient with untreated HIV develops fever, weight loss and persistent diarrhoea. His CD4 count is very low.

What does the low CD4 count indicate?
why_correct: A markedly reduced CD4 count indicates substantial impairment of cellular immunity and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.
why_wrong: A. CD4 count does not measure bone density. B. A low CD4 count indicates impaired rather than improved immunity. C. Renal failure is assessed using renal function tests. D. Hyperthyroidism is assessed using thyroid function tests.
pearl: The CD4 count reflects cellular immunity in HIV; as it falls, the risk of opportunistic infections rises, guiding the need for prophylaxis such as co-trimoxazole.
thinking: Untreated HIV ↓ Fever, weight loss and persistent diarrhoea ↓ Very low CD4 count ↓ Significant immune suppression
exam_trap: B, improved immune function — confusing the direction is easy under pressure, but a low CD4 count means impaired, not improved, immunity.
takeaway: Low CD4 count = significant immunosuppression and opportunistic infection risk.

stem:
A patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is coughing extensively while awaiting further assessment.

What infection-control principle is particularly important?

options.A: No precautions are needed if the patient is afebrile
options.B: Reduce transmission by appropriate respiratory precautions
options.C: Encourage close contact with other patients
options.E: Treat the patient as non-infectious until all investigations are complete

correct_answer: B. Reduce transmission by appropriate respiratory precautions
why_correct: Suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis requires appropriate infection-control measures to reduce airborne transmission.
why_wrong: A. Absence of fever does not exclude infectious TB. C. Close contact can increase transmission risk. D. TB transmission is primarily airborne rather than simply contact-based. E. Infection-control measures should begin when clinically indicated rather than waiting for definitive confirmation.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs airborne precautions from the outset: a single room, negative pressure if available, and staff respiratory protection.
thinking: Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis ↓ Coughing extensively ↓ Spread is airborne ↓ Respiratory precautions to reduce transmission
exam_trap: D, contact precautions only — sound practice for many infections, but TB spreads by the airborne route, so contact precautions alone are insufficient.
takeaway: Suspected pulmonary TB: start airborne precautions before confirmation.

stem:
A 39-year-old man develops jaundice and dark urine several weeks after returning from travel. Blood tests show markedly raised ALT.

Which viral infection should be considered?
why_correct: Hepatitis A can cause an acute hepatitis syndrome with jaundice and markedly elevated transaminases, particularly after relevant travel or food/water exposure.
why_wrong: A. Influenza is a respiratory viral infection. B. Otitis externa is a local ear infection. D. Measles causes a febrile illness with a characteristic rash. E. Herpes zoster causes a dermatomal vesicular rash.
pearl: Hepatitis A spreads by the faecal–oral route, often after travel, with an incubation of a few weeks; it causes acute hepatitis that is usually self-limiting and does not become chronic.
thinking: Recent travel ↓ Jaundice and dark urine weeks later ↓ Markedly raised ALT = acute hepatitis ↓ Hepatitis A
exam_trap: A, influenza — a common travel-related viral illness, but it causes respiratory symptoms, not jaundice with a marked ALT rise.
takeaway: Jaundice with a high ALT weeks after travel: think hepatitis A.

stem:
A 30-year-old healthcare worker sustains a needlestick injury from a patient whose blood is known to be infected with hepatitis B.

What is an important immediate consideration?

options.A: Test for hepatitis B later if symptoms of acute hepatitis develop
options.B: Give a 7-day course of oral antibiotics to prevent infection
options.C: Clean the wound and take no further action if small
options.D: Assess hepatitis B vaccination and post-exposure management
options.E: Start HIV post-exposure prophylaxis as the main step

correct_answer: D. Assess hepatitis B vaccination and post-exposure management
why_correct: Occupational exposure to hepatitis B requires prompt assessment of vaccination status and appropriate post-exposure management.
why_wrong: A. Post-exposure management should not wait for symptoms. B. Antibiotics have no role in preventing hepatitis B infection. C. Even a small needlestick can transmit blood-borne infection. E. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis does not address hepatitis B exposure from a known HBV source.
pearl: After a needlestick, encourage bleeding, wash with soap and water and report urgently; for a hepatitis B source, management depends on the recipient's vaccination and antibody status.
thinking: Needlestick injury ↓ Source known to have hepatitis B ↓ Protection depends on the worker's vaccine response ↓ Assess vaccination and give post-exposure management
exam_trap: E, start HIV post-exposure prophylaxis — needlestick prompts thoughts of PEP, but the known risk is hepatitis B, managed with vaccine and/or immunoglobulin.
takeaway: Hepatitis B needlestick: check vaccination status and give post-exposure management promptly.

stem:
A 63-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with vomiting blood and black stools.

Which diagnosis is particularly important to consider?
why_correct: Portal hypertension associated with cirrhosis can produce oesophageal varices, which may cause life-threatening upper GI bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Haemorrhoids cause lower gastrointestinal bleeding. C. Vomiting blood indicates an upper rather than lower gastrointestinal source. D. Ureteric colic causes loin-to-groin pain and haematuria, not haematemesis or melaena. E. Anal fissure causes painful bright-red rectal bleeding.
pearl: Suspected variceal bleeding in cirrhosis needs resuscitation, terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics before urgent endoscopy with band ligation.
thinking: Cirrhosis = portal hypertension ↓ Vomiting blood ↓ Black stools = upper GI source ↓ Oesophageal variceal bleeding
exam_trap: C, lower gastrointestinal bleeding — black stools tempt this, but melaena with haematemesis points to an upper GI source.
takeaway: Haematemesis in cirrhosis is variceal until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman has persistent tiredness, weight gain, constipation and feeling unusually cold. Her thyroid examination is unremarkable.

Which investigation is most appropriate initially?
why_correct: TSH is an appropriate initial test when hypothyroidism is suspected.
why_wrong: B. Hypercalcaemia can cause fatigue and constipation but not weight gain and cold intolerance. C. Morning cortisol assesses adrenal insufficiency, which typically causes weight loss rather than gain. D. TPO antibodies help establish an autoimmune cause after thyroid dysfunction is confirmed and are not the first test. E. HbA1c assesses glycaemic control and does not explain cold intolerance or weight gain.
pearl: TSH is the first-line test for suspected primary hypothyroidism; if it is raised, measure free T4, and TPO antibodies can then support an autoimmune cause.
thinking: Tiredness and weight gain ↓ Constipation ↓ Feeling unusually cold ↓ Suspected hypothyroidism: check TSH
exam_trap: D, thyroid peroxidase antibodies — they relate to the likely cause, but they do not establish thyroid status; TSH comes first.
takeaway: Suspected hypothyroidism: the first-line test is TSH.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations and a fine tremor.

Which investigation is most appropriate initially?
why_correct: Thyroid function testing, beginning with TSH in most initial assessments, is appropriate when hyperthyroidism is suspected.
why_wrong: B. TPO antibodies do not establish thyroid status and are not the first test. C. Metanephrines are measured for suspected phaeochromocytoma, which is far less likely than thyrotoxicosis; thyroid function should be checked first. D. Isotope uptake scanning helps determine the cause after hyperthyroidism is confirmed biochemically. E. Calcium does not assess thyroid function.
pearl: In suspected hyperthyroidism, a suppressed TSH with raised free T4 and/or T3 confirms thyrotoxicosis; antibodies or uptake scanning then define the cause.
thinking: Weight loss and heat intolerance ↓ Palpitations and fine tremor ↓ Suspected thyrotoxicosis ↓ Check TSH first
exam_trap: D, radioisotope thyroid uptake scan — it is used in hyperthyroidism, but only to find the cause after biochemical confirmation.
takeaway: Suspected thyroid disease: confirm with TSH first, find the cause later.

stem:
A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has persistent hyperkalaemia. ECG shows tall, peaked T waves.

What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Start a low-potassium diet and repeat bloods in a week
options.C: Oral sodium bicarbonate and review in renal clinic
options.D: Increase the furosemide dose and recheck tomorrow

correct_answer: B. Urgent treatment of the hyperkalaemia
why_correct: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias and requires urgent treatment.
why_wrong: A. Dietary restriction is a long-term measure and does not address the immediate arrhythmia risk. C. Oral bicarbonate is a chronic CKD measure and provides no urgent cardiac protection or potassium shift. D. Adjusting a diuretic with a delayed recheck does not treat hyperkalaemia with ECG changes as the emergency it is. E. ECG changes make this an emergency rather than routine follow-up.
pearl: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes such as peaked T waves is an emergency: IV calcium to protect the heart, insulin with glucose to shift potassium, then measures to remove it.
thinking: CKD with persistent hyperkalaemia ↓ Tall peaked T waves on ECG ↓ Risk of fatal arrhythmia ↓ Urgent treatment of hyperkalaemia
exam_trap: A, low-potassium diet and repeat bloods in a week — reasonable for chronic mild hyperkalaemia, but ECG changes make this an emergency.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is an emergency, whatever the background.

stem:
A 70-year-old man develops sudden severe breathlessness and is hypotensive. Examination reveals distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Hypotension, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds are classic features of cardiac tamponade.
why_wrong: A. Tension pneumothorax causes hypotension and raised JVP but with unilateral absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation rather than muffled heart sounds. B. Pneumonia usually causes fever, cough and focal chest signs. C. Constrictive pericarditis develops gradually with chronic right heart failure rather than sudden shock with muffled heart sounds. E. Asthma causes wheeze and airflow obstruction rather than raised JVP with muffled heart sounds.
pearl: Beck's triad of hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds suggests cardiac tamponade; confirm with bedside echocardiography and treat with pericardiocentesis.
thinking: Sudden breathlessness with hypotension ↓ Distended neck veins ↓ Muffled heart sounds = Beck's triad ↓ Cardiac tamponade
exam_trap: A, tension pneumothorax — it also causes hypotension and raised JVP, but with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation, not muffled heart sounds.
takeaway: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds = cardiac tamponade.

stem:
A 19-year-old woman with asthma is increasingly breathless and using her reliever inhaler several times each day.

What does this suggest?
why_correct: Frequent reliever use and increasing symptoms indicate inadequate asthma control and require review.
why_wrong: A. Frequent symptoms indicate ongoing rather than resolved disease. C. Stable angina causes exertional chest discomfort, not recurrent wheeze and breathlessness. D. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. E. CKD does not explain this pattern of airway symptoms.
pearl: Needing a reliever several times a day signals poorly controlled asthma; check inhaler technique, adherence and triggers, then step up anti-inflammatory treatment.
thinking: Known asthma ↓ Increasing breathlessness ↓ Using reliever several times each day ↓ Poorly controlled asthma
exam_trap: C, stable angina — breathlessness can be cardiac, but in a young woman with asthma, rising reliever use points to the airways.
takeaway: Frequent reliever use means poor control: review technique, adherence and treatment.

stem:
A 14-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss. Blood tests show anaemia and raised inflammatory markers.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
why_correct: Chronic abdominal pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, anaemia and inflammatory markers suggest inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease.
why_wrong: A. Lactose intolerance does not typically cause systemic inflammation or anaemia. B. IBS does not cause anaemia or raised inflammatory markers. C. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. E. GORD causes upper gastrointestinal reflux symptoms.
pearl: Children with IBD often present with weight loss or growth faltering as well as diarrhoea; anaemia and raised inflammatory markers point to organic disease and need specialist referral.
thinking: Teenager with recurrent abdominal pain and diarrhoea ↓ Weight loss ↓ Anaemia and raised inflammatory markers = organic disease ↓ Crohn's disease
exam_trap: B, irritable bowel syndrome — recurrent pain with diarrhoea tempts, but IBS does not cause weight loss, anaemia or raised inflammatory markers.
takeaway: Diarrhoea with weight loss, anaemia and raised inflammation is organic: think Crohn's.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman has chronic bloody diarrhoea and urgency. She reports mucus in her stools.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Bloody diarrhoea, urgency and mucus are characteristic features of ulcerative colitis.
why_wrong: A. Renal colic causes flank-to-groin pain. C. IBS does not typically cause persistent rectal bleeding. D. Coeliac disease more commonly causes diarrhoea and malabsorption rather than persistent bloody diarrhoea. E. GORD causes reflux symptoms.
pearl: Ulcerative colitis starts in the rectum and extends continuously; bloody diarrhoea with urgency, mucus and tenesmus is the typical picture.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Chronic bloody diarrhoea ↓ Urgency and mucus = rectal inflammation ↓ Ulcerative colitis
exam_trap: C, irritable bowel syndrome — chronic diarrhoea with urgency tempts, but IBS does not cause persistent rectal bleeding.
takeaway: Chronic bloody diarrhoea with urgency and mucus = ulcerative colitis.

stem:
A 57-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice and right upper abdominal pain. He is confused and hypotensive.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?
why_correct: Fever, jaundice and right upper abdominal pain indicate biliary infection, while confusion and hypotension indicate severe systemic illness.
why_wrong: B. Acute cholecystitis causes fever and RUQ pain, but jaundice with confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) indicates cholangitis. C. Hepatitis A can cause jaundice but not typically RUQ pain with septic shock. D. Acute pancreatitis typically causes epigastric pain radiating to the back; fever, jaundice and RUQ pain point to biliary infection. E. Biliary colic is transient pain without fever, jaundice or systemic illness.
pearl: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot's triad) indicate cholangitis; with confusion and shock (Reynolds' pentad) it needs sepsis management and urgent biliary drainage, usually by ERCP.
thinking: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain = Charcot's triad ↓ Plus confusion ↓ Plus hypotension = Reynolds' pentad ↓ Severe acute cholangitis
exam_trap: B, acute calculous cholecystitis — fever and RUQ pain fit, but jaundice with confusion and shock indicates an obstructed, infected bile duct.
takeaway: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain = cholangitis; confusion and shock make it severe.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of painful swelling of her lips and face. There is no urticaria or itching.

Which condition should be considered?
why_correct: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria or itching is characteristic of hereditary angioedema.
why_wrong: A. Chronic spontaneous urticaria typically produces itchy wheals, which are absent. B. Contact dermatitis causes an itchy eczematous rash at sites of exposure. D. Orofacial granulomatosis causes persistent, usually painless lip swelling rather than recurrent self-limiting episodes. E. Facial cellulitis causes a single episode of warm, tender, erythematous swelling, often with fever, rather than recurrent episodes.
pearl: Recurrent angioedema without urticaria or itch suggests bradykinin-mediated disease such as hereditary angioedema; a low C4 supports it, and antihistamines are ineffective.
thinking: Young woman ↓ Recurrent painful lip and facial swelling ↓ No urticaria or itching = not histamine-mediated ↓ Hereditary angioedema
exam_trap: A, chronic spontaneous urticaria — it often comes with angioedema, but it causes itchy wheals, which are absent here.
takeaway: Recurrent angioedema without wheals or itch: think hereditary angioedema.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman develops recurrent episodes of wheeze, nasal congestion and itchy eyes during spring.

Which condition is most likely contributing to her symptoms?
why_correct: Asthma and allergic rhinitis occurring alongside seasonal allergic symptoms are characteristic of an atopic tendency.
why_wrong: A. Renal impairment does not explain this pattern. B. Iron deficiency does not cause seasonal allergic symptoms. C. Osteoarthritis affects joints. E. Hypothyroidism does not explain episodic wheeze and allergic rhinitis.
pearl: Asthma, allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis and eczema cluster together as atopic conditions; seasonal spring symptoms point to pollen as the trigger.
thinking: Recurrent wheeze ↓ Nasal congestion and itchy eyes ↓ Seasonal, during spring = pollen allergy ↓ Atopy
exam_trap: E, hypothyroidism — a common chronic condition in women, but it does not cause episodic seasonal wheeze, rhinitis and itchy eyes.
takeaway: Seasonal wheeze, rhinitis and itchy eyes reflect an atopic tendency.

stem:
A 71-year-old man develops new back pain and progressive difficulty walking. He has a history of prostate cancer.

Which diagnosis should be considered urgently?
why_correct: New spinal pain with neurological symptoms in a patient with cancer is an important warning pattern for metastatic spinal cord compression.
why_wrong: A. Spinal stenosis causes chronic neurogenic claudication rather than new, progressive deficit in a patient with cancer. B. Mechanical back pain does not account for the cancer history and progressive difficulty walking. C. An osteoporotic fracture can cause back pain, but with known prostate cancer and progressive neurology, cord compression must be assumed until excluded. D.
