thinking: Regular benzodiazepine for months ↓ Tolerance develops ↓ Body adapts to the drug ↓ Physical and psychological dependence ↓ Dependence
exam_trap: A, Reduced sedation — tolerance can blunt some effects, which tempts, but the key long-term risk is dependence.
takeaway: Long-term benzodiazepines cause dependence; taper, never stop abruptly.

stem: A patient taking a combined oral contraceptive pill has missed pills. What is the appropriate principle?

options.A: Stop the pill and rely on condoms until the next period starts
options.B: Take two pills each day for the remainder of the pack to catch up
options.C: It depends on how many pills were missed and when in the pack
options.D: Emergency contraception is needed after one missed pill
options.E: No further action is needed if fewer than three pills were missed

correct_answer: C. It depends on how many pills were missed and when in the pack
why_correct: The need for additional precautions or emergency contraception depends on the specific circumstances of the missed pills.
why_wrong: A. Stopping the pill is unnecessary and leaves the patient unprotected. B. Doubling doses for the rest of the pack is not recommended. D. Emergency contraception is not automatically required after one missed pill. E. Missing two or more pills can require additional precautions and possibly emergency contraception.
pearl: Missed combined pill advice depends on how many pills were missed and where in the pack; one missed pill usually needs only taking it now, while more may need extra precautions or emergency contraception.
thinking: Combined oral contraceptive ↓ Missed pills ↓ Risk depends on number missed and week of pack ↓ Determines need for condoms or emergency contraception ↓ It depends on how many and when
exam_trap: E, No action if fewer than three missed — it sounds like a familiar rule, but missing two or more pills can require extra precautions and possibly emergency contraception.
takeaway: Missed pill advice hinges on how many were missed and where in the pack.

stem: A woman has had unprotected intercourse and is concerned about pregnancy. What is the key principle?

options.A: Emergency contraception is effective only after pregnancy is established
options.C: It is only available to women over 40
options.D: Emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible
options.E: Emergency contraception is never needed after unprotected intercourse

correct_answer: D. Emergency contraception should be considered as soon as possible
why_correct: Emergency contraception is time-sensitive, so appropriate options should be considered promptly.
why_wrong: A. Emergency contraception is intended to prevent pregnancy before an established pregnancy. B. Emergency contraception does not permanently prevent fertility. C. Age does not create such a restriction. E. It can be appropriate after unprotected intercourse.
pearl: Emergency contraception options are the copper IUD, the most effective, and oral ulipristal or levonorgestrel; all should be used as soon as possible after unprotected intercourse.
thinking: Unprotected intercourse ↓ Concern about pregnancy ↓ Emergency contraception is time-sensitive ↓ Effectiveness falls with delay ↓ Consider it as soon as possible
exam_trap: A, Effective only after pregnancy is established — it confuses emergency contraception with abortion; it prevents pregnancy and does not work once pregnancy is established.
takeaway: Offer emergency contraception promptly; the copper IUD is the most effective option.

stem: A 38-year-old woman who smokes asks about starting a combined hormonal contraceptive. Why does smoking matter?

options.A: Smoking causes immediate infertility in every woman
options.C: Smoking increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risk
options.D: Smoking eliminates the risk of venous thrombosis
options.E: Smoking makes combined contraception completely risk-free

correct_answer: C. Smoking increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risk
why_correct: Smoking contributes to cardiovascular risk, particularly as age and smoking intensity increase, and this is relevant when considering combined hormonal contraception.
why_wrong: A. It does not cause immediate infertility in every woman. B. Smoking does not abolish contraceptive efficacy. D. Smoking does not protect against thrombosis. E. Smoking does not make contraception safer.
pearl: Combined hormonal contraception adds thrombotic and arterial risk; UKMEC advises against it in smokers aged 35 or over, so progestogen-only or non-hormonal methods are preferred.
thinking: Woman aged 38 ↓ Smoker ↓ Combined hormones raise venous and arterial risk ↓ Age and smoking add to that risk ↓ Smoking increases cardiovascular and thrombotic risk
exam_trap: B, Smoking prevents all contraceptive effects — smoking clearly matters, which tempts, but it raises cardiovascular risk rather than reducing efficacy.
takeaway: Smokers aged 35 or over should generally avoid combined hormonal contraception.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has irregular periods followed by 12 months without menstruation. She has no other concerning features. What does this most likely represent?
why_correct: Menopause is clinically defined retrospectively after 12 months of amenorrhoea when there is no other obvious cause, in the appropriate age group.
why_wrong: A. Cervical cancer can cause abnormal bleeding but does not explain this typical menopausal transition by itself. B. Ovarian torsion causes acute pelvic pain. D. PID typically causes pelvic pain and genital tract symptoms. E. Ectopic pregnancy presents with pregnancy-related symptoms and potentially pain or bleeding.
pearl: Menopause is diagnosed clinically in women over 45 after 12 months without periods; FSH testing is not usually needed in this age group.
thinking: Woman aged 52 ↓ Irregular periods, then none ↓ 12 months of amenorrhoea ↓ No other concerning features ↓ Menopause
exam_trap: A, Cervical cancer — cancer worries tempt, but it causes abnormal bleeding, not amenorrhoea; bleeding after the menopause would need investigation.
takeaway: Over 45 with 12 months of amenorrhoea, menopause is a clinical diagnosis.

stem: Which medication exposure is an important risk factor for osteoporosis?

options.C: Long-term dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker use
options.D: Short-term topical emollient use for eczema
options.E: Long-term thiazide diuretic therapy for hypertension

why_correct: Prolonged systemic corticosteroid treatment increases bone loss and fracture risk.
why_wrong: A. Salbutamol is not a recognised osteoporosis risk factor. C. Calcium channel blockers are not a recognised osteoporosis risk factor. D. Emollients do not cause osteoporosis. E. Thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and are not a risk factor.
pearl: Long-term systemic corticosteroids are a major cause of osteoporosis and fragility fracture; consider bone protection early when prolonged courses are expected, especially in older adults.
thinking: Asked for a drug cause of osteoporosis ↓ Steroids reduce bone formation and calcium absorption ↓ Long-term systemic use ↓ Raised fracture risk ↓ Long-term systemic corticosteroid therapy
exam_trap: E, Thiazide diuretics — diuretics feature in bone questions, which tempts, but thiazides reduce urinary calcium loss and are not an osteoporosis risk factor.
takeaway: Long-term systemic steroids cause osteoporosis: think about bone protection.

stem: A patient receiving gentamicin develops a rising serum creatinine. Which adverse effect of gentamicin should be considered?
why_correct: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside that can cause renal toxicity.
why_wrong: A. Gentamicin does not characteristically cause hyperglycaemia. B. Hypothyroidism is not a characteristic gentamicin toxicity. C. Peptic ulceration is not a typical effect. D. Cataract is unrelated.
pearl: Gentamicin is nephrotoxic and ototoxic; monitor renal function and drug levels, and review the dose or stop it if creatinine rises.
thinking: Gentamicin ↓ Aminoglycoside ↓ Rising serum creatinine ↓ Renal tubular toxicity ↓ Nephrotoxicity
exam_trap: A, Hyperglycaemia — some drugs disturb glucose, which tempts, but gentamicin's characteristic toxicities are renal and ototoxic.
takeaway: Aminoglycosides cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity: monitor levels and renal function.

stem: A patient develops flushing and itching during a rapid intravenous vancomycin infusion. What reaction should be considered?

options.C: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
options.D: Septic shock from a central line infection

why_correct: Rapid IV vancomycin administration can cause flushing and pruritus due to an infusion-related reaction.
why_wrong: A. SJS develops over days with mucocutaneous blistering. C. DRESS develops weeks after starting a drug. D. Sepsis does not explain flushing and itching linked to infusion rate. E. Flushing and itching alone do not establish anaphylaxis without airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
pearl: Flushing and itch during rapid vancomycin infusion is a rate-related histamine release, not true allergy; stop or slow the infusion and give it more slowly.
thinking: Intravenous vancomycin ↓ Given rapidly ↓ Flushing and itching ↓ Rate-related histamine release ↓ Rate-related vancomycin infusion reaction
exam_trap: E, Confirmed anaphylaxis — flushing during an infusion raises alarm, but without airway, breathing or circulation compromise this is not anaphylaxis.
takeaway: Flushing with a fast vancomycin infusion is rate-related: slow the infusion.

stem: A patient taking rifampicin notices that their urine and tears have become orange-red. What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: Rifampicin commonly causes orange-red discolouration of body fluids.
why_wrong: B. Interstitial nephritis does not cause orange-red tears. C. Renal stones may cause haematuria but not orange-red tears. D. Cholestatic jaundice darkens urine but does not cause orange-red tears. E. Myoglobinuria darkens urine but does not affect tears.
pearl: Rifampicin colours urine, tears and sweat orange-red; warn patients in advance, including that soft contact lenses may be permanently stained.
thinking: Taking rifampicin ↓ Orange-red urine and tears ↓ Several body fluids affected ↓ Known drug pigment effect ↓ Harmless rifampicin-related discolouration
exam_trap: C, Haematuria from renal stones — red urine tempts this, but stones would not colour the tears.
takeaway: Orange-red body fluids on rifampicin are harmless; warn contact lens wearers.

stem: A patient taking rifampicin notices reduced effectiveness of their usual combined oral contraceptive. What explains this?

options.A: Rifampicin inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
options.B: Rifampicin blocks the renal excretion of the hormones
options.C: Rifampicin binds the oral hormones in the gut lumen
options.D: Rifampicin induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
options.E: Rifampicin increases hormone binding to plasma albumin

correct_answer: D. Rifampicin induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
why_correct: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer and can reduce the effectiveness of several medicines, including hormonal contraception.
why_wrong: A. Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer, not an inhibitor; inhibition would raise hormone levels. B. Its important interaction is hepatic enzyme induction rather than blocking renal excretion. C. Rifampicin does not bind contraceptive hormones in the gut. E. Its key interaction is not altered plasma protein binding.
pearl: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer that makes combined pills unreliable; advise a method unaffected by enzyme inducers, such as a copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS or progestogen injection.
thinking: Rifampicin ↓ Combined pill less effective ↓ Faster hepatic metabolism of hormones ↓ Cytochrome P450 induction ↓ Rifampicin induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
exam_trap: A, Rifampicin inhibits P450 — the enzyme system is right, which tempts, but inhibition would raise hormone levels; rifampicin is an inducer.
takeaway: Rifampicin induces P450 enzymes, reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy.

stem: A patient taking a macrolide antibiotic develops palpitations. Which cardiac adverse effect can occur with some macrolides?
why_correct: Some macrolides can prolong the QT interval and increase the risk of ventricular arrhythmias.
why_wrong: A. Aortic dissection is unrelated. B. Mitral stenosis is structural heart disease. C. Macrolides do not prevent arrhythmias. D. Persistent hypertension is not a characteristic effect.
pearl: Macrolides such as clarithromycin and erythromycin can prolong the QT interval; take care with other QT-prolonging drugs, and note clarithromycin also inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes.
thinking: Macrolide antibiotic ↓ New palpitations ↓ Known effect on cardiac repolarisation ↓ Risk of ventricular arrhythmia ↓ QT interval prolongation
exam_trap: A, Aortic dissection — antibiotic-related aortic risk exists, which tempts, but it is linked to fluoroquinolones, not macrolides.
takeaway: Macrolides can prolong the QT interval; check for other QT-prolonging drugs.

stem: Why are tetracyclines generally avoided in young children?

options.A: They cause sensorineural ototoxicity at standard doses
options.B: They cause dose-related nephrotoxicity in developing kidneys
options.C: They damage cartilage in growing weight-bearing joints
options.D: They cause grey baby syndrome in neonates and young infants
options.E: They cause tooth discolouration and enamel hypoplasia

correct_answer: E. They cause tooth discolouration and enamel hypoplasia
why_correct: Tetracyclines can bind to developing teeth and bones, causing tooth discolouration.
why_wrong: A. Ototoxicity is associated with aminoglycosides. B. Nephrotoxicity in children is not the characteristic concern. C. Cartilage damage is associated with fluoroquinolones. D. Grey baby syndrome is associated with chloramphenicol.
pearl: Tetracyclines bind calcium in developing teeth and bone, causing staining and enamel hypoplasia; avoid them in children under 12 and in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
thinking: Tetracyclines ↓ Chelate calcium ↓ Deposit in developing teeth and bone ↓ Permanent staining ↓ Tooth discolouration and enamel hypoplasia
exam_trap: C, Cartilage damage in growing joints — a recognised antibiotic concern in children, which tempts, but it is associated with fluoroquinolones, not tetracyclines.
takeaway: Avoid tetracyclines in young children: they stain developing teeth.

stem: A patient develops sudden Achilles tendon pain while taking a fluoroquinolone antibiotic. What adverse effect should be considered?
why_correct: Fluoroquinolones are associated with tendinitis and tendon rupture, including Achilles tendon injury.
why_wrong: B. Iron deficiency is unrelated. C. Peptic ulcer disease is unrelated. D. Cataract is not the characteristic adverse effect. E. Hypothyroidism is unrelated.
pearl: Fluoroquinolones can cause tendinitis and tendon rupture, especially in older people and those taking corticosteroids; stop the drug at the first sign of tendon pain.
thinking: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic ↓ Sudden Achilles pain ↓ Known drug-related tendinopathy ↓ Risk of rupture ↓ Tendon injury
exam_trap: D, Cataract — some drugs cause eye adverse effects, which tempts, but cataract is not a fluoroquinolone effect and does not explain tendon pain.
takeaway: Tendon pain on a fluoroquinolone: stop the drug because of rupture risk.

stem: A patient taking metronidazole asks about drinking alcohol. What advice is appropriate?

options.A: Up to two units a day is acceptable if taken with food
options.B: Avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least 48 hours after
options.C: Avoid alcohol for the first two days of the treatment course
options.D: Alcohol is safe once the infection symptoms have fully resolved
options.E: Limit intake to within the weekly recommended limit of units

correct_answer: B. Avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least 48 hours after
why_correct: Patients are advised to avoid alcohol with metronidazole because of the potential for an unpleasant interaction.
why_wrong: A. Even small amounts can provoke a disulfiram-like reaction. C. Avoidance is needed throughout treatment and afterwards. D. The interaction depends on the drug, not on symptom resolution. E. Keeping within weekly limits does not prevent the interaction.
pearl: Metronidazole with alcohol can cause a disulfiram-like reaction with flushing, nausea, vomiting and palpitations; avoid alcohol during treatment and for 48 hours afterwards.
thinking: Metronidazole ↓ Question about alcohol ↓ Risk of disulfiram-like reaction ↓ Effect persists after the last dose ↓ Avoid during treatment and for at least 48 hours after
exam_trap: C, Avoid for the first two days only — it echoes the 48-hour rule, which tempts, but avoidance is needed throughout treatment and afterwards.
takeaway: No alcohol on metronidazole, nor for 48 hours after the course ends.
